native_language_example: Shortly before the end of the game, it started to rain.

additional_notes: Used for giving directions indoors (e.g., in an apartment, office, or hotel). It’s a noun phrase with genitive: **das Ende** (the end) + **des Flurs** (of the corridor). Often appears with a preposition like **am** (= an dem): **Am Ende des Flurs** = “at the end of the hallway.”
target_language_example: Die Toiletten sind am Ende des Flurs links.
native_language_example: The restrooms are at the end of the hallway on the left.

meaning: the end of the month; by the end of the month.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a deadline or latest time within the current month. Very often used with time phrases like „bis zum Ende des Monats“ or shorter „bis Ende des Monats“ (= no later than the last day of the month).
target_language_example: Ich bezahle die Rechnung bis zum Ende des Monats.
native_language_example: I’ll pay the bill by the end of the month.

additional_notes: Used when talking about grammar and punctuation. It’s the genitive form: „Ende“ + „des Satzes“ (= of the sentence). Often appears in phrases like „am Ende des Satzes“ (at the end of the sentence).
target_language_example: Am Ende des Satzes steht ein Punkt.
native_language_example: At the end of the sentence there is a period.

additional_notes: A common saying used when problems happened along the way, but the final result is good—so the earlier trouble feels less important. Often said as a short closing comment after a story or situation. You may also see it written with commas ("Ende gut, alles gut").
target_language_example: Wir hatten viele Pannen auf der Reise, aber am Ende hat alles geklappt: Ende gut alles gut.
native_language_example: We had lots of mishaps on the trip, but in the end everything worked out: all’s well that ends well.

additional_notes: A common verb phrase: the language name + „lernen“ (to learn). Often used with a modal verb like „müssen“ (must/have to) or „möchten/wollen“ (want/would like): „Du musst Englisch lernen.“ You can swap in other languages: „Deutsch lernen“, „Französisch lernen“, etc.
target_language_example: Du musst jeden Tag Englisch lernen.
native_language_example: You have to learn English every day.

additional_notes: A common verb + language pattern: "[Sprache] sprechen" (Deutsch sprechen, Französisch sprechen, etc.). Often used with "können" to say you can/can’t speak a language ("Ich kann Englisch sprechen"). You can add "gut/besser/am besten" to compare ability: "besser Englisch sprechen".
target_language_example: Ich kann ein bisschen Englisch sprechen, aber nicht so gut.
native_language_example: I can speak a little English, but not that well.

additional_notes: Uses the infinitive with „zu“ (zu lernen) after verbs/phrases like „versuchen“ (to try), „anfangen“ (to start), „Interesse haben“ (to be interested), or „mit der Absicht“ (with the intention). Can be changed to other languages: „Deutsch zu lernen“, „Spanisch zu lernen“, etc.
target_language_example: Ich habe letztes Jahr angefangen, Englisch zu lernen.
native_language_example: I started learning English last year.

additional_notes: A "zu" + infinitive phrase meaning "to speak" (in order/ability) English. Often used after verbs/expressions like "versuchen" (to try), "lernen" (to learn), "(es) ermöglichen" (to enable), or "(es) macht mir Mühe" (it’s hard for me).
target_language_example: Ich versuche, im Urlaub mehr Englisch zu sprechen.
native_language_example: I’m trying to speak more English on vacation.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "treffen" (to make, lit. "to hit/meet") in the common phrase "eine Entscheidung treffen" = "to make a decision." You usually add an article/adjective: "eine gute / schlechte / falsche Entscheidung getroffen". In the Perfekt (past) it appears as "hat/habe ... getroffen".
target_language_example: Ich habe eine Entscheidung getroffen.
native_language_example: I made a decision.

meaning: "your decision again/once more" (usually implying: reconsider the decision).
additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs like „überdenken“ or „überlegen“: „die Entscheidung noch einmal überdenken“ = to reconsider a decision. „noch einmal“ means “again/one more time,” often as a polite request to think again before deciding.
target_language_example: Könnten Sie Ihre Entscheidung noch einmal überdenken?
native_language_example: Could you reconsider your decision?

additional_notes: A very common formal/neutral collocation: you usually say eine Entscheidung treffen (often with adjectives like wichtige/schwierige). In sentence 4, die Entscheidung treffen lassen means “let someone make the decision.”
target_language_example: Ich muss heute eine Entscheidung treffen.
native_language_example: I have to make a decision today.

additional_notes: Typically occurs as part of the fixed collocation „eine Entscheidung treffen“ (“to make a decision”), with „zu“ marking the infinitive after another verb or in certain constructions (e.g., „im Begriff sein, … zu treffen“, „brauchen, … zu treffen“, „versuchen, … zu treffen“). Very common in both formal and everyday German. Literally “to meet/hit a decision,” but idiomatically “to make a decision.”
target_language_example: Er war im Begriff, eine endgültige Entscheidung zu treffen.
native_language_example: He was about to make a final decision.

additional_notes: A very common, neutral phrase. Often used with adjectives to describe the type of decisions (e.g., schwierige/kluge Entscheidungen treffen). Frequently appears with modal verbs like müssen/sollen and with possessives: seine/deine/eure Entscheidungen treffen.
target_language_example: Wir müssen auf die Zukunft achten und kluge Entscheidungen treffen.
native_language_example: We have to pay attention to the future and make smart decisions.

meaning: to be able to bring (relevant) experience; to have experience to offer.
additional_notes: Used especially in job or application contexts to say you can contribute your previous experience to a role or project. In everyday German, people more often say „Erfahrung mitbringen können“ or „Ich kann Erfahrung mitbringen“ (same meaning).
target_language_example: Für diese Stelle sollte man Erfahrung bringen können.
native_language_example: For this position, you should be able to bring experience.

meaning: to be successful; to have success.
additional_notes: Used to say that someone (or something) achieves a desired result. It’s common with "werden" for predictions ("Er wird Erfolg haben") and with "möchten/wollen" to express wanting to succeed ("Ich möchte Erfolg haben").
target_language_example: Mit diesem neuen Produkt werden wir bestimmt Erfolg haben.
native_language_example: With this new product, we’ll definitely be successful.

additional_notes: Used in formal or official contexts to say that a request has been approved (e.g., by an authority, a system, or a supervisor). Often appears as a short status message after asking for permission ("Erlaubnis") and having it granted ("erteilt" = issued/granted).
target_language_example: Nach der Prüfung wurde mir die Erlaubnis erteilt, das Gebäude zu betreten.
native_language_example: After the check, I was granted permission to enter the building.

additional_notes: Usually used as part of the phrase „in Erwägung ziehen“ = “to consider”. „In Erwägung gezogen“ is the past participle form and is often used with „werden/sein“, e.g. „wurde … in Erwägung gezogen“ (“was considered”). Common in more formal contexts (plans, options, decisions).
target_language_example: Ein Umzug wurde in Erwägung gezogen, aber wir bleiben doch hier.
native_language_example: A move was considered, but we’re staying here after all.

meaning: “Your Excellency” (a very formal title of address).
additional_notes: Used when speaking directly to someone with high rank (especially a diplomat/ambassador, high official, or similar). It’s extremely formal and sounds old-fashioned or ceremonial in everyday life. In writing you may also see: „Eure Exzellenz“ (depending on the addressee/grammar). Often used with respectful phrases like „Wie Euer Exzellenz befehlen“ (“As Your Excellency commands”).
target_language_example: Darf ich Sie bitten, Euer Exzellenz, mir zu folgen?
native_language_example: May I ask you, Your Excellency, to follow me?

meaning: “Your Majesty.” (formal way to address a king or queen)
additional_notes: A very formal form of address used when speaking directly to royalty. It’s typically used like a name (often with a comma: „…, Eure Majestät.“). In modern everyday German you’ll mostly see it in historical contexts, films, books, ceremonies, or formal letters. Related forms: „Ihre Majestät“ (“His/Her Majesty,” talking about them) and „Euer/Ihr Majestät“ depending on grammar/case.
target_language_example: Darf ich Euch etwas zeigen, Eure Majestät?
native_language_example: May I show you something, Your Majesty?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a man you were married to before (usually after a divorce). Commonly used with possessive pronouns: mein/dein/ihr Ex-Mann. Often written with a hyphen in German: Ex-Mann.
target_language_example: Mein Ex-Mann und ich verstehen uns jetzt besser.
native_language_example: My ex-husband and I get along better now.

additional_notes: Used with another verb and "zu" (e.g., hoffen/versuchen/planen), meaning you succeed in the exam. Without "zu", you often say: "ein Examen bestehen" (to pass an exam). Note: "bestehen" can also mean "to exist" or "to consist of", but with exams it means "to pass".
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, das Examen zu bestehen.
native_language_example: I hope to pass the exam.

meaning: to ride a bike; to go cycling.
additional_notes: Common verb phrase meaning using a bicycle for transport or sport. Often used without an article: „Ich fahre Fahrrad.“ You can also say „mit dem Fahrrad fahren“ (= to go by bike). In questions about ability, it works like „schwimmen“: „Kannst du Fahrrad fahren?“
target_language_example: Kannst du Fahrrad fahren?
native_language_example: Can you ride a bike?

additional_notes: Often used as a shortened note, label, or headline indicating that a bike was stolen (e.g., on a sign, in a chat, or in an online post). In a full sentence you’ll more often say: „Mein Fahrrad wurde gestohlen.“ or „Mein Fahrrad ist gestohlen worden.“
target_language_example: Fahrrad gestohlen – bitte melden, falls gesehen.
native_language_example: Bicycle stolen—please get in touch if seen.

meaning: to have/get your bike repaired (by someone else).
additional_notes: Uses the pattern „etwas + Infinitiv + lassen“ to mean you arrange for a service to be done by another person (e.g., a mechanic), not that you repair it yourself. Common conjugations: „Ich lasse … reparieren“, past: „Ich habe … reparieren lassen“, necessity: „Ich muss … reparieren lassen“.
target_language_example: Ich habe mein Fahrrad reparieren lassen.
native_language_example: I had my bike repaired.

additional_notes: Usually said as **mit dem Fahrrad zur Schule (fahren)** (“to go/ride to school by bike”). Used with the verb **fahren** (to go/ride/drive): *Er fährt mit dem Fahrrad zur Schule.* Without **mit dem**, it can sound incomplete, but the meaning is clear in context.
target_language_example: Ich fahre jeden Tag mit dem Fahrrad zur Schule.
native_language_example: I ride my bike to school every day.

meaning: “has color” (is colored / has taken on color).
additional_notes: Often used with a subject like *es* or *das*: *Es hat Farbe* / *Das hat Farbe*. Literally it can mean something is (now) colored (e.g., paint, food while cooking). Depending on context, it can also be used more loosely to say something looks vivid or has some flair/impact.
target_language_example: Die Sauce ist fertig, sie Farbe hat schon.
native_language_example: The sauce is ready; it has already taken on some color.

additional_notes: Used with the verb *begehen* (“to commit”), often in the perfect tense: *einen Fehler begangen haben* = “to have made a mistake.” Common in more formal or serious contexts. Note: *Fehler* means “mistake/error,” not “failure.”
target_language_example: Ich habe einen Fehler begangen und möchte mich entschuldigen.
native_language_example: I made a mistake and I want to apologize.

additional_notes: Used with the verb „haben“ to talk about mistakes in the past: „Ich habe einen Fehler gemacht“ (one mistake) or „Ich habe Fehler gemacht“ / „eine Menge Fehler gemacht“ (more than one). „Fehler“ means a mistake/error (not „failure“ in the English sense).
target_language_example: Ich habe einen Fehler gemacht, aber ich kann es korrigieren.
native_language_example: I made a mistake, but I can fix it.

meaning: to make a mistake; to make mistakes.
additional_notes: Common everyday phrase. Often used with an article for a specific mistake (e.g., „den/diesen Fehler machen“) or in the plural for mistakes in general („Fehler machen“). The verb „machen“ matches English “make,” so the structure is straightforward.
target_language_example: Sogar ein erfahrener Fahrer kann Fehler machen.
native_language_example: Even an experienced driver can make mistakes.

additional_notes: "(einen) Fehler zu begehen" is a more formal way to say "einen Fehler zu machen". It often appears in evaluative or accusatory contexts (e.g., with "jemandem vorwerfen" = to accuse someone of), and it uses "begehen" in the sense of "to commit" (also used with crimes: "eine Straftat zu begehen").
target_language_example: Es ist schrecklich, einen Fehler zu begehen.
native_language_example: It’s terrible to make a mistake.

additional_notes: Uses the verb phrase "Fehler machen" (to make mistakes). In sentences with another verb, it often appears as an infinitive with "zu": "Angst haben, Fehler zu machen" (to be afraid of making mistakes), "dazu neigen, Fehler zu machen" (to tend to make mistakes). You can also say: "Ich habe einen Fehler gemacht" (I made a mistake).
target_language_example: Du lernst schneller, wenn du keine Angst hast, Fehler zu machen.
native_language_example: You learn faster when you’re not afraid of making mistakes.

additional_notes: Used with the verb „lassen“ to say someone didn’t close a window: „(jmd.) hat das/die Fenster offen gelassen.“ „offen“ = open, „gelassen“ = left (past participle of „lassen“). Often appears in questions like „Haben Sie das Fenster offen gelassen?“ and with „Wer…?“ to ask who did it.
target_language_example: Ich glaube, ich habe das Fenster offen gelassen.
native_language_example: I think I left the window open.

additional_notes: A common everyday phrase, often used as an instruction or request. You’ll also hear it in the imperative: "Schließ bitte das Fenster!" (informal) or "Schließen Sie bitte das Fenster!" (formal).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte das Fenster schließen?
native_language_example: Can you please close the window?

additional_notes: Infinitive phrase with „zu“ (like “to …” in English). Often used after another verb (e.g., „Ich habe vergessen, das Fenster zu schließen.“) or in instructions/reminders. In a direct command you’d usually say: „Schließ das Fenster!“
target_language_example: Ich habe vergessen, das Fenster zu schließen.
native_language_example: I forgot to close the window.

additional_notes: This is an infinitive phrase with „zu“ („to open“). It’s commonly used after another verb, e.g. „versuchen“ (to try), „vergessen“ (to forget), „bitten“ (to ask), or „Zeit haben“ (to have time): „… die Fenster zu öffnen“. Often you’ll see it with an article/case, e.g. „das Fenster zu öffnen“ (the window) or „die Fenster zu öffnen“ (the windows).
target_language_example: Vergiss nicht, die Fenster zu öffnen.
native_language_example: Don’t forget to open the windows.

additional_notes: "Fenster" = "window" and "öffnen" = "to open". You’ll often hear it as a request or instruction in the imperative: "Öffnen Sie bitte das Fenster." (formal) or "Öffne bitte das Fenster." / "Mach bitte das Fenster auf." (informal, very common). "Fenster öffnen" can also appear as an infinitive phrase, e.g. on signs or in instructions.
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte das Fenster öffnen?
native_language_example: Can you please open the window?

additional_notes: "ausschalten" is a separable verb: in a normal sentence the prefix goes to the end (Ich schalte den Fernseher aus.). In commands, it stays together at the front (Schalt(e) den Fernseher aus! / Schalten Sie den Fernseher aus!). You’ll often use it with the accusative object "den Fernseher".
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte den Fernseher ausschalten?
native_language_example: Can you please turn off the TV?

meaning: “(Turn the) TV down” / “make the TV quieter.”
additional_notes: Often used as an abbreviated request (missing the verb), especially in speech. Full forms include: „Mach den Fernseher leiser.“ / „Kannst du den Fernseher leiser machen?“ (leiser = quieter; Fernseher = TV set).
target_language_example: Kannst du den Fernseher leiser machen?
native_language_example: Can you turn the TV down?

additional_notes: Used for things that start burning (a house, a pan, paper). It can also be used figuratively to mean someone “catches fire” emotionally—becomes very enthusiastic or passionate about something (e.g., für ein Thema Feuer fangen).
target_language_example: Pass auf, das Öl kann schnell Feuer fangen.
native_language_example: Be careful, the oil can catch fire quickly.

additional_notes: A strong warning or command telling someone to leave something (or someone) alone. It’s often used when you feel protective or angry: "Finger weg von meinem ...!". Can also be used about a person: "Finger weg von meiner Tochter!".
target_language_example: Finger weg von meinem Handy!
native_language_example: Hands off my phone!

additional_notes: From the verb **fangen** (to catch). In natural German you usually say **einen Fisch fangen** (present) or **einen Fisch gefangen** / **Ich habe einen Fisch gefangen** (perfect tense with **haben**). Without context, **Fisch gefangen** can sound like a short note or headline ("Fish caught").
target_language_example: Ich habe heute einen Fisch gefangen.
native_language_example: I caught a fish today.

additional_notes: This is the past participle phrase from **Fische fangen** (“to catch fish”). It’s typically used with **haben** in the present perfect: **Ich habe Fische gefangen** (“I caught fish / I have caught fish”). **Fische** is the accusative object; you can add a number: **drei Fische gefangen**.
target_language_example: Wir haben heute Morgen zwei Fische gefangen.
native_language_example: We caught two fish this morning.

additional_notes: Used for quantities when buying, bringing, or sharing wine. Often appears with an article and adjectives: eine Flasche Wein (a bottle of wine), noch eine Flasche Wein (another bottle), eine gute Flasche Wein (a good bottle of wine).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte eine Flasche Wein für das Abendessen kaufen?
native_language_example: Can you please buy a bottle of wine for dinner?

meaning: “flesh and blood”: a real human (not a robot/ghost), or one’s own close family.
additional_notes: Common patterns: **aus Fleisch und Blut (sein)** = “to be made of flesh and blood,” meaning someone/something is real and human. **(mein/dein/sein) Fleisch und Blut** = “my/your/his own flesh and blood,” meaning a close relative (often a child). It can also refer to the human body/physical nature: **Fleisch und Blut lassen mich im Stich** = “my body is failing me.”
target_language_example: Sie ist keine Maschine, sie ist aus Fleisch und Blut.
native_language_example: She’s not a machine; she’s flesh and blood.

additional_notes: Used capitalized as a proper name in these examples. If you mean the weather phenomenon, you typically wouldn’t use this as a fixed term; more idiomatic options are „Schneetreiben“ or „Schneefall“ (and then it would be lowercase if used descriptively).
target_language_example: Wie geht es Fliegender Schnee?
native_language_example: How is Flying Snow?

additional_notes: Used for giving directions indoors. Often appears as "den Flur entlang" (accusative) or with a verb like "(den) Flur entlanggehen" = "walk along the hallway". Similar: "den Gang entlang".
target_language_example: Gehen Sie den Flur entlang, dann ist die Tür links.
native_language_example: Go down the hallway, then the door is on the left.

additional_notes: Used to describe moving or stretching parallel to a river. Very often you’ll see it as **am Fluss entlang** (= an dem Fluss entlang, “along the river”). **entlang** can come after the noun phrase (am Fluss entlang) or before it with genitive: **entlang des Flusses** (more formal).
target_language_example: Wir sind am Fluss entlang bis zur Brücke gelaufen.
native_language_example: We walked along the river as far as the bridge.

additional_notes: Common pattern: **Der/Ein Fluss fließt + location/direction**. Use it with prepositions to say where the river flows: **in/ins** (into), **durch** (through), **unter ... hindurch** (under ... through), **entlang** (along). Verb: **fließen** (to flow), 3rd person singular: **(er/sie/es) fließt**.
target_language_example: Der Fluss fließt durch die Stadt.
native_language_example: The river flows through the city.

additional_notes: Usually used as an infinitive with „zu“ after another verb (e.g., versuchen, planen, schaffen): „… den Fluss zu durchschwimmen.“ The river is typically in the accusative: „einen/den Fluss durchschwimmen“ (to swim across the whole river).
target_language_example: Ich versuche, den Fluss zu durchschwimmen.
native_language_example: I’m trying to swim across the river.

meaning: to swim in a river / to swim across a river.
additional_notes: In real sentences you normally need a preposition: **in einem Fluss schwimmen** = to swim in a river; **über einen Fluss schwimmen** = to swim across a river. The structure **zu schwimmen** is an infinitive (“to swim”), often used with **es ist …, … zu schwimmen** (“it is … to swim …”).
target_language_example: Es ist keine gute Idee, bei Nacht über den Fluss zu schwimmen.
native_language_example: It’s not a good idea to swim across the river at night.

additional_notes: Used to say who/what is in a photo. Most often it’s followed by the dative: ein Foto von ihm/ihr/dir, ein Foto von meiner Familie. You may also hear the more formal genitive without "von": ein Foto meines Bruders.
target_language_example: Hast du ein Foto von deiner Schwester?
native_language_example: Do you have a photo of your sister?

meaning: to take a photo of me.
additional_notes: Commonly used as a request. Very often you’ll hear it with a question or polite modal: „Machst du ein Foto von mir?“ (informal) or „Können/Könnten Sie ein Foto von mir machen?“ (formal). „ein Foto machen“ = to take a photo; „von mir“ = of me.
target_language_example: Könnten Sie bitte ein Foto von mir machen?
native_language_example: Could you please take a photo of me?

additional_notes: Used when the subject and the person in the photo are the same. Often appears with verbs like „machen“ (to take), „schicken“ (to send), or „posten“ (to post): „Er macht ein Foto von sich.“ In everyday speech you also commonly hear a specific pronoun instead: „ein Foto von mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen“.
target_language_example: Sie hat ein Foto von sich auf Instagram gepostet.
native_language_example: She posted a photo of herself on Instagram.

additional_notes: Common collocation meaning ‘to answer a question.’ Typically takes an accusative direct object: eine/diese/meine Frage beantworten. Frequently used in polite requests (e.g., Könnten Sie …?) or when discussing ability to answer questions.
target_language_example: Könnten Sie bitte meine Frage beantworten?
native_language_example: Could you please answer my question?

additional_notes: Most often used as **„(nur) eine Frage der Zeit“** to mean something will happen sooner or later. Common pattern: **„Es ist nur eine Frage der Zeit, bis …“** (“It’s only a matter of time until …”).
target_language_example: Es ist nur eine Frage der Zeit, bis er zurückkommt.
native_language_example: It’s only a matter of time until he comes back.

additional_notes: Usually used as part of the common phrase **eine Frage stellen** (“to ask a question”). In the past tense you often see **ich habe … eine Frage gestellt** (Perfekt with **haben** + past participle **gestellt**).
target_language_example: Hast du ihm schon eine Frage gestellt?
native_language_example: Have you already asked him a question?

additional_notes: A very common, polite way to say “ask a question,” especially in formal situations (e.g., to a teacher, in a meeting, to a stranger). Often used with the pattern: jemandem (Dat.) eine Frage stellen (“to ask someone a question”).
target_language_example: Darf ich Ihnen kurz eine Frage stellen?
native_language_example: May I quickly ask you a question?

additional_notes: Common infinitive construction with **zu** (often after certain verbs/adjectives): **Es ist schwierig/schwer, eine Frage zu beantworten**; **Ich weigere mich, deine Frage zu beantworten**; **versuchen, die Frage zu beantworten**. In a normal main clause without **zu**, you typically use the finite verb: **Ich beantworte die Frage** / **Ich habe die Frage beantwortet**. Word order note: the infinitive phrase is often set off with a comma.
target_language_example: Es fällt mir schwer, Ihre Frage zu beantworten.
native_language_example: It’s hard for me to answer your question.

additional_notes: Most commonly used as **eine Frage stellen** (“to ask a question”). With **zu** it often appears in constructions like **jemandem eine Frage zu stellen** (“to ask someone a question”), where the person is typically in the **dative**. Don’t confuse it with **in Frage stellen**, which means “to question/challenge/doubt” something.
target_language_example: Erlaube mir, dir eine einfache Frage zu stellen.
native_language_example: Allow me to ask you a simple question.

additional_notes: Common verb phrase: beantworten + accusative (direct object). You can say Fragen beantworten (answer questions) or a specific question: eine Frage beantworten. Often used in school/work contexts or when offering help: Ich kann deine Fragen beantworten.
target_language_example: Kannst du meine Fragen beantworten?
native_language_example: Can you answer my questions?

additional_notes: Used with the verb phrase „jemandem Fragen stellen“ = “to ask someone questions.” The person you ask is in the dative case (e.g., „Ich habe dem Arzt Fragen gestellt.“). „gestellt“ is the past participle of „stellen“, so you’ll often see it with „haben“ in the perfect tense: „Ich habe … Fragen gestellt.“
target_language_example: Ich habe der Lehrerin ein paar Fragen gestellt.
native_language_example: I asked the teacher a few questions.

additional_notes: Used to indicate that someone needs clarification or has things they want to ask. Very common in polite offers like „Wenn Sie Fragen haben, …“ (“If you have questions, …”) and in direct prompts such as „Welche Fragen haben Sie an mich?“ (“What questions do you have for me?”). Often appears with formal „Sie“ in work/school/customer-service contexts, but it can also be used informally (e.g., „Wenn du Fragen hast, …“).
target_language_example: Wenn Sie Fragen haben, rufen Sie mich an.
native_language_example: If you have questions, call me.

additional_notes: Common verb phrase meaning to ask one or more questions (literally “to set/pose questions”). Often used with "Darf ich ...?" to ask for permission ("May I ask questions?"). You can also specify what kind of questions: "viele", "ein paar", "keine", "persönliche", etc.
target_language_example: Im Kurs darfst du jederzeit Fragen stellen.
native_language_example: In the course you may ask questions at any time.

additional_notes: An infinitive phrase with "zu" ("to"), often used after another verb (e.g., "anfangen, Fragen zu stellen" = "to start asking questions") or as the subject of a sentence ("Fragen zu stellen ist ..." = "Asking questions is ..."). Without "zu" you often see "Fragen stellen" after modal verbs (e.g., "Ich kann Fragen stellen" = "I can ask questions").
target_language_example: Du brauchst keine Angst zu haben, Fragen zu stellen.
native_language_example: You don’t need to be afraid to ask questions.

meaning: French as well as English; both French and English.
additional_notes: Usually used with the correlative conjunction pattern **„sowohl … als auch …“** (= “both … and …”). In standard German you would say: **„sowohl Französisch als auch Englisch“**. Without **sowohl**, it can sound incomplete or less natural in careful writing.
target_language_example: Ich spreche sowohl Französisch als auch Englisch.
native_language_example: I speak both French and English.

additional_notes: "beibringen" means to teach someone a skill or knowledge (often by showing/explaining). It commonly takes a person in the dative: "mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen Französisch beibringen". You can also say what exactly you’re teaching: "ein paar Wörter Französisch beibringen" (teach a few French words).
target_language_example: Meine Freundin kann mir Französisch beibringen.
native_language_example: My girlfriend can teach me French.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "lernen" (to learn), often in the present perfect: "haben ... gelernt" = "have learned." You’ll also commonly see "etwas Französisch" meaning "some French" (a bit of the language).
target_language_example: Ich habe in der Schule Französisch gelernt.
native_language_example: I learned French in school.

additional_notes: Used mainly with the verb **sprechen** in the passive: **(Es) wird Französisch gesprochen** = “French is spoken.” You can use it to say which language is used in a place or situation. Often contrasts with the active form **(jemand) spricht Französisch** (“someone speaks French”) or **auf Französisch sprechen** (“to speak in French”).
target_language_example: In diesem Kurs wird nur Französisch gesprochen.
native_language_example: Only French is spoken in this course.

meaning: to know French; to be able to speak French.
additional_notes: Uses the modal verb „können“ to talk about ability in a language. Word order changes with person/tense (e.g., „Ich kann Französisch“, „Er kann Französisch“), but the infinitive construction „Französisch können“ is common after another verb (e.g., „möchte“, „muss“) or as a general statement about a skill.
target_language_example: Ich möchte unbedingt Französisch können.
native_language_example: I really want to be able to speak French.

additional_notes: Used to talk about studying or learning the French language. After modal verbs like müssen (must/have to) and wollen (want), the verb lernen stays in the infinitive at the end: „Du musst Französisch lernen.“
target_language_example: Ich möchte Französisch lernen, aber ich habe wenig Zeit.
native_language_example: I would like to learn French, but I have little time.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone can (or cannot) speak the French language. You can also replace "Französisch" with other languages (e.g., „Englisch sprechen“).
target_language_example: Sie können Französisch sprechen.
native_language_example: They can speak French.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **hören** in the pattern **jemanden + (Sprache) sprechen hören** (“to hear someone speak (a language)”). The person you hear is in the **accusative**: *Ich habe ihn Französisch sprechen hören.*
target_language_example: Ich habe sie im Zug Französisch sprechen hören.
native_language_example: I heard her speaking French on the train.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone can speak the French language. Often appears in relative clauses with "der/die" ("someone who speaks French") or in questions like "Spricht sie Französisch?". Word order can change depending on the sentence (e.g., "..., ob sie Französisch spricht").
target_language_example: Wir brauchen jemanden, der Französisch spricht.
native_language_example: We need someone who speaks French.

meaning: “to … in French / to … French” (Französisch + zu + infinitive).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (zu + verb) to say you manage/try/learn to do something in French, or to have the ability to do it in French. Examples: „Französisch zu lernen“ = to learn French; „auf Französisch zu sprechen“ = to speak in French. Often appears after verbs like „schaffen“, „versuchen“, „helfen“, „Gelegenheit nutzen“ etc.
target_language_example: Ich versuche, auf Französisch zu schreiben.
native_language_example: I’m trying to write in French.

additional_notes: An infinitive phrase: **zu + infinitive** (hier: *zu lernen* = “to learn”). *Französisch* (the language) is capitalized in German. This phrase is often used after another verb or expression (e.g., *schwerfallen*, *Gelegenheit haben*, *Lust haben*, *jemanden überreden*).
target_language_example: Ich versuche, Französisch zu lernen.
native_language_example: I'm trying to learn French.

additional_notes: Uses the infinitive construction "zu + infinitive" ("zu sprechen" = "to speak"). You can replace "Französisch" with another language: "Deutsch zu sprechen" (to speak German). Often used after verbs/adjectives like "Spaß machen" (be fun), "Lust haben" (feel like), "schwierig" (difficult), "sich weigern" (refuse), "beibringen" (teach).
target_language_example: Es ist nicht leicht, Französisch zu sprechen.
native_language_example: It’s not easy to speak French.

meaning: to translate (something) into/from French (intended meaning; wording is unidiomatic in German).
additional_notes:
This exact wording is not idiomatic German and sounds like a fragment. In standard German you would normally say:
- **etwas ins Französische übersetzen** = to translate something **into** French
- **etwas aus dem Französischen übersetzen** = to translate something **from** French
Also note: **Französisch** is the language (“French”). **Französische** usually means “French people/things” (plural or nominalized adjective) and doesn’t fit well as the language name here.

If you must keep the exact term (e.g., because it appears in instructions or a bad prompt), it’s best treated as a quoted label rather than natural German.
target_language_example: In der Aufgabenstellung steht wörtlich, „Französische zu übersetzen“; gemeint ist wahrscheinlich, den Text ins Französische zu übersetzen.
native_language_example: The assignment literally says “Französische zu übersetzen”; it probably means to translate the text into French.

meaning: “translated into French” (or, less commonly and only with missing context, could be interpreted as relating to French translation).
additional_notes:
As written, **Französische übersetzt** is not a complete, idiomatic standalone phrase in standard German. In natural usage you would typically add a preposition and use the noun form of the language:
- **aus dem Französischen übersetzt** = translated **from** French
- **ins Französische übersetzt** = translated **into** French
If you must keep the exact string **Französische übersetzt**, it most naturally appears as part of a longer phrase like **ins Französische übersetzt** (where *Französische* is the required inflected form after *ins*).
target_language_example: Der Text wurde ins Französische übersetzt.
native_language_example: The text was translated into French.

additional_notes: Used to start a relative clause describing a specific woman. Typically follows a noun phrase like "eine Frau" or "die erste/hübscheste Frau" and then gives more information about her: "eine Frau, die dort saß" (= a woman who was sitting there). The verb in the relative clause usually goes to the end: "die ich kenne", "die allein über den Atlantik flog".
target_language_example: Ich kenne eine Frau, die drei Sprachen spricht.
native_language_example: I know a woman who speaks three languages.

meaning: formal way to address a female doctor (“Doctor”).
additional_notes: Used as a respectful form of address, especially in professional settings (e.g., at a doctor’s office). It can refer to a medical doctor and, in German-speaking contexts, also to someone with a doctoral degree. Often paired with formal "Sie/Ihnen" and can sound quite formal or old-fashioned in some situations.
target_language_example: Entschuldigen Sie, Frau Doktor, hätten Sie kurz Zeit für mich?
native_language_example: Excuse me, Doctor, do you have a moment for me?

additional_notes: “Frau” can mean either “woman” (a general woman) or “wife” (someone’s spouse). In sentences like “Ihre Frau ist …”, it usually means “your wife is …”. The meaning depends on context and any possessive/article (die/eine/ihre/seine).
target_language_example: Meine Frau ist heute bei der Arbeit.
native_language_example: My wife is at work today.

additional_notes: Used to add extra information about a group of women: "Frauen, die ..." = "women who ...". In German, a comma is usually required before the relative pronoun: "Frauen, die ...". Here "die" is the relative pronoun for plural "Frauen" (it can also be used for other plural nouns, not only women).
target_language_example: Ich kenne Frauen, die jeden Tag Fahrrad fahren.
native_language_example: I know women who ride a bike every day.

additional_notes: Used to describe women in general or a group of women. It’s the plural subject "Frauen" (women) + the 3rd-person plural of "sein" (to be): "sind" (are). Often without an article to make a general statement ("Frauen sind ..." = "Women are ..."); with "die" it means a specific group ("Die Frauen sind ..." = "The women are ...").
target_language_example: Frauen sind heute im Büro.
native_language_example: Women are in the office today.

additional_notes: A fixed phrase used to refer to the non-combatant/civilian group “women and children,” often in contexts like war, danger, evacuation, or rescue (sometimes implying priority for protection or evacuation). Usually plural; can take articles/cases: „die Frauen und Kinder“, „Frauen und Kinder“.
target_language_example: In solchen Notfällen bringt man zuerst Frauen und Kinder in Sicherheit.
native_language_example: In emergencies like that, women and children are brought to safety first.

additional_notes: An infinitive phrase with **zu** (“to …”), often used after another verb: **Ich versuche/plane/hoffe, eine Fremdsprache zu lernen.** Without **zu**, you commonly say **eine Fremdsprache lernen** (“to learn a foreign language”). You’ll also often see the plural: **Fremdsprachen lernen** (“to learn foreign languages”).
target_language_example: Ich versuche, eine Fremdsprache zu lernen.
native_language_example: I’m trying to learn a foreign language.

meaning: "friend who..." (a male friend described with a relative clause).
additional_notes: Used when you add extra information about a male friend by starting a relative clause with the relative pronoun "der" (here: masculine, nominative). In other cases you may need a different form: "den" (accusative), "dem" (dative), "dessen" (genitive). Written German usually has a comma before the relative clause: "ein Freund, der ..."
target_language_example: Ich habe einen Freund, der in Berlin wohnt.
native_language_example: I have a friend who lives in Berlin.

additional_notes: Used to refer to one (unspecified) person from your group of friends. Very often used with an article: „ein Freund von mir“ = “a friend of mine.” You can change the noun and pronoun: „eine Freundin von mir“ (a female friend of mine), „ein Kollege von mir“ (a colleague of mine), „ein Freund von uns“ (a friend of ours).
target_language_example: Ein Freund von mir wohnt in Berlin.
native_language_example: A friend of mine lives in Berlin.

additional_notes: Used to describe a group of friends with a certain characteristic or ability. The comma is required before the relative clause in German: „Freunde, die …“. Here, „die“ is the relative pronoun for plural („Freunde“) and often corresponds to English “who/that.” Depending on the role inside the clause, it can change (e.g., „Freunde, denen ich vertraue“ = friends whom I trust / friends I довер trust; „Freunde, die ich kenne“ = friends (that) I know).
target_language_example: Ich suche Freunde, die gerne wandern gehen.
native_language_example: I'm looking for friends who like to go hiking.

additional_notes: Used to add a relative clause describing the friends. **mit** takes the dative case, so the relative pronoun is **denen** (dative plural) because it refers to **Freunde** (plural). Word order: the verb in the relative clause goes to the end (e.g., „mit denen er reden kann“).
target_language_example: Er hat ein paar Freunde, mit denen er am Wochenende Fußball spielt.
native_language_example: He has a few friends that he plays soccer with on the weekend.

additional_notes: Used to describe or identify friends in the plural: "Freunde" (friends) + "sind" (are). Often followed by an adjective or a place/person: "Freunde sind nett." / "Unsere Freunde sind in Boston." In questions, the verb usually comes first: "Sind Freunde immer ehrlich?"
target_language_example: Gute Freunde sind schwer zu finden.
native_language_example: Good friends are hard to find.

additional_notes: Used as a proper name for a specific location (often a park on an island). It’s feminine because of *die Insel*: *die Freundschafts-Insel*. With movement/going there you’ll often hear: *zur Freundschafts-Insel* (= *zu der*).
target_language_example: Wir gehen nachher zur Freundschafts-Insel und machen einen Spaziergang.
native_language_example: Later we’re going to Friendship Island and taking a walk.

meaning: to bear fruit; to pay off (to produce good results).
additional_notes: Used for efforts, research, learning, plans, or hard work that eventually lead to success. Can also be literal for trees/plants producing fruit (e.g., "Diese Bäume tragen keine Früchte"). Often used with "werden" for future results: "wird/werden Früchte tragen".
target_language_example: Wenn du regelmäßig übst, wird deine Arbeit bald Früchte tragen.
native_language_example: If you practice regularly, your work will soon pay off.

meaning: (usually: „zu Fuß nach Hause“) ‘home on foot’ / ‘walk home’.
additional_notes: In German you normally say **„zu Fuß“** = “on foot.” So the natural phrase is **„zu Fuß nach Hause“** (“walk home”). **nach Hause** means “(to) home” (movement toward home).
target_language_example: Ich gehe heute zu Fuß nach Hause.
native_language_example: I’m walking home today.

additional_notes: In natural German you normally say **„zu Fuß nach Hause gegangen“** (= went home on foot). It uses the past participle **gegangen** with **sein** in the Perfekt: **„Ich bin zu Fuß nach Hause gegangen.“** Also, **„nach Hause“** is used without an article (not *nach dem Hause*).
target_language_example: Wir sind gestern zu Fuß nach Hause gegangen.
native_language_example: We walked home yesterday.

meaning: (usually: „zu Fuß zur Arbeit“) on foot / walking to work.
additional_notes: In natural German you normally say **„zu Fuß“** (= on foot). The full phrase is typically **„zu Fuß zur Arbeit gehen/fahren“**. Without **„zu“**, it sounds incomplete.
target_language_example: Ich gehe jeden Tag zu Fuß zur Arbeit.
native_language_example: I walk to work every day.

additional_notes: In real German you almost always say **„zu Fuß zur Schule“** (literally: “on foot to school”). It’s used with verbs like **gehen/kommen**: **„Ich gehe zu Fuß zur Schule.“** (You wouldn’t normally say *„Ich fahre zu Fuß…“*.)
target_language_example: Heute gehe ich zu Fuß zur Schule.
native_language_example: Today I’m walking to school.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "haben" to form the Perfekt (past): "Ich habe Fußball gespielt." You can also see it in the passive: "Es wird (viel) Fußball gespielt" = "(A lot of) soccer is played." In German, "Fußball" usually means soccer (not American football).
target_language_example: Als Kind habe ich jeden Samstag Fußball gespielt.
native_language_example: As a child, I played soccer every Saturday.

meaning: to give (someone) something for their birthday / as a birthday present.
additional_notes: In natural German you usually use a prepositional phrase: **(jemandem) etwas zum Geburtstag schenken**. The bare combination **Geburtstag schenken** is uncommon on its own; it typically appears as part of a longer sentence (e.g., with **zum**). Common patterns: **Ich schenke dir (etwas) zum Geburtstag.** / **Was schenkst du ihm/ihr zum Geburtstag?**
target_language_example: Ich will meiner Schwester zum Geburtstag schenken, was sie sich wirklich wünscht.
native_language_example: I want to give my sister, for her birthday, what she really wants.

meaning: to read minds; to read someone’s thoughts.
additional_notes: Often used to talk about a (real or imagined) ability to know what someone is thinking without them saying it. Used with können (can): „Er kann Gedanken lesen.“ You can also add a possessive to specify whose thoughts: „meine/deine/eure Gedanken lesen“.
target_language_example: Du musst es nicht sagen – ich kann Gedanken lesen.
native_language_example: You don’t have to say it—I can read minds.

meaning: a poem by heart; a memorized poem.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like **auswendig lernen** (to memorize/learn by heart) and **auswendig kennen** (to know by heart). You often add **das/ein**: **ein Gedicht auswendig lernen**.
target_language_example: Kannst du das Gedicht auswendig?
native_language_example: Can you recite the poem by heart?

meaning: to be patient; to have patience.
additional_notes: Used with a person as the subject and often with a modal verb: „Ich/du/wir muss(t) Geduld haben“ = I/you/we need to be patient. You can add „(nur) etwas Geduld“ to mean “(just) a little patience.”
target_language_example: Wir müssen nur etwas Geduld haben.
native_language_example: We just need to be a little patient.

additional_notes: Very common polite phrase. Pattern: jemanden (Akk.) um einen Gefallen (Akk.) bitten. You can add adjectives like großen/kleinen/weiteren: „Ich muss dich um einen großen Gefallen bitten.“ Often used with „möchte“ to sound more polite: „Ich möchte dich um einen Gefallen bitten.“
target_language_example: Könnte ich dich um einen Gefallen bitten?
native_language_example: Could I ask you for a favor?

additional_notes: Usually used as "jemandem einen Gefallen tun" (dative + "einen"), meaning you help someone or do something nice/useful for them. Often appears in polite requests: "Könntest du mir bitte einen (kleinen/großen) Gefallen tun?" You can also say "Ich tue dir einen Gefallen" = "I’m doing you a favor."
target_language_example: Kannst du mir einen Gefallen tun und die Tür zumachen?
native_language_example: Can you do me a favor and close the door?

additional_notes: Usually used as "jmds. Gefühle verletzen" (literally: to hurt/injure someone’s feelings). With "zu" it commonly appears in infinitive clauses after verbs like "fürchten" or "Angst haben": "Er fürchtete, ihre Gefühle zu verletzen." Because the feelings belong to someone, you typically use a possessive pronoun: "seine/ihre/deine Gefühle".
target_language_example: Er fürchtete, ihre Gefühle zu verletzen.
native_language_example: He feared hurting her feelings.

meaning: in contrast to; as opposed to.
additional_notes: Most commonly used as **im Gegensatz zu** + dative (“in contrast to ...”). It’s a fairly formal way to compare two things and highlight a difference.
target_language_example: Im Gegensatz zu meinem Bruder fahre ich lieber mit dem Zug.
native_language_example: In contrast to my brother, I prefer traveling by train.

meaning: to reveal a secret; to tell someone a secret.
additional_notes: Often used with an indirect object in the dative (the person you tell): jemandem ein Geheimnis verraten. You can also say sein/ihr Geheimnis verraten (“reveal his/her secret”). In many contexts it implies you’re not supposed to tell (like “spill the secret”).
target_language_example: Ich will dir ein Geheimnis verraten.
native_language_example: I want to tell you a secret.

additional_notes: Used when the noun „Geld“ is followed by a relative clause introduced by „das“. The comma before the relative pronoun is required: „das Geld, das …“. Since „Geld“ is neuter singular, the relative pronoun is typically „das“ when it functions as subject or direct object within the relative clause. Other relative-pronoun forms (e.g., „dem Geld, dem …“) can occur depending on the role inside the relative clause.
target_language_example: Das ist das ganze Geld, das ich habe.
native_language_example: That is all the money that I have.

meaning: “money that I …” (a relative clause: money that I have / had / carry, etc.).
additional_notes: Used when you add extra information about which money you mean. It’s typically followed by a verb later in the clause (German word order): „… Geld, das ich jetzt habe / das ich bei mir hatte.“ Here „das“ refers back to „Geld“ (neuter), so you use „das“, not „der/die“.
target_language_example: Ich habe nur das Geld, das ich heute dabei habe.
native_language_example: I only have the money that I have with me today.

additional_notes: Common pattern: **Geld, um ... zu + infinitive** = money needed *in order to* do something. The comma often comes before the **um ... zu** clause: *Sie brauchte Geld, um ... zu kaufen.*
target_language_example: Ich brauche Geld, um ein Ticket zu kaufen.
native_language_example: I need money to buy a ticket.

meaning: money in the bank (in your bank account).
additional_notes: Means you have savings or funds available in your bank account. Literally “money on the bank,” but in English you say “in the bank.” Often used when talking about financial security: „Ich habe noch Geld auf der Bank.“
target_language_example: Ich habe nicht viel Geld, aber noch etwas Geld auf der Bank.
native_language_example: I don’t have much money, but I still have some money in the bank.

additional_notes: Perfekt/past participle form of "Geld ausgeben" used with "haben": "Ich habe (viel/zu viel) Geld ausgegeben" = "I spent (a lot/too much) money." Often followed by "für" to specify what it was spent on: "Geld für etwas ausgeben".
target_language_example: Ich habe heute zu viel Geld ausgegeben.
native_language_example: I spent too much money today.

additional_notes: Used to say what you spend/pay/collect money for. Very common in patterns like „Geld für etw. ausgeben“ (to spend money on sth) and „Geld für etw. einwerfen/spenden“ (to put in/donate money for sth). „für“ takes the accusative: Geld für + accusative object (e.g., „für Bücher“).
target_language_example: Wir sparen Geld für den Urlaub.
native_language_example: We’re saving money for the vacation.

additional_notes: This is the past participle of „Geld geben“ (to give money / to pay). It’s usually used with „haben“ to form the Perfekt: „Ich habe … Geld gegeben.“ The person who receives the money is in the dative (mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen/Ihnen), and the money is often „das Geld“ (accusative): „Ich habe ihm das Geld gegeben.“
target_language_example: Ich habe dir das Geld gegeben.
native_language_example: I gave you the money.

additional_notes: Usually used with "haben" in the Perfekt: "jmd. hat Geld gestohlen" = someone stole/has stolen money. If you want to say "stolen money" as a noun phrase, German typically uses the adjective form: "gestohlenes Geld".
target_language_example: Sie hat kein Geld gestohlen.
native_language_example: She didn’t steal any money.

additional_notes: This is the German perfect infinitive: **zu haben** + past participle (**gestohlen**). It’s often used after certain verbs (e.g., **zugeben** = to admit, **beschuldigen** = to accuse, **verdächtigen** = to suspect) to talk about something someone is said/admitted/suspected to have done in the past. The object **Geld** (money) is what was stolen.
target_language_example: Er hat zugegeben, Geld gestohlen zu haben.
native_language_example: He admitted to having stolen money.

additional_notes: Used to talk about making money through work (salary, wages, etc.). In questions it’s often about how much you want to earn: „viel Geld verdienen“ = “earn a lot of money.”
target_language_example: Ich muss Geld verdienen, um die Miete zu bezahlen.
native_language_example: I have to earn money to pay the rent.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "verdienen" (to earn). In the present perfect it’s usually "Ich habe … Geld verdient" (I earned/have earned money). "Eigenes Geld verdienen" means to earn your own money; "eine Menge" = a lot; "kaum" = hardly.
target_language_example: Er hat mit dem Nebenjob Geld verdient.
native_language_example: He earned money with the part-time job.

meaning: “money to …” (used before a zu‑infinitive, e.g. “Geld zu sparen” = “to save money”).
additional_notes: This isn’t a fixed expression; it’s the noun **Geld** followed by a **zu + infinitive** phrase. It often appears as **Geld zu + infinitive** to say what someone is doing with money (save it, send it, launder it, earn it, etc.). Word order: **Geld zu + verb** at the end of the clause (e.g., „Er versucht, Geld zu sparen.“).
target_language_example: Ich versuche, Geld zu verdienen.
native_language_example: I’m trying to earn money.

additional_notes: Infinitive phrase with „zu“ used after many verbs/expressions (e.g., „bitten“, „dazu bringen“, „so freundlich/nett sein“) to mean lending money to someone: „jemandem Geld leihen“ = to lend someone money. The recipient is in the dative: „mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen Geld leihen“. Don’t confuse with „sich Geld leihen“ = to borrow money.
target_language_example: Ich bat ihn, mir Geld zu leihen.
native_language_example: I asked him to lend me money.

additional_notes: Used with "um ... zu" to express purpose: "um Geld zu verdienen" = "in order to earn money". The verb is "(Geld) verdienen" (to earn money); "zu verdienen" is the infinitive form used in these constructions.
target_language_example: Sie hat einen Nebenjob, um Geld zu verdienen.
native_language_example: She has a part-time job to earn money.

additional_notes: Common in shops, ads, and customer service to promise a refund (often as part of a guarantee): „Geld zurück!“ or „Sie bekommen Ihr Geld zurück.“ You’ll also see it with a time period: „30 Tage Geld zurück“ (= 30-day money-back guarantee).
target_language_example: Wenn du nicht zufrieden bist, bekommst du dein Geld zurück.
native_language_example: If you’re not satisfied, you get your money back.

additional_notes: Most often used as a stage direction or in scripts/subtitles to show that people stop laughing and it becomes quiet. "aus" here means "off/ended" (like switching something off).
target_language_example: Gelächter aus. Dann wird es plötzlich ganz still.
native_language_example: The laughter stops. Then it suddenly gets very quiet.

additional_notes: Used when you say who the present is for. It’s commonly followed by a person in the accusative: für + mich/dich/ihn/sie/es/uns/euch/sie/Sie or a name (für Tom). Often used with kaufen/bringen/haben: ein Geschenk für jemanden kaufen.
target_language_example: Ich habe ein kleines Geschenk für dich.
native_language_example: I have a small gift for you.

additional_notes: Used when giving or talking about a gift meant for the person you’re speaking to. You’ll often hear it with demonstratives like „Das ist …“ / „Dies ist …“ (“This is …”), or with adjectives like „ein kleines“ (“a small”). „für dich“ uses the accusative after „für“.
target_language_example: Ich habe ein kleines Geschenk für dich.
native_language_example: I have a small present for you.

meaning: to like a gift; (literally) “the gift pleased someone”.
additional_notes: Used with the verb **gefallen**: the thing that is liked (here: **das Geschenk**) is the grammatical subject, and the person who likes it is in the **dative** (mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/**Ihnen**). Common question: **Hat Ihnen das Geschenk gefallen?** = “Did you like the gift?” Note: **gefallen** is not “to fall” (that’s **fallen**), so it can be confusing.
target_language_example: Hat Ihnen Ihr Geschenk gefallen?
native_language_example: Did you like your gift?

meaning: to tell a story; to tell someone your story.
additional_notes: Used for telling a (often longer) story or narrative, either fictional (e.g., a children’s story) or personal (your life/story). Common patterns: „jemandem eine Geschichte erzählen“ (tell someone a story) and „seine/ihre Geschichte erzählen“ (tell your story).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir eine Geschichte erzählen?
native_language_example: Can you tell me a story?

additional_notes: Commonly appears as part of a larger phrase, especially with an object: „eine Geschichte erzählt“ (told a story) or „die Geschichte erzählt“ (told the story). „Geschichte“ can mean a (fictional) story, an anecdote/account, or „history“ (the subject/past events); which meaning is intended is usually clear from context. Note: on its own, „Geschichte erzählt“ is typically not a standalone phrase in German; it’s most natural within a full clause (e.g., „Er hat die Geschichte erzählt.“).
target_language_example: Ich habe Tom die Geschichte erzählt.
native_language_example: I told Tom the story.

meaning: to show your face; to make an appearance (often: to take a stand publicly).
additional_notes: Literally “to show (your) face.” Used both for simply appearing somewhere (“He finally showed up”) and in a more figurative sense meaning to show courage/support and be visibly present, e.g. “gegen Rassismus Gesicht zeigen” = “to take a stand against racism.”
target_language_example: Komm zur Veranstaltung und zeig dein Gesicht – es ist wichtig, Gesicht zu zeigen.
native_language_example: Come to the event and show your face—it’s important to make an appearance / take a stand.

additional_notes: A common, literal phrase for the highest point of a mountain. "Gipfel" = summit/peak; "des Berges" is genitive ("of the mountain"). You’ll often also see: "der Gipfel des Bergs" or simply "der Gipfel" when the mountain is clear from context.
target_language_example: Am Gipfel des Berges machten wir eine Pause.
native_language_example: At the top of the mountain, we took a break.

additional_notes: Common way to talk about playing an instrument: [instrument] + spielen. Often used after modal verbs like können (can) or mögen (to like), or with verbs like lernen (to learn): „Kannst du Gitarre spielen?“ / „Ich lerne Gitarre spielen.“ In simple present without a modal/infinitive construction, German usually says „Ich spiele Gitarre.“ (split form), but the phrasebook term here is the infinitive construction „Gitarre spielen“.
target_language_example: Ich lerne jetzt Gitarre spielen.
native_language_example: I’m learning to play the guitar now.

additional_notes: Used when ordering or talking about beer served in a glass. Very common with quantities/articles: „ein Glas Bier“, „noch ein Glas Bier“, „ein großes/kaltes Glas Bier“. In restaurants you’ll also hear „ein Bier“ (a beer) when the size/type is understood.
target_language_example: Ich nehme ein Glas Bier, bitte.
native_language_example: I’ll have a glass of beer, please.

additional_notes: Used when ordering, offering, or asking for milk as a drink. Very common with an article: „ein Glas Milch“ (a glass of milk), „das Glas Milch“ (the glass of milk). Often with adjectives like „ein großes Glas Milch“ (a big glass of milk).
target_language_example: Ich hätte gern ein Glas Milch, bitte.
native_language_example: I’d like a glass of milk, please.

additional_notes: Usually said as **ein Glas Wasser** (“a glass of water”). In everyday speech you may also hear **ein Glas Wasser, bitte** when ordering/asking for water. Example 4 uses it idiomatically: **in einem Glas Wasser ertrinken** (“to drown in a glass of water”) = to be overwhelmed by a very small problem.
target_language_example: Kann ich bitte ein Glas Wasser haben?
native_language_example: Can I have a glass of water, please?

additional_notes: Usually said with an article/number: „ein Glas Wein“ (a glass of wine), „noch ein Glas Wein“ (another glass of wine). Plural: „zwei Gläser Wein“ (two glasses of wine). Common when ordering in a bar/restaurant.
target_language_example: Ich hätte gern ein Glas Wein, bitte.
native_language_example: I’d like a glass of wine, please.

additional_notes: Used to say someone was fortunate that a situation happened (or didn’t happen). Often followed by a subordinate clause with the verb at the end: „… dass ich dich gefunden habe.“ Common patterns: „Du hast Glück, dass …“, „Ich hatte Glück, dass …“, „Was für ein Glück, dass …“, „Welch Glück, dass …“.
target_language_example: Du hast Glück, dass ich heute Zeit habe.
native_language_example: You’re lucky that I have time today.

meaning: (He is/was) lucky that … / Good thing that …
additional_notes: Used with a dass-clause to say someone is fortunate something happened (or is true). Common variants include: „Er hatte Glück, dass …“ (= He was lucky that …), „Ein Glück, dass …“ (= Good thing that …), and „Dein Glück, dass …“ (= You’re lucky that …). The subject changes depending on who is lucky (ich/du/er/sie/wir/ihr/sie).
target_language_example: Er hatte Glück, dass er den Zug noch erwischt hat.
native_language_example: He was lucky that he still caught the train.

additional_notes: Used when you hope an action, object, or event will result in good luck for someone. The person who receives the luck is in the dative: "mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen" (e.g., "Das bringt dir Glück"). Common in wishes: "Möge dir … Glück bringen!"
target_language_example: Dieser Anhänger soll dir Glück bringen.
native_language_example: This charm is supposed to bring you good luck.

additional_notes: Used with "haben" (e.g., "Du hast Glück gehabt") to say someone was lucky in a situation. Often said alone as an exclamation—"Glück gehabt!"—meaning "Lucky you!" or "That was lucky!" especially after something almost went wrong. Commonly followed by "dass ..." to explain what the luck was.
target_language_example: Glück gehabt, dass nichts passiert ist!
native_language_example: Lucky that nothing happened!

meaning: to be lucky; to have good luck.
additional_notes: Used to say that something turned out well by chance. Often used with a specific situation: „Ich habe Glück gehabt“ (I was lucky) or „Du hast Glück, dass …“ (You’re lucky that …). In the past, it’s very common as „Glück gehabt!“ meaning „Lucky you!“ / „That was close!“
target_language_example: Du musst heute wirklich Glück haben, wenn du noch ein Ticket bekommen willst.
native_language_example: You really have to be lucky today if you still want to get a ticket.

additional_notes: Used to congratulate someone on their birthday. It’s a bit more formal than the very common "Alles Gute zum Geburtstag!" or simply "Alles Gute!" You can also say "Herzlichen Glückwunsch zum Geburtstag!" to sound warmer/more enthusiastic.
target_language_example: Herzlichen Glückwunsch zum Geburtstag, Maria!
native_language_example: Happy birthday, Maria!

additional_notes: Used as an exclamation of relief or gratitude when something turns out well (often like “thank goodness”). It can be used in both religious and non-religious contexts. Often appears with a comma when followed by extra information: “Gott sei Dank, …” or “Gott sei Dank ist/hat …”. Literally it’s an older-style form meaning “God be thanked.”
target_language_example: Gott sei Dank habe ich meinen Pass doch noch gefunden.
native_language_example: Thank God, I found my passport after all.

meaning: God knows (used to emphasize truth or uncertainty).
additional_notes: Often used to stress that something is true ("God knows that...") or that nobody really knows ("Gott weiß, wohin" = "God knows where"). Can also be said alone as a short answer: "Gott weiß." = "God knows." Typically followed by a comma when introducing a clause.
target_language_example: Gott weiß, wie lange das noch dauert.
native_language_example: God knows how long that will take.

meaning: to get a flu shot (to have yourself vaccinated against the flu).
additional_notes: Often used with a reflexive pronoun: "sich gegen Grippe impfen lassen" (most explicit). "lassen" indicates you have it done by a medical professional. Common with time phrases like "im Herbst" or "jedes Jahr".
target_language_example: Ich werde mich im Herbst gegen Grippe impfen lassen.
native_language_example: I’m going to get a flu shot in the fall.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an explanation, usually followed by a clause with a verb at the end: „der Grund, warum ich zu spät war“. Often used with „der Grund“ (the reason) or „ein Grund“ (a reason). The comma is standard because „warum“ introduces a relative clause here.
target_language_example: Das ist der Grund, warum ich heute nicht kommen kann.
native_language_example: That’s the reason why I can’t come today.

meaning: reason for concern / reason to worry.
additional_notes: Used to say there is (or isn’t) a reason to be worried. Very common in the phrase „Kein Grund zur Sorge.“ (= “No need to worry.”). You can also add a reason with „Es gibt Grund zur Sorge, weil …“ (= “There is reason for concern because …”).
target_language_example: Kein Grund zur Sorge, das ist ganz normal.
native_language_example: No need to worry, that’s completely normal.

additional_notes: A common fixed phrase used when talking about morality. Often appears with verbs like „(unter)scheiden“ or „auseinanderhalten“ (to tell apart/distinguish): „Gut und Böse unterscheiden“ = to distinguish right from wrong.
target_language_example: Manchmal ist es schwer, Gut und Böse zu unterscheiden.
native_language_example: Sometimes it's hard to tell right from wrong.

meaning: (Not standard on its own.) Usually meant as: “Happy birthday!”
additional_notes: The common, correct phrase is **„Alles Gute zum Geburtstag!“** (“Happy birthday!” / “All the best for your birthday!”). People may shorten it to **„Alles Gute!“** (especially if it’s clear it’s about a birthday). Using just **„Gute zum Geburtstag“** is unusual/incorrect; you might also hear **„Alles Gute zum Geburtstag, …“** followed by the person’s name.
target_language_example: Alles Gute zum Geburtstag, Anna!
native_language_example: Happy birthday, Anna!

meaning: to cut hair / get a haircut.
additional_notes: Often used with the structure „sich die Haare schneiden lassen“ (= to have your hair cut by someone else): „Ich lasse mir die Haare schneiden.“ The person whose hair it is can appear in the dative („mir/dir/ihm…“) and the hair is usually „die Haare“ (plural). In formal situations use „Lassen Sie …“, and in informal use „Lass …“.
target_language_example: Ich lasse mir morgen die Haare schneiden.
native_language_example: I’m getting a haircut tomorrow.

meaning: to get your hair cut (have someone cut it).
additional_notes: Uses the structure "etwas + Verb + lassen" to mean you arrange for someone else to do something for you. A common fuller version is "sich die Haare schneiden lassen". Often used with a place or person: "beim Friseur" (at the hairdresser’s).
target_language_example: Ich möchte mir morgen die Haare schneiden lassen.
native_language_example: I’d like to get my hair cut tomorrow.

meaning: to cut hair (to get your hair cut).
additional_notes: This is the infinitive with **zu** (“to cut hair”). You often use it after another verb (e.g., *versuchen, planen, vergessen, Zeit haben*): *Ich habe keine Zeit, mir die Haare zu schneiden.* For talking about the general activity, you’ll also see **Haare schneiden** (without *zu*). Commonly you add **mir die Haare** = “my hair” when it’s your own hair.
target_language_example: Ich habe heute keine Zeit, mir die Haare zu schneiden.
native_language_example: I don’t have time to cut my hair today.

meaning: hand in hand; closely connected / going together.
additional_notes: Used literally for people walking while holding hands (often with "gehen"). Very common figuratively with "gehen" ("X und Y gehen Hand in Hand") to mean two things are closely linked and usually happen together.
target_language_example: In dieser Stadt gehen Tradition und Moderne Hand in Hand.
native_language_example: In this city, tradition and modernity go hand in hand.

meaning: hand-to-mouth (living with only enough money for daily needs).
additional_notes: Usually used as part of fixed phrases like „von der Hand in den Mund leben“ or „aus der Hand in den Mund leben“, meaning you have no savings and can only cover expenses day by day.
target_language_example: Nach der Kündigung lebten sie eine Zeit lang von der Hand in den Mund.
native_language_example: After the layoff, they lived hand-to-mouth for a while.

additional_notes: Used mainly when talking about books, movies, or stories that end well. In German it’s a common loanword from English and is usually used with an article: „ein Happy End“, „mit einem Happy End“.
target_language_example: Der Film hat zum Glück ein Happy End.
native_language_example: Luckily, the movie has a happy ending.

additional_notes: Used to name the capital city of a country or region. Usually followed by the thing it belongs to with **von + dative**: *die Hauptstadt von Deutschland*. You’ll also see the alternative **genitive** form: *Deutschlands Hauptstadt* (more formal/written).
target_language_example: Berlin ist die Hauptstadt von Deutschland.
native_language_example: Berlin is the capital of Germany.

additional_notes: Usually used as part of a full sentence like: “Das Haus befindet sich …” + a place (often with in/auf/bei + dative). “sich befinden” is a common, slightly formal way to say where something is. With people, “sich befinden” can also mean “to be/feel” (e.g., “Wie befinden Sie sich?”).
target_language_example: Das Haus befindet sich in der Nähe des Bahnhofs.
native_language_example: The house is located near the train station.

meaning: “built a house” (past tense of „ein Haus bauen“).
additional_notes: Usually appears in the Perfekt (common spoken past): „(jemand) hat ein Haus gebaut“ = “(someone) built a house.” You can add an object to show who it was built for: „Er hat ihnen ein Haus gebaut“ (for them). With „sich“ it means building it for yourself: „Er hat sich ein Haus gebaut“ = “He built himself a house.”
target_language_example: Wir haben letztes Jahr ein Haus gebaut.
native_language_example: We built a house last year.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific house by its street location. In German, streets are often expressed with **in der + street name** (dative), e.g. *in der Parkstraße* = “on Park Street.”
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns vor dem Haus in der Parkstraße.
native_language_example: We’re meeting in front of the house on Park Street.

meaning: 'house is' (used to say what a house/home is like or what it is).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom—it's simply the noun "Haus" (house/home) + the verb "ist" (is), as in "Das Haus ist groß." It’s used to describe a house or to identify it (e.g., where it is, what it’s made of, how it is). You’ll often see it with articles or possessives: "Das Haus ist ...", "Mein/Dein Haus ist ...".
target_language_example: Mein Haus ist nicht weit von hier.
native_language_example: My house is not far from here.

additional_notes: In correct German you normally need an article: **Das Haus ist in der Nähe.** The key phrase is **in der Nähe** = “nearby / close (by)”. You can also say **in der Nähe von + Dativ** (“near …”): **Das Haus ist in der Nähe vom Bahnhof.**
target_language_example: Das Haus ist in der Nähe vom Park.
native_language_example: The house is near the park.

meaning: to leave the house (to go out); also: to leave someone’s house/premises (can sound firm in a request/command).
additional_notes: Commonly used with the accusative: „das Haus verlassen“. Neutral in everyday contexts (go out/leave home), but can be forceful when telling someone to leave: „Ich will, dass Sie mein Haus verlassen!“ In the past it often appears in Perfekt/Plusquamperfekt: „hat verlassen“, „hatte verlassen“.
target_language_example: Layla hat das Haus verlassen.
native_language_example: Layla left the house.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like vorhaben/plan (to plan), überreden (to persuade), and erwägen (to consider) to express the intention or decision to buy a house. Often appears as „(sich) ein Haus zu kaufen“ (for oneself) or with an adjective: „ein neues Haus zu kaufen“.
target_language_example: Wir sparen gerade, um uns ein Haus zu kaufen.
native_language_example: We’re saving right now to buy a house.

additional_notes: Usually used with **mit** + dative: **mit den Hausaufgaben fertig sein** = “to be done with the homework.” You can also say **die Hausaufgaben fertig machen** = “to finish (doing) the homework.” Often appears with **schon** (“already”) and **rechtzeitig** (“on time”).
target_language_example: Ich bin schon mit meinen Hausaufgaben fertig.
native_language_example: I'm already done with my homework.

additional_notes: Very common with the verb „machen“: „Ich muss noch meine Hausaufgaben machen.“ The word „Hausaufgaben“ is almost always plural. You can add a possessive/determiner: „meine/deine/seine Hausaufgaben machen“ or just say it without one if it’s clear from context.
target_language_example: Ich kann erst später kommen, ich muss noch Hausaufgaben machen.
native_language_example: I can only come later; I still have to do homework.

additional_notes: In German you usually say **bei den Hausaufgaben helfen** or **mit den Hausaufgaben helfen**; the sequence **Hausaufgaben zu helfen** typically appears as part of an infinitive clause (e.g., **jemandem versprechen/bitten, bei/mit den Hausaufgaben zu helfen**). Common patterns: **jemandem bei/mit den Hausaufgaben helfen** (= help someone with their homework) and **jemanden bitten, bei/mit den Hausaufgaben zu helfen** (= ask someone to help with homework).
target_language_example: Ich versprach, meinem Bruder bei seinen Hausaufgaben zu helfen.
native_language_example: I promised to help my brother with his homework.

additional_notes: Common with structures like „Ich habe … zu machen“ (= I have … to do) or „um … zu machen“ (= in order to do …). In everyday speech you also often just say „Hausaufgaben machen“ without „zu“.
target_language_example: Ich habe heute Abend noch Hausaufgaben zu machen.
native_language_example: I still have homework to do this evening.

additional_notes: Note: **„Hause bleiben“** is not standard on its own; in correct German you normally say **„zu Hause bleiben“**. If you must use the exact term as given, it most naturally appears in the fixed expression **„nach Hause bleiben“** (rare/regionally influenced and generally not recommended). Use **„zu Hause bleiben“** in real-life German.
target_language_example: Ich werde heute lieber **Hause bleiben**.
native_language_example: I’d rather stay at home today.

additional_notes: In standard German you normally say **nach Hause bringen** (“to bring/take home”). **Hause bringen** on its own is incomplete/incorrect; it typically appears as part of **nach Hause bringen** and needs an object in the accusative (e.g., *dich*, *ihn*, *sie*).
target_language_example: Ich muss dich nach Hause bringen.
native_language_example: I have to take you home.

additional_notes: Standard is **nach Hause fahren** (often written as two words): *Ich fahre nach Hause.* It refers to traveling home by some means (car, bus, train, bike, etc.). For walking, use **nach Hause gehen**. Don’t confuse **nach Hause** (direction = “(to) home”) with **zu Hause** (location = “at home”).
target_language_example: Ich muss jetzt nach Hause fahren.
native_language_example: I have to go/drive home now.

meaning: (nonstandard; usually said as **nach Hause gehen**) to go home.
additional_notes: **Hause gehen** without **nach** is generally not standard in modern German. The idiomatic, correct form is **nach Hause gehen** (also: **nach Hause fahren/kommen**). **Hause** is a fixed form in this expression.
target_language_example: Ich muss jetzt Hause gehen.
native_language_example: I have to go home now.

additional_notes: In standard German you normally say **nach Hause kommen** (with **nach**). The form **Hause kommen** without **nach** is uncommon/elliptical and may sound nonstandard; prefer **nach Hause kommen** in most situations. Use **nach Hause** for movement (going/coming home) and **zu Hause** for location (being at home): **Ich bin zu Hause.**
target_language_example: Ich werde spät Hause kommen.
native_language_example: I will come home late.

meaning: (Incorrect word order; intended meaning is usually “at home”.)
additional_notes: “Hause zu” is not standard German and will sound wrong to native speakers. The correct fixed expression is “zu Hause” (“at home”): „Ich bin zu Hause.“ For motion toward home, use “nach Hause” (“(go) home”). If you saw “Hause zu” somewhere, it may be a typo or a learner’s mistake.
target_language_example: *Ich bin heute Hause zu. (incorrect; correct: „Ich bin heute zu Hause.“)
native_language_example: *I am at home today. (incorrect word order in German; correct: “Ich bin heute zu Hause.”)

additional_notes: Note: **„Hause zu bleiben“** is **not standard German**. The correct, common form is **„zu Hause bleiben“** (or in an infinitive construction: **„zu Hause zu bleiben“**). You’ll hear/see it when talking about not going out (e.g., because you’re sick, tired, or because of bad weather). Examples of correct forms: **Ich bleibe zu Hause.** / **Ich bleibe heute zu Hause.** / **Ich bin zu Hause geblieben.** / **Ich habe beschlossen, zu Hause zu bleiben.**
target_language_example: Ich habe beschlossen, Hause zu bleiben, weil ich krank bin.
native_language_example: I decided to stay at home because I'm sick.

meaning: (intended) “to go/drive home” — but this phrasing is not idiomatic/grammatical in standard German.
additional_notes: **„Hause zu fahren“** is generally not used on its own. The natural/standard phrasing is **„nach Hause fahren“** (or in an infinitive construction: **„nach Hause zu fahren“**), meaning “to go/drive home.” **nach Hause** = “(to) home” (no article: not *nach dem Hause*). With **fahren**, it can mean going by car, bus, train, etc. Alternatives: **nach Hause gehen** (to walk home).
target_language_example: Man sagt nicht „Hause zu fahren“, sondern „nach Hause zu fahren“.
native_language_example: You don’t say “Hause zu fahren,” but rather “nach Hause zu fahren.”

meaning: to go home (lit. “to go to home”).
additional_notes: In standard German, this is normally phrased as **nach Hause gehen** (or **nachhause gehen**) = “to go home.” **Hause zu gehen** is not idiomatic on its own; you may see it only in nonstandard/learner usage or if the word order is forced by context. Don’t confuse it with **zu Hause** = “at home” (a location, not movement).
target_language_example: Ich habe vor, heute früh nach der Arbeit nach Hause zu gehen, statt noch auszugehen; manchmal sagt man auch (nicht standardsprachlich): Ich habe vor, heute früh nach der Arbeit Hause zu gehen.
native_language_example: I plan to go home early after work today instead of going out; sometimes people also say (not standard): I plan to go home early after work today.

additional_notes: Used for safety rules (e.g., biking, skiing, construction). You can specify the situation with "beim" + activity: "Beim Fahrradfahren muss man einen Helm tragen."
target_language_example: Beim Fahrradfahren musst du einen Helm tragen.
native_language_example: When cycling, you have to wear a helmet.

meaning: “Mr. Director/Principal” — a formal way to address a male director or school principal.
