additional_notes: Usually used with a possessive: „seine/ihre/deine Meinung ändern“. The infinitive phrase „(die/eine) Meinung zu ändern“ is commonly used after verbs like „versuchen“, „schaffen“, „bereit sein“ or in fixed expressions like „nicht leicht/schwer, die Meinung zu ändern“.
target_language_example: Es ist nicht leicht, seine Meinung zu ändern.
native_language_example: It’s not easy to change your mind.

meaning: a lot of money; a (large) sum of money.
additional_notes: Most commonly used as "eine Menge Geld" (= a lot of money), often with verbs like "kosten" (to cost) or "schulden" (to owe). You can also say "eine große Menge Geld" for extra emphasis. It’s a neutral, everyday expression.
target_language_example: Für das neue Handy habe ich eine Menge Geld bezahlt.
native_language_example: I paid a lot of money for the new phone.

meaning: a lot of time (usually: „eine Menge Zeit“).
additional_notes: „Menge“ means an “amount/quantity.” In everyday German, you most often say „eine Menge Zeit“ = “a lot of time.” It’s used to emphasize that something takes (or gives you) lots of time: „Das kostet eine Menge Zeit.“
target_language_example: Das wird eine Menge Zeit kosten.
native_language_example: That will take a lot of time.

additional_notes: Usually used with an article: „eine Menge zu tun“ (= lots to do). Common with „haben“: „Ich habe eine Menge zu tun.“ You can also say „noch“ to mean “still”: „Ich habe noch eine Menge zu tun.“
target_language_example: Heute habe ich eine Menge zu tun.
native_language_example: Today I have a lot to do.

additional_notes: Used with an article or quantifier: **ein Mensch ist …** (a person is …), **der Mensch ist …** (humankind is … / humans are …), **jeder Mensch ist …** (every person is …), **kein Mensch ist …** (no person is … / nobody is …). In everyday speech, **kein Mensch** often means **“nobody”**.
target_language_example: Kein Mensch ist perfekt.
native_language_example: Nobody is perfect.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause that describes or identifies a group of people. “Die” changes with case/number (e.g., Menschen, denen … / Menschen, die …). Often used after words like "die Menschen" or "einer der Menschen".
target_language_example: Ich mag Menschen, die ehrlich sind.
native_language_example: I like people who are honest.

meaning: people in the world / on Earth.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the number or existence of people worldwide, often with expressions like „Es gibt …“ (there are …) or „Es leben …“ (… live). In English you usually say “people in the world” or “people on Earth,” not “on the world.”
target_language_example: Wie viele Menschen auf der Welt sprechen Deutsch?
native_language_example: How many people in the world speak German?

additional_notes: Used to make general statements about people. "Menschen" is plural, so the verb is plural: "haben" (not "hat"). Often followed by a noun (e.g., "Angst", "ein großes Gehirn", "kein Benehmen").
target_language_example: Menschen haben unterschiedliche Meinungen.
native_language_example: People have different opinions.

meaning: 'People are' / 'Humans are' (used to make general statements).
additional_notes: Used with a plural noun (Menschen = people/humans) plus the verb sein (to be) to describe people in general: Menschen sind + adjective/noun phrase. Note: Menschen means people/humans (not specifically 'men').
target_language_example: Menschen sind nicht perfekt.
native_language_example: People aren't perfect.

additional_notes: Used with a number to say how tall/high something is: „X Meter hoch“. Common with measurements of buildings, walls, snow, waves, etc. The number changes: „einen Meter hoch“, „drei Meter hoch“, „hundert Meter hoch“, etc.
target_language_example: Der Zaun ist zwei Meter hoch.
native_language_example: The fence is two meters high.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the amount of money (usually in US dollars). In German you typically say it with an article and number, e.g. „eine Million Dollar“. „Dollar“ is often left unchanged in the plural: „zwei Million(en) Dollar“. Also common in fixed expressions like „die Millionen-Dollar-Frage“ (the million-dollar question) or „ein Million-Dollar-Lächeln“ (a million-dollar smile).
target_language_example: Das Haus kostet eine Million Dollar.
native_language_example: The house costs a million dollars.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens a short time after an earlier event. Often appears with a number or quantifier: „einige/ wenige/ ein paar/ drei Minuten später“. It can also be used for arriving a bit late: „Ich komme … Minuten später.“
target_language_example: Zehn Minuten später begann der Film.
native_language_example: Ten minutes later, the movie started.

meaning: (to have/feel) pity for; to feel sorry for.
additional_notes: Usually used with the verb "haben": "Mitleid mit jemandem haben" (= to feel sorry for someone). "mit" takes the dative case: "mit mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen". Common in requests like "Hab/Habt Mitleid mit mir!"
target_language_example: Bitte hab Mitleid mit ihm.
native_language_example: Please have pity on him / please feel sorry for him.

meaning: to eat lunch; to have lunch.
additional_notes: Common everyday phrase for the midday meal. You can also say „zu Mittag essen“. Often used when making plans: „Mittag essen gehen“ = to go out for lunch (to eat lunch somewhere).
target_language_example: Wollen wir Mittag essen gehen?
native_language_example: Shall we go out for lunch?

meaning: middle of the (of the + masculine/neuter noun).
additional_notes: Used with the genitive case: des = “of the” for masculine/neuter nouns (e.g., des Gartens, des Parks, des Hauses). Often appears in phrases like „in die Mitte des …“ (into the middle of) or „in der Mitte des …“ (in the middle of). A common alternative is „in der Mitte von …“ (more general, uses von + dative).
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns in der Mitte des Parks.
native_language_example: We’ll meet in the middle of the park.

additional_notes: Uses the genitive case: des Zimmers = “of the room.” Common with location phrases like In der Mitte des Zimmers steht … (“In the middle of the room there is …”). You can also say: in der Mitte vom Zimmer (more spoken/colloquial).
target_language_example: In der Mitte des Zimmers steht ein Tisch.
native_language_example: There is a table in the middle of the room.

additional_notes: Very informal/colloquial and strongly influenced by English; often used by younger speakers or jokingly/ironically. Neutral/common German alternatives are "Mama und Papa" (more everyday) or "Mutter und Vater" (more formal).
target_language_example: Ich fahre am Wochenende mit Mom und Dad zu meiner Oma.
native_language_example: I'm going to my grandma's this weekend with Mom and Dad.

additional_notes: Used to say which month something is within a year (often with ordinals: der erste/zweite/dritte Monat des Jahres). Grammar: "Monat" is masculine (der Monat); "des Jahres" is the genitive form of "das Jahr" (the year).
target_language_example: Der Dezember ist der letzte Monat des Jahres.
native_language_example: December is the last month of the year.

additional_notes: Used with a number or quantity word to say how long something lasts: „drei Monate lang“, „ein paar Monate lang“. It’s an adverbial expression of duration and often goes with the simple past or present (e.g., „Ich war …“, „Ich lag …“, „Er spart …“).
target_language_example: Wir haben vier Monate lang auf die Lieferung gewartet.
native_language_example: We waited for the delivery for four months.

Montag gekommen und am nächsten Tag wieder abgereist

target_language_multi_word_term: Montag gekommen und am nächsten Tag wieder abgereist
meaning: arrived on Monday and left again the next day.
additional_notes: A set phrase-like travel description using the past participles (Perfekt): (ist) gekommen (to come/arrive) and (ist) abgereist (to depart/leave). You often add the helper verb once for both parts: „Er ist Montag gekommen und am nächsten Tag wieder abgereist.“ „am nächsten Tag“ = “the next day”; „wieder“ here means “again” (i.e., left shortly after arriving).
target_language_example: Sie ist Montag gekommen und am nächsten Tag wieder abgereist, weil sie einen Termin hatte.
native_language_example: She arrived on Monday and left again the next day because she had an appointment.

additional_notes: A formal legal phrase. It’s commonly used with the genitive: „des Mordes angeklagt (werden)“ = to be charged with murder. You may also see „wegen Mordes angeklagt“ (because of/on suspicion of murder).
target_language_example: Der Verdächtige wurde des Mordes angeklagt.
native_language_example: The suspect was charged with murder.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the morning of the next day. Often in plans and requests: „Morgen früh muss ich…“, „Morgen früh um acht…“. In context it can also mean simply “early” (as in: early that morning).
target_language_example: Morgen früh habe ich um acht einen Termin.
native_language_example: Tomorrow morning I have an appointment at eight.

meaning: to keep quiet; to shut up.
additional_notes: Colloquial and often rude/harsh, especially as an order ("Halt den Mund!"). Also used more neutrally in the sense of "not tell anyone" (keep your mouth shut about something).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte den Mund halten? Ich telefoniere gerade.
native_language_example: Can you please be quiet? I’m on the phone right now.

additional_notes: Used with Konjunktiv II (würde) in polite, hypothetical requests—most often in sentences like „Hättest du etwas dagegen, wenn ich … würde?“ or „Würde es dir etwas ausmachen, wenn ich … würde?“ Meaning: you’re asking for permission and trying to be polite. „Musik anmachen“ = to switch/turn music on (e.g., start playing music from a phone/speaker).
target_language_example: Hättest du etwas dagegen, wenn ich Musik anmachen würde?
native_language_example: Would you mind if I turned on some music?

additional_notes: Common infinitive phrase used to describe the activity of listening to music. Often appears in hobby/activity lists (e.g., „lesen, Musik hören“) and with modal verbs: „Ich möchte Musik hören“ (I want to listen to music), „Wir können Musik hören“ (we can listen to music). Typical question: „Was für Musik hören Sie/du gern?“ (What kind of music do you like listening to?).
target_language_example: Mein Hobby ist Musik hören.
native_language_example: My hobby is listening to music.

additional_notes: An infinitive phrase with **zu**. Often used with **um … zu** to express purpose: *um Musik zu studieren* = “in order to study music.” You can also use it after verbs/expressions like *lieben es,* *vorhaben,* *versuchen,* etc.: *Sie liebt es, Musik zu studieren.*
target_language_example: Ich möchte nach Wien gehen, um Musik zu studieren.
native_language_example: I want to go to Vienna to study music.

meaning: to encourage someone; to give someone courage.
additional_notes: Usually used with a person in the dative: „jemandem Mut machen“ = to encourage someone (literally: to make courage for someone). Common when someone is nervous, scared, or unsure: „Mach dir Mut“ / „Ich will dir Mut machen.“
target_language_example: Ich will dir Mut machen: Du schaffst das!
native_language_example: I want to encourage you: You can do it!

meaning: As written, this is an incomplete/incorrect way to say “Mom, (take) the trash outside.”
additional_notes: This string is missing a verb and needs punctuation/case marking to sound natural. A correct, idiomatic version would be: „Mutter, bring den Müll nach draußen!“ or more commonly „Mama, bring den Müll nach draußen!“. „den Müll“ = “the trash” (accusative), „nach draußen“ = “outside/to the outdoors.” The exact term given is not a standard German phrase on its own.
target_language_example: Mutter den Müll nach draußen
native_language_example: Mom, (take) the trash outside.

meaning: "(My/our) mother has" / "Mother has" (start of a sentence in the past perfect or with "haben").
additional_notes: Used with the verb "haben" (has) as the auxiliary to form the perfect tense (past): "Mutter hat ... gemacht/gebracht/gesagt". In family context, German often says "Mutter" without "die" or a possessive (like "my").
target_language_example: Mutter hat heute keine Zeit.
native_language_example: Mom doesn't have time today.

meaning: “Mom/Mother has … to me / for me …” (start of a sentence in the present perfect).
additional_notes: This is an incomplete sentence fragment that usually continues with a past participle (e.g., gesagt, gegeben, geholfen). “hat” is the auxiliary verb for the present perfect (Perfekt). “mir” is dative “(to) me,” used with many verbs that take an indirect object (e.g., jemandem etwas geben = to give someone something; jemandem helfen = to help someone). In everyday speech, people often say “Mama” instead of “Mutter.”
target_language_example: Mutter hat mir das Buch gegeben.
native_language_example: My mom gave me the book.

additional_notes: Used to say what your (or someone’s) mother is doing or what she is like (job, nationality, etc.). Often you’ll see it with an article/possessive: „Die Mutter ist …“ (the mother), „Meine/Eure Mutter ist …“ (my/your mother). In family-style speech German sometimes drops the article: „Mutter ist einkaufen gegangen“ (= Mom went shopping), which can sound a bit old-fashioned or childlike.
target_language_example: Meine Mutter ist heute zu Hause.
native_language_example: My mom is at home today.

additional_notes: Used when you add extra information about a specific girl: „ein/das Mädchen, das …“. Even though a girl is female, the noun „das Mädchen“ is grammatically neuter, so the relative pronoun is often „das“ (not „die“). The verb in the relative clause usually goes at the end: „das … kam/sitzt/sprechen kann“.
target_language_example: Das ist das Mädchen, das neben mir wohnt.
native_language_example: That’s the girl who lives next to me.

meaning: “(the) girl that/who I …” (start of a relative clause).
additional_notes: Used to add extra information about a specific girl: *das Mädchen, das ich …* = “the girl that/who I …”. Even though *Mädchen* means “girl,” it is grammatically neuter (*das Mädchen*), so the relative pronoun is often *das* (not *die*). The verb in the relative clause goes at the end: *das Mädchen, das ich am Bahnhof gesehen habe*.
target_language_example: Das ist das Mädchen, das ich gestern kennengelernt habe.
native_language_example: That’s the girl that I met yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the female students in your (school) class. Often appears with plural (die Mädchen) or in structures like "kein Mädchen in meiner Klasse" (no girl in my class) and "keines der Mädchen in meiner Klasse" (none of the girls in my class). You can swap "meiner" for other possessives: "in deiner/seiner/ihrer/unserer Klasse".
target_language_example: Die Mädchen in meiner Klasse sind sehr nett.
native_language_example: The girls in my class are very nice.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **sein** (“to be”) to describe men in general (often a general statement or stereotype). For specific men, you’ll often see an article or determiner: **Die Männer sind ...** (“The men are ...”), **Diese Männer sind ...** (“These men are ...”).
target_language_example: Männer sind nicht alle gleich.
native_language_example: Men are not all the same.

additional_notes: A neutral, general phrase used to refer to people of both genders together. Often used in formal writing or speeches (e.g., talking about a group, society, or a workforce).
target_language_example: In diesem Kurs lernen Männer und Frauen gemeinsam Deutsch.
native_language_example: In this course, men and women learn German together.

meaning: to make an effort; to try hard.
additional_notes: Usually used reflexively: **sich Mühe geben** (e.g., *Ich gebe mir Mühe*, *Gib dir Mühe!*). You can intensify it with **alle** (*sich alle Mühe geben* = make every effort), **größere** (*sich größere Mühe geben* = try harder), or **nach Kräften** (*sich nach Kräften Mühe geben* = try as hard as you can). Often followed by **zu + infinitive**: *Sie geben sich Mühe, pünktlich zu sein.*
target_language_example: Du musst dir etwas mehr Mühe geben.
native_language_example: You have to make a bit more effort.

additional_notes: Common in household contexts as a shortened phrase or instruction. Often used with a verb, especially: „den Müll nach draußen bringen“ (to take the trash outside) or „den Müll nach draußen stellen“ (to put the trash outside). „Müll“ is usually used with an article: „den Müll“.
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte den Müll nach draußen bringen?
native_language_example: Can you please take the trash outside?

meaning: to take the trash/garbage outside (to put it out).
additional_notes: Common household chore meaning you carry the trash out of the apartment/house, usually to the bins outside. Also often said as: „den Müll rausbringen“ (more common in everyday speech).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte den Müll nach draußen bringen?
native_language_example: Can you please take the trash outside?

additional_notes: Used when you can’t speak to someone directly and you leave a voicemail or ask someone else to pass on a message. Common patterns: jemandem eine Nachricht hinterlassen; eine Nachricht hinterlassen (e.g., on voicemail). Often used in polite questions on the phone: „Möchten/Wollen Sie ihm eine Nachricht hinterlassen?“
target_language_example: Möchten Sie ihm eine Nachricht hinterlassen?
native_language_example: Would you like to leave him a message?

additional_notes: "hörte" is the simple past (Präteritum) of "hören" (to hear). This phrasing is common in written stories and in time clauses with "als": "Als ich die Nachricht hörte, ...". In everyday spoken German, people often use the present perfect instead: "Als ich die Nachricht gehört habe, ...". "Nachricht" can mean a piece of news or a message (e.g., a text message), depending on context.
target_language_example: Als ich die Nachricht hörte, habe ich sofort meine Familie angerufen.
native_language_example: When I heard the news, I immediately called my family.

meaning: to hear (some) news / to get a message
additional_notes: Typically used with an object or complement, especially: „eine Nachricht von dir zu hören“ = „to hear from you / to get a message from you“. You’ll also commonly see „Ich hoffe, bald von dir zu hören“ (without „Nachricht“). Note: „die Nachrichten hören“ usually means „to listen to the news“ (e.g., on radio/TV), which is a different meaning.
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, bald Nachricht zu hören.
native_language_example: I hope to hear some news soon.

additional_notes: Usually written as one word: „nachtlang wach“ (also: „die ganze Nacht lang wach“). Used to say you didn’t sleep during the night. Often appears with a form of „sein“: „Ich war die ganze Nacht (lang) wach.“
target_language_example: Ich war die ganze Nacht lang wach.
native_language_example: I was awake all night long.

meaning: awake at night; (stay) awake all night.
additional_notes: Usually used with an article/adverb, e.g. „die ganze Nacht wach (bleiben)“ = “(to) stay awake all night” or „nachts wach sein“ = “to be awake at night.” On its own, „Nacht wach“ sounds incomplete in German.
target_language_example: Ich war die ganze Nacht wach.
native_language_example: I was awake all night.

meaning: “You hit the nail on the head.” (You described it exactly.)
additional_notes: Fixed idiom used to say someone’s comment/analysis is exactly right. Often said as an exclamation: „Du hast den Nagel auf den Kopf getroffen!“ You may also see slight variations like „den Nagel auf den Kopf treffen“ (infinitive) or „… hat den Nagel auf den Kopf getroffen“ (past).
target_language_example: Mit deiner Erklärung hast du den Nagel auf den Kopf getroffen.
native_language_example: With your explanation, you hit the nail on the head.

additional_notes: Used in statements to identify a person or thing ("Der Name ist …"). Also appears in set phrases like "Der Name ist mir entfallen" = "I forgot the name / the name slipped my mind."
target_language_example: Mein Name ist Laura.
native_language_example: My name is Laura.

meaning: nose and mouth (often in phrases like “over/covering the nose and mouth”).
additional_notes: A common fixed pair referring to the parts of the face used for breathing/speaking. Frequently used with prepositions like „über“ or „vor“ (e.g., „eine Maske über Nase und Mund“ = a mask covering the nose and mouth). Also appears in hygiene/health advice, especially with „berühren“ (touch).
target_language_example: Die Ärzte trugen weiße Masken über Nase und Mund.
native_language_example: The doctors wore white masks over their nose and mouth.

additional_notes: Almost always used as **„von Natur aus“**: **„Er/Sie ist von Natur aus …“** = someone is that way innately (e.g., calm, shy, curious). You’ll also see it with **sein**: **„Ich bin von Natur aus nicht so geduldig.“**
target_language_example: Ich bin von Natur aus eher ruhig.
native_language_example: By nature, I'm rather calm.

meaning: "number one"; the best/top-ranked, or the first one.
additional_notes: Used for rankings ("die Nummer eins" = the top/best in a competition or category). It can also be used as a label or call sign for a person/object (like "Number One, take over"), and in family contexts to mean the first child (e.g., "Sohn Nummer eins" = first son).
target_language_example: Unser Team will dieses Jahr die Nummer eins werden.
native_language_example: Our team wants to become number one this year.

meaning: “near (the) … / in the vicinity of …” (used with a masculine or neuter noun in the genitive).
additional_notes: Most often used in the fixed phrase **in der Nähe des + [Genitiv]**, meaning “near …”. **des** is the genitive form of “der/das” (for masculine/neuter nouns). With feminine plural nouns you use **in der Nähe der + [Genitiv]** (e.g., *in der Nähe der Schule*).
target_language_example: Ich wohne in der Nähe des Bahnhofs.
native_language_example: I live near the train station.

meaning: near my house / in the vicinity of my house.
additional_notes: Usually used with the fixed phrase "in der Nähe" + genitive: "in der Nähe meines Hauses" = "near my house". In everyday speech you may also hear "in der Nähe von meinem Haus" (more colloquial).
target_language_example: Es gibt einen Supermarkt in der Nähe meines Hauses.
native_language_example: There is a supermarket near my house.

additional_notes: Most often used as part of the fixed phrase **in der Nähe von** (“near”), followed by the **dative**: *in der Nähe von dem Bahnhof* → often contracted in speech/writing to *in der Nähe **vom** Bahnhof*. You’ll also see it in phrases like *in unmittelbarer Nähe von* (“in the immediate vicinity of”).
target_language_example: Wir wohnen in der Nähe von dem Bahnhof.
native_language_example: We live near the train station.

additional_notes: A common pairing in shopping and food contexts, especially at the supermarket or market. "Obst" = fruit, "Gemüse" = vegetables; often used as a category or department (e.g., im Supermarkt).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte Obst und Gemüse für heute Abend einkaufen?
native_language_example: Can you please buy fruit and vegetables for tonight?

additional_notes: Usually said as **in Ohnmacht fallen** (“to fall into a faint”). In the perfect tense it’s formed with **sein**: **Ich bin in Ohnmacht gefallen.**
target_language_example: Mir war schwindelig, und ich bin in Ohnmacht gefallen.
native_language_example: I felt dizzy, and I fainted.

meaning: (informal) to go to bed / go to sleep (usually: sich aufs Ohr hauen).
additional_notes: Most commonly used as the reflexive phrase „sich aufs Ohr hauen“ meaning to lie down and sleep (similar to “hit the sack”). Literally it would be “to hit (yourself) on the ear,” but that’s not the real meaning. In other contexts, „jemandem (eine) aufs Ohr hauen“ can mean to hit someone (on/near the ear) or sometimes to trick someone, depending on context.
target_language_example: Ich bin total müde — ich geh jetzt und will mir aufs Ohr hauen; kurz gesagt: Ohr hauen.
native_language_example: I’m really tired—I’m going to go and hit the sack; in short: go to bed.

additional_notes: Past participle form of the phrase "Opfer erbringen". Used in formal contexts (e.g., war, hardship, achieving a goal) to say that people have suffered losses or given up something important. Often appears with "haben": "Viele Menschen haben große Opfer erbracht."
target_language_example: Für die Freiheit haben viele Menschen große Opfer erbracht.
native_language_example: Many people made great sacrifices for freedom.

meaning: “place where” (a place in which something is/ happens).
additional_notes: Used to describe a specific place and add a relative clause with information about it. Often seen as „der Ort, wo …“ or „einen Ort, wo …“. In more formal German, you may also hear/see „Ort, an dem …“ instead of „Ort, wo …“.
target_language_example: Kennst du einen Ort, wo man hier gut Kaffee trinken kann?
native_language_example: Do you know a place where you can get good coffee around here?

additional_notes: Used with numbers and quantities: "ein Paar Schuhe" (one pair), "drei Paar Schuhe" (three pairs). After numbers, German often keeps "Paar" in the singular: "drei Paar Schuhe" (also possible: "drei Paare Schuhe" but less common). In questions you’ll often see "welches Paar Schuhe …?" = "which pair of shoes …?".
target_language_example: Ich brauche ein neues Paar Schuhe für den Winter.
native_language_example: I need a new pair of shoes for the winter.

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression—just the noun **Park** + the past participle **gesehen** (“seen”). You typically use it with **haben** in the Perfekt: **Ich habe den Park gesehen.** With a specific park, you usually say **den Park** (accusative) rather than just **Park**.
target_language_example: Ich habe den Park gesehen, aber nicht das Museum.
native_language_example: I saw the park, but not the museum.

meaning: to take a walk in the park.
additional_notes: This exact phrase is not natural in German. You usually say **im Park spazieren gehen** (or simply **im Park spazieren**). **spazieren gehen** = “to go for a walk,” and the location is added with **im** (= in the).
target_language_example: Wir gehen im Park spazieren.
native_language_example: We’re going for a walk in the park.

meaning: (to be) invited to a party; (to) invite (someone) to a party.
additional_notes: Usually used with **zu** + dative: **jemanden zu einer/der Party einladen** (to invite someone to a/the party). In the past/perfect, the participle is **eingeladen**: **Ich habe sie zu meiner Party eingeladen.** In the passive you’ll hear: **Er/Sie wurde zu einer Party eingeladen.**
target_language_example: Ich habe dich zu meiner Party eingeladen.
native_language_example: I invited you to my party.

additional_notes: Used when you stop working/doing an activity for a short time to rest. Commonly appears as "eine Pause machen" or "eine kleine Pause machen". You can ask about timing with "Wann wirst du Pause machen?" or suggest it with "Du solltest (mal) Pause machen."
target_language_example: Ich finde, du solltest Pause machen.
native_language_example: I think you should take a break.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has been unlucky, often with a blunt or unsympathetic tone (like “Tough luck!”). Literally “had bad luck” (Pech = bad luck, gehabt = had). You can use it about yourself or someone else: „Ich habe Pech gehabt.“ / „Er hat Pech gehabt.“
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, aber du hast Pech gehabt.
native_language_example: Sorry, but tough luck.

meaning: to have bad luck; to be unlucky; to be out of luck.
additional_notes: Common everyday phrase used when something unfortunate happens to you. In the present tense it’s typically used as „Ich habe Pech“ / „Du hast Pech“. In the past, Germans often say „Pech gehabt“ (literally: ‘had bad luck’). You can intensify it with „richtig“, „total“: „Ich habe total Pech.“
target_language_example: Ich will heute ins Schwimmbad, aber ich habe Pech haben: Es regnet den ganzen Tag.
native_language_example: I want to go to the swimming pool today, but I have bad luck: it’s raining all day.

additional_notes: Used when you add information about a specific person. Since **Person** is grammatically feminine, the relative pronoun is often **die** (e.g., *die Person, die…*). In other cases you’ll see other forms like **der/dem/den/deren** depending on gender/case (e.g., *die Person, der ich vertraue* = “the person (to) whom I trust”).
target_language_example: Das ist die Person, die mir immer hilft.
native_language_example: That’s the person who always helps me.

meaning: a backup plan; an alternative plan.
additional_notes: Used when the first plan ("Plan A") might fail, or when you need another option. Often said with "Es gibt (k)einen Plan B" (There is/isn't a Plan B) or asked as "Und was ist Plan B?" (So what’s Plan B?).
target_language_example: Wenn das Restaurant voll ist, haben wir einen Plan B.
native_language_example: If the restaurant is full, we have a backup plan.

meaning: 'space/room for' (enough capacity or an available spot for someone/something).
additional_notes: Used with an object to say there is (or isn’t) space/capacity for something: "Platz für + Akkusativ" (e.g., Platz für alle). It can mean physical space (bags, dessert) or an available spot/opportunity (a reserved seat; no room for tourists in these jobs). Common verbs: "Platz für ... haben" (to have room for), "Platz für ... schaffen" (to make room for), "einen Platz für ... reservieren" (to reserve a spot for).
target_language_example: Kannst du noch etwas Platz für meinen Rucksack machen?
native_language_example: Can you make a bit of room for my backpack?

meaning: to have space/room; to have a free seat/spot.
additional_notes: Used to say that there is enough room for someone/something. Very common in questions like „Hast du noch Platz?“ (Do you still have room?) or statements like „Hier haben wir Platz.“ You conjugate only „haben“: ich habe, du hast, er/sie/es hat, wir haben, ihr habt, sie/Sie haben.
target_language_example: Haben wir im Auto noch Platz haben für zwei Koffer?
native_language_example: Do we still have space in the car for two suitcases?

meaning: to make room (for someone/something); to move aside.
additional_notes: Used when you need more space, often with a dative pronoun: „Mach mir bitte Platz.“ You can also say what it’s for with „für“: „Platz machen fürs Bett.“ As an imperative, it can be a direct command: „Platz machen!“ or more polite: „Würdet ihr mir etwas Platz machen?“
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, könnten Sie bitte kurz Platz machen?
native_language_example: Excuse me, could you please make room for a moment?

meaning: to take a seat; to sit down (polite).
additional_notes: Commonly used as a polite invitation or instruction, especially in service or formal situations (doctor’s office, meetings, restaurants). Often appears in imperative form: „Nehmen Sie Platz.“ / „Bitte nehmen Sie Platz.“ More casual alternatives: „Setz dich (bitte).“ / „Setzen wir uns.“
target_language_example: Bitte nehmen Sie Platz, der Arzt kommt gleich.
native_language_example: Please take a seat; the doctor will be here shortly.

additional_notes: This looks like a misspelling. In standard German it’s usually **„Poker dieses Wochenende“** (“poker this weekend” / “poker this weekend (as an activity)”). **Wochende** is not the usual spelling; the correct noun is **Wochenende**. If you mean “on the weekend,” German commonly uses **„am Wochenende“**. As written, the phrase is understandable but nonstandard.
target_language_example: Poker dieses Wochende klingt gut.
native_language_example: Poker this weekend sounds good.

additional_notes: Used when you want someone to contact/summon the police, often in urgent situations. You’ll also hear the more common phrasing „die Polizei anrufen“ (to phone the police). In commands: „Ruf die Polizei!“ (informal singular) / „Rufen Sie die Polizei!“ (formal).
target_language_example: Wir müssen die Polizei rufen.
native_language_example: We have to call the police.

additional_notes: This is an infinitive phrase with „zu“ (literally “to call (the) police”). It’s often used after another verb, e.g. „Ich versuche, die Polizei zu rufen.“ In everyday speech you’ll also hear „die Polizei rufen“ or „die Polizei anrufen“. In commands: „Ruf die Polizei!“
target_language_example: Wenn du dich bedroht fühlst, solltest du die Polizei zu rufen versuchen.
native_language_example: If you feel threatened, you should try to call the police.

additional_notes: A very common food word in German (often just called „Pommes“). Used in restaurants when ordering a side dish: „Pommes frites dazu?“ = “French fries with that / as a side?”
target_language_example: Ich nehme einen Burger mit Pommes frites, bitte.
native_language_example: I’ll have a burger with French fries, please.

additional_notes: Used with the verb „gewinnen“ in the Perfekt tense: „(Ich/Er/Sie) habe/hat … einen/den Preis gewonnen“ = “(I/he/she) have/has won … a prize/the prize.” Often refers to prizes in contests, competitions, or awards.
target_language_example: Sie hat einen Preis gewonnen und ist sehr glücklich.
native_language_example: She won a prize and is very happy.

additional_notes: Common in news and everyday talk about inflation and costs. Often used with a percentage or amount ("Preise steigen um 5 %" / "... um 10 Euro") or with time phrases ("dieses Jahr", "in den letzten Monaten").
target_language_example: Die Preise steigen dieses Jahr wieder.
native_language_example: Prices are going up again this year.

meaning: to set priorities; to decide what’s most important.
additional_notes: Used when you need to choose what to do or focus on first, especially when time, money, or other resources are limited. Often used with müssen/should: „Du musst Prioritäten setzen.“ You can also specify which ones: „die richtigen Prioritäten setzen“ = set the right priorities.
target_language_example: Wir haben nur zwei Tage, also müssen wir Prioritäten setzen.
native_language_example: We only have two days, so we have to set priorities.

additional_notes: Uses the past participle gelöst (from lösen = “to solve”). It can be a short statement like “Problem gelöst!” meaning “Problem solved!” It also appears in full sentences with haben in the present perfect: Ich/Wir habe(n) das Problem gelöst. You can also use it in questions about how something was solved: Wie haben Sie das Problem gelöst?
target_language_example: Keine Sorge—Problem gelöst.
native_language_example: Don’t worry—problem solved.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the main difficulty or issue. Often appears as **Das Problem ist, dass …** (“The problem is that …”) or **Mein/Dein Problem ist …** (“My/your problem is …”). In spoken German, people also say **Problem ist:** like “Problem is:” to set up an explanation.
target_language_example: Das Problem ist, dass ich meinen Schlüssel verloren habe.
native_language_example: The problem is that I lost my key.

additional_notes: Common phrase for finding a solution. Often used with an article: „ein Problem lösen“ (solve a problem) or „das Problem lösen“ (solve the problem). „Problem“ is neuter (das Problem) and typically appears as the direct object (accusative).
target_language_example: Wir müssen ein Problem lösen.
native_language_example: We need to solve a problem.

additional_notes: Often used with verbs like versuchen (to try) or helfen (to help): „versuchen, das Problem zu lösen“, „jdm. helfen, ein Problem zu lösen“. The „zu“ marks the infinitive (“to solve”). Usually you’ll see it with an article or possessive: „das Problem zu lösen“, „dein Problem zu lösen“.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir helfen, das Problem zu lösen?
native_language_example: Can you help me solve the problem?

additional_notes: Often used with verbs like versuchen (to try), helfen (to help), or the expression gut darin sein/begabt darin sein (to be good/gifted at). It’s also common with a subject + haben: Ich habe viele Probleme zu lösen. = “I have many problems to solve.” Here, zu + infinitive shows purpose or something that needs to be done.
target_language_example: Wir arbeiten zusammen, um Probleme zu lösen.
native_language_example: We work together to solve problems.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **bestehen** + **Akkusativ**: **eine Prüfung bestehen** = to pass an exam. In the perfect tense you often see **hat … bestanden**. Common opposite: **durch die Prüfung durchfallen** = to fail the exam. Also used more generally for tests like a driving test: **die Führerscheinprüfung bestehen**.
target_language_example: Ich habe die Prüfung bestanden und bin total erleichtert.
native_language_example: I passed the exam and I’m really relieved.

additional_notes: "bestehen" means to pass (i.e., succeed) an exam/test. It’s commonly used with an object in the accusative: "eine Prüfung bestehen". Contrast: "eine Prüfung machen/ablegen" = to take an exam (no result implied); "durch die Prüfung fallen" = to fail an exam.
target_language_example: Wenn ich genug lerne, kann ich die Prüfung bestehen.
native_language_example: If I study enough, I can pass the exam.

additional_notes: Used as an infinitive phrase with „zu“ (often after verbs like „versuchen“, „hoffen“, „schaffen“, or after adjectives): „Ich hoffe, die Prüfung zu bestehen.“ Without „zu“, you’ll often see it as a main verb phrase: „Ich bestehe die Prüfung.“
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, die Prüfung zu bestehen.
native_language_example: I hope to pass the exam.

additional_notes: A playful, childlike made-up compound from **Quatsch** (“nonsense”) + **mach(en)** (“to make/do”). It’s not standard German, but you might see it in kids’ language or as a humorous label. It can be used as a noun (“Quatsch-Mach ist top.”) or as part of bigger compounds (e.g., **Quatsch-Mach-Insel** = “silly-make island”).
target_language_example: Lass uns heute Quatsch-Mach spielen!
native_language_example: Let’s do silly stuff today!

meaning: to ride a bike; to cycle.
additional_notes: Common verb phrase with the noun "Rad" (bike): "Rad fahren" / "Ich fahre Rad" = "to ride a bike / to cycle." You can also say "Fahrrad fahren" (same meaning, a bit more explicit). In writing, "Rad" is capitalized because it’s a noun.
target_language_example: Ich gehe jeden Morgen Rad fahren.
native_language_example: I go cycling every morning.

meaning: Turn the radio down (make it quieter).
additional_notes: Common as an instruction/request. Often used as an elliptical imperative (missing the verb), like: „(Mach das) Radio leiser!“ You can also say „Mach das Radio leiser.“ or more politely „Kannst du das Radio bitte leiser machen?“
target_language_example: Radio leiser, bitte! Ich telefoniere gerade.
native_language_example: Turn the radio down, please! I’m on the phone right now.

additional_notes: Used with **hätte ... angenommen** (Konjunktiv II, past) to express **regret about the past**, often after **Wenn ich (doch) nur ...!** (“If only I had ...!”). Pattern: **(deinen/euren/Ihren) Rat annehmen** = to take someone’s advice. Note: **Rat** means **advice**, not the animal “rat” (false friend).
target_language_example: Wenn ich doch nur deinen Rat angenommen hätte, wäre alles einfacher gewesen.
native_language_example: If only I had taken your advice, everything would have been easier.

additional_notes: Used with a possessive pronoun or name in the genitive: meinen/deinen/euren/Ihren/seinen Rat befolgen (“follow my/your/your (pl.)/your (formal)/his advice”). Common in more formal or written German; in everyday speech you also hear „einen Rat annehmen“ (accept advice).
target_language_example: Ich sollte deinen Rat befolgen und früher ins Bett gehen.
native_language_example: I should follow your advice and go to bed earlier.

meaning: to stop smoking; to quit smoking.
additional_notes: An infinitive phrase used to talk about quitting smoking. Commonly used as: „Ich höre auf zu rauchen.“ (I’m quitting smoking.) You can also use it with modals/plans: „Ich will mit dem Rauchen aufhören.“
target_language_example: Ich möchte mit dem Rauchen aufhören.
native_language_example: I’d like to quit smoking.

meaning: to give up smoking; to quit smoking.
additional_notes: An infinitive phrase often used after verbs like „versuchen“ (to try), „planen“ (to plan), or „schaffen“ (to manage): „Ich versuche, Rauchen aufzugeben.“ In everyday speech, people also commonly say „mit dem Rauchen aufhören“ or „aufhören zu rauchen“ (to stop smoking).
target_language_example: Ich versuche, Rauchen aufzugeben.
native_language_example: I’m trying to quit smoking.

additional_notes: This is an infinitive phrase: „die Rechnung“ (the bill/check) + „zu bezahlen“ (to pay). It often appears after another verb, e.g. „Ich habe vergessen, die Rechnung zu bezahlen.“ In restaurants you’ll also hear: „Zahlen, bitte.“ / „Ich möchte bitte bezahlen.“
target_language_example: Ich habe leider vergessen, die Rechnung zu bezahlen.
native_language_example: Unfortunately, I forgot to pay the bill.

additional_notes: "Rechnungen" are bills/invoices; "zu bezahlen" is the "zu"-infinitive used after certain verbs/structures (e.g., haben, vergessen, sich erinnern, sich weigern; also: genug Geld haben, um … zu + Infinitiv). In this phrase it commonly refers to everyday expenses like rent, utilities, phone, etc.
target_language_example: Ich habe heute einige Rechnungen zu bezahlen.
native_language_example: I have some bills to pay today.

additional_notes: Used with „ein Recht haben, …“ or „das Recht haben, …“ to say someone is entitled to know a piece of information. „es“ refers to whatever is being talked about (the news/facts/secret). Often appears as „ein Recht, es zu erfahren“ after a noun: „Die Öffentlichkeit hat ein Recht, es zu erfahren.“
target_language_example: Ich habe ein Recht, es zu erfahren, bevor ihr entscheidet.
native_language_example: I have a right to know it before you decide.

meaning: to be right; to have the right (to do something).
additional_notes: Two common uses: (1) "(du/Sie) hast/haben Recht" = "you are right" (agreeing with someone). (2) "das Recht haben, ... zu ..." = "to have the right to ..." (a legal/moral entitlement), often with an infinitive clause like "selbst zu entscheiden".
target_language_example: Ich denke, du könntest Recht haben.
native_language_example: I think you might be right.

meaning: “umbrella on the bus” (e.g., an umbrella you left/forgot on the bus).
additional_notes: Used to specify the location where something was forgotten or left behind. Often appears with verbs like **vergessen** (to forget) or **liegen lassen** (to leave behind).
target_language_example: Ich glaube, ich habe meinen Regenschirm im Bus liegen gelassen.
native_language_example: I think I left my umbrella on the bus.

additional_notes: A simple noun phrase often used with verbs like **vergessen** (to forget) or **liegenlassen** (to leave behind), typically with a possessive: **meine/deine/ihre/unsere Regenschirme im Bus**. In German, **im Bus** is idiomatic for “on the bus.”
target_language_example: Wir haben unsere Regenschirme im Bus liegenlassen.
native_language_example: We left our umbrellas on the bus.

additional_notes: Used with a destination: „eine Reise nach + Stadt/Land“. With cities you usually don’t add an article (z.B. „nach Berlin“). With some places you use an article and then often switch to „in“ + accusative (z.B. „eine Reise in die USA / in die Schweiz“ rather than „nach die USA/Schweiz“).
target_language_example: Nächste Woche mache ich eine Reise nach Berlin.
native_language_example: Next week I’m taking a trip to Berlin.

additional_notes: A verb phrase in the present perfect: **(ein) Rennen gewinnen** = “to win a race”, **gewonnen** is the past participle, and **hat** is the helping verb for **gewinnen**. Often appears in a relative or subordinate clause where the conjugated verb (**hat**) goes to the end: *der Mann, der das Rennen gewonnen hat* = “the man who has won the race.”
target_language_example: Sie ist die Läuferin, die das Rennen gewonnen hat.
native_language_example: She is the runner who has won the race.

additional_notes: Means the time from now until you die. Often used with verbs like „(ver)bringen“ (to spend) or with a future idea: „für den Rest deines Lebens“ = “for the rest of your life.” Grammar note: „deines Lebens“ is genitive (“of your life”). You’ll also see: „den Rest meines/deines/seines Lebens“ (accusative object: “the rest of my/your/his life”).
target_language_example: Du hast den Rest deines Lebens Zeit, dich zu entscheiden.
native_language_example: You have the rest of your life to decide.

meaning: "the rest of the day" (the remaining time today).
additional_notes: Usually used with an article and in the accusative: "den Rest des Tages". Common with prepositions like "für" (for) or "den ganzen" context: "für den Rest des Tages" = for the rest of the day. Often refers to the time from now until the end of today.
target_language_example: Ich bleibe den Rest des Tages zu Hause.
native_language_example: I’m staying home for the rest of the day.

additional_notes: Usually used as part of the full phrase „das Richtige getan“ (literally “the right [thing] done”), often with a form of „haben“: „Du hast das Richtige getan.“ It means someone acted correctly in a situation.
target_language_example: Du hast das Richtige getan.
native_language_example: You did the right thing.

additional_notes: Used with an object: ein Risiko / dieses Risiko. Common with müssen (have to), wollen (want to), sollen (should), or würde (would). Often means doing something even though there could be negative consequences.
target_language_example: Ich will kein Risiko eingehen.
native_language_example: I don’t want to take any risks.

additional_notes: This is an infinitive phrase with „zu“ (…„to“ do something). It’s often used after verbs like „empfehlen“ (recommend), „versuchen“ (try), or expressions like „Es fällt mir schwer, …“ (I find it hard to …). With a specific novel, you’ll often see an article: „einen Roman zu lesen“ (a novel) / „den Roman zu lesen“ (the novel). Note: German „Roman“ means „novel“ (not „Roman“ as in ancient Roman).
target_language_example: Ich habe keine Zeit, einen Roman zu lesen.
native_language_example: I don’t have time to read a novel.

meaning: to stay calm; to keep your cool.
additional_notes: Used as advice or an instruction, especially in stressful or urgent situations. Very common as an imperative: „Ruhe bewahren!“ You can also use it with „müssen“/„sollten“: „Wir müssen Ruhe bewahren.“
target_language_example: Bitte Ruhe bewahren und langsam sprechen.
native_language_example: Please stay calm and speak slowly.

meaning: to be left alone; to be left in peace.
additional_notes: Usually used as **in Ruhe gelassen werden** (“to be left in peace”). It’s the passive form of **(jdn.) in Ruhe lassen** (“to leave (someone) alone”). Often used to express that you don’t want to be bothered.
target_language_example: Ich möchte einfach in Ruhe gelassen werden.
native_language_example: I just want to be left alone.

meaning: to leave (someone/something) alone; to let (someone) be; to stop bothering (someone/something).
additional_notes: Most commonly used as "jdn/etw in Ruhe lassen" = "leave someone/something alone" / "leave someone/something in peace." Frequently appears in the imperative: "Lass mich in Ruhe!" You can also use it for not touching or messing with something: "Lass das in Ruhe."
target_language_example: Bitte Ruhe lassen.
native_language_example: Please leave it alone / Please don’t disturb.

meaning: “is supposed to leave (someone/sething) alone” / “is supposed to let (someone/something) rest.”
additional_notes: This sequence is typically part of a larger clause and sounds most natural with **in Ruhe lassen** (“to leave alone / not disturb”) plus **soll** (3rd person singular of **sollen**, meaning “is supposed to / should”). Word order can vary depending on what is emphasized; the exact string **„Ruhe lassen soll“** often appears when **in** is omitted (less common) or when **in Ruhe** is split so that **Ruhe lassen** stays together before **soll**. A very common alternative wording is **„… in Ruhe lassen soll.“**
target_language_example: Er sagte, dass ich ihn Ruhe lassen soll.
native_language_example: He said that I’m supposed to leave him alone.

meaning: to manage; to make ends meet (especially financially).
additional_notes: Note: In standard German this is normally "rund zu kommen" (often written as one word in the infinitive: "rundzukommen") and conjugated as "(ich) komme rund" / "(um) rundzukommen". The exact spelling/capitalization "Runden zu kommen" is unusual; it may be a misspelling or mishearing of "rund zu kommen". Typical pattern: "mit" + resource (money/income/time): "mit dem Geld/mit dem Einkommen rundkommen"; often negative: "nicht (mehr) rundkommen".
target_language_example: Ich versuche, mit meinem Gehalt Runden zu kommen.
native_language_example: I’m trying to make ends meet on my salary.

meaning: salt on his eggs (i.e., to put/sprinkle salt on his eggs).
additional_notes: Used literally when someone seasons eggs with salt. You’ll often see it with verbs like „streuen“ (to sprinkle) or „tun“ (to put): „Er streute Salz auf seine Eier.“ The preposition „auf“ takes the accusative here („auf seine Eier“) because the salt is being placed onto the eggs (movement/change of place). The possessive can change with the person: „Salz auf meine/deine/ihre Eier“.
target_language_example: Er streute Salz auf seine Eier.
native_language_example: He sprinkled salt on his eggs.

meaning: “(the) sentence is …” / “in the sentence there is …”.
additional_notes: Used when talking about grammar or writing. With a subject: „Der Satz ist …“ = “The sentence is …” (e.g., too long, correct, unclear). In German you’ll often see it in the pattern „In dem Satz ist …“ = “In the sentence, there is …” (e.g., a mistake). „Satz“ can also mean “set” (e.g., a set of tools), but in these examples it clearly means “sentence.”
target_language_example: Der Satz ist zu lang; kannst du ihn kürzer machen?
native_language_example: The sentence is too long; can you make it shorter?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the activity of playing the board game chess. Common in questions and invitations (e.g., „Kannst du …?“ / „Willst du …?“).
target_language_example: Willst du Schach spielen?
native_language_example: Do you want to play chess?

additional_notes: Used when talking about leaving something behind on public transport. Often appears with verbs like „vergessen“ (to forget) or „(stehen) lassen“ (to leave behind): „Ich habe meinen Schirm im Bus vergessen.“ „Im Bus“ = „in/on the bus“ (location; „in“ + dative).
target_language_example: Ich glaube, ich habe meinen Schirm im Bus liegen lassen.
native_language_example: I think I left my umbrella on the bus.

meaning: to go ice skating; to ice-skate.
additional_notes: Used for the activity/sport of ice skating. Often used with verbs like „gehen“ (to go) or „können“ (to be able to): „Wir gehen Schlittschuh laufen.“ / „Ich kann Schlittschuh laufen.“ (Without “gehen”, it can still mean “to ice-skate” in general.)
target_language_example: Im Winter gehen wir oft Schlittschuh laufen.
native_language_example: In winter, we often go ice skating.

additional_notes: Used with "mit" + dative to say who you broke up with: "mit Tom Schluss gemacht". Most often in the perfect tense: "Ich habe Schluss gemacht." / "Hast du Schluss gemacht?" It refers to ending a relationship, not just finishing an activity.
target_language_example: Warum hast du mit ihm Schluss gemacht?
native_language_example: Why did you break up with him?

meaning: to stop/finish (for now); also: to break up (end a relationship).
additional_notes: Used in two common ways: (1) to end an activity/work for the day: „Wollen wir für heute Schluss machen?“ = “Shall we call it a day?” (2) to end a romantic relationship, usually with „mit + Dativ“: „mit jemandem Schluss machen“ = “to break up with someone.” Often used with time words like „jetzt“ (now).
target_language_example: Ich muss jetzt Schluss machen.
native_language_example: I have to stop now.

additional_notes: From the verb **finden** (“to find”). Often appears in the **Perfekt** tense with **haben**: *Ich habe den Schlüssel gefunden.* It can also be used as a short label/notice (e.g., in a lost-and-found context): *Schlüssel gefunden!* Use **den Schlüssel** for one key and **die Schlüssel** for multiple keys.
target_language_example: Ich habe den Schlüssel gefunden!
native_language_example: I found the key!

additional_notes: Used when talking about missing keys, often in questions or statements. You can use it with a possessive pronoun: „meinen Schlüssel verloren“ (lost my key), „meine Schlüssel verloren“ (lost my keys). Common in the perfect tense: „Ich habe … verloren“ / „Hast du … verloren?“
target_language_example: Ich habe meinen Schlüssel verloren—kannst du mir aufmachen?
native_language_example: I lost my key—can you open the door for me?

additional_notes: Used with forms of "bedecken" (to cover): "von Schnee bedeckt" = covered with/by snow; also common: "mit Schnee bedeckt". Often used to describe landscapes, trees, mountains, roads, etc. (e.g., "Der Berg ist mit Schnee bedeckt.")
target_language_example: Am Morgen waren die Straßen mit Schnee bedeckt.
native_language_example: In the morning, the streets were covered in snow.

additional_notes: This is the formal imperative of **schreiben** used with **Sie** (e.g., in instructions, forms, or polite requests). It’s addressed to one person (or used as the polite form in general). It can take a direct object (e.g., *Schreiben Sie Ihren Namen.*) and is often combined with separable-prefix verbs like **mitschreiben** (*Schreiben Sie das bitte mit.* = “Write that down too / take notes.”) or **aufschreiben** (*Schreiben Sie mir das auf.* = “Write that down for me.”).
target_language_example: Schreiben Sie bitte Ihre E-Mail-Adresse hier.
native_language_example: Please write your email address here.

meaning: step by step; gradually, one step at a time.
additional_notes: Used to say you should do or explain something in a slow, orderly sequence. Often with verbs like lernen (learn), erklären/erzählen (explain/tell), vorgehen (proceed). It can describe learning, instructions, or how something happens over time.
target_language_example: Wir lösen das Problem Schritt für Schritt.
native_language_example: We'll solve the problem step by step.

additional_notes: Usually part of the separable verb phrase **(sich) die Schuhe anziehen** = “to put on (your) shoes.” In many sentences **an** goes to the end: *Ich ziehe mir die Schuhe an.* Often used with a reflexive pronoun (**mir/dir/sich/uns/euch**). In commands you’ll hear: **Zieh dir deine Schuhe an!** (informal singular), **Ziehen Sie Ihre Schuhe an!** (formal), **Zieht euch eure Schuhe an!** (plural).
target_language_example: Zieh dir bitte die Schuhe an, wir müssen los.
native_language_example: Please put on your shoes, we have to go.

additional_notes: Used with the separable verb "ausziehen" (to take off clothes/shoes): "(die) Schuhe ausziehen". In speech you may hear shortened forms like "Ich zieh mir die Schuhe aus." The opposite is "Schuhe anziehen" (to put shoes on).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte die Schuhe ausziehen?
native_language_example: Can you please take off your shoes?

additional_notes: Often used as an instruction or polite question when entering someone’s home: „(Bitte) Schuhe ausziehen.“ / „Soll ich meine Schuhe ausziehen?“. It can also appear in the idiom „jemandem die Schuhe ausziehen“, meaning to amaze someone or knock someone’s socks off (not literal).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte deine Schuhe ausziehen, bevor du reinkommst?
native_language_example: Can you please take off your shoes before you come in?

additional_notes: Past action with "kaufen" (to buy). Often used with a form of "haben" (e.g., "ich habe", "du hast", "Sie haben") to form the present perfect: "Ich habe Schuhe gekauft" = "I bought/have bought shoes." You can add details like "ein Paar" (a pair), "neue" (new), or say where: "… im Laden / online".
target_language_example: Ich habe gestern neue Schuhe gekauft.
native_language_example: I bought new shoes yesterday.

meaning: to be to blame for; to be responsible for (the).
additional_notes: Used with the noun "Schuld" (fault/blame/guilt) plus "an" + dative to say who/what caused a problem: "Die Verspätung ist Schuld an dem Stau." In everyday German you’ll very often see the contracted form "Schuld an dem" → "Schuld an dem" = "Schuld an dem" (formal), but especially: "Schuld an dem" → "Schuld an dem" is commonly shortened to "Schuld an dem" → "Schuld an dem"; and with the article it’s usually contracted: "an dem" → "am" (so: "Schuld am ...").
target_language_example: Die Verspätung ist Schuld an dem Unfall.
native_language_example: The delay is due to the accident.

additional_notes: Usually used with an indirect object (dative) and the noun **die Schuld**: **jemandem die Schuld geben** = “to blame someone.” You can add **für + Akkusativ** to specify the reason: **jemandem die Schuld für etwas geben**. Related: **Schuld haben** = “to be at fault / to be guilty.”
target_language_example: Warum willst du mir die Schuld geben?
native_language_example: Why do you want to blame me?

meaning: to be to blame; to be at fault.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is responsible for a mistake/problem/accident. Often with a situation using „an + Dativ“: „Er hat Schuld an dem Unfall.“ You can also use it with „daran“: „Du hast daran Schuld“ (= it’s your fault). Common question: „Wer hat Schuld?“ (= Who is to blame?).
target_language_example: Ich habe Schuld an dem Fehler.
native_language_example: It’s my fault for the mistake.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "gehen" in the Perfekt (past): "sein + gegangen" → "Ich bin … gegangen." With a specific school, German often uses "auf" + school: "Er ist auf meine Schule gegangen" = "He went to/attended my school." For school in general (starting/going to school), you often hear "in die Schule gehen".
target_language_example: Ich bin auf diese Schule gegangen.
native_language_example: I went to (attended) this school.

meaning: to go to school; to attend school.
additional_notes: Most commonly expressed as „zur Schule gehen“ in everyday German. The bare form „Schule gehen“ is less idiomatic on its own, but it can occur (e.g., in shortened, headline-like, or learner contexts).
target_language_example: Meine Tochter will jeden Tag Schule gehen.
native_language_example: My daughter wants to go to school every day.

meaning: to go to school; to attend school.
additional_notes: This wording is grammatically possible but less idiomatic on its own. In everyday German you usually say **zur Schule gehen**. The form **Schule zu gehen** often appears in contexts like **(um) zur Schule zu gehen** (“in order to go to school”) or after certain verbs/adjectives that take **zu + Infinitiv**.
target_language_example: Ich habe keine Lust, Schule zu gehen.
native_language_example: I don't feel like going to school.

additional_notes: Most often used in the fixed phrase „etwas in Schutt und Asche legen“ = to destroy something completely (to raze it, reduce it to rubble). It’s a dramatic/literary-sounding expression and is common in war or revenge contexts.
target_language_example: Der Brand hat das Haus in Schutt und Asche gelegt.
native_language_example: The fire reduced the house to rubble and ashes.

additional_notes: Often used with verbs like suchen (to look for) or finden (to find): Schutz vor dem Regen suchen. It can refer to any place that keeps you dry (e.g., under a tree, under a roof, in a doorway).
target_language_example: Wir suchten Schutz vor dem Regen in einem Hauseingang.
native_language_example: We looked for shelter from the rain in a doorway.

meaning: to be lucky; to have good luck.
additional_notes: Common, fairly informal idiom meaning you got lucky (often unexpectedly), e.g., you avoided a problem or something worked out in your favor. Often used in the perfect tense as "Schwein gehabt" (e.g., "Du hast aber Schwein gehabt!") even though the base idiom is "Schwein haben".
target_language_example: Wir haben Schwein haben und noch den letzten Zug erwischt.
native_language_example: We were lucky and still caught the last train.

additional_notes: Used to report that you heard shots being fired (often in a police/witness context). You’ll see it with or without an article: **Schüsse** (some shots) vs. **die Schüsse** (the specific shots everyone is talking about). It’s typically used with **haben** in the perfect: **Ich habe Schüsse gehört.** In reported speech it often appears in the subjunctive: **Er sagte, er habe Schüsse gehört.**
target_language_example: Ich habe gestern Abend Schüsse gehört.
native_language_example: I heard gunshots last night.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the genre in movies, books, etc. In German it’s often written with a hyphen (Science-Fiction) and can be used in compounds like Science-Fiction-Film / Science-Fiction-Roman. You can also say: „Ich mag Science-Fiction.“
target_language_example: Ich lese gern Science-Fiction-Bücher.
native_language_example: I like reading sci-fi books.

meaning: side by side; together next to each other.
additional_notes: Used to describe people being physically next to each other (sitting, walking, standing) and often implies doing something together closely (e.g., working alongside someone). Common with verbs like sitzen, gehen/schreiten, stehen, arbeiten.
target_language_example: Wir haben Seite an Seite an dem Projekt gearbeitet.
native_language_example: We worked side by side on the project.

additional_notes: Usually used in the full phrase **an der Seite des/der ...** to mean being physically next to someone or (often) loyally accompanying/supporting them. **des** is the masculine/neuter genitive form (“of the”); for feminine/plural you use **der**: *an der Seite der Frau / der Kinder*. In everyday speech you’ll also hear **an der Seite von + Dativ** (*an der Seite von dem Mann*).
target_language_example: Ich will an der Seite des Teams bleiben.
native_language_example: I want to stay by the side of the team.

additional_notes: Literally “side of the river” (Seite = side, Fluss = river). You’ll often also hear similar phrases like „auf der anderen Seite des Flusses“ (on the other side of the river) or „am Ufer“ (by the riverbank), which is very common for talking about being next to a river.
target_language_example: Auf der anderen Seite des Flusses ist ein kleines Dorf.
native_language_example: On the other side of the river there is a small village.

additional_notes: Used with the verb „begehen“ (past participle: „begangen“) to talk about suicide, often in news or formal contexts: „Er/Sie hat Selbstmord begangen.“ In everyday German, many people also say „sich das Leben nehmen“ (to take one’s own life).
target_language_example: Laut der Polizei hat er Selbstmord begangen.
native_language_example: According to the police, he committed suicide.

additional_notes: A common, direct way to talk about having sex, typically meaning sexual intercourse. It’s fairly explicit; in more polite or softer contexts people may prefer alternatives like „miteinander schlafen“ or „Sex miteinander haben“.
target_language_example: Glaubst du, wir werden Sex haben?
native_language_example: Do you think we’ll have sex?

additional_notes: This isn’t a fixed idiom on its own; it’s a common sentence structure where a main clause addressing someone formally with **Sie** is followed by a comma and a **dass**-clause (“that”-clause). The comma before **dass** is required. Common with verbs like **wollen**, **bitten**, **hoffen**, **fordern**, **beweisen** (e.g., *Was wollen Sie, dass ich tue?* / *Beweisen Sie, dass …*).
target_language_example: Was wollen Sie, dass ich tue?
native_language_example: What do you want me to do?

meaning: Formal pattern: “(… you …), that you …” — polite address with a verb + comma + "dass" clause whose subject is again "Sie".
additional_notes: Used when addressing someone formally ("Sie") and then adding a subordinate clause introduced by "dass" (“that”). The first "Sie" is the object of the main-clause verb (e.g., bitten/entschuldigen/fragen/hoffen/glauben/leugnen), and the second "Sie" is the subject inside the "dass" clause. In the "dass" clause, the conjugated verb typically goes to the end (verb-final word order).
target_language_example: Entschuldigen Sie, dass Sie warten mussten!
native_language_example: Sorry that you had to wait!

meaning: a formal way to say “(you) … that I …” (a polite verb + a dass-clause).
additional_notes: This isn’t a fixed phrase by itself, but a common pattern: **[Verb] Sie, dass ich …**. **Sie** is formal “you” (to one person) and **dass ich …** means “that I …”. It’s often used after polite imperatives like **Entschuldigen Sie, dass ich …** (“Sorry that I …”), but also with other verbs, e.g. **Vergessen Sie, dass ich …** (“Forget that I …”) or **Wollten Sie, dass ich …?** (“Did you want me to …?”).
target_language_example: Entschuldigen Sie, dass ich zu spät bin.
native_language_example: Sorry that I’m late.

meaning: formal “you … that …” (used when addressing someone with **Sie** and introducing a subordinate clause with **daß**).
additional_notes: This pattern combines the formal pronoun **Sie** with a **daß**-clause (traditional spelling; modern: **dass**), often after verbs like **wollen** (“to want”), **möchten** (“would like”), or **bitten** (“to ask/request”). In the **daß** clause, the conjugated verb typically goes to the end: *… daß wir Ihnen dabei helfen.*
target_language_example: Wollen Sie, daß wir Ihnen dabei helfen?
native_language_example: Do you want us to help you with that?

meaning: formal pattern “you …, what …” (Sie + clause introduced by was = “what”), often used to introduce an object clause.
additional_notes: **Sie** is the formal “you” (singular/plural). **was** introduces a subordinate clause meaning “what …”. This pattern is typically used after a verb, e.g. **Tun Sie, was …** (“Do what …”), **Wussten Sie, was …?** (“Did you know what …?”). Word order: the **was**-clause is subordinate (verb usually at the end). Comma before **was** is standard.
target_language_example: Tun Sie, was ich sage!
native_language_example: Do what I say!

meaning: 'you, if you …' (formal), used to introduce a condition.
additional_notes: Used with formal address (Sie) and commonly set off by a comma when the „wenn“-clause is inserted into or follows another clause. In the „wenn“-clause (a subordinate clause), the finite verb typically goes to the end: „wenn Sie Zeit haben“. The sequence „Sie, wenn Sie“ often appears when the „wenn“-clause is embedded after „Sie“ as an interruption: „… dass Sie, wenn Sie …, …“.
target_language_example: Ich schlage vor, dass Sie, wenn Sie keine Fragen haben, anfangen.
native_language_example: I suggest that you, if you have no questions, start.

meaning: formal “you” (Sie) + “where” (wo); commonly appears with a comma before a subordinate clause, e.g., “..., wo Sie ...” = “..., where you ...” / “... where (you) ...”
additional_notes: “Sie” is the polite/formal form of “you” (always capitalized) used with strangers, customers, officials, etc. The sequence “Sie, wo” itself is not an idiom but a frequent grammatical pattern: a main clause ending with “Sie,” followed by a subordinate clause introduced by “wo” (“where”). A classic example is an imperative: “Bleiben Sie, wo Sie sind!” = “Stay where you are!” In such clauses, German typically sends the conjugated verb to the end (e.g., “wo Sie sind”).
target_language_example: Bleiben Sie, wo Sie sind!
native_language_example: Stay where you are!

additional_notes: Used when speaking politely/formally to one person (or more) you don’t address as “du”. In instructions and imperatives you often see both together, e.g. “Wiegen Sie Ihr Gepäck” (“Weigh your luggage”). Both are capitalized in this meaning: Sie/Ihr. (Lowercase sie/ihr usually refers to “she/they” and “her/their”.)
target_language_example: Bitte zeigen Sie Ihr Ticket.
native_language_example: Please show your ticket.

meaning: formal (polite) “you / your” used when addressing someone formally (one person or a group): “you” (Sie) + “your” (Ihre, one of the possible possessive forms).
additional_notes: "Sie" (capital S) is the formal/polite "you." "Ihre" is a possessive form meaning "your"; the ending varies with gender/number and case of the noun (Ihr / Ihre / Ihren / Ihrem / Ihres). The pair "Sie Ihre" often appears in polite requests or questions, but it’s not a fixed idiom—it's compositional.
target_language_example: Vermissen Sie Ihre Eltern?
native_language_example: Do you miss your parents?

additional_notes: Used when speaking politely to one person (or sometimes to a group). "Sie" is the formal form of "you" and is always capitalized, as is the possessive "Ihr-/Ihr(e)". "Ihren" is a declined form meaning "your" in the accusative masculine/neuter (e.g., Ihren Wagen = your car, Ihren Sohn = your son). Word order often looks like: Sie + verb + Ihren + noun.
target_language_example: Können Sie Ihren Ausweis bitte zeigen?
native_language_example: Could you please show your ID?

additional_notes: This is not a complete expression by itself; it needs a following noun/adjective. You’ll most often see it as part of longer phrases, e.g. “Sie auf dem Laufenden halten” = “to keep you informed/up to date.” “Sie” is the formal “you,” and “auf dem” literally means “on the.”
target_language_example: Ich halte Sie auf dem Laufenden.
native_language_example: I’ll keep you informed (up to date).

meaning: formal command pattern with separable verbs: “(verb) …!” (e.g., “Wake up!”, “Pay attention!”).
additional_notes: In formal/Polite German, commands often use **Sie** (“you”) with the verb first: **Verb + Sie + …**. With **separable verbs**, the prefix (often something like **auf**) goes to the **end** of the clause: **Passen Sie auf!** = “Pay attention / Watch out!”, **Wachen Sie auf!** = “Wake up!”. In longer sentences, **auf** still comes at the end: **Wir fordern Sie auf, mitzumachen.** = “We ask/urge you to join in.” Note: **Sie** (formal “you”) is capitalized.
target_language_example: Bitte passen Sie auf!
native_language_example: Please pay attention!

meaning: formal "please" used when politely telling someone to do something ("Please ...").
additional_notes: Used with the formal pronoun "Sie" (you) in polite requests/instructions, often in workplaces, customer service, announcements, and written instructions. It commonly follows an imperative verb: "Kommen Sie bitte rein." In English you usually translate it simply as "Please ..." (not "You please").
target_language_example: Warten Sie bitte einen Moment.
native_language_example: Please wait a moment.

meaning: Part of a polite formal instruction: “(verb) … please … your …” (to one person).
additional_notes: This isn’t a standalone phrase; it appears inside formal commands (imperatives). Pattern: **Verb + Sie + bitte + Ihren + noun**. **Sie** = formal “you” (singular), **bitte** = “please”, **Ihren** = “your” for a masculine/neuter noun in the accusative (direct object), e.g. **Ihren Pass / Ihren Spind / Ihren Urlaub**.
target_language_example: Nehmen Sie bitte Ihren Ausweis heraus.
native_language_example: Please take out your ID.

additional_notes: Used with the polite form of “you” (Sie) in instructions, signs, manuals, and formal speech. It’s typically an imperative verb + Sie + object “das” (e.g., „Füllen Sie das Formular aus.“ = “Fill out the form.”). In English you usually omit “you” and translate “das” as “it/that/the …” depending on context. Note: „Sie“ is always capitalized when it means “you” (formal).
target_language_example: Bitte bringen Sie das Paket morgen mit.
native_language_example: Please bring the package along tomorrow.

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression on its own. It is the formal pronoun Sie ("you") plus das ("that" or "it"). You often see this combination in questions or with a verb, as in Können Sie das ...? = "Can you ... that? / Can you do it?".
target_language_example: Können Sie das erklären?
native_language_example: Can you explain that?

additional_notes: This is a common building block in polite requests. **Sie** is the formal “you” (to a stranger, customer service, a professional, etc.). You normally add a verb: **tun / machen / erledigen** (“do / make / take care of”). In questions the verb often comes first: *Tun/Können Sie das für mich …?* In subordinate clauses it goes to the end: *…, wenn Sie das für mich täten.*
target_language_example: Können Sie das für mich erledigen?
native_language_example: Could you take care of that for me?

additional_notes: This is a common fragment with formal **Sie** (“you”), **das** (“that/it”), and **nicht** (“not”). It appears in questions and commands where the verb is placed elsewhere: **Fanden Sie das nicht …?** (“Didn’t you find that …?”) / **Vergessen Sie das nicht!** (“Don’t forget that!”). In imperatives, the verb comes first; in many questions, the verb also comes first (inversion).
target_language_example: Bitte sagen Sie das nicht.
native_language_example: Please don’t say that.

additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom, but a very common word sequence: **Sie** (formal “you”) + **das** (“that/it”) + **wirklich** (“really”). It often appears in questions or slightly critical/surprised remarks: *Interessiert Sie das wirklich?* (“Do you really care about that?”). Word order changes depending on the sentence (e.g., *Müssen Sie das wirklich tun?*).
target_language_example: Wollen Sie das wirklich kaufen?
native_language_example: Do you really want to buy that?

meaning: "you" (formal) + "the" (masculine accusative: den), often in polite instructions or questions.
additional_notes: "Sie" is the polite/formal form of "you" used with strangers, customers, or in official contexts. "den" is the accusative form of "der" (= “the”) for masculine nouns (e.g., den Satz, den Bahnhof, den Rechner). This combination is very common in commands with an implied "please" (imperative) like "Korrigieren Sie den …" or in questions like "Mussten Sie den …?".
target_language_example: Öffnen Sie den Brief bitte erst zu Hause.
native_language_example: Please open the letter only at home.

meaning: “you, then?” / “you (in the world)…?” (polite), adding surprised or curious emphasis in a question.
additional_notes: Used in questions with formal/polite „Sie“. „denn“ here is a modal particle (often untranslatable) that shows surprise, impatience, or strong interest: „Was machen Sie denn…?“, „Wo waren Sie denn…?“. It does NOT mean English “then” in this use.
target_language_example: Wie haben Sie denn das gemacht?
native_language_example: How on earth did you do that?

meaning: “you … then/actually …?” (adds emphasis in a polite question).
additional_notes: Used with the modal particle „denn“ in questions addressed to „Sie“ (formal “you”). It doesn’t change the basic meaning, but adds a tone like surprise, impatience, curiosity, or “come on—really?”. In English it’s often left untranslated or rendered with “then”, “actually”, “so”, or “really”. (Not to be confused with „denn“ meaning “because” in statements.)
target_language_example: Wie heißen Sie denn?
native_language_example: So what’s your name, then? / What’s your name again?

additional_notes: This is not a fixed expression; it’s a very common sequence in formal German (Sie-form). **Sie** is the polite "you" used with strangers, customers, older people, etc. **die** is the definite article for **feminine singular** or **plural** nouns, and in these examples it’s in the **accusative** (direct object) after a verb or in a question/command: *Schließen Sie die Tür.* / *Wie fanden Sie die Gedichte?* Word order often stays verb-first in polite commands and questions: **Verb + Sie + (object)**.
target_language_example: Können Sie die Rechnung bitte unterschreiben?
native_language_example: Could you please sign the invoice?

meaning: “…the door” in a formal command (with **Sie** = ‘you’ formal).
additional_notes: In formal instructions, German often uses the imperative with the verb first: **Schließen Sie die Tür.** = “Close the door.” Here **Sie** is the polite ‘you’ (to one person or multiple people). The chunk **Sie die Tür** by itself is incomplete—you normally need a verb before it (e.g., **Schließen**, **Streichen**). Word order: **Verb + Sie + object**.
target_language_example: Öffnen Sie die Tür bitte.
native_language_example: Please open the door.

additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself. You’ll most often see it in formal/polite instructions with a verb in the imperative: **Verb + Sie + diese + noun**. Example: **Übersetzen Sie diese Sätze.** = “Translate these sentences.”
target_language_example: Lesen Sie diese E-Mail bitte zuerst.
native_language_example: Please read this email first.

meaning: “you (formal) … this …” (masculine accusative), used in polite requests/questions.
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase, but a very common pattern: **Verb + Sie + diesen + noun**. **Sie** = formal “you” (singular or plural). **diesen** is the accusative form of “this” for a masculine noun (e.g., *den Ausgang, den Beitrag, den Text, den Vers, den Korb*). In polite imperatives: *Bitte + Verb + Sie diesen …* = “Please [verb] this …”. In questions: *Wie/Wofür + Verb + Sie diesen …?* = “How/For what do you [verb] this …?”.
target_language_example: Bitte werfen Sie diesen Zettel nicht weg.
native_language_example: Please don’t throw this note away.

meaning: Formal “you” + *doch* (modal particle) expressing emphasis, reminder, mild contradiction, or an expectation that the other person agrees/has done something; often felt as “you do … (after all),” “surely you …,” or “come on, you …”.
additional_notes: *Sie* is the formal “you.” *Doch* is a very common German modal particle with no single fixed English translation. In patterns like **“Verb + Sie doch …”** it can (a) gently urge or prompt (*Kommen Sie doch rein.* = “Do come in.”), (b) signal the speaker expects confirmation (*Das werden Sie doch wissen?* = “You do know that, right?”), or (c) contradict an assumption (*Ich kenn Sie doch überhaupt nicht!* = “But I don’t know you at all!”).
target_language_example: Die werden Sie doch haben?
native_language_example: You do have them, right?

additional_notes: This isn’t a fixed expression, but a very common grammar chunk in polite questions/requests and formal instructions. **Sie** is the formal “you” (used with strangers, customers, officials). **einen** is used before a masculine noun that is the direct object (accusative), e.g. *einen Fachmann, einen Reisepass, einen Termin, einen Tipp*. You often see it after a verb: *Fragen Sie einen … / Suchen Sie einen … / Haben Sie einen …?*
target_language_example: Haben Sie einen Moment?
native_language_example: Do you have a moment?

meaning: “(to speak to) you for a moment” (polite/formal “you”).
