native_language_example: When my father died, I was still in school.

additional_notes: Used to describe what someone’s father was like or what state he was in in the past. You’ll often see it as **der Vater war** (“the father was”). In family context, German can drop the article: **Vater war …** can mean “Dad/Father was …”.
target_language_example: Vater war sehr müde nach der Arbeit.
native_language_example: Dad was very tired after work.

meaning: to contact; to get in touch (often: to put someone in touch).
additional_notes: Most often used with the preposition **in**: **(sich) mit jemandem in Verbindung setzen** = to get in touch/contact someone. With an object it can mean to connect people: **jemanden mit jemandem in Verbindung setzen** = to put someone in touch with someone. Common in formal or written German.
target_language_example: Ich werde mich morgen mit Ihnen in Verbindung setzen.
native_language_example: I will contact you tomorrow.

additional_notes: A formal legal/political term for extremely serious crimes (e.g., torture, slavery, genocide), typically judged under international law. Usually used in the pattern „etw. ist ein Verbrechen gegen die Menschheit“ (something is a crime against humanity).
target_language_example: Die Anklage lautet: Verbrechen gegen die Menschheit.
native_language_example: The charge is: crimes against humanity.

additional_notes: A formal, legal-sounding expression used for extremely serious acts that violate basic human rights (e.g., slavery, forced disappearances, mass violence). Often used in news, history, politics, and law. In German it’s commonly used with the article: „ein Verbrechen gegen die Menschlichkeit“.
target_language_example: Viele halten Folter für ein Verbrechen gegen die Menschlichkeit.
native_language_example: Many consider torture a crime against humanity.

additional_notes: Most commonly used as **im Vergleich zu + dative** to say how something differs when compared with something else: *Im Vergleich zu letztem Jahr ist es teurer.* In headlines or shorter phrases you may also see just *Vergleich zu ...*.
target_language_example: Im Vergleich zu Berlin ist München teurer.
native_language_example: Compared to Berlin, Munich is more expensive.

meaning: to have lost your mind (to act crazy/irrational).
additional_notes: Usually used as part of the verb phrase „den Verstand verloren haben“ (literally: “to have lost (one’s) reason”). Often rhetorical/exaggerated: „Hast du den Verstand verloren?“ = “Have you lost your mind?”
target_language_example: Bist du verrückt geworden? Hast du den Verstand verloren?
native_language_example: Have you gone crazy? Have you lost your mind?

additional_notes: Used with a person, group, or thing you believe is reliable or will do something well. Common patterns: „(großes) Vertrauen in + Akkusativ haben“ (to have (great) trust/confidence in), „Vertrauen in + Akk. verlieren“ (to lose trust in), „Vertrauen in + Akk. steigt/sinkt“ (trust increases/decreases), „jmds. Vertrauen in mich zu schätzen wissen“ (to appreciate someone’s trust in me).
target_language_example: Ich habe Vertrauen in dich, aber ich brauche mehr Zeit.
native_language_example: I trust you, but I need more time.

additional_notes: Used for changing or improving video files (cutting, trimming, adding music/effects, etc.). Common with modal verbs like „wollen“ (to want) and „können“ (to be able to): „Videos bearbeiten wollen/können“. Also common: „ein Video bearbeiten“ (edit a video).
target_language_example: Wenn du deine Videos bearbeiten willst, kannst du dieses Programm benutzen.
native_language_example: If you want to edit your videos, you can use this program.

meaning: Polyjuice Potion (a potion that lets you take someone else’s appearance).
additional_notes: A fixed name from the Harry Potter universe. In the examples, it’s treated like a specific item you can look for, see, or have ready (“in ein paar Tagen fertig”). Grammatically masculine: der Vielsaft-Trank.
target_language_example: Der Vielsaft-Trank ist fast fertig, aber wir brauchen noch eine Zutat.
native_language_example: The Polyjuice Potion is almost ready, but we still need one ingredient.

meaning: pros and cons; advantages and disadvantages.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the positive and negative sides of an option or situation, often when comparing choices or making a decision. Common patterns: „Vor- und Nachteile haben“ (to have pros and cons), „über Vor- und Nachteile nachdenken“ (to think about the pros and cons), „die Vor- und Nachteile von + Dativ“ (the pros and cons of ...).
target_language_example: Lass uns die Vor- und Nachteile abwägen, bevor wir buchen.
native_language_example: Let’s weigh the pros and cons before we book.

additional_notes: This is often used as a short instruction (e.g., on a note or checklist). In a full sentence you usually add a verb, for example: „den Wagen in die Garage fahren“ (drive the car into the garage) or „den Wagen in die Garage stellen“ (put/park the car in the garage). „in die Garage“ indicates motion/direction (into the garage).
target_language_example: Fahr den Wagen in die Garage, bitte.
native_language_example: Drive the car into the garage, please.

additional_notes: This isn’t a fixed idiom; it’s just a common sentence pattern. **Wagen** means “car/vehicle” (more general/formal than **Auto**). **fuhr** is simple past (Präteritum) of **fahren** (“to drive/go”). You often see it after **(ein)steigen**: **Ich stieg in den Wagen und fuhr ...** = “I got into the car and drove ...”.
target_language_example: Er stieg in den Wagen und fuhr zur Arbeit.
native_language_example: He got into the car and drove to work.

meaning: to find out / learn the truth.
additional_notes: Usually used with the article: „die Wahrheit erfahren“ (= to find out the truth). It often implies that something was hidden or unclear before, and you finally get the real facts.
target_language_example: Ich will die Wahrheit erfahren.
native_language_example: I want to find out the truth.

additional_notes: Usually used as part of the phrase **die Wahrheit sagen** (“to tell the truth”). In the examples it appears in the perfect tense (**hat ... die Wahrheit gesagt**) and in hypothetical/conditional sentences (**hätte ... die Wahrheit gesagt**). You normally include the article: **die Wahrheit**.
target_language_example: Warum hast du mir nicht die Wahrheit gesagt?
native_language_example: Why didn’t you tell me the truth?

additional_notes: Often used with „die (ganze) Wahrheit“ = “the (whole) truth.” The verb is „sagen“ (to say/tell), and it commonly takes a person in the dative: „jemandem die Wahrheit sagen“ = “to tell someone the truth.”
target_language_example: Du mußt uns nur die ganze Wahrheit sagen.
native_language_example: You just have to tell us the whole truth.

meaning: to be supposed to tell the truth; should (have) tell/told the truth.
additional_notes: Uses the modal verb „sollen“ to express obligation/expectation (what you’re supposed to do). Often appears with „hätte/hatte … sollen“ to talk about the past: „Ich hätte die Wahrheit sagen sollen“ = “I should have told the truth.” In the present: „Du sollst die Wahrheit sagen“ = “You’re supposed to tell the truth.”
target_language_example: Ich hätte die Wahrheit sagen sollen.
native_language_example: I should have told the truth.

additional_notes: An infinitive phrase with „zu“ expressing purpose/goal/intent: e.g., someone wants/tries/hopes „die Wahrheit zu erfahren“. „erfahren“ here means “to find out/learn” (information), not “to drive.” Common with verbs like „versuchen“, „wollen“, „hoffen“ or in constructions like „um … zu“ (in order to). Often appears as „die Wahrheit zu erfahren“ (with the article), though the core multi-word term is the infinitive phrase „Wahrheit zu erfahren“.
target_language_example: Ich möchte endlich die Wahrheit zu erfahren.
native_language_example: I want to finally find out the truth.

additional_notes: Usually used in the fixed phrase „Um die Wahrheit zu sagen, …“ at the start of a sentence to introduce an honest opinion or confession (similar to “To be honest, …”). You can also say „die Wahrheit sagen“ (“to tell the truth”).
target_language_example: Um die Wahrheit zu sagen, habe ich keine Zeit heute.
native_language_example: To be honest, I don’t have time today.

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary verb **haben** in the **Perfekt** (present perfect/simple past in spoken German): **(ich/du/er …) habe/hast/hat … Wasser getrunken**. **getrunken** is the past participle of **trinken** (“to drink”). You can add amounts or time: **ein Glas**, **viel**, **heute**, **drei Liter**.
target_language_example: Ich habe nach dem Sport viel Wasser getrunken.
native_language_example: I drank a lot of water after exercising.

meaning: "Water is" (used to say what water is like or what it means).
additional_notes: Used with the verb **ist** ("is", 3rd person singular of **sein** = "to be") to make statements/definitions about water: **Wasser ist flüssig.** It can also appear in questions when **ist** comes before the subject: **Wie viel Wasser ist ...?** ("How much water is ...?").
target_language_example: Wasser ist wichtig für unsere Gesundheit.
native_language_example: Water is important for our health.

additional_notes: Commonly used with washing/cleaning verbs like „(sich) waschen“ (to wash) and „(sich) die Hände waschen“ (to wash your hands). Often appears after „mit“ (with): „mit Wasser und Seife“ = with water and soap. In everyday advice, it can mean simple, basic hygiene/cleaning.
target_language_example: Du brauchst nur Wasser und Seife, um die Flecken rauszubekommen.
native_language_example: You only need water and soap to get the stains out.

meaning: “the way here / the route here” (the trip to this place).
additional_notes: Often used with **auf dem Weg hierher** = “on the way here.” You also hear **den Weg hierher zeigen** = “show (someone) the way here,” and **weiter Weg hierher** = “a long way here.”
target_language_example: Wir sind schon auf dem Weg hierher.
native_language_example: We’re already on the way here.

additional_notes: Used with destinations (usually cities/countries/regions): „der Weg nach Berlin“. Very common in phrases like „den Weg nach X nehmen“ (take the way to X) and „sich auf den Weg nach X machen“ (set off/head to X). Can also be figurative: „den Weg nach Europa finden“ = “make its way to Europe / become available in Europe.”
target_language_example: Wir suchen den schnellsten Weg nach Hause.
native_language_example: We’re looking for the fastest way home.

meaning: way home; the route back to your home.
additional_notes: Used with or without a preposition: often with "auf meinem Weg nach Hause" (= on my way home). "Weg" can mean a path/route or the act of going somewhere; here it’s specifically the trip back home. Also used in fixed phrases like "den Weg nach Hause finden" (= find your way home).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir den Weg nach Hause zeigen?
native_language_example: Can you show me the way home?

additional_notes: "zum" is the contraction of "zu dem" and is used with masculine/neuter nouns ("zum Kino", "zum Büro"). Used both literally for directions/routes and figuratively for a means to reach a goal ("der Weg zum Frieden").
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ist das der Weg zum Bahnhof?
native_language_example: Excuse me, is this the way to the train station?

meaning: the way to the train station
additional_notes: Used when asking for or talking about directions to the train station. "der Weg" means "path/way" and "zum" = "zu dem" ("to the"). Common in questions like "Ist das der (richtige) Weg zum Bahnhof?".
target_language_example: Können Sie mir bitte den Weg zum Bahnhof zeigen?
native_language_example: Could you please show me the way to the train station?

meaning: the way to work; the commute to work.
additional_notes: Refers to the route or time spent going to your workplace. Often used with "auf dem Weg zur Arbeit" (on the way to work) or "der Weg zur Arbeit" (the commute). "zur" = "zu der" (to the).
target_language_example: Auf dem Weg zur Arbeit höre ich oft Podcasts.
native_language_example: On the way to work, I often listen to podcasts.

meaning: way to school; route to school.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the path/route you take when going to school. Very common in phrases like „auf dem Weg zur Schule“ (= on the way to school). „zur“ is a contraction of „zu der“ and is used with feminine nouns like „die Schule“.
target_language_example: Auf dem Weg zur Schule habe ich meine Freundin getroffen.
native_language_example: On the way to school, I met my friend.

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb phrase **(jemanden) zum Weinen bringen** (“to make (someone) cry”). **gebracht** is the past participle of *bringen* (“to bring”), so you’ll often see it in the perfect tense: **Er hat mich zum Weinen gebracht.** Without **zum**, it can sound incomplete; the common full form is **zum Weinen gebracht**.
target_language_example: Der Film hat mich zum Weinen gebracht.
native_language_example: The movie made me cry.

additional_notes: Used with „sein“ and usually with a dative pronoun: „Mir ist (nicht) zum Weinen zumute.“ = “I (don’t) feel like crying.” More generally: „Mir ist zum + Infinitiv zumute“ expresses your mood/feeling (often negative): „Mir ist zum Lachen zumute“ (I feel like laughing).
target_language_example: Nach der schlechten Nachricht war mir zum Weinen zumute.
native_language_example: After the bad news, I felt like crying.

additional_notes: This is the noun + verb part of a sentence: **Welt** (world) + **ist** (is). It almost always appears with an article or possessive/demonstrative before it, e.g. **die Welt ist** (the world is), **unsere Welt ist** (our world is), **meine Welt ist** (my world is), **diese Welt ist** (this world is). In set phrases, it can be part of expressions like **das Ende der Welt ist nah** (“the end of the world is near”).
target_language_example: Die Welt ist manchmal laut, aber auch schön.
native_language_example: The world is sometimes loud, but also beautiful.

additional_notes: Usually used as **Die Welt ist voller + Genitive** to say there are many of something: **Die Welt ist voller Möglichkeiten.** In everyday speech, people often use **von + Dative** instead: **Die Welt ist voll von Möglichkeiten.**
target_language_example: Die Welt ist voller Überraschungen.
native_language_example: The world is full of surprises.

meaning: to say goodbye (literally: to say “see you again”).
additional_notes: Most commonly you’ll hear and use this as „Auf Wiedersehen sagen“ (or simply „Auf Wiedersehen!“), especially in more formal or neutral situations (e.g., shops, offices). „Wiedersehen“ is a noun meaning “seeing again.” With „zu sagen“, it’s used like an infinitive phrase: „…, um Auf Wiedersehen zu sagen.“
target_language_example: Ich rufe nur kurz an, um Auf Wiedersehen zu sagen.
native_language_example: I’m just calling briefly to say goodbye.

additional_notes: Uses the verb „wehen“ (to blow, for wind). Most common is „Der Wind weht.“ You can add direction or strength: „Der Wind weht aus Norden.“ (from the north), „Der Wind weht stark.“ (The wind is blowing strongly).
target_language_example: Der Wind weht heute sehr stark.
native_language_example: The wind is blowing very strongly today.

meaning: to become reality; to come true.
additional_notes: Used for plans, hopes, wishes, or ideas when they actually happen. Often with a subject like „ein Traum / ein Wunsch / ein Plan“: „Mein Traum wird Wirklichkeit.“ You can also use it with „lassen“ (make something come true): „Sie hat ihren Traum Wirklichkeit werden lassen.“
target_language_example: Endlich wird unser Plan Wirklichkeit werden.
native_language_example: Finally our plan will become reality / will come true.

additional_notes: Usually used with an article/number: „eine Woche krank im Bett“ = “sick in bed for a week.” You can also say „eine Woche lang“ for extra emphasis (“for a whole week”). Common with verbs like „liegen“ (to lie) or „sein“ (to be): „Ich liege seit einer Woche krank im Bett.“
target_language_example: Ich war eine Woche krank im Bett und konnte nicht zur Arbeit gehen.
native_language_example: I was sick in bed for a week and couldn’t go to work.

meaning: for a week; a week long.
additional_notes: Used with a time expression (often with an article or modifiers) to say how long something lasts: „eine Woche lang“, „die ganze Woche lang“, „zwei Wochen lang“. It usually goes after the time unit (Woche/Monat/Jahr) and can be used with durations like validity, weather, waiting, etc.
target_language_example: Wir waren eine Woche lang in Berlin.
native_language_example: We were in Berlin for a week.

meaning: to … for a week; (in/next week) to …
additional_notes: Used with movement/travel verbs (gehen, fahren, fliegen, müssen, wollen) and the destination preposition **nach** (typically for cities/countries without an article): **für eine Woche nach Berlin** = “to Berlin for a week.” With a time phrase like **in der nächsten Woche**, it means “(sometime) next week to …”. Note: **nach** here means “to,” not “after.”
target_language_example: Wir fliegen für eine Woche nach Spanien.
native_language_example: We’re flying to Spain for a week.

additional_notes: Used to express duration: a number + time unit + ("lang") = how long something lasts (e.g., „zwei Wochen lang“ = for two weeks). In modern German it’s often written as one word („wochenlang“, „zwei Wochen lang“ is also common).
target_language_example: Ich habe zwei Wochen lang jeden Tag Deutsch gelernt.
native_language_example: I studied German every day for two weeks.

additional_notes: This is more of a sentence fragment than a fixed phrase. In natural German you typically say **am Wochenende** (“on the weekend”) and include a main verb, e.g. **Ich gehe am Wochenende wieder angeln.** You can also use it as a short note/plan: **Am Wochenende wieder angeln.**
target_language_example: Ich gehe am Wochenende wieder angeln.
native_language_example: I’m going fishing again this weekend.

additional_notes: A common weather phrase. Usually used with "es gibt" (there are) or "es sind" (there are) to describe the sky. You can add adjectives like "dunkle" (dark) or "keine" (no) before "Wolken".
target_language_example: Heute sind nur ein paar Wolken am Himmel.
native_language_example: Today there are only a few clouds in the sky.

meaning: to keep your word (to do what you promised).
additional_notes: Often appears with a possessive pronoun: „sein/ihr Wort halten“ (to keep one’s word). Refers to a promise or commitment. Verb forms: halten – hielt – gehalten.
target_language_example: Khan, werden Sie Ihr Wort halten?
native_language_example: Khan, will you keep your word?

meaning: to say a word; to utter a word (often implying breaking silence).
additional_notes: This is an infinitive construction with „zu“ and is most commonly used with verbs like „haben“ (e.g., „nichts/kein Wort zu sagen haben“ = to have nothing to say) or in contexts about not speaking. In practice, German more often uses the finite verb phrase „ein/kein Wort sagen“, but „Wort zu sagen“ appears naturally inside larger sentence structures.
target_language_example: Ich hatte in diesem Moment kein Wort zu sagen.
native_language_example: At that moment, I didn’t have a word to say.

meaning: "the number of" (followed by a plural noun).
additional_notes: Used to talk about how many of something there are. It’s typically followed by a plural noun in the genitive case: "die Zahl der Studierenden" = "the number of students". Common in more formal or written German; in everyday speech you also hear "die Anzahl der" or simply "wie viele".
target_language_example: Die Zahl der Besucher steigt jedes Jahr.
native_language_example: The number of visitors increases every year.

meaning: 'time to' / 'time in order to' (used before an action).
additional_notes: Usually followed by an infinitive clause: „Zeit, um … zu + Infinitiv“ (often with a comma). Common with verbs like „Zeit haben“ (to have time) or „Zeit geben“ (to give time): „Ich habe keine Zeit, um zu warten.“ / „Geben Sie mir Zeit, um …“.
target_language_example: Ich brauche Zeit, um das zu verstehen.
native_language_example: I need time to understand that.

meaning: “time than with me” — a fragment used in comparisons (not a complete standalone phrase).
additional_notes: This string is not a fixed idiom and sounds incomplete on its own. In natural German it normally appears after a comparative like „mehr/weniger Zeit … als mit mir“, e.g., „mehr Zeit mit X als mit mir“. Note that this fragment omits what the time is spent *with* on the first side (e.g., „Zeit mit deinen Freunden“).
target_language_example: Du verbringst mehr Zeit mit deinen Freunden Zeit als mit mir.
native_language_example: You spend more time with your friends than with me.

meaning: (usually as) “in the wrong place at the wrong time.”
additional_notes: This wording is most commonly seen as the fixed phrase **„zur falschen Zeit am falschen Ort (sein)“**. It means someone is unlucky or gets involved in something just because they happened to be there at that moment.
target_language_example: Er war zur falschen Zeit am falschen Ort und wurde in den Streit hineingezogen.
native_language_example: He was in the wrong place at the wrong time and got pulled into the argument.

meaning: to need time; to take time.
additional_notes: Used to say that something takes a certain amount of time or that someone needs time. Often with a time expression ("Ich brauche zwei Stunden") or with "um ... zu" + infinitive ("Ich brauche Zeit, um das zu lernen"). Also common in the sense "I need some time" (e.g., to think or decide).
target_language_example: Ich werde Zeit brauchen, um mich zu entscheiden.
native_language_example: I will need time to decide.

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has time available, or to say whether something is a good/bad moment for an activity. It’s followed by a noun phrase: Zeit für + accusative (e.g., Zeit für einen Besuch / ein Frühstück). Common in questions like „Haben Sie Zeit für …?“ and statements like „Ich habe (keine) Zeit für …“.
target_language_example: Hast du heute Abend Zeit für einen kurzen Spaziergang?
native_language_example: Do you have time for a short walk this evening?

meaning: time for me; time to myself.
additional_notes: Often used when asking someone to spend time with you ("Hast du Zeit für mich?") or when talking about personal time/space ("Ich brauche Zeit für mich"). It can also mean a difficult period in your life ("eine dunkle Zeit für mich" = a dark time for me), where "Zeit" means "period/time in life" rather than free time.
target_language_example: Heute Abend brauche ich Zeit für mich, aber morgen habe ich Zeit für dich.
native_language_example: Tonight I need time to myself, but tomorrow I have time for you.

meaning: to give (someone) time; to allow time.
additional_notes: Used when asking someone to wait or to allow more time before you decide, answer, or finish something. Very common with a person in the dative: „Gib mir Zeit.“ It can also be used in the fixed saying „Man muss der Zeit Zeit geben“ (= you have to let time do its work / give it time).
target_language_example: Können Sie mir ein bisschen mehr Zeit geben?
native_language_example: Could you give me a little more time?

meaning: to have time (to do something); to be available.
additional_notes: Used to say you have enough free time or availability for an activity. Very often followed by "für" + noun ("Zeit haben für ...") or "um" + infinitive ("Zeit haben, um ... zu ..."). In polite requests it appears in conditional clauses like "wenn Sie Zeit haben" ("when/if you have time").
target_language_example: Sie möchten sie bitte anrufen, wenn Sie Zeit haben.
native_language_example: Please call her when you have time.

meaning: to take your time; not to rush.
additional_notes: Most common as the reflexive phrase „sich Zeit lassen“ (e.g., „Lass dir Zeit!“ = “Take your time!”). Used to tell someone to go slowly, or to say you won’t hurry. Often paired with „mit“ + dative: „Lass dir Zeit mit der Entscheidung.“
target_language_example: Du kannst dir ruhig Zeit lassen.
native_language_example: You can take your time.

meaning: “time with (someone)” (usually in: Zeit mit jemandem verbringen = to spend time with someone).
additional_notes:
Most commonly used with the verb **verbringen**: **Zeit mit + Dativ** (jemandem) **verbringen**.
- ich verbringe Zeit mit **dir**
- wir verbringen Zeit mit **Tom**
- Zeit mit **meiner Familie**
It’s about being together/doing things together. In sentence 7, a different expression is used: **die Zeit totschlagen** = “to kill time.”
target_language_example: Am Wochenende verbringe ich viel Zeit mit meinen Freunden.
native_language_example: On the weekend I spend a lot of time with my friends.

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase meaning to do something more efficiently so you need less time. Used with the person who saves time: „Ich spare Zeit“, „Wir sparen Zeit“. Often with „indem“ (by doing): „Wir sparen Zeit, indem wir online bestellen.“
target_language_example: Wenn wir den Bus nehmen, können wir Zeit sparen.
native_language_example: If we take the bus, we can save time.

meaning: to kill time; to pass the time (until something happens).
additional_notes: Used when you’re waiting and want to do something to make time go by faster. Often used with an activity: „Ich schlage die Zeit mit Lesen tot.“ In a full sentence, the verb is commonly split: „Ich schlage die Zeit tot.“
target_language_example: Wir schlagen die Zeit totschlagen, bis der Zug kommt.
native_language_example: We’re killing time until the train arrives.

meaning: to spend time (doing something / with someone).
additional_notes: Used to say how you occupy your time, often with **mit + Dativ** (with someone) or with a place/activity: **Zeit mit Freunden verbringen**, **Zeit im Park verbringen**. Common forms: present **ich verbringe Zeit**, past **ich habe Zeit verbracht**.
target_language_example: Am Wochenende verbringe ich gern Zeit mit meiner Familie — wir können richtig Zeit verbringen.
native_language_example: On the weekend I like to spend time with my family — we can really spend time together.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the passage of time. Very common with adverbs like „schnell“ (quickly) or „langsam“ (slowly): „Die Zeit vergeht schnell.“ The verb is „vergehen“ (to pass by, elapse), and here it’s in 3rd person singular: „(die) Zeit vergeht“.
target_language_example: Die Zeit vergeht schnell, wenn man Spaß hat.
native_language_example: Time flies when you’re having fun.

meaning: to waste time; to lose time (by delaying).
additional_notes: Often used with "keine": "keine Zeit verlieren" = "don’t waste any time / don’t delay" (a sense of urgency). It can mean you’re wasting time in general, or that waiting/delaying will make you miss a deadline or opportunity.
target_language_example: Lass uns keine Zeit verlieren und sofort losgehen.
native_language_example: Let’s not waste any time and leave right away.

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase. Often used with "mit" + dative to say what you’re wasting time on: "Zeit mit etwas verschwenden". You can also say "meine/deine Zeit verschwenden" (waste my/your time).
target_language_example: Ich möchte keine Zeit verschwenden.
native_language_example: I don't want to waste time.

additional_notes: Used when you don’t know the outcome yet and want to say you’ll find out later. Often followed by a clause with "ob" (whether/if): "Zeit wird zeigen, ob ...". Also common: "Die Zeit wird zeigen, ob ...".
target_language_example: Zeit wird zeigen, ob das eine gute Idee war.
native_language_example: Time will tell whether that was a good idea.

meaning: from time to time; now and then.
additional_notes: Most commonly used as **von Zeit zu Zeit** (“from time to time”). It means something happens occasionally, not regularly.
target_language_example: Von Zeit zu Zeit gehe ich mit Freunden ins Kino.
native_language_example: From time to time I go to the movies with friends.

additional_notes: Often used with „um … zu …“ to express purpose: „um Zeit zu sparen“ = “in order to save time.” You’ll also commonly see it without „zu“ as „Zeit sparen“ (e.g., „Ich will Zeit sparen.“).
target_language_example: Wir nehmen die U-Bahn, um Zeit zu sparen.
native_language_example: We’re taking the subway to save time.

meaning: time to read / time for reading.
additional_notes: Used with (haben) to say you have (little/no/rarely) time to read: „Ich habe (kaum/keine/selten) Zeit zum Lesen.“ „zum“ = „zu dem“ and is used here to mean “for” doing an activity (reading). You can also say „Zeit zum + infinitive“ for other activities (e.g., „Zeit zum Kochen“).
target_language_example: Heute Abend habe ich endlich Zeit zum Lesen.
native_language_example: This evening I finally have time to read.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone has successfully reached a goal (personal, work, travel, etc.). Often appears with haben + Ziel erreicht (e.g., Wir haben unser Ziel erreicht) or as a short status/message: Ziel erreicht!
target_language_example: Nach vielen Wochen Training habe ich mein Ziel erreicht.
native_language_example: After many weeks of training, I achieved my goal.

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb "haben" in the present perfect: "Ich habe mein Zimmer aufgeräumt" = "I tidied up my room / I have tidied up my room." The verb is "aufräumen" (separable: "räumen" + "auf"); the past participle is "aufgeräumt". Possessives change: mein/dein/ihr/sein/unser Zimmer.
target_language_example: Ich habe mein Zimmer aufgeräumt.
native_language_example: I tidied up my room.

additional_notes: A common everyday phrase meaning to put things away and make your room neat. Usually used with a possessive: „mein/dein/unser/euer Zimmer aufräumen“. Note that „aufräumen“ is a separable verb, so in main clauses it often appears split (e.g., „Ich räume mein Zimmer auf.“), but the infinitive phrase is „Zimmer aufräumen“.
target_language_example: Ich muss mein Zimmer aufräumen.
native_language_example: I have to tidy my room.

meaning: to tidy/clean up (a) room (to put it in order).
additional_notes: From the verb phrase „(ein) Zimmer aufräumen“ = to tidy up a room. In your sentences it appears as „… das Zimmer aufzuräumen“ (zu + infinitive), used after phrases like „beschäftigt sein“, „brauchen“, or „helfen“: „Ich war damit beschäftigt, das Zimmer aufzuräumen.“ Word order: in main clauses you often say „Ich räume mein Zimmer auf.“ (separable verb: auf + räumen).
target_language_example: Ich brauche eine Stunde, um mein Zimmer aufzuräumen.
native_language_example: I need an hour to tidy up my room.

meaning: "(he/she) entered the room" (simple past of "das Zimmer betreten").
additional_notes: Used in written stories/narration. "betreten" is a formal-ish verb meaning "to enter"; in everyday speech people often use "ins Zimmer gehen/kommen" instead. In the phrase "das Zimmer betrat", the verb is in Präteritum (simple past) and the subject is understood from context (e.g., "er/sie").
target_language_example: Als sie das Zimmer betrat, wurde es still.
native_language_example: When she entered the room, it got quiet.

meaning: '(the) room is' / 'in the room there is…'.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "sein" ("ist" = "is") to describe a room ("Mein Zimmer ist klein.") or, very often, after a place phrase to say what is in that place: "In meinem Zimmer ist …" = "In my room there is …". In this second use, German often uses "ist" (singular) even when English would say "there are"—German agrees with the thing that follows (e.g., "In meinem Zimmer ist keine Uhr."; plural would be "… sind zwei Stühle.").
target_language_example: In unserem Zimmer ist ein großes Fenster.
native_language_example: In our room there is a big window.

meaning: (to) keep the room clean / (to) clean the room.
additional_notes:
Usually used with a verb, especially: 
- „das Zimmer sauber machen“ = to clean/tidy the room (do the cleaning)
- „das Zimmer sauber halten“ = to keep the room clean (maintain cleanliness)
Used in commands and questions: „Halt dein Zimmer sauber!“ / „Ist dein Zimmer sauber?“
target_language_example: Ich muss mein Zimmer sauber machen.
native_language_example: I have to clean my room.

meaning: to go to the room / to go into the room
additional_notes: **Zimmer zu gehen** is not idiomatic as a standalone phrase in modern German. Normally you would say **ins Zimmer gehen** or **in (mein/dein/das) Zimmer gehen**. If you must use the exact wording, it typically appears only as part of an expanded structure (e.g., with an added preposition or in awkward/non-native phrasing). A more natural version of the example below would be: **Ich gehe ins Zimmer, um meine Jacke zu holen.**
target_language_example: Es ist Zeit, Zimmer zu gehen, um meine Jacke zu holen.
native_language_example: It’s time to go to the room to get my jacket.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "fahren" with "Zug" (train). You’ll see it in schedules and questions like "Welcher Zug fährt ...?" (= Which train goes ...?). Note: With an object it can also mean "to drive/operate the train": "jemand fährt den Zug" (= someone drives the train).
target_language_example: Welcher Zug fährt zum Flughafen?
native_language_example: Which train goes to the airport?

additional_notes: Used with a place name to say where the train is going: **der Zug nach Berlin** = “the train to Berlin.” Common in questions and travel situations: **Ist das der Zug nach …?** (“Is this the train to …?”) You’ll also see related patterns like **mit dem Zug nach …** (“by train to …”) and **in den Zug nach … steigen** (“to get on the train to …”).
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ist das der Zug nach München?
native_language_example: Excuse me, is this the train to Munich?

additional_notes: Used with the verb **verpassen** (to miss) in the **Perfekt** tense: **Ich habe den Zug verpasst.** The train is usually in the accusative: **den Zug / meinen Zug**. Often used with **fast** (almost) or **vielleicht** (maybe): **Ich hätte fast meinen Zug verpasst. / Sie hat vielleicht ihren Zug verpasst.**
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich komme zu spät — ich habe meinen Zug verpasst.
native_language_example: Sorry, I'm late — I missed my train.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone can enter/reach a place or use a service/thing. "zur" = "zu der" and is used with feminine nouns (e.g., "zur Bibliothek"). With masculine/neuter nouns you usually use "zum" (= "zu dem"), e.g., "Zugang zum Internet".
target_language_example: Haben Sie Zugang zur Bibliothek?
native_language_example: Do you have access to the library?

additional_notes: Used for guessing or predicting what will happen later. Often used with an object in the accusative, especially with the definite article: „die Zukunft vorhersagen“ (predict the future). You may also see: „jemandem die Zukunft vorhersagen“ (tell someone their future), e.g., with tarot cards, a horoscope, or a model/forecast.
target_language_example: Niemand kann Zukunft vorhersagen.
native_language_example: Nobody can predict the future.

additional_notes: Used with the verb „zur Welt bringen“ (= to give birth to). In the perfect tense, you’ll often see: „Sie hat Zwillinge zur Welt gebracht.“ In the simple past: „Sie brachte Zwillinge zur Welt.“ You can add details like „zwei Jungen / zwei Mädchen“ (two boys / two girls) or „eineiige Zwillinge“ (identical twins).
target_language_example: Sie hat letztes Jahr Zwillinge zur Welt gebracht.
native_language_example: She gave birth to twins last year.

additional_notes: Used with forms of "haben" (e.g., "hast du…?", "haben Sie…?") to talk about the completed action of brushing teeth. Often appears with "schon" (= already) and "das letzte Mal" (= the last time). With "deine" it means "your teeth"; without a possessive, "Zähne" is still understood as your own in everyday questions.
target_language_example: Ich habe mir heute Morgen schon die Zähne geputzt.
native_language_example: I already brushed my teeth this morning.

additional_notes: Common daily routine phrase. Often used as an instruction with "gehen": "Geh dir die Zähne putzen!" You’ll also hear the reflexive pattern "sich die Zähne putzen"; in commands, "dir" is common and "die" is often used instead of "deine".
target_language_example: Zieh dir deinen Schlafanzug an und geh dir die Zähne putzen.
native_language_example: Put on your pajamas and go brush your teeth.

additional_notes: Used to say something begins today and continues into the future. Often followed by a present or future meaning: „Ab heute“ + verb (e.g., „Ab heute schlafe ich hier.“). Similar to „von heute an“.
target_language_example: Ab heute arbeite ich jeden Tag bis 18 Uhr.
native_language_example: From today on, I work every day until 6 p.m.

meaning: from here (on); starting at this point/place.
additional_notes: Used to mark a starting point in space or time: from this location onward or from this moment onward (often with rules, responsibility, or what happens next). Common on signs/instructions and in speech (e.g., handing something over: „Ich übernehme ab hier.“).
target_language_example: Ab hier gilt Tempo 30.
native_language_example: From here on, the speed limit is 30.

additional_notes: Used to mark a new starting point in time (often a decision, rule, or change). Common at the beginning of a sentence, but it can also appear mid-sentence. Similar in meaning to "von jetzt an".
target_language_example: Ab jetzt spreche ich nur noch Deutsch im Unterricht.
native_language_example: From now on, I’m only speaking German in class.

additional_notes: Used to say that something begins tomorrow and continues from that point. Often followed by present tense or future meaning (e.g., "Ab morgen ist...", "Ab morgen wird...").
target_language_example: Ab morgen arbeite ich wieder im Büro.
native_language_example: Starting tomorrow, I’m working in the office again.

additional_notes: Used to announce a change that starts right away (often for new rules, decisions, or behavior). It can come at the beginning of the sentence or before the thing that changes: „Ab sofort arbeite ich …“ / „Ich habe beschlossen, ab sofort …“.
target_language_example: Ab sofort sind Handys im Unterricht verboten.
native_language_example: From now on, phones are forbidden in class.

meaning: Off to bed! (go to bed now).
additional_notes: A common, often parental, command telling someone (often children) to go to bed immediately. Used as a standalone phrase or after/with a verb like „heißt es“ ("it’s time to...").
target_language_example: Du bist müde—ab ins Bett!
native_language_example: You’re tired—off to bed!

additional_notes: Used to say something happens sometimes, but not regularly or often. Often placed with the verb (e.g., "Das passiert ab und an.") or before what it describes (e.g., "ab und an Geld"). Similar to "manchmal" but usually suggests a bit less frequent.
target_language_example: Ich sehe ihn ab und an in der Stadt.
native_language_example: I see him every now and then in town.

meaning: every now and then; from time to time (occasionally).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens sometimes, but not regularly. Very common in everyday German; it can appear at the beginning of a sentence ("Ab und zu …") or later ("… passiert ab und zu"). You’ll also often hear "ab und zu mal" = "every now and then."
target_language_example: Ab und zu gehe ich nach der Arbeit noch spazieren.
native_language_example: Every now and then I go for a walk after work.

additional_notes: A common, spoken command meaning someone should go to bed now (often said to children, but can also be used jokingly with adults). It’s usually used on its own as an exclamation, sometimes with “mit euch” (“you lot”) or “alle” (“everyone”).
target_language_example: Du siehst müde aus—ab ins Bett!
native_language_example: You look tired—off to bed!

additional_notes: In many verbs, **ab-** is a separable prefix that often suggests doing something **off/away** or **completing** an action (e.g., *abschließen* = to lock, *abkochen* = to boil, *abnehmen* = to take off/remove, *abhauen* = to get away). In a main clause, the **ab** part usually goes to the end: *Schließe die Tür **ab***. **Bevor** introduces a subordinate clause meaning **before**, and the verb goes to the end of that clause: *..., bevor du **gehst***.
target_language_example: Schalte das Licht ab, bevor du gehst.
native_language_example: Turn off the light before you go.

meaning: "every now and then; occasionally" (ab und zu / ab und an).
additional_notes: On its own, "ab und" is usually incomplete; the fixed expressions are "ab und zu" and "ab und an" (= occasionally). In other sentences you may see "ab" as a separable verb prefix (e.g., "Er nahm die Brille ab und ..." = "He took his glasses off and ..."), where "ab" means "off/away" and is not the same as the time expression.
target_language_example: Wir gehen ab und zu ins Kino.
native_language_example: We go to the cinema every now and then.

meaning: to already have plans (for the evening).
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone is free at a certain time, often as a lead-in to an invitation. "schon" adds the idea of "already" (maybe you might have plans). The verb is "vorhaben" (separable in some forms): Ich habe … vor / Hast du … vor?
target_language_example: Hast du heute Abend schon etwas vor, oder hast du Zeit?
native_language_example: Do you already have plans this evening, or do you have time?

meaning: “but not / however not” (used to contrast or as a warning).
additional_notes: Used to contrast with what was just said: “X, but not Y” (often after the subject, e.g. „Tiere aber nicht“). It can also add emphasis in a warning/command: „Aber nicht …!“ = “Just don’t … / Make sure you don’t …”.
target_language_example: Du kannst heute ausgehen, aber nicht zu spät nach Hause kommen.
native_language_example: You can go out today, but don’t come home too late.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast or consequence after what was just said. In dialogues it often means “OK, but then (on that condition) …” and can sound like setting a rule or warning.
target_language_example: Du kannst kommen, aber dann musst du pünktlich sein.
native_language_example: You can come, but then you have to be on time.

additional_notes: A very common, compositional phrase: aber adds contrast ('but'), and das refers to something already mentioned or understood from context. In English, das is often translated as 'that' or more naturally 'it' depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Ich verstehe deinen Punkt, aber das stimmt nicht ganz.
native_language_example: I understand your point, but that isn't quite right.

meaning: 'but that is…' (to add a contrast or correction).
additional_notes: Used to introduce information that contrasts with what was just said or expected. Very common in conversation and writing. Often followed by an adjective or noun phrase (e.g., „aber das ist nicht wichtig / nicht nötig / meine Kündigung“) or by an evaluation („aber das ist Selbstmord!“). In spoken German you may also hear it starting a new sentence to push back: „Aber das ist doch…“.
target_language_example: Ich verstehe dich, aber das ist nicht mein Problem.
native_language_example: I understand you, but that's not my problem.

additional_notes: Used to react to a statement or situation and push back or emphasize your point. **doch** adds the idea of “after all / really / you know,” often implying that something is obvious, surprising, or contrary to what someone suggested. Common before an adjective or noun phrase (e.g., *unmöglich, zu viel, ein Haufen Arbeit*).
target_language_example: Aber das ist doch viel zu teuer!
native_language_example: But that’s really way too expensive!

additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence to push back against what was just said and then deny or correct something: “Aber das ist nicht das Problem / der richtige Ort / ungefährlich.” Often followed by a noun phrase (“… das Problem”), an adjective (“… ungefährlich”), or expanded with “sondern …” (“but rather …”).
target_language_example: Aber das ist nicht meine Frage.
native_language_example: But that’s not my question.

meaning: "but that was…" (introduces a contrast about something in the past).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a clause to correct, limit, or add an opposing point to what was just said. It’s typically followed by more information (often with negation: „…war es nicht“, „…war nicht…“) or by a time/condition („…war, bevor…“).
target_language_example: Ich wollte helfen, aber das war nicht möglich.
native_language_example: I wanted to help, but that wasn’t possible.

meaning: "but you…" (contrasting what you did/are with someone else or with what was expected).
additional_notes: Used before a statement about the other person to show a contrast or objection: "I did X, but you (didn't/did Y)." At the start of a sentence, it can also sound like mild surprise or reproach, similar to "But you…!" / "Come on, you…" in English. Often followed by a verb: "aber du hörst (nicht) zu".
target_language_example: Ich wollte gehen, aber du bist geblieben.
native_language_example: I wanted to leave, but you stayed.

meaning: 'but you are …' (introduces a contrast or objection).
additional_notes: Used to push back against what was just said, or to point out a surprising/important fact about the other person. Often followed by an adjective, age, role, or group membership (e.g., "Aber du bist erst elf."). In speech, stress on "du" can add emphasis ("But YOU are...").
target_language_example: Ich dachte, du kommst nicht — aber du bist ja doch hier.
native_language_example: I thought you weren’t coming — but you’re actually here after all.

additional_notes: Used to object or correct someone by pointing out a fact about what they did or what has happened. Often followed by a past action (Perfekt with "hast" + past participle) or a state/result ("hast" + object). In English it’s usually "But you did..." or "But you have...", depending on context.
target_language_example: Aber du hast mir doch gesagt, dass du Zeit hast.
native_language_example: But you told me you had time.

meaning: "but you have" / "but you do have" (introduces a contrast).
additional_notes: Used to point out something the other person possesses or a fact about them that changes the situation: "Aber du hast …" is often followed by a noun (eine Familie), or something more abstract (Integrität, andere Prioritäten). In spoken German it can sound like a mild objection or reminder, similar to "But you *do* have…" in English.
target_language_example: Aber du hast doch genug Zeit, um kurz anzurufen.
native_language_example: But you do have enough time to call briefly.

meaning: 'but you can …' (introduces a contrast: you’re able/allowed to do something).
additional_notes: Used to contrast two statements: something is true, but you still have the ability/option/permission to do something else. Often followed by an infinitive at the end of the clause (e.g., „Aber du kannst es morgen machen.“). It can also soften suggestions/offers (e.g., „…, aber du kannst mich Bill nennen.“).
target_language_example: Es ist spät, aber du kannst morgen anrufen.
native_language_example: It’s late, but you can call tomorrow.

meaning: "but you have to / but you must".
additional_notes: Used to add a contrast or correction ("aber" = "but") and then state a necessity/obligation for "you". "Du musst" is 2nd-person singular of "müssen". Often followed by an infinitive later in the clause (e.g., "aber du musst gehen"). Important: "du musst nicht" usually means "you don’t have to" (no obligation), not "you must not" (prohibition).
target_language_example: Ich verstehe dich, aber du musst jetzt losgehen.
native_language_example: I understand you, but you have to leave now.

additional_notes: Used to contrast what comes before with something about a male person (er = he). Typically comes after a comma: „..., aber er ...“. You can swap in other pronouns: „aber sie“ (but she/they), „aber ich“ (but I).
target_language_example: Ich wollte gehen, aber er hatte keine Zeit.
native_language_example: I wanted to go, but he didn’t have time.

additional_notes: Used to contrast with what was said before: "aber" = "but" + "er" = "he" + "hat" = "has" (present) or auxiliary for the past (Perfekt), depending on the rest of the sentence. Often followed by a past participle (e.g., „... aber er hat es vergessen.“ = "... but he forgot.").
target_language_example: Ich habe ihn gefragt, aber er hat nichts gesagt.
native_language_example: I asked him, but he didn't say anything.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast about a man/boy ("er"). Often follows a statement about him and adds a surprising or opposite detail: "Er sieht aus wie …, aber er ist …". In writing, a comma is typically used before "aber" when it connects two main clauses.
target_language_example: Er wirkt sehr freundlich, aber er ist sehr streng.
native_language_example: He seems very friendly, but he is very strict.

additional_notes: Used to start the next clause after a statement, to add a contrasting or limiting point about something referred to as "es" (= "it" / the situation). Very common in spoken and written German: first clause, then a comma + „aber es …“. „Es“ is a placeholder for an idea, event, or whole situation, not only a physical object.
target_language_example: Ich war müde, aber es ging mir besser als gestern.
native_language_example: I was tired, but I felt better than yesterday.

meaning: “but there is / but there are” (introduces an exception, limitation, or new point).
additional_notes: Used when you want to add a contrasting fact after what was just said. You’ll often see it followed by a noun phrase: “aber es gibt ein Problem” (but there’s a problem), “aber es gibt keine Wahl” (but there’s no choice). Word order stays the same as normal “es gibt …” (there is/are …); “aber” just connects the contrast.
target_language_example: Ich verstehe deine Idee, aber es gibt ein Risiko.
native_language_example: I understand your idea, but there’s a risk.

meaning: "but it is" (used to contrast or correct what came before).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast after a statement: something may seem one way, **but it is** actually/also another way. Very common in explanations and everyday speech. Often followed by an adjective or noun phrase (e.g., *aber es ist interessant / sehr kalt / wahr*).
target_language_example: Es klingt komisch, aber es ist richtig.
native_language_example: It sounds strange, but it’s correct.

meaning: "but it's true" (said to insist that something really is true).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize or defend a statement that sounds surprising, doubtful, or that someone else denies. Often comes after another clause ("..., aber es ist wahr") or as an exclamation ("Aber es ist wahr!").
target_language_example: Du glaubst mir vielleicht nicht, aber es ist wahr.
native_language_example: You might not believe me, but it’s true.

meaning: 'but it was …' (introduces a contrast about a past situation).
additional_notes: Used to add a contrasting fact after a previous statement. Very common pattern: "..., aber es war + Adjektiv/Adverb" ("..., but it was too late/occupied/over quickly"). Note that "war" is the simple past of "sein" ("to be").
target_language_example: Ich wollte dir helfen, aber es war schon zu spät.
native_language_example: I wanted to help you, but it was already too late.

additional_notes: A simple, non-idiomatic combination of aber + ich. It is used to contrast what the speaker says or does with what was said before: “..., but I ...”. Often starts a new clause after a comma, but it can also begin a sentence for emphasis.
target_language_example: Du gehst nach Hause, aber ich bleibe noch hier.
native_language_example: You're going home, but I'm staying here a bit longer.

meaning: “but I am …” / “but I’m …” (used to contrast with what was just said).
additional_notes: Often comes after someone’s statement or an assumption to correct it or add a contrasting fact. Very common in conversation: “..., aber ich bin …” + adjective/noun/prepositional phrase (e.g., „unschuldig“, „der Auserwählte“, „noch nicht da“).
target_language_example: Ich verstehe dich, aber ich bin heute zu müde.
native_language_example: I understand you, but I’m too tired today.

meaning: “but I am not …” (used to disagree or correct).
additional_notes: Used to push back, clarify, or correct what someone thinks about you. Typically followed by a noun/adjective/phrase (e.g., „…der Dieb“, „…wie du“, „…begeistert“). In speech it often contrasts with what was said or implied before: „…, aber ich bin nicht …“.
target_language_example: Ich verstehe deinen Punkt, aber ich bin nicht damit einverstanden.
native_language_example: I understand your point, but I don't agree with it.

additional_notes: Used to contrast what was just said with a necessity or requirement. After "brauche" you typically put the thing you need in the accusative (e.g., "ich brauche ihn / sie / es"), or use "für" + accusative to say what it’s needed for (e.g., "ich brauche es für die Arbeit").
target_language_example: Ich würde gern kommen, aber ich brauche heute Ruhe.
native_language_example: I’d like to come, but I need some peace and quiet today.

meaning: “but I think …” / “but I believe …” (polite, slightly unsure disagreement or correction).
additional_notes: Used to soften a contradiction or to correct someone: you add a polite “but” (aber) and then your opinion/assumption (ich glaube). Often followed by a full clause ("…, aber ich glaube, dass …") or directly by a statement ("…, aber ich glaube, das ist …"). You can add words like "schon" or "eigentlich" to nuance it ("aber ich glaube schon" = “but I do think so”).
target_language_example: Ich verstehe, aber ich glaube, das ist nicht richtig.
native_language_example: I understand, but I think that’s not correct.

additional_notes: "Ich hab" is a very common spoken/written-informal shortening of "ich habe" (sometimes written "ich hab'" with an apostrophe). It’s used to contrast with what was just said: "Aber ich hab …" = "But I have …" / "But I haven't …".
target_language_example: Aber ich hab heute keine Zeit.
native_language_example: But I don't have time today.

meaning: "but I have..." (used to contrast with what was just said).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrasting point from the speaker’s perspective. "Ich habe" can mean (1) "I have" (possession): "Ich habe Zeit." or (2) "I have" as the auxiliary for the Perfekt (past): "Ich habe viel nachgedacht." After "aber", German keeps normal word order here: "aber ich habe ..."
target_language_example: Aber ich habe keine Zeit, heute zu kommen.
native_language_example: But I don’t have time to come today.

meaning: "but I have" (used to contrast with what was just said).
additional_notes: Use this after a statement (yours or someone else’s) to introduce a contrasting point or exception. "aber" = "but" and "ich habe" = "I have" (present tense of "haben"). Often followed by a noun: "Aber ich habe keine Zeit."
target_language_example: Aber ich habe heute keine Zeit.
native_language_example: But I don’t have time today.

meaning: 'but I can …' (contrast: something is true, but you’re able to do something).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast or limitation after what was just said: “but I can/can’t …”. Often followed by an infinitive or phrase like helfen (help), bleiben (stay), zustimmen (agree). With a direct object, you may see it as: „aber ich kann es nicht tun“ (but I can’t do it).
target_language_example: Ich bin müde, aber ich kann noch ein bisschen arbeiten.
native_language_example: I’m tired, but I can still work a little.

meaning: “but I can’t …” / “but I’m not able to …”.
additional_notes: Used to contrast with what was just said ("aber" = “but”) and then express inability or impossibility ("ich kann nicht" = “I can’t”). Often followed by an infinitive (kommen, gehen, zustimmen) or a prepositional phrase (von hier fort).
target_language_example: Ich würde dir gern helfen, aber ich kann nicht bleiben.
native_language_example: I’d like to help you, but I can’t stay.

additional_notes: Used to add a constraint or obligation after saying yes, agreeing, or stating a preference. Often used to politely decline or explain why you can’t do something: "Gerne, aber ich muss …". In everyday speech, German often uses "müssen" where English would say "have to".
target_language_example: Ich würde gern länger bleiben, aber ich muss morgen früh arbeiten.
native_language_example: I’d like to stay longer, but I have to work early tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to contrast with what was just said or expected ("but..."). It’s often followed by a clause with "dass ..." or by an object like "es" (e.g., "aber ich weiß es nicht" = "but I don’t know"). Word order is flexible in spoken German, but this phrase typically starts a new thought.
target_language_example: Ich bin nicht sicher, aber ich weiß, dass er heute kommt.
native_language_example: I’m not sure, but I do know that he’s coming today.

additional_notes: Used to add a contrast and then say you’re not sure or don’t have the information. It’s often followed by an indirect question clause with a question word like „wo“, „warum“, „wie“, „woher“: „… aber ich weiß nicht, woher er kommt.“
target_language_example: Ich würde gern helfen, aber ich weiß nicht, wie das geht.
native_language_example: I'd like to help, but I don't know how that works.

additional_notes: Used to contrast with what was just said and then state your intention or future action. "werde" is the 1st-person singular form of "werden" and is often used with an infinitive at the end (future/intent): „Aber ich werde es tun.“ / „Aber ich werde nicht warten.“ It can also be used on its own with an object: „Aber ich werde es herausfinden.“
target_language_example: Ich bin müde, aber ich werde trotzdem weiterarbeiten.
native_language_example: I'm tired, but I'll keep working anyway.

meaning: “but I want …” / “but I do want …” (to object, correct, or insist).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence to push back against what someone else said (“But I want…/But I don’t want…”). Very often followed by a direct object or an infinitive phrase: “Aber ich will euch helfen …” (But I want to help you …). Note: German “will” means “want,” not the English future tense “will” (which is usually “werde”).
target_language_example: Aber ich will das nicht machen.
native_language_example: But I don’t want to do that.

additional_notes: Used to correct or contrast what someone thinks/claims/what seems true with what is really true. Often comes after a statement or assumption: "X, aber in Wirklichkeit Y." You can also say "in Wirklichkeit" without "aber" if no strong contrast is needed.
target_language_example: Sie wirkt sehr selbstbewusst, aber in Wirklichkeit ist sie ziemlich nervös.
native_language_example: She seems very confident, but in reality she’s pretty nervous.

additional_notes: Used to contrast a previous situation with the current one ("before..., but now..."). It can also mean "but right now" when talking about the present moment (often followed by a reason like "keine Zeit"). Usually starts the second part of a sentence after something like "früher/einmal" (before/once).
target_language_example: Früher hatte ich Angst, aber jetzt fühle ich mich sicher.
native_language_example: I used to be scared, but now I feel safe.

additional_notes: Used to contrast two statements and negate the second one: something is true or possible in one way, but the opposite (or a limit) applies in the next part. Often comes after the verb in a clause: "... können ..., sich aber nicht ...".
target_language_example: Ich kann heute kommen, aber nicht lange bleiben.
native_language_example: I can come today, but I can't stay long.

additional_notes: Used to show a contrast: something happened or you expected a response, but no person did it (often after a comma). "Niemand" is singular, so the verb is singular: "aber niemand öffnete" / "aber niemand machte auf".
target_language_example: Ich habe dreimal angerufen, aber niemand ist rangegangen.
native_language_example: I called three times, but nobody picked up.

additional_notes: Often used as an emphatic, friendly answer meaning “definitely/you bet!” (e.g., “Aber sicher doch!”). You’ll also see it in the fixed phrase “langsam aber sicher” = “slowly but surely/gradually but surely.”
target_language_example: Kommst du morgen mit? – Aber sicher!
native_language_example: Are you coming along tomorrow? – Of course!

additional_notes: Used as a strong, often friendly-sounding way to confirm or agree with something. Common in spoken German; the tone can range from enthusiastic reassurance (“yes, absolutely”) to slightly sarcastic depending on context and intonation.
target_language_example: Kommst du morgen mit? – Aber sicher doch!
native_language_example: Are you coming along tomorrow? – Of course!

additional_notes: Used to contrast two statements. "Aber" is a coordinating conjunction, so you often put a comma before it when it connects two full clauses: "Ich wollte …, aber sie …". "Sie" can mean "she", "they", or formal "you"—in these examples it means "she" (e.g., Maria).
target_language_example: Ich wollte dir helfen, aber sie wollte es allein machen.
native_language_example: I wanted to help you, but she wanted to do it alone.

meaning: "but she is" / "but it is" (introduces a contrast).
additional_notes: Used to correct or add contrasting information after a statement. "sie" can mean "she" (a female person) or "it" when referring to a feminine noun (e.g., "die Verbindung"), and "ist" is the 3rd-person singular of "sein" (to be).
target_language_example: Der Plan klingt gut, aber sie ist zu teuer.
native_language_example: The plan sounds good, but it’s too expensive.

additional_notes: Used to express contrast: something is true or happens despite what was just said. Often follows a comma after the first clause (…, aber trotzdem …). In speech it can also stand in the middle of a sentence for emphasis (Ich habe mich aber trotzdem verspätet = “I was late anyway, even so”).
target_language_example: Ich war müde, aber trotzdem bin ich mitgekommen.
native_language_example: I was tired, but I still came along.

additional_notes: Used to contrast what “we” do/are with what was just said. Often comes after a comma (…, aber wir …) or at the start of a sentence (Aber wir …).
target_language_example: Sie haben mehr Geld, aber wir haben mehr Zeit.
native_language_example: They have more money, but we have more time.

meaning: "but we have..." (introduces a contrast and then says what 'we have').
additional_notes: Used to contrast a problem or negative point with something positive or useful that you possess or can rely on. Often used for reassurance: „Aber wir haben uns.“ = “But we have each other.” You typically continue with an object: „Aber wir haben einen Plan / die Schlüssel / genug Zeit.“
target_language_example: Es ist schwierig, aber wir haben genug Zeit.
native_language_example: It’s difficult, but we have enough time.

meaning: 'but we have to / but we must'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast or objection ("but") and then state a necessity/obligation ("we must"). Typically followed by an infinitive at the end of the clause: "Aber wir müssen gehen." / "Aber wir müssen schnell handeln."
target_language_example: Aber wir müssen jetzt los.
native_language_example: But we have to leave now.

meaning: “but we are …” (to contrast what comes next with what was just said).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrasting point about “us/we” ("wir"). Often followed by an adjective or noun phrase (e.g., „alt“, „keine Kinder mehr“, „eine Familie“) or another comment that corrects/limits the previous statement.
target_language_example: Aber wir sind bereit, es zu versuchen.
native_language_example: But we are ready to try.

meaning: did it on purpose; did it intentionally.
additional_notes: Used to say an action wasn’t an accident. Common pattern: **Das habe(n) ... absichtlich gemacht** (subject changes: ich habe, du hast, ihr habt, sie/Sie haben). You can also use **es** instead of **das** when referring to something already known: **Sie hat es absichtlich gemacht.**
target_language_example: Ich habe das nicht absichtlich gemacht.
native_language_example: I didn’t do that on purpose.

additional_notes: Used to accuse or state that someone’s action was deliberate (not an accident). Often appears as: "Das hast du absichtlich getan" (informal "du") or "Das haben Sie absichtlich getan" (formal "Sie").
target_language_example: Ich habe das nicht absichtlich getan.
native_language_example: I didn’t do that on purpose.

meaning: “Oh, that…” / “Oh, is that…?” (reaction: surprise, realization, emphasis).
additional_notes: Used as an interjection at the start of a sentence: “Ach” expresses a reaction (surprise, disbelief, admiration, annoyance, or “oh well”), and “das” refers to what comes next (“that/this”). The exact feeling depends a lot on intonation and context: e.g. disbelief (Ach, das hast du gesagt?), downplaying (Ach, das ist gar nichts.), admiration (Ach, das war aber lecker.), or annoyance (Ach, das muss doch nicht sein!).
target_language_example: Ach, das wusste ich nicht!
native_language_example: Oh, I didn’t know that!

meaning: “oh, you…” — used to show surprise, disbelief, or annoyance.
additional_notes: A very common spoken opener before you react to what someone said or did. Often followed by more words (e.g., “Ach, du meine Güte!” = “Oh my goodness!”) or by a comment addressing the person (“Ach, du machst Witze.” / “Ach, du verarschst uns doch.”). The tone depends on context: it can be amused, shocked, or irritated.
target_language_example: Ach, du machst doch nur Spaß!
native_language_example: Oh, you’re just kidding!

meaning: "Oh, I..." (a reaction before saying something about yourself).
additional_notes: "Ach" is a very common interjection used to show a feeling like surprise, realization, disappointment, impatience, or relief. It often comes at the start of a sentence; adding "ich" means you’re about to say something about yourself ("Ach, ich..." → "Oh, I..."). In writing, it’s usually followed by a comma: "Ach, ich ..."
target_language_example: Ach, ich habe es vergessen.
native_language_example: Oh, I forgot it.

additional_notes: Used to react emotionally (admiration, annoyance, irony, nostalgia, self-criticism). Often followed by an adjective (Ach, wie schön!) or a full sentence with inverted word order (Ach, wie vermisse ich dich!).
target_language_example: Ach, wie schön, dich wiederzusehen!
native_language_example: Oh, how nice to see you again!

meaning: "Oh right!" / "Oh yeah" (sudden remembering, realization, or an afterthought).
additional_notes: Used as an interjection when you suddenly remember something or add something you almost forgot: "Ach ja, ..." It can also react to something someone said. As a question ("Ach ja?") it often means "Oh really?" / "Is that so?" and can sound skeptical depending on tone.
target_language_example: Ach ja, ich muss noch einkaufen gehen.
native_language_example: Oh right, I still need to go shopping.

meaning: “Oh, I see / oh, right.” (shows you’ve just understood or remembered something).
additional_notes: Used as a quick reaction when something becomes clear after an explanation or when you suddenly remember a detail. Often stands alone (“Ach so!”) or comes at the start of a sentence (“Ach so, die Auktion.”). Tone depends on context: neutral to mildly surprised; can sometimes sound a bit dismissive if said flatly.
target_language_example: Ach so, jetzt verstehe ich dich.
native_language_example: Oh, I see—now I understand you.

additional_notes: Used to say a duration of time (how long something lasts) or a time remaining until an event. Often appears with prepositions like „seit“ (for: „seit acht Stunden“ = for eight hours) or with per-time phrases like „pro Tag / am Tag“ (per day).
target_language_example: Ich habe heute acht Stunden gearbeitet.
native_language_example: I worked eight hours today.

additional_notes: Used to state a time. With context it can mean 8:00 in the morning or in the evening; you can clarify with „morgens“ (in the morning) or „abends“ (in the evening). After „um“ (at) it becomes „um acht Uhr“.
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns um acht Uhr vor dem Kino.
native_language_example: We’re meeting at eight o’clock in front of the cinema.

additional_notes: Formal imperative (Sie-form) meaning you are telling someone politely to pay attention to something or be careful of it. Used with a noun after it (often with die/den/das depending on the noun): achten Sie auf die Details / den Verkehr / das Schild.
target_language_example: Achten Sie auf die Verkehrszeichen.
native_language_example: Pay attention to the traffic signs.

additional_notes: Polite/formal imperative (Sie-form) used for instructions and reminders. Often followed by **dass + clause**: *Achten Sie darauf, dass …* (“Make sure that …”). Can also be followed by **zu + infinitive**: *Achten Sie darauf, das Licht zu löschen* (“Make sure to turn off the light”), or by a noun/pronoun: *Achten Sie darauf* (“Pay attention to it/that”).
target_language_example: Achten Sie darauf, dass Sie Ihren Pass dabeihaben.
native_language_example: Make sure you have your passport with you.

additional_notes: Refers back to things already known from the conversation or context. Often used to sum up a situation (“all that”) and can sound emotional or emphatic: Warum all das? = “Why all this/that?”
target_language_example: Ich kann all das nicht vergessen.
native_language_example: I can’t forget all that.

additional_notes: Used when referring back to a whole set of things/situations already mentioned or understood from context. It’s the dative form of "all das" and is common after prepositions that take the dative (e.g., "von all dem" = "of all that", "zu all dem" = "to all that"), or with verbs that require the dative (e.g., "all dem widerstehen" = "resist all that").
target_language_example: Nach all dem brauche ich erst mal eine Pause.
native_language_example: After all that, I need a break first.

meaning: all those years / all the years (over a long period of time).
additional_notes: Used with prepositions like „in“, „vor“, or „aus“ to talk about something that happened or was true throughout a long stretch of time in the past: „in all den Jahren“ = throughout all those years; „vor all den Jahren“ = all those years ago; „aus all den Jahren“ = from all those years. Grammatically it’s dative plural („den Jahren“).
target_language_example: In all den Jahren habe ich dich nie vergessen.
native_language_example: In all those years, I never forgot you.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to refer to the whole set of specific things/people (often things already known from context): all those questions/tracks, etc. Common with plural nouns: all die Fragen, all die Leute, all die Spuren. In everyday speech it can also sound like simply “all the …”.
target_language_example: All die Leute warten schon vor der Tür.
native_language_example: All those people are already waiting in front of the door.

meaning: all those years; all these years.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize a long period of time in the past (often up to now). It often sounds emotional or reflective, like looking back and realizing something took a long time. It can be used in statements and questions: „Was hast du all die Jahre gemacht?“
target_language_example: Ich habe all die Jahre gedacht, du würdest zurückkommen.
native_language_example: All those years, I thought you would come back.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to emphasize the whole group of nearby/mentioned things or people: all these roses/letters/people/questions/things. It’s a common combination of **all** (all) + **diese** (these). Often appears with a noun right after it: **all diese + Nomen (Plural)**.
target_language_example: Ich verstehe all diese Regeln nicht.
native_language_example: I don’t understand all these rules.

meaning: very rarely; once in a blue moon.
additional_notes: Used (often with "nur" and sometimes with "(ein)mal") to say something happens extremely infrequently. Literally refers to a "jubilee year" (a rare, special year), but in everyday German it’s just an idiom for "hardly ever."
target_language_example: Wir sehen uns leider nur alle Jubeljahre.
native_language_example: Unfortunately, we only see each other once in a blue moon.

additional_notes: Used to make a general statement about people as a whole. It often starts a sentence (e.g., „Alle Menschen sind …“). With an added phrase it can be more specific: „Alle Menschen dieser Erde“ = all people on Earth. In comparisons/generalizations you may see „Wie alle Menschen …“ = like everyone (else) / as most people do.
target_language_example: Alle Menschen brauchen Liebe und Respekt.
native_language_example: All people need love and respect.

meaning: all (the) students / every student (in a group).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the entire group of students being talked about (e.g., at a school or in a class). Often followed by extra information like a place or group: „alle Schüler in der Klasse“, „alle Schüler an unserer Schule“. With negation, it means “not all students”: „Nicht alle Schüler …“.
target_language_example: Alle Schüler müssen pünktlich sein.
native_language_example: All students have to be on time.

additional_notes: "Alle" means "all" and "Türen" is the plural of "Tür" (door). It’s used literally for actual doors (e.g., in a house) and figuratively in phrases like "(etwas) öffnet alle Türen" = "(something) opens all doors" meaning it creates many opportunities or makes everything possible.
target_language_example: Ein gutes Netzwerk kann dir alle Türen öffnen.
native_language_example: A good network can open all doors for you.

additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs like „zumachen“/„schließen“ (to close) or „verriegeln“ (to lock/bolt), often as an instruction for safety, noise, weather, or security. „Mach … zu“ = informal singular; „Macht … zu!“ = informal plural; „Schließen Sie …!“ = formal (Sie) command.
target_language_example: Bitte schließen Sie alle Türen und Fenster, bevor Sie gehen.
native_language_example: Please close all doors and windows before you leave.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a large, unspecified group of people—often meaning “it feels like everyone” rather than literally the entire world. Sometimes it can also mean “the whole world” in a more literal sense, but very commonly it means “everyone”.
target_language_example: Auf einmal kennt alle Welt diese Geschichte.
native_language_example: Suddenly everyone knows this story.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the rest of a group (people or things), excluding the one(s) you’re talking about. Very common in comparisons with "als" (e.g., "größer als alle anderen" = "taller than all the others"). You can use it with nouns ("alle anderen Plätze") or on its own ("alle anderen").
target_language_example: Ich nehme den roten Stift; alle anderen brauche ich nicht.
native_language_example: I’ll take the red pen; I don’t need the others.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the rest of a group besides the person/people already mentioned (often meaning “everyone else”). It can stand alone (“Dann alle anderen!”) or follow a noun list (“Mama, Papa und alle anderen …”). It also appears in comparisons: “als alle anderen” = “than all the others.”
target_language_example: Ich habe keine Zeit, aber alle anderen können kommen.
native_language_example: I don't have time, but everyone else can come.

additional_notes: Used to compare one person/thing with the rest of a group. Often appears with comparisons: "besser/schlechter/schneller … als alle anderen" (better/worse/faster than everyone else). Can also be used with prepositions like "über" (above) in phrases like "über alle anderen hinaus" (above all others).
target_language_example: Ich will nicht auffallen; ich möchte einfach sein wie alle anderen.
native_language_example: I don’t want to stand out; I just want to be like everyone else.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that a statement applies to the two people/things being talked about. It often comes after the subject or pronoun (e.g., „Sie sind alle beide …“, „Tom und Maria sind alle beide …“). Common with people, but it can also be used for things.
target_language_example: Wir haben alle beide keine Zeit.
native_language_example: Both of us don’t have time.

additional_notes: Used when you mean exactly three people or things together. Often follows the noun/pronoun it refers to ("Tom, Maria und Johannes sind alle drei da"), but it can also appear at the beginning of the sentence ("Alle drei sahen Tom an"). It inflects for case: nominative/accusative "alle drei", dative "allen drei".
target_language_example: Tom, Maria und Johannes sind alle drei da.
native_language_example: Tom, Maria, and Johannes are all three here.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to mean you include every one of your things/people: „alle meine Geschwister“ (all my siblings), „alle meine Lehrer“ (all my teachers). The forms can change with case: e.g. nominative/accusative plural „alle meine …“, dative plural „mit allen meinen …“. For singular, German often uses „mein ganzes / meine ganze / mein ganzer …“ (my whole …) instead of *alle meine*.
target_language_example: Alle meine Freunde sind schon da.
native_language_example: All my friends are already here.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your entire group of friends. Often placed at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis (Alle meine Freunde …). In a longer sentence it can also come after the verb: Ich habe alle meine Freunde eingeladen. (accusative object).
target_language_example: Alle meine Freunde kommen heute Abend zu mir.
native_language_example: All my friends are coming to my place tonight.

meaning: all sorts of; all kinds of; all manner of.
additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to mean “a wide variety of” things, often implying “many different types” (not literally every possible one). It commonly appears with rumors, names, ideas, books, insults, etc.: „alle möglichen Gerüchte / Bücher / Schimpfwörter“.
target_language_example: Im Internet findet man alle möglichen Tipps zum Deutschlernen.
native_language_example: On the internet you can find all kinds of tips for learning German.

meaning: every two (e.g., every two days); sometimes: both (of them).
additional_notes: Most commonly used with a time word: „alle zwei Tage/Wochen/Monate“ = “every two days/weeks/months” (= every other day/week/month). In some contexts, especially in speech, „alle zwei“ can also mean “both” (similar to „beide“), but „beide/alle beide“ is clearer and more common for “both.”
target_language_example: Ich gehe alle zwei Tage ins Fitnessstudio.
native_language_example: I go to the gym every two days (every other day).

meaning: every two days; every other day.
additional_notes: Used to describe a repeated schedule with a two-day interval (one day in between). Common with routines and appointments, often with a verb like kommen/gehen/anrufen/besuchen. Compare: „jeden zweiten Tag“ (same meaning).
