target_language_example: Wir treffen uns alle zwei Tage zum Lernen.
native_language_example: We meet every other day to study.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a whole group of people or things that share a condition, followed by a relative clause with verb at the end (e.g., „alle, die … leben/sehen/müssen“). It can refer to people („all who…“) or, depending on context, to things („all the ones that…“). Often used without a noun: „Alle, die kommen, …“ = „Everyone who comes …“.
target_language_example: Alle, die heute Zeit haben, können mitkommen.
native_language_example: Everyone who has time today can come along.

additional_notes: Used to say that a whole group is identical/similar in some way (often with verbs like „sein“ or „aussehen“) or that everyone has the same status/rights (e.g., „Vor dem Gesetz sind wir alle gleich.“ = equal before the law). In statements like „Frauen sind alle gleich“, it can sound like a sweeping generalization.
target_language_example: Für mich sehen sie alle gleich aus.
native_language_example: To me they all look the same.

meaning: all of you / all together (everyone as a group).
additional_notes: Used to address a group or to refer to everyone doing something together. Often set off by commas when speaking to a group (like “everyone”): „Hallo, alle miteinander!“ It can also mean “together as a group” in a sentence: „Wir essen alle miteinander.“
target_language_example: Kommt rein, alle miteinander!
native_language_example: Come in, all of you!

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement or sending, especially **gehen** (to go) and **schicken** (to send): **Alle gehen nach Hause** = everyone goes home; **Jemand schickt alle nach Hause** = someone sends everyone home. In commands it often appears as **Geht alle nach Hause!** (“Everyone go home!”).
target_language_example: Es ist spät—wir gehen jetzt alle nach Hause.
native_language_example: It’s late—we’re all going home now.

additional_notes: Used to say that a whole group has a state/feeling: **Alle sind aufgeregt/nervös.** Grammatically, **alle** is plural, so it goes with **sind** (3rd person plural of **sein**, “to be”). In the Perfekt tense, **sind** can also be the helping verb with movement/change verbs: **Alle sind auf die Party gegangen.**
target_language_example: Alle sind schon hier.
native_language_example: Everyone is already here.

additional_notes: “Alle” means “everyone” or “all (of them)”. “Waren” is the simple past (Präteritum) of “sein” (“to be”) for wir/sie/Sie: “we/they/you (formal) were”. Used to describe a past state of a whole group (often followed by an adjective or phrase): “Alle waren müde.”
target_language_example: Alle waren froh, als der Test vorbei war.
native_language_example: Everyone was happy when the test was over.

additional_notes: Used to say something is common knowledge. It’s typically followed by a subordinate clause introduced by **dass** (“that”). In German you usually write a comma before **dass**, and the verb in the **dass**-clause goes to the end: **Alle wissen, dass er heute kommt.**
target_language_example: Alle wissen, dass wir morgen eine Prüfung haben.
native_language_example: Everyone knows that we have an exam tomorrow.

meaning: all together; everyone (here), as a group.
additional_notes: Used to address or refer to a whole group at once (like “everyone” or “all of you together”). Common in greetings (“Guten Morgen, alle zusammen!”) and when giving a group instruction (“Los, alle zusammen!”).
target_language_example: Kommt alle zusammen nach vorne!
native_language_example: Everyone, come up to the front together!

meaning: to leave (someone) alone; to let (someone) be alone.
additional_notes: Used when you ask or tell someone not to leave you by yourself, or when you ask people to give you privacy (e.g., “Could you leave us alone for a moment?”). Common with pronouns: jemanden allein lassen (mich/dich/ihn/sie/uns/euch). In the examples it often appears with polite requests (Könnten/Würden Sie … bitte …?).
target_language_example: Kannst du mich bitte kurz allein lassen?
native_language_example: Can you please leave me alone for a moment?

meaning: to be alone; to be by yourself.
additional_notes: Used to describe being without other people present, or not having company (sometimes emotionally: feeling alone). Often appears with verbs like „wollen“ (want), „müssen“ (need), „können“ (can): „Ich will/muss/kann nicht allein sein.“ Also used for requesting privacy: „Könnten wir kurz allein sein?“
target_language_example: Ich möchte heute Abend nicht allein sein.
native_language_example: I don’t want to be alone tonight.

additional_notes: Used when talking about going somewhere without anyone else. "dorthin" means "to there" (to that place), and "allein" means "alone"—so it often appears with verbs of movement like "gehen" (to go) or "fahren" (to go/drive).
target_language_example: Ich möchte nicht allein dorthin gehen.
native_language_example: I don’t want to go there alone.

additional_notes: An infinitive phrase with "zu" used after many verbs (e.g., "sich entschließen", "die Absicht haben", "zu jung sein, um … zu …"). "dorthin" means “to there” (to that place), and "allein" emphasizes you go without anyone else.
target_language_example: Ich traue mich nicht, allein dorthin zu gehen.
native_language_example: I don’t dare to go there alone.

meaning: alone in the forest (in the woods).
additional_notes: A common location phrase used with verbs like sein (to be), leben (to live), wohnen (to live/reside), or verbringen (to spend): „Er lebt allein im Wald.“ „im“ is a contraction of „in dem“ and „Wald“ means “forest/woods.”
target_language_example: Sie hat sich allein im Wald verlaufen.
native_language_example: She got lost alone in the woods.

meaning: to stand alone; to be able to stand by itself.
additional_notes: Used both literally (a person/thing stands without support) and figuratively (a word, sentence, or idea can be used independently and still make sense). In everyday speech about relationship status, German more often uses the adjective "alleinstehend" (single) rather than the verb phrase "allein stehen".
target_language_example: Dieser Satz kann allein stehen.
native_language_example: This sentence can stand on its own.

additional_notes: Describes being at home with no other people there. Commonly used with verbs like „sein“ (to be) and „bleiben“ (to stay). Word order can vary: „allein zu Hause“ and „zu Hause allein“ both work, but „allein zu Hause“ is very common.
target_language_example: Ich bin heute Abend allein zu Hause.
native_language_example: I’m home alone tonight.

meaning: "to ... alone / by yourself" (used before an infinitive).
additional_notes: Used to say someone does an action without help or without other people. Pattern: "allein" + "zu" + infinitive (often at the end of the clause): "allein zu wohnen" = "to live alone". Can express being physically alone (no company) or doing something without assistance (on one’s own).
target_language_example: Kannst du das allein zu Ende bringen?
native_language_example: Can you finish that on your own?

additional_notes: Used to talk about being by yourself (without other people). Often used with phrases like „Ich mag es …“ (I like it…), „Ich wünsche …“ (I wish…), or „Macht es dir/Ihnen nichts aus …?“ (Do you mind…?).
target_language_example: Heute Abend möchte ich gern allein zu sein.
native_language_example: This evening I’d like to be alone.

meaning: to leave (someone) alone; to leave (someone) by themselves; to stop bothering someone (context-dependent).
additional_notes: Takes a direct object in the accusative: jemanden alleine lassen. Can mean (1) physically leaving someone without company/help/supervision (e.g., a child) or (2) leaving someone in peace ("stop bothering me"). Common in polite requests: „Würden Sie uns kurz alleine lassen?“ = “Would you leave us alone for a moment?”
target_language_example: Würden Sie uns ein paar Minuten alleine lassen?
native_language_example: Would you leave us alone for a few minutes?

meaning: apparently; it seems (based on what you can see/know).
additional_notes: Used to say you’re making a conclusion from appearances or available evidence, not stating a proven fact. It often comes at the beginning of the sentence, but can also be inserted later: „Tom hat allem Anschein nach …“. More formal than „anscheinend“.
target_language_example: Allem Anschein nach kommt der Bus heute zu spät.
native_language_example: Apparently, the bus is late today.

additional_notes: This is the dative form of **alles** (“everything”) + **was** (“that/which”) in a relative clause: **(mit/aus/nach) allem, was …** = “with/from/after everything that …”. The comma is standard before the relative clause (**was ...**). The case (allem / alles / allem, etc.) depends on the role in the main clause (often set by a preposition like **mit** or **aus**).
target_language_example: Ich bin mit allem, was du gesagt hast, einverstanden.
native_language_example: I agree with everything that you said.

additional_notes: Used with reporting verbs like **sagen** or **erzählen**: **jemandem (Dat.) sagen/erzählen, dass …**. **allen** is dative plural (“to everyone”), followed by a **dass**-clause. Word order: the verb in the **dass**-clause goes to the end (e.g., **dass er morgen keine Zeit hat**).
target_language_example: Maria sagte allen, dass es ihr gut gehe.
native_language_example: Maria told everyone that she was doing well.

meaning: of the whole world; of all the world.
additional_notes: “Aller” is the genitive form of “alle” (all). You most often see this in set phrases like “aus aller Welt” (“from all over the world”) or “Menschen aus aller Welt” (“people from all over the world”). It’s a somewhat fixed, formal-sounding genitive expression, not something beginners usually build freely in new sentences.
target_language_example: In dieser Stadt treffen sich Menschen aus aller Welt.
native_language_example: In this city, people from all over the world meet.

meaning: “on earth have you …?” (strong emphasis in a question).
additional_notes: Used in surprised/annoyed questions, usually with a question word in front: e.g. „Was aller Welt hast du gemacht?“ = “What on earth did you do?” „Aller Welt“ is an old-fashioned genitive (“of all the world”) used as an intensifier; it’s not meant literally.
target_language_example: Was aller Welt hast du denn gemacht?
native_language_example: What on earth did you do?

meaning: of the whole world; (with „aus“) from all over the world.
additional_notes: „aller Welt“ is genitive and is common in two patterns: (1) „aus aller Welt“ = “from all over the world” (people/things coming from many countries). (2) With a superlative: „der/die/das …ste … aller Welt“ = “the …est … in the whole world.”
target_language_example: In diesem Museum gibt es Kunst aus aller Welt.
native_language_example: This museum has art from all over the world.

meaning: “of all time” / “ever” (used to emphasize a superlative).
additional_notes: Usually comes after a superlative: "die beste/größte/schlimmste … aller Zeiten" = “the best/biggest/worst … of all time.” Grammatically it’s genitive plural of "alle Zeiten" (“all times”), meaning across all eras/periods.
target_language_example: Das ist mein Lieblingsfilm aller Zeiten.
native_language_example: That’s my favorite movie of all time.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has an allergy. Usually with a noun: „Ich bin allergisch gegen Milch.“ You can add contrasts with „aber nicht gegen …“ (but not to …). In everyday speech, people also say „allergisch auf“ with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: Bist du allergisch gegen Katzen?
native_language_example: Are you allergic to cats?

additional_notes: A common, friendly way to wish someone well—often when saying goodbye, for birthdays, or before an important event. You can say it on its own as a greeting/farewell (“Alles Gute, Anna!”) or use it with wünschen: “Ich wünsche dir/Ihnen alles Gute.” (to a friend vs. formal).
target_language_example: Alles Gute zum Geburtstag!
native_language_example: All the best for your birthday!

meaning: "Happy birthday" (literally: "all the best for your birthday").
additional_notes: A common birthday greeting said or written directly to the person whose birthday it is. Often followed by the person’s name or a form of address (e.g., "Alles Gute zum Geburtstag, Anna!"). You may also hear "Alles Gute zum Geburtstag!" by itself.
target_language_example: Alles Gute zum Geburtstag, Mama! Ich hab dich lieb.
native_language_example: Happy birthday, Mom! I love you.

additional_notes: Used to say the exact thing isn’t known or doesn’t matter—there are many possibilities. Often appears after an indefinite pronoun like "etwas"/"nichts"/"alles" (e.g., "etwas alles Mögliche") or on its own ("Das kann alles Mögliche sein"). In "sich alles Mögliche einfallen lassen", it means thinking up all kinds of ideas.
target_language_example: Im Urlaub kann alles Mögliche passieren.
native_language_example: All sorts of things can happen on vacation.

additional_notes: Used to wish someone well, often as a short closing in messages/cards or when saying goodbye. Common with verbs like wünschen: „Ich/Wir wünschen dir/Ihnen alles Gute.“ Also used alone as „Alles Gute!“. In other contexts it can literally mean “everything good” (e.g., „Alles Gute passiert…“).
target_language_example: Alles Gute zum Geburtstag!
native_language_example: All the best for your birthday!

additional_notes: Used to refer to the total set of things that meet a condition, often followed by a full clause (subject + verb): "alles, was ich will" = "everything (that) I want." The comma is typical because it introduces a relative clause with "was". In everyday speech, you may also hear "alles, was" without a pause, but the comma is still written.
target_language_example: Alles, was du brauchst, ist hier.
native_language_example: Everything you need is here.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause: **alles, was Sie + verb** = “everything (that) you + verb.” **Sie** is the formal “you” (for strangers, customers, etc.); with friends you’d usually say **alles, was du …**. Often appears in warnings, questions, and customer-service contexts.
target_language_example: Alles, was Sie hier unterschreiben, ist verbindlich.
native_language_example: Everything you sign here is binding.

additional_notes: Uses the relative pronoun “was” after “alles” to mean “everything that…”. “Sie” is the formal “you” (for one person or a group), so this phrase is formal/polite. Often appears in longer forms like “alles, was Sie wissen müssen” = “everything you need to know.” Comma is required before the relative clause: “alles, was Sie wissen”.
target_language_example: Sagen Sie mir alles, was Sie wissen.
native_language_example: Tell me everything you know.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause referring to “everything” someone knows/has/does, etc. After "was du", the verb goes to the end of the clause (e.g., "alles, was du weißt"). Often followed by a prepositional phrase like "darüber" (about it) or "über ihn" (about him).
target_language_example: Erzähl mir alles, was du gehört hast.
native_language_example: Tell me everything that you heard.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has (or can find) all the things they need. "alles" = everything, and "was du brauchst" is a relative clause meaning "that you need" (literally: "what you need"). Often used in questions like "Hast du alles, was du brauchst?"
target_language_example: Keine Sorge—ich habe alles, was du brauchst.
native_language_example: Don’t worry—I have everything you need.

alles, was du tun musst, ist

target_language_multi_word_term: alles, was du tun musst, ist
additional_notes: Used to say that only one action is needed (often to make something sound simple). Very common with an infinitive clause: "Alles, was du tun musst, ist, + zu + Infinitiv" (e.g., "... ist, den Knopf zu drücken"). In speech and informal writing, the comma after "ist" is sometimes omitted: "... ist den Knopf zu drücken." You can change "du" to other pronouns: "alles, was ich/er/sie/wir tun muss/müssen, ist ..."
target_language_example: Alles, was du tun musst, ist, mir kurz zu schreiben.
native_language_example: All you have to do is send me a quick message.

additional_notes: Means “all the things that you want.” Often used with verbs like geben (to give), tun/machen (to do), or kaufen (to buy): „Ich gebe/tu/kaufe dir alles, was du willst.“ You can change the person: „alles, was ich will“ (everything I want), „alles, was Sie wollen“ (everything you want, formal).
target_language_example: Sag einfach Bescheid, ich mache alles, was du willst.
native_language_example: Just let me know, I’ll do anything you want.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause with **alles, was** (“everything that/whatever”). The comma is required: **Alles, was er tut, …**. The verb in the relative clause goes to the end (e.g., **was er weiß**). Replace **er** with another subject as needed (sie, ich, Tom, etc.).
target_language_example: Alles, was er sagt, stimmt nicht immer.
native_language_example: Everything that he says isn’t always true.

additional_notes: Common pattern: "alles, was + subject + (verb in past)" = "everything that ...". Here, "besaß" is simple past of "besitzen" (to own/possess). Used when talking about all of someone’s belongings/property, often with verbs like "verkaufen" (sell), "verlieren" (lose), or "tragen" (carry). You can change the subject: "alles, was ich besaß" (everything I owned), "alles, was sie besaß" (everything she owned).
target_language_example: Nach dem Brand hatte er alles, was er besaß, verloren.
native_language_example: After the fire, he had lost everything he owned.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause referring to “everything” (alles). The comma is required: „alles, was ich …“. After „was ich“, you usually continue with a verb at/near the end of the clause (e.g., „alles, was ich brauche“ = everything I need).
target_language_example: Das ist alles, was ich heute brauche.
native_language_example: That’s everything I need today.

additional_notes: Used to say you have (or don’t have) all necessary things. "alles, was ..." introduces a relative clause meaning "everything that ...". Often appears with verbs like "haben" (to have): "Ich habe alles, was ich brauche."
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, ich habe alles, was ich brauche.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I have everything I need.

meaning: everything I have; all that I have.
additional_notes: A relative clause meaning “everything that I have.” Often used to emphasize that something is your only possession/asset (Alles, was ich habe, ist …) or that you’re giving absolutely everything you have (Ich gebe dir alles, was ich habe.).
target_language_example: Bitte nimm alles, was ich habe, aber lass mich in Ruhe.
native_language_example: Please take everything I have, but leave me alone.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause with **ihr** (= “you” plural/informal, or “you” formal in some dialects). **Alles** refers to a general set of things, and **was** links to what follows: *alles, was ihr gesehen habt* = “everything that you saw.” Often used to ask if something is the total amount: *Ist das alles, was ihr …?*
target_language_example: Erzähl mir alles, was ihr heute gemacht habt.
native_language_example: Tell me everything you (all) did today.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause with an indefinite subject (man = “one/you/people in general”). It refers to the total of things in a general sense: Alles, was man + VERB, … (“Everything that you eat/need/know/lose …”). Often followed by a verb at the end of the clause.
target_language_example: Alles, was man braucht, ist ein bisschen Geduld.
native_language_example: Everything you need is a bit of patience.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause (comma + "was") referring back to "alles" (“everything”): "Alles, was sie sagt" = “Everything (that) she says.” The pronoun "sie" here can mean “she” or formal “you” (singular/plural), depending on context. The verb in the relative clause usually comes at the end: "Alles, was sie braucht, ist Zeit."
target_language_example: Ich glaube alles, was sie mir erzählt.
native_language_example: I believe everything she tells me.

additional_notes: Used when you refer to the total of things/actions connected to “we,” and then add more information with a verb at the end of the clause. Common patterns: “alles, was wir haben/tun/sagen/brauchen …”. In German, the verb in the “was”-clause typically comes last: “alles, was wir brauchen”.
target_language_example: Alles, was wir heute brauchen, ist Zeit.
native_language_example: Everything we need today is time.

additional_notes: Used to say/check that you have all necessary items or requirements. Often appears in questions (Hast du/Habt ihr …? Ist das …?) and can be used on its own as a short statement (e.g., on a checklist).
target_language_example: Okay, wir haben alles, was wir brauchen.
native_language_example: Okay, we have everything we need.

additional_notes: Used to contrast one thing with the rest: "X ist wichtig, alles andere ..." It can be the subject or object of a sentence. Often means "everything besides that" (everything else). In questions/negatives it can also mean "anything else" (e.g., "Hast du alles andere?" = "Do you have everything else?").
target_language_example: Ich habe keine Zeit; alles andere muss warten.
native_language_example: I have no time; everything else has to wait.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that something is NOT the case (often with adjectives like sicher, unschuldig, glücklich). It suggests the opposite or that reality is very different from what’s being mentioned.
target_language_example: Der Film war alles andere als langweilig.
native_language_example: The movie was anything but boring.

additional_notes: Used to strongly say that someone/something is NOT what follows (often the opposite). Common with adjectives ("alles andere als zufriedenstellend") or noun phrases ("alles andere als ein Lügner"). It adds emphasis, like “definitely not” or “not at all.”
target_language_example: Der Film war alles andere als langweilig.
native_language_example: The movie was anything but boring.

meaning: “everything for …” / “all for …” (doing, buying, or dedicating something to someone/something).
additional_notes: Used with a noun/pronoun in the accusative after **für**: **alles für dich** (everything for you), **alles für die Kinder** (everything for the children). It can mean (1) things intended for a purpose/person (“I bought all this for …”) or (2) being willing to do anything for someone (“I’d do anything for …”).
target_language_example: Ich würde alles für meine Familie tun.
native_language_example: I would do anything for my family.

additional_notes: Used to express strong willingness to do a lot for someone, or that you did/made sacrifices for them. Common with verbs like tun (to do), aufgeben (to give up), opfern (to sacrifice), vorbereiten (to prepare). Depending on context it can sound loving, dramatic, or even threatening/manipulative.
target_language_example: Ich würde alles für dich tun, aber das geht zu weit.
native_language_example: I’d do anything for you, but that goes too far.

meaning: “did everything that …” (i.e., did all they could / did all that was necessary).
additional_notes: Used with a relative clause introduced by **was** to explain what “everything” refers to: **Ich habe alles getan, was ich konnte** = “I did everything I could.” Often followed by **um … zu** to give a goal/purpose: **… um jemanden zu retten** (“… to save someone”).
target_language_example: Ich habe alles getan, was ich konnte, um dir zu helfen.
native_language_example: I did everything I could to help you.

additional_notes: Used with a relative clause: **alles tun, worum + person (Akk.) + bitten**. Here **worum** means “what/that which” referring back to **alles** (“everything”) and links to the verb **bitten** (“to ask/request”). The request is usually expressed as **jemanden um etwas bitten** (“to ask someone for something / to ask someone to do something”). Word order: *Hast du alles getan, worum ich dich gebeten habe?*
target_language_example: Danke, du hast alles getan, worum ich dich gebeten habe.
native_language_example: Thanks, you did everything I asked you to do.

additional_notes: Common, casual reassurance. Used as an exclamation (“Alles gut!” = “It’s okay!”), as a check-in question (“Alles gut?” = “You okay?”), or to say a problem is solved (“Dann ist alles gut.” = “Then everything will be fine.”). Often used to tell someone not to worry or that there’s no harm done.
target_language_example: Alles gut, ich hab’s schon erledigt.
native_language_example: All good, I’ve already taken care of it.

meaning: “everything in/into …” (used before a place/thing you mean).
additional_notes:
You use it to say that all things/people are inside something (“alles in diesem Zimmer …” = everything in this room). It’s usually followed by a noun phrase.

Grammar tip: with **in** + a place, German often uses **dative** for location (where?): *alles in diesem Zimmer*, and **accusative** for direction (where to?): *alles in die Hand nehmen*.

Common set phrase: **alles in Ordnung** = “everything is OK / in order.”
target_language_example: Alles in meiner Tasche ist nass.
native_language_example: Everything in my bag is wet.

additional_notes: Used to ask whether everything is fine or acceptable, or to reassure someone that there’s no problem. Very common in everyday speech; can be a standalone check-in (“Alles in Ordnung?”) or reassurance (“Alles in Ordnung.”).
target_language_example: Nein, es ist alles in Ordnung.
native_language_example: No, everything is all right.

additional_notes: Used to ask (or say) whether someone is fine or whether a situation is okay. Usually followed by a person in the dative: bei dir (informal), bei Ihnen (formal), bei euch, etc. Often used as a question: „Ist alles in Ordnung bei dir?“
target_language_example: Ist alles in Ordnung bei dir?
native_language_example: Is everything OK with you?

additional_notes: Used in a subordinate clause with "dass" or "ob" to check or reassure that everything is fine. Often appears with "mit + Dativ" to mean "with (someone)" = regarding someone’s situation/health: "ob mit Tom alles in Ordnung ist" = "whether Tom is OK." The full main-clause version is: "Alles ist in Ordnung."
target_language_example: Sag mir bitte, ob alles in Ordnung ist.
native_language_example: Please tell me if everything is OK.

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone/something is okay. Often used as a question: „Ist alles in Ordnung mit dir?“ (Are you okay?). You can also use it with things: „Ist alles in Ordnung mit dem Auto?“ (Is everything okay with the car?). The basic phrase is „Alles in Ordnung.“ = “Everything’s fine.”
target_language_example: Ist alles in Ordnung mit dir?
native_language_example: Is everything okay with you?

meaning: everything in the world (used for strong emphasis: “anything/everything”).
additional_notes: Often used as a strong, emotional exaggeration. Common patterns: „Mehr als alles in der Welt …“ = “more than anything in the world …” and „Ich gebe dir/Ihnen alles in der Welt dafür.“ = “I’d give anything for that.”
target_language_example: Mehr als alles in der Welt liebe ich dich.
native_language_example: I love you more than anything in the world.

additional_notes: Very common in spoken German. As a question (often with a friendly tone): “Alles klar?” = “You OK?” / “Everything clear?” As a response/confirmation: “Alles klar.” = “OK.” / “Alright.” / “Got it.” With words like “Alter”, “Mann”, “Kleiner” it sounds quite casual and can be slangy depending on context.
target_language_example: Alles klar, ich komme gleich.
native_language_example: OK, I’ll be right there.

additional_notes: Used to check if someone is fine, especially if they look worried, hurt, or something seems wrong. Often used as a short question (sometimes without “Ist”). You can also answer with “Alles ok.” (= Everything’s fine.)
target_language_example: Alles ok bei dir?
native_language_example: Everything OK with you?

additional_notes: Common, friendly check-in about how someone is doing or whether a situation is fine. Often used as a question ("Alles okay?" / "Alles okay mit dir/Ihnen?") or as reassurance ("Ja, alles okay."). Also spelled "Alles OK?". With "Ihnen" it’s formal; with "dir/deiner" it’s informal.
target_language_example: Alles okay bei dir, oder brauchst du Hilfe?
native_language_example: Everything okay with you, or do you need help?

meaning: to do everything yourself / on your own.
additional_notes: Used when someone has to handle all tasks without help. "selbst" adds emphasis: no one else helps. Often appears with modal verbs like "müssen" (had to): "Ich muss alles selbst machen."
target_language_example: Ich muss heute alles selbst machen, weil niemand Zeit hat.
native_language_example: I have to do everything myself today because nobody has time.

meaning: to do anything; to do everything.
additional_notes: Often used with an added clause to say someone will do whatever is necessary ("alles tun, um ..." = do anything in order to ...) or to express permission/ability ("alles tun dürfen/können" = be allowed/able to do anything).
target_language_example: Ich würde alles tun, um dir zu helfen.
native_language_example: I would do anything to help you.

meaning: to do everything that … / to do whatever …
additional_notes: Used with a relative clause introduced by **was** to express doing everything possible/necessary to achieve something: **Ich werde alles tun, was in meiner Macht steht** (“I’ll do everything in my power”). Often followed by an infinitive clause with **um … zu …**. Also appears in imperatives like **Lass/Lasst … alles tun, was er/sie will** (“Let … do whatever he/she wants”).
target_language_example: Ich werde alles tun, was in meiner Macht steht, um dir zu helfen.
native_language_example: I’ll do everything in my power to help you.

meaning: 'everything is under control' / 'I've got everything under control'.
additional_notes: Used to reassure someone that a situation is handled and there’s no need to worry. You can say it alone as a short statement ("Alles unter Kontrolle."), or with a subject to emphasize who is managing things ("Ich habe alles unter Kontrolle.", "Hier ist alles unter Kontrolle.").
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, ich habe alles unter Kontrolle.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ve got everything under control.

additional_notes: Used when you want to start a story or explanation at the very beginning, often with verbs like „erzählen“ (to tell) or „erklären“ (to explain): „Lass mich alles von Anfang an erzählen.“ It can also mean that something was already going wrong right from the start: „Alles ging von Anfang an schief.“
target_language_example: Wir müssen alles von Anfang an neu planen.
native_language_example: We have to plan everything again from the beginning.

meaning: 'everything is OK again' / 'all is well again'.
additional_notes: Used after a problem or difficult moment to say things have returned to normal or been resolved. Often used reassuringly. You can also say it about the future: "Alles wird wieder gut" (Everything will be OK again).
target_language_example: Keine Sorge—morgen ist alles wieder gut.
native_language_example: Don’t worry—tomorrow everything will be OK again.

additional_notes: A common reassuring phrase said to comfort someone or express optimism. Often used on its own ("Alles wird gut.") or with additions like "... sein/werden" to emphasize the future, or with conditions like "..., solange ..." ("... as long as ...").
target_language_example: Mach dir keine Sorgen—alles wird gut.
native_language_example: Don’t worry—everything will be okay.

additional_notes: Used with a noun or pronoun to say someone knows/tells/reports all details about a topic/person/thing: alles über den Plan, alles über mich. Common with verbs like wissen (to know), erzählen/berichten (to tell/report), erfahren (to find out).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir alles über die Stadt erzählen?
native_language_example: Can you tell me everything about the city?

meaning: first (the first one to do something).
additional_notes: Used to say someone (masculine singular) was the first to arrive/do something, often with verbs like kommen/ankommen/sein/überqueren/vorstellen. It answers “in what order?” and agrees in gender/case: als Erster (masc. nom.), als Erste (fem. nom.), als Erstes (neuter / “first of all”), plural: als Erste; with dative: als Erstem/Erster/Erstem, etc.
target_language_example: Tom überquerte die Ziellinie als Erster.
native_language_example: Tom crossed the finish line first.

additional_notes: Used with an ordinal after "als" to say someone does something before anyone else (order in a sequence). It changes with gender/case: als Erste (female), als Erster (male), als Erstes (neuter/"the first thing"), als Erste (plural).
target_language_example: Ich gehe als Erster rein.
native_language_example: I’ll go in first.

additional_notes: Used to say what should be done or checked first, often in instructions, plans, or investigations. It can appear at the start of a sentence ("Als Erstes musst du …") or later for emphasis ("… gehen wir immer als Erstes nach"). Similar to "zuerst" but often highlights “the very first step/priority.”
target_language_example: Als Erstes rufe ich meine Mutter an.
native_language_example: First, I’ll call my mother.

additional_notes: Used with „als“ to describe the role/function of an animal (or even something unusual) in a situation: someone keeps/chooses something „als Haustier“ (= in the role of a pet). Often used with verbs like „halten“ (to keep), „sich halten“ (to keep for oneself), „sich (etw.) erwählen“ (to choose for oneself).
target_language_example: Ich möchte eine Katze als Haustier.
native_language_example: I want a cat as a pet.

meaning: as a child; when (I/you/etc.) was a child.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that was true or happened during someone’s childhood. Often followed by a verb in the past: "Als Kind war ich …" / "Als Kind habe ich …". You can also specify whose childhood with a possessive: "als mein Kind" is wrong—say "als Kind" (me) or "als Kind" + context, or "als Kind meines Bruders" (as my brother’s child) / "als Kind von …" (as the child of …).
target_language_example: Als Kind hatte ich Angst vor Hunden.
native_language_example: As a child, I was afraid of dogs.

meaning: "When I was a child, I ..." / "As a child, I ..."
additional_notes: Used to talk about things you regularly did or that happened to you in childhood. Often followed by the past tense (e.g., Perfekt: „bin ich … gegangen/geschwommen“ or passive: „bin ich … gestochen worden“). You can also use it with other persons: „Als Kind war er …“, „Als Kind habe ich …“.
target_language_example: Als Kind bin ich jeden Samstag zu meiner Oma gefahren.
native_language_example: When I was a child, I went to my grandma’s every Saturday.

additional_notes: Used to talk about habits, likes/dislikes, or beliefs from your childhood. "Als Kind" = "as a child" (time phrase) and is often placed at the beginning of the sentence; then the verb comes second: "Als Kind habe ich …". Typically followed by a past form (Perfekt: "habe ich + Partizip II"), but you can also use Präteritum in writing.
target_language_example: Als Kind habe ich jeden Sommer bei meinen Großeltern gewohnt.
native_language_example: As a child, I used to live with my grandparents every summer.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the next thing in a sequence or plan. Very common in questions like „Was kommt als Nächstes?“ (= What’s next?) and after verbs like „kommen“, „passieren“, or „zu tun sein“: „Ich frage mich, was als Nächstes passiert.“
target_language_example: Okay, und was machen wir als Nächstes?
native_language_example: Okay, and what are we doing next?

meaning: as the only one; the only person (who).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that one person (or thing) is the only one in a group with a certain situation or quality. It often comes right after the subject: „Tom war als einziger dort.“ For other genders/numbers it changes: „als einzige“ (female), „als einziges“ (neuter), „als einzige“ (plural = the only ones).
target_language_example: Tom war als einziger dort.
native_language_example: Tom was the only one there.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is the first to do something. It changes to match the person’s gender/number/case: **als Erster** (male), **als Erste** (female), **als Erstes** (neuter/impersonal: “first of all”), **als Erste/Erste** (plural). Often followed by what happened (e.g., *als erster gehen/ankommen/gratulieren/erfahren*).
target_language_example: Ich möchte dir als Erster gratulieren.
native_language_example: I’d like to be the first to congratulate you.

additional_notes: Used to say what happens first in a sequence or priority. Often placed in the middle of the sentence (e.g., "Ich wasche mir als erstes die Hände") or at the beginning for emphasis ("Als erstes ..."). Can also be used in questions/offers to choose who goes first or what to start with ("Wer will als erstes?").
target_language_example: Als erstes machen wir die Hausaufgaben, dann schauen wir einen Film.
native_language_example: First we do the homework, then we watch a movie.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is last in a sequence (e.g., in a line, on a list, to fall asleep, to arrive/finish). It agrees with the person/thing: als letzter (masc.), als letzte (fem.), als letztes (neut.), als letzte(r) (plural). Often used with verbs like anstehen (to line up), einschlafen (to fall asleep), ankommen/ins Ziel kommen (to arrive), gehen (to leave), fertig werden (to finish).
target_language_example: Ich bin als Letzter angekommen.
native_language_example: I arrived last.

meaning: as the last one out of the (e.g., building/room).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is the last person to leave a place. It’s usually followed by a noun phrase naming the place: „als Letzter aus dem Büro/aus dem Haus …“. Adjust the gender/ending: „als Letzter“ (male), „als Letzte“ (female), „als Letztes“ (neuter/thing). Also adjust „aus dem“ depending on the noun: „aus der“ (feminine), „aus den“ (plural).
target_language_example: Ich bin gestern als Letzter aus dem Büro gegangen.
native_language_example: Yesterday I was the last one to leave the office.

additional_notes: Used to indicate the final step in a sequence or the last item in a list. Often appears in instructions or when describing the order of actions: "Erst ..., dann ..., und als Letztes ...".
target_language_example: Und als Letztes schalten wir das Licht aus.
native_language_example: And lastly, we switch off the light.

meaning: next; next up; the next thing.
additional_notes: Used to talk about what happens next in a sequence (who goes next, what you do next, what stop comes next). Often appears in questions: „Was machen wir als nächstes?“ or „Bin ich als nächstes dran?“ It refers to the next item/action/person after the current one.
target_language_example: Ich bin als nächstes dran.
native_language_example: I’m next (it’s my turn next).

meaning: to do next; what to do next.
additional_notes: Used when planning the next step in a process. Very common in questions with "Was" (e.g., "Was soll ich als nächstes tun?") and after verbs like "wissen", "entscheiden" or "sagen" (e.g., "Ich weiß nicht, was ich als nächstes tun soll.").
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht, was ich als nächstes tun soll.
native_language_example: I don't know what I should do next.

additional_notes: Used with a comparative (Komparativ) to emphasize that something is stronger/more/less now than at any time in the past: e.g., besser/schlimmer/schneller/größer als je zuvor. Similar to “mehr denn je” (“more than ever”).
target_language_example: Ich bin motivierter als je zuvor.
native_language_example: I’m more motivated than ever before.

meaning: "as well as" / part of "sowohl … als auch" = "both … and".
additional_notes: Most commonly used with "sowohl" to pair two (or more) items: "sowohl X als auch Y" = "both X and Y". It can link nouns, adjectives, or verbs (activities). Usually the same grammatical form follows on both sides (e.g., two nouns, two adjectives).
target_language_example: Wir haben sowohl Zeit als auch Lust.
native_language_example: We have both time and desire (we feel like it).

additional_notes: Used to add another item, often in the pattern "sowohl A als auch B" (= both A and B). Without "sowohl", "A als auch B" can still mean "A as well as B", but "sowohl ... als auch ..." is more common and clearer.
target_language_example: Ich spreche sowohl Deutsch als auch Englisch.
native_language_example: I speak both German and English.

additional_notes: Used after a comparative (mehr, weniger, größer, schwieriger, klüger, älter, etc.) to say something is different from what the listener expects. Formal/polite because it uses "Sie"; informal is "als du denkst" (or plural "als ihr denkt"). Often preceded by intensifiers like "viel", "weitaus", or "wahrscheinlich".
target_language_example: Es dauert länger, als Sie denken.
native_language_example: It takes longer than you think.

meaning: than anything else; more than everything else.
additional_notes: Used after comparatives (mehr, lieber, besser, schneller, wichtiger, etc.) to say something stands out above all other options. Often appears as: „mehr/lieber/besser … als alles andere“.
target_language_example: Ich mag Kaffee mehr als alles andere.
native_language_example: I like coffee more than anything else.

meaning: “when the phone rang” (at that moment in the past).
additional_notes: Uses **als** to introduce a time clause for a **single, specific event in the past**. Often used with another past action that was in progress or had just (barely) happened (e.g., **gerade**, **kaum**, **mitten**). Word order: **Als das Telefon klingelte, ...** or **..., als das Telefon klingelte.**
target_language_example: Ich war gerade eingeschlafen, als das Telefon klingelte.
native_language_example: I had just fallen asleep when the phone rang.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a subordinate clause (verb goes to the end). Common with preferences/comparisons, especially with „lieber …, als dass …“ (= “I’d rather … than …”). It’s also used after „zu“ to express that something is so much/so [adjective/adverb] that the result is impossible: „zu …, als dass …“ (= “too … for … to …”), often with Konjunktiv II in the clause (e.g., „hätte … können“).
target_language_example: Es war zu laut, als dass wir hätten schlafen können.
native_language_example: It was too loud for us to have been able to sleep.

additional_notes:
1) Time meaning: **als du + verb (at the end)** = *when you…* for a single event or time in the past. (Not used for repeated events—German usually uses **wenn** for that.)
2) Comparison meaning: **… größer/schneller … als du** = *… bigger/faster than you.* Here **als** means *than* (not *as*).
target_language_example: Als du angekommen bist, haben wir schon gegessen.
native_language_example: When you arrived, we had already eaten.

additional_notes: Used after a comparative (e.g., besser, größer, klüger, reicher) to say someone/something is more/less X than the listener expects. Often follows a comma: „…, als du denkst.“
target_language_example: Das ist schwieriger, als du denkst.
native_language_example: That is harder than you think.

additional_notes: Compositional phrase: als + er. It often means "when he" when introducing a past event or situation, and "than he" after a comparative expression such as mehr, älter, jünger, or besser. In the subordinate clause, the conjugated verb goes to the end.
target_language_example: Als er nach Hause kam, schliefen alle schon.
native_language_example: When he came home, everyone was already asleep.

additional_notes: Uses **als** to mean **“when”** for a **single event in the past** (not repeated). It introduces a subordinate clause, so the **verb goes to the end**: *… den Polizisten sah*. The clause is usually separated by a **comma** and can come first or last: *Als er … sah, …* / *…, als er … sah.* Note: **als** can look like English “as,” but here it means “when.”
target_language_example: Als er den Polizisten sah, bekam er Angst.
native_language_example: When he saw the police officer, he got scared.

additional_notes: "Als" introduces a time clause, often for a single event in the past. After "als", the verb goes to the end of the clause (e.g., "als er die Tür öffnete"). "die" is the feminine/plural form of "the" (or "those"), and it’s followed by a noun (e.g., "die Tür", "die Leute").
target_language_example: Als er die Nachricht hörte, wurde er ganz still.
native_language_example: When he heard the news, he became completely quiet.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a specific moment in the past. "als" introduces a one-time past event; "er" = he; "starb" is the simple past of "sterben" (to die). You can swap the pronoun: "als sie starb" (when she died), or use a name: "als Tom starb".
target_language_example: Er war bei seiner Mutter, als er starb.
native_language_example: He was with his mother when he died.

additional_notes: Uses **als** for a single event in the past. **es** is a dummy pronoun meaning "it" (the event/situation), and **passierte** is past tense of *passieren* (to happen). Common after statements or questions about where/with whom you were at that moment: *Ich war ..., als es passierte.* / *Warst du da, als es passierte?*
target_language_example: Ich war im Zug, als es passierte.
native_language_example: I was on the train when it happened.

additional_notes: Used in storytelling with **als** to introduce a one-time event in the past: **…, als es zu regnen begann/anfing.** The verb is usually **beginnen** (more formal) or **anfangen** (more common in speech). Word order: main clause + comma + **als** + subject (**es**) + rest of the verb at the end (**… begann/anfing**).
target_language_example: Ich wollte gerade losfahren, als es zu regnen anfing.
native_language_example: I was just about to leave when it started to rain.

meaning: "as if I had" (as though I had).
additional_notes: Used to compare to an unreal/uncertain situation. It uses Konjunktiv II ("hätte"), often after expressions like "Mir ist/war, als ..." to describe a feeling or impression (e.g., something seems as if it happened). The verb often comes at the end of the clause: "..., als hätte ich ...".
target_language_example: Mir ist, als hätte ich das schon einmal erlebt.
native_language_example: It feels as if I had experienced that before.

meaning: “as if you had …” / “like you had …” (talking to one person).
additional_notes: Used to compare reality with an imagined situation, often in a guess, impression, or exaggeration. It introduces a clause in the subjunctive (Konjunktiv II) with hättest (from haben) + past participle (e.g., verloren, genossen, gehabt). Common after expressions like du wirkst/klangst/siehst aus, mir war, als … .
target_language_example: Du siehst aus, als hättest du die ganze Nacht nicht geschlafen.
native_language_example: You look as if you hadn’t slept all night.

additional_notes: Usually introduces a subordinate clause. For a specific situation or time in the past, als ich means 'when I', and the verb goes to the end of the clause: als ich ankam. After a comparative, it means 'than I' or 'than me': besser als ich. For repeated events or future situations, German usually uses wenn instead of als.
target_language_example: Als ich gestern nach Hause kam, war niemand da.
native_language_example: When I came home yesterday, nobody was there.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a past time in your life. It often introduces a clause in the past tense (e.g., Präteritum or Perfekt) and is commonly followed by a comma: “Als ich Kind war, …”. You can also say “als ich ein Kind war” (a bit more explicit).
target_language_example: Als ich Kind war, habe ich jeden Sommer meine Großeltern besucht.
native_language_example: When I was a child, I visited my grandparents every summer.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a single event in the past: **Als ich ankam, ...** = “When I arrived, ...”. Often sets the time for what happened next. In an **als**-clause, the verb goes to the end (**ankam**). Compare: **als** (one-time past) vs **wenn** (whenever / if, repeated or general).
target_language_example: Als ich ankam, war das Konzert schon vorbei.
native_language_example: When I arrived, the concert was already over.

meaning: when I woke up (in the past).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a time clause about a single moment/event in the past. With "als" (not "wenn"), you usually talk about something that happened once (or a specific point in the past). In this subordinate clause, the verb goes to the end: "als ich aufwachte".
target_language_example: Als ich aufwachte, war es schon dunkel.
native_language_example: When I woke up, it was already dark.

meaning: "When I woke up, ..." (setting the scene for what was the case then).
additional_notes: Used to describe a situation in the past right after you woke up. "Als" introduces a past time point (“when”), and the verb comes second in the main clause, so you often get: "Als ich aufwachte, war ..." / "Als ich aufwachte, hatte ..." / "Als ich aufwachte, war er weg." You can follow it with a noun/adjective ("war ich müde"), a place ("war ich zu Hause"), or something that had happened/changed ("war mein Handy weg").
target_language_example: Als ich aufwachte, war es schon hell draußen.
native_language_example: When I woke up, it was already bright outside.

additional_notes: Used after a comparison (often with words like einfacher/schwieriger, weniger/mehr, länger/kürzer, besser/schlechter) to say reality is different from your expectation. Common pattern: "(mehr/weniger/…)-er, als ich dachte."
target_language_example: Die Reise war teurer, als ich dachte.
native_language_example: The trip was more expensive than I thought.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a time clause about a single event in the past (with **als**). The verb goes to the end of the clause: **als ich die Nachricht hörte**. Often paired with an emotional reaction in the main clause. Note: **als** can look like English “as,” but here it usually means “when” (in the past), not “as/like.”
target_language_example: Als ich die Nachricht hörte, war ich sprachlos.
native_language_example: When I heard the news, I was speechless.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a period of time in the past. It often introduces a clause with background information, and the verb in that clause goes to the end (e.g., „als ich ein Kind war“). Use „als“ (not „wenn“) for a one-time time period in the past like your childhood.
target_language_example: Als ich ein Kind war, habe ich jeden Sommer meine Großeltern besucht.
native_language_example: When I was a child, I visited my grandparents every summer.

additional_notes: Used after a comparison (often with a comparative like "besser", "einfacher", "interessanter") to say the reality is different from what you thought. Here "als" means "than" (not "as"). You’ll also often hear it as "als ich erwartet hatte" (past perfect) in the same meaning.
target_language_example: Die Prüfung war leichter, als ich erwartet habe.
native_language_example: The exam was easier than I expected.

additional_notes: Used after a comparative (mehr, weniger, besser, leichter, teurer, etc.) to compare reality with what you expected in the past. In these sentences, als means “than” (not “when”). Often paired with “(nicht) so …, wie ich erwartet hatte” (= “(not) as … as I had expected”).
target_language_example: Der Test war schwieriger, als ich erwartet hatte.
native_language_example: The test was harder than I had expected.

meaning: "when I" / "than I" + "it" (referring back to something already mentioned).
additional_notes: This is a common chunk inside a longer clause. **Als** can mean **"when"** (for a one-time past event) or **"than"** (in comparisons). **Es** usually points back to a previously mentioned thing/idea, and in comparisons it often stands for an implied verb phrase: *geduldiger, als ich es bin* = “more patient than I am (patient)”; *besser ausgedrückt, als ich es könnte* = “better expressed than I could (express it).” Word order: the verb typically comes at the end of the *als*-clause (e.g., *als ich es bemerkte / als ich es bin / als ich es könnte*).
target_language_example: Das ist schwieriger, als ich es gedacht habe.
native_language_example: That is harder than I thought.

additional_notes: Used after a comparison (often with a comparative adjective/adverb like billiger/teurer/länger) to say the reality was different from your expectation: „…, als ich gedacht hatte.“ It refers to what you previously assumed or expected.
target_language_example: Die Aufgabe war schwieriger, als ich gedacht hatte.
native_language_example: The task was harder than I had thought.

meaning: “when I … this morning” (talking about a past moment).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a time clause in the past with als (“when” for a one-time past situation). You typically add a verb at the end of the clause: als ich heute Morgen aufgewacht bin / als ich heute Morgen angerufen habe. The main clause and als-clause often describe what was happening at that time.
target_language_example: Ich war noch müde, als ich heute Morgen das Haus verlassen habe.
native_language_example: I was still tired when I left the house this morning.

meaning: "when I (… ) him" (talking about a past moment).
additional_notes: Used to start a time clause about the past. **als** is used for a single time period/event in the past (“when”), not for repeated events (then you often use **wenn**). **ich** = “I”. **ihn** is the accusative form of “he” and means “him” (the direct object). The verb usually comes at the end of the **als**-clause: *Als ich ihn sah, …*
target_language_example: Als ich ihn gestern getroffen habe, war er sehr freundlich.
native_language_example: When I met him yesterday, he was very friendly.

meaning: "when I was in …" / "when I lived in …" (introduces a time in the past).
additional_notes: Used to start a subordinate clause with **als** for a single time period/event in the past. Word order: **Als ich in + place + verb …,** then the main clause follows (often with the verb in position 2). Common with **war** (was), **wohnte/lebte** (lived). Not used for repeated situations in the past (that’s usually **wenn**).
target_language_example: Als ich in Berlin war, habe ich jeden Tag Museen besucht.
native_language_example: When I was in Berlin, I visited museums every day.

meaning: “when I was young” / “back when I was young.”
additional_notes: Used to talk about a past period in your life. It’s a time clause introduced by **als** (for a single time/period in the past), often paired with the simple past (**war**) or past tense in the main clause (**habe … gespielt**, **lebte**, **konnte**). You can put it at the start of the sentence (then the verb comes second in the main clause) or later in the sentence.
target_language_example: Als ich jung war, wollte ich Feuerwehrmann werden.
native_language_example: When I was young, I wanted to be a firefighter.

meaning: when I was little / when I was young.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened regularly or at a specific time in your childhood. It often introduces a past situation (“Als ich klein war, …”) and commonly goes with past tense verbs (Perfekt or Präteritum). Word order can vary: “Als ich klein war, …” or “…, als ich klein war.”
target_language_example: Als ich klein war, wollte ich jeden Tag ein Eis essen.
native_language_example: When I was little, I wanted to eat ice cream every day.

additional_notes: Used with **als** to talk about a **single event in the past** (“when…”). It often starts a time clause, and the verb goes to the end in that clause: **Als ich nach Hause kam, …**. In the main clause, the verb comes right after this clause: **…, bemerkte ich / sah er / lernte Tom …**.
target_language_example: Als ich nach Hause kam, war niemand da.
native_language_example: When I got home, nobody was there.

meaning: “when I still …” / “back when I still …” (talking about a past time that continued up to that point).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a time clause in the past: *als* = “when” (one-time/past period), *ich* = “I”, *noch* = “still”. It’s usually followed by a verb at the end of the clause (e.g., **als ich noch klein war** = “when I was still little”). Often used for childhood memories or earlier stages of life.
target_language_example: Als ich noch Student war, hatte ich kaum Geld.
native_language_example: When I was still a student, I hardly had any money.

als ich so alt war wie du

target_language_multi_word_term: als ich so alt war wie du
additional_notes: Used to compare the speaker’s past age with the listener’s current age. Often introduces a story, advice, or a personal memory. The tense is usually past (war, hab …).
target_language_example: Als ich so alt war wie du, wollte ich unbedingt ins Ausland ziehen.
native_language_example: When I was your age, I really wanted to move abroad.

additional_notes: Used after a comparative to say something is more/less/different than the listener expects. Very common pattern: **(viel) + comparative + als ihr denkt** (e.g., *viel besser/mehr/länger … als ihr denkt*). **ihr** addresses more than one person informally; with one person you’d use **als du denkst**, and in formal speech **als Sie denken**.
target_language_example: Das ist schwieriger, als ihr denkt.
native_language_example: That is harder than you (all) think.

additional_notes: Used after a comparative ("-er" forms like größer, besser, schöner, schneller) to compare two people/things. German uses **als** for comparisons of inequality (bigger/better/etc.), where English uses **than**—not *as*. Common pattern: **X ist (nicht) ...-er als ihre Mutter** / **X ist nicht weniger ... als ihre Mutter**.
target_language_example: Er ist schneller als ihre Mutter.
native_language_example: He is faster than her mother.

additional_notes: Used with comparatives ("-er" forms or "mehr/weniger") to emphasize that something is stronger/more intense now than at any time in the past: "schöner/stärker/mehr … als je zuvor". It can also appear as a short headline-style phrase (e.g., "Lebendiger als je zuvor.").
target_language_example: Wir sind heute besser vorbereitet als je zuvor.
native_language_example: Today we’re better prepared than ever before.

additional_notes: Used after a comparative (mehr …, größer …, besser …) to compare one thing with all others in the same group: "X ist … als jede andere Y" = X is more/bigger/better than any other Y. Agreement matters: **als jede andere** + feminine noun (z.B. *Sprache, Stadt*), **als jeder andere** + masculine noun (z.B. *Tag*), **als jedes andere** + neuter noun (z.B. *Modell, Land*), plural typically **als alle anderen** rather than *als jede anderen*. Word order: usually no comma; a comma may appear if the comparison is treated as an inserted parenthetical, but it’s not required.
target_language_example: Tōkyō ist größer als jede andere Stadt in Japan.
native_language_example: Tokyo is larger than any other city in Japan.

additional_notes: Used in comparisons with "mehr/besser/schneller … als" to say someone does something more/better/etc. than all others in a group. "jeder" = everyone/anyone; "andere" = other. It can refer to people in general or in a specific group (e.g., "hier", "in der Klasse").
target_language_example: Sie arbeitet härter als jeder andere im Team.
native_language_example: She works harder than anyone else on the team.

meaning: than anyone else; than everyone else.
additional_notes: Used with comparatives (besser, schneller, mehr, usw.) to say someone does something more/better than all others. Often followed by extra information like „den ich kenne“ (“that I know”).
target_language_example: Sie kann das schneller lösen als jeder andere in der Klasse.
native_language_example: She can solve that faster than anyone else in the class.

additional_notes: Used to compare something to an imagined situation: "..., als ob ..." (= as if ...). Often followed by Konjunktiv (e.g., "als ob er es wüsste") or sometimes indicative in everyday speech. It can also be used on its own ("Als ob!") to express disbelief or sarcasm ("Yeah, right!").
target_language_example: Er tut so, als ob er alles wüsste.
native_language_example: He acts as if he knows everything.

additional_notes: Used to compare reality with an (often unlikely) impression or hypothetical situation: "It looks/sounds as if you..." It can also be used sarcastically to express disbelief: "Yeah, as if you had a choice." The verb typically goes to the end of the clause (e.g., „als ob du es nicht mehr willst“). In more formal German you may see Konjunktiv II (e.g., „als ob du es nicht mehr wolltest“).
target_language_example: Du redest, als ob du alles besser wüsstest.
native_language_example: You talk as if you knew everything better.

additional_notes: Used to compare something to an imagined situation: “He talks as if he knew everything.” Very often followed by Konjunktiv II (subjunctive) to show it’s not (necessarily) true: wäre/wär’ (were), hätte (had), wüsste (knew). In everyday speech you may hear contractions like “wär’”.
target_language_example: Er schaut mich an, als ob er mich nicht kennen würde.
native_language_example: He looks at me as if he didn’t know me.

additional_notes: Used to compare something to a (often unreal or exaggerated) situation: *als ob es gestern gewesen wäre* (“as if it had been yesterday”). Very common with **Konjunktiv II** (*wäre, hätte, würde*) for unreal comparisons. Can also be used sarcastically/ironically to mean “yeah right”: *Als ob es die kümmert!* (“As if they care!”).
target_language_example: Er tut so, als ob es ihn nichts angehen würde.
native_language_example: He acts as if it had nothing to do with him.

additional_notes: Used to say that something seems a certain way, or that someone behaves/speaks in a way that isn’t really true. Very often followed by Konjunktiv II to show it’s unreal: „als ob ich verrückt wäre“ (not really crazy). You’ll also see it after feelings/perceptions like „Mir war, als ob …“ (“It felt as if …”).
target_language_example: Er tut so, als ob ich ihn beleidigt hätte.
native_language_example: He acts as if I had insulted him.

additional_notes: Used to compare reality with an appearance, impression, or imagined situation. It’s often followed by Konjunktiv II (e.g., wäre/hätte) to show something is not real or is just assumed: "als ob sie reich wäre" = as if she were rich. In speech you may also hear "als wenn sie" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Er tut so, als ob sie ihn nicht kennen würde.
native_language_example: He acts as if she didn’t know him.

additional_notes: Used after a comparative (mehr, weniger, besser, größer, etc.) to compare two people/things. In German, **als** = “than” in comparisons (not “as”). The noun phrase can change: *als seine Schwester / als ihre Eltern* etc.
target_language_example: Sie ist größer als sein Bruder.
native_language_example: She is taller than his brother.

additional_notes: Lowercase sie can mean 'she' or 'they', so the exact meaning depends on context. With als, it commonly means 'when she/they' for a specific past event, or 'than she/her/them' after a comparison. In German, als is used for one-time events in the past; beginners often confuse this with wenn. In phrases like 'als sie auszuführen', sie can refer back to a plural noun, so English may translate it as 'them'.
target_language_example: Ich war froh, als sie endlich ankam.
native_language_example: I was glad when she finally arrived.

additional_notes: Used at the beginning of a time clause with **als** (= when, for a single event in the past). **Sie** = she/they (here: she). **Die** is the definite article (often feminine singular or plural), introducing the noun that comes next. In an **als**-clause, German typically sends the conjugated verb to the end: *Als sie die Nachricht hörte, …*
target_language_example: Als sie die Tür öffnete, war niemand da.
native_language_example: When she opened the door, nobody was there.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a past event (often a one-time event) with **als** (“when” for past situations). The verb goes to the end of the **als**-clause: **als sie die Nachricht hörte**. Often sets the scene for an emotional reaction in the main clause.
target_language_example: Als sie die Nachricht hörte, konnte sie zuerst nichts sagen.
native_language_example: When she heard the news, she couldn’t say anything at first.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a past time in someone’s life (here: a woman). With **als** you usually refer to a specific time period or one-time situation in the past. You can swap **sie** for another subject: **als ich/j er/wir jung war(en)** (“when I/he/we were young”).
target_language_example: Als sie jung war, hat sie in Berlin gelebt.
native_language_example: When she was young, she lived in Berlin.

additional_notes: Used with **als** to talk about a one-time period or situation in the past. Often appears in comparisons ("… schneller, als sie noch jung war") or to describe something that happened back then ("… als sie noch jung waren"). You’ll usually need the verb in the clause (e.g., **war/gewesen ist**).
target_language_example: Als sie noch jung war, ist sie jeden Tag schwimmen gegangen.
native_language_example: When she was still young, she went swimming every day.

additional_notes: Used after a comparative ("-er" forms or "mehr/weniger") to compare something to what is normal or typical: "länger als sonst", "voller als sonst", "später als sonst". You can also hear "nicht mehr als sonst (auch)" = "no more than usual".
target_language_example: Heute bin ich früher als sonst aufgestanden.
native_language_example: Today I got up earlier than usual.

meaning: "when we" (typically for a one-time event in the past).
additional_notes: Used to start a time clause about something that happened once in the past (Als wir ankamen, …). In the clause with "als", the verb goes to the end: "als wir angekommen sind" / "als wir ankamen". For repeated events or present/future, German usually uses "wenn" instead.
target_language_example: Als wir nach Hause kamen, war niemand da.
native_language_example: When we got home, nobody was there.

additional_notes: Used after a comparative (länger, näher, schlimmer, ernster, reicher, etc.) to say reality is different from what you expected. Pattern: [comparative] + als wir dachten. In everyday speech you can also say: „als gedacht“ (“than expected”).
target_language_example: Der Weg war kürzer, als wir dachten.
native_language_example: The route was shorter than we thought.

additional_notes: Used with **als** to introduce a **one-time event in the past** (“when”). The clause is a **subordinate clause**, so the verb goes to the end: *als wir dort an**kamen***. Often used to set the time for another past action (e.g., something had already happened). Contrast: **wenn** = “when/if” for repeated events or general situations.
target_language_example: Als wir dort ankamen, war das Konzert schon angefangen.
native_language_example: When we arrived there, the concert had already started.

additional_notes: Used to start a time clause in the past: **als** = “when (at that time)”. **wir** = “we”. **uns** is a reflexive pronoun that often means “each other” with plural subjects (e.g., **als wir uns kennenlernten** = “when we met / got to know each other”, **als wir uns den Film angesehen haben** = “when we watched the movie”). The verb usually comes at the end of the clause after **als wir uns …**.
target_language_example: Als wir uns das erste Mal trafen, waren wir beide nervös.
native_language_example: When we met for the first time, we were both nervous.

additional_notes: Used to compare something to an unreal or hypothetical situation: “(just) as if …”. It typically introduces a clause in the subjunctive (Konjunktiv II), most often with forms of sein: wäre (would be/weren’t). Common patterns: „als wäre nichts gewesen“ = “as if nothing had happened”; „als wäre ich …“ = “as if I were …”.
target_language_example: Er tut so, als wäre alles in Ordnung.
native_language_example: He acts as if everything is fine.

additional_notes: Used to make an unreal/imaginary comparison (often implying it’s not true). It uses Konjunktiv II (wäre = subjunctive of „sein“) and typically comes after a comma: „…, als wäre er …“ You can replace „er“ with other subjects: „als wäre ich/du/sie/wir/ihr/sie“.
target_language_example: Sie redet mit mir, als wäre er nicht im Raum.
native_language_example: She talks to me as if he weren’t in the room.

meaning: “as if it were/was” (as though it were).
additional_notes: Used to describe something that seems unreal, hypothetical, or only appears true. Very common in comparisons and impressions (e.g., “It feels as if…”). The verb is in Konjunktiv II (subjunctive), so you’ll often see it with time words like „gestern“ or „erst“ to mean “as if it were only yesterday.”
target_language_example: Er tut so, als wäre es ganz einfach.
native_language_example: He acts as if it were really easy.

additional_notes: Used to describe how something seems or how someone is treated, not as a real fact. It uses Konjunktiv II (wäre) after als (often also als ob) to show that the situation is hypothetical or contrary to reality: "Sie behandelt mich, als wäre ich ..." = "She treats me as if I were ...".
target_language_example: Er schaut mich an, als wäre ich verrückt.
native_language_example: He looks at me as if I were crazy.

additional_notes: Used to describe an unreal or hypothetical comparison. It uses Konjunktiv II of "sein" ("wäre") and refers to a female subject ("sie" = she). Often comes after a main clause: "Er tut so, als wäre sie nicht da."
target_language_example: Er redet mit ihr, als wäre sie seine beste Freundin.
native_language_example: He talks to her as if she were his best friend.

meaning: as if / as though (introduces an unreal or imagined comparison).
additional_notes:
Used to start a comparison that feels unreal, hypothetical, or only seems true. It’s typically followed by Konjunktiv II: 
- als würde + infinitive (e.g., „als würde sie schlafen“ = as if she were sleeping)
Often equivalent to „als ob“ or „als wenn“. In the past you may also see „als hätte/als wäre …“.
target_language_example: Er redet, als würde er alles besser wissen.
native_language_example: He talks as if he knows everything better.

meaning: 'as if he would' / 'as if he were' (as if he were doing something).
additional_notes: Used to describe an appearance, impression, or pretense: something seems or is acted out as if he were doing something. Common after verbs like „scheinen“ (to seem) and in expressions like „so tun, als würde er …“ (to pretend as if he …). The verb after „würde“ goes at the end: „als würde er mich nicht kennen“.
target_language_example: Sie schaut mich an, als würde er ihr etwas bedeuten.
native_language_example: She looks at me as if he meant something to her.

meaning: "as if you (were/did)" (suggesting something isn’t really true).
additional_notes: Used to introduce an unreal comparison or to say someone is acting/behaving in a way that suggests something. It uses Konjunktiv II with würde + infinitive (e.g., „als würdest du ihn kennen“ = as if you knew him). Often interchangeable with „als ob du …“ or „als wenn du …“. Frequently used with phrases like „Tu nicht so, als würdest du …“ (Don’t act as if you …).
target_language_example: Er tut so, als würdest du ihn stören.
native_language_example: He acts as if you were bothering him.

meaning: "Well, I…" (a spoken filler to start or soften what you’re about to say).
additional_notes: Common in conversation when beginning an explanation, confession, or uncertain statement. It often signals hesitation, a transition, or that you’re organizing your thoughts. Not the same as English “also” (= “too/as well”); German “also” can mean “so/well/anyway” depending on context.
target_language_example: Also, ich bin mir nicht sicher, ob das stimmt.
native_language_example: Well, I’m not sure if that’s true.

additional_notes: Used to open a question, often to move the conversation along or get to the point. Depending on tone, it can sound neutral (“So, what are we doing?”) or a bit impatient/expecting an explanation (“So, what’s this all about?”). Note: German „also“ usually means “so/well/therefore,” not English “also.”
target_language_example: Also, was machen wir jetzt?
native_language_example: So, what are we doing now?

meaning: "all right then" / "okay, fine" (accepting a plan or moving on).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence as a conversational marker to signal a decision, agreement, or reluctant acceptance, often followed by "dann" (then). It can also introduce a conclusion or lesson ("Also gut, was lernen wir daraus?").
target_language_example: Also gut, dann machen wir das so.
native_language_example: All right then, we'll do it like that.

additional_notes: Usually you say this with „wie“: „Wie alt bist du?“. On its own („Alt bist du?“) it can sound incomplete or like a surprised/echo question, depending on context and intonation.
target_language_example: Wie alt bist du?
native_language_example: How old are you?

additional_notes: Used to say someone has reached the required age for something. Common patterns: **alt genug + für + noun** ("old enough for school/the tournament") and **alt genug + zu + infinitive** ("old enough to drink"). Often appears with **noch nicht**: "noch nicht alt genug" ("not old enough yet").
target_language_example: Bist du schon alt genug, um allein zu reisen?
native_language_example: Are you old enough to travel alone?

meaning: "old enough to" (to be old enough to do something).
additional_notes: Used to say someone has reached the age/maturity needed to do something. It’s followed by an infinitive clause with „zu“: „alt genug, um + zu + Verb“ (e.g., „alt genug, um allein zu reisen“).
target_language_example: Bist du alt genug, um Auto zu fahren?
native_language_example: Are you old enough to drive a car?

additional_notes: "alt" is an adjective meaning “old.” With "sein" (to be), you say someone/something “is old”: "Er/Sie/Es ist alt." The sequence "alt ist" often appears in subordinate clauses because the verb goes to the end: "..., dass er alt ist." You can also specify an age: "fünf Jahre alt" = “five years old,” "wenige Monate alt" = “a few months old.” Often used in comparisons: "so alt wie" / "genauso alt wie" = “(just) as old as."
target_language_example: Ich denke, dass Tom alt ist.
native_language_example: I think that Tom is old.

meaning: "… old is your …" (used in questions to ask someone’s age).
additional_notes: Usually appears in the full question pattern: **Wie alt ist dein/deine/dein…?** = “How old is your …?” **dein** is informal “your” for one person you’re on *du* terms with, and it changes with gender/case (e.g., *dein Bruder*, *deine Schwester*).
target_language_example: Wie alt ist dein Bruder?
native_language_example: How old is your brother?

meaning: “was … years/months old” (talking about someone’s age in the past).
additional_notes: Used in time clauses with **als** to mean “when I/he/she was … old.” The age phrase often comes before **alt**: **fünf Jahre alt**, **drei Monate alt**. Common pattern: **Als ich/er/sie … Jahre alt war, …**
target_language_example: Als sie zehn Jahre alt war, hat sie Klavier gelernt.
native_language_example: When she was ten years old, she learned piano.

meaning: to grow old; to get old.
additional_notes: Literally “to become old.” Used to talk about aging in general or about wanting to spend your life with someone (“Mit dir möchte ich alt werden” = “I want to grow old with you”). Often appears with adverbs/phrases like „in Würde“ (with dignity).
target_language_example: Ich will gesund alt werden.
native_language_example: I want to grow old in good health.

additional_notes: Used in comparisons to say two people/things have the same age. Very commonly appears with a modifier like **so** or **genauso**: **so alt wie … / genauso alt wie …**. It needs something after it (e.g., a person/thing): **alt wie du**, **alt wie mein Bruder**.
target_language_example: Ich bin genauso alt wie du.
native_language_example: I’m the same age as you.

additional_notes: Used to compare ages: something/someone is the same age as the person you’re speaking to. Often part of a longer sentence (e.g., „Ich bin (genau) so alt wie du.“). Depending on tone, it can sound teasing or rude if used to call someone old.
target_language_example: Ich bin genauso alt wie du.
native_language_example: I’m the same age as you.

meaning: as old as me / as old as I am.
additional_notes: Used to compare ages with the pattern **so + adjective + wie** (e.g., **so alt wie ich** = “as old as me”). Often appears with **sein**: **Er ist (so) alt wie ich.** You can swap **ich** for other pronouns: **alt wie du/er/sie/wir/ihr**.
target_language_example: Meine Schwester ist so alt wie ich.
native_language_example: My sister is as old as me.

additional_notes: Literally means an older woman (alte + Dame). Often a neutral/polite way to refer to an elderly woman (commonly with an article: „die alte Dame“). Can also be used as a form of address („Das wird schon, alte Dame.“), which may sound teasing or affectionate depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Ich ging zur Seite, um die alte Dame vorbei zu lassen.
native_language_example: I stepped aside to let the old lady pass.

additional_notes: Used to describe a female person who is old/elderly. It can sound blunt or disrespectful in some situations, especially when talking directly about someone; polite alternatives include "eine ältere Frau" (an older woman) or "eine Seniorin" (a senior woman).
target_language_example: Eine alte Frau sitzt auf der Bank und liest.
native_language_example: An old woman is sitting on the bench and reading.

additional_notes: Plural of „das Gebäude“ (building) with the adjective „alt“ (old). Often used for historic or traditional buildings in cities. In German, adjective endings change with the article/case: e.g., „viele alte Gebäude“ (many old buildings), „die alten Gebäude“ (the old buildings). Singular: „das alte Gebäude“.
target_language_example: In der Altstadt stehen viele alte Gebäude.
native_language_example: There are many old buildings in the old town (historic city center).

additional_notes: This is an inflected form of **alte Dame** (“old lady”). You often see it with articles/cases, e.g. **einer alten Dame** (dative: “to/for an old lady”) or **der alten Dame** (“to/for the old lady”). It’s a polite/neutral way to refer to an elderly woman.
target_language_example: Ich habe einer alten Dame die Tür aufgehalten.
native_language_example: I held the door open for an old lady.
