native_language_example: No matter when you go to him, he’s always sitting at his desk.

meaning: on/at his …; in some phrases also “from/of his …” (e.g., dying from injuries).
additional_notes: “an” + “seinen” is usually “on/at his” with a following noun (often plural: an seinen Türen/Nägeln/Wunden = on/at his doors/nails/wounds). With certain verbs—especially health-related ones like “an … sterben/versterben”—“an” means “from” (cause): “an seinen Verletzungen” = from his injuries.
target_language_example: Die Bilder hängen an seinen Wänden.
native_language_example: The pictures are hanging on his walls.

meaning: in his place; if you were him.
additional_notes: Used to express what someone would do in another person’s situation (often in hypotheticals, frequently with Konjunktiv II): „Was hättest du an seiner Stelle getan?“ You can swap the possessive pronoun depending on whose situation you mean: an meiner/deiner/ihrer/unserer/eurer Stelle = in my/your/her/our/your (pl.) place.
target_language_example: Was hättest du an seiner Stelle getan?
native_language_example: What would you have done in his place?

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens or exists at your school. Here, "an" means "at" (location/association), and "unserer Schule" is dative feminine ("die Schule" → "unserer Schule"). Common with institutions like schools/universities: "an der Schule", "an unserer Schule".
target_language_example: An unserer Schule gibt es eine große Bibliothek.
native_language_example: At our school there is a big library.

additional_notes: Used when a verb or situation requires the preposition "an" before a person. Very common with verbs like "sich erinnern an" (to remember) and "schicken an" (to send to). With "erinnern an" it takes the accusative: "An wen erinnerst du dich?"
target_language_example: An wen soll ich die E-Mail schicken?
native_language_example: Who should I send the email to?

meaning: “Anna!” (calling someone named Anna; to get their attention).
additional_notes: Used as a direct form of address (a name), often with emphasis or drawn out (“An-na!”) when calling out to someone or reacting emotionally. In writing, the hyphen can show the syllables being stressed.
target_language_example: An-na, komm bitte her!
native_language_example: Anna, please come here!

additional_notes: This isn’t a fixed phrase. **an** is a separable verb prefix/particle (e.g. *anlächeln* = “to smile at”, *ansehen* = “to look at”, *sich anfreunden* = “to become friends (with)”). In the main clause, **an** often moves to the end: *Er lächelte mich **an***. Then you can add a time clause with **als** (“when” for a single moment/period in the past), separated by a comma: *Er lächelte mich an, **als** ich hereinkam.*
target_language_example: Sie sah ihn an, als er ihren Namen sagte.
native_language_example: She looked at him when he said her name.

meaning: ..., when he ... (talking about a specific past time).
additional_notes: This pattern often appears with separable-prefix verbs that end in **an** (e.g. **anrufen**, **anfangen**, **anlächeln**, **sich anfreunden**): the **an** moves to the end of the clause, then a comma introduces a time clause with **als er**. **Als er** is used for a single event/time in the past (= “when he ...”), not for repeated events (use **wenn er** for that). Note: **als** looks like English “as”, but here it usually means “when”.
target_language_example: Ich fing an, als er ankam.
native_language_example: I started when he arrived.

meaning: Used with certain verbs to introduce a 'that…' clause (e.g., "Ich nehme an, dass…" = "I assume that…").
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself. It’s the pattern you see when a separable-prefix verb with **an-** is split: the verb stem stays in position 2 and **an** goes to the end of the clause, right before a comma + **dass**-clause. Common ones: **annehmen, dass…** (to assume/think that), **jdm etw. ansehen, dass…** (to be able to tell/see from someone that), **damit angeben, dass…** (to brag that). The comma before **dass** is required.
target_language_example: Ich nehme an, dass wir morgen früher losfahren.
native_language_example: I assume that we’ll leave earlier tomorrow.

meaning: “to start/begin (to do something),” especially in the pattern **anfangen …, sich … zu …** (“to start to [do something reflexive]”).
additional_notes: Common with the separable verb **anfangen**: **(jemand) fängt/fing an, sich … zu …**. In main clauses, **an** splits off and moves to the end of the verb phrase: *Er fängt an … / Er fing an …*; perfect: *hat angefangen*. Typically followed by a reflexive infinitive phrase with **sich** (e.g., *sich interessieren*, *sich lustig machen*, *sich küssen*).
target_language_example: Als ich Deutsch hörte, fing ich an, sich für die Sprache zu interessieren.
native_language_example: When I heard German, I started to become interested in the language.

additional_notes: Reflexive verb phrase: „anfangen“ + „sich langweilen“. Commonly used with time expressions (e.g., „nach ein paar Minuten“, „nach einer Viertelstunde“) to say boredom begins after some time. In the past tense you’ll often see „fing … an“; in the present tense „fängt … an“.
target_language_example: Maria fing nach ein paar Minuten an, sich zu langweilen.
native_language_example: Maria started getting bored after a few minutes.

additional_notes: Most often seen as the pattern **anrufen / bei … anrufen, um … zu + infinitive** to say why you’re calling or contacting someone. **um … zu** expresses purpose (“in order to”). The comma is standard: *Er rief an, um …*
target_language_example: Ich rufe bei der Praxis an, um einen Termin zu vereinbaren.
native_language_example: I’m calling the doctor’s office to make an appointment.

meaning: Used with separable verbs like „anrufen/anfangen“ to mean “(do X) when … / if …”.
additional_notes: In many common verbs, **an-** is a separable prefix (e.g., **anrufen** = to call, **anfangen** = to start). In main clauses, **an** moves to the end: **Ruf mich an. / Wir fangen an.** A **wenn**-clause (“when/if”) adds the condition or time: **Ruf mich an, wenn …** (“Call me when/if …”). If the **wenn**-clause comes first, the main clause verb comes second: **Wenn Bob kommt, fangen wir an.**
target_language_example: Ruf mich an, wenn du Zeit hast.
native_language_example: Call me when you have time.

additional_notes: Common with the separable verb **anrufen** (“to call”). In main clauses, the prefix **an** goes to the end: **Ruf mich an.** The **wenn du…** clause (“when you…”) often comes after it: **Ruf mich an, wenn du zu Hause bist.** If the **wenn** clause comes first, word order flips in the main clause: **Wenn du zu Hause bist, ruf mich an.**
target_language_example: Ruf mich an, wenn du Zeit hast.
native_language_example: Call me when you have time.

meaning: Used when a separable verb with the prefix **an-** is split: the **an** goes to the end, often right before **und** (“and”).
additional_notes: In German main clauses, many verbs with **an-** are *separable*: the main verb stays in position 2 and the prefix **an** moves to the end. When you add another action with **und**, the **an** often appears immediately before **und**: **Ich rufe Tom an und erzähle …** (= *I call Tom and tell …*). Common verbs: **anrufen** (rufen … an = to call), **ankommen** (kommen … an = to arrive), **anziehen** (ziehen … an = to put on), **anlegen** (legen … an = to put on/put on equipment). In subordinate clauses, it usually stays together: **…, weil ich Tom anrufe.**
target_language_example: Ich mache das Licht an und lese noch ein bisschen.
native_language_example: I turn on the light and read a little more.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **anfangen** to say someone starts doing an action: **anfangen + zu + infinitive**. Because **anfangen** is separable, **an** often goes to the end: *Ich fange an zu laufen.* In 3rd person singular: *er/sie/es fängt an zu …*. (In everyday speech, **zu** is sometimes dropped: *Ich fange an zu lernen* / *Ich fange an, lerne…*).
target_language_example: Wir fangen an zu kochen, sobald die Gäste da sind.
native_language_example: We start cooking as soon as the guests are here.

meaning: to start laughing; to begin to laugh.
additional_notes: Usually used with the verb "anfangen" (to start): "anfangen, + zu + infinitive". In the present/past, the separable prefix "an" goes to the end: "Ich fange ... an, zu lachen." / "Ich fing ... an, zu lachen." In perfect tense: "Ich habe angefangen zu lachen."
target_language_example: Als er den Witz erzählte, fing ich an zu lachen.
native_language_example: When he told the joke, I started laughing.

additional_notes: Usually used with an impersonal "es" and often with "anfangen": "Es fängt an zu regnen." In everyday speech, you’ll also hear the shorter version: "Es fängt an zu regnen" / "Es fängt an zu regnen."
target_language_example: Es fängt an zu regnen, nimm einen Regenschirm mit.
native_language_example: It’s starting to rain—take an umbrella with you.

meaning: to start screaming / to begin to scream.
additional_notes: Usually used with the verb **anfangen**: **anfangen zu schreien** (“to start to scream”). In the past tense you often see the separable verb split: **Er fing an zu schreien** (“He started screaming”). You can add an adverb like **lauthals** (“at the top of one’s lungs”).
target_language_example: Als er das hörte, fing er an zu schreien.
native_language_example: When he heard that, he started screaming.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like „anfangen“/„beginnen“: „anfangen + an zu + infinitive“ (e.g., „Er fing an zu weinen.“). In modern German you’ll also often hear „anfangen zu weinen“ without the extra „an“.
target_language_example: Als sie die Nachricht hörte, fing sie an zu weinen.
native_language_example: When she heard the news, she started to cry.

additional_notes: Most often used in phrases like „keine andere Wahl“ (“no other choice”) or „Ich habe keine andere Wahl, als …“ (“I have no choice but to …”). „Wahl“ can mean “choice” as well as “election,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Ich habe keine andere Wahl, als heute zu Hause zu bleiben.
native_language_example: I have no choice but to stay at home today.

additional_notes: Used with the adjective "anders" (other/different) + "Mädchen" (girl). The form "anderen" is a declined ending (here: dative). It often appears after prepositions like "mit" (with) or after certain verbs. "Mädchen" is grammatically neuter (das Mädchen), and its singular and plural form are the same; context shows whether it means one girl or multiple girls.
target_language_example: Er hat mit einem anderen Mädchen getanzt.
native_language_example: He danced with another girl.

additional_notes: Usually used with a preposition like auf (on) and often with an indefinite article and adjective ending: auf anderen Planeten (on other planets) or auf einem anderen Planeten (on another planet). Also common in comparisons: wie auf einem anderen Planeten (“like on another planet”) to say a place feels alien/strange.
target_language_example: Auf anderen Planeten könnten ganz andere Bedingungen herrschen.
native_language_example: On other planets, completely different conditions could prevail.

additional_notes: Usually used with a preposition: **auf der anderen Seite** (= on the other side), **von der anderen Seite** (= from the other side), **zur anderen Seite** (= to the other side). It can mean a physical side (of a room, street, etc.) or a figurative side/aspect of a person: **jemanden von einer anderen Seite kennenlernen** (= to get to know someone in a different way).
target_language_example: Auf der anderen Seite der Straße ist ein Café.
native_language_example: There’s a café on the other side of the street.

additional_notes: Used with a following noun in the genitive case (des + masculine/neuter noun): „… der anderen Seite des Flusses / des Parks“. Very often appears in the full phrase „auf der anderen Seite des …“ (“on the other side of the …”).
target_language_example: Das Café ist auf der anderen Seite des Parks.
native_language_example: The café is on the other side of the park.

meaning: the other side of the river.
additional_notes: Usually used with a preposition like **auf** or **an**: **auf der anderen Seite des Flusses** = “on the other side of the river.” Often you also need the article **der**: **der anderen Seite** (dative). **des Flusses** is genitive (“of the river”).
target_language_example: Auf der anderen Seite des Flusses ist ein kleiner Park.
native_language_example: On the other side of the river there is a small park.

meaning: the other side of the street.
additional_notes: Usually used with a preposition, especially: **auf der anderen Straßenseite** = “on the other side of the street.” You’ll also hear **zur anderen Straßenseite** (“to the other side of the street,” e.g., when crossing). The article and adjective ending change with the case (der anderen … in dative; die andere … in accusative).
target_language_example: Die Bank ist auf der anderen Straßenseite.
native_language_example: The bank is on the other side of the street.

meaning: of a different kind/type; different in nature.
additional_notes: Used with a noun (often after it) to say something is a different kind from what was expected or previously mentioned: e.g., „Probleme anderer Art“ = “problems of a different kind.” Note: „Art“ here means “kind/type,” not “art” (painting, music, etc.).
target_language_example: Wir brauchen Hilfe anderer Art.
native_language_example: We need a different kind of help.

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb "sein": "anderer Meinung sein" = to think differently / not share the same opinion. Common patterns: "Ich bin (da) anderer Meinung." (I disagree.), "Ich bin anderer Meinung als du." (I have a different opinion than you.), "Zu diesem Thema bin ich anderer Meinung." (On this topic, I disagree.).
target_language_example: Ich bin da anderer Meinung – ich finde, das ist keine gute Idee.
native_language_example: I disagree—I don't think that's a good idea.

meaning: to have a different opinion; to disagree.
additional_notes: Used to express that someone’s view differs from someone else’s. Commonly used with „als + Person“: „Ich bin anderer Meinung als du.“ Neutral to slightly formal; colloquial alternatives include „Ich sehe das anders“ or „Da bin ich anderer Meinung.“
target_language_example: Ich bin anderer Meinung sein als du, aber ich verstehe deinen Punkt.
native_language_example: I disagree with you, but I understand your point.

meaning: the other shore/bank (of a river or lake).
additional_notes: Often used with a preposition and inflected: ans andere Ufer (to the other bank), am anderen Ufer (on the other bank). Note: It can also appear in the dated euphemism vom anderen Ufer sein (“to be gay/lesbian”); this can sound old-fashioned or awkward today.
target_language_example: Wir rudern ans anderes Ufer.
native_language_example: We’re rowing to the other bank.

additional_notes: Used to compare or exclude: "X ist (et)was anderes als Y" = X is different from Y. In questions/negatives it often means "anything other than": "nichts anderes als" = nothing other than; "was anderes als" = something/anything other than. Word order: "etwas anderes als + noun/pronoun"; with verbs it can be split: "Kannst du noch was anderes als Nein sagen?"
target_language_example: Ich möchte heute etwas anderes als Pizza essen.
native_language_example: I want to eat something other than pizza today.

additional_notes: Used to compare two people or things and say they are not the same. It’s often followed by a noun or pronoun in the dative case (e.g., anders als mir/dir/ihm), and it commonly comes after an adjective phrase: „Er ist anders als …“.
target_language_example: Dieses Jahr ist anders als letztes Jahr.
native_language_example: This year is different from last year.

additional_notes: Used to compare two people/things and say they are not the same. Often follows a description of how something is done/seen ("anders") and then names what it’s compared to ("als" + noun/pronoun): "anders als Männer" (differently than men), "anders als diese" (different from these).
target_language_example: Das ist anders als gestern.
native_language_example: That’s different from yesterday.

meaning: to change your mind; to reconsider.
additional_notes: Usually used as the reflexive phrase **es sich anders überlegen** (e.g., *ich überlege es mir anders*, *du überlegst es dir anders*, *wir überlegen es uns anders*). It often comes with **noch/immer noch** to mean “you can still change your mind.”
target_language_example: Wenn du möchtest, kannst du es dir bis morgen noch anders überlegen.
native_language_example: If you want, you can still change your mind by tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with the fixed reflexive phrase **es sich anders überlegen** = “to change one’s mind / decide differently.” The **sich** changes with the person: **ich überlege es mir anders**, **du überlegst es dir anders**, **er/sie überlegt es sich anders**, **wir überlegen es uns anders**, **ihr überlegt es euch anders**, **Sie überlegen es sich anders**. Often appears with **wieder** (“again”) or **plötzlich** (“suddenly”).
target_language_example: Ich habe es mir anders überlegt und komme doch mit.
native_language_example: I changed my mind and I’m coming along after all.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "anfangen" (= to start/begin) + a comma + an infinitive phrase ("... zu lernen" = to learn). Very common pattern: "anfangen, etwas zu tun" (to start doing something). Often said in the past with "haben" ("Ich habe angefangen, ...").
target_language_example: Ich habe letztes Jahr angefangen, Französisch zu lernen.
native_language_example: I started learning French last year.

additional_notes: Past form of the phrase "angeln gehen" (“to go fishing”). In the Perfekt, German uses **sein**: "Ich bin angeln gegangen" / "Wir sind angeln gegangen". Often used with time words like "letztes Wochenende" and with "nicht" to say you didn’t go: "Wir sind nicht angeln gegangen."
target_language_example: Wir sind gestern früh angeln gegangen.
native_language_example: We went fishing early yesterday.

additional_notes: Common past-time sequence to show that by the time someone arrived, another state/situation was already true. Typically used with **als** (= when, for one-time past events). **ankam** is Präteritum of *ankommen* (to arrive), and **war** is Präteritum of *sein* (to be). Frequently paired with **schon/bereits** (= already). Pattern: **Als** + (subject) + … + **ankam**, **war** + …
target_language_example: Als ich am Bahnhof ankam, war der Zug schon abgefahren.
native_language_example: When I arrived at the train station, the train had already left.

meaning: to come to light; to be revealed.
additional_notes: Used when hidden information (often the truth, facts, or a secret) becomes known or is uncovered. Common with nouns like "die Wahrheit" (the truth) and in contexts like investigations, journalism, or court ("Vor Gericht wird noch mehr ans Licht kommen").
target_language_example: Früher oder später wird die Wahrheit ans Licht kommen.
native_language_example: Sooner or later, the truth will come to light.

meaning: to the sea; to the seaside.
additional_notes: "Ans" = "an das" (to/at the) and is used with neuter nouns like "das Meer". It usually describes going to the sea/seaside (a destination): "Ich fahre ans Meer." For being already there, you often use "am Meer" ("at the sea").
target_language_example: Wir fahren am Wochenende ans Meer.
native_language_example: We’re going to the seaside this weekend.

meaning: to the phone; to answer/pick up the phone.
additional_notes: Used especially with verbs like „gehen/kommen“ to mean you go to the phone and answer it. „ans“ is a contraction of „an das“ (accusative, movement toward something): „ans Telefon gehen“ = to go to the phone / to pick up the phone.
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte ans Telefon gehen?
native_language_example: Can you please answer the phone?

meaning: to answer the phone; to go to the phone.
additional_notes: Used when the phone is ringing and you pick up/answer it. Very common with "müssen/sollen/können" (Ich muss/soll/kann ans Telefon gehen). "ans" = "an das" (to the).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte ans Telefon gehen?
native_language_example: Can you please answer the phone?

meaning: to go to the phone (often: to answer/pick up the phone).
additional_notes: Used when someone stops what they’re doing in order to respond to a ringing phone. "ans" is a contraction of "an das" (= to the). In everyday English you’ll often translate it as "to answer the phone" or "to pick up the phone," even though the German wording is literally "to go to the phone."
target_language_example: Er unterbrach seine Arbeit, um ans Telefon zu gehen.
native_language_example: He interrupted his work to answer the phone.

additional_notes: Imperative form of „antworten“ (to answer) addressed to one person („du“). „mir“ is dative = “to me.” Often sounds demanding or impatient; in polite situations you’d say „Antworten Sie mir“ or „Bitte antworten Sie mir.“
target_language_example: Antworte mir bitte, wenn du Zeit hast.
native_language_example: Please answer me when you have time.

meaning: to work in order to (do something)
additional_notes: Used with an "um ... zu" infinitive clause to express purpose: "arbeiten, um ... zu ..." = "work (so as) to ...". The "zu" goes right before the second verb at the end of the clause (e.g., "um Geld zu verdienen").
target_language_example: Wir arbeiten, um Geld zu verdienen.
native_language_example: We work to earn money.

additional_notes: Used with **Sie** (capital S) to speak politely to one person or to address people formally. Often appears in questions like **Arbeiten Sie hier?** (“Do you work here?”) or with details: **Wo/Für wen/Wie viele Stunden arbeiten Sie?**.
target_language_example: Arbeiten Sie heute im Büro oder zu Hause?
native_language_example: Are you working in the office today or at home?

meaning: to go to work; to go and work.
additional_notes: Uses "gehen" + infinitive to express going somewhere in order to do an activity. Very common for everyday routines (similar patterns: "einkaufen gehen" = go shopping, "schwimmen gehen" = go swimming). Often used with a time word: "morgens/gleich/heute arbeiten gehen".
target_language_example: Ich muss morgen früh arbeiten gehen.
native_language_example: I have to go to work tomorrow morning.

meaning: "do you work" (asking someone about their job/work).
additional_notes: This is the verb-first word order used for yes/no questions: **Arbeitest du ...?** = “Do you work ...?” / “Are you working ...?”. **du** is the informal "you" (used with friends, family, classmates); with **Sie** it becomes **Arbeiten Sie ...?**.
target_language_example: Arbeitest du heute?
native_language_example: Are you working today?

additional_notes: Used to say someone’s profession/role: [Person] arbeitet als + job title (often feminine/masculine forms, e.g., Übersetzerin/Übersetzer). You can add where they work afterwards (e.g., in einem Büro).
target_language_example: Mein Bruder arbeitet als Lehrer in Berlin.
native_language_example: My brother works as a teacher in Berlin.

additional_notes: Use **arbeiten an + dative** to say someone is working on/developing something (a project, book, plan, idea). With masculine/neuter nouns you often see **an einem neuen + Noun** (e.g., *an einem neuen Plan/Buch*). In everyday speech, English often prefers the continuous form: “is working on …”.
target_language_example: Sie arbeitet an einem neuen Projekt.
native_language_example: She is working on a new project.

additional_notes: Used to say where someone is employed. "bei" is used for workplaces/companies (roughly “at/for”). "einer" is the dative form of "eine" and is used because "bei" takes the dative case; it’s followed by a feminine noun (e.g., Tankstelle, Firma). For masculine/neuter you’d use "bei einem" (e.g., bei einem Restaurant).
target_language_example: Meine Mutter arbeitet bei einer Bank.
native_language_example: My mother works at a bank.

meaning: "works hard to / in order to" (to achieve a goal).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is making a strong effort with a purpose. The comma is common when "um … zu" introduces the goal: "Er arbeitet hart, um … zu + infinitive" (e.g., "um die Prüfung zu bestehen"). You can also use other forms of "arbeiten" (ich arbeite, wir arbeiten, etc.).
target_language_example: Sie arbeitet hart, um einen besseren Job zu bekommen.
native_language_example: She works hard to get a better job.

meaning: “works in” (at/in a place, city, or department).
additional_notes: Used with the verb **arbeiten** in the 3rd person singular (**er/sie**): **Er/Sie arbeitet in …**. It’s commonly followed by a city/country (**arbeitet in Tokio**) or a specific area/department (**arbeitet in der Personalabteilung**). For people: **Ich arbeite in …** (I work in …), **Wir arbeiten in …** (we work in …).
target_language_example: Sie arbeitet in Berlin.
native_language_example: She works in Berlin.

meaning: “works in the” (for places/organizations with feminine nouns).
additional_notes: Used with the verb *arbeiten* + *in* to say where someone works. After *in* (location, not movement), German usually uses the dative case: *in der* is dative feminine (e.g., *in der Fabrik*, *in der Personalabteilung*, *in der Stadt*). For masculine/neuter nouns you often see *in dem* → *im* (e.g., *im Büro*).
target_language_example: Er arbeitet in der Schule.
native_language_example: He works at/in the school.

additional_notes: Used to say someone’s workplace. "arbeitet" is the verb "to work". "in" + dative often expresses location; "einem" is the dative form of "ein" used here (often before a neuter noun like "Krankenhaus" or "Restaurant"). You’ll also see other forms depending on the noun: e.g., "arbeitet in einer Klinik" (feminine) or "arbeitet in einem Büro" (neuter).
target_language_example: Sie arbeitet in einem Büro in Berlin.
native_language_example: She works in an office in Berlin.

meaning: “works in a …” (a workplace in the dative case).
additional_notes: Used to say where someone works. It’s typically followed by a feminine noun for a place of work (e.g., Bäckerei, Fabrik, Bibliothek, Pizzeria). Because of the preposition "in" (location), "eine" becomes "einer" (dative feminine). For masculine/neuter places you’d use "in einem" (e.g., in einem Büro).
target_language_example: Sie arbeitet in einer Schule.
native_language_example: She works in a school.

additional_notes: "arbeitet" is the 3rd-person singular present tense of "arbeiten" (to work), so it goes with "er/sie/es" or a singular noun/name (e.g., "Anna arbeitet..."). With other subjects, the verb changes: "ich arbeite", "du arbeitest", "wir arbeiten". "jeden Tag" = "every day" (accusative: "jeder Tag" → "jeden Tag").
target_language_example: Mein Bruder arbeitet jeden Tag.
native_language_example: My brother works every day.

meaning: as poor as a church mouse; extremely poor.
additional_notes: An idiom used to emphasize that someone has very little or no money. Often used with „sein“ (e.g., „Er ist/war arm wie eine Kirchenmaus.“).
target_language_example: Nach der Miete bin ich arm wie eine Kirchenmaus.
native_language_example: After paying the rent, I'm as poor as a church mouse.

additional_notes: Used to describe breathing in deeply, often to calm down, prepare for something, or before an action (e.g., speaking, blowing out candles). The verb is the separable verb „einatmen“ (to breathe in): in simple past, the stem is „atmete“ and the prefix „ein“ goes to the end of the clause.
target_language_example: Ich atmete tief ein, bevor ich antwortete.
native_language_example: I took a deep breath before I answered.

additional_notes: Used when a main clause is followed by a "dass"-clause, and "auch" shows that this information is in addition to something else ("I also think/know/feel that …"). The comma comes before "dass". In English you usually translate it as "also" or "too" (not literally as "also, that").
target_language_example: Ich hoffe auch, dass du Zeit hast.
native_language_example: I also hope that you have time.

additional_notes: Used to add something/someone to a list: it means that the person/thing is one more example in addition to others. It comes right before a noun phrase with an indefinite article: auch ein (masc./neut.), auch eine (fem.), also plural: auch (keine article). In questions, it often means “also/too”: e.g., “Spielst du auch ein Instrument?” = “Do you play an instrument too?”
target_language_example: Das ist auch ein Problem.
native_language_example: That is also a problem.

meaning: also good; that’s fine too / okay as well.
additional_notes: Used to say something is fine in addition to (or as an alternative to) something else. Often appears as a short reaction meaning “fine/okay then.” With "auch gut so" it means “that’s a good thing too / that’s fine the way it is.” In questions, it can mean “also” in the sense of “as well” (e.g., "Geht es dir auch gut?" = “Are you well too?”).
target_language_example: Wir können heute nicht ins Kino gehen? Auch gut, dann bleiben wir zu Hause.
native_language_example: We can’t go to the movies today? That’s fine; then we’ll stay home.

meaning: "always, too"; or (with question words) "whatever / whichever" (emphasis: no matter which).
additional_notes:
1) With time expressions like "immer": "... und wird es auch immer geben" = "... and it will always exist too" (adds "also/too" to "immer").
2) Often used after a question word to mean “no matter which/what”: "was auch immer" (whatever), "welches auch immer" (whichever), "wer auch immer" (whoever), etc. It adds emphasis: any choice is fine.
target_language_example: Nimm, was auch immer du brauchst.
native_language_example: Take whatever you need.

meaning: “too / as well (sometime),” often with “for once” nuance.
additional_notes: Combines **auch** (“also/too”) + **mal** (a common spoken particle that makes requests/questions sound more casual or means “once/sometime”). In statements it can express wanting to do something too (sometimes with impatience: “I want to as well, for once!”). In questions it can mean “ever/sometime” in the sense of “Will you come by sometime?”
target_language_example: Ich möchte das auch mal ausprobieren.
native_language_example: I’d like to try that too (sometime/for once).

additional_notes: combines auch and nicht. It is used to add another negative statement: if something is not true for one thing, it is also not true for another. In English, it is often translated as 'not ... either' rather than word-for-word.
target_language_example: Ich kann morgen auch nicht kommen.
native_language_example: I can't come tomorrow either.

additional_notes: Used to add emphasis that something is no longer true, often in addition to another negative statement ("me neither" / "not anymore"). It can stand alone as a short reply ("Auch nicht mehr.") or appear in longer sentences to show a change over time: "Es ist hier auch nicht mehr so ...". In some contexts it implies "if X happens, then you won’t be able to Y anymore" (e.g., "kommst du auch nicht mehr heraus" = "you won’t get out again").
target_language_example: Ich habe dafür auch nicht mehr die Zeit.
native_language_example: I don’t have the time for that anymore either.

additional_notes: Used to react to something positively in a modest way—often as mild praise or pleasant surprise. Can stand alone as a comment, or refer back to something mentioned before ("Meins ist auch nicht schlecht" = "Mine isn’t bad either").
target_language_example: Das Angebot ist auch nicht schlecht.
native_language_example: That offer isn’t bad either.

additional_notes: In negative sentences, **auch** often means **“either”** (not “also”). So **auch nichts** is used to add emphasis like “nothing either” or “doesn’t help either.” Common patterns: **Das bringt/nutzt/taugt auch nichts.** = “That doesn’t help either / That’s no good either.” It can also mean “also nothing” in a simple listing: **Und das ist auch nichts.** = “And that is also nothing (special).”
target_language_example: Wenn wir uns beeilen, hilft das auch nichts.
native_language_example: Even if we hurry, that won’t help either.

meaning: also; as well; on top of that (an additional thing).
additional_notes: Used to add one more item/person/action to what’s already the case. Often implies “in addition to everything else” and can sound slightly emphatic or annoyed depending on context (e.g., "Du hast ihm auch noch geholfen!" = "You even helped him, too!").
target_language_example: Ich muss heute auch noch einkaufen.
native_language_example: I also have to go shopping today (on top of everything else).

meaning: “even just a / even a single …” (emphasizes a very small amount).
additional_notes: Used to stress that even the smallest amount/instance would be enough or would matter. Often followed by a noun or combined with quantity words: „auch nur ein bisschen“ (even just a little), „auch nur einen Moment“ (even just a moment), „auch nur ein Wort“ (even just one word). Word order can vary with what’s being emphasized (e.g., „auch nur ein wenig“).
target_language_example: Kannst du auch nur einen Moment warten?
native_language_example: Can you wait even just a moment?

meaning: “already” (often with extra emphasis: “as well / even / anyway”).
additional_notes: Combines **auch** (“also/even/anyway”) + **schon** (“already”). It often means **“already”** with a tone of surprise, impatience, or emphasis: *Auch schon kapiert?* ≈ “Got it yet?” / “Finally got it?” In other contexts it can mean “also already” (= someone has done something before, too): *Er hat auch schon Kindern geholfen.* In questions like *Was soll sich auch schon verändert haben?* it can sound like **“anyway” / “really”** (“What could have changed anyway?”).
target_language_example: Bist du auch schon fertig?
native_language_example: Are you finished already?

meaning: also like that; the same way too.
additional_notes: Used to say something is true in the same way for someone/something else (a comparison): "bei deiner Mutter auch so" = "it was the same with your mother". It can also add emphasis with adjectives/adverbs, often meaning "anyway / all the same": "Ist ja auch so egal" = "It’s (all) the same anyway."
target_language_example: Bei mir war das früher auch so.
native_language_example: It used to be the same for me too.

additional_notes: Introduces a contrast: something is true or happens despite another condition or fact. Use it at the start of a clause, often followed by a comma: "Auch wenn ..., ...". With the verb in the "auch wenn" clause typically at the end (subordinate clause).
target_language_example: Auch wenn ich müde bin, gehe ich heute noch spazieren.
native_language_example: Even though I'm tired, I'm still going for a walk today.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a concessive clause: something is true or will happen despite a difficult condition. It’s often followed by strong consequences ("even if it kills me"). Grammar tip: in the full clause after "auch wenn", the verb typically goes to the end (e.g., "Auch wenn es nur fünf Minuten dauert, ...").
target_language_example: Ich komme, auch wenn es regnet.
native_language_example: I'll come even if it rains.

meaning: right away; immediately; on the first try.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens instantly/without difficulty (e.g., verstehen, mögen, gelingen). Often implies “without needing a second attempt” or “from the very start.”
target_language_example: Ich habe die Aufgabe nicht auf Anhieb gelöst.
native_language_example: I didn’t solve the task on the first try.

additional_notes: Uses the verb **klettern** (“to climb”) with **auf** + accusative to express direction/goal: **auf Bäume** (“onto trees”). Commonly used with **können** to talk about ability: **Ich kann (nicht) gut auf Bäume klettern.**
target_language_example: Können Sie gut auf Bäume klettern?
native_language_example: Can you climb trees well?

additional_notes: Used to say that something is written, spoken, sung, or done in the English language. Often appears with verbs like schreiben (to write), sprechen (to speak), lesen (to read), singen (to sing), or eine Rede halten (to give a speech). You can swap the language: auf Deutsch, auf Französisch, etc.
target_language_example: Kannst du das bitte auf Englisch erklären?
native_language_example: Can you please explain that in English?

additional_notes: Used to say what language a text (book, letter, email, etc.) is written in. With "auf" + a language name (auf Deutsch / auf Englisch / auf Französisch) + "geschrieben". It can describe something ("Das Buch ist auf Englisch geschrieben") or be used with "schreiben" ("Ich habe einen Brief auf Englisch geschrieben").
target_language_example: Der Artikel ist auf Englisch geschrieben, aber ich kann ihn gut verstehen.
native_language_example: The article is written in English, but I can understand it well.

meaning: on Earth; in this world (not in heaven).
additional_notes: Used to talk about life and events in the earthly world, often in contrast to heaven ("im Himmel"). Common in elevated, religious, or poetic contexts (e.g., "Frieden auf Erden", "Paradies auf Erden").
target_language_example: Nichts ist für immer, zumindest nicht auf Erden.
native_language_example: Nothing lasts forever, at least not on Earth.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is true anywhere in the world, often with superlatives or comparisons ("der beste/der schönste … auf Erden"). It can also be used as an intensifier in questions ("Was machst du auf Erden?" = "What on earth are you doing?").
target_language_example: Für mich gibt es kein besseres Essen auf Erden als Pizza.
native_language_example: For me, there’s no better food on earth than pizza.

additional_notes: Used with "auf" + language to say something is spoken, written, or done in that language. Common with verbs like sprechen, sagen, schreiben, erklären, heißen ("What is it called in French?").
target_language_example: Kannst du das bitte auf Französisch sagen?
native_language_example: Can you please say that in French?

meaning: because of; due to (also: 'aground' in boating/ship contexts).
additional_notes: In the causal sense, it’s very common and often written as one word: "aufgrund" + genitive (e.g., "aufgrund des Wetters"), or with dative in everyday speech ("aufgrund dem Wetter"). In fixed expressions about ships/boats, "auf Grund" is literal: "auf Grund gehen" (to sink/go down), "auf Grund liegen" (to be aground), "auf Grund laufen" (to run aground).
target_language_example: Auf Grund des starken Regens fällt das Spiel aus.
native_language_example: Because of the heavy rain, the game is canceled.

meaning: your health; (also as a toast) “to your health!”
additional_notes: Most often used with **achten auf** (“to pay attention to / take care of”): **Achten Sie auf Ihre Gesundheit.** = “Take care of your health.” On its own (**Auf Ihre Gesundheit!**) it can be used like a formal toast meaning “To your health!” (similar to “Cheers!”). **Ihre** is the formal “your” (to one person); informal would be **deine**.
target_language_example: Bitte achten Sie besser auf Ihre Gesundheit.
native_language_example: Please take better care of your health.

additional_notes: Most common in shopping/business contexts to ask if something is available right now: „Haben Sie das auf Lager?“. It can also be used more figuratively for things someone has prepared or can produce (ideas, jokes, tricks): „noch etwas auf Lager haben“ = to still have something up one’s sleeve / in reserve.
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, haben Sie das noch auf Lager?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you still have that in stock?

additional_notes: In standard German, this is most commonly used with an article: **auf die Seite** (direction: move something aside) or **auf der Seite** (location: on the side). Without an article (**auf Seite**) it can sound shortened/elliptical and may appear in notes, instructions, or colloquial speech. Common with verbs like **legen/stellen/schieben**. In phrases like **Geld auf die Seite legen**, it means “to set money aside (save).”
target_language_example: Leg das bitte auf Seite.
native_language_example: Put that aside, please.

meaning: up to speed; running at full speed (especially in fixed phrases like „auf Touren kommen/bringen“).
additional_notes: Often used about machines, work, or people when they start working well or reach their full pace. Common patterns: „auf Touren kommen“ = to get going / get up to speed; „jdn./etw. auf Touren bringen“ = to get someone/something going, to rev something up.
target_language_example: Nach dem Kaffee komme ich endlich auf Touren.
native_language_example: After coffee I finally get going.

meaning: "Goodbye" on the phone (literally: "until we hear each other again").
additional_notes: Used when ending a phone call. It’s the telephone version of "Auf Wiedersehen" (used in person). Often said alone or after "Danke" / "Vielen Dank". You can also use it in a sentence like "ohne auf Wiederhören zu sagen" (“without saying goodbye”).
target_language_example: Gut, dann bis morgen—auf Wiederhören!
native_language_example: Alright, then see you tomorrow—goodbye (on the phone)!

meaning: Goodbye (formal/neutral; literally “until we see each other again”).
additional_notes: A standard, polite way to say goodbye when leaving. Often shortened in speech to "Wiedersehen!". In casual situations, people may also say "Tschüss" instead.
target_language_example: Danke für Ihren Besuch. Auf Wiedersehen!
native_language_example: Thank you for your visit. Goodbye!

additional_notes: Usually appears in patterns like "ohne … zu sagen" ("without saying goodbye"). Common related forms: "(auf) Wiedersehen sagen" (finite verb), and "für jemanden auf Wiedersehen sagen" (to say goodbye on someone’s behalf).
target_language_example: Sie ging hinaus, ohne auf Wiedersehen zu sagen.
native_language_example: She went outside without saying goodbye.

meaning: “onto the / on the” (with movement or a target); also “to the / at the” in some fixed phrases.
additional_notes: “auf” + “das” (neuter accusative). You use **auf das** when something is directed onto/toward a neuter noun (often with movement: *auf das Regal stellen*). It’s also common with verbs that take *auf* to name the thing you focus on or listen to (*auf das Resultat ankommen*, *auf das Geschwätz hören*) and with toasts like *Ein Hoch auf das …*.
target_language_example: Leg die Jacke bitte auf das Bett.
native_language_example: Please put the jacket on the bed.

meaning: to the concert; to go to the concert.
additional_notes: Common with verbs of movement like **gehen**: **auf + das (Akkusativ)** = going to an event (similar to **zu einem Konzert**). Also appears with **sich freuen auf + Akk.**: **Ich freue mich auf das Konzert** = “I’m looking forward to the concert.”
target_language_example: Gehst du heute Abend auf das Konzert?
native_language_example: Are you going to the concert tonight?

additional_notes: Used with **gehen** to say someone went to an event. In spoken German this is often in the **Perfekt** tense: **sein + gegangen** (e.g., **Er ist ... gegangen**). With events, German commonly uses **auf + Akkusativ**: **auf das Konzert / auf die Party / auf den Markt gehen**.
target_language_example: Wir sind gestern Abend auf das Konzert gegangen.
native_language_example: We went to the concert last night.

meaning: for the worst (case); expecting the worst.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like „sich vorbereiten (auf)“ (to prepare for) and „sich gefasst machen (auf)“ (to brace oneself for). It refers to the most negative possible outcome: „auf das Beste hoffen und auf das Schlimmste vorbereitet sein“ (“hope for the best and be prepared for the worst”).
target_language_example: Ich bereite mich auf das Schlimmste vor, aber ich hoffe, dass alles gut geht.
native_language_example: I’m preparing for the worst, but I hope everything will be fine.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement like gehen/kommen/bringen/stellen to mean going or putting something in your (personal) room. Often heard as a parent’s command: „Geh auf dein Zimmer!“ = “Go to your room!” (similar to being sent to your room). With verbs like stellen/legen it means placing something in your room.
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte auf dein Zimmer gehen und die Hausaufgaben holen?
native_language_example: Can you please go to your room and get the homework?

meaning: 'on/at your …' (used before a feminine or plural noun).
additional_notes: This is the preposition **auf** + the possessive determiner **deine** (“your”). It often appears in fixed verb + preposition patterns, e.g. **auf deine Finger achten** (watch your fingers), **auf deine Intuition/Kraft vertrauen** or **sich auf deine Intuition verlassen** (rely on your intuition), **auf deine Eltern hören** (listen to your parents), and in phrases like **auf deine Art** (your way) or **auf deine Verantwortung** (= at your own responsibility/risk). In these uses, **auf** is typically followed by the **accusative**: *auf deine …*.
target_language_example: Pass auf deine Tasche auf!
native_language_example: Watch your bag!

meaning: “on/to your …” (with a masculine noun in the accusative: deinen).
additional_notes: Used with verbs and expressions that take **auf + accusative**, e.g. **antworten auf** (to reply to), **(nicht) auf etwas hören** (to (not) listen to), **(sich) freuen auf** (to look forward to). It’s the start of a longer phrase: **auf deinen Brief/Rat/Besuch** etc. In some fixed phrases it can sound rude (e.g. **Scheiß auf …!** = “Screw …!”).
target_language_example: Ich freue mich schon auf deinen Anruf.
native_language_example: I’m already looking forward to your call.

additional_notes: Used for location with auf + the dative article dem (masculine/neuter). It usually describes where something is, not movement toward something. In English, it is often translated as "on the," but with some nouns it can also mean "at the" or "in the" depending on natural English usage.
target_language_example: Die Schlüssel liegen auf dem Tisch.
native_language_example: The keys are on the table.

additional_notes: A common location phrase. Uses dative case (dem) because it describes a static location (where something is happening). If you mean movement/direction onto the balcony, use accusative: „auf den Balkon“ (e.g., „Ich gehe auf den Balkon.“).
target_language_example: Wir sitzen abends oft auf dem Balkon.
native_language_example: We often sit on the balcony in the evening.

meaning: on your stomach; lying face down.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like liegen/schlafen to describe the position of your body: face down with your stomach on the bed/floor. Common contrasting phrases: auf dem Rücken (on your back) and auf der Seite (on your side).
target_language_example: Ich kann nicht auf dem Bauch schlafen.
native_language_example: I can't sleep on my stomach.

meaning: on the mountain; up on the mountain.
additional_notes: A location phrase: auf + dative (dem) shows position (not movement). Used to say something is located/stands/lives up on a mountain. For movement to a mountain, you’d typically use „auf den Berg“ (accusative).
target_language_example: Wir machen ein Picknick auf dem Berg.
native_language_example: We’re having a picnic on the mountain.

meaning: on the mountain peak / at the summit.
additional_notes: A location phrase: auf + dative (dem) because it describes where something is (not movement). Used for being located at the top of a mountain (snow, trees, people, etc.). For movement to the summit, you’d often use „auf den Berggipfel“ (accusative).
target_language_example: Wir machen eine Pause auf dem Berggipfel.
native_language_example: We’re taking a break on the mountain peak (at the summit).

additional_notes: Used to describe a location/position. With a fixed location, German often uses **auf + dative**: **auf dem Bett** (“on the bed”). If there is movement to the bed (direction), it’s usually **auf + accusative**: **aufs Bett / auf das Bett** (“onto the bed”).
target_language_example: Das Buch liegt auf dem Bett.
native_language_example: The book is on the bed.

meaning: in the picture; in the photo.
additional_notes: Used to point out someone or something that appears in a picture/photo (not necessarily physically "on top of" it). Often with verbs like „sein“ (to be), „aussehen“ (to look), or questions like „Wer ist … auf dem Bild?“ / „Welcher bist du …?“
target_language_example: Auf dem Bild sieht man meine Schwester neben dem Auto.
native_language_example: In the picture you can see my sister next to the car.

meaning: on the floor; on the ground.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is located on the surface you walk on (inside: the floor; outside: the ground). Often used with verbs like sein/liegen/schlafen/sehen: „Er liegt auf dem Boden.“ Also contrasts with „auf dem Boden“ (on the surface) vs. „am Boden“ (down/knocked down, at ground level).
target_language_example: Die Schlüssel liegen auf dem Boden.
native_language_example: The keys are on the floor.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is located on a boat, or that an action happens there. After the preposition "auf" (on) with a fixed location, German often uses the dative case: "dem Boot" (not *den Boot*). For movement onto the boat, you’d usually say "auf das Boot" (accusative).
target_language_example: Wir sind auf dem Boot und genießen die Sonne.
native_language_example: We’re on the boat and enjoying the sun.

additional_notes: Used to say something/someone is located or happening on the sidewalk (the pedestrian path next to the street). With movement verbs it can also mean you are walking along the sidewalk (e.g., gehen auf dem Bürgersteig). In German, "Bürgersteig" is common in many regions; "Gehweg" is another common word for sidewalk.
target_language_example: Bitte fahr nicht auf dem Bürgersteig Fahrrad.
native_language_example: Please don’t ride your bike on the sidewalk.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is located on top of a building (the roof). Often used with verbs like sein (to be), liegen (to lie/be), stehen (to stand), landen (to land), or gehen (to walk). Note the dative case after the fixed location preposition auf + dem (on the roof, not onto the roof).
target_language_example: Die Kinder spielen auf dem Dach der Garage.
native_language_example: The children are playing on the roof of the garage.

meaning: in the attic / up in the attic.
additional_notes: Used to say something is located or happens in the attic (the space under the roof, often for storage). Grammar: "auf" + dative for location → "auf dem Dachboden" (masc. dative). With movement/direction you often hear accusative: "auf den Dachboden" (up to the attic).
target_language_example: Die alten Kisten stehen auf dem Dachboden.
native_language_example: The old boxes are in the attic.

meaning: (to be) feeling well; in good shape (especially health-wise).
additional_notes: Commonly used with "sein" and very often in the negative: "nicht (ganz/richtig) auf dem Damm" = not feeling well / under the weather / not quite back to normal. Colloquial idiom; it does not literally mean "on the dam."
target_language_example: Nach der Grippe bin ich noch nicht wieder ganz auf dem Damm.
native_language_example: After the flu, I’m still not quite back to normal.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is physically on ice (e.g., on an icy surface). Very common with verbs like „ausrutschen“ (to slip) and „laufen/gehen“ (to walk).
target_language_example: Pass auf, auf dem Eis kann man leicht ausrutschen!
native_language_example: Be careful, you can easily slip on the ice!

additional_notes: Used to say someone is physically located in a cultivated field (e.g., doing farm work). Often contrasts with being indoors (im Haus). With location you’ll usually hear: auf dem Feld sein/arbeiten.
target_language_example: Die Bauern sind schon früh auf dem Feld.
native_language_example: The farmers are already out in the field early.

meaning: at the airport (on the airport grounds).
additional_notes: Literally “on the airport,” used with places/grounds you are physically on or within. In everyday German, people more often say **am Flughafen** (“at the airport”) for general location. **auf dem** is dative (location, not movement); for going there you’d use **zum Flughafen** / **auf den Flughafen** (less common).
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns auf dem Flughafen am Eingang.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at the airport at the entrance.

additional_notes: Used to say something is happening in a building’s corridor (often inside an apartment building, hotel, office, etc.). With location you typically hear: „auf dem Flur“ (in the hallway). Related: „im Flur“ can also mean “in the hallway,” especially when describing where something is in the entrance/hall area of a home.
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns auf dem Flur vor dem Aufzug.
native_language_example: We’ll meet in the hallway in front of the elevator.

meaning: in the photo; in the picture.
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone or something that appears in a photo. Often modifies a noun: "der Junge auf dem Foto" (the boy in the photo). You can also use it after "sein": "Ich bin auf dem Foto."
target_language_example: Auf dem Foto steht meine Schwester neben dem Auto.
native_language_example: In the photo, my sister is standing next to the car.

meaning: on the floor (on the ground inside a room).
additional_notes: Used to say something is lying/placed directly on the floor indoors. Often with verbs like liegen (to lie), finden (to find), sitzen (to sit), schlafen (to sleep). Note: Fußboden = indoor floor; Boden can be more general (ground/soil/floor).
target_language_example: Die Schlüssel liegen auf dem Fußboden neben dem Sofa.
native_language_example: The keys are on the floor next to the sofa.

meaning: on the sidewalk / on the footpath.
additional_notes: Uses the dative case (auf + dem) to describe location/where something happens: on the pedestrian path (as opposed to the street/road). Common with verbs like gehen (to walk), finden (to find), liegen (to lie), herunterfallen (to fall down).
target_language_example: Bitte fahr nicht auf dem Fußweg, dort gehen viele Leute.
native_language_example: Please don’t ride on the sidewalk; a lot of people walk there.

additional_notes: Used with sein/unterwegs sein to say you are currently heading home ("Ich bin auf dem Heimweg"). It’s also common to add where you’re coming from: "auf dem Heimweg vom Büro" (on the way home from the office). Often used when asking someone to stop somewhere while heading home: "Kannst du auf dem Heimweg ...?".
target_language_example: Ich bin noch auf dem Heimweg und komme in zehn Minuten an.
native_language_example: I’m still on my way home and I’ll arrive in ten minutes.

meaning: on your mind; something you want to talk about (often a worry or concern).
additional_notes: Used almost always with "etwas" and "haben": "(Hast/Haben) du/Sie/ihr etwas auf dem Herzen?" = a polite way to ask if someone has something they want to say or if something is bothering them. It literally means "on the heart," but the natural English equivalent is usually "on your mind" or "we need to talk."
target_language_example: Wenn du etwas auf dem Herzen hast, kannst du es mir jederzeit sagen.
native_language_example: If you have something on your mind, you can tell me anytime.

meaning: in the yard/courtyard; on the farm (property).
additional_notes: "Hof" can mean a courtyard/yard (e.g., between apartment buildings) or a farm/farmyard. "auf dem Hof" describes being/doing something on the premises (a location, not movement). Which meaning fits depends on context: kids playing usually = courtyard/yard; helping/working, giving up a job usually = farm.
target_language_example: Die Katze läuft den ganzen Tag auf dem Hof herum.
native_language_example: The cat walks around in the yard all day.

additional_notes: A location phrase: **auf** + dative (dem) is used for being in a place (not moving). Often used with verbs like **sein** (to be) and **stehen** (to stand). For movement onto a hill, German typically uses **auf den Hügel** (accusative).
target_language_example: Wir sitzen auf dem Hügel und schauen ins Tal.
native_language_example: We’re sitting on the hill and looking into the valley.

meaning: on the piano; (playing) on the piano.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like spielen (to play) and begleiten (to accompany): etwas auf dem Klavier spielen = to play something on the piano; jemanden auf dem Klavier begleiten = to accompany someone on the piano. You’ll also hear an + instrument without an article in some contexts (e.g., am Klavier), but auf dem Klavier is a common, clear way to say “on the piano.”
target_language_example: Kannst du das bitte auf dem Klavier spielen?
native_language_example: Can you play that on the piano, please?

meaning: in the toilet / in the restroom (using the toilet).
additional_notes: "Klo" is a common, casual word for "toilet" (more informal than "die Toilette"; less crude than some slang). "auf dem Klo sein" usually means being in the bathroom because you’re using the toilet. You’ll also hear "Ich bin auf dem Klo" = “I’m in the restroom.”
target_language_example: Warte kurz, ich bin auf dem Klo.
native_language_example: Wait a second, I’m in the restroom.

additional_notes: Used for things that are inverted (e.g., a picture, text) and for the position where a person is balancing with their head on the ground (often with verbs like stehen: auf dem Kopf stehen). For objects you can also say: Das Bild hängt auf dem Kopf. For text: Der Text steht auf dem Kopf.
target_language_example: Das Bild hängt auf dem Kopf.
native_language_example: The picture is hanging upside down.

meaning: in the countryside; in a rural area.
additional_notes: Used to describe living or being outside cities/towns, in a rural setting. Often contrasts with "in der Stadt" (in the city).
target_language_example: Am Wochenende fahren wir oft auf dem Land spazieren.
native_language_example: On the weekend we often go for a walk in the countryside.

meaning: to go for a walk in the countryside (in a rural area).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like gehen/fahren to describe taking a leisurely walk outside the city. "auf dem Land" contrasts with "in der Stadt" (in the city) and means "in the country / in the countryside". "spazieren gehen" is a common split verb phrase: "Ich gehe spazieren."
target_language_example: Am Wochenende gehen wir oft auf dem Land spazieren.
native_language_example: On the weekend, we often go for a walk in the countryside.

meaning: in the countryside; in a rural area.
additional_notes: A fixed phrase meaning someone lives outside cities/towns, in a rural region. Often used with verbs like „wohnen/leben“ (to live).
target_language_example: Wir verbringen den Sommer auf dem Lande.
native_language_example: We spend the summer in the countryside.

meaning: up to date; informed (about the latest developments).
additional_notes: Used with "sein/bleiben" (to be/stay up to date) or very commonly with "jemanden auf dem Laufenden halten" (to keep someone updated). Often followed by "über" + topic: "auf dem Laufenden über die Schwangerschaft". In requests you’ll often hear the imperative: "Halte(n) Sie uns auf dem Laufenden."
target_language_example: Kannst du mich bitte auf dem Laufenden halten?
native_language_example: Can you please keep me updated?

meaning: to keep (someone) up to date; to keep (someone) informed.
additional_notes: Used with a direct object person: jemanden auf dem Laufenden halten. Common in work and everyday contexts for updates on news, progress, plans, etc. Related phrase: auf dem Laufenden sein = to be up to date. Word order note: the verb part can split (e.g., Ich halte dich auf dem Laufenden.)
target_language_example: Kannst du mich bitte über die Änderungen auf dem Laufenden halten?
native_language_example: Can you please keep me up to date about the changes?

meaning: on the market; available for sale.
additional_notes: Used to say a product/service is available to buy (often with verbs like „sein“, „kommen“ or „bringen“): „Ist es schon auf dem Markt?“, „Das Produkt kommt nächstes Jahr auf den Markt.“ Can also mean physically at a (street/farmers’) market, but in product contexts it usually means “available commercially.”
target_language_example: Das neue Handy ist noch nicht auf dem Markt.
native_language_example: The new phone isn’t on the market yet.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a location on the Moon (the celestial body). With a place meaning, German often uses "auf" (on) rather than "in". You’ll often see it with verbs like "landen" (to land) and "sein" (to be): "auf dem Mond landen/sein".
target_language_example: Es wäre spannend, einmal auf dem Mond zu stehen.
native_language_example: It would be exciting to stand on the moon someday.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens while you are traveling home (walking, driving, taking the bus, etc.). It uses the dative: auf + dem, because it describes a location/time during a journey. Similar: „auf dem Heimweg“.
target_language_example: Auf dem Nachhauseweg habe ich noch Brot gekauft.
native_language_example: On the way home, I also bought some bread.

additional_notes: Used to say where something/someone is located. It’s literally “on the parking lot,” but in English you usually say “in/at the parking lot.” Often answers the question “Wo?” (where?).
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns auf dem Parkplatz vor dem Supermarkt.
native_language_example: We’re meeting in the parking lot in front of the supermarket.

meaning: on the lawn; on the grass (a grassy area).
additional_notes: Means being located on a grassy surface, often a lawn in a garden or park. It’s the contraction of "auf" + "dem" (dative) = "auf dem" because the location is stationary (where?), not movement onto it ("auf den Rasen" = onto the lawn).
target_language_example: Die Kinder spielen auf dem Rasen hinter dem Haus.
native_language_example: The children are playing on the lawn behind the house.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like tragen (to carry), liegen (to lie), or schlafen (to sleep) to say something/someone is on the back. With a person + dative: auf dem Rücken (e.g., auf dem Rücken tragen = to carry on one’s back).
target_language_example: Das Baby schläft auf dem Rücken.
native_language_example: The baby is sleeping on its back.

meaning: on the way back (back home/return trip).
additional_notes: Used to say you are returning to where you came from. Often followed by “von …” to show where you’re coming back from (e.g., „auf dem Rückweg von der Schule“). Common in everyday updates: „Ich bin schon auf dem Rückweg.“
target_language_example: Ich bin auf dem Rückweg nach Hause.
native_language_example: I’m on my way back home.

meaning: burned at the stake (burned on a pyre).
additional_notes: Historical expression: someone is executed by being tied up and burned on a pile of wood (Scheiterhaufen = pyre). Often used in passive forms like „auf dem Scheiterhaufen verbrannt worden/ wurde“.
target_language_example: Im Mittelalter wurden manche Menschen auf dem Scheiterhaufen verbrannt.
native_language_example: In the Middle Ages, some people were burned at the stake.

additional_notes: Means someone/something is located on a ship. Common with verbs like sein (to be), schlafen (to sleep), arbeiten (to work). The preposition auf + dative (dem) is used here because it describes location (not movement); for movement onto a ship you’d often use auf das Schiff (accusative).
target_language_example: Wir sind auf dem Schiff und suchen unsere Kabine.
native_language_example: We’re on the ship and looking for our cabin.

additional_notes: Literally refers to the place where a battle is fought. It’s a fixed prepositional phrase: auf + dem (dative) because it describes location (where?), not movement. It can also be used more broadly/metaphorically for a place of direct conflict, but it’s most often used in a military/war context.
target_language_example: Viele Entscheidungen werden auf dem Schlachtfeld in Sekunden getroffen.
native_language_example: Many decisions are made on the battlefield in seconds.

additional_notes: Used to say where something is located (a position on top of a desk). It uses dative case because it answers “where?” (Wo?): auf dem Schreibtisch. For movement onto the desk (“where to?” / Wohin?), you’d use accusative: auf den Schreibtisch.
target_language_example: Mein Handy liegt auf dem Schreibtisch.
native_language_example: My phone is lying on the desk.

meaning: "is lying on the desk" / "there is … on the desk."
additional_notes: Used to say that an object is located on top of a desk (Schreibtisch). "auf" + dative ("dem") shows location (not movement). In German, you can start with the place: "Auf dem Schreibtisch liegt …" and then the verb comes second, so the subject comes after the verb.
target_language_example: Auf dem Schreibtisch liegt mein Handy.
native_language_example: My phone is lying on the desk. / There’s my phone on the desk.

meaning: on the way to/from school (school route).
additional_notes: Used with the preposition "auf" + dative ("dem"), meaning you are on the route between home and school. It often implies a regular school commute and is commonly used with verbs like "gehen", "sein", "treffen", "begleiten" (e.g., meeting someone or seeing something on the way).
target_language_example: Auf dem Schulweg habe ich meinen Freund an der Haltestelle getroffen.
native_language_example: On the way to school, I met my friend at the stop.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is located on the sofa, or that an action happens there (e.g., sitting, napping, falling asleep). Uses dative after a fixed location: auf + dem (dem = “the”, masculine/neuter dative). Contrast: „aufs Sofa“ (= onto the sofa, motion/direction).
target_language_example: Ich sitze heute Abend auf dem Sofa und schaue einen Film.
native_language_example: I’m sitting on the sofa tonight and watching a movie.

additional_notes: Used when someone sleeps on a sofa (often as a guest, or because there’s no bed available). With a specific sofa, you’ll often hear it with the dative article: „auf dem Sofa“ (on the sofa).
target_language_example: Wenn du willst, kannst du heute Nacht auf dem Sofa schlafen.
native_language_example: If you want, you can sleep on the couch tonight.

meaning: "on the couch/sofa and …" (used to link to the next action).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is on the sofa and then add what they are doing next (often with another verb): "auf dem Sofa und + Verb". Note the dative case after "auf" for a location (where?): "auf dem Sofa".
target_language_example: Ich sitze auf dem Sofa und lese ein Buch.
native_language_example: I'm sitting on the couch and reading a book.

additional_notes: Used with locations/positions (often with sein/liegen/stehen/sitzen). Note: with sitzen it usually means “sitting on the chair” (not necessarily “on top of” it), while “on top of the chair” can also be expressed as „oben auf dem Stuhl“.
target_language_example: Mein Rucksack liegt auf dem Stuhl.
native_language_example: My backpack is on the chair.

additional_notes: Refers to something being located/left/placed on top of a table. Common with verbs like „liegen“ (to lie/be lying), „stellen“ (to put upright/place), „legen“ (to lay/put), and „lassen“ (to leave).
target_language_example: Die Schlüssel sind noch auf dem Tisch.
native_language_example: The keys are still on the table.

additional_notes: Used with destinations: „auf dem Weg zum/zur …“ = “on the way to …”. It can also mean “in the process of” or “making progress” in fixed phrases like „auf dem Weg der Besserung“ (“on the road to recovery”).
target_language_example: Ich bin schon auf dem Weg zu dir.
native_language_example: I’m already on my way to you.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens while traveling to the place where the speaker currently is (often “here” = where we are now). Common with verbs like treffen/begegnen (“meet/run into”) for things that happened during the trip, or with sein for someone who is currently traveling here (“Er ist auf dem Weg hierher.”).
target_language_example: Auf dem Weg hierher habe ich mir einen Kaffee geholt.
native_language_example: On the way here, I got a coffee.

meaning: on the way to; heading to.
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is currently traveling toward a destination. Often with sein: „Ich bin/Er ist auf dem Weg nach …“ Can also describe vehicles: „Der Zug ist auf dem Weg nach …“. Use „nach“ for most cities and countries without an article (nach Berlin, nach Japan).
target_language_example: Wir sind auf dem Weg nach Berlin, aber wir machen noch einen kurzen Stopp.
native_language_example: We’re on the way to Berlin, but we’re making a short stop first.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens while traveling home (e.g., from work, school, or a visit). Often combined with requests or advice: "Kannst du auf dem Weg nach Hause …?" (Can you … on your way home?) and "Sei/Seien Sie …" (Be …).
target_language_example: Ich rufe dich auf dem Weg nach Hause an.
native_language_example: I'll call you on the way home.

meaning: to be on the way; to be en route.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is currently traveling to a place. Common with a destination ("Ich bin auf dem Weg nach Hause.") or with "zu" + person/appointment ("Ich bin auf dem Weg zum Arzt."). Also used in messages to mean “I’m coming now / I’m on my way.”
target_language_example: Ich bin schon auf dem Weg sein zum Bahnhof.
native_language_example: I’m already on my way to the train station.

meaning: on the way to; (figuratively) on the path to (becoming/achieving).
additional_notes: Used for movement toward a destination: **auf dem Weg zu + place/person**. Grammar: **auf dem Weg** uses dative (**dem Weg**), and **zu** also takes dative (e.g., **zu meiner Freundin**, **zum Bahnhof**). It can also be used figuratively for progress toward a goal (e.g., **auf dem Weg zu einem Erfolg** = “on the way to success”).
target_language_example: Ich bin auf dem Weg zum Bahnhof.
native_language_example: I’m on the way to the train station.

meaning: 'on the way to' / 'on the road to'.
additional_notes: Used to say you are traveling toward a destination or are in the process of reaching a goal. It’s a fixed phrase with dative: auf dem Weg + zu + dem (= zum) + noun. For feminine nouns you’ll see: auf dem Weg zur (zu der). Can also be used metaphorically for progress toward something (e.g., a goal).
target_language_example: Wir sind auf dem Weg zum Bahnhof.
native_language_example: We’re on the way to the train station.

meaning: on the way to the train station.
additional_notes: Used to say you are traveling/heading toward the train station and something happens during that trip. Often used with verbs like sein (Ich bin auf dem Weg …), etwas erledigen (… auf dem Weg …), and treffen (… auf dem Weg … getroffen).
target_language_example: Ich bin gerade auf dem Weg zum Bahnhof und komme in zehn Minuten an.
native_language_example: I’m on my way to the train station right now and will arrive in ten minutes.

meaning: on the way to work (while commuting).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens during your commute to work. Often used with verbs like haben/sehen/passieren (something happens), abholen (pick someone up), or vorbeikommen/vorbeifahren (pass by somewhere): „auf dem Weg zur Arbeit an der Post vorbei“.
target_language_example: Auf dem Weg zur Arbeit habe ich meine Kollegin im Bus getroffen.
native_language_example: On the way to work, I met my colleague on the bus.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens while someone is going from one place to school. Often with verbs like "sein" or "gehen": "Auf dem Weg zur Schule bin ich …" / "… ging er …". The phrase uses dative: "auf dem Weg" (on the way) + "zur" (= zu der) Schule (to the school).
target_language_example: Auf dem Weg zur Schule habe ich meinen Lehrer gesehen.
native_language_example: On the way to school, I saw my teacher.

meaning: “on(to) the” / “at the” (auf + der → den, masculine accusative).
additional_notes: Used with masculine nouns after **auf** (e.g., *auf den Stuhl*). Often **accusative** for movement/direction (“onto”): *Setz dich auf den Stuhl!* It can also appear in common verb patterns like **auf + Akk.**: *auf den Verkehr achten* (“pay attention to the traffic”), *auf etw. nichts geben* (“not care about something”).
target_language_example: Bitte achte auf den Weg!
native_language_example: Please pay attention to the path!

meaning: 'onto the tree' / 'up the tree' (moving to the tree).
additional_notes: Used with verbs of motion like klettern (to climb) to show direction/goal. Because it indicates movement to a place, German uses accusative: auf den Baum. If someone is already in the tree (location, not movement), you usually say auf dem Baum (dative).
target_language_example: Die Katze klettert auf den Baum.
native_language_example: The cat climbs up the tree.

meaning: (to be) up and about; on your feet (awake, active, or recovered).
additional_notes: Used mainly with "sein" ("auf den Beinen sein"). It can mean (1) awake and out of bed / already active (often with "schon", "früh"), or (2) back on your feet after illness/injury ("wieder auf den Beinen"). It can also describe how steady you are standing/walking ("wackelig auf den Beinen" = unsteady).
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, in ein paar Tagen bist du wieder auf den Beinen.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, in a few days you’ll be back on your feet.

meaning: to stay on your feet; to keep standing (not fall over).
additional_notes: Often used with a reflexive pronoun: sich (nicht/kaum) auf den Beinen halten = to (barely/not) be able to remain standing, usually because of dizziness, weakness, or exhaustion. Common pattern: „so …, dass … sich kaum auf den Beinen halten konnte“.
target_language_example: Nach der langen Wanderung konnte ich mich kaum noch auf den Beinen halten.
native_language_example: After the long hike, I could barely stay on my feet.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (e.g., fallen, werfen, legen) to show direction: something ends up on the floor/ground. Often heard as a short command in urgent situations: „Auf den Boden!“ (= Get down to the floor!). Contrast: „auf dem Boden“ = on the floor/ground (location).
target_language_example: Leg das bitte auf den Boden.
native_language_example: Please put that on the floor.

meaning: 'for the bus' (as in: waiting for the bus).
additional_notes: Commonly used with the verb "warten" in the phrase "auf den Bus warten" (= to wait for the bus). With "warten auf", German uses "auf" + accusative: "auf den Bus" (masc.), "auf die Bahn" (fem.), "auf das Taxi" (neut.), "auf die Busse" (pl.). Note: although it literally looks like "on the bus", in this context it means "for the bus".
target_language_example: Ich warte schon seit zehn Minuten auf den Bus.
native_language_example: I’ve already been waiting for the bus for ten minutes.

additional_notes: Past participle phrase of **auf etw. warten** (= to wait for something). Used with **haben** to form the present perfect: **Ich habe auf den Bus gewartet.** The preposition **auf** takes the accusative here (**den Bus**). You can ask about duration with **Wie lange ...?**
target_language_example: Wir haben zehn Minuten auf den Bus gewartet.
native_language_example: We waited for the bus for ten minutes.

meaning: onto the floor; on the floor (with movement/placing).
additional_notes: Uses accusative (den) with "auf" to show direction or putting something somewhere (movement/change of position): "Leg das auf den Fußboden." For a static location (no movement), German often uses dative: "auf dem Fußboden" = "on the floor." "Auf den Fußboden!" is a short command meaning "Put it on the floor!"
target_language_example: Stell die Tasche bitte auf den Fußboden.
native_language_example: Please put the bag on the floor.

meaning: to get the idea that … / to think that … (as a possibility).
additional_notes: Most commonly used with verbs like **kommen** or **bringen**: **(nicht) auf den Gedanken kommen, dass …** = “(not) to think of the possibility that … / it (never) occurred to (someone) that …”; **jemanden auf den Gedanken bringen, dass …** = “to make someone think that … / to give someone the idea that …”. Often conveys that the thought was unexpected or surprising.
target_language_example: Ich kam nie auf den Gedanken, dass du woanders als in Cornwall sein könntest.
native_language_example: It never occurred to me that you could be anywhere other than Cornwall.

meaning: on the button (as in: press the button).
additional_notes: Usually used with the verb „drücken“: „auf den Knopf drücken“ = to press the button. „auf“ + accusative („den“) expresses direction/contact (pushing onto something). Often also said as „den Knopf drücken“ (without „auf“).
target_language_example: Drück bitte auf den Knopf links.
native_language_example: Please press the button on the left.

additional_notes: Used with the accusative (den Kopf) to show movement toward a target or contact/impact: jemanden auf den Kopf schlagen, jemanden auf den Kopf küssen, sich etwas auf den Kopf setzen (e.g., a cap/hat). With a static location you often hear the dative: auf dem Kopf (“on the head,” not moving). In the idiom „Mir fällt die Decke auf den Kopf“ it means you feel cooped up/restless from being inside too long.
target_language_example: Setz dir bitte eine Mütze auf den Kopf, es ist kalt.
native_language_example: Please put a hat on your head, it’s cold.

meaning: squandered/spent (a lot of money), often carelessly.
additional_notes: Usually used with money: „(das Geld) auf den Kopf schlagen“ = to blow/squander money (often on fun things). It can also literally mean „hit on the head“ in other contexts, but the idiomatic money-meaning is very common.
target_language_example: Er hat sein ganzes Geld im Urlaub auf den Kopf geschlagen.
native_language_example: He blew all his money on vacation.

meaning: (idiom) “hit the nail on the head”; be exactly right.
additional_notes: Commonly used to say someone described something perfectly: **Das hast du auf den Kopf getroffen.** Grammatically it comes from **etwas auf den Kopf treffen** (“to hit something right on the head” = get it exactly right). In a literal (non-idiomatic) sense, **jemanden auf den Kopf treffen** can also mean physically hitting someone on the head, but the fixed phrase is very often meant figuratively.
target_language_example: Mit deiner Beschreibung hast du es genau auf den Kopf getroffen.
native_language_example: With your description, you hit the nail on the head.

meaning: to the market; onto the market (to be introduced for sale).
additional_notes: Used with movement/action toward the market (accusative): „(auf den Markt) gehen/fahren“. For location, German often uses „auf dem Markt“ (= at the market). Also common in business/product contexts: „etw. auf den Markt bringen“ = to bring/launch a product onto the market.
