With feminine nouns use "Da ist eine ...", and with neuter nouns "Da ist ein ..." too (e.g., "Da ist ein Licht."). Often followed by a location phrase like "unter dem Schreibtisch" or "an der Tür".
target_language_example: Da ist ein Hund vor der Haustür.
native_language_example: There is a dog in front of the front door.

meaning: "There is a man" / "A man is there" (pointing out someone’s presence).
additional_notes: Used to draw attention to a man who is present or has appeared somewhere (often: at the door). "Da" = “there,” and "da ist ..." is a very common way to say “there is/are ...” in everyday speech. You can swap in other nouns: "Da ist eine Frau" / "Da ist jemand".
target_language_example: Da ist ein Mann an der Tür und er will mit dir sprechen.
native_language_example: There’s a man at the door and he wants to talk to you.

additional_notes: Used to point something out or show where something/someone is: "Da ist es!" = “There it is!”. It can also refer to a place and describe it: "Da ist es ruhiger." = “It’s quieter there.”
target_language_example: Da ist es! Ich habe meinen Schlüssel gefunden.
native_language_example: There it is! I found my key.

meaning: “then/there you can …” / “in that situation, you can …” (impersonal “one can …”).
additional_notes: Used to talk generally about what is possible (or likely) in a situation or place just mentioned. "da" refers back to the context (“then/there”), and "man" means “you/one/people in general” (not a specific person). Often followed by an infinitive: "Da kann man … sehen/suchen/entkommen". It can also express a natural reaction: "Da kann man sich fürchten" (“That can be scary / You could be afraid in that situation”).
target_language_example: In dem Museum, da kann man viele alte Bilder sehen.
native_language_example: In that museum, you can see many old paintings.

additional_notes: Used to point out that someone or something is arriving or approaching. Often said when you see the person/thing: "Da kommt ein Auto." / "Da kommt er schon!" In English you usually say "Here comes…" even though German uses "da" (literally "there").
target_language_example: Da kommt der Bus!
native_language_example: Here comes the bus!

meaning: "you have to" (in that situation / for that).
additional_notes: "Da" here usually means “in that case / with that / for that” (not necessarily a physical “there”). It introduces a requirement or necessity: "Da musst du …" = “Then you have to … / You need to …”. Often followed by an infinitive ("hingehen") or by "wissen" + a clause ("… wissen, was …").
target_language_example: Da musst du einfach ruhig bleiben.
native_language_example: In that situation, you just have to stay calm.

additional_notes: Used to point to or refer to a higher place/location (e.g., upstairs, on top of something, up in the air). Often said while indicating the direction with your eyes or hand.
target_language_example: Da oben auf dem Regal liegt das Buch.
native_language_example: Up there on the shelf is the book.

additional_notes: A location phrase: **da oben** = “up there” (pointing to a specific place you can see/mean), **auf dem Dach** = “on the roof.” Often used in questions to ask what someone is doing in that place. **denn** (as in “Was machen Sie denn …?”) adds surprise/curiosity: “What on earth are you doing up there on the roof?”
target_language_example: Warum bist du da oben auf dem Dach?
native_language_example: Why are you up there on the roof?

meaning: (get/stay) out of there; (stay) out of it.
additional_notes: Often used to indicate a place: „Da raus, bei der Hecke.“ = “Out there, by the hedge.” Very common in the expression „(Sich) da raushalten“ / „Halt dich da raus!“ meaning “stay out of it / don’t get involved.” Also used with movement verbs: „Sie muss da raus.“ = “She has to get out of there.”
target_language_example: Bitte misch dich nicht ein—halt dich da raus!
native_language_example: Please don’t get involved—stay out of it!

meaning: out of there; out of it.
additional_notes: Common with verbs like „holen“ (to get someone out), „kommen“ (to come/get out), or in „(sich) da raushalten“ = to stay out of it / not get involved. „da“ refers to the place or situation you mean (there/that), and „raus“ is short for „heraus“ (out). Often written together as „daraus“ in more formal writing, but spoken as „da raus“/„da raus-“.
target_language_example: Ich will da raus!
native_language_example: I want to get out of there!

additional_notes: Used to point to a specific place or container and tell someone to go or put something inside it. Common in spoken German as a shorter, more casual form of „da hinein“. Often used as an instruction: „Schnell, da rein!“ (= Get in there!).
target_language_example: Leg die Schlüssel da rein, bitte.
native_language_example: Put the keys in there, please.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (gehen, fahren, kommen, tun, etc.) to mean moving something/someone into a place that’s indicated by context (e.g., a room, a car, a bag). "rein" is a shortened, more conversational form of "hinein"; you may also hear "da hinein" (more neutral) or word order like "Rein da!".
target_language_example: Stell die Kiste da rein.
native_language_example: Put the box in there.

meaning: (go) over there; (go) over to the other side.
additional_notes: Common in spoken German as a shorter, more casual form of **darüber/dorthinüber**. Used to tell someone to move to another spot or to cross to the other side (e.g., across a room, street, river). Often with verbs like **gehen**, **kommen**, **rennen**, **schwimmen**, **stellen**: *Geh/Kommt da rüber!*
target_language_example: Komm da rüber, ich kann dich kaum hören.
native_language_example: Come over here/there; I can barely hear you.

additional_notes: Used to talk about being present at a place, or about reaching a place by a certain time. With things like letters or packages, it can also mean that something has arrived.
target_language_example: Kannst du morgen um neun da sein?
native_language_example: Can you be there tomorrow at nine?

additional_notes: Combination of **da** (“there”) + **sind** (“are”). Used to point out that people/things are present or located somewhere: **Da sind Löcher.** (“There are holes.”) / **Ach, da sind sie!** (“Oh, there they are!”). With **bis wir da sind** it means “until we get there/arrive.” You also see **die/der/das … da sind** to mean “those … over there” (pointing at something).
target_language_example: Da sind meine Schlüssel—auf dem Tisch!
native_language_example: There are my keys—on the table!

meaning: “there is …” / “... is standing there” (pointing out where something/someone is).
additional_notes: Used with "da" (= there) to indicate something’s location. With people it usually means they are literally standing; with objects it often just means they are placed/located somewhere (not necessarily “standing” upright). Common in spoken German when pointing things out.
target_language_example: Da steht mein Auto vor dem Haus.
native_language_example: My car is parked in front of the house (There’s my car in front of the house).

additional_notes: Used to point to a location below you (e.g., on the ground, in a lower part of a building, downstairs, down in the valley). Often said while indicating a place with your hand or eyes. Can also be used in warnings like “Sachte da unten!” = “Careful down there!/Easy down there!”
target_language_example: Die Schuhe stehen da unten im Flur.
native_language_example: The shoes are down there in the hallway.

additional_notes: Used to point to a place that is in front of the speaker (often a short distance away). Common when giving directions or indicating where someone/something is: "Da vorne ist …" / "Stell dich da vorne hin." You can emphasize with "gleich" (= right) as in "gleich da vorne" (= right up ahead).
target_language_example: Der Eingang ist gleich da vorne.
native_language_example: The entrance is right up ahead.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something was present at a place/time (e.g., "als Frith da war" = "when Frith was there"). With existential/dummy subjects or negatives, it can correspond to English "there was/were" (e.g., "da war niemand" = "there was nobody"). Word order varies: "da war" often appears when "da" is placed first ("Da war niemand."); with a normal subject-first clause you may get "war ... da" ("Sie war schon da.").
target_language_example: Ich ging auf die Straße, aber da war niemand.
native_language_example: I went out into the street, but there was nobody there.

additional_notes: "Da" means "there" (in that place/situation). With "waren" (simple past of "sein"), it often introduces what existed/was present: "Da waren Ratten" = "There were rats." With a subject like "wir": "Da waren wir ..." = "We were there ..." It can also appear with "noch da waren" meaning "were still there/present."
target_language_example: Als wir ankamen, da waren schon viele Leute da.
native_language_example: When we arrived, there were already many people there.

additional_notes: Common spoken phrase said when you arrive at a place or reach the end of a journey/task. Often used with fillers like "so" or "also" ("So, da wären wir!"). You may hear it from a driver/guide right before getting out: "Da wären wir, bitte aussteigen!"
target_language_example: So, da wären wir — das ist das Museum.
native_language_example: So, here we are — this is the museum.

additional_notes: Used to start a subordinate clause that gives the reason for something. The verb goes to the end of the clause: „Da er keine Zeit hat, …“. Often followed by a comma, and the main clause comes after (or before).
target_language_example: Da er heute arbeiten muss, kann er nicht mitkommen.
native_language_example: Since he has to work today, he can’t come along.

additional_notes: Used to give the reason for something, often at the beginning of a sentence. It starts a subordinate clause, so the conjugated verb goes to the end: "Da es regnete, ...". "es" is a dummy subject meaning "it" (e.g., weather/time/situations).
target_language_example: Da es schon spät war, sind wir nach Hause gegangen.
native_language_example: Since it was already late, we went home.

additional_notes: A causal (reason) clause introduced by **da**. It’s a subordinate clause, so the verb goes to the end (**… müde war**). Usually separated by a comma, and it can come first or last: **Da ich müde war, …** / **…, da ich müde war.**
target_language_example: Da ich müde war, habe ich zu Hause geblieben.
native_language_example: Because I was tired, I stayed at home.

meaning: to stick with it; to keep at it.
additional_notes: Used to say you continue an activity, plan, or decision instead of stopping or changing. Often refers back to something already mentioned: „Ich lerne Deutsch – und ich bleibe dabei.“ It can also literally mean staying present/remaining there in some contexts, but most commonly it means continuing/persisting.
target_language_example: Auch wenn es schwierig ist, musst du dabei bleiben.
native_language_example: Even if it's difficult, you have to stick with it.

additional_notes: Used with helfen to say someone helped with a specific task or action already mentioned or clear from context. Common pattern: „Jemand hat mir/uns/euch dabei geholfen, …“ + infinitive with „zu“. Note: „helfen“ takes the dative case (mir, dir, ihm/ihr, uns, euch, ihnen).
target_language_example: Danke, dass du mir dabei geholfen hast, die Wohnung zu finden.
native_language_example: Thanks for helping me find the apartment.

meaning: to have with you (on you); to be carrying
additional_notes: Used when you have something with you at the moment (in your bag, pocket, etc.). Very common in questions/requests: "Haben Sie Ihren Ausweis dabei?" (= Do you have your ID with you?). In normal word order the parts often separate ("Ich habe meinen Ausweis dabei"), but the exact term "dabei haben" appears together in constructions like "dabei zu haben" or in infinitive clauses.
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, ich werde meinen Ausweis dabei haben.
native_language_example: I hope I will have my ID with me.

meaning: to help (with that/with it); to help with it.
additional_notes: Used with a verb or activity to mean helping with that specific thing: jemanden dabei helfen, etwas zu tun. Common with können/sollen and questions/requests (e.g., „Soll ich euch dabei helfen?“).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir dabei helfen, das Formular auszufüllen?
native_language_example: Can you help me fill out the form?

meaning: to be there; to be present (at an event/when something happens).
additional_notes: Used for being present/attending (meetings, ceremonies, situations). Often with a modal verb: „muss/soll/darf/kann dabei sein“ (= has to/should/may/can be there). In the past: „Ich war dabei“ = I was there / I was present (sometimes implying you witnessed it).
target_language_example: Ich kann morgen leider nicht dabei sein.
native_language_example: Unfortunately, I can’t be there tomorrow.

meaning: to help (someone) with that; to help (someone) do it
additional_notes: Used with a verb of helping (often **helfen**) to refer back to an activity/task already mentioned or clear from context: **jemandem dabei helfen, etwas zu tun**. **dabei** = “with it/with that” (about that task), and **zu helfen** is the infinitive “to help.” The person being helped is in the dative: **dir / euch / Ihnen / Maria**.
target_language_example: Ich finde, du solltest Tom bitten, dir dabei zu helfen.
native_language_example: I think you should ask Tom to help you with that.

meaning: "(how) did you feel when …?" (in that moment).
additional_notes: Used especially in the question pattern: „Wie war + DATIV (mir/dir/Ihnen/euch/…) + dabei zumute, als …?“ It asks about someone’s emotional state during a specific situation. The key expression is „jemandem ist (nicht) zumute“ = someone feels (not) up to it / feels a certain way; „dabei“ refers back to the situation, and „als“ introduces what happened.
target_language_example: Wie war dir dabei zumute, als du das gehört hast?
native_language_example: How did you feel when you heard that?

additional_notes: Used to introduce what someone believed or assumed in the past. Very common with a comma before **dass**. In a **dass**-clause, the conjugated verb usually goes to the end: **Er dachte, dass sie kommt.**
target_language_example: Ich dachte, dass du heute keine Zeit hast.
native_language_example: I thought that you didn’t have time today.

additional_notes: Used to report what a man/boy believed or assumed. After „dachte“, German often continues with a clause without „dass“: „Er dachte, er …“. You’ll frequently see Konjunktiv II forms like „könnte“ and „hätte“ to express an unreal/uncertain thought (similar to “he thought he could / had”). The comma is required before the second clause.
target_language_example: Er dachte, er hätte recht.
native_language_example: He thought he was right.

additional_notes: Used after a past-tense thinking verb ("denken": "dachte") to introduce a clause starting with "es" (= "it"). The comma is typical before the clause: "Er dachte, es wäre…" / "Ich dachte, es würde…". Very often followed by "wäre" (was/would be), "würde" (would), "könnte" (could), etc.
target_language_example: Ich dachte, es wäre eine gute Idee, früher zu gehen.
native_language_example: I thought it would be a good idea to leave earlier.

additional_notes: Used when reporting what someone believed about you. Very often followed by indirect speech with Konjunktiv I/II (e.g., „sei“, „wäre“, „würde“) to show it’s reported belief, not necessarily true: „Sie dachte, ich sei Ärztin.“ In casual speech, many people also use normal past forms instead of Konjunktiv.
target_language_example: Ich dachte, ich hätte meinen Schlüssel verloren.
native_language_example: I thought I had lost my key.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like „denken“ to report what someone believed at the time. German often uses Konjunktiv (here: „sei“) in indirect speech/thought, especially in writing. In everyday speech, many people also say „dachte, ich wäre“ or even „dachte, ich bin“. It’s usually followed by a noun/adjective clause (e.g., „… krank“, „… tot“) or an „es“-clause („… es“ = “I was the one”).
target_language_example: Ich dachte, ich sei zu spät.
native_language_example: I thought I was too late.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone (or you) believed in the past. German often uses Konjunktiv II ("wäre") after verbs like "denken" in reported speech to show it was just a belief/assumption, not necessarily true. In more formal indirect speech you may also hear "dachte, ich sei".
target_language_example: Ich dachte, ich wäre zu spät, aber der Zug hatte Verspätung.
native_language_example: I thought I was too late, but the train was delayed.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what a woman/girl believed or assumed. Often appears in narration as a shortened form of **Sie dachte, sie …**. What follows is frequently in **Konjunktiv** (e.g., *sie wäre / sie sei / sie könnte*) or with **würde** to show reported thoughts or an unreal/uncertain idea.
target_language_example: Er dachte, sie hätte keine Zeit.
native_language_example: He thought she didn’t have time.

additional_notes: Past tense of the separable verb **(darüber) nachdenken**. **darüber** = “about it/that” and refers to the topic you’re thinking about. Often followed by a **question word clause** (wie/ob/was …) or an **infinitive with zu** (z.B. *darüber nachdenken, ein Haus zu kaufen*).
target_language_example: Ich dachte darüber nach, ob ich morgen frei nehmen soll.
native_language_example: I thought about whether I should take tomorrow off.

meaning: “did you think…?” (past tense of “denken” addressed to “you”).
additional_notes: Used to ask what someone believed/assumed at the time. Often followed by a subordinate clause with „dass“/„daß“ (older spelling) or by a clause without „dass“ (e.g., „Dachtest du, du wärst fertig?“). Depending on tone, it can sound surprised or critical (like “What were you thinking?”).
target_language_example: Dachtest du wirklich, das würde funktionieren?
native_language_example: Did you really think that would work?

additional_notes: Rhetorical/accusatory question using the simple past of *denken* (du dachtest). Often used to express surprise, disbelief, or criticism: you assumed something about me, but you were wrong. The verb for the following clause usually comes at the end: *Dachtest du, ich merke das nicht?* / *Dachtest du, ich wäre böse?*
target_language_example: Dachtest du, ich würde dir nicht helfen?
native_language_example: Did you think I wouldn't help you?

additional_notes: Uses the simple past of *denken* (*du dachtest*) to challenge a past belief or assumption. Often sounds skeptical or surprised and can be mildly reproachful. Note: modern standard spelling is **dass**; **daß** is pre-1996/reform spelling and still seen in older texts.
target_language_example: Dachtest du wirklich, daß ich helfen würde?
native_language_example: Did you really think I would help?

additional_notes: Used to ask what a group of people believed or assumed in the past. "dachtet" is the simple past of "denken" (to think) for "ihr" (you plural). It’s typically followed by a "daß/dass" clause; in many contexts you’ll see Konjunktiv II in the second clause to express an assumption or unreal situation (e.g., "…dass ich gestorben wäre"). Modern spelling is usually "dass" instead of "daß".
target_language_example: Dachtet ihr, daß ich euch nicht helfen würde?
native_language_example: Did you all think that I wouldn’t help you?

meaning: “that …” (introduces a dass-clause referring back to dafür, often meaning “the reason/cause that …”).
additional_notes: Used when a previous word like Ursache, Grund, Schuld, Verantwortung, Dank, Scham, etc. is linked to a full clause with dass. In English you often drop “for that” and just say “that …” or “the fact that …”. Common pattern: „der Grund/Ursache dafür, dass …“ = “the reason/cause that …”.
target_language_example: Das ist der Grund dafür, dass ich heute nicht komme.
native_language_example: That’s the reason I’m not coming today.

meaning: for the fact that you… / for what you did…; (with verbs like „sorgen“) to make sure that you…
additional_notes: Used before a „dass“-clause with „du“ to give a reason or explanation (often like “for (the fact) that you…”). Common patterns: „Danke dafür, dass du …“ = “Thanks for …”; „Das ist dafür, dass du …“ = “This is for what you did …” (often punishment/revenge); „(Wir) sorgen dafür, dass du …“ = “(We) make sure that you …”. Sometimes it can also mean “considering that you …” (e.g., „Dafür, dass du so jung bist, …“).
target_language_example: Danke dafür, dass du mir geholfen hast.
native_language_example: Thanks for helping me.

meaning: to pay for it / to pay for that.
additional_notes: "dafür" means "for it/for that" and refers back to something already mentioned (e.g., a service, repair, mistake). "bezahlen" is "to pay". Common pattern: "jemanden dafür bezahlen, dass …" = "to pay someone to …".
target_language_example: Wir müssen dafür bezahlen, dass der Techniker es repariert.
native_language_example: We have to pay for the technician to fix it.

meaning: “paid for it/that” / “paid for this/that (service, item, etc.)”.
additional_notes: “dafür” means “for it/that” and refers back to something already mentioned (a thing or an action). Often used in questions like “Hast du schon dafür bezahlt?” (= Have you paid for it yet?) or with a person as the payer: “Er hat mich dafür bezahlt …” (= He paid me to do/say …). In formal speech you may also see “dafür, dass …” (= for the fact that / because …).
target_language_example: Ich habe dafür bezahlt, also möchte ich eine Quittung.
native_language_example: I paid for it, so I’d like a receipt.

meaning: “took (that long) (to do it)” / “needed (that long) for it.”
additional_notes: Used with **brauchen** (typically in the perfect tense: **haben ... gebraucht**) to say how much time someone needed to do something. **dafür** refers back to the task (“for that” / “to do that”). Common with time expressions like **lange**, **zehn Minuten**, **zwei Stunden**, **Wochen**. Typical patterns: **Ich habe dafür zwei Stunden gebraucht.** / **Wie lange hast du dafür gebraucht?**
target_language_example: Du hast lange genug dafür gebraucht.
native_language_example: You took long enough (to do it).

meaning: 'not for that/it' (i.e., not responsible/ready/eligible for that).
additional_notes: Used with a negative or in questions to say something does not apply "for that" situation. Often expresses lack of responsibility (Ich bin dafür nicht verantwortlich.), lack of suitability/authority (Wir sind dafür nicht zuständig.), or that something is too early/too much "for that" (Ist es dafür nicht zu früh?). In English you usually translate the whole idea rather than word-for-word.
target_language_example: Ich bin dafür nicht verantwortlich.
native_language_example: I'm not responsible for that.

meaning: to be in favor of (something); to support (a plan/idea).
additional_notes: Used to state your opinion in a discussion or decision. "dafür" refers back to a specific idea/proposal already mentioned (e.g., a rule, plan, or suggestion). Often contrasted with "dagegen sein" (to be against): "Ich bin dafür, aber sie ist dagegen." Also commonly used with a comma + "dass" or an infinitive clause: "Ich bin dafür, dass wir ..." / "Ich bin dafür, ... zu ...".
target_language_example: Ich bin dafür, den Plan morgen umzusetzen.
native_language_example: I’m in favor of carrying out the plan tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used when someone takes responsibility to make something happen (or prevent something). Typically followed by a „dass“-clause with the verb at the end. Implies actively arranging, managing, or seeing to it. Common patterns: „Ich werde dafür sorgen, dass …“ / „Kannst du dafür sorgen, dass …?“
target_language_example: Ich werde dafür sorgen, dass du pünktlich ankommst.
native_language_example: I’ll make sure you arrive on time.

meaning: responsible for that / responsible for it.
additional_notes: Used with "sein" to say someone is responsible for something already known from context: "für etwas verantwortlich sein" → "dafür verantwortlich sein". Common patterns: "dafür verantwortlich sein, dass ..." (responsible that ...) and "dafür verantwortlich sein, etwas zu tun" (responsible to do something). With "jemanden dafür verantwortlich machen" it means "to blame/hold someone responsible (for it)".
target_language_example: Wer ist dafür verantwortlich, dass die Tür offen ist?
native_language_example: Who is responsible for the door being open?

additional_notes: Used to refer back to something just mentioned (“dafür” = “for that/for it”). It’s often followed by a verb like bezahlen (“pay”) or büßen (“pay the price/atone”), and can sound like a warning or threat: “You’ll pay for that!” It can also be neutral in contexts like being paid for something: „Dafür wirst du bezahlt.“
target_language_example: Dafür wirst du dich entschuldigen müssen.
native_language_example: You'll have to apologize for that.

meaning: to do something about it/that (to take action against it).
additional_notes: Used when reacting to a problem or situation and asking or saying what action can/should be taken. Often appears with "was/irgendwas" (something) and in questions like "Was kann man dagegen tun?". "dagegen" refers back to a previously mentioned issue ("against it").
target_language_example: Ich kann nichts dagegen tun.
native_language_example: I can’t do anything about it.

meaning: to do something about it; to take action against it.
additional_notes: Usually used as **etwas dagegen unternehmen** (“do something about it”). **dagegen** refers back to a problem already mentioned (“against it/about it”), and **unternehmen** is a separable verb: *Ich unternehme etwas dagegen.* / *Wir müssen etwas dagegen unternehmen.*
target_language_example: Wir müssen etwas dagegen unternehmen, sonst wird es schlimmer.
native_language_example: We have to do something about it, otherwise it will get worse.

meaning: to where / to the place where.
additional_notes: Used to point to a destination or goal: "Geh/geh(en) Sie dahin, wo …" = "Go to where …". "dahin" means "(to) there" and is often paired with a "wo"-clause to specify the place more precisely. You’ll also hear fixed phrases like "dahin, wo’s weh tut" (“right where it hurts,” i.e., in a very painful spot).
target_language_example: Ich möchte dahin, wo es ruhiger ist.
native_language_example: I’d like to go to where it’s quieter.

meaning: to the effect that; regarding (something specific).
additional_notes: Used mostly in formal or written German to specify the content or direction of a statement, request, decision, etc. Common patterns: „eine Aussage/Erklärung dahin gehend, dass …“ (= a statement to the effect that …) and „ein Antrag/Entscheidung dahin gehend, …“ (= a request/decision regarding …).
target_language_example: Er machte eine Aussage dahin gehend, dass er morgen keine Zeit hat.
native_language_example: He made a statement to the effect that he doesn’t have time tomorrow.

meaning: “back to where …” (put/return something to its original place).
additional_notes:
Used when you want someone to put something back in the exact place it was before. 
- **dahin** = “(to) there”, **zurück** = “back”, **wo** = “where”. 
- Very common with verbs like **legen** (lay/put), **stellen** (set/put upright), **tun** (put/do; informal), **bringen** (bring). 
- Often used in commands: **Leg/Stell/Tu … dahin zurück, wo …** / formal **Legen/Stellen Sie … dahin zurück, wo …**.
target_language_example: Bring die Schlüssel bitte dahin zurück, wo sie vorher waren.
native_language_example: Please put the keys back where they were before.

meaning: Back then, there was / there were.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that existed (or did not exist) in the past. Often combined with negatives like „kein/keine“ or „noch nicht“ to say something didn’t exist yet: „Damals gab es noch kein Internet.“ The verb is „es gab“ (past tense of „es gibt“ = “there is/are”); the thing that existed is in the accusative: „Damals gab es viele Menschen.“
target_language_example: Damals gab es hier nur ein kleines Dorf.
native_language_example: Back then, there was only a small village here.

meaning: to start (with it); to begin doing it.
additional_notes: Uses the pronoun "damit" (= "with it/with that") to refer back to something already mentioned. Common in questions and warnings: "Soll ich jetzt damit anfangen?" = "Should I start now?" / "Fang nicht wieder damit an" = "Don’t start that again." With "können" it can also mean "to be able to do something with it / make sense of it": "Ich konnte nichts damit anfangen" = "I couldn’t make anything of it."
target_language_example: Können wir bitte endlich damit anfangen?
native_language_example: Can we please finally start?

meaning: to stop doing that; to quit it.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to stop a specific action that’s happening or was just mentioned. "damit" refers back to the action (“with that/doing that”), and "aufhören" means “to stop.” Common in requests such as "Könntest/Könnten … bitte damit aufhören?"
target_language_example: Könntet ihr bitte damit aufhören?
native_language_example: Could you please stop doing that?

meaning: busy (with doing something); occupied with it/that.
additional_notes: Used with "sein" (or past forms like "war") to say someone is currently occupied with an activity. "damit" refers back to something already mentioned or understood, and it’s often followed by an infinitive clause: "damit beschäftigt, etwas zu tun".
target_language_example: Ich bin gerade damit beschäftigt, meine E-Mails zu beantworten.
native_language_example: I'm busy answering my emails right now.

meaning: to agree with that; to be okay with that.
additional_notes: Used to ask or state whether someone agrees/consents to something previously mentioned. "damit" refers to "with that/with it" (the thing/plan/idea). Common in questions: "Bist du damit einverstanden?" You can also use it as a statement: "Ich bin damit einverstanden."
target_language_example: Ich bin damit einverstanden, dass wir morgen früher losfahren.
native_language_example: I agree that we leave earlier tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **sein**: **mit etwas fertig sein** = “to be done/finished with something.” **damit** refers back to what you’re talking about (“with that/it”). Common in questions: **Bist/Seid ihr damit fertig?** = “Are you done with that?”
target_language_example: Ich bin damit fertig, du kannst jetzt anfangen.
native_language_example: I’m finished with it; you can start now.

meaning: to finish it; to get done with it.
additional_notes: Used with a task or thing you’re working on: „mit etwas fertig werden“ = to finish something. „damit“ refers back to the thing (it = “with that/with it”). Often used with time pressure or deadlines (e.g., „bis Ende der Woche“, „bevor … hier sind“).
target_language_example: Ich muss damit fertig werden, bevor wir losfahren.
native_language_example: I have to finish it before we leave.

meaning: to manage to finish it; to get it done (also: to cope with it).
additional_notes: Used with "mit" + dative, often with a pronoun: "damit" (= with it/with that). Common in questions about whether someone can finish a task or handle a situation: "Schaffst du es, damit fertig zu werden?" Also appears with time expressions: "bis morgen", "wie lange brauchst du".
target_language_example: Ich versuche, heute noch damit fertig zu werden.
native_language_example: I’m trying to finish it today.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase „mit etwas rechnen“ = to expect/anticipate something (often something likely or possible). „damit“ refers back to the thing you’re expecting: „Ich habe damit gerechnet, dass …“ = “I expected that …”. You can soften it with „halb“: „Ich habe halb damit gerechnet …“ = “I half expected …”.
target_language_example: Ich habe nicht damit gerechnet, dass es heute schneit.
native_language_example: I didn’t expect it to snow today.

meaning: to mean by that; to intend (something) by that.
additional_notes: Used to clarify what someone intends with a statement or action. Very common in questions like „Was meinst du damit?“ (= “What do you mean by that?”). Often takes an object or clause: „Ich meine damit …“ (= “What I mean by that is …”).
target_language_example: Was willst du damit meinen, dass es zu spät ist?
native_language_example: What do you mean by saying it’s too late?

meaning: to have nothing to do with it/that; to not be involved.
additional_notes: Used to deny involvement or to say something is unrelated to the current topic. Often appears as „Das hat damit nichts zu tun“ (That has nothing to do with that/it) or with a person as subject: „Er/Ich hat/habe damit nichts zu tun.“ „damit“ refers back to something already mentioned.
target_language_example: Ich habe damit nichts zu tun.
native_language_example: I have nothing to do with it.

meaning: to expect (something); to count on it.
additional_notes: Used when you consider something likely and plan for it. Often followed by a clause: „Ich rechne damit, dass …“ (= I expect that …). It can also refer back to something already mentioned („damit“ = with that / with it). Related pattern: „mit etwas rechnen“ (e.g., „mit Problemen rechnen“ = to expect problems).
target_language_example: Ich muss damit rechnen, dass der Zug heute Verspätung hat.
native_language_example: I have to expect that the train will be delayed today.

meaning: to mean (by that); to be trying to say.
additional_notes: Used when clarifying the point or intended message behind what someone said. Very common in questions like „Was willst du mir damit sagen?“ (= “What are you trying to tell me/What do you mean by that?”). Often appears with „wollen“: „Ich weiß nicht, was du damit sagen willst.“
target_language_example: Ich verstehe, was du damit sagen willst.
native_language_example: I understand what you mean by that.

additional_notes: Used to check or clarify what someone implies. Often expresses surprise or disbelief. Commonly used with "wollen": "Willst du damit sagen, daß …?" (informal singular), "Wollen Sie damit sagen, daß …?" (formal), "Wollt ihr damit sagen, daß …?" (informal plural). Note: "daß" is the old spelling; modern standard is "dass".
target_language_example: Wollen Sie damit sagen, daß Tom verrückt ist?
native_language_example: Are you saying that Tom is crazy?

additional_notes: Used with a time expression + „haben“: „Ich habe [Zeit] damit verbracht, ...“ It usually goes with an infinitive clause (often with „zu“): „damit verbracht, etwas zu tun“ (= to spend time doing something). „Damit“ refers to the activity that follows.
target_language_example: Wir haben den Nachmittag damit verbracht, die Stadt zu erkunden.
native_language_example: We spent the afternoon exploring the city.

meaning: 'to have to do with it/that' (to be involved; to be connected; to be relevant to).
additional_notes: Used with "haben" to ask or state whether someone/something is involved in an event or whether something is relevant to the topic: "Hast du damit zu tun?" (Are you involved?) / "Was hat das damit zu tun?" (What does that have to do with it?). "damit" refers back to something previously mentioned ("with that/with it").
target_language_example: Was habe ich denn damit zu tun?
native_language_example: What does that have to do with me, then?

meaning: "so that you" / "in order for you to".
additional_notes: Used to introduce a purpose/goal (a reason for doing something): main clause + comma + "damit du" + verb at the end. Example pattern: „Ich lerne Deutsch, damit du mich verstehst.“ (= I’m learning German so that you understand me.)
target_language_example: Ich schreibe es dir auf, damit du es nicht vergisst.
native_language_example: I’ll write it down for you so that you don’t forget it.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a purpose clause: main clause + „damit er …“. In the „damit“-clause, the verb normally goes to the end (e.g., „… damit er pünktlich ankommt.“). Often used when someone does something in order for him to be able to do something else.
target_language_example: Ich rufe ihn an, damit er Bescheid weiß.
native_language_example: I’ll call him so that he knows.

meaning: "so that I" / "in order for me to".
additional_notes: Introduces a purpose/goal: something happens (or you do something) so that you can do something else. It’s a subordinating conjunction, so the verb goes to the end of the clause (…damit ich gehen kann). Often used after a comma, and can be used with requests/commands (Gib mir …, damit ich … kann!).
target_language_example: Kannst du das Fenster öffnen, damit ich besser atmen kann?
native_language_example: Can you open the window so that I can breathe better?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a purpose clause (a reason/goal). It’s often followed by a verb in the subjunctive (Konjunktiv II) in hypothetical or cautious statements (e.g., „damit sie nicht fallen würde“). „Sie“ can mean either “she” (singular) or “they” (polite/plural) depending on context; the verb form helps clarify.
target_language_example: Sprich leiser, damit sie schlafen kann.
native_language_example: Speak more quietly so that she can sleep.

meaning: to be grateful; to feel thankful.
additional_notes: Used with **für** + noun/pronoun or **für das, was ...** to say what you’re grateful for: *dankbar sein für das, was man hat* (“be grateful for what you have”). Often appears with **sollte(n)** to give advice or criticism: *Du solltest dankbar sein.* You can also say who should be grateful **to** someone with the dative: *Er sollte mir dankbar sein* (“He should be grateful to me”).
target_language_example: Ich sollte dankbar sein für deine Hilfe.
native_language_example: I should be grateful for your help.

meaning: “thanks for …” / “thank you that …” (to thank someone for something they did).
additional_notes: Used to thank someone for an action or fact that follows in a full clause. The verb goes to the end of the clause after "dass". Often followed by formal "Sie" or informal "du/ihr": "Danke, dass Sie …" / "Danke, dass du …" / "Danke, dass ihr …".
target_language_example: Danke, dass du mir geholfen hast.
native_language_example: Thanks for helping me.

additional_notes: Used to thank someone politely for a specific action, followed by a clause with a verb at the end: "Danke, dass Sie + ...". Use "Sie" for formal situations (e.g., strangers, customers, officials, older people). For informal situations with friends/family, say "Danke, dass du ...".
target_language_example: Danke, dass Sie sich Zeit genommen haben.
native_language_example: Thank you for taking the time.

meaning: “Thank you for …” (formal: thanking someone for something they did for you).
additional_notes: Used to thank someone politely ("Sie" = formal "you"). It’s usually followed by a verb at the end of the clause (e.g., „… eingeladen haben“, „… gerettet haben“). In spoken German you can also say „Danke, dass Sie …“ without „mich“ if it’s not specifically about you.
target_language_example: Danke, dass Sie mich so freundlich unterstützt haben.
native_language_example: Thank you for supporting me so kindly.

meaning: "Thank you for being so …" / "Thank you for … (doing it) so …" (formal).
additional_notes: A polite, formal thank-you using **Sie**. The pattern is **Danke, dass Sie so + adjective/adverb + sind/kommen/gekommen sind**. Common with qualities (e.g., *aufmerksam* = attentive, *bedacht* = considerate) or with adverbs like *kurzfristig* = at short notice.
target_language_example: Danke, dass Sie so schnell geantwortet haben.
native_language_example: Thank you for replying so quickly.

meaning: "Thanks for (that) you..." / "Thank you for..." (talking to one person you address as "du").
additional_notes: Used to thank someone for a specific action, followed by a dass-clause. In the dass-clause, the conjugated verb usually goes to the end: „Danke, dass du mir geholfen hast.“ If you’re speaking formally to one person, use „Danke, dass Sie ...“ instead of „du“.
target_language_example: Danke, dass du mir heute geholfen hast!
native_language_example: Thanks for helping me today!

meaning: “thanks for (you) … me …” (starting a thank-you sentence with ‘that you … me …’).
additional_notes: Used to thank someone for an action they did involving you, followed by a verb at the end of the clause (e.g., „… eingeladen hast“, „… angerufen hast“). Often followed by what they did: „Danke, dass du mich eingeladen hast.“ You can swap „du“ for other forms: „Danke, dass Sie mich …“ (formal) or „Danke, dass ihr mich …“ (plural).
target_language_example: Danke, dass du mich heute unterstützt hast.
native_language_example: Thanks for supporting me today.

meaning: "Thanks for" / "Thank you for" (to you) … (for doing something for me).
additional_notes: Used to thank someone directly (du = informal "you") for an action that benefits you: "Danke, dass du mir …" + verb at the end (e.g., geholfen hast, zuhörst). "mir" means "me" (dative), often with verbs like helfen, zuhören, kaufen, zeigen.
target_language_example: Danke, dass du mir heute so viel erklärt hast.
native_language_example: Thanks for explaining so much to me today.

additional_notes: Used to thank a group of people for a specific action. It introduces a subordinate clause with **dass** (“that”), so the verb typically goes to the end: **Danke, dass ihr gekommen seid.** For one person you’d say **Danke, dass du …**, and in formal situations **Danke, dass Sie …**.
target_language_example: Danke, dass ihr mir so schnell geantwortet habt.
native_language_example: Thanks for answering me so quickly.

additional_notes: Used to thank more than one person for something they did. Grammar: „Danke, dass …“ introduces a full clause (often with Perfekt, e.g. „gemacht habt“). „ihr“ = you (plural/informal), „mich“ = me. In the clause, the verb typically goes at the end: „…, dass ihr mich geweckt habt.“
target_language_example: Danke, dass ihr mich abgeholt habt!
native_language_example: Thanks for picking me up!

meaning: “Thanks for …” (used before a clause introduced by daß/daß).
additional_notes: Used to thank someone for an action or situation described in the following subordinate clause: “Danke, daß …”. Note: modern spelling is usually “Danke, dass …”; “daß” is older/less common (pre-1996 spelling). Often you can also say “Danke dafür, daß …” (= “Thanks for the fact that …”). Typically written with a capital D (“Danke”), but the entry here keeps your given form.
target_language_example: Danke, daß ihr euch die Zeit genommen habt, meine Fragen zu beantworten!
native_language_example: Thanks for taking the time to answer my questions!

additional_notes: Used with formal "Sie" to thank someone for an action. It’s typically followed by a clause with a verb at the end: "danke, daß Sie mir geholfen haben." Note: modern spelling is "dass" (instead of older "daß"), but "daß" is still seen in older texts.
target_language_example: Danke, daß Sie mir alles erklärt haben!
native_language_example: Thank you for explaining everything to me!

meaning: “Thanks for (the fact that) you …” / “Thank you for …” (followed by a clause).
additional_notes: Used to thank someone for something they did (or do) when you continue with a full clause introduced by „daß du …“ (verb typically at the end of the clause). Often translated as “Thanks for …-ing”: „Danke, daß du auf meine Kinder aufgepaßt hast!“ = “Thanks for looking after my kids!” Spelling note: modern German usually writes „dass“ (not „daß“), but „daß“ is correct in older/Swiss-style orthography.
target_language_example: Danke, daß du mir alles erklärt hast!
native_language_example: Thanks for explaining everything to me!

meaning: “Thanks that you (plural)…”, i.e. “Thanks for … / Thank you for …” (addressing two or more people).
additional_notes: Used to thank a group of people ("ihr" = you all). Common pattern: "Danke, daß ihr + ..." with a verb at the end (e.g., "gekommen seid") or with an adjective phrase (e.g., "so großzügig seid"). Note: Modern spelling is usually "dass" instead of "daß"; "daß" is older/Swiss-uncommon spelling.
target_language_example: Danke, daß ihr so kurzfristig gekommen seid!
native_language_example: Thanks for coming on such short notice!

additional_notes: Used to thank someone for a noun or noun phrase (thing, help, action): Danke für + accusative (e.g., Danke für die Hilfe / für deinen Beitrag). Often followed by a polite addressee like Ihnen (formal) or dir/euch (informal).
target_language_example: Danke für deine Hilfe heute!
native_language_example: Thanks for your help today!

additional_notes: Used to politely thank someone you address with Sie/Ihr (e.g., a customer, colleague, or stranger). You usually follow it with a noun: Danke für Ihre E-Mail / Nachricht / Unterstützung / Einladung. In speech you may also hear: Vielen Dank für Ihre ...
target_language_example: Danke für Ihre Hilfe, das weiß ich sehr zu schätzen.
native_language_example: Thank you for your help, I really appreciate it.

meaning: "Thank you for your ..." (formal, to a man).
additional_notes: Used to thank someone politely using the formal address Sie/Ihr. The form "Ihren" is accusative masculine (e.g., "Ihren Besuch", "Ihren Einkauf"). For a woman you often see "Ihre" (e.g., "Danke für Ihre Hilfe"), and for plural nouns: "Ihre" (e.g., "Danke für Ihre Fragen").
target_language_example: Danke für Ihren Anruf.
native_language_example: Thank you for your call.

additional_notes: Used to thank someone for a specific action, thing, or abstract noun that follows. Often followed by a noun in the accusative (e.g., das Kompliment, das Vertrauen) or by a nominalized verb phrase (e.g., das Kochen). You can also say "Danke für die/den/das …" depending on the noun’s gender and case.
target_language_example: Danke für das schnelle Antworten.
native_language_example: Thanks for replying so quickly.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to thank someone for something specific. "Deine" is the informal possessive "your" (to one person: du). After "für" it’s in the accusative, often with feminine nouns (e.g., die E-Mail) or plural nouns (e.g., die Bemühungen). For polite/formal addressing, use "Danke für Ihre …".
target_language_example: Danke für deine Hilfe.
native_language_example: Thanks for your help.

meaning: "Thanks for the ..." (used before a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used to thank someone for something specific. "für" takes the accusative case, so with masculine singular nouns you often get "den" (e.g., "den Anruf", "den Kommentar"). With feminine or neuter nouns it changes: "Danke für die ..." / "Danke für das ...".
target_language_example: Danke für den Tipp!
native_language_example: Thanks for the tip!

meaning: "Thanks for the ..." (used before a feminine noun or plural noun).
additional_notes: Used to thank someone for a specific thing. After "für" you use the accusative: "die" is the accusative article for feminine singular (die Korrektur, die harte Arbeit) and plural (die Kekse). For masculine/neuter singular you’d use "den/das": "Danke für den Tipp!", "Danke für das Geschenk!".
target_language_example: Danke für die Hilfe!
native_language_example: Thanks for the help!

meaning: “Thanks for …” (thanking someone for an action or thing).
additional_notes: “fürs” is a contraction of “für das” and is followed by a noun or nominalized verb: “Danke fürs Kommen” (= for coming). In speech and informal writing it’s very common; in more formal writing you may also see “Danke für das …”.
target_language_example: Danke fürs Helfen, das war wirklich nett.
native_language_example: Thanks for helping, that was really nice.

additional_notes: Used to express gratitude, often a bit warmer or more formal than just "danke". You can also follow it with "dass ..." to say what you’re thanking someone for ("Danke schön, dass du ..." = "Thank you for ...").
target_language_example: Danke schön, dass Sie mir geholfen haben.
native_language_example: Thank you very much for helping me.

meaning: “thank you” (formal; to one person you address as Sie).
additional_notes: Used in formal or polite situations. Grammar note: danken takes the dative case, so it’s danke dir (informal, one person) / danke Ihnen (formal, one person) / danke euch (informal, plural) / danke Ihnen (formal, plural). You can also say Vielen Dank! without specifying a person.
target_language_example: Danke Ihnen für Ihre Hilfe.
native_language_example: Thank you for your help.

meaning: "Thanks" / "thank you" (to one person you address as "du").
additional_notes: Used when thanking a single person informally (with "du"). It’s a bit warmer/more personal than just "Danke." For more emphasis you can say "Danke dir!" or "Vielen Dank (dir)!" For formal situations ("Sie"), use "Danke Ihnen."
target_language_example: Danke dir für deine Hilfe!
native_language_example: Thanks for your help!

additional_notes: Used to say what your state or situation is after something else happens (a consequence or next step). Often follows an implied or stated condition: "Wenn …, dann bin ich …" (“If …, then I am …”). You’ll frequently see it with places or states ("dann bin ich drin/frei") or followed by where you went ("dann bin ich zur U-Bahn gegangen").
target_language_example: Okay, dann bin ich morgen um 9 Uhr da.
native_language_example: Okay, then I’ll be there tomorrow at 9 o’clock.

additional_notes: Used after a reason/condition or something just said to state the result or conclusion about the person addressed (du). Often appears as: „Wenn …, dann bist du …“ (“If …, then you are …”) or after a statement: „…, dann bist du …“.
target_language_example: Du magst Kaffee? Dann bist du hier genau richtig.
native_language_example: You like coffee? Then you're in exactly the right place here.

meaning: "then go" (often: "then just go!" as an imperative).
additional_notes: Used when reacting to what someone just said ("then, in that case..."). Most commonly it’s a direct command: "Wenn du nach Hause willst, dann geh!" Adding "doch" ("Dann geh doch!") makes it more like urging/challenging someone (“well then, go on!”) and can still sound blunt depending on tone. You may also see it with "ich": "Dann geh ich (da) mal hin" = “Then I’ll go (over) there (now).”
target_language_example: Wenn du keine Zeit hast, dann geh jetzt schon.
native_language_example: If you don’t have time, then leave now already.

additional_notes: Used to say what you and others will do next (often as a decision or next step). "Dann" = "then"; "gehen wir" = "we go" (often understood as "we'll go"). Can be followed by a destination with "zu/nach" (e.g., "Dann gehen wir nach London"), or used on its own to mean leaving: "Dann gehen wir (eben)."
target_language_example: Okay, dann gehen wir jetzt nach Hause.
native_language_example: Okay, then we'll go home now.

meaning: "then I" / "then I have" (used to continue a story or sequence of events).
additional_notes: Common in storytelling to move to the next step: *Dann habe ich …* + past participle (Perfekt), e.g. *Dann habe ich angefangen … / Dann habe ich nachgedacht.* Word order note: in a main clause, *dann* takes position 1, so the verb (*habe*) comes before the subject (*ich*).
target_language_example: Dann habe ich schnell meine Tasche gepackt und bin gegangen.
native_language_example: Then I quickly packed my bag and left.

meaning: 'then he…' / 'so he…' (introducing what happened next or a conclusion).
additional_notes: Common in spoken and written storytelling to continue events or react to new information. Grammar: starting with "Dann" puts the conjugated verb second and the subject after it: "Dann hat er …". Often used with the Perfekt (past) tense: "hat" + past participle later in the sentence (e.g., "Dann hat er gelogen"). Depending on context it can mean "then he did…" or "then he has…" in English.
target_language_example: Dann hat er mich sofort angerufen.
native_language_example: Then he called me right away.

meaning: "then it's" / "then it is" (introduces a result or conclusion).
additional_notes: Used to state what follows from something: a consequence, decision, or conclusion. Very common after a condition (often with „wenn …, dann …“): „Wenn X passiert, dann ist es Y.“ It can also be followed by an adjective or phrase: „… dann ist es vorbei / in Ordnung / nicht so schlimm / nutzlos.“
target_language_example: Wenn du keine Zeit hast, dann ist es kein Problem.
native_language_example: If you don’t have time, then it’s not a problem.

additional_notes: Usually said when a problem is resolved or something turns out not to be serious. It’s commonly completed with an adjective like "gut", "super", "okay" (e.g., "Dann ist ja alles gut!"). The modal particle "ja" adds a tone of relief/"as we can see now".
target_language_example: Ah, du hast den Schlüssel doch gefunden? Dann ist ja alles gut!
native_language_example: Oh, you found the key after all? Then everything’s fine!

additional_notes: "Dann" means "then/after that" and "kam" is the simple past (Präteritum) of "kommen" (to come). It’s used in storytelling to show what happened next. With "dann" at the start, German often puts the verb second: "Dann kam er ..." (= Then he came ...). It can be literal movement ("Then I came here") or more general events ("Then came the diagnosis").
target_language_example: Dann kam der Brief, und alles wurde klar.
native_language_example: Then the letter came, and everything became clear.

meaning: "then I can" / "in that case, I can".
additional_notes: Used to say what you’re able to do as a result of something (often after a condition like „wenn …, dann …“ or after someone does something first). After „dann“, German word order usually flips: „dann kann ich …“ (not „dann ich kann …“). Often followed by an infinitive at the end: „Dann kann ich dir helfen.“
target_language_example: Wenn du mir die Adresse gibst, dann kann ich dir helfen.
native_language_example: If you give me the address, then I can help you.

meaning: 'then you can' (after that, you’re able/allowed to).
additional_notes: Used to say what someone can/should do next, often as a suggestion or instruction after something else happens. With "dann" at the start, German word order flips: "Dann kannst du ..." (verb 2nd, subject after it), not *"Dann du kannst ...".
target_language_example: Dann kannst du mir später helfen.
native_language_example: Then you can help me later.

additional_notes: Used to say you will come after something else happens or after you finish something. Often refers to coming soon or coming back: "Dann komme ich gleich" (I’ll come right away), "Dann komme ich zurück" (then I’ll come back). Common in casual planning and sequencing actions.
target_language_example: Ich mache kurz einen Anruf, dann komme ich.
native_language_example: I’ll make a quick call, then I’ll come.

meaning: 'then we can' / 'in that case, we can'.
additional_notes: Used to say what is possible or allowed next, often as the next step in a plan or as a consequence of something ("If X happens, then we can..."). It’s commonly followed by an infinitive verb at the end: „Dann können wir einkaufen.“
target_language_example: Dann können wir morgen früher losfahren.
native_language_example: Then we can leave earlier tomorrow.

meaning: "then I have to / then I must".
additional_notes: Used to state a necessary result or consequence, often after a condition (especially after a "wenn ..." clause). It’s commonly followed by an infinitive at the end of the sentence: "Dann muss ich gehen." / "Wenn du willst, dann muss ich das machen." (In formal situations you may also see "Dann muss ich Sie ...".)
target_language_example: Wenn es regnet, dann muss ich drinnen bleiben.
native_language_example: If it rains, then I have to stay inside.

meaning: "then you have to" / "then you must" (telling someone what is necessary next).
additional_notes: Used to draw a conclusion from what was just said or from a condition: if X is true, then the next necessary step is Y. Often gives advice or instructions. The verb changes with the subject (e.g., dann musst ihr…, dann muss er…, dann müssen wir…).
target_language_example: Wenn du morgen früh raus musst, dann musst du heute Abend früher schlafen gehen.
native_language_example: If you have to get up early tomorrow, then you have to go to bed earlier tonight.

additional_notes: Used to state what is necessary as a result of something (a consequence or next step). Often followed by an infinitive at the end of the clause (e.g., „Dann müssen wir gehen.“). „Dann“ = “then”, „müssen“ = “to have to/must”, „wir“ = “we”.
target_language_example: Wenn es weiterregnet, dann müssen wir drinnen bleiben.
native_language_example: If it keeps raining, then we have to stay inside.

meaning: “then we are / then we’re …” (a conclusion from what was just said).
additional_notes: Used after a condition or new information to state the result. It’s often followed by a noun (“Dann sind wir Nachbarn.”), an adjective/participle phrase (“Dann sind wir falsch informiert.”), or a place/situation (“Dann sind wir in das Gebäude gezogen.”). In speech it can also introduce agreement: “Dann sind wir uns einig.”
target_language_example: Wenn du auch in der Goethestraße wohnst, dann sind wir Nachbarn.
native_language_example: If you also live on Goethe Street, then we’re neighbors.

additional_notes: Means something happens sometimes, but not regularly. It’s close to "ab und zu" and "hin und wieder". Often used in casual conversation.
target_language_example: Dann und wann gehe ich nach der Arbeit noch spazieren.
native_language_example: Every now and then I go for a walk after work.

meaning: "then I will …" / "then I’m going to …" (and sometimes: "then I become …").
additional_notes: Used to say what you’ll do next, often as a consequence of something ("If/when X happens, then I will …"). Most often, "werde" is the future auxiliary ("Ich werde + infinitive"): "Dann werde ich dich beschützen" = "Then I will protect you." If no infinitive follows, "werde" can mean "become/get": "Dann werde ich traurig" = "Then I get sad."
target_language_example: Wenn es regnet, dann werde ich zu Hause bleiben.
native_language_example: If it rains, then I will stay at home.

additional_notes: Used to say what you (we) will do next or what will happen as a result. Often follows a condition, threat, or plan (e.g., "Wenn..., dann werden wir..."). "Dann" = then, "werden" + infinitive forms the future/intent ("we will ...").
target_language_example: Wenn es weiter regnet, dann werden wir zu Hause bleiben.
native_language_example: If it keeps raining, then we’ll stay at home.

meaning: "then ... will" / "then it will ..." (introduces the result that comes next).
additional_notes: Used to talk about what will happen as a consequence after something else: "[First thing], dann wird ...". Very common with "es": "Dann wird es ..." (= "Then it will be ..." / "Then things will get ..."). The verb is usually in position 2: "Dann wird er ...", "Dann wird es ...".
target_language_example: Mach die Tür zu, dann wird es nicht so laut.
native_language_example: Close the door, then it won’t be so loud.

meaning: "Alright then, let's…" (to get started / see what happens).
additional_notes: A common, conversational way to move things along or start an action. Often followed by an infinitive (e.g., „… loslegen“, „… sehen“, „… anfangen“), but it can also stand alone („Okay, dann wollen wir mal.“). It can sound like mild encouragement or “here we go.”
target_language_example: Okay, dann wollen wir mal anfangen.
native_language_example: Okay, let's get started then.

meaning: "that" after a preposition + da- (e.g., "because of the fact that…", "think/remember that…", "doubt that…").
additional_notes: German often uses a da-compound + comma + „dass“ to introduce a clause: „daran, dass …“, „darüber, dass …“, „dafür, dass …“. Common with verbs/adjectives/nouns that normally take a preposition: „denken an“ → „(an etwas) denken“ → „daran, dass …“; „zweifeln an“ → „daran, dass …“; „glauben an“ → „daran, dass …“. Also very common in „(Es) liegt daran, dass …“ = “That’s because … / It’s due to the fact that …”.
target_language_example: Es liegt daran, dass ich heute keine Zeit habe.
native_language_example: It’s because I don’t have time today.

meaning: to work on it/that; to keep working at it (to improve or achieve something).
additional_notes: Used to refer back to a specific issue, goal, or task already known from context. Closely related to „an etwas arbeiten“ (to work on something): „daran arbeiten“ = work on that/it. Often used with an infinitive clause with „zu“: „daran arbeiten, … zu …“ (work on …ing / work to …).
target_language_example: Du musst daran arbeiten, dein Deutsch zu verbessern.
native_language_example: You have to work on improving your German.

meaning: to remember (to do something); to think about it.
additional_notes: Uses the da- form to refer back to something: daran = "about it" / "of it". Very common with an infinitive + zu for things you must remember to do: "Ich muss daran denken, ...". With a clause it can mean "think about (how/that...)": "daran denken, wie/dass ...".
target_language_example: Ich muss daran denken, den Brief abzuschicken.
native_language_example: I have to remember to send the letter.

meaning: to remember (it/that); to remind someone (of it/that).
additional_notes:
Used in two common patterns:
1) **sich daran erinnern** = “to remember (it/that)”: *Ich kann mich daran erinnern, dass …* / *Kannst du dich daran erinnern?*
2) **jemanden daran erinnern** = “to remind someone (of it/that/to do something)”: *Erinnerst du mich daran, …?* / *Tom musste Maria daran erinnern, dem Hund Futter zu geben.*
**daran** refers back to something already known (“it/that”). The verb is often followed by **dass** (that-clause) or **zu** (to do something).
target_language_example: Kannst du mich bitte daran erinnern, den Termin zu buchen?
native_language_example: Can you please remind me to book the appointment?

meaning: “(have) thought about it” / “(have) remembered to (do it)”
additional_notes: Past participle of the phrase "an etwas denken" (to think of/about something). "daran" refers back to an idea/thing, or to an action that follows, often with "zu" + infinitive: "Hast du daran gedacht, ... zu ...?" = "Have you thought about/remembered to ...?" It can mean either considering an idea (e.g., moving abroad) or remembering a task (e.g., telling someone).
target_language_example: Hast du daran gedacht, den Arzttermin abzusagen?
native_language_example: Did you remember to cancel the doctor’s appointment?

target_language_multi_word_term: daran gedacht, die Fenster … (zu schließen / zuzumachen / abzuschließen)
meaning: remembered to … the windows (close / shut / lock).
additional_notes: Used to ask/check whether someone remembered to do something: „Hast du daran gedacht, …?“ = “Did you remember to …?” The „daran“ refers to the action that follows (often with „zu“ + infinitive). Common verbs here: „schließen“ (close), „zumachen“ (shut/close, everyday), „abschließen“ (lock).
target_language_example: Hast du daran gedacht, die Fenster abzuschließen?
native_language_example: Did you remember to lock the windows?

additional_notes: Usually used as the reflexive verb phrase **sich daran gewöhnen** (= to get used to it). **daran** refers back to something already mentioned (like “to it/that”). You can also say **sich an + Akkusativ gewöhnen**: *Ich gewöhne mich an den Lärm.*
target_language_example: Am Anfang war es schwer, aber ich werde mich daran gewöhnen.
native_language_example: At first it was hard, but I’ll get used to it.

meaning: used to it / accustomed to it.
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of the reflexive verb phrase „sich an etwas gewöhnen“ (to get used to something). „daran“ is a pronominal adverb meaning “to it/that,” referring back to something already mentioned. „gewöhnt“ is the past participle; common forms: „Ich habe mich daran gewöhnt.“ (I got used to it.) / „Hast du dich (schon) daran gewöhnt, …?“ (Have you (already) gotten used to …?) / „Daran gewöhnt ihr euch.“ (You’ll get used to it.).
target_language_example: Ich habe mich schnell daran gewöhnt.
native_language_example: I got used to it quickly.

meaning: to believe in it; to have faith in that.
additional_notes: Used with the pronominal adverb "daran" (= "in that/it") to refer back to an idea, plan, or goal. Often used with a "dass" clause: "daran glauben, dass ...". Word order can vary (e.g., "Ich muss daran glauben"), but the core term is "daran glauben".
target_language_example: Wir müssen daran glauben, dass wir gewinnen können.
native_language_example: We have to believe that we can win.

meaning: interested in it / interested in doing that.
additional_notes: Used with a reference to something mentioned before or a following action. "daran" literally means "on that/at that" and often refers to a clause with "zu" (e.g., "daran interessiert, das zu tun") or a thing already known from context ("daran interessiert sein"). Common forms: "(nicht) daran interessiert sein" = "to be (not) interested in it"; questions like "Woran bist du interessiert?" = "What are you interested in?"
target_language_example: Ich bin daran interessiert, Deutsch zu lernen.
native_language_example: I’m interested in learning German.

meaning: to be to blame for it; to be responsible for that (in a negative sense).
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something caused a problem or bad outcome. "daran" refers back to something previously mentioned (a situation, mistake, accident, etc.). Common patterns: "Ich bin daran schuld." / "Er ist daran schuld." / "Wer ist daran schuld?" You may also see the related structure "an etwas schuld sein" (e.g., "an dem Unfall schuld sein").
target_language_example: Ich will nicht, dass du denkst, ich würde daran schuld sein.
native_language_example: I don't want you to think that I'd be to blame for it.

meaning: to remember it/that; to remind (someone) of it/that.
additional_notes: Uses the pronominal adverb "daran" (= "of it/that", referring back to something already mentioned). Common with reflexive "sich erinnern": "Ich versuche, mich daran zu erinnern" (I’m trying to remember it). With a person as the object (often with "um …"), it means "to remind": "Ich rufe an, um dich daran zu erinnern" (I’m calling to remind you). Often appears in the structure "(um) … daran zu erinnern".
target_language_example: Ich rufe an, um dich daran zu erinnern, dass wir morgen einen Termin haben.
native_language_example: I’m calling to remind you that we have an appointment tomorrow.

meaning: to doubt it / to have doubts about that
additional_notes: Used with the preposition „an“ + dative: „(an etwas) zweifeln“. „daran“ is a da-compound meaning “about it/that” (da- + an) and refers back to something already mentioned. Common patterns: „Ich fange an, daran zu zweifeln.“ (I’m starting to doubt it.) and „Ich zweifle nicht daran, dass …“ (I don’t doubt that …).
target_language_example: Ich fange an, daran zu zweifeln.
native_language_example: I’m starting to doubt it.

meaning: “that …” after verbs like “pay attention to,” “wait for,” or “insist,” using darauf as “to it/for it.”
additional_notes:
Common patterns:
- achten darauf, dass … = make sure / pay attention that …
- warten darauf, dass … = wait for … to happen
- bestehen darauf, dass … = insist that …
“Darauf” refers back to an implied “it/that,” and “dass” introduces a clause. In speech you’ll often hear: „Achte darauf, dass …“
target_language_example: Bitte achte darauf, dass du die Tür abschließt.
native_language_example: Please make sure you lock the door.

meaning: 'on that… (she/they …)' — used to introduce a dass-clause after certain verbs/phrases.
additional_notes: Used when a verb/phrase takes the preposition "auf" and then refers forward to a "dass" clause (instead of a noun). Common with: "hoffen darauf, dass …" (hope that …), "warten darauf, dass …" (wait for … to happen / wait until …), "bestehen darauf, dass …" (insist that …), "Mein Wort darauf, dass …" (I swear / My word that …). Here "sie" can mean "she" or "they" depending on context.
target_language_example: Wir verlassen uns darauf, dass sie rechtzeitig ankommt.
native_language_example: We’re counting on her to arrive on time.

meaning: 'that' (used after certain verbs where 'darauf' points forward to a following daß-clause).
additional_notes: Used when a verb takes a preposition (often "auf") and you refer forward to an entire subordinate clause. "darauf" is a pronominal adverb meaning roughly "to that / on that" and it anticipates the following clause introduced by "daß" (modern spelling: "dass"). Common patterns: "auf etwas warten" → "darauf warten, daß ..." (= to wait for ... to happen); "auf etwas kommen" → "Wie kommst du darauf, daß ...?" (= What makes you think that ...? / How do you get the idea that ...?).
target_language_example: Wie kommst du darauf, daß ich das auch müßte?
native_language_example: What makes you think that I would have to do that too?

meaning: to pay attention to (that); to be careful about; to make sure (that).
additional_notes: Used to express being mindful of something or ensuring something happens. Often followed by a clause with "dass" or an indirect question/relative clause with "was/wie/wer" etc. (e.g., "darauf achten, dass …" / "darauf achten, was …"). "Darauf" refers back to the thing you should pay attention to.
target_language_example: Du musst besonders darauf achten, was du isst und trinkst.
native_language_example: You have to pay particular attention to what you eat and drink.

meaning: to depend on that; to be what matters.
additional_notes: Used to express that something depends on a particular factor or that something is what matters. Very common in the pattern "Es kommt darauf an, ob ..." (= It depends on whether ...). Note that in many sentences the verb is split: "Es kommt ... darauf an"; when using the infinitive, it appears as the exact multi-word term "darauf ankommen".
target_language_example: Ob wir heute losfahren, kann darauf ankommen, wie das Wetter wird.
native_language_example: Whether we leave today can depend on what the weather will be like.

meaning: to answer (to that); to respond to it.
additional_notes: Used when you answer a specific thing that was just said/asked/written. "darauf" refers back to that statement/question/message (often: auf die Frage / auf das, was er gesagt hat). Common with "was/ wie soll ich darauf antworten?".
target_language_example: Sie hat noch nicht auf meine E-Mail geantwortet—ich weiß nicht, was ich darauf antworten soll.
native_language_example: She still hasn’t replied to my email—I don’t know what I should answer to that.

additional_notes: Used when you strongly demand something or won’t accept an alternative. Very common with a “dass …” clause: „Ich muss darauf bestehen, dass …“ = “I must insist that …”. It can also stand alone when the context is clear: „Ich muss (leider) darauf bestehen.“ You’ll also hear the polite reply „Wenn Sie darauf bestehen.“ = “If you insist.”
target_language_example: Ich muss darauf bestehen, dass du pünktlich kommst.
native_language_example: I must insist that you come on time.

additional_notes: Used when asking whether someone noticed/kept track of the exact time something happened. Structure: „auf etwas achten“ = to pay attention to something; „darauf“ refers back to the idea of watching/monitoring. „um wieviel Uhr“ introduces an indirect question about the time (also commonly written as „um wie viel Uhr“).
target_language_example: Haben Sie darauf geachtet, um wieviel Uhr Tom weggefahren ist?
native_language_example: Did you pay attention to what time Tom left?

darauf geachtet, wo ich meine Schlüssel

target_language_multi_word_term: darauf achten, wo ich meine Schlüssel …
meaning: to pay attention to where I left/put my keys.
additional_notes: "auf etwas achten" means "to pay attention to / watch out for something." With "darauf" ("to that"), it refers back to what follows in the sentence: "darauf achten, wo …" = paying attention to the location of something. Often used when asking someone if they noticed/remembered where something was placed.
target_language_example: Hast du darauf geachtet, wo ich meine Schlüssel hingelegt habe?
native_language_example: Did you pay attention to where I put my keys?

meaning: to point out; to indicate; to draw attention to (something).
additional_notes: Used when you want to make someone notice an important fact, rule, problem, or detail. It often takes a clause with „dass“ (e.g., „Ich möchte darauf hinweisen, dass …“) or a noun with „auf + Akkusativ“ (e.g., „… darauf hinweisen, auf den Fehler“).
target_language_example: Ich möchte darauf hinweisen, dass der Zug heute später kommt.
native_language_example: I would like to point out that the train is arriving later today.

meaning: to wait for it/that; to wait for something previously mentioned (often followed by a dass-clause).
additional_notes: Used when you don’t repeat what you’re waiting for; it refers back to something already mentioned. Common with a clause: „darauf warten, dass …“ (= to wait for … to happen). Related pattern when naming the object directly: „auf + Akk. warten“ (e.g., „auf den Bus warten“ = to wait for the bus).
target_language_example: Ich werde darauf warten, dass er zurückruft.
native_language_example: I will wait for him to call back.

meaning: toward it/that (towards the thing just mentioned).
additional_notes: Used to refer back to something already mentioned and show movement in its direction. Very common with movement verbs like „gehen“, „laufen“, „kommen“: „auf etwas zugehen“ = to walk toward something. „darauf“ replaces „auf + das/den/die …“ when the thing is already known from context (often translated as “towards it/that”).
target_language_example: Ich sah ein Licht in der Ferne und ging darauf zu.
native_language_example: I saw a light in the distance and walked toward it.

additional_notes: Used to ask for permission in a polite way. It is built from dürfen + ich. In service or very polite contexts, it can also introduce an offer, as in Wie darf ich Ihnen helfen? = "how may I help you?"
target_language_example: Darf ich hier sitzen?
native_language_example: May I sit here?

meaning: “May I … (for you)?” / “Am I allowed to … ?” (polite, formal).
additional_notes: Used with the formal dative pronoun „Ihnen“ (to you). Common at the start of polite questions when offering, asking permission, or introducing a request: „Darf ich Ihnen etwas zeigen/anbieten?“ In a shop or restaurant you also hear „Was darf ich Ihnen anbieten?“ = “What can I get you?” (very polite).
target_language_example: Darf ich Ihnen kurz helfen?
native_language_example: May I help you for a moment?

additional_notes: Used to politely ask permission before doing something involving the other person. It’s formal because it uses **Sie** (not **du**). **dürfen** = “to be allowed to / may”; **Sie** is the object (“you”) in the sentence, often followed by an infinitive: *Darf ich Sie kurz sprechen?* / *Darf ich Sie etwas fragen?*
target_language_example: Darf ich Sie kurz sprechen?
native_language_example: May I speak to you briefly?

meaning: "May I ... you?" / "Can I ... you?" (asking permission politely).
additional_notes: Used to politely ask if you’re allowed to do something involving the other person. It’s usually followed by an infinitive phrase, e.g. "Darf ich dich etwas fragen?" (May I ask you something?) or "Darf ich dich kurz stören?" (May I bother/interruption you briefly?). "dich" is informal singular "you" (to one person you address as du).
target_language_example: Darf ich dich kurz etwas fragen?
native_language_example: May I ask you something quickly?

additional_notes: Used to politely ask if it’s okay to do something for someone ("dir" = "to you" informal singular). Often followed by a verb phrase like "einen Rat geben" (give advice), "etwas anbieten" (offer something), or "jemanden vorstellen" (introduce someone).
target_language_example: Darf ich dir kurz helfen?
native_language_example: May I help you for a moment?

meaning: “May I … (you all)?” / “Am I allowed to … (to you)?”
additional_notes: Used to politely ask permission or whether something is okay. „darf“ is from „dürfen“ (to be allowed to / may), „ich“ = I, „euch“ = you (plural, informal) in the accusative or dative depending on the verb (e.g., „euch unterbrechen“ = interrupt you; „euch eine Frage stellen“ = ask you a question; „euch bringen“ = take/drive you somewhere). For one person: „darf ich dich …?“ For formal: „darf ich Sie …?“
target_language_example: Darf ich euch kurz etwas zeigen?
native_language_example: May I quickly show you (all) something?

additional_notes: Used to politely ask permission to ask a question, often before a sensitive, personal, or direct question. Typically followed by a question word (warum/was/wer/wo, etc.) or a comma and a full question. Common in formal situations; with friends you can also just ask the question directly.
target_language_example: Darf ich fragen, wie alt Sie sind?
native_language_example: May I ask how old you are?

meaning: “May I ask what …?” (polite way to start a question).
additional_notes: Very polite/formal phrase (uses the formal “Sie”). Often followed by a full question clause after “was”, e.g. “Darf ich fragen, was das bedeutet?” You can also use “darf ich fragen, was du …” with friends (informal “du”).
target_language_example: Darf ich fragen, was Sie beruflich machen?
native_language_example: May I ask what you do for a living?

meaning: “May I ask where …?” (a polite way to ask for a location).
additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect question about place. It’s polite and common with strangers or in formal situations. After „wo“ (where), the verb goes to the end: „Darf ich fragen, wo Sie wohnen?“ You can use different pronouns depending on formality: „Sie“ (formal), „ihr“ (informal plural).
target_language_example: Darf ich fragen, wo die nächste Apotheke ist?
native_language_example: May I ask where the nearest pharmacy is?

additional_notes: Used to politely ask permission. "mal" softens the request and often means "just" or "for a moment". You can use it with a verb/object ("Darf ich mal Ihren Ausweis sehen?"), or by itself when the action is clear from context ("Darf ich mal?"). Common in requests like asking to pass by: "Darf ich mal durch?" (= Can I get through?).
target_language_example: Darf ich mal kurz Ihr Handy benutzen?
native_language_example: May I use your phone for a moment?

meaning: "May I..." (polite way to ask permission to do something involving yourself).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a question to ask permission: "+ infinitive" (e.g., setzen, ausruhen, umsehen). The pronoun „mich“ is needed with reflexive verbs like „sich setzen“, „sich ausruhen“, „sich umsehen“ (often translated as “sit down,” “rest,” “look around”). „Darf ich mich mal …?“ sounds a bit more casual (“just/for a moment”). With „Sie/Ihnen“ it becomes more formal/polite: „Darf ich mich zu Ihnen setzen?“
target_language_example: Darf ich mich kurz hinsetzen?
native_language_example: May I sit down for a moment?

meaning: “may I … (for myself)?” (a polite way to ask permission).
