additional_notes: Used with verbs like „machen“ or „erledigen“ to mean washing the dishes after a meal. „Wer macht den Abwasch?“ = Who’s doing the dishes? Note: „Abwasch“ is masculine (der Abwasch); „den Abwasch“ is the accusative form after these verbs.
target_language_example: Ich mache heute Abend den Abwasch.
native_language_example: I’m doing the dishes this evening.

additional_notes: “den Alten” is the accusative masculine singular (or can refer to an elderly person in a general way). It can also be plural in context (“unter den Alten” = among the elderly/older people). Often used as a noun meaning “the old (one/person)”; depending on context it can sound neutral (“the elderly”) or familiar (“the old man” meaning someone’s dad/husband, etc.).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte den Alten anrufen und ihm Bescheid sagen?
native_language_example: Can you please call the old man and let him know?

additional_notes: This is the masculine singular definite article in the accusative case (den + Apfel). You use it when the apple is the direct object (what someone eats, cuts, steals, etc.), or after many prepositions that take accusative. In the nominative (subject), it’s "der Apfel".
target_language_example: Ich esse den Apfel.
native_language_example: I’m eating the apple.

meaning: changed jobs (switched to a different workplace).
additional_notes: Used with **wechseln** + accusative (**den Arbeitsplatz**) and usually in the perfect tense with **haben**: *Ich habe den Arbeitsplatz gewechselt.* It means you started working somewhere else (a new employer/position). In everyday speech you can also hear *den Job gewechselt*.
target_language_example: Sie hat vor kurzem den Arbeitsplatz gewechselt.
native_language_example: She changed jobs recently.

additional_notes: "Den Arm" is the masculine accusative form of "der Arm". You use it when the arm is the direct object of the verb (e.g., "den Arm brechen" = to break someone’s arm; "den Arm hinlegen/legen" = to put/lay the arm down). With body parts, German often uses the definite article (der/die/das) where English might use a possessive (my/your/his).
target_language_example: Ich habe mir den Arm verletzt.
native_language_example: I injured my arm.

additional_notes: Used with the reflexive verb pattern "sich den Arm brechen" (literally “to break oneself the arm”), meaning you broke your own arm (usually by accident). In the perfect tense it’s commonly: "Ich habe mir den Arm gebrochen" / "Hast du dir den Arm gebrochen?". Often used with time or cause: "vor drei Wochen", "beim Fußballspielen", "beim Laufen hingefallen".
target_language_example: Ich habe mir gestern den Arm gebrochen.
native_language_example: I broke my arm yesterday.

meaning: "the poor" (people who are poor) in the dative plural.
additional_notes: Used after many verbs and prepositions that take the dative case (e.g., helfen + dative: "jemandem helfen" → "den Armen helfen"; also "mit den Armen" = "with the poor"). The base form is "die Armen" (nominative/accusative plural); "den Armen" is the dative plural form.
target_language_example: Wir spenden regelmäßig den Armen in unserer Stadt.
native_language_example: We regularly donate to the poor in our city.

additional_notes: Accusative form of **der Arsch** (“ass/butt”). Used for the body part in often crude/vulgar contexts (e.g., **auf den Arsch gucken** = stare at someone’s butt; **jemandem an den Arsch fassen** = grab someone’s butt; **den Arsch zeigen/rausstrecken** = show/stick out your butt). Also appears in insulting or degrading expressions (e.g., **jemandem den Arsch lecken** = “lick someone’s ass”).
target_language_example: Hör auf, ihr auf den Arsch zu gucken.
native_language_example: Stop staring at her butt.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "anhalten" (or "halten") as in "den Atem anhalten" / "den Atem anhalten" = to stop breathing for a moment. Common in instructions (e.g., breathing exercises) and to describe suspense or nervous anticipation ("alle hielten den Atem an").
target_language_example: Bitte halten Sie kurz den Atem an.
native_language_example: Please hold your breath for a moment.

meaning: the assignment / order / mission (direct object form).
additional_notes: “den Auftrag” is the accusative form of “der Auftrag” and is used when it’s the thing being received, given, or completed. Common verbs: (einen Auftrag) bekommen/kriegen (to get an assignment), annehmen (to accept), erledigen/ausführen (to carry out), zu Ende bringen (to finish). Depending on context, it can mean a work order/contract, an official task, or a mission.
target_language_example: Ich habe den Auftrag bekommen, den Bericht bis morgen fertig zu machen.
native_language_example: I got the assignment to finish the report by tomorrow.

meaning: the eyes (dative plural, used after certain prepositions).
additional_notes: **den Augen** is the dative plural form of **die Augen** (“the eyes”). It commonly appears after dative prepositions like **mit** (“with/by”) and in set phrases like **vor den Augen** (“before someone’s eyes / right in front of them”). Also used in idioms such as **jdn. mit den Augen ausziehen** (“to undress someone with your eyes,” i.e., look at them lustfully).
target_language_example: Das Brot wird dort direkt vor den Augen zubereitet.
native_language_example: The bread is prepared right there before your eyes.

meaning: lost sight of (someone/something); lost track of.
additional_notes: Usually used with the verb phrase **„aus den Augen verlieren“**: literally “to lose from (your) eyes,” meaning you no longer see someone/something or you lose contact/lose track of them over time. Common in the perfect tense: **„Ich habe ihn aus den Augen verloren.“**
target_language_example: Nach dem Umzug habe ich meine alten Freunde aus den Augen verloren.
native_language_example: After the move, I lost track of my old friends.

meaning: 'the ball' (accusative of "der Ball"); also used in "auf den Ball" = 'to the (dance) ball'.
additional_notes: "Den Ball" is the masculine accusative form of "der Ball". You use it when the ball is the direct object (you throw/catch/kick it): "Wirf den Ball!" In the fixed phrase "auf den Ball" it means a formal dance event (a ball): "mit jemandem auf den Ball gehen" = to go to the ball with someone.
target_language_example: Kannst du den Ball fangen?
native_language_example: Can you catch the ball?

additional_notes: Used when "der Baum" is the direct object of a verb (accusative case), often with actions like climbing up/down (den Baum hinauf / den Baum herunter), cutting down (einen Baum fällen), or when something hits a tree (in den Baum einschlagen). Nominative: der Baum; accusative: den Baum.
target_language_example: Wir haben den Baum im Garten gefällt.
native_language_example: We cut down the tree in the garden.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like „geben“ (to give an order) or „haben“ (to have orders / be under orders). „Befehl“ is common in military, police, or strict hierarchical contexts. The form „den“ shows it’s masculine accusative (der Befehl → den Befehl).
target_language_example: Wer hat den Befehl gegeben?
native_language_example: Who gave the order?

meaning: “the legs” (dative plural of „die Beine“), used after many prepositions.
additional_notes: Often appears with prepositions that take the dative, e.g. an (on), mit (with), von (from), zwischen (between): „an den Beinen“ = on the legs, „mit den Beinen“ = with the legs, „von den Beinen“ = off/from the legs, „zwischen den Beinen“ = between the legs. Contrast: without a preposition you usually use accusative „die Beine“ (e.g. „Ich bewege die Beine.“).
target_language_example: Ich habe mir am Strand Sonnencreme auf den Beinen verteilt.
native_language_example: I spread sunscreen on my legs at the beach.

additional_notes: „den Berg“ is the accusative form of „der Berg“. You often see it with actions done to/with the mountain (e.g., climb it, photograph it) and with movement/direction phrases like „den Berg hinab“ (down the hill/mountain) or „den Berg hinauf“ (up the hill/mountain).
target_language_example: Wir sind den Berg hinaufgelaufen.
native_language_example: We ran up the hill/mountain.

additional_notes: Used after prepositions that take the dative (often for location or direction): „auf den Bergen“ = (up) in/on the mountains, „hinter den Bergen“ = behind the mountains, „zu den Bergen“ = to the mountains. Base form: „die Berge“ (the mountains).
target_language_example: Wir fahren morgen zu den Bergen.
native_language_example: We’re going to the mountains tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used when “the report” is the direct object of the verb (e.g., write/read/look at a report). The base form is **der Bericht** (nominative); in the accusative masculine it becomes **den Bericht**.
target_language_example: Ich muss den Bericht heute noch fertig schreiben.
native_language_example: I still have to finish writing the report today.

meaning: the ground / the floor (accusative: direct object).
additional_notes: “Boden” can mean the ground outside (earth/soil) or the floor inside. “Den Boden” is the accusative form used when the ground/floor is what the action affects (e.g., fegen = to sweep, berühren = to touch, erwärmen = to warm). With location you often see dative: “auf dem Boden” = on the floor/ground; movement onto it: “auf den Boden” = onto the floor/ground.
target_language_example: Bitte wisch den Boden in der Küche.
native_language_example: Please mop the kitchen floor.

additional_notes: „den“ is the masculine accusative form of „der“. You use „den Brief“ when the letter is the thing being read/written/answered/burned/etc. Base form: „der Brief“ = the letter. Beware: German „Brief“ means „letter“ (mail), not English „brief“ (= short).
target_language_example: Ich schreibe den Brief heute Abend.
native_language_example: I’m writing the letter this evening.

additional_notes: Uses the separable verb "abschicken" (= to send off). With a modal verb or in an infinitive construction, you often see it as "abzuschicken" at the end of the clause: "Denk daran, den Brief abzuschicken." In a main clause without an infinitive, it splits: "Ich schicke den Brief ab."
target_language_example: Ich gehe zur Post, um den Brief abzuschicken.
native_language_example: I’m going to the post office to mail the letter.

additional_notes: Used with verbs that take a direct object (accusative), especially with actions involving catching, missing, taking, or stopping a bus: „den Bus erreichen/verpassen/nehmen/stoppen“. The base form is „der Bus“ (nominative), but after many verbs it changes to „den Bus“.
target_language_example: Ich habe den Bus verpasst und bin zu spät gekommen.
native_language_example: I missed the bus and arrived late.

additional_notes: From the verb "(etw.) verpassen" = to miss (something), e.g., a bus/train/appointment. Commonly used with "haben" in the perfect tense: "Ich habe den Bus verpasst." In past narration you may see past perfect to mark an earlier event: "... weil ich den Bus verpasst hatte."
target_language_example: Ich habe den Bus verpasst.
native_language_example: I missed the bus.

additional_notes: This is the dative plural form of "die Bäume" (the trees). You often see it after prepositions that take the dative for location, e.g. "in den Bäumen" (in the trees), "auf den Bäumen" (on the trees), "zwischen den Bäumen" (between the trees).
target_language_example: Im Herbst hängen bunte Blätter an den Bäumen.
native_language_example: In autumn, colorful leaves hang on the trees.

additional_notes: Used when "Computer" is the direct object of the verb. For masculine nouns like "der Computer" (nominative), the definite article changes to "den" in the accusative (e.g., "Ich benutze den Computer.").
target_language_example: Kannst du den Computer einschalten?
native_language_example: Can you turn on the computer?

meaning: to have the impression (that); to get the feeling (that).
additional_notes: Used to express your subjective impression, not a proven fact. Often followed by a "dass" clause ("Ich habe den Eindruck, dass …") or with "von" ("Ich habe den Eindruck von …"). You can also say "Ich hatte den Eindruck" (past) or "Ich habe den Eindruck, als ob …" (as if …).
target_language_example: Ich kann mich irren, aber ich habe den Eindruck, dass er heute schlecht gelaunt ist.
native_language_example: I might be wrong, but I have the impression that he’s in a bad mood today.

meaning: 'the case' (e.g., an investigation, legal matter, or problem to handle).
additional_notes: “Den Fall” is the accusative form of “der Fall.” It’s commonly used with verbs like **einen Fall lösen** (solve a case), **sich um einen Fall kümmern** (take care of/handle a case), and **einen Fall übergeben** (hand a case over). In German, **Fall** usually means “case,” not the English “fall.”
target_language_example: Die Polizei hat den Fall noch nicht gelöst.
native_language_example: The police haven't solved the case yet.

meaning: the holidays / school break (dative plural of „die Ferien“).
additional_notes: Used with certain prepositions that take the dative, especially: „in den Ferien“ = during the holidays/during the school break, and „bis zu den Ferien“ = until the holidays. „Ferien“ is usually plural in German (like „die Sommerferien“).
target_language_example: In den Ferien besuche ich meine Familie.
native_language_example: During the holidays, I visit my family.

meaning: “the TV” / “the television” (accusative masculine form of der Fernseher).
additional_notes: Used when the TV is the direct object of the verb (e.g., turn on/off, repair, make louder). Typical verbs: den Fernseher anmachen/anstellen (turn on), ausmachen/ausstellen (turn off), lauter/leiser stellen (turn up/down).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte den Fernseher leiser stellen?
native_language_example: Can you please turn the TV down?

additional_notes: Used with separable verbs like **ausschalten** or **ausstellen**: *den Fernseher ausschalten/ausstellen* = to turn off the television. In the present tense, **aus** often goes to the end: *Ich schalte den Fernseher aus.* Imperative forms you may see: **Schalten Sie den Fernseher aus!** (formal) / **Schaltet den Fernseher aus!** (plural) / **Schalt den Fernseher aus!** (informal singular).
target_language_example: Bitte schalt den Fernseher aus.
native_language_example: Please turn off the TV.

additional_notes: Used when asking someone to switch the television off. The verb is "ausschalten" (to switch off/turn off). In main clauses with a separable verb, you’ll often see the split form: "Ich schalte den Fernseher aus." In requests, however, the full infinitive commonly appears after a modal verb: "Kannst du bitte den Fernseher ausschalten?" Formal address uses "Sie": "Könnten Sie bitte den Fernseher ausschalten?"
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte den Fernseher ausschalten? Ich möchte schlafen.
native_language_example: Can you please turn off the TV? I want to sleep.

additional_notes: Usually used with the separable verb **einschalten**: **den Fernseher einschalten**. In the present/imperative, **ein** often goes to the end: **Ich schalte den Fernseher ein. / Schalte bitte den Fernseher ein!**
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte den Fernseher einschalten?
native_language_example: Can you please turn on the TV?

meaning: “the TV quieter” → turn the TV down (lower the volume).
additional_notes: Usually used with a verb like **stellen**: **den Fernseher leiser stellen** = to lower the TV volume. Common in polite requests (e.g., **Könntest du…?**, **Würden Sie…?**).
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, könnten Sie den Fernseher leiser stellen?
native_language_example: Excuse me, could you turn the TV down?

additional_notes: Used when “the film” is the direct object (what someone liked, saw, talked about, etc.). It’s the accusative form of **der Film** → **den Film** (masculine). Common with verbs like **sehen** (to see/watch), **mögen** (to like), and in questions like **Wie fandest du den Film?** (“What did you think of the movie?”).
target_language_example: Wir haben gestern Abend den Film im Kino gesehen.
native_language_example: We watched the movie at the cinema last night.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **sehen** in the **Perfekt** (conversational past): **haben + gesehen**. The direct object is in the accusative: **den Film** (masculine). In questions and main clauses, **gesehen** typically appears at the end: *Hast du den Film gesehen?*
target_language_example: Hast du den Film gesehen?
native_language_example: Have you seen the movie?

meaning: 'the fingers' (dative plural), often after prepositions like *mit* or *zwischen*.
additional_notes: You usually see **den Fingern** in phrases like **mit den Fingern** (“with your fingers”) or **zwischen den Fingern** (“between your fingers”). It’s the dative plural form of *die Finger* used because of the preposition (*mit* always takes dative; *zwischen* is often dative for a position). Common with verbs describing touching or stroking, e.g. *mit den Fingern durchs Haar fahren* (“run your fingers through your hair”).
target_language_example: Sie drehte den Ring zwischen den Fingern.
native_language_example: She turned the ring between her fingers.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement to describe going along the length of a corridor. It often appears as a postposition after the noun phrase in the accusative (den Flur entlang). You may also see the variant with genitive before it: entlang des Flurs.
target_language_example: Wir gingen den Flur entlang bis zur Küche.
native_language_example: We walked along the hallway to the kitchen.

meaning: “the river” (accusative: the river as the object).
additional_notes: You see **den Fluss** when **der Fluss** (“the river”) is the direct object of a verb, e.g. **den Fluss überqueren** (“to cross the river”). It’s masculine: **der Fluss** (nom.), **den Fluss** (acc.).
target_language_example: Wir gehen über die Brücke und überqueren den Fluss.
native_language_example: We’re going over the bridge and crossing the river.

additional_notes: Describes movement or something stretching next to the river. With entlang, German often uses the accusative (den Fluss) when it comes after the noun: den Fluss entlang. You can swap the order and use dative: entlang dem Fluss.
target_language_example: Wir fuhren den Fluss entlang bis zur alten Brücke.
native_language_example: We drove along the river to the old bridge.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "durchschwimmen" (= to swim through/across). With "zu" it often appears after verbs like "versuchen" (to try), "schaffen" (to manage), "scheitern" (to fail), or expressions like "es fiel ihm (nicht) schwer" (it was (not) hard for him). You can swap in another place: "den See zu durchschwimmen" (to swim across the lake).
target_language_example: Sie hat es geschafft, den Fluss zu durchschwimmen.
native_language_example: She managed to swim across the river.

additional_notes: This phrase is understandable, but it’s not the most natural wording in German. More common options are: „über den Fluss schwimmen“ (swim across the river) or „den Fluss durchschwimmen“ (swim the whole way across). „zu schwimmen“ is the infinitive (“to swim”), often used after another verb (e.g., „versuchen, … zu schwimmen“ = “to try to swim …”).
target_language_example: Es ist gefährlich, den Fluss zu schwimmen.
native_language_example: It’s dangerous to swim across the river.

additional_notes: "Den Garten" is "der Garten" (garden/yard) in the accusative. You use it after many verbs when the garden is the thing being acted on (e.g., betreten = enter, gießen = water, zeigen = show) and after some prepositions that take the accusative. It often translates as "the garden" or sometimes "the yard," depending on context.
target_language_example: Ich muss den Garten heute noch gießen.
native_language_example: I still have to water the garden today.

additional_notes: Used when "smell" is the direct object of a verb (e.g., riechen, erkennen, lieben, sich an etw. gewöhnen). Often followed by "von" or "der" to say what the smell is from: "den Geruch von Kaffee" / "den Geruch der Angst". Related forms: nominative "der Geruch" (the smell), dative "dem Geruch" (to/with the smell).
target_language_example: Ich kann den Geruch von Rauch nicht ausstehen.
native_language_example: I can't stand the smell of smoke.

additional_notes: Used when someone knows, gives, asks for, or explains a reason/cause: den Grund nennen/kennen/erklären. Also appears in the fixed phrase „bis auf den Grund“ = “down to the ground / completely” (e.g., „bis auf den Grund niederbrennen“ = “burn down completely”).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir den Grund sagen?
native_language_example: Can you tell me the reason?

additional_notes: Used after many verbs and in common fixed expressions. Examples: jdm ein Messer an den Hals halten (“hold a knife to someone’s throat”), sich jdm an den Hals werfen (“throw yourself around someone’s neck” = hug them passionately), jdm den Hals umdrehen (threat: “wring someone’s neck”), sich den Hals abschneiden / brechen (idioms meaning to ruin yourself / break your neck, not usually literal). Also used for everyday actions: sich den Hals waschen (“wash your neck”).
target_language_example: Ich habe mir den Hals gewaschen.
native_language_example: I washed my neck.

additional_notes: In German, *Hausaufgaben* (“homework”) is usually used in the plural. *Den Hausaufgaben* is the dative plural form, commonly used after dative verbs like **widmen** (“to devote”) and after prepositions like **nach** (“after”): *nach den Hausaufgaben* = “after (doing) the homework.”
target_language_example: Ich helfe dir nach den Hausaufgaben.
native_language_example: I’ll help you after the homework.

meaning: to help with the homework (to help someone with their homework).
additional_notes: This wording is grammatically possible but less idiomatic than **jemandem bei den Hausaufgaben helfen**. You’ll most often hear: *Kannst du mir bei den Hausaufgaben helfen?* In the given term, **zu helfen** is an infinitive used with another verb (often *versuchen, anbieten, Zeit haben*). **helfen** takes the **dative** for the person being helped (e.g., *mir/dir/ihr*). The homework part is commonly expressed with **bei + dative** (*bei den Hausaufgaben*).
target_language_example: Ich versuche, dir heute Abend den Hausaufgaben zu helfen.
native_language_example: I’m trying to help you with the homework this evening.

additional_notes: Used as the direct object (accusative) after verbs like "betrachten" (to look at/observe) or "sehen" (to see): "den Himmel betrachten" = to look at the sky. Depending on context, "Himmel" can mean the physical sky or (in religious contexts) heaven.
target_language_example: Nachts kann man den Himmel voller Sterne sehen.
native_language_example: At night you can see the sky full of stars.

additional_notes: „Hintern“ is a common, fairly informal word for someone’s butt. You’ll often see it in fixed expressions like „den Hintern retten“ (“save (our) asses”) or with movement/impact: „auf den Hintern fallen/fliegen“ (“fall/land on your butt”). It’s used with different cases depending on the verb (e.g., accusative „auf den Hintern“ with direction/impact; dative „auf dem Hintern“ with location). It can sound rude if translated as “ass,” so choose tone based on context.
target_language_example: Beeil dich, wir müssen den Hintern retten!
native_language_example: Hurry up, we have to save our asses!

additional_notes: "Hof" has a few common meanings. In everyday situations it often means an inner courtyard/yard (e.g., windows look onto the courtyard; search the yard; sweep the yard). In rural contexts it can mean a farmer’s whole place/holding (the farmstead), so "den Hof verkaufen/aufgeben" = to sell/give up the farm. Also appears in the fixed phrase "jemandem den Hof machen" = to court/woo someone (not literally "make the yard").
target_language_example: Die Kinder spielen im Hof, und später muss ich den Hof fegen.
native_language_example: The kids are playing in the courtyard, and later I have to sweep the yard.

additional_notes: "den" is the masculine accusative form of "der". You use "den Hund" when the dog is the direct object of the verb (the one being petted, found, taught, etc.). In the nominative (subject) it’s "der Hund".
target_language_example: Ich sehe den Hund im Park.
native_language_example: I see the dog in the park.

meaning: 'the dog bark' (used in patterns like 'hear/let/make the dog bark').
additional_notes: Used with verbs like hören/sehen (to hear/see) or lassen (to let/make): the dog is the direct object (den Hund) and the action stays in the infinitive (bellen). Common patterns: „Er hört den Hund bellen.“ (= He hears the dog bark.) / „Der Lärm lässt den Hund bellen.“ (= The noise makes the dog bark.)
target_language_example: Er hörte den Hund bellen.
native_language_example: He heard the dog bark.

meaning: 'the hands' (dative plural); used after certain prepositions like in/mit/bei/aus.
additional_notes: Most commonly appears in set patterns with prepositions: **in den Händen** = in (someone’s) hands; **mit den Händen** = with (your) hands/using your hands; **bei den Händen (halten)** = hold (someone) by the hands; **aus den Händen** = out of (someone’s) hands (often with verbs like *nehmen, schlagen, reißen*). Often refers literally to holding something, but can also imply control/possession (something is “in someone’s hands”).
target_language_example: Gib mir das bitte nicht aus den Händen!
native_language_example: Please don’t take that out of my hands!

additional_notes: “Hügel” means “hill” (a smaller, gentler rise than a “Berg” = mountain). You often see “den Hügel” after verbs of motion to show direction/goal, especially with: “auf den Hügel” (onto/up to the hill), “den Hügel hinauf” (up the hill), “den Hügel hinunter” (down the hill). Without movement (location), German typically uses dative: “auf dem Hügel” = “on the hill.”
target_language_example: Wir gehen den Hügel hinauf.
native_language_example: We’re walking up the hill.

additional_notes: "Den" is the masculine accusative form of "der". You use "den Islam" when Islam is the object of the verb (e.g., talk about Islam, criticize Islam, be interested in Islam). In other cases you’ll see "der Islam" (subject) or "dem Islam" (after certain prepositions/verbs).
target_language_example: Viele Menschen wissen wenig über den Islam.
native_language_example: Many people know little about Islam.

meaning: “the job” (accusative: the job as the object of the sentence).
additional_notes: Used after many verbs that take a direct object, e.g. den Job bekommen (get the job), den Job annehmen (accept the job), den Job wechseln (change jobs), den Job aufgeben (give up/quit the job). Base form: der Job (nominative), ein Job (a job).
target_language_example: Ich will den Job nicht aufgeben.
native_language_example: I don’t want to give up the job.

additional_notes: Used when the boy is the direct object (the person something happens to, or who someone knows/sees). It’s the accusative form of “der Junge” → “den Jungen”. In relative clauses you may see it with “der …” (e.g., “den Jungen, der …”).
target_language_example: Ich sehe den Jungen jeden Tag auf dem Weg zur Schule.
native_language_example: I see the boy every day on the way to school.

additional_notes: Used when "the boy" is the direct object (accusative: den Jungen) and you add extra information with a relative clause. The relative pronoun "der" refers back to "der Junge" and starts the relative clause; the verb in the relative clause usually goes to the end (e.g., „… der dort drüben steht“).
target_language_example: Ich sehe den Jungen, der neben dem Fenster steht.
native_language_example: I see the boy who is standing next to the window.

additional_notes: Used when "Kampf" is the direct object (what someone prepares for, goes into, or wins): sich auf den Kampf vorbereiten (prepare for the fight), in den Kampf ziehen (go into battle), den Kampf gewinnen (win the fight). In the examples it’s often about military fighting, but it can also mean a struggle/contest more generally (e.g., der Kampf gegen den Krebs = the fight against cancer).
target_language_example: Wir müssen uns auf den Kampf vorbereiten.
native_language_example: We have to prepare for the fight.

additional_notes: Used with „probieren“ to ask whether someone has tasted a specific food. In questions you’ll often see it as: „Hast/Haben … den Kartoffelsalat probiert?“ Adding „mal“ makes it sound more casual/soft, like “ever/once”: „Hast du mal … probiert?“ („den Kartoffelsalat“ is accusative, the direct object of „probieren“.)
target_language_example: Hast du den Kartoffelsalat probiert?
native_language_example: Have you tried the potato salad?

additional_notes: “Der Keller” means basement/cellar. It becomes “den Keller” in the accusative case, often after verbs that take a direct object (e.g., durchsuchen = to search) or with movement/direction (e.g., in den Keller = down into the basement). Contrast: “im Keller” = in the basement (location, dative).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte den Keller aufräumen?
native_language_example: Can you please tidy up the basement?

meaning: “the guy / that guy” (often a rough or dismissive way to say “man”).
additional_notes: “Der Kerl” means “guy/fellow,” and “den Kerl” is the accusative form used when he is the direct object (e.g., someone catches him, grabs him, keeps him away). It can sound impolite or hostile depending on tone and context (like talking about a suspect or someone you’re angry at).
target_language_example: Die Polizei hat den Kerl endlich erwischt.
native_language_example: The police finally caught the guy.

meaning: to the children (dative plural of "die Kinder").
additional_notes: Used when the children are the indirect object/recipient (who something is said/told/brought/ordered). Common with verbs like sagen (to say/tell), erzählen (to tell), bringen/mitbringen (to bring), and befehlen (to order). Contrast: "die Kinder" = the children (nominative/accusative).
target_language_example: Ich gebe den Kindern heute ein Eis.
native_language_example: I'm giving the children an ice cream today.

additional_notes: „Knast“ is an informal word for prison/jail. „Den“ shows masculine accusative case, often used after verbs like „in den Knast kommen“ (to go to jail) or „jemanden in den Knast bringen“ (to send someone to jail). The more neutral terms are „das Gefängnis“ or „das Gefängnis“ (prison).
target_language_example: Wenn du das nochmal machst, kommst du in den Knast.
native_language_example: If you do that again, you’ll go to jail.

meaning: “the button” (direct object: the one you press).
additional_notes: "Den Knopf" is the accusative form of "der Knopf" and is used after many verbs like "drücken" (to press): "den Knopf drücken" = to press the button. Often used in instructions and warnings ("Bitte...", "nicht...").
target_language_example: Wenn es brennt, drücken Sie den Knopf.
native_language_example: If there’s a fire, press the button.

additional_notes: Often used with a reflexive pronoun: „sich den Knöchel verstauchen“ = to sprain one’s ankle. Structure: „Ich habe mir den Knöchel verstaucht.“ (mir = to myself, dative; den Knöchel = the ankle, accusative). You can add context with „beim …“ (e.g., „beim Wandern“ = while hiking).
target_language_example: Ich habe mir gestern beim Sport den Knöchel verstaucht.
native_language_example: I sprained my ankle yesterday while playing sports.

additional_notes: “Koffer” is a masculine noun. “Den Koffer” is the accusative form, used when the suitcase is the object of the verb (e.g., den Koffer nehmen/tragen/packen/aufmachen/schließen/hinstellen). In polite requests you might hear: “Den Koffer, bitte.”
target_language_example: Kannst du den Koffer ins Auto stellen?
native_language_example: Can you put the suitcase in the car?

additional_notes: You see **den Kopf** when *Kopf* is the direct object or follows many prepositions that take the accusative, especially with motion or direction (e.g., **an den Kopf** = to/on the head, **über den Kopf** = over the head). Common with verbs like **den Kopf drehen** (turn your head), **den Kopf wegdrehen** (turn your head away), **Wasser über den Kopf schütten** (pour water over your head), **die Hände über den Kopf machen/halten** (put/hold your hands over your head).
target_language_example: Er hob den Kopf und sah mich an.
native_language_example: He raised his head and looked at me.

additional_notes: Typically used with a reflexive dative pronoun (mir/dir/sich/uns/euch): „Ich habe mir den Kopf (an/auf etwas) geschlagen.“ It describes an accidental bump. Often you specify what you hit it on: „… an der Tür / am Schrank / an der Kante“.
target_language_example: Ich habe mir den Kopf geschlagen, als ich durch die Tür gegangen bin.
native_language_example: I hit my head when I walked through the door.

meaning: to shake your head (to show “no”, disagreement, or disbelief).
additional_notes: Used when someone disagrees, refuses, doesn’t understand, or finds something hard to believe. Often appears with words like „nur“ (just) or „leicht“ (slightly): „Er schüttelte nur den Kopf.“
target_language_example: Als ich die Nachricht hörte, musste ich den Kopf schütteln.
native_language_example: When I heard the news, I had to shake my head.

meaning: to lose your head (panic; stop thinking clearly).
additional_notes: Used when someone is getting overwhelmed, acting irrationally, or panicking—often in stressful situations. Commonly appears in negatives or warnings: „Nicht den Kopf verlieren!“ = “Don’t panic / Keep a cool head.”
target_language_example: Bleib ruhig—wir dürfen jetzt nicht den Kopf verlieren.
native_language_example: Stay calm—we mustn’t panic now.

additional_notes: Used when *war* is the direct object or after many prepositions (e.g., *gegen den Krieg* “against the war”, *in den Krieg ziehen* “go off to war”). In statements like *über den Krieg sprechen* (“talk about the war”), you’ll often see other cases too (e.g., *über den Krieg*).
target_language_example: Viele Menschen sind gegen den Krieg.
native_language_example: Many people are against the war.

additional_notes: Used when *Kuchen* is the direct object (what someone eats, tries, cuts, or divides). Common with verbs like *essen* (to eat), *probieren* (to try), *backen* (to bake), *schneiden/aufschneiden* (to cut), and *teilen/aufteilen* (to divide/share). The base form is *der Kuchen* (nominative); in the accusative it becomes *den Kuchen*.
target_language_example: Ich nehme noch ein Stück von den Kuchen.
native_language_example: I’ll have another piece of the cake.

additional_notes: Used when “the king” is the direct object of a verb (e.g., protect/kill/betray) or after certain prepositions (e.g., an den König = “to the king”). The base form is der König (the king).
target_language_example: Sie haben den König gesehen.
native_language_example: They saw the king.

additional_notes: Used when the fridge is the direct object of the verb (e.g., öffnen, reparieren, in ... stellen). Base form: der Kühlschrank (nom.), dem Kühlschrank (dat.). Often used with prepositions like in den Kühlschrank (= into the fridge).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte die Milch in den Kühlschrank stellen?
native_language_example: Can you please put the milk in the fridge?

meaning: "the shop/store"; also "the place/business" (often: the operation you run).
additional_notes: "Laden" literally means a shop/store. With verbs like "schließen" (to close) or "betreten" (to enter), it usually means a physical store. In phrases like "den Laden schmeißen" it’s a common, slightly casual way to mean "run the place/business" (not necessarily a literal shop).
target_language_example: Kannst du heute den Laden aufschließen?
native_language_example: Can you open (unlock) the shop today?

meaning: 'to the people' / 'for the people' (dative plural of "die Leute").
additional_notes: "Die Leute" means "people" (in general). "Den Leuten" is the dative plural, often used after verbs like "geben" (to give), "zeigen" (to show), and with "gefallen" (to please): "Es gefällt den Leuten" = "The people like it" (literally: "It pleases the people"). It’s also used after certain prepositions like "mit": "mit den Leuten" = "with the people".
target_language_example: Ich helfe den Leuten im Museum.
native_language_example: I help the people in the museum.

additional_notes: "Lärm" means noise—often loud, disruptive, or annoying sound. "den Lärm" is the accusative form used when it’s the direct object (e.g., after many verbs like "hören", "ertragen", or in phrases like "sich an den Lärm gewöhnen" = to get used to the noise).
target_language_example: Ich brauchte lange, um mich an den Lärm zu gewöhnen.
native_language_example: It took me a long time to get used to the noise.

additional_notes: Used when "der Mann" is the direct object of the verb (someone sees, knows, removes, looks at, hits, etc.). It’s the accusative form of "der Mann". In relative clauses, you may also see it with extra information: "den Mann, der ..." (the man who ...).
target_language_example: Ich kenne den Mann dort drüben.
native_language_example: I know the man over there.

meaning: “the person / man” or “to/for the people / humans” (depending on the case).
additional_notes:
This form appears often because **Mensch** is a “weak noun” (it often adds **-en** in the singular):
- **Accusative singular**: *den Menschen* = “the person / man (in general)”, e.g. after verbs like **machen**, **sehen**, **kennen**.
- **Dative plural**: *den Menschen* = “to/for the people/humans”, e.g. after verbs like **helfen** or in expressions like **fällt den Menschen schwer** (“is difficult for people”).
Context usually makes it clear whether it means one person/humankind (singular) or people (plural).
target_language_example: Diese Regel hilft den Menschen, sicherer zu arbeiten.
native_language_example: This rule helps people work more safely.

additional_notes: Used as the direct object (accusative) of many common verbs: den Motor ausschalten/ausmachen (turn off the engine), den Motor starten (start the engine), den Motor zerlegen (take the engine apart). It’s the accusative form of "der Motor" → "den Motor".
target_language_example: Bitte mach den Motor aus.
native_language_example: Please turn off the engine.

additional_notes: Used as the direct object after many verbs, especially in common phrases like „den Mund öffnen“ (open your mouth) and „den Mund aufmachen“ (open your mouth / speak up). „Den Mund aufmachen“ can also be figurative: to start talking, often to complain or to say something.
target_language_example: Mach bitte den Mund auf.
native_language_example: Please open your mouth.

meaning: "open your mouth"; also "speak up / say something" (often in the negative: "not say a word").
additional_notes: Used with verbs like "machen" (most common) or "halten": "Mach den Mund auf!" = open your mouth (e.g., at the doctor). Figuratively, especially with "(nicht) den Mund aufmachen", it means to (not) speak: "Er macht kaum den Mund auf" = he barely says anything. Depending on tone, it can sound like a sharp command.
target_language_example: Sag’s ruhig—mach den Mund auf!
native_language_example: Go on, say it—speak up!

meaning: to shut up; to keep your mouth shut.
additional_notes: A strong, often rude way to tell someone to stop talking (an order). Often used with sollen/müssen (e.g., „Du sollst den Mund halten!“). In polite situations, prefer softer phrases like „Bitte sei leise“ or „Könnten Sie bitte leise sein?“
target_language_example: Du sollst den Mund halten!
native_language_example: You’re supposed to shut up!

additional_notes: This isn’t usually used on its own; it’s the start of a longer phrase. "den Mund" is the accusative form of "der Mund" (the mouth), typically used after verbs like "aufmachen" (to open), e.g. "Mach den Mund auf" (Open your mouth) or in longer expressions like "den Mund und die Augen aufmachen" (literally: open your mouth and eyes; often meaning: pay attention / wake up / speak up, depending on context).
target_language_example: Mach den Mund und die Augen auf!
native_language_example: Open your mouth and eyes! (Often: Pay attention / Wake up!)

additional_notes: "Mut" means "courage" (masculine: der Mut). You often see it in phrases like "den Mut haben" (to have the courage), "den Mut finden" (to find/work up the courage), and "den Mut verlieren" (to lose courage). It’s commonly followed by "zu" + infinitive: "den Mut haben, etwas zu tun".
target_language_example: Ich habe nicht den Mut, ihn zu fragen.
native_language_example: I don't have the courage to ask him.

meaning: to have the courage (to do something).
additional_notes: Uses the noun "Mut" (courage) with the accusative article: "den Mut". Very often followed by "zu" + infinitive: "den Mut haben, etwas zu tun" (to have the courage to do something). You can also use other tenses (e.g., "Ich hatte den Mut, ...").
target_language_example: Ich will den Mut haben, ihn nach dem Weg zu fragen.
native_language_example: I want to have the courage to ask him for directions.

additional_notes: Used when trash is the direct object (accusative), often with verbs like „rausbringen“ (take out) or in the phrase „in den Müll (werfen)“ = (to throw) in the trash / to throw away. The base form is „der Müll“ (nominative).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte den Müll rausbringen?
native_language_example: Can you please take out the trash?

meaning: (to take) the trash outside / take out the trash.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like „bringen“ or „rausbringen“: „den Müll nach draußen bringen“ = take the trash outside. Very common everyday household phrase. In speech you often shorten it to „den Müll rausbringen“.
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte den Müll nach draußen bringen?
native_language_example: Can you please take out the trash?

meaning: to take the trash out (bring the garbage outside).
additional_notes: Common household chore. Usually means carrying the trash bag/bin outside (often to the outside trash can). Often used with "noch" (= still/also) and "müssen" (= have to): "Du musst noch den Müll nach draußen bringen." Can also appear with "jdn. etw. machen lassen" (= to have/let someone do something): "Lässt dich deine Mutter den Müll nach draußen bringen?"
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte den Müll nach draußen bringen?
native_language_example: Can you please take the trash out?

additional_notes: Used with the separable verb **rausbringen** (“to bring/take out”). In main clauses the **raus** part often goes to the end: **Ich bringe den Müll raus.** Common in commands: **Bring/Bringt den Müll raus!**
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte den Müll rausbringen?
native_language_example: Can you please take out the trash?

den Nagel auf den Kopf getroffen

target_language_multi_word_term: den Nagel auf den Kopf getroffen
meaning: “to hit the nail on the head” (to be exactly right).
additional_notes: Used when someone has described a situation perfectly or made an exactly correct point. Very common in both formal and informal conversations; you can change the person: „Da haben Sie …“ (formal you), „Da hast du …“ (informal you), „Er/Sie hat …“ (he/she). Often said with „Da …“ = “There/Now (with that statement) …”.
target_language_example: Mit deiner Analyse hast du den Nagel auf den Kopf getroffen.
native_language_example: With your analysis, you hit the nail on the head.

den Nagel auf den Kopf treffen

target_language_multi_word_term: den Nagel auf den Kopf treffen
meaning: to hit the nail on the head; to be exactly right.
additional_notes: An idiom used when someone has described a situation perfectly or made the correct point. Often used as a reaction to what someone just said: „Du triffst den Nagel auf den Kopf.“
target_language_example: Mit deiner Analyse wirst du den Nagel auf den Kopf treffen.
native_language_example: With your analysis, you’ll hit the nail on the head.

meaning: 'the name' (accusative: the name as the object of the sentence).
additional_notes: Used when the name is what you say, know, give, use, or mention (often after verbs like sagen, kennen, geben). With "auf den Namen + Name" it means "named/called" (e.g., "auf den Namen John" = "named John"). Also used in set phrases like "den Namen einer Blume" (the name of a flower).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir den Namen des Restaurants sagen?
native_language_example: Can you tell me the name of the restaurant?

meaning: “the name of the …” (of a masculine/neuter person or thing).
additional_notes: Used when „Name“ is in the accusative („den Namen“) and the owner is expressed with the genitive „des“ + noun/name (masculine or neuter): „den Namen des Mannes“, „den Namen des Dorfs“. For feminine nouns, you use „den Namen der …“ (e.g., „den Namen der Frau“).
target_language_example: Ich kenne den Namen des Hotels nicht.
native_language_example: I don’t know the name of the hotel.

additional_notes: This is the accusative form of **der Ofen** (“the oven”). You commonly use it after verbs like **anlassen** (leave on), **abstellen** (turn off/stop), **ausmachen** (switch off), and **ausschalten** (switch off). Example patterns: **Hast du den Ofen ausgemacht?** = “Did you turn off the oven?”
target_language_example: Ich mache den Ofen jetzt aus.
native_language_example: I’m turning off the oven now.

additional_notes: Used after certain prepositions that take the dative case, especially **mit** (“with”): **mit den Ohren** = “with (your/our) ears,” i.e., “using your ears / by ear.” You also see it in phrases like **in den Ohren** (“in your ears,” e.g., a sound ringing) and **bei den Ohren** (“by the ears”).
target_language_example: Wir hören mit den Ohren.
native_language_example: We hear with our ears.

additional_notes: Used when *Park* is the direct object or after certain prepositions, especially with motion: **durch den Park** = “through the park”, **um den Park (herum)** = “around the park”. With a place where you are (no movement), you often see dative: **im Park** = “in the park.”
target_language_example: Wir gehen heute durch den Park.
native_language_example: We’re walking through the park today.

additional_notes: "Den Plan" is used when "the plan" is the direct object of a verb (accusative), often after verbs like "ausführen" (carry out), "ändern" (change), "aufgeben/fallen lassen" (give up), or "unterstützen" (support). In nominative (as the subject) it’s "der Plan".
target_language_example: Wir müssen den Plan ändern.
native_language_example: We have to change the plan.

additional_notes: This is a sentence fragment with the verb "sehen" (to see) in the simple past: "sah" = "saw". "Den Polizisten" is the accusative form (direct object) of "der Polizist" (the police officer). This word order often appears in longer sentences (e.g., after "als" or in relative clauses), where the verb can come later.
target_language_example: Als ich den Polizisten sah, blieb ich stehen.
native_language_example: When I saw the police officer, I stopped.

additional_notes: Used when *Preis* is the direct object of a verb, especially in shopping/negotiation phrases like **über den Preis sprechen** (talk about the price) or **den Preis senken** (lower the price). In the nominative (as the subject), it’s **der Preis** (e.g., *Der Preis ist zu hoch.*).
target_language_example: Könnten Sie den Preis noch etwas senken?
native_language_example: Could you lower the price a bit more?

meaning: “the lawn / grass” (accusative: the grass/lawn as the thing affected or entered).
additional_notes: "Rasen" means a lawn or grassy area (often maintained/short grass). "den Rasen" is the accusative form (masculine): used after many verbs (e.g., mähen = to mow) and after some prepositions like "auf" (onto) or "in" (into) when there is movement (e.g., "sich auf den Rasen setzen" = sit down onto the grass). For location without movement you often see dative: "auf dem Rasen" (on the lawn).
target_language_example: Bitte nicht auf den Rasen laufen.
native_language_example: Please don’t walk on the grass.

additional_notes: Used when "the room" is the direct object of a verb, especially with movement/actions involving a room (e.g., "den Raum betreten" = to enter the room, "den Raum verlassen" = to leave the room). With location (no movement), German often uses dative: "in dem Raum" = in the room.
target_language_example: Bitte verlassen Sie sofort den Raum.
native_language_example: Please leave the room immediately.

additional_notes: Used with a masculine noun: "der Rest" = the remaining part. Often followed by "von" + dative to say what it’s the rest of ("den Rest von meinem Sandwich"). In the fixed phrase "jemandem den Rest geben", it can mean "to finish someone/something off" (make the last bit of damage).
target_language_example: Ich esse den Rest später.
native_language_example: I’ll eat the rest later.

additional_notes: Accusative noun phrase meaning “the rest of your life,” used for something continuing from now until death. Addressed to one person informally (deines = “your” with du). You can swap the possessive: den Rest meines Lebens (my), den Rest seines/ihres Lebens (his/her), den Rest unseres Lebens (our), den Rest eures Lebens (your plural). Often used with verbs like verbringen (to spend) or bleiben (to stay).
target_language_example: Hast du wirklich vor, den Rest deines Lebens hier zu verbringen?
native_language_example: Do you really intend to spend the rest of your life here?

meaning: “the rest of the …” (with a feminine or plural noun in the genitive).
additional_notes: Used when “the rest” (den Rest, accusative) is the object, followed by what it’s the rest *of* in the genitive: der Geschichte (feminine), der Pizza (feminine), der Eimer (plural). For masculine/neuter nouns you usually say **den Rest des …** (e.g., den Rest des Kuchens). You may also see **der Rest der/des …** when “the rest” is the subject.
target_language_example: Ich esse später den Rest der Suppe.
native_language_example: I’ll eat the rest of the soup later.

meaning: “the rest of the …” (the remaining part of something).
additional_notes: Used to talk about what remains of a route, time period, food, etc. It’s often an accusative object with masculine "Rest" (den Rest). The thing that remains is in the genitive after it: "des" + noun (e.g., "den Rest des Weges", "den Rest des Kuchens").
target_language_example: Ich mache den Rest des Tages zu Hause weiter.
native_language_example: I’ll continue the rest of the day at home.

additional_notes: Means the remaining time from now (or from a mentioned point) until the end of the day. Often used with what someone does or how they feel for that remaining period: „Ich schlafe den Rest des Tages“ (I sleep for the rest of the day). You’ll also see it with a time reference: „Nach der Arbeit habe ich den Rest des Tages frei.“
target_language_example: Ich bleibe den Rest des Tages zu Hause.
native_language_example: I’m staying at home for the rest of the day.

meaning: the rest of his life (for the remainder of his lifetime).
additional_notes: Used to say that something continues from now (or from a certain point in the past) until someone dies. The possessive pronoun changes with the person: den Rest meines/deines/ihres/unseres/eures Lebens. Often used with verbs like verbringen (spend) or bereuen (regret).
target_language_example: Er wird das für den Rest seines Lebens bereuen.
native_language_example: He will regret that for the rest of his life.

additional_notes: "Den Ring" is used when "the ring" is the direct object of a verb (e.g., have, take, bring, mention): "Ich habe den Ring." The base form is "der Ring" (nominative/subject), and you often see it in phrases like "den Ring nehmen" (to take the ring), "den Ring bringen" (to bring the ring), or "den Ring vom Finger nehmen" (to take the ring off your finger).
target_language_example: Gib mir bitte den Ring.
native_language_example: Please give me the ring.

additional_notes: Used with many common verbs and idioms. Literal uses include physical actions or sensations on the back: über den Rücken laufen (to run down/over someone’s back), den Rücken kratzen (scratch someone’s back), Schweiß läuft über den Rücken (sweat runs down the back). In expressions like „Es lief mir kalt den Rücken herunter“, it means a shiver ran down your spine (you feel sudden fear/disgust). „Jemandem den Rücken zudrehen“ means to turn your back on someone, and „jemandem ein Messer in den Rücken stoßen“ is an idiom meaning to stab someone in the back (betray them).
target_language_example: Als ich das hörte, lief es mir kalt den Rücken herunter.
native_language_example: When I heard that, a shiver ran down my spine.

additional_notes: Used in many common expressions: „sich in den Schlaf weinen“ = to cry oneself to sleep; „um den Schlaf gebracht“ = deprived of sleep/kept from sleeping; „den Schlaf finden“ = to get to sleep; „sich den Schlaf aus den Augen reiben“ = to rub the sleep out of one’s eyes (when you’ve just woken up).
target_language_example: Nach dem langen Flug konnte ich endlich den Schlaf finden.
native_language_example: After the long flight, I could finally get to sleep.

additional_notes: You use **den Schlüssel** after many verbs when the key is the thing being acted on (e.g., *behalten* = keep, *geben* = give, *nehmen* = take). It’s **accusative masculine singular**; the dictionary form is **der Schlüssel** (nominative).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte den Schlüssel holen?
native_language_example: Can you please get the key?

additional_notes: Used when *der See* is the direct object (e.g., *Wir überquerten den See*) or after certain prepositions when talking about movement/direction: *in den See* = “into the lake” (going in), *an den See* = “to the lake/shore”. For location (no movement), German often uses dative: *im See* (“in the lake”), *am See* (“at the lake”). Note: *der See* = “lake” (not the sea). The sea is *das Meer*.
target_language_example: Wir sind ins Boot gestiegen und haben den See überquert.
native_language_example: We got into the boat and crossed the lake.

meaning: "the summer" (accusative; often used to mean "during/over the summer").
additional_notes: "Den Sommer" is the accusative form of "der Sommer". You see it after many verbs (e.g., "den Sommer verbringen" = to spend the summer) and in the common phrase "den Sommer über" = over/during the summer.
target_language_example: Wir haben den Sommer am Meer verbracht.
native_language_example: We spent the summer by the sea.

additional_notes: You use **den Spiegel** when *der Spiegel* is the direct object of a verb (e.g., **den Spiegel halten** = to hold the mirror, **den Spiegel zeigen** = to show the mirror, **den Spiegel haben** = to have the mirror). In more figurative contexts, **jemandem den Spiegel (vor)halten** means “to hold up a mirror to someone,” i.e., to make someone see the truth about themselves.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir bitte den Spiegel halten?
native_language_example: Can you please hold the mirror for me?

additional_notes: “Den Stein” is the accusative form of “der Stein” (the stone). You use it when the stone is the thing being acted on (e.g., heben = lift, werfen = throw, zurückgeben = give back, holen = get/pick up). In the nominative (subject) it’s “der Stein”.
target_language_example: Ich habe den Stein ins Wasser geworfen.
native_language_example: I threw the stone into the water.

additional_notes: “Den Sternen” is the dative plural form of “die Sterne” (the stars). It often appears after prepositions that require the dative case, especially “zu” (to), as in “zu den Sternen” (“to the stars”).
target_language_example: Nachts schaue ich oft zu den Sternen.
native_language_example: At night I often look up at the stars.

additional_notes: Used when *Strand* is the direct object (accusative), often after certain prepositions that take the accusative, e.g. **für den Strand** (“for the beach”) or **auf den Strand** (“onto the beach”). The base form is **der Strand** (“the beach”).
target_language_example: Wir gehen heute an den Strand.
native_language_example: We’re going to the beach today.

meaning: “the dough” / “the batter” (direct object form of *der Teig*).
additional_notes: *Teig* is the mixture you knead or mix for bread, pizza, cake, etc. You often see it with baking verbs like **ruhen lassen** (let rest), **gehen lassen** (let rise/proof), **teilen** (divide), and sometimes **braten** (fry/pan-cook). *Den* is the masculine accusative article used when the dough is the object of the sentence.
target_language_example: Knete den Teig kurz und lass ihn dann 30 Minuten gehen.
native_language_example: Knead the dough briefly and then let it rise for 30 minutes.

additional_notes: Used when *der Test* is the direct object (accusative), especially with verbs like **machen** (to take/do a test), **bestehen** (to pass a test), and with **sich auf … vorbereiten** (to prepare for something): *Ich bereite mich auf den Test vor.*
target_language_example: Morgen schreibe ich den Test in Mathe.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I have a math test.

additional_notes: Used when someone should repeat a test/exam. "noch mal" = "again/one more time" (also written "nochmal"). Often comes with "sollen" (should): "Du solltest den Test noch mal machen."
target_language_example: Wenn du unsicher bist, kannst du den Test noch mal machen.
native_language_example: If you’re unsure, you can take the test again.

meaning: the text; the lyrics (of a song).
additional_notes: “Den Text” is the accusative form of “der Text” and is used as the direct object (e.g., kennen/lesen/lernen den Text). In music contexts, “der Text” often means the lyrics; you can also say “der Liedtext” for “song lyrics.”
target_language_example: Ich muss den Text noch auswendig lernen.
native_language_example: I still have to memorize the lyrics/text.

meaning: “the table” (masculine, accusative/direct object form of „der Tisch“).
additional_notes: Used when the table is the direct object of a verb (e.g., „den Tisch stellen/bewegen/abräumen/decken“). With location, you often see contrasts like: „unter den Tisch“ (motion/direction, accusative) vs. „unter dem Tisch“ (location, dative).
target_language_example: Ich stelle den Tisch in die Küche.
native_language_example: I’m putting the table in the kitchen.

meaning: to clear the table (take dishes etc. away).
additional_notes:
You’ll most often see this with a separable-prefix verb: 
- **den Tisch abräumen** = clear the table (remove plates, glasses, leftovers)
- **den Tisch abwischen** = wipe the table (clean the surface)
In the examples, most sentences use **(den Tisch) abräumen**. The **ab** goes to the end in the present/imperative: **Räumen Sie den Tisch ab.**
target_language_example: Nach dem Essen räumen wir den Tisch ab.
native_language_example: After eating, we clear the table.

meaning: to clear the table (remove dishes, etc.).
additional_notes: Used after eating to mean taking plates, glasses, cutlery, and leftovers off the table (often to the kitchen). Common in polite requests: „Kannst du bitte den Tisch abräumen?“ (informal) / „Könnten Sie bitte den Tisch abräumen?“ (formal).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte den Tisch abräumen?
native_language_example: Can you please clear the table?

additional_notes: Used when preparing a table for a meal (putting out plates, cutlery, glasses, etc.). Common with helping/requests, e.g., „Hilf mir, den Tisch zu decken.“ / „Können Sie mir helfen, den Tisch zu decken?“ Note: in main clauses you’ll also hear the variant without „zu“: „Kannst du den Tisch decken?“
target_language_example: Du musst helfen, den Tisch zu decken.
native_language_example: You have to help set the table.

additional_notes: Used when *Tod* is the direct object (e.g., *den Tod fürchten* = “to fear death”). Also appears in fixed phrases like *den Tod bringen* (“to bring death”) and with nouns like *den Tod (jemandes) beklagen* (“to mourn someone’s death”).
target_language_example: Viele Menschen fürchten den Tod.
native_language_example: Many people fear death.

meaning: the sound/audio; also: the clay (in pottery).
additional_notes: "Ton" has a few common meanings. In everyday media/tech contexts it usually means "sound/audio" (e.g., turn the sound on/off, louder/quieter: "den Ton ein-/ausschalten", "den Ton lauter/leiser stellen"). In art/craft contexts, "Ton" can mean "clay" (as in the sentence about letting it glide between your fingers). In the fixed expression "den Ton angeben", it means "to set the tone" / "to call the shots".
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte den Ton leiser stellen?
native_language_example: Can you turn the sound down, please?

additional_notes: "Umschlag" usually means a (mailing) envelope. In these examples it’s something you can open, rip open ("aufreißen"), or cut open ("aufschneiden"). "Den" is the accusative masculine form of "der" and is used after many verbs like "öffnen" (to open).
target_language_example: Ich habe den Umschlag noch nicht geöffnet.
native_language_example: I haven’t opened the envelope yet.

additional_notes: This is the accusative form of **der Unfall** (“the accident”). You use **den Unfall** when the accident is the direct object, e.g. with verbs like **sehen** (to see), **erwähnen** (to mention), **sich erinnern an** (to remember), etc. In the nominative (as the subject), it’s **der Unfall**.
target_language_example: Ich habe den Unfall gestern auf der Straße gesehen.
native_language_example: I saw the accident on the street yesterday.

additional_notes: Used when someone notices, sees, understands, or points out a difference between two things. It’s the accusative form of „der Unterschied“, so it often follows verbs like „sehen“, „bemerken“, „erkennen“, „verstehen“ and phrases like „beachte …!“. In questions you’ll often hear: „Siehst/Sehen du/Sie den Unterschied?“
target_language_example: Ich sehe den Unterschied zwischen den beiden Bildern.
native_language_example: I see the difference between the two pictures.

additional_notes: Used to compare two (or more) people/things and talk about how they are not the same. Common patterns: „den Unterschied zwischen A und B“ or as a question „Was ist der Unterschied zwischen A und B?“ Note the case: „Unterschied“ often takes accusative with „den“ here.
target_language_example: Ich kenne den Unterschied zwischen „ihr“ und „Ihr“ nicht.
native_language_example: I don't know the difference between “ihr” and “Ihr”.

meaning: (to have) the suspicion that; to suspect that.
additional_notes: Usually used with "(den) Verdacht haben, dass …" to introduce a clause with "dass" (that). The noun is masculine: "der Verdacht" → in this pattern it often appears in the accusative "den Verdacht".
target_language_example: Ich habe den Verdacht, dass er mich anlügt.
native_language_example: I suspect that he’s lying to me.

meaning: (to have) lost your mind; to be crazy.
additional_notes: Used to express disbelief or criticism, often as a (rhetorical) question: „Hast du den Verstand verloren?“ = “Have you lost your mind?!” It’s strong and emotional, but not slang. Grammatically it’s the perfect tense of „den Verstand verlieren“ (to lose your mind).
target_language_example: Hast du den Verstand verloren, bei dem Wetter ohne Jacke rauszugehen?
native_language_example: Have you lost your mind, going outside without a jacket in this weather?

additional_notes: Used when a contract/agreement is the direct object (e.g., you read/sign/check it). Common verbs: „den Vertrag unterschreiben/unterzeichnen“ (to sign), „den Vertrag lesen“ (to read), „einen Blick auf den Vertrag werfen“ (to take a look at the contract). Base form: „der Vertrag“ (nominative); accusative: „den Vertrag“.
target_language_example: Ich unterschreibe den Vertrag erst morgen.
native_language_example: I’m not signing the contract until tomorrow.

meaning: “to … the contract” (usually: to sign the contract).
additional_notes: This is the start of a common structure: **den Vertrag zu + infinitive**. In your examples it’s **den Vertrag zu unterschreiben / zu unterzeichnen** (“to sign the contract”). **unterschreiben** is the everyday verb; **unterzeichnen** is more formal (often in official/legal contexts).
target_language_example: Ich habe zugestimmt, den Vertrag zu unterschreiben.
native_language_example: I agreed to sign the contract.

additional_notes: You use „den Vogel“ when the bird is the direct object of the verb (accusative), e.g. with „freilassen“ (to release), „entkommen lassen“ (to let escape), „auf … schießen“ (to shoot at), and „sich an … heranschleichen“ (to creep up on).
target_language_example: Ich habe den Vogel im Garten gesehen.
native_language_example: I saw the bird in the garden.

additional_notes: “Den Wagen” is the accusative form of “der Wagen” and is used when the car is the object of the verb (e.g., wash it, park it, drive it, pay for it). Depending on context, “Wagen” can also mean “wagon/cart,” but in everyday modern German it often refers to a (personal) car—so it can be confusing for English speakers who think of “wagon.”
target_language_example: Kannst du den Wagen heute Abend in die Garage stellen?
native_language_example: Can you put the car in the garage this evening?

additional_notes: "Wald" means "forest/woods." In many sentences it appears as "den Wald" because it’s masculine and in the accusative case (often the direct object), e.g., after verbs like "umgeben" (to surround) or when talking about going into/through a forest.
target_language_example: Wir gehen morgen durch den Wald.
native_language_example: We’re going through the forest tomorrow.

additional_notes: This is the accusative form of der Weg. It is used when Weg is the direct object, for example den Weg kennen or den Weg finden. In the expression sich in den Weg stellen, it means to stand in the way or block someone's path.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir den Weg zum Bahnhof zeigen?
native_language_example: Can you show me the way to the train station?

meaning: the way clear; (to) clear the way / make room.
additional_notes: Usually used with verbs like „machen“ or „schießen“: „Mach den Weg frei!“ = “Move/Make room!” It can be literal (clearing a path) or figurative: „Das macht den Weg frei für …“ = “That clears the way for …”.
target_language_example: Könnt ihr bitte den Weg frei machen?
native_language_example: Could you please clear the way / make room?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "laufen" + an accusative object ("den Weg") to say you covered a certain route or distance: "Ich bin den Weg gelaufen." In the Perfekt tense, "laufen" usually takes "sein" ("bin ... gelaufen"). Depending on context, "laufen" can mean either "to run" or (often in everyday speech) "to walk".
target_language_example: Ich bin den Weg gelaufen.
native_language_example: I walked the way / I ran the route.

meaning: the way to the train station.
additional_notes: Used when asking for or giving directions. Often appears with verbs like „zeigen“ (to show) or „weisen“ (to direct/point out), typically with „mir“: „Können Sie mir den Weg zum Bahnhof zeigen?“ You can swap „zum Bahnhof“ for another destination: „den Weg zum Hotel / zur Post / zur U-Bahn“.
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, können Sie mir den Weg zum Bahnhof zeigen?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you show me the way to the train station?

additional_notes: Used when the fence is the direct object of the verb (e.g., paint, repair, knock over). Many common phrases use verbs with it: „den Zaun streichen“ (paint the fence), „den Zaun reparieren“ (repair the fence). Note the case change: der Zaun (subject) → den Zaun (object).
target_language_example: Ich repariere heute den Zaun im Garten.
native_language_example: I’m repairing the fence in the garden today.

additional_notes: *Den Zoo* is used when the zoo is the direct object of a verb (e.g., *Wir besuchen den Zoo.*) or after certain prepositions that take the accusative for movement/direction (e.g., *in den Zoo* = “into/to the zoo”). The nominative form is *der Zoo* (“the zoo” as the subject).
target_language_example: Wir besuchen am Samstag den Zoo.
native_language_example: We’re visiting the zoo on Saturday.

meaning: went to the zoo / have gone to the zoo (with context).
additional_notes: This is a fragment you normally use with an auxiliary verb, usually **sein** in the perfect tense: **(Ich/Wir) sind … gegangen**. In correct German you typically say **in den Zoo gegangen** ("gone to the zoo"), because **gehen** needs a destination (often with **in + accusative** for places you go into).
target_language_example: Wir sind gestern in den Zoo gegangen.
native_language_example: We went to the zoo yesterday.

additional_notes: Used when the train is the direct object of the sentence, especially with verbs like „nehmen“ (to take), „verpassen“ (to miss), „schaffen“ (to make it), and „erreichen“ (to catch/reach in time). In the nominative, it’s „der Zug“ (e.g., „Der Zug kommt an.“).
target_language_example: Ich muss los, sonst verpasse ich den Zug.
native_language_example: I have to go, otherwise I’ll miss the train.

additional_notes: Used with the verb „verpassen“ (to miss) + an object (here: „den Zug“). Most commonly appears in the perfect tense: „Ich habe den Zug verpasst.“ Can be modified with adverbs like „gerade“ (just) or used in deductions: „Er muss den Zug verpasst haben“ (He must have missed the train).
target_language_example: Wir sind zu spät aufgestanden und haben den Zug verpasst.
native_language_example: We got up too late and missed the train.

meaning: “the others” / “the other one” (in the accusative or dative case).
additional_notes: “Den anderen” is the declined form of “die anderen / der andere” (“the others / the other one”). It often refers to people in a group: e.g., accusative after verbs like “sehen” (to see): “Du hättest den anderen sehen sollen.” It can also be dative plural (“to the others”) after verbs like “mitteilen” (to inform): “Ich werde es den anderen mitteilen.” In “von den anderen” it means “of/from the others.”
target_language_example: Kannst du den anderen bitte Bescheid sagen?
native_language_example: Can you please let the others know?

additional_notes: Used when referring to the other person/thing(s) in a pair or group, often contrasting with one already mentioned (e.g., "Den anderen Arm" = "the other arm"). It’s the accusative form of "der/die/das andere"; the ending changes with gender, number, and case (e.g., "der andere", "die andere", "das andere", "die anderen"). Common fixed phrase: "von einem Tag auf den anderen" = "from one day to the next".
target_language_example: Kannst du mir bitte den anderen Stift geben?
native_language_example: Can you please give me the other pen?

meaning: “the first” (masculine, accusative), often with an implied noun (“the first one”).
additional_notes: Used before a masculine noun in the accusative case (direct object), e.g. „den ersten Zug“ = “the first train”. It can also stand alone when the noun is understood from context (e.g., “Take the first one.”). For other genders/cases you’ll see forms like „der erste“ (masc. nom.), „die erste“ (fem.), „das erste“ (neut.).
target_language_example: Nimm bitte den ersten Bus.
native_language_example: Please take the first bus.

meaning: 'at first glance' (usually in: „auf den ersten Blick“).
additional_notes: This phrase is most commonly used with a preposition, especially „auf den ersten Blick“ = “at first glance / at first sight,” to describe a first impression before you look more closely. You’ll often see it contrasted with „aber…“ or „doch…“ when the first impression is misleading.
target_language_example: Auf den ersten Blick sieht das einfach aus, aber es ist ziemlich kompliziert.
native_language_example: At first glance it looks easy, but it’s pretty complicated.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like gewinnen (“to win”) and erhalten (“to receive”) to talk about getting the top prize in a contest. It’s in the accusative case (den) when it’s the direct object (e.g., den ersten Preis gewinnen); in the nominative you’d say der erste Preis.
target_language_example: Wer den ersten Preis gewinnt, bekommt ein Stipendium.
native_language_example: Whoever wins first prize gets a scholarship.

additional_notes: Used to say someone came in first place and received the top prize/award (often in a contest or competition). In full sentences it’s usually with a form of "haben": "Er hat den ersten Preis gewonnen." You can also specify the event with "bei" + dative: "beim Wettbewerb".
target_language_example: Sie hat beim Fotowettbewerb den ersten Preis gewonnen.
native_language_example: She won first prize in the photo contest.

meaning: the first step; making the first move.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like tun/unternehmen/machen (“to take/do”) to mean starting something—often taking initiative (e.g., being the one who reaches out, starts a conversation, begins a project). In the accusative: den ersten Schritt (e.g., den ersten Schritt tun).
target_language_example: Wenn du Hilfe brauchst, musst du den ersten Schritt tun und danach fragen.
native_language_example: If you need help, you have to take the first step and ask for it.

additional_notes: Used as the object of verbs like nehmen (take), erwischen (catch), erreichen (reach). Very often appears with um … zu + infinitive to express purpose: „Ich stand früh auf, um den ersten Zug zu nehmen.“
target_language_example: Wir müssen los, um den ersten Zug zu erwischen.
native_language_example: We have to go to catch the first train.

additional_notes: Used when a masculine noun in the accusative case is "wrong"—often with the noun stated (den falschen Zug = the wrong train), and sometimes with the noun understood from context (Ich nehme den falschen. = I’m taking the wrong one.). The base adjective is falsch = wrong/incorrect; forms change with gender/case (e.g., der falsche / die falsche / das falsche). Note: It looks like English "false," but in everyday use it usually means "wrong" rather than "false".
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich glaube, ich habe den falschen Schlüssel genommen.
native_language_example: Sorry, I think I took the wrong key.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "nehmen" (to take) in the past (Perfekt): "Ich habe den falschen Bus genommen." It means you got on the wrong bus line/direction by mistake. You can also use it with modal verbs to guess: "Sie muss den falschen Bus genommen haben" = "She must have taken the wrong bus."
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich habe den falschen Bus genommen.
native_language_example: Sorry, I took the wrong bus.

additional_notes: Usually used with "sein" in the present perfect: "Ich bin (in) den falschen Zug eingestiegen." Often includes "in" (into/onto). "den falschen Zug" is accusative (the wrong train).
target_language_example: Ich bin in den falschen Zug eingestiegen und musste umsteigen.
native_language_example: I got on the wrong train and had to change trains.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine noun in the accusative case to mean you mean all of it (not just a part). Common with time expressions and objects: den ganzen Tag (all day), den ganzen Winter (the whole winter), den ganzen Bericht (the whole report). Other forms are die ganze (fem.), das ganze (neut.), and plural die ganzen.
target_language_example: Ich habe den ganzen Tag gearbeitet.
native_language_example: I worked the whole day.

meaning: all evening; the whole evening (for the entire evening).
additional_notes: Accusative time expression meaning something lasts throughout the evening (typically from early evening until later at night). Often used with verbs like sein (to be), dauern (to last), verbringen (to spend), warten (to wait): „Ich war den ganzen Abend zu Hause.“
target_language_example: Ich habe den ganzen Abend gelernt.
native_language_example: I studied all evening.

additional_notes: Accusative form used as a direct object (e.g., with essen/aufessen). It emphasizes that none is left. The base form is “der ganze Kuchen” (nominative); after many verbs and with “den” it becomes “den ganzen Kuchen.”
target_language_example: Ich kann nicht glauben, dass du den ganzen Kuchen gegessen hast!
native_language_example: I can’t believe you ate the whole cake!

additional_notes: Used to say something happened or continued throughout the morning (from morning until around noon). It often goes with verbs like „suchen“, „arbeiten“, „sein“: „Ich war den ganzen Morgen …“. You can also use it in questions: „Warst du den ganzen Morgen …?“.
target_language_example: Ich habe den ganzen Morgen gearbeitet.
native_language_example: I worked all morning.

additional_notes: Accusative time expression meaning something lasts for the entire afternoon (duration). Often used with verbs like sein, warten, arbeiten, verbringen. You can also say "den ganzen Nachmittag über" (= all afternoon long).
target_language_example: Ich habe den ganzen Nachmittag gelernt.
native_language_example: I studied all afternoon.

additional_notes: Accusative phrase used with a time period to mean the entire duration. Very often appears with “über” (“den ganzen Sommer über” = “all summer (long)”), but it can also be used without it in many contexts.
target_language_example: Wir haben den ganzen Sommer am See verbracht.
native_language_example: We spent the whole summer at the lake.

meaning: all summer (long); throughout the whole summer.
additional_notes: Time expression meaning something lasts for the entire summer period. Often used with verbs like bleiben/sein/arbeiten, and you can swap in other time words: den ganzen Tag über, den ganzen Winter über. Word order is flexible in sentences (e.g., Ich war den ganzen Sommer über zu Hause / Den ganzen Sommer über war ich zu Hause).
target_language_example: Den ganzen Sommer über hat es kaum geregnet.
native_language_example: It barely rained all summer long.

additional_notes: Used to say something lasts throughout the day. Often answers “Wie lange?” (How long?) and is very common with verbs like arbeiten, regnen, zuhören, warten, bleiben. It’s in the accusative because it expresses duration of time (Akkusativ der Zeit).
target_language_example: Ich war den ganzen Tag zu Hause.
native_language_example: I was at home all day.

additional_notes: Used to say you spent the entire day at the beach. „den ganzen Tag“ = “the whole day” (time expression), and „am Strand“ = “at the beach” (short for „an dem Strand“). Often used with verbs like „bleiben“ (to stay), „(Zeit) verbringen“ (to spend time), or „spielen“ (to play).
target_language_example: Wir sind den ganzen Tag am Strand geblieben.
native_language_example: We stayed at the beach all day.

meaning: all day (long), spending the whole day on (something).
additional_notes: Usually used before what you’re doing, often with an "an + dative" phrase: "den ganzen Tag an etwas arbeiten/denken/sitzen" (= to work/think/sit on something all day). On its own it can feel incomplete, because it typically needs the thing you’re focusing on after "an".
target_language_example: Ich habe den ganzen Tag an dem Bericht gearbeitet.
native_language_example: I worked on the report all day long.

meaning: "all day (long) on/at …" (introduces a place/thing you’re on/at for the whole day).
