meaning: the Fourth Mistress (the man’s fourth wife/concubine in a traditional household).
additional_notes: Used as a title in historical/fictional settings (often in translations of Chinese palace/household dramas) to refer to a woman by her rank among a man’s wives/concubines. Capitalized as a form of address/title ("die vierte Herrin"), and it’s typically used with third person ("die vierte Herrin ist gekommen").
target_language_example: Die vierte Herrin möchte den Herrn jetzt sprechen.
native_language_example: The Fourth Mistress would like to speak to the master now.

additional_notes: Plural of der Arzt (“doctor”/“physician”). Used for a group of medical professionals, often in hospitals or emergencies. Singular: der Arzt (male) / die Ärztin (female). Common with verbs like sagen (say), untersuchen (examine), behandeln (treat).
target_language_example: Die Ärzte haben ihm geraten, im Krankenhaus zu bleiben.
native_language_example: The doctors advised him to stay in the hospital.

additional_notes: Feminine form of "der Arzt" (male doctor). Used for a woman who treats patients (e.g., in a clinic or hospital). Common collocations include "zur Ärztin gehen" (to go to the female doctor) and "bei der Ärztin" (at the female doctor’s office).
target_language_example: Die Ärztin untersuchte das Baby.
native_language_example: The (female) doctor examined the baby.

additional_notes: Refers to transport services that are open to everyone, such as buses, trains, subways (U-Bahn), trams (Straßenbahn), and sometimes ferries. Usually used in the plural with an article (die), often with verbs like nutzen (to use), nehmen (to take), or mit … fahren (to go by).
target_language_example: Heute nehme ich die öffentlichen Verkehrsmittel, weil es regnet.
native_language_example: Today I’m taking public transportation because it’s raining.

meaning: "those who" / "the ones that" (feminine plural or mixed group; also used for plural things).
additional_notes: Used when the second „die“ starts a relative clause: „die, die …“ = „those (people/things) who/that …“. It often refers back to a group you just mentioned or that’s understood from context. For masculine plural you’ll often see „die, die …“ as well (because plural article is „die“ for all genders); singular forms are „der, der …“ (masc.), „die, die …“ (fem.), „das, das …“ (neut.).
target_language_example: Ich vertraue den Leuten, die, die mich gut kennen, ehrlich sind.
native_language_example: I trust the people who are honest—those who know me well.

additional_notes: Used to point out a specific person or thing (feminine noun), often while gesturing: Wer ist die da? = Who is that (woman/that thing) there? It can also appear in a relative clause meaning “who/that … there”: die da singt = who is singing there. Variants: der da (masc.), das da (neut.), die da (plural).
target_language_example: Wer ist die da vor der Tür?
native_language_example: Who is that (woman) there in front of the door?

meaning: "those up there" (people up there / people in charge).
additional_notes: Often used while pointing out people/things located higher up (e.g., on the right, on a shelf, in a photo). Very commonly it also refers (often critically) to people with power or authority like "the bosses" or "politicians"—similar to "those up there" in English. Colloquial tone; can sound dismissive depending on context.
target_language_example: Die da oben haben wieder neue Regeln beschlossen.
native_language_example: Those up there have made new rules again.

additional_notes: Here, die is a pronoun meaning “they” or “those people,” not the article “the.” In many sentences, die haben introduces the German perfect tense, so it often corresponds to English simple past as well: Die haben Tom gesehen = “They saw Tom” / “They have seen Tom.” It usually refers to a specific group already known from context and can sound a bit more pointed than sie haben.
target_language_example: Die haben schon angerufen.
native_language_example: They've already called.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **haben** to say that a group possesses something or is experiencing something (**Die haben Spaß.**). **Die** here often refers to “they/those people” (a demonstrative), especially when talking about a specific group you mean from context. It takes plural verb forms: **die haben**, **die hatten**, **die haben gehabt**.
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, die haben genug Essen für alle.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, they have enough food for everyone.

additional_notes: Used at the start of a relative clause after a noun: die is a relative pronoun and ich means I. In this pattern, die usually refers back to a feminine singular noun or a plural noun, as in die Kamera, die ich gekauft habe or die Bücher, die ich gekauft habe. In English, it is often translated as that I or which I.
target_language_example: Wo ist die Tasche, die ich gestern hier gelassen habe?
native_language_example: Where is the bag that I left here yesterday?

meaning: “that I ever …” (relative clause, often after a superlative).
additional_notes: Used to say something is the most/least/etc. you have ever experienced: *die beste/schlechteste/größte …, die ich je …*. **die** is the relative pronoun (“that/which”) and changes with gender/case of the noun: *der ich je…* (masc.), *das ich je…* (neut.), *den ich je…* (acc. masc.), etc. **je** means “ever” in this kind of comparison.
target_language_example: Das ist zweifelsohne die schlechteste Mahlzeit, die ich je zu mir genommen habe.
native_language_example: That is without a doubt the worst meal I’ve ever had.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to add extra information: "...die ich kenne" = "...that/whom I know." The relative pronoun changes with gender/case and can be plural: der/die/das/den/dem… (e.g., "einer der besten Musiker, die ich kenne"; "der Mann, den ich kenne").
target_language_example: Das ist eine der nettesten Personen, die ich kenne.
native_language_example: That’s one of the nicest people I know.

meaning: "who/that" + "themselves" (introduces a relative clause with a reflexive verb).
additional_notes: Used mainly in relative clauses: "die" refers back to a noun (often plural, or feminine singular), and "sich" is the reflexive pronoun used with many verbs (e.g., sich verlieben = to fall in love, sich verkaufen lassen = to let oneself be bought/sold). In English you often translate it as "who" or "that" plus a reflexive idea ("themselves") or just a normal verb, depending on the verb.
target_language_example: Ich kenne Leute, die sich nie entschuldigen.
native_language_example: I know people who never apologize.

additional_notes: Used when referring to a group of people or things. **die** can mean **“they”** (personal pronoun) or **“those”** (demonstrative), depending on context and emphasis. Often used to point out or identify someone: *Ich will sicher sein, dass Sie die sind, die …* (“I want to be sure you’re the ones who …”).
target_language_example: Die sind schon unterwegs.
native_language_example: They’re already on the way.

meaning: "they are" with ja = emphasis ("they really are", "as you know", "after all").
additional_notes: Used when talking about “they” (die) and adding the modal particle ja to comment on the statement. ja often signals that something is obvious/expected (“after all”), or expresses surprise/emphasis (“wow, they really are…”), or a reassuring reason (“it’s fine—they’re good anyway”). The exact English translation depends on tone and context.
target_language_example: Die sind ja echt laut!
native_language_example: Wow, they’re really loud!

additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom. In many sentences, die means "they" and werden marks the future or a prediction: Die werden kommen = "They'll come." In some contexts, especially with a past participle, werden is part of the passive: Die werden benötigt = "They are needed." Also note that die can sometimes mean "those" instead of "they," depending on context.
target_language_example: Die werden das sofort merken.
native_language_example: They'll notice that right away.

additional_notes: “die” here is an informal spoken way to mean “they/those people” (often people you’ve just mentioned or are pointing to). It can sound slightly dismissive depending on tone. In more neutral/formal German you’d often say “Sie wissen, dass …”. Used before a subordinate clause with “dass” (verb goes to the end): “Die wissen, dass wir hier sind.”
target_language_example: Die wissen, dass du recht hast.
native_language_example: They know that you’re right.

additional_notes: Used to point out one specific female person and then add a relative clause. It’s the feminine singular form (nominative/accusative). Other common forms: derjenige, der (male), dasjenige, das (neuter/thing), diejenigen, die (plural). In formal address you may see it with Sie: „Sind Sie diejenige, die …?“
target_language_example: Bist du diejenige, die gestern angerufen hat?
native_language_example: Are you the one (female) who called yesterday?

additional_notes: Used to say an action/state started in the past and is still continuing. Very often followed by a time expression with „seit“ (e.g., „seit Jahren“, „seit Stunden“, „seit 2010“). With durations, German commonly uses „seit“ where English uses “for”.
target_language_example: Dies geschieht bereits seit Monaten, und niemand hat etwas dagegen unternommen.
native_language_example: This has already been happening for months, and nobody has done anything about it.

additional_notes: "Dies" is a more formal/neutral version of "das" meaning "this" (often in writing, presentations, announcements, or when emphasizing). Common patterns: "Dies ist + noun" (Dies ist mein Bruder.) and "Dies ist, was/was ..." (Dies ist, was ich meine. / Dies ist das, was ich meine.). In everyday speech, "Das ist ..." is more common.
target_language_example: Dies ist mein erstes Mal in Deutschland.
native_language_example: This is my first time in Germany.

meaning: “this is the …” (pointing out/identifying something; for a neuter noun: das).
additional_notes: Used to introduce or identify a specific thing: “This is the cinema…”. The article changes with the noun’s gender: dies ist der (masc.), dies ist die (fem.), dies ist das (neut.), dies sind die (plural). Often followed by extra information, e.g., a relative clause (…in dem…, …wo…) or a superlative (das interessanteste…).
target_language_example: Dies ist das Museum, in dem wir gestern waren.
native_language_example: This is the museum where we were yesterday.

meaning: “this is the” (used with masculine nouns, nominative).
additional_notes: Used to introduce or identify something: “This is the …”. "der" is the masculine definite article in the nominative case (the subject form). For feminine nouns you usually use "dies ist die …", and for neuter nouns "dies ist das …".
target_language_example: Dies ist der erste Schritt.
native_language_example: This is the first step.

meaning: 'this is a' (introducing a masculine or neuter noun).
additional_notes: Used to point something out or identify/introduce something: "Dies ist ein Apfelbaum." The "ein" is the indefinite article for masculine/neuter nouns in the nominative case; with feminine nouns you use "dies ist eine ...". In everyday speech, "das ist ein ..." is more common than "dies ist ein ...".
target_language_example: Dies ist ein neues Buch.
native_language_example: This is a new book.

additional_notes: Used to identify or introduce something: “This is a …”. It’s followed by a singular feminine noun (die …), so the article is “eine” (e.g., eine Blume, eine Rose). For masculine/neuter nouns use “dies ist ein …” (ein Mann / ein Haus); for plural use “dies sind …” (dies sind Blumen). In everyday speech you’ll often hear “Das ist eine …”.
target_language_example: Dies ist eine gute Idee.
native_language_example: This is a good idea.

meaning: 'this is my' (introducing or pointing out something that belongs to you).
additional_notes: Use before a masculine or neuter noun in the nominative (subject) case: "Dies ist mein Computer." For feminine nouns use "Dies ist meine ..." and for plural use "Dies sind meine ...". Common for showing ownership and for introducing people: "Helen, dies ist mein Cousin."
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, dies ist mein Platz.
native_language_example: Sorry, this is my seat.

meaning: this matter; this issue; this affair (topic/problem).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific matter or situation already known from context. Often sounds neutral to slightly formal, common in discussions, meetings, or when talking seriously about a topic (e.g., „diese Angelegenheit diskutieren“, „auf diese Angelegenheit aufmerksam machen“).
target_language_example: Wir sollten diese Angelegenheit morgen in Ruhe besprechen.
native_language_example: We should discuss this matter calmly tomorrow.

meaning: “this work” / “this job” / “this task” (referring to a specific one).
additional_notes: Used to point to a particular piece of work or a particular job you mean in the situation (often something already mentioned or currently being done). "Arbeit" can mean work in general, a job/employment, or a task/assignment; "diese" makes it specific: “this (one)”.
target_language_example: Ich kann diese Arbeit heute nicht fertig machen.
native_language_example: I can’t finish this work today.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to refer to a specific kind or type of something (often with a noun right after it: „diese Art Fehler/Waffen/Hilfe“). It can also mean a biological species in context („Diese Art ist … bedroht“). With weather and similar things, it can mean “this kind of” experience („diese Art Wetter“).
target_language_example: Diese Art Musik höre ich gern.
native_language_example: I like listening to this kind of music.

additional_notes: Used to describe a category of things: "this kind of + noun". It’s often followed by a noun in singular (e.g., diese Art von Käse) and the noun after "von" is usually in the dative in careful/formal German, though in everyday speech you may also hear other cases.
target_language_example: Ich mag diese Art von Musik.
native_language_example: I like this kind of music.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific style/genre of music you mean in the current context. Common with opinions: mögen (to like), lieben (to love), nicht mögen (to not like). Often appears as „diese Art von + Noun“ (e.g., „diese Art von Film“ = this kind of movie).
target_language_example: Ich kann diese Art von Musik nicht hören.
native_language_example: I can’t listen to this kind of music.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific task/assignment that’s clear from context (e.g., a school exercise, homework, or a work task). "Aufgabe" can mean a task to complete or an assignment to hand in; "diese" changes with gender/case (e.g., "diese Aufgabe" (nom./acc.), "dieser Aufgabe" (dat./gen.)).
target_language_example: Diese Aufgabe ist so einfach, dass ich sie lösen kann.
native_language_example: This task is so easy that I can solve it.

additional_notes: “diese” is the demonstrative/article meaning “these” (plural). Use it when pointing to or referring to specific pictures/images that are nearby, visible, or already known from context. Noun: das Bild (sing.), die Bilder (pl.).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir diese Bilder schicken?
native_language_example: Can you send me these pictures?

additional_notes: Used to describe or identify a specific flower that’s close by or being pointed at. "diese" is the feminine form of "this" (nominative singular), because "die Blume" is feminine. Often followed by an adjective (with no extra ending after "ist"): "Diese Blume ist schön/rot/blau."
target_language_example: Diese Blume ist wirklich schön.
native_language_example: This flower is really beautiful.

meaning: "these flowers" (specific flowers nearby or already mentioned).
additional_notes: "Diese" is the demonstrative/article meaning "these" for plural nouns. It’s used to point to particular flowers (often ones you can see) or flowers you’ve already talked about. In different cases you may see changes like: "Ich kaufe diese Blumen" (accusative), "mit diesen Blumen" (dative).
target_language_example: Ich nehme diese Blumen, nicht die anderen.
native_language_example: I’ll take these flowers, not the others.

additional_notes: "Diese" is the demonstrative determiner meaning "these" (plural). It’s used with plural nouns like "Briefe" (letters) to point to specific letters (often ones you can see or have already mentioned). The case changes with the sentence: e.g., nominative "Diese Briefe sind …" (subject), accusative "Ich möchte diese Briefe schicken" (direct object).
target_language_example: Kannst du diese Briefe bitte zur Post bringen?
native_language_example: Can you take these letters to the post office, please?

additional_notes: Phrase built around the past participle "gepflanzt" (from "pflanzen" = to plant). Typically used in the Perfekt tense: "haben" + "gepflanzt". Example structure: "Ich habe diese Bäume gepflanzt." In yes/no questions, the auxiliary verb comes first: "Hast du diese Bäume gepflanzt?"
target_language_example: Hast du diese Bäume gepflanzt?
native_language_example: Did you plant these trees?

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase: "diese" is the demonstrative/article for plural "Bücher" (books). Used to point out specific books nearby or already known in context. Case changes depending on role: nominative/accusative "diese Bücher" (subject/direct object), dative "diesen Büchern" (to/with these books), genitive "dieser Bücher" (of these books).
target_language_example: Kannst du diese Bücher bitte hier lassen?
native_language_example: Can you please leave these books here?

additional_notes: Refers to multiple items, actions, topics, or issues that are known from context. Often used in a general way when you don’t want to name each thing. Grammar: plural; nominative/accusative. Dative: "diesen Dingen".
target_language_example: Wir müssen diese Dinge heute erledigen.
native_language_example: We have to get these things done today.

additional_notes: "Diese" is the plural form of "this/these" for feminine nouns; "Foto" is neuter, but in the plural it becomes "die Fotos". Used to point to specific photos (e.g., ones you’re holding, showing on a phone, or already mentioned). With verbs like "sich ansehen" it often appears as "Schau dir diese Fotos an!" (look at these photos!).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir diese Fotos schicken?
native_language_example: Can you send me these photos?

meaning: "this question" (the specific question being talked about).
additional_notes: Used when referring to a particular question in the conversation or text. Often appears with verbs like beantworten (to answer) or stellen (to ask). You can also use it politely when redirecting a question: „Diese Frage richten Sie bitte an …“
target_language_example: Diese Frage kann ich leider nicht beantworten.
native_language_example: Unfortunately, I can’t answer this question.

additional_notes: Used when referring to a specific question (often one that was just asked or is in front of you, e.g., on a test). "beantworten" may look like a separable verb, but it is NOT separable. You can swap "diese" for other determiners: "die Frage beantworten" (answer the question), "eine Frage beantworten" (answer a question). In polite/formal speech, use "Können Sie …?"; informal is "Kannst du …?"
target_language_example: Können Sie diese Frage beantworten?
native_language_example: Can you answer this question?

additional_notes: Usually used with "haben" in the perfect tense: "Ich habe … diese Frage gestellt." The full pattern is "jemandem (Dat.) eine Frage stellen" = to ask someone a question (the person is in the dative: mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen).
target_language_example: Ich habe dir diese Frage gestellt, weil ich es genau wissen wollte.
native_language_example: I asked you this question because I wanted to know exactly.

meaning: "this woman" (a specific woman being pointed out or referred to).
additional_notes: "Diese" is a demonstrative determiner meaning "this" (or sometimes "that" in context). Use "diese Frau" when referring to a particular woman you mean in the situation or conversation. It changes with case: nominative/accusative "diese Frau", dative "dieser Frau", genitive "dieser Frau".
target_language_example: Ich kenne diese Frau nicht.
native_language_example: I don't know this woman.

additional_notes: Used to describe or identify a specific woman. "diese" = "this" (feminine, nominative), "Frau" = "woman", "ist" = "is" (from "sein"). What comes after can be an adjective ("… merkwürdig"), a noun/person ("… meine Tante"), or information like age ("… über achtzig").
target_language_example: Diese Frau ist sehr nett.
native_language_example: This woman is very nice.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific story, explanation, or situation that’s being discussed or has been mentioned. In everyday speech it can be slightly skeptical or dismissive, like: “Diese Geschichte ergibt keinen Sinn!” = “This doesn’t make any sense!” (literally “this story”). “diese” is the feminine demonstrative for “this,” matching “die Geschichte.”
target_language_example: Ich glaube diese Geschichte nicht.
native_language_example: I don’t believe this story.

meaning: 'this camera' (a specific camera close by or just mentioned).
additional_notes: "diese" is the demonstrative "this" used with a noun. It points to a particular camera (often one you’re holding, pointing at, or talking about). Changes with case/gender: nominative "diese Kamera"; accusative also "diese Kamera" (e.g., "Ich kaufe diese Kamera."); dative "dieser Kamera" (e.g., "Mit dieser Kamera."). In polite requests you may hear "Ich hätte gerne diese Kamera."
target_language_example: Kann ich diese Kamera ausprobieren?
native_language_example: Can I try out this camera?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific box/crate nearby or already mentioned. Often appears with verbs about moving or leaving something somewhere (e.g., lassen = leave, wegnehmen = take away, wegstellen = put away). Note: "Kiste" can also be used informally to mean an old car or something junky, but here it’s the literal box/crate.
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte diese Kiste in den Keller stellen?
native_language_example: Can you please put this box in the basement?

additional_notes: Used to describe or judge a specific box/crate you’re pointing at. Common pattern: “Diese Kiste ist (zu) schwer/leicht/groß/klein …” Often followed by “zu + adjective + zu + infinitive” to say something is too (heavy) to do something: “Diese Kiste ist zu schwer zu tragen.”
target_language_example: Diese Kiste ist zu schwer, um sie allein zu tragen.
native_language_example: This box is too heavy to carry by myself.

additional_notes: Used to point out a specific group of people that the speaker can identify from the situation or context. It’s often used when asking about or commenting on a particular group: "Kennst du diese Leute?" / "Wer sind diese Leute?" In polite speech you’ll also hear it with "Sie": "Wissen Sie, wer diese Leute sind?"
target_language_example: Warum sind diese Leute so wütend?
native_language_example: Why are these people so angry?

meaning: 'this machine' (a specific machine nearby or already mentioned).
additional_notes: Used with a feminine noun in the nominative/accusative case: diese Maschine. You use it to point to one particular machine (not any machine). In other cases it changes: dieser Maschine (dative), dieser Maschine (genitive). Often used when asking what it does or talking about how to operate it (bedienen).
target_language_example: Diese Maschine funktioniert heute nicht richtig.
native_language_example: This machine isn’t working properly today.

additional_notes: Used to point to a specific medicine that’s known from context (e.g., the one you’re holding or the one just mentioned). In other cases, it changes with case: „dieser Medizin“ (genitive/dative) and „diese Medizin“ (accusative). Often seen in instructions with „nehmen“ (to take) and dosage information.
target_language_example: Nehmen Sie diese Medizin bitte nach dem Essen.
native_language_example: Please take this medicine after eating.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "werden" to talk about what the medicine will do in the future. Pattern: "Diese Medizin wird + infinitive" (e.g., "Diese Medizin wird helfen." = "This medicine will help."). Note: "wird" can also appear in the passive ("wird gemacht" = "is made"), but here it’s the future construction.
target_language_example: Diese Medizin wird dir schnell helfen.
native_language_example: This medicine will help you quickly.

additional_notes: "Nachricht" can mean a message (text, email, voicemail) or news/information. "diese" points to a specific one (this particular message/news). Often used with verbs like bekommen/erhalten (to receive), geben/schicken (to give/send), hören (to hear), and makes sense in spy-style lines like "Diese Nachricht wird sich ... selbst zerstören".
target_language_example: Ich habe diese Nachricht gerade gelesen.
native_language_example: I just read this message.

meaning: “this person” (a specific person you’re referring to).
additional_notes: Used when you’re pointing out or referring to one particular person (often someone already known from context). It changes with gender/case (e.g., “dieser Person” in dative, “diese Person” in nominative/accusative). Common in questions like “Kennen Sie diese Person?” = “Do you know this person?”.
target_language_example: Ich kenne diese Person nicht.
native_language_example: I don’t know this person.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a particular topic, problem, event, or situation that’s already known from context or has been mentioned. It can sound slightly vague, like “this matter/this business.” Case changes depending on the verb or preposition (e.g., über diese Sache = “about this matter”).
target_language_example: Wir müssen diese Sache heute klären.
native_language_example: We need to clear up this matter today.

additional_notes: "Diese" is the plural form of "this/these" used with masculine nouns in the plural: "der Schuh" → "die Schuhe". Common in shopping or when pointing out a specific pair: "Und diese Schuhe?" / "Wie finden Sie diese Schuhe?". In "Diese Schuhe bringen mich um!" it’s an idiomatic exaggeration meaning the shoes hurt a lot (e.g., too tight).
target_language_example: Ich nehme diese Schuhe, bitte.
native_language_example: I’ll take these shoes, please.

additional_notes: Commonly used with the Perfekt tense to describe a completed purchase; it typically appears with a form of „haben“ (e.g., „habe/hast/hat/haben/habt … gekauft“). In questions, the usual word order is: question word + „haben“ (conjugated) + subject + object + past participle („gekauft“).
target_language_example: Wann hast du diese Schuhe gekauft?
native_language_example: When did you buy these shoes?

additional_notes: Used to describe shoes with an adjective or phrase after **sind** (plural of *sein* = to be). Common patterns: **Diese Schuhe sind teuer/groß/unbequem.** You can modify the adjective with words like **sehr** (very), **etwas** (a bit), or **zu** (too): **Diese Schuhe sind zu groß.**
target_language_example: Diese Schuhe sind wirklich bequem.
native_language_example: These shoes are really comfortable.

meaning: “this city” (a specific city, usually near the speaker or already known from context).
additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative article “diese” (feminine singular) + “Stadt”. It points to a particular city the speaker means (e.g., the city you are in, one on a map, or one just mentioned). Case changes with the role in the sentence: nominative “diese Stadt”, accusative “diese Stadt”, dative “dieser Stadt” (e.g., “in dieser Stadt”), genitive “dieser Stadt” (e.g., “die Einwohner dieser Stadt”).
target_language_example: Diese Stadt ist in Frankreich.
native_language_example: This city is in France.

additional_notes: Used to describe or identify a city (location, condition, atmosphere, etc.). “Diese” agrees with the feminine noun “Stadt” (die Stadt). Often followed by an adjective or a place phrase (e.g., “in den USA”). Note: “Stadt” means “city,” not “state.”
target_language_example: Diese Stadt ist sehr teuer.
native_language_example: This city is very expensive.

additional_notes: Used to point out a specific street/road that is near, visible, or already being discussed. In questions it often appears with verbs like „führen (zu)“ (to lead to) or „gehen“ (to go): „Wohin führt diese Straße?“ = “Where does this road lead?”
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, führt diese Straße zum Bahnhof?
native_language_example: Excuse me, does this street lead to the train station?

additional_notes: Used to say where a street/road goes. It’s usually followed by a destination with **zu/ zum/ zur** (e.g., *zum Bahnhof*, *zur Schule*). *führt* is from **führen** (“to lead”).
target_language_example: Diese Straße führt zur Altstadt.
native_language_example: This street leads to the old town.

additional_notes: Used to describe a specific street with an adjective or phrase after **ist** (e.g., *laut, schmal, furchtbar*). **diese** is the feminine form of “this” to match **die Straße** (feminine). Often followed by an adjective, or by a longer description with **für** (e.g., *für den Verkehr*).
target_language_example: Diese Straße ist jeden Morgen sehr voll.
native_language_example: This street is very crowded every morning.

additional_notes: Use it to describe the flavor of a specific soup. Add an adjective like gut/lecker/salzig (“good/delicious/salty”), or use **schmeckt nach + dative** to say what it tastes like (e.g., nach Fisch/Knoblauch/Wein/Zwiebeln).
target_language_example: Diese Suppe schmeckt wirklich lecker.
native_language_example: This soup tastes really delicious.

additional_notes: Used when pointing to a particular fact already mentioned or understood from context. Often appears with verbs like berücksichtigen (take into account), im Auge behalten (keep in mind), bekannt sein (be known), or leugnen (deny). In speech, you can also say simply „diese Tatsache“ to emphasize that this point matters.
target_language_example: Wir müssen diese Tatsache akzeptieren.
native_language_example: We have to accept this fact.

additional_notes: "diese" is the feminine demonstrative article meaning "this"; "Tür" (door) is feminine, so you say "diese Tür" (nominative/accusative). Used to point to a specific door nearby or obvious from context, especially in instructions or questions (e.g., "Open this door").
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte diese Tür zumachen?
native_language_example: Can you please close this door?

additional_notes: Usually used with a preposition, most commonly **auf diese Weise** = “in this way.” *Weise* here means “manner/way (of doing something),” not “wise.” You can also see **in dieser Weise** (more formal/less common).
target_language_example: Auf diese Weise sparen wir Zeit.
native_language_example: This way, we save time.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the current week (the week you are in now). It can refer to the whole week in general (past days and remaining days) depending on context.
target_language_example: Ich habe diese Woche keine Zeit.
native_language_example: I don't have time this week.

meaning: "this time" / "this period" (the time being referred to).
additional_notes: Used to point to a specific time or time period that’s clear from context. Often appears with prepositions like „um diese Zeit“ (= around this time), „in dieser Zeit“ (= during this time), or in fixed contexts like „diese Zeit im Monat“ (= that time of the month, i.e., around menstruation).
target_language_example: Um diese Zeit ist der Park fast leer.
native_language_example: Around this time, the park is almost empty.

additional_notes: Used when pointing to or referring back to exactly two items (plural). It agrees with the noun that follows: e.g., "diese beiden Hemden" (two shirts), "diese beiden Schauspieler" (two actors). You can also use it without repeating the noun if it’s clear from context: "Diese beiden passen zusammen."
target_language_example: Diese beiden Bücher sind sehr ähnlich.
native_language_example: These two books are very similar.

additional_notes: Used to compare two people: Person A goes to/attends the same school as Person B. Very common with **auf dieselbe Schule gehen** (“to go to the same school”) or **dieselbe Schule besuchen** (“to attend the same school”). You can also use it in past tense: **hat dieselbe Schule wie ich besucht** (“attended the same school as me”).
target_language_example: Ich gehe auf dieselbe Schule wie meine Schwester.
native_language_example: I go to the same school as my sister.

additional_notes: „Diesem Buch“ is used when the noun „Buch“ is in the dative case, often after common dative prepositions like „mit“ (with), „von“ (from/about), and „unter“ (under, in a location sense), or in expressions like „viel von etwas halten“ (to think highly of something).
target_language_example: Ich lerne gerade mit diesem Buch für die Prüfung.
native_language_example: I’m studying for the exam with this book.

meaning: “this case” (dative), usually in the phrase “in diesem Fall” = “in this case”.
additional_notes: “diesem” is the dative form of “dieser” (this). You most often see “diesem Fall” after a preposition that requires dative, especially “in diesem Fall” (“in this case”) when talking about what happens in a particular situation.
target_language_example: In diesem Fall ruf bitte die Polizei.
native_language_example: In this case, please call the police.

additional_notes: Dative form of "dieses Gebiet" (from "das Gebiet" = area/region; also used figuratively for a subject area or professional field). Common after prepositions like "in" or "auf" when they indicate location/area: "in diesem Gebiet" = in this area; "auf diesem Gebiet" = in this field.
target_language_example: In diesem Gebiet gibt es viele Wanderwege.
native_language_example: In this area there are many hiking trails.

additional_notes: Used when "Haus" is in the dative case, often after certain prepositions. Common patterns: "in diesem Haus" = "in this house" (location), "von diesem Haus" = "of/from this house." The base form is "dieses Haus" (nominative/accusative).
target_language_example: In diesem Haus gibt es drei Wohnungen.
native_language_example: There are three apartments in this house.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition "in": "in diesem Jahr" = "this year." "Diesem" is the dative form of "dieses" because "in" takes dative when it means a time period (not movement). You can also say "dieses Jahr" without "in" (e.g., "Dieses Jahr ist der Sommer heiß").
target_language_example: In diesem Jahr mache ich Urlaub in Deutschland.
native_language_example: This year I'm going on vacation in Germany.

additional_notes: Used when "Laden" (shop/store) is in the dative case—often after prepositions like in, bei, aus, mit, zu, or after certain verbs. Base form: "dieser Laden" (nominative). Note: German "Laden" is not the same as English "laden" (= loaded).
target_language_example: Ich kaufe oft in diesem Laden ein.
native_language_example: I often shop in this store.

additional_notes: “Diesem Land” is the dative form of “dieses Land” (“this country/land”). It often appears after certain prepositions (e.g., in, aus, zu) and with verbs like “gefallen” (to like/appeal to): “Was gefällt dir an diesem Land?” = “What do you like about this country?”
target_language_example: In diesem Land spricht man Deutsch.
native_language_example: In this country people speak German.

meaning: (usually in: „in diesem Moment“) “at this moment / right now”.
additional_notes: You’ll most often see this as **„in diesem Moment“** (“at this moment”). Because **in** is used for a time point here, German uses the **dative**: **in + diesem Moment** (not *dieser Moment*). Often used to make a scene feel immediate: “In this moment, …”.
target_language_example: In diesem Moment habe ich keine Zeit.
native_language_example: At this moment I don’t have time.

additional_notes: “Diesem” is the dative form of “dieser” used with the masculine noun “der Raum” (room/space). You often see “diesem Raum” after prepositions that take the dative, like **in diesem Raum** (in this room), **aus diesem Raum** (out of this room), **zu diesem Raum** (to this room), **mit diesem Raum** (with this room). It can also appear as an indirect object.
target_language_example: In diesem Raum ist es sehr ruhig.
native_language_example: It’s very quiet in this room.

additional_notes: “diesem” is the dative form of “dieser” (this). You use “diesem Restaurant” after many prepositions that take the dative (e.g., in, bei, zu, nach) or as an indirect object. In English you’ll often translate it as “in/at/to this restaurant,” depending on the preposition and context.
target_language_example: Wir essen heute in diesem Restaurant.
native_language_example: We’re eating in this restaurant today.

additional_notes: “diesem Tag” is the dative form of “dieser Tag” (“this day”). You often see it after prepositions that take the dative, e.g. **an diesem Tag** (“on this day”), **seit diesem Tag** (“since that day”), and **von diesem Tag an** (“from this day on”).
target_language_example: An diesem Tag habe ich zum ersten Mal Deutsch gesprochen.
native_language_example: On that day I spoke German for the first time.

additional_notes: "diesem Thema" is the dative form of "dieses Thema". It’s often used after prepositions like "bei" (with/when it comes to), "zu" (on the topic of), and some verbs that take dative (e.g., "sich mit etwas auskennen" = to know a lot about something).
target_language_example: Bei diesem Thema bin ich mir nicht sicher.
native_language_example: I’m not sure about this topic.

additional_notes: Used when "this room" is the object of a dative-taking preposition (common here: "aus diesem Zimmer" = out of/from this room, "zu diesem Zimmer" = to this room) or when the sentence requires dative. Base form: "dieses Zimmer" (nominative/accusative). "diesem" is the dative form of "dieses" for neuter nouns like "das Zimmer".
target_language_example: Ich komme gerade aus diesem Zimmer.
native_language_example: I'm just coming out of this room.

additional_notes: A verb phrase using the past participle **gepflanzt** (from **pflanzen** = “to plant”). In the **Perfekt** past tense it’s usually **hat ... gepflanzt** (with **haben**): *Er hat diesen Baum gepflanzt.* **Diesen Baum** is accusative (“this tree” as the direct object). Often used in questions like **Wer hat diesen Baum gepflanzt?** (“Who planted this tree?”).
target_language_example: Mein Großvater hat diesen Baum gepflanzt.
native_language_example: My grandfather planted this tree.

additional_notes: Used when "der Bericht" (report) is the direct object of the verb (e.g., write, correct, translate, discuss). "diesen" is the accusative masculine form of "dieser" (this). In the nominative you’d say "dieser Bericht" (this report).
target_language_example: Ich habe diesen Bericht gestern fertig geschrieben.
native_language_example: I finished writing this report yesterday.

additional_notes: Used when the letter is the direct object (what you give, read, send, answer, etc.). It’s the accusative masculine form of the demonstrative/article: der Brief → diesen Brief. Common with verbs like geben (to give), lesen (to read), schicken/senden (to send), beantworten (to answer).
target_language_example: Kannst du diesen Brief bitte zur Post bringen?
native_language_example: Can you take this letter to the post office, please?

meaning: "this letter for me" / "this letter on my behalf".
additional_notes: Used as the object in polite requests asking someone to mail a specific letter for you. "Diesen Brief" is accusative (direct object). "für mich" here means "for me / on my behalf" (i.e., you want the other person to do the mailing). Often used with verbs like "abschicken", "abschicken/absenden", or with "aufgeben" (to post at the post office) and separable forms like "abschicken"/"abschicken" and "abschicken" with "ab" (e.g., "Schick ... ab!").
target_language_example: Kannst du diesen Brief für mich abschicken?
native_language_example: Can you mail this letter for me?

additional_notes: Used with the Perfekt tense: **haben** + **geschrieben**. **Diesen Brief** is the direct object (accusative) meaning “this letter.” You’ll often hear it in questions, e.g. **Für wen/Wem haben Sie diesen Brief geschrieben?** (“for whom/to whom did you write this letter?”) and **Wo haben Sie diesen Brief geschrieben?** (“where did you write this letter?”). Note: **Brief** means “letter,” not “brief” (a false friend).
target_language_example: Für wen haben Sie diesen Brief geschrieben?
native_language_example: Who did you write this letter for?

additional_notes: Used when the noun is the direct object of the verb (e.g., sehen, mögen, hassen): *Ich sehe diesen Film.* Depending on context, *Film* can mean a movie or a roll of photographic film; in a photo shop/lab, *diesen Film entwickeln und drucken* means “develop and print this roll of film.”
target_language_example: Ich möchte diesen Film heute Abend sehen.
native_language_example: I want to watch this movie tonight.

additional_notes: “diesen” is the dative plural form of “diese” (“these”). You use “diesen Leuten” after many prepositions that take the dative case, e.g. **mit** (with), **bei** (with/at), **von** (from/of), **unter** (among), to refer to a specific group of people in the situation/context.
target_language_example: Ich will mit diesen Leuten nichts zu tun haben.
native_language_example: I don’t want to have anything to do with these people.

additional_notes: Used when the man is the direct object of the verb (masculine accusative): e.g., „Ich kenne diesen Mann.“ It often points to a specific man (like “this man here/that man we’re talking about”). Nominative would be „dieser Mann“ (as the subject).
target_language_example: Ich habe diesen Mann gestern im Park gesehen.
native_language_example: I saw this man in the park yesterday.

meaning: "this place" (accusative: the place as the object of the sentence).
additional_notes: "Diesen" is the masculine accusative form of "dieser" (this), used with "der Ort" (place/location). You use "diesen Ort" after many verbs that take a direct object (e.g., besuchen, kennen, hassen, beschreiben). If it’s the subject, you’d say "dieser Ort" (e.g., "Dieser Ort ist schön.").
target_language_example: Ich möchte diesen Ort noch einmal besuchen.
native_language_example: I’d like to visit this place one more time.

additional_notes: Used when the sentence is the direct object of the verb (accusative), often with requests/commands: „Diesen Satz bitte …“ (e.g., delete/rewrite/translate this sentence). In nominative it’s „dieser Satz“ (this sentence as the subject).
target_language_example: Kannst du diesen Satz bitte wiederholen?
native_language_example: Can you repeat this sentence, please?

additional_notes: Used when asking someone to translate a specific sentence. Common in questions with polite forms: "Könnten Sie diesen Satz übersetzen?" (formal) vs. "Könntest du diesen Satz übersetzen?" (informal). You can add a person in the dative with "mir/uns": "Könntest du mir diesen Satz übersetzen?" = "Could you translate this sentence for me?"
target_language_example: Könntest du diesen Satz übersetzen?
native_language_example: Could you translate this sentence?

meaning: this summer (referring to the current/coming summer).
additional_notes: Accusative time phrase meaning “this summer.” Used to say when something happens or is planned (often about plans for the upcoming summer, but it can also refer to the summer that just happened in context). Common with future intentions: „Ich will/werde diesen Sommer …“
target_language_example: Diesen Sommer fahren wir nach Italien.
native_language_example: This summer we’re going to Italy.

additional_notes: "Angelegenheit" means a matter/issue/affair (often something practical or official). "dieser" is the dative feminine form of "dies-" because it’s used after "bei" (bei + dative). Common pattern: "bei dieser Angelegenheit" = "with/on this matter".
target_language_example: Kannst du mir bei dieser Angelegenheit bitte helfen?
native_language_example: Can you please help me with this matter?

additional_notes: Used to describe a specific apple. **dieser** = “this” (masculine, nominative) and **ist** = “is”. Often followed by an adjective (groß, rot, schlecht, etc.).
target_language_example: Dieser Apfel ist süß.
native_language_example: This apple is sweet.

additional_notes: "dieser" is the masculine nominative form of "this" (used with masculine nouns like "der Baum"). Often used while pointing something out ("hier" = "here"). In questions: "Wie alt ist dieser Baum?" = "How old is this tree?"
target_language_example: Schau mal, dieser Baum hat schon keine Blätter mehr.
native_language_example: Look, this tree doesn’t have any leaves anymore.

additional_notes: Used to describe or compare a specific tree. "dieser" means "this" (masculine nominative singular, agreeing with "der Baum"). Often followed by an adjective, age/height information, or a comparison like "so … wie" (as … as) or "… als" (… than).
target_language_example: Dieser Baum ist sehr hoch.
native_language_example: This tree is very tall.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific letter you’re talking about or holding. "dieser" is the masculine nominative singular form of "dies-" (this) because "Brief" is masculine (der Brief). In other cases it changes, e.g. accusative: "Ich habe diesen Brief bekommen."
target_language_example: Dieser Brief trägt keine Unterschrift.
native_language_example: This letter has no signature.

meaning: "this movie/this film" (referring to a specific film).
additional_notes: Used to point out or refer back to a particular movie that’s clear from the context (e.g., the one you’re watching or just mentioned). "Dieser" is the masculine nominative form of "dies-" (this) because "der Film" is masculine. In other cases you’ll see forms like "diesen Film" (accusative) or "diesem Film" (dative).
target_language_example: Dieser Film ist viel besser als der letzte.
native_language_example: This movie is much better than the last one.

additional_notes: Used to introduce information about a film (e.g., a description, opinion, or dedication). "Dieser" is a demonstrative/article meaning “this” (nominative masculine), and "ist" is “is.” Often followed by an adjective ("sehenswert"), a noun phrase, or "… gewidmet" (“dedicated to …”).
target_language_example: Dieser Film ist sehr spannend.
native_language_example: This film is very exciting.

additional_notes: "Gegend" means an area or region (often like a neighborhood or part of a city). "dieser Gegend" is the dative form of "diese Gegend" and is commonly used after prepositions like "in" (in this area) and "aus" (from this area), and in expressions like "sich in dieser Gegend auskennen" (to know your way around this area).
target_language_example: Ich wohne schon lange in dieser Gegend.
native_language_example: I've lived in this area for a long time.

meaning: "this dog is" (used to describe a dog).
additional_notes: Used to make statements about a specific dog. "dieser" = "this" (masculine, nominative singular, used with "Hund"); "ist" is the 3rd person singular of "sein" (to be). Often followed by an adjective or description: "Dieser Hund ist groß / nicht zu verkaufen / voller Zecken."
target_language_example: Dieser Hund ist sehr freundlich.
native_language_example: This dog is very friendly.

meaning: this boy; that boy (referring to a specific boy).
additional_notes: Used to point out or refer back to a particular boy in context. In speech, stress/intonation often shows whether it means “this boy here” vs “that boy (we’re talking about)”. Case changes with grammar: nominative dieser Junge, accusative diesen Jungen, dative diesem Jungen, genitive dieses Jungen.
target_language_example: Dieser Junge dort heißt Lukas.
native_language_example: That boy over there is called Lukas.

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative pronoun "dieser" (= this) with the masculine noun "Mann". It points to a particular man you mean (often someone present, visible, or already mentioned). In questions you often hear: "Wer ist dieser Mann?". For other cases: "diesem Mann" (to/for this man), "diesen Mann" (this man as the direct object).
target_language_example: Dieser Mann dort ist mein Nachbar.
native_language_example: That man over there is my neighbor.

meaning: 'this man is …' (introducing/identifying a man and describing him).
additional_notes: Used before a noun (often without an article for jobs/nationalities: „Dieser Mann ist Chinese/Anwalt.“), a name („… ist Tom.“), an adjective („… ist lebendig/unfähig.“), or a state/condition („… ist in Panik.“ / „… ist seit fünf Jahren blind.“). „Dieser“ points to a specific man (often one you can see or have mentioned).
target_language_example: Dieser Mann ist mein Nachbar.
native_language_example: This man is my neighbor.

additional_notes: Used to describe or evaluate a specific coat. It’s typically followed by an adjective (e.g., „altmodisch“, „wasserdicht“) or by „zu + adjective“ meaning “too …” (e.g., „zu klein“, „zu teuer“). In „Dieser Mantel ist mir zu klein“, „mir“ (dative) means “for me” = “It’s too small for me.”
target_language_example: Dieser Mantel ist sehr warm.
native_language_example: This coat is very warm.

additional_notes: Used to describe a place that is close/known in the context. "Dieser Ort" is masculine (der Ort), so it takes "dieser". You then add an adjective or description: "Dieser Ort ist laut/schmutzig/wunderbar". In speech you might also hear "Der Ort ist ..." (the place is ...) or "Dieser Platz ist ..." (this spot is ...).
target_language_example: Dieser Ort ist perfekt für einen Spaziergang.
native_language_example: This place is perfect for a walk.

additional_notes: Used to describe a specific room (often the one you’re in) by adding an adjective or phrase after ist (e.g., groß/klein, ruhig, gemütlich, noch nicht renoviert). "Dieser" is the masculine form of "this" in the nominative case because "Raum" is masculine (der Raum).
target_language_example: Dieser Raum ist sehr hell.
native_language_example: This room is very bright.

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative article "dieser" with the masculine noun "Roman" (novel). "Dieser" changes with case (e.g., nominative: "dieser Roman"; accusative: "diesen Roman"; dative: "diesem Roman"). Note: German "Roman" means "novel" (not something "Roman" as in Ancient Rome), so it can be a false cognate for English speakers.
target_language_example: Dieser Roman besteht aus drei Teilen.
native_language_example: This novel consists of three parts.

meaning: 'this novel is …' (used to describe or compare a novel).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence to give an opinion or a fact about a specific novel. "Dieser" is masculine nominative for "Roman" and points to a particular novel (often "this" one here / the one we’re talking about). Common patterns: "Dieser Roman ist langweilig/interessant/schwer zu verstehen", and comparisons with "… interessanter als …".
target_language_example: Dieser Roman ist spannend, aber manchmal schwer zu verstehen.
native_language_example: This novel is exciting, but sometimes hard to understand.

additional_notes: Used when pointing to a particular sentence (spoken, written, or shown on a page/screen). 'Dieser' is the masculine nominative form of 'this' and matches 'Satz' (masculine). Often appears with extra words like 'hier' to emphasize the exact sentence being referred to.
target_language_example: Weißt du, was dieser Satz hier bedeutet?
native_language_example: Do you know what this sentence here means?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a statement about the sentence itself (often in exercises, grammar explanations, or logic puzzles). “Dieser” is the masculine form of “this,” because “der Satz” (sentence) is masculine. German nouns like “Satz” are capitalized, and “ist” is the 3rd-person singular of “sein” (to be).
target_language_example: Dieser Satz ist zu lang.
native_language_example: This sentence is too long.

additional_notes: Used to describe or compare a specific desk that’s close by or clearly identified. "dieser" is a demonstrative meaning "this" (masculine nominative singular: der Schreibtisch), and "ist" is the 3rd-person singular form of "sein" (to be). Often followed by an adjective or comparison: "… ist besser/defekt/anders als …".
target_language_example: Dieser Schreibtisch ist zu klein für mein Zimmer.
native_language_example: This desk is too small for my room.

meaning: “of this city/town” (genitive: belonging to this city).
additional_notes: “dieser” is the genitive singular feminine form of “dies-” used with “die Stadt”. It’s used to show possession/association, often after another noun: “der Name dieser Stadt” = “the name of this city”. In everyday speech, Germans also often use “von dieser Stadt” instead of the genitive (“der Name von dieser Stadt”).
target_language_example: Ich kenne die Geschichte dieser Stadt nicht.
native_language_example: I don’t know the history of this city.

meaning: “this street” (in/on this street; along this street).
additional_notes:
This is the form of **diese Straße** (“this street”) used in certain cases:
- **Dative** (often after prepositions or with directions): *in dieser Straße* = “on/in this street”; *Folgen Sie dieser Straße* = “Follow this street.”
- **Genitive** (showing “of this street”): *der Name dieser Straße* = “the name of this street.”
In everyday speech, people sometimes also say *der Name von dieser Straße*.
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, wo ist die Apotheke in dieser Straße?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is the pharmacy on this street?

additional_notes: Used to describe or compare a specific chair that’s close by or clearly identified. “dieser” is the masculine nominative form of “this,” matching “der Stuhl.” It’s usually followed by an adjective (bequem, hässlich, klein) or a phrase like “aus Plastik” or a comparison like “besser als …”.
target_language_example: Dieser Stuhl ist zu unbequem für mich.
native_language_example: This chair is too uncomfortable for me.

additional_notes: Used to describe or compare a specific table. “dieser” is the masculine nominative form of “this” (because “der Tisch” is masculine). “ist” is “is” (3rd person singular of “sein”). Often followed by an adjective (sauber, schwer) or a comparison (so groß wie …).
target_language_example: Dieser Tisch ist zu klein für vier Personen.
native_language_example: This table is too small for four people.

additional_notes: "Typ" can mean a person (“guy”, often slightly casual) or a category/model (“type/kind”, common in technical/product contexts). For a more formal/neutral “this man/person,” use "dieser Mann" or "diese Person".
target_language_example: Wer ist dieser Typ da drüben?
native_language_example: Who is that guy over there?

meaning: “of this world” / “to/from this world” (depending on the preposition).
additional_notes:
“dieser Welt” is the form of “diese Welt” (“this world”) used in different cases. Commonly:
- Genitive: “(something) dieser Welt” = “(something) of this world” (e.g., “das Treiben dieser Welt” = “the hustle and bustle of this world”).
- After prepositions that take the dative, like “zu” and “von”: “zu dieser Welt” = “to this world”, “von dieser Welt” = “from this world”.
It’s also used in the pattern “die X dieser Welt” meaning “the Xs of this world” (a generalizing expression).
target_language_example: Manchmal habe ich das Gefühl, ich gehöre nicht zu dieser Welt.
native_language_example: Sometimes I feel like I don’t belong in this world.

additional_notes: A noun phrase with the demonstrative "dieser" (masculine nominative singular) + adjective "alt" + noun "Mann". Used to point to a specific old man (often someone you can see or have just mentioned). In other cases you’ll see different case forms like "diesem alten Mann" (dative) or "diesen alten Mann" (accusative).
target_language_example: Dieser alte Mann wohnt allein in dem Haus am Fluss.
native_language_example: This old man lives alone in the house by the river.

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative article "dieses" (neuter nominative/accusative) with the noun "Auto" (neuter). Common when pointing to or talking about a particular car you mean (e.g., in a comparison, description, question, or advice).
target_language_example: Dieses Auto ist sehr sparsam.
native_language_example: This car is very fuel-efficient.

additional_notes: Used to describe a specific car that’s close by or clearly identified. Add an adjective or a phrase after **ist** (e.g., a color, condition, value, or features). Note the verb agrees with **Auto** (singular): **ist**.
target_language_example: Dieses Auto ist sehr sparsam.
native_language_example: This car is very fuel-efficient.

additional_notes: "Dieses" is the neuter form of "this" (for "das Bild"). Used when pointing to or referring to a specific picture/photo/painting. In speech it’s often used with a gesture or context (e.g., on a screen, in a book, in a gallery).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir etwas über dieses Bild erzählen?
native_language_example: Can you tell me something about this picture?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "malen" (to paint). Often appears in the perfect tense as "hat dieses Bild gemalt" (has painted this picture) or in the passive voice as "wurde dieses Bild gemalt" (was this picture painted). In questions, it’s commonly used to ask who created a painting: "Wer hat dieses Bild gemalt?"
target_language_example: Wer hat dieses Bild gemalt?
native_language_example: Who painted this picture?

additional_notes: Used to point to a specific book. "dieses" is the demonstrative/article form used with the neuter singular noun "Buch"; in sentences like these, the phrase can be nominative or accusative depending on its role.
target_language_example: Ich lese dieses Buch gerade.
native_language_example: I'm reading this book right now.

additional_notes: Used to say who owns something. After gehört, the owner is in the dative case: Dieses Buch gehört Paul / der Bibliothek / euch / ihr (= to her). Note: gehört can also mean 'heard' (Ich habe das gehört), so it can be confusing.
target_language_example: Dieses Buch gehört meiner Schwester.
native_language_example: This book belongs to my sister.

additional_notes: Used with the Perfekt tense: (ich/du/er/sie/wir/ihr/sie) habe/hast/hat/haben + dieses Buch + gekauft. "dieses Buch" is accusative (the direct object). In questions, "gekauft" typically stays at the end: "Wo hast du dieses Buch gekauft?"
target_language_example: Ich habe vor drei Tagen dieses Buch gekauft.
native_language_example: I bought this book three days ago.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "haben" to form the Perfekt (past) tense: "Ich habe dieses Buch geschrieben." In questions you often hear it as "Hast du dieses Buch geschrieben?" (informal) or "Haben Sie dieses Buch geschrieben?" (formal). "geschrieben" is the past participle of "schreiben" (to write), and "dieses Buch" means "this book" (accusative object).
target_language_example: Ich habe dieses Buch geschrieben.
native_language_example: I wrote this book / I have written this book.

additional_notes: Used to describe what a book (or story, film, article, etc.) is about. The verb is **handeln von + dative**: *Das Buch handelt von einem König.* You can swap *dieses Buch* for another subject: *Der Film handelt von ...*
target_language_example: Dieses Buch handelt von einer Familie, die in die Berge zieht.
native_language_example: This book is about a family that moves to the mountains.

meaning: "this book in the …" (incomplete phrase; needs a noun after "in der").
additional_notes: "dieses Buch" means "this book". "in der" is "in the" with dative case (used with feminine nouns like "der Tasche" = "the bag", or certain locations). This expression is typically followed by a place/thing: "… in der Tasche", "… in der Schule", etc.
target_language_example: Ich habe dieses Buch in der Tasche.
native_language_example: I have this book in my bag.

additional_notes: Used to describe or identify a specific book. "Dieses" means "this" and agrees with the noun: "das Buch" (neuter, nominative) → "dieses Buch". "ist" is the 3rd-person singular form of "sein" (to be). Often followed by an adjective ("interessant"), a noun/pronoun ("meins"), or a phrase like "auf Englisch" / "in einfachem Englisch".
target_language_example: Dieses Buch ist sehr hilfreich für Anfänger.
native_language_example: This book is very helpful for beginners.

meaning: “this book is in …” / “this book is translated into …” / “this book is divided into …” (depending on what follows).
additional_notes: This is a sentence frame. After **ist in** you add the place or the “category” it goes into. Common patterns: **ist in [place] (nicht) zu haben** = “(not) available in [place]”; **ist in [language(s)] übersetzt (worden)** = “translated into [language(s)]”; **ist in [parts] unterteilt** = “divided into [parts]”. Grammar note: **in + dative** is used for location (e.g., *in Japan*), and **in + accusative** is common for “into” in these passive phrases (e.g., *in mehrere Sprachen*, *in vier Teile*).
target_language_example: Dieses Buch ist in Englisch übersetzt worden.
native_language_example: This book has been translated into English.

additional_notes: This isn’t a fixed phrase by itself; it’s usually a fragment that needs a verb in the infinitive. In German, **zu** often corresponds to English **“to”** before a verb: **dieses Buch zu lesen** = “to read this book.” You’ll commonly see this structure after verbs/adjectives like **versuchen** (to try), **vergessen** (to forget), **leicht/schwer** (easy/hard), etc.
target_language_example: Ich versuche, dieses Buch zu lesen.
native_language_example: I’m trying to read this book.

additional_notes: An infinitive phrase with „zu“ used to talk about the action in general (often with verbs like „dauern“ = to take, „lohnen“ = to be worth it, „brauchen“ = to need, or in questions). Pattern: „Es dauert …, [etwas] zu lesen“ = “It takes … to read …”.
target_language_example: Ich habe keine Zeit, dieses Buch zu lesen.
native_language_example: I don't have time to read this book.

additional_notes: An infinitive phrase with **zu** (“to …”) often used after verbs like **brauchen** (to need/take [time]) and **kosten** (to cost [someone time/effort]): *Wie lange hast du gebraucht, dieses Buch zu schreiben?* = “How long did it take you to write this book?”
target_language_example: Ich brauche noch ein paar Wochen, um dieses Buch zu schreiben.
native_language_example: I still need a few weeks to write this book.

additional_notes: This is the genitive singular of "dieses Buch". It’s used to show possession/relationship, often after another noun: "der Preis dieses Buches" (the price of this book), "die letzte Seite dieses Buches" (the last page of this book). You also see it in set phrases like "mit Hilfe dieses Buches" (with the help of this book).
target_language_example: Die Bedeutung dieses Buches ist heute noch groß.
native_language_example: The importance of this book is still great today.

meaning: “this thing” (an object you can point to, often when you don’t know or don’t want to say its name).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific item nearby or in the current situation. Often sounds slightly annoyed, casual, or dismissive depending on tone (e.g., something that doesn’t work, looks weird, or is in the way). Grammar: “dieses” matches neuter “das Ding” in nominative/accusative; in other cases you’ll see changes like “mit diesem Ding” (dative).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir bitte dieses Ding geben?
native_language_example: Can you please give me this thing?

meaning: 'this document' (a specific document you’re referring to).
additional_notes: "Dieses" is the demonstrative article meaning “this” (neuter singular), used with the noun "Dokument" (neuter). It changes with the case: nominative/accusative "dieses Dokument"; dative "diesem Dokument"; genitive "dieses Dokuments". Common in formal contexts (forms, contracts, official papers), often with verbs like "unterschreiben" (sign), "ausdrucken" (print), "abschicken" (send).
target_language_example: Bitte lesen Sie dieses Dokument sorgfältig durch.
native_language_example: Please read this document carefully.

meaning: "this document into French" (as the target language for a translation).
additional_notes: This is a phrase fragment you typically use with verbs like „übersetzen“ (to translate): „Bitte übersetzen Sie dieses Dokument ins Französische.“ „ins“ = „in das“. „(das) Französische“ is the French language (a nominalized adjective). You can also say „auf Französisch“ (= in French), but with translation requests „ins Französische“ is very common.
target_language_example: Können Sie dieses Dokument ins Französische übersetzen?
native_language_example: Can you translate this document into French?

meaning: "this form" (a document you need to fill out).
additional_notes: "Dieses" is the neuter form of "this" and is used with "das Formular" (the form). Very common in offices, applications, registrations, and appointments, often with the verb "(ein) Formular ausfüllen" = "to fill out a form."
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, wo soll ich dieses Formular abgeben?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where should I hand in this form?

additional_notes: Common in offices, doctor’s visits, hotels, and government services. Often used in polite requests with "Bitte" or "Würden Sie bitte ...?" and with "müssen" to show that it’s required. "ausfüllen" is separable (ich fülle ... aus).
target_language_example: Könnten Sie bitte dieses Formular ausfüllen und unterschreiben?
native_language_example: Could you please fill out this form and sign it?

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative article "dieses" (neuter) with "das Foto" to point to a particular photo you mean or are holding/looking at. In speech it often has emphasis: "THIS photo (not that one)". Common with verbs like "sehen" (see), "machen" (take), "ausdrucken" (print), "vergrößern" (enlarge).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir sagen, wer auf dieses Foto ist?
native_language_example: Can you tell me who is in this photo?

meaning: “this building” (a specific building nearby or being talked about).
additional_notes: “Dieses” is the neuter form of “this” (for nouns like “das Gebäude”). Used with a noun to point out or refer to a particular building; often appears with descriptions (alt/neu, hoch) or extra details (mit dem grünen Dach).
target_language_example: Kennen Sie dieses Gebäude?
native_language_example: Do you know this building?

additional_notes: "Dieses" is the demonstrative article meaning "this" (neuter nominative/accusative), used to point to a particular poem that’s being discussed, shown, or just mentioned. "Gedicht" means "poem". Common with verbs like schreiben/verfassen (to write/compose), übersetzen (to translate), and with questions like "Wer hat dieses Gedicht geschrieben?"
target_language_example: Dieses Gedicht gefällt mir sehr.
native_language_example: I like this poem a lot.

meaning: "this house" (a specific house near/known in the context).
additional_notes: "dieses" is the demonstrative word "this" used with a noun. With "Haus" (neuter), it becomes "dieses" in the nominative and accusative (e.g., "Dieses Haus ist groß." / "Ich sehe dieses Haus."). In other cases it changes: "in diesem Haus" (dative), "wegen dieses Hauses" (genitive). Often used to point out or compare one particular house.
target_language_example: Ich mag dieses Haus, aber es ist zu teuer.
native_language_example: I like this house, but it’s too expensive.

meaning: 'this house is …' (used to describe this house).
additional_notes: Use it to start a sentence describing a specific house that is close by, visible, or already known. "Dieses" is the neuter nominative form of "dieser" to match "das Haus". What follows after "ist" is typically an adjective (berühmt, unbewohnt, wunderschön), an age/measure phrase (fünfhundert Jahre alt), or something with "zu" + adjective (zu groß/zu klein).
target_language_example: Dieses Haus ist sehr teuer.
native_language_example: This house is very expensive.

additional_notes: Used to point out a specific shirt that’s near you, in your hand, or otherwise clear from context. "dieses" is the neuter form of "this" (for nouns like "das Hemd"). In other cases you’ll see: "dieser" (masculine), "diese" (feminine/plural).
target_language_example: Kann ich dieses Hemd anprobieren?
native_language_example: Can I try on this shirt?

additional_notes: Refers to the current calendar year. Often used to talk about plans, experiences, or comparisons within the same year (e.g., weather, travel, how many times something happened). You can place it at the beginning or end of a sentence: „Dieses Jahr fahre ich nach Berlin.“ / „Ich fahre dieses Jahr nach Berlin.“
target_language_example: Dieses Jahr lerne ich mehr Deutsch.
native_language_example: This year I’m learning more German.

additional_notes: Used with the perfect tense: **(ich/du/er/sie/es/wir/ihr/Sie) habe/hast/hat/haben/habt/haben dieses Jahr Weihnachtsgeschenke gekauft**. **dieses Jahr** (“this year”) is a time expression; **Weihnachtsgeschenke** means “Christmas presents/gifts”; **gekauft** is the past participle of **kaufen** (“to buy”). Common in questions with **Für wie viele Leute …?** (“For how many people …?”) or **Für wen …?** (“For whom …?”).
target_language_example: Für wie viele Leute hast du dieses Jahr Weihnachtsgeschenke gekauft?
native_language_example: For how many people have you bought Christmas presents this year?

meaning: “this dress” (referring to a specific dress near you or just mentioned).
additional_notes: Used to point out one particular dress. In a sentence, the form changes with case: nominative/accusative: „dieses Kleid“, dative: „diesem Kleid“ (e.g., „mit diesem Kleid“).
target_language_example: Ich mag dieses Kleid sehr.
native_language_example: I like this dress a lot.

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative article/pronoun "dieses" (neuter) to point to a specific place you mean (nearby, just mentioned, or obvious from context). "Land" can mean both "land" (territory) and "country"; the exact meaning depends on context. In these examples it appears as nominative or accusative: "Dieses Land gehört mir" (subject) vs. "Ich liebe dieses Land" (object).
target_language_example: Ich möchte dieses Land besser kennenlernen.
native_language_example: I want to get to know this country better.

additional_notes: Used to talk about ownership/possession. It’s often followed by the dative (the owner): „Dieses Land gehört Tom / Herrn Ikeda / ihm.“ (Tom/Mr. Ikeda/him = dative). The verb is „gehören“ = to belong; don’t confuse „gehört“ with English “heard”.
target_language_example: Dieses Land gehört meiner Familie.
native_language_example: This land belongs to my family.

meaning: “this country is …” (used to describe a country).
additional_notes: “Dieses” is a demonstrative meaning “this” before a noun; “Land” (capitalized) often means “country” in this context; “ist” is the 3rd-person singular of “sein” (to be). Commonly followed by an adjective or a phrase giving a description (size, resources, atmosphere, etc.).
target_language_example: Dieses Land ist sehr vielfältig.
native_language_example: This country is very diverse.

additional_notes: A noun phrase: "dieses" (this, referring to a specific song) + "Lied" (song). Used when pointing out one particular song in the situation or one that’s already known from context. With "singen" it means "to sing this song"; with "hören" it means "to hear/listen to this song".
target_language_example: Ich mag dieses Lied sehr.
native_language_example: I like this song a lot.

meaning: “I listen to this song” (sentence fragment; usually completed as “Dieses Lied höre ich …”).
additional_notes: German word order can put the object first for emphasis: “Dieses Lied höre ich …” = “I listen to this song …”. The verb is **hören** (“to listen/hear”); with music you often also say **(sich) etwas anhören** (“to listen to something”).
target_language_example: Dieses Lied höre ich jeden Tag.
native_language_example: I listen to this song every day.

additional_notes: Used to describe a specific song. "Dieses Lied" is the subject (nominative, neuter singular), and "ist" links it to a description (often an adjective like "schön", "traurig", "leicht zu lernen"). You can replace "dieses" with other determiners (e.g., "das Lied ist...", "mein Lied ist...") and change the verb for other tenses (e.g., "dieses Lied war...", "dieses Lied wird...").
target_language_example: Dieses Lied ist mein Lieblingslied.
native_language_example: This song is my favorite song.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the current/next occasion in contrast to other times (earlier or usual situations). Often implies “as opposed to last time / usually.” Can appear at the start of the sentence for emphasis, or in the middle: „Dieses Mal mache ich es.“ / „Es traf dieses Mal eine Journalistin.“
target_language_example: Dieses Mal komme ich pünktlich.
native_language_example: This time I’ll be on time.

additional_notes: "Dieses" is the demonstrative "this" for a neuter noun (das Medikament). Used to point to a specific medicine already known from the situation (e.g., a prescription or something the doctor is referring to). In advice/medical instructions you’ll often see it with "nehmen" (to take): "Nehmen Sie dieses Medikament …"
target_language_example: Nehmen Sie dieses Medikament zweimal täglich.
native_language_example: Take this medication twice a day.

meaning: "this medicine will" (used to say what the medicine is expected to do).
additional_notes: Often followed by a verb describing the effect of the medicine (e.g., heilen = cure, lindern = relieve, (den Schmerz) beseitigen/nehmen = remove (the pain), verschwinden lassen = make (pain) go away). It’s a neutral, common way to talk about expected results.
target_language_example: Dieses Medikament wird dir helfen, besser zu schlafen.
native_language_example: This medicine will help you sleep better.

meaning: “this girl” (referring to a specific girl nearby or just mentioned).
additional_notes: “Dieses” is the demonstrative article “this” and changes with case and gender. “Mädchen” is neuter (das Mädchen), so you get forms like: nominative/accusative: dieses Mädchen; dative: diesem Mädchen; genitive: dieses Mädchens. Used to point out or identify a particular girl (“this girl is Maria”) or to refer back to someone in context.
target_language_example: Kennst du dieses Mädchen da drüben?
native_language_example: Do you know that/this girl over there?

meaning: "this problem" (a specific issue being talked about).
additional_notes: Used to point to a particular problem that’s already known in the conversation or situation. Often appears with case endings depending on its role: nominative/accusative: „dieses Problem“; genitive: „dieses Problems“ (e.g., „die Lösung dieses Problems“); dative: „diesem Problem“ (e.g., „bei diesem Problem“).
target_language_example: Wir müssen dieses Problem heute lösen.
native_language_example: We need to solve this problem today.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a statement about a specific problem. "dieses" is the demonstrative "this" (nominative neuter, matching "das Problem"), and "ist" is the 3rd person singular of "sein" (to be). Often followed by an adjective or comparison: "Dieses Problem ist zu schwer" (too difficult), "Dieses Problem ist ebenso ... wie ..." (just as ... as ...).
target_language_example: Dieses Problem ist nicht so schwierig, wie es aussieht.
native_language_example: This problem isn’t as difficult as it looks.

additional_notes: Uses the verb „lösen“ (to solve) with an accusative object: „ein/dieses Problem lösen“. The phrase is neutral in register and common in everyday and professional contexts. You can replace the object as needed (e.g., „das Rätsel lösen“, „den Konflikt lösen“).
target_language_example: Ich kann dieses Problem lösen.
native_language_example: I can solve this problem.

additional_notes: "Zu lösen" is the infinitive phrase of "lösen" (to solve), used after adjectives and expressions like "schwierig/schwer", "Mühe haben", "helfen", or with time limits: "Ich gebe dir fünf Minuten, ...". You can replace "dieses Problem" with another noun phrase (e.g., "die Aufgabe", "das Rätsel").
target_language_example: Ich brauche Hilfe, dieses Problem zu lösen.
native_language_example: I need help to solve this problem.

meaning: "this program" (a software program, TV show, or a planned program).
additional_notes: "Dieses" is the demonstrative "this" for neuter nouns (das Programm). Use it to point to a specific program that’s clear from context: "dieses Programm" (this program) vs. "das Programm" (the program). In the examples, it refers to a particular program you like, pay for, or can use (e.g., for editing videos).
target_language_example: Dieses Programm ist sehr einfach zu benutzen.
native_language_example: This program is very easy to use.

additional_notes: Common in instructions and help texts. The verb is **benutzen** (“to use”). You’ll often see it with different forms of “you”: **du kannst** (informal singular), **Sie können** (formal), **ihr könnt** (informal plural).
target_language_example: Um die Datei zu öffnen, kannst du dieses Programm benutzen.
native_language_example: To open the file, you can use this program.

additional_notes: Used with masculine/neuter nouns in the genitive singular after a genitive article/pronoun like „dieses“. Here the base noun is „der Satz“ (masculine), so it becomes „des/dieses Satzes“ in the genitive. Common in formal/written German, often after nouns like „Übersetzung“, „Subjekt“, or when talking about reading/meaning of a sentence.
target_language_example: Die Bedeutung dieses Satzes ist nicht ganz klar.
native_language_example: The meaning of this sentence isn’t completely clear.

additional_notes: "dieses" is the demonstrative determiner "this" used with a neuter noun in the nominative/accusative singular. Use it to point out a specific game (e.g., the one you’re looking at or talking about).
target_language_example: Magst du dieses Spiel auch?
native_language_example: Do you like this game too?

meaning: "this piece" (e.g., a piece of music/theatre, a piece/part of something, or a plot of land).
additional_notes: Stück means “piece/part,” and depending on context it can refer to an artwork (ein Stück = a play; ein Musikstück = a piece of music), an object/portion (a piece of cake), or an area of land (ein Stück Land/Wüste). Dieses is the neuter form of “this” used with neuter nouns like das Stück; in other cases you may see forms like „diesem Stück“ (dative) or „dieses Stück“ (accusative).
target_language_example: Kannst du dieses Stück noch einmal spielen?
native_language_example: Can you play this piece again?

additional_notes: "Dieses" is the demonstrative "this" used with neuter nouns like "das T-Shirt". It often points to a specific item you mean or are holding/looking at (e.g., in a shop).
