If there’s an adjective before the noun, it usually takes the ending -er after "ein" in nominative masculine: "Du bist ein guter Freund." It can be positive ("ein Schatz") or insulting ("ein Idiot").
target_language_example: Du bist ein guter Freund.
native_language_example: You are a good friend.

meaning: “you are a good …” (talking about a man/masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used to compliment someone by saying they are a good friend/driver/etc. It normally needs a noun after it: „Du bist ein guter Freund.“ The adjective ending „-er“ is because it’s masculine nominative with „ein“. For feminine: „Du bist eine gute …“ (e.g., „eine gute Freundin“). For plural: „Ihr seid gute …“
target_language_example: Du bist ein guter Lehrer.
native_language_example: You’re a good teacher.

meaning: “you are a …” (to a woman/girl, with a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Uses the informal “du” and introduces a feminine predicate noun (often an insult or a compliment): Du bist eine Nervensäge. / Du bist eine Wucht! For masculine nouns, you’d say “Du bist ein …”. For a polite/formal address, use “Sie sind ein/e …”.
target_language_example: Du bist eine gute Freundin.
native_language_example: You are a good friend.

additional_notes: Often used when recognizing or identifying someone (“Ah, it’s you!”). Also appears in the pattern “Du bist es + jemandem + schuldig, …” meaning “You owe it to someone to …” (e.g., “Du bist es Maria schuldig, ihr die Wahrheit zu sagen.”).
target_language_example: Ach, du bist es! Ich habe dich gar nicht erkannt.
native_language_example: Oh, it’s you! I didn’t recognize you at all.

meaning: “You’re pretty/quite (really) …” (often with surprise, emphasis, sometimes criticism).
additional_notes: Used in spoken German to intensify an adjective: „Du bist ganz schön + Adjektiv.“ Depending on tone and the adjective, it can be a compliment („…cool“, „…mutig“) or a reproach/criticism („…dreist“, „…verlogen“). „Ganz schön“ here means “pretty/quite/really,” not literally “completely nice.”
target_language_example: Du bist ganz schön spät dran.
native_language_example: You’re pretty late.

additional_notes: Literally states that someone is in this place. Often used with extra information to explain why someone is here ("Du bist hier, weil …"), to say someone is welcome/safe here ("Du bist hier willkommen." / "Du bist hier keinen Gefahren ausgesetzt."), or to emphasize someone’s role/status in this situation ("Du bist hier der/die …"). Uses "du" (informal singular); for formal you’d say "Sie sind hier".
target_language_example: Du bist hier, um mir zu helfen.
native_language_example: You are here to help me.

meaning: "you are in" (a place), or "you were/have" in the past with a past participle.
additional_notes: Used with places: "Du bist in Boston." = you are in Boston. Very often it’s also the start of the Perfekt with verbs that use *sein*: "Du bist in Boston aufgewachsen." = you grew up in Boston. With *in*, German chooses case: *in* + dative for location (in/at: "in Boston"), *in* + accusative for movement into (into: "in einen Brunnen").
target_language_example: Du bist in Berlin, oder?
native_language_example: You’re in Berlin, right?

meaning: "You really are…" / "Wow, you are…" (emphasis, often surprise).
additional_notes: Here "ja" is a modal particle (not the answer "yes"). It adds emphasis and often signals surprise, admiration, criticism, or “as you can see / as we both know.” Common in spoken German: "Du bist ja verrückt!" = “You’re really crazy!”
target_language_example: Du bist ja schon wieder hier!
native_language_example: Wow, you’re here again already!

additional_notes: Used to say someone has entered a new situation or status, or to emphasize the current moment. Often introduces what is true from this point on (change or realization): *Du bist jetzt erwachsen* (you’re an adult now), *Du bist jetzt in Paris* (you’re in Paris now). In questions it can show surprise: *Du bist jetzt Ärztin?* (So you’re a doctor now?).
target_language_example: Du bist jetzt nicht mehr allein.
native_language_example: You’re not alone anymore now.

meaning: "you are not a" (used before a masculine or neuter noun).
additional_notes: Used to negate a noun with the verb "sein" (to be): "Du bist kein + Nomen". "Kein" is for masculine/neuter nouns in the nominative singular (e.g., "kein Student", "kein Genie"). For feminine nouns use "keine" ("Du bist keine Lehrerin"), and for plural use "keine" ("Ihr seid keine Studenten"). Often corresponds to English "not a/an" rather than the literal-sounding "no".
target_language_example: Du bist kein Arzt, oder?
native_language_example: You're not a doctor, are you?

additional_notes: Used with the informal singular pronoun "du" to say someone belongs to you in a relationship sense (e.g., "mein Schatz") or, more commonly, to state a connection/role: "mein Nachbar" (my neighbor), "mein Kind" (my child), "mein Stuntdouble" (my stunt double). "Mein" must match the noun’s gender/case, so it may change (e.g., "du bist meine Freundin", "du bist mein Bruder").
target_language_example: Du bist mein Freund.
native_language_example: You are my friend.

additional_notes: Used to negate a statement about “you” (singular, informal). Put “nicht” after the verb “bist” and typically before what is being negated (e.g., an adjective or noun phrase): “Du bist nicht müde.” / “Du bist nicht der Erste …”. For formal “you,” use “Sie sind nicht …”.
target_language_example: Du bist nicht allein.
native_language_example: You are not alone.

meaning: “you are not the … (masculine)” / “you’re not the one who …”.
additional_notes: This is an incomplete phrase that normally needs a noun or further information after it. Use it when the missing word is masculine (der): e.g. “Du bist nicht der Chef.” (You’re not the boss.) or with a relative clause: “Du bist nicht der, der das entscheidet.” (You’re not the one who decides that.) For feminine/neuter/plural you’d use: “du bist nicht die / das / die”.
target_language_example: Du bist nicht der Chef.
native_language_example: You’re not the boss.

meaning: you are no longer / not anymore.
additional_notes:
Used to say that a previous state no longer applies. Very common with adjectives and noun phrases: 
- Du bist nicht mehr allein. = You’re not alone anymore.
- Du bist nicht mehr der Alte. = You’re not the same person as before.
It can also sound very final/harsh in sentences like: Du bist nicht mehr meine Tochter. (“You’re not my daughter anymore.”).
target_language_example: Es tut mir leid, aber du bist nicht mehr eingeladen.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but you’re not invited anymore.

additional_notes: Used with **noch** to say someone is still in a state, place, or situation: **Du bist noch fiebrig.** (still feverish), **Du bist noch hier.** (still here), **Du bist noch bei der Polizei?** (still with/at the police?). It can also mean “still/only (so) …” about age or readiness: **Du bist noch so jung.** / **Du bist noch jung genug, um …**.
target_language_example: Du bist noch nicht fertig, oder?
native_language_example: You’re not finished yet, are you?

additional_notes: Used to describe someone with emphasis: **Du bist** (informal “you are”) + **sehr** (“very”) + adjective/adverb. For formal “you,” use **Sie sind sehr …**. Often sounds like the start of a sentence and needs a word after **sehr** (e.g., *müde, nett, krank*).
target_language_example: Du bist sehr müde heute.
native_language_example: You are very tired today.

meaning: 'you are so …' (used to emphasize a description).
additional_notes: Used before an adjective ("Du bist so hübsch." = “You’re so pretty.”) or before "ein/eine" + noun ("Du bist so ein Lügner!" = “You’re such a liar!”). Often expresses strong emotion (praise, surprise, annoyance). Can also be said as a question to show disbelief or surprise: "Du bist so schlau?" = “You’re that smart?” / “You’re so smart?”
target_language_example: Du bist so nett, dass du mir hilfst.
native_language_example: You’re so nice to help me.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine noun (often an insult) to strongly emphasize what you think someone is: "Du bist so ein + Nomen!" With feminine nouns: "Du bist so eine …"; with plural: "Ihr seid so …". Very rude if followed by a swear word (e.g., "Arsch").
target_language_example: Du bist so ein Idiot!
native_language_example: You’re such an idiot!

meaning: “you’re dead” (literal), or “you’re done for / you’re going to pay” (as a threat).
additional_notes: Literally states that someone is dead, but it’s also commonly used figuratively as a strong, usually informal threat (“you’re in big trouble”). The tone is aggressive and can sound violent; use with caution and pay attention to context.
target_language_example: Wenn du das nochmal machst, du bist tot!
native_language_example: If you do that again, you’re dead!

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize a description or judgment about someone, usually followed by an adjective or phrase (e.g., "nett", "weit weg"). Depending on intonation and context, it can sound like praise ("You’re really nice") or criticism/surprise ("You’re really far away" / "You really are something..."). You can also switch the word order: "Du bist echt/wirklich ..."; "wirklich" = "really".
target_language_example: Du bist wirklich sehr hilfsbereit.
native_language_example: You really are very helpful.

meaning: "I guess you're…" / "You must be…" (often with a skeptical or sarcastic tone).
additional_notes: Uses **wohl** as a modal particle to express an assumption or guess about the other person. Depending on tone and context, it can sound neutral (**"you probably…"**) or sarcastic/accusatory (**"oh, so you think you’re…"**). It’s usually followed by a description: *Du bist wohl müde.* / *Du bist wohl schon fertig.*
target_language_example: Du bist wohl total müde, oder?
native_language_example: You must be really tired, right?

additional_notes: Use **zu** before an adjective/adverb to say someone has an excessive amount of a quality: **Du bist zu langsam / zu aggressiv / zu dünn.** It often sounds critical or rude, so use carefully (you can soften it with words like **ein bisschen**).
target_language_example: Du bist zu müde, geh lieber ins Bett.
native_language_example: You’re too tired; you’d better go to bed.

meaning: “please (you)”—a polite request to one person you address with du.
additional_notes: Used when asking a single person (informal “you”) to do something. Often appears in requests with verb-first word order, like a question: “Machst du bitte …?” or “Schließt du bitte …?”. It softens the request, similar to “Could you please …?” in English (but not a literal translation of “you please”).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte das Fenster zumachen?
native_language_example: Could you please close the window?

meaning: An incomplete, colloquial fragment meaning something like: “You—please (do something with) the window.”
additional_notes:
This isn’t a standard phrase in German because it’s missing the verb (what you want the person to do with the window). In speech, people sometimes leave words out, but as a learner you should use a full request, e.g.:
- „Mach bitte das Fenster zu.“ (Please close the window.)
- „Mach bitte das Fenster auf.“ (Please open the window.)
- „Kannst du bitte das Fenster zumachen?“ (Can you please close the window?)
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte das Fenster zumachen?
native_language_example: Can you please close the window?

meaning: 'you stay' / 'you are staying' (2nd person singular of bleiben).
additional_notes: Used to tell or ask one person to remain somewhere. Common patterns: "Du bleibst bitte ..." (polite request), "Du bleibst noch hier?" ("Are you staying here a bit longer?"), and "Du bleibst bei ..." ("You stay with ..."). In questions, the rising intonation makes it a yes/no question.
target_language_example: Du bleibst bitte hier, ja?
native_language_example: Please stay here, okay?

additional_notes: From the verb "brauchen" (to need). Used with a noun: "Du brauchst Urlaub." (= you need a vacation). With "nicht" + infinitive, it often means "don’t have to / needn’t": "Du brauchst die Teller nicht zu spülen." Also common as "was du brauchst" (= what you need).
target_language_example: Du brauchst heute nicht zu arbeiten.
native_language_example: You don’t have to work today.

additional_notes: Used when the thing you need is a masculine noun in the accusative case (object of brauchen). It’s usually followed by a noun like „einen Führerschein“ or „einen Meister“. For other genders: „du brauchst eine …“ (feminine), „du brauchst ein …“ (neuter), „du brauchst …“ (plural/no article).
target_language_example: Du brauchst einen Termin, um den Pass abzuholen.
native_language_example: You need an appointment to pick up the passport.

additional_notes: Used when addressing one person informally (*du*). With a direct object (person/thing) it often means to physically bring or take something/someone to a place: *du bringst sie nach Busan* (“you take/bring her to Busan”). It can also appear in common phrases like *du bringst das (alleine) fertig* meaning “you manage to do that (on your own).”
target_language_example: Du bringst die Unterlagen morgen ins Büro.
native_language_example: You’ll bring the documents to the office tomorrow.

meaning: “you’re getting/making me …” (you cause me to be/do something).
additional_notes: Used with a complement to say someone causes a reaction or situation: **du bringst mich + in + Akk.** (into trouble: *in Schwierigkeiten*), **du bringst mich + durcheinander** (you confuse me), **du bringst mich + auf die Palme** (you’re driving me crazy / making me really angry; idiomatic). With **umbringen** (*du bringst mich um*) it means **to kill** (“Are you going to kill me?”).
target_language_example: Du bringst mich zum Lachen.
native_language_example: You make me laugh.

meaning: 'you there' / 'you (right) there'; also 'you being here/present' ("dass du da bist").
additional_notes: "Da" points to a place, moment, or situation. With "du" it often highlights what the person is doing/holding/wearing right now ("Was treibst du da?" = 'What are you doing there/just now?'). In "schön/gut, dass du da warst/bist" it means 'here' in the sense of being present.
target_language_example: Was machst du da gerade?
native_language_example: What are you doing right now (there)?

additional_notes: Often used with „schön, dass …“ / „gut, dass …“ to say you’re happy or relieved that someone is present: „Schön, dass du da bist.“ = “Nice to have you here.” Literally „da“ means “there,” but in many situations it’s best translated as “here” in English.
target_language_example: Gut, dass du da bist — ich brauche kurz deine Hilfe.
native_language_example: Good thing you’re here — I need your help for a moment.

meaning: “(have) you remembered / thought of it?” (usually: “Hast du daran gedacht …?”).
additional_notes: This is typically part of a question with the verb: “Hast du daran gedacht, …?” = “Did you remember to …?” / “Did you think about …?” The pronoun “daran” means “about it” or “of it” and refers back to something already mentioned. Common with infinitives: “Hast du daran gedacht, den Müll rauszubringen?”
target_language_example: Hast du daran gedacht, deinen Ausweis mitzunehmen?
native_language_example: Did you remember to bring your ID?

meaning: "you may" / "you’re allowed to" (permission); also used as "you must not" in negatives.
additional_notes: From the verb "dürfen" (to be allowed to). Used to give permission (often polite) or to state rules/prohibitions with "nicht" ("du darfst nicht …" = "you mustn’t …" / "you’re not allowed to …"). Common with another verb in the infinitive at the end: "Du darfst gehen."
target_language_example: Du darfst hier parken, aber du darfst nicht über Nacht bleiben.
native_language_example: You may park here, but you must not stay overnight.

meaning: “you mustn’t / you’re not allowed to” (telling someone not to do something).
additional_notes: Used to forbid or strongly warn someone against an action. Structure: **du** (you) + **darfst** (may/are allowed) + **dich** (yourself; used with many reflexive verbs like *sich setzen, sich bewegen, sich benehmen*) + **nicht** (not). Often followed by an infinitive: *Du darfst dich nicht bewegen.* In English this is usually “mustn’t” or “don’t,” not “you may not” in the old-fashioned sense.
target_language_example: Du darfst dich nicht so spät hinlegen.
native_language_example: You mustn’t go to bed so late.

meaning: "you must not" / "you're not allowed to" (to do something).
additional_notes: Uses the modal verb "dürfen" (to be allowed to). "Du darfst nicht + infinitive" expresses a prohibition (a rule, permission denied). It can be said by a parent/teacher, or used for rules and commandments. For a softer warning in English you might translate it as "you shouldn't," but the core meaning is "not allowed."
target_language_example: Du darfst nicht so schnell fahren.
native_language_example: You must not drive that fast.

additional_notes: "Du" is the informal singular "you". "Das" can be (1) the neuter definite article "the" (das Buch = the book) or (2) the pronoun "that/it" referring to something already known from context (Danke, dass du das geklärt hast = thanks for clearing that up). In sentences like "Kannst du das...?", "das" usually means "that/it".
target_language_example: Kannst du das bitte noch einmal sagen?
native_language_example: Can you say that again, please?

additional_notes: This isn’t a fixed expression; it’s just the pronoun **du** (“you”, informal singular) together with the direct object **das Buch** (“the book”, accusative). In German, **du** often comes right after the verb, especially in questions: **Fandest du das Buch …?** (“Did you find the book …?”). In relative clauses you may see it in the middle of a longer structure: **denen du das Buch gegeben hast** (“to whom you gave the book”), where **das Buch** is what was given (accusative).
target_language_example: Hast du das Buch schon gelesen?
native_language_example: Have you read the book yet?

meaning: “you … all of that / all this” (addressing you, referring to everything mentioned).
additional_notes: This isn’t a fixed idiom—it's just the pieces in a sentence: **du** = “you” (subject) and **das alles** = “all of that / all this” (object, referring to a whole set of things). In yes/no questions, German often puts the verb first: **Riechst du das alles?** = “Do you smell all that?”
target_language_example: Verstehst du das alles?
native_language_example: Do you understand all of that?

meaning: “You—this is the last time …” / “For the last time …” (an annoyed, emphatic way to address someone and insist they stop or finally do something).
additional_notes: Colloquial and confrontational. It’s typically used as a scolding opener before an instruction or warning. In standard written German you’d usually punctuate and capitalize it (e.g., “Du, das letzte Mal …”), but the core multi-word term is the same. Use with care because it can sound rude.
target_language_example: Ich sag’s dir: du das letzte Mal, hör auf damit!
native_language_example: I’m telling you: for the last time, stop it!

meaning: “…you last time a …” (a sentence fragment used in questions, usually after a verb like *hattest* / *war* / *brauchtest*).
additional_notes: This isn’t a complete phrase by itself—it’s a chunk that typically appears in a question like: *Hattest du das letzte Mal eine Reservierung?* (“Did you have a reservation last time?”). *das letzte Mal* means “last time,” and *eine* is “a/an” for feminine nouns (e.g., *eine Reservierung, eine Karte, eine Frage*). In normal word order, the verb usually comes first in yes/no questions: *Hattest du …?*
target_language_example: Hattest du das letzte Mal eine Reservierung?
native_language_example: Did you have a reservation last time?

meaning: Not correct standard German as written; likely intended: „du, das letzte Mal …“ ("you, last time …") or „das letzte Mal“ ("last time / the last time").
additional_notes: The string „du das letztemal“ is ungrammatical in standard German. If you mean "last time," write „das letzte Mal“ (two words; adjective ending -e). If you are addressing someone and referring back to a previous occasion, you might say „Du, das letzte Mal …“ with a comma after „Du“ (a direct address): e.g., „Du, das letzte Mal hast du gesagt …“.
target_language_example: Du, meintest du das letztemal oder das letzte Mal?
native_language_example: Hey, did you mean 'du das letztemal' or 'das letzte Mal'?

meaning: Not a standard German multi-word term; as written it’s ungrammatical and likely a typo/fragment. It looks like it was intended to mean something like “you … last time … a (masc. accusative) …”.
additional_notes:
Problems in the original fragment:
- Word order/grammar: German needs a verb and proper structure; “du …” (you) must pair with a verb.
- Spelling: standard German is usually “das letzte Mal” (two words), not “das letztemal”.
- “einen” is the masculine accusative form of “ein” (“a/an”) and must be followed by a masculine noun (e.g., “einen Kaffee”).

Likely intended full versions (depending on context):
- “Du hast das letzte Mal einen Kaffee bestellt.” = “Last time you ordered a coffee.”
- “Du warst das letzte Mal ein bisschen müde.” (would use “ein”, not “einen”, because it’s not a direct object)

If you share the full original sentence, it’s possible to correct it precisely.
target_language_example: Ich habe nur den Satzfetzen „du das letztemal einen“ gesehen—vermutlich war gemeint: „Du hast das letzte Mal einen Kaffee bestellt.“
native_language_example: I only saw the sentence fragment “du das letztemal einen”—it was probably meant to be: “Last time you ordered a coffee.”

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression. du is the informal singular 'you', and das points to something already mentioned or understood from context. In English, das is often translated as 'it' rather than literal 'that'. This sequence often appears in questions and subordinate clauses before the main verb.
target_language_example: Ich verstehe nicht, warum du das gesagt hast.
native_language_example: I don't understand why you said that.

additional_notes: This isn’t a fixed idiom—it's just the normal combination of **du** (you) + **das** (that/it) + **auch** (also/too). It’s used to include the listener in the same action/ability/knowledge as someone else: **Kannst du das auch?** (Can you do that too?). In questions, the verb usually comes first (**Riechst du das auch?**), and in statements you often see it like **Wenn ich das kann, kannst du das auch.**
target_language_example: Ich kann schwimmen — kannst du das auch?
native_language_example: I can swim—can you too?

meaning: "you (do) that, please" — used in requests like "Can you do that, please?"
additional_notes: **"du das bitte"** on its own is not a complete, well-formed sentence in German; it typically appears inside a larger request, e.g. **"Kannst du das bitte …?"** (informal **du**). A more direct imperative would be **"Tu das bitte."** or **"Mach das bitte."** (still informal). In formal situations you’d use **"Können Sie das bitte …?"** / **"Machen Sie das bitte."**
target_language_example: Kannst du das bitte wiederholen?
native_language_example: Can you please repeat that?

meaning: “(Can) you (do) that for me, please?” (informal, with du).
additional_notes: This is usually part of a longer question and needs a verb, e.g. "Kannst du das bitte für mich machen?" (= Can you do that for me, please?). The word order "du … für mich" is typical in spoken requests with "du" (informal “you”). With a formal/polite "you", use "Sie": "Können Sie das bitte für mich machen?"
target_language_example: Kannst du das bitte für mich machen?
native_language_example: Can you do that for me, please?

meaning: “you … that for me” (part of a request, usually with a verb).
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase on its own. It commonly appears inside questions/requests like “Kannst du das für mich …?” (“Can you … that for me?”). In correct word order, a verb is needed (e.g., machen, erledigen, erklären).
target_language_example: Kannst du das für mich machen?
native_language_example: Can you do that for me?

meaning: “you did that / you’ve done that” (in a subordinate clause).
additional_notes: This is a dependent-clause form of the Perfekt (present perfect): **du** (you) + **das** (that) + **gemacht** (done/made) + **hast** (have). In German subordinate clauses (often after **wie** “how” or **dass** “that”), the helping verb **hast** typically goes at the end: *… wie du das gemacht hast* / *… dass du das gemacht hast*.
target_language_example: Ich verstehe nicht, wie du das gemacht hast.
native_language_example: I don’t understand how you did that.

meaning: “…you don’t/can’t (do) that…?” (fragment, usually in a question).
additional_notes: This isn’t a complete phrase by itself; it’s typically part of a longer sentence, especially a question like: „Kannst du das nicht …?“ (= “Can’t you …?”) or „Willst du das nicht …?“ (= “Don’t you want to …?”). Word-by-word: „du“ = you, „das“ = that/it, „nicht“ = not.
target_language_example: Kannst du das nicht morgen erledigen?
native_language_example: Can’t you take care of that tomorrow?

additional_notes: A clause with the verb at the end (…tust) because it’s often used after conjunctions like wenn (when/if), falls (in case), dass (that), etc. Refers to an action mentioned or understood from context: das = “that/it”.
target_language_example: Ich bin froh, dass du das tust.
native_language_example: I’m glad that you’re doing that.

meaning: "you really" (emphasizing that it’s truly you / that you truly do/want/know something).
additional_notes: This is usually a fragment inside a longer sentence, often in a subordinate clause: e.g. "..., dass du das wirklich willst" (“...that you really want that”). "wirklich" adds emphasis (“really / truly”), and "das" refers to “that/it” (something already known from context). In yes/no questions you often see: "Wusstest du das wirklich nicht?" (“Did you really not know that?”).
target_language_example: Ich kann nicht glauben, dass du das wirklich gesagt hast.
native_language_example: I can’t believe you really said that.

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression. du is the informal singular 'you', and dein means 'your' when speaking to one person addressed as du. dein changes its ending depending on the noun: dein Land, deine Tasche, dein Haus. In English, the words often will not stay next to each other because English may need extra words like 'do' in questions.
target_language_example: Warum räumst du dein Zimmer nicht auf?
native_language_example: Why don't you clean your room?

additional_notes: "Du" is the informal way to say "you" to one person (friends, family, kids). "Deine" means "your" and is used with feminine nouns (die Jacke, die Prüfung) and with plural nouns (die Ziele, die Beine, die Kleidung). Other forms include: dein (masc./neut. nominative/accusative), deinen (masc. accusative), deinem (dative), deiner (fem. dative/genitive).
target_language_example: Warum hast du deine Hausaufgaben noch nicht gemacht?
native_language_example: Why haven’t you done your homework yet?

meaning: "you" + "your" (informal singular) with a masculine noun: "you … your …"
additional_notes: "Du" is the informal singular "you" (used with friends, family, kids). "Deinen" is the form of "dein" (= your) used with masculine nouns in the accusative case (direct object), and also masculine/neuter nouns in the dative case. Common masculine nouns you’ll see here: der Name (deinen Namen), der Schlüssel (deinen Schlüssel), der Hund (deinen Hund), der Geburtstag (deinen Geburtstag), der Ehemann (deinen Ehemann). Word order: "du" is the subject; "deinen + noun" usually comes later as the object (e.g., "Ich weiß, wo du deinen Schlüssel versteckst.").
target_language_example: Kannst du deinen Pass kurz zeigen?
native_language_example: Can you show your passport briefly?

additional_notes:
This isn’t a fixed expression; it’s just two very common words next to each other in sentences, often in questions: verb + du + den + noun. 
- **du** = informal singular “you” (to a friend, child, etc.)
- **den** = “the” for a **masculine** noun in the **accusative** case (usually the direct object), e.g. *den Sommer, den Zucker*.
target_language_example: Kennst du den Mann dort?
native_language_example: Do you know the man over there?

meaning: Fragment meaning “you (… ) the TV” — it needs a verb (e.g., “turn off”).
additional_notes: This isn’t a fixed phrase by itself; it’s typically part of a full sentence or question. **du** = “you” (subject). **den Fernseher** = “the TV” in the accusative case (direct object), used after many verbs (e.g., *anmachen* “turn on”, *ausmachen* “turn off”, *sehen* “watch”). Word order often looks like: **Machst du den Fernseher aus?** (“Are you turning off the TV?”).
target_language_example: Machst du den Fernseher aus?
native_language_example: Are you turning off the TV?

meaning: Not a fixed expression; literally "you (… ) the whole …". In practice, it’s usually the pronoun *du* followed by *den ganzen* + a masculine noun in the accusative ("the whole/the entire"), most often in colloquial/elliptical speech.
additional_notes: *Den ganzen* is the masculine accusative form of *der ganze* ("the whole/the entire") and normally requires a noun right after it: *den ganzen Tag* (all day), *den ganzen Abend* (all evening). The sequence *du den ganzen* by itself is incomplete in standard written German; it most naturally appears in casual speech where parts are omitted (ellipsis), e.g., complaining or emphasizing duration: "Du den ganzen Tag …" (= "You, all day long …"). In careful writing you’d often use punctuation or a fuller clause (e.g., *Du bist den ganzen Tag …*).
target_language_example: Du den ganzen Tag nur am Meckern!
native_language_example: You complaining all day long!

meaning: 'you ... all day' / 'you ... the whole day' (fragment used in questions/statements).
additional_notes: This is not a complete sentence by itself; it’s a common fragment you’ll see inside a full sentence, often in questions. "den ganzen Tag" means "all day / the whole day" and is a common time expression in the accusative (answering "how long?"). Example patterns: "Was machst du den ganzen Tag?" (What do you do all day?) or "Schläfst du den ganzen Tag?" (Are you sleeping all day?).
target_language_example: Was machst du den ganzen Tag?
native_language_example: What do you do all day?

additional_notes: Used to state what the other person believes or assumes. Often starts a clause like "Ich weiß, du denkst, ..." ("I know you think..."); in everyday speech this can replace a "dass"-clause ("Ich weiß, dass du denkst, ..."). Also common in comparisons: "... wie du denkst" ("... than you think" / "... as you think").
target_language_example: Du denkst, es ist leicht, aber es ist schwer.
native_language_example: You think it’s easy, but it’s hard.

meaning: (in questions) “you, then/so…?” — a casual way to ask what someone is doing/like these days.
additional_notes: Used after a question word (was/wie/wo, etc.) to sound more friendly and conversational, often like “so, what about you?” or “what are you up to (these days)?” You’ll most often hear it in questions such as “Was machst du denn so?” or “Wie geht’s dir denn so?” It doesn’t translate word-for-word into a fixed English phrase; it mainly adds a casual, interested tone.
target_language_example: Was machst du denn so am Wochenende?
native_language_example: So what are you up to this weekend?

additional_notes: Not a fixed phrase: du is simply "you". In questions, denn is a modal particle that adds curiosity, surprise, impatience, or a softer, more natural tone. It is often not translated directly in English.
target_language_example: Was machst du denn hier?
native_language_example: What are you doing here, then?

meaning: adds emphasis in questions like “what are you … there?” (often showing surprise or criticism).
additional_notes: Used mainly in spoken German in questions such as: “Was machst du denn da?” / “Was erzählst du denn da?” The modal particle “denn” doesn’t mean “then” here; it makes the question sound more involved/insistent (often: “what on earth…?”). “da” is often “there” (what you’re doing/saying right now). Word order stays: question word + verb + subject + denn + da.
target_language_example: Was machst du denn da am Computer?
native_language_example: What are you doing there on the computer?

meaning: “(Where) are you going (then)?” (part of a question about where someone is headed).
additional_notes: Usually appears inside a full question like **„Wo willst du denn hin?“** or **„Wo gehst du denn hin?“**. **denn** is a common modal particle that adds emphasis/interest/surprise (often not translated directly). **hin** indicates movement away from the speaker (roughly “to/into (somewhere)”). On its own, **„du denn hin“** is incomplete—you need a verb and usually **wo**.
target_language_example: Wo gehst du denn hin?
native_language_example: Where are you going (then)?

meaning: “haven’t you …?” / “don’t you …?” (said with surprise or emphasis).
additional_notes: Used inside a question, usually after the verb: “Hast du denn nicht …?” The particle “denn” doesn’t change the basic meaning, but adds an emotional tone (surprise, impatience, insistence: “come on, haven’t you…?”). “du” is informal (talking to one person you address as “du”).
target_language_example: Hast du denn nicht meine Nachricht bekommen?
native_language_example: Didn’t you get my message (then)? / Haven’t you gotten my message?

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression. Dich is the accusative/reflexive form of du. It is used when the action refers back to the same person, often with reflexive verbs: du beziehst dich, du schämst dich, du verhältst dich. In English, it may be translated as just "you" or sometimes "yourself," depending on the verb.
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, dass du dich bald besser fühlst.
native_language_example: I hope you feel better soon.

meaning: yourself to / about (used with **sich an … erinnern** = “to remember …”).
additional_notes: This is the reflexive + preposition part of the verb phrase **sich an etwas/jemanden erinnern** (“to remember something/someone”). With **du** (you, informal singular) it becomes **du erinnerst dich an …**. The thing/person remembered is in the accusative: **an ihn**, **an sie**, **an den Moment**, **an das**.
target_language_example: Erinnerst du dich an mich?
native_language_example: Do you remember me?

meaning: (fragment) “you … that” — often used in questions like “Do you remember that?”
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself; it usually appears with a verb before it, especially the reflexive verb **sich an etw. erinnern** (“to remember something”): **Erinnerst du dich an das?** = “Do you remember that?” The structure is **du + dich** (reflexive “yourself”) + **an das** (“about/at that”).
target_language_example: Erinnerst du dich an das Lied?
native_language_example: Do you remember that song?

meaning: “you hurry” / “you’re in a hurry” (literally: “you hurry yourself”).
additional_notes: From the reflexive verb **sich beeilen** = “to hurry.” You’ll often see this as part of a longer sentence, e.g. **Wenn du dich beeilst, ...** (“If you hurry, ...”) or **Ich möchte, dass du dich beeilst.** (“I want you to hurry.”).
target_language_example: Wenn du dich beeilst, schaffen wir den Zug.
native_language_example: If you hurry, we’ll catch the train.

additional_notes: From the reflexive verb **sich an etwas erinnern** = “to remember something.” **daran** means “about it/that” and refers to something already mentioned. This exact form usually appears in a question or a clause, e.g. **Kannst du dich daran erinnern?** (“Can you remember?”) or **…, dass du dich daran erinnerst.** (“…that you remember it.”)
target_language_example: Kannst du dich daran erinnern, wie er hieß?
native_language_example: Can you remember what his name was?

meaning: “…you … in/for …” (a fragment used with reflexive verbs like *sich interessieren* / *sich entscheiden*).
additional_notes:
This isn’t a complete phrase by itself. You’ll see it inside questions or statements such as:
- **Interessierst du dich für …?** = Are you interested in …?
- **Entscheidest du dich für …?** = Are you choosing/deciding on …?
Here **dich** is reflexive (“yourself”) because the full verbs are **sich interessieren (für)** and **sich entscheiden (für)**.
target_language_example: Interessierst du dich für Musik?
native_language_example: Are you interested in music?

meaning: “you still …” (often starting a casual question/remark, usually with an implied/understood verb).
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself; it’s a spoken, informal fragment where the speaker starts with the subject + reflexive pronoun (du + dich) and then adds information like *immer noch* (“still”), with the main verb coming later (sometimes implied). It often conveys surprise/annoyance that something hasn’t changed yet. In a full sentence you’d typically have something like *Du hast dich immer noch …* / *Du willst dich immer noch …* / *Du kannst dich immer noch …* etc.
target_language_example: Du dich immer noch nicht entschieden?
native_language_example: You still haven’t decided?

meaning: “you … yourself with …” — used in many reflexive verb phrases (often meaning “with …”).
additional_notes: This is the 2nd-person form of the reflexive pattern **sich mit …**. You’ll see it in different verbs, and the overall meaning depends on the verb, e.g. **sich mit etwas auskennen** (“to know about / be familiar with something”), **sich mit jemandem treffen** (“to meet someone”), **sich mit jemandem abgeben** (“to hang out/associate with someone,” often disapproving). **mit** takes the dative case (mit wem? mit Tom).
target_language_example: Triffst du dich mit Tom nach der Arbeit?
native_language_example: Are you meeting Tom after work?

additional_notes: This is a common pattern in questions and suggestions with reflexive verbs: **Verb + du + dich + nicht** (e.g., *Bewegst du dich nicht?* = “Aren’t you moving?”). With **Warum … nicht?** it often means “Why don’t you …?” or “How come you don’t …?”. **dich** is the reflexive pronoun used with **du**.
target_language_example: Warum ziehst du dich nicht an?
native_language_example: Why don’t you get dressed?

meaning: “you … yourself … still/yet” (often part of a longer question).
additional_notes: This isn’t a complete set phrase by itself; it’s a common sequence you see in sentences like questions with reflexive verbs. For example, with **sich erinnern** (“to remember”), **Kannst du dich noch …?** means “Do you still remember …?” Here **du** = “you”, **dich** = reflexive “yourself” (used because the verb is reflexive), and **noch** = “still/yet”. Word order can vary depending on the full sentence.
target_language_example: Kannst du dich noch an ihn erinnern?
native_language_example: Do you still remember him?

meaning: “do you still remember …?” (as in: “Do you remember …?”).
additional_notes: This is a common fragment from the question pattern **Erinnerst du dich noch an …?** = “Do you still remember …?” It uses the reflexive verb **sich erinnern an + accusative** (to remember). You must add what is being remembered after **an** (e.g., **an mich**, **an den Tag**, **an unseren Urlaub**). Word order can vary in full sentences (e.g., **Erinnerst du dich noch an …?** / **Kannst du dich noch an … erinnern?**).
target_language_example: Erinnerst du dich noch an unseren ersten Tag hier?
native_language_example: Do you still remember our first day here?

meaning: "you still (remember) it" (as in: "Do you still remember that?")
additional_notes: This is a sentence fragment commonly used with a reflexive verb like **sich erinnern (an)** (“to remember”). You’ll often hear it in questions such as: **Kannst du dich noch daran erinnern?** (“Do you still remember it/that?”). **daran** refers back to something previously mentioned (“to it/that”). Word order changes depending on the full sentence.
target_language_example: Kannst du dich noch daran erinnern, wo wir uns getroffen haben?
native_language_example: Do you still remember where we met?

additional_notes: This is not a standalone fixed phrase, but a common sequence in informal (du) questions with a reflexive verb (sich): **Hast du dich schon …?** = “Have you already …?/Have you … yet?”. Here **dich** is the reflexive pronoun (“yourself”), used because the verb is reflexive (e.g., sich anmelden, sich entscheiden, sich vorbereiten).
target_language_example: Hast du dich schon entschieden?
native_language_example: Have you decided yet?

additional_notes: This is a sentence fragment typically used in questions with a verb like **hast** or **kannst**: **Hast du dich schon einmal …?** = “Have you ever … (before)?” The **dich** is the reflexive pronoun (“yourself”), so it’s used with reflexive verbs like **sich verlaufen** (to get lost), **sich irren** (to be mistaken), **sich vorstellen** (to imagine/introduce oneself). **schon einmal** often means “ever before” in questions.
target_language_example: Hast du dich schon einmal verlaufen?
native_language_example: Have you ever gotten lost?

meaning: "you" (informal singular) + reflexive "yourself" (accusative: dich) + "so" ("like that" / "so much") as part of a larger clause, often in questions like "Warum/Was ... du dich so ...?"
additional_notes: Not a standalone fixed phrase; it’s a very common word sequence in questions with reflexive verbs. **so** can mean **“like that”** (manner/behavior) or **“so much”** (degree/intensity), depending on the verb and context. Typical verbs: **sich benehmen** (behave), **sich verhalten** (act/behave), **sich aufregen** (get upset), **sich sorgen (um + Akk.)** (worry (about)).
target_language_example: Warum benimmst du dich so seltsam?
native_language_example: Why are you behaving so strangely?

meaning: (fragment) “you … the door” — used in commands to emphasize that *you* should handle the door (usually “close/open the door”).
additional_notes: This isn’t a complete phrase by itself; it normally appears inside a full sentence with a verb, e.g. **Mach du die Tür zu.** (“You close the door.”). Using **du** here adds emphasis/contrast (like “*you* do it”). Common verbs: **zumachen** (close), **aufmachen/öffnen** (open).
target_language_example: Mach du die Tür zu, bitte.
native_language_example: You close the door, please.

meaning: “you … all the time / the whole time” (used with a verb).
additional_notes: This is not a complete sentence on its own; it needs a verb. In standard word order, it typically appears as: “Du + Verb + die ganze Zeit …”. The fixed time expression is “die ganze Zeit” (“the whole time / all the time”), and adding “du” addresses someone directly (informal singular “you”).
target_language_example: Warum redest du die ganze Zeit?
native_language_example: Why are you talking all the time?

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression. It is just du ('you', singular informal) followed by diesen, the accusative masculine form of 'this', used before a masculine noun: du diesen Brief liest = 'you read this letter'. In English, the word order often changes depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Hast du diesen Schlüssel gesehen?
native_language_example: Have you seen this key?

meaning: “you … this letter” (a fragment used inside a longer sentence).
additional_notes: This isn’t a complete phrase by itself. It’s typically part of a question or request like: “Kannst du diesen Brief …?” (“Can you … this letter?”). **du** = “you” (informal singular). **diesen Brief** = “this letter” in the accusative (masculine), used as the direct object (e.g., lesen/schicken/unterschreiben).
target_language_example: Kannst du diesen Brief bitte unterschreiben?
native_language_example: Can you please sign this letter?

meaning: “you (… ) this sentence” — a fragment, usually part of a longer sentence like “Kannst du diesen Satz …?”
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase in German; by itself it’s incomplete. It typically appears inside a question or statement with a verb, e.g. “Kannst du diesen Satz übersetzen?” (Can you translate this sentence?) or “Verstehst du diesen Satz?” (Do you understand this sentence?). “diesen” is the accusative masculine form of “this,” used with “Satz” (sentence).
target_language_example: Kannst du diesen Satz bitte wiederholen?
native_language_example: Can you please repeat this sentence?

meaning: Literally: “you (singular), this book” — not a normal standalone German phrase; it reads like an incomplete fragment.
additional_notes: As written, it isn’t a grammatical sentence because it’s missing a verb and case marking doesn’t form a standard structure. You could, however, use it as a kind of fragment in very colloquial speech to draw attention or point something out (similar to “You—this book!”), but in normal German you’d say something like “Du hast dieses Buch.” or “Nimm dieses Buch.” Also note capitalization: “Du” is normally capitalized at the start of a sentence.
target_language_example: Du dieses Buch—das musst du zurückgeben.
native_language_example: You—this book—you have to return it.

meaning: "you" + "this year" (talking to someone about what they are doing this year).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed expression—it's just the pronoun "du" (you, informal singular) followed by the time phrase "dieses Jahr" (this year). In a full sentence, a verb normally comes between them: "Was machst du dieses Jahr?" (What are you doing this year?). "Du" is informal and used with friends, family, children, etc.
target_language_example: Was machst du dieses Jahr in den Ferien?
native_language_example: What are you doing this year during the holidays/vacation?

meaning: “you … yourself / for yourself” (du + dir = informal ‘you’ + dative reflexive pronoun ‘to/for yourself’).
additional_notes: Used when the verb requires a dative reflexive pronoun (dir), often expressing that you do something to/for yourself or in your own interest. Typical with everyday actions and set phrases, e.g. „(sich) die Zähne putzen“ (brush your teeth), „sich Mühe geben“ (make an effort), „sich etw. wünschen“ (wish for something), „sich etw. ansehen“ (watch/look at something). In many sentences, „dir“ appears shortly after the conjugated verb, and you’ll often see the exact sequence „du dir“ in subordinate clauses or questions where „du“ precedes „dir“: „Warum siehst du dir … an?“
target_language_example: Warum siehst du dir diesen Quatsch an?
native_language_example: Why are you watching this nonsense?

meaning: a common bit in spoken questions meaning roughly “you … (then/anyway)”, adding emphasis or surprise.
additional_notes: This isn’t a fixed expression on its own; it’s usually part of a longer question. "du" = “you”, "dir" is the dative reflexive pronoun used with many verbs (e.g., "sich denken", "sich vorstellen"), and "denn" is a modal particle that makes the question sound more interested/surprised/insistent (often like “then/anyway” in English, but not always translated). Very common in: "Was hast du dir denn gedacht?"
target_language_example: Was hast du dir denn dabei gedacht?
native_language_example: What were you thinking (then/anyway)?

meaning: Not a fixed phrase; it’s three separate words that can appear next to each other in a sentence: “du” (you), “dir” (to/for yourself/you), “die” (the / she / they).
additional_notes:
This exact three-word sequence is usually not used on its own; it appears inside longer sentences due to German word order.
- **du** = “you” (subject, nominative)
- **dir** = “to/for you/yourself” (indirect object, dative)
- **die** = “the” (feminine singular or plural), depending on the noun that follows.
In the example, **dir** is reflexive (“yourself”), and **die** is the article for **Mühe** (feminine).
target_language_example: Du gibst du dir die Mühe, Deutsch zu lernen.
native_language_example: You make the effort to learn German.

meaning: Literally “you (to yourself) the hair” → used in sentences about washing/doing/cutting your own hair, with a reflexive dative pronoun instead of a possessive (“your”).
additional_notes: German often uses a reflexive dative pronoun with body parts: mir/dir/sich/uns/euch/sich + the body part, instead of a possessive. So “Du wäschst dir die Haare” means “You wash your hair.” Common with verbs like waschen (wash), kämmen (comb), föhnen (blow-dry), schneiden (cut), färben (dye), machen lassen (have done).
target_language_example: Wie oft wäschst du dir die Haare?
native_language_example: How often do you wash your hair?

additional_notes: Usually used as ("Bist du dir sicher?"). It comes from the reflexive expression "sich (über etw.) sicher sein" = "to be sure (about something)". You can also specify what you’re unsure about with "Bist du dir sicher, dass …?" ("Are you sure that …?") or "Bist du dir sicher wegen …?" ("Are you sure about …?").
target_language_example: Bist du dir sicher, dass du heute keine Zeit hast?
native_language_example: Are you sure you don’t have time today?

meaning: you can imagine / picture (to yourself); can you imagine…? / could you… (consider…)?
additional_notes: From the verb phrase **sich etwas vorstellen** (= to imagine/picture something). **dir** is the reflexive pronoun (“to yourself”), used with **du**. Common patterns: **Kannst du dir vorstellen, …?** (Can you imagine…?/Could you see yourself…?) + infinitive clause, and **Kannst du dir vorstellen, wie …?** (Can you imagine how…?). With **Könntest du dir vorstellen, …?** it often becomes a polite way to suggest or request something (≈ “Could you possibly…?” / “Would you consider…?”).
target_language_example: Kannst du dir vorstellen, ohne Handy zu leben?
native_language_example: Can you imagine living without a phone?

meaning: 'actually' / 'really' (often in questions, to add emphasis or a casual 'by the way').
additional_notes: Not a fixed phrase: it's usually the pronoun "du" with the modal particle "eigentlich". In questions, "eigentlich" softens the tone and/or shows curiosity, surprise, or that you’re asking for the real/underlying answer (similar to “actually” or “really”). It can also introduce a side question like “by the way”. Word order varies (e.g., "Wie heißt du eigentlich?", "Hast du eigentlich ...?").
target_language_example: Was machst du eigentlich am Wochenende?
native_language_example: What are you actually doing this weekend?

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression. This is just du (informal singular “you”) followed by einen, the accusative masculine form of ein (“a/an”). It appears before a masculine singular noun when that noun is the direct object, as in du einen Reisepass hast (“you have a passport”).
target_language_example: Ich glaube, dass du einen Fehler gemacht hast.
native_language_example: I think you made a mistake.

additional_notes: From the verb **sich erinnern** (to remember). Often used with **an + accusative** for who/what you remember: *Du erinnerst dich an Jackie?* It can also be followed by a clause with **was/wie/dass**: *Du erinnerst dich, was passiert ist.* In questions it can mean “Do you remember?” and with **nicht/kaum** it means “don’t/hardly remember.”
target_language_example: Du erinnerst dich an unseren ersten Tag hier, oder?
native_language_example: You remember our first day here, right?

additional_notes: Used to say a person or thing makes you think of another person/thing because of similarities. Grammar: erinnern + Akkusativ + an + Akkusativ (Du erinnerst mich an meinen Sohn.). Can also be used with things/ideas (Du erinnerst mich an eine Geschichte.).
target_language_example: Du erinnerst mich an meinen besten Freund.
native_language_example: You remind me of my best friend.

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression, just the pronouns du ('you') and es ('it'). It is common when es refers to something already mentioned or understood from context. You often see it in subordinate clauses like dass/ob/bevor du es + verb, and also in questions such as Wie mochtest du es?
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, dass du es verstehst.
native_language_example: I hope that you understand it.

meaning: “you … it … (to) yourself” — pronoun order often used with reflexive verbs (e.g. *es dir ansehen* = “look at it”).
additional_notes: *Du* = “you” (subject). *Es* = “it” (direct object). *Dir* = “to you/yourself” (dative; often the reflexive pronoun with many verbs). This word order commonly appears in questions and with separable verbs: **Schaust du es dir an?** / **Siehst du es dir an?** = “Will you look at it?”. With *wünschen*: **Da du es dir wünschst** = “since you want/wish it (that way)”.
target_language_example: Kannst du es dir kurz ansehen?
native_language_example: Can you take a quick look at it?

meaning: "you found it" (in a subordinate clause / with perfect tense).
additional_notes: This is the perfect tense of **finden** (to find): **du hast es gefunden**. In a subordinate clause (often after **dass** = “that” or **wo** = “where”), the word order changes and the helping verb goes to the end: **…, dass du es gefunden hast** / **…, wo du es gefunden hast**. Often used in the set phrase **(dahin) zurücklegen/-tun, wo du es gefunden hast** = “put it back where you found it.”
target_language_example: Ich bin froh, dass du es gefunden hast.
native_language_example: I’m glad that you found it.

additional_notes: In correct German, this is almost always used as **„Du hast es geschafft!“** (with **hast**) in the perfect tense of **schaffen** (“to manage/accomplish”). Without **hast**, it’s incomplete/nonstandard, but you may still see it in very informal speech, captions, or messages where the auxiliary is dropped for effect.
target_language_example: Endlich: du es geschafft.
native_language_example: Finally: you did it.

meaning: “you (should) tell me (it)” (often with emphasis on you).
additional_notes: Usually appears in sentences like **„Sag du es mir!“** (= “You tell me!” / “You tell it to me!”). **du** is stressed to mean “you (not someone else)”. The pronouns **es** (“it/that”) and **mir** (“to me”) commonly come before/after each other like this in German: **Sag es mir. / Sag du es mir.**
target_language_example: Wenn du es mir sagst, kann ich dir helfen.
native_language_example: If you tell me, I can help you.

meaning: Fragment meaning “you … it not / you don’t … it” (used with a verb).
additional_notes: This isn’t a complete sentence on its own in standard German. It normally appears with a verb in the middle: **du + verb + es nicht** (e.g., **du weißt es nicht**, **du verstehst es nicht**). Note that in a full sentence German capitalization applies (**Du …**), but the term itself is given here in lowercase as provided.
target_language_example: Ich glaube, du verstehst es nicht.
native_language_example: I think you don’t understand it.

additional_notes: This comes from the verb phrase **etwas wagen / es wagen** = “to dare (something) / to risk (something)”. In correct, natural German you’ll usually see it as a full question or sentence, e.g. **Wirst du es wagen?** (“Will you dare?”) or with **zu + infinitive**: **Wagst du es, das zu sagen?** (“Do you dare to say that?”). The **es** here is often just a placeholder object (not a specific “it”).
target_language_example: Wirst du es wagen, allein zu reisen?
native_language_example: Will you dare to travel alone?

meaning: "you, (surely) not?" / "you, by any chance?" (surprised, skeptical; often rhetorical).
additional_notes: Used to challenge or question what the other person thinks/does, often with surprise or disbelief. The particle "etwa" adds doubt/skepticism (like "surely"/"by any chance"), not genuine expectation. Common in questions such as "Du etwa nicht?" (= "You don’t, really?").
target_language_example: Du etwa nicht?
native_language_example: You don’t, really? / You don’t, do you?

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression; it is just du + etwas. It commonly appears before a verb in clauses like dass du etwas weißt or ehe du etwas sagst. In questions, etwas may sound more natural as 'anything' in English, depending on context.
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, dass du etwas lernst.
native_language_example: I hope that you learn something.

additional_notes: This is often used inside a subordinate clause (especially after "wenn" = "if/when"), which is why the verb "brauchst" comes at the end: "Wenn du etwas brauchst, ...". By itself it’s a sentence fragment; as a full sentence you’d usually say: "Brauchst du etwas?" (Do you need anything?) or "Du brauchst etwas." (You need something.).
target_language_example: Wenn du etwas brauchst, sag mir bitte Bescheid.
native_language_example: If you need anything, please let me know.

additional_notes: This is not a complete sentence by itself. It’s usually part of the question: “Hast du etwas zu essen?” = “Do you have something to eat?” Here, “etwas zu essen” literally means “something to eat” (etwas + zu + infinitive). Often used when asking for food or offering help.
target_language_example: Hast du etwas zu essen?
native_language_example: Do you have something to eat?

additional_notes: Literally “you are missing (to) me.” German uses the verb **fehlen** with the person being missed as the subject (**du**) and the person who feels the miss in the dative (**mir**). Often intensified with words like **wirklich** (really) or **ganz doll** (a lot).
target_language_example: Du fehlst mir jeden Tag.
native_language_example: I miss you every day.

additional_notes: This is not a complete sentence on its own; it’s a fragment used for emphasis (often in romantic or emotional contexts). It’s typically embedded in a larger sentence, e.g. “Du bist für mich …” (“You are … to me”) or in an appositive/emphatic structure like “Du für mich bist …”. “für mich” can mean “for me” or “to me” depending on context.
target_language_example: Du für mich bist etwas ganz Besonderes.
native_language_example: You, to me, are something very special.

additional_notes: Used when talking to one person (informal *du*) about going somewhere, leaving, or walking. It’s often followed by a destination (*Du gehst nach Hause.*). It can also appear in set expressions where *gehen* is part of a larger meaning, e.g. *Du gehst mir auf die Nerven* (“You’re getting on my nerves”).
target_language_example: Du gehst heute nicht zur Arbeit.
native_language_example: You’re not going to work today.

additional_notes: This is the Perfekt form of **kommen** (to come): **du bist gekommen**. It often appears inside a longer sentence as a subordinate clause, e.g. after **dass** (“that”), or in relative/prepositional clauses like **mit der du gekommen bist** (“with whom you came”), **weswegen du gekommen bist** (“why you came”), **von wo du gekommen bist** (“from where you came”). In a subordinate clause, the participle **gekommen** usually goes at the end.
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht, warum du gekommen bist.
native_language_example: I don’t know why you came.

additional_notes: Used with a verb to say someone enjoys doing something: „Du liest gerne.“ = “You like reading.” In questions, it asks about preferences: „Isst du gerne scharf?“ = “Do you like spicy food?” Note: „gerne“ literally means “gladly,” but in this common pattern it usually translates as “like to.”
target_language_example: Spielst du gerne Fußball?
native_language_example: Do you like to play soccer?

additional_notes: This is a relative-clause piece used after words like "was" or "das, was" to refer back to what someone said. It uses the Perfekt tense ("hast ... gesagt"): the helping verb "hast" goes at the end in subordinate/relative clauses. In a main clause you’d say: "Du hast das gesagt."
target_language_example: Ich verstehe, was du gesagt hast.
native_language_example: I understand what you said.

additional_notes: A verb-at-the-end subordinate clause (Perfekt: **hast gesehen**) used after complementizers/wh-words like **was** (what), **wen** (whom), **dass** (that), etc.: **Ich weiß, was du gesehen hast.** In a direct (main) question, the word order switches to verb-second: **Was hast du gesehen?**
target_language_example: Ich weiß, was du gesehen hast.
native_language_example: I know what you saw.

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression—it's just the pronoun **du** (“you”, informal singular) used with the time word **gestern** (“yesterday”). In German, **gestern** can appear in different places: often after the verb (*Warst du gestern da?*), but it can also come earlier for emphasis (*Gestern warst du nicht da.*).
target_language_example: Hast du gestern Zeit gehabt?
native_language_example: Did you have time yesterday?

meaning: 'you … yesterday evening' (often in questions about what someone did).
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom—it's just the pronoun "du" (you, informal singular) plus the time phrase "gestern Abend" (yesterday evening). Typically used in questions like "Was hast du gestern Abend gemacht?"; the verb usually comes at the end in subordinate clauses ("…, was du gestern Abend gemacht hast").
target_language_example: Was hast du gestern Abend gemacht?
native_language_example: What did you do yesterday evening?

additional_notes: This is the Perfekt (present perfect) form of "tun" (to do): "du hast ... getan". In subordinate clauses (often after "was" = "what"), German sends the conjugated verb to the end, so "du hast getan" becomes "du getan hast". It’s commonly used in sentences like "Ich weiß, was du getan hast" (I know what you did/have done).
target_language_example: Ich verstehe nicht, was du getan hast.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what you did.

additional_notes: 2nd-person singular (du) present tense of **glauben**. Used for (1) beliefs/opinions (**Du glaubst, das ist verrückt.** = You think it’s crazy), (2) believing someone (**Du glaubst mir nicht.** = You don’t believe me), and (3) skeptical or accusing questions (**Du glaubst das wirklich?** = You really believe that?). In **Du glaubst aber auch alles!** it’s often sarcastic: “You’ll believe anything!”
target_language_example: Du glaubst wirklich, das stimmt?
native_language_example: Do you really think that’s true?

additional_notes: second-person singular of haben with du. In the examples, it is used as an auxiliary with a past participle to form the present perfect (for example, du hast erkannt = 'you have recognized'). It can also be used as a main verb to mean 'you have' in the sense of possession.
target_language_example: Du hast meine Nachricht gelesen.
native_language_example: You've read my message.

additional_notes: Often used with the Perfekt (present perfect): **du hast + alles + past participle** (sometimes the participle comes later in the sentence). It means you did something to/with *everything* or *told everything*: *Du hast alles erzählt.* = “You told everything.” As a standalone sentence it can also literally mean “You have everything.”
target_language_example: Du hast alles vergessen.
native_language_example: You forgot everything.

additional_notes: Used when addressing one person informally (du). "hast" is the present tense of "haben" (to have). "deine" is a possessive meaning "your" and is used with certain noun forms (often feminine singular like "deine Tür" or plural like "deine Schlüssel"). It’s typically followed by a noun: "Du hast deine Tür offengelassen."
target_language_example: Du hast deine Schlüssel vergessen.
native_language_example: You forgot your keys.

meaning: "you have your …" (speaking to one person; usually introducing a masculine noun in the accusative).
additional_notes: Used with the Perfekt: "du hast" + past participle, and "deinen" is the possessive "your" for masculine nouns in the direct-object form (accusative), e.g. "deinen Koffer", "deinen Regenschirm", "deinen Teil". Common in sentences like "Du hast deinen X vergessen" (You forgot your X) or "Du hast deinen X verlassen" (You left your X / your post/position).
target_language_example: Du hast deinen Schlüssel vergessen.
native_language_example: You forgot your key.

meaning: “you have the …” / “you …-ed the …” (with a masculine direct object).
additional_notes: Used with the Perfekt tense: **du hast + past participle** (e.g., *du hast … gelassen/geschmückt/ausgelassen/gestanden*). **den** is the accusative masculine form of **der** (“the”), used for a masculine direct object (*der Rucksack → den Rucksack*). In English this often translates as simple past (“you left/decorated/omitted/confessed …”).
target_language_example: Du hast den Schlüssel vergessen.
native_language_example: You forgot the key.

meaning: “you have … (yourself)” — used to form the Perfekt (past) of reflexive verbs with *dich*.
additional_notes: *Du hast dich* is not a fixed phrase by itself; it’s the start of many past-tense sentences with reflexive verbs. Structure: **du hast dich + Partizip II** (past participle), e.g. *du hast dich geschnitten / versteckt / konzentriert / gestritten*. The **dich** refers back to *du* (“yourself”) and is required by reflexive verbs. In questions, the word order often changes: *Hast du dich …?*
target_language_example: Du hast dich gestern verspätet.
native_language_example: You were late yesterday.

additional_notes: Common start of the spoken past tense (Perfekt): **du hast** + past participle later in the sentence. **die** is the accusative article for **feminine singular** nouns (e.g., *die Regel, die Uniform, die Waschmaschine*) and also for **plural** nouns. Although it literally says “you have…”, it often translates as simple past in English (“you broke/put on/broke”).
target_language_example: Du hast die Tür zugemacht.
native_language_example: You closed the door.

meaning: “you have … yourself” / “you have … for yourself” (using the reflexive pronoun “dir”).
additional_notes: Used with many reflexive or ‘to/for oneself’ expressions where German needs the dative reflexive pronoun (mir/dir/sich/uns/euch/sich). Common patterns: **sich (Dat.) + body part (Akk.)** (e.g., *Du hast dir die Hände gewaschen.*) and other verbs like *sich etwas verdienen*, *sich (selbst) eine Falle stellen*. Often implies the action affects you or is done for your own benefit.
target_language_example: Du hast dir die Hände gewaschen.
native_language_example: You washed your hands.

meaning: “But you said …” / “You did say …” (reminding someone what they previously said).
additional_notes: Used to point out a possible contradiction or to remind someone of their earlier statement. The word **doch** adds emphasis like “though/actually/after all,” often implying “I thought you said…” or “But you told me…”. Commonly followed by a subordinate clause (often with **dass** or in indirect speech).
target_language_example: Du hast doch gesagt, dass wir um acht losfahren.
native_language_example: But you said we were leaving at eight.

meaning: "but you did (though)" / "you know you did" (reminding or insisting).
additional_notes: Used when the speaker is reminding someone of something they already know or did/said/heard, often with a slightly reproachful or insistent tone. "doch" here adds emphasis like "after all" or "come on". Often followed by a past action or statement (e.g., "Du hast doch gesagt …", "Du hast doch die Anweisung gehört …").
target_language_example: Du hast doch gesagt, dass du heute keine Zeit hast.
native_language_example: But you said you don’t have time today (remember?).

meaning: "you have a" / "you’ve got a" (with a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used with "du" (informal singular "you") + "hast" (from "haben", to have). "Einen" is the accusative form of "ein" for masculine nouns, because the noun is the direct object: "Du hast einen Ohrring." It’s typically followed by a masculine noun (often with adjectives in between: "Du hast einen wichtigen Hinweis ...").
target_language_example: Du hast einen Termin um drei Uhr.
native_language_example: You have an appointment at three o’clock.

additional_notes: Used when speaking directly to someone (“du”). “Es” refers to something already known from context (“it/that”), and is often used with a verb that comes later: e.g., “Du hast es versprochen” = “You promised it.” It can also act like a general “it” with verbs like “schaffen/möglich machen/übersehen.”
target_language_example: Du hast es geschafft!
native_language_example: You did it!

meaning: “you said” / “you told (me/us)” (referring to something said earlier).
additional_notes: Perfekt (past tense) of **sagen** addressed to **du**. Often used to remind someone of their earlier words, and commonly followed by a comma and a clause with what they said (sometimes in reported speech: *Du hast gesagt, …*). It can sound neutral or slightly reproachful depending on tone/context.
target_language_example: Du hast gesagt, dass du heute keine Zeit hast.
native_language_example: You said that you don’t have time today.

additional_notes: Used with the Perfekt (conversational past): **du hast** + past participle (usually at the end of the sentence), and **ihn** is the accusative pronoun meaning “him” (or “it” for masculine nouns). Example pattern: *Du hast ihn gesehen.* = “You saw him.”
target_language_example: Du hast ihn angerufen.
native_language_example: You called him.

meaning: “you have my …” / “you (have) … my …” (starting a sentence about something of mine).
additional_notes: This is an incomplete phrase that must be followed by a neuter noun (or a neuter direct object), e.g. mein Buch, mein Auge, mein Gesicht, mein Kleid. In many common sentences, **hast** is also the auxiliary verb for the **Perfekt** (past) tense: **Du hast mein Buch gelesen** = “You (have) read my book.” Note: **mein** changes depending on gender/case (e.g. *meine* Mutter, *meinen* Bruder).
target_language_example: Du hast mein Handy kaputtgemacht.
native_language_example: You broke my phone.

additional_notes: Used at the start of the Perfekt (past tense) with a past participle at the end: "Du hast mich + Partizip II" (e.g., gefragt, beleidigt, behandelt). "Mich" is the accusative form of "ich" (= me).
target_language_example: Du hast mich angelogen.
native_language_example: You lied to me.

meaning: “you have … to/for me” (you did something to me / for me).
additional_notes: Common start of a sentence where the speaker tells someone what they did or have done that affected the speaker. Uses the informal singular “du” and “mir” = “to me.” The verb usually comes right after: “Du hast mir geholfen” (helped me), “Du hast mir versprochen …” (promised me …), “Du hast mir die Nase gebrochen” (broke my nose), “Du hast mir gefehlt” (I missed you / you were missing to me). Word order: “Du hast mir + past participle” in the perfect tense.
target_language_example: Du hast mir so viel bedeutet.
native_language_example: You meant so much to me.

du hast mir nie gesagt, daß

target_language_multi_word_term: du hast mir nie gesagt, daß
additional_notes: Used to point out that someone didn’t share information before. Common in conversation and can sound mildly reproachful depending on tone. After „dass/daß“, German uses a subordinate clause, so the verb goes to the end: „… daß Tom Anwalt ist.“ Note: „daß“ is older spelling; modern standard is „dass“ (same pronunciation).
target_language_example: Du hast mir nie gesagt, daß Tom Anwalt ist.
native_language_example: You never told me that Tom is a lawyer.

meaning: "you promised me" (you made me a promise).
additional_notes: Used to remind someone of a promise they made, often with a reproachful tone. It uses Perfekt (past) with "haben": "du hast ... versprochen". It’s typically followed by a clause with what was promised (often with a comma), e.g., "..., dass ..." or an infinitive clause.
target_language_example: Du hast mir versprochen, dass du heute anrufst.
native_language_example: You promised me that you would call today.

meaning: "you have her/them" / "you did … to her/them" (addressing one person).
additional_notes: In the examples, **sie** is the lowercase pronoun meaning **"her"** or **"them"** (accusative object). **Du hast …** is often used to form the **Perfekt** (spoken past): **du hast + past participle**, e.g. *Du hast sie gesehen* = "You saw her/them." (Note: capital **Sie** would mean formal "you," but here it’s lowercase **sie**.)
target_language_example: Du hast sie angerufen, oder?
native_language_example: You called her/them, right?

meaning: “you have … us” / “you … us” (you did something to us).
additional_notes: This chunk commonly appears in the **Perfekt** (present perfect): **du hast** (auxiliary) + **uns** (object pronoun = “us”) + a **past participle** later in the sentence. It often conveys “you have [done something] to us,” e.g. *Du hast uns verraten.* = “You betrayed us.”
target_language_example: Du hast uns verpfiffen, was?
native_language_example: You ratted us out, right?

additional_notes: Used with du, the informal singular word for "you." It is the present-tense form of haben. For formal "you," German uses Sie haben.
target_language_example: Du hast heute viel Zeit.
native_language_example: You have a lot of time today.

additional_notes: Common way to agree with someone or admit they’re correct. Often used alone as an answer ("Ja, du hast Recht."), or followed by a reason/explanation (", ich sehe es ein."). Literally “you have right,” but the natural English meaning is “you’re right.”
target_language_example: Du hast Recht, das ist keine gute Idee.
native_language_example: You’re right, that’s not a good idea.

meaning: "you have the ..." (talking to one person; "die" = "the" for feminine singular or plural nouns).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "haben" (to have). "Du" is informal singular "you". "Die" is the definite article for feminine singular (e.g., die Lösung) and for plural nouns (e.g., die Tabletten). After "haben", the noun is usually in the accusative case, but for many feminine/plural nouns the article stays "die" (so you often don’t see a change).
target_language_example: Du hast die Schlüssel, oder?
native_language_example: You have the keys, right?

meaning: you have a choice / it’s up to you.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone they can decide. Often followed by **zwischen + dative**: *Du hast die Wahl zwischen Tee und Kaffee.* It can also stand alone (*Du hast die Wahl.*) or be followed by an infinitive idea: *Du hast die Wahl, zu bleiben oder zu gehen.*
target_language_example: Du hast die Wahl: Wir können heute kochen oder essen gehen.
native_language_example: It’s your choice: we can cook today or go out to eat.

meaning: "but you (do) have..." / "you know you have..." (reminding or contradicting someone).
additional_notes: Used when the speaker assumes the other person already knows the fact, or when correcting them. The particle "doch" adds emphasis like "but" / "after all" / "come on". Often followed by something that contradicts what was just said or implied: "Du hast doch heute frei" = "But you’re off today (aren’t you)?"
target_language_example: Du hast doch mein Buch – kannst du es mir morgen geben?
native_language_example: But you have my book—you can give it to me tomorrow, right?

additional_notes: Used to say someone possesses something or has a quality/trait. It’s followed by a noun in the accusative case. The article changes with gender/case (e.g., ein Mann, eine Idee, einen Hund). “Du” is used with friends, family, children, or people you’re on informal terms with; otherwise use “Sie haben …”.
target_language_example: Du hast ein Problem.
native_language_example: You have a problem.

additional_notes: Used with **du** (“you” singular, informal) + **hast** (2nd person singular of *haben*, “to have”) + **eine** (indefinite article for **feminine** nouns in the accusative). You then add the noun and any adjectives: *Du hast eine Eintrittskarte / eine Wahl / eine schöne Stimme.* For masculine/neuter nouns you use **einen/ein** instead (*Du hast einen Hund / ein Auto*).
target_language_example: Du hast eine gute Idee.
native_language_example: You have a good idea.

meaning: “you have a good …” (talking to one person).
additional_notes: Used with feminine nouns (eine). You usually add a noun after it: e.g., eine gute Arbeitsstelle (job), eine gute Aussprache (pronunciation), eine gute Bibliothek (library), eine gute Kamera (camera). For masculine/neuter nouns, you change the article: du hast einen guten … / du hast ein gutes ….
target_language_example: Du hast eine gute Idee.
native_language_example: You have a good idea.

meaning: “you have a …” (talking to one person; with a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used with an indefinite masculine noun in the accusative (einen + noun), e.g., einen Hund, einen Abschluss, einen Versuch. It can mean possession (“you have a …”) or describe a condition/feature (“you’ve got a … / you have a …”), depending on the noun (e.g., einen offenen Reißverschluss = your zipper is open).
target_language_example: Du hast einen Termin um drei Uhr.
native_language_example: You have an appointment at three o’clock.

meaning: "you don't have any" / "you have no" (with a masculine or neuter noun).
additional_notes: Used to say someone does not have something: **Du hast kein + noun**. **Kein** is the negative form of **ein** (“a/an”) and changes by gender/case: **kein** (masc./neut. nominative/accusative), **keine** (feminine/plural), etc. Examples: *Du hast kein Geld.* / *Du hast keine Zeit.*
target_language_example: Du hast kein Geld dabei.
native_language_example: You don't have any money with you.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone they are not entitled or permitted to do something. Often followed by an infinitive with „zu“ (e.g., „Du hast kein Recht, so mit mir zu reden.“). It can sound very strict or accusatory.
target_language_example: Du hast kein Recht, meine Sachen anzufassen.
native_language_example: You have no right to touch my things.

meaning: “you have no … / you don’t have any …”
additional_notes: Used to say someone has zero of something. It’s “du hast” (you have) + “keine” (no/none). “Keine” is the form of “kein-” used with feminine singular nouns (e.g., keine Zeit) and with plural nouns (e.g., keine Beweise). With masculine/neuter singular you use “keinen/kein”: Du hast keinen Ausweis. / Du hast kein Geld.
target_language_example: Du hast keine Zeit für mich.
native_language_example: You have no time for me.

meaning: “you have no idea” / “you don’t know (at all)” (said to “you”).
additional_notes: Used to tell someone they don’t understand something, often for emphasis. It can sound annoyed or dramatic (“You have no idea how hard that was!”). Often followed by a clause with „was/wie/wie sehr …“ (what/how/how much), or it can stand alone: „Du hast keine Ahnung.“
target_language_example: Du hast keine Ahnung, wie sehr ich mich darauf freue.
native_language_example: You have no idea how much I’m looking forward to it.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone they don’t know/understand something (often for emphasis). Common in spoken German; you can also soften it: „Du hast keine Ahnung, was hier passiert.“ / make it stronger: „Du hast ja keine Ahnung, was …“. Often followed by a clause with „was“ (what) describing the unknown thing.
target_language_example: Du hast keine Ahnung, was das für mich bedeutet.
native_language_example: You have no idea what that means to me.

meaning: “you don’t have a / you have no …” (with a masculine noun).
