additional_notes: Used with verbs like "haben" (to have) and "bekommen/kriegen" (to get) to say you feel guilty, often because you think you did something wrong. Related: "Ich habe ein schlechtes Gewissen, weil …" (I feel guilty because …).
target_language_example: Ich habe ein schlechtes Gewissen, weil ich sie angelogen habe.
native_language_example: I feel guilty because I lied to her.

additional_notes: Used with a masculine noun in the nominative case (often after “sein”): ein schrecklicher Fehler / ein schrecklicher Film. The adjective ending changes with gender and case (e.g., eine schreckliche Idee, ein schreckliches Problem).
target_language_example: Das ist ein schrecklicher Tag.
native_language_example: This is a terrible day.

meaning: a weak heart (a heart condition / poor heart health).
additional_notes: Used to say someone has a heart problem or a weak cardiovascular condition (often meaning they get tired easily or have limited physical capacity). In German you often say: „Er/Sie hat ein schwaches Herz.“ It can be literal/medical, but is also used generally for someone in frail health.
target_language_example: Ich kann nicht so schnell laufen, weil ich ein schwaches Herz habe.
native_language_example: I can’t run that fast because I have a weak heart.

meaning: a heavy blow; a big (emotional) setback.
additional_notes: Used to say that news or an event affects someone very strongly (often emotionally), like a major disappointment or shock. Common pattern: „Das/Die … war/ist ein schwerer Schlag für + Akkusativ“ (e.g., „für ihn“, „für mich“, „für Sie“).
target_language_example: Die Kündigung war ein schwerer Schlag für ihre Familie.
native_language_example: The dismissal/layoff was a heavy blow for her family.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine noun in the nominative case: ein schöner Tag, ein schöner Baum. The adjective ending changes with gender/case (e.g., eine schöne Blume, ein schönes Haus). In exclamations like “Das wird ein schöner Sommer!”, it can be sincere or (depending on tone/context) sarcastic.
target_language_example: Das ist ein schöner Tag für einen Spaziergang.
native_language_example: That’s a beautiful day for a walk.

meaning: "a beautiful/nice name" (a compliment about someone’s name).
additional_notes: Used to compliment a person’s name. Often said as an exclamation: “(Name), ein schöner Name!” or “Was für ein schöner Name!” You can swap in other adjectives too (e.g., „ein toller Name“, „ein netter Name“).
target_language_example: Mila – ein schöner Name!
native_language_example: Mila—what a beautiful name!

additional_notes: Used to describe pleasant weather or a good day in general. Often appears with „Es ist/war …“ (It is/was …) or as an exclamation: „Was für ein schöner Tag!“ / „Welch ein schöner Tag!“ (= What a beautiful day!). You can also add a purpose with „für“: „ein schöner Tag für ein Picknick“.
target_language_example: Es ist heute ein schöner Tag, also gehen wir spazieren.
native_language_example: It’s a nice day today, so we’re going for a walk.

additional_notes: Used before a singular neuter noun, as in ein schönes Bild or ein schönes Gefühl. schön can mean "beautiful," "nice," or "lovely" depending on context. The ending changes with gender and case: compare ein schöner..., eine schöne..., ein schönes....
target_language_example: Das ist ein schönes Geschenk.
native_language_example: That's a lovely gift.

additional_notes: Common phrase with the indefinite article: "ein" (a) + "schönes" (beautiful/nice, neuter form) + "Haus" (house). Used to describe a house positively; in exclamations you often hear "Was für ein schönes Haus!" = "What a beautiful house!"
target_language_example: Sie haben ein schönes Haus am See.
native_language_example: They have a beautiful house by the lake.

additional_notes: Used to describe a country positively (often when talking about travel, nature, or culture). Grammar note: „Land“ is neuter (das Land), so after „ein“ the adjective takes the ending -es: „ein schönes Land“. With a definite article: „das schöne Land“.
target_language_example: Deutschland ist ein schönes Land, aber im Winter ist es oft kalt.
native_language_example: Germany is a beautiful country, but in winter it’s often cold.

additional_notes: A common compliment about someone’s smile. Often used with “Du hast …” (to a friend) or “Sie haben …” (polite/formal). You can intensify it with “so”: “so ein schönes Lächeln!”
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, Sie haben wirklich ein schönes Lächeln.
native_language_example: Excuse me, you really have a beautiful smile.

additional_notes: "Mädchen" means "girl" (grammatically neuter: das Mädchen), so you often see "ein" and the adjective ending "-es" (ein schönes). Used to describe a girl’s appearance; it can be a compliment but may sound a bit objectifying depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: Er hat ein schönes Mädchen im Park kennengelernt.
native_language_example: He met a pretty girl in the park.

meaning: a nice couple; a good match.
additional_notes: Used to say two people look good together or fit well as partners. Often said about romantic partners (dating, married), but can also be used playfully/suggestively (“You two would make a nice couple”).
target_language_example: Ihr seid wirklich ein schönes Paar.
native_language_example: You really are a nice couple.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone how their weekend was (past) or to wish them a pleasant weekend (often when saying goodbye on Friday). With verbs like **haben** (to have): *Hattest du …?* / *Ich hoffe, dass du … hattest.* With **wünschen** (to wish): *Ich wünsche dir/Ihnen …* Use **du/dir** for friends and family, and **Sie/Ihnen** for formal situations.
target_language_example: Ich wünsche dir ein schönes Wochenende!
native_language_example: Have a nice weekend!

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression on its own; it is simply ein + sehr, used before an adjective and a singular noun: ein sehr guter Lehrer = "a very good teacher." The form of the article can change depending on gender and case, for example eine sehr nette Frau or einen sehr alten Hund.
target_language_example: Das ist ein sehr gutes Buch.
native_language_example: That is a very good book.

meaning: a very big/large (one) / a very large (noun).
additional_notes: Used before a neuter noun (das Wort) in the nominative or accusative, e.g., „ein sehr großes Tier/Land/Feld“. It’s the indefinite article „ein“ + intensifier „sehr“ + adjective „groß“ with the ending „-es“ (for neuter). For masculine/feminine nouns, the ending changes: „ein sehr großer Hund“, „eine sehr große Stadt“.
target_language_example: Das ist ein sehr großes Problem.
native_language_example: That is a very big problem.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun to describe someone/something as very good: ein sehr guter Arzt / Boden / Fahrer. It can also stand alone when the noun is implied: „Tom ist Rechtsanwalt, noch dazu ein sehr guter.“ = “Tom is a lawyer—what’s more, a very good one.” Changes with gender/case: ein sehr guter (m.), eine sehr gute (f.), ein sehr gutes (n.).
target_language_example: Das ist ein sehr guter Plan.
native_language_example: That’s a very good plan.

additional_notes: "hübsch" means "pretty" (often about a person’s appearance). "Mädchen" is "girl" (grammatically neuter: das Mädchen), but here it’s in the accusative/nominative with "ein". Common pattern: "ein/eine sehr hübsche(r/s) ..." depending on the noun’s gender and case (e.g., "eine sehr hübsche Frau").
target_language_example: Sie ist ein sehr hübsches Mädchen.
native_language_example: She is a very pretty girl.

additional_notes: A friendly compliment. Use "ein" with masculine nouns like "Mensch" (here: "a person"). "sehr" = "very". "netter" is the adjective "nett" with the ending used after "ein" (masculine, nominative). Can be said about someone ("Tom ist …") or directly to someone ("Du bist …" / polite "Sie sind …").
target_language_example: Unsere Nachbarin ist ein sehr netter Mensch.
native_language_example: Our neighbor is a very nice person.

additional_notes: Used before a neuter noun with an indefinite article: ein + sehr + adjective + noun (e.g., ein sehr schönes Lied). The adjective ending “-es” shows neuter nominative/accusative singular. For masculine/feminine/plural, the ending changes (ein sehr schöner…, eine sehr schöne…, sehr schöne…).
target_language_example: Das ist ein sehr schönes Hotel.
native_language_example: That’s a very nice hotel.

additional_notes: A descriptive noun phrase. **Land** is neuter (**das Land**), so after **ein** the adjective takes the ending **-es**: **ein schönes Land**. **sehr** (“very”) intensifies the adjective **schön** (“beautiful”). You can use this in nominative or accusative with the same form: **Das ist ein sehr schönes Land.** / **Ich besuche ein sehr schönes Land.**
target_language_example: Deutschland ist ein sehr schönes Land.
native_language_example: Germany is a very beautiful country.

additional_notes: Used to describe a man who seems unusual, odd, or suspicious. It can be neutral (“unusual”) or negative (“creepy/strange”), depending on context. With an exclamation like “Was für ein seltsamer Mann!”, it expresses strong surprise or disapproval. Grammar note: it’s masculine nominative with an indefinite article (ein + seltsam + -er + Mann).
target_language_example: Da steht ein seltsamer Mann vor der Tür.
native_language_example: There’s a strange man standing at the door.

additional_notes: Used when you hear something unusual and can’t identify it. Often used with verbs like „hören“ (to hear) or „machen“ (to make), e.g. „Der Motor macht …“ = “The engine makes …”. Word order can change: „Ich hörte ein seltsames Geräusch aus der Küche.“
target_language_example: Ich habe draußen ein seltsames Geräusch gehört.
native_language_example: I heard a strange noise outside.

additional_notes: Used to describe noticeably windy weather. Often appears with verbs like „wehen“ (to blow, of wind) and „blasen“ (to blow), or in the expression „Es kam ein starker Wind auf“ (= a strong wind started up).
target_language_example: Am Strand weht heute ein starker Wind.
native_language_example: There’s a strong wind blowing at the beach today.

meaning: "a great / really nice" (used before a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used to compliment someone or something: ein toller Tag/Lehrer/Mann/Typ/Kerl. It’s the masculine nominative form of the adjective toll; with feminine and plural you’d say eine tolle … / tolle …. Can also be used sarcastically depending on tone (e.g., Das muss ja ein toller Tag gewesen sein.).
target_language_example: Das ist echt ein toller Freund.
native_language_example: He’s a really great friend.

meaning: "a great / awesome" (used before a neuter noun).
additional_notes: "toll" is a very common adjective meaning "great, awesome, fantastic". In "ein tolles ...", "tolles" has the -es ending because it follows "ein" and modifies a neuter noun (das): e.g., "ein tolles Lied", "ein tolles Haus". For masculine/feminine/plural you change the ending: "ein toller Abend", "eine tolle Arbeit", "tolle Leute". Not to be confused with English "toll" (a road fee).
target_language_example: Das war ein tolles Geschenk!
native_language_example: That was a great gift!

additional_notes: Used to praise two or more people (or a group) for working well together. Often said directly to the people: „Ihr (beiden/zwei) seid ein tolles Team.“ With formal „Sie“: „Sie (beide/zwei) sind ein tolles Team.“
target_language_example: Ihr seid wirklich ein tolles Team!
native_language_example: You really are a great team!

meaning: a four-leaf clover (a symbol of good luck).
additional_notes: Often used when talking about luck or finding something rare. In German you commonly say it "bringt Glück" (brings luck) or "finden" (to find) one. The adjective agrees with the noun: "ein vierblättriges Kleeblatt" (neuter, nominative/accusative).
target_language_example: Wenn du ein vierblättriges Kleeblatt findest, hast du Glück.
native_language_example: If you find a four-leaf clover, you're lucky.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine noun to emphasize that someone/something really fits the description (often as praise, sometimes as strong criticism): ein wahrer Freund, ein wahrer Gentleman, ein wahrer Alptraum. It changes with gender/case (e.g., eine wahre Freundin, ein wahres Wunder, in einem wahren Albtraum).
target_language_example: Sie ist ein wahrer Profi.
native_language_example: She’s a real professional.

meaning: a “walking dictionary” (someone who knows a lot of words/facts).
additional_notes: Figurative expression used to describe a person who seems to know every word or has a huge vocabulary (often in languages), or who always has the right definition/answer. Often used with “sozusagen” (“so to speak”).
target_language_example: Anna ist echt ein wandelndes Wörterbuch – sie kennt jedes Wort.
native_language_example: Anna is really a walking dictionary—she knows every word.

meaning: a long way (to go); a long journey.
additional_notes: Used both literally (a long physical distance) and figuratively (a lot of progress still needed to reach a goal or solution). Often appears with "bis" or "zu": "Es ist ein weiter Weg bis/zur …" / "Zu … ist es noch ein weiter Weg." You can also say "ein weiter Weg vor uns" = "a long way ahead of us."
target_language_example: Bis wir fertig sind, ist es noch ein weiter Weg.
native_language_example: It’s still a long way to go until we’re finished.

additional_notes: Used with a masculine noun (der): ein weiterer Kunde = another customer. With feminine/neuter/plural nouns it changes: eine weitere Minute, ein weiteres Mal, weitere Leute. Often used to emphasize that something/someone is just one more in a series ("just another...").
target_language_example: Anton Ego ist nur ein weiterer Kunde.
native_language_example: Anton Ego is just another customer.

additional_notes: Used before a noun (neuter singular) to mean “one more / another,” often with time/attempts: „ein weiteres Mal“ = “another time/once again.” Common fixed phrase: „Ohne ein weiteres Wort“ = “without another word / without saying anything else.”
target_language_example: Können wir ein weiteres Treffen nächste Woche vereinbaren?
native_language_example: Can we arrange another meeting next week?

additional_notes: A common clothing phrase. "Hemd" usually means a (men’s) dress shirt/button-up shirt (not a T-shirt). With the indefinite article it changes by case: nominative/accusative "ein weißes Hemd"; dative "einem weißen Hemd" (e.g., "mit einem weißen Hemd").
target_language_example: Für das Vorstellungsgespräch brauche ich ein weißes Hemd.
native_language_example: For the job interview, I need a white shirt.

additional_notes: Used to soften statements and mean “somewhat/slightly” with adjectives and adverbs (ein wenig sonderbar, ein wenig zu groß, ein wenig besser). Also used with verbs to mean doing something “for a little while” or “a bit” (ein wenig fernsehen, ruh dich ein wenig aus). With quantities it means “a little of” something (von allem ein wenig gegessen).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte ein wenig langsamer sprechen?
native_language_example: Can you please speak a little more slowly?

additional_notes: Describes a mild (not strong) feeling of surprise. Often used with "sein" (to be): "Ich bin ein wenig überrascht." You can also add what caused it with "von" + dative ("überrascht von ...") or use a clause: "überrascht, dass ...".
target_language_example: Ich bin ein wenig überrascht, dass du schon hier bist.
native_language_example: I'm a little surprised that you're already here.

additional_notes: Used to soften statements or requests and to mean a small amount/degree. Common with adjectives/adverbs ("ein wenig egoistisch" = "a bit selfish") and with verbs ("ein wenig schlafen" = "sleep a little"). In polite requests, it makes the request sound less direct ("ein wenig senken" = "lower it a bit").
target_language_example: Warten Sie bitte ein wenig, ich bin gleich da.
native_language_example: Please wait a little; I'll be right there.

additional_notes: Used to soften statements or describe a small amount/degree. Often comes before a noun ("ein wenig Hilfe") or with a noun phrase ("ein wenig Kopfschmerzen"). Similar to "ein bisschen".
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte ein wenig langsamer sprechen?
native_language_example: Could you please speak a little more slowly?

meaning: a wild animal; (figuratively) a wild, uncontrollable person.
additional_notes: Literally describes an animal that lives in the wild (not a pet or farm animal): „Der Fuchs ist ein wildes Tier.“ It’s also used metaphorically to say someone is acting untamed, aggressive, or out of control: „Du bist jetzt wie ein wildes Tier!“ Often used with „wie“ (= like/as) for comparisons.
target_language_example: Pass auf, der Hund verhält sich wie ein wildes Tier.
native_language_example: Be careful, the dog is behaving like a wild animal.

additional_notes: This is usually a noun phrase that needs a noun after it (e.g., "ein ziemlich guter Film"). "guter" is the masculine nominative form of "gut" after "ein"; the ending changes with gender and case (e.g., "eine ziemlich gute Idee", "ein ziemlich gutes Buch"). "ziemlich" means "quite / pretty" and is neutral in tone.
target_language_example: Das war ein ziemlich guter Film.
native_language_example: That was a pretty good movie.

additional_notes: Used when the exact number isn’t important or you’re estimating (often meaning “not many”). It can refer to time (ein oder zwei Jahre) or countable things (ein oder zwei Schüsse).
target_language_example: Ich habe nur ein oder zwei Fragen.
native_language_example: I only have one or two questions.

meaning: Used with some separable verbs (e.g., einsehen/eingestehen/einfallen) to introduce a „dass“-clause: “(to realize/admit/it occurs) that …”.
additional_notes: In sentences like „Er gestand ein, dass …“, the verb has a separable prefix „ein-“ (eingestehen/einsehen/einfallen). In the main clause, the prefix can appear later as „… ein“, and then a new clause starts after the comma with „dass …“. Common patterns: „(jdm.) fällt ein, dass …“ = “it occurs to (someone) that …”; „(etw.) einsehen, dass …“ = “to realize/accept that …”; „eingestehen, dass …“ = “to admit that …”.
target_language_example: Sie sah ein, dass sie sich geirrt hatte.
native_language_example: She realized that she had been wrong.

meaning: “… up/in and …” (shows the separated prefix **ein-** of a separable verb, e.g. **einpacken**).
additional_notes: In German, many verbs have a separable prefix like **ein-**. In the present tense it often splits: **Ich packe es ein.** In the past tense too: **Er packte es ein.** If another action follows, you’ll often see the prefix right before **und**: **Er packte es ein und legte es…** Here **ein** belongs to the verb (**einpacken**), not to **und**.
target_language_example: Ich packe alles ein und gehe dann nach Hause.
native_language_example: I pack everything up and then go home.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “a shortcut” (a quicker route), especially with verbs like nehmen/gehen/fahren (eine Abkürzung nehmen = to take a shortcut). It can also mean “an abbreviation” (a shortened form of a word or name), depending on context.
target_language_example: Wir können durch den Park gehen – das ist eine Abkürzung.
native_language_example: We can go through the park—it's a shortcut.

meaning: to have an affair (a secret romantic/sexual relationship), often while in another relationship.
additional_notes: Often used as „mit jemandem eine Affäre haben“ (to have an affair with someone). „Affäre“ can also mean a public scandal/incident in other contexts, but „eine Affäre haben“ is about a (usually secret) relationship.
target_language_example: Er soll eine Affäre haben.
native_language_example: He is said to be having an affair.

additional_notes: Used for answering a question or replying to a message/letter. Common patterns: „eine Antwort geben“ (to give an answer), „eine Antwort bekommen“ (to get a reply), „eine Antwort schreiben“ (to write a reply), „eine Antwort auf + Akk.“ (an answer to …).
target_language_example: Ich habe noch keine Antwort auf meine E-Mail bekommen.
native_language_example: I still haven't gotten a reply to my email.

additional_notes: Used to say who the reply comes from. After "von" you use the dative case (e.g., "von meinem Chef", "von meiner Schwester"). Often used with verbs like "bekommen" (to get/receive) or "haben" (to have): "Ich habe eine Antwort von ..." / "Ich habe eine Antwort von ... bekommen."
target_language_example: Ich habe eine Antwort von meinem Chef bekommen.
native_language_example: I got an answer from my boss.

meaning: a kind of; sort of; a type of.
additional_notes: Used to describe something approximately or as a category, often when you don’t want to be too exact ("a sort of..."). It’s commonly followed by a noun: „eine Art + Nomen“ (e.g., „eine Art Belohnung“).
target_language_example: Das ist eine Art Einladung, aber nicht offiziell.
native_language_example: That’s a kind of invitation, but not official.

additional_notes: "eine" is the indefinite article meaning "a/an" for feminine nouns in the nominative and accusative case. "Banane" is feminine: die Banane. Used when talking about one banana (e.g., describing it, offering it, or telling someone to eat one).
target_language_example: Ich kaufe eine Banane im Supermarkt.
native_language_example: I'm buying a banana at the supermarket.

additional_notes: Used literally for the insect. Very common in the fixed comparison "fleißig wie eine Biene" (“as busy as a bee”). Noun: die Biene; plural: die Bienen. The article changes with case (e.g., "Ich sehe eine Biene" but "mit einer Biene").
target_language_example: Im Garten fliegt eine Biene von Blume zu Blume.
native_language_example: In the garden, a bee is flying from flower to flower.

additional_notes: "Blume" is feminine (die Blume). With "eine" it means one/any single flower. Often used with "in der Hand" (in the hand) or to point something out: "Das ist eine Blume."
target_language_example: Ich habe eine Blume für dich.
native_language_example: I have a flower for you.

meaning: a bomb; (also figuratively) a bombshell (shocking news).
additional_notes: Literally refers to an explosive device. In the common expression „eine Bombe platzen lassen“ it means to reveal something shocking or surprising (“to drop a bombshell”). In questions like „Eine Bombe?“ it can express surprise or disbelief (“A bomb?!”).
target_language_example: Warum hast du das gesagt? Du hast eine Bombe platzen lassen.
native_language_example: Why did you say that? You dropped a bombshell.

additional_notes: Used with the verb „tragen“ (to wear): „eine Brille tragen“. In German, „Brille“ is usually singular even though English often says “glasses.” Indefinite article: „eine“ because „die Brille“ is feminine.
target_language_example: Ich habe meine Brille zu Hause vergessen.
native_language_example: I forgot my glasses at home.

additional_notes:
Used when asking someone (often a company/office) to mail or email you an informational brochure. 

Grammar tips: "schicken" usually takes a direct object (eine Broschüre) and can also take an indirect object in the dative for the recipient: "jemandem (Dat.) eine Broschüre schicken" (send someone a brochure). In polite requests you often use "Können Sie …?" or "Könnten Sie …?".
target_language_example: Könnten Sie mir bitte eine Broschüre schicken?
native_language_example: Could you please send me a brochure?

additional_notes: Used with geben (“to give”): jemandem eine Chance geben = to give someone a chance (e.g., to try, to prove themselves, or to succeed). Also common with haben (“to have”): eine Chance haben = to have a chance.
target_language_example: Gib mir bitte eine Chance.
native_language_example: Please give me a chance.

meaning: to give someone a chance (another chance).
additional_notes: Used with a person in the dative (jemandem): "jemandem eine Chance geben" = to give someone an opportunity, often meaning to give them a try or forgive and let them try again in a relationship, job, or situation. You can add "noch" to mean "another": "noch eine Chance geben".
target_language_example: Ich finde, du solltest Tom eine Chance geben.
native_language_example: I think you should give Tom a chance.

meaning: a stupid thing (a mistake; something foolish).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like "machen" to mean you did something foolish or careless (often with regret). "Dummheit" is a noun meaning "stupidity," but in the singular it commonly refers to one specific foolish action. You can emphasize it with words like "so/solch": "so eine Dummheit!" = "what a stupid thing to do!"
target_language_example: Es tut mir leid—ich habe eine Dummheit gesagt.
native_language_example: I’m sorry—I said something stupid.

additional_notes: Noun: **die E-Mail** (feminine). In the accusative (direct object) it’s **eine E-Mail**: *eine E-Mail schicken* = “to send an email”, *eine E-Mail bekommen/kriegen* = “to get/receive an email”. Often used with **an + Akk.** for the recipient: *eine E-Mail an Tom schicken*.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir bitte eine E-Mail schicken?
native_language_example: Can you please send me an email?

additional_notes: Past tense with "schicken" (to send): "Ich habe … eine E-Mail geschickt" = "I sent/have sent … an email." Often used with an indirect object in the dative (mir/dir/ihm/ihr/Ihnen) to say who you sent it to, and with "gerade" to mean "just now".
target_language_example: Ich habe meiner Kollegin eine E-Mail geschickt.
native_language_example: I sent my colleague an email.

additional_notes: Used to express respect or that you feel privileged (often with "Es ist eine Ehre, ..." / "Es wäre mir eine Ehre, ..."). You can also say "Was für eine Ehre!" to react to something flattering. Often used in formal or polite situations.
target_language_example: Es ist mir eine Ehre, Sie kennenzulernen.
native_language_example: It’s an honor to meet you.

meaning: to get an A / the top grade (1) in school.
additional_notes: Used in the German grading system where 1 is the best grade (often like an A). You’ll often add the subject with "in" (in Mathe) or the test/exam with "bei" or "in" (bei der Prüfung / in der Klausur). Common with "haben" too: "Ich habe eine Eins (in Mathe)."
target_language_example: Sie hat in Mathe eine Eins bekommen.
native_language_example: She got an A in math.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase for “a decision.” Often used with the verbs **eine Entscheidung treffen** (to make a decision) and **eine Entscheidung fällen** (to make/reach a decision, more formal). You may also hear **eine Entscheidung fällt** / **eine Entscheidung muss fallen** meaning “a decision is made / must be made.”
target_language_example: Wir müssen heute eine Entscheidung treffen.
native_language_example: We have to make a decision today.

additional_notes: Common collocation with the verb "treffen" (to make, lit. "to hit/meet"): "eine Entscheidung treffen" = to make a decision. Used with different subjects and tenses (e.g., "Ich habe eine Entscheidung getroffen"). Also often appears in the passive: "Es muss eine Entscheidung getroffen werden" = "A decision has to be made."
target_language_example: Ich habe endlich eine Entscheidung getroffen.
native_language_example: I finally made a decision.

additional_notes: Common, neutral phrase used with verbs like müssen (must/have to) or sollen (should). Often used when choosing between options or when a decision is required soon.
target_language_example: Wir müssen heute eine Entscheidung treffen.
native_language_example: We have to make a decision today.

additional_notes: Means saying sorry for something you did. Common with verbs like „sich entschuldigen“ (to apologize), „eine Entschuldigung verlangen“ (to demand an apology), or „eine Entschuldigung ist fällig“ (an apology is due/needed).
target_language_example: Du schuldest ihr eine Entschuldigung.
native_language_example: You owe her an apology.

meaning: an explanation; a statement/account (why something happened).
additional_notes: Used when you want reasons or clarification. In “Hierfür gibt es … eine Erklärung”, it means there’s a reason for it. In “jemandem eine Erklärung schuldig sein”, it means “to owe someone an explanation” (often because you did something surprising or wrong). Also commonly used with verbs like „brauchen“, „geben“, „haben“, „finden“: „Ich brauche eine Erklärung.“
target_language_example: Ich brauche eine Erklärung dafür, was passiert ist.
native_language_example: I need an explanation for what happened.

additional_notes: Used with "haben" (to have a cold): "Ich habe eine Erkältung." You can also say "sich eine Erkältung zuziehen" = to catch a cold. Often used with "gegen" when talking about medicine/remedies: "gut gegen eine Erkältung" (good for a cold).
target_language_example: Ich glaube, ich habe eine Erkältung und bleibe heute zu Hause.
native_language_example: I think I have a cold and I’m staying home today.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something takes or lasts a very long time, or that something happened a long time ago. Common with verbs like dauern (to take), warten (to wait), kennen (to know), and with time expressions like her (ago).
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich habe eine Ewigkeit auf dich gewartet.
native_language_example: Sorry, I waited for you for ages.

additional_notes: Used when buying or asking the price of a public-transport ticket to a destination. Add the place name after nach (e.g., „eine Fahrkarte nach Berlin“). With a return ticket you’ll often hear „… nach X und zurück“ (“to X and back”).
target_language_example: Ich brauche bitte eine Fahrkarte nach München.
native_language_example: I need a ticket to Munich, please.

additional_notes: Used with "sein" ("Es ist eine Falle!" / "Das könnte eine Falle sein") to warn that something is a trick, a setup, or a dangerous situation. Often appears with words like "vielleicht" (maybe) or "könnte" (could) when you’re not sure.
target_language_example: Pass auf — das klingt wie eine Falle.
native_language_example: Be careful — that sounds like a trap.

additional_notes: Indefinite form of "Familie" (feminine). Used when talking about a family in general or introducing one: "eine Familie haben" (to have a family), "eine Familie gründen" (to start a family), "eine Familie unterhalten" (to support/provide for a family).
target_language_example: Sie wollen nächstes Jahr eine Familie gründen.
native_language_example: They want to start a family next year.

additional_notes: Used with countable drinks or liquids in a container: eine Flasche Bier/Whisky/Wasser. The noun is feminine: die Flasche; so in the accusative with “eine” it stays “eine Flasche”. You can also use it with “mit” to say what’s inside: eine Flasche mit Wasser.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir bitte eine Flasche Wasser geben?
native_language_example: Can you please give me a bottle of water?

additional_notes: Common when ordering or talking about quantities. "eine" changes depending on case (e.g., "Ich trinke eine Flasche Bier"; "mit einer Flasche Bier").
target_language_example: Ich hätte gern eine Flasche Bier, bitte.
native_language_example: I’d like a bottle of beer, please.

additional_notes: Used when ordering, asking for, offering, or talking about water in a bottle. The article changes depending on case: nominative/accusative "eine Flasche Wasser" (I want a bottle of water), dative "einer Flasche Wasser" (with/from a bottle of water).
target_language_example: Könnte ich bitte eine Flasche Wasser haben?
native_language_example: Could I please have a bottle of water?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a single bottle of wine. Often appears with verbs like „mitbringen“ (to bring along), „kaufen“ (to buy), „haben“ (to have), „geben“ (to give), or with location phrases like „auf dem Tisch“ (on the table). Word order can change (e.g., „Da steht …“ vs. „… steht da …“) without changing the basic meaning.
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte eine Flasche Wein kaufen?
native_language_example: Can you please buy a bottle of wine?

additional_notes: Most often a literal insect: *Da ist eine Fliege...* (“There’s a fly...”). Common with simple verbs like **fliegen** (to fly), **fangen** (to catch), **töten** (to kill), **essen** (to eat), and with locations using **auf** + dative: **auf der Decke** (“on the ceiling”). Also appears in proverbs/idioms (e.g., **mit einer Kanone eine Fliege töten** = “use excessive force for a small problem”).
target_language_example: Mach bitte das Fenster zu – hier ist eine Fliege.
native_language_example: Please close the window—there’s a fly in here.

additional_notes: Used with "haben" (to have) and "stellen" (to ask/pose): "Ich habe eine Frage." / "Ich stelle eine Frage." Also common to introduce a final question: "Eine Frage habe ich noch." In expressions like "eine Frage von Leben oder Tod" it means "a matter/question of life or death."
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich habe noch eine Frage.
native_language_example: Sorry, I still have one more question.

additional_notes: Used to say that something will probably happen sooner or later; often with "Es ist nur eine Frage der Zeit, bis ..." (= It’s only a matter of time until ...).
target_language_example: Es ist nur eine Frage der Zeit, bis er die Prüfung besteht.
native_language_example: It’s only a matter of time until he passes the exam.

additional_notes: This is the past participle phrase used with the verb **stellen** (“to ask/pose” a question) in the **Perfekt** tense: **jdm. eine Frage stellen** → **Ich habe dir eine Frage gestellt.** Word order often puts the participle **gestellt** at the end in subordinate clauses (e.g., *…, weil ich dir eine Frage gestellt habe.*).
target_language_example: Ich habe dir eine Frage gestellt.
native_language_example: I asked you a question.

additional_notes: A very common, polite way to introduce a question. The person you’re asking can be added in the dative: jemandem eine Frage stellen (e.g., Ihnen/dir/euch). Often used with modal verbs: Darf ich ...? (May I ...?), Ich möchte ... (I would like to ...), Ich muss ... (I need to ...).
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, darf ich Ihnen eine Frage stellen?
native_language_example: Excuse me, may I ask you a question?

additional_notes: Means “a woman” in general. In some contexts, *Frau* can also mean “(someone’s) wife” (similar to “my wife”), depending on what’s being talked about. *eine* is the indefinite article (“a/an”) in the feminine form; in the accusative it stays *eine* (e.g., *eine Frau sehen* = “to see a woman”).
target_language_example: Ich habe eine Frau im Park gesehen.
native_language_example: I saw a woman in the park.

meaning: “a woman whose …” (introducing a relative clause with “deren” = “whose”).
additional_notes: Used to describe a woman by adding extra information about someone or something connected to her. “Deren” is the genitive relative pronoun (feminine/plural), meaning “whose” and showing possession (e.g., whose husband, whose children). The noun after “deren” is usually in the nominative/accusative, but the ownership is marked by “deren.”
target_language_example: Eine Frau, deren Sohn im Ausland lebt, vermisst ihn sehr.
native_language_example: A woman whose son lives abroad misses him a lot.

additional_notes: Used to describe/identify a particular woman by adding more information in a relative clause. The verb in the “die …” clause goes to the end: „eine Frau, die dort saß“, „eine Frau, die dich liebt“. In other cases you may see other forms like „einer Frau, die …“ (dative) or „eine Frau, die …“ (accusative), depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Ich suche eine Frau, die Deutsch spricht.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a woman who speaks German.

additional_notes: Used for any language that is not your native language (your "Muttersprache"). Often appears with verbs like „lernen“ (to learn), „erlernen“ (to learn/acquire), and „beherrschen“ (to master).
target_language_example: Ich lerne gerade eine Fremdsprache für meinen Job.
native_language_example: I’m currently learning a foreign language for my job.

additional_notes: Uses "zu" + infinitive ("zu lernen") meaning “to learn.” Often appears as the subject of a sentence (like English “Learning a foreign language is…”). "Fremdsprache" means a foreign language (e.g., English, French, Spanish).
target_language_example: Eine Fremdsprache zu lernen macht Spaß.
native_language_example: Learning a foreign language is fun.

additional_notes: Used to express that something is enjoyable or makes you happy. Common patterns: „Es war/ist eine Freude, …“ = “It was/is a pleasure to …”; „Es wird mir eine Freude sein!“ = “It will be my pleasure!”; „Was für eine Freude!“ = “What a joy!”
target_language_example: Es ist mir eine Freude, Ihnen zu helfen.
native_language_example: It’s a pleasure for me to help you.

additional_notes: "Freundin" is the feminine form of "Freund". It can mean a platonic female friend (e.g., "eine Freundin in England", "eine Freundin begegnet") or a romantic partner (girlfriend), especially when talking about having/being with someone, relationships, or breaking up (e.g., "Hast du eine Freundin?", "wir haben uns getrennt"). Context usually makes the meaning clear.
target_language_example: Er hat seit einem Jahr eine Freundin.
native_language_example: He’s had a girlfriend for a year.

additional_notes: Used to introduce someone as a friend and to say who they are connected to: „eine Freundin von mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen“. In German, „eine Freundin“ usually means a female friend; „meine Freundin“ can also mean “my girlfriend” (romantic partner), but „eine Freundin von mir“ is typically just “a friend of mine.”
target_language_example: Anna ist eine Freundin von mir.
native_language_example: Anna is a friend of mine.

additional_notes: Used in work contexts for an increase in your salary. Common verbs: „eine Gehaltserhöhung bekommen“ (to get a raise), „um eine Gehaltserhöhung bitten“ (to ask for a raise), „eine Gehaltserhöhung verlangen“ (to demand a raise). Note: „Gehalt“ is typical for salaried jobs; „Lohnerhöhung“ is often used for hourly wages.
target_language_example: Ich möchte nächstes Jahr um eine Gehaltserhöhung bitten.
native_language_example: I’d like to ask for a pay raise next year.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like lesen (read), erzählen (tell), hören (hear), and vorlesen (read aloud). It often refers to a fictional story (e.g., a children’s story), but "Geschichte" can also mean "history" depending on context (then often with an article like "die Geschichte" or in phrases like "Geschichte lernen").
target_language_example: Kannst du mir eine Geschichte erzählen?
native_language_example: Can you tell me a story?

additional_notes: Used for a (usually female) witch in fairy tales, fantasy, or folklore. It can also be used as an insult about a woman ("She’s such a witch"), so be careful with tone and context. The plural is "Hexen" (witches).
target_language_example: In dem Märchen wohnt eine Hexe im Wald.
native_language_example: In the fairy tale, a witch lives in the forest.

meaning: an idea; a thought or suggestion.
additional_notes: Very common. Used literally for “an idea” and in set phrases like: „auf eine Idee kommen“ / „Mir kam eine Idee“ = “to get/have an idea”, „jemanden auf eine Idee bringen“ = “to give someone an idea”, and „eine Idee haben“ = “to have an idea” (often meaning a suggestion or plan).
target_language_example: Ich habe eine Idee: Wir treffen uns morgen um zehn.
native_language_example: I have an idea: Let’s meet tomorrow at ten.

additional_notes: Used to say you have a suggestion/plan, or that you know how to do something. In questions it often means “Do you have any idea…?” (i.e., do you know?). Common pattern: „Hast du eine Idee, wie/wo/was …?“
target_language_example: Hast du eine Idee, was wir heute Abend machen können, oder soll ich eine Idee haben?
native_language_example: Do you have an idea what we can do tonight, or should I come up with an idea?

additional_notes: "Kamera" is a feminine noun, so with "eine" it means "a/one camera" (indefinite article, nominative/accusative). Often used after verbs like "kaufen" (to buy), "haben" (to have), or "mitbringen" (to bring). In casual speech you may hear "’ne Kamera" instead of "eine Kamera".
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte eine Kamera mitbringen?
native_language_example: Can you please bring a camera?

meaning: a ticket; a map; a card.
additional_notes:
"Karte" has several common meanings. In these examples it can mean:
- a ticket (often for concerts, events, public transport): "eine Karte (für das Konzert)"
- a map (especially when someone draws you directions): "eine Karte zeichnen" / "eine Karte von deiner Straße"
- a card (depending on context: e.g., bank card, ID card, playing card). The meaning is usually clear from what follows ("für ...", "von ...") or from the situation.
target_language_example: Hast du schon eine Karte fürs Kino?
native_language_example: Do you already have a ticket for the cinema?

meaning: a disaster; (also) a total mess/complete failure.
additional_notes: Used for real disasters (earthquakes, accidents) and very often as an exaggeration for something going terribly wrong. With people, it means someone is hopeless at something: "Ich bin eine Katastrophe" = "I’m a mess / I’m terrible (at this)." "Das wäre eine Katastrophe!" warns that something would have very bad consequences.
target_language_example: Ohne dich wäre das eine Katastrophe gewesen.
native_language_example: Without you, that would have been a disaster.

additional_notes: Indefinite article + noun: use when talking about one unspecified cat, introducing a cat for the first time, or asking whether someone has a cat. Forms: nominative/accusative feminine "eine Katze"; dative "einer Katze" (e.g., Ich gebe einer Katze Wasser).
target_language_example: Ich sehe eine Katze im Garten.
native_language_example: I see a cat in the garden.

additional_notes: Used for a duplicate of a document, file, or other information. Often appears with verbs like „schicken“ (send), „senden“ (send), „machen“ (make), or „bekommen/erhalten“ (get/receive). Note: „Kopie“ is feminine (die Kopie); other forms include „die Kopie“ (the copy) and „Kopien“ (copies).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir bitte eine Kopie von dem Vertrag machen?
native_language_example: Can you please make me a copy of the contract?

additional_notes: Used for having a tie on (often because it’s required for work, an event, or a dress code). You can ask about rules with „Muss ich …?“ or „Soll ich …?“. In the perfect tense: „Ich habe eine Krawatte getragen.“
target_language_example: In diesem Restaurant muss man eine Krawatte tragen.
native_language_example: In this restaurant you have to wear a tie.

additional_notes: Kugel can describe a round object (a ball) or a spherical shape (Die Erde ist eine Kugel = “The Earth is a sphere”). In crime/weapon contexts it often means “a bullet” (durch eine Kugel verwundet = “wounded by a bullet”). Common phrases: jemandem eine Kugel verpassen (“to shoot someone”), sich eine Kugel einfangen (“to get shot / catch a bullet”).
target_language_example: Die Erde ist eine Kugel.
native_language_example: The Earth is a sphere.

additional_notes: "Kuh" is a feminine noun (die Kuh). "eine Kuh" is the indefinite form (“a cow”), used when talking about any cow in general or introducing one. Common related word: "melken" = to milk (a cow).
target_language_example: Auf dem Bauernhof sehen wir eine Kuh.
native_language_example: On the farm we see a cow.

meaning: to be a lesson (learned), especially from a bad experience.
additional_notes: Usually said as a warning or after a mistake: something unpleasant should teach someone not to do it again. Very common in the fixed phrases: „Das soll dir eine Lehre sein!“, „Das wird dir eine Lehre sein.“, and „Lass es dir eine Lehre sein!“. Uses dative for the person learning the lesson (mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen).
target_language_example: Wenn du wieder zu spät kommst, wird dir das eine Lehre sein.
native_language_example: If you’re late again, that will teach you a lesson.

meaning: a lesson; (also) “a lesson” as a punishment to teach someone not to do something again.
additional_notes: Can be neutral in learning contexts (“eine Lektion über …” = a lesson about …). Very often used in the fixed phrase “jemandem eine Lektion erteilen” = to teach someone a lesson (often with the idea of punishment/revenge). Common pattern: jemand braucht eine Lektion (“someone needs to be taught a lesson”).
target_language_example: Wenn du so weitermachst, wird dir jemand eine Lektion erteilen.
native_language_example: If you keep doing that, someone will teach you a lesson.

additional_notes: Used for a written (or digital) list of items, tasks, names, places, etc. Common with verbs like „eine Liste machen“ (to make a list) or „eine Liste von …“ (a list of …).
target_language_example: Ich mache eine Liste, damit ich nichts vergesse.
native_language_example: I’m making a list so I don’t forget anything.

meaning: a solution (an answer/way to solve a problem).
additional_notes: Used when talking about solving a problem or finding an answer. Very common with verbs like „finden“ (to find), „haben“ (to have), „suchen“ (to look for), and „anbieten“ (to offer). Grammar note: „Lösung“ is feminine (die Lösung), so „eine Lösung“ is singular; plural: „Lösungen“.
target_language_example: Wir brauchen schnell eine Lösung für dieses Problem.
native_language_example: We need a solution for this problem quickly.

additional_notes: Used for solving a problem or reaching an agreement. Common with teamwork phrasing like "Lass(t) uns ..." or with modal verbs/future: "Wir können eine Lösung finden" / "Wir werden eine Lösung finden". Verb pattern: "eine Lösung" (accusative) + "finden".
target_language_example: Ich bin sicher, dass wir eine Lösung finden werden.
native_language_example: I’m sure that we will find a solution.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase with the indefinite article: "Das ist eine Lüge" = "That’s a lie." Often used with emphasis like "nichts als" (nothing but) or in contrasts: "Das war eine Lüge" (That was a lie). Related verb: "lügen" = to lie.
target_language_example: Ich glaube dir nicht – das ist eine Lüge.
native_language_example: I don’t believe you — that’s a lie.

additional_notes: Usually means a face covering (e.g., for health/safety) or a disguise to hide your identity. In the phrase „eine Maske tragen/anhaben“ it means “to wear a mask.”
target_language_example: Im Zug muss man eine Maske tragen.
native_language_example: On the train you have to wear a mask.

additional_notes: “Maus” is a feminine noun (die Maus). “eine Maus” is the indefinite form (“a mouse”) used when it’s not a specific mouse. Common with verbs like sehen (to see), fangen (to catch), and hören (to hear).
target_language_example: In der Küche ist eine Maus!
native_language_example: There’s a mouse in the kitchen!

additional_notes: Used with a noun to mean “a large amount/number of” something: eine Menge Leute/Probleme/Möbel. It can refer to a “crowd” in some contexts (eine Menge versammelte sich … = a crowd gathered). Often interchangeable with „viel(e)“, but „eine Menge“ sounds a bit more emphatic.
target_language_example: Ich habe heute eine Menge zu tun.
native_language_example: I have a lot to do today.

meaning: a lot of books; lots of books.
additional_notes: “eine Menge” is a very common way to say “a lot of / lots of” before a noun. It’s used for a large quantity (often similar to “viele”). You can swap in other nouns: “eine Menge Arbeit” (a lot of work), “eine Menge Leute” (lots of people).
target_language_example: In der Bibliothek gibt es eine Menge Bücher.
native_language_example: There are a lot of books in the library.

meaning: a lot of money; a large sum of money.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the amount of money is large. Very common in everyday German; often used with verbs like haben (to have), verdienen (to earn), ausgeben (to spend), kosten (to cost), erben/hinterlassen (to inherit/leave behind).
target_language_example: Für das Auto habe ich eine Menge Geld bezahlt.
native_language_example: I paid a lot of money for the car.

meaning: a lot of time; lots of time.
additional_notes: “Eine Menge” means “a lot/lots,” so this phrase is used to say you have, save, spend, or waste a large amount of time (e.g., Zeit sparen = save time, Zeit verschwenden = waste time, Zeit verbringen = spend time).
target_language_example: Mit dem Zug sparen wir eine Menge Zeit.
native_language_example: By taking the train, we save a lot of time.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like *wissen* (to know) or *lernen* (to learn) to say someone knows/learns a lot about a topic. *eine Menge* is an indefinite amount (“a lot”), and *über* is “about” + accusative (e.g., *über Blumen*, *über Boston*).
target_language_example: Ich weiß eine Menge über Deutschland.
native_language_example: I know a lot about Germany.

additional_notes: Literally the number 1,000,000. Very often used informally as hyperbole to mean “very many” (e.g., eine Million Mal/Fragen/Ideen = ‘a million times/questions/ideas’). As with all German nouns, Million is capitalized; with the number it’s usually used as: eine Million + noun (often plural): eine Million Fragen. You can also use other amounts: zwei Millionen, drei Millionen, etc.
target_language_example: Ich habe dir das schon eine Million Mal gesagt.
native_language_example: I’ve told you that a million times.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an amount of money (USD). As a direct object it often appears without extra endings: „eine Million Dollar“. With larger numbers: „zwei Millionen Dollar“. You’ll also see it in hypothetical questions: „Hättest du eine Million Dollar …?“
target_language_example: Wenn ich eine Million Dollar hätte, würde ich ein Haus kaufen.
native_language_example: If I had a million dollars, I would buy a house.

additional_notes: Used to state an amount of money in yen. In German, big numbers can be written out like this, and the currency name stays the same (Yen). With values, you’ll often see it with "wert" (worth) or in conditional sentences ("Hätte ich ..., würde ich ...").
target_language_example: Das kostet eine Million Yen.
native_language_example: That costs one million yen.

additional_notes: Literally “one minute.” Used both for an actual 60 seconds and as a polite way to ask someone to wait briefly (“One moment.”). Common with verbs like geben/nehmen/bleiben/warten: „Geben Sie mir eine Minute.” (formal) vs. „Gib/Gebt mir eine Minute.” (informal).
target_language_example: Warten Sie bitte eine Minute, ich komme gleich.
native_language_example: Please wait a moment; I’ll be right there.

additional_notes: Used to say how long something lasts. Often used with verbs like warten (wait), zuhören (listen), stehen (stand), allein lassen (leave alone). You can swap in other time amounts: eine Stunde lang (for an hour), zwei Tage lang (for two days).
target_language_example: Warte bitte eine Minute lang hier.
native_language_example: Please wait here for one minute.

meaning: an option; a possibility; a way (to do something).
additional_notes: Used to talk about one possible choice or solution. Very common with phrases like „Das ist (auch) eine Möglichkeit“ (That’s also an option) and „Es gibt noch eine Möglichkeit“ (There’s still one option left). Often followed by „zu“ + infinitive: „eine Möglichkeit, es zu beenden“ (a way to finish it).
target_language_example: Wir haben noch eine Möglichkeit, das Problem zu lösen.
native_language_example: We still have one way to solve the problem.

additional_notes: Refers to a single piece of money made of metal. Often used with verbs like fallen (to fall), aufheben (to pick up), jemandem etwas in die Hand drücken (to press/put something into someone’s hand), or werfen (to throw/toss), e.g., into a fountain or well. In German you also hear: "eine Münze werfen" (to toss a coin / flip a coin).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir eine Münze geben?
native_language_example: Can you give me a coin?

meaning: a message; a piece of news (a notification).
additional_notes: Most commonly means a message you send/receive (text, email, chat). Typical patterns: „eine Nachricht für + Akk.“ (a message for someone), „eine Nachricht von + Dat.“ (a message from someone), „jemandem eine Nachricht schicken“ (to send someone a message). „Nachricht“ can also mean “news” in general, especially in plural: „die Nachrichten“ = the news (TV/radio).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir bitte eine Nachricht schicken, wenn du angekommen bist?
native_language_example: Can you please send me a message when you’ve arrived?

additional_notes: Used to say you have a message intended for a particular person. Very common with the verb "haben" (to have): "Ich habe eine Nachricht für dich." You can change "eine" depending on the noun (e.g., "eine wichtige Nachricht"). The person after "für" is in the accusative (für + Akk.): für mich/dich/ihn/sie/uns/euch/sie/Sie.
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich habe eine Nachricht für Frau Schmidt.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I have a message for Mrs. Schmidt.

additional_notes: Used when you can’t reach someone directly (e.g., by phone/voicemail, at a reception desk, or via a note) and you leave information for them to get later. Often used with a person in the dative: jemandem eine Nachricht hinterlassen (e.g., mir/dir/ihm/ihr).
target_language_example: Wenn du mich nicht erreichst, kannst du mir bitte eine Nachricht hinterlassen.
native_language_example: If you can’t reach me, could you please leave me a message?

additional_notes: Usually means hitting someone with an open hand on the face (often as punishment or insult). It can also be used figuratively to mean a strong insult or humiliation ("That’s a slap in the face"), especially in politics or public situations. Common verbs: „jemandem eine Ohrfeige geben“ / „jemandem eine Ohrfeige verpassen“.
target_language_example: Das war eine Ohrfeige für ihn, als man ihn nicht eingeladen hat.
native_language_example: It was a slap in the face for him when they didn’t invite him.

additional_notes: "Party" is a very common English loanword in German. Use "eine Party" for an indefinite party (“a party”); for a specific one, use "die Party" (“the party”). Typical collocations: "auf eine Party gehen" (go to a party), "eine Party machen/feiern" (have/celebrate a party), informal "eine Party schmeißen" (throw a party).
target_language_example: Gestern gab es bei uns im Haus eine Party.
native_language_example: Yesterday there was a party in our building.

additional_notes: Used for taking time off from work/activity (Mach eine Pause. / Wir machen jetzt eine Pause.) or for a longer break from someone or something (eine Pause voneinander = “a break from each other”). Common verbs: eine Pause machen (to take a break), eine Pause brauchen (to need a break), jemandem eine Pause gönnen (to give someone a break).
target_language_example: Ich mache kurz eine Pause und komme gleich zurück.
native_language_example: I’m taking a short break and I’ll be right back.

additional_notes: Used when you want to stop what you’re doing for a short time to rest. Very common at work or during studying. You can ask politely with: „Kann ich eine Pause machen?“ or more formally: „Hätten Sie etwas dagegen, wenn ich eine Pause machen würde?“
target_language_example: Ich muss eine Pause machen.
native_language_example: I need to take a break.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a single individual. Often contrasts with more people ("nur eine Person" = only one person; "mehr als nur eine Person" = more than one person). With numbers/quantities it often means “except for one person” ("alle bis auf eine Person"). Also used in general statements about what a person should do (similar to English “a person/one”).
target_language_example: Nur eine Person kann hier rein.
native_language_example: Only one person can come in here.

additional_notes: A firearm that you can hold with one hand. In German you’ll often see it with verbs like "haben" (to have), "tragen" (to carry), and "ziehen" (to pull out/draw), e.g. "eine Pistole ziehen" = "to draw/pull out a pistol". "Pistole" is feminine: "die Pistole"; accusative is "eine Pistole".
target_language_example: Der Mann hat eine Pistole in der Tasche.
native_language_example: The man has a pistol in his pocket.

additional_notes: Used when you mean one pizza (indefinite article). As a direct object, it often appears with verbs like essen (to eat) and bestellen (to order). If you add toppings, you can use „eine Pizza mit …“ (a pizza with …).
target_language_example: Ich möchte eine Pizza bestellen.
native_language_example: I'd like to order a pizza.

meaning: a rat; (insult) a despicable or sneaky person.
additional_notes: Literally the animal “ratte” (feminine noun: die Ratte). Can also be used as an insult to call someone nasty, treacherous, or contemptible (similar to “rat” in English).
target_language_example: In der Küche ist eine Ratte — fass sie nicht mit der Hand an!
native_language_example: There’s a rat in the kitchen—don’t touch it with your hand!

meaning: a speech (a formal talk to an audience).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like „eine Rede halten“ (= to give/deliver a speech). Common in formal settings (meetings, weddings, ceremonies). Related word: „Lampenfieber“ = stage fright.
target_language_example: Sie hält morgen eine Rede bei der Hochzeit.
native_language_example: She’s giving a speech at the wedding tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used when someone speaks to an audience in a formal or semi-formal situation (e.g., at school, a wedding, a meeting). Often used with "müssen" (to have to) or "vor" + dative to say who you’re speaking in front of: "vor der Klasse eine Rede halten".
target_language_example: Ich dachte schon, ich müsste eine Rede halten.
native_language_example: I already thought I would have to give a speech.

meaning: a row/line; a series (a number of).
additional_notes: Used for things arranged next to each other or one behind the other ("in eine Reihe" / "eine Reihe nebeneinander" = in a row). Also means “a series/a number of” when referring to multiple items or people ("eine Reihe wohlhabender Klienten" = a number of wealthy clients). With a location/position it can mean “one row” in seating/rows ("Eine Reihe vor mir" = one row in front of me).
target_language_example: Eine Reihe vor mir saß eine schöne Frau.
native_language_example: A row in front of me sat a beautiful woman.

additional_notes: Used with a destination: "eine Reise nach + place". With countries and cities you typically use "nach" (e.g., nach Amerika, nach Europa, nach New York). Often used with verbs like "machen/unternehmen/planen/buchen".
target_language_example: Nächstes Jahr machen wir eine Reise nach Japan.
native_language_example: Next year we’re taking a trip to Japan.

meaning: a roll (e.g., of paper); a role/part (in a play/film); also in expressions: “does it matter?”
additional_notes: “Rolle” can mean a physical roll (“eine Rolle Toilettenpapier”) or a character/part (“eine Rolle spielen”). In the common phrase “eine Rolle spielen”, it often means “to matter / to play a role”: “Spielt es eine Rolle?” = “Does it matter?” You also see it with auditions: “für eine Rolle vorspielen” = “to audition for a role.”
target_language_example: Spielt es eine Rolle, ob wir heute oder morgen gehen?
native_language_example: Does it matter whether we go today or tomorrow?

meaning: to play a role; to matter (be important).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is important or has an influence. Very common in negatives: „Das spielt (keine) Rolle.“ = “That (doesn’t) matter.” You can also specify what role it plays: „Dabei spielt Geld eine große Rolle.“ = “Money plays a big role in that.”
target_language_example: Bei dieser Entscheidung kann Geld eine Rolle spielen.
native_language_example: In this decision, money can play a role.

meaning: a round; a lap; a quick loop (walk/drive).
additional_notes: Used for repeated units in games or activities (eine Runde dauert …; eine Runde Karten spielen) and for going around once (eine Runde drehen/gehen = do one lap / take a short walk or drive around). Often also used when inviting someone: „Gehen wir eine Runde?“ = “Shall we go for a walk / take a quick round?”
target_language_example: Komm, wir gehen noch eine Runde um den Block.
native_language_example: Come on, let’s go one more time around the block.

meaning: a thing; a matter; one point (to mention/do).
additional_notes: Used very broadly for an item, issue, or point in a list. Common in phrases like „noch eine Sache“ (one more thing), „eine Sache erledigen“ (take care of something), and contrasts like „X ist eine Sache, Y eine andere“ (X is one thing, Y another).
target_language_example: Ich habe noch eine Sache zu sagen.
native_language_example: I have one more thing to say.

additional_notes: Used to express strong disapproval, embarrassment, or regret about a situation. Common with “Es ist eine Schande!” (= “It’s a shame!”) or with emphasis like “So eine Schande!” / “Wirklich eine Schande, dass …”. Can refer both to something unfortunate and to something morally unacceptable or humiliating.
target_language_example: Es ist eine Schande, dass niemand geholfen hat.
native_language_example: It’s a shame that nobody helped.

additional_notes: Most commonly means the animal (“a snake”). It can also mean a queue (especially in phrases like „eine Schlange stehen“ = “to stand in line”). As an insult („Du bist eine Schlange!“), it suggests someone is treacherous or two-faced.
target_language_example: Ich habe Angst, dass im Garten eine Schlange ist.
native_language_example: I’m afraid there’s a snake in the garden.

meaning: to have a soft spot for; to be especially fond of (someone/something).
additional_notes: Used with **für + accusative**: *eine Schwäche für jemanden/etwas haben*. It often implies a special liking or weakness you can’t resist (people, foods, styles, etc.).
target_language_example: Ich habe eine Schwäche für Schokolade.
native_language_example: I have a soft spot for chocolate.

meaning: “a second” (a very short moment); also used to mean “one moment / just a second.”
additional_notes: Often used in requests to ask someone to wait briefly or to pause for a moment. It can be literal (one second) or just a general “very short time.” In polite speech you may hear it with formal "Sie" (e.g., "Warten Sie eine Sekunde.").
target_language_example: Warte bitte eine Sekunde, ich bin gleich da.
native_language_example: Please wait a second, I'll be right there.

additional_notes: Indefinite form: "eine" + feminine noun "Sprache". Used when talking about an unspecified language or choosing/learning one (e.g., "eine Sprache lernen", "eine Sprache auswählen"). The plural is "Sprachen".
target_language_example: Ich lerne eine Sprache für die Arbeit.
native_language_example: I’m learning a language for work.

additional_notes: Uses the verb pattern "etwas zu lernen" (= to learn something). Here, "eine Sprache" is the object and "zu lernen" often appears in general statements with "ist" (e.g., "Eine Sprache zu lernen ist…") or after "um" to express purpose ("um … zu …" = "in order to …").
target_language_example: Ich versuche, eine Sprache zu lernen, aber ich brauche mehr Zeit.
native_language_example: I’m trying to learn a language, but I need more time.

additional_notes: Used to describe the role/title of a job. Common with verbs like **sich bewerben um/auf** (to apply for) and **finden/bekommen** (to find/get): *eine Stelle als Kellner* = “a job as a waiter.” **Stelle** can mean “position” or “job opening,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Ich suche eine Stelle als Verkäufer.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a job as a salesperson.

additional_notes: Used to say a duration of 60 minutes (how long something lasts). Often used with time expressions like „eine Stunde warten“ (to wait for an hour) or „in einer Stunde“ (in an hour). In the examples, it describes how long someone waited.
target_language_example: Ich brauche noch eine Stunde, dann bin ich fertig.
native_language_example: I need another hour, then I’ll be finished.

additional_notes: Used to say how long an action lasted. It often comes after the time amount: „eine Stunde lang“, „zwei Stunden lang“. Similar meaning to „eine Stunde“ (accusative duration), but adding „lang“ emphasizes the length. Not the same as „in einer Stunde“ (= in one hour / within an hour).
target_language_example: Wir sind eine Stunde lang spazieren gegangen.
native_language_example: We went for a walk for an hour.

additional_notes: Used to say someone waits for about 60 minutes. Often appears as "eine Stunde warten" (exactly one hour) or "über eine Stunde warten" (more than an hour). You can also use it in polite requests: "Würden Sie (bitte) eine Stunde warten?" = "Would you (please) wait an hour?"
target_language_example: Wir mussten eine Stunde warten.
native_language_example: We had to wait an hour.

additional_notes: A common noun used when you need portable light, especially in the dark or during a power outage. Often used with verbs like „brauchen“ (need), „dabeihaben“ (have with you), „benutzen“ (use), or „(sich) borgen“ (borrow).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir bitte eine Taschenlampe geben?
native_language_example: Can you please give me a flashlight?

meaning: “a cup” (a drinking cup; often also a cupful as a measure).
additional_notes: Used with drinks: „eine Tasse Kaffee/Tee/Kakao“ = “a cup of coffee/tea/cocoa.” In everyday speech it can mean either the physical cup or the amount it holds (“a cupful”). Noun: „die Tasse“ (feminine).
target_language_example: Ich hätte gern eine Tasse Tee, bitte.
native_language_example: I’d like a cup of tea, please.

additional_notes: Used when ordering, offering, or talking about a single serving of coffee. In sentences it often appears with polite phrases like „Bitte“ or „Wäre Ihnen … gefällig?“ and with the accusative after verbs like „bringen“ (to bring) or „stellen“ (to put/place).
target_language_example: Ich hätte gern eine Tasse Kaffee, bitte.
native_language_example: I’d like a cup of coffee, please.

additional_notes: Used when ordering, offering, or talking about drinking tea. Grammar: "eine" (a) is feminine because "die Tasse" is feminine; in the accusative you say "eine Tasse Tee" (e.g., "Ich möchte eine Tasse Tee").
target_language_example: Ich hätte gern eine Tasse Tee, bitte.
native_language_example: I’d like a cup of tea, please.

additional_notes: Used to say you have (or someone has) one female child. With the verb "haben" (to have): "Ich habe eine Tochter." In questions: "Haben Sie eine Tochter?" (formal) / "Hast du eine Tochter?" (informal). "eine" is the feminine form of "a"; compare "ein Sohn" (a son).
target_language_example: Wir haben eine Tochter und einen Sohn.
native_language_example: We have a daughter and a son.

meaning: a bag; a packet (e.g., of chips).
additional_notes: Common in shops: "Möchten Sie eine Tüte?" means “Would you like a bag?” (often a paper/plastic carrier bag). It can also mean a sealed packet of snacks: "eine Tüte Chips" = “a bag/packet of chips.” The plural is "Tüten".
target_language_example: Kann ich bitte eine Tüte haben?
native_language_example: Can I have a bag, please?

meaning: to have an appointment / a date (an arranged meeting).
additional_notes: Used when you’ve already arranged to meet someone at a certain time. Often with "mit" + dative: "Ich habe eine Verabredung mit ...". In everyday speech it can mean a romantic date, but it can also be any planned meeting; for a more formal/professional meeting, "einen Termin haben" is common.
target_language_example: Ich kann nicht mitkommen, ich habe eine Verabredung heute Abend.
native_language_example: I can't come along; I have an appointment (a date) this evening.

additional_notes: "Waffe" is a feminine noun (die Waffe). "Eine Waffe" is the indefinite form meaning "a weapon"; in the plural: "Waffen" (weapons). Often used with verbs like "haben" (to have/carry) or "tragen" (to carry).
target_language_example: Der Mann hatte eine Waffe dabei.
native_language_example: The man had a weapon with him.

meaning: for a while; for some time.
additional_notes: Used to talk about an unspecified, limited period of time. Often used with verbs like bleiben (stay), warten (wait), schweigen (be silent), fahren (drive). You may also see "eine Weile lang" (= for a while), which adds emphasis but keeps the same meaning.
target_language_example: Ich setze mich eine Weile und warte auf dich.
native_language_example: I’ll sit for a while and wait for you.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration of seven days (how long something lasts, how long someone stays, etc.). Often appears with time expressions like „für eine Woche“ (for a week) or „eine Woche später“ (a week later). Note: after certain prepositions/cases it may change form (e.g., „seit einer Woche“), but the base term is „eine Woche“.
target_language_example: Willst du wirklich eine Woche hier bleiben?
native_language_example: Do you really want to stay here for a week?

meaning: for a week; for one week (for the duration of a week).
additional_notes: Used to say how long something lasts or continues. It often goes with the present or future for planned duration ("Es wird eine Woche lang schneien") or with the past to describe how long something happened ("Ich war eine Woche lang im Krankenhaus"). Also common with "gültig" for tickets/validity: "Das Ticket ist eine Woche lang gültig."
target_language_example: Ich bin eine Woche lang in Berlin.
native_language_example: I’m in Berlin for a week.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happened one week after a previously mentioned time or event. Often placed at the beginning of a sentence as a time expression, but it can also appear after what it refers to.
target_language_example: Wir haben uns gestritten, und eine Woche später haben wir wieder miteinander gesprochen.
native_language_example: We argued, and a week later we talked to each other again.

meaning: an apartment/flat; a place to live (a unit in a building).
additional_notes: "Wohnung" is a feminine noun (die Wohnung). It commonly refers to an apartment/flat you rent or live in, and is often used with verbs like "mieten" (to rent), "suchen" (to look for), and "finden" (to find). For a whole standalone house, German usually uses "ein Haus" instead.
target_language_example: Wir suchen eine Wohnung in der Nähe der Arbeit.
native_language_example: We’re looking for an apartment near work.

meaning: for a while; for some time.
additional_notes: Used to say something happened/was true for a limited period of time (often temporary). It can be placed at the beginning of a sentence for emphasis (“Eine Zeit lang, …”) or in the middle like an adverb (“Ich lebte eine Zeit lang in …”).
target_language_example: Wir haben eine Zeit lang in Berlin gewohnt.
native_language_example: We lived in Berlin for a while.

meaning: for a while; for some time.
additional_notes: Used to say something lasts for an unspecified, temporary period. Often placed in the middle of the sentence (after the verb) or near the end: „Ich bleibe eine Zeit lang hier.“ / „Lass es eine Zeit lang stehen.“
target_language_example: Ich werde eine Zeit lang in Berlin wohnen.
native_language_example: I’m going to live in Berlin for a while.

meaning: for a while; for some time.
additional_notes: Used as an adverbial time expression to say something lasted temporarily (often an unspecified period). It can be placed early or mid-sentence: „Eine Zeitlang war es still.“ / „Er war eine Zeitlang weg.“
target_language_example: Ich habe eine Zeitlang in Berlin gearbeitet.
native_language_example: I worked in Berlin for a while.

additional_notes: A "Zeitschrift" is a regularly published magazine (weekly/monthly, etc.), often on a specific topic. The article changes with case: nominative/accusative "eine Zeitschrift" (Ich kaufe eine Zeitschrift), dative "einer Zeitschrift" (in einer Zeitschrift), plural "Zeitschriften".
target_language_example: Ich lese gern eine Zeitschrift im Zug.
native_language_example: I like to read a magazine on the train.

additional_notes: "Zigarette" is feminine: die Zigarette. "eine" is used for one/ a cigarette (indefinite article). Often used when offering/asking for one: "Willst du eine Zigarette?" (informal) or "Haben Sie vielleicht eine Zigarette?" (polite). Common verb: "eine Zigarette rauchen" = to smoke a cigarette.
target_language_example: Kann ich bitte eine Zigarette haben?
native_language_example: Can I please have a cigarette?

additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun (or a noun understood from context): *eine alte Straße* (an old street), *eine alte Kirche* (an old church). German adjectives change endings: with feminine *eine*, it becomes **alte**. On its own, it can also mean “an old one (female thing)” when the noun is omitted: *eine alte (Lampe)*.
target_language_example: Ich suche eine alte Tasche.
native_language_example: I’m looking for an old bag.

additional_notes: "eine" is the feminine indefinite article meaning "a/an". "alte" is the adjective "old" and takes the -e ending here because it follows an article (eine). Used to describe an elderly female person; depending on context, "alt" can sound a bit blunt, so you may also hear "eine ältere Frau" (an older/elderly woman) as a more neutral/polite option.
target_language_example: Dort wohnt eine alte Frau.
native_language_example: An old woman lives there.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a different item/person (often where the noun is feminine or understood from context). It’s the feminine form of "ein anderer / eine andere / ein anderes" and changes with case: e.g., "Ich nehme eine andere." (= I’ll take another one [feminine noun like "Uhr"]).
target_language_example: Ich hätte gern eine andere, bitte.
native_language_example: I’d like another one, please.

additional_notes: Uses the indefinite article + adjective: „eine“ + „andere“ + noun. Often implies “a different woman” from the one expected; in relationship contexts it can imply “another woman (someone else he’s involved with).” In questions, verb-first word order is common: „Liebst du eine andere Frau?“
target_language_example: Er hat eine andere Frau kennengelernt.
native_language_example: He met another woman.

additional_notes: Used when talking about any language that is different from the one already mentioned or assumed (e.g., “another language than French”). With verbs like lernen (to learn), sprechen (to speak), or übersetzen (to translate) it’s very common. Case changes depending on the verb/preposition: e.g., in eine andere Sprache (into another language, accusative).
target_language_example: Ich möchte nächstes Jahr eine andere Sprache lernen.
native_language_example: I want to learn another language next year.

additional_notes: Used to describe a woman who is well-known for acting. In sentences with jobs/roles, German often uses "werden" (to become) and "sein" (to be): "Sie wollte eine berühmte Schauspielerin werden" (She wanted to become a famous actress), "Sie ist/war eine berühmte Schauspielerin" (She is/was a famous actress). "Eine" is the feminine form of "a" because "Schauspielerin" is feminine.
target_language_example: Nach dem Film war sie eine berühmte Schauspielerin.
native_language_example: After the movie, she was a famous actress.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine noun (or an implied one) to compare and say something is improved: e.g., eine bessere Welt (a better world), eine bessere Erklärung (a better explanation), eine bessere Arbeit (a better job), eine bessere Stelle (a better position). You’ll also see it with other endings depending on gender/case (ein besserer / ein besseres / einen besseren, etc.).
target_language_example: Ich brauche eine bessere Idee.
native_language_example: I need a better idea.

additional_notes: Used when you want to propose an alternative suggestion or ask someone for a better suggestion. Often said as a stand-alone comment: "Ich habe eine bessere Idee." You can also ask politely: "Haben Sie eine bessere Idee?"
target_language_example: Warte kurz—ich habe eine bessere Idee.
native_language_example: Wait a second—I have a better idea.

meaning: a better method / a better way.
additional_notes: Used when suggesting an improved approach. Often appears after verbs like „zeigen“ (to show) or „kennen“ (to know). The ending on „besser-“ changes with gender/case (e.g., „eine bessere Methode“, „einer besseren Methode“).
target_language_example: Wir brauchen eine bessere Methode, um Zeit zu sparen.
native_language_example: We need a better method to save time.

meaning: “a stupid/silly question” (often said as a polite, self-deprecating way to ask something).
additional_notes: Used literally to criticize a question ("Das war eine dumme Frage.", "Was für eine dumme Frage!"). Very often it’s used politely before asking for clarification: "Ich habe mal eine dumme Frage" / "Darf ich (Ihnen/dir) eine dumme Frage stellen?"—meaning “This might be obvious, but…” (It doesn’t necessarily mean the question is actually dumb.)
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, darf ich Ihnen eine dumme Frage stellen?
native_language_example: Sorry, may I ask you a silly question?

additional_notes: This is the feminine form of the adjective "echt" used with an indefinite article. It must match the gender/case of the noun: e.g., "eine echte Chance" (a real chance), "eine echte Kämpferin" (a real fighter), "eine echte Perle" (a real gem). With products/brands it often means "genuine, not fake" ("eine echte Rolex").
target_language_example: Das ist eine echte Chance für uns.
native_language_example: That’s a real chance for us.

additional_notes: Means a woman who is genuinely blonde (often implying naturally blonde, not dyed). The word "echt" adds emphasis (“really/actually”). Depending on context, it can also hint at the “dumb blonde” stereotype, so it may sound impolite if used that way.
target_language_example: Sie ist eine echte Blondine, aber sie ist sehr clever.
native_language_example: She’s a real blonde, but she’s very smart.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine noun (or a noun treated as feminine in the phrase) to emphasize that it’s the full amount: eine ganze CD (a whole CD), eine ganze Weile / Stunde (a whole while/hour), eine ganze Reihe (a whole series/number of). Forms change with gender/case: ein ganzer Tag, ein ganzes Jahr, einen ganzen Tag, etc.
target_language_example: Ich habe eine ganze Woche daran gearbeitet.
native_language_example: I worked on it for a whole week.

meaning: a lot; quite a lot (a large amount).
additional_notes: Used to say there is a large amount/number of something. Common with verbs like wissen/lernen/haben (e.g., „eine ganze Menge über … wissen“ = to know a lot about …). It often sounds a bit stronger than „viel“ and can refer to things (snow, money) or information/experience.
target_language_example: Ich habe heute eine ganze Menge zu tun.
native_language_example: I have a lot to do today.
