meaning: 'a great' / 'an excellent' (feminine form, used before a noun).
additional_notes: Used with a feminine noun in the nominative or accusative case: e.g., eine großartige Idee, eine großartige Stimme. The adjective ending -e comes after the indefinite article eine. Without a following noun, the phrase is incomplete in normal speech.
target_language_example: Das ist eine großartige Idee.
native_language_example: That’s a great idea.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine noun in the accusative or nominative (e.g., eine große Universität/Explosion/Ehre/Nachfrage/Ratte). With abstract nouns it often means “great” (eine große Ehre). As an adjective, „groß“ changes endings to match gender/case: masc. „ein großer …“, neut. „ein großes …“, plural „große …“.
target_language_example: Das war eine große Überraschung.
native_language_example: That was a big surprise.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has (or wants) many family members (often many children). In contexts like "unterstützen / versorgen / unterhalten", it implies having a lot of people to provide for financially.
target_language_example: Sie haben eine große Familie und brauchen deshalb ein größeres Auto.
native_language_example: They have a big family and therefore need a bigger car.

meaning: a big help; a great help.
additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something is very helpful. Often with "für" + accusative to show who benefits: "eine große Hilfe für mich/die Familie". You can also say "Das wäre eine große Hilfe" = "That would be a big help."
target_language_example: Danke, das war wirklich eine große Hilfe!
native_language_example: Thanks, that was really a big help!

additional_notes: Used to describe many people in one place. Often with verbs like „sich versammeln“ (to gather), „sich drängen“ (to press/crowd together), or „sich befinden“ (to be located). You can swap in other adjectives: „eine kleine Menschenmenge“ (a small crowd).
target_language_example: Vor dem Stadion wartete eine große Menschenmenge auf den Einlass.
native_language_example: A large crowd was waiting in front of the stadium to get in.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the amount of money is high/considerable. Often followed by "Geld" ("eine große Summe Geld") or the amount is clear from context. Also commonly used with verbs like "spenden" (donate), "ausgeben" (spend), and "leihen" (borrow/lend).
target_language_example: Für die Reparatur musste ich eine große Summe bezahlen.
native_language_example: I had to pay a large sum for the repair.

meaning: “a good …” (before a feminine noun) / “a good one” (feminine).
additional_notes: “Gute” is the adjective “gut” with the ending -e, used after the feminine article “eine” (nominative/accusative). It’s most often followed by a feminine noun (eine gute Frage, eine gute Reise, eine gute Atmosphäre). It can also be used without a noun if it’s clear from context, meaning “a good one” (feminine).
target_language_example: Ich brauche eine gute Idee.
native_language_example: I need a good idea.

additional_notes: Often means “a good job” in the sense of employment (Er hat/sucht/findet eine gute Arbeit). With verbs like leisten/machen, it can also mean doing work well (“to do good work”). In many situations, “einen guten Job” is a common alternative, especially when praising someone’s work.
target_language_example: Sie hat endlich eine gute Arbeit gefunden.
native_language_example: She finally found a good job.

additional_notes: Used to say that a plan or thought is good/sensible. Common with verbs like sein (Es ist/war eine gute Idee.), haben (Ich habe eine gute Idee.), or scheinen (Es schien mir eine gute Idee zu sein.). Also appears with "dass" in reported speech: "Ich entschied, dass es eine gute Idee sei."
target_language_example: Es ist eine gute Idee, früher loszufahren.
native_language_example: It’s a good idea to leave earlier.

meaning: some good news; a piece of good news.
additional_notes: Used to share or react to positive information. You’ll often hear it with "für dich" (for you): "Ich habe eine gute Nachricht für dich." You can also use it as an exclamation: "Endlich mal eine gute Nachricht!"
target_language_example: Ich habe eine gute Nachricht für dich: Wir haben das Zimmer bekommen.
native_language_example: I have some good news for you: we got the room.

meaning: "a good night" (said to wish someone a good night).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "wünschen" (to wish) when saying goodbye at bedtime: "Jemandem eine gute Nacht wünschen". Often shortened in speech to "Gute Nacht!".
target_language_example: Ich wünsche dir eine gute Nacht!
native_language_example: I wish you a good night! / Good night!

meaning: a good trip; (wish:) have a good trip.
additional_notes: Used as a friendly travel wish. Often said as part of a full sentence like „Gute Reise!“ or „Ich wünsche dir/Ihnen eine gute Reise.“ You can ask about someone’s trip with „Hattest du/Hatten Sie eine gute Reise?“
target_language_example: Ich wünsche euch eine gute Reise!
native_language_example: I wish you a good trip!

additional_notes: Used to describe a woman or girl who dances well. �Eine matches the feminine noun �Tnzerin. In questions youll often hear �Bist du (informal singular) or �Sind Sie (formal singular).
target_language_example: Sie ist wirklich eine gute Tänzerin.
native_language_example: Shes really a good dancer.

additional_notes: Often used with "haben" ("eine gute Zeit haben") to say you enjoyed yourself or that an experience/trip was pleasant. You can intensify it with words like "wirklich" (really) or specify where: "eine gute Zeit in Berlin".
target_language_example: Wir hatten gestern Abend eine gute Zeit.
native_language_example: We had a good time last night.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine noun (die …) to mean “half a/an …” or “half of the …”. It’s often followed by a unit or amount: eine halbe Flasche (half a bottle), eine halbe Meile (half a mile), eine halbe Million (half a million), eine halbe Tüte (half a bag). With masculine/neuter nouns you use different forms (einen halben / ein halbes).
target_language_example: Ich hätte gern eine halbe Stunde Pause.
native_language_example: I’d like a half-hour break.

additional_notes: Used to talk about duration (how long something lasts) or waiting time. Often appears with time-related verbs like dauern (to last), warten (to wait), lernen (to study), or with prepositions like in/für: „in einer halben Stunde“ (in half an hour), „für eine halbe Stunde“ (for half an hour). The form changes with case, e.g. nominative „eine halbe Stunde“, dative „in einer halben Stunde“.
target_language_example: Ich brauche nur eine halbe Stunde, um nach Hause zu kommen.
native_language_example: I only need half an hour to get home.

additional_notes: "hübsch" means "pretty" (often about someone’s looks). "eine" is the indefinite article in the accusative case (e.g., after "haben": "Er hat eine hübsche Frau"). With "sein" you can also describe someone: "Sie ist eine hübsche Frau". As an exclamation you can say: "Was für eine hübsche Frau!" = "What a pretty woman!"
target_language_example: Ich habe eine hübsche Frau gesehen.
native_language_example: I saw a pretty woman.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun (or plural with no article) to say something is interesting. It changes depending on gender/case: e.g. **ein interessanter** (masc.), **ein interessantes** (neut.), **eine interessante** (fem.). Often followed by nouns like **Geschichte** (story), **Reise** (trip), **Information** (information), **Tatsache** (fact).
target_language_example: Das ist eine interessante Idee.
native_language_example: That’s an interesting idea.

additional_notes: Used to describe something you read, heard, or were told (a story, anecdote, or plot). Often used after verbs like „lesen“ (to read), „hören“ (to hear), and „erzählen“ (to tell). Also common as a reaction: „Was für eine interessante Geschichte!“
target_language_example: Kannst du mir eine interessante Geschichte erzählen?
native_language_example: Can you tell me an interesting story?

additional_notes: Used to describe an unspecified young adult female person. With the indefinite article "eine", the adjective takes the ending -e: "eine junge Frau" (nominative/accusative). You can use it in statements or questions to refer to someone you see or are talking about.
target_language_example: Da drüben steht eine junge Frau und wartet auf den Bus.
native_language_example: A young woman is standing over there and waiting for the bus.

additional_notes: "jünger" means "younger". With a feminine noun like "Schwester", it becomes "jüngere" (ending -e) after the article "eine". Commonly used to talk about family members: "Ich habe eine jüngere Schwester" = "I have a younger sister."
target_language_example: Meine jüngere Schwester wohnt in Berlin.
native_language_example: My younger sister lives in Berlin.

meaning: "a small / a little" (before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used with a feminine noun in the nominative or accusative case (e.g., eine kleine Pause, eine kleine Frage). "Eine" = "a" and "kleine" is the adjective ending that matches a feminine noun.
target_language_example: Ich brauche eine kleine Hilfe.
native_language_example: I need a little help.

additional_notes: Used to suggest or ask for a brief rest/stop (often with the verb "eine kleine Pause einlegen" = "to take a short break"). Common in work, meetings, travel, or while telling a story (pausing briefly, then continuing).
target_language_example: Nach einer Stunde machen wir eine kleine Pause.
native_language_example: After an hour, we’ll take a short break.

additional_notes: This is the feminine form of the adjective "kurz" after "eine" (nominative/accusative). It’s used before feminine nouns, e.g. "eine kurze Antwort/Nachricht/Entfernung/Hose/Dusche". With other genders you change the ending: "ein kurzer ..." (masc.), "ein kurzes ..." (neut.), "kurze ..." (plural). Note: "eine Kurze" (capital K) can also mean a small shot of liquor in some contexts, but that’s not what’s meant in the examples.
target_language_example: Ich schreibe nur eine kurze E-Mail.
native_language_example: I’m only writing a short email.

additional_notes: Used when suggesting or announcing a brief interruption in an activity (work, studying, traveling, etc.). Often with verbs like „machen“ (to take/make) or „einlegen“ (to take). You can also say „Zeit für eine kurze Pause!“ to signal it’s time to stop briefly.
target_language_example: Lass uns eine kurze Pause machen, dann arbeiten wir weiter.
native_language_example: Let’s take a short break, then we’ll keep working.

additional_notes: This is the feminine form of the adjective "lang" after the indefinite article "eine". It normally needs a noun right after it, e.g. "eine lange Geschichte" (a long story), "eine lange Fahrt" (a long drive), "eine lange Reise" (a long trip), "eine lange Nachricht" (a long message).
target_language_example: Das war eine lange Nacht.
native_language_example: That was a long night.

meaning: to have a long drive (ahead of you).
additional_notes: Used with "vor" + dative pronoun to say a long journey is coming up: "Ich habe … vor mir" (I have … ahead of me), "du … vor dir", "er/sie … vor sich", "wir … vor uns", "ihr … vor euch", "sie/Sie … vor sich". Often used to explain why you need to rest or leave early.
target_language_example: Ich gehe jetzt schlafen, weil ich morgen eine lange Fahrt vor mir habe.
native_language_example: I'm going to sleep now because I have a long drive ahead of me tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to describe a long duration. Common with adverbs like „schon“ (for quite a while/already) or in constructions with „bis“ (until) to indicate how long something takes. Can also be used as a short standalone answer: „Eine lange Zeit.“
target_language_example: Wir brauchen eine lange Zeit, bis wir eine Fremdsprache beherrschen.
native_language_example: We need a long time until we master a foreign language.

additional_notes: This is the feminine form of the phrase "ein(e) + Adjektiv" in the nominative case. "Leicht" can mean "light" (not strong, not intense) with things like wind/illness ("eine leichte Brise", "eine leichte Erkältung"), and it can also mean "easy" with tasks/subjects ("eine leichte Sprache" = an easy language). It normally needs a noun after it; on its own it’s only used when the noun is understood from context.
target_language_example: Ich hätte gern eine leichte Suppe.
native_language_example: I’d like a light soup.

meaning: a last chance; a final opportunity.
additional_notes: Used when there’s only one more opportunity left before it’s too late or before you stop trying. Often said to ask someone to try again or to forgive you ("Gib mir eine letzte Chance!"). Also common with "noch" (still): "Wir haben noch eine letzte Chance."
target_language_example: Bitte gib mir eine letzte Chance, es besser zu machen.
native_language_example: Please give me one last chance to do it better.

additional_notes: Used when someone tells or reads a story that is amusing. „lustig“ can mean funny/amusing, not necessarily “joke.” You can change the article/case depending on the sentence (e.g., „eine lustige Geschichte“ as the object of „erzählen/vorlesen“).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir eine lustige Geschichte erzählen?
native_language_example: Can you tell me a funny story?

additional_notes: Used before a feminine noun (e.g., *eine nette Überraschung*, *eine nette Person*). *nett* means “nice/kind/pleasant.” The ending **-e** is the adjective ending after **eine** with feminine nouns in the nominative (and also accusative). Often used to describe someone’s personality or a pleasant event.
target_language_example: Danke, das ist wirklich eine nette Idee.
native_language_example: Thanks, that’s a really nice idea.

additional_notes: Used with feminine nouns (nominative/accusative), e.g. „eine neue Wohnung“, „eine neue Ära“, „eine neue Filiale“, „eine neue Schwester“. It can also stand alone when the feminine noun is understood from context: „Ich brauche eine neue.“ = “I need a new one.”
target_language_example: Ich brauche eine neue Wohnung.
native_language_example: I need a new apartment.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is unfamiliar to someone (they haven’t experienced it before). Often appears with „für“ + a person: „Das war eine neue Erfahrung für mich/ihn/uns.“
target_language_example: Das ist eine neue Erfahrung für mich, aber es macht Spaß.
native_language_example: This is a new experience for me, but it’s fun.

meaning: a new girlfriend; a new (female) friend.
additional_notes: “Freundin” can mean either “girlfriend” (romantic partner) or “female friend.” The intended meaning depends on context (e.g., with “haben” or “suchen” it often implies a girlfriend). “Eine” and “neue” change depending on case and gender (e.g., “mit einer neuen Freundin”).
target_language_example: Er ist sehr glücklich, weil er eine neue Freundin hat.
native_language_example: He’s very happy because he has a new girlfriend.

additional_notes: Often used after verbs like anfangen/beginnen (to start) or as the subject of a sentence. The verb lernen goes at the end in this infinitive phrase (… zu lernen).
target_language_example: Ich versuche gerade, eine neue Sprache zu lernen.
native_language_example: I’m currently trying to learn a new language.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine noun to say something is very big. It’s the indefinite article + adjective ending: eine riesige + feminine noun (e.g., eine riesige Spinne, eine riesige Halle). With masculine/neuter nouns it changes: ein riesiger Hund, ein riesiges Haus.
target_language_example: Das ist eine riesige Überraschung.
native_language_example: That’s a huge surprise.

additional_notes: Used to talk about languages in the Romance family (e.g., French, Spanish, Italian, Portuguese, Romanian). The adjective changes ending depending on the article/case (e.g., „eine romanische Sprache“, „die romanischen Sprachen“).
target_language_example: Spanisch ist eine romanische Sprache.
native_language_example: Spanish is a Romance language.

additional_notes: This is the feminine accusative/nominative form of the adjective "schlecht" used with "eine". It must be followed by a feminine noun: e.g., "eine schlechte Note" (a bad grade), "eine schlechte Entscheidung" (a bad decision), "eine schlechte Zeit" (a bad time). With masculine/neuter/plural nouns, the ending changes: "ein schlechter Tag", "ein schlechtes Gefühl", "schlechte Nachrichten".
target_language_example: Ich habe heute eine schlechte Nachricht bekommen.
native_language_example: I got bad news today.

additional_notes: Used to say that a plan or action is not smart or likely to end well. Often appears with verbs like „finden“/„halten“ (to think it’s a bad idea) or „sagen“ (to say it’s a bad idea). In your own sentence you can also use „Ich habe da eine schlechte Idee“ to mean “I have a (bad) idea,” often jokingly.
target_language_example: Ich glaube, das ist eine schlechte Idee.
native_language_example: I think that’s a bad idea.

meaning: bad news (a bad piece of information).
additional_notes: Used when you need to tell someone something negative or disappointing. Often appears with: „Ich habe eine schlechte Nachricht (für dich/Sie).“ (I have bad news (for you).) „jemandem eine schlechte Nachricht mitteilen“ means “to inform someone of bad news.” Note the article changes with case: nominative/accusative „eine schlechte Nachricht“, dative „einer schlechten Nachricht“.
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, ich habe eine schlechte Nachricht: Der Zug fällt heute aus.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have bad news: the train is canceled today.

additional_notes: This is the adjective phrase used before a feminine noun: **eine schwere + Nomen** (e.g., *eine schwere Frage* = a difficult question, *eine schwere Bürde* = a heavy burden, *eine schwere Geburt* = a difficult birth). **schwer** can mean literally “heavy” (weight) and also “difficult/serious” depending on context. The **-e** ending agrees with a feminine noun after **eine**.
target_language_example: Das war eine schwere Entscheidung.
native_language_example: That was a difficult decision.

meaning: a difficult situation; a tricky spot.
additional_notes: Often used with the verb phrase „jemanden in eine schwierige Lage bringen“ = “to put someone in a difficult situation.” „Lage“ here means “situation/position,” not “location.”
target_language_example: Ich will dich nicht in eine schwierige Lage bringen.
native_language_example: I don't want to put you in a difficult situation.

additional_notes: Used to describe a language as hard to learn. The adjective changes with the noun: *eine schwierige Sprache* (feminine, nominative/accusative). You can also use it after verbs like *sein* (to be), *finden* (to find/think), or *sagen* (to say): *Deutsch ist eine schwierige Sprache.* / *Ich finde Deutsch eine schwierige Sprache.*
target_language_example: Für viele Leute ist Arabisch eine schwierige Sprache.
native_language_example: For many people, Arabic is a difficult language.

additional_notes: This is the feminine form of the adjective "schön" after the indefinite article "eine". It must be followed by a feminine noun (or used as a noun, e.g. "eine Schöne" = “a beautiful woman”). The exact ending can change with case (e.g., nominative: "eine schöne Geschichte"; accusative: "eine schöne Geschichte"; dative: "einer schönen Geschichte").
target_language_example: Ich möchte eine schöne Wohnung.
native_language_example: I would like a nice apartment.

additional_notes: Used to describe a woman’s appearance. Because of German case endings, you may also see it as "eine schöne Frau" (nominative/accusative), "einer schönen Frau" (dative/genitive), etc. Often appears in exclamations like "Was für eine schöne Frau!" (= "What a beautiful woman!").
target_language_example: Er sagt, dass sie eine schöne Frau ist.
native_language_example: He says that she is a beautiful woman.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase with an adjective. "Stadt" is feminine (die Stadt). With the indefinite article "eine", the adjective often takes -e (eine schön-e Stadt). You can use it after verbs like "sein" (to be) or when describing a city you visit/live in.
target_language_example: Berlin ist eine schöne Stadt.
native_language_example: Berlin is a beautiful city.

additional_notes: Used to say you enjoyed a period of time or an event, or to wish someone an enjoyable time. Common with verbs like „haben“ (Ich hatte eine schöne Zeit.), „verleben“ (more formal: Ich habe eine schöne Zeit verlebt.), and „wünschen“ (Ich wünsche dir eine schöne Zeit!). You can add details like place/time: „im Urlaub“, „in Australien“, „gestern Abend“.
target_language_example: Wir hatten im Urlaub eine schöne Zeit.
native_language_example: We had a good time on vacation.

meaning: to have a nice/good time in (a place).
additional_notes: Used with a form of "haben" (habe/hat/hast/hatten, etc.) to ask about or wish someone an enjoyable stay in a location. Common in questions ("Hattest du …?") and in wishes ("Ich hoffe, du hast …"). The place follows after "in" (e.g., "in Berlin").
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, ihr habt eine schöne Zeit in Berlin.
native_language_example: I hope you have a nice time in Berlin.

meaning: “a very …” (feminine: used before an adjective + noun).
additional_notes: Used with feminine nouns when you want to strongly describe something: eine sehr + adjective + noun (e.g., eine sehr gute Idee). The adjective often takes the -e ending with feminine “eine” in nominative/accusative (eine sehr wichtige Person).
target_language_example: Das ist eine sehr gute Idee.
native_language_example: That’s a very good idea.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun (e.g., *eine sehr gute Frage/Idee/Stimme*). The adjective ending changes with gender/case: e.g., *ein sehr guter* (masc.), *ein sehr gutes* (neut.), *sehr gute* (plural or without article).
target_language_example: Das ist eine sehr gute Idee.
native_language_example: That’s a very good idea.

additional_notes: Used to describe something as very interesting. This exact form fits feminine nouns with an indefinite article (eine), e.g. eine sehr interessante Frage/Geschichte/Dokumentation. The adjective ending changes with gender/case: ein sehr interessantes Buch (neuter), ein sehr interessanter Film (masc. nom.), einen sehr interessanten Film (masc. acc.).
target_language_example: Ich finde das eine sehr interessante Idee.
native_language_example: I think that’s a very interesting idea.

additional_notes: Used to describe a feminine noun (e.g., Zeit, Blume, Wohnung, Handschrift, Schauspielerin). The adjective takes the weak ending -e after the indefinite article eine: eine sehr schöne Zeit/Blume. The noun that follows determines the gender/case; the phrase can appear in nominative or accusative depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Das ist eine sehr schöne Stadt.
native_language_example: That’s a very beautiful city.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine noun with the indefinite article ("eine"): e.g., "eine tolle Reise" (a great trip), "eine tolle Zeit" (a great time), "eine tolle Kamera" (a great camera). "toll" is a very common, friendly adjective meaning "great/awesome". Note: German "toll" is not the same as English "toll" (road fee).
target_language_example: Wir hatten eine tolle Party.
native_language_example: We had a great party.

additional_notes: Used to describe a story, situation, or someone’s life as sad or unfortunate. Often appears with forms of "sein" (ist/war) or with "erzählen" (to tell): "Er erzählte mir eine traurige Geschichte." You can also use it as an exclamation: "Was für eine traurige Geschichte!"
target_language_example: Das ist wirklich eine traurige Geschichte.
native_language_example: That’s really a sad story.

meaning: a rough idea; an approximate sense.
additional_notes: Used when you don’t know exactly, but you have some general sense (e.g., about time, location, a number, etc.). Often used in questions like „Hast du eine ungefähre Ahnung …?“ to ask if someone can estimate. „ungefähr“ = approximate/roughly; „Ahnung“ = idea/clue.
target_language_example: Ich habe nur eine ungefähre Ahnung, wann er ankommt.
native_language_example: I only have a rough idea of when he’ll arrive.

meaning: “a true story” (a story that really happened).
additional_notes: Used to say or ask that a story is real, not invented. Often with verbs like „erzählen“ (to tell) or „scheinen“ (to seem): „Erzähl mir eine wahre Geschichte.“ / „Das scheint eine wahre Geschichte zu sein.“
target_language_example: Kannst du mir eine wahre Geschichte erzählen?
native_language_example: Can you tell me a true story?

additional_notes: Used to praise a choice as smart and well-considered. Often appears with the verb "(eine) Entscheidung treffen" (to make a decision): "eine weise Entscheidung getroffen".
target_language_example: Das war eine weise Entscheidung.
native_language_example: That was a wise decision.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine noun (or as a stand-in for one) to mean an additional/next one: eine weitere Chance (another chance), eine weitere Person (another person), eine weitere (Tasse) (another cup). Changes with gender/case: ein weiterer (masc.), ein weiteres (neut.), weitere (plural).
target_language_example: Kann ich bitte eine weitere Flasche Wasser haben?
native_language_example: Can I please have another bottle of water?

additional_notes: Used when you learned something important from an experience (often after a mistake or a difficult situation). Commonly said with „lernen“: „eine wertvolle Lektion lernen“.
target_language_example: Ich habe aus diesem Fehler eine wertvolle Lektion gelernt.
native_language_example: I learned a valuable lesson from that mistake.

additional_notes: This is the start of a noun phrase: **eine** (indefinite article for feminine nouns) + **wichtige** (adjective “important” with the -e ending after **eine**). You need to add a feminine noun, e.g. **eine wichtige Prüfung** (an important exam), **eine wichtige Entscheidung** (an important decision), **eine wichtige Nachricht** (an important message). Used in nominative or accusative with feminine nouns.
target_language_example: Ich habe heute eine wichtige Frage.
native_language_example: I have an important question today.

additional_notes: Commonly used with the verb "spielen": "eine wichtige Rolle spielen" = "to play an important role" (to be important in a situation). The article changes with case (eine/einer/eine).
target_language_example: In dieser Entscheidung spielt Zeit eine wichtige Rolle.
native_language_example: In this decision, time plays an important role.

meaning: a second chance; another opportunity (to try again).
additional_notes: Used when someone made a mistake or failed and you allow them to try again. Common with verbs like „geben“ (to give) and „verdienen“ (to deserve): „jemandem eine zweite Chance geben“ = to give someone a second chance.
target_language_example: Bitte gib mir eine zweite Chance.
native_language_example: Please give me a second chance.

additional_notes: Used with the indefinite article (eine) to mean “a surprise” (something unexpected). Common patterns: „eine Überraschung für dich/euch/Sie“ (“a surprise for you”) and „Es soll eine Überraschung bleiben“ (“It should stay a surprise,” i.e., not be revealed).
target_language_example: Keine Sorge — ich habe eine Überraschung für dich.
native_language_example: Don’t worry—I have a surprise for you.

additional_notes: Used to announce that you have planned or prepared something unexpected for the other person. Very common with "Ich habe ..." ("I have...") and often said with excitement; you can replace "dich" with other people (e.g., "für euch", "für Sie").
target_language_example: Warte kurz—ich habe eine Überraschung für dich.
native_language_example: Wait a moment—I have a surprise for you.

additional_notes: Colloquial shorthand: "eine" stands for "eine Zigarette" (a cigarette). Common in spoken German, often with verbs of going/stepping out: "Ich geh eine rauchen" = "I’m going to have a smoke / step out for a cigarette."
target_language_example: Entschuldige, ich wollte bloß mal eine rauchen.
native_language_example: Sorry, I just wanted to smoke one (have a cigarette).

meaning: blind in one eye; (figuratively) biased/turning a blind eye.
additional_notes: Most often used as **auf einem Auge blind sein** (“to be blind in one eye”). Literally it can describe a physical condition. Figuratively, it means someone is unfairly ignoring something (showing bias), similar to “turning a blind eye.” Note the structure: **auf + dative** → *auf einem Auge*.
target_language_example: Die Polizei ist bei diesem Thema auf einem Auge blind.
native_language_example: The police are turning a blind eye on this issue.

meaning: hit by a car (run into by a car).
additional_notes: Used with the verb **anfahren** (separable: *fährt ... an*, *fuhr ... an*, *angefahren*) to describe a vehicle colliding with someone/something. Very often you’ll see it in the passive: **Ich wurde von einem Auto angefahren.** Without **von** it’s incomplete; **von einem Auto angefahren** = “hit by a car.” (Active: **Ein Auto hat mich angefahren.**)
target_language_example: Der Mann wurde von einem Auto angefahren, aber es geht ihm gut.
native_language_example: The man was hit by a car, but he’s fine.

meaning: to have been hit by a car (run into by a car).
additional_notes: Used with the passive perfect: **sein + Partizip II + worden**. The thing/person that hit you is in the dative: **von einem Auto / von einem Fahrer** or simply **einem Auto**. Full sentence often includes **Ich bin ...** (I have been ...).
target_language_example: Ich bin gestern von einem Auto angefahren worden.
native_language_example: Yesterday, I was hit by a car.

meaning: to run someone over with a car.
additional_notes: This wording is not the most idiomatic: in everyday German you’ll more often hear **jemanden mit dem Auto überfahren**. Grammatically, **überfahren** normally takes a direct object in the accusative (**jemanden überfahren**), while the vehicle is expressed with **mit**. The phrase **einem Auto überfahren** is understood as a dative/instrumental-like use (“run over by/with a car”), but it can sound nonstandard or context-dependent.
target_language_example: Der Hund wurde von einem Auto überfahren.
native_language_example: The dog was run over by a car.

meaning: (in the dative) “a car accident” / “in a car accident” (depending on the preposition).
additional_notes: This is the dative form of **ein Autounfall** (“a car accident”). You often see it after dative prepositions like **bei** (during/in the event of), **nach** (after), or **wegen** + dative in some dialects/colloquial use (standard German: **wegen eines Autounfalls** with genitive). Example patterns: **bei einem Autounfall** = “in a car accident”, **nach einem Autounfall** = “after a car accident”.
target_language_example: Nach einem Autounfall musste er ins Krankenhaus.
native_language_example: After a car accident, he had to go to the hospital.

meaning: “a tree” (in the dative case, often after prepositions like in/an/hinter/von).
additional_notes:
“einem Baum” is the dative form of “ein Baum” (“a tree”). You’ll often see it after prepositions:
- in + dative (location): „in einem Baum“ = in a tree
- an + dative (at/by, fixed location): „an einem Baum“ = at/by a tree
- hinter + dative (behind, location): „hinter einem Baum“ = behind a tree
- von + dative (from/of): „von einem Baum“ = from a tree / of a tree
With two-way prepositions (in, an, hinter, etc.), dative is used for location (where?), while accusative is used for direction/movement (where to?).
target_language_example: Das Fahrrad steht an einem Baum.
native_language_example: The bike is (standing) by a tree.

additional_notes: “Freund” means “friend”; “einem” is the dative form of “ein” (used for an indirect object). You’ll often see it with verbs like **geben** (to give) and **schreiben** (to write): *jemandem (Dat.) etwas geben/schreiben*. It can also appear after prepositions that take dative, e.g. **bei einem Freund** = “at a friend’s place,” **mit einem Freund** = “with a friend.”
target_language_example: Ich gebe einem Freund einen Tipp.
native_language_example: I’m giving a friend a tip.

meaning: (as in: sich mit einem Handtuch abtrocknen) “to dry off with a towel.”
additional_notes: Used with the separable verb **abtrocknen** (“to dry off”). In the examples it’s reflexive: **sich abtrocknen** = “to dry oneself off.” The towel is introduced with **mit** + dative: **mit einem Handtuch**. Word order: in the simple past/present, **ab** goes to the end: **Er trocknet sich … ab.**
target_language_example: Nach dem Baden trockne ich mich mit einem Handtuch ab.
native_language_example: After swimming, I dry myself off with a towel.

meaning: “a year” (dative singular of „ein Jahr“), used in time expressions.
additional_notes: Often appears after prepositions that take the dative, especially for time: „vor einem Jahr“ = a year ago, „seit einem Jahr“ = for/since a year, „nach einem Jahr“ = after a year. It’s the same noun „Jahr“ (“year”), but the article changes to dative: „ein Jahr“ → „einem Jahr“.
target_language_example: Ich lerne seit einem Jahr Deutsch.
native_language_example: I’ve been learning German for a year.

meaning: “not anymore for a year” / “not for a year now”.
additional_notes: Used with a time phrase (often with **seit** = “for/since”) to say something has **not happened / not worked / not been true anymore** for the last year: **seit einem Jahr nicht mehr** (“not for a year now”). With **nach** (“after”), it means something stopped after one year: **nach einem Jahr nicht mehr** (“no longer after one year”). It usually comes at the end of the clause.
target_language_example: Ich benutze diese App seit einem Jahr nicht mehr.
native_language_example: I haven’t used this app for a year now.

additional_notes: This is the dative form of "ein Lächeln" and is commonly used after prepositions like "mit" (with), "hinter" (behind), or "zu" (into/to), e.g. "mit einem Lächeln" = "with a smile". You’ll see it when describing how someone speaks/acts, or when someone hides feelings "behind a smile."
target_language_example: Er begrüßte mich mit einem Lächeln.
native_language_example: He greeted me with a smile.

meaning: “with a knife in …” / “a knife in …” (introduces where the knife is).
additional_notes: This is an incomplete phrase fragment that normally continues with a place/body part, e.g. **„mit einem Messer in der Hand“** (with a knife in your hand) or **„ein Messer im Rücken“** (a knife in the back). Note the case change depending on the full phrase: **mit** + dative (**mit einem Messer …**), but without **mit** it can appear as **ein Messer im/in den …** depending on location/movement.
target_language_example: Der Mann stand mit einem Messer in der Hand vor der Tür.
native_language_example: The man stood in front of the door with a knife in his hand.

additional_notes: Used with prepositions that take the dative, especially time expressions: vor einem Monat (“a month ago”), seit einem Monat (“for a month / since a month ago”), über einem Monat (“for over a month”), in einem Monat (“in one month / a month from now”). The base form is ein Monat (“one month”); it becomes einem Monat after these prepositions.
target_language_example: Ich habe ihn seit einem Monat nicht gesehen.
native_language_example: I haven’t seen him for a month.

meaning: to look for a parking spot/space.
additional_notes: Used when you are trying to find somewhere to park a car. The verb is usually used with dative: „Ich suche **einen** Parkplatz“ (accusative, common) is also very common in everyday speech, but the fixed phrasing „einem Parkplatz suchen“ appears too. You can also say: „einen Parkplatz finden“ (to find a parking spot).
target_language_example: Wir müssen noch einem Parkplatz suchen.
native_language_example: We still have to look for a parking spot.

meaning: “a restaurant” (dative: “to/at/in a restaurant,” depending on the preposition).
additional_notes: “einem” is the dative form of “ein” for a neuter noun. “Restaurant” is neuter (das Restaurant). You’ll often see “einem Restaurant” after prepositions that take the dative, e.g. “in einem Restaurant” (in/at a restaurant), “bei einem Restaurant” (near/at a restaurant), “aus einem Restaurant” (out of a restaurant).
target_language_example: Wir essen heute in einem Restaurant.
native_language_example: We’re eating in a restaurant today.

meaning: (to/with) an old friend; a long-time friend.
additional_notes: This phrase is in the dative case (einem Freund). It’s commonly used after verbs like **begegnen** (to meet/run into) and the expression **jemandem über den Weg laufen** (to run into someone by chance). It can also appear with **von**: *von einem alten Freund* (by/from an old friend).
target_language_example: Gestern bin ich im Supermarkt einem alten Freund begegnet.
native_language_example: Yesterday I ran into an old friend at the supermarket.

additional_notes: This is the dative form of "ein anderer" and is often used after prepositions that take the dative, especially for location or company: "in einem anderen …" (in another …), "mit einem anderen …" (with another …), "auf einem anderen …" (on another …). It usually modifies a masculine/neuter noun: "in einem anderen Flügel" / "in einem anderen Haus".
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns in einem anderen Café.
native_language_example: We’ll meet in another café.

additional_notes: "einem anderen Land" is the dative form of "ein anderes Land" (another country). It commonly follows prepositions like "aus" (from) and "in" (in) when talking about where someone comes from or lives: "aus einem anderen Land", "in einem anderen Land". Often used with the verb "kommen" (to come from).
target_language_example: Ich komme aus einem anderen Land, aber ich wohne jetzt hier.
native_language_example: I come from another country, but I live here now.

meaning: “another planet” (dative: “to/on/from another planet,” depending on the preposition).
additional_notes: This is the dative form of „ein anderer Planet“ (“another planet”). You’ll often see it after prepositions that take the dative, especially: „von einem anderen Planeten“ (from another planet) and „auf einem anderen Planeten“ (on another planet). It’s also common in a figurative sense meaning someone seems totally different, strange, or out of touch: „Er wirkt wie von einem anderen Planeten.“
target_language_example: Er wirkt manchmal wie von einem anderen Planeten.
native_language_example: Sometimes he seems like he’s from another planet.

meaning: a single; one and only (dative masculine/neuter).
additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that there is just one (not several). It’s the dative form of "ein einziger" and is used when the noun is in the dative case (often after prepositions like "aus", "an", "mit", or with certain verbs). Other forms include: "ein einziger" (masc. nom.), "ein einziges" (neut. nom.), "einer einzigen" (fem. dat.).
target_language_example: Ich habe heute mit einem einzigen Kaffee überlebt.
native_language_example: I survived today on a single coffee.

additional_notes: Used when the noun is masculine or neuter and is in the dative case (often after dative prepositions like mit, in (when location), neben, zu, bei). The adjective takes the ending -en in this form: einem großen Mann / einem großen Büro.
target_language_example: Ich wohne in einem großen Haus.
native_language_example: I live in a big house.

meaning: a big/large house (dative: “in/at a big house”).
additional_notes: Used after prepositions that take the dative case for location (most commonly: **in einem großen Haus** = “in a big house,” meaning you are *inside* it). The adjective ending **-en** in **großen** comes from the dative form after **ein-** words: **ein großes Haus** (nom./acc.) → **in einem großen Haus** (dat.).
target_language_example: Wir sind in einem großen Haus.
native_language_example: We are in a big house.

meaning: 'a hot coffee' (in the dative case), often in suggestions like “How about a hot coffee?”
additional_notes: This is the dative form of “ein heißer Kaffee.” It commonly appears after prepositions like **von** and **zu** in questions such as **Was hältst du von …?** / **Was sagst du zu …?** to make a suggestion or ask someone’s opinion. If you order one as a direct object, you usually say **einen heißen Kaffee** (accusative): *Ich möchte einen heißen Kaffee.*
target_language_example: Was hältst du von einem heißen Kaffee nach dem Spaziergang?
native_language_example: How about a hot coffee after the walk?

meaning: “a small …” (in the dative case: “to/with/from a small …”).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase; it’s the form of **ein** + **klein** used before a **masculine or neuter** noun in the **dative** (e.g., *mit/zu/bei/nach/von*, or after some verbs). It usually needs a noun right after it: *einem kleinen Raum*, *einem kleinen Kind*.
target_language_example: Wir gehen zu einem kleinen Café in der Nähe.
native_language_example: We’re going to a small café nearby.

meaning: “a small village” (dative: “in/to/at a small village,” depending on the preposition).
additional_notes: This is the dative form of "ein kleines Dorf". You’ll often see it after dative prepositions like "in" (location), "aus" (from), "bei" (at/near), or "zu" (to). The ending "-en" on "kleinen" matches dative after "einem".
target_language_example: Wir wohnen in einem kleinen Dorf.
native_language_example: We live in a small village.

additional_notes: This is the dative form of "ein neuer / ein neues" and is used when a masculine or neuter noun is in the dative case—often after prepositions like "in" (with location), "mit" (with), and "zu" (to). It’s usually followed by a noun, e.g. "in einem neuen Licht" (in a new light), "zu einem neuen Bürgerkrieg" (to a new civil war), "mit einem neuen Namen" (with a new name).
target_language_example: Mit einem neuen Plan geht alles leichter.
native_language_example: With a new plan, everything is easier.

meaning: a safe place (dative: “to/at a safe place”).
additional_notes: Used in the dative case (ein sicherer Ort → einem sicheren Ort), often after prepositions like „an“ or „zu“ or with verbs that imply moving/putting something somewhere (e.g., „bringen“, „legen“, „aufbewahren“). Common pattern: „an einen sicheren Ort“ (accusative) = to a safe place (movement), vs. „an einem sicheren Ort“ (dative) = in/at a safe place (location).
target_language_example: Bewahr deine Dokumente an einem sicheren Ort auf.
native_language_example: Keep your documents in a safe place.

additional_notes: Most often used in the phrase „jemandem einen Antrag machen“ = to propose to someone. Grammar: „einen Antrag“ (accusative) + the person in dative („mir/dir/ihr/ihm“). Note: „einen Antrag stellen“ is more common for an official application/request (e.g., a visa application), while „einen Antrag machen“ in everyday speech often means a marriage proposal.
target_language_example: Er hat ihr im Urlaub einen Antrag gemacht.
native_language_example: He proposed to her on vacation.

meaning: a lawyer / an attorney (accusative: “a lawyer” as the object).
additional_notes: "Anwalt" means lawyer/attorney. "Einen Anwalt" is the accusative form used after many verbs (e.g., "einen Anwalt engagieren" = to hire a lawyer; "einen Anwalt zu Rate ziehen" = to consult a lawyer). For a female lawyer you can say "eine Anwältin".
target_language_example: Wenn du Ärger mit dem Vertrag hast, solltest du einen Anwalt kontaktieren.
native_language_example: If you have trouble with the contract, you should contact a lawyer.

meaning: 'an apple' (accusative masculine: one apple as the direct object).
additional_notes: Used when "Apfel" is the direct object (what someone eats, gives, draws, etc.). "einen" is the accusative form of "ein" for masculine nouns. In the dative (indirect object), it becomes "einem Apfel" (e.g., "mit einem Apfel").
target_language_example: Kannst du mir bitte einen Apfel geben?
native_language_example: Can you please give me an apple?

additional_notes: "Arzt" = (medical) doctor/physician. You use "einen Arzt" after verbs that take the accusative, especially when you need someone: "einen Arzt schicken" (send a doctor), "einen Arzt brauchen" (need a doctor), "einen Arzt holen" (get a doctor), "einen Arzt zu Rate ziehen" (consult a doctor). For a female doctor, say "eine Ärztin".
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte einen Arzt rufen?
native_language_example: Can you please call a doctor?

meaning: to see a doctor; to consult a doctor.
additional_notes: Used when you advise or tell someone to get medical help. Common with modal verbs like müssen/ sollen (e.g., "Du musst/solltest ..."). In everyday speech, people also say "zum Arzt gehen" with a very similar meaning.
target_language_example: Wenn die Schmerzen nicht besser werden, solltest du einen Arzt aufsuchen.
native_language_example: If the pain doesn’t get better, you should see a doctor.

additional_notes: Used when you need medical help and want someone to contact a doctor to come to you (e.g., at home or in an emergency). Often used with "bitte" for polite requests. The verb "rufen" literally means "to call/shout", but here it means "to call (someone)".
target_language_example: Könnten Sie bitte einen Arzt rufen?
native_language_example: Could you please call a doctor?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to wait briefly or to say something will take only a short time. Often appears with polite phrases like „bitte“ or with verbs like „warten“ (wait), „Zeit haben“ (have time), „still sein“ (be quiet). Also common as „nur für einen Augenblick“ = “only for a moment.”
target_language_example: Warten Sie bitte einen Augenblick, ich bin gleich da.
native_language_example: Please wait a moment, I’ll be right there.

additional_notes: Used to say that something lasts only a very short time. Often appears with verbs like denken (think), schweigen (be silent), warten (wait), hinhorchen (listen closely), or with states like „alles war dunkel“ (everything was dark). It describes duration (how long), similar to „für einen Moment“ or „kurz“.
target_language_example: Einen Augenblick lang war ich verwirrt, dann verstand ich es.
native_language_example: For a moment I was confused, then I understood it.

meaning: a trip / an outing (usually short, for fun).
additional_notes: Often used with verbs like „machen“ (einen Ausflug machen = to go on an outing) or after „Lust auf …?“ to suggest doing something together. „Ausflug“ is typically a short day trip, often into nature or to a nearby place.
target_language_example: Am Sonntag machen wir einen Ausflug an den See.
native_language_example: On Sunday we're going on a trip to the lake.

additional_notes: Used with a reflexive pronoun + "lassen": "sich (einen Bart) wachsen lassen" = to let a beard grow / to grow a beard. In conversation you’ll often hear "Willst du dir einen Bart wachsen lassen?" (Are you going to grow a beard?).
target_language_example: Ich lasse mir gerade einen Bart wachsen.
native_language_example: I’m growing a beard right now.

additional_notes: Used when the tree is the direct object or the target of movement/impact. Common after verbs like „sehen“ (to see), „an … binden“ (to tie to), and with prepositions that take accusative to show motion/direction (e.g., „unter einen Baum gehen“ = to go under a tree). Also used with accidents/collisions: „in einen Baum fahren“ / „gegen einen Baum fahren“.
target_language_example: Wir setzen uns unter einen Baum.
native_language_example: We sit down under a tree.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **fällen** (“to fell, cut down”). In the perfect tense you say **einen Baum gefällt haben**: *Ich habe einen Baum gefällt.* Be careful: **gefällt** can also come from **gefallen** (“to like”) as in *Das gefällt mir* (“I like that”), but with **haben** + an object it usually means “felled.”
target_language_example: Warum hast du einen Baum gefällt?
native_language_example: Why did you cut down a tree?

additional_notes: "Bleistift" means "pencil." You use "einen Bleistift" when the pencil is the direct object (what someone has/needs/wants): "Haben Sie einen Bleistift?" = "Do you have a pencil?" With a masculine noun like "der Bleistift," the accusative indefinite article is "einen" (nominative: "ein Bleistift").
target_language_example: Kann ich mir kurz einen Bleistift leihen?
native_language_example: Can I borrow a pencil for a moment?

additional_notes: Very common with the verb „(einen) Blick werfen“ (= to take a look / to glance), often with a preposition: „einen Blick auf … werfen“ (at), „in …“ (into), „nach …“ (toward). Also in „einen Blick für … haben“ = to have an eye for something (be good at noticing it).
target_language_example: Kannst du kurz einen Blick auf meine E-Mail werfen?
native_language_example: Can you quickly take a look at my email?

additional_notes: Used with a verb like werfen/werfen ("to throw") or richten ("to direct") to mean looking at something briefly: "einen Blick auf etw. werfen" = "to take a look at sth." The thing you look at is in the accusative after auf: "einen Blick auf den Vertrag / das Foto". Common in polite requests: "Lassen Sie mich (nochmal) einen Blick auf … werfen."
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte einen Blick auf meine E-Mail werfen, bevor ich sie abschicke?
native_language_example: Can you please take a look at my email before I send it?

additional_notes: Used when you want to say you look briefly at something. It usually appears with a verb like **werfen** or **haben**: **einen Blick auf den + masculine noun (Akkusativ)**, e.g. *einen Blick auf den Plan werfen* (to take a look at the map/plan). The article changes with the noun’s gender: **auf den** (masc.), **auf die** (fem./plural), **auf das** (neut.).
target_language_example: Wirf bitte einen Blick auf den Fahrplan.
native_language_example: Please take a look at the timetable.

meaning: a look at it; (to) take a look at it.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like „werfen“ or „werfen auf“: „(mal) einen Blick darauf werfen“ = “(just) take a quick look at it.” „darauf“ refers back to something already mentioned (a document, screen, problem, etc.). Common in both informal and polite requests: „Lass mich …“ (informal) vs. „Lassen Sie mich …“ (formal).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte einen Blick darauf werfen?
native_language_example: Can you please take a look at it?

meaning: to take a look; to glance (at).
additional_notes: Often used with a preposition: „einen Blick auf + Akk.“ (take a look at), „einen Blick in + Akk.“ (take a look into). Common in requests: „Kannst du bitte einen Blick werfen …?“ / „Wirf mal einen Blick …“. Note: the fixed multi-word term is „einen Blick werfen“; you can then add what you’re looking at via „auf/in“.
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte einen Blick werfen auf meinen Text?
native_language_example: Can you please take a look at my text?

additional_notes: "Brief" means a written letter (not an email). "einen" is the accusative form of "ein" because "Brief" is masculine (der Brief). Common verbs: "einen Brief bekommen/erhalten" (receive a letter), "(jemandem) einen Brief schicken" (send someone a letter), "(jemandem) einen Brief schreiben" (write someone a letter).
target_language_example: Ich muss heute noch einen Brief an meine Versicherung schreiben.
native_language_example: I still have to write a letter to my insurance company today.

additional_notes: Used with the accusative after **an** to show the recipient of the letter: **einen Brief an + Akkusativ**. Commonly used with **schreiben** (to write) or **schicken** (to send). Note: German **Brief** means “letter” (not “brief”).
target_language_example: Ich schreibe gerade einen Brief an meine Oma.
native_language_example: I’m writing a letter to my grandma right now.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **schicken** (“to send”). In the Perfekt (past) you often say **haben + geschickt**: *Ich habe ... geschickt.* The thing being sent is in the **accusative** (*einen Brief*), and the person receiving it is in the **dative** (*mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen* or *meiner Mutter*).
target_language_example: Ich habe meinem Bruder einen Brief geschickt.
native_language_example: I sent my brother a letter.

additional_notes: Used with "haben" to form the present perfect: "Ich habe einen Brief geschrieben." You often add the recipient in the dative: "jemandem einen Brief schreiben" (to write someone a letter). Note: German "Brief" means "letter" (mail), not English "brief".
target_language_example: Ich habe meiner Oma einen Brief geschrieben.
native_language_example: I wrote my grandma a letter.

additional_notes: Common phrase meaning to write a (single) letter. "einen" is the masculine accusative indefinite article (der Brief → einen Brief). You can add details like the recipient ("einen Brief an meine Großmutter schreiben") or the language ("einen Brief auf Englisch schreiben"). Plural: "Briefe schreiben" (to write letters).
target_language_example: Ich muss heute noch einen Brief schreiben.
native_language_example: I still have to write a letter today.

additional_notes: Used with bekommen/kriegen/erhalten (“to get/receive”) to say who sent the letter. The sender comes after von + dative: von meiner Schwester, von einem Freund, von Maria.
target_language_example: Ich habe einen Brief von meiner Oma bekommen.
native_language_example: I got a letter from my grandma.

meaning: “a brother” (accusative: the direct object of the sentence).
additional_notes: Used after verbs that take a direct object (e.g., haben, lieben): „Ich habe einen Bruder.“ / „Ich liebe ihn wie einen Bruder.“ Note the ending „-en“ because „Bruder“ is masculine and here in the accusative (der Bruder → einen Bruder). In questions, it often appears with „Hast du…?“ or „Hat sie…?“
target_language_example: Ich habe keinen Bruder, aber zwei Schwestern.
native_language_example: I don’t have a brother, but two sisters.

additional_notes: Common in invitations or suggestions: „Auf einen Drink.“ = “Let’s have a drink / Cheers.” Often used with verbs like „holen“ (to get) or „sich auf … treffen“ / „treffen“ (to meet for). „Drink“ is a borrowed English word in German and often implies a cocktail or alcoholic drink, though context can vary.
target_language_example: Hast du nach der Arbeit Zeit, noch einen Drink zu trinken?
native_language_example: Do you have time to have a drink after work?

additional_notes: Usually used with verbs like „einen Fehler machen/begehen“ (to make/commit a mistake) or „einen Fehler sehen“ (to spot an error). Because „Fehler“ is masculine, the accusative form is „einen Fehler“.
target_language_example: Ich habe einen Fehler gemacht.
native_language_example: I made a mistake.

additional_notes: Usually used with "haben" (present perfect): "Ich habe einen Fehler gemacht" = "I made a mistake." Often appears with "wo" or "irgendwo" to say where you made the mistake: "wo/irgendwo ich einen Fehler gemacht habe." You can strengthen it with words like "absichtlich" (on purpose) or "zweifellos" (without a doubt).
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, ich habe einen Fehler gemacht.
native_language_example: Sorry, I made a mistake.

additional_notes: This is the past perfect (Plusquamperfekt) of „einen Fehler machen“: *machen* → *gemacht*, and *hat* → *hatte*. It often appears in subordinate clauses (after words like „weil“, „dass“, „als“) to show the mistake happened before another past event. Note: German „Fehler“ means “mistake/error,” not “failure.”
target_language_example: Ich merkte, dass ich einen Fehler gemacht hatte.
native_language_example: I realized that I had made a mistake.

additional_notes: Common, neutral expression. Often used with modal verbs (können/dürfen/sollen) and in warnings or predictions (e.g., „Du könntest einen Fehler machen.“). Alternatives: „einen Fehler begehen“ (more formal), „sich irren“ (to be wrong).
target_language_example: Jeder kann einen Fehler machen.
native_language_example: Anyone can make a mistake.

meaning: a movie; (also) a roll of film (for a camera).
additional_notes: Most often means “a movie” in phrases like: einen Film sehen/ansehen (to watch a movie), einen Film ausleihen (to rent/borrow a movie), auf einen Film vorbeikommen (come over to watch a movie). In photo/camera context it can mean “a roll of film”: einen Film für diese Kamera (a roll of film for this camera). "Einen" is the masculine accusative form of "ein" used because Film is masculine (der Film).
target_language_example: Wollen wir heute Abend einen Film ansehen?
native_language_example: Do you want to watch a movie tonight?

additional_notes: Commonly used to talk about successfully catching a fish (usually while fishing). It’s the perfect tense: **fangen** (to catch) → **hat ... gefangen** with **haben**. **Einen Fisch** is accusative; you can swap in other objects or add adjectives: *einen großen Fisch gefangen* (caught a big fish).
target_language_example: Wir haben heute Morgen einen Fisch gefangen.
native_language_example: We caught a fish this morning.

additional_notes: "Freund" can mean a (male) friend in general, but in questions like "Hast du einen Freund?" it often means "Do you have a boyfriend?" (a romantic partner). The exact meaning depends on the situation; if you want to be clear, you can say "einen Freund (als Partner)" for boyfriend, or "einen Freund (nur als Freund)" for just a friend.
target_language_example: Sie hat seit einem Jahr einen Freund.
native_language_example: She has had a boyfriend for a year.

meaning: to have a boyfriend; or to have a (male) friend.
additional_notes: Most commonly used to mean “to have a boyfriend” (romantic partner). If you just mean a friend in general, you’ll often specify with context or say "einen Freund" (male friend) / "eine Freundin" (female friend). For “to have friends” (plural), use "Freunde haben".
target_language_example: Sie sagt, dass sie einen Freund haben will.
native_language_example: She says that she wants to have a boyfriend.

additional_notes: Usually appears with the auxiliary verb in the Perfekt tense: „Ich habe … gekauft.“ Often used with a dative reflexive pronoun to mean “bought myself”: „Ich habe mir einen Gebrauchtwagen gekauft.“ (also „Er hat sich … gekauft“).
target_language_example: Ich habe mir letzte Woche einen Gebrauchtwagen gekauft.
native_language_example: I bought myself a used car last week.

meaning: a favor (a helpful thing you do for someone).
additional_notes: Most often used in the expressions „jemandem einen Gefallen tun“ (to do someone a favor) and more formal „jemandem einen Gefallen erweisen“ (to do/render someone a favor). The person who benefits is in the dative: „mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/Ihnen“. You can also say „(jemandem) einen Gefallen schuldig sein“ = to owe someone a favor.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir einen Gefallen tun und die Tür zumachen?
native_language_example: Can you do me a favor and close the door?

additional_notes: Usually used with **um** and often with a person: **jemanden um einen Gefallen bitten** (to ask someone for a favor). You can also say **Kann ich dich/Sie um einen Gefallen bitten?** = “Can I ask you for a favor?” (dich = informal you, Sie = formal you).
target_language_example: Kann ich dich um einen Gefallen bitten?
native_language_example: Can I ask you for a favor?

additional_notes: Past participle phrase used with "tun" (to do) in the perfect tense. Full structure: "jemandem einen Gefallen tun" (dative person) = to do someone a favor. In perfect: "Ich habe dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen einen Gefallen getan." Can be neutral, or used pointedly to remind someone of help you gave them.
target_language_example: Ich habe dir einen Gefallen getan.
native_language_example: I did you a favor.

additional_notes: Used with a person in the dative: jemandem einen Gefallen tun (e.g., „Kannst du mir einen Gefallen tun?“). Common for polite requests, often with „können“/„würden“: „Könnten/Würdest du mir einen Gefallen tun und …?“
target_language_example: Könntest du mir einen Gefallen tun und das Fenster schließen?
native_language_example: Could you do me a favor and close the window?

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "geben" (to give) and "nennen" (to name) when asking someone for a reason. Basic form: "der Grund" = the reason; accusative singular: "einen Grund". Common patterns: "Gib/Nenn mir einen Grund ..." and "einen Grund haben" (to have a reason).
target_language_example: Ich habe einen Grund, warum ich heute nicht kommen kann.
native_language_example: I have a reason why I can't come today.

meaning: a lot of; lots of (a bunch/pile of).
additional_notes: Used informally to mean a large amount or number of something. Often followed directly by a noun: „einen Haufen + Nomen“ (e.g., „einen Haufen Bücher“ = lots of books). It can be used both for things you can count and for general quantities/experiences like „Spaß“.
target_language_example: Wir haben einen Haufen Arbeit heute.
native_language_example: We have a lot of work today.

meaning: a lot of money; a pile of money.
additional_notes: Common, informal-ish way to say someone has/paid/wants a large amount of money. Often used with verbs like haben (to have), bezahlen (to pay), wollen (to want), and machen/verdienen (to make/earn). The noun phrase is accusative here: einen Haufen (a heap/pile).
target_language_example: Das Auto kostet einen Haufen Geld.
native_language_example: That car costs a lot of money.

meaning: a marriage proposal (an offer/request to marry).
additional_notes: Usually used with the verb „machen“: „jemandem einen Heiratsantrag machen“ = to propose to someone. Often described with gestures like „knien“ (to kneel). The noun is masculine: „der Heiratsantrag“ (accusative: „einen Heiratsantrag“).
target_language_example: Er hat ihr gestern Abend einen Heiratsantrag gemacht.
native_language_example: He proposed to her last night.

additional_notes: Used when talking about safety rules or advice (e.g., cycling, motorbikes, construction). Often with "müssen" (must/have to): "Du musst beim Radfahren einen Helm tragen." In formal situations you may hear "Sie müssen einen Helm tragen."
target_language_example: Du musst beim Radfahren einen Helm tragen.
native_language_example: You have to wear a helmet when cycling.

additional_notes: Used when the dog is the direct object (the thing someone has, buys, draws, sees, etc.). The base noun is der Hund; after many verbs you’ll see the accusative form: einen Hund.
target_language_example: Wir haben gestern einen Hund im Park gesehen.
native_language_example: We saw a dog in the park yesterday.

additional_notes: Perfect tense of kaufen: haben + gekauft. „Einen Hund“ is the accusative direct object. In questions and many past-tense sentences, the participle „gekauft“ often comes at the end (e.g., „Haben Sie … gekauft?“). With two objects, you can say who you bought it for in the dative: „jemandem einen Hund kaufen“ (e.g., „Habt ihr Tom einen Hund gekauft?“).
target_language_example: Ich habe mir einen Hund gekauft.
native_language_example: I bought myself a dog.

additional_notes: Used as the direct object with verbs like **tragen** (to wear) and **brauchen** (to need). **Hut** is masculine: **ein Hut** (nominative), **einen Hut** (accusative). Often appears after frequency words like **manchmal/nie/selten/stets**.
target_language_example: Ich trage heute einen Hut.
native_language_example: I’m wearing a hat today.

meaning: to be wearing a hat (to have a hat on).
additional_notes: Uses the common pattern „etwas an/aufhaben“ = “to have something on (wearing it)”. The hat is in the accusative: „einen Hut“. Often used with frequency words like „oft“, „manchmal“, „nie“.
target_language_example: Heute habe ich einen Hut auf.
native_language_example: Today I’m wearing a hat.

meaning: a job (accusative: the direct object form).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like „finden“ (to find) and „kriegen/bekommen“ (to get): „einen Job finden/kriegen“. Base form is „ein Job“; it changes to „einen Job“ in the accusative.
target_language_example: Ich suche einen Job in Berlin.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a job in Berlin.

additional_notes: "Junge" means "boy". "Einen Jungen" is the accusative form, used when the boy is the direct object (e.g., to have/kiss/adopt a boy). With different articles you’ll see: "einen Jungen" (a boy), "den Jungen" (the boy).
target_language_example: Sie hat einen Jungen im Park getroffen.
native_language_example: She met a boy in the park.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like wollen (to want), trinken (to drink), or anbieten (to offer). The form „einen“ is the accusative masculine article because „Kaffee“ is masculine (der Kaffee) and it’s the direct object.
target_language_example: Kann ich dir einen Kaffee anbieten?
native_language_example: Can I offer you a coffee?

additional_notes: A common everyday phrase for having coffee, often used as an invitation. Frequently appears with "gehen" ("einen Kaffee trinken gehen") meaning "to go out for a coffee." In questions/invitations you’ll often see polite forms like "Hättest du Lust …?" or "Ich würde gerne …".
target_language_example: Nach der Arbeit können wir einen Kaffee trinken gehen.
native_language_example: After work, we can go out for a coffee.

additional_notes: "Keks" means a cookie/biscuit. "Einen" is the accusative form of "ein" (a/one) used for masculine nouns when it’s the direct object (e.g., eating, wanting, offering). Often used in polite offers/requests: "Möchtest du einen Keks?" / "Kann ich einen Keks haben?"
target_language_example: Willst du einen Keks zum Kaffee?
native_language_example: Do you want a cookie with your coffee?

additional_notes: Used when you need a professional for plumbing problems (leaks, clogged drains, broken pipes). "einen" is the accusative form of "ein" (because the plumber is the direct object). Often appears with modal verbs like "sollte/solltest/sollten" (should) or as a suggestion. You may also hear "einen Klempner anrufen" (to phone a plumber) with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: Kannst du das reparieren, oder sollte ich einen Klempner rufen?
native_language_example: Can you fix that, or should I call a plumber?

meaning: 'a head taller than' (about one head’s height taller than).
additional_notes: Used to compare people’s height in an approximate, everyday way. Often with intensifiers like „mindestens“ (at least) or „gut“ (a good bit). Grammar: „Er/Sie ist einen Kopf größer als + Person“ (accusative: „einen Kopf“).
target_language_example: Meine Schwester ist einen Kopf größer als ich.
native_language_example: My sister is a head taller than me.

additional_notes: Used when you need emergency medical transport. "einen" is the accusative form of "ein" (because it’s the direct object), e.g. "Rufen Sie einen Krankenwagen" (“Call an ambulance”). The base word is "der Krankenwagen" (nominative).
target_language_example: Können Sie bitte sofort einen Krankenwagen rufen?
native_language_example: Can you please call an ambulance immediately?

additional_notes: Used when someone is injured or seriously ill and you want emergency medical help. Commonly used as a suggestion or question with „sollen“ (e.g., „Soll ich einen Krankenwagen rufen?“). You can also say „den Notruf wählen“ (dial the emergency number).
target_language_example: Du solltest einen Krankenwagen rufen.
native_language_example: You should call an ambulance.

additional_notes: Used when a cake is the direct object of the verb (e.g., backen/machen): Ich backe/mache einen Kuchen. After masculine words like Kuchen, the indefinite article changes from "ein" (nominative) to "einen" (accusative).
target_language_example: Ich backe heute einen Kuchen.
native_language_example: I’m baking a cake today.

additional_notes: Used for making a cake in the oven. The verb is backen (“to bake”); in the present tense you often see: ich backe, du backst, er/sie/es backt. In questions you may hear the polite form with Sie: „Könnten Sie …?“
target_language_example: Vielleicht sollte ich heute mal einen Kuchen backen.
native_language_example: Maybe I should bake a cake today.

additional_notes: Commonly used in the Perfekt (spoken past) with **haben**: *Ich habe einen Kuchen gebacken.* It’s the past participle of **backen** (“to bake”) with the direct object **einen Kuchen** (“a cake”). You’ll often hear it with time phrases like *zum/zu meinem Geburtstag* (“for my birthday”).
target_language_example: Ich habe gestern einen Kuchen gebacken.
native_language_example: I baked a cake yesterday.

additional_notes: Most often used with the verb „geben“: „jemandem einen Kuss geben“ = to give someone a kiss. Also common with „von“ to say who it’s from: „Gib deiner Mutter einen Kuss von mir“ (“Give your mom a kiss from me”). You may also see fixed contexts like „zum Abschied“ (“as a goodbye kiss”).
target_language_example: Kann ich dir einen Kuss geben?
native_language_example: Can I give you a kiss?

additional_notes: Used when “man” is the direct object (accusative) of the verb (e.g., lieben, sehen, heiraten, jagen) or after many prepositions that take the accusative (e.g., für: Was für einen Mann?). Compare: nominative “ein Mann” (subject) vs. accusative “einen Mann” (object).
target_language_example: Ich kenne einen Mann aus Berlin.
native_language_example: I know a man from Berlin.

meaning: “a man who …” (used to introduce a relative clause).
additional_notes: Used when the man is the direct object in the main clause ("einen Mann" = accusative), and then you add a description with a relative clause starting with "der". Even though you see "einen Mann" (accusative), the relative pronoun "der" is often nominative because it is the subject inside the relative clause: "Ich kenne einen Mann, der gut Französisch spricht."
target_language_example: Ich suche einen Mann, der mir helfen kann.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a man who can help me.

additional_notes: Very common with requests and waiting: „Warten Sie bitte einen Moment.“ / „Einen Moment (bitte)!“ = “One moment (please)!” It can also mean “for a moment” in the middle of a sentence: „Ich habe einen Moment nicht aufgepasst.“ = “I didn’t pay attention for a moment.”
target_language_example: Einen Moment, ich komme gleich.
native_language_example: One moment, I'll be right there.

additional_notes: Used with time expressions to say how long something lasts, how long ago something happened, or how long someone is/was somewhere. Often appears with words like „erst“ (only/just), „nicht einmal“ (not even), „mehr als“ (more than), „länger als“ (longer than), and „lang“ (for).
target_language_example: Ich war einen Monat in Deutschland.
native_language_example: I was in Germany for one month.

meaning: for a month; for one month (long).
additional_notes: Used to say how long something lasts. It usually follows a time amount (einen Monat, zwei Wochen, drei Tage) + lang. Often used with the accusative: einen Monat lang, den ganzen Tag lang.
target_language_example: Ich war einen Monat lang in Berlin.
native_language_example: I was in Berlin for a month.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like „haben“ (to have), „brauchen“ (to need), „geben“ (to give), „aussuchen“ (to choose): „einen Namen haben/brauchen/geben/aussuchen“. Very common when naming a person, thing, project, or even a dish. In questions you’ll often see „Was für einen Namen …?“ = “What kind of name …?”
target_language_example: Wir brauchen noch einen Namen für das Baby.
native_language_example: We still need a name for the baby.

additional_notes: Used when "Plan" is the direct object, often with verbs like "haben" (to have), "machen" (to make), or "brauchen" (to need): "Ich habe einen Plan." Note the case change: "ein Plan" (nominative) → "einen Plan" (accusative, masculine).
target_language_example: Ich habe einen Plan für morgen.
native_language_example: I have a plan for tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used when the first plan (Plan A) might fail. Often appears with questions like „Hast du einen Plan B?“ or with „es gibt“: „Einen Plan B gibt es (noch) nicht“ = there is (not yet) a backup plan. Capital letters A/B are commonly used in German too.
target_language_example: Wenn das nicht klappt, brauchen wir einen Plan B.
native_language_example: If that doesn’t work, we need a backup plan.

meaning: to have a plan; to know what you’re going to do.
additional_notes: Used to say you’ve thought something through or have a clear idea of the next steps. Often used with a context word: „einen Plan für + Akk.“ (a plan for something) or „einen Plan, wie …“ (a plan for how to …). In speech you may also hear the opposite: „keinen Plan haben“ = to have no idea.
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, ich werde einen Plan haben, bevor wir losfahren.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll have a plan before we set off.

meaning: a place / a spot / a seat.
additional_notes: Accusative form of "ein Platz" (masculine). Used when "a place" is the direct object, often with verbs like: "einen Platz suchen" (look for a seat/spot), "einen Platz haben" (have a place/seat), "einen Platz finden" (find a place), and "(für jdn.) einen Platz frei machen" / "Platz machen" (make room). Depending on context it can mean a physical seat, an empty spot, or a figurative “place” (e.g., in a group or in your life).
target_language_example: Kann ich hier einen Platz nehmen?
native_language_example: Can I take a seat here?

additional_notes: Used when someone saves a seat or place for another person (e.g., on a bus, in a café, in a meeting). The person you save it for is in the dative: „mir/dir/Ihnen“. Often said in the present perfect: „Ich habe dir einen Platz freigehalten.“ The verb is „freihalten“ (separable): „Ich halte dir einen Platz frei“ (present).
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, ich habe dir einen Platz freigehalten.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I saved you a seat.

meaning: "a sweater / a jumper" (accusative: something you put on or make).
additional_notes: "Pullover" is a masculine noun (der Pullover). You’ll often see it as "einen Pullover" after verbs that take the accusative, especially with clothing (e.g., "einen Pullover anziehen" = to put on a sweater). It can also be the direct object of verbs like "stricken" (to knit).
target_language_example: Ich ziehe mir einen Pullover an, weil es draußen kalt ist.
native_language_example: I’m putting on a sweater because it’s cold outside.

meaning: (to give/need) a piece of advice; a tip.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like „einen Rat geben“ (to give advice) and „einen Rat brauchen/gebrauchen“ (to need advice). „Rat“ is masculine (der Rat), so in the accusative it becomes „einen Rat“. In polite/formal speech you may see „Ihnen“ and refer back to it with „ihn“ (masculine).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir einen Rat geben?
native_language_example: Can you give me some advice?

additional_notes: Used when offering advice, often with an indirect object in the dative: jemandem einen Rat geben (e.g., dir/ihm/ihr/Ihnen). Common in polite questions like „Können Sie mir einen Rat geben?“ and also as an offer: „Darf ich dir einen Rat geben?“
target_language_example: Ich kann dir einen Rat geben: Sprich langsam und deutlich.
native_language_example: I can give you some advice: Speak slowly and clearly.

meaning: "a novel" (accusative: the direct object form of "ein Roman").
additional_notes: Used with many verbs like lesen (to read), schreiben (to write), veröffentlichen (to publish). Because "Roman" is masculine (der Roman), the accusative singular is "einen Roman". The base form is "ein Roman"; plural: "Romane".
target_language_example: Ich habe gestern Abend einen Roman angefangen.
native_language_example: I started a novel yesterday evening.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like „nehmen“ (to take/have), „trinken“ (to drink), or „möchten“ (would like) to mean taking a small amount of a drink. You can add what it’s a sip of with „von“: „einen Schluck von …“. In phrases like „einen Schluck nötig haben“, it means someone could use a drink (often implying alcohol, depending on context).
target_language_example: Ich brauche nur einen Schluck.
native_language_example: I just need a sip.

additional_notes: Used when "key" is the direct object (something you need, have, give, or take out). Common with verbs like brauchen (need), haben (have), geben (give), holen (fetch/take out). The accusative masculine article is "einen" (not "ein").
target_language_example: Kannst du mir einen Schlüssel geben?
native_language_example: Can you give me a key?

additional_notes: Used with verbs like gehen or machen to describe taking a step, often with a direction (e.g., „einen Schritt nach vorn/zurück“). It’s also common in the phrase „einen Schritt weitergehen“ = “to go one step further” (literally: to go one step farther).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte einen Schritt zur Seite gehen?
native_language_example: Could you please take one step to the side?

meaning: a shot (e.g., a gunshot); also a splash/dash of alcohol added to a drink.
additional_notes: With hören (“to hear”), it usually means a gunshot or loud bang: „Ich habe einen Schuss gehört.“ In food/drink contexts with geben/tun (“to add/put”), it means a small added amount, often alcohol: „einen Schuss Brandy/Rum in den Tee“. (Related but different: „einen Schuss haben“ = to be a bit crazy.)
target_language_example: Kannst du mir einen Schuss Rum in den Kakao geben?
native_language_example: Can you add a shot of rum to my cocoa?

additional_notes: This is the accusative form of “ein Sohn” (a son). You use it after many verbs like haben (“to have”): „Er hat einen Sohn.“ After some prepositions you also need accusative, e.g. „für einen Sohn“ (“for a son”).
target_language_example: Wir haben einen Sohn und eine Tochter.
native_language_example: We have a son and a daughter.

meaning: “a son who …” (introduces a relative clause about the son).
additional_notes: Used to give more information about “einen Sohn” (“a son”). The comma is required before the relative clause. “der” is the relative pronoun (here: masculine, nominative), because it is the subject of the relative clause (e.g., “der John heißt” = “who is called John”).
target_language_example: Sie hat einen Sohn, der in Berlin lebt.
native_language_example: She has a son who lives in Berlin.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like „machen“ or „unternehmen“: „einen Spaziergang machen/unternehmen“ = to go for a walk. It’s an accusative phrase (einen Spaziergang), so it often follows the verb directly, and you can add details with „im Park“, „am Morgen“, „entlang des Flusses“, etc.
target_language_example: Nach dem Abendessen machen wir einen Spaziergang.
native_language_example: After dinner we go for a walk.

meaning: to go for a walk (to take a walk).
additional_notes: Common everyday phrasing. Often appears as an infinitive clause with „zu“ (e.g., after verbs like „mögen“, „pflegen“, „die Gewohnheit haben“): „einen Spaziergang zu machen“. The core phrase is „einen Spaziergang machen“ (accusative: „einen Spaziergang“). Typically implies walking for pleasure/exercise, not necessarily to reach a destination.
