target_language_example: Er hat die Gewohnheit, vor dem Frühstück einen Spaziergang zu machen.
native_language_example: He has the habit of going for a walk before breakfast.

meaning: to get stuck in a traffic jam.
additional_notes: Usually used as **in einen Stau geraten** (with *in*): *Wir sind in einen Stau geraten.* The verb *geraten* means “to get into (a situation) unexpectedly,” often something inconvenient.
target_language_example: Wir sind auf der Autobahn in einen Stau geraten.
native_language_example: We got stuck in a traffic jam on the highway.

additional_notes: "Stein" is a masculine noun (der Stein). You use "einen" when it’s the direct object in the accusative case: Ich sehe **einen Stein**. In the nominative (subject) it’s "ein Stein": **Ein Stein** liegt da. Watch out: German "Stein" can look like English "stein" (a beer mug), but it usually means "stone/rock".
target_language_example: Ich habe einen Stein im Garten gefunden.
native_language_example: I found a stone in the garden.

meaning: to get a ticket (a fine notice).
additional_notes: Used when you receive an official fine notice from the police/authorities, often for parking or traffic violations. Common patterns: „einen Strafzettel bekommen, weil …“ (because …) and „Wenn du hier geparkt hättest, hättest du einen Strafzettel bekommen.“ (You would have gotten a ticket). „Strafzettel“ is the ticket/fine notice itself; you can also say „einen Strafzettel kriegen“ (more casual).
target_language_example: Ich habe einen Strafzettel bekommen, weil ich im Halteverbot stand.
native_language_example: I got a ticket because I was parked in a no-parking zone.

meaning: a prank; a trick (often in „jemandem einen Streich spielen“ = to play a trick on someone / to deceive someone).
additional_notes: Most often used with „spielen“: „jemandem einen Streich spielen“ (to prank someone). It can also be used when something misleads you, especially your imagination or senses: „Die Phantasie/Augen spielen mir einen Streich“ = “My imagination/eyes are playing tricks on me” (something isn’t actually as it seems).
target_language_example: Ich glaube, meine Ohren spielen mir einen Streich – ich dachte, ich hätte meinen Namen gehört.
native_language_example: I think my ears are playing tricks on me—I thought I heard my name.

meaning: "a chair" (accusative: a chair as the object of the sentence).
additional_notes: Used after many verbs when the chair is what you get, need, move, or interact with (e.g., holen, brauchen, nehmen, werfen). It’s the accusative form of the masculine noun "der Stuhl"; in the nominative you say "ein Stuhl" (a chair).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir bitte einen Stuhl geben?
native_language_example: Can you please give me a chair?

meaning: one day (for one day; one more day).
additional_notes: Accusative form of "ein Tag" used with durations of time ("for a day") and with "noch" to mean "one more day." Often appears with verbs like bleiben (stay) or nehmen (take) and with Urlaub: "einen Tag Urlaub nehmen" = "take a day off."
target_language_example: Können wir einen Tag länger bleiben?
native_language_example: Can we stay one day longer?

additional_notes: Used with verbs like **haben** (to have) and **(sich) nehmen** (to take): **einen Tag frei haben** = to have a day off; **(sich) einen Tag frei nehmen** = to take a day off (e.g., from work/school). Often appears as **einen Tag frei nehmen** or **sich einen Tag frei nehmen**.
target_language_example: Ich nehme morgen einen Tag frei.
native_language_example: I’m taking a day off tomorrow.

additional_notes: Usually used with the reflexive pronoun ("sich") and often in questions/suggestions: "Kannst du dir einen Tag freinehmen?" / "Sie sollten sich einen Tag freinehmen." The direct statement form is also common: "Ich werde mir einen Tag freinehmen."
target_language_example: Kannst du dir einen Tag freinehmen?
native_language_example: Can you take a day off?

additional_notes: Used with verbs like „haben“ (to have) or „machen/vereinbaren“ (to make/arrange), especially for a doctor, office, or official meeting. „Haben Sie einen Termin?“ often means “Do you have an appointment (scheduled)?”
target_language_example: Ich habe morgen um zehn Uhr einen Termin beim Arzt.
native_language_example: I have an appointment at the doctor’s tomorrow at ten o’clock.

meaning: to have an appointment (a scheduled time).
additional_notes: Used for scheduled meetings or time slots (e.g., with a doctor, at an office, with a client). Often used with a time or place: „Ich habe um 10 Uhr einen Termin.“ You can also say who/where the appointment is with: „Ich habe einen Termin beim Arzt / bei der Bank.“
target_language_example: Ich werde morgen einen Termin haben.
native_language_example: I will have an appointment tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "haben" ("einen Unfall haben" = "to have an accident"). In questions like "Handelte es sich um einen Unfall?", it means "Was it an accident?" (i.e., not intentional). "Unfall" is masculine: der Unfall; accusative: einen Unfall.
target_language_example: Ich hatte gestern auf dem Weg zur Arbeit einen Unfall.
native_language_example: I had an accident yesterday on the way to work.

additional_notes: Accusative form of "ein Weg". It can be literal (a physical route) or figurative (a solution or method). Very common in phrases like "einen Weg finden" (to find a way) and "es gibt einen Weg" (there is a way). Often followed by an infinitive with "zu": "einen Weg finden, ... zu ...".
target_language_example: Wir finden einen Weg, das Problem zu lösen.
native_language_example: We’ll find a way to solve the problem.

meaning: to find a way (to do something); to figure out a solution.
additional_notes: Used when you don’t yet know how to achieve a goal but believe a solution is possible. Very often followed by an infinitive clause with „um … zu …“ (purpose): „einen Weg finden, um X zu tun“ = “find a way to do X”. Also common with a „damit“-clause: „einen Weg finden, damit …“ = “find a way so that …”. Can refer to practical steps, solving a problem, or making something possible.
target_language_example: Wir müssen einen Weg finden, das Missverständnis zu klären.
native_language_example: We have to find a way to clear up the misunderstanding.

meaning: a joke (as the object: to tell/make/crack a joke).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like „einen Witz erzählen“ (to tell a joke), „einen Witz machen“ (to make a joke / be joking), and more informal options like „einen Witz reißen“ or „einen Witz vom Stapel lassen“ (to crack a joke). The full base form is „der Witz“; here it appears in the accusative with „einen“.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir einen Witz erzählen?
native_language_example: Can you tell me a joke?

additional_notes: Used before a masculine noun in the accusative case, usually as the direct object: einen alten Wagen / Film / Brief / Schuhkarton. The adjective ending (-en) comes from this grammar pattern (ein + masculine accusative). It normally needs a noun after it: "einen alten ...".
target_language_example: Ich habe einen alten Mantel gefunden.
native_language_example: I found an old coat.

meaning: an old friend (someone you’ve known for a long time).
additional_notes: Often used when you meet someone you knew in the past or have known for many years. "Alt" here usually means the friendship is long-standing, not that the friend is elderly. The article "einen" shows it’s masculine accusative, commonly after verbs like "treffen" (to meet) or "besuchen" (to visit).
target_language_example: Gestern habe ich in der Stadt einen alten Freund getroffen.
native_language_example: Yesterday I met an old friend in the city.

meaning: met an old friend (ran into an old friend).
additional_notes: Past participle phrase used with "haben" in the Perfekt: "Ich habe ... getroffen." "treffen" often means "to meet" in the sense of encountering someone (often by chance), and it takes the accusative: "einen alten Freund". "alt" here means "long-time/former" rather than literally old in age.
target_language_example: Gestern habe ich in der Stadt einen alten Freund getroffen.
native_language_example: Yesterday I ran into an old friend in the city.

additional_notes: Used when the noun is masculine and in the accusative case (often after verbs like haben, brauchen, nehmen, sehen, küssen). It can stand alone if the noun is understood from context (e.g., „Ich brauche einen anderen.“ = I need a different one/another one). For feminine/neutral/plural you use other forms: „eine andere“, „ein anderes“, „andere“.
target_language_example: Kann ich einen anderen Stuhl bekommen?
native_language_example: Can I get a different chair?

additional_notes: Used when you’re looking for or suggesting an alternative way to do something. Often appears with verbs like „geben“ (there must be another way), „finden“ (to find another way), or „wissen“ (to know another way). Here, „Weg“ is usually figurative (a solution/method), not a physical road.
target_language_example: Wir brauchen einen anderen Weg, um das Problem zu lösen.
native_language_example: We need another way to solve the problem.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine noun in the accusative case after verbs like haben/bekommen or in questions like „Gibt es …?“. Pattern: „einen besseren + [masculine noun]“ (e.g., „einen besseren Vorschlag“, „einen besseren Preis“). Other forms: „ein besseres“ (neuter), „eine bessere“ (feminine), „bessere“ (plural).
target_language_example: Ich brauche einen besseren Plan.
native_language_example: I need a better plan.

meaning: a steady/serious boyfriend (in an established relationship).
additional_notes: Used to ask or say whether someone has a boyfriend they’re in a committed relationship with (not just dating casually). Grammatically it’s accusative masculine: einen … Freund. With a female partner you say: eine feste Freundin.
target_language_example: Ich habe seit zwei Jahren einen festen Freund.
native_language_example: I’ve had a steady boyfriend for two years.

meaning: "a big/large/great" (before a masculine noun in the accusative).
additional_notes: This is the accusative masculine form of the adjective "groß" used with the indefinite article: "einen" + "großen" + masculine noun (e.g., "einen großen Fehler", "einen großen Park"). You’ll see it after many verbs that take the accusative (like "haben", "sehen", "machen"). Note: German "groß" looks like English "gross" but does NOT mean "gross" (disgusting).
target_language_example: Ich habe einen großen Hund.
native_language_example: I have a big dog.

additional_notes: Used with the verb „machen“ (to make) or after phrases like „Ich halte das für …“ (I consider that …). The noun „Fehler“ is masculine: „ein großer Fehler“ (nominative), but often „einen großen Fehler“ (accusative) after verbs like „machen“.
target_language_example: Wenn du jetzt gehst, machst du einen großen Fehler.
native_language_example: If you leave now, you’re making a big mistake.

meaning: "a big fish"; also figuratively "a big shot / important person" (someone influential).
additional_notes: Literally refers to catching/seeing a large fish. Figuratively used especially with verbs like „fangen“ (to catch) or „an Land ziehen“ (to land) to mean securing an important person, client, or deal. Note: with „sein“ you’d typically say „ein großer Fisch“ (nominative), but the given term „einen großen Fisch“ is accusative and fits better as an object.
target_language_example: Wenn wir diesen Kunden gewinnen, haben wir einen großen Fisch an Land gezogen.
native_language_example: If we win this client, we’ll have landed a big fish (a major win).

meaning: to have landed a big catch; to score a big success (often: an important client/person).
additional_notes: Literally “to have caught a big fish.” Commonly used idiomatically when someone has achieved something significant—especially in business or networking (e.g., winning a major customer, making a valuable contact). Often used with verbs like „Ich habe einen großen Fisch gefangen.“
target_language_example: Mit diesem Auftrag haben wir wirklich einen großen Fisch gefangen.
native_language_example: With this contract, we really landed a big catch.

additional_notes: Used with masculine nouns in the accusative case: "einen guten + Noun" (e.g., einen guten Gedanken = a good idea/thought, einen guten Dienst = a good service/favor, einen guten Lebenslauf = a good CV). It’s not usually used alone; a noun follows. Contrast: nominative masculine "ein guter ..." and accusative feminine "eine gute ...".
target_language_example: Ich brauche einen guten Arzt.
native_language_example: I need a good doctor.

additional_notes: Used when someone needs, has, or can recommend a competent lawyer. "Anwalt" = lawyer/attorney; the form "einen guten" is accusative masculine, common after verbs like "haben", "empfehlen", or "sich (etwas) besorgen".
target_language_example: Wenn du Ärger bekommst, brauchst du einen guten Anwalt.
native_language_example: If you get into trouble, you need a good lawyer.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like „machen“ (to make) and „hinterlassen“ (to leave) to talk about how someone/something seems to others, especially at first (e.g., at a job interview, meeting new people). You often say: „einen guten Eindruck machen“ / „einen guten Eindruck hinterlassen“.
target_language_example: Beim Vorstellungsgespräch will ich einen guten Eindruck machen.
native_language_example: At the job interview, I want to make a good impression.

additional_notes: Used when you want to justify an action or decision, or when you demand a convincing explanation. Often appears with: „einen guten Grund dafür“ (a good reason for it/that), „einen guten Grund nennen“ (to name/state a good reason), or „Gib mir einen guten Grund, …“ (Give me a good reason to …). The noun „Grund“ is masculine; in the accusative singular it becomes „einen Grund“.
target_language_example: Ich brauche einen guten Grund, um das zu machen.
native_language_example: I need a good reason to do that.

meaning: a good job (a good position); also: doing a good job.
additional_notes: Used either literally for employment ("Ich brauche/fand/habe einen guten Job") or as praise for performance ("einen guten Job machen" = to do a good job). In sentence 2, it appears in the fixed phrase "einen guten Job gemacht" (past of "einen guten Job machen"). "Job" is a common loanword in German; "Arbeit" is also used, but "Job" often sounds more like a position/employment.
target_language_example: Du machst einen guten Job!
native_language_example: You're doing a good job!

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (often with verbs like „bekommen“ = to get or „sich … sichern“ = to secure) to explain why you arrived early, e.g. at the theater, a concert, or on public transport. „Platz“ can mean a seat or a good spot, depending on context.
target_language_example: Wir sind früh da, um uns einen guten Platz zu sichern.
native_language_example: We’re there early to secure a good seat/spot.

additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself—it normally comes right before a masculine noun in the accusative case: einen kleinen Unterschied (a small difference), einen kleinen Spaziergang (a little walk). The -en ending on kleinen is the adjective ending used after the indefinite article einen. (With a neuter noun you’d use: ein kleines …)
target_language_example: Ich brauche einen kleinen Moment.
native_language_example: I need a little moment.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine noun when it’s the direct object (accusative): **einen langen + noun** (e.g., *einen langen Brief, einen langen Spaziergang, einen langen Tunnel*). The **-en** ending on *langen* is the normal adjective ending after *einen* in this case.
target_language_example: Ich habe heute einen langen Brief geschrieben.
native_language_example: Today I wrote a long letter.

additional_notes: Perfect tense of **einen langen Brief schreiben**. Often used with a recipient in the **dative**: **jemandem** einen langen Brief schreiben (e.g., *Ich habe ihm/ihr/Tom einen langen Brief geschrieben*). Note: **Brief** in German means **letter** (not “brief” in English).
target_language_example: Ich habe meiner Oma einen langen Brief geschrieben.
native_language_example: I wrote my grandma a long letter.

additional_notes: This is the adjective phrase used before a masculine noun in the accusative case (after verbs like haben/machen): einen leichten + Noun. Meaning depends on the noun: einen leichten Schlaf = “a light sleep,” einen leichten Akzent = “a slight accent,” einen leichten Herzinfarkt = “a mild heart attack,” einen leichten Bogen = “a slight curve.”
target_language_example: Ich habe nur einen leichten Schnupfen.
native_language_example: I just have a slight cold.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine noun when it is the direct object (accusative): e.g., "einen neuen Mantel" = "a new coat". You’ll often see it after verbs like kaufen (to buy), suchen (to look for), brauchen (to need). The ending changes with gender/case (e.g., nominative: "ein neuer ..."; neuter accusative: "ein neues ...").
target_language_example: Ich brauche einen neuen Pass.
native_language_example: I need a new passport.

additional_notes: Used when someone buys, wears, or has a suit made. It’s the accusative form because it’s usually the direct object (e.g., Ich kaufe/nehme/trage einen neuen Anzug). In the nominative you say: ein neuer Anzug.
target_language_example: Für das Vorstellungsgespräch brauche ich einen neuen Anzug.
native_language_example: For the job interview, I need a new suit.

meaning: “a new computer” (accusative form, used as the object of the verb).
additional_notes: Used when a verb takes a direct object (accusative), especially with verbs like kaufen (to buy), brauchen (to need), möchten (would like), or sich (etw.) zulegen (to get/acquire). The base noun phrase is ein neuer Computer (nominative), but as an object it becomes einen neuen Computer (masculine accusative: ein→einen, neuer→neuen).
target_language_example: Ich spare gerade für einen neuen Computer.
native_language_example: I’m currently saving for a new computer.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "kaufen" in the Perfekt (past) tense: "hat ... gekauft" (most common in spoken German). "einen neuen Computer" is the accusative object (“a new computer”). Word order: subject + hat/habe + object + gekauft.
target_language_example: Ich habe mir einen neuen Computer gekauft.
native_language_example: I bought myself a new computer.

meaning: "a new friend" (male friend/boyfriend, depending on context).
additional_notes: "Freund" can mean either "friend" or "boyfriend"; the context decides. In questions like "Hast du einen neuen Freund?" it often implies "new boyfriend". "Such dir lieber einen neuen Freund!" is an imperative meaning "You’d better find yourself a new friend/boyfriend!" The ending "-en" on "einen" and "neuen" is used because it’s masculine accusative (direct object) after many verbs (e.g., "haben", "suchen").
target_language_example: Sie hat sich einen neuen Freund gesucht.
native_language_example: She found herself a new friend/boyfriend.

additional_notes: "Einen neuen Hut" is the accusative form used as the direct object after verbs like brauchen (to need), wollen (to want), haben (to have), kaufen (to buy). The base noun is "der Hut" (hat). Adjective ending: "neu" becomes "neuen" after "einen" (masculine accusative).
target_language_example: Ich brauche einen neuen Hut für den Winter.
native_language_example: I need a new hat for the winter.

additional_notes: "Rechner" often means "computer" (especially in the sense of a PC) in everyday German. In this phrase, "einen" shows the accusative case (used after many verbs like "brauchen" = to need, or in phrases like "sich einen neuen Rechner zulegen" = to get/buy oneself a new computer).
target_language_example: Ich habe mir einen neuen Rechner gekauft, weil der alte zu langsam war.
native_language_example: I bought myself a new computer because the old one was too slow.

additional_notes: Used when the noun is understood from context and left out. It refers to a masculine thing in the accusative case (often after verbs like haben/kaufen/tragen): e.g., (Badeanzug/Wagen) → „einen roten“. The adjective ending -en matches masculine accusative.
target_language_example: Ich nehme den blauen, und du nimmst einen roten.
native_language_example: I’ll take the blue one, and you take a red one.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine noun in the accusative case (direct object): einen schlechten Tag, einen schlechten Traum, einen schlechten Ruf. It’s the declined form of schlecht (“bad”) and needs a noun after it.
target_language_example: Ich hatte einen schlechten Tag.
native_language_example: I had a bad day.

additional_notes: Used with "haben" ("einen schlechten Ruf haben") to say that a person, group, place, or thing is seen negatively by others. Often followed by "bei" + dative to specify whose opinion (e.g., "bei seinen Schülern"). The noun "Ruf" means "reputation" (literally "call"), and "schlecht" changes to "schlechten" because of the masculine accusative noun phrase "einen ... Ruf".
target_language_example: Das Restaurant hat bei vielen Leuten einen schlechten Ruf.
native_language_example: That restaurant has a bad reputation with many people.

meaning: "a black one" (masculine accusative), or "a black [noun]" when the noun is understood.
additional_notes: Used when talking about a masculine noun in the accusative case (often after verbs like "haben" or "tragen"). It can either come before a masculine noun (e.g., "einen schwarzen Anzug" = "a black suit") or stand alone with the noun left out because it’s obvious from context (e.g., "Ich habe einen schwarzen und einen weißen." = "I have a black one and a white one.").
target_language_example: Ich nehme einen schwarzen.
native_language_example: I'll take a black one.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like „machen“ (to make) or „begehen“ (to commit): „einen schweren Fehler machen/begehen“. It implies the mistake has important consequences, not just a small slip-up. Adjective endings change with case, e.g. nominative: „ein schwerer Fehler“, accusative: „einen schweren Fehler“.
target_language_example: Wenn wir jetzt abbrechen, machen wir einen schweren Fehler.
native_language_example: If we stop now, we’ll be making a serious mistake.

meaning: "a nice/beautiful" (masculine accusative), or in wishes: "have a nice …!"
additional_notes: This is the masculine accusative form of "ein schöner" and is used before a masculine noun in the accusative case (often after verbs like "haben": "Du hast einen schönen Hund."). It’s also very common as a shortened wish where the noun is understood or added, e.g. "Einen schönen Tag!" = "Have a nice day!" You’ll change the ending depending on gender/case (e.g. "eine schöne …", "ein schönes …").
target_language_example: Einen schönen Abend noch!
native_language_example: Have a nice evening!

additional_notes: A common polite good-bye or well-wish in the evening. Often used with extra words like „noch“ ("Einen schönen Abend noch!") meaning “Have a nice evening (still)”. You can also use it after „ich wünsche …“ ("Ich wünsche dir/euch/Ihnen einen schönen Abend").
target_language_example: Danke für den Besuch — einen schönen Abend noch!
native_language_example: Thanks for visiting—have a nice evening!

additional_notes: Used as a friendly wish or greeting, often on its own: "Einen schönen Tag!" You also commonly hear it with "wünschen": "Ich wünsche dir/euch/Ihnen einen schönen Tag" (= I wish you a nice day). In questions it means "a nice day" in the sense of how your day went: "Hattest du einen schönen Tag?"
target_language_example: Einen schönen Tag noch, und bis morgen!
native_language_example: Have a nice rest of your day, and see you tomorrow!

additional_notes: Used before a masculine noun after “einen” (accusative of “ein”): e.g., „einen sehr guten Eindruck/Lehrer/Job/Start“. The adjective ending „-en“ comes from the masculine accusative form. You’ll also see other forms depending on gender/case (e.g., „eine sehr gute …“, „ein sehr gutes …“).
target_language_example: Ich habe einen sehr guten Eindruck von ihr.
native_language_example: I have a very good impression of her.

additional_notes: This is an adjective phrase used before a masculine noun in the accusative case, because of “einen” (e.g., einen sehr schönen Abend / Ort / Namen). Often used in wishes and greetings: “Ich wünsche Ihnen/euch einen sehr schönen …” (Ihnen = formal “you”, euch = informal/plural “you”).
target_language_example: Ich wünsche dir einen sehr schönen Tag!
native_language_example: I wish you a very nice day!

meaning: "a strange/weird dream" (accusative: a dream as the object of the sentence).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like "haben" (to have) and "träumen"/"einen Traum träumen" (to dream / to have a dream). The adjective changes with the case: nominative "ein seltsamer Traum" (a strange dream), accusative "einen seltsamen Traum" (I had a strange dream). Common time phrases: "letzte Nacht" (last night).
target_language_example: Ich hatte letzte Nacht einen seltsamen Traum über die Schule.
native_language_example: I had a strange dream about school last night.

meaning: “to make/commit such a mistake …” (introduces a zu-infinitive).
additional_notes: This is an incomplete chunk that must be followed by an infinitive verb, typically **machen** (“to make”) or **begehen** (“to commit”): *einen solchen Fehler zu machen / zu begehen*. It’s often used after verbs like **vermeiden** (“to avoid”) or with judgments like **dumm** (“stupid”). Note: **Fehler** usually means “mistake/error,” not “failure” (which is **Misserfolg**).
target_language_example: Ich versuche, einen solchen Fehler zu vermeiden.
native_language_example: I’m trying to avoid making such a mistake.

meaning: 'a strong' (masculine, accusative), used before a noun.
additional_notes: This is the accusative masculine form of the adjective "stark" after "einen". It must be followed by a masculine noun (e.g., "einen starken Willen" = "a strong will", "einen starken Menschen" = "a strong person"). Note: German "stark" looks like English "stark" but usually means "strong" (not "stark" in English).
target_language_example: Er hat einen starken Akzent.
native_language_example: He has a strong accent.

additional_notes: Used to describe a sudden, intense pain that feels like stabbing. Very common in medical contexts when saying where it hurts: „einen stechenden Schmerz in/im + body part“ (e.g., „im Bauch“, „in der Brust“).
target_language_example: Seit heute Morgen habe ich einen stechenden Schmerz im Rücken.
native_language_example: Since this morning, I’ve had a sharp, stabbing pain in my back.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine noun when that noun is the direct object (accusative), e.g. after verbs like haben, kennen, backen, machen, verbringen. The adjective changes with gender/case: ein toller Mann (nom.), einen tollen Mann (acc.), eine tolle Idee, ein tolles Hotel. Note: German toll means “great/awesome” (or sometimes “crazy”), not the English “toll” (road fee).
target_language_example: Ich habe einen tollen Film gesehen.
native_language_example: I saw a great movie.

meaning: a full schedule; a packed calendar.
additional_notes: Used with "haben" (to have) to say someone is very busy and has many appointments/commitments. You can vary the adjective: "einen ziemlich/sehr vollen Terminkalender" (a pretty/very full schedule).
target_language_example: Diese Woche habe ich einen vollen Terminkalender, aber am Freitag habe ich Zeit.
native_language_example: This week I have a packed schedule, but on Friday I have time.

additional_notes: Used when "older brother" is the direct object, often after verbs like haben (to have): "Ich habe einen älteren Bruder." In questions with "hast/hat", it also takes accusative: "Hast du einen älteren Bruder?" Nominative (subject) would be "ein älterer Bruder".
target_language_example: Hast du einen älteren Bruder oder eine ältere Schwester?
native_language_example: Do you have an older brother or an older sister?

additional_notes: “Bank” has two common meanings in German: (1) a financial bank, and (2) a bench (seat), often in a park. “einer” is the dative form of “eine,” so you’ll often see it after prepositions like “in” (in a bank), “bei” (at/with a bank), or “auf” (on a bench). Context and the preposition usually make the meaning clear: “in/bei einer Bank” = bank (financial), “auf einer Bank” = bench.
target_language_example: Ich sitze auf einer Bank im Park.
native_language_example: I’m sitting on a bench in the park.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like „sein/werden“ to describe what happened to someone: „Ich bin (von) einer Biene gestochen (worden).“ The full, most common form is „von einer Biene gestochen“ (“stung by a bee”); the „von“ can sometimes be omitted in short speech, but including it is safest.
target_language_example: Ich bin von einer Biene gestochen worden.
native_language_example: I got stung by a bee.

additional_notes: Usually used as part of a longer phrase, especially with verbs like „im Bett liegen“ (to be lying in bed) or „bleiben“ (to stay): „mit einer Erkältung im Bett liegen/bleiben“. „einer Erkältung“ is the dative form of „eine Erkältung“ (often after „mit“). „im Bett“ = „in dem Bett“ (in bed).
target_language_example: Ich liege mit einer Erkältung im Bett und gehe heute nicht zur Arbeit.
native_language_example: I’m in bed with a cold and I’m not going to work today.

meaning: “of a woman” / “a woman’s” (genitive) or “to/for a woman” (dative).
additional_notes:
"einer" is the feminine form used for two cases:
- Genitive singular: shows possession/association ("das Leben einer Frau" = "a woman’s life").
- Dative singular: after many prepositions/verbs that take dative (e.g., "mit einer Frau" = "with a woman", "einer Frau helfen" = "help a woman").
Which meaning it has depends on the sentence.
target_language_example: Er hat einer Frau geholfen, die ihre Tasche verloren hatte.
native_language_example: He helped a woman who had lost her bag.

additional_notes: Used with "sein" to say you (don’t) share the same opinion: "(nicht) einer Meinung sein". Common patterns: "mit jemandem (völlig) einer Meinung sein" (= agree with someone) and "in solchen Dingen einer Meinung sein" (= agree on such matters). Often refers to viewpoints rather than concrete facts.
target_language_example: Ich bin nicht deiner Meinung, aber wir können ruhig darüber reden.
native_language_example: I don't agree with you, but we can talk about it calmly.

meaning: 'one hour' (in/within/for an hour; an hour ago).
additional_notes: This is the dative form of **eine Stunde** (“one hour”). It’s very common in time expressions with prepositions: **in einer Stunde** = in one hour; **vor einer Stunde** = an hour ago; **seit einer Stunde** = for/since an hour; **innerhalb einer Stunde** = within an hour. Often used with approximations like **etwa** (about) or **mindestens** (at least).
target_language_example: Ich bin in etwa einer Stunde wieder da.
native_language_example: I'll be back in about an hour.

meaning: an hour behind; one hour back.
additional_notes: Used to say something is one hour earlier/behind in time (e.g., your schedule is delayed: „Wir sind einer Stunde zurück.“). For “an hour ago,” German usually says „vor einer Stunde“ instead. Related: „die Uhr eine Stunde zurückstellen“ = to set the clock back one hour.
target_language_example: Wir sind wegen des Staus einer Stunde zurück.
native_language_example: We’re an hour behind because of the traffic jam.

additional_notes: Used with time prepositions: **seit einer Weile** = “for a while / for some time now” (ongoing); **vor einer Weile** = “a while ago” (in the past). Often implies an unspecified but noticeable amount of time.
target_language_example: Seit einer Weile lerne ich jeden Tag Deutsch.
native_language_example: I've been learning German every day for a while now.

meaning: (for) a week / one week (in time expressions).
additional_notes:
"Einer Woche" is the dative form of "eine Woche" and is very common after time prepositions:
- seit einer Woche = for a week (and still continuing)
- innerhalb einer Woche = within a week (deadline)
- vor einer Woche = a week ago
- nach einer Woche = after a week
target_language_example: Ich bin seit einer Woche in Berlin.
native_language_example: I’ve been in Berlin for a week.

additional_notes: A time expression about how long someone has been ill. Most commonly used with **seit**: **seit einer Woche krank** = “(have been) sick for a week.” You may also hear **eine Woche krank** without *seit* (more like “sick for one week”).
target_language_example: Ich bin seit einer Woche krank.
native_language_example: I’ve been sick for a week.

additional_notes: This is the declined form of **ein anderer / eine andere / ein anderes** (“another/different”). **Einer anderen** is used when the noun is **feminine** and in the **dative case**, often after prepositions like **mit** (with), **in** (in/into), **von** (from/of), **zu** (to): *mit einer anderen Frau*, *in einer anderen Stadt*, *von einer anderen Welt*. The noun may be stated (*einer anderen Stadt*) or sometimes understood from context.
target_language_example: Ich spreche lieber mit einer anderen Person.
native_language_example: I’d rather talk to another person.

additional_notes: Used with feminine nouns after the indefinite article in the dative case: einer + adjective ending -en + noun (e.g., in/bei/von/zu einer großen Firma/Armee/Wohnung). The preposition or verb decides the dative case; the adjective ending changes accordingly.
target_language_example: Er arbeitet bei einer großen Bank.
native_language_example: He works at a large bank.

meaning: in/at a big city (feminine singular, dative); sometimes also “of a big city” (genitive).
additional_notes: This is the noun phrase "eine große Stadt" (“a big city”) in a case form: most commonly dative after prepositions like "in", "aus", "bei", "zu" (e.g., "in einer großen Stadt"). It can also be genitive (“of a big city”), depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Ich wohne in einer großen Stadt.
native_language_example: I live in a big city.

additional_notes: Used with time expressions like "in" (in half an hour), "vor" (half an hour ago), and "seit" (for half an hour). It’s dative feminine because of "(die) Stunde": "in/vor/seit einer halben Stunde".
target_language_example: Ich bin in einer halben Stunde zu Hause.
native_language_example: I’ll be home in half an hour.

additional_notes: This is the declined form of "eine kleine" used with feminine nouns when the noun is in the dative case (often after prepositions like "aus" = from, "auf" = on, "seit" = for/since). Common patterns: "aus einer kleinen Stadt" (from a small town), "auf einer kleinen Insel" (on a small island), "seit einer kleinen Weile" (for a little while).
target_language_example: Wir kommen aus einer kleinen Stadt.
native_language_example: We come from a small town.

additional_notes: This is the dative form of „eine kleine Stadt“. It’s used after prepositions like „in“ (location) and „aus“ (origin): „in einer kleinen Stadt“ = “in a small town,” „aus einer kleinen Stadt“ = “from a small town.” In everyday English, this is usually “small town,” even though „Stadt“ can mean “city.”
target_language_example: Sie arbeitet in einer kleinen Stadt in Bayern.
native_language_example: She works in a small town in Bavaria.

meaning: a short break (after a short pause).
additional_notes: Dative form of **eine kurze Pause**. Commonly used with **nach** (“after”): *nach einer kurzen Pause* = “after a short break,” and with **mit** (“with/about” in suggestions): *Wie wäre es mit einer kurzen Pause?* = “How about a short break?”
target_language_example: Nach einer kurzen Pause ging es weiter.
native_language_example: After a short break, we continued.

additional_notes: Refers to an (often unspecified) male person and then adds a relative clause: „einer, der …“. Used in statements and exclamations; can sound emphatic or slightly ironic/annoyed depending on context (e.g., „Schon wieder einer, der …!“). For other genders: „eine, die …“ (female) and „eins/eines, das …“ (neuter), with case changing as needed (e.g., „einen, der …“ in the accusative).
target_language_example: Endlich einer, der uns versteht.
native_language_example: Finally someone who understands us.

additional_notes: Used to pick out one person/thing from a group: "one of the + plural noun". The following clause often describes the group: "einer der Männer, die ...". Changes with gender and case: e.g., "eine der" (feminine), "eines der" (neuter), "einen der" (accusative masculine).
target_language_example: Er ist einer der besten Freunde meines Bruders.
native_language_example: He is one of my brother’s best friends.

meaning: "one of the best" (masculine; among the top).
additional_notes: Used to say a male person or a masculine noun is in a top group: "einer der besten + plural noun" (e.g., einer der besten Schüler). It’s the masculine form ("einer"); feminine: "eine der besten"; neuter: "eines der besten". Often followed by a relative clause ("…, die/den/das …") or a genitive phrase ("… meines Lebens").
target_language_example: Das war einer der besten Momente meines Lebens.
native_language_example: That was one of the best moments of my life.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something is one member of a group that belongs to you: e.g., one of my brothers/sons/neighbors/suitcases. It’s the masculine/neuter form (einer) + the possessive in the genitive plural (meiner). For feminine nouns, use "eine meiner" (e.g., eine meiner Schwestern). For plural-only groups without a singular member word, you usually say "eins von meinen …" (e.g., eins von meinen Büchern).
target_language_example: Einer meiner Freunde kommt aus Kanada.
native_language_example: One of my friends is from Canada.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an unspecified person from your group of friends. This is a genitive construction: "meiner Freunde" = "of my friends". The form of "einer" changes with gender/case (e.g., "eine meiner Freundinnen" = one of my (female) friends; "einen meiner Freunde" = one of my friends (accusative)).
target_language_example: Einer meiner Freunde wohnt in Berlin.
native_language_example: One of my friends lives in Berlin.

additional_notes: Used to say a male person/thing is among your top favorites or top performers. It typically takes a plural noun after it (e.g., Freunde, Schüler, Lehrer) and is masculine nominative. The form changes with gender/case: einer meiner besten (masc. nom.), eine meiner besten (fem. nom.), eines meiner besten (neut. nom.), and it will also change in other cases (e.g., Ich spreche mit einem meiner besten Freunde = ‘one of my best friends’ in dative).
target_language_example: Tom ist einer meiner besten Freunde.
native_language_example: Tom is one of my best friends.

meaning: one after another; one by one.
additional_notes: Used to describe people or things doing the same action in sequence (not all at once). It can change for gender/number, e.g. "eine nach der anderen" (all feminine) or "eines nach dem anderen" (neuter).
target_language_example: Bitte kommt einer nach dem anderen nach vorne.
native_language_example: Please come to the front one by one.

additional_notes: Used to single out one member of a larger group: **einer von + plural noun/pronoun**. After **von**, the noun phrase is typically dative (e.g., *von den Leuten / von euch*). In everyday speech you may also hear *von* + number + plural noun without an article (e.g., *von vier Menschen*). Form varies by gender/case: **einer von** (masc./nom.), **eine von** (fem.), **eines von** (neut.). Common with pronouns: *einer von euch* = “one of you.”
target_language_example: Kennt einer von euch Tom?
native_language_example: Does one of you know Tom?

additional_notes: Used when speaking politely to a group you address as „Sie“. „einer“ refers to one person (often a man, or gender not specified); you may also hear „eine von Ihnen“ (one woman) or „eines von Ihnen“ (one of you, e.g., a child/baby). Often used in questions: „Kennt einer von Ihnen …?“
target_language_example: Kann einer von Ihnen mir bitte helfen?
native_language_example: Can one of you please help me?

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something belongs to a group of several people/things. It’s a common spoken variant of the more standard “einer von den/der + plural noun” (e.g., “einer von den Leuten”) and can also be used with things (“Einer von den Koffern …”). Often you’ll also hear/see “einer von den” instead of the more formal “einer der …” / “einer von denjenigen, die …”. Case and gender change as needed: e.g., “eine von den …”, “eines von den …”.
target_language_example: Ich bin einer von den neuen Mitarbeitern.
native_language_example: I’m one of the new employees.

meaning: "one of those (people)" / "one of them" (often said in a dismissive way).
additional_notes: Used to classify someone as belonging to a certain (usually negatively viewed) group: "He’s one of those." Often refers back to a group already mentioned or understood from context. Variations: "eine von denen" (female), "eines von denen" (neuter, less common), plural: "welche von denen" = "which ones of them".
target_language_example: Mach dir keine Sorgen—er ist nicht einer von denen, die immer Ärger machen.
native_language_example: Don’t worry—he’s not one of those people who always cause trouble.

meaning: "one of you" (one person from your group).
additional_notes: Used when speaking to two or more people you address with informal plural "ihr/euch" (“you all”). It often appears in questions like "Hat/Kann/Kennt einer von euch ...?" = “Does/Can/Does anyone (among you) …?”. For mixed-gender or unspecified gender groups, you may also hear "eine von euch" (female) or "einer/eine von Ihnen" with formal "Sie".
target_language_example: Kann einer von euch mir kurz helfen?
native_language_example: Can one of you help me for a moment?

meaning: one of you two (one of the two of you).
additional_notes: Used when addressing two people informally (euch) and asking whether either person fits something or has done something. It’s often used with yes/no questions (Hat …? Ist …? Spricht …?). The feminine form is “eine von euch beiden” (one of you two women / one of you, feminine), and the plural form for more than two people is “einer von euch” (one of you).
target_language_example: Kann einer von euch beiden mir kurz helfen?
native_language_example: Can one of you two help me for a moment?

meaning: 'one of them' (referring to a male person, or a person of unknown gender).
additional_notes:
Used to single out one person from a group previously mentioned. It changes with gender/case: 
- masculine nominative: einer von ihnen (one of them)
- feminine nominative: eine von ihnen
- neuter nominative: eines von ihnen
Also commonly appears with other pronouns: einer von uns (one of us), einer von euch (one of you all).
target_language_example: Ich glaube, einer von ihnen kennt dich.
native_language_example: I think one of them knows you.

meaning: 'one of us' (a person from our group).
additional_notes: Used when choosing or pointing out a single person from a group that includes the speaker ("uns" = "us"). Can be replaced depending on gender/number: "eine von uns" (female), "eines von uns" (neuter/child), "einer/eine von euch" (one of you all). Often used in situations where someone has to volunteer or take responsibility.
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, einer von uns kann dir helfen.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, one of us can help you.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone in a group needs to do something, without saying who yet (often followed by an infinitive like fragen/hingehen/bleiben). It can imply shared responsibility or that the task is unavoidable.
target_language_example: Einer von uns muss heute früher gehen.
native_language_example: One of us has to leave early today.

meaning: "of a man" (genitive: belonging to/connected with a man).
additional_notes: This is the genitive form of "ein Mann". It’s used to show possession or relationship, often after a noun: "das Gesicht eines Mannes" = "the face of a man." In the genitive, masculine/neuter "ein" becomes "eines," and "Mann" commonly takes the ending "-es" → "Mannes."
target_language_example: Ich kenne den Namen eines Mannes, der hier wohnt.
native_language_example: I know the name of a man who lives here.

meaning: one night (once, on a particular night).
additional_notes: Used to set the scene for a past event, often in stories. It means “one night” in the sense of “on a certain night” (not necessarily the following night). The genitive form “eines” is fixed in this phrase.
target_language_example: Eines Nachts hörten wir ein seltsames Geräusch.
native_language_example: One night we heard a strange noise.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that will happen at an unspecified time in the future. It’s common in promises, predictions, or hopes. Often appears with future meaning (e.g., with "wird"), but can also be used in stories to mean "one day" (at some point).
target_language_example: Eines Tages werde ich nach Berlin ziehen.
native_language_example: One day I’ll move to Berlin.

meaning: “one day / someday to” (a place) — used to express a future hope, plan, or possibility of going somewhere.
additional_notes: Phrase pattern: eines Tages + nach + place. Eines Tages means “one day/someday” and is often used for dreams or long-term plans. Nach is used with most cities and many countries without an article (e.g., nach Japan, nach Berlin). Some destinations take a different construction instead (e.g., in die Schweiz, in die USA).
target_language_example: Ich will eines Tages nach Japan gehen.
native_language_example: I want to go to Japan one day.

meaning: “one day (will) …” (saying something will happen in the future).
additional_notes: Used to express a hope, prediction, or warning about the future. Often placed at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis. It’s commonly followed by the future auxiliary verb "wird" (from "werden") plus an infinitive at the end of the clause (e.g., "Eines Tages wird er verstehen.").
target_language_example: Eines Tages wird sie nach Berlin ziehen.
native_language_example: One day she will move to Berlin.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that will happen at an unspecified time in the future. Often sounds like a prediction, promise, warning, or encouragement. Grammar: "eines Tages" = "one day"; "wirst du" is the 2nd-person singular future with "werden" (du wirst …).
target_language_example: Eines Tages wirst du stolz auf dich sein.
native_language_example: One day you will be proud of yourself.

meaning: one of the (used with plural nouns).
additional_notes: Common pattern: **eines der + plural noun (Genitive)**, e.g. *eines der Fenster* (“one of the windows”), *eines der Teams* (“one of the teams”). Often used with superlatives: *eines der schönsten …* (“one of the most beautiful …”).
target_language_example: Das ist eines der besten Restaurants in der Stadt.
native_language_example: That’s one of the best restaurants in the city.

meaning: to open one of the windows.
additional_notes: "eines" means "one" (a neuter pronoun), and "der Fenster" is the genitive plural meaning "of the windows" (from "das Fenster"). Often used in polite requests with "Könnten/Könntest/Könntet ... bitte ...?".
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, könnten Sie bitte eines der Fenster öffnen?
native_language_example: Excuse me, could you please open one of the windows?

meaning: “just … whatever you …” (used to tell someone to do/say/eat what they want).
additional_notes: Used in commands (imperatives) to make them sound more relaxed or encouraging: “Mach/Sag/Tu/Iss einfach …” + “was du …” (“whatever you …”). Here, **einfach** often means “just/simply” (not “easy”). The second part **was du** introduces a clause like “want,” “saw,” “normally do,” etc.
target_language_example: Sag einfach, was du denkst.
native_language_example: Just say what you think.

meaning: “just/simply not” (emphatic: “not at all / not no matter what”).
additional_notes: Used to stress that something is not true or not happening, often with a tone of frustration, surprise, or emphasis. Common with verbs to show that someone/something won’t do something (e.g., „Er kommt einfach nicht.“ = “He just won’t come.”). Word order: typically after the verb or after the statement element you’re emphasizing.
target_language_example: Ich verstehe das einfach nicht.
native_language_example: I just don’t understand that.

additional_notes: Used to downplay or narrow something to the simplest explanation or to a single intention: “just (do/think/be) …”. Often adds emphasis like “only” or “merely.” Common with verbs (einfach nur ansehen, hinter mir lassen, sich anfreunden) and with nouns/adjectives to mean “not just …” (Nicht einfach nur Köche …).
target_language_example: Ich möchte heute Abend einfach nur zu Hause bleiben.
native_language_example: I just want to stay at home tonight.

meaning: just like that; simply (without a reason/without doing anything about it).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens or is done without a special reason, explanation, or effort (“for no particular reason”), or that someone lets something happen without intervening (“just let it happen”). Often expresses surprise, criticism, or disbelief: "einfach so stehen/liegen lassen" (just leave it there), "einfach so gehen" (just leave).
target_language_example: Du kannst nicht einfach so gehen, ohne dich zu verabschieden.
native_language_example: You can’t just leave like that without saying goodbye.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone broke into a place (home, shop, bank), usually when the person is unknown or not mentioned. Commonly appears in the impersonal passive: "Es ist ... eingebrochen worden" or with the place first: "Bei uns / In die Bank ist ... eingebrochen worden." This is the perfect passive: "sein" + Partizip II (eingebrochen) + "worden".
target_language_example: In unsere Wohnung ist letzte Nacht eingebrochen worden.
native_language_example: Our apartment was broken into last night.

additional_notes: Used to say you have more than one question (usually a small number). Often appears with verbs like "haben" (to have) and "stellen" (to ask/pose): "einige Fragen haben" / "jemandem einige Fragen stellen". More formal alternative for "ein paar Fragen".
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich habe noch einige Fragen.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I still have a few questions.

additional_notes: Used when you want to ask multiple questions. Common in interviews, formal situations, and polite requests. You’ll often see it with polite modal verbs like: „Darf ich …?“ / „Dürfte ich …?“ (May I …?), or more formal: „Ich würde Ihnen gern einige Fragen stellen.“ (I’d like to ask you a few questions.) „jemandem Fragen stellen“ uses the dative: „Tom einige Fragen stellen“, „Ihnen einige Fragen stellen“.
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, dürfte ich Ihnen einige Fragen stellen?
native_language_example: Excuse me, may I ask you a few questions?

additional_notes: Used to refer to an unspecified number of people (not everyone, not a specific group). Often introduces a general opinion or observation. For a few specific individuals you can also say "ein paar Leute"; for more emphasis on “many,” use "viele Leute".
target_language_example: Einige Leute mögen Kaffee, andere lieber Tee.
native_language_example: Some people like coffee; others prefer tea.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an unspecified small number of days (often around 2–5), in the past or future. It’s less specific than „zwei/drei Tage“ and often implies a short period. Common in phrases like „für einige Tage“ (for a few days) or with verbs like „bleiben“ (to stay).
target_language_example: Gib mir einige Tage.
native_language_example: Give me a few days.

additional_notes: Used to show that something happens after a short time has passed (typically several days) from a previously mentioned event. Often comes at the beginning of a sentence as a time expression; you can also place it after the verb in some contexts.
target_language_example: Einige Tage später haben wir uns wieder gesehen.
native_language_example: A few days later we saw each other again.

additional_notes: Refers to an unspecified (often not very long) period of time. Common with verbs like dauern (to take time) and with für: für einige Zeit = for a while. Can also be used without für when it clearly refers to a time span (e.g., Einige Zeit lebten sie… = They lived… for some time).
target_language_example: Warte bitte noch einige Zeit, dann bin ich fertig.
native_language_example: Please wait a little while longer, then I’ll be finished.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an unspecified part of a larger group. It’s usually followed by a definite group like a noun with a possessive/name/article (e.g., „einige von Toms Mitarbeitern“) or a pronoun (e.g., „einige von ihnen/uns“). The verb is plural: „Einige von ihnen sind …“.
target_language_example: Einige von meinen Nachbarn sprechen Englisch.
native_language_example: Some of my neighbors speak English.

additional_notes: Usually used in time expressions, often with prepositions like **seit** (for/since), **vor** (ago), or **in** (in): **seit einigen Jahren** = “for a few years,” **vor einigen Jahren** = “a few years ago,” **in einigen Jahren** = “in a few years.” Grammar note: **Jahren** is the dative plural of **Jahr** and is required after these prepositions.
target_language_example: Vor einigen Jahren habe ich in Berlin gewohnt.
native_language_example: A few years ago, I lived in Berlin.

meaning: (in) a few days; after a few days.
additional_notes: Usually used with a time preposition, most commonly **in**: **in einigen Tagen** = “in a few days / a few days from now.” With **nach** it means “after a few days” (**nach einigen Tagen**). **einigen** is the dative plural form of **einige** (“some, a few”), so you’ll often see it in time phrases like this.
target_language_example: Ich melde mich in einigen Tagen bei dir.
native_language_example: I’ll get back to you in a few days.

additional_notes: Used to talk about frequency (how often something happens). Often placed after the verb or at the end of the sentence: „Ich mache das einmal am Tag.“ You may also see the more formal synonym „einmal täglich“. In spoken German it can appear as a short, unfinished phrase when the verb is understood from context (like in sentence 3).
target_language_example: Ich trinke einmal am Tag Kaffee.
native_language_example: I drink coffee once a day.

additional_notes: Used to introduce someone/something in a story (often like a fairy tale: "Es war einmal ein …" = "Once there was a …"). It can also mean something used to be something in the past ("X war einmal ein Y" = "X was once a Y").
target_language_example: Hier stand einmal ein kleines Kino.
native_language_example: There used to be a small movie theater here.

additional_notes: Used when talking about a single past occasion ("once") or something that existed in the past ("used to be / there once was"). "Einmal" is an adverb; "einen" is the masculine accusative form of "ein" before a noun (e.g., "einen Wal", "einen Hut", "einen See"). Often appears as "einmal einen + noun".
target_language_example: Ich habe einmal einen netten Mann im Zug kennengelernt.
native_language_example: I once met a nice man on the train.

additional_notes:
Used to say you saw someone or something only a single time. Often appears as:
- „nur/bloß einmal gesehen“ = only seen once
- „einmal gesehen zu haben“ (with an infinitive) = to have seen (him/it) once
target_language_example: Ich habe diese Schauspielerin nur einmal gesehen.
native_language_example: I’ve only seen that actress once.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens one time per year (frequency). Often used with verbs like kommen/fahren/besuchen. You can add emphasis with words like „wenigstens“ (at least): „wenigstens einmal im Jahr“.
target_language_example: Ich gehe einmal im Jahr zum Zahnarzt.
native_language_example: I go to the dentist once a year.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how often something happens (frequency). Often goes near the verb or at the beginning/end of the sentence: "Ich gehe einmal im Monat ins Kino." / "Einmal im Monat gehe ich ins Kino."
target_language_example: Einmal im Monat rufe ich meine Großeltern an.
native_language_example: Once a month I call my grandparents.

meaning: "once in …" / "at one time in …" (referring to a single occasion or a past period).
additional_notes: Use "einmal" with "in" + dative to say something happened once in a place ("einmal in Rom"), or once in a situation/state (e.g., "einmal in dich verliebt" = once in love with you). It can also mean "sometime/one day" in questions about future plans ("Wollen Sie sich einmal in der Politik engagieren?").
target_language_example: Ich habe einmal in Berlin gearbeitet.
native_language_example: I once worked in Berlin.

meaning: considered (as an option), at least once.
additional_notes: From the verb phrase „in Erwägung ziehen“ = „to consider“. It’s often used in the passive: „X wurde (einmal) in Erwägung gezogen“ = „X was (at least once) considered.“ „Einmal“ here usually means “at some point / at least once,” not necessarily “one time only.”
target_language_example: Der Umzug wurde einmal in Erwägung gezogen, aber dann haben wir uns dagegen entschieden.
native_language_example: Moving was considered at one point, but then we decided against it.

additional_notes: Used to talk about frequency (how often something happens). It often answers the question „Wie oft?“ (How often?). You can swap in other time units: „einmal am Tag“ (once a day), „einmal im Monat“ (once a month).
target_language_example: Ich rufe meine Oma einmal in der Woche an.
native_language_example: I call my grandma once a week.

meaning: "once in a ..." / "one time in a ..." (talking about frequency).
additional_notes: Used before a time period in the dative case: einmal in einem Monat/Jahr/Woche = once a month/year/week. In everyday German, this is often shortened with a contraction: einmal im Monat (in dem Monat), einmal im Jahr (in dem Jahr).
target_language_example: Ich gehe einmal in einem Monat ins Kino.
native_language_example: I go to the cinema once a month.

additional_notes: Used to say how often something happens. You can swap in other time units: einmal pro Woche (once a week), einmal pro Jahr (once a year). Also common: einmal im Monat (same meaning).
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns einmal pro Monat zum Mittagessen.
native_language_example: We meet once a month for lunch.

additional_notes: Used to say how often something happens. Often placed near the verb: „Ich schwimme einmal pro Woche.“ You can swap the time unit: „einmal pro Tag“ (once a day), „einmal pro Monat“ (once a month).
target_language_example: Wir telefonieren einmal pro Woche.
native_language_example: We talk on the phone once a week.

meaning: to see (someone) dance (once / at least once).
additional_notes: Usually used with an object: jemanden einmal tanzen sehen = “to see someone dance at least once.” The word einmal often means “once” or “sometime/at least once” (a casual, not very exact “once”). Common word order: Ich möchte dich einmal tanzen sehen. In speech, you might also hear: Ich will dich mal tanzen sehen. (mal = shortened einmal).
target_language_example: Ich möchte dich einmal tanzen sehen.
native_language_example: I'd like to see you dance at least once.

meaning: to try (it) once / to give it a try.
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive clause ("zu" + verb): "... einmal zu versuchen". "Einmal" often makes the request or intention sound softer or more casual, like "just" or "for once": "Ich will es einmal versuchen" = "I’ll just give it a try."
target_language_example: Ich möchte es einmal zu versuchen.
native_language_example: I’d like to try it once.

meaning: "one, two, three" (counting; often to start together).
additional_notes: Used for counting items (e.g., drops, steps) and as a spoken countdown to begin an action together (similar to “1, 2, 3!” in English). Also common in music, dance, workouts, and kids’ games to keep rhythm. Sometimes followed by more numbers (eins, zwei, drei, vier...) or by a cue word (e.g., Cha-Cha-Cha).
target_language_example: Eins, zwei, drei – jetzt springen wir!
native_language_example: One, two, three—now we jump!

additional_notes: Used to count out loud, often to set a rhythm (e.g., in music, dancing, or exercise) or to count steps/actions ("on six you turn it"). You can extend it with more numbers (eins … zehn).
target_language_example: Eins, zwei, drei, vier—und los!
native_language_example: One, two, three, four—and go!

meaning: 'one after the other' (also: 'one thing at a time').
additional_notes: Most commonly used as the fixed phrase „eins nach dem anderen“ to tell someone to do things step by step, not all at once (often to calm things down or organize tasks). Can be said on its own as an exclamation: „Eins nach dem anderen!“
target_language_example: Keine Sorge—eins nach dem anderen, dann schaffen wir das.
native_language_example: Don’t worry—one thing at a time, then we’ll manage it.

additional_notes: Used with "ein/kein/nur" to emphasize the number of times something happens: "ein einziges Mal" = just once / a single time; "kein einziges Mal" = not once. Often used for emphasis in warnings or strong statements ("noch ein einziges Mal" = one more single time).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir das noch ein einziges Mal erklären?
native_language_example: Can you explain that to me just one more time?

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that there were no words at all or not even one word (often in phrases like „kein einziges Wort“ = “not a single word”). „Einziges“ is the neuter form of „einzig“ and matches „das Wort“.
target_language_example: Ich habe kein einziges Wort verstanden.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand a single word.

additional_notes: Used to say what time it is (Jetzt ist es elf Uhr.), suggest a time (Wie wäre elf Uhr? = How about 11 o’clock?), or show a time limit with bis (bis elf Uhr = until 11 o’clock). You can add parts of the day: vormittags (a.m.), nachmittags (p.m.).
target_language_example: Treffen wir uns um elf Uhr?
native_language_example: Shall we meet at eleven o’clock?

meaning: “finally … up” — used with separable verbs ending in **auf** (e.g. *aufhören, aufmachen, aufwachen, aufgehen, aufgeben*) to mean “finally” + that action.
additional_notes: **Endlich** means “finally / at last.” **Auf** here is usually the separated prefix of a **separable verb**, and it moves to the end of the clause: *Die Sonne geht auf.* → *Die Sonne ging endlich auf.* Common patterns from the examples: **hör … auf** = stop, **mach … auf** = open (a door/window), **wach … auf** = wake up, **geh … auf** = rise (sun), **gib … auf** = give up. In commands, **endlich** often adds impatience: *Hör endlich auf!* = “Stop it already!”
target_language_example: Hör endlich auf, so laut zu sein!
native_language_example: Stop being so loud already!

additional_notes: Used with "sein" (to be) to describe a strong friendship (not romantic): "Wir sind eng befreundet." You can intensify it with "sehr" (very) or add time expressions like "seit Jahren" (for years).
target_language_example: Wir sind seit der Schulzeit eng befreundet.
native_language_example: We’ve been close friends since school.

additional_notes: Describes a strong, personal friendship (people you trust and are close to). Often used with verbs like „sein“ (Tom und Maria sind enge Freunde) or „werden“ (Sie wurden enge Freunde = they became close friends). You can also strengthen it with words like „richtig“ or „sehr“: „richtig enge Freunde“, „sehr enge Freunde“.
target_language_example: Wir sind enge Freunde und erzählen uns alles.
native_language_example: We’re close friends and tell each other everything.

additional_notes: Used to describe something located or happening next to the river over some distance. "entlang" often goes with the genitive in more formal German ("entlang des Flusses"), but you may also hear the dative in everyday speech ("entlang dem Fluss").
target_language_example: Es gibt einen Radweg entlang des Flusses.
native_language_example: There is a bike path along the river.

meaning: to be fired (from a job); to be dismissed/released.
additional_notes: Passive form: *werden* + past participle *entlassen*. Most commonly used for losing your job (*aus der Firma entlassen werden*). It can also mean being released/discharged (e.g., from the hospital or the army), depending on context.
target_language_example: Wenn du zu spät kommst, kannst du entlassen werden.
native_language_example: If you come late, you can be fired.

meaning: “to have been discharged/released” (often from a hospital) or “to have been fired” (from a job).
additional_notes: This is the passive form (Perfekt) of **entlassen**: *jemanden entlassen* = to discharge/release/fire someone. **entlassen worden** focuses on what happened to the person (not who did it). Very common with **aus dem Krankenhaus entlassen werden** (“to be discharged from the hospital”). In a work context, it usually means “to be fired/laid off.”
target_language_example: Er ist gestern aus dem Krankenhaus entlassen worden.
native_language_example: He was discharged from the hospital yesterday.

additional_notes: Past tense of the reflexive verb „sich entscheiden“ (to decide). Common patterns: „sich für + Akk.“ = decide on/choose something (e.g., „für den roten Mantel“), and „sich (dafür) entscheiden, zu + Infinitiv“ = decide to do something (e.g., „Sie entschied sich, Tom zu heiraten.“). Often used with adverbs like „schließlich“ (finally) or „stattdessen“ (instead).
target_language_example: Er entschied sich dafür, heute zu Hause zu bleiben.
native_language_example: He decided to stay home today.

meaning: “Sorry that I …” / “Excuse me for …” (apologizing for something you did).
additional_notes: Used with **du** (informal) when you want to apologize and then explain the reason with a **dass**-clause: *Entschuldige, dass ich zu spät bin.* For a more formal version, use **Entschuldigen Sie, dass ich …**. In English you usually wouldn’t say the literal “excuse that I…”, but rather “sorry that I…” or “excuse me for…”.
target_language_example: Entschuldige, dass ich so spät anrufe.
native_language_example: Sorry that I’m calling so late.

additional_notes: Used to start a sentence with an apology, often to soften what you’re about to say (a mistake, misunderstanding, interruption, or awkward situation). Common with verbs like dachte (thought), wollte (wanted), weiß nicht (don’t know). Also appears as the more formal Sie-form: „Entschuldigen Sie, ich …“.
target_language_example: Entschuldige, ich habe dich falsch verstanden.
native_language_example: Sorry, I misunderstood you.

additional_notes: Used when addressing someone with „Sie“ (formal “you”), e.g., to apologize, to interrupt politely, or to get someone’s attention. Often used on its own („Entschuldigen Sie!“) or with more information: „Entschuldigen Sie (bitte) …“ / „Entschuldigen Sie mich …“ / „Entschuldigen Sie wegen …“.
target_language_example: Entschuldigen Sie bitte, wo ist der Bahnhof?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is the train station?

additional_notes: A very polite, formal phrase used with **Sie** when speaking to strangers, customers, officials, etc. It can be used to apologize (often followed by a noun or **dass**-clause: *Entschuldigen Sie bitte, dass …*) or to politely get someone’s attention (*Entschuldigen Sie bitte!*).
target_language_example: Entschuldigen Sie bitte, können Sie mir helfen?
native_language_example: Excuse me, could you help me?

additional_notes: Used with „Sie“ to be polite/formal, followed by a noun naming what you’re apologizing for (e.g., „die Störung“ = the interruption, „die Umstände“ = the inconvenience, „die Unordnung“ = the mess). Common in service situations or when speaking to strangers/authority figures.
target_language_example: Entschuldigen Sie die Verspätung.
native_language_example: Sorry for the delay.

additional_notes: Polite, formal phrase used to apologize and/or to politely get someone’s attention, often before asking something or when you need to leave. Used with "Sie" (formal "you"), so it’s common with strangers, customers, officials, or in professional settings. You can add "bitte" or "kurz" to soften it: "Bitte entschuldigen Sie mich" / "Entschuldigen Sie mich kurz".
target_language_example: Entschuldigen Sie mich, könnten Sie mir bitte helfen?
native_language_example: Excuse me, could you please help me?

additional_notes: Simple past (Präteritum) of the reflexive verb "sich entschuldigen" (to apologize). Used in written narratives and reports; in everyday speech you often hear the perfect: "Er/Sie hat sich entschuldigt." You can add adverbs like "überschwenglich" (profusely) or a time phrase like "einige Augenblicke später" (a few moments later).
target_language_example: Sie entschuldigte sich bei mir für die Verspätung.
native_language_example: She apologized to me for being late.

additional_notes: Präteritum (simple past) of **sich für etwas entschuldigen** = to apologize for something. Used with **für + accusative**: *sich für den Fehler / das Verhalten entschuldigen*. Common in writing and narration; in everyday speech you often hear **hat sich für … entschuldigt** (Perfekt).
target_language_example: Er entschuldigte sich für seinen Fehler.
native_language_example: He apologized for his mistake.

additional_notes: Used to apologize and then say what you did wrong or what happened. Very common with the present perfect: „ich habe“ + past participle (e.g., „vergessen“, „gesagt“, „gedacht“), or with an object („ich habe einen Fehler gemacht“). „Entschuldigung“ is polite; „Sorry“ is more casual.
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich habe die falsche Datei geschickt.
native_language_example: Sorry, I sent the wrong file.

additional_notes: Used to politely get someone’s attention and make a request, especially with strangers or in formal situations. Often followed by an infinitive phrase: „… das bitte wiederholen?“, „… mir den Weg zeigen?“. „Sie“ is the formal “you”.
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, könnten Sie mir bitte helfen?
native_language_example: Excuse me, could you please help me?

meaning: Relax! / Calm down! (said to one person).
additional_notes: An informal imperative meaning “(you) relax.” Used when telling one person (du-form) to calm down or not worry. For more than one person: „Entspannt euch!“; formal: „Entspannen Sie sich!“
target_language_example: Hey, entspann dich — wir haben noch genug Zeit.
native_language_example: Hey, relax—we still have enough time.

additional_notes: "Er" = "he" and "arbeitet" is the 3rd-person singular present tense of "arbeiten" (to work). It can describe a general fact (He works here.) or what he is doing right now (He’s working right now.), depending on context. Often followed by details like place (hier), time (nachts, jeden Tag), or purpose/employer (für eine Universität).
target_language_example: Er arbeitet heute bis spät.
native_language_example: He’s working until late today.

meaning: "he works as" (he has the job of).
additional_notes: Used to say someone’s profession or role: "arbeiten als + [job]". You can change the subject and verb (e.g., "Ich arbeite als…", "Sie arbeitet als…"). Often followed by a noun for a job, sometimes with more info ("als Lehrer an einer Schule").
target_language_example: Mein Bruder arbeitet als Koch in einem Restaurant.
native_language_example: My brother works as a cook in a restaurant.

additional_notes: „arbeitete“ is the Präteritum (simple past) of „arbeiten“ (to work). It’s common in writing and storytelling; in everyday speech people often use the perfect instead: „Er hat gearbeitet.“ You can add time/amount phrases like „den ganzen Tag“ (all day) or „bis spät in die Nacht“ (until late at night).
target_language_example: Er arbeitete bis spät in die Nacht.
native_language_example: He worked until late into the night.

meaning: “he … out of/from the …” (a common sentence fragment: *er* = “he”, *aus dem* = “out of/from the” used with masculine/neuter nouns in the dative).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed standalone phrase; it’s a fragment that needs a verb and a noun to form a full sentence. The preposition *aus* takes the dative case, so *dem* is dative masculine/neuter. In speech/writing, *aus dem* is often contracted to *aus’m* or *ausm*.
target_language_example: Er kommt aus dem Büro.
native_language_example: He’s coming out of/from the office.

additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of **bitten**: **er bat** = “he asked/requested,” and **mich** = “me.” Very often followed by **zu + infinitive** (e.g., *Er bat mich aufzustehen.*) or by a clause with a comma (e.g., *Er bat mich, ihm zu helfen.*). Slightly more formal than **er hat mich gebeten** in everyday speech, but common in writing and storytelling.
target_language_example: Er bat mich, die Tür zuzumachen.
native_language_example: He asked me to close the door.

additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of the reflexive verb **sich benehmen** (“to behave”). Often used with an adverb: **Er benahm sich sehr sonderbar.** = “He behaved very strangely.” Said on its own (**Er benahm sich.**), it often implies “He behaved well / properly” (as in a reminder to behave).
target_language_example: Er benahm sich sehr sonderbar.
native_language_example: He behaved very strangely.

additional_notes: "Er blieb" is the simple past (Präteritum) of "er bleibt" (present) from the verb "bleiben" (to stay/remain). It’s often used in writing and storytelling. Common expression: "bei seiner Meinung bleiben" = to stick to your opinion (not change your mind).
target_language_example: Er blieb den ganzen Abend zu Hause.
native_language_example: He stayed at home the whole evening.

meaning: “he made me … / he brought me to …” (either caused me to do/feel something, or led/took me to a place/person).
additional_notes: Fixed pattern: **jdn. zum + Nomen / nominalisierter Infinitiv**. With reactions/feelings it means “to make someone …”: *jdn. zum Lachen/Weinen/Lächeln bringen* = “make someone laugh/cry/smile.” It can also be literal “bring/lead someone to” a destination or person: *jdn. zum Arzt bringen* = “take someone to the doctor.” Other persons/tenses: *Sie bringt mich zum Lachen. / Er hat mich zum Weinen gebracht.*
target_language_example: Er brachte mich zum Lachen.
native_language_example: He made me laugh.

additional_notes: "Er" = "he" and "braucht" is the 3rd-person singular of "brauchen" (to need). It’s usually followed by the thing needed in the accusative (e.g., "Er braucht Zeit" = He needs time). With "kein/keine" it means "doesn’t need" ("Er braucht keine Hilfe" = He doesn’t need any help). In sentences like "Was er braucht, ist ..." it means "What he needs is ...".
target_language_example: Er braucht heute deine Hilfe.
native_language_example: He needs your help today.

meaning: “he saw the police officer” (a clause with the verb at the end).
additional_notes: This is a clause fragment that typically appears as a subordinate clause, where the conjugated verb comes at the end (e.g., after weil, dass, als). “den Polizisten” is accusative (the person being seen). You could also say “er sah den Polizisten” in a main clause (verb in position 2).
target_language_example: Als er den Polizisten sah, blieb er stehen.
native_language_example: When he saw the police officer, he stopped.

additional_notes: This chunk is part of a larger verb phrase and most commonly appears in the present perfect as **Er hat den Zug verpasst.** **verpassen** = “to miss” (a train/bus/appointment/opportunity). In main clauses, the finite auxiliary **hat** is in 2nd position and the past participle **verpasst** goes to the end. The string **er den Zug verpasst** can also occur as a subordinate-clause word order segment (with the auxiliary at the end).
target_language_example: Ich glaube, dass er den Zug verpasst hat.
native_language_example: I think that he missed the train.

additional_notes: From the verb **denken** (to think). Common patterns: **er denkt, dass ...** / **er denkt, ...** (he thinks that ...), **er denkt an + Akk.** (he thinks about/of someone/something), **er denkt daran, ... zu + infinitive** (he’s thinking of doing something). Word order changes in the **dass**-clause: *Er denkt, dass es hilft.*
target_language_example: Er denkt, dass das eine gute Idee ist.
native_language_example: He thinks that’s a good idea.

additional_notes: This is a clause fragment and typically appears with a complementizer like „dass“ and a finite verb at the end: „…, dass er die Prüfung bestanden hat.“ In normal main-clause word order you’d say: „Er hat die Prüfung bestanden.“
target_language_example: Ich bin froh, dass er die Prüfung bestanden hat.
native_language_example: I’m glad that he passed the exam.

additional_notes: Often used after verbs like „sehen“ or „man sah“ with „wie“: „Ich sah, wie er die Straße überquerte.“ Here „überquerte“ is Präteritum (simple past) of „überqueren“ (“to cross”).
target_language_example: Ich merkte, wie er die Straße überquerte und dann verschwand.
native_language_example: I noticed how he crossed the street and then disappeared.

additional_notes: This is a clause in the past perfect (Plusquamperfekt): **hatte gemacht** = “had made.” It’s often used after **dass** (“that”), e.g. *Er bemerkte, dass …* / *Er wollte nicht zugeben, dass …*. **einen Fehler machen** is the common phrase for “to make a mistake” (Fehler = mistake/error, not “failure”).
target_language_example: Sie merkte, dass er einen Fehler gemacht hatte.
native_language_example: She realized that he had made a mistake.

additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of the reflexive verb **sich entscheiden** (“to decide”). Often followed by **zu + infinitive** or a comma + infinitive clause: *Er entschied sich zu gehen.* / *Er entschied sich, das Haus nicht zu behalten.* It can also stand alone when the choice is clear from context: *Er entschied sich.*
target_language_example: Er entschied sich, mit dem Zug zu fahren.
native_language_example: He decided to take the train.

additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of **sich entschuldigen**. Often followed by **bei + Dativ** for the person you apologize to (*bei dem Angestellten*) and **für + Akkusativ** for what you apologize for (*für sein Benehmen*). In spoken German you often hear the perfect tense instead: **Er hat sich entschuldigt.** Note: it does not usually mean “he excused himself (to leave)”.
target_language_example: Er entschuldigte sich bei ihr für die Verspätung.
native_language_example: He apologized to her for being late.

additional_notes: From the reflexive verb **sich erinnern an** = “to remember.” It takes **an + accusative** (e.g., *an mich/dich/Sie/euch*). **noch** adds the idea of “still.”
target_language_example: Er erinnert sich noch an unseren ersten Tag in Berlin.
native_language_example: He still remembers our first day in Berlin.
