target_language_example: Ich fange gar nicht erst an zu diskutieren.
native_language_example: I’m not even going to start arguing.

additional_notes: Used to say that something has stopped completely compared to before. It often adds emphasis: not just “not anymore,” but “not anymore at all.” Word order: usually comes after the verb or after the part you’re negating (e.g., “Ich gehe gar nicht mehr …”, “Das tut gar nicht mehr weh.”).
target_language_example: Seit dem Umzug sehe ich ihn gar nicht mehr.
native_language_example: Since the move, I don’t see him anymore (at all).

meaning: “not that … / not so …” (not as much/bad/wrong/etc. as expected).
additional_notes: Used to soften a negative statement or to say something is less extreme than you thought. Often followed by an adjective/adverb (gar nicht so übel = not that bad; gar nicht so falsch = not that wrong) or by quantity words (gar nicht so viele = not that many).
target_language_example: Der Test war gar nicht so schwer.
native_language_example: The test wasn’t that hard.

meaning: really not that easy; not so easy at all.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is difficult or complicated. "gar nicht" = "not at all" (strong negation), and "so" softens it to "not that..." → overall: "it’s actually pretty hard." Often said as a standalone comment: "Gar nicht so einfach, was?" (= "Not so easy, huh?").
target_language_example: Einen Termin zu bekommen ist gar nicht so einfach.
native_language_example: Getting an appointment isn’t that easy.

additional_notes: Used in comparisons to say someone isn’t as hungry as expected. "gar nicht" strengthens the negation ("not at all" / "really not"). The comma often appears because a comparison with "wie" commonly introduces a clause (e.g., "wie du meinst"). Word order is flexible in full sentences (e.g., "Er ist gar nicht so hungrig, wie ich dachte").
target_language_example: Ich bin gar nicht so hungrig, wie du denkst.
native_language_example: I’m not nearly as hungry as you think.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that there is zero of something (no knowledge, no ability, no options, etc.). Often appears with verbs like „sehen“ (see), „wissen“ (know), or „tun“ (do): „Ich weiß gar nichts.“ / „Wir können gar nichts tun.“
target_language_example: Ich habe gar nichts verstanden.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand anything at all.

meaning: didn’t do anything at all; did absolutely nothing.
additional_notes: "gar nichts" means "absolutely nothing" (stronger than just "nichts"). You usually use this in the perfect tense with "haben" (e.g., "Ich habe gar nichts gemacht") to deny responsibility or emphasize that you did nothing. In spoken German, "ich hab" is a common contraction of "ich habe". Often appears with "doch" for emphasis: "Ich hab doch gar nichts gemacht!" = "But I didn’t do anything!"
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, ich habe heute gar nichts gemacht.
native_language_example: Sorry, I didn’t do anything at all today.

meaning: nothing anymore; nothing at all anymore.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone has (or does) nothing/doesn’t do anything anymore. "gar" strengthens "nichts" (= not at all), and "mehr" adds the idea of "anymore/no longer". Can be a short standalone answer: "Gar nichts mehr."
target_language_example: Seit dem Stromausfall funktioniert hier gar nichts mehr.
native_language_example: Since the power outage, nothing works here anymore.

meaning: to have no right to tell someone what to do ("you can’t tell me anything!")
additional_notes: Used in arguments to reject someone’s authority or interference. Most often said as: „Du hast mir gar nichts zu sagen!“ (= “You don’t get to tell me what to do.”). It’s stronger than the literal “to have nothing to say” and can sound rude/hostile.
target_language_example: Du hast mir gar nichts zu sagen — das ist meine Entscheidung.
native_language_example: You can’t tell me what to do — it’s my decision.

additional_notes: "Geben Sie" is the formal (Sie) form of the verb "geben". It’s used when speaking politely to one person (or to a group) in requests, commands, and service situations: "Geben Sie mir ..." = "Give me ..." / "Please give me ...". Word order: "Geben Sie + indirect object (mir/ihm/ihr/uns/ihnen) + direct object" (e.g., "Geben Sie mir die Datei").
target_language_example: Geben Sie mir bitte Ihren Ausweis.
native_language_example: Please give me your ID.

additional_notes: Used with "Sie" (formal "you") to make polite requests: "Geben Sie mir ..." + object (e.g., time, a minute, a drink). With money/value it can mean "offer/pay me": "Wie viel geben Sie mir dafür?" = "How much will you give/offer me for that?"
target_language_example: Geben Sie mir bitte einen Moment.
native_language_example: Please give me a moment.

additional_notes: A polite/formal request using the Sie form (to a stranger, customer, official, etc.). It’s the imperative of geben (“to give”) + mir (“to me”) + Ihre (“your”, formal possessive). It is typically followed by a noun phrase (e.g., Adresse, Telefonnummer, Ausweis, Autoschlüssel). Adding bitte softens the request; adding an exclamation mark can make it sound more forceful. In standard writing, Ihre is often capitalized when used as the formal possessive (your).
target_language_example: Bitte geben Sie mir Ihre feste Adresse.
native_language_example: Please give me your permanent address.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone politely to hand you something or provide something. "Sie" is the formal/polite "you" (for strangers, staff, older people). Word order is common in requests: verb first (Geben) + Sie + mir + bitte + object. In casual situations you’d usually say: "Gib mir bitte ..." (to one person) or "Gebt mir bitte ..." (to a group).
target_language_example: Geben Sie mir bitte die Speisekarte.
native_language_example: Please give me the menu.

additional_notes: Used with "Sie" to politely ask someone to hand you something or provide information. It’s the imperative of "geben" (to give) + "Sie" (you, formal) + "mir" (to me) + "die" (the, for feminine singular or plural nouns), so the noun that follows must match "die" (e.g., die Adresse, die Datei, die Details). In a question, it’s often said with rising intonation: "Geben Sie mir die Adresse?"
target_language_example: Geben Sie mir die Quittung, bitte.
native_language_example: Please give me the receipt.

additional_notes: "Geben" means "to give"; "Sie" is the formal "you" (to one person or to a group); "uns" means "us." Used for polite requests and instructions (often with "bitte"): "Geben Sie uns das Menü" = "Please give us the menu." Commonly appears in fixed phrases like "Geben Sie uns Bescheid" = "Let us know."
target_language_example: Geben Sie uns bitte kurz Bescheid, ob Sie Zeit haben.
native_language_example: Please let us know briefly whether you have time.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "bitten" (to ask/request) + a "zu"-infinitive: "jemanden bitten, zu gehen". The person being asked is in the accusative (e.g., "Hast du ihn/sie gebeten zu gehen?"). In context it often implies you want the person to leave the room/place, not just “go somewhere”.
target_language_example: Der Chef hat mich gebeten zu gehen, weil das Meeting vorbei war.
native_language_example: The boss asked me to leave because the meeting was over.

additional_notes: Used to say where someone spent their childhood and grew up. Very common with sein: „Ich bin in/auf … geboren und aufgewachsen“ (in a country/city; auf dem Land = in the countryside).
target_language_example: Ich bin in Berlin geboren und aufgewachsen, aber jetzt wohne ich in Hamburg.
native_language_example: I was born and raised in Berlin, but now I live in Hamburg.

additional_notes: Used with the verb „sein“ to form the passive/perfect meaning: „Ich bin … geboren worden“ = „I was born …“. It often takes a place (in + dative): „in Berlin geboren worden“, or a time: „1989 geboren worden“. Common in questions and statements about someone’s birthplace or birth events.
target_language_example: Ich bin in Hamburg geboren worden.
native_language_example: I was born in Hamburg.

additional_notes: Simple past (Präteritum) of the passive verb phrase „geboren werden“ (to be born). Common in subordinate/relative clauses, where the finite verb „wurde“ often appears at the end: „…, wo/wo er geboren wurde“ = „…, where he was born.“ Used to state someone’s birthplace or birth circumstances.
target_language_example: Das ist das Dorf, in dem er geboren wurde.
native_language_example: That is the village where he was born.

meaning: 'took ... to' / 'needed ... to' (time needed to do something).
additional_notes: Used with a time expression to say how long it took someone to do something: „Ich habe + Zeit + gebraucht, um + zu-Infinitiv“ (e.g., „Ich habe zehn Minuten gebraucht, um … zu …“). The verb is „brauchen“ (to need), and the main action comes after „um … zu …“ (in order to). In questions: „Wie lange hast du gebraucht, um …?“
target_language_example: Ich habe nur fünf Minuten gebraucht, um die E-Mail zu schreiben.
native_language_example: It only took me five minutes to write the email.

additional_notes: "Gebt" is the informal imperative (command) for "ihr" (you plural). Use it when speaking to two or more people you address as "ihr" (friends, kids, etc.). Common with objects (Gebt mir das Buch.), or with amounts/time (Gebt mir nur eine Minute.). For a polite version to strangers/one person: "Geben Sie mir …"; for one informal person: "Gib mir …".
target_language_example: Gebt mir bitte noch eine Minute!
native_language_example: Give me another minute, please!

additional_notes: Used with forms of *denken* + *dass*, especially in past/perfect (*ich habe gedacht, dass …* / *er hat gedacht, dass …*) or conditional (*ich hätte nicht gedacht, dass …* = “I wouldn’t have thought that …”). A comma comes before *dass*, and the verb in the *dass*-clause goes to the end. With *sich gedacht* (*ich habe mir gedacht, dass …*) it often means “I figured/thought to myself that …”.
target_language_example: Ich hätte nicht gedacht, dass das so schwierig ist.
native_language_example: I wouldn’t have thought that it’s so difficult.

additional_notes: Used with the verb „denken“ to introduce a „daß“-clause (“that …”). A comma normally precedes „daß“: „Ich hätte gedacht, daß …“. Note: „daß“ is the pre-1996 spelling; modern standard German usually writes „dass“. Common with „hätte“ to express an expectation or assumption, often with surprise (“I would have thought that … / I never thought that …”).
target_language_example: Ich hätte nie gedacht, daß so etwas passieren würde.
native_language_example: I would never have thought that something like that would happen.

additional_notes: Used with the pattern: „Es hat + (time) + gedauert, bis + clause.“ It describes how long it took until a change or event happened. In questions: „Wie lange hat es gedauert, bis …?“ The verb is „dauern“ (to last/take), and „gedauert“ is the past participle.
target_language_example: Es hat nur zehn Minuten gedauert, bis der Bus kam.
native_language_example: It only took ten minutes for the bus to come.

additional_notes: Used with the verb *fragen* + a comma + *ob* to report a question: *Ich habe ihn gefragt, ob …* = “I asked him whether/if …”. The *ob*-clause is a subordinate clause, so the conjugated verb goes to the end (*… ob er Zeit hat*).
target_language_example: Ich habe sie gefragt, ob sie morgen kommen kann.
native_language_example: I asked her if she can come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used after a verb like "(jemanden) fragen" to introduce an indirect yes/no question with "ob" (= whether/if). "er" is “he” and refers to the person being talked about; in indirect speech you may see Konjunktiv forms like "könne" or "sei".
target_language_example: Ich habe sie gefragt, ob er schon zu Hause ist.
native_language_example: I asked her whether he is already at home.

meaning: 'asked (me), if I…' (introduces an indirect yes/no question).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like "fragen" (to ask) to report a yes/no question indirectly. Word order: "… gefragt, ob ich + verb at the end" (e.g., "ob ich mitkomme / ob ich kommen kann"). Often appears as "hat mich gefragt, ob ich…" = "asked me whether/if I…".
target_language_example: Sie hat mich gefragt, ob ich heute Zeit habe.
native_language_example: She asked me if I have time today.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **fragen** + a **warum**-clause to ask for a reason: **jemanden fragen, warum ...** (ask someone why ...). With the reflexive form **sich fragen, warum ...**, it means “to wonder why ...”. In questions you often see **Hast du ... gefragt, warum ...?** / **Habt ihr euch gefragt, warum ...?**.
target_language_example: Ich habe ihn gefragt, warum er so früh gehen muss.
native_language_example: I asked him why he has to leave so early.

meaning: to be found; to get found.
additional_notes: Passive form of "finden" (to find). Used when the focus is on the person/thing that is found (or not found), often with modal verbs: "will/muss/kann gefunden werden". Common with abstract nouns too: "Eine Lösung muss gefunden werden" = "A solution must be found."
target_language_example: Es muss eine Lösung gefunden werden.
native_language_example: A solution must be found.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **gefallen** in the **formal** form (**Ihnen** = “to you”). German uses a different structure than English: the *thing you like* is the grammatical subject. Pattern: **Was/Welches ... gefällt Ihnen (am besten)?** = “What/Which ... do you like (best)?”
target_language_example: Welcher Film gefällt Ihnen am besten?
native_language_example: Which movie do you like best?

additional_notes: Used in polite/formal situations (with Ihnen) when offering or showing someone something, especially in shops, at exhibitions, or presentations. It’s the verb gefallen (“to be pleasing to”) in a question; the thing liked is the subject: Gefällt Ihnen diese Bluse? = “Does this blouse please you?” (i.e., “Do you like this blouse?”). The phrase needs a noun after diese/dieser/dieses depending on gender/case.
target_language_example: Gefällt Ihnen diese Jacke?
native_language_example: Do you like this jacket?

additional_notes: Used with the verb **gefallen** to say that something is pleasing to someone. The thing you like is the **subject**: **Gefällt dir Englisch?** (= English pleases you). Word order: **Gefällt dir …?** (question) / **… gefällt dir.** (statement). You can add **gut/besser/am besten**: **Was gefällt dir besser, … oder …?**
target_language_example: Gefällt dir dieses Lied?
native_language_example: Do you like this song?

meaning: (that you) like best / you like the most.
additional_notes: Used with "Was/Welche/Welcher/Welches ... gefällt dir am besten?" to ask someone’s favorite option. It uses the verb "gefallen" (to be pleasing): the thing you like is the grammatical subject (e.g., "Welche Krawatte"), and "dir" means "to you". Often interchangeable with "am liebsten" in many contexts.
target_language_example: Welcher Film gefällt dir am besten?
native_language_example: Which movie do you like best?

additional_notes: Used with the verb **gefallen** (to please) plus **an** to ask or say what someone likes about a person/thing. The person who likes it is in the **dative** (dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen): **Was gefällt dir an ...?** = What do you like about ...? Common pattern: **Was gefällt dir an dem Film/an ihr/an mir?**
target_language_example: Was gefällt dir an Berlin am besten?
native_language_example: What do you like best about Berlin?

meaning: "Do you like your …?" / "How do you like your …?"
additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion about something they own or that belongs to them (with "dein" = your, informal singular). Grammar note: "gefallen" works like "to please"—the thing is the subject (e.g., "dein Anzug"), and the person is in the dative ("dir"). Often appears as "Gefällt dir dein …?" or "Wie gefällt dir dein …?" (more like "How do you like …?").
target_language_example: Gefällt dir dein neues Fahrrad?
native_language_example: Do you like your new bike?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone likes something that belongs to you. With **gefallen**, the thing you like is the grammatical subject: **Mein Kleid gefällt dir.** (literally: “My dress pleases you.”). **dir** is dative (“to you”). In questions you’ll often hear: **Gefällt dir mein/meine …?** Choose **mein** for masculine/neuter nouns (mein Hund, mein Buch) and **meine** for feminine/plural nouns (meine Jacke, meine Schuhe).
target_language_example: Gefällt dir mein neues Handy?
native_language_example: Do you like my new phone?

additional_notes: Used with the verb **gefallen** to say someone likes something. The person who likes it is in the **dative**: **mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen/Ihnen**. **Es** is often a “dummy” subject meaning “it/that” and can refer to a place, an activity, or a whole situation: **Gefällt es dir hier?** / **Mir gefällt es, spazieren zu gehen.** / **Ihm gefällt es nicht, wenn …**.
target_language_example: Gefällt es dir, wenn ich so laut Musik höre?
native_language_example: Do you like it when I play music that loudly?

additional_notes: Uses the verb **gefallen** (“to be pleasing to”), so the grammar is reversed compared to English: **es** = “it” (the thing/place), and **Ihnen** is **dative** = “to you.” You can add a location: *Gefällt es Ihnen hier in Berlin?* This is the polite **Sie/Ihnen** form (for strangers, customers, etc.).
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, gefällt es Ihnen hier im Hotel?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you like it here at the hotel?

meaning: "Do you like it?" / "Do you like that?"
additional_notes: From the verb "gefallen" (= to be pleasing). Literally: "Is it pleasing to you?" The thing that is liked is the grammatical subject (es / das / wenn… clause), and the person is in the dative: "dir". Used to ask if someone likes a place, a situation, or an action: "Gefällt es dir in …?" "Gefällt es dir, wenn …?"
target_language_example: Gefällt es dir hier im Café?
native_language_example: Do you like it here in the café?

meaning: “Do you like it here?” / “How do you like it here?”
additional_notes: Uses the verb **gefallen** (“to be pleasing to”). Literally: “Is it pleasing to you here?” Often expanded with a place (**… in Berlin?**) or time/so far (**… soweit?**). A common follow-up question when someone is visiting or has moved somewhere.
target_language_example: Gefällt es dir hier in der Stadt, oder ist es dir zu laut?
native_language_example: Do you like it here in the city, or is it too loud for you?

additional_notes: Used with the verb **gefallen** to ask what a group of people thinks of something. The thing liked is the grammatical subject: **Gefällt euch San Francisco?** (literally: “Does San Francisco please you?”). **euch** is the 2nd-person plural object in the dative (“to you all”). For plural subjects, use **gefallen euch**: **Gefallen euch die Schuhe?**
target_language_example: Gefällt euch das Restaurant?
native_language_example: Do you all like the restaurant?

additional_notes: Used with the verb **gefallen** to express liking something. The thing you like is the grammatical subject: **Das gefällt mir** = “I like that” (literally “That pleases me”). You can strengthen or negate it: **(gar) nicht** = “not (at all)”, **sehr/ganz gut** = “a lot/really well”.
target_language_example: Der Film gefällt mir sehr.
native_language_example: I like the movie a lot.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "gefallen" (to be pleasing). The thing you like is the grammatical subject: "Deine Handtasche gefällt mir sehr" (= Your handbag pleases me a lot). Use it for objects, sounds, activities, places, etc. For people, you usually say "Ich mag dich/sie/ihn" instead of "Du gefällst mir".
target_language_example: Das Restaurant gefällt mir sehr.
native_language_example: I like the restaurant very much.

additional_notes: Almost always used in the fixed pattern **„ob es dir/Ihnen gefällt oder nicht“** (also: **„ob es euch gefällt oder nicht“**). It expresses that something will happen or must be done regardless of someone’s opinion or preference. **gefallen** means “to please” (literally: “it pleases you”), but the whole phrase is best translated idiomatically as “whether you like it or not.”
target_language_example: Du musst jetzt gehen, ob es dir gefällt oder nicht.
native_language_example: You have to go now, whether you like it or not.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive clause: **(jemand) ist … gegangen, um … zu + Infinitiv** to say why someone went somewhere. A comma typically comes before **um**. Very common with movement verbs like **gehen/fahren/kommen**.
target_language_example: Ich bin in die Stadt gegangen, um ein Geschenk zu kaufen.
native_language_example: I went into town to buy a gift.

meaning: to get vaccinated against the flu
additional_notes: Typically used with a reflexive pronoun (mich/dich/sich/uns/euch) plus „lassen“ to mean you have a doctor/pharmacist administer the vaccine: „Ich habe mich gegen Grippe impfen lassen.“ Often appears in questions; adding „schon“ asks whether it’s already been done: „Hast du dich schon gegen Grippe impfen lassen?“
target_language_example: Hast du dich schon gegen Grippe impfen lassen?
native_language_example: Have you already gotten vaccinated against the flu?

additional_notes: Used with neuter nouns (das + noun) after the preposition "gegen". Common meanings: (1) physical contact/direction: leaning/pressing/being positioned against something ("gegen das Geländer" = against the railing); (2) opposition: being against an idea/action or fighting against something ("gegen das Klonen" = against cloning). With movement/impact it can also mean "into" (e.g., "gegen das Fenster" = into/against the window).
target_language_example: Ich bin gegen das Rauchen im Restaurant.
native_language_example: I’m against smoking in the restaurant.

additional_notes: Used to say an action is not allowed by law. Common patterns: „Es ist gegen das Gesetz, …“ (It’s against the law to …) and „gegen das Gesetz verstoßen“ (to break/violate the law).
target_language_example: Es ist gegen das Gesetz, hier ohne Fahrschein zu fahren.
native_language_example: It’s against the law to ride here without a ticket.

meaning: "against the" (used with masculine/neuter nouns in the accusative).
additional_notes: Used with the preposition "gegen" + accusative to mean opposition or moving/acting in the opposite direction. Common in set phrases like "gegen den Strom" (against the current), "gegen den Uhrzeigersinn" (counterclockwise), and the idiom "jemandem gegen den Strich gehen" (to get on someone’s nerves / rub someone the wrong way).
target_language_example: Wir sind gegen den Wind gelaufen.
native_language_example: We walked against the wind.

meaning: against the plan; opposed to the plan.
additional_notes: Used to say you disagree with a plan or do not support it. Often with „sein“: „Ich bin gegen den Plan.“ / „Bist du gegen den Plan?“ You can also use „Einwände gegen den Plan haben“ = “to have objections to the plan.” „gegen“ takes the accusative here, so: „den Plan“ (not „dem Plan“).
target_language_example: Ich bin gegen den Plan, weil er zu teuer ist.
native_language_example: I’m against the plan because it’s too expensive.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition "gegen" + accusative. Common for physical contact/movement toward a surface (e.g., rain hitting a window, a ball bouncing off something, leaning an object against a wall). Also used in the fixed pattern "etwas gegen die/den/das ... haben" = "to have something against ..." (to object to / be opposed to).
target_language_example: Der Wind drückt gegen die Tür.
native_language_example: The wind is pushing against the door.

meaning: for pain; against the pain (to relieve pain).
additional_notes: Commonly used when talking about medicine or remedies that reduce pain: etwas gegen die Schmerzen nehmen (to take something for the pain), ein Mittel gegen die Schmerzen (a remedy/painkiller). Often implies pain relief rather than fighting pain directly.
target_language_example: Haben Sie etwas gegen die Schmerzen?
native_language_example: Do you have something for the pain?

meaning: 'against the wall' (toward a wall, hitting it).
additional_notes: Used with verbs of impact or motion (e.g., schlagen, werfen, stoßen) to show that something hits a wall. Often implies force: something is thrown/banged so it ends up striking the wall.
target_language_example: Sie stieß die Leiter gegen die Wand.
native_language_example: She pushed the ladder against the wall.

additional_notes: Used to say someone did something despite not wanting to. The possessive changes with the person: gegen meinen/deinen/seinen/ihren/unseren/euren/ihren Willen. Often used with passive to show coercion: „Sie wurde gegen ihren Willen …“.
target_language_example: Maria wurde gegen ihren Willen verheiratet.
native_language_example: Maria was married off against her will.

meaning: against me (opposed to me / directed at me).
additional_notes: Used with **gegen** + accusative (**mich**) to express opposition to you personally or something directed at you: e.g., people being on the other side (*Alle sind gegen mich*), plotting (*sich verschwören gegen mich*), or having a grievance/issue with you (*Was haben Sie gegen mich?* = “What do you have against me?/What’s your problem with me?”). Can also appear in more literary language about fate/fortune turning against someone.
target_language_example: Was haben Sie gegen mich?
native_language_example: What do you have against me? / What’s your problem with me?

additional_notes: Used to express opposition to an idea, plan, or action. Typically appears as **sein + gegen + accusative noun/pronoun** (e.g., gegen den Plan / gegen mich). You can also use **dagegen sein** when referring back to something already mentioned: *Ich bin dagegen.* = I’m against it.
target_language_example: Ich bin gegen sein Verhalten.
native_language_example: I’m against his behavior.

additional_notes: Used with a dass-clause (a subordinate clause). In the perfect tense, you say: „Ich habe (nicht) geglaubt, dass …“. The verb in the dass-clause goes to the end: „…, dass ich einmal heiraten werde.“ Often translates as “thought” or “believed” depending on context.
target_language_example: Ich habe nicht geglaubt, dass es so spät ist.
native_language_example: I didn’t think it was so late.

meaning: 'go and …' (du-imperative: telling one person to go do something).
additional_notes: Used in commands/instructions with the informal singular "du" form. It’s typically followed by another verb in the imperative: "Geh und schau/ sieh/ such …". In speech you may also hear it shortened as "Geh' und …".
target_language_example: Geh und hol bitte Wasser.
native_language_example: Go and get some water, please.

meaning: "Oh, come on!" / "Give me a break!" (expressing disbelief or annoyance).
additional_notes: Usually said as an exclamation: „Geh bitte!“ It’s a colloquial reaction when you think something is exaggerated, unfair, or hard to believe. Literally it’s „go, please“, but in everyday speech it’s mostly used idiomatically with the meaning above; tone/intonation matters.
target_language_example: Geh bitte! Das ist doch viel zu teuer.
native_language_example: Oh, come on! That’s way too expensive.

meaning: “just go” / “go on (then)” (imperative with emphasis; sometimes dismissive).
additional_notes: Used in spoken German with the modal particle „doch“ to add emphasis. Depending on tone and context, it can sound like encouragement/suggestion (≈ “why don’t you go… / go ahead”) or impatient/dismissive (≈ “then just go”). In insults it can be stronger, e.g. „Geh doch zum Teufel!“ (“Go to hell!”).
target_language_example: Wenn du müde bist, geh doch nach Hause.
native_language_example: If you’re tired, just go home.

additional_notes: An (informal) command using the imperative of "gehen" (du-form). Often used when telling someone to go to sleep or at least go lie down. You can add things like "jetzt" (now) or another instruction: "Mach das Licht aus und geh ins Bett."
target_language_example: Du siehst müde aus—geh ins Bett.
native_language_example: You look tired—go to bed.

additional_notes: An imperative to one person you address as du. Depending on context it can mean "go (somewhere) now" (often with a destination: Geh jetzt in die Klasse.) or "leave now" (Geh jetzt! = Go away/leave now). Often used with nicht to tell someone not to leave: Geh jetzt nicht weg.
target_language_example: Es ist spät—geh jetzt nach Hause.
native_language_example: It’s late—go home now.

additional_notes: Imperative form of „jemandem aus dem Weg gehen“ (“to get out of someone’s way”). Uses dative „mir“ (“for me / out of my way”). Often sounds rude or angry, especially with swear words (e.g., „verdammt“, insults). You can soften it with „Bitte“ or use a more polite option like „Entschuldigung, könnten Sie bitte kurz Platz machen?“
target_language_example: Geh mir aus dem Weg, ich habe es eilig!
native_language_example: Get out of my way, I’m in a hurry!

additional_notes: Imperative (command) with du: "geh" = "(you) go". "nach Hause" means "(to) home" (movement/direction). Often used as an instruction or, in angry contexts, as "Go home!"/"Get out of here and go home!".
target_language_example: Es ist spät—geh nach Hause.
native_language_example: It’s late—go home.

meaning: “don’t go” (telling one person not to leave/do it).
additional_notes: Imperative (command) for “du”: geh = “go”, nicht = “not”. Used to stop someone from leaving or from going somewhere/doing something: “Geh nicht!” / “Geh nicht zu nah an den Rand!” You can add more info after it (where/when/how).
target_language_example: Bitte, geh nicht ohne mich.
native_language_example: Please, don’t go without me.

additional_notes: Imperative of „gehen“ + „nur“ (“just/only”). Often used to give permission or encouragement: „Ja, geh nur.“ (“Yes, go ahead.”). Depending on tone, it can also sound a bit dismissive (“Fine, just go then.”). Related pattern in statements: „Ich geh nur …“ = “I’m just going … (briefly/only).”
target_language_example: Wenn du müde bist, geh nur nach Hause.
native_language_example: If you’re tired, just go home.

additional_notes: Imperative of "weggehen" (to go away). Used to tell one person (du) to leave, move away, or keep distance. Often said as a warning or when annoyed; with "von + dative" it means "move away from" someone/something (e.g., "Geh weg vom Wagen!"). Polite/plural forms: "Gehen Sie weg!" (formal), "Geht weg!" (to several people).
target_language_example: Geh weg von der Tür!
native_language_example: Get away from the door!

meaning: “go/get away from” (imperative: telling someone to move away from something/someone).
additional_notes: Used to tell one person (du-form) to move away. Very common as a warning or when something is unpleasant or dangerous. Often used with a noun: „Geh weg von dem Hund!“ You can also say „Geh weg!“ without „von …“ if the object is clear.
target_language_example: Geh weg von der Kante, das ist gefährlich!
native_language_example: Get away from the edge, that’s dangerous!

additional_notes: Imperative (du-form) of **zurückgehen** (“to go back”). Used to tell one person to return to a previous place or situation: **Geh zurück an die Arbeit!** (“Go back to work!”). Can sound strict/angry depending on tone (e.g., **Geh zurück in dein Loch.** is very insulting). You can soften it with **bitte**.
target_language_example: Geh zurück ins Zimmer, bitte.
native_language_example: Go back to the room, please.

additional_notes: Imperative (du-form) of **zurückgehen** (“to go back”). **in den** is used with masculine/neuter places when there is movement *into* somewhere (accusative), and it must be followed by a noun (e.g., **in den Park/Laden/Zug**). For feminine you’d use **in die …**, and for plural **in die …**.
target_language_example: Geh zurück in den Laden!
native_language_example: Go back into the shop!

additional_notes: "Gehe ich" is the verb + subject order, often used when something comes first in the sentence (time, place, reason, or a condition), e.g. "Nach dem Abendessen gehe ich …" or "Deswegen gehe ich …". In a main clause, the conjugated verb stays in position 2, so the subject "ich" moves after it.
target_language_example: Am Wochenende gehe ich manchmal ins Kino.
native_language_example: On the weekend I sometimes go to the movies.

additional_notes: “Sie” is the formal/polite form of “you.” Depending on context and punctuation, “Gehen Sie …” can be a polite command/request (often with Bitte) or a question about what someone does/where they go. The verb “gehen” also appears in fixed combinations like “ans Telefon gehen” (to go to/answer the phone) and “ins Bett gehen” (to go to bed). Don’t confuse “gehen Sie davon aus, dass …” with literal walking: it means “assume that …”.
target_language_example: Gehen Sie bitte hier entlang.
native_language_example: Please go this way.

meaning: (formal) go home; (also in questions) are you going home? / do you go home?
additional_notes: Polite/formal form using "Sie" (used with strangers, customers, older people, etc.). As an imperative: "Gehen Sie nach Hause." = "Go home." In a question: "Wann gehen Sie nach Hause?" = "When are you going home?" "Nach Hause" means "(to) home" with movement/direction.
target_language_example: Wann gehen Sie nach Hause?
native_language_example: When are you going home?

meaning: to go to work; to go and work.
additional_notes: Used with a conjugated form of „gehen“ + the infinitive „arbeiten“ to express that you’re going somewhere in order to work: „Ich gehe arbeiten.“ Often interchangeable with „arbeiten gehen“ or „zur Arbeit gehen“. You can add a time or place: „Morgen gehe ich arbeiten.“ / „Ich gehe im Büro arbeiten.“
target_language_example: Ich gehe arbeiten.
native_language_example: I’m going to work.

meaning: to let (someone) go; to allow (someone) to leave.
additional_notes: Usually used with a person as the object: jemanden gehen lassen. It can mean giving permission ("I let him go home") or releasing someone (e.g., from custody or from a situation). Typical forms include: "lass ihn gehen" (imperative), "Er soll mich gehen lassen" (modal/command), and perfect: "Ich habe ihn gehen lassen."
target_language_example: Er soll mich gehen lassen.
native_language_example: He should let me go.

meaning: to have to go (somewhere); to be forced/required to go.
additional_notes: "gehen müssen" expresses necessity/obligation to go/leave. It can be used with a destination (e.g., "zum Bahnhof", "nach Hause") or without one (simply meaning you must leave). In main clauses, the conjugated form of "müssen" typically appears in 2nd position and the infinitive "gehen" at the end; the multi-word term is often seen together in subordinate clauses ("...dass ich gehen müssen werde") or as an infinitive phrase ("gehen müssen").
target_language_example: Bitte sag ihnen, wohin sie gehen müssen.
native_language_example: Please tell them where they have to go.

meaning: to go to bed; to go to sleep.
additional_notes: This word order (**gehen schlafen**) is understandable but less idiomatic in everyday German; the usual order is **schlafen gehen** (e.g., *Ich gehe schlafen.*) or **ins Bett gehen** (to go to bed). Used to express that you are going somewhere (typically to bed) in order to sleep.
target_language_example: Ich bin müde; ich werde jetzt gehen schlafen.
native_language_example: I’m tired; I’m going to bed now.

additional_notes: Often used with verb-first word order to suggest doing something together, like an inclusive command or proposal. Depending on tone and punctuation, it can be a statement or a question. In other contexts, it may simply be part of a normal sentence meaning 'we go/are going'.
target_language_example: Gehen wir jetzt nach Hause?
native_language_example: Shall we go home now?

meaning: "are we going now?" / "what do we do next (now)?"
additional_notes: Used in questions with inverted word order (verb first): "Gehen wir jetzt …?" Depending on context, it can be literal (moving somewhere: "Where are we going now?") or more general about the next step ("How do we proceed now?"). "wir" can be inclusive, like English "shall we…?".
target_language_example: Okay, gehen wir jetzt rein?
native_language_example: Okay, shall we go in now?

additional_notes: Used when *hoffen* is followed by a **dass**-clause to say what you hoped would happen. In the perfect tense you often see **haben + gehofft**: *Ich habe gehofft, dass ...* In a **dass**-clause, the conjugated verb usually goes to the end: *..., dass er heute kommt / kommen würde.*
target_language_example: Ich habe gehofft, dass du Zeit hast.
native_language_example: I hoped that you have time.

additional_notes: Question form with the du-form of gehen ('to go'). Used to ask if someone is going somewhere, leaving, or regularly goes somewhere. In German questions, the verb comes before du.
target_language_example: Gehst du heute Abend mit uns ins Kino?
native_language_example: Are you going to the cinema with us tonight?

meaning: “are you going today?” / “do you go today?”
additional_notes: A common question pattern: **Gehst du …?** (verb first) is the informal **du** form of “to go” (**gehen**). **heute** = “today”. It’s usually followed by where/what you’re going to (e.g., **zur Arbeit**, **zur Schule**, **feiern**).
target_language_example: Gehst du heute ins Kino?
native_language_example: Are you going to the movies today?

meaning: "Are you going (out) tonight?" / "Are you going tonight…?"
additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s plans for this evening. With "gehen" you can mean simply “go” (to a place) or, with words like "fort" or "irgendwo hin", “go out.” You can add a destination or activity after it: "…ins Kino" (to the cinema), "…mit mir essen" (to eat with me).
target_language_example: Gehst du heute Abend in eine Bar?
native_language_example: Are you going to a bar tonight?

additional_notes: Used to ask a question with negation: **gehst** (you go) + **du** (you) + **nicht** (not). Often expresses surprise, doubt, or mild criticism (like “You’re not going…?”). The verb **gehen** changes meaning by context: **hingehen** = go there/attend, **ausgehen** = go out, **in die Schule gehen** = go to school, **rangehen** (am Telefon) = pick up the phone.
target_language_example: Gehst du nicht mit uns ins Kino?
native_language_example: Aren’t you coming to the movies with us?

meaning: "do you go on foot?" / "are you walking?"
additional_notes: "zu Fuß" means "on foot" (walking, not using a vehicle). "Gehst du …?" is an informal/singular question to one person. Often used to ask how someone is getting somewhere, commonly contrasted with "mit dem Bus" / "mit dem Auto" / "mit dem Fahrrad".
target_language_example: Gehst du zu Fuß zur Arbeit oder nimmst du die U-Bahn?
native_language_example: Are you walking to work, or are you taking the subway?

meaning: 'that's none of your business' / 'that doesn't concern you'.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone strongly that something is private and they shouldn’t ask or get involved. Very common in spoken German. Grammar note: it’s based on "etwas geht jemanden an" = "something concerns someone"; with "nichts" it becomes "it doesn’t concern you." You’ll also hear "Das geht Sie nichts an" (formal) and past tense "Das ging dich nichts an."
target_language_example: Was ich verdiene, geht dich nichts an.
native_language_example: What I earn is none of your business.

additional_notes: This is usually part of a larger pattern. In jemandem geht es gut/schlecht/besser, it means someone is doing or feeling well/badly/better: Mir geht es gut = I'm doing well. In es geht um + noun, it means it's about or it concerns something: Es geht ums Geld = It's about money.
target_language_example: Heute geht es mir schon viel besser.
native_language_example: I'm feeling much better today.

additional_notes: Used in polite/formal questions about someone’s state or well-being, often with adjectives or adverbs: "Geht es Ihnen gut/schlecht?" (Are you well/feeling bad?), "Geht es Ihnen besser?" (Are you feeling better?), "Wie geht es Ihnen?" (How are you?). "Ihnen" is the formal "you" (to one person or a group). The verb is in 3rd person singular ("geht"), like “How is it going for you?”
target_language_example: Geht es Ihnen heute besser?
native_language_example: Are you feeling better today?

meaning: "how are you?" (literally: "is it going well for you?")
additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s well-being. Often appears as "Wie geht es dir?" (informal, to one person) or "Wie geht’s dir?" in speech. Common add-ons: "gut" (well), "schlecht" (bad), "auch" (too), "wirklich" (really). For more formal situations or strangers, use "Wie geht es Ihnen?".
target_language_example: Hey, geht es dir heute besser?
native_language_example: Hey, are you feeling better today?

additional_notes: Common way to ask about someone’s well-being. Literally “is it going well for you?” You can also say “Geht’s dir gut?” in casual speech. Use “dir” (informal you); for formal you: “Geht es Ihnen gut?”
target_language_example: Hey, du wirkst müde—geht es dir gut?
native_language_example: Hey, you look tired—are you OK?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the well-being of more than one person ("euch" = you plural/informal). Often followed by an adverb like "gut" (well), "schlecht" (badly), or a comparison like "besser" (better): "Geht es euch gut?" / "Geht es euch heute besser?" The word order is a typical question pattern (verb first).
target_language_example: Geht es euch nach der Reise wieder gut?
native_language_example: Are you all feeling well again after the trip?

additional_notes: Used with the dative to say how someone is (health/mood): „Mir geht es gut“ (I’m fine), „Clara geht es gut“ (Clara is fine), „Uns geht es gut“ (We’re fine), „Denen geht es gut“ (They’re fine). Often answers „Wie geht’s (dir)?“ Note: word order can change for emphasis, but the core is „jemandem geht es gut“.
target_language_example: Danke, mir geht es gut.
native_language_example: Thanks, I'm doing fine.

meaning: “(Someone) is doing well / is fine.” or “Are you/they doing well?”
additional_notes: Used with the verb *gehen* in a “how things are going” sense. You usually add a dative pronoun/person: *Mir geht es gut* (I’m fine), *Dir geht es gut?* (Are you okay?), *Ihm/Ihr geht es gut* (He/She is fine). In questions, verb comes first: *Geht es dir gut?*
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, mir geht es gut.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m fine.

meaning: "it doesn’t work / it’s not possible"; also in context: "it’s not about …"
additional_notes:
Used with "es geht" to talk about whether something is possible or works.
- "Anders geht es nicht." = There’s no other way.
- "Ohne ihn geht es nicht." = It won’t work without him.
- In questions: "Geht es nicht schneller?" = Can’t it be faster?
- With "um": "(Da) geht es nicht um …" = It’s not about …
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, heute geht es nicht.
native_language_example: Sorry, it’s not possible today.

meaning: "is about" / "is it about" (what the topic is).
additional_notes: Used to say what something is about: "In dem Film geht es um …" = "The movie is about …". The thing after "um" is usually in the accusative (e.g., "um Tom", "um mich"). It often appears in questions: "Geht es um …?" = "Is it about …?"
target_language_example: In diesem Gespräch geht es um dein neues Projekt.
native_language_example: This conversation is about your new project.

additional_notes: Used to say an event is about to begin very soon. Often said as a short standalone phrase (subject understood): "Geht gleich los." = "It’s starting soon." "losgehen" literally means "to get going / to start"; "gleich" here means "soon/right away" (not "equal").
target_language_example: Der Film geht gleich los, beeil dich!
native_language_example: The movie starts soon, hurry up!

additional_notes:
"Geht" is the verb *gehen* (to go) in the *ihr* form (2nd person plural: you all). It’s often used in questions like: *Geht ihr jetzt?* (Are you leaving now?) or *Geht ihr zur Arbeit?* (Do you go to work?).

Be careful: the same words can also appear with a different meaning in *es geht ihr …* = “she is doing/feeling …” (literally “it goes (for) her”), e.g. *Es geht ihr nur um Aufmerksamkeit.* = “All she cares about is attention.”
target_language_example: Geht ihr heute Abend ins Kino?
native_language_example: Are you (all) going to the movies tonight?

additional_notes: Uses "gehen" in 3rd person singular (er/sie/es geht). "jeden Morgen" is a common time expression meaning "every morning" (accusative with no preposition). Often used with a destination ("in den Park") or an activity like "spazieren gehen" (to go for a walk).
target_language_example: Sie geht jeden Morgen zur Arbeit.
native_language_example: She goes to work every morning.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **gehen** to talk about a routine: someone goes somewhere every day (**geht jeden Tag zur Schule / in die Bibliothek**) or does an activity every day where German often uses **gehen** (**joggen gehen**, **spazieren gehen**). Can be followed by a place (**zu**, **nach**, **in**, **auf**) or by an activity (**joggen**, **spazieren**). The verb form **geht** is for **er/sie/es** (he/she/it).
target_language_example: Er geht jeden Tag ins Fitnessstudio.
native_language_example: He goes to the gym every day.

additional_notes: Common in spoken, informal German as a quick reply meaning you agree, you understand, or you’ll do it (similar to “OK”, “sure”, “sounds good”). It can also mean that something will work out or is settled: "Die Sache geht klar" = “It’ll be fine / it’s taken care of.”
target_language_example: Alles klar, ich bringe das morgen vorbei — geht klar.
native_language_example: All right, I’ll drop it off tomorrow — OK.

meaning: “starts/begins” (for an event), or “sets off / starts going” (for a person/thing).
additional_notes: From the separable verb **losgehen** (los + gehen). **Es geht los.** = “It’s starting.” Used for the start of meetings, trips, wars, shows, etc. It can also mean someone/thing begins moving: **Er geht los.** = “He sets off.” As a command you’ll often hear **Geh los!** (to one person) / **Geht los!** (to multiple people) meaning “Get going!” / “Let’s go!”.
target_language_example: Das Treffen geht los.
native_language_example: The meeting is starting.

meaning: "...affects me / gets to me" (used with *mir* = “to me”).
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of fixed expressions where *gehen* + dative (*mir*) shows how something feels to you or how you react to it. Common patterns include: *Das geht mir auf die Nerven* (That really annoys me), *Das geht mir am Arsch vorbei* (I don’t care at all — very vulgar), *Geh mir aus den Augen!* (Get out of my sight!), *Mir geht’s gut* / *Geht mir auch so* (I’m doing well / Same here).
target_language_example: Diese Musik geht mir auf die Nerven.
native_language_example: This music is really getting on my nerves.

meaning: “is getting on my nerves / is annoying me” (very colloquial).
additional_notes: This expression is usually incomplete without a noun after „den“, e.g. „Keks“, „Sack“, „Geist“, or „Nerven“: „Das geht mir auf den Keks.“ It’s used to complain that something/someone is irritating you. Word order: „[Etwas/Jemand] geht mir auf den …“.
target_language_example: Diese laute Musik geht mir auf den Keks.
native_language_example: This loud music is getting on my nerves.

additional_notes: Used when something (a person, sound, behavior, etc.) is irritating you. Common pattern: "X geht mir auf die Nerven" (X is annoying me). You can change the pronoun: "geht dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen auf die Nerven". Often a bit stronger than just "stört mich".
target_language_example: Diese laute Musik geht mir auf die Nerven.
native_language_example: This loud music is getting on my nerves.

additional_notes: Used to say how you are feeling, often as an answer to “Wie geht’s?” or “Wie geht es dir/Ihnen?”. It’s short for “Es geht mir gut.” Word order: “geht” (is going) + “mir” (to me) + “gut” (well).
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, geht mir gut.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m fine.

additional_notes: Imperative with ihr (plural “you”) of gehen: "Geht ...!" Used to tell a group to go home. Often said as a command (with !), but can also be a firm instruction in a sentence ("Ich sagte, geht nach Hause."). For one person you’d say "Geh nach Hause!"; for formal/plural "you" you’d say "Gehen Sie nach Hause!".
target_language_example: Leute, es ist spät—geht nach Hause!
native_language_example: Guys, it’s late—go home!

additional_notes: Often used on its own to say something won’t work, isn’t possible, or isn’t allowed: „Das geht nicht.“ = “That won’t work / You can’t do that.” In other contexts it can be the normal verb phrase „gehen + nicht“, meaning someone/thing doesn’t go somewhere or doesn’t do something: „Er geht nicht raus.“ (He doesn’t go out.) / „Tom geht nicht ans Telefon.“ (He doesn’t answer/pick up the phone.)
target_language_example: Aber das geht nicht.
native_language_example: But that won’t work.

meaning: "is not about" (it’s not a question of / not the point).
additional_notes: Most often used with an impersonal subject: "Es geht nicht um …" = "It’s not about …". The positive form is "Es geht um …" ("It’s about …"). You can also use it in questions: "Worum geht es?" ("What is it about?").
target_language_example: Es geht nicht um Geld, sondern um Zeit.
native_language_example: It’s not about money, but about time.

additional_notes: Most often used as **"Es geht um …"** = “It’s about … / It concerns …”. Common with **"es geht um + Akkusativ"** (e.g., *Es geht um meinen Bruder.*). In fixed phrases like **"Es geht um Leben und Tod"**, it means “It’s a matter of life and death.” Note: **"um"** can also mean **“at”** with times (*Tom geht um 10 Uhr zu Bett*), but that’s just **gehen + time**, not the phrase **"es geht um"**.
target_language_example: Es geht um deine Sicherheit.
native_language_example: It’s about your safety.

additional_notes: Used most often in the pattern "Es geht um die …" to introduce the topic or what something concerns. The "die" is the definite article for feminine singular (die Frage, die Sache) or plural nouns (die Kosten, die Leute). The verb phrase "es geht um" is idiomatic—it's not about physically going somewhere.
target_language_example: Es geht um die Rechnung.
native_language_example: It’s about the bill.

additional_notes: Used to say that something continues (an activity, a process, life in general). Often appears as a complete sentence: „Es geht weiter!“ = “Let’s continue / It goes on.” It can also be an instruction in the imperative: „Geht weiter!“ (to several people) = “Move on / Keep going.”
target_language_example: Keine Sorge — es geht weiter.
native_language_example: Don’t worry — it goes on.

meaning: contraction of „geht es“: “how’s it going?” / “is everything OK?” / “what’s going on?” (depending on context).
additional_notes: Very common in spoken German. Used in questions like „Wie geht’s (dir)?“ = “How are you?” and „Um was geht’s (hier)?“ = “What is this about/what’s going on here?”. With a person it often takes the dative: „Geht’s dir gut?“ (“Are you doing well?”). „Geht’s noch?“ is usually an annoyed/surprised “Are you serious?/What’s wrong with you?” (can sound rude). Also appears in fixed expressions: „Hoffentlich geht’s gut aus.“ (“Hopefully it turns out well.”) and „Jetzt geht’s um die Wurst!“ (“Now it really matters / it’s do-or-die.”).
target_language_example: Wie geht’s dir heute?
native_language_example: How are you today?

meaning: colloquial short form of „geht es“ (“is it going / how is it”).
additional_notes: In standard writing it’s usually spelled with an apostrophe: „geht’s“ (spoken/written informally also as „gehts“). Used in common expressions like „Wie gehts?“ (“How are you?”), „Wie gehts dir/ihm/ihr?“ (“How are you / how is he/she?”), „Los gehts!“ (“Let’s go!”), and „Darum gehts“ (“That’s what it’s about”).
target_language_example: Wie gehts dir?
native_language_example: How are you?

meaning: to belong to; to be part of.
additional_notes: Used with the dative case (zu + dative): zu mir, zu ihm/ihr, zu uns/euch/ihnen. It can mean ownership (something belongs to someone) or membership/association (someone belongs to a group). Common with people, groups, or things that are considered part of something else.
target_language_example: Wir gehören zu Doras Bande.
native_language_example: We belong to Dora's gang.

meaning: to be among (the); to rank among (the)
additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something is part of a group, often an outstanding (best, biggest, most popular) or negative (worst, most dangerous) group: „X gehört/gehören zu den besten/schlechtesten …“. Grammar: „gehören“ + „zu“ + dative plural (often „den“) + adjective in superlative (besten, größten, beliebtesten, gefährlichsten, etc.) + noun or used substantively (e.g., „zu den Besten“).
target_language_example: Elefanten gehören zu den intelligentesten Tieren.
native_language_example: Elephants are among the most intelligent animals.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **gehören** to say who something belongs to (ownership/possession). Often used about objects: *Das Buch gehört mir.* It can also be used about a person (*Er gehört mir!*), which in English is “He’s mine!” and can sound jealous/possessive depending on context.
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, diese Jacke gehört mir.
native_language_example: Excuse me, this jacket is mine.

additional_notes: Used to show that someone or something is part of a group/category or belongs to a person. It takes the dative case: zu mir, zu euch, zu einer Bande, zu einer Generation.
target_language_example: Dieses Buch gehört zu mir, nicht zu dir.
native_language_example: This book belongs to me, not to you.

additional_notes: Used with the verb hören in the perfect tense (haben + gehört) before a dass-clause. Common in questions to ask if someone already knows a piece of news: „Hast du schon gehört, dass …?“ Word order: „… gehört, dass + subject + verb (at the end)“.
target_language_example: Hast du schon gehört, dass der Zug heute ausfällt?
native_language_example: Have you heard that the train is cancelled today?

additional_notes: Used after a form of **haben** + **gehört** (past participle of *hören*) to introduce an indirect object clause with **was** (“what”). In German you typically write a comma before the **was**-clause: *Du hast gehört, was … gesagt hat.* Word order: the main clause ends with **gehört**, and the verb in the **was**-clause goes to the end (*… gesagt hat*).
target_language_example: Hast du gehört, was der Lehrer gesagt hat?
native_language_example: Did you hear what the teacher said?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "hören" (or "gehört" in perfect tense) to introduce a subordinate clause with "wie". The "wie"-clause often describes the way something happened ("how"), but in everyday German it can also introduce what you heard, similar to English "heard that". Word order: the verb goes to the end of the "wie"-clause (e.g., "… wie er angekommen ist").
target_language_example: Ich habe gehört, wie ihr Chef mit ihr gesprochen hat.
native_language_example: I heard how her boss spoke to her.

additional_notes: Used with a form of "kommen" + ", um" + infinitive to say why someone came. In writing, there’s usually a comma before "um". The verb after "um" stays in the infinitive at the end (e.g., "um dich zu sehen"). In speech you often hear it as one chunk: "Wir sind gekommen, um …"
target_language_example: Ich bin gekommen, um dir zu helfen.
native_language_example: I came to help you.

additional_notes: This is the Perfekt (present perfect) form of **kommen** for **du**: **du bist gekommen** (auxiliary verb **sein** + past participle **gekommen**). It’s used for arrival/movement (often to a person/place). You’ll often see it in clauses like **…, dass du gekommen bist** (“…that you came”) or **von wo du gekommen bist** (“from where you came”).
target_language_example: Ich freue mich, dass du heute gekommen bist.
native_language_example: I'm happy that you came today.

gekommen und am nächsten Tag wieder abgereist

target_language_multi_word_term: gekommen und am nächsten Tag wieder abgereist
meaning: (Someone) came/arrived and left again the next day.
additional_notes: Used to say a visit or stay was very short: first you arrive (gekommen) and then you depart again the next day (am nächsten Tag wieder abgereist). Typically describes travel/visits; often used with a specific day: „am Montag … und am nächsten Tag …“.
target_language_example: Wir sind nur kurz geblieben: Wir sind am Freitag gekommen und am nächsten Tag wieder abgereist.
native_language_example: We only stayed briefly: we arrived on Friday and left again the next day.

additional_notes: Passive infinitive ("zu" + "werden"). Often used after expressions like "es ist wert" (it’s worth) or "um … zu" (in order to …), e.g. "Dieses Buch ist es wert, gelesen zu werden." You can add frequency words like "nochmals" (again) or "zweimal" (twice): "… zweimal gelesen zu werden."
target_language_example: Der Artikel ist wichtig und verdient es, gelesen zu werden.
native_language_example: The article is important and deserves to be read.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a completed action in the past (very common in spoken German). It often appears with objects like *das* or *was*: *Was hast du gemacht?* (“What did you do?”). It also shows up in fixed expressions like *sich die Mühe gemacht haben* (“to have made the effort / to have taken the trouble”) and in phrases like *Fortschritte gemacht haben* (“to have made progress”). Word order changes in subordinate clauses: *…, dass er es gemacht hat.*
target_language_example: Ich glaube, dass Tom und Maria das schon mindestens einmal gemacht haben.
native_language_example: I think that Tom and Maria have already done that at least once.

additional_notes: This is the 2nd-person singular Perfekt form of "machen": "du hast ... gemacht". In main clauses, the helper verb comes second and the participle goes to the end ("Du hast einen Fehler gemacht."). In subordinate clauses with "dass/weil/als/warum", both parts typically go to the end, with "hast" last ("..., dass du einen Fehler gemacht hast"). "machen" can mean both 'do' and 'make', and is often used in phrases like "einen Fehler machen" (make a mistake) or "Hoffnung machen" (give someone hope).
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht, warum du das gemacht hast.
native_language_example: I don't know why you did that.

meaning: “has made/done” (past participle + auxiliary in subordinate clauses).
additional_notes: "gemacht" is the past participle of "machen" (to do/make). In main clauses, German uses the perfect tense like "Tom hat das gemacht" (verb in 2nd position, participle at the end). In subordinate clauses (often after "dass", "wer", "wo", or relative clauses with "die"), the auxiliary "hat" moves to the end: "…, dass Tom das gemacht hat" / "die Suppe, die sie gemacht hat". Often refers to something someone did (an action) or made (a thing), depending on context.
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht, wer das gemacht hat.
native_language_example: I don’t know who did that.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is treating you badly/unkindly. Pattern: **(jemand) ist/war gemein zu (mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen)**. Also common with **sei nicht so gemein zu mir!** (“don’t be so mean to me!”).
target_language_example: Bitte sei nicht gemein zu mir.
native_language_example: Please don’t be mean to me.

additional_notes: Used when you want to be very specific about information, intent, or an action. Very common in sentences like „Ich weiß nicht genau, was …“ (“I don’t know exactly what …”) and after verbs such as wissen (to know), sagen (to say/tell), verstehen (to understand), tun (to do). The comma is standard when „genau“ modifies a following clause introduced by „was“.
target_language_example: Also, ich weiß nicht genau, was es bedeutet.
native_language_example: So, I don’t know exactly what it means.

meaning: "exactly what I" (introduces a clause about what you need/mean/do).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something matches perfectly what you needed, expected, or did: "Das ist genau, was ich …" / "Er tat genau, was ich …". Often you’ll also see "genau das, was ich …" (with "das"), especially in careful writing. The comma is used because "was ich …" is a clause.
target_language_example: Das ist genau, was ich gesucht habe.
native_language_example: That's exactly what I was looking for.

additional_notes: Used when someone knows or describes something very precisely. Often appears in indirect questions or statements about knowing/seeing/feeling: „Ich weiß genau, wie …“, „Niemand wusste genau, wie …“. With some verbs it can mean “exactly as” (= in the same way): „Er tat genau, wie ich gesagt hatte.“ Note: without the comma („genau wie“) it can also mean “just like / exactly like” in comparisons.
target_language_example: Sie erklärt genau, wie man das Formular ausfüllt.
native_language_example: She explains exactly how to fill out the form.

additional_notes: Used when someone knows or specifies a precise location. Often appears with verbs like „wissen“ (to know) or „sagen/zeigen“ (to say/show): „Ich weiß genau, wo …“ / „Sag mir genau, wo …“. „genau“ intensifies „wo“ to mean not just 'where' but 'exactly where'.
target_language_example: Ich weiß genau, wo der Bahnhof ist.
native_language_example: I know exactly where the train station is.

additional_notes: Used to point out an exact location or position. Often with verbs like bleiben (stay), gehen (go), sein (be), lassen (leave): „Bleib genau da, wo du bist!“ = stay exactly where you are. Can also be used more figuratively: „Ich hatte dich genau da, wo ich wollte.“ = I had you exactly where I wanted you.
target_language_example: Warte genau da, wo du stehst!
native_language_example: Wait right where you are standing!

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is completely contrary to what was said, expected, or compared to someone/something else. Common patterns: „genau das Gegenteil (tun/machen/sagen)“ and „genau das Gegenteil von …“.
target_language_example: Ich wollte heute früh aufstehen, aber ich habe genau das Gegenteil gemacht.
native_language_example: I wanted to get up early today, but I did the exact opposite.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is precisely the thing you mean (often agreeing with someone or pointing to the exact requirement). Frequently placed at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis: "Genau das ...".
target_language_example: Wenn du mehr Ruhe brauchst, dann ist genau das der richtige Schritt.
native_language_example: If you need more peace and quiet, then that’s exactly the right step.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something matches perfectly. Usually followed by a clause: „genau das, was + subject + verb …“. Often appears with verbs like bekommen (to get), tun (to do), sagen (to say), haben (to have).
target_language_example: Das ist genau das, was ich gemeint habe.
native_language_example: That’s exactly what I meant.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something matches your expectation or instruction perfectly. Typically followed by a verb at the end of the clause (e.g., „…genau das, was ich wollte/gesagt habe/kaufen will“). Often used with „das ist…“ or with verbs like „machen/tun“.
target_language_example: Das ist genau das, was ich meinte.
native_language_example: That’s exactly what I meant.

meaning: to do exactly what I (tell you / said).
additional_notes: A firm instruction or insistence on following directions precisely. "genau" = exactly, "das tun" = do that, and "was ich …" introduces a clause specifying what you must follow. The verb after "was ich" depends on context (e.g., "was ich dir/euch/Ihnen sage" = what I tell you; "was ich gesagt habe" = what I said). Often used with "müssen" to sound strict: "Du musst …" / "Sie müssen …".
target_language_example: Du musst genau das tun, was ich dir sage.
native_language_example: You must do exactly what I tell you.

additional_notes: Used to correct or qualify a statement with more precision. Often placed at the beginning of the sentence as a comment on what follows (like “technically…”), but it can also be inserted mid-sentence.
target_language_example: Genau genommen habe ich das nicht gesagt.
native_language_example: Strictly speaking, I didn’t say that.

meaning: at exactly the right moment (just in time).
additional_notes: Used to say someone arrived/acted at the perfect time. Often appears with verbs of arriving like „kommen“ (Du bist … gekommen / Du kamst …). „genau“ adds emphasis: not just the right time, but precisely the right time.
target_language_example: Wir haben genau im richtigen Augenblick angerufen.
native_language_example: We called at exactly the right moment.

meaning: exactly like that; just like that.
additional_notes: Used to say something is the same in the exact way described or shown. Often used when agreeing or confirming an instruction ("Yes, exactly like that.") or to emphasize that something is precisely the kind/way you mean ("genau so ein Auto" = "exactly that kind of car"). As a short exclamation ("Genau so!") it can mean "Exactly! / That's it!".
target_language_example: Mach es genau so, wie ich es dir gezeigt habe.
native_language_example: Do it exactly like I showed you.

additional_notes: Used to compare reality with an idea, expectation, or preference: “exactly the way I thought/want.” It can also reassure/accept someone as they are (“genau so, wie du bist” = “just the way you are”). Often followed by a full clause with a verb at the end (weil it introduces a comparison with wie).
target_language_example: Mach es bitte genau so, wie ich es dir gezeigt habe.
native_language_example: Please do it exactly the way I showed you.

additional_notes: Used to say two people/things are the same or very similar. Often followed by a noun/pronoun ("genau wie deine Mutter") or a whole clause ("genau wie ich es gesagt habe"). In short replies, you can just say "Genau wie ich." = "Just like me."
target_language_example: Er kocht genau wie sein Vater.
native_language_example: He cooks just like his father.

meaning: “(just) as old as” (the same age as).
additional_notes: Used to compare ages and say they are equal: X ist genauso alt wie Y. Often appears with approximations like etwa/ungefähr (“about”): etwa/ungefähr genauso alt wie. With two people as the subject (Tom und Maria …), it means both are the same age as the person mentioned after wie.
target_language_example: Meine Schwester ist genauso alt wie dein Bruder.
native_language_example: My sister is (just) as old as your brother.

meaning: “look exactly the same as / just like.”
additional_notes: Used with the verb **aussehen** (“to look/appear”) to compare someone’s appearance to someone/something else: **X sieht genauso aus wie Y**. It can also compare to a photo (**wie auf diesem Bild**) or to a usual situation (**wie immer** = “as always”). **Fast genauso** means “almost exactly the same.”
target_language_example: Meine Schwester sieht genauso aus wie meine Mutter.
native_language_example: My sister looks exactly like my mother.

meaning: “(just) as big/tall as” (the same size/height as).
additional_notes: Used to compare size or height: A ist genauso groß wie B = A and B are equal in size/height. With people it usually means “as tall as”; with objects it means “as big/large as.” You’ll often see modifiers like fast (“almost”), ungefähr (“approximately”), or nicht (“not”) before genauso.
target_language_example: Meine Schwester ist genauso groß wie ich.
native_language_example: My sister is just as tall as me.

meaning: just as well; equally well; might as well (in some contexts).
additional_notes: Often used in comparisons with **wie**: **genauso gut wie ...** = “as well as ... / just as well as ...”. With modals like **könnte/hätte**, it can mean an alternative is just as possible or sensible: **Wir könnten genauso gut warten.** = “We might as well wait.”
target_language_example: Ich kann genauso gut heute kommen wie morgen.
native_language_example: I can come just as well today as tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to compare language ability: **genauso gut X wie Y** = X and Y are at the same level. Often with verbs like **sprechen** (to speak) or **können** (to be able to). You can swap in other skills/languages: **genauso gut Deutsch wie Englisch**.
target_language_example: Ich spreche genauso gut Französisch wie du.
native_language_example: I speak French just as well as you.

additional_notes: Used to compare two people/things/situations and say they are equal in the relevant way. Common patterns include **genauso wie + noun/pronoun** (“just like …”) and **genauso + adjective/adverb + wie + noun/pronoun** (“just as … as …”). Also used to express having the same opinion/feeling as someone: *Es geht mir genauso wie dir.* / *Ich denke genauso wie du.*
target_language_example: Es geht mir genauso wie dir.
native_language_example: I feel the same way as you do.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something has enough of a quality for an action to be possible. Pattern: (Adjektiv/Adverb) + genug, um + zu + Infinitiv: „alt genug, um zu fahren“, „stark genug, um zu helfen“. With negation: „nicht genug, um …“ = “not enough to …”. Often follows a description like jung/alt/groß/stark/dumm/verrückt + genug.
target_language_example: Ich bin nicht müde genug, um jetzt zu schlafen.
native_language_example: I'm not tired enough to sleep now.

additional_notes: Used to say something is sufficient for someone/something. Common patterns: **genug für + Akkusativ** (e.g., *genug für mich / drei Personen*) and **Adjektiv + genug für + Akkusativ** (e.g., *groß genug für dich* = 'big/tall enough for you'). In phrases like *Das ist genug für mich*, it can also mean 'That’s enough for me' (i.e., 'I’ve had enough / stop').
target_language_example: Diese Mahlzeit ist genug für drei Personen.
native_language_example: This meal is enough for three people.

additional_notes: Used to ask or say whether someone has sufficient money for a specific purpose (often with „für“ + noun: „genug Geld für eine Fahrkarte“). With „nicht genug Geld“ it means “not enough money.” In hypothetical/conditional sentences you’ll often see „Wenn ich genug Geld hätte …“ (“If I had enough money …”).
target_language_example: Ich habe nicht genug Geld für das Hotel.
native_language_example: I don’t have enough money for the hotel.

additional_notes: Used to express that someone has sufficient money to do an action. The verb after "um" goes to the end of the clause ("… genug Geld, um es zu kaufen"). Often appears with comparisons like "fast genug" (almost enough) or "mehr als genug" (more than enough).
target_language_example: Ich habe nicht genug Geld, um heute essen zu gehen.
native_language_example: I don't have enough money to eat out today.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has sufficient money to do something for themselves. Common pattern: **genug Geld, um sich + (etwas) zu + Infinitiv**. Often used with **sich (etwas) kaufen** (“to buy oneself something”). **sich** stays as written in the fixed term, but in a full sentence it can appear as the appropriate reflexive dative/accusative form (e.g., *mir/dir/sich/uns/euch*), depending on the verb and person.
target_language_example: Glaubst du, Tom und Maria haben genug Geld, um sich das zu kaufen?
native_language_example: Do you think Tom and Maria have enough money to buy that for themselves?

additional_notes: Used to say you have sufficient time to do something. Often with **haben** (to have): *Ich habe genug Zeit.* You can add an infinitive with **zu**: *genug Zeit, um … zu …* (“enough time to …”), or a purpose phrase: *genug Zeit zum Essen* (“enough time to eat”). With **hätte** it becomes hypothetical: *Wenn ich genug Zeit hätte …* (“If I had enough time …”).
target_language_example: Hast du genug Zeit, um mir kurz zu helfen?
native_language_example: Do you have enough time to help me quickly?

additional_notes: Used to say there is sufficient food for someone (often for everyone). Common in questions like „Gibt es genug zu essen?“ and with verbs like „dasein“ (to be there/available), „dabeihaben“ (to have with you), and „mitbringen“ (to bring along).
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, wir haben genug zu essen für alle.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, we have enough to eat for everyone.

additional_notes: Used with places (usually with verbs of coming/going, e.g. "kommen") to say someone has just come from somewhere: "Er kommt gerade aus dem Internat." It can also appear with verbs like "schleichen" to mean someone was just (about) to go out of a place: "... wollte gerade aus dem Haus(e) schleichen." Note: in fixed expressions like "nicht gerade aus dem Häuschen sein" it means "not exactly" rather than a physical "out of".
target_language_example: Ich komme gerade aus dem Supermarkt.
native_language_example: I just came from the supermarket.

meaning: “a letter right now / at the moment” (usually: “(to be) writing a letter right now”).
additional_notes: Used with **gerade** to say something is happening **right now**. In English you often use the present progressive (“I’m writing…”). Word order varies: **Ich schreibe gerade einen Brief** / **Ich schreibe einen Brief gerade** (less common). Note: German **Brief** means “letter” (mail), not English “brief” (= short).
target_language_example: Ich kann nicht telefonieren; ich schreibe gerade einen Brief.
native_language_example: I can’t talk on the phone; I’m writing a letter right now.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something happened a very short time ago (or that not much time has passed yet). Often used with the present perfect (ich habe …) or with time expressions like „letztes Jahr“. Similar to „erst gerade“.
target_language_example: Ich habe gerade erst gegessen, ich bin noch satt.
native_language_example: I just ate, I’m still full.

additional_notes: Used to refer to something someone said very recently. Common in questions like „Was hast du gerade gesagt?“ (“What did you just say?”) or in references like „Wie Sie gerade gesagt haben …“ (“As you just said …”).
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich habe nicht verstanden, was du gerade gesagt hast.
native_language_example: Sorry, I didn’t understand what you just said.

meaning: “right now/currently in the …” or “especially/just in the …” (depending on context).
additional_notes: “gerade” is a flexible adverb. With places/activities it often means “right now/currently” (e.g., *gerade in der Buchhandlung* = currently in the bookstore). With time expressions it can mean “just/precisely” or “especially” (e.g., *gerade in der letzten Woche* = just/especially in the last week). “in der” is simply “in the” (dative, feminine noun), so the noun after it changes (e.g., *in der Schweiz, in der Stadt, in der Bibel*).
target_language_example: Ich bin gerade in der Küche und koche.
native_language_example: I’m in the kitchen right now and cooking.

additional_notes: Used to say someone arrived home a moment ago. Common with present perfect: „Er ist gerade nach Hause gekommen.“ (= He just came home.) It can also appear in past perfect to show one past event happened just before another: „Sie war gerade nach Hause gekommen, als …“. Literal parts: „gerade“ = just/just now, „nach Hause“ = (to) home, „gekommen“ = come (past participle of „kommen“).
target_language_example: Ich bin gerade nach Hause gekommen und muss erst meine Schuhe ausziehen.
native_language_example: I just got home and first I have to take off my shoes.

meaning: just now / only just; barely (at the last moment).
additional_notes: Used either for time (something happened a moment ago) or for a narrow margin (you almost didn’t make it, but you did). Common with verbs like „erreichen“, „schaffen“, „reichen“: „Ich habe es gerade noch geschafft.“ It can also appear in the fixed, often ironic pattern „Da hat uns gerade noch X gefehlt!“ meaning “Just what we needed!” / “That’s the last thing we needed.”
target_language_example: Wir haben den Bus gerade noch bekommen.
native_language_example: We only just caught the bus.

meaning: just in time; at the very last moment.
additional_notes: Used to say something happened barely in time, with almost no time left (you nearly missed it or it almost went wrong). Often appears with verbs like ankommen (arrive), erreichen (catch/reach), entkommen (escape), or schaffen (manage).
target_language_example: Ich habe den Bus gerade noch rechtzeitig erwischt.
native_language_example: I caught the bus just in time.

meaning: at home right now; currently at home.
additional_notes: Used in questions to ask whether someone is at home at the moment. "gerade" = "right now/just" and "zu Hause" = "at home". In conversation, you’ll also often hear "Ist er/sie gerade zuhause?" (spelling variation: "zu Hause" vs. "zuhause").
target_language_example: Ist Frau Keller gerade zu Hause, oder soll ich später anrufen?
native_language_example: Is Ms. Keller at home right now, or should I call later?

meaning: having lunch right now / just having lunch.
additional_notes: Used with a verb like „essen“ to mean someone is currently eating lunch: „(Ich/Er/Sie) esse/isst gerade zu Mittag.“ „gerade“ = at the moment/just now; „zu Mittag (essen)“ = to have/eat lunch (midday meal). In speech you’ll often hear „gerade Mittag essen“ as well.
target_language_example: Ich kann nicht telefonieren—ich esse gerade zu Mittag.
native_language_example: I can’t talk on the phone—I’m having lunch right now.

meaning: got into; ended up in (often an unpleasant situation).
additional_notes: „Geriet in“ is the simple past (Präteritum) of „in etw. geraten“ and is common in written German (news, stories). It’s used with the accusative after „in“ (in + Akkusativ): „in Schwierigkeiten“, „in einen Stau“, „in schlechte Gesellschaft“.
target_language_example: Sie geriet in Panik, als sie ihr Handy nicht finden konnte.
native_language_example: She panicked when she couldn’t find her phone.

additional_notes: “gern” means “gladly” and is commonly used to express that you enjoy doing something. As a standalone sentence you’ll often hear: “Ich arbeite gern.” With an infinitive phrase, it appears as “gern arbeiten,” for example after modal verbs: “Ich will gern arbeiten.”
target_language_example: Ich möchte gern arbeiten, aber nicht am Wochenende.
native_language_example: I would like to work, but not on the weekend.

additional_notes: Used as a polite reply after someone says “Danke.” It can be said on its own (“Gern geschehen!”) or with softeners like “doch” (e.g., “Ist doch gern geschehen.” = “It was no trouble / gladly.”).
target_language_example: Danke für deine Hilfe! – Gern geschehen.
native_language_example: Thanks for your help! – You’re welcome.

meaning: to like; to be fond of (someone).
additional_notes: Used mostly with people: jemanden gern haben = to like someone (often warmly, sometimes close to “care about”). In many contexts it can feel warmer/stronger than “mögen”.
