native_language_example: Did you (all) watch a movie yesterday?

additional_notes: Used at the start of a question to ask what a group of people has done today. "habt" is the 2nd person plural form of "haben" (you all have), and "ihr" = you (plural, informal). Often followed by a past participle (Perfekt), e.g. "gesehen", "gegessen", or sometimes another verb depending on the context.
target_language_example: Habt ihr heute Zeit für ein Treffen?
native_language_example: Do you all have time for a meeting today?

additional_notes: Used to ask a question to a group (ihr = “you all”). "Habt" is the 2nd-person plural form of "haben" and often appears at the start of yes/no questions. It’s commonly followed by a past participle to form the Perfekt (e.g., "Habt ihr hier geschlafen?" = “Did you sleep here?”). "hier" means “here” and points to the location.
target_language_example: Habt ihr hier schon gegessen?
native_language_example: Have you (all) eaten here already?

meaning: “have you (all) … him?” (question to more than one person).
additional_notes: Used when asking a group (“ihr” = you plural/informal) about something they did involving a male person (“ihn” = him, accusative). It usually introduces a verb phrase in the Perfekt with a past participle (e.g., „Habt ihr ihn angerufen?“ = Did you call him?/Have you called him?) or with an infinitive (e.g., „Habt ihr ihn tanzen sehen?“ = Have you seen him dance?).
target_language_example: Habt ihr ihn schon gefragt?
native_language_example: Have you (all) asked him yet?

meaning: “Do you (all) have … in …?” (asking whether something is available in a particular size/color/version).
additional_notes: Common in shops when addressing staff as a group (“ihr”). Typically used as: “Habt ihr [Artikel] in [Farbe/Größe/Ausführung]?” or “Habt ihr das in …?” where “in” introduces the requested variant (e.g., in Blau, in Größe M).
target_language_example: Habt ihr in Größe M noch dieses T-Shirt?
native_language_example: Do you still have this T-shirt in size M?

additional_notes: Used to ask a group of people (ihr) whether something has happened in the recent past. It’s the perfect tense question form of "ihr habt" + "in letzter Zeit" (lately/recently), and is typically followed by a past participle (e.g., geschrieben, geguckt) or phrases like "von jemandem gehört" (heard from/about someone).
target_language_example: Habt ihr in letzter Zeit viel gearbeitet?
native_language_example: Have you all worked a lot lately?

additional_notes: Used to ask about experiences at any time up to now. "habt" is the present tense of "haben" for "ihr" (you all), and it’s typically followed by a past participle (Perfekt): "Habt ihr jemals + Partizip II …?" It can also be used rhetorically to mean “when have you ever…?” (implying “never”).
target_language_example: Habt ihr jemals in Berlin gewohnt?
native_language_example: Have you (all) ever lived in Berlin?

additional_notes: "Habt ihr" is the 2nd person plural form of "haben" and is used when speaking to more than one person ("you all"). "Jemanden" is the accusative form of "jemand" and is used when "someone/anyone" is the direct object of the verb that follows (e.g., benachrichtigt, geküsst, getroffen, gehört). Often translated with “anyone” in questions.
target_language_example: Habt ihr jemanden gesehen, der mir helfen kann?
native_language_example: Have you (all) seen anyone who can help me?

meaning: “have you (all) my …?” (addressing more than one person).
additional_notes: "Habt ihr" is the 2nd person plural form of "haben" (you all have). "meine" means "my" and must match the noun’s gender/number (e.g., meine Bilder/Blumen/Handschuhe; but: meinen Koffer, mein Handy). This phrase is typically followed by a noun and often a past participle or other verb phrase: "gesehen?" (seen), "bekommen/gekriegt?" (received; "gekriegt" is more informal), "hingestellt/gestellt?" (put/placed).
target_language_example: Habt ihr meine Jacke gesehen?
native_language_example: Have you all seen my jacket?

additional_notes: Used to ask two or more people (or one person with informal/plural "ihr") whether they did something involving something you own. "Meinen" is the masculine accusative form of "mein" and is followed by a masculine noun (e.g., meinen Computer / meinen Müll / meinen Roman / meinen Text). In perfect tense questions, the main verb often appears as a past participle at the end: "Habt ihr meinen Computer eingeschaltet?"
target_language_example: Habt ihr meinen Schlüssel gesehen?
native_language_example: Have you (all) seen my key?

meaning: “have you (all) … me?” / “did you … me?” (question to a group).
additional_notes: Used when speaking to more than one person (ihr = “you” plural). In questions, the verb often comes first: Habt ihr …? It’s commonly followed by a past participle for the spoken past (Perfekt): “Habt ihr mich geholt?” = “Did you pick me up/get me?” It can also be used with an infinitive structure, especially with verbs like sehen: “Habt ihr mich weinen sehen?” = “Have you ever seen me cry?”
target_language_example: Habt ihr mich schon angerufen?
native_language_example: Have you (all) called me already?

meaning: “have you (all) … with …” (used to start a question like “Have you talked to/with …?”).
additional_notes: This is a question start made of **habt ihr** (“have you” plural, *ihr*) + **mit** (“with”). It’s usually followed by a person and a past participle, e.g. **mit Tom gesprochen/geredet** (“talked with Tom”), **mit jemandem getanzt** (“danced with someone”). Word order in questions: **Habt ihr mit Tom darüber gesprochen?**
target_language_example: Habt ihr mit ihr schon darüber gesprochen?
native_language_example: Have you already talked to her about it?

additional_notes: Used to ask a question addressed to more than one person (ihr = you all). It’s often followed by a past participle to form the Perfekt (present perfect): "Habt ihr schon … gefunden/gegessen/zugebracht?" With time expressions (seit/wie lange/wie viele Tage/Jahre), it can ask about how long something has been the case up to now.
target_language_example: Habt ihr schon gegessen?
native_language_example: Have you eaten yet?

additional_notes: Used to ask a group of people (ihr = you all) whether they have had an experience at least once in their lives. "schon einmal" adds the idea of “ever / already at least once.” Typically followed by a past participle to form the present perfect question: "Habt ihr schon einmal + Partizip II ...?"
target_language_example: Habt ihr schon einmal in Berlin gelebt?
native_language_example: Have you (all) ever lived in Berlin?

additional_notes: Used to ask a group of people you address as "ihr" (informal plural) whether they have ever done/seen something. The verb usually comes at the end: "Habt ihr schon einmal einen Hai gesehen?" / "Habt ihr schon einmal einen Reifen gewechselt?". Often you’ll also see it without "einen" depending on the noun (e.g., "eine" / "ein" / plural).
target_language_example: Habt ihr schon einmal einen Film auf Deutsch gesehen?
native_language_example: Have you (guys) ever watched a movie in German?

additional_notes: Used to ask a group of people about past experience. "habt ihr" is 2nd person plural (you all), and "schon mal" is a common, spoken shortening of "schon einmal" meaning "ever/before (at least once)". Often followed by a past participle (Perfekt): "Habt ihr schon mal … gemacht/gesehen/gehört?"
target_language_example: Habt ihr schon mal Sushi gegessen?
native_language_example: Have you ever eaten sushi?

additional_notes: Used when speaking to more than one person ("ihr" = you plural). "habt" is the present tense of "haben" and is often used as an auxiliary verb in the perfect tense: "Habt ihr sie gefunden?" = "Did you find her/it/them?". "sie" can mean "her" or "them" (or formal "you" in other contexts), so the exact meaning depends on context.
target_language_example: Habt ihr sie schon gesehen?
native_language_example: Have you (all) seen her/them yet?

additional_notes: Used to ask a group ("ihr" = you plural) if they have any additional questions, requests, or items. It’s usually followed by a noun (e.g., "Fragen") or can stand on its own in conversation when the context is clear.
target_language_example: Habt ihr sonst noch Fragen?
native_language_example: Do you have any other questions?

additional_notes: Used to address a group of people (“ihr” = you all). It’s the Perfekt of “vergessen” (to forget): “ihr habt vergessen …”. The comma introduces an indirect question or relative clause starting with “was” (“what”), and the main verb of that clause goes to the end: “was er gesagt hat”. Often used as a reminder or reproach.
target_language_example: Habt ihr vergessen, was wir gestern abgemacht haben?
native_language_example: Have you (all) forgotten what we agreed on yesterday?

additional_notes: Used to ask a surprised or doubtful question to a group you’re speaking to with the informal plural "ihr". "Habt" is the "ihr" form of "haben" and is often used with the past participle (Perfekt): "Habt ihr wirklich + Partizip II …?"
target_language_example: Habt ihr wirklich so früh angefangen?
native_language_example: Did you really start that early?

additional_notes: Question form of ihr habt, from haben. Used when speaking to two or more people informally. It often appears in common expressions like Angst haben (to be afraid), frei haben (to have time off), or etwas dagegen haben (to mind/object).
target_language_example: Habt ihr heute Abend Zeit?
native_language_example: Do you all have time this evening?

additional_notes: Used to ask a group of people (ihr = you plural) if they are afraid. Often followed by an infinitive with zu: „Habt ihr Angst, allein zu gehen?“ (= are you afraid to go alone?). You can also say what you’re afraid of with „Angst vor + Dativ“: „Habt ihr Angst vor Hunden?“ or ask with „Wovor habt ihr Angst?“ (= what are you afraid of?).
target_language_example: Habt ihr Angst vor dem Dunkeln?
native_language_example: Are you afraid of the dark?

meaning: "Do you (all) have a ...?" / "Have you got a ...?"
additional_notes: Used to ask a group of people (2nd person plural: ihr) whether they have something. It’s followed by a noun in the accusative with the correct article, e.g. "ein" (masc./neut.), "eine" (fem.): "Habt ihr ein Feuerzeug?" / "Habt ihr eine Lampe?"
target_language_example: Habt ihr ein Ladegerät?
native_language_example: Do you (all) have a charger?

meaning: "Do you (all) have a…?" (asking about a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to ask a group of people (ihr = you plural/informal) whether they have something. The verb comes first for yes/no questions: „Habt ihr …?“. „eine“ is the feminine form of “a/an”, so it’s followed by a feminine noun (e.g., „eine Schere“). For masculine/neuter nouns: „Habt ihr einen…?“ / „Habt ihr ein…?“. For formal plural: „Haben Sie…?"
target_language_example: Habt ihr eine Karte von der Stadt?
native_language_example: Do you all have a map of the city?

meaning: "Do you (all) have a …?" (asking a group for one item).
additional_notes: Used to ask people you address as „ihr“ (informal plural: friends, family, kids). It’s the verb „haben“ (to have) in 2nd person plural: „ihr habt“. You usually add a noun after it: „Habt ihr einen Drucker?“ For mixed/unknown groups in a polite/formal setting, use „Haben Sie einen …?“ instead.
target_language_example: Habt ihr einen Stift für mich?
native_language_example: Do you (all) have a pen for me?

additional_notes: Used to ask a group of people (ihr = you all) whether they have something today, or what is happening today. It's the verb "haben" in 2nd-person plural (habt) + "today" (heute). Often followed by a noun (Unterricht, Schule, Vorlesungen) or plans/appointments (heute Abend schon etwas vorhaben).
target_language_example: Habt ihr heute Zeit für ein kurzes Treffen?
native_language_example: Do you all have time for a short meeting today?

additional_notes: Used to ask a group of people (ihr = “you” plural) whether they have any kind of something (an explanation, an idea, good news, etc.). It’s the question form of "ihr habt" (you have) → "habt ihr…?" (do you have…?). "irgendeine" means “any (at all)” and is used with feminine singular nouns (e.g., eine Erklärung, eine Vorstellung, eine Nachricht). With other nouns it changes: "irgendein" (masc./neut. singular), "irgendwelche" (plural).
target_language_example: Habt ihr irgendeine Idee, was wir jetzt machen sollen?
native_language_example: Do you guys have any idea what we should do now?

meaning: 'Do you (all) still have…?' / 'Do you (all) have any … left?'
additional_notes: Used when speaking to more than one person ("ihr"), often to check if something remains or if someone is still interested/has room/time. "noch" can mean "still" (state continues: Durst/Interesse) or "any left" (quantity remains: Milch, Geld). Common in shops/restaurants and group situations. For one person: "Hast du noch …?"; formal/plural: "Haben Sie noch …?" / "Habt Sie noch …?" (rare).
target_language_example: Habt ihr noch Zeit, kurz zu bleiben?
native_language_example: Do you all still have time to stay for a moment?

additional_notes: From the verb **vorhaben** (= to plan/intend). Used a lot in questions, usually followed by an infinitive clause: **Habt ihr vor, ... zu + Infinitiv?** (e.g., *zu helfen, zu kaufen*). With verbs of staying/going you’ll often see: **Habt ihr vor, in + place + zu bleiben?**
target_language_example: Habt ihr vor, heute Abend auszugehen?
native_language_example: Are you planning to go out tonight?

additional_notes: In German, "halb" is said *before* the next hour: "halb drei" means “half (an hour) before three,” i.e., 2:30—not 3:30. Common with time prepositions like "um" (at), "bis" (until), and "vor" (before): "bis halb drei" = until 2:30; "vor halb drei" = before 2:30.
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns um halb drei.
native_language_example: We’re meeting at 2:30.

additional_notes: In German, "halb" + the next hour means half an hour *before* that hour (literally "half (to) seven"). So "halb sieben" = 6:30, not 7:30. (Likewise: "halb acht" = 7:30.)
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns um halb sieben vor dem Kino.
native_language_example: We’re meeting at 6:30 in front of the cinema.

additional_notes: Used with comparisons and quantities to say something is 50% of another: "halb so + adjective/adverb" (halb so schwer/teuer/schnell) or "halb so + viel/viele" (half as much/many). Often appears with a reference point like "wie ..." (as ... as) or implied from context.
target_language_example: Mit dem Zug ist es halb so teuer wie mit dem Taxi.
native_language_example: By train it's half as expensive as by taxi.

additional_notes: Used to compare sizes: **X ist halb so groß wie Y** = X is 50% of Y’s size. The pattern is **halb so + adjective + wie** (you can swap in other adjectives too: *halb so teuer wie* = half as expensive as). Often modified with words like **fast** (almost) or **etwa** (about).
target_language_example: Der Koffer ist halb so groß wie der andere.
native_language_example: The suitcase is half as big as the other one.

additional_notes: Used with time expressions like "eine halbe Stunde" (for half an hour) and in schedules like "jede halbe Stunde" (every half hour). In informal speech you may also hear "eine halbe Stunde" used loosely to mean “about” 30 minutes.
target_language_example: Ich brauche noch eine halbe Stunde.
native_language_example: I need another half hour.

additional_notes: *helfen* takes the dative case, so it’s **ihm** (“to him”). **half** is the simple past (Präteritum), common in writing; in everyday speech you often hear **hat ihm geholfen**. It can be followed by **zu + infinitive** (*half ihm zu entkommen*) or a comma + infinitive clause (*half ihm, die Badewanne zu reinigen*).
target_language_example: Er half ihm beim Umzug.
native_language_example: He helped him with the move.

additional_notes: Präteritum (simple past) of **helfen**: **(er/sie/es) half** + **mir** (dative = “to me”). Common in writing and narration; in speech you’ll also hear **hat mir geholfen** (present perfect). Word order can vary: **Er half mir** / **… half mir, …**.
target_language_example: Tom half mir wirklich, mein Französisch zu verbessern.
native_language_example: Tom really helped me improve my French.

additional_notes: Used when you say your name for the first time. Usually followed by your name: “Hallo, ich bin + Name.” You can also drop “Hallo” and just say “Ich bin …”.
target_language_example: Hallo, ich bin Daniel.
native_language_example: Hello, I’m Daniel.

additional_notes: Used as an interjection to urgently stop someone or interrupt what’s happening. Repeating it ("Halt, halt!" or "Halt, halt, halt!") makes it stronger, similar to “Stop, stop!” or “Wait, wait!” in English. Often paired with "Stopp" for extra emphasis.
target_language_example: Halt, halt! Geh da nicht weiter!
native_language_example: Stop, stop! Don’t go any further!

additional_notes: An imperative phrase used to tell someone to stop talking. Much harsher than neutral options like "Sei bitte still" or "Bitte sei leise"; can sound aggressive or insulting, especially with added words like "du!". Use with great caution.
target_language_example: Halt den Mund und lass mich ausreden.
native_language_example: Shut up and let me finish speaking.

additional_notes: An aggressive, impolite imperative used to tell someone to stop talking and then do something else (“… und hör zu”, “… und komm mit”, etc.). Avoid in polite situations; safer alternatives are “Sei bitte still” or “Bitte sei ruhig”.
target_language_example: Halt den Mund und hör mir zu!
native_language_example: Shut up and listen to me!

meaning: “hold on / hang on” or “stay away / keep out.”
additional_notes:
Imperative with reflexive pronoun: **halt** (from *halten*) + **dich** (“yourself”). Meaning depends on what comes next:
- **Halt dich fest!** = “Hold on tight!” (physical or also “Brace yourself!”)
- **Halt dich da raus! / Halt dich aus … raus!** = “Stay out of it / Keep out of …”
- **Halt dich von … fern!** = “Stay away from …”
Common in spoken German; can sound very forceful depending on tone/context.
target_language_example: Halt dich da raus, das geht dich nichts an.
native_language_example: Stay out of it—this is none of your business.

additional_notes: Imperative of **halten** addressed to **du** (one person). Used with a noun after **die** (feminine singular or plural): *Halt die Lampe höher.* / *Halt die Augen offen.* With **Schnauze** it becomes a rude command meaning “Shut up!” (*Halt die Schnauze!*). Don’t confuse German **halt** here (from **halten**) with English “halt” (= stop).
target_language_example: Halt die Tür bitte offen.
native_language_example: Please keep the door open.

additional_notes: A highly offensive, aggressive way to tell someone to be quiet. “Fresse” is a crude word for a mouth/snout (used for animals), so it dehumanizes the person. Avoid using it; a less vulgar alternative is “Halt den Mund.” or “Sei bitte still.”
target_language_example: Halt die Fresse und lass mich in Ruhe!
native_language_example: Shut the fuck up and leave me alone!

additional_notes: A very direct, often aggressive command telling someone to stop talking. Common in arguments; can sound insulting. Literally “hold the flap,” but you can’t translate it word-for-word. Less harsh options: „Sei bitte still.“ / „Sei leise.“ / „Ruhe, bitte.“
target_language_example: Halt die Klappe und lass mich in Ruhe!
native_language_example: Shut up and leave me alone!

additional_notes: An aggressive/insulting command: imperative "Halt die Klappe!" = "Shut up!". Often followed by another command with "und" (e.g., "... und hör zu!" = "... and listen!"). Use only if you intentionally want to be rude; neutral alternatives include "Sei bitte still" or "Bitte hör kurz zu".
target_language_example: Halt die Klappe und lass mich ausreden!
native_language_example: Shut up and let me finish talking!

meaning: “I consider him (to be) … / I think he is …”.
additional_notes: From the verb pattern **jemanden für + Akk. + (Adj./Nomen)** = “to regard someone as …”. **halte** is 1st person singular present of **halten** (“I consider”), and **ihn** is “him”. You usually add an adjective or noun after **für** (e.g., *ehrlich*, *einen Experten*).
target_language_example: Ich halte ihn für sehr zuverlässig.
native_language_example: I consider him very reliable.

meaning: formal imperative of „halten“: “hold/keep” (also used in fixed phrases like “hang in there”, “keep still”, “stick to”).
additional_notes: Used when addressing one person formally (Sie). It usually needs an object or a particle/reflexive phrase to be clear: „Halten Sie das Kind fern …“ = keep … away; „Halten Sie durch!“ = hang in there/keep going; „Halten Sie still!“ = keep still; „Halten Sie sich an …“ = stick to/follow … .
target_language_example: Halten Sie bitte die Tür zu.
native_language_example: Please keep the door closed.

additional_notes: Used when addressing someone politely (Sie). It must be followed by a noun in the “your” form (Ihre + noun, e.g., Ihre Fahrkarten). Very common in announcements/instructions, often with an extra word like **bereit** (“ready”): **Halten Sie Ihre Fahrkarten bereit.** Note that **halten** also appears in other verb phrases with different meanings, e.g. **Sitzungen abhalten** = “to hold/organize meetings.”
target_language_example: Halten Sie Ihre Ausweise bereit.
native_language_example: Please have your IDs ready.

meaning: formal: “hold/keep yourself …”; used in commands like “keep (left/right)” or “stick to/obey …”.
additional_notes:
This is the formal imperative (Sie-form) of the reflexive verb *sich halten*. It almost always needs an add-on:
- **Halten Sie sich an + Akk.** = “stick to / follow / obey” (rules, schedule).
- **Halten Sie sich links/rechts** = “keep left/right” (often with directions).
- **Für wen halten Sie sich (eigentlich)?** = “Who do you think you are?” (can sound annoyed/accusatory).
target_language_example: Halten Sie sich bitte an die Öffnungszeiten.
native_language_example: Please stick to the opening hours.

additional_notes:
This is the 2nd-person plural form of **halten** (addressing a group: “you all”). It’s very common in opinions/judgments with:
- **halten … für + adjective/noun** = “to consider … (to be) …” (e.g., *Haltet ihr das für glaubwürdig?* = “Do you consider that believable?”)
- **halten … von + noun** = “to think of/about …” (e.g., *Was haltet ihr von …?* = “What do you think of …?”)
Often used as a question to ask for someone’s opinion.
target_language_example: Was haltet ihr von dem Plan?
native_language_example: What do you think of the plan?

additional_notes: Used to ask for an opinion. It’s the 2nd person plural form of the expression **(et)was von etwas halten**. Often used as **Was haltet ihr von ...?** (you all). Other common forms: **Was hältst du von ...?** (you, singular/informal) and **Was halten Sie von ...?** (formal).
target_language_example: Was haltet ihr von der Idee, heute Abend Pizza zu bestellen?
native_language_example: What do you all think of the idea of ordering pizza tonight?

meaning: 'it is' / 'this is about' (used to clarify what something is)
additional_notes: Used to identify or specify what something actually is: „Es handelt es sich um + Akkusativ“ ≈ “It is/this is (a case of) …”. Very common in more formal/neutral writing and speech (reports, explanations). Often appears with adverbs like „hier“, „dabei“, „hierbei“ (“Here it is about…”). In questions, the verb comes first: „Handelt es sich um …?“ = “Is it …?”
target_language_example: Hier handelt es sich um einen Fehler in der Datei.
native_language_example: Here, it’s an error in the file.

meaning: 'it is/this is' (used to clarify what something is).
additional_notes: Almost always used with "es": "Es handelt sich um …". Common in formal/neutral contexts (explanations, customer service, writing). Often followed by a noun phrase: "Es handelt sich um einen Fehler." You can also use it to introduce the topic: "Es handelt sich um das Thema Steuern."
target_language_example: Es handelt sich um ein Missverständnis.
native_language_example: It's a misunderstanding.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone is putting in a lot of effort at work or while studying. Often appears with time expressions like „Tag und Nacht“ (day and night) or in future plans: „Ich werde hart arbeiten.“
target_language_example: Ich muss hart arbeiten, um die Prüfung zu bestehen.
native_language_example: I have to work hard to pass the exam.

meaning: to work hard in order to; to work hard to (do something).
additional_notes: Used to express purpose: "hart arbeiten" + "um ... zu" + infinitive. The verb goes to the end of the "um ... zu" clause (e.g., "um den Test zu bestehen"). Often used with "müssen" to say you have to work hard to achieve something.
target_language_example: Ich muss hart arbeiten, um den Test zu bestehen.
native_language_example: I have to work hard to pass the test.

additional_notes: Past participle phrase used to say someone has/had worked hard. Often appears with auxiliaries like „haben“ (present perfect: „Sie haben hart gearbeitet.“) or „hatte“ (past perfect: „Er hatte hart gearbeitet.“).
target_language_example: Wir haben diese Woche sehr hart gearbeitet.
native_language_example: We worked very hard this week.

additional_notes: Means physically or mentally demanding work/effort. Often used with common phrases like „Danke für die harte Arbeit“ (thanks for the hard work) and „(sich) an harte Arbeit gewöhnen“ (to get used to hard work). Also appears with „sich auszahlen“: „Harte Arbeit zahlt sich aus“ = hard work pays off.
target_language_example: Danke für die harte Arbeit.
native_language_example: Thanks for the hard work.

additional_notes: Verb phrase: **ich hasse** = “I hate” (from *hassen*). **es** is the direct object pronoun “it,” referring to something neutral or an entire situation (often: *Ich hasse es, wenn …* = “I hate it when …”).
target_language_example: Ich hasse es, wenn es regnet.
native_language_example: I hate it when it rains.

additional_notes: Used to address one person informally (du). It’s the present tense of haben (du hast), often used in questions with inversion: „Hast du …?“ = “Have you …?” or, in many contexts, “Did you …?” (past meaning depends on context or with a past participle: „Hast du geschlafen?“ = “Did you sleep?/Have you slept?”). In statements, word order changes: „Vielleicht hast du ihn nicht gesehen.“ = “Maybe you didn’t see him.”
target_language_example: Hast du heute Zeit?
native_language_example: Do you have time today?

meaning: “But you said …” / “You did say …” (reminding someone of what they said).
additional_notes: Used in conversation to refer back to what someone said earlier, often to point out a contradiction or to insist that it was said. The particle "doch" adds emphasis like “but/after all/you know”. Often followed by a clause: "Du hast doch gesagt, dass …".
target_language_example: Du hast doch gesagt, dass du heute Zeit hast.
native_language_example: But you said you have time today.

additional_notes: question form of du hast ('you have'). It's used to ask yes/no questions, very often with the perfect tense. In everyday English, it is often translated as 'did you' when talking about past actions.
target_language_example: Hast du heute schon gegessen?
native_language_example: Have you eaten yet today?

meaning: "Do you have everything?" / "Did you do everything?"
additional_notes: Used at the start of a question to check whether everything is complete. The exact meaning depends on the verb that follows: with a past participle it often means “Did you do/finish everything?” (e.g., „Hast du alles eingepackt/geschafft/verstanden?“). It can also be used with a participle like „gesetzt“ in games or betting to mean “Have you placed all your bets?”
target_language_example: Hast du alles dabei, was du brauchst?
native_language_example: Do you have everything with you that you need?

additional_notes: Question form of the separable verb **anfangen** (“to start”). This is **Perfekt** (spoken past): **du hast … angefangen**. Often followed by **mit + dative** (“with”): *Womit hast du angefangen?* = “What did you start with?”
target_language_example: Was hast du angefangen?
native_language_example: What did you start?

meaning: "do you also…?" / "did you… too?" (often: "have you…?" or "did you…?")
additional_notes: Used in questions with "du" to add "also/too". Depending on context it can be a simple "also" question (Hast du auch was mitgebracht? = Did you bring something too?), or it can sound surprised/critical (Die Vorschule hast du auch übersprungen. = You skipped preschool too.). With "auch nur" it often means "even": "Hast du auch nur ein Wort verstanden?" = Did you understand even a single word?
target_language_example: Hast du auch schon gegessen?
native_language_example: Have you eaten too?

meaning: "are you wearing (…)? / do you have (… ) on?"
additional_notes: From the separable verb "aufhaben" (= to have on / to be wearing, especially items like glasses, a hat, or headphones). Used as a question with an object placed between "du" and "auf": "Hast du [etwas] auf?" Also possible: "Was hast du auf?" = "What are you wearing?" (though "Was hast du an?" is more common for clothing).
target_language_example: Hast du auf dem Foto eine Mütze auf?
native_language_example: Are you wearing a hat in the photo?

meaning: “did you … there/then?” (asking about what someone did/experienced in that situation).
additional_notes: Used in questions to refer back to a specific place, time, or situation that’s already clear from context. "da" can mean "there" or "then/in that situation", and it often sounds like you’re asking for more details or following up on what happened.
target_language_example: Hast du da auch Freunde gefunden?
native_language_example: Did you make friends there/then too?

additional_notes: Used to check whether someone remembered to do something (often a practical task). It’s commonly followed by a comma and an infinitive clause (e.g., „…, Zucker zu kaufen?“). „daran“ refers to the action mentioned after it; with nouns you can also hear „Hast du an X gedacht?“ (e.g., „Hast du an den Schlüssel gedacht?“).
target_language_example: Hast du daran gedacht, den Herd auszuschalten?
native_language_example: Did you remember to turn off the stove?

meaning: "have you … that/it?" (starting a question to someone).
additional_notes: Used to begin a yes/no question with "du" (you, informal singular). Very common in the Perfekt (spoken past) with a past participle later in the sentence: "Hast du das Buch gelesen?" = "Have you read the book?" It can also literally mean "Do you have that?" depending on what follows.
target_language_example: Hast du das schon gemacht?
native_language_example: Have you done that already?

meaning: “have you (the car) … ?” (a question starting with “Have you … the car …?”).
additional_notes: This is the start of a yes/no question with **haben** in the **Perfekt**: **hast du + das Auto + past participle** (e.g., *gesehen, gewaschen, mitgebracht*). **das Auto** is the direct object (accusative). By itself it’s incomplete—you normally add what happened to the car.
target_language_example: Hast du das Auto schon gesehen?
native_language_example: Have you seen the car yet?

meaning: “have you (got) the book …?” (starting a question about a specific book).
additional_notes: Common question starter: **hast du** = “have you” (2nd person singular, informal), **das Buch** = “the book” (a specific book both speakers know). It’s usually followed by another verb/participle to ask what happened with the book (e.g., *bezahlt* paid for, *zurückgegeben* returned, *gelesen/zu Ende gelesen* read/finished). English often uses “Do you have…?” rather than “Have you…?” in this basic sense, so a word-for-word translation may sound unnatural.
target_language_example: Hast du das Buch schon zurückgebracht?
native_language_example: Have you brought the book back yet?

additional_notes:
Common start of a yes/no question asking what someone did with the window. Typically followed by a past participle: 
- "offengelassen" = left open
- "zugemacht" = closed/shut. 
Grammar: "hast du" is the 2nd person singular of "haben" (perfect tense helper verb) and "das Fenster" is the object. In perfect tense, the participle often comes at the end of the sentence.
target_language_example: Hast du das Fenster aufgemacht?
native_language_example: Did you open the window?

meaning: "did you ... last time" / "the last time, did you ..."
additional_notes: Used to ask about what someone did on the previous occasion (the last time something happened). It’s usually followed by a verb or other details: "Hast du das letzte Mal auch ...?" (Did you also ... last time?).
target_language_example: Hast du das letzte Mal auch mit Karte bezahlt?
native_language_example: Did you also pay by card last time?

meaning: “did you … last time?” (asking about what someone did on the previous occasion).
additional_notes: This phrase is used to compare with a previous occasion: „Hast du das letzte Mal …?“ Note: the standard spelling is „das letzte Mal“ (two words). Your term „das letztemal“ is nonstandard, but it may still appear in informal writing/typos. Typically followed by a verb phrase: „Hast du das letzte Mal/letztemal auch … gemacht/genommen/bezahlt?“
target_language_example: Hast du das letztemal auch mit Karte bezahlt?
native_language_example: Did you pay by card last time too?

meaning: “Did you have a ___ last time?” (incomplete; needs a noun after „einen“).
additional_notes: As written, this is not standard German spelling/spacing. Correct would be: „Hast du das letzte Mal einen …?“ (two words: „letzte Mal“). „einen“ is masculine accusative and must be followed by a masculine noun (e.g., „einen Regenschirm“, „einen Termin“). The word order (verb first) matches a yes/no question, but the phrase remains incomplete without the noun.
target_language_example: Ich frage nur: hast du das letztemal einen Regenschirm dabei gehabt?
native_language_example: I’m just asking: did you have an umbrella with you last time?

meaning: "have you (got) that" / "did you (do) that" (asking about something specific).
additional_notes: Common question start: "Hast du das …?" = "Have you … (it/that)?" or sometimes "Did you …?" in English. "das" refers to a specific thing or action already known from context (it = that). Often followed by a past participle: "Hast du das gelesen/gesehen/gekauft?"
target_language_example: Hast du das schon bezahlt?
native_language_example: Have you paid for that already?

meaning: "have you already (done) that?" / "have you (done) that yet?"
additional_notes: Common question pattern: **hast du** (have you) + **das** (that/it) + **schon** (already). You usually add a past participle at the end: *bezahlt, gelesen, getan, gemacht*. With time expressions you can extend it: *Hast du das schon im Voraus gewusst?* = “Did you already know that in advance?”
target_language_example: Hast du das schon bestellt?
native_language_example: Have you ordered that already / yet?

additional_notes: Used to question whether someone truly did/said/saw something. Commonly followed by a past participle (Perfekt): „Hast du das wirklich gemacht/gesagt/geschrieben?“ or by „nicht“ for “Did you really not …?”. Tone can sound skeptical or amazed depending on context.
target_language_example: Hast du das wirklich schon bezahlt?
native_language_example: Did you really pay for that already?

meaning: "Have you ... your ...?" (question with "you" + "your" for a masculine/neuter noun).
additional_notes: Used to start a yes/no question in the Perfekt (past) or with another verb phrase: "Hast du dein + Noun + (Partizip II / Infinitiv ...)?". "hast" = "have" (2nd person singular of "haben"), "du" = "you", and "dein" = "your" when the possessed noun is masculine or neuter (e.g., dein Hund, dein Fahrrad). For feminine/plural nouns you use other forms (e.g., "deine Tasche", "deine Freunde").
target_language_example: Hast du dein Handy gefunden?
native_language_example: Have you found your phone?

meaning: “Have you (your)…?” (asking if someone has/has done something related to their things).
additional_notes: Common question pattern: **hast du** = “have you” (informal singular), and **deine** is a possessive meaning “your” for plural nouns or feminine singular nouns (e.g., *deine Schlüssel*, *deine Medizin*). Used to ask if someone has seen, taken, measured, brought, or achieved something; the specific verb often comes at the end (e.g., *gesehen*, *genommen*, *gemessen*).
target_language_example: Hast du deine Hausaufgaben schon gemacht?
native_language_example: Have you done your homework yet?

meaning: “have you (your)…?” (asking if someone has done something with their masculine/neuter item).
additional_notes: Used to ask a yes/no question in the present perfect: **Hast du …?** = “Have you …?” or often “Did you …?”. **deinen** is the accusative form of **dein** (“your”) used with masculine nouns (e.g., *deinen Hund*) and can also appear before plural nouns in the dative (e.g., *mit deinen Kindern*). You usually add a noun after it: *Hast du deinen Kaffee ausgetrunken?*
target_language_example: Hast du deinen Schlüssel schon gefunden?
native_language_example: Have you found your key yet?

meaning: "have you ..." / "did you ..." (talking to one person) + "the" for a masculine direct object.
additional_notes: Used to ask someone (du = you, singular) whether they have/they did something with a masculine noun in the accusative: den Besen, den Kellner, den Pullover, den Scheck. Often appears with the Perfekt (hast du ... gesehen/bekommen/gespielt?), but can also be used with other verbs. "Den" changes with gender/case (e.g., "hast du die ...?", "hast du das ...?").
target_language_example: Hast du den Schlüssel schon gefunden?
native_language_example: Have you found the key yet?

meaning: “Have you (the) letter…?” / “Did you (do something with) the letter…?”
additional_notes: Common question starter meaning “have you…?” used with an action or result, e.g. **abgeschickt** (sent/posted), **bekommen** (received), **beantwortet** (answered). **den Brief** is accusative (“the letter”). Note: **Brief** looks like English “brief” but means **letter**.
target_language_example: Hast du den Brief schon abgeschickt?
native_language_example: Have you sent the letter yet?

meaning: "have you (the) movie…?" (start of a question about a movie).
additional_notes: Used at the beginning of questions where you ask what someone did with a movie. Often followed by a past participle in the Perfekt: "Hast du den Film gesehen/gemocht?" (= Did you see/like the movie?). It can also be used with other verbs, e.g. "jemandem den Film zeigen" (to show someone the movie): "Wie vielen Frauen hast du den Film gezeigt?" Here "den Film" is the direct object (accusative) and the person is in the dative.
target_language_example: Hast du den Film schon gesehen?
native_language_example: Have you already seen the movie?

meaning: "do you have the whole ..." / "have you been ... the whole ..." (sentence starter).
additional_notes: This is an incomplete fragment that usually needs a noun after it, most often a time word like **Tag** (day) or **Abend** (evening): *Hast du den ganzen Tag Zeit?* It uses **den ganzen** (accusative masculine) meaning “the whole/entire.” The exact meaning depends on the verb phrase that follows (e.g., having time vs. doing something for the entire time).
target_language_example: Hast du den ganzen Tag Zeit?
native_language_example: Do you have time all day?

meaning: "have you" (in a question, with extra emphasis/curiosity/surprise).
additional_notes: "Denn" here is a modal particle often used in questions. It doesn’t mean "then" in the time/order sense; it makes the question sound more interested, surprised, or slightly reproachful (depending on tone): *Warum hast du denn...?* ≈ "Why on earth have you...?" / "So why did you...?". Word order stays the same as a normal question; you can often omit "denn" without changing the basic meaning.
target_language_example: Was hast du denn gemacht?
native_language_example: So what did you do? / What on earth did you do?

meaning: "have you (then)…?" used to add surprise/curiosity in a question.
additional_notes: Used in questions (often spoken) with the modal particle „denn“ to make the question sound more like: “so/then…?”, “how come…?”, “what on earth…?”. It doesn’t change the basic meaning of „hast du …?“, but adds emphasis or expresses surprise. Note: „denn“ here is not the conjunction meaning “because” and it’s not the English word “then”.
target_language_example: Hast du denn keine Zeit heute?
native_language_example: So you don’t have any time today?

meaning: "have you" + reflexive "yourself/you" (used with reflexive verbs in the past).
additional_notes: Used to form a yes/no question in the Perfekt with a reflexive verb: **Hast du dich + (… ) + Partizip II?** The pronoun **dich** is the reflexive “you” (accusative) and stays with the verb (e.g., **sich entschuldigen, sich einleben, sich kümmern (um), sich verlieben (in), sich verlaufen, sich verletzen**). Often followed by prepositions like **bei** (apologize to someone), **um** (take care of something), **in** (fall in love with), etc.
target_language_example: Hast du dich schon entschieden?
native_language_example: Have you already decided?

meaning: “Have you … with/to …?” (asking if you contacted, apologized to, thanked, complained to someone, etc.).
additional_notes: This is a common question frame used with reflexive verbs that take **bei + dative** (e.g., *sich bei jemandem bedanken/entschuldigen/melden/beschweren*). **dich** shows the verb is reflexive (you do it “yourself”), and **bei** introduces the person you do it with/to. The person after **bei** is in the dative: *bei Tom*, *bei jemandem*, *bei meiner Mutter*.
target_language_example: Hast du dich bei deiner Mutter entschuldigt?
native_language_example: Did you apologize to your mother?

meaning: "have you fallen for / fallen in love with …?" (start of a question; needs a noun/pronoun after „in“).
additional_notes: This is the beginning of a question with the reflexive pronoun „dich“ (“yourself/you”). It’s most commonly used with a reflexive verb that takes „in + Akkusativ“, especially „sich in jdn./etw. verlieben“ (“to fall in love with someone/something”): „Hast du dich in ihn/sie …?“ You normally finish it with a verb like „verliebt“.
target_language_example: Hast du dich in sie verliebt?
native_language_example: Have you fallen in love with her?

meaning: "Have you … with …?" (used with a reflexive verb).
additional_notes: This is a common question pattern: **hast du** (have you) + **dich** (yourself, reflexive) + a reflexive verb + **mit + Person (dative)**. It’s often used with verbs like **sich streiten** (argue), **sich prügeln** (get into a fight), **sich gut amüsieren** (have a good time). The person after **mit** is in the dative (e.g., *mit Maria*, *mit Tom*).
target_language_example: Hast du dich mit deinem Bruder gestritten?
native_language_example: Did you argue with your brother?

meaning: 'Have you already…?' / 'Have you … yet?' (with a reflexive verb).
additional_notes: Used to ask whether someone has already done something expressed with a reflexive verb in the perfect tense (haben + past participle). "dich" is the reflexive pronoun (yourself), and "schon" adds the idea of "already/yet". You’ll usually follow it with a past participle: "Hast du dich schon entschieden?" / "…gewöhnt?" / "…verliebt?"
target_language_example: Hast du dich schon angemeldet?
native_language_example: Have you signed up yet?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has ever had a certain experience. It’s built from: "hast du" (have you), "dich" (yourself—needed with many reflexive verbs), "schon" (already), "einmal" (ever/once). The verb that comes next often needs "dich" (e.g., dich verirren = get lost, dich fragen = ask yourself). In some questions you may also hear "Hast du schon einmal …?" without "dich" if the next verb isn’t reflexive.
target_language_example: Hast du dich schon einmal in einer fremden Stadt verlaufen?
native_language_example: Have you ever gotten lost in a strange city?

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression: hast du means "have you," and die is the definite article "the" before a feminine singular or plural noun. In many everyday questions, hast du + object + past participle is the German perfect tense, often translated as "did you ...?" in natural English.
target_language_example: Hast du die Hausaufgaben gemacht?
native_language_example: Did you do the homework?

meaning: “have you the door…?” — the start of a question about the door (often: whether you closed/locked it).
additional_notes: This is an incomplete phrase on its own; it’s usually followed by a past participle or other info, e.g. **zugemacht** (closed), **abgeschlossen** (locked), **aufgemacht** (opened). German often forms yes/no questions by putting the verb first: **Hast du…?** (“Have you…?”). **die Tür** is accusative (“the door”).
target_language_example: Hast du die Tür abgeschlossen?
native_language_example: Did you lock the door?

additional_notes: This is the start of a question. **hast du** = “have you” (du = informal “you”), and **diese** is a demonstrative meaning “this/these” that must match the noun that follows (e.g., *diese Torte* = “this cake”). With a past participle like **probiert**, it often means “Have you tried …?”
target_language_example: Hast du diese App schon ausprobiert?
native_language_example: Have you tried this app yet?

additional_notes: Used in questions addressed to one person (du). "hast du" is the present perfect auxiliary for many verbs (e.g., "ausprobiert"), often translating as "have you" or simple past "did you" in English. "diesen" refers to a masculine noun in the accusative case (direct object), e.g., "diesen Laden" (this shop), "diesen Beruf" (this job), "diesen Witz" (this joke).
target_language_example: Hast du diesen Film schon gesehen?
native_language_example: Have you already seen this movie?

additional_notes: Used to start a yes/no question with the auxiliary verb **haben** in the **Perfekt** (e.g., **hast du gelesen/geschrieben/bekommen …?**). **Dieses** is a demonstrative meaning **“this”**; here it’s typically **accusative neuter singular** (e.g., **dieses Buch**, **dieses Märchen**, **dieses Geschenk**). In questions, the verb comes first: **Hast du …?**
target_language_example: Hast du dieses Foto schon gesehen?
native_language_example: Have you already seen this photo?

meaning: 'have you' + reflexive 'yourself' (used with reflexive verbs in the perfect tense).
additional_notes: Used in questions with **du** in the **Perfekt** when the verb is reflexive and takes **dir** (dative), e.g. **sich denken** (to think to oneself), **sich kaufen** (to buy oneself), **sich ansehen** (to watch). Word order often is: **Was/Wie/Welches ... hast du dir ... [Partizip II]?**
target_language_example: Was hast du dir für morgen vorgenommen?
native_language_example: What have you planned for tomorrow?

additional_notes: From the verb "(sich) aussuchen" = "to choose / pick out". "dir" shows it’s for yourself. Used as a question in the perfect tense: "Was/Welche(n/s) ... hast du dir ausgesucht?" = "Which ... did you choose?" (The exact form of "welch-" depends on the noun’s gender/case.)
target_language_example: Welches T-Shirt hast du dir ausgesucht?
native_language_example: Which T-shirt did you choose (for yourself)?

additional_notes: Used at the start of a question to sound surprised, curious, or slightly impatient. "denn" adds emphasis (often like “actually/then”), and "dir" is a dative reflexive pronoun used with certain verbs (e.g., sich etwas vorstellen/überlegen/merken). You’ll usually see it followed by a verb phrase: "Hast du dir denn schon …?"
target_language_example: Hast du dir denn schon überlegt, was du morgen machen willst?
native_language_example: Have you actually thought about what you want to do tomorrow?

meaning: "Have you looked at/watched the …?" (asking if someone checked something out).
additional_notes: Used with the verb (often) "ansehen": "Hast du dir die … angesehen?" The "dir" is a common German way to say you took the time to view/check something (videos, shows, drawings, data, etc.). You add the noun after "die" (feminine singular or plural), e.g. "die Sendung" or "die Daten".
target_language_example: Hast du dir die E-Mail schon angesehen?
native_language_example: Have you looked at the email yet?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has already done something, often with a reflexive verb ("dir" = "yourself/to you"). Common patterns: (1) with everyday actions: "Hast du dir schon die Hände gewaschen?" (2) with thinking/deciding: "Hast du dir schon einen Namen überlegt?" / "Hast du dir schon überlegt, was ...?" In questions, the past participle usually comes at the end ("... gewaschen/geputzt/überlegt").
target_language_example: Hast du dir schon überlegt, was du morgen machen willst?
native_language_example: Have you already thought about what you want to do tomorrow?

meaning: "Have you … a/an …?" (often starting a past-tense question in the Perfekt).
additional_notes: Used at the beginning of a yes/no question with du. Very often, hast is the auxiliary verb for the Perfekt: hast du + (direct object starting with ein/eine/einen…) + past participle at the end (e.g., „Hast du ein Thema ausgesucht?“). In other contexts it can also mean simple possession („Hast du ein Auto?“ = “Do you have a car?”).
target_language_example: Hast du ein Foto gemacht?
native_language_example: Did you take a photo?

meaning: “do you have a…?” / “have you … a …?” (starting a yes/no question with a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a question with **du** (you, informal singular). **eine** is the accusative form of “a/one” for **feminine** nouns (eine Einladung, eine Karte, eine Stelle, eine Wassermelone). Very often it appears in the **Perfekt** (past) with a past participle later in the sentence: **Hast du eine Einladung erhalten?** = “Have you received an invitation?” For masculine/neuter nouns you’d use **hast du einen… / hast du ein…**.
target_language_example: Hast du eine Frage?
native_language_example: Do you have a question?

meaning: "do you have a…?" / "did you get a…?" (to a masculine thing).
additional_notes: Used to ask whether someone has/has packed/has obtained something masculine (accusative): einen Adapter, einen Preis, einen Tisch, etc. It often comes before the noun, but can also stand alone when the noun is understood from context ("Hast du einen?" = "Do you have one?"). For feminine/neuter nouns: "hast du eine…?" / "hast du ein…?".
target_language_example: Hast du einen Stift für mich?
native_language_example: Do you have a pen for me?

additional_notes: Used to form a question with **du** (you, informal singular) + **haben** (auxiliary verb) + **es** (“it”). Often appears with a past participle at the end: **Hast du es bemerkt?** (“Did you notice it?”). **Es** refers to something already known from context.
target_language_example: Hast du es schon gesehen?
native_language_example: Have you seen it yet?

meaning: "have you (already) ... ?" (with a reflexive meaning like "take a look" / "think it over" / "change your mind").
additional_notes: This is the start of a very common pattern: **hast du + es + dir + past participle/verb?** It uses **dir** (dative) as a reflexive pronoun and often appears with verbs like **(sich) ansehen** (to take a look at it), **(sich) überlegen** (to think it over), and **es sich anders überlegen** (to change your mind). In English, you usually don’t translate **dir** directly; you translate the whole verb phrase (e.g., “Have you taken a look at it?” / “Have you thought it over?”). Word order tip: in questions, **hast** comes first; **es** typically comes before **dir**.
target_language_example: Hast du es dir schon überlegt?
native_language_example: Have you thought it over already?

meaning: "Did you manage (to do it)?" / "Did you make it?"
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone succeeded in doing something. Often followed by an infinitive with **zu**: **Hast du es geschafft, … zu …?** (“Did you manage to …?”). **es** is a placeholder object meaning “it” (the task/goal). On its own (**Hast du es geschafft?**), it usually means “Did you make it?” (e.g., arrive in time, finish it, succeed).
target_language_example: Hast du es geschafft, den Zug zu erwischen?
native_language_example: Did you manage to catch the train?

meaning: “have you already …?” / “have you done it yet?”
additional_notes: Used to ask whether someone has already done something. It’s the start of a yes/no question in the Perfekt: **Hast du … schon + past participle?** (e.g., *Hast du es schon gemacht?*). **schon** often implies “already / by now” and can also feel like “yet” in English questions. **es** is a placeholder for “it/that” and can be replaced with a specific object (e.g., *Hast du den Kaffee schon bezahlt?*).
target_language_example: Hast du es schon gehört?
native_language_example: Have you already heard it? / Have you heard it yet?

additional_notes: A very common question pattern: **hast du** (have you) + **etwas** (anything/something) + optional verb/object. It’s used to ask whether someone has done something or had/consumed something: *Hast du etwas gelesen?* (read anything), *Hast du etwas gegessen?* (eaten anything). Depending on context it can also imply suspicion (especially with *angestellt* = “been up to something/caused trouble”).
target_language_example: Hast du etwas gegessen oder hast du keinen Hunger?
native_language_example: Have you eaten anything, or are you not hungry?

additional_notes: Used in questions where the verb commonly takes *für* (e.g. *für jemanden stimmen* = vote for someone, *für etwas bezahlen* = pay for something, *für etwas üben* = practice for something). Also in the pattern *Was hast du für + Nomen?* meaning “What kind of … do you have?” (e.g. *Was hast du für Geschichten zu erzählen?* = What stories do you have to tell?). Word order changes with other question words (e.g. *Wie viel hast du für … bezahlt?*).
target_language_example: Hast du für die Reise schon bezahlt?
native_language_example: Have you paid for the trip yet?

additional_notes: Literally “have you thought” (Perfekt of denken), but in English it’s usually translated as “did you think…?”. Common in questions that challenge an assumption or expectation: “Hast du gedacht, …?” = “Did you think …?”. It can also be used to ask about someone’s reaction: “Was hast du gedacht?” = “What did you think?”
target_language_example: Hast du gedacht, ich würde das einfach akzeptieren?
native_language_example: Did you think I would just accept that?

meaning: "did you eat?" / "have you eaten?" (addressing one person informally: "du").
additional_notes: This is the perfect tense of "essen" (to eat): "du hast gegessen" = "you ate / you have eaten." In questions, the verb comes first: "Hast du gegessen?" You can add a question word: "Was/wo/mit wem/wie viele ... hast du gegessen?" Use only when speaking to one person you address as "du" (friends, family, children).
target_language_example: Was hast du gegessen?
native_language_example: What did you eat? / What have you eaten?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone heard something (a sound) or heard some news. Often used as a question: "Hast du gehört?" (sometimes like "Did you hear that?"). It can be followed by a clause with question words: "Hast du gehört, ob …" (whether …), "Hast du gehört, wie …" (how …), or "Was hast du gehört?" (What did you hear?).
target_language_example: Hast du gehört, dass es morgen schneien soll?
native_language_example: Have you heard that it’s supposed to snow tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to introduce reported speech or information you heard (often gossip or news). It’s typically followed by a clause (e.g., “was er gesagt hat” = “what he said”). You can change the person: “Haben Sie gehört, was …” (formal), “Habt ihr gehört, was …” (plural).
target_language_example: Hast du gehört, was er gestern über den Chef gesagt hat?
native_language_example: Have you heard what he said about the boss yesterday?

additional_notes: Used in questions in the Perfekt (present perfect): **du hast** (you have) + **gekauft** (bought). In German questions with a question word, the finite verb (**hast**) comes right after the question word, and the participle (**gekauft**) typically goes at the end: *Welches Buch hast du gekauft?* This is **informal** because it uses *du*; the formal version is *haben Sie gekauft*.
target_language_example: Welches Buch hast du gekauft?
native_language_example: Which book did you buy?

additional_notes: Question form with the Perfekt tense: "du hast gelernt" (you learned / you have learned) → "hast du gelernt?" Used to ask what, where, when, how, or from whom someone learned something. Often followed by an infinitive clause: "hast du gelernt, wie man das macht?" (did you learn how to do that?).
target_language_example: Hast du gelernt, wie man das sagt?
native_language_example: Did you learn how to say that?

additional_notes: Used in questions to ask if someone did something a moment ago. It’s typically followed by a past participle (Perfekt): "Hast du gerade … gesagt/gehört/gemacht?" Here, "gerade" means "just" (a moment ago).
target_language_example: Hast du gerade meinen Namen gesagt?
native_language_example: Did you just say my name?

meaning: "did you say" / "you said" (asking about or repeating what someone said).
additional_notes: Used to refer back to someone’s words, often as a question to confirm, clarify, or show surprise. It can appear in direct questions ("Was hast du gesagt?") or inside a longer question ("Hast du gesagt, du würdest…?"). In German, you may also hear it at the end of a question to mean “you said” ("Wie viele waren es, hast du gesagt?").
target_language_example: Wie spät ist es, hast du gesagt?
native_language_example: What time is it, you said?

additional_notes: Used to ask whether someone saw something. It’s a question form with inversion (verb first): "Hast du ...?" Literally "have you seen" and uses the present perfect: "du hast gesehen" (you have seen). Often followed by a question word like "wer" (who) or "wie viele" (how many).
target_language_example: Hast du gesehen, wo mein Handy ist?
native_language_example: Did you see where my phone is?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone noticed or witnessed something, often as an introduction to surprising or important information. The verb phrase is second person singular informal (du). It’s commonly followed by a clause with a past action (e.g., „… gesagt/geschrieben/getan hat“) or by „was mit … passiert ist“ (“what happened to …”).
target_language_example: Hast du gesehen, was er heute im Unterricht gesagt hat?
native_language_example: Did you see what he said in class today?

additional_notes: Used to ask whether someone witnessed the way something happened. It’s usually followed by a clause with the verb at the end: „Hast du gesehen, wie das passiert ist?“ Sometimes used to emphasize or brag about what someone did.
target_language_example: Hast du gesehen, wie schnell er gerannt ist?
native_language_example: Did you see how fast he ran?

meaning: “did you … yesterday?” (starting a yes/no question about yesterday).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a question in the Perfekt (present-perfect style) with inversion: **hast** (auxiliary verb) + **du** + **gestern** + past participle later in the sentence. Common with verbs that form the Perfekt with **haben** (e.g., *essen → gegessen*, *erhalten → erhalten*).
target_language_example: Hast du gestern Zeit gehabt?
native_language_example: Did you have time yesterday?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a fact (often something surprising or interesting) and ask whether the other person already knew it. **gewußt** and **daß** are older spellings; in modern German you usually see **gewusst** and **dass** (Rechtschreibreform).
target_language_example: Hast du gewußt, daß Tom in Australien geboren wurde?
native_language_example: Did you know that Tom was born in Australia?

meaning: "Have you (today)…?" (starting a yes/no question about today).
additional_notes: Common question starter with inversion: **hast** (have) + **du** (you) + **heute** (today). It’s usually followed by a past participle or other phrase, e.g. **Hast du heute deine Übungen gemacht?** (perfect tense), or with **schon** = “already”: **Hast du heute schon …?**.
target_language_example: Hast du heute schon gegessen?
native_language_example: Have you eaten today already?

meaning: "did you (this) morning" (asking if someone has done something earlier today).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a yes/no question: „Hast du heute Morgen …?“ + past participle or other verb phrase. Literally "have you this morning"; very common with the conversational past (Perfekt) to ask about things done earlier today.
target_language_example: Hast du heute Morgen schon gefrühstückt?
native_language_example: Did you already have breakfast this morning?

additional_notes: Used to start a yes/no question with "du" (informal "you") and "hier" (here). Often followed by a past participle at the end: "Hast du hier gewohnt?" = "Have you lived here?" / "Did you live here?" In speech it often means "Did you … here?" depending on context.
target_language_example: Hast du hier gearbeitet?
native_language_example: Did you work here? / Have you worked here?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone (du) whether they have done something involving a male person as the indirect object (ihm = “to him/for him”, dative). Typically followed by a past participle (gegeben, geschrieben, geholfen, geraten, erzählt) and often also a direct object (e.g., das Geld, einen Brief).
target_language_example: Hast du ihm schon geantwortet?
native_language_example: Have you already replied to him?

meaning: 'have you ... him' / 'did you ... him' (you → singular, informal).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a yes/no question with inverted word order: **hast** (auxiliary) + **du** (you) + **ihn** (him, accusative). It’s usually followed by a past participle (Perfekt) like **gesehen** (seen), or by another verb phrase: **Hast du ihn rausgeschmissen?**
target_language_example: Hast du ihn schon angerufen?
native_language_example: Have you called him yet?

meaning: "Have you already … him?" / "Have you … him yet?"
additional_notes: Used to start a yes/no question in the present perfect: "Hast du ihn schon + Partizip II?" (e.g., gesehen, geküsst, kennengelernt). "ihn" is the accusative pronoun for a masculine person/thing (“him/it”). "schon" often means “already” (or “yet” in questions) and can suggest something might be expected by now.
target_language_example: Hast du ihn schon gesehen?
native_language_example: Have you seen him yet?

meaning: “have you … to/for her?” (question: you + auxiliary “hast” + dative “ihr”).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a question in the Perfekt (past) tense. “hast du” = “have you,” and “ihr” is the dative pronoun meaning “to her / for her” (not “she”). The main verb often comes at the end: “Hast du ihr geholfen?” = “Did you help her?”
target_language_example: Hast du ihr schon geschrieben?
native_language_example: Have you written to her yet?

meaning: "have you … in …?" (a common question pattern in the past/Perfect tense).
additional_notes: Used to ask what someone did in a place (or sometimes within a context like a room). Grammar: "hast" (auxiliary for Perfekt) + "du" + past participle later in the sentence, with "in" introducing the location (usually with dative: "in Deutschland", "in Boston"). Example pattern: "Hast du in [place] [verb-participle]?"
target_language_example: Hast du in Berlin studiert?
native_language_example: Did you study in Berlin?

additional_notes: Used to ask if something has happened in the recent past (over the last days/weeks). It’s often followed by a past participle or a phrase like "etwas von ihm gehört" (heard from him). Common in casual conversation; you may also hear "Hast du in letzter Zeit mal ...?" for an even more conversational tone.
target_language_example: Hast du in letzter Zeit viel gearbeitet?
native_language_example: Have you been working a lot lately?

meaning: “have you ever …?” (asking if something has happened at any time).
additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s experience at any point up to now. "je" adds emphasis like “ever” in English and is common in questions; in everyday speech you may also hear "Hast du schon mal …?" meaning “Have you ever…/Have you ever once…?”. The verb form changes with the person: "Hast du je…?" (you), "Haben Sie je…?" (formal you).
target_language_example: Hast du je in einem anderen Land gelebt?
native_language_example: Have you ever lived in another country?

meaning: "have you ever" (asking if something has happened at any time in your life up to now).
additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s past experiences. Typical pattern: "Hast du jemals + Partizip II?" (present perfect), e.g. "Hast du jemals … gesehen/gehört/gemacht?" In everyday speech, "jemals" is often optional: "Hast du mal …?" can sound more casual.
target_language_example: Hast du jemals Berlin besucht?
native_language_example: Have you ever visited Berlin?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has met/seen/hugged/etc. a person, usually followed by a past participle or another verb phrase: „Hast du jemanden getroffen/gesehen/umarmt …?“ „jemanden“ is the accusative form meaning “someone/anyone.”
target_language_example: Hast du jemanden gesehen, der mir helfen kann?
native_language_example: Have you seen anyone who can help me?

meaning: “did you last night…?” (asking about something someone did or experienced last night).
additional_notes: Common question start: "Hast du letzte Nacht + (something) + ?" Uses "hast du" (have you) with past participle to talk about the recent past (Perfekt), e.g., "geschlafen" (slept), "gespürt" (felt), "angestellt" (got up to/did). You can also use it with a noun phrase like "ein Erdbeben" (an earthquake).
target_language_example: Hast du letzte Nacht einen Albtraum gehabt?
native_language_example: Did you have a nightmare last night?

meaning: "Have you ever…?" / "Have you (by any chance)…?" (a casual way to ask if someone has done something).
additional_notes: Used mainly in spoken, informal German to make a question sound less direct. Often suggests “at some point / already / just once” and is frequently used when checking, reminding, or making a suggestion (e.g., “Hast du mal nachgesehen…?” = “Did you check…?”). It’s not about a specific time like “now”; it’s more like “ever / at least once”.
target_language_example: Hast du mal versucht, den Computer neu zu starten?
native_language_example: Have you tried restarting the computer (at least once)?

meaning: “have you my …?” / “did you … my …?” (asking if someone has/received/used your thing).
additional_notes: Common start of a yes/no question: **Hast du …?** = “Do you have …?” With **meine** (my), you’re referring to a noun that is either **plural** (e.g., *meine Bilder*) or **feminine singular** (e.g., *meine Einladung, meine Zahnbürste*). You typically add the noun right after **meine**.
target_language_example: Hast du meine Schlüssel gesehen?
native_language_example: Have you seen my keys?

additional_notes: Used to start a yes/no question with "du" (you, singular informal). "meinen" is the masculine accusative form of "mein" and is followed by a masculine noun (e.g., meinen Stift, meinen Pass). The main verb often comes at the end in these questions (gesehen, gelesen, versteckt).
target_language_example: Hast du meinen Schlüssel gefunden?
native_language_example: Have you found my key?

meaning: “have you … me?” → “did you … to me?” / “have you … me?” (starting a question with “me” as the object).
additional_notes: This is not usually a complete phrase by itself, but the beginning of many questions where **mich** (“me”) is the direct object and **hast** is the 2nd-person singular of **haben** (“to have”). In everyday German, **hast du mich + past participle** often forms the *Perfekt* (present perfect), which is commonly used like English “did you…?”. Example patterns: **Hast du mich gesehen?** (“Did you see me?”), **Hast du mich gerettet?** (“Did you save me?”).
target_language_example: Hast du mich angerufen?
native_language_example: Did you call me?

meaning: "Didn't you ... me?" / "Haven't you ... me?" (a negative question).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a yes/no question to express surprise or to check something you expected: "Hast du mich nicht + Partizip II ...?" (e.g., "beachtet", "vermisst") or with hearing verbs: "Hast du mich nicht + Infinitiv + hören/gehört?" ("Hast du mich nicht rufen hören?" / "Hast du mich nicht rufen gehört?"). "mich" = "me", and "nicht" makes it negative.
target_language_example: Hast du mich nicht gesehen?
native_language_example: Didn't you see me?

additional_notes: Common sentence start in questions: **hast** (2nd-person singular of *haben*) + **du** (you) + **mir** (to me/for me, dative). It’s used when the action affects you as an indirect object: *Hast du mir zugehört?* = “Did you listen to me?”; *Hast du mir die Wahrheit gesagt?* = “Did you tell me the truth?” The exact English translation depends on the verb that follows.
target_language_example: Hast du mir schon geschrieben?
native_language_example: Have you written to me yet?

additional_notes: This is the start of a yes/no question with "du" (you). It’s used with verbs that take "mit" (with), especially "sprechen" (to talk/speak): "Hast du mit X gesprochen?" = "Have you talked to X?". With some verbs the meaning changes, e.g. "mit jemandem Schluss machen" = "to break up with someone". The person after "mit" is in the dative case (e.g. "mit deinen Eltern").
target_language_example: Hast du mit deiner Lehrerin darüber gesprochen?
native_language_example: Have you talked to your teacher about it?

additional_notes: Used to start a question about whether someone has talked with a specific person (or thing) using **mit + dative**. **mit dem** = “with the” (dative masculine/neuter). For plural you use **mit den** (e.g., **mit den Kindern**, not *mit dem Kindern*). You can also use the polite form: **Haben Sie mit dem … gesprochen?**
target_language_example: Hast du mit dem Lehrer gesprochen?
native_language_example: Have you spoken to the teacher?

additional_notes: This is a common sentence start when asking if someone has interacted with a specific feminine person/thing. "mit" takes the dative case, so "die" becomes "der" (feminine dative): *mit der Frau*, *mit der Ärztin*, *mit der Besitzerin*. It’s usually followed by a past participle like *gesprochen* (spoken) or another verb phrase: *Hast du mit der Ärztin gesprochen?*
target_language_example: Hast du mit der Nachbarin gesprochen?
native_language_example: Have you spoken with the (female) neighbor?

meaning: "have you (done something) with my …?" / "did you (do something) with my …?" (followed by a masculine/neuter noun).
additional_notes: This is an unfinished question fragment. "hast du" = "have you" (informal singular "you"). "mit" takes the dative case, so "mein" becomes "meinem" for masculine/neuter nouns (e.g., "mit meinem Bruder" = "with my brother", "mit meinem Handy" = "with my phone"). You normally need a verb at the end or more context: e.g., "Hast du mit meinem Bruder gesprochen?" (spoken), "Hast du mit meinem Handy telefoniert?" (made a call).
target_language_example: Hast du mit meinem Bruder gesprochen?
native_language_example: Did you talk to my brother?

additional_notes: Used with inversion in yes/no questions to express surprise or to check/confirm something you think is true: "Hast du nicht …?" = "Didn't you …?" / "Haven't you …?". The tense depends on context: it can refer to the past (often like English "didn't you") or to a current state/result (like "haven't you"). It can also appear in short replies: "Nein, hast du nicht." = "No, you haven't."
target_language_example: Hast du nicht gesagt, dass du morgen kommst?
native_language_example: Didn't you say you were coming tomorrow?

meaning: "Didn’t you say …?" (reminding someone of what they said).
additional_notes: Used to refer back to something the other person previously said, often to check a contradiction or confirm a detail. It’s a question with "nicht" that expects the answer "yes" (i.e., you did say that). Commonly followed by a "dass"-clause ("…, dass …") or a direct reported clause ("…, du wärst …").
target_language_example: Hast du nicht gesagt, dass du heute keine Zeit hast?
native_language_example: Didn’t you say you don’t have time today?

meaning: “have you already …?” (asking if something has been done yet).
additional_notes: Used to ask whether someone has already completed an action, usually with the present perfect: **Hast du schon + Partizip II?** (e.g., *Hast du schon gegessen?*). **schon** = “already/yet” and often suggests you expect it might be done by now.
target_language_example: Hast du schon gegessen?
native_language_example: Have you eaten already? / Have you eaten yet?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has ever done/experienced something at least once up to now. Very common in conversation; typically followed by a past participle (Perfekt) like „gesehen“, „gemacht“, „gedacht“.
target_language_example: Hast du schon einmal in Berlin gewohnt?
native_language_example: Have you ever lived in Berlin?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has ever done/seen/visited/heard something at least once in their life. The key phrase is **schon einmal** (“ever/at least once”). **die** is the accusative article for feminine nouns (e.g., *die Freiheitsstatue*) or plural nouns (e.g., *die Alpen*). You can swap in other articles: *Hast du schon einmal den/das …?*
target_language_example: Hast du schon einmal die Nordlichter gesehen?
native_language_example: Have you ever seen the Northern Lights?

additional_notes: Used to ask whether someone has had an experience at least once in their life. Literally it’s like “have you already once a…”, but in English you normally translate it as “have you ever…?”. The noun after "ein" is in the accusative, and the main verb typically comes at the end: "Hast du schon einmal ein Insekt gegessen?"
target_language_example: Hast du schon einmal ein Konzert besucht?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to a concert?

meaning: “Have you ever … ?” (about doing something with a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has ever done something before. Literally: “have you already once a …,” but in English it’s usually “have you ever …?” The verb goes at the end: “Hast du schon einmal eine Auster geknackt?” For masculine nouns use “einen” (…einen Hund gesehen?), for neuter use “ein” (…ein Auto gefahren?).
target_language_example: Hast du schon einmal eine Pizza selbst gemacht?
native_language_example: Have you ever made a pizza yourself?

additional_notes: A common question starter: "Hast du schon einmal …?" = “Have you ever …?” It uses "schon einmal" to mean “ever / at least once.” "hast du" is informal singular (“have you”), and "einen" is the masculine accusative form of “a” (used before a masculine noun like "Igel"). The verb often comes at the end in the past participle form (Perfekt), e.g. "… gesehen?", "… getragen?"
target_language_example: Hast du schon einmal einen Delfin gesehen?
native_language_example: Have you ever seen a dolphin?

meaning: "Have you ever (been) in …?" / "Have you ever … in …?"
additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s past experience. "schon einmal" means "ever / at least once (before)". You usually add a place after "in" and then finish the sentence with a verb at the end (e.g., gewesen, gewohnt, gearbeitet). With places: "in" + dative for being somewhere (in Berlin), and "in" + accusative for going somewhere (in die Schweiz).
target_language_example: Hast du schon einmal in Deutschland gearbeitet?
native_language_example: Have you ever worked in Germany?

additional_notes: Used to ask about life experience in a casual question. "schon einmal" means "ever" (literally "already once"). "jemanden" is "someone" in the accusative case, so a verb usually follows (e.g., gesehen, gehört, besucht, geliebt). Word order often continues with the main verb at the end: "Hast du schon einmal jemanden singen hören?"
target_language_example: Hast du schon einmal jemanden im echten Leben getroffen, den du aus dem Internet kennst?
native_language_example: Have you ever met someone in real life that you know from the internet?

meaning: "have you ever..." (have you done/seen/heard this before?).
additional_notes: Common way to ask about someone’s past experience. Often used with a past participle (Perfekt), e.g. „Hast du schon mal X gemacht/gesehen/gehört?“ „schon mal“ is short for „schon einmal“ and means “ever/before at least once” (not necessarily “already” in this question).
target_language_example: Hast du schon mal in Deutschland gelebt?
native_language_example: Have you ever lived in Germany?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has ever done/seen/touched something before. "schon mal" is very common in speech and means roughly “ever / at some point (before)”. The phrase is usually followed by a masculine accusative noun ("einen") and then the past participle at the end: "Hast du schon mal einen Elefanten gesehen?" You can swap "einen" depending on the noun: "ein" (neuter), "eine" (feminine), or no article with plurals.
target_language_example: Hast du schon mal einen Film auf Deutsch gesehen?
native_language_example: Have you ever watched a movie in German?

additional_notes: Used to start a yes/no question in the Perfekt (spoken past): **hast du** + past participle + **sie**. **du** = you (informal singular). **sie** (lowercase) usually means **her** or **them** (not the formal **Sie**). The main verb often comes as a past participle later in the sentence (e.g., *gesehen, gebeten, kaputtgemacht*).
target_language_example: Hast du sie schon angerufen?
native_language_example: Have you called her/them yet?

meaning: "do you have anything else" / "do you have any other …"
additional_notes: Used to ask if there’s something additional besides what was already mentioned. Very common in service situations (e.g., at a shop) or in conversations: it’s usually followed by a noun like "Fragen" (questions), "Wünsche" (wishes/requests), "Ideen" (ideas), etc. Informal because it uses "du"; the formal version is "Haben Sie sonst noch …?"
target_language_example: Hast du sonst noch Fragen?
native_language_example: Do you have any other questions?

meaning: "have you … us" / "did you … to us" (addressing several people).
additional_notes: This is a common question/statement frame: **hast du** (2nd person singular of *haben*) + **uns** (*us*). It’s usually used with a past participle in the **Perfekt** (spoken past): *Hast du uns gesehen?* = “Did you see us?” / *Das hast du uns nie erzählt* = “You never told us that.” In questions, the verb comes first (**Hast du …?**). **uns** can be a direct object (“see us”) or an indirect object (“tell us”).
target_language_example: Hast du uns gestern im Park gesehen?
