Grammar note: after „Ich wünschte,“ German typically uses Konjunktiv II; with verbs like „würdest“ + infinitive (e.g., „würdest kommen“) it corresponds closely to English “would.”
target_language_example: Ich wünschte, du würdest öfter anrufen.
native_language_example: I wish you would call more often.

meaning: "I wish he ..." (expressing an unreal or unlikely wish).
additional_notes:
Used to express wishes about situations that aren’t true (or are unlikely). It’s typically followed by Konjunktiv II: 
- Present/now: "Ich wünschte, er wäre hier." = I wish he were here.
- Past: "Ich wünschte, er wäre da gewesen." = I wish he had been there.
- With actions/verbs: often "würde" + infinitive (or a Konjunktiv II form): "Ich wünschte, er würde mich bemerken." = I wish he would notice me.
More formal/literary than "Ich wünsche mir, dass ..."
target_language_example: Ich wünschte, er hätte mehr Zeit für uns.
native_language_example: I wish he had more time for us.

meaning: “I wish there were …” (expressing an unreal/imagined situation).
additional_notes: Used to express a wish about something that is not true right now. It’s the subjunctive (Konjunktiv II): ich wünschte (“I wish”) + es gäbe (from geben → es gibt / “there is/are”). You normally follow it with a noun phrase: „… es gäbe mehr Zeit / eine bessere Lösung / mehr Leute wie dich“.
target_language_example: Ich wünschte, es gäbe heute keine Hausaufgaben.
native_language_example: I wish there were no homework today.

meaning: "I wish it were…" (expressing an unreal wish).
additional_notes: Used to say you wish something were different from reality. It’s followed by the subjunctive form of "sein" (wäre). Common with adjectives or situations: "…anders", "…wahr", "…so wie früher". Often implies regret or longing.
target_language_example: Ich wünschte, es wäre schon Freitag.
native_language_example: I wish it were already Friday.

meaning: "I wish I…" (a wish about something unreal or unlikely).
additional_notes: Used to express a wish about the present or future that is not true (or not likely). It’s followed by a verb in the subjunctive (Konjunktiv II), often in forms like spräche/sähe/wohnte/wäre. In everyday speech, people often use "wäre" instead of the more formal "wäre"/"wäre" patterns, and contractions like "wär" are common.
target_language_example: Ich wünschte, ich hätte mehr Zeit.
native_language_example: I wish I had more time.

meaning: "I wish I had ..." (regret about the past).
additional_notes: Used to express regret or a missed opportunity about something in the past. It’s followed by the subjunctive II form of "haben" ("hätte") plus a past participle (Perfekt), e.g. "Ich wünschte, ich hätte gelernt/gehört/gekauft." Often implies “but I didn’t.”
target_language_example: Ich wünschte, ich hätte früher Bescheid gesagt.
native_language_example: I wish I had told you earlier.

meaning: “I wish I had …” (wishing for something you don’t have).
additional_notes: Used to express an unreal/imaginary wish about the present: you want something to be true now, but it isn’t. Grammar pattern: „Ich wünschte, ich hätte + noun …“ (subjunctive II of „haben“). You can add a purpose with „…, um … zu …“ (e.g., „genug Geld, um … zu kaufen“).
target_language_example: Ich wünschte, ich hätte mehr Zeit.
native_language_example: I wish I had more time.

additional_notes: Used to express a wish about an unreal/possible situation—usually something you would like to do but can’t right now. Often followed by an infinitive at the end of the clause (e.g., „helfen“, „mitkommen“, „aufhören“). The verb form „wünschte“ is the subjunctive (Konjunktiv II) of „wünschen“ to show it’s not reality.
target_language_example: Ich wünschte, ich könnte länger bleiben, aber ich muss arbeiten.
native_language_example: I wish I could stay longer, but I have to work.

meaning: “I wish I could do that (like that / as well).”
additional_notes: Used to express an unreal wish about your ability. It’s usually followed by more detail, e.g. a comparison with wie + person/thing (“…wie du”) or an adjective/adverb (“so gut / so fließend”). Grammar note: wünschte and könnte are in Konjunktiv II (subjunctive) to show it’s not real right now.
target_language_example: Ich wünschte, ich könnte so gut Klavier spielen wie du.
native_language_example: I wish I could play the piano as well as you.

meaning: "I wish I were …" (expressing an unreal wish).
additional_notes: Used to express a wish about something that is not true (now or in general). It’s the subjunctive form: „ich wäre“ = “I were / I would be”. Often followed by a comparison („… wie …“ = “like/as …”) or an adjective/noun phrase. For past regrets, German often uses „… gewesen“ (e.g., „Ich wünschte, ich wäre früher gegangen.“ = “I wish I had left earlier.”).
target_language_example: Ich wünschte, ich wäre zu Hause.
native_language_example: I wish I were at home.

additional_notes: Used to express regret about not knowing something (an unreal/contrary-to-fact situation in the present). It uses Konjunktiv II: **wünschte** (from *wünschen*) + **wüsste** (from *wissen*). Very often followed by a question word or clause: *… was / wie / wo …*
target_language_example: Ich wünschte, ich wüsste, wo mein Handy ist.
native_language_example: I wish I knew where my phone is.

additional_notes: Used to express a wish/regret about something that isn’t possible or isn’t happening (often a polite or realistic limitation). It’s followed by an infinitive at the end of the clause (e.g., „… kommen“, „… helfen“). Grammar note: „wünschte“ + „könnten“ is Konjunktiv II (subjunctive) to talk about hypothetical/desired situations.
target_language_example: Ich wünschte, wir könnten dir heute helfen.
native_language_example: I wish we could help you today.

meaning: "I would" (conditional / hypothetical; also used for polite requests).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to talk about what you would do in a situation (real or imagined): "Ich würde dir helfen" = "I would help you." It’s also very common for polite or softer wording, especially with verbs like "gern(e)": "Ich würde gern ..." = "I would like to ..." (polite). This is Konjunktiv II of "werden".
target_language_example: Ich würde gern einen Kaffee bestellen.
native_language_example: I would like to order a coffee.

meaning: “I would … you” (I’d … you) — used for hypothetical or polite/soft statements.
additional_notes: This is the start of a sentence with the conditional/subjunctive II form “würde”. It usually needs an infinitive later: “Ich würde dich gern sehen” = “I’d like to see you.” It can express (1) a hypothetical situation (“I thought I would find you there”), (2) a wish (“I’d really like to see you”), or (3) something you would/wouldn’t do (“I would never kiss/hurt you”).
target_language_example: Ich würde dich sofort anrufen, wenn ich Zeit hätte.
native_language_example: I would call you right away if I had time.

meaning: "I’d like to (do something) with you" / "I would like to (do something)."
additional_notes: Used to express a polite or gentle wish/intention toward the person you’re speaking to (dich = “you”). Usually followed by an infinitive verb at the end of the clause: „Ich würde dich gerne anrufen.“ It uses the conditional („würde“) and often sounds softer/less direct than „Ich möchte dich …“.
target_language_example: Ich würde dich gerne zum Essen einladen.
native_language_example: I’d like to invite you to dinner.

additional_notes: Used with Konjunktiv II (würde + infinitive) to talk about what you would do in a situation, or to sound more cautious/polite. The "es" often refers to a previously mentioned action or idea (like “do it”, “say it”, “prefer it”). Typical patterns: „Ich würde es (nicht) tun/sagen.“ / „Ich würde es vorziehen, …“ / „Ich würde es gern …“
target_language_example: Ich würde es nicht machen, wenn ich du wäre.
native_language_example: I wouldn’t do it if I were you.

additional_notes: Used to express a polite wish or request, often followed by an infinitive verb: „Ich würde gern + Verb …“ (e.g., „Ich würde gern zahlen.“). It’s a common, soft-sounding alternative to „Ich möchte …“.
target_language_example: Ich würde gern einen Kaffee bestellen.
native_language_example: I would like to order a coffee.

meaning: "I would like (to)" (polite way to say what you want).
additional_notes: Used to express a wish or preference in a friendly, polite way. Often followed by an infinitive verb (Ich würde gerne schlafen.) or by a noun with a verb like haben/möchten implied (Ich würde gerne einen Kaffee. = I’d like a coffee.). In formal situations you can add "mit Ihnen" (with you) or make it a question: "Würden Sie gerne …?"
target_language_example: Ich würde gerne einen Termin vereinbaren.
native_language_example: I would like to make an appointment.

meaning: "I would like to know" (polite way to ask for information).
additional_notes: A very common polite phrase using Konjunktiv II (würde) to sound less direct. Often followed by a question word or clause, e.g. „… ob …“ (whether), „… wann …“ (when), „… wie …“ (how), „… wo …“ (where). You can also shorten it to „Ich würde gern wissen …“.
target_language_example: Ich würde gerne wissen, wann der nächste Zug fährt.
native_language_example: I would like to know when the next train leaves.

additional_notes: Used to express a preference in a polite, hypothetical way (Konjunktiv II of "werden"). Often followed by an infinitive: "Ich würde lieber bleiben." You can compare two options with "als": "Ich würde lieber A (machen) als B (machen)" (= rather A than B). For negation, use "lieber nicht": "Ich würde lieber nicht ...".
target_language_example: Ich würde lieber heute zu Hause bleiben, als spät auszugehen.
native_language_example: I’d rather stay at home today than go out late.

meaning: "I would" (used with a reflexive verb: "I would ... myself").
additional_notes: This is the Konjunktiv II form of "ich" + "werden" ("würde") plus the reflexive pronoun "mich". It’s used before a reflexive verb to talk about a hypothetical situation or to sound more polite/less direct: e.g. "Ich würde mich gern ..." = "I’d like to ...". The exact English translation depends on the reflexive verb that follows (e.g. "mich unterhalten" = have a conversation, "mich verlaufen" = get lost, "mich begeben" = go/put myself into).
target_language_example: Ich würde mich gern entschuldigen.
native_language_example: I would like to apologize.

meaning: “I’d say …” (a polite/soft way to give your opinion).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a guess, assessment, or recommendation without sounding too direct. Often followed by a comma and then your statement ("Ich würde sagen, …"). It can also imply “in my view / if you ask me.”
target_language_example: Ich würde sagen, wir treffen uns um sieben.
native_language_example: I’d say we’ll meet at seven.

meaning: “I would know / I knew” (subjunctive of *wissen*), often to sound less direct.
additional_notes: *Ich wüsste* is **Konjunktiv II** of *ich weiß* (“I know”). It’s used for (1) **polite/softened wishes or requests**: *Ich wüsste (wirklich) gerne …* (“I’d really like to know …”), (2) **hypothetical/assumed knowledge**: *Ich dachte, ich wüsste …* (“I thought I knew …”), and (3) the fixed phrase **Nicht, dass ich wüsste.** = “Not that I know of.”
target_language_example: Ich wüsste gern, ob du morgen Zeit hast.
native_language_example: I’d like to know if you have time tomorrow.

meaning: “I’d like to know” / “I’d like to find out.”
additional_notes: Polite way to ask for information. Uses Konjunktiv II of *wissen* (“wüsste”) to sound softer/more indirect than *ich möchte wissen* or *ich will wissen*. Often followed by an indirect question with *ob/was/wie/wann/wer*, etc.
target_language_example: Ich wüsste gern, ob der Zug heute pünktlich ist.
native_language_example: I’d like to know if the train is on time today.

meaning: “I would like to know …” / “I’d like to know …”.
additional_notes: A polite way to say you want information, often followed by an indirect question (was/wer/wo/wie/warum/ob). It uses the subjunctive of wissen ("wüsste") to sound softer/more tentative than "Ich möchte wissen".
target_language_example: Ich wüsste gerne, ob du morgen Zeit hast.
native_language_example: I’d like to know if you have time tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to ask indirectly and politely for information. It’s a common alternative to "Ich möchte gern wissen, ob …". The verb "wüsste" is Konjunktiv II (subjunctive) of "wissen" and makes the request sound softer/more polite. The clause after "ob" has normal subordinate-clause word order (verb at the end).
target_language_example: Ich wüsste gerne, ob Sie morgen Zeit haben.
native_language_example: I’d like to know if you have time tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask for an explanation or reason. Literally “I would know gladly why…”. It’s more formal/soft than "Warum...?" and is often followed by a clause (subject + verb), e.g., "..., warum er so spät ist."
target_language_example: Ich wüsste gerne, warum du heute nicht kommen kannst.
native_language_example: I’d like to know why you can’t come today.

additional_notes: A polite, somewhat formal-sounding way to introduce an indirect question. Uses Konjunktiv II ("wüsste") to soften the statement. "warum" = why. "man" is an impersonal subject meaning "one/people/they" (you usually translate it as "they" or "people" in English). You typically continue with a verb in past tense or perfect: "… warum man ihn gewählt hat" (why they chose/elected him).
target_language_example: Ich wüsste gerne, warum man das so gemacht hat.
native_language_example: I’d like to know why they did it that way.

additional_notes: From the verb **zeigen** (“to show”). Very often used with two objects: **jemandem** (to someone, dative) + **etwas** (something, accusative): *Ich zeige dir/euch/ihr das.* With pronouns, German commonly puts the dative pronoun first: *Ich zeige es dir.* Also exists as the reflexive **sich zeigen** (“to show oneself / to appear”): *Ich zeige mich nie in der Öffentlichkeit ohne Maske.*
target_language_example: Warte kurz, ich zeige dir, wie das geht.
native_language_example: Wait a second, I’ll show you how it works.

additional_notes: Used when speaking politely to one person (or a group) with Sie. Ihnen is the dative form meaning “to you.” Often followed by what you’re showing (usually in the accusative): Ich zeige Ihnen den Weg / den Campus / ein Foto.
target_language_example: Warten Sie kurz, ich zeige Ihnen das Zimmer.
native_language_example: Wait a moment, I’ll show you the room.

additional_notes: Used when you’re about to demonstrate something or explain how to do something. Often followed by a comma + a clause (e.g., “wie …” = “how …”, “was …” = “what …”), or by a noun/pronoun (“welche” = “which ones”). You can add a time word like “jetzt” (now) or “gleich” (in a moment).
target_language_example: Warte kurz, ich zeige dir, wie das geht.
native_language_example: Wait a second, I’ll show you how it works.

additional_notes: Used to state your personal preference. Very often followed by a verb in the infinitive with „zu“: „Ich ziehe es vor, … zu …“ (e.g., „Ich ziehe es vor, zu Hause zu bleiben.“). You can also prefer a noun: „Ich ziehe Kaffee vor.“
target_language_example: Ich ziehe es vor, zu Hause zu bleiben.
native_language_example: I prefer to stay at home.

meaning: "I pull / I draw" (forms many common verbs like "put on", "take off", "move house", "tease").
additional_notes: "Ich ziehe" is the 1st-person singular of *ziehen* (present tense). On its own it most literally means "I pull" or "I draw" (e.g., draw a card), but in everyday German it very often appears with prefixes/particles that change the meaning: **anziehen** = put on clothes, **ausziehen** = take off clothes / move out, **umziehen** = move house / change clothes, **durchziehen** = carry through/finish, **(jemanden) aufziehen** = tease someone. Watch for separable parts that may appear later in the sentence (e.g., *Ich ziehe ... an/aus/um/durch*).
target_language_example: Ich ziehe nächsten Monat um.
native_language_example: I’m moving house next month.

meaning: “I’m getting dressed / changing (clothes)” (with an added particle like an/um) or “I’m withdrawing” (with zurück).
additional_notes:
This is the reflexive verb "sich ziehen" (“to pull oneself”), but in everyday German it’s mostly used with separable particles: 
- sich anziehen → to get dressed: "Ich ziehe mich an." 
- sich umziehen → to change clothes: "Ich ziehe mich um." 
- sich zurückziehen → to withdraw / retreat: "Ich ziehe mich zurück." 
Without the particle (an/um/zurück), "Ich ziehe mich" sounds incomplete in these common meanings.
target_language_example: Warte kurz, ich ziehe mich schnell um.
native_language_example: Wait a second, I’m going to change quickly.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like **sein** (to be) and **bleiben** (to stay): **Ich bin zu Hause.** = I’m at home; **Ich bleibe zu Hause.** = I’m staying home. Note the spelling: usually **zu Hause** (separate words), often with **H** capitalized.
target_language_example: Am Wochenende bleibe ich zu Hause.
native_language_example: On the weekend I’m staying at home.

additional_notes: Used to say you are doing/experiencing something for the first time. The verb changes depending on the situation, and „zum ersten Mal“ is often placed later in the sentence: „Das höre ich zum ersten Mal.“ / „Vor zwei Wochen war ich zum ersten Mal im Disneyland.“ You may also add „in meinem Leben“ (“in my life”) for emphasis.
target_language_example: Das höre ich zum ersten Mal.
native_language_example: I’m hearing that for the first time.

meaning: “to him, that …” — used to introduce reported speech or a statement directed to him, followed by a “dass” (that) clause.
additional_notes: Typical structure with verbs like sagen/erklären/versprechen: Verb + „ihm“ + comma + „dass“ + subordinate clause. The comma before „dass“ is required. In the „dass“-clause, the conjugated verb usually goes to the end: „Sie sagte ihm, dass du recht hast.“
target_language_example: Sie sagte ihm, dass du recht hast.
native_language_example: She told him that you are right.

meaning: “(to) him, that he …” (dative pronoun + comma + dass-clause with “he …”).
additional_notes: Used when a verb takes an indirect object (ihm = “to him”) and is followed by a dass-clause. The comma before “dass” is required. In the dass-clause, the conjugated verb typically goes to the end: „… dass er heute kommt.“ Common with verbs like sagen/erzählen/erklären/schreiben, etc. Not a fixed idiom; it’s a grammatical pattern.
target_language_example: Ich sagte ihm, dass er kommen soll.
native_language_example: I told him that he should come.

meaning: 'to him, that he…' — used in sentences like “tell him that he …”, where **ihm** is the dative object (“to him”) and **daß er …** introduces a subordinate clause (“that he …”).
additional_notes: Common with reporting/communicating verbs: **jemandem (Dativ) sagen/erzählen/erklären, daß …** = “to tell someone that …”. **ihm** = “to him”. **daß er …** starts a subordinate clause; the conjugated verb in that clause typically goes to the end. Note: **daß** is the traditional spelling; modern standard German usually writes **dass**.
target_language_example: Sie sagte ihm, daß er recht habe.
native_language_example: She told him that he was right.

meaning: "(Tell) him to ..." / "Tell him that he should ..."
additional_notes: Used after verbs like **(jemandem) sagen** or **bitten** to pass on an instruction/request: **Ich sage ihm, er soll ...** = “I’ll tell him to ...”. German often uses **soll** here (from **sollen**) where English uses an infinitive (“to call you back”). Word order: **ihm** (to him) + comma + **er soll** + verb at the end: **er soll Sie zurückrufen**.
target_language_example: Ich sage ihm, er soll morgen früher kommen.
native_language_example: I’ll tell him to come earlier tomorrow.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "leihen" (= to lend). "ihm" is the dative pronoun meaning "to him" (the person receiving the loan). Often appears after verbs like "bitten" (to ask/request): "jemanden bitten, ihm Geld zu leihen" = "to ask someone to lend him money."
target_language_example: Ich kann es mir nicht leisten, ihm Geld zu leihen.
native_language_example: I can’t afford to lend him money.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **schlagen** (“to hit/strike”). **ihm** is the dative pronoun (“to him”), and **auf den Kopf** means “on the head.” In reported speech you may see **hast** (direct speech), **haben** (reported with *sagte*), or **hätten** (subjunctive/indirect speech).
target_language_example: Warum hast du ihm auf den Kopf geschlagen?
native_language_example: Why did you hit him on the head?

additional_notes: Used when you mean being honest with a male person (ihm = “to him” in the dative case). You can also change the person: ihr die Wahrheit sagen (tell her the truth), ihnen die Wahrheit sagen (tell them the truth). Common with modal verbs like sollen: Du solltest ihm die Wahrheit sagen. (“You should tell him the truth.”).
target_language_example: Ich werde ihm die Wahrheit sagen, auch wenn es schwer ist.
native_language_example: I will tell him the truth, even if it’s hard.

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression, but a common combination in sentences with verbs like geben, schenken, or schicken. "ihm" is the dative form of "er" and means "to him," while "eine" is "a/an" for a following feminine singular noun, as in "ihm eine Uhr" = "him a watch."
target_language_example: Ich kaufe ihm eine neue Jacke.
native_language_example: I'm buying him a new jacket.

additional_notes: Used when a man/boy is the indirect object (recipient) and the following noun phrase is a masculine direct object in the accusative: e.g., jemandem (ihm) einen Brief / einen Applaus / einen Welpen geben, kaufen, schreiben. Compare: „ihm eine …“ (feminine) and „ihm ein …“ (neuter).
target_language_example: Kannst du ihm einen Gefallen tun?
native_language_example: Can you do him a favor?

additional_notes: Common pattern with two objects: dative pronoun (ihm = to him) + accusative thing (einen Brief = a letter). Used with verbs like schreiben (to write), schicken (to send), geben (to give): Ich schreibe/schicke/gebe ihm einen Brief. Word order can change in longer sentences, but this is a very common order. Note: German "Brief" means "letter" (not English "brief" = short).
target_language_example: Ich habe ihm einen Brief geschrieben.
native_language_example: I wrote him a letter.

additional_notes: Past participle phrase from "jemandem helfen" (to help someone), which takes the dative; "ihm" is the dative pronoun meaning "to him". Commonly used in the Perfekt tense with "haben" + "geholfen" (e.g., "Ich habe ihm geholfen"). Word order changes in questions: "Hast du ihm geholfen?"
target_language_example: Gestern habe ich ihm geholfen.
native_language_example: Yesterday I helped him.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **gehören** (“to belong”). The owner is in the **dative**: *mir gehört* (belongs to me), *dir gehört*, *ihm gehört*, *ihr gehört*, *uns gehört*, *euch gehört*, *ihnen/Ihnen gehört*. Often the thing owned is the subject: **Das Buch gehört ihm.** Word order can vary; placing the dative pronoun first (*Ihm gehört …*) can add emphasis.
target_language_example: Ihm gehört das Auto.
native_language_example: The car belongs to him.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like **sagen** (“to say/tell”) and the dative pronoun **ihm** (“to him”). You’ll often see it in the **Perfekt/Plusquamperfekt**: **(ich) habe ihm gesagt …** / **(ich) hatte ihm gesagt …**. It can be followed by a clause (**…, dass …**) or a question word (**was/wie/warum …**).
target_language_example: Ich habe ihm gesagt, dass wir später kommen.
native_language_example: I told him that we’re coming later.

additional_notes: "Ihm" is the dative form of "er" (he) and means "to him". Many verbs (including "helfen") take the dative, so you say "jemandem helfen" (to help someone).
target_language_example: Du kannst ihm helfen.
native_language_example: You can help him.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **geben**: **jemandem (Dat.) noch eine Chance geben** = “to give someone another chance.” **ihm** is dative (“to him”); you can replace it with **ihr** (to her), **dir** (to you), **mir** (to me), **ihnen** (to them/you formal). **noch** here means “still/yet/another,” i.e., one more chance.
target_language_example: Gib ihm noch eine Chance, bitte.
native_language_example: Give him another chance, please.

additional_notes: Used to report what you tell a male person (ihm = “to him”). Put the message after dass, and send the main verb to the end of the dass-clause: „Sag ihm, dass er kommt.“ In questions/requests it’s common with können/müssen/werden: „Können Sie ihm sagen, dass …?“
target_language_example: Kannst du ihm sagen, dass ich heute später komme?
native_language_example: Can you tell him that I’m coming later today?

meaning: "to him" (dative), often before "zu" + infinitive or with a separable verb.
additional_notes: "ihm" means "to him" (dative object). In many sentences, "zu" belongs to the verb phrase, not to "ihm": (1) "ihm zu" + infinitive = "to ... him" (e.g., "ihm zu gehorchen" = "to obey him", "ihm zu verzeihen" = "to forgive him"); (2) with separable verbs, the prefix can appear at the end: "Ich schaute ihm zu" (zuschauen) = "I watched him." So "ihm zu" is usually not a fixed expression by itself—it's "ihm" plus the verb’s "zu" or separable prefix.
target_language_example: Ich versuche, ihm zu helfen.
native_language_example: I’m trying to help him.

additional_notes: "ihm" is the dative form of "er" (= him), used because helfen takes the dative: "jemandem helfen". "zu helfen" is the infinitive with "zu" (often after verbs like anbieten, vorhaben, bereit sein, bitten), meaning "to help" as an action/plan.
target_language_example: Ich versuche, ihm zu helfen.
native_language_example: I'm trying to help him.

additional_notes: Used in the common pattern **jemanden als + (noun/role) + verb**: *choose/see/consider/call/use someone as…* The noun after **als** is often **without an article** (e.g., *als Vorsitzenden*), but can also take one (e.g., *als den besten Arzt*). Note: **als** can also mean **“than”** in comparisons (*größer als…*), but here it means **“as.”**
target_language_example: Alle sehen ihn als guten Freund.
native_language_example: Everyone sees him as a good friend.

meaning: 'ihn' = 'him' + the separable prefix 'an' belonging to certain verbs (e.g., anrufen, ansehen, anlächeln). In main clauses, the prefix often appears at the end.
additional_notes:
This is not a fixed phrase by itself; it’s a common split pattern you get with separable-prefix verbs.

Examples of verbs where this happens:
- **anrufen** → *Ich rufe ihn an.* (I call him.)
- **ansehen** → *Sie sieht ihn an.* (She looks at him.)
- **anlächeln** → *Er lächelt ihn an.* (He smiles at him.)

Word order note: in main clauses (present/simple past), the prefix (**an**) typically goes to the end. In infinitive/perfect forms, it stays attached: *ich will ihn anrufen*, *ich habe ihn angerufen*.
target_language_example: Jetzt nimm dein Telefon und ruf ihn an.
native_language_example: Now take your phone and call him.

meaning: "him out of the …" / "remove him from the …"
additional_notes: A very common pattern: **ihn** ("him") + **aus dem** ("out of the" for masculine/neuter nouns). **aus** always takes the **dative**, so you get **aus dem** (often contracted to **ausm** in speech). Used with many verbs, e.g. **holen** (get him out), **lassen** (let him out), **bringen** (throw him off, knock him out of), **schlagen** (knock him out of).
target_language_example: Kannst du ihn aus dem Wasser holen?
native_language_example: Can you get him out of the water?

meaning: "him alone" / "in peace" (often in: "Lass ihn in Ruhe!")
additional_notes: Most commonly used with verbs like „lassen“ or „in Ruhe lassen“ to mean “leave him alone” or “stop bothering him.” „in Ruhe“ can also mean “quietly / without being disturbed.” The pronoun changes with the person: „mich in Ruhe“, „dich in Ruhe“, „sie in Ruhe“, etc.
target_language_example: Lass ihn in Ruhe, er will gerade nicht reden.
native_language_example: Leave him alone; he doesn’t want to talk right now.

meaning: “him with a …” (using something as the tool/means).
additional_notes: This is the pattern **jemanden + mit + einem/einer/einem + noun** to say what you use to do something to someone (instrument/means): *Sie überraschte ihn mit einem Geschenk.* It’s a fragment that depends on a verb (e.g., wecken, erschießen, überraschen). Case: **ihn** = accusative (direct object); **mit** always takes **dative** → *mit einem Eimer, mit einem Gewehr, mit einem Kissen, mit einem Trick*.
target_language_example: Er öffnete die Dose und fütterte ihn mit einem Löffel.
native_language_example: He opened the can and fed him with a spoon.

additional_notes: Used with a verb of movement (e.g., bringen, mitnehmen, schicken) to say someone (here: a male person = ihn) is going back home. "nach Hause" means "(to) home" (direction), not "zu Hause" (= "at home").
target_language_example: Ich bringe ihn nach Hause, weil er müde ist.
native_language_example: I'm taking him home because he's tired.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "(jdn.) fragen" + "nach" + dative to ask for information: "jemanden nach etwas fragen" = "to ask someone about something / to ask for something." Here: "ihn" (accusative) = "him" and "seinem Namen" (dative) = "his name." Often appears as "Frag ihn nach seinem Namen" (informal) or "Fragen Sie ihn nach seinem Namen" (formal).
target_language_example: Kannst du ihn nach seinem Namen fragen?
native_language_example: Can you ask him his name?

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression. ihn is the accusative form of er and can mean 'him', or 'it' when it refers to a masculine noun. With nicht, it is used in negative sentences: Wir kennen ihn nicht = 'We don't know him.' English usually changes the word order.
target_language_example: Ich verstehe ihn nicht.
native_language_example: I don't understand him.

additional_notes: Used when someone stops doing something to/with him, or when something about him is no longer true (e.g., no longer love him, can’t calm him down anymore). It often goes with a verb: "ihn nicht mehr anrufen" (not call him anymore), "ihn nicht mehr lieben" (not love him anymore). Word order: pronoun "ihn" comes before "nicht mehr".
target_language_example: Ich kann ihn nicht mehr sehen.
native_language_example: I can’t see him anymore.

additional_notes: This is the accusative pronoun ihn (“him”) combined with nie (“never”). It’s used to say you never do/did something to him: Ich habe ihn nie gesehen. In normal word order, ihn often comes before nie (pronoun before adverb), but the exact position can vary depending on what’s emphasized.
target_language_example: Ich werde ihn nie vergessen.
native_language_example: I will never forget him.

additional_notes: Used to say you have seen a man/person before. Common with questions ("Hast du ihn schon einmal gesehen?") or in the past ("weil ich ihn schon einmal gesehen hatte"). "schon einmal" means "before" or "once already".
target_language_example: Ich glaube, ich habe ihn schon einmal gesehen.
native_language_example: I think I've seen him before.

meaning: him for help (as in: to ask him for help).
additional_notes: Usually used with the verb "bitten": "jemanden um Hilfe bitten" = "to ask someone for help". "ihn" is the accusative form of "er" (him). You can swap the person: "sie um Hilfe bitten" (ask her), "dich um Hilfe bitten" (ask you).
target_language_example: Kann ich dich bitten, ihn um Hilfe zu bitten?
native_language_example: Can I ask you to ask him for help?

additional_notes:
This is not a fixed phrase by itself. It shows the common German pattern with **separable verbs**, where the object pronoun (**ihn** = “him/it”) comes in the middle and the separable prefix (**um**) goes to the end: 
- **umdrehen** → *Tom drehte ihn um.* = “Tom turned it over/around.” 
- **umbringen** → *Ihr bringt ihn um.* = “You’re killing him.” 
- **umlegen** (in some contexts) → *Siehst du ihn, legst du ihn um.* can mean “If you see him, you take him down/kill him.” 
So the exact meaning depends on the full verb (the part before *ihn* plus *um* together).
target_language_example: Dreh ihn um, ich will die Rückseite sehen.
native_language_example: Turn it over; I want to see the back.

additional_notes: „umbringen“ means “to kill” (often in the sense of murdering). „ihn“ is the accusative pronoun “him.” The word order can change for emphasis (e.g., „Ihn umbringen würde sie“ = “She would kill him”). In questions you’ll often see: „Willst/Wirst du ihn umbringen?“
target_language_example: Sie will ihn umbringen, aber er kann fliehen.
native_language_example: She wants to kill him, but he can escape.

meaning: “him all the more / even more (because of that)”
additional_notes: Used to say you like/love someone even more due to a specific reason (often introduced with „weil“, „wegen“ + Genitive, or „denn“). Related pattern: „je …, umso …“ (“the …er, the …er”), but here it’s simply „umso mehr“ = “all the more / even more”. Word order often: „Ich mag ihn umso mehr, weil …“.
target_language_example: Ich schätze ihn umso mehr, weil er immer ehrlich ist.
native_language_example: I appreciate him even more because he’s always honest.

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression. ihn is the accusative form of er and means 'him'. In zu + infinitive constructions, German often puts the object before zu, so ihn zu + verb usually corresponds to English 'to [verb] him': ihn zu warnen = 'to warn him', ihn zu beeindrucken = 'to impress him'.
target_language_example: Es ist schwer, ihn zu verstehen.
native_language_example: It's hard to understand him.

additional_notes: "heiraten" means "to marry". "ihn" = "him" (accusative object). The "zu" + infinitive form is used after many verbs to express an action someone decides, promises, tries, or manages to do (e.g., "beschließen", "versprechen", "bitten", "überzeugen"). You can swap "ihn" for other pronouns/nouns: "sie zu heiraten" (to marry her), "dich zu heiraten" (to marry you), "Tom zu heiraten" (to marry Tom).
target_language_example: Ich kann mir vorstellen, ihn zu heiraten.
native_language_example: I can imagine marrying him.

additional_notes: A common German structure is **zu + infinitive** (“to + verb”), often used after verbs like *versuchen* (to try), *erlauben* (to allow), or in statements like *Ihn zu töten ist …* (“To kill him is …”). **ihn** is the accusative form of “he/him” (referring to a male person or animal). Putting **ihn** before **zu töten** can sound more emphatic, like “him, to kill (him)”.
target_language_example: Sie wollten ihn zu töten, aber die Polizei kam rechtzeitig.
native_language_example: They wanted to kill him, but the police arrived in time.

additional_notes: Used when a verb takes „zu“ + dative and the noun is masculine/neuter with „dem“, which contracts to „zum“. Common patterns: „jdn. zu etw. zwingen“ (force someone to do something) and „jdn. zu etw. wählen/ernennen“ (elect/appoint someone as something). Here, „ihn“ is the accusative object (him), and the following noun phrase after „zum“ is in the dative.
target_language_example: Der Chef ernannte ihn zum Teamleiter.
native_language_example: The boss appointed him (as) team leader.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like "sagen" (to say/tell) to report an instruction or request to a group: "Sag/Sagen Sie ihnen, sie sollen + Infinitiv". "ihnen" = to them; "sie" here means "they" (not "her"). "sollen" expresses what someone is supposed to do (an instruction), not what they want to do.
target_language_example: Sag ihnen, sie sollen leise sein.
native_language_example: Tell them to be quiet.

additional_notes: Used to address a group directly (“ihr” = you plural) in an angry, insulting way—often like shouting at people. Extremely offensive; avoid in polite or normal conversation.
target_language_example: Lasst mich in Ruhe, ihr Arschlöcher!
native_language_example: Leave me alone, you assholes!

meaning: her car; also: their car / your (formal) car (depending on context).
additional_notes:
"ihr" is a possessive determiner. It can mean:
- her (referring to "sie" = she)
- their (referring to "sie" = they)
- your (formal) (referring to "Sie" = you)
Which meaning is intended depends on the surrounding sentence and who is being talked about.
target_language_example: Ich sehe ihr Auto vor dem Haus.
native_language_example: I see her car in front of the house.

additional_notes:
"ihr" can mean "her" (to her) or "their" (to them), depending on context: 
- Maria musste ihr Auto verkaufen. = her car.
- Sie mussten ihr Auto verkaufen. = their car (if "Sie" = they).
Often used with modal verbs like "müssen" (have to) or "würde" (would). Word order: in a main clause with a modal, the full verb goes to the end ("... ihr Auto verkaufen").
target_language_example: Warum musste Maria ihr Auto verkaufen?
native_language_example: Why did Maria have to sell her car?

meaning: her money; their money (depending on context).
additional_notes: "ihr" is a possessive determiner meaning "her" (singular feminine) or "their" (plural). It changes with the case: e.g., nominative/accusative "ihr Geld", dative "ihrem Geld". Don’t confuse with capitalized "Ihr Geld" (= "your money" in formal address).
target_language_example: Sie spart ihr Geld für eine Reise.
native_language_example: She saves her money for a trip.

additional_notes: "ihr" is a possessive pronoun meaning "her" (or "their" depending on context). With "Gesicht" (face), it’s used both literally (a person’s face) and figuratively, e.g. "Die Sonne zeigte ihr Gesicht" = "The sun showed its face" (the sun comes out). Common with descriptions of emotions or appearance: "Ihr Gesicht hellte sich auf" (her face brightened), "Ihr Gesicht war feucht von Tränen" (her face was wet with tears).
target_language_example: Ich konnte ihr Gesicht kaum im Dunkeln erkennen.
native_language_example: I could barely make out her face in the dark.

additional_notes: "ihr" is a possessive determiner meaning "her" (or "their" depending on context). "Haar" is usually used as a mass noun in the singular to mean hair in general (like English "hair"), even though it can also mean a single hair. Often used with verbs like waschen (to wash), tragen (to wear), or werden (to become): e.g., "Ihr Haar wird grau" = "Her hair is turning gray."
target_language_example: Sie hat ihr Haar kurz geschnitten.
native_language_example: She cut her hair short.

meaning: her house; their house; your (formal) house.
additional_notes: "ihr" is a possessive word and its meaning depends on context: (1) her (3rd person singular feminine: "Sie" = she), (2) their (3rd person plural: "sie" = they), or (3) your (formal "Sie"). In the examples with "Sie" meaning "she" (e.g., "Sie verkaufte ..."), it means "her house". The form "ihr" agrees with the noun "Haus" (neuter), so it stays "ihr" in the nominative/accusative: "ihr Haus".
target_language_example: Sie möchte ihr Haus nächstes Jahr verkaufen.
native_language_example: She wants to sell her house next year.

meaning: her heart (literal or figurative: feelings, love, courage, character).
additional_notes:
Most literally it means the physical heart. Very often it’s used figuratively: 
- emotions/inner feelings (jemandem ihr Herz öffnen = to open her heart to someone)
- sadness (ihr Herz brach = her heart broke)
- personality/character (ein schwarzes Herz = a black heart)
- inner voice/instinct (auf ihr Herz hören = listen to her heart)
Also common in physical expressions like an ihr Herz drücken (= hold/press someone to her chest).
target_language_example: Sie nahm ihren Mut zusammen und öffnete ihm ihr Herz.
native_language_example: She gathered her courage and opened her heart to him.

additional_notes: "ihr" is the possessive form of "sie" (she/they). So "ihr Kind" usually means "her child." Depending on context, "ihr" can also mean "their" (plural) or "your" (formal); capitalization helps: "Ihr Kind" (capital I) = "your child" (formal).
target_language_example: Das ist eine Frau und ihr Kind!
native_language_example: That is a woman and her child!

additional_notes: “ihr” is the possessive pronoun “her” (also can mean “their,” depending on context). Common in set phrases like “jemandem ihr Leben anvertrauen” (to trust someone with her life) and “um ihr Leben kommen” (literally “to come around her life,” meaning “to die”).
target_language_example: Sie hat Angst um ihr Leben.
native_language_example: She is afraid for her life.

additional_notes: “ihr” is a possessive pronoun and can mean “her,” “their,” or “your” (formal) depending on context; in these examples it means “her.” “Mann” literally means “man,” but “ihr Mann” is commonly used to mean “her husband.” In the nominative (as the subject), it stays “ihr Mann”; in other cases it changes (e.g., “mit ihrem Mann” = with her husband).
target_language_example: Sie spricht oft über ihr Mann.
native_language_example: She often talks about her husband.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a woman’s husband and then describe him (job/nationality/where he is, etc.). Note: lowercase **ihr** usually means “her” (or “their” in other contexts). Capital **Ihr** would be the formal “your,” but with **Mann** it most often means “your husband.”
target_language_example: Ihr Mann ist heute im Büro.
native_language_example: Her husband is at the office today.

meaning: "her name" (or, formally, "your name" to one person).
additional_notes: "ihr" can mean (1) "her" (referring to a woman) or (2) formal "your" when addressing one person with "Sie". In questions like "Ihr Name?" it’s often a short, polite way to ask for someone’s name (e.g., at a reception desk). Watch capitalization: "Ihr" is also used for formal "your"; "ihr" can mean "her" or "their" depending on context.
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, wie ist Ihr Name?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what is your name?

meaning: “her name is” (sometimes: “their name is” / “your name is” formal).
additional_notes: “ihr” can mean **her**, **their**, or **your** (formal, to one person). In many everyday introductions, “Ihr Name ist …” is understood as **her name is …** from context (talking about a woman). In sentence 3 (“Ihr Name ist immer noch auf der Liste.”), it means the person’s name is still on the list.
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich glaube, ihr Name ist Anna.
native_language_example: Sorry, I think her name is Anna.

meaning: her son; their son (sometimes: your son, formal).
additional_notes: "ihr" is a possessive word that can mean "her", "their", or (with polite address) "your". Which one it is depends on context (and polite "your" is often written "Ihr" in formal writing). "ihr Sohn" is nominative (subject). Other common forms: "ihren Sohn" (accusative), "ihrem Sohn" (dative).
target_language_example: Ihr Sohn geht noch zur Schule.
native_language_example: Her son is still in school.

additional_notes: "ihr" can mean "her" (to/for a single female person) or "their" (to/for a group). In many sentences like these, it means "her" because the subject is "sie" (she). Note the capitalization: "ihr" (possessive) vs. "Ihr" (formal "your"), e.g. "Ihr Vater" = "your father" (formal).
target_language_example: Ihr Vater arbeitet in Berlin.
native_language_example: Her father works in Berlin.

additional_notes: "ihr" can mean "her" (to/for her) or "their" depending on context; "Vater" is a masculine noun (capitalized). Used to identify who someone’s father is or to state his nationality, job, or status. In questions you’ll often see: "Wer ist ihr Vater?" (Who is her/their father?)
target_language_example: Ihr Vater ist Arzt.
native_language_example: Her father is a doctor.

additional_notes: "ihr" is a possessive that can mean **her**, **their**, or **your** (to more than one person, or formal "your" = *Ihr*). In writing, **Ihr** (capital I) usually signals formal "your". "war" is the past tense of *sein* (to be), used to describe what someone/something **was** (job, state, opinion, etc.).
target_language_example: Sie sagte, ihr Vater war sehr streng.
native_language_example: She said her father was very strict.

additional_notes: "ihr" is a possessive word meaning "her" or "their" depending on context. In sentences with "sie" (she), it usually means "her": "Sie ging in ihr Zimmer." With "sie" meaning "they", it means "their": "Sie sind in ihr Zimmer gegangen." "Zimmer" means a room (often a bedroom in this context).
target_language_example: Nach dem Essen ging sie in ihr Zimmer.
native_language_example: After dinner she went to her room.

meaning: her whole life; her entire life.
additional_notes: Uses the possessive pronoun „ihr“ (= her / their) + „ganzes Leben“ (= whole life). It’s often used to talk about how long someone has lived somewhere or spent time/effort on something: „ihr ganzes Leben hier gelebt“, „ihr ganzes Leben dem Studium gewidmet“. Capitalize „Leben“ because it’s a noun.
target_language_example: Er hat ihr ganzes Leben in Berlin verbracht.
native_language_example: He spent her whole life in Berlin.

additional_notes: Means a novel written by a woman (“ihr” = “her”). Can refer to a specific author already known from context. Often used with verbs like „erscheinen“ (to be published/come out), „herauskommen“ (to come out), and „veröffentlicht werden“ (to be published). Note: If you capitalize „Ihr“ (Ihr neuer Roman), it can also mean “your (formal) new novel” in a sentence addressed to someone politely.
target_language_example: Ihr neuer Roman erscheint im April.
native_language_example: Her new novel comes out in April.

meaning: “you (plural) … that …” or “to her … that …” (with a dass-clause).
additional_notes: This is a very common pattern: a main clause with **ihr** plus a verb, followed by a subordinate clause starting with **dass** (“that”). **ihr** can mean **you (plural)** (e.g., *Denkt ihr, dass …?* = “Do you all think that …?”) or it can be the dative pronoun **to her** (e.g., *Du sagtest ihr, dass …* = “You told her that …”). Word order: after **dass**, the verb usually goes to the end of the subordinate clause.
target_language_example: Glaubt ihr, dass wir heute fertig werden?
native_language_example: Do you all believe that we’ll finish today?

meaning: 'you (plural)… that…' — addressing a group informally and introducing a subordinate clause with **daß**.
additional_notes: **ihr** is the informal 2nd-person plural pronoun (you all), used for friends, family, children, etc. **daß** (traditional spelling; modern: **dass**) introduces a subordinate clause; in that clause the conjugated verb typically goes to the end. Formal plural would be **Sie**.
target_language_example: Findet ihr, daß die Leute gemein zu euch sind?
native_language_example: Do you (all) think that people are mean to you?

additional_notes:
This is the combination of **ihr** + **was**.
- **ihr** can mean **“to her”** (dative singular): *Gib ihr …* / *Sag ihr …*
- **ihr** can also mean **“you (all)”** (2nd person plural): *Wusstet ihr …?*
- **was** means **“what”** and is used in questions (*Wusstet ihr, was …?* = “Did you know what …?”) and in indirect statements/requests (*Sag ihr, was …* = “Tell her what …”).
The comma often separates a main clause from the *was*-clause.
target_language_example: Sag ihr, was du gesehen hast.
native_language_example: Tell her what you saw.

additional_notes: Used when addressing several people directly ("ihr" = you plural). "Alle" emphasizes that you mean everyone in the group; it can also be used as an add-on for emphasis (e.g., "Ihr habt mir gefehlt, ihr alle."). Often used with a verb in plural: "ihr alle wisst", "ihr alle stellt".
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, ihr alle könnt morgen kommen.
native_language_example: I hope all of you can come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used when speaking to exactly two people and emphasizing that it’s both of them. Grammatically it’s the pronoun “ihr” (you, plural informal) + “beide” (both). Often appears in questions and instructions like “Kommt ihr beide?” or “Ihr beide geht jetzt…”.
target_language_example: Ich brauche, dass ihr beide mir kurz helft.
native_language_example: I need both of you to help me for a moment.

additional_notes: Used when speaking to exactly two people, often for emphasis. It’s made from the plural pronoun “ihr” (you all) + “beiden” (the two of you). You’ll also see other forms depending on case: “euch beide(n)” (you two, accusative/dative), “ihr zwei” (more casual), and similar patterns like “wir beide” (we two) or “sie beide” (those/they two).
target_language_example: Kommt ihr beiden morgen mit?
native_language_example: Are you two coming along tomorrow?

meaning: “you two … each other” (addressing two people informally).
additional_notes: Used when speaking to two people ("ihr beiden" = “you two”). With verbs like kennen, begegnen, anschauen, it often comes with the reflexive pronoun "euch" to mean “each other/one another” (e.g., "Kennt ihr beiden euch?" = “Do you two know each other?”). Word order is flexible in speech: "Kennt ihr euch beide?" is also common.
target_language_example: Habt ihr beiden euch schon mal getroffen?
native_language_example: Have you two met (each other) before?

additional_notes: "Ihr" is the informal plural "you" (addressing more than one person). "brauchen" means "to need" (often + a noun: "Ihr braucht einen Schlüssel.") or + "zu" + infinitive: "Ihr braucht euch nicht zu verstecken." In everyday speech, "ihr braucht nicht …" can mean "you don’t have to …"; with emphasis like "gar nicht" it means "really don’t need to".
target_language_example: Ihr braucht einen Schlüssel.
native_language_example: You (all) need a key.

additional_notes: Usually appears as part of a question or statement like "Habt ihr daran gedacht?" or "Ihr habt daran gedacht." It comes from the verb phrase **an etwas denken** (to think of something / remember something). **daran** = "da-" + "an" and refers back to a thing/idea already known ("about it/at it"). **ihr** is the informal "you" for a group of people.
target_language_example: Habt ihr daran gedacht, die Tickets mitzunehmen?
native_language_example: Did you remember to take the tickets with you?

meaning: you (all) paid attention to it / made sure of it.
additional_notes: From the verb phrase „auf etwas achten“ = “to pay attention to something / to make sure of something.” „darauf“ refers back to something previously mentioned (≈ “to it/that”). Often used in questions like „Habt ihr darauf geachtet …?“ or statements like „Ihr habt darauf geachtet, dass …“.
target_language_example: Habt ihr darauf geachtet, die Tür abzuschließen?
native_language_example: Did you make sure to lock the door?

meaning: “to her … last time” / “(I/you/etc.) … to her the last time.”
additional_notes: This is a nonstandard spelling. In standard German you would normally write: “ihr das letzte Mal” (separate words; “Mal” capitalized). “ihr” is the dative form meaning “to her,” and “das letzte Mal” means “the last time.” Often used in sentences like “Ich habe ihr das letzte Mal gesagt, …” (“I told her last time …”).
target_language_example: Ich habe ihr das letztemal gesagt, dass ich keine Zeit habe.
native_language_example: I told her last time that I don’t have time.

additional_notes: A compositional combination of ihr (“you” when speaking to more than one person informally) and das (“it/that”). In German these words can appear next to each other before or after the verb, but in natural English you usually translate them with the verb in between, e.g. ihr das tun = “do it/that”, ihr das getan habt = “you did it/that”.
target_language_example: Ich frage mich, ob ihr das schon wisst.
native_language_example: I wonder whether you already know that.

meaning: "to/for her, that, for me" (pronoun phrase: ‘her that for me’).
additional_notes: This isn’t a fixed idiom—it's a common combination of pronouns used inside a larger sentence. Typical use: with a verb like geben/sagen/bringen/schicken: „Kannst du ihr das für mich geben?“ = ‘Can you give her that for me?’ Grammar: „ihr“ is dative (‘to/for her’), „das“ is accusative (‘that/it’), „für mich“ means ‘for me’. Word order often places the dative pronoun before the accusative pronoun: ihr + das.
target_language_example: Kannst du ihr das für mich geben?
native_language_example: Can you give her that for me?

meaning: “(to her / you all) … really (that)?” (a sentence fragment used for emphasis).
additional_notes:
This isn’t a fixed expression by itself; it’s typically part of a longer sentence, often a question. 
- ihr can mean “to her” (dative of sie) or “you (plural)” depending on context.
- das = “that/it”; wirklich = “really”.
Common full sentences include: “Meinst du/ihr das wirklich?” (Do you really mean that?) or “Sagt ihr das wirklich?” (Are you really saying that?)
target_language_example: Meint ihr das wirklich?
native_language_example: Do you really mean that?

meaning: “you (all) think” / “you think” (to more than one person).
additional_notes: "Ihr" is the informal plural form of "you" (addressing two or more people). "Denkt" is the verb "denken" (to think) in the present tense: "ihr denkt". Often used in comparisons like "..., als ihr denkt" (“...than you think”) or to ask for opinions: "Was denkt ihr?" / "Sagt mir, was ihr denkt."
target_language_example: Es ist einfacher, als ihr denkt.
native_language_example: It’s easier than you think.

meaning: 'you (plural) ... (then/anyway?)' — used in questions to add emphasis, surprise, or impatience.
additional_notes: In questions, **denn** is a modal particle: it doesn’t mean the time word “then”. It makes the question sound more emotional/insistent (e.g., surprise, disbelief, annoyance). **ihr** is the informal plural “you” (addressing more than one person). Word order varies depending on the question word: *Was macht ihr denn?*, *Wie kommt ihr denn darauf?*
target_language_example: Warum seid ihr denn so spät?
native_language_example: Why are you (all) so late, then?/Why on earth are you so late?

additional_notes: Uses the modal verb **dürfen** with **ihr** (2nd person plural). It’s used to give permission or say what is allowed (often to a group, friends, family, children). With **nicht** it means **must not / are not allowed to**: *Ihr dürft hier nicht rauchen.* (You’re not allowed to smoke here.) Not used for the formal “you” (**Sie dürfen**).
target_language_example: Ihr dürft jetzt reinkommen.
native_language_example: You (all) may come in now.

additional_notes: “wagen” means “to dare.” “ihr” is the 2nd-person plural pronoun (“you all”). “es” often functions as a placeholder for the action you’re daring to do, which is then expressed with an infinitive clause (often with “zu”): “Wagt ihr es, … zu …?” The phrase is common in challenges, dares, or dramatic questions.
target_language_example: Wagt ihr es wagen, nachts allein nach Hause zu gehen?
native_language_example: Do you (all) dare to walk home alone at night?

meaning: 'you (plural) … something' or 'something for her/them' (depends on context).
additional_notes:
"ihr" has two common uses:
1) "ihr" = "you" (plural, informal) as the subject: "Hört ihr etwas?" = "Do you (all) hear something?".
2) "ihr" = "to her" / "to them" (dative pronoun): "Holen Sie ihr etwas zu essen!" = "Get her something to eat!".
"etwas" means "something" and is often used in questions: "Sucht ihr etwas?" = "Are you looking for something?".
target_language_example: Könnt ihr ihr etwas sagen?
native_language_example: Can you (all) tell her something?

additional_notes: A combination of pronouns: ihr is informal plural subject ('you all') and euch is the object/reflexive form. Together they often appear with reflexive verbs, where English may say 'yourselves', or with reciprocal meaning, where English says 'each other'. The exact translation depends on the verb and context.
target_language_example: Versteht ihr euch gut?
native_language_example: Do you get along well?

meaning: "you (plural) … yourselves already" (often in questions like "Have you already …?").
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it’s a common word sequence: **ihr** = “you” (plural), **euch** = reflexive “yourselves/each other” (used with reflexive verbs), and **schon** = “already.” You’ll often see it in questions such as **"Habt ihr euch schon …?"** or **"Seid ihr euch schon …?"** depending on the verb.
target_language_example: Habt ihr euch schon entschieden?
native_language_example: Have you already decided?

additional_notes: This is a common fragment from the reflexive expression **sich sicher sein** (“to be sure/certain”). With **ihr** (2nd person plural, informal), you often hear it in questions like **Seid ihr euch sicher?** (“Are you sure?”) or statements like **Ihr seid euch sicher.** (“You’re sure.”). For formal “you,” use **Sind Sie sich sicher?**
target_language_example: Seid ihr euch sicher, dass das der richtige Weg ist?
native_language_example: Are you sure that this is the right way?

additional_notes: Used when speaking to more than one person with the informal "ihr" (like "you all"). "Eure" is the possessive "your" that matches the noun it describes (usually plural or feminine nominative/accusative): eure Kinder (your children), eure Medikamente (your medications), eure Freizeit (your free time). Other common forms are euer (masc./neut.), euren (masc. acc./dat. pl.), eurem (dat. masc./neut.), eurer (dat./gen. fem.).
target_language_example: Habt ihr eure Hausaufgaben schon gemacht?
native_language_example: Have you (all) already done your homework?

meaning: “you (plural) … your …” (addressing a group, with a masculine/neuter thing in the accusative).
additional_notes: Used when speaking to more than one person: **ihr** = “you all/you (plural)”. **euren** is the accusative form of **euer** (“your”) used with a masculine singular noun (e.g., *euren Bericht, euren Kaffee, euren Sohn, euren Ölfilter*) or with plural nouns in accusative. Often appears in questions: *Besucht ihr euren …?* = “Do you (all) visit your …?”
target_language_example: Habt ihr euren Ausweis dabei?
native_language_example: Do you all have your ID with you?

meaning: "you (all) came" / "you (all) have come" (used in a subordinate clause).
additional_notes: Perfect tense of **kommen** with **sein**: **ihr seid gekommen** = “you all came/you have come.” In a **dass**-clause (or other subordinate clause), the conjugated verb (**seid**) goes to the end: **dass ihr gekommen seid** = “that you came / that you’ve come.” **ihr** is the informal plural “you” (talking to a group).
target_language_example: Schön, dass ihr gekommen seid.
native_language_example: Nice that you came.

additional_notes: "ihr" is the informal 2nd-person plural pronoun (used when talking to more than one person). "gestern Abend" means "yesterday evening" (often also translated as "last night"). Word order depends on the sentence, e.g. "Was habt ihr gestern Abend gemacht?" (= What did you do last night?). Note: If you see "ihr" used as "to her" (dative), it’s usually in a different structure (e.g. "Ich habe ihr gestern Abend geschrieben." = I wrote to her last night).
target_language_example: Was habt ihr gestern Abend gemacht?
native_language_example: What did you do last night?

additional_notes: Used when talking to more than one person (plural "you"). This is the Perfekt of **tun** (to do): **ihr** (you-plural) + **habt** (have) + **getan** (done). In subordinate clauses with words like **was** (“what”) the conjugated verb **habt** often goes to the end: **… was ihr getan habt** (“… what you have done”).
target_language_example: Danke für alles, was ihr getan habt.
native_language_example: Thank you for everything you’ve done.

additional_notes: The informal plural form of haben, used when speaking to more than one person. It can mean possession, but very often it is also the helping verb in the present perfect: ihr habt gemacht = 'you have done' or simply 'you did'.
target_language_example: Ihr habt heute viel gelernt.
native_language_example: You all learned a lot today.

meaning: 'you (all) have...' (talking to more than one person).
additional_notes: "Ihr" addresses a group (plural "you"). "habt" is the present tense of "haben" used as an auxiliary for the Perfekt (past): "ihr habt ... gelassen/getroffen/getauscht/gebrochen/kaputtgemacht" = "you (all) have/you (all) did ...". "die" is the definite article "the" for feminine singular or plural nouns; in these examples it’s used in the accusative (direct object), e.g., "die Kekse", "die Regel", "die Show".
target_language_example: Ihr habt die Tür offen gelassen.
native_language_example: You (all) left the door open.

additional_notes: "Ihr" addresses more than one person (you all). "Habt" is the 2nd-person plural form of "haben" and is often used to form the Perfekt (past tense): "ihr habt" + past participle (e.g., "geschafft", "erklärt", "versprochen"). "Es" usually refers to something already known from context (it/that), and can be a placeholder object ("Ihr habt es geschafft" = you managed to do it).
target_language_example: Ihr habt es schon gehört, oder?
native_language_example: You’ve already heard it, right?

meaning: "you (all) have ..." (perfect tense with the reflexive pronoun "euch").
additional_notes: Used with reflexive or reciprocal verbs in the Perfekt (present perfect). "Ihr" = you (plural, informal), "habt" = have, and "euch" = yourselves/each other. It must be followed by a past participle (e.g., "ihr habt euch geirrt" = you were mistaken; "ihr habt euch Zeit gelassen" = you took your time).
target_language_example: Ihr habt euch verlaufen.
native_language_example: You (all) got lost.

additional_notes: "ihr" = you (plural/informal). "habt" is the 2nd person plural form of "haben" (to have). "eure" means "your" and is used with feminine singular nouns (e.g., "eure Arbeit") and with plural nouns (e.g., "eure Ziele", "eure Regenschirme"). For masculine/neuter singular, use "euer" (e.g., "euer Handy"). Often followed by a noun, and sometimes by a past participle to form the present perfect (e.g., "ihr habt eure Regenschirme vergessen").
target_language_example: Ihr habt eure Hausaufgaben schon gemacht.
native_language_example: You all have already done your homework.

meaning: “you (all) have … me” / “you guys have … me” (addressing more than one person).
additional_notes: Used with **ihr** (2nd person plural) when talking to a group you address informally. **habt** is the plural form of **haben** and often forms the **Perfekt** (present perfect) with a past participle: *Ihr habt mich gesehen/found/überrascht.* You usually add the participle or another object to complete the meaning.
target_language_example: Ihr habt mich total falsch verstanden.
native_language_example: You guys completely misunderstood me.

meaning: “you (all) have … (to/for me)” (plural informal ‘you’ + Perfekt with haben).
additional_notes: Used when talking to more than one person (plural informal: ihr). “habt” is the present tense of “haben” used to form the Perfekt (present perfect/past) with a past participle at the end: “Ihr habt mir geholfen.” “mir” is the dative pronoun meaning “to me / for me,” common with verbs like fehlen (miss), leid tun (feel sorry for), versprechen (promise), geben (give), verderben (ruin).
target_language_example: Ihr habt mir wirklich geholfen.
native_language_example: You all really helped me.

additional_notes: Used when speaking to more than one person ("ihr" = you plural). "habt" is the present of "haben" used to form the Perfekt (present perfect): "ihr habt" + past participle (e.g., geglaubt/gesagt/vertraut). "mir" is dative = "to me". "nie" (never) usually comes before the past participle at the end.
target_language_example: Ihr habt mir nie geholfen.
native_language_example: You never helped me.

additional_notes: Used when addressing two or more people informally (“you all”). It’s the present-tense form of **haben** with **ihr**. Common for possession (Ihr habt drei Stifte.), family (Ihr habt doch Kinder.), or abstract things (Ihr habt keine Manieren. = you have no manners; Ihr habt nur noch einen Ausweg. = you only have one way out left). Not used for the formal plural **Sie haben**.
target_language_example: Ihr habt doch Kinder.
native_language_example: You do have children, don’t you?

meaning: “you (plural) have a …” (talking to more than one person; before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: "ihr" is the informal plural “you” (to friends, family, kids, or a group you’re on first-name terms with). "habt" is the 2nd-person plural form of "haben" (to have). "eine" is “a/an” for feminine nouns (e.g., eine Basis, eine Alternative). For formal plural “you,” use "Sie haben eine …".
target_language_example: Ihr habt eine gute Idee.
native_language_example: You all have a good idea.

additional_notes: *Ihr* is the informal plural “you” (talking to more than one person). *Hattet* is the simple past (Präteritum) of *haben* (“to have”). Common in storytelling and in set phrases like *Ihr hattet Glück/Pech/Recht* (“You were lucky/unlucky/right”). In questions it often implies “had” in the sense of “were you going to / did you have”: *Ihr hattet mir etwas zu sagen?* = “Did you have something to tell me?” (literally “You had something to tell me?”).
target_language_example: Ihr hattet gestern keine Zeit.
native_language_example: You (all) didn’t have time yesterday.

additional_notes: "ihr" is the informal second-person plural pronoun (addressing two or more people: "you all"). "heute" means "today" and is often placed after the verb in questions ("Arbeitet ihr heute?") or after the subject in statements. Don’t confuse "ihr" (you-plural / her-their) with "Ihr" (capitalized, an old-fashioned polite "you").
target_language_example: Seid ihr heute Abend frei?
native_language_example: Are you (all) free this evening?

additional_notes: "ihr" is the informal 2nd-person plural pronoun (talking to more than one person). "heute Abend" means "this evening/tonight" (also commonly written "heute abend" in casual contexts). Often used in questions like "Kommt ihr heute Abend...?".
target_language_example: Kommt ihr heute Abend mit?
native_language_example: Are you guys coming along tonight?

additional_notes: "ihr" usually means "you" when speaking to more than one person (informal plural). "heute Morgen" is a very common time expression meaning "this morning"—in standard spelling, "Morgen" is capitalized because it’s a noun. Word order often varies: "Ihr wart heute Morgen ..." / "Heute Morgen wart ihr ...".
target_language_example: Wart ihr heute Morgen schon im Supermarkt?
native_language_example: Were you (all) already at the supermarket this morning?

additional_notes: "Ihr" is the informal plural "you" (to more than one person). "Hättet" is Konjunktiv II (subjunctive) of "haben" for "ihr". It’s commonly used with a past participle to talk about unreal/imagined past situations or to express criticism/advice about the past: "Ihr hättet … (nicht) sollen" = "You (guys) should (not) have …" It can also appear in reported speech where English often uses simple past: "Ich dachte, ihr hättet …" = "I thought you had …".
target_language_example: Ihr hättet mich vorher anrufen sollen.
native_language_example: You (guys) should have called me earlier.

additional_notes: "ihr" addresses more than one person ("you all / you guys"). "in letzter Zeit" means "lately / recently" and is often used in questions like "Habt ihr in letzter Zeit ...?" ("Have you (all) ... lately?"). Word order varies; you’ll also commonly hear "Habt ihr ... in letzter Zeit?".
target_language_example: Habt ihr in letzter Zeit viel Stress gehabt?
native_language_example: Have you guys been very stressed lately?

additional_notes: Used with **ihr** (2nd person plural “you all”) plus **jeden Tag** (“every day”). In a statement, the verb is usually in position 2 (e.g., *Ihr duscht jeden Tag.*). In a yes/no question, the verb comes first (e.g., *Duscht ihr jeden Tag?*). **jeden Tag** is a common time expression (literally “each day”).
target_language_example: Geht ihr jeden Tag zur Schule?
native_language_example: Do you (all) go to school every day?

meaning: "you (plural) can" / "you all can" (are able to; may).
additional_notes: Used when speaking to more than one person ("ihr" = you plural). "könnt" is the present-tense form of "können" for "ihr". Depending on context, it can mean ability ("You can speak German"), permission ("You may stay with me"), or a suggestion/option ("You can wait in the car").
target_language_example: Wenn ihr wollt, ihr könnt morgen vorbeikommen.
native_language_example: If you want, you can come by tomorrow.

meaning: "you (plural) can ..." (often used with a reflexive verb: "you can ... yourselves").
additional_notes: "Ihr" is "you" when talking to more than one person. "Könnt" is the present-tense form of "können" (can/to be able to). "Euch" is the reflexive object for "ihr" (yourselves/you all). It’s very common before reflexive verbs like "euch ausruhen" (to rest), "euch freuen" (to be happy), or expressions like "ihr könnt euch sicher sein" (you can be sure). Word order: Ihr könnt euch + infinitive at the end (e.g., "Ihr könnt euch heute freinehmen.").
target_language_example: Ihr könnt euch später bei mir melden.
native_language_example: You (all) can get back to me later.

meaning: "you (all) can … me" (you are able to … / you’re allowed to …).
additional_notes: Used with a following verb to say what a group of people can do to/with you: Ihr könnt mich anrufen. = You can call me. On its own (often with "alle mal": "Ihr könnt mich alle mal!") it’s an insulting way to dismiss people (roughly: “You can all get lost / screw you”).
target_language_example: Ihr könnt mich jederzeit anrufen.
native_language_example: You can call me anytime.

additional_notes: "Ihr" is the informal 2nd-person plural pronoun ("you all"). "Könntet" is Konjunktiv II of "können" and is often used to make suggestions more polite/less direct (like "you could...") or to talk about possibilities in an imagined situation ("you might..."). In conditional warnings it can mean "could end up" (e.g., "ihr könntet entlassen werden" = "you could be fired").
target_language_example: Ihr könntet später vorbeikommen, wenn ihr Zeit habt.
native_language_example: You could come by later if you have time.

meaning: her last year / their last year (e.g., final year at school, last year of something).
additional_notes: "ihr" can mean "her" (referring to *sie* = she) or "their" (referring to *sie* = they). "letztes" means "last" (not "latest"). With the neuter noun *das Jahr*, you get *ihr letztes Jahr* (nominative/accusative). Often used for someone’s final year in school/university or the last year of a job, project, etc.
target_language_example: Sie denkt oft an ihr letztes Jahr an der Universität.
native_language_example: She often thinks about her last year at university.

meaning: "you (plural)" + "me" (used when talking to several people: you … me).
additional_notes: "ihr" is the subject pronoun for addressing multiple people informally (like "you all" / "you guys"). "mich" is the direct-object form of "ich" ("me"). You’ll usually see them with a verb in between or nearby (e.g., "ihr habt mich…", "ignoriert ihr mich?", "dass ihr mich…"). For polite/formal address to one or more people, German uses "Sie" instead of "ihr" ("Sie mich" in similar patterns).
target_language_example: Habt ihr mich verstanden?
native_language_example: Did you (all) understand me?

additional_notes: This is a common pronoun combination: **ihr** = “you all” (plural, informal; used with friends/family), and **mir** = “to me” (dative object). You see it with verbs that take a dative object (e.g., *helfen*, *bringen*, *sagen*) or in expressions like *ihr seid mir wichtig* (“you are important to me”). Word order can change depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Vielen Dank, dass ihr mir geholfen habt!
native_language_example: Thanks a lot for helping me!

additional_notes: A verb phrase with the subject pronoun "ihr" (you all), the dative pronoun "mir" (to me), and the infinitive "sagen" (to say/tell). It’s most commonly used with another verb, especially in questions like: "Könnt ihr mir sagen, …?" (Can you tell me …?).
target_language_example: Könnt ihr mir sagen, wo der Bahnhof ist?
native_language_example: Can you tell me where the train station is?

additional_notes: "ihr" usually means "you" (plural, informal) and is often used in contrasts like "ich ... aber ihr ..." ("I ..., but you ..."). "mit dem" means "with the" or can imply "by/using the" with a masculine/neuter noun in the dative case (e.g., "mit dem Auto" = "by car"). Without more context, this is just a sentence fragment that needs a following noun.
target_language_example: Ich komme zu Fuß, aber ihr mit dem Auto.
native_language_example: I'm coming on foot, but you (all) by car.

additional_notes: Used when talking to a group ("ihr" = you all). After "mit" you use the dative case, so it becomes "eurem/eurer/euren" depending on the noun; with plural nouns it’s often "euren" (e.g., "mit euren Freunden"). It can be neutral in questions ("Seid ihr mit euren Hausaufgaben fertig?") or sound annoyed/blaming in complaints ("Ihr mit euren …!").
target_language_example: Ihr mit euren Fragen – ich brauche erst mal eine Pause.
native_language_example: You and your questions—I need a break first.

additional_notes: "Ihr" addresses a group of people informally (friends, kids, classmates), like "you all". "Müsst" is the 2nd-person plural form of "müssen" (to have to / must). Used for obligations, strong advice, or a strong assumption (e.g., "Ihr müsst verrückt sein" = "You must be crazy").
target_language_example: Ihr müsst jetzt leise sein.
native_language_example: You all have to be quiet now.

additional_notes: Used when speaking to a group in the informal “ihr” form, and it’s followed by a reflexive verb (a verb that takes “sich”, here “euch”): z.B. euch fragen, euch umdrehen, euch an etwas halten, euch helfen lassen. The formal version is “Sie müssen sich …”.
target_language_example: Ihr müsst euch beeilen, sonst verpassen wir den Zug.
native_language_example: You (all) have to hurry, otherwise we’ll miss the train.

additional_notes: Addressing more than one person (2nd person plural). Expresses obligation/necessity. Note: In modern German spelling, this is usually written „ihr müsst“ (with -ss); „ihr müßt“ is the older spelling. Often followed by an infinitive: „ihr müßt mehr üben“.
target_language_example: Ihr müßt diesen Bericht noch einmal neu schreiben.
native_language_example: You (all) have to rewrite this report once again.

meaning: 'you (plural) have to / must' (often used with a reflexive verb: 'you must … yourselves').
additional_notes: "Ihr" is "you" addressing a group (friends, kids, students). "müßt" (also spelled "müsst" in modern German) is from "müssen" = "must / have to". "euch" is the reflexive pronoun for "you (plural)" and is used with reflexive verbs like "sich beeilen" (to hurry), "sich anstrengen" (to make an effort), "sich an etwas halten" (to stick to something), and "sich verhalten" (to behave). This phrase is common in instructions and rules.
target_language_example: Ihr müßt euch jetzt entscheiden.
native_language_example: You (all) have to decide now.

additional_notes: "ihr" is the informal 2nd-person plural pronoun ("you" to a group). "noch" usually means "still" or "yet". Together it commonly appears in questions like "Macht ihr noch ...?" (Are you still ...?) or "Wie weit müsst ihr noch?" (How much farther do you still have to go?).
target_language_example: Seid ihr noch im Büro?
native_language_example: Are you still at the office?

additional_notes: "ihr" is the informal plural "you" (talking to two or more people). "noch immer" means "still" and is often interchangeable with "immer noch". You’ll usually see this phrase as part of a full sentence, e.g., in questions: "Seid ihr noch immer …?" ("Are you still …?").
target_language_example: Seid ihr noch immer hier?
native_language_example: Are you still here?

additional_notes: “Ihr” is the informal/plural “you” (talking to more than one person). “Sagtet” is simple past of sagen (“you said”). The particle “doch” adds emphasis that this was already said/known and can sound like a reminder or mild contradiction (“after all / you did say …”). Often followed by reported speech with Konjunktiv I/II (e.g., brauche, seien, wäret).
target_language_example: Ihr sagtet doch, ihr hättet schon bezahlt.
native_language_example: But you said you’d already paid.

meaning: 'you (plural) already' / used to say that a group has already done something or has been doing something for some time.
additional_notes: "ihr" = informal plural "you" (addressing more than one person). "schon" commonly means "already" and is often used with "Wie lange ...?" to ask how long an ongoing situation has been true up to now (English often omits "already" here). It can also add mild emphasis/reminder in statements (e.g., "Das hättet ihr schon gestern tun sollen.").
target_language_example: Wie lange wartet ihr schon?
native_language_example: How long have you been waiting?

additional_notes: Used mostly in questions, especially with the present perfect: „Habt ihr schon einmal …?“ It addresses a group of people with „ihr“ (plural ‘you’). „schon einmal“ literally means ‘already once’, but in this pattern it usually means ‘ever/before’ (asking about life experience).
target_language_example: Habt ihr schon einmal in Deutschland gelebt?
native_language_example: Have you ever lived in Germany?

meaning: "have you (plural) ever (had/seen) a …?" (beginning of a question).
additional_notes: This is a sentence fragment often used at the start of a question, typically with a verb before it, e.g. "Habt ihr schon einmal einen …?" = "Have you ever had/seen a …?". "ihr" addresses a group of people (you all). "schon einmal" means "ever / at some point before". "einen" is the masculine accusative form of "ein" and must be followed by a masculine noun (e.g. "einen Hund", "einen Film").
target_language_example: Habt ihr schon einmal einen Film auf Deutsch gesehen?
native_language_example: Have you ever watched a movie in German?

additional_notes: Used in questions to ask a group of people (ihr = plural “you”) whether they have ever visited a place. It’s typically followed by a location, e.g. „Wart ihr schon einmal in Berlin?“ (often with the verb „sein“: „wart/seid ihr …“).
target_language_example: Wart ihr schon einmal in Hamburg?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Hamburg?

additional_notes: Common in spoken questions, usually as part of a larger sentence like „Habt ihr schon mal …?“ or „Seid ihr schon mal …?“ It asks whether the group has had the experience at least once in the past. „schon mal“ is a very common way to say “ever (before)” in casual conversation.
target_language_example: Habt ihr schon mal Berliner Pfannkuchen gegessen?
native_language_example: Have you guys ever eaten Berlin doughnuts?

additional_notes: "Ihr" is the informal "you" for more than one person (talking to friends, family, kids). "Seht" is the 2nd-person plural form of "sehen" (to see).
