target_language_example: Die Frau liegt im Sterben, bitte rufen Sie einen Arzt.
native_language_example: The woman is dying; please call a doctor.

meaning: in the lurch; abandoned/let down (usually in: „jdn. im Stich lassen“).
additional_notes: Most often used with „lassen“: „jemanden im Stich lassen“ = to abandon someone or not support them when they need you. Can also be used for things: „Mein Gedächtnis lässt mich im Stich“ = my memory is failing me. Neutral register (not slang).
target_language_example: Bitte lass mich jetzt nicht im Stich.
native_language_example: Please don’t leave me in the lurch now.

additional_notes: Usually appears as part of the verb phrase „jemanden im Stich lassen“ (Perfekt: „hat … im Stich gelassen“) = to abandon/let someone down. The person being abandoned is in the accusative: „Er hat mich im Stich gelassen.“ It often implies you needed help/support and the other person failed you, sometimes at a crucial moment.
target_language_example: Eine meiner besten Freundinnen hat mich im Stich gelassen.
native_language_example: One of my best (female) friends abandoned me / let me down.

meaning: to abandon / let (someone) down (when they need you)
additional_notes: Used with a person or group as the direct object: jemanden im Stich lassen. Typical in contexts of need, trouble, or responsibility (friends, family, children). Very common in the negative: jemanden nicht im Stich lassen (“not to abandon/let someone down”).
target_language_example: Ich kann meine Familie nicht im Stich lassen.
native_language_example: I can’t abandon my family / I can’t let my family down.

additional_notes: "im" = "in dem" and is used with places/buildings when you mean being inside/at that location. Common with verbs like einkaufen (to shop), kaufen (to buy), bekommen (to get), verlieren (to lose). It can also be used for events happening there (e.g., es hat im Supermarkt gebrannt).
target_language_example: Ich treffe dich im Supermarkt an der Kasse.
native_language_example: I’ll meet you in the supermarket at the checkout.

additional_notes: Used to say where something is located in the southern part of a place. Often followed by a genitive country/region name: „im Süden Italiens/Russlands“ (= in the south of Italy/Russia).
target_language_example: Meine Großeltern wohnen im Süden Deutschlands.
native_language_example: My grandparents live in the south of Germany.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what happens in the classroom/lesson time. Grammar: "im" = "in dem" (dative) + "Unterricht" (lesson/class). Often with verbs like "aufpassen" (pay attention), "fehlen" (be absent), "langweilig/öde" (boring).
target_language_example: Im Unterricht darfst du dein Handy nicht benutzen.
native_language_example: In class you’re not allowed to use your phone.

meaning: fell asleep in class (during a lesson).
additional_notes: Uses the verb phrase „einschlafen“ (to fall asleep) in the past („eingeschlafen“). With „im Unterricht“ it means it happened during class/while the teacher was teaching. Often used with „schon mal“ to ask if it has ever happened: „Bist du schon mal im Unterricht eingeschlafen?“
target_language_example: Ich bin gestern im Unterricht eingeschlafen.
native_language_example: I fell asleep in class yesterday.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "sein" to say someone is away from work/school for vacation ("Ich bin im Urlaub"). "im" = "in dem" and is used here with the dative to mean being in a state/period of vacation. Common in questions about duration: "Wie lange bist du im Urlaub?"
target_language_example: Nächste Woche bin ich im Urlaub.
native_language_example: Next week I’m on vacation.

additional_notes: Used to compare two things, often to show a difference in size, importance, quality, etc. It is followed by the thing you’re comparing to (dative): im Vergleich zu meinem Bruder, im Vergleich zu dem alten Modell.
target_language_example: Im Vergleich zu letztem Jahr ist es heute viel wärmer.
native_language_example: Compared to last year, it’s much warmer today.

additional_notes: Used for actions done before a later event or deadline (e.g., paying, reserving, informing someone). Common collocations: „im Voraus bezahlen“ (pay in advance), „im Voraus reservieren“ (reserve/book in advance), „im Voraus Bescheid geben“ (let someone know in advance).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir bitte im Voraus sagen, wann du kommst?
native_language_example: Can you please tell me in advance when you're coming?

additional_notes: "im" is a contraction of "in dem" (dative). Use it to say that something happens or is located inside the forest (a place).
target_language_example: Wir machen einen Spaziergang im Wald.
native_language_example: We’re going for a walk in the woods.

meaning: to go for a walk in the forest; to take a stroll in the woods.
additional_notes: Used with forms of „spazieren gehen“ (to go for a walk). „im Wald“ means “in the forest/woods.” Common patterns: „Ich gehe im Wald spazieren.“ (present), „Wir sind im Wald spazieren gegangen.“ (past with „sein“). You can add time words like „jeden Tag“ (every day) or „gern(e)“ (gladly/like to).
target_language_example: Am Wochenende gehe ich mit meinem Hund im Wald spazieren.
native_language_example: On the weekend I go for a walk in the woods with my dog.

additional_notes: Often used with the reflexive verb "sich verirren" (= to get lost): "Ich habe mich im Wald verirrt" (Perfect tense with "haben" + "sich verirrt"). "im Wald" means "in the forest/woods" (a location). You can swap the place: "in der Stadt verirrt" (lost in the city).
target_language_example: Wir haben uns im Wald verirrt und finden den Weg nicht mehr.
native_language_example: We got lost in the woods and can’t find the way anymore.

meaning: to get lost in the forest/woods.
additional_notes: Usually used with the reflexive pronoun: sich verlaufen (ich habe mich verlaufen, wir haben uns verlaufen). It often implies getting lost while walking/hiking. You can also say just: Ich habe mich verlaufen. ("I got lost.")
target_language_example: Wir sind gestern wandern gegangen und haben uns im Wald verlaufen.
native_language_example: We went hiking yesterday and got lost in the woods.

meaning: to be in the way; to block/obstruct.
additional_notes: Used when a person/thing is physically blocking a path or more generally preventing something from happening. Commonly used with a dative object: „jemandem im Weg stehen“ = to be in someone’s way / to hinder someone.
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte zur Seite gehen? Du musst mir nicht im Weg stehen.
native_language_example: Can you please step aside? You don't have to stand in my way.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is true in its most important points, even if not in every detail. Common in neutral/formal statements: "X ist im Wesentlichen vorbei" (more or less over), "X besteht im Wesentlichen aus ..." (consists mainly of ...), "im Wesentlichen recht" (basically right).
target_language_example: Im Wesentlichen sind wir fertig, aber wir müssen noch ein paar Kleinigkeiten prüfen.
native_language_example: Basically, we’re done, but we still need to check a few small things.

meaning: 'in the west' (to the west / in the western part).
additional_notes: "im" = "in dem" (dative). Used for location (“in the western part of a place/region”) and for directions with fixed expressions like "Die Sonne geht im Westen unter" (“the sun sets in the west”). With motion, German often uses "in den Westen" (accusative) = “to the west.”
target_language_example: Unser Hotel liegt im Westen der Stadt.
native_language_example: Our hotel is in the west of the city.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something happening during the winter season. Often answers “When?” (Wann?). You’ll also see it at the start of a sentence as a time phrase: “Im Winter …”.
target_language_example: Im Winter trage ich fast jeden Tag eine Mütze.
native_language_example: In winter I wear a hat almost every day.

additional_notes: “Im” is a contraction of “in dem” and is used with neuter nouns in the dative case to mean “in the.” “Wohnzimmer” (living room) is neuter: das Wohnzimmer. Used to say where someone/something is happening (location).
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns im Wohnzimmer.
native_language_example: We’re meeting in the living room.

additional_notes: "im" is a contraction of "in dem" (dative). It’s used for location (being somewhere), often with verbs like "sein" (to be), "sitzen" (to sit), "stehen" (to stand), and "sich umsehen" (to look around). For movement into a room, you usually use "ins Zimmer" (= "in das Zimmer").
target_language_example: Ich bin gerade im Zimmer und lerne.
native_language_example: I’m in the room right now and studying.

additional_notes: "im" = "in dem" (in the). Use it to say someone is inside the zoo or visited it. With places like the zoo, English often says "at the zoo" while German commonly uses "im".
target_language_example: Wir sind heute im Zoo und sehen uns die Elefanten an.
native_language_example: We’re at the zoo today and we’re going to look at the elephants.

meaning: on the train (while in the train).
additional_notes: Used to say that something happens while you are traveling by train or that something is located/left inside the train. It’s the contraction of "in dem Zug" (in the train). Often used with verbs like schlafen (sleep), einschlafen (fall asleep), reden/sich unterhalten (talk), vergessen (forget).
target_language_example: Im Zug habe ich ein Buch gelesen.
native_language_example: On the train, I read a book.

meaning: in the course of; as part of (something).
additional_notes: Used in fairly formal contexts to say something happens during a process or as a consequence of an event or change (often with nouns like „im Zuge der Reform/Umstrukturierung/Untersuchung“). It’s usually followed by a genitive noun phrase (e.g., „im Zuge der …“).
target_language_example: Im Zuge der Renovierung bleibt das Café zwei Wochen geschlossen.
native_language_example: As part of the renovation, the café will be closed for two weeks.

additional_notes: Used to say where something is located inside a building. With floors, German often uses "im" + ordinal number + "Stock" (e.g., im ersten/zweiten/dritten Stock).
target_language_example: Das Büro ist im dritten Stock.
native_language_example: The office is on the third floor.

meaning: on the first floor (one level above the ground floor).
additional_notes: Used to say where something is located inside a building. In Germany, "1. Stock" is typically the floor above the "Erdgeschoss" (ground floor), so it often corresponds to the US "second floor".
target_language_example: Die Toiletten sind im ersten Stock, gleich neben dem Aufzug.
native_language_example: The restrooms are on the first floor, right next to the elevator.

meaning: throughout the whole country; all over the country.
additional_notes: Used to say something applies everywhere in a country (in all regions), often with verbs like „bekannt sein“ (to be known), „sich verbreiten“ (to spread), or „herrschen“ (to prevail). It’s a fixed prepositional phrase: „im“ = „in dem“ + dative, and „ganz“ changes to „ganzen“ with dative neuter („dem ganzen Land“).
target_language_example: Die Nachricht ging im ganzen Land herum.
native_language_example: The news spread throughout the whole country.

meaning: "in the same" / "at the same" (same age, office, speed, etc.).
additional_notes: "im" = "in dem" (in the). "gleichen" is the dative form of "gleich" and is used before a noun (often with a noun implied by context). Common patterns: "im gleichen Alter" (the same age), "im gleichen Büro" (in the same office), "im gleichen Tempo" (at the same pace). Often paired with "wie" to compare: "im gleichen … wie …".
target_language_example: Wir arbeiten im gleichen Gebäude wie Anna.
native_language_example: We work in the same building as Anna.

meaning: "last" / "in the last …" (referring to the previous time period).
additional_notes: Used with a time word to mean the previous one: im letzten Winter (last winter), im letzten Oktober (last October), im letzten Frühling (last spring). Also very common in fixed phrases like im letzten Moment / im letzten Augenblick = “at the last moment.” It’s the contraction of in dem letzten + dative.
target_language_example: Wir haben uns im letzten Sommer gesehen.
native_language_example: We saw each other last summer.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened during the previous calendar year. Literally "in the last year" ("im" = "in dem"), and it’s a common time expression for past events.
target_language_example: Im letzten Jahr habe ich Deutsch gelernt.
native_language_example: Last year I learned German.

meaning: last month; in the previous month.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened during the month before the current one. "im" = "in dem" (dative), because "in" with a time period takes dative: im letzten Monat.
target_language_example: Im letzten Monat habe ich viel gearbeitet.
native_language_example: Last month I worked a lot.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened during the previous summer (the summer before now). Often used with past tenses like Präteritum or Perfekt. Grammar: "im" = "in dem" + dative; "letzten" is the dative form of "letzter" (last).
target_language_example: Im letzten Sommer habe ich viel Zeit am See verbracht.
native_language_example: Last summer I spent a lot of time at the lake.

meaning: "next" (used with a time period), e.g. "next summer / next vacation."
additional_notes: Used with a time word in the dative case, most often with masculine/neuter nouns: im nächsten Sommer/Winter/Monat/Jahr/Urlaub (= in dem nächsten ...). With feminine nouns you use "in der nächsten ..." (e.g. in der nächsten Woche), and with plural nouns "in den nächsten ..." (e.g. in den nächsten Tagen). In English you usually drop "in" and just say "next ...".
target_language_example: Im nächsten Jahr möchte ich nach Berlin ziehen.
native_language_example: Next year I want to move to Berlin.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something planned for the next spring season relative to now. Often used with future plans and schedules, and can be combined with "erst" to mean "not until next spring" (e.g., "erst im nächsten Frühjahr").
target_language_example: Wir ziehen im nächsten Frühjahr in eine neue Wohnung.
native_language_example: We’re moving into a new apartment next spring.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something happening in the year after this one. Very common with future plans and predictions (often with the future tense "werden" or with present tense used for the future).
target_language_example: Im nächsten Jahr fahren wir nach Berlin.
native_language_example: Next year we’re going to Berlin.

additional_notes: Time phrase meaning “in/within the next month” (the month after the current one). Often used to talk about plans or scheduled events. Uses dative after the preposition “in” for time: im (= in dem) nächsten Monat.
target_language_example: Wir ziehen im nächsten Monat um.
native_language_example: We’re moving next month.

meaning: at the right moment; at just the right time.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens exactly when it should. Often appears with verbs like kommen (to come), passieren (to happen), sagen (to say), or ankommen (to arrive). You can also hear the similar phrase „im richtigen Moment“.
target_language_example: Du bist im richtigen Augenblick gekommen.
native_language_example: You came at just the right moment.

meaning: 'in the same' (in the same place/room/building, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to say that two or more people/things are in the identical location or setting. It’s the contraction of "in dem selben" (dative case after "in" when it means location, not movement). Often followed by a noun: "im selben Büro/Zimmer/Zug". Also used in comparisons with "wie": "im selben Stadtteil wie ...".
target_language_example: Wir waren im selben Restaurant, aber wir haben uns nicht gesehen.
native_language_example: We were in the same restaurant, but we didn’t see each other.

meaning: in the same boat (in the same situation).
additional_notes: An idiom used to say that people share the same situation—often the same problem or difficulty—so they should understand each other or work together. Commonly used with the verb "sitzen" ("im selben Boot sitzen").
target_language_example: Keine Sorge — wir sind im selben Boot und finden eine Lösung.
native_language_example: Don’t worry—we’re in the same boat and we’ll find a solution.

meaning: last year; in the past year.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the previous calendar year (like English “last year”), often with events or totals. It can also be used more generally to mean “in the past year” (the last 12 months), depending on context. Grammar: "im" = "in dem" + dative; "Jahr" is neuter.
target_language_example: Im vergangenen Jahr war ich zweimal in Berlin.
native_language_example: Last year I was in Berlin twice.

additional_notes: Used with thanks to express gratitude before something happens, especially in emails/messages: (Vielen) Dank/Danke (schon) im Voraus für + accusative noun (e.g., für Ihre Hilfe, für die Unterstützung). “im Voraus” is often written as two words and “Voraus” is capitalized.
target_language_example: Vielen Dank im Voraus für Ihre schnelle Antwort.
native_language_example: Thank you in advance for your quick reply.

additional_notes: Used to say where something is inside a building. German uses the dative with locations: "im" = "in dem" + "Stock" (floor/storey). Note: in many German-speaking countries, "zweiter Stock" is typically one level above the "erster Stock" (which is above the "Erdgeschoss"/ground floor).
target_language_example: Der Unterricht findet im zweiten Stock statt.
native_language_example: The class takes place on the second floor.

meaning: 'always ... that ...' / 'every time ... that ...' (repeatedly introducing a 'dass' clause).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom, but a very common pattern: **immer** (‘always’) + a verb (e.g., *erwarten, glauben, denken, sagen, schaffen*) + **, dass** to introduce a subordinate clause. In writing, there is usually a **comma before dass**: *Ich denke immer, dass ...* It expresses that something happens or is thought/said repeatedly.
target_language_example: Sie glaubt immer, dass alles gut wird.
native_language_example: She always believes that everything will turn out fine.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens regularly each time a condition occurs. It’s usually written as **immer, wenn** with a comma before the **wenn**-clause. The **wenn**-clause is a subordinate clause, so the verb goes to the end: *… wenn er nach Madrid kommt.*
target_language_example: Immer, wenn ich Kaffee trinke, kann ich nicht schlafen.
native_language_example: Whenever I drink coffee, I can’t sleep.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens repeatedly each time a certain situation occurs. Often followed by the main clause later (e.g., "Immer, wenn ich ..., (dann) ..."). In speech and writing, "immer" is often set off with a comma: "Immer, wenn ich ...".
target_language_example: Immer, wenn ich Musik höre, bekomme ich gute Laune.
native_language_example: Whenever I listen to music, I get in a good mood.

meaning: 'always on / always at' (used with an 'auf'-phrase; exact meaning depends on the verb).
additional_notes:
This is not one fixed idiom: **immer** (“always”) often comes right before a verb phrase that includes **auf**. With different verbs, **auf** changes meaning:
- **(sich) setzen auf** = to sit down on (place)
- **liegen auf** = to lie on (location)
- **zählen auf** = to count on / rely on (a person/thing)
- **warten auf** = to wait for
- **schieben auf** (jdn./etw.) = to blame on
Case tip: with **auf** you often see **accusative** after verbs of direction/target (sich setzen auf, warten auf, zählen auf), and **dative** after location (liegen auf).
target_language_example: Ich sitze immer auf demselben Platz.
native_language_example: I always sit in the same seat.

meaning: better and better; getting better (and better).
additional_notes: Used to say that someone’s condition or situation is improving over time. Very common with verbs like „gehen“ (Es geht mir immer besser.) and „sich fühlen“ (Ich fühle mich immer besser.)
target_language_example: Seit ich mehr schlafe, geht es mir immer besser.
native_language_example: Since I’ve been sleeping more, I’ve been feeling better and better.

meaning: “always the same (thing)” / “the same thing every time.”
additional_notes: Used to complain that something keeps repeating or never changes (often as a standalone comment: “Immer das Gleiche!” = “Same old thing!”). It can also be neutral, e.g., someone always orders the same item. Common pattern: "jmd. macht/sagt/bestellt immer das Gleiche".
target_language_example: Warum änderst du nie etwas? Es ist immer das Gleiche.
native_language_example: Why do you never change anything? It’s always the same.

meaning: always the truth; always telling the truth.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like sagen/erzählen to emphasize that someone is consistently honest. Word order is flexible: "immer die Wahrheit sagen" is very common.
target_language_example: Ich versuche, immer die Wahrheit zu sagen.
native_language_example: I try to always tell the truth.

meaning: “...ever you want” / “... you want” (in phrases like “whatever/wherever/whenever you want”).
additional_notes: Used after a question word to mean “no matter which/what/when/where”. Most common patterns: „was immer du willst“ (whatever you want), „wo immer du willst“ (wherever you want), „wann immer du willst“ (whenever you want). Word order: [question word] + „immer“ + „du willst“.
target_language_example: Du kannst bleiben, wo immer du willst.
native_language_example: You can stay wherever you want.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a safety habit. Often said with verbs like **tragen** (to wear) or **aufhaben** (to have on): *Ich habe immer einen Helm auf* / *Ich trage immer einen Helm*. Common with biking or motorcycling (*Fahrrad/Rad fahren*, *Motorrad fahren*).
target_language_example: Beim Skaten habe ich immer einen Helm auf.
native_language_example: When skating, I always wear a helmet.

meaning: always up early / always wake up early.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like **aufwachen** (to wake up) and **aufstehen** (to get up): *Ich wache immer früh auf.* / *Ich stehe immer früh auf.* Word order: **immer** (always) often comes after the verb (*Ich wache immer...*), and **früh** (early) often comes before **auf** (*...früh auf*). You can add a time word like **morgens** (in the mornings): *Ich stehe morgens immer früh auf.*
target_language_example: Am Wochenende stehe ich auch immer früh auf.
native_language_example: On the weekend, I also always get up early.

additional_notes: Most often used after a question word + „immer“: „was immer ihr wollt“ = „whatever you want“. It adds emphasis/total freedom (“anything at all”). You’ll usually see it in phrases like „tun, was immer ihr wollt“ (do whatever you want) or „fragen, was immer ihr wollt“ (ask whatever you want).
target_language_example: Ihr könnt sagen, was immer ihr wollt.
native_language_example: You can say whatever you want.

additional_notes: Used to show that the amount or number keeps growing over time. Often with plurals ("immer mehr Leute") or with nouns in general ("immer mehr Geld"). It can also be used in comparisons or trends: "Immer mehr Menschen haben ...".
target_language_example: Immer mehr Menschen nutzen das Fahrrad, um zur Arbeit zu kommen.
native_language_example: More and more people use a bicycle to get to work.

additional_notes: Used to say that something grows, increases, or becomes stronger over time (quantity, frequency, intensity, or a situation). Often with verbs like „werden“ (Es werden immer mehr.), „sich stapeln“ (Die Rechnungen stapeln sich immer mehr.), or with feelings like „Ich liebe dich immer mehr.“
target_language_example: Mit jedem Tag werden die Aufgaben im Büro immer mehr.
native_language_example: With each day, the tasks at the office become more and more.

additional_notes: Used to say that a situation continues up to now or up to the time being talked about. In questions, it asks whether something is continuing.
target_language_example: Ich wohne immer noch in Berlin.
native_language_example: I still live in Berlin.

meaning: “still … that …” (you continue to hope/want/think that something is true).
additional_notes: Used when a main clause (often with a verb like hoffen/wollen/möchten) is followed by a dass-clause. German normally puts a comma before „dass“: „Ich hoffe immer noch, dass …“. „Immer noch“ emphasizes that the feeling/opinion/plan hasn’t changed up to now.
target_language_example: Ich denke immer noch, dass es eine gute Idee ist.
native_language_example: I still think it’s a good idea.

additional_notes: Used to say something continues to be the case ("still a ..."): *Das ist immer noch ein Problem.* It comes before a noun, and **ein** changes with gender and case: **immer noch ein** (masc./neut. nom./acc.), **immer noch eine** (fem.), **immer noch einen** (masc. acc.), etc. It can also mean “one more” in some contexts: *Noch einen Kaffee? – Ja, immer noch einen.*
target_language_example: Das ist immer noch ein Problem.
native_language_example: That is still a problem.

additional_notes: Used to say someone remains in the same location as before, often when you expected they might have left. Common in questions ("Bist du immer noch in …?") and statements ("Er ist/lebt/wohnt immer noch in …"). Word order: "immer noch" usually comes before the location phrase with "in".
target_language_example: Wir sind immer noch in Berlin.
native_language_example: We’re still in Berlin.

meaning: “still with” (still together/engaged/seeing someone; still doing something with someone).
additional_notes: Used to say a situation continues up to now. Common with relationships: „Bist du immer noch mit … zusammen?“ = “Are you still together with …?” It can also mean you still meet or do an activity with someone: „Machst du das immer noch mit Tom?“ = “Are you still doing that with Tom?” Often followed by a person in the dative case: mit + wem? (mit Tom, mit Maria).
target_language_example: Bist du immer noch mit ihr befreundet?
native_language_example: Are you still friends with her?

additional_notes: Used to say something has not happened up to now, often implying it’s taking longer than expected. Common in questions and statements: „Bist du immer noch nicht fertig?“ = “Are you still not done?” (often a bit impatient).
target_language_example: Ich habe immer noch nicht verstanden, wie das funktioniert.
native_language_example: I still haven’t understood how that works.

additional_notes: Used with the verb phrase **wehtun** (“to hurt”): **(etwas) tut weh** / **(etwas) tut mir weh**. **immer noch** = “still” (the pain continues). Word order is flexible: **Mein Rücken tut immer noch weh** / **Tut dein Rücken immer noch weh?**
target_language_example: Mein Fuß tut immer noch weh, ich kann nicht gut laufen.
native_language_example: My foot still hurts; I can’t walk well.

meaning: “always only” / “nothing but”; repeatedly doing or being just one thing.
additional_notes: Used to stress that something happens repeatedly (immer) and is limited to just one thing (nur). Often sounds like a complaint or criticism: "Du sagst mir immer nur …" = "All you ever do is tell me …". It can also mean “only ever” with quantity/choice: "Elisa hat immer nur einen Mann geliebt" = she loved only one man (in her whole life).
target_language_example: Du redest immer nur über die Arbeit.
native_language_example: All you ever talk about is work.

meaning: getting worse and worse; increasingly worse.
additional_notes: Used to say that something (a situation, a person’s behavior, etc.) keeps worsening over time. Often with verbs like „werden“: „Es wird immer schlimmer.“
target_language_example: Seit gestern wird mein Husten immer schlimmer.
native_language_example: Since yesterday my cough has been getting worse and worse.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a repeated/typical way something happens or how someone behaves. Often refers back to what you just observed: "Machst du das immer so?" = "Do you always do it like that?" It can also mean "it’s not always like that" (i.e., not in every case).
target_language_example: Machst du das immer so?
native_language_example: Do you always do it like that?

additional_notes: Used to show a gradual decrease over time or as a situation develops. Common with verbs like sich erinnern (remember), verstehen (understand), sich treffen (meet), sehen (see).
target_language_example: Seit dem Umzug habe ich immer weniger Zeit für meine Freunde.
native_language_example: Since the move, I have less and less time for my friends.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a repeated or general situation: something happens each time another thing happens. It usually starts a dependent clause ("immer wenn ..."), and the verb goes to the end of that clause. It often pairs with a main clause stating the result (e.g., "Immer wenn es regnet, ...").
target_language_example: Immer wenn ich Kaffee trinke, kann ich abends nicht einschlafen.
native_language_example: Whenever I drink coffee, I can’t fall asleep in the evening.

meaning: again and again; repeatedly; over and over.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens repeatedly (often more than expected, sometimes annoyingly). Can describe repeated actions ("immer wieder auf die Uhr schauen"), repeated events (making the same mistakes), or someone repeatedly succeeding at something ("schafft es immer wieder"). Often stronger than just "wieder" (again), emphasizing repetition.
target_language_example: Ich habe ihn immer wieder angerufen, aber er ging nicht ran.
native_language_example: I called him again and again, but he didn’t answer.

additional_notes: Used to say you are at home regularly/consistently (often with a time expression like sonntags, abends). Note: zu Hause = 'at home' (location). If you mean 'to home/homewards' (movement), use nach Hause.
target_language_example: Ich bin nach der Arbeit immer zu Hause.
native_language_example: After work, I'm always at home.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is late every time or very often. Common with verbs like „sein“ and „kommen“: „Du bist immer zu spät“ / „Du kommst immer zu spät“. Often followed by „zu“ + event/place: „zu spät zum Unterricht“ (late for class).
target_language_example: Ich bin heute wieder immer zu spät gewesen.
native_language_example: Today, I was late again—as always.

additional_notes: Used to complain that the amount of something (time, money, food, sleep, etc.) is consistently insufficient. Common pattern: „Immer zu wenig + noun“ (e.g., „immer zu wenig Zeit“). You can also use it as a standalone comment: „Immer zu wenig!“
target_language_example: Ich habe immer zu wenig Zeit für Sport.
native_language_example: I always have too little time for sports.

meaning: to make use of; to take up (a service/offer); to claim (a right/benefit).
additional_notes: Used in fairly formal contexts (services, rights, benefits, legal/official language). Typical patterns: "etwas in Anspruch nehmen" (use/claim something) and "jemanden in Anspruch nehmen" (take up someone’s time/attention). In the perfect tense it splits: "Ich habe die Beratung in Anspruch genommen."
target_language_example: Ich möchte die kostenlose Beratung in Anspruch nehmen.
native_language_example: I’d like to make use of the free consultation.

meaning: to consider; to take into consideration.
additional_notes: Used as: „etwas in Betracht ziehen“ (= consider something as a possibility or option), often in planning, decisions, or polite/formal requests. Common with things like „Optionen“, „Möglichkeiten“, „Vorschläge“.
target_language_example: Wir sollten auch eine günstigere Lösung in Betracht ziehen.
native_language_example: We should also consider a cheaper solution.

additional_notes: Often used with verbs like (sich) in Bewegung setzen (“to start moving”) or sein (“to be moving”). Common for people, vehicles, elevators, and machines when they begin to move.
target_language_example: Der Zug setzt sich langsam in Bewegung.
native_language_example: The train slowly starts moving.

meaning: to set in motion; to get (something) moving.
additional_notes: Often used with an object (e.g., „eine Maschine in Bewegung setzen“ = start a machine). With the reflexive pronoun („sich in Bewegung setzen“) it means “to start moving / to set off” (people, a group, etc.). Can also be used figuratively for starting a process (e.g., reforms, changes).
target_language_example: Der Fahrer will den Bus in Bewegung setzen.
native_language_example: The driver wants to get the bus moving.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic/aspect you’re talking about (often more formal than „über“ or „wegen“). It takes the accusative: „in Bezug auf + Akk.“ (e.g., „in Bezug auf sein Alter“).
target_language_example: In Bezug auf deine Frage habe ich noch eine Bitte.
native_language_example: Regarding your question, I still have one request.

additional_notes: Used with "sein" (e.g., "Ich bin in Eile") to say you don’t have much time and need to go quickly. Often followed by "um … zu …" to express what you’re hurrying to do ("in Eile, um den Zug zu erreichen").
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich bin in Eile und muss los.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m in a hurry and have to go.

meaning: to be able to find out (learn/discover information).
additional_notes: Used when you managed (or were asked whether you managed) to obtain information through research, asking around, investigation, etc. Very common in questions like „Hast du in Erfahrung bringen können, warum …?“ The core phrase is „etw. in Erfahrung bringen“ (= to find out something); „können“ adds the idea of being able to / having managed to.
target_language_example: Ich habe in Erfahrung bringen können, dass der Zug heute ausfällt.
native_language_example: I was able to find out that the train is canceled today.

additional_notes: Used mainly with wishes, hopes, plans, or dreams (often with the subject "ein Traum/Wunsch/Hoffnung"). Common pattern: "(Mein/Dein/Sein) Traum/Wunsch geht in Erfüllung"; also with "möge" to express a wish: "Möge es in Erfüllung gehen."
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, dass alle deine Träume in Erfüllung gehen.
native_language_example: I hope that all your dreams come true.

additional_notes: Almost always used with the verb "(etwas) in Erwägung ziehen" = "to consider (something)". It means you’re weighing options, not deciding yet. Common with questions like "Ziehst du ernsthaft in Erwägung ...?" (Are you seriously considering ...?).
target_language_example: Ich ziehe in Erwägung, nächstes Jahr nach Berlin zu ziehen.
native_language_example: I’m considering moving to Berlin next year.

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb "ziehen": "etwas in Erwägung ziehen" = to consider something. Often appears in questions about possible actions or decisions (e.g., moving, going to the doctor). In speech you’ll often hear it with "schon" or "mal/je": "Hast du schon mal in Erwägung gezogen …?"
target_language_example: Ich habe in Erwägung gezogen, den Job zu wechseln.
native_language_example: I considered changing jobs.

additional_notes: Used for seriously thinking about a possibility or option, often as advice or a recommendation. Common patterns: (1) „etwas in Erwägung ziehen“ (noun/pronoun object), e.g., „einen Umzug in Erwägung ziehen“; (2) „in Erwägung ziehen, … zu …“ (infinitive with „zu“). Formal/neutral register, frequent in written and professional contexts.
target_language_example: Du solltest in Erwägung ziehen, dir einen neuen Arbeitsplatz zu suchen.
native_language_example: You should consider looking for a new job.

meaning: to be in flames; to be on fire.
additional_notes: Used to describe something (often a building, car, forest, etc.) burning strongly. German commonly uses the verb „stehen“ in this expression (literally “to stand”), where English would say “be in flames/on fire.”
target_language_example: Als die Feuerwehr ankam, musste sie feststellen, dass die Garage in Flammen stehen würde, wenn sie nicht sofort löschte.
native_language_example: When the fire department arrived, it had to realize that the garage would be in flames if it didn’t put it out immediately.

additional_notes: Used mainly about physical condition/fitness: „gut/sehr gut in Form sein“ = to be fit; „sich in Form halten“ = to keep fit; „in Form kommen“ = to get into shape (often after a break). You can also use it for someone’s performance being good (e.g., in sports), but beginners will mostly hear it about fitness.
target_language_example: Nach dem Urlaub muss ich wieder in Form kommen.
native_language_example: After vacation I need to get back into shape.

meaning: to be an option; to be possible/eligible
additional_notes: Used to say that something is a realistic possibility or could be considered. Commonly negated: “Das kommt nicht in Frage.” = “That’s not an option.” Also common as a question: “Was kommt in Frage?” = “What are the options?” Note: although it contains “Frage” (question), it usually means “option/consideration,” not a literal question.
target_language_example: Für mich kann nur der Zug in Frage kommen.
native_language_example: For me, only the train is an option.

additional_notes: Literally “in peace.” Used to describe living without conflict ("in Frieden leben"). In the imperative, it can mean a blessing or farewell ("Geh in Frieden!" = “Go in peace!”). With verbs like "lassen" it often means “leave someone alone” ("Lass mich in Frieden"), and in "in Frieden ruhen" it’s a respectful phrase meaning “rest in peace.”
target_language_example: Bitte lass mich in Frieden arbeiten.
native_language_example: Please leave me alone so I can work.

meaning: lost in thought; in your thoughts (not paying attention).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is mentally elsewhere—thinking deeply, daydreaming, or distracted. Often with verbs like „sein“ (Ich war in Gedanken.) or to describe doing something only in your mind: „In Gedanken hab ich …“ = “In my mind, I …”.
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich war gerade in Gedanken und habe nicht zugehört.
native_language_example: Sorry, I was lost in thought and wasn’t listening.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "sein" ("in Gefahr sein" = to be in danger) and often with "Leben" ("Mein Leben ist in Gefahr" = My life is in danger). You’ll also see it with "geraten"/"kommen" (to get into danger) or "sich in Gefahr begeben" (to put yourself in danger).
target_language_example: Pass auf! Du bist in Gefahr.
native_language_example: Watch out! You’re in danger.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **ausbrechen**: **in Gelächter ausbrechen** = to suddenly start laughing. Common with a subject like *ich/er/sie/wir* or a group (*die Zuhörer*, *die Masse*). The noun **Gelächter** means “laughter” (often loud/group laughter).
target_language_example: Als sie das hörte, brach sie in Gelächter aus.
native_language_example: When she heard that, she burst into laughter.

additional_notes: Used with the formal “Sie/Ihr” to mean “in your” when the noun is masculine or neuter and in the dative case (location/where). Example patterns: “in Ihrem Text/Haus/Büro/Zimmer/Mund”. With “in” + dative it usually answers “where?” (location). For feminine nouns you’ll see “in Ihrer …” (e.g., in Ihrer E-Mail).
target_language_example: Ich habe die Unterlagen in Ihrem Büro gelassen.
native_language_example: I left the documents in your office.

additional_notes: Used to talk politely/formally about someone’s age group. Uses the formal possessive „Ihr-“ (to one person: „in Ihrem Alter“; to a woman also possible: „in Ihrem Alter“). Often used when comparing people (“I have a daughter your age”) or giving advice/expectations (“At your age you should…”).
target_language_example: Meine Schwester ist ungefähr in Ihrem Alter.
native_language_example: My sister is about your age.

additional_notes: Used with formal 'Sie/Ihr' to mean 'in your' when the following noun is feminine singular (in Ihrer Stadt/Gegend) or plural (in Ihrer Klasse, if you mean the group). It takes the dative case after 'in' for location (Where?); for movement into somewhere you'd often use 'in Ihre …' (accusative), e.g., 'Ich komme in Ihre Stadt.'
target_language_example: In Ihrer Straße gibt es einen Supermarkt.
native_language_example: There is a supermarket on your street.

additional_notes: Formal/official phrasing, typically used with the verb construction „jemanden über etw. in Kenntnis setzen“ (to inform someone about something). Very common in the passive: „jemand wird/wurde in Kenntnis gesetzt“ = someone is/was informed.
target_language_example: Er wurde über die Änderungen in Kenntnis gesetzt.
native_language_example: He was informed about the changes.

meaning: in force; in effect (legally valid and active).
additional_notes: Used mostly in legal/official contexts for laws, rules, decisions, contracts, or ceasefires. Common patterns: „in Kraft sein“ = to be in force; „in Kraft treten“ = to come into force / take effect (often with a time like „sofort“ or „in sechs Stunden“).
target_language_example: Die neuen Regeln sind seit Montag in Kraft.
native_language_example: The new rules have been in effect since Monday.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen soon, often in announcements or predictions. It means “in a short time” and is common with verbs like beginnen/anfangen/sein.
target_language_example: Der Zug kommt in Kürze an.
native_language_example: The train will arrive shortly.

meaning: in math (class/at math, as a school subject).
additional_notes: Used with the preposition „in“ to talk about performance, homework, tests, etc. in the subject math. „Mathe“ is the common (slightly informal) short form of „Mathematik“, especially in school contexts.
target_language_example: Ich bin in Mathe ganz gut, aber in Englisch nicht so sehr.
native_language_example: I'm pretty good at math, but not so much at English.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition "in" + dative to talk about the subject area (school, skills, comparisons): "gut/schlecht in Mathematik" (good/bad at math), "überlegen/unterlegen in Mathematik" (superior/inferior in math). You can also place it first for emphasis: "In Mathematik ist er sehr gut."
target_language_example: Ich war in Mathematik nie besonders gut.
native_language_example: I was never particularly good at math.

additional_notes: Used with "sein" to say something is (or isn’t) fashionable right now: "Das ist in Mode" / "Das ist nicht (mehr) in Mode". You can also use it with "kommen" to mean it becomes fashionable again: "wieder/erneut in Mode kommen".
target_language_example: Diese Schuhe sind gerade total in Mode.
native_language_example: These shoes are totally in fashion right now.

meaning: to come into fashion; to become trendy.
additional_notes: Used when something (a style, item, color, activity) starts being seen as fashionable (often again). Common with subjects like Kleidung/Trends/Marken. Also used as „wieder in Mode kommen“ (come back into fashion).
target_language_example: Weite Jeans kommen gerade wieder in Mode.
native_language_example: Wide-leg jeans are coming back into fashion right now.

additional_notes: Almost always used with the verb **fallen**: **in Ohnmacht fallen** = “to faint / to pass out.” You’ll also see the past forms: **Ich fiel in Ohnmacht.** (I fainted.) and **Ich bin in Ohnmacht gefallen.** (I have fainted.).
target_language_example: Mir ist plötzlich schwindlig geworden, und ich bin fast in Ohnmacht gefallen.
native_language_example: I suddenly got dizzy, and I almost fainted.

additional_notes: Past tense phrase (Perfekt/Plusquamperfekt) of "in Ohnmacht fallen" = to faint/lose consciousness. Used with "sein" (e.g., "ist/war in Ohnmacht gefallen") and often with a cause: "wegen der Hitze" (because of the heat), "vor Schreck" (from shock).
target_language_example: Im Bus ist ihr plötzlich schwindlig geworden und sie ist in Ohnmacht gefallen.
native_language_example: On the bus she suddenly got dizzy and fainted.

additional_notes: Usually means something is fine, acceptable, or correct. It can describe a situation, object, or person; with a person, it can also suggest they are okay or trustworthy. As a reply on its own, it often means 'all right' or 'okay.'
target_language_example: Alles ist jetzt in Ordnung.
native_language_example: Everything is okay now.

meaning: to fix; to put in order; to sort out.
additional_notes: Used when you make a problem, situation, or mess okay again. With concrete things (e.g., a room) it often means tidying/organizing; with abstract things (eine Sache, die Dinge, ein Schlamassel) it means resolving or putting things right. Common patterns: etwas in Ordnung bringen; sein Zimmer/die Dinge/die Sache in Ordnung bringen.
target_language_example: Ich kann die Sache noch immer in Ordnung bringen.
native_language_example: I can still sort things out.

additional_notes: Used with forms of "sein" (to be) to describe a state ("Er ist in Panik" = He’s in a panic). Very common with "in Panik geraten" (to panic) and "in Panik ausbrechen" (to break into panic / panic suddenly). Often used in advice: "Nicht in Panik geraten!" (Don’t panic!).
target_language_example: Als der Alarm losging, gerieten viele Leute in Panik.
native_language_example: When the alarm went off, many people panicked.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like gehen (go) or sein (be) to talk about retirement: in Rente gehen = to retire/to go into retirement; in Rente sein = to be retired. Often refers to stopping work because of age (but can also be early retirement).
target_language_example: Meine Mutter ist seit 2020 in Rente.
native_language_example: My mother has been retired since 2020.

additional_notes: Used to show movement or orientation toward a place or direction (often with a destination like a compass point, a building, etc.). You’ll often see it with a noun in the genitive after it (especially in more formal German): „in Richtung des Bahnhofs“ = “toward the station.” It can also be used figuratively for a development or trend: „in Richtung Chaos“ = “toward chaos.”
target_language_example: Gehen Sie in Richtung Stadtzentrum, dann links.
native_language_example: Go toward the city center, then left.

meaning: alone; in peace; without being bothered.
additional_notes: Often used with verbs like „lassen“ (to leave) or „lassen … in Ruhe“ to mean “leave (someone/something) alone.” It can be a polite request with „Bitte“/„lassen Sie …“ or a more irritated command with „Lass mich (einfach) in Ruhe!“ It can also refer to not touching/using something: „Lass die Sachen in Ruhe.“
target_language_example: Können wir bitte in Ruhe essen?
native_language_example: Can we please eat in peace (without being disturbed)?

meaning: to be left alone; to be left in peace.
additional_notes: A passive phrase ("werden" + past participle "gelassen") from "jemanden in Ruhe lassen" = "to leave someone alone". Often used to say you don’t want to be disturbed or bothered. Common variants: "Ich möchte in Ruhe gelassen werden" (I’d like to be left alone) and the direct request "Lass mich in Ruhe!" (Leave me alone!).
target_language_example: Bitte lass mich jetzt in Ruhe gelassen werden.
native_language_example: Please let me be left alone now.

meaning: to leave (someone) alone; to let (someone) be.
additional_notes: Used when you want someone to stop bothering, disturbing, or contacting someone else. The person being left alone is in the accusative (mich/dich/ihn/sie/uns/euch/Sie): „Lass mich in Ruhe!“ / „Lassen Sie ihn in Ruhe.“ It can be a request, complaint, or command. Literally it’s like “leave (someone) in peace.”
target_language_example: Warum können Sie mich nicht in Ruhe lassen?
native_language_example: Why can't you leave me alone?

additional_notes: Used to say that someone is supposed to stop bothering another person. It appears with a person in the accusative: „mich/dich/ihn/sie/uns/euch/Sie in Ruhe lassen“. Often used after verbs like „sagen“: „Sag ihm, dass er mich in Ruhe lassen soll!“ In direct speech you can also say: „Lass mich in Ruhe!“
target_language_example: Ich habe ihr gesagt, dass sie mich in Ruhe lassen soll.
native_language_example: I told her that she should leave me alone.

meaning: in trouble; in a difficult situation.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like „sein/stecken/geraten/bringen“ to talk about being (or getting) in trouble (e.g., with the police, at work, or in a personal situation). Often used without an article: „in Schwierigkeiten“.
target_language_example: Wenn du lügst, kommst du in Schwierigkeiten.
native_language_example: If you lie, you’ll get in trouble.

meaning: safe; in a safe place/out of danger.
additional_notes: Used with forms of „sein“ to say someone is safe ("Ich bin in Sicherheit"), and with verbs like „bringen“/„in Sicherheit bringen“ to mean taking someone/something to safety. Often implies being out of danger and protected.
target_language_example: Keine Sorge – wir sind jetzt in Sicherheit.
native_language_example: Don’t worry—we’re safe now.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something can be seen or is visible from where you are. Very common in negative phrases like „kein(e) … in Sicht“ = “no … in sight” and „niemand in Sicht“ = “nobody in sight.” Also used in fixed expressions like „(k)ein Ende in Sicht“ = “(no) end in sight.”
target_language_example: Noch ist kein Taxi in Sicht.
native_language_example: There’s still no taxi in sight.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like (zer)reißen, reißen, hauen, schlagen to show something/someone is torn, smashed, or beaten badly. Often in fixed phrases like „in Stücke reißen“ (tear to pieces) or „in Stücke hauen“ (smash to bits). Can be literal (paper, photos) or figurative/threatening (a person).
target_language_example: Sie hat den Brief in Stücke gerissen.
native_language_example: She tore the letter into pieces.

meaning: in deeds; through actions (not just words).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize doing something in practice. Often appears in the phrase „in Worten und Taten“ (“in words and deeds”). „Tat“ means a (notable) deed/action; the plural „Taten“ can sound a bit formal or emphatic.
target_language_example: Er zeigt seine Dankbarkeit nicht nur in Worten, sondern auch in Taten.
native_language_example: He shows his gratitude not only in words, but also through actions.

additional_notes: Used with the separable verb **ausbrechen**: **in Tränen ausbrechen**. In the past tense it’s often **brach … aus** (singular) / **brachen … aus** (plural). Typical pattern: **Als/Bei … brach sie in Tränen aus.**
target_language_example: Bei dem Film brach er in Tränen aus.
native_language_example: During the movie, he burst into tears.

additional_notes: Most often used with the verb phrase **sich mit jemandem in Verbindung setzen** = “to get in touch/contact someone” (formal: **Setzen Sie sich...**, informal: **Setz dich...**, plural: **Setzt euch...**). Also used with **bleiben**: **in Verbindung bleiben** = “to stay in touch.”
target_language_example: Ich setze mich morgen mit dir in Verbindung.
native_language_example: I’ll get in touch with you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with the reflexive verb phrase **sich mit jemandem in Verbindung setzen** = “to contact/get in touch with someone.” **in Verbindung gesetzt** is the past participle form, often used in the **Perfekt** tense: *Hat/ Haben … sich … in Verbindung gesetzt?* It’s fairly neutral to formal and common in emails, customer service, and professional contexts.
target_language_example: Ich habe mich gestern mit der Firma in Verbindung gesetzt.
native_language_example: I contacted the company yesterday.

meaning: to contact; to get in touch (with someone).
additional_notes: Usually used with the reflexive pronoun: „sich mit jemandem in Verbindung setzen“ = to contact someone / get in touch with someone. Common in polite or formal contexts (emails, customer service, business): „Wir setzen uns mit Ihnen in Verbindung.“
target_language_example: Ich muss mich mit Tom in Verbindung setzen.
native_language_example: I have to get in touch with Tom.

meaning: to get in touch (with); to contact.
additional_notes: Used with **mit + dative** to say you initiate contact or establish a connection with someone (often by phone, email, etc.). Commonly appears as **mit jemandem in Verbindung treten**. Similar in meaning to **Kontakt aufnehmen (mit)**, but typically a bit more formal.
target_language_example: Ich werde morgen mit der Schule in Verbindung treten.
native_language_example: I'll get in touch with the school tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what is really true, often contrasting with what someone said, believed, or what it seemed like before. Common in explanations and confessions: „Aber in Wahrheit …“ = “But actually …”.
target_language_example: In Wahrheit habe ich keine Zeit, heute zu kommen.
native_language_example: Actually, I don’t have time to come today.

meaning: in reality; actually (as opposed to what seems or was said).
additional_notes: Used to correct a misunderstanding or reveal the true situation. Often contrasts with appearances, rumors, assumptions, or earlier statements; frequently followed by a fact that sets things straight.
target_language_example: In Wirklichkeit habe ich keine Zeit, aber ich will dich nicht enttäuschen.
native_language_example: Actually, I don’t have time, but I don’t want to disappoint you.

additional_notes: Used to say something is expressed (or can’t be expressed) using language rather than actions, images, etc. Common with phrases like „gut/schlecht in Worten sein“ (to be good/bad with words) and verbs like „etwas in Worten ausdrücken/beschreiben“ (to put/describe something in words). Can also appear alone for emphasis: „In Worten.“ (“In words.”).
target_language_example: Ich kann das Gefühl nicht in Worten ausdrücken.
native_language_example: I can’t put that feeling into words.

meaning: in the future; from now on.
additional_notes: Used to talk about what will happen later or to give advice/instructions for how someone should behave going forward. Often appears with requests or warnings (e.g., „Sei/Seien Sie in Zukunft …“).
target_language_example: In Zukunft möchte ich weniger arbeiten.
native_language_example: In the future, I want to work less.

additional_notes: A fixed, quite formal/poetic phrase, often used in religious contexts (e.g., prayers: „in alle Ewigkeit. Amen.“). In everyday speech, people more often say „für immer“ or „für ewig“.
target_language_example: Ich werde dich in alle Ewigkeit lieben.
native_language_example: I will love you forever.

additional_notes: Used to say something/someone moves, spreads, or looks everywhere (left, right, forward, back). Often with verbs like fliegen (fly), laufen (run), schauen (look), gehen (go).
target_language_example: Als es plötzlich laut wurde, rannten die Leute in alle Richtungen.
native_language_example: When it suddenly got loud, people ran in all directions.

additional_notes: Used with the dative plural of "alle" to mean "in all" or "in every" when talking about being inside something or within a group/category (e.g., rooms, boxes, restaurants, newspapers). Often followed by a plural noun: "in allen Zimmern" = "in all rooms".
target_language_example: In allen Ländern gibt es unterschiedliche Regeln.
native_language_example: There are different rules in all countries.

meaning: 'on earth' (used to add strong emphasis in questions).
additional_notes: Used in wh-questions (warum/wer/wo/woher, etc.) to express surprise, disbelief, irritation, or strong curiosity. It doesn’t mean the literal physical location “in the whole world” here; it functions like English “on earth” or “in the world.”
target_language_example: Wie in aller Welt soll ich das schaffen?
native_language_example: How on earth am I supposed to manage that?

meaning: “on earth did you …?” (strong surprise/annoyance in a question).
additional_notes: Used inside a question (often with wo/was/wie) to emphasize disbelief or frustration: e.g., “Wo in aller Welt hast du …?” = “Where on earth did you …?” The word order depends on the question (verb-second in German), so this chunk is often followed by a past participle or infinitive phrase.
target_language_example: Wo in aller Welt hast du meinen Schlüssel gefunden?
native_language_example: Where on earth did you find my key?

meaning: (on earth / in the world) — used for strong surprise, confusion, or annoyance in questions.
additional_notes: Used almost always in questions with words like warum/was/wer/wie/wo to intensify them: "Warum in aller Welt ...?" = "Why on earth ...?" It adds emphasis and emotion (often irritation or disbelief). It can be set off by commas: "Was, in aller Welt, ...?"
target_language_example: Wie in aller Welt soll das funktionieren?
native_language_example: How on earth is that supposed to work?

additional_notes: Used with movement/direction (going from outside to inside), so it takes the accusative: *in das* (often contracted to *ins*). Contrast: *im Zimmer* (= in the room, location). Common with verbs like *gehen*, *kommen*, *schauen*, *treten*.
target_language_example: Sie lief schnell in das Zimmer.
native_language_example: She ran quickly into the room.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of motion (e.g., gehen, kommen, laufen) to show movement into the room. With motion, German uses accusative: dein Zimmer. If you’re already inside and talking about location, you’d usually say „in deinem Zimmer“ (dative) = “in your room.”
target_language_example: Geh bitte in dein Zimmer und mach die Tür zu.
native_language_example: Please go into your room and close the door.

additional_notes: "In" + "deinem" (dative) is used for a location (where something is), usually with a masculine or neuter noun: in deinem Briefkasten (m), in deinem Bett (n), in deinem Zimmer (n). "Deinem" refers to one person you address as "du" (informal singular).
target_language_example: In deinem Auto liegt mein Handy.
native_language_example: My phone is in your car.

additional_notes: Used to compare someone’s current age to another person’s age, often when talking about what you did or what was true when you were that age. Common pattern: „Als ich in deinem Alter war, …“ (“When I was your age, …”). It can also mean “about your age” when estimating someone’s age: „Er scheint etwa in deinem Alter zu sein.“
target_language_example: Als ich in deinem Alter war, musste ich jeden Tag früh aufstehen.
native_language_example: When I was your age, I had to get up early every day.

additional_notes: Used to ask about what something is like where the other person is from (weather, common names, languages, time, etc.). Often appears in questions: „Wie ist … in deinem Land?“ It can be adapted: „in meinem Land“ (in my country), „in ihrem Land“ (in her/their country).
target_language_example: Was isst man in deinem Land zum Frühstück?
native_language_example: What do people eat for breakfast in your country?

additional_notes: Often used literally (someone/something is part of your life) or in expressions like "nie (wieder) in deinem Leben" = "never (again) in your life" / "never ever" for strong emphasis.
target_language_example: Sag das nie wieder in deinem Leben!
native_language_example: Never say that again in your life!

additional_notes: "in" + dative shows a location (where someone/something is). "deinem" is the dative form of "dein" (your) used with the neuter noun "das Zimmer" → "in deinem Zimmer". Often used with verbs like "bleiben" (stay), "sein" (be), "Ordnung halten" (keep tidy), and questions like "Was ... in deinem Zimmer gemacht?".
target_language_example: Bitte bleib in deinem Zimmer.
native_language_example: Please stay in your room.

additional_notes: Used both literally (you can physically see something in someone’s eyes, like tears) and figuratively (you can tell/see what someone feels or thinks by looking at their eyes). Often appears with verbs like „sehen“ (to see) and „lesen“ (to read). Can be changed to other people: „in meinen Augen“ (in my eyes), „in seinen/ihren Augen“ (in his/her eyes).
target_language_example: Ich sehe die Angst in deinen Augen.
native_language_example: I can see the fear in your eyes.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine noun in the dative case (e.g., in deiner Hand, in deiner Freizeit). With "in", German often uses dative for location/state (where?) and accusative for direction/movement (where to?), so you’ll also see "in deine ..." when talking about going into something.
target_language_example: In deiner Tasche ist mein Schlüssel.
native_language_example: My key is in your pocket/bag.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition "in" + the dative article "dem" (= masculine/neuter singular). Very often shortened to "im" in everyday German ("in dem Wald" → "im Wald"). With "in", German uses dative for a location (where?), and accusative for direction/motion into something (where to?).
target_language_example: Im Winter ist es in dem Haus sehr kalt.
native_language_example: In winter it’s very cold in the house.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific situation or condition just mentioned (or understood from context). Often used when drawing a conclusion or deciding what to do next: “In dem Fall …”. In speech it’s frequently shortened to “in dem Fall” (as written) and can be stressed for emphasis.
target_language_example: In dem Fall können wir morgen früher losfahren.
native_language_example: In that case, we can leave earlier tomorrow.

meaning: in the house; in that house.
additional_notes: Means “inside the house” (location). In speech it’s often shortened to **im Haus** (= in dem Haus). **in diesem Haus** means “in this house,” while **in dem Haus** often points to a specific/known house (“that house”). It can be expanded with extra info: **in dem Haus gegenüber** = “in the house across the street.”
target_language_example: In dem Haus nebenan wohnt meine Freundin.
native_language_example: My girlfriend lives in the house next door.

additional_notes: “in dem” is a contraction of “in” + “dem” (dative masculine/neuter). It’s used for location with “in” when you mean being inside/at a place (not going into it). In everyday speech and writing you often see the shortened form “im Hotel” (= in dem Hotel).
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns um acht in dem Hotel.
native_language_example: We’re meeting at eight in the hotel.

additional_notes: A location phrase: "in" + dative "dem" + "Laden" (shop/store). In everyday German it’s very often contracted to "im Laden" (= "in dem Laden"). "Laden" here is a noun meaning a store, not the verb "laden" (to load).
target_language_example: Ich habe ihn in dem Laden gesehen.
native_language_example: I saw him in the shop.

meaning: "the moment that" / "just as" (at the exact time when).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause that happens at the exact same time as something else, often emphasizing how immediate it is. It’s common in storytelling or descriptions of sudden events. The verb in the second clause goes to the end (because it’s a subordinating structure with "als").
target_language_example: In dem Moment, als das Telefon klingelte, ging das Licht aus.
native_language_example: The moment the phone rang, the lights went out.

additional_notes: Means someone/something is located inside a particular room. It’s the contraction of the preposition + article: **in + dem = im**, so you’ll very often see **im Raum**. You may keep **in dem** (instead of **im**) for emphasis or clarity (e.g., to stress *that* specific room).
target_language_example: In dem Raum steht ein großer Tisch.
native_language_example: There is a big table in the room.

additional_notes: Means being inside a specific car. "in dem" is the dative form of "in + der" (masculine/neuter), often shortened to "im" in everyday German: "im Wagen". Used with dative to describe location (where?), not movement into it ("in den Wagen" = into the car). "Wagen" can mean "car" (sometimes a more formal word than "Auto") or, depending on context, a wagon/cart.
target_language_example: Die Tasche liegt in dem Wagen.
native_language_example: The bag is in the car.

additional_notes: Used to say where something is happening or located (a place, not movement). It uses dative case after the preposition „in“ for location. Very often contracted to „im Zimmer“ (= „in dem Zimmer“).
target_language_example: In dem Zimmer ist es heute sehr warm.
native_language_example: It’s very warm in the room today.

additional_notes: Often used with a relative clause: "..., in dem ..." = "..., in which ..." (referring back to a masculine/neuter noun like "das Büro"). It can also simply be the preposition + article: "in dem Haus" = "in the house" (masc./neut. dative). Commonly contracted to "im" ("in dem" → "im"), especially for locations ("im Büro").
target_language_example: Das ist das Zimmer, in dem ich schlafe.
native_language_example: That’s the room in which I sleep.

meaning: "in which he" / "where he" (introduces a relative clause).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to add information about a place/thing. "in" takes the dative here (location, not movement), so it becomes "in dem" (= "in + the", often shortened to "im"). "dem" is the relative pronoun for masculine/neuter singular in the dative case, and "er" is the subject inside the relative clause. Common with nouns like "das Zimmer", "das Land", "das Haus": "..., in dem er ...".
target_language_example: Das ist das Café, in dem er jeden Morgen frühstückt.
native_language_example: That’s the café where he has breakfast every morning.

meaning: "in which I" / "where I" (introduces a relative clause).
additional_notes: Used to add extra information about a masculine/neuter noun (der/das) and means that you are *in* that thing/place. It’s a relative-clause form of **in dem** (= in which), similar to **in welchem** but more common. The verb goes to the end of the relative clause: *das Hotel, in dem ich gewohnt habe*.
target_language_example: Das ist die Stadt, in dem ich geboren bin.
native_language_example: That’s the city where I was born.

meaning: "in which we" / "where we" (referring to a place/thing).
additional_notes: Used in a relative clause to describe a noun (a place or thing) that "we" are inside of. "In" + a stationary location takes the dative, so you get "in dem" (often shortened to "im" in simple sentences, but not here because you need the relative pronoun). The form "dem" is dative masculine/neuter; for feminine it’s "in der wir" and for plural it’s "in denen wir".
target_language_example: Das ist das Café, in dem wir immer lernen.
native_language_example: That’s the café where we always study.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition in + den. It can mean in the for location/state (usually with plural nouns in the dative, e.g. in den Vereinigten Staaten, in den Zeitungen) or into the for movement into something (with masculine singular nouns in the accusative, e.g. in den Mantel).
target_language_example: Im Sommer arbeiten viele Studenten in den Restaurants der Stadt.
native_language_example: In the summer, many students work in the city's restaurants.

meaning: (jemanden) in den Arm nehmen = to hug (someone).
additional_notes: Most commonly used with the verb phrase **jemanden in den Arm nehmen** (“to take someone into your arms” = to hug). The same words can also simply describe a location with other verbs, e.g. **jemanden in den Arm kneifen** = “to pinch someone in the arm.”
target_language_example: Kann ich dich kurz in den Arm nehmen?
native_language_example: Can I give you a quick hug?

meaning: “in the ass / up the ass” (very vulgar).
additional_notes: A highly offensive, explicit phrase used with verbs describing movement into that body part (e.g., jemanden in den Arsch treten = “to kick someone in the ass”). Uses accusative (den) because it expresses direction/motion (“into”). Avoid in polite conversation.
target_language_example: Tritt mich nicht in den Arsch!
native_language_example: Don’t kick me in the ass!

meaning: in the eyes (of); in someone’s view/opinion.
additional_notes: Used literally for something physically in your eyes (pain, sand, etc.), and figuratively to mean “in someone’s eyes” = “according to their perspective/opinion.” Often followed by a possessive or a name in the genitive/dative phrase: “in den Augen meiner Mutter / in seinen Augen.”
target_language_example: In den Augen vieler Leute ist Deutsch schwer.
native_language_example: In the eyes of many people, German is difficult.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something is located within a mountainous area (not necessarily on a specific mountain). Often follows verbs like sein (to be), liegen (to be located), wohnen (to live), or passieren (to happen).
target_language_example: Wir machen Urlaub in den Bergen.
native_language_example: We’re going on vacation in the mountains.

meaning: (going) into/onto the bus; getting on the bus.
additional_notes: Used with movement (destination) and typically with verbs like „(in den Bus) steigen“ (to get on), „einsteigen“ (to get on), or „jemandem in den Bus helfen“ (to help someone onto the bus). Because it’s a destination, German uses accusative: „in den Bus“ (masculine „der Bus“ → „den“). For location (already inside), you usually say „im Bus“ (= in the bus).
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, wo kann ich in den Bus einsteigen?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where can I get on the bus?

additional_notes: This is part of the separable verb **einsteigen** = “to get in/on (a vehicle)”. In main clauses, **ein-** often goes to the end: **Steig in den Bus ein!** In the past: **stieg … ein**. With the formal/polite form: **Steigen Sie … ein!** You can also say **in den Bus einsteigen** when the verb stays together (e.g., in infinitives).
target_language_example: Bitte steigen Sie in den Bus ein.
native_language_example: Please get on the bus.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens within a holiday/vacation period (often school holidays). It’s more general than a specific trip: Wohin fährst du in den Ferien? = Where will you go during the vacation?
target_language_example: In den Ferien habe ich mehr Zeit für meine Freunde.
native_language_example: During the holidays, I have more time for my friends.

additional_notes: Used with movement/change of location toward the inside of a river (e.g., jump/dive/throw/fall into it). It often goes with verbs like springen, tauchen, werfen, fallen. Contrast: "im Fluss" = in the river (location, not movement).
target_language_example: Pass auf—dein Handy könnte in den Fluss fallen!
native_language_example: Watch out—your phone could fall into the river!

meaning: into the garden; to the garden (direction/movement).
additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement to show you are going from somewhere else into the garden (destination). In German this is typically accusative with "in" ("in den" = masculine accusative of "der Garten"). Often contrasts with "im Garten" (= in the garden, location).
target_language_example: Kommst du kurz mit in den Garten?
native_language_example: Are you coming with me to the garden for a moment?

meaning: to get (something) under control; to get a handle on (something).
additional_notes: Used when you manage a problem, situation, or feeling successfully. It takes an accusative object (e.g., den Stress, die Situation). Common with things like Stress, Angst, Probleme, eine Situation. The verb is often used with modal verbs: muss/kann ... in den Griff bekommen.
target_language_example: Ich muss meine Zeit besser in den Griff bekommen.
native_language_example: I need to get my time management under control.

additional_notes: Used with the accusative (den Himmel) after "in" to show direction/movement: looking up into the sky (literal) or going to heaven (religious/after death). It can also be used figuratively to mean feeling ecstatic (e.g., through kisses).
target_language_example: Der Ball flog in den Himmel.
native_language_example: The ball flew up into the sky.

additional_notes: A common (informal, slightly crude) body-part phrase, often used in threats or jokes with verbs like „(jmdm.) in den Hintern treten“ (to kick someone’s butt) or „(jmdm.) eine Kugel in den Hintern schießen“ (to shoot someone in the butt). The form changes with the case after different prepositions (e.g., „in den Hintern“ with movement/impact).
target_language_example: Wenn du nicht aufpasst, trete ich dir in den Hintern.
native_language_example: If you don’t watch out, I’ll kick your butt.

additional_notes: Used with haben/halten/sehen to describe that someone has an object in their hands (is holding it). Often paired with a possessive or dative pronoun: in den Händen haben/halten (z. B. „in den Händen halten“, „in den Händen haben“, „in den Händen“).
target_language_example: Er hat sein Handy in den Händen und schreibt eine Nachricht.
native_language_example: He has his phone in his hands and is writing a message.

meaning: into the basement / down to the cellar.
additional_notes: Used with movement (destination) toward the basement (usually with verbs like gehen, bringen). Often implies going downstairs. Contrast: „im Keller“ = in the basement (location, not movement).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte die Kisten in den Keller bringen?
native_language_example: Can you please take the boxes down to the basement?

additional_notes: "Knast" is an informal word for prison/jail. You often see it with movement/causation verbs like "gehen/kommen" (to go/end up) or "bringen" (to take/send someone): "jemanden in den Knast bringen" = to send someone to jail. Uses accusative after "in" because it implies direction (into).
target_language_example: Wenn du so weitermachst, kommst du in den Knast.
native_language_example: If you keep going like this, you’ll end up in jail.

meaning: into the head; to someone’s head.
additional_notes: Used with the accusative (den Kopf) to express direction/movement toward the head. Very common in set phrases/idioms, e.g. jemandem Flöhe in den Kopf setzen (to put ideas into someone’s head), jemandem/etwas wird in den Kopf steigen (to go to someone’s head, e.g. success), jemandem in den Kopf schießen (to shoot someone in the head).
target_language_example: Setz dir das nicht in den Kopf!
native_language_example: Don’t get that idea into your head!

meaning: to go to war; to march off to war.
additional_notes: Used for starting a military campaign or joining a war. Often implies being sent/going off as part of an army ("ziehen" = to march/move), and it’s commonly used with a subject like "wir/sie" and sometimes with "gegen" + an opponent (e.g., "gegen Saladin").
target_language_example: Viele junge Männer mussten in den Krieg ziehen.
native_language_example: Many young men had to go off to war.

meaning: into the fridge / into the refrigerator.
additional_notes: Used with verbs of motion/placement (e.g., legen, stellen) to say you’re putting something into the fridge. Because it’s movement into a place, German uses the accusative: den Kühlschrank (der Kühlschrank). Often heard as (zurück) in den Kühlschrank = (back) into the fridge.
target_language_example: Kannst du den Käse bitte in den Kühlschrank stellen?
native_language_example: Can you put the cheese in the fridge, please?

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (gehen, kommen, laufen) to show direction/destination: you’re going into the shop. For location (being in the shop), German usually uses "im Laden" (= in the shop). "in" + "den" (accusative) indicates motion into a place.
target_language_example: Ich gehe kurz in den Laden und kaufe Brot.
native_language_example: I’m going into the shop for a moment and buying bread.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement/putting something somewhere (accusative): etwas in den Mund stecken/schieben/stopfen/nehmen. Contrast: im Mund (“in the mouth,” location, not movement). Also appears in the idiom jemandem die Worte in den Mund legen (“to put words in someone’s mouth”).
target_language_example: Steck dir das bitte nicht in den Mund!
native_language_example: Please don’t put that in your mouth!

meaning: in the news; on the news.
additional_notes: Used to say something is being reported by the media (TV, radio, newspapers, news websites). Often with verbs like „sehen“, „hören“, „lesen“: „Ich habe es in den Nachrichten gesehen/gehört/gelesen.“ Also works as a short reply: „In den Nachrichten.“ (= “On the news.”).
target_language_example: Ich habe es gestern Abend in den Nachrichten gehört.
native_language_example: I heard it on the news yesterday evening.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of putting/moving something (e.g., schieben/stellen/tun/legen) to say something goes *into* the oven. Grammar note: it uses the accusative (den) because it implies movement/direction. For location (already inside), you usually say **im Ofen** (= in the oven).
target_language_example: Kannst du das Brot in den Ofen schieben?
native_language_example: Can you put the bread into the oven?

meaning: to the park; into the park (going there).
additional_notes: Used with movement/direction: "in" + accusative (den Park) means you’re going into the park. For location (already there), German usually uses dative: "im Park" (= in the park).
target_language_example: Wir gehen nach der Schule in den Park.
native_language_example: We’re going to the park after school.

additional_notes: Used with **sein** in the Perfekt tense for movement: **(ich) bin … gegangen**. **in den Park** uses the accusative after **in** because it indicates motion/direction (going into/to the park), not location (that would be **im Park** = in the park). Often combined with a purpose phrase using **zum** + noun (e.g., **zum Spielen**, **zum Musikhören**).
target_language_example: Wir sind nach der Schule in den Park gegangen.
native_language_example: We went to the park after school.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like „in den Ruhestand gehen/treten“ to mean someone stops working and becomes retired (often from a job/career). In everyday German you’ll also hear „in Rente gehen“ with a very similar meaning.
target_language_example: Meine Mutter geht dieses Jahr in den Ruhestand.
native_language_example: My mother is retiring this year.

meaning: in/into the back (often: shot or stabbed in the back).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like „schießen“ (to shoot) and „stechen/stoßen/rammen“ (to stab/thrust) to say someone was hit in the back. It can also appear in the common idiom „jemandem in den Rücken fallen“ = to betray someone / stab someone in the back (figuratively).
target_language_example: Er wurde von hinten in den Rücken geschossen.
native_language_example: He was shot in the back from behind.

meaning: into the sand; in "in den Sand setzen": to mess up / ruin (something).
additional_notes: Literally used for writing/drawing in sand: "(etw.) in den Sand schreiben/zeichnen". Very common idiom with "setzen": "etw. in den Sand setzen" = to botch something, waste an opportunity, or make a plan fail.
target_language_example: Wir haben den Plan komplett in den Sand gesetzt.
native_language_example: We completely messed up the plan.
