target_language_example: Mach dir keine Sorgen um die Prüfung.
native_language_example: Don’t worry about the exam.

meaning: to not worry; not to be worried (about something).
additional_notes: Commonly used with the reflexive pronoun: „sich keine Sorgen zu machen“ (e.g., „Ich versuche, mir keine Sorgen zu machen.“). The „zu“ appears when the verb phrase is in an infinitive construction (often after verbs like „versuchen“, „scheinen“, „anfangen“ or after fixed expressions like „es gibt keinen Grund“). In direct reassurance, German more often uses the imperative without „zu“: „Mach dir keine Sorgen!“
target_language_example: Ich versuche, mir keine Sorgen zu machen.
native_language_example: I’m trying not to worry.

additional_notes: Uses *brauchen* + *zu* + infinitive to express that something is unnecessary. Here the phrase is in a relative clause-like structure where *braucht* comes at the end: *... der/die keine Sorgen zu machen braucht.* Closely related to the common wording *Du brauchst dir keine Sorgen zu machen.* (*Sich Sorgen machen* = “to worry,” literally “to make oneself worries”). Often used to reassure someone.
target_language_example: Er ist in guten Händen und jemand, der sich keine Sorgen zu machen braucht.
native_language_example: He’s in good hands and someone who doesn’t need to worry.

additional_notes: A polite, common reply after someone thanks you, meaning it wasn’t any trouble. Often used on its own (“Keine Ursache!”) or followed by a name. Also used to downplay what you did: “Keine Ursache, das war nicht so schlimm.”
target_language_example: Danke für deine Hilfe! – Keine Ursache.
native_language_example: Thanks for your help! – No problem.

additional_notes: Used to say you can’t decide freely because the situation (or someone else) forces you. Common patterns: „Ich habe/hatte keine Wahl.“ (I have/had no choice.), „Du hast keine Wahl.“ (You have no choice.), „Jemand lässt mir/uns keine Wahl.“ (Someone leaves me/us no choice.).
target_language_example: Wir mussten gehen — wir hatten keine Wahl.
native_language_example: We had to leave — we had no choice.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t have time (right now) or that there isn’t time for something: „Ich habe keine Zeit.“ / „Wir haben keine Zeit dafür.“ Often followed by „für“ + noun („keine Zeit für Sport“) or „zum/zur“ + noun („keine Zeit zum Reden“, „keine Zeit zur Diskussion“). Common related phrases: „keine Zeit haben“, „keine Zeit mehr haben“ (no time left), „noch keine Zeit dazu haben“ (haven’t had time for it yet).
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, ich habe gerade keine Zeit dafür.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t have time for that right now.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t have time for an activity/thing/person. Often in the pattern: (Ich/Wir/Er/Sie) habe(n) keine Zeit für + noun (or nominalized verb). It can also mean “I’m not in the mood for that / I won’t tolerate that” when used with things like Spielchen/Spiele (“games”).
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, ich habe heute keine Zeit für ein Gespräch.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t have time for a talk today.

meaning: to have no time; to be too busy.
additional_notes: Used to say you’re too busy to do something or can’t make time. Conjugate "haben" (ich habe, du hast, er/sie hat, wir haben, ihr habt, sie/Sie haben) while keeping "keine Zeit" together: "Ich habe keine Zeit." You can add what for with "für" + accusative: "Ich habe keine Zeit für dich/heute."
target_language_example: Es ist schade, aber ich werde diese Woche keine Zeit haben.
native_language_example: It’s a shame, but I won’t have time this week.

additional_notes: Used when time has run out or you can’t spare any more time. Often followed by an action with **zum + infinitive** or **für + noun**: *keine Zeit mehr zum Lernen*, *keine Zeit mehr für Fragen*. Common in urgent situations: *Wir haben keine Zeit mehr!*
target_language_example: Ich habe keine Zeit mehr, dich abzuholen.
native_language_example: I don’t have any more time to pick you up.

meaning: “no time to lose” / “no time to waste.”
additional_notes: Used to express urgency: you need to act immediately. Often appears as a standalone sentence ("Es ist keine Zeit zu verlieren.") or with "haben" in the past/present: "Wir haben keine Zeit zu verlieren."
target_language_example: Beeil dich—wir haben keine Zeit zu verlieren!
native_language_example: Hurry up—we have no time to lose!

additional_notes: Used to say someone is forced to do something because there isn’t another option. Very common with forms of "haben" ("keine andere Wahl haben") and often followed by "als" + infinitive ("… als zu …").
target_language_example: Ich habe keine andere Wahl, als jetzt zu gehen.
native_language_example: I have no other choice but to leave now.

additional_notes: Used to say there is only one possible option. Very common in the pattern: (ich/du/er ...) habe/hatte/wir haben/hatten **keine andere Wahl, als** + infinitive (often with **zu**): *... als zu Hause zu bleiben / ... als nach Hause zurückzukehren*.
target_language_example: Ich hatte keine andere Wahl, als den Arzt anzurufen.
native_language_example: I had no choice but to call the doctor.

additional_notes: Used to warn against or discourage a plan/action. Common patterns: „Das ist keine gute Idee.“ / „Ich halte das für keine gute Idee.“ (“I don’t think that’s a good idea.”) / „Vielleicht ist es keine gute Idee.“ (“Maybe it’s not a good idea.”). Often refers to something already suggested or about to happen.
target_language_example: Es ist keine gute Idee, so spät noch Kaffee zu trinken.
native_language_example: It’s not a good idea to drink coffee so late.

meaning: “no way / under no circumstances” (usually in: „auf keinen Fall“).
additional_notes: You’ll most often see it as the fixed phrase „auf keinen Fall“ to strongly refuse or say something must not happen: „Auf keinen Fall!“ = “No way!” / “Absolutely not!” Grammar note: „keinen“ is the accusative form of „kein“ because it goes with „Fall“ (masculine: der Fall).
target_language_example: Auf keinen Fall darfst du das vergessen.
native_language_example: Under no circumstances may you forget that.

additional_notes: Usually used with **zu + infinitive** to say there’s no reason to do something: **keinen Grund, zu lügen / hier zu bleiben**. It can also appear with **dazu** (“to that / to do that”) to refer back to a situation: **Ich hatte keinen Grund dazu** (“I had no reason to do that”). The noun **Grund** literally means “ground,” but in this phrase it means “reason.”
target_language_example: Ich habe keinen Grund, mich zu beschweren.
native_language_example: I have no reason to complain.

additional_notes: Used to say there is no good reason for something to happen or be different. Common patterns: „Es gibt keinen Grund, warum …“ and „Ich sehe keinen Grund, warum …“. The part after „warum“ is a clause (often with „sollte“, „müsste“, etc.).
target_language_example: Wir haben keinen Grund, warum wir uns beeilen sollten.
native_language_example: We have no reason why we should hurry.

additional_notes: Used with "haben" to say you are not hungry: "Ich habe keinen Hunger." In questions, it often expresses surprise/expectation that someone might be hungry: "Hast du keinen Hunger?" Can also be used with "noch" (= yet) or "vielleicht" (= maybe).
target_language_example: Danke, ich habe keinen Hunger, aber ich trinke gern etwas.
native_language_example: Thanks, I'm not hungry, but I'd like to drink something.

meaning: to have no idea; to have no clue.
additional_notes: Colloquial way to say you don’t know something at all. Often used with a question-word clause: „Ich habe keinen Schimmer haben, wie/wo/warum …“ (more natural in usage is the conjugated form „Ich habe keinen Schimmer, wie …“, but this entry keeps the exact multi-word term). Similar to „keine Ahnung haben“; can be intensified with „überhaupt“.
target_language_example: Ich werde dir ehrlich sagen: Ich kann dir nicht helfen, weil ich keinen Schimmer haben, wie das funktioniert.
native_language_example: I’ll be honest: I can’t help you because I have no idea how that works.

meaning: “Not one step further!” / “Don’t come any closer!”
additional_notes: A strong command (often shouted) used to stop someone from moving forward. Literally “no step further.” You’ll often hear it in confrontations (e.g., police, guards, arguments). Can also be said alone as an order: “Keinen Schritt weiter!”
target_language_example: Keinen Schritt weiter, oder ich rufe die Polizei!
native_language_example: Not one step further, or I’ll call the police!

meaning: “no sense” / “no point” (doesn’t make sense; is pointless).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like „machen/ergeben/haben“: „Das macht keinen Sinn.“ = it doesn’t make sense. „Es hatte keinen Sinn, …“ = there was no point in … (it was pointless). Note the forms change with gender/case: „kein Sinn“ (subject), „keinen Sinn“ (object). Also common: „Sinn für etw. haben“ = to have a sense for something (e.g., „keinen Sinn für die Gefahr“ = no sense of danger).
target_language_example: Es hat keinen Sinn, weiter zu warten.
native_language_example: There’s no point in waiting any longer.

meaning: to have no sense/feel for (something); to not understand or appreciate (something).
additional_notes: Used with the accusative: keinen Sinn für + noun (e.g., keinen Sinn für Humor). Often describes lacking understanding, appreciation, or talent for something (humor, art, details, etc.). You can also say „keinen Sinn für etwas haben“ or „dafür keinen Sinn haben“. Related: „Sinn für“ = a sense/feel for.
target_language_example: Er hat keinen Sinn für Humor.
native_language_example: He has no sense of humor.

additional_notes: Used with negation (kein-) to say something isn’t fun or someone isn’t enjoying it. Common patterns: „(Das) macht keinen Spaß.“ = “(That) isn’t fun.” / „Ich habe keinen Spaß.“ = “I’m not having fun.” With people: „Es macht keinen Spaß mit ihr/ihm.“ = “It’s no fun with her/him.” Also: „Verstehst du keinen Spaß?“ means “Can’t you take a joke?” (you don’t tolerate joking).
target_language_example: Heute macht das Spiel irgendwie keinen Spaß.
native_language_example: Today the game somehow isn’t fun.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like „machen“ (to make), „sehen“ (to see), and „es gibt“ (there is/are): „Das macht keinen Unterschied.“ = “That makes no difference.” The form „keinen“ is accusative masculine because „Unterschied“ is masculine (der Unterschied). Often appears with intensifiers like „gar“: „gar keinen Unterschied“ = “no difference at all.”
target_language_example: Ob wir heute oder morgen fahren, macht keinen Unterschied.
native_language_example: Whether we go today or tomorrow makes no difference.

additional_notes: Most often used with **haben**: **(Es) hat keinen Zweck.** = “It’s no use / There’s no point.” You can also hear it shortened in conversation: **Hat keinen Zweck.** Often said with particles like **ja/doch** for emphasis (e.g., “It really is pointless”).
target_language_example: Wir müssen nicht weiter diskutieren – das hat keinen Zweck.
native_language_example: We don’t need to discuss it further—it’s pointless.

additional_notes: Used with different prepositions and clauses: **keinen Zweifel an + Dativ** (no doubt about something/someone), **keinen Zweifel daran, dass …** (no doubt that …), **keinen Zweifel daran lassen, dass …** (to make it very clear; to leave no doubt that …). Often used to emphasize certainty.
target_language_example: Ich habe keinen Zweifel daran, dass alles gut wird.
native_language_example: I have no doubt that everything will be fine.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like machen/bringen to mean “don’t cause trouble” or “not cause any trouble (for someone).” Common in warnings/requests: „Mach bloß keinen Ärger!“ = “Don’t you dare cause any trouble!” You can also say „keinen Ärger mehr“ = “no more trouble (anymore).”
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, ich mache keinen Ärger.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I won’t cause any trouble.

meaning: in no way; not at all (usually in: „in keiner Weise“).
additional_notes: Most commonly used with a preposition, especially „in keiner Weise“, meaning something is absolutely not the case. „Weise“ here means “way/manner” (not the adjective „weise“ = “wise”). Often used in more formal or emphatic statements.
target_language_example: Das ist in keiner Weise akzeptabel.
native_language_example: That is in no way acceptable.

additional_notes: Used to say that not a single person did something or has something. "Keiner" means "no one" (masculine nominative; also used generically for mixed groups), and it’s often followed by "hat" + past participle in the present perfect: "Keiner hat angerufen" = "No one called." In casual speech you may hear "Keiner hat was ..." meaning "No one has anything ... / No one has ...".
target_language_example: Keiner hat mir heute Morgen geschrieben.
native_language_example: No one wrote to me this morning.

meaning: "none of" / "not one of" (for masculine or mixed groups).
additional_notes: Used to say that from a certain group, not a single person/thing applies. It’s commonly followed by a dative phrase after von (e.g., keiner von meinen Freunden, keiner von Ihnen, keiner von beiden). For feminine groups use keine von, and for neuter use keines von.
target_language_example: Keiner von meinen Freunden hat heute Zeit.
native_language_example: None of my friends has time today.

additional_notes: Used to say that not a single person in a group addressed as "euch" (you plural/informal) does something or is something. Often followed by a verb: "Keiner von euch hat ..." = "None of you has ...". You can add a number: "Keiner von euch beiden" = "Neither of you two". With "Recht haben": "Recht hat keiner von euch" = "None of you is right."
target_language_example: Keiner von euch weiß, wie das Passwort lautet.
native_language_example: None of you knows what the password is.

additional_notes: Refers to a group of people/things already known from context and says that zero of them fit. Use it as the subject: "Keiner von ihnen ist ...". For feminine groups use "keine von ihnen", and for mixed/neutral in plural often "keines von ihnen" (e.g., things). In everyday speech you also hear "Keiner von denen ...".
target_language_example: Keiner von ihnen hat heute Zeit.
native_language_example: None of them has time today.

additional_notes: Used to say that zero people in the group (including the speaker) have/do something. Often takes a singular verb in German: "Keiner von uns ist …". Can also be used as a short standalone answer: "Keiner von uns." (="None of us."). For mixed/unknown gender groups you may also hear "keine(r) von uns" depending on context, but "keiner von uns" is very common in general statements.
target_language_example: Keiner von uns hat heute Zeit.
native_language_example: None of us has time today.

meaning: 'neither of us (two)' / 'none of the two of us'.
additional_notes: Used when you’re talking about exactly two people (you + one other person). It’s often the subject of the sentence and is followed by singular verb forms: "Keiner von uns beiden kann ...". The form changes with case: nominative "keiner", accusative "keinen" (e.g., "Ich sehe keinen von uns beiden"), dative "keinem" (e.g., "Ich helfe keinem von uns beiden").
target_language_example: Keiner von uns beiden hat heute Zeit.
native_language_example: Neither of us has time today.

additional_notes: "Keiner" means "no one" (masculine) and is often used as the subject. It’s commonly followed by a direct object (Keiner weiß die Antwort.) or by an indirect question with a comma: Keiner weiß, dass/ob/wer/wie/wohin … . In more formal/written German you may also see "Niemand weiß …".
target_language_example: Keiner weiß, warum der Zug heute so spät ist.
native_language_example: No one knows why the train is so late today.

additional_notes: From the verb **kennen** (“to know/be familiar with people, places, things”). You’ll often hear it as **Das kenne ich.** (“I know that / I’ve heard of that.”) or in questions like **Woher kenne ich dich/den Namen?** (“How do I know you/that name?”). With **nicht**, it means “I don’t know (it/them)”: **Den Ausdruck kenne ich nicht.** For skills/subjects, German often uses **sich auskennen**: **Mit Mathe kenne ich mich nicht aus.** (“I’m not good with math / I don’t know my way around math.”).
target_language_example: Den Film kenne ich schon.
native_language_example: I already know that movie / I’ve seen that movie before.

additional_notes: From the verb **kennen** (to know/be familiar with a person, place, or thing). It’s used when you know someone personally or recognize them. **ihn** means “him” and is the accusative (direct object) pronoun. With **nicht**: *Ich kenne ihn nicht.* (“I don’t know him.”) Contrast: **wissen** is for knowing facts/information (*Ich weiß es.* = “I know it.”).
target_language_example: Ich kenne ihn aus der Schule.
native_language_example: I know him from school.

additional_notes: "Kennen" is used for knowing people, places, or being familiar with things (songs, poems, riddles, tricks). "Sie" is the formal “you” (used with strangers, in shops, at work). For facts/answers, German often uses "wissen" (e.g., "Wissen Sie die Antwort?"), but you may still hear "Kennen Sie die Antwort?" in some contexts. In questions like "Kennen Sie zwei sich schon?", it means “Do you two already know each other?”
target_language_example: Kennen Sie dieses Lied?
native_language_example: Do you know this song?

additional_notes: Used when politely asking if someone is familiar with a person or a specific thing (often followed by a noun: Kennen Sie die Dame?/die Postleitzahl?). With people it can mean “Have you met/Do you know (personally) … ?”; with things it means “Are you familiar with/Do you know … ?”. In informal speech you’d usually say “Kennst du die … ?”.
target_language_example: Kennen Sie die Frau dort drüben?
native_language_example: Do you know the woman over there?

additional_notes: A polite way to ask if someone can recommend a person with a certain skill or experience. It’s followed by a relative clause: use **der** (masc.), **die** (fem./plural), or **das** (neut.), depending on **jemand**’s implied gender/number or the noun you mean (e.g., *Kennen Sie jemanden, **die** gut Italienisch spricht?*).
target_language_example: Kennen Sie jemanden, der mir beim Umzug helfen kann?
native_language_example: Do you know anyone who can help me with the move?

additional_notes: Past participle of **kennenlernen**. Used with **haben** in the perfect tense: **Ich habe ihn kennen gelernt / kennengelernt.** Often used reflexively with **sich** to mean “to meet (each other)”: **Wir haben uns kennen gelernt.** Both spellings are common: **kennen gelernt** (two words) and **kennengelernt** (one word).
target_language_example: Wir haben uns letztes Jahr auf einer Party kennen gelernt.
native_language_example: We met at a party last year.

meaning: to get to know (someone); to meet and start to know them.
additional_notes: Used for the process of becoming acquainted (not for already knowing someone). Often said with the reflexive pronoun when it’s mutual: „Wir müssen uns erst kennen lernen.“ Also commonly written as one word in modern German: „kennenlernen“ (both are seen).
target_language_example: Ich möchte dich gern besser kennen lernen.
native_language_example: I’d like to get to know you better.

meaning: to get to know; to meet (and become acquainted).
additional_notes: Infinitive form of **kennenlernen** used with **zu** (often after another verb): *ich freue mich, dich kennen zu lernen*. It means becoming familiar with a person/place/thing over time—not just a first encounter (that’s often **treffen** = “to meet”). Spelling is also common as one word: **kennenzulernen** / **kennenlernen**.
target_language_example: Schön, dich kennen zu lernen!
native_language_example: Nice to meet you!

additional_notes: Used to ask one person informally whether they know or are familiar with someone or something. It comes from kennen, which is used for being acquainted with people, places, words, films, feelings, etc. For knowing facts or information, German usually uses wissen instead.
target_language_example: Kennst du dieses Lied?
native_language_example: Do you know this song?

meaning: “Do you know him/it?” (referring to a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone is familiar with a specific person or thing already identified in context. "Kennst du" is for knowing/familiar with people/places/things (not facts). "den" is the masculine accusative form of "der" and can mean “him” or “that (masc.)” depending on what follows (e.g., a noun or a relative clause).
target_language_example: Kennst du den Mann da drüben?
native_language_example: Do you know the man over there?

meaning: “Do you know the …?” (asking if someone knows certain people/things).
additional_notes: Uses du (informal “you”) and kennen (“to know/be familiar with”). The object is in the accusative; die is used for plural nouns and for feminine singular nouns (e.g., die Bedeutung). You can also ask without the article: “Kennst du Maria?”
target_language_example: Kennst du die Leute hier?
native_language_example: Do you know the people here?

additional_notes: Used to ask if the other person knows a person with a certain skill/quality. After "jemanden" you use a relative clause with "der/die/das" (here: "der" for a masculine person; also common: "Kennst du jemanden, der/die …?" when the gender is unknown). Verb goes to the end of the relative clause.
target_language_example: Kennst du jemanden, der mir beim Umzug helfen kann?
native_language_example: Do you know someone who can help me with the move?

additional_notes: Uses the verb "kennen" (to be familiar with / to know a person or thing). Here it means someone is familiar with the truth/facts. "kennt" is 3rd person singular (er/sie/es). With "ihr" (you plural), it becomes "ihr kennt"; with "ich", "ich kenne". Often used with "schon" (already) or "noch nicht" (not yet).
target_language_example: Sie kennt die Wahrheit, aber sie sagt nichts.
native_language_example: She knows the truth, but she’s not saying anything.

additional_notes: "kennt" is the 2nd-person plural present tense of **kennen** (ihr = you all). It’s used mainly for knowing/familiarity with **people, places, or things** (e.g., "Kennt ihr meine Schwester?"). For facts/information, German often uses **wissen** instead. In questions, German commonly uses verb-first word order: **Kennt ihr ...?**
target_language_example: Kennt ihr dieses Restaurant hier?
native_language_example: Do you (all) know this restaurant here?

additional_notes: From the verb "kennen" (to know/be acquainted with) + reflexive "euch" (each other/yourselves) in the plural "ihr" (you all). It’s used to ask if two or more people are acquainted, often with follow-ups like "schon lange?" (for a long time?), "Wie gut...?" (How well...?), or "Woher...?" (From where/How do you know each other?). For two people you’d say "Kennt ihr euch?"; for one person to one person: "Kennt ihr euch?" is also used when speaking to a pair, while to a single person about another single person you’d ask "Kennt ihr euch?" addressing both, or "Kennst du ihn/sie?" (Do you know him/her?).
target_language_example: Kennt ihr euch schon?
native_language_example: Do you already know each other?

meaning: has no limits / knows no bounds.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is extremely strong, intense, or excessive. Common with abstract nouns like Unverschämtheit (rudeness), Arroganz (arrogance), Eitelkeit (vanity), Liebe (love), but can also be used more literally with things like Natur (nature) or borders. Structure: [something] kennt keine Grenzen.
target_language_example: Seine Geduld kennt keine Grenzen.
native_language_example: His patience has no limits.

additional_notes: Used before a subordinate clause with **dass** to introduce what is clear/obvious. Common patterns: **Es ist klar, dass …** (“It’s clear that …”) and **Mir wurde klar, dass …** (“I realized that …”). The comma often appears because the **dass**-clause is a subordinate clause.
target_language_example: Es ist klar, dass wir heute nicht mehr ankommen.
native_language_example: It’s clear that we won’t arrive today.

meaning: “(it’s) clear that he …” / “it becomes clear to (someone) that he …”
additional_notes: Used with a **dass**-clause to say something is obvious or becomes obvious. Common patterns: **Es ist klar, dass er ...** (“It’s clear that he ...”) and **Jemandem wird/ist klar, dass er ...** (“Someone realizes / it is clear to someone that he ...”; note the person is often in the **dative**: *mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch*).
target_language_example: Mir ist klar, dass er heute nicht kommt.
native_language_example: It’s clear to me that he isn’t coming today.

additional_notes: Used with a form of "klar sein/werden" (e.g., "Mir ist klar …", "Mir wurde klar …", "Mir war nicht klar …") followed by an embedded question with "wie" to express that you (suddenly) understand the degree/way something is: "It’s clear to me how …" / "I didn’t realize how …". Often takes a dative experiencer: "mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen".
target_language_example: Mir ist jetzt klar, wie viel Zeit das kostet.
native_language_example: I realize now how much time that takes.

additional_notes: Often used to emphasize that something is easy to understand/hear, or that a result is decisive (a clear win). Common with verbs like hören (to hear), sagen (to say), verstehen (to understand), and gewinnen (to win).
target_language_example: Bitte sag es noch einmal klar und deutlich.
native_language_example: Please say it again clearly and distinctly.

additional_notes: Colloquial way to strongly say yes or confirm something. Often used as a short reply to a request or question (similar to "Sure, no problem!"). "Doch" adds emphasis, like "after all" or "you bet" in English.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir kurz helfen? – Klar doch!
native_language_example: Can you help me quickly? – Of course!

additional_notes: Refers to Western classical music (e.g., Mozart, Beethoven). Often used with verbs like „hören“ (to listen) and to express preferences: „am liebsten klassische Musik“ = “classical music most of all.”
target_language_example: Ich höre gern klassische Musik, wenn ich lerne.
native_language_example: I like listening to classical music when I study.

meaning: 'small, but …' (a contrast: small yet with a positive/strong quality).
additional_notes: Used to contrast being small with another (often surprising or positive) trait: "klein, aber stark/hübsch/schnell". Often appears with the pattern "zwar …, aber …" (= "it’s true that …, but …"). The comma is standard before "aber" when it connects two clauses.
target_language_example: Der Laden ist klein, aber sehr beliebt.
native_language_example: The shop is small, but very popular.

additional_notes: Used in time clauses to talk about when someone was a child, most often with **als** (one-time period in the past): **als ich (noch) klein war** = “when I was little.” **noch** adds the idea of “still” (= still a small child back then). Conjugation depends on the subject: **als er klein war**, **als wir klein waren**, etc.
target_language_example: Als ich klein war, wollte ich Tierarzt werden.
native_language_example: When I was little, I wanted to become a vet.

additional_notes: Refers to children who are still quite young (often preschool/early elementary age). It can be used literally (“Tom hat kleine Kinder”) or figuratively to criticize someone’s behavior (“Ihr seid wie kleine Kinder” = you’re acting childish). Common with the verb “auf … aufpassen” = to look after/babysit (e.g., „auf kleine Kinder aufpassen“).
target_language_example: Ich kann heute Abend nicht, ich muss auf kleine Kinder aufpassen.
native_language_example: I can’t tonight; I have to babysit little kids.

additional_notes: Plural of „das Mädchen“ (“girl”). „kleine“ is the plural adjective form used with no article (e.g., „Kleine Mädchen spielen …“). With an article it changes: „die kleinen Mädchen“ = “the little girls”. Note: „Mädchen“ is grammatically neuter in the singular („das Mädchen“) because of the diminutive ending -chen.
target_language_example: Kleine Mädchen spielen oft im Park.
native_language_example: Little girls often play in the park.

additional_notes: Used to say a sister is younger than someone else (not necessarily physically small). Often appears with possessive pronouns: „meine/deine/ihre kleine Schwester“. Contrast: „große Schwester“ = older sister.
target_language_example: Meine kleine Schwester ist zehn Jahre alt.
native_language_example: My younger sister is ten years old.

meaning: “small village” (with the adjective ending -en because of the grammar in the sentence).
additional_notes:
This is an inflected form of **kleines Dorf** (“small village”). You often see **kleinen Dorf** after certain prepositions or articles that require a specific case, especially **dative** (location) or **accusative** (movement):
- **in einem kleinen Dorf** = in a small village (location)
- **aus einem kleinen Dorf** = from a small village
- **in ein kleines Dorf** = into a small village (note: then it’s *kleines*, not *kleinen*)
The base word is **das Dorf** (village).
target_language_example: Ich wohne in einem kleinen Dorf.
native_language_example: I live in a small village.

meaning: (a/the) little boy (in a declined form, e.g. accusative/dative).
additional_notes: This is the declined form of **kleiner Junge** (“little boy”). German changes adjective and noun endings depending on case and article. Common patterns you’ll see: **den kleinen Jungen** (accusative, direct object: “I see the little boy”), **dem kleinen Jungen** (dative, indirect object: “to the little boy”), **eines kleinen Jungen** (genitive: “of a little boy”).
target_language_example: Ich sehe den kleinen Jungen im Park.
native_language_example: I see the little boy in the park.

additional_notes: Literally “small + brother,” but used to mean the younger (or sometimes just younger/smaller) brother. Often used with a possessive (mein/dein/sein/ihr) or as a friendly way to address someone (“Hey, little brother”). In neutral statements you’ll often see it as “der kleine Bruder” or with possessives: “sein kleiner Bruder”.
target_language_example: Mein kleiner Bruder geht noch zur Schule.
native_language_example: My younger brother is still in school.

additional_notes: Literally “small finger.” Used for the fifth finger on the hand. Common idiom: „Das hat mir mein kleiner Finger erzählt“ = “I have a hunch / my gut tells me” (not meant literally). Often used with possessives: „mein/dein/sein kleiner Finger“.
target_language_example: Mein kleiner Finger ist geschwollen.
native_language_example: My little finger (pinky) is swollen.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a male child, often with a gentle/affectionate tone. With a name or context it can mean “someone’s little boy” (Lisas kleiner Junge). It can also be used figuratively to compare an adult to a child (“wie ein kleiner Junge” = “like a little boy”), sometimes teasing or criticizing. Grammar note: it’s the adjective + noun phrase; in nominative it’s often “ein kleiner Junge”, and after “kein” it’s “kein kleiner Junge”.
target_language_example: Ziri war ein kleiner Junge.
native_language_example: Ziri was a little boy.

meaning: “little cook” — used as a nickname/term of address for someone (often affectionately or a bit patronizing).
additional_notes: Used when speaking directly to someone (like “buddy” or “kiddo”), often in a slightly teasing, protective, or bossy tone. It’s common to pair it with instructions or encouragement. Capitalize it (Koch) because it’s a noun, and it can be used on its own: „Kleiner Koch?“
target_language_example: Komm schon, kleiner Koch, das schaffst du!
native_language_example: Come on, little cook, you can do it!

meaning: “little shit” (a very rude insult, often aimed at a child).
additional_notes: Very informal and offensive. Used as an insult for someone (often a boy/child) who is being annoying or misbehaving. Avoid in polite situations; can easily escalate conflict. Related forms: „du Scheißer!“ (very rude), „kleine Scheißerin“ (female).
target_language_example: Hör auf damit, du kleiner Scheißer!
native_language_example: Stop that, you little shit!

additional_notes: Used to compare sizes/height/amounts: A ist kleiner als B. The opposite is „größer als“ (bigger/taller than). Often used with people for height (e.g., „Ich bin kleiner als du.“). You can add intensifiers like „viel“ or „sehr viel“: „viel kleiner als …“ = much smaller than.
target_language_example: Dieses Handy ist viel kleiner als das andere.
native_language_example: This phone is much smaller than the other one.

meaning: a small child; a little kid.
additional_notes: Literally “small child.” Often used for a very young child (toddler/young kid) and also in comparisons like „wie ein kleines Kind“ (“like a little kid”) to say someone is acting childish or crying a lot.
target_language_example: Er hat Angst im Dunkeln, wie ein kleines Kind.
native_language_example: He’s afraid of the dark, like a little kid.

meaning: (a) little girl; (as a form of address) “little girl”.
additional_notes: Literally “small/little girl.” Used with an article (ein kleines Mädchen) or without an article in comparisons/roles (wie ein kleines Mädchen) and when talking about someone’s age in the past (als kleines Mädchen / seit sie ein kleines Mädchen war). It can also be used as direct address (“Kleines Mädchen?”) and, depending on tone/context, can sound patronizing or insulting (e.g., “Hör auf, wie ein kleines Mädchen zu heulen!”).
target_language_example: Als kleines Mädchen wollte ich immer Ärztin werden.
native_language_example: When I was a little girl, I always wanted to become a doctor.

additional_notes: Uses the simple past (Präteritum) of *klingeln* (“to ring”) with *das Telefon* as the subject. Common in written narratives and storytelling (spoken German often uses: *Das Telefon hat geklingelt*). Often used with time phrases like *als* (“when”), *gerade* (“just”), *kaum …, da* (“hardly … when”), and *schon wieder* (“again already”).
target_language_example: Gerade als ich eingeschlafen war, klingelte das Telefon.
native_language_example: Just as I had fallen asleep, the phone rang.

meaning: "sounds like a" (followed by a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to react to an idea/plan and say it seems like something. It’s the verb "klingen" (to sound) + "nach" (like/as if) + "einer" (dative feminine). You normally continue with a noun, e.g. "klingt nach einer guten Idee". For masculine/neuter use "klingt nach einem ..."; for plural just "klingt nach ...".
target_language_example: Klingt nach einer guten Idee.
native_language_example: Sounds like a good idea.

additional_notes: From the verb "anklopfen" / "klopfen" (to knock). It’s commonly used to say someone is at the door. The verb is conjugated: "ich klopfe", "du klopfst", "er/sie/es klopft". You can also say: "Es klopft an der Tür" (= There's a knock at the door).
target_language_example: Warte kurz, jemand klopft an die Tür.
native_language_example: Wait a moment, someone is knocking on the door.

additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of "an die Tür klopfen". Used to say someone knocked on a door (often before entering). With "an" + accusative (die Tür). In conversation, you’ll often also hear the perfect tense: "hat an die Tür geklopft".
target_language_example: Ich klopfte an die Tür, dann wartete ich.
native_language_example: I knocked on the door, then I waited.

additional_notes: Used to compare two people or things. Pattern: [Person/thing] ist klüger als [comparison]. The word after "als" is often in the nominative (e.g., "als ich", "als er"), though you may also hear accusative in casual speech ("als mich").
target_language_example: Ich bin nicht klüger als du, aber ich lerne jeden Tag.
native_language_example: I'm not smarter than you, but I learn every day.

additional_notes: A common spoken way to invite or tell someone to sit. Often followed by a place: „… da hin“ / „… auf den Stuhl“ / „… zu mir“. You’ll also hear „Komm, setz dich hin“ (very common), and „doch“ can make it sound more encouraging/insistent (“go on, have a seat”).
target_language_example: Komm, setz dich (hin) und erzähl mir, was passiert ist.
native_language_example: Come, sit down and tell me what happened.

additional_notes: Used in spoken German to encourage someone to act with you: imperative "Komm" + "wir" + verb (often in position 2): "Komm, wir gehen." It can sound friendly (making a suggestion) or urgent (hurrying someone).
target_language_example: Komm, wir gehen nach Hause.
native_language_example: Come on, let's go home.

additional_notes: Used to prompt someone to leave or to go do something together. Often followed by an activity (e.g., essen gehen = go eat) or used alone to mean “let’s go (now)”. The comma after “Komm” reflects a brief pause in speech.
target_language_example: Komm, wir gehen nach Hause.
native_language_example: Come on, let's go home.

additional_notes: Imperative of **kommen** + **her** (“toward me/this place”). Used to call someone closer to you; can be friendly (“Komm her, schau dir das an!”) or aggressive/insulting depending on tone and words around it. More polite alternatives: **Komm bitte her.** / **Kommen Sie bitte her.**
target_language_example: Komm her, ich zeig dir etwas.
native_language_example: Come here, I’ll show you something.

additional_notes: Imperative of the separable verb "mitkommen" (to come along). Often said on its own as an invitation or instruction; you can add who you’re speaking to ("Komm mit, Bianca") and sometimes a destination: "Komm mit zum Bahnhof" (Come with me to the station).
target_language_example: Komm mit, wir gehen jetzt nach Hause.
native_language_example: Come with me, we’re going home now.

additional_notes: Used to push someone to do something, keep going, or hurry up (often with a name: “Komm schon, Harry …”). Can also be said to someone who should wake up or be brave (“Komm schon, das ist doch nicht deine erste Spritze.”). Imperative of “kommen” + “schon” for emphasis.
target_language_example: Komm schon, wir schaffen das!
native_language_example: Come on, we can do it!

additional_notes: Used to push someone to do something, speed up, continue, or stop hesitating (e.g., “Komm schon, schnell!”, “Komm schon, weiter!”, “Komm schon, wach auf.”). Often sounds impatient or pleading depending on tone. Very common in spoken German; also used as a standalone “Komm schon.”
target_language_example: Komm schon, wir müssen jetzt los!
native_language_example: Come on, we have to leave now!

additional_notes: "Kommt" is a form of the verb "kommen". It’s used with "er/sie/es" and names ("Tom kommt.") and in yes/no questions ("Kommt Tom?"). With places it can mean "comes here" ("Kommt Tom hierher?") or "ends up/goes to" ("Kommt Tom ins Gefängnis?"). With "aus" it means "comes from" ("Kommt dein Mann auch aus Australien?"). As an imperative to a group, "Kommt!" means "Come!".
target_language_example: Kommt ihr heute Abend mit?
native_language_example: Are you (all) coming along tonight?

additional_notes: Often used to push or motivate a group (plural imperative of *kommen*): *Kommt schon, Leute!* = “Come on, guys!” It can also show impatience or disbelief (“Come on…”). With **noch** (as in *Kommt schon noch*), it means something will still happen/arrive later: “It’ll come eventually / It’ll happen in time.”
target_language_example: Kommt schon, wir müssen los!
native_language_example: Come on, we have to go!

additional_notes: Imperative (command) with **du**: *Komm her!* is used to call someone over to you. You can add a name (*Nico, komm her!*). To sound softer, use **Komm bitte her!** or **Komm mal her!**
target_language_example: Komm her, bitte — ich will dir etwas zeigen.
native_language_example: Come here, please — I want to show you something.

additional_notes: A common, casual way to call someone over. "mal" softens the command and makes it sound like "just" / "for a sec". You can add a name before it (e.g., "Lara, komm mal her!").
target_language_example: Komm mal her, ich zeig dir was.
native_language_example: Come here for a second, I’ll show you something.

additional_notes: An informal singular (du) command: "komm" (come) + "mit" (with) + "mir" (me/dative). Used to invite or tell one person to accompany you; you can add a destination with "nach/zu/in ..." (e.g., "Komm mit mir nach Hause."). For polite or plural: "Kommen Sie mit mir." / "Kommt mit mir."
target_language_example: Komm mit mir ins Café.
native_language_example: Come with me to the café.

additional_notes: Imperative (command) form of "mitkommen". Used to invite or tell someone to accompany you. Often followed by a destination with "nach/zu/auf" (e.g., "komm mit nach Hause", "komm mit aufs Foto").
target_language_example: Komm mit ins Café, ich lade dich ein.
native_language_example: Come with me to the café—it's on me.

additional_notes: Imperative (du-form) of **reinkommen**. Used to invite someone into a room/house, often after opening the door. Can sound friendly (“Come in!”) or impatient/urgent depending on tone/context. For more formal situations, you’d say **Kommen Sie rein.**
target_language_example: Komm rein, es ist kalt draußen.
native_language_example: Come in, it’s cold outside.

additional_notes: Used in informal speech to push someone along, encourage them, or show impatience: “Komm schon, gehen wir.” / “Komm schon, Mann.” It can also be used when calling someone to come closer: “Komm schon her!” Don’t confuse it with the similar-sounding phrase “Ich komme schon zurecht” = “I’ll manage / I’ll be fine.”
target_language_example: Komm schon, wir sind spät dran!
native_language_example: Come on, we’re running late!

meaning: "Come on!" (used to urge, encourage, or show impatience).
additional_notes: Very common informal phrase. Used when you want someone to hurry up ("Komm schon, beeil dich!"), to keep going, or to protest/press someone ("Nein, komm schon!"). Often appears with particles like "ach", "na", or "also" to add emotion: "Ach komm schon!" / "Na, komm schon."
target_language_example: Komm schon, wir müssen jetzt los!
native_language_example: Come on, we have to leave now!

additional_notes: Imperative form of "zurückkommen" (to come back). Used to ask or tell someone to return (often to the speaker or to a place): "komm zurück!" You can add where: "komm zurück ins Bett" (come back to bed). In speech you’ll often hear "komm" instead of "komme" ("Ich komm zurück" = "I’m coming back").
target_language_example: Liebling, komm zurück ins Bett.
native_language_example: Darling, come back to bed.

additional_notes: Form of the verb **kommen**. In commands, **Kommt!** is the imperative for **ihr** (= “you all”): *Kommt jetzt mit mir.* It can also be present tense: *Er kommt gleich.* Often used with particles like **mit** (come along), **wieder** (come back), or in phrases like **zu nahe kommen** (come too close).
target_language_example: Kommt bitte schnell nach Hause!
native_language_example: Please come home quickly!

meaning: "Is he coming?" / "Does he come?" (verb-first question form).
additional_notes: Used to ask about a male person (er = he) with the verb first (Kommt ...?). German often uses the present tense to talk about the near future: "Kommt er bald?" = "Is he coming soon?" You’ll also see it with separable-prefix verbs like wiederkommen (come back), zurückkommen (return), runterkommen (come down), where the prefix goes to the end: "Kommt er wieder/ zurück/ runter?"
target_language_example: Kommt er heute Abend mit?
native_language_example: Is he coming along tonight?

additional_notes: This is the verb-first word order used to form a yes/no question: **Kommt** (comes/is coming) + **sie** (she). Depending on context it can mean (1) coming/arriving ("Kommt sie heute?"), (2) coming along/with someone (often with **mit**: "Kommt sie auch mit?"), or (3) coming from somewhere/origin (with **von**: "Kommt sie von der Agentur?"). The present tense **kommt** can also refer to the near future ("Kommt sie nächste Woche?").
target_language_example: Kommt sie später noch mit?
native_language_example: Is she coming along later too?

additional_notes: Used with places to say where you come from or where someone/something originates. It’s the verb phrase "kommen aus" (to come from); in the first person singular present it’s "ich komme aus ...". Often appears without repeating "ich" in the second clause: "Ich bin Polin und komme aus Warschau."
target_language_example: Ich komme aus den USA, aber ich wohne jetzt in Berlin.
native_language_example: I’m from the USA, but I live in Berlin now.

meaning: “I come / I’m coming” (from the verb *kommen*); used in statements and questions, e.g. “do I come / am I coming?”.
additional_notes:
Common in many fixed combinations depending on what follows:
- **komme ich zu dir** = I come to you / I’ll come over to you.
- **komme ich ins Spiel** = I come into play (I get involved / become relevant).
- **komme ich … zurecht** (from *zurechtkommen*) = I manage / cope / get by.
- In questions: **Wo komme ich …?** = How/where do I get across/pass?; **Woher komme ich?** = Where do I come from?
target_language_example: Ich glaube, damit komme ich alleine zurecht.
native_language_example: I think I can manage that on my own.

meaning: "I feel like a …" / "I feel as if I’m a …" (to myself).
additional_notes: Used to compare yourself to something/someone to express a subjective feeling, often awkwardness, smallness, incompetence, etc. Common in the fuller construction: „ich komme mir vor wie …“. Grammar: „mir“ is dative (reflexive). After „wie“ you typically use nominative with an indefinite article: „wie ein Idiot“, „wie eine Königin“, etc. Often paired with „vor“ (… „komme ich mir … vor“), but in colloquial speech the „vor“ may be implied depending on context.
target_language_example: Bei diesem Thema komme ich mir wie ein Anfänger vor.
native_language_example: When it comes to this topic, I feel like a beginner.

meaning: 'to come if/when you …' (conditional: coming depends on what you do).
additional_notes: Used with a subordinate clause introduced by **wenn du ...** (“if you … / when you …”). It often expresses a condition: **Du kannst kommen, wenn du willst.** = “You can come if you want.” With future situations it can also mean “when”: **Er wird kommen, wenn du ...** = “He will come when/if you ...”. Word order: the verb in the **wenn**-clause goes to the end (e.g., **wenn du willst / wenn du ein Visum hast / wenn du ihn darum bittest**).
target_language_example: Du kannst kommen, wenn du willst.
native_language_example: You can come if you want.

additional_notes: Uses capitalized Sie, the polite/formal way to say "you" (singular or plural). At the start of a sentence, it is often a formal imperative: "come" / "come on." In questions, it can mean "do you come / are you coming," and with places it may be translated more naturally as "get" or "go" in English (for example, Wie kommen Sie nach Mailand? = "How do you get to Milan?").
target_language_example: Kommen Sie bitte herein.
native_language_example: Please come in.

additional_notes: A polite, formal way to tell someone to come somewhere. Uses **Sie** (formal 'you') and the imperative **kommen**. Often followed by a place or direction: **Kommen Sie bitte ins Büro / hierher / wieder**. You can also combine it with another action: **Kommen Sie bitte und setzen Sie sich.**
target_language_example: Kommen Sie bitte kurz zu mir.
native_language_example: Please come over to me for a moment.

additional_notes: A formal command/request using **Sie** (polite “you”). **her** indicates movement toward the speaker (“here, to me”). Often used with **bitte** to sound more polite: *Kommen Sie bitte her.* The informal version is *Komm her.*
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, kommen Sie her.
native_language_example: Excuse me, come here.

additional_notes: Formal/polite ("Sie") imperative of "mitkommen" (= to come along). Used to invite someone to accompany you (e.g., "Kommen Sie mit zur Bar?"), or to instruct someone to follow you (often implies "with me": "Kommen Sie mit nach hinten."). You can add a destination with "mit + nach/zu". Informal version: "Komm mit!"
target_language_example: Kommen Sie mit nach hinten.
native_language_example: Come with me to the back.

additional_notes: A polite/formal invitation or instruction to enter a room/building. Uses the formal address Sie (for strangers, customers, officials, etc.). Often said with Bitte: „Bitte kommen Sie rein!“ You might also hear the informal version: „Komm rein!“
target_language_example: Guten Tag—bitte kommen Sie rein und nehmen Sie Platz.
native_language_example: Good day—please come in and have a seat.

additional_notes: Polite/formal usage with Sie. As an imperative, it can be an instruction or a friendly invitation to return (e.g., in shops, offices, or appointments). It’s also common in questions about when someone will return: „Um wie viel Uhr kommen Sie wieder?“ Often combined with hinein/rein: „Kommen Sie wieder herein/rein.“
target_language_example: Kommen Sie wieder, wann immer Sie möchten.
native_language_example: Come back whenever you like.

additional_notes: Formal/polite form addressing someone with "Sie". Can be used as an instruction/command ("Kommen Sie zurück.") or in questions about return ("Wann kommen Sie zurück?"). Often paired with a destination using "auf"/"in" etc.: "Kommen Sie zurück aufs Schiff", "Kommen Sie zurück ins Büro".
target_language_example: Kommen Sie zurück aufs Schiff.
native_language_example: Come back onto the ship.

additional_notes: Used when someone is traveling to see a person (or sometimes a place). In natural German it’s very common to use this as a split verb phrase: „Ich komme dich/euch besuchen.“ (person in the accusative). You can also often just use „besuchen“ alone, or say „zu Besuch kommen“ (= to come for a visit).
target_language_example: Ich werde dich am Wochenende kommen besuchen.
native_language_example: I will come visit you this weekend.

meaning: "we come" / "shall we come...?" / "let’s ..." (1st person plural of "kommen").
additional_notes: Used as a normal statement ("Wir kommen." = we’re coming), or as a question with verb-first word order: "Kommen wir zu spät?" = Are we going to be late? It also appears in set phrases like "Kommen wir zur Sache" = Let’s get to the point. With separable verbs, the extra part goes to the end: "kommen wir an" (arrive), "kommen wir ... aus" (get along), "kommen wir in die Tausende" (reach the thousands).
target_language_example: Kommen wir morgen zu dir?
native_language_example: Shall we come to your place tomorrow?

meaning: to be late; to arrive too late
additional_notes: Means arriving after the expected or agreed time. Very common order is also „zu spät kommen“ (same meaning). Typical forms: Präsens „Ich komme zu spät.“ / Perfekt „Ich bin zu spät gekommen.“
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich komme zu spät, weil der Bus nicht kam.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m late because the bus didn’t come.

meaning: "are you coming" / "do you come" (2nd-person singular of "kommen" in a question).
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone is coming/going somewhere (often with a destination: "Kommst du nach Hause?", "Kommst du hierher?"), or if they’re joining you: "Kommst du mit?". It can also ask about someone’s origin: "Woher kommst du?" (= Where are you from?). Word order is typical for yes/no questions (verb first).
target_language_example: Kommst du heute Abend mit ins Kino?
native_language_example: Are you coming with us to the cinema tonight?

additional_notes: Question form of **aus … kommen** (“to be from” a place). **Kommst du** uses **du** (informal “you”), so it’s used with friends, classmates, kids, etc. For formal situations, use **Kommen Sie aus …?**. You can ask about countries, cities, or regions: **Kommst du aus Deutschland/Berlin/Bayern?**
target_language_example: Kommst du aus Kanada?
native_language_example: Are you from Canada?

meaning: “Are you coming with (me/us)?” / “Do you want to come along?”
additional_notes: Common invitation question using the separable verb **mitkommen** (“to come along”). The **mit** often appears at the end: **Kommst du mit?** You can add where/to whom: **Kommst du mit zu einer Party? / zu uns? / zur Lerngruppe?** Very common in spoken German.
target_language_example: Ich gehe kurz in den Supermarkt—kommst du mit?
native_language_example: I’m going to the supermarket for a moment—are you coming with me?

meaning: “are you coming to …?” (to a city or country).
additional_notes: This is the 2nd-person singular question form of **nach … kommen** (“to come to …”). Use **nach** mainly with **cities** and **most countries** *without* an article: **nach Rom**, **nach Arizona**. For people/places treated like a destination (e.g., someone’s home), you often use **zu**: *Kommst du zu mir?* For countries with an article, use **in** + accusative instead: *in die Schweiz*, *in den Iran* (not *nach die Schweiz*).
target_language_example: Wie oft kommst du nach Rom?
native_language_example: How often do you come to Rome?

additional_notes: Used in questions with the verb **kommen** (“to come”), often with an extra word that changes the meaning, especially separable parts or prepositions: **Kommst du nicht mit?** (“Aren’t you coming along?”), **… rein?** (“… in?”), **… durch?** (“… through / get through?”), **… davon/weg?** (“… get away / get rid of it?”). It can sound like the speaker expects the answer “yes” or is surprised that you aren’t coming/able to do it.
target_language_example: Kommst du nicht mit ins Kino?
native_language_example: Aren’t you coming along to the cinema?

meaning: “Are you coming back?” / “Will you be back?”
additional_notes: Used as a question to ask if someone will return. Depending on context, it can also mean “Are you coming again?” or “Are you coming back (later)?” Often appears with a time expression (e.g., „morgen“, „später“). You may also hear reinforced variants like „Kommst du wieder zurück?“ or „Kommst du später wieder?“
target_language_example: Kommst du wieder, wenn du Zeit hast?
native_language_example: Will you come back when you have time?

additional_notes: 3rd-person singular of "kommen" used to state origin: "X kommt aus Y". Used with a place, region, or country. With most cities/countries you usually use no article ("aus China", "aus Boston"); with regions or common nouns you often use an article ("aus dem Süden", "aus einer anderen Dimension").
target_language_example: Sie heißt Jessica und kommt aus Illinois.
native_language_example: Her name is Jessica and she’s from Illinois.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "kommen" + "aus" + dative. "Einer" is the dative form of "eine" for feminine nouns (e.g., "aus einer Familie"). You can use it for origin in a general sense (family, social background, sometimes an institution), not just physical location.
target_language_example: Sie kommt aus einer Arbeiterfamilie.
native_language_example: She comes from a working-class family.

meaning: (He/she) just came from university; is a recent graduate/newly qualified.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is very new in their profession and has only recently finished studying (often implying little work experience yet). You can change the verb for other people/tense: „Ich komme frisch von der Uni.“ / „Sie kommen frisch von der Uni.“
target_language_example: Unsere neue Kollegin kommt frisch von der Uni.
native_language_example: Our new colleague just came from university (she’s a recent graduate).

additional_notes: Used to say someone will arrive very soon. Often answers “Wann kommt er/sie?” (“When is he/she coming?”). It can mean “right away” or simply “soon,” depending on the context and tone.
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, der Arzt kommt gleich.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, the doctor will be here in a moment.

meaning: “do you (all) come/are you (all) coming?” or “are you (all) from …?”
additional_notes: “kommt” is the 2nd‑person plural form of **kommen** (“to come”), used with **ihr** (“you” plural). You’ll often see **Kommt ihr …?** at the start of a question (inversion). Depending on context it can mean (1) traveling/visiting: **Kommt ihr morgen vorbei?** (“Are you coming by tomorrow?”), or (2) origin: **Woher kommt ihr?** (“Where are you from?”). For polite/formal “you,” use **kommen Sie** instead.
target_language_example: Kommt ihr heute Abend mit ins Kino?
native_language_example: Are you all coming to the cinema tonight?

additional_notes: Used to say someone consistently arrives late. It’s built from **kommen** (to come/arrive) + **immer** (always) + **zu spät** (too late). Change the verb ending with the subject: **ich komme**, **du kommst**, **er/sie/es kommt**, **wir kommen**, **ihr kommt**, **sie/Sie kommen**. Often followed by where/what you’re late for: **zu spät zur Schule / zur Arbeit / zum Treffen**.
target_language_example: Er kommt immer zu spät zum Unterricht.
native_language_example: He is always late to class.

meaning: "you/one get(s)" / "how do you get (to …)?" (impersonal use of *kommen*).
additional_notes: Used with *man* to talk in general (like English “you/one”), often in questions about directions or access: *Wie/Womit/Auf welchem Weg kommt man …?* = “How do you get …?/Which way/with what do you get …?” It can also be part of common verb phrases, e.g. *mit jemandem klarkommen* (“get along with someone”) or *an jemanden rankommen* (“be able to reach/get to someone”).
target_language_example: Wie kommt man von hier aus zum Bahnhof?
native_language_example: How do you get to the train station from here?

additional_notes: Used when something (a name, song, place, or person) feels familiar, but you may not remember exactly where you know it from. The verb is **vorkommen**: **Das kommt mir bekannt vor.** = “That seems familiar to me.” The person who feels it is in the **dative** (**mir**, **dir**, **ihm/ihr**, **uns**, **euch**, **ihnen**).
target_language_example: Die Stimme kommt mir bekannt vor, aber ich weiß nicht warum.
native_language_example: The voice sounds familiar to me, but I don’t know why.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **kommen** (“to come”) in **3rd person singular** (**er/sie/es kommt**). In everyday German, the **present tense** often expresses a planned **future** event: *Er kommt morgen.* = “He’s coming tomorrow.” **Morgen** can mean **“tomorrow”** (here) or **“morning”** depending on context.
target_language_example: Sie kommt morgen wieder.
native_language_example: She’s coming back tomorrow.

meaning: is out of the question; not an option.
additional_notes: Used to say something is not possible or not acceptable. Often used as: „Das kommt nicht in Frage.“ or „Es kommt nicht in Frage, …“ (with an infinitive clause). You can also use it with a noun: „Ein Urlaub kommt nicht in Frage.“
target_language_example: Heute Abend ausgehen kommt nicht in Frage.
native_language_example: Going out tonight is out of the question.

additional_notes: Used to say someone always arrives on time. It’s the 3rd-person singular form of **kommen** (“to come/arrive”): **Er/Sie kommt nie zu spät.** You can add a destination with **zu** + dative (e.g., **zu einem Date**) or **zu** + **zur/zum** (e.g., **zur Schule**).
target_language_example: Meine Schwester kommt nie zu spät zur Arbeit.
native_language_example: My sister is never late to work.

meaning: could solve the problem / was able to solve the problem.
additional_notes: "konnte" is the simple past of "können" (can/to be able to). "das Problem lösen" means "to solve the problem". Together, it expresses that someone was able to solve it in that situation (and typically implies success). You can swap in other objects: "konnte die Aufgabe lösen" (could solve the task).
target_language_example: Er konnte das Problem lösen.
native_language_example: He could solve the problem. / He was able to solve the problem.

meaning: could hardly wait (was very excited/impatient for something).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is really looking forward to something and feels impatient because they’re excited. It’s usually followed by an infinitive with „zu“ (e.g., „…sie zu sehen“, „…es ihm zu sagen“) or sometimes by „bis …“ (e.g., „…bis es anfängt“). Present tense: „Ich kann es kaum erwarten …“.
target_language_example: Ich konnte es kaum erwarten, dir die Nachricht zu erzählen.
native_language_example: I could hardly wait to tell you the news.

meaning: “I couldn’t” / “I wasn’t able to” (in the past).
additional_notes: Präteritum (simple past) of können: ich konnte. This word order often appears when something comes first in the sentence (e.g., Als ich fünf war, konnte ich nicht … / Mehr konnte ich nicht …). It’s usually followed by an infinitive (konnte ich nicht lesen) but can also stand alone when the verb is understood from context (Mehr konnte ich nicht.). In a neutral main clause without anything in front, you’d say: Ich konnte nicht …
target_language_example: Wegen des Lärms konnte ich nicht schlafen.
native_language_example: Because of the noise, I couldn’t sleep.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say someone was almost unable to do something (because it was difficult, they were tired, it was quiet, etc.). It’s the simple past (Präteritum) of "kann kaum" (can hardly). Often followed by verbs like: sehen, hören, sprechen, schlafen, finden, atmen, glauben, etc.
target_language_example: Nach der langen Nacht konnte ich kaum die Augen offenhalten.
native_language_example: After the long night, I could barely keep my eyes open.

additional_notes: Past tense of "können" (can/to be able to) + "nicht" (not). Used to say someone was unable to do something, didn’t have the ability/permission, or (with verbs like "wissen") couldn’t have known. Often followed by an infinitive at the end: "Sie konnte nicht schwimmen." Also appears in fixed expressions like "nicht umhin können" (= can’t help but): "Er konnte nicht umhin, an Maria zu denken."
target_language_example: Ich konnte nicht kommen, weil ich arbeiten musste.
native_language_example: I couldn’t come because I had to work.

meaning: “couldn’t (himself/herself/themself)” / “wasn’t able to (bring oneself to)” in a reflexive construction.
additional_notes: Used with a reflexive pronoun (sich) to say someone was not able to do something involving themself, typically followed by an infinitive at the end (e.g., sich befreien, sich entscheiden, sich beherrschen, sich überwinden). The reflexive pronoun changes with the person: ich konnte mich nicht…, du konntest dich nicht…, er/sie/es konnte sich nicht…, wir konnten uns nicht…, ihr konntet euch nicht…, sie/Sie konnten sich nicht…. Often appears with mehr/länger (“anymore/any longer”).
target_language_example: Tom konnte sich nicht entscheiden, wen er wählen sollte.
native_language_example: Tom couldn’t decide whom he should vote for.

meaning: "could" (past of *können*) + "in order to" (to emphasize doing one’s best/maximum effort to reach a goal).
additional_notes: Typical structure: **(alles) was ich/er/sie konnte, um ...** = "(everything) I/he/she could, in order to ..." Often paired with **tun**: *Ich/Er/Sie tat/habe alles getan, was ... konnte, um ...* Also with speed/extent: *so schnell, wie ich konnte, um ...* Verb form changes with person/tense (*konnte*, *konnten*, *kann*), but this entry focuses on the exact sequence **konnte, um**.
target_language_example: Er tat alles, was er konnte, um seinen Sohn zu schützen.
native_language_example: He did everything he could to protect his son.

additional_notes: This is the past tense of **können** (“can/to be able to”) with **Sie** (formal “you”). In questions, it often means “Could you…?” (polite) or “Were you able to…?” depending on context. It can refer to a specific past situation (ability/success) or function like a polite request.
target_language_example: Konnten Sie mir bitte helfen?
native_language_example: Could you please help me?

meaning: “could you” / “were you able to” (past, informal singular “you”).
additional_notes: Used to ask whether someone was able to do something in the past. It’s the simple past of **können** for **du** (2nd person singular). Often followed by an infinitive at the end: *Konntest du … lösen/kommen/sagen?* In questions, the verb comes first.
target_language_example: Konntest du gestern kommen?
native_language_example: Could you come yesterday?

meaning: "could you just/only" (addressing one person, past tense).
additional_notes: Made of **konntest** (simple past of *können* = "to be able to / can"), **du** ("you", informal singular), and **nur** ("only/just"). Used when asking (or referring to) whether someone was able to do something *only briefly / just once / just a bit*. In many polite requests about the present or future, German more often uses the subjunctive: **könntest du nur ...?** ("could you just ...?").
target_language_example: Konntest du nur kurz warten, bis ich fertig war?
native_language_example: Could you just wait briefly until I was finished?

additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of "ihr könnt" from the verb "können" (to be able to). Used when speaking to two or more people ("you all"). Often followed by an infinitive (e.g., "konntet ihr kommen?") or used with another verb idea like "jemanden erreichen" (reach/contact someone). In casual speech you may also hear the perfect: "Habt ihr ... gekonnt?" (less common) or rephrase with "Konntet ihr ...?" as in the examples.
target_language_example: Konntet ihr gestern früher nach Hause gehen?
native_language_example: Could you (all) go home earlier yesterday?

additional_notes: Imperative (command) form of **sich auf etwas/jemanden konzentrieren** = to focus on something/someone. Use **dich** for informal singular 'you' (du). For formal singular/plural, say **Konzentrieren Sie sich auf ...**. It takes **auf + Akkusativ**: *auf den Moment, auf ihn, auf uns*. (In sentence 3, standard German would be: **Konzentriere dich auf meine Hand**.)
target_language_example: Konzentriere dich auf deine Aufgabe, nicht auf dein Handy.
native_language_example: Focus on your task, not on your phone.

additional_notes: A fixed, emphatic phrase meaning you will do something regardless of consequences, effort, or expense. Often used after a statement with „müssen“/„wollen“ (e.g., „Ich muss …, koste es, was es wolle.“) or on its own as a dramatic vow. The verb form „koste“ is a subjunctive/command-like form of „kosten“ here.
target_language_example: Wir werden das Problem lösen, koste es, was es wolle.
native_language_example: We’ll solve the problem, whatever it takes.

additional_notes: Used when stating a price or cost. "kostet" is the 3rd-person singular form of the verb "kosten" (to cost), and "ein" is "a/one". Common patterns: "Das kostet ein Euro." / "Das kostet ein Ticket." For other amounts you’ll change "ein" (e.g., "Das kostet zwei Euro.").
target_language_example: Das kostet ein Euro.
native_language_example: That costs one euro.

additional_notes: Used with forms of **sein** to talk about a past state of being sick (often implying you’re not sick anymore): **Ich bin krank gewesen** = “I was sick / I’ve been sick.” It also appears in constructions like **scheint ... krank gewesen zu sein** (“seems to have been sick”) and with **Modalverben**: **Er kann nicht krank gewesen sein** (“He can’t have been sick”).
target_language_example: Ich bin gestern krank gewesen und bin heute wieder fit.
native_language_example: I was sick yesterday, and today I’m fit again.

additional_notes: Past participle phrase used with the verb „sein“ in the perfect tense: „ich bin krank geworden“ = “I got sick.” Often refers to the moment/change of becoming ill (not the state of being ill, which is „krank sein“).
target_language_example: Ich bin gestern krank geworden und konnte nicht zur Arbeit gehen.
native_language_example: I got sick yesterday and couldn’t go to work.

meaning: sick in bed; bedridden (because of illness).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "liegen" (to be lying) to say someone is staying in bed because they’re ill: "Er liegt krank im Bett." Often combined with time expressions like "seit" (for/since) or "schon" (already).
target_language_example: Ich kann nicht kommen — ich liege krank im Bett.
native_language_example: I can’t come — I’m sick in bed.

meaning: to make (someone) sick; to call in sick (often: to take sick leave).
additional_notes: Literally “make sick.” With a direct object it means causing illness or nausea: „Das Essen hat mich krank gemacht.“ Without an object, it’s often used in the workplace sense of calling in sick / taking sick leave: „Ich mache heute krank.“ It can sometimes imply you’re not really ill (i.e., you’re faking), depending on context; „sich krankmelden“ is more neutral/formal.
target_language_example: Ich kann heute nicht kommen, ich mache heute krank.
native_language_example: I can’t come today; I’m calling in sick today.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "sein" to describe someone’s state of health (temporary illness). Often appears with "(nicht) krank sein" and with modal verbs like "müssen" to express an assumption: "Er muss krank sein" = "He must be sick" (I assume so).
target_language_example: Er muss krank sein.
native_language_example: He must be sick.

additional_notes: Used to express strong anxiety or concern (often a bit exaggerated). The person you’re worried about comes after **um** in the accusative: **um Tom / um dich / um Sie / um euch**. Often intensified with **ganz** (“really”).
target_language_example: Sie war ganz krank vor Sorge um ihre Tochter.
native_language_example: She was really sick with worry about her daughter.

meaning: to get sick; to become ill.
additional_notes: "krank" = sick/ill, "werden" = to become. Used for the process of becoming ill (often about the future or a possibility): "ich werde krank" (I’m getting sick / I’ll get sick), "könnte krank werden" (could get sick), "nicht krank werden" (not get sick). For already being ill, use "krank sein".
target_language_example: Wenn du im Regen ohne Jacke gehst, kannst du schnell krank werden.
native_language_example: If you go out in the rain without a jacket, you can get sick quickly.

meaning: to be sick/ill; to be unwell.
additional_notes: Infinitive phrase meaning “to be sick.” It commonly appears after verbs like **scheinen** (to seem) and **vorgeben** (to pretend): *Er scheint krank zu sein.* / *Sie gab vor, krank zu sein.* It can also be used in prepositional phrases such as **unter dem Vorwand** (under the pretext of): *Unter dem Vorwand, krank zu sein, ...*
target_language_example: Er scheint krank zu sein.
native_language_example: He seems to be sick.

meaning: informal for "bekomme ich" / "schaffe ich": "I get" / "I can manage" / in questions "How do I get…?"
additional_notes: "Kriegen" is common in spoken German and more informal than "bekommen" (receive/get) or "schaffen" (manage). Depending on context, it can mean (1) receiving/obtaining something ("Kriege ich meinen Anteil?"), (2) managing to do something ("Das kriege ich nicht zusammen."), or (3) catching/getting someone (often as a threat/joke: "Das nächste Mal kriege ich euch." / "I'll get you"). Word order "kriege ich" often appears after another element ("Jetzt kriege ich…") or at the start of a question ("Wie kriege ich…?").
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, das kriege ich hin.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I can handle that.

additional_notes: From the verb **kriegen** (colloquial for **bekommen**). It can mean **to receive** something (*Nächstes Jahr kriegst du ein neues.*), **to catch** something (often illnesses: *sonst kriegst du die Pest*), or **to understand** (*Kriegst du mich?* = “Do you get/understand me?”). Very common in spoken German and also appears in threats/idioms (e.g., *Jetzt kriegst du dein Fett weg* = “Now you’re going to get what’s coming to you.”).
target_language_example: Wenn du so weitermachst, kriegst du Ärger.
native_language_example: If you keep this up, you’ll get in trouble.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens a short time after a previous event or point in the story. Often placed at the start of the sentence (Kurz darauf ...) or after the verb (… starb kurz darauf).
target_language_example: Ich ging nach Hause, und kurz darauf rief sie mich an.
native_language_example: I went home, and shortly afterward she called me.

meaning: just about to; on the verge of.
additional_notes: Used to say something is going to happen very soon, or that someone almost did something. Common patterns: „(etwas) steht kurz davor, … zu + Infinitiv“ (is about to …) and past: „Ich war kurz davor, …“ (I almost … / I was about to …). It can describe actions, events, or emotional reactions (e.g., „an die Decke gehen“ = to blow up).
target_language_example: Ich war kurz davor, dir anzurufen, aber dann war es schon zu spät.
native_language_example: I was just about to call you, but then it was already too late.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a short summary or simplified conclusion of what was just said. Often placed at the start of a sentence (followed by a comma): "Kurz gesagt, ..." It can also appear mid-sentence as a parenthetical: "..., kurz gesagt, ...".
target_language_example: Kurz gesagt, wir haben keine Zeit mehr.
native_language_example: In short, we don’t have any time left.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens a little while after a point in time (kurz nach Mittag), an event (kurz nach der Geburt), or another person (kurz nach ihm). It often answers “when?” and can be followed by a noun phrase in the dative (kurz nach der Party) or by a time expression (kurz nach acht).
target_language_example: Wir haben uns kurz nach dem Essen verabschiedet.
native_language_example: We said goodbye shortly after eating.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens a little bit before a point in time (kurz vor Ende, kurz vor Tagesanbruch, kurz vor dem Tod) or just before reaching a place/limit (kurz vor der Küste = just off the coast). Typically followed by dative: kurz vor dem Ende / kurz vor der Küste.
target_language_example: Wir waren kurz vor dem Bahnhof, als der Bus plötzlich anhielt.
native_language_example: We were just before the train station when the bus suddenly stopped.

meaning: 'shortly before' / 'just about to' (right before something happens).
additional_notes: Used to say something is imminent—very close to happening. Typically followed by a noun in the dative case (often a nominalized verb): kurz vor dem Bankrott, kurz vor dem Fall, kurz vor dem Ausbruch, kurz vor dem Ertrinken. You can also use it with time: kurz vor dem Essen (= shortly before eating).
target_language_example: Wir waren kurz vor dem Aufbruch, als es plötzlich anfing zu regnen.
native_language_example: We were just about to leave when it suddenly started to rain.

meaning: shortly before (a feminine noun); just about to.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens a short time before an event or point in time. It’s followed by a noun in the dative case with the feminine article: kurz vor der Wahl/Abreise/Aufführung. With masculine/neuter nouns: kurz vor dem; with plural: kurz vor den.
target_language_example: Wir sind kurz vor der Abfahrt noch schnell tanken gegangen.
native_language_example: Shortly before departure, we quickly went to get gas.

additional_notes: Used to say something lasts only briefly. Often appears with "eine" ("eine kurze Zeit") or with "(eine) kurze Zeit lang" (= "for a short time"). You can also use it with "vor" to mean "a short time ago" ("vor kurzer Zeit").
target_language_example: Warte bitte eine kurze Zeit, ich bin gleich zurück.
native_language_example: Please wait a short time; I'll be right back.

additional_notes: A polite/formal way to ask someone about ability, possibility, or whether they can do something. Sie is the formal 'you' and is capitalized.
target_language_example: Können Sie mir bitte helfen?
native_language_example: Can you help me, please?

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone you address as Sie (a stranger, service staff, someone you don’t know well). It’s typically followed by an infinitive verb or a short command: “Können Sie bitte + Verb …?” You can also say “Könnten Sie bitte …?” for an even more polite/softer tone. Note: Sentence 1 contains rude slang (“auf meinen Sack aufpassen?”) and is not appropriate in polite conversation.
target_language_example: Können Sie bitte langsamer sprechen?
native_language_example: Could you please speak more slowly?

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone (formal “Sie”) to do something with “das” = “that/it.” Often followed by an infinitive verb: „Können Sie das beweisen/öffnen/liefern?“ In questions, the verb comes first (Können …?).
target_language_example: Können Sie das bitte wiederholen?
native_language_example: Could you please repeat that?

additional_notes: A polite/formal question starter using **Sie** (“you”). **Den** is the accusative article for a masculine noun (“the”), used when the noun is the object of the verb. You normally follow this with a **verb** and then a **masculine noun** (e.g., *Können Sie den Schmerz beschreiben?*).
target_language_example: Können Sie den Weg zum Bahnhof erklären?
native_language_example: Can you explain the way to the train station?

additional_notes: Used to make a polite request or ask if someone is able to do something. "Sie" is the formal "you" (to a stranger, customer, etc.). "die" is the definite article for feminine singular or plural nouns, so the noun after it will be feminine (e.g., die Tür) or plural (e.g., die Schlüssel). Often said as a request: "Können Sie die … (bitte) …?"
target_language_example: Können Sie die Tür bitte schließen?
native_language_example: Can you please close the door?

additional_notes: Used to make polite requests or ask if someone is able to do something with a previously mentioned object, situation, or action. The pronoun “es” = “it” and refers back to whatever is being talked about (e.g., a problem, a smell, an item). Often followed by an infinitive verb like „halten / beheben / buchstabieren / reparieren / riechen“.
target_language_example: Können Sie es bitte noch einmal erklären?
native_language_example: Can you explain it again, please?

meaning: "can you … me" (start of a polite question/request with "you").
additional_notes: Used with the formal/polite "Sie". It’s the beginning of many questions where "mich" is the object (the person affected), e.g. "Können Sie mich hören?" (hear me), "Können Sie mich anrufen?" (call me), "Können Sie mich fragen?" (ask me). In everyday speech you may also hear the informal version: "Kannst du mich …?"
target_language_example: Können Sie mich bitte kurz warten lassen?
native_language_example: Can you have me wait for a moment, please?

additional_notes: Used with formal/polite “Sie” to ask someone to do something for you. It’s typically followed by an infinitive at the end of the clause: “Können Sie mir das erklären?” = “Can you explain that to me?” In questions, the verb comes first (Können…), and “mir” (“to me/for me”) usually comes before the direct object.
target_language_example: Können Sie mir bitte den Weg zum Bahnhof erklären?
