additional_notes: „mich“ is the reflexive pronoun for „ich“ (me/myself). With many reflexive verbs, „an“ introduces what the action relates to: „Ich erinnere mich an + Akk.“ = “I remember …”, „Ich gewöhne mich an + Akk.“ = “I get used to …”, „Ich halte mich an + Akk.“ / „festhalten an + Dat.“ can mean “hold on to …” (case depends on the specific verb). On its own, „mich an“ is incomplete—you need the verb and the object after „an“.
target_language_example: Ich erinnere mich an deinen Namen.
native_language_example: I remember your name.

meaning: “myself on …” — appears as part of reflexive constructions with **mich** + **auf** (often expressing “on … / for … / about …”, depending on the verb).
additional_notes: **mich auf** is not a complete phrase on its own; it typically occurs in verb phrases with **sich + auf** (here: **mich auf** for “I myself”). Common patterns include: **sich auf jdn./etw. verlassen** (“to rely on sb/sth”), **sich auf etw. vorbereiten** (“to prepare for sth”), **sich auf etw. berufen** (“to invoke/cite sth”), and **sich auf (eine Sprache) verständigen** (“to communicate in (a language) / make oneself understood”). The exact English meaning depends on the verb.
target_language_example: Ich muss mich auf den Test vorbereiten.
native_language_example: I have to prepare for the test.

meaning: 'me (to/with) …' — used to say who you direct something at (e.g., apologize/thank someone).
additional_notes: Used with certain reflexive verbs + „bei“ + dative to name the person you address: „sich bedanken bei jemandem“ (thank someone), „sich entschuldigen bei jemandem“ (apologize to someone). The word after „bei“ is in the dative (e.g., „bei Tom“, „bei meiner Mutter“, „bei Ihnen“). Note: „bei“ can also mean “while/with/during” in other contexts (e.g., „Ich kann mich bei dem Lärm nicht konzentrieren.“).
target_language_example: Ich entschuldige mich bei Ihnen für die Verspätung.
native_language_example: I apologize to you for being late.

meaning: “to you” (formal), used with reflexive verbs like thank/apologize/report back.
additional_notes: This is a common pattern: **sich bei jemandem + Verb**. With **Ihnen** it’s formal/polite (“you”). You’ll often see it in phrases like **mich bei Ihnen bedanken** (thank you), **mich bei Ihnen entschuldigen** (apologize to you), and **mich bei Ihnen melden** (get in touch/report back to you).
target_language_example: Ich möchte mich bei Ihnen für Ihre Unterstützung bedanken.
native_language_example: I would like to thank you for your support.

meaning: used with certain reflexive verbs to mean “(myself) for” → usually “for / about / of” something (e.g., apologize for, be ashamed of, get ready for).
additional_notes: “mich” is the reflexive pronoun (“myself”) and changes with the subject: ich → mich, du → dich, er/sie/es → sich, wir → uns, ihr → euch, sie/Sie → sich. Common patterns: **sich entschuldigen für** + Akk. = “to apologize for”; **sich schämen für** + Akk. = “to be ashamed of”; **sich fertig machen für** + Akk. = “to get ready for.” The noun after **für** is usually in the accusative case.
target_language_example: Ich entschuldige mich für den Lärm.
native_language_example: I apologize for the noise.

additional_notes: Used with the reflexive verb "sich irren" (= to be mistaken). Most common in the Perfekt: "Ich habe mich geirrt" (I was wrong). Often said to admit a mistake: "Ich gebe zu, dass ich mich geirrt habe."
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, ich habe mich geirrt.
native_language_example: Sorry, I was wrong.

meaning: "me (myself) with" — used in reflexive verb constructions (e.g., "sich treffen", "sich streiten") to express doing something "with" someone.
additional_notes: "mich" is the 1st-person singular accusative reflexive pronoun used with reflexive verbs (dictionary form: "sich"). The person you do it with comes after "mit" and is in the dative case (e.g., "mit Maria", "mit einem Freund", "mit Leuten"). Common patterns: "sich mit jemandem treffen" (to meet up with someone), "sich mit jemandem streiten" (to argue with someone).
target_language_example: Gestern habe ich mich mit Maria getroffen.
native_language_example: Yesterday I met up with Maria.

meaning: 'not me/myself' (used to negate a verb with 'mich').
additional_notes: This is the combination of the reflexive pronoun "mich" (myself/me) + "nicht" (not). It often appears with reflexive verbs like "sich scheiden lassen" (to get divorced), "sich sehen" (to see oneself), "sich sehnen" (to long for), "sich aufregen" (to get upset). In many sentences, "mich" comes before "nicht": "Ich reg mich nicht auf." = "I’m not getting upset."
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, ich beschwere mich nicht.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m not complaining.

meaning: “still (remember) …” (used with erinnern: Ich erinnere mich noch an …).
additional_notes: This is a common fragment used when the full verb phrase is omitted in a quote or text. It normally appears as: „Ich erinnere mich noch an + Akkusativ“ (= “I still remember …”). The noun/pronoun after „an“ is in the accusative (an den Tag, an dich, an das Gespräch).
target_language_example: Ich erinnere mich noch an deinen Namen.
native_language_example: I still remember your name.

meaning: “me/myself very …” (used with reflexive verbs to mean “I … a lot / very much”).
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom, but a common pattern: **sich + sehr + Verb**. It appears with reflexive verbs like **sich amüsieren** (to have fun), **sich langweilen** (to be bored), **sich freuen** (to be happy/glad), **sich schwer tun** (to have a hard time). Word order is usually **ich habe mich sehr + Partizip** / **ich freue mich sehr**.
target_language_example: Ich habe mich sehr gefreut, dich wiederzusehen.
native_language_example: I was very happy to see you again.

meaning: “for/about …” in certain reflexive verb phrases (e.g., apply for; take care of).
additional_notes: Not used on its own: it appears with specific reflexive verbs + „um“ + accusative noun/pronoun. Common patterns: „sich um etwas kümmern“ = to take care of / look after something; „sich um etwas bewerben“ = to apply for something (a job, a spot). The reflexive pronoun changes with the subject: ich mich, du dich, er/sie/es sich, wir uns, ihr euch, sie/Sie sich.
target_language_example: Ich kümmere mich um meine kleine Schwester.
native_language_example: I take care of my little sister.

additional_notes: Used to say the minimum number of times something should happen or has happened. Often used with time expressions (e.g., "im Monat", "pro Woche"): "mindestens einmal im Monat" = "at least once a month."
target_language_example: Du solltest das mindestens einmal ausprobiert haben.
native_language_example: You should have tried that at least once.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a minimum frequency. "mindestens" = "at least"; "einmal" = "once"; "in der Woche" = "per week / in a week". Often used with routines and habits (e.g., how often you do something).
target_language_example: Ich rufe meine Eltern mindestens einmal in der Woche an.
native_language_example: I call my parents at least once a week.

meaning: “to me that …” (dative “mir” + a “dass”-clause), often used with verbs like “sagen/erzählen/erklären” or in patterns like “Mir dämmerte, dass …” = “It dawned on me that …”.
additional_notes: Used when the speaker (“mir”) is the indirect object (Dativ) and the content is expressed in a subordinate clause introduced by “dass”. A comma is normally placed before “dass” (orthography: “… mir, dass …”). Common with: “Sag/Erzähl/Erklär mir, dass …”. Also occurs with verbs expressing realization: “Allmählich dämmerte mir, dass …” = “It gradually dawned on me that …”.
target_language_example: Allmählich dämmerte mir, dass ich ihn falsch verstanden hatte.
native_language_example: It gradually dawned on me that I had misunderstood him.

meaning: "to me, that you …" — used when a verb takes "mir" (dative) and is followed by a "dass"-clause starting with "dass du …".
additional_notes: Common with verbs/expressions like "versprechen" (promise), "zeigen" (show), "sagen" (tell), "schreiben" (write), "erklären" (explain), "scheinen" (seem). A comma typically precedes the "dass"-clause: "… mir, dass du …". Word order: in the main clause, the conjugated verb is in position 2; in the "dass"-clause, the conjugated verb goes to the end.
target_language_example: Bitte versprich mir, dass du nie mehr eine Lüge erzählen wirst.
native_language_example: Please promise me that you will never tell a lie again.

meaning: "to me, that he..." (a common structure: verb + mir + dass-clause).
additional_notes: Used with verbs of telling/showing/promise (e.g., erklären, sagen, verraten, versprechen): the person receiving the information is in the dative (mir = to me), and the content is introduced with a dass-clause (dass er ... = that he ...). The verb in the dass-clause goes to the end: „..., dass er zurückkommen würde.“
target_language_example: Sie sagte mir, dass er heute keine Zeit hat.
native_language_example: She told me that he doesn’t have time today.

meaning: “me, that I …” — a pattern used when a verb takes “mir” and then a “dass”-clause.
additional_notes: This isn’t a fixed phrase, but a common structure: **[verb] + mir** (to/for me) + **, dass ich ...** (that I ...). You see it with verbs like **(ver)zeihen** (forgive): *Verzeih mir, dass ich ...*; **sich wünschen** (wish): *Ich wünsche mir, dass ich ...*; and with **von mir erwarten** (expect of me): *Sie erwarten von mir, dass ich ...*. The comma before **dass** is normal because **dass ich ...** is a subordinate clause.
target_language_example: Entschuldigen Sie mir, dass ich zu spät gekommen bin.
native_language_example: Forgive me for arriving late.

meaning: 'to me, that…' — used when a verb takes the dative object "mir" (to me) and is followed by a subordinate clause introduced by "daß" (that).
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase but a very common grammatical pattern: [verb] + mir + , daß + [subordinate clause]. The comma before „daß“ is standard. Typical verbs include „sagen“ (tell), „versprechen“ (promise), „erklären“ (explain), „zeigen“ (show), and the idiomatic „sich denken“ → „Ich dachte mir, daß…“ (“I thought to myself that…”). Note: modern spelling usually writes „dass“; „daß“ is the older/pre-1996 spelling and still appears in older texts or by stylistic choice.
target_language_example: Versprich mir, daß du mich holst.
native_language_example: Promise me that you'll pick me up.

meaning: "to me, what…" → used like "tell/show me what…" (introduces an indirect question).
additional_notes: Fixed pattern after verbs like erzählen (tell), verraten (reveal), zeigen (show), sagen (say): verb + mir, was + subordinate clause. The comma is required because "was" introduces an indirect question (subordinate clause). "mir" is dative = "to me".
target_language_example: Verrätst du mir, was das soll?
native_language_example: Will you tell me what that’s supposed to mean?

meaning: "me what you …" / "to me what you …" (used in requests like “Show me what you can do”).
additional_notes: This is a common pattern in formal German requests: **mir** (“to me”) + **was Sie ...** (“what you ...”, with formal **Sie**). It often follows verbs like **zeigen** (show) or **geben** (give): *Zeigen Sie mir, was Sie können.* In casual speech, **Sie** is usually replaced by **du**: *Zeig mir, was du kannst.*
target_language_example: Sagen Sie mir, was Sie möchten.
native_language_example: Tell me what you would like.

meaning: 'to me' + 'when/if' (often in requests like “tell me when/if …”).
additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom, but a very common pattern: a verb + **mir** (“to me”) followed by a **wenn**-clause (“when/if …”). Often used with verbs like *sagen* (tell), *schreiben* (write), *anrufen* (call), *verzeihen* (forgive): „Sag/Schreib/Verzeih **mir, wenn** …“. In the *wenn*-clause, the conjugated verb goes to the end: „… **wenn** er Zeit **hat**.“
target_language_example: Sag mir, wenn der Lehrer anruft.
native_language_example: Tell me if/when the teacher calls.

meaning: “(to) me, how to …” (typically after verbs like “explain/tell/show”), i.e. “(to) me how to …”.
additional_notes: Common pattern: **(jemandem) erklären/sagen/zeigen/verraten** + **mir, wie man** + verb. **wie man** is an impersonal “how one/you …” often translated as “how to …” in English. The comma is standard because **wie man …** introduces a subordinate clause.
target_language_example: Erklärst du mir, wie man zu dir nach Hause kommt?
native_language_example: Can you explain to me how to get to your place?

meaning: “(tell) me where …” (introduces an indirect question about a location).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like **sagen** (“to tell/say”) or **zeigen** (“to show”) to introduce an indirect question: **Sagen Sie mir, wo … ist.** / **Sag mir, wo … ist.** The comma is standard before the indirect question, and the verb goes to the end of the **wo**-clause (e.g., **wo die Haltestelle ist**). Note: **mir** is the dative pronoun “to me,” and **wo** means “where.”
target_language_example: Bitte sagen Sie mir, wo die Bushaltestelle ist.
native_language_example: Please tell me where the bus stop is.

additional_notes: Fixed phrase used most often with the verbs sagen or geben: „Sag/Gib mir Bescheid“ = “Let me know.” Common with wenn (“if/when”): „Sag mir Bescheid, wenn …“. Conjugates for formality/person: informal singular (du) „Sag/Gib mir Bescheid“, informal plural (ihr) „Sagt/Gebt mir Bescheid“, formal (Sie) „Sagen/Geben Sie mir Bescheid“.
target_language_example: Wenn etwas passiert, gib mir Bescheid.
native_language_example: If something happens, let me know.

additional_notes: Usually used as **(Es) tut mir leid** (“I’m sorry / I regret it”). On its own, **mir leid** is incomplete in modern German—you’ll almost always hear **tut mir leid**. You can also use it to express sympathy: **Das tut mir leid** = “I’m sorry to hear that.”
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, ich habe keine Zeit.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t have time.

meaning: 'me worries' → used to say something worries me / I’m worried.
additional_notes: Usually appears with verbs like **machen** or **bereiten**: **Das macht/bereitet mir Sorgen** = “That worries me.” Related pattern: **sich Sorgen machen (um + Akk.)** = “to worry (about …)”, e.g. **Ich mache mir Sorgen um dich** (“I’m worried about you”). **mir** is dative (“to me”).
target_language_example: Die Verspätung macht mir Sorgen.
native_language_example: The delay worries me.

additional_notes: Used in the pattern **sich Sorgen um + Akkusativ machen**: *Ich mache mir Sorgen um Tom.* The reflexive pronoun changes with the person: **ich mache mir**, **du machst dir**, **er/sie macht sich**, **wir machen uns**, **ihr macht euch**, **sie machen sich** Sorgen um …
target_language_example: Ich mache mir Sorgen um dich.
native_language_example: I’m worried about you.

additional_notes: Used with the verb phrase **sich Sorgen machen um + Akkusativ**: **Ich mache mir Sorgen um dich.** = “I’m worried about you.” The **mir** is dative (“for myself”), and **um dich** is accusative (“about you”). In speech, **ich mach** is a common shortened form of **ich mache**.
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, aber ich mache mir Sorgen um dich.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, but I’m worried about you.

additional_notes: Part of the common verb phrase **Spaß machen** (“to be fun”). **Mir** is dative (“for me”), and **gemacht** is the past participle, usually used with **haben**: *Es hat mir Spaß gemacht.* Note: don’t confuse it with English **“to make fun (of someone)”** (= *sich lustig machen über*), which means to mock.
target_language_example: Das hat mir Spaß gemacht.
native_language_example: I enjoyed that.

meaning: "to me" + "everything" (used like “tell/explain me everything”, “everything to me”).
additional_notes: “mir” is the dative form of “ich” (= to/for me). “alles” means “everything.” You often see “mir alles” with verbs like sagen/erzählen/erklären/zeigen (“tell/describe/explain/show me everything”) and with “bedeuten” (“mean everything to me”: *Du bedeutest mir alles / Meine Familie bedeutet mir alles*). Word order is flexible, but “mir” typically comes before “alles” (*Er hat mir alles gesagt*).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir alles erklären?
native_language_example: Can you explain everything to me?

meaning: 'to me too / to me as well' (also me).
additional_notes: Uses the dative pronoun "mir" (= to me) with "auch" (= also). Often means "me too" as a reply (e.g., "Ich komme morgen." – "Mir auch."), but it can also appear inside a longer sentence to mean that something applies to you as well.
target_language_example: Ich möchte mir auch ein Stück Kuchen nehmen.
native_language_example: I'd like to take a piece of cake too.

meaning: to get on my nerves; to annoy me.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "gehen": "etwas/jemand geht mir auf den Geist" = something/someone is annoying me. Change "mir" to the person affected: "geht dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen auf den Geist". Common in spoken German and mildly informal.
target_language_example: Diese ständigen Anrufe gehen mir auf den Geist.
native_language_example: These constant calls are getting on my nerves.

meaning: (to) get on my nerves; annoy me.
additional_notes: Used with **gehen**: **jemandem auf die Nerven gehen** = “to get on someone’s nerves.” The person who is annoyed is in the **dative** (mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen). Very common in everyday speech; can sound a bit strong depending on tone.
target_language_example: Die Geräusche gehen mir auf die Nerven.
native_language_example: The noises are getting on my nerves.

meaning: out of my way; (also) avoiding me.
additional_notes: Used with gehen (“to go/walk”) in phrases like: Geh/Gehen Sie mir aus dem Weg! = “Get out of my way!” It can also be figurative: Jemand geht mir aus dem Weg = “Someone is avoiding me.” The pronoun changes in the dative: mir (me), dir (you), ihm/ihr (him/her), uns (us), euch (you all), ihnen/Ihnen (them/you formal).
target_language_example: Warum gehst du mir aus dem Weg?
native_language_example: Why are you avoiding me?

meaning: 'out of my sight' / 'go away (so I don’t have to see you)'.
additional_notes: Used in sharp commands like „Geh mir aus den Augen!“ or more formal „Gehen Sie mir aus den Augen!“. Very strong and rude/angry: you’re telling someone to leave immediately so you don’t have to look at them. You may also hear it with other verbs: „Schafft ihn mir aus den Augen!“ (= Get him out of my sight!).
target_language_example: Geh mir aus den Augen!
native_language_example: Get out of my sight!

additional_notes: Used with the verb „vorkommen“ (separable): „Das kommt mir bekannt vor.“ = “That seems familiar to me.” The „mir“ is dative (“to me”), and „bekannt“ means “known/familiar.” Often used when you recognize something but can’t place it.
target_language_example: Dieser Name kommt mir bekannt vor, aber ich weiß nicht, woher.
native_language_example: That name seems familiar to me, but I don’t know from where.

additional_notes: Used when you politely ask someone to do something for you, often right after the verb: "Hilf mir bitte" / "Sag mir bitte …". "mir" is dative = 'to me'; "bitte" softens the request. Word order can vary: "Bitte hilf mir" is also common. Often combined with "mal" to sound more casual: "Leih mir bitte mal …".
target_language_example: Schick mir bitte die Adresse.
native_language_example: Please send me the address.

meaning: “(to) me, please, the salt” → “Pass me the salt, please.”
additional_notes: This is a sentence fragment that’s commonly used in requests, but in full German you normally add a verb: **Gib mir bitte das Salz.** (informal singular) / **Geben Sie mir bitte das Salz.** (formal). **mir** is dative = “to me,” **bitte** softens the request, and **das Salz** is “the salt.”
target_language_example: Gib mir bitte das Salz.
native_language_example: Pass me the salt, please.

meaning: “(to) me, please, the …” — used when asking for a specific masculine item (usually in a request like “Give me …”).
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself; it normally needs a noun after **den** (e.g., **den Kaffee**, **den Stift**) and often a verb at the start: **Gib mir bitte den …** (“Please give me the …”). **mir** = “to me” (dative pronoun), **bitte** = “please”, **den** = “the” for masculine nouns in the accusative (direct object). Word order can vary: **Gib mir bitte den Stift** / **Gib mir den Stift, bitte**.
target_language_example: Gib mir bitte den Kaffee.
native_language_example: Please give me the coffee.

meaning: “…for me, please.” (often said when asking someone to pour you a drink)
additional_notes: This is usually the end of a sentence with a separable verb that has the prefix **ein-**, especially **einschenken** (“to pour (a drink)”). In German, the **ein** part often goes to the end: **Schenk mir bitte … ein.** On its own, **mir bitte ein** sounds incomplete—you normally need the verb and what you want poured.
target_language_example: Schenk mir bitte ein Glas Wasser ein.
native_language_example: Please pour me a glass of water.

meaning: “(to) me, please, a glass …” (used when ordering/asking for a drink).
additional_notes: This is a common sentence fragment you use with a verb like **geben** (give) or **bringen** (bring): **Geben/Bringen Sie mir bitte ein Glas Wasser.** It usually needs what the glass is of (e.g., **Wasser**, **Wein**) and often includes **Sie** for politeness in restaurants.
target_language_example: Bringen Sie mir bitte ein Glas Wasser.
native_language_example: Please bring me a glass of water.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to give/show/bring/buy something for you. "mir" = "to/for me" (dative). "eine" is the feminine form of "a/an" and is also used like "one" when the noun is understood from context (e.g., "eine billigere" = "a cheaper one"; "eine Decke" = "a blanket"). You’ll often see it with verbs like "kaufen", "bringen", "zeigen", "geben": "Kauf/Bring/Zeig/Gib mir bitte eine ...".
target_language_example: Bring mir bitte eine Flasche Wasser.
native_language_example: Please bring me a bottle of water.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to give you information. Typically followed by a question word (wie, ob, wann, wo, etc.) or a full clause: „Kannst du mir bitte sagen, wie …?“ Also common with more formal phrasing like „Könnten Sie mir bitte sagen …?“
target_language_example: Könnten Sie mir bitte sagen, wo der Bahnhof ist?
native_language_example: Could you please tell me where the train station is?

additional_notes: Used to ask or tell someone to assist you with a specific task or situation. "mir" is the dative pronoun "to me," and "dabei" means "with that/with it" (referring back to something already mentioned). You can change the pronoun/person: "dir dabei helfen" (help you), "ihm/ihr dabei helfen" (help him/her), etc. Works with informal "du" or formal "Sie."
target_language_example: Kannst du mir dabei helfen, das Formular auszufüllen?
native_language_example: Can you help me fill out the form?

additional_notes: Used with verbs that take two objects: something is done/sent/taught to you (mir) and 'it/that' is the thing (das). Often translates as “me it/that” or more naturally “it/that to me” / “for me” depending on the verb (e.g., 'Gib mir das' = 'Give it to me'). Word order can vary: 'Kannst du mir das erklären?' / 'Kannst du das mir erklären?' (the first is much more common).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir das bitte erklären?
native_language_example: Can you please explain that to me?

meaning: 'to me the book' / 'me the book' (indirect object + direct object).
additional_notes: Used when someone gives/ brings/ sends something to you. "mir" is the dative pronoun for "to me" (the receiver), and "das Buch" is the accusative direct object (the thing). Often appears with verbs like geben, bringen, schicken/senden: "Gib mir das Buch." = "Give me the book."
target_language_example: Kannst du mir das Buch geben?
native_language_example: Can you give me the book?

meaning: 'the money to me' / 'me the money' (dative: I receive it).
additional_notes: Used when you are the indirect object (recipient) of the money: *mir* = “to me,” *das Geld* = “the money.” Common with verbs like **geben** (to give), **bringen** (to bring), **schieben/stecken** (to slip/put). Often appears in sentences like **Gib mir das Geld.** Word order can also be **Gib das Geld mir** (more emphasis on *mir*), but **Gib mir das Geld** is the most common.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir das Geld heute noch geben?
native_language_example: Can you give me the money today?

meaning: "my life" (literally: "to me the life"), used with verbs like retten (save) or nehmen (take).
additional_notes: "Mir" is the dative form of "ich" (me), and "das Leben" means "life." You often see this chunk in fixed expressions: **jemandem das Leben retten** = "to save someone’s life" (e.g., "Er hat mir das Leben gerettet."), and **sich das Leben nehmen** = "to take one’s own life" / "to kill oneself" (e.g., "Ich habe versucht, mir das Leben zu nehmen."). In other contexts it can refer to "life" in a situation, e.g. "mir das Leben auf dem Mond vorstellen" = "imagine what life on the moon would be like."
target_language_example: Danke, du hast mir das Leben gerettet!
native_language_example: Thanks, you saved my life!

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb "(jemandem) das Leben retten" = "to save (someone’s) life." "mir" is dative (“to me/for me”), and "das Leben" is the thing being saved. Common full sentence: "Du hast mir das Leben gerettet."
target_language_example: Du hast mir das Leben gerettet.
native_language_example: You saved my life.

meaning: (to) make my life a living hell.
additional_notes: Used in the full expression „jemandem das Leben zur Hölle machen“ = to make someone’s life miserable/very difficult. „mir“ is dative (“to me”): Er macht **mir** das Leben zur Hölle. Strong, emotional phrasing; often used about ongoing bad treatment, stress, or harassment.
target_language_example: Der Chef macht mir das Leben zur Hölle, weil er mich ständig kritisiert.
native_language_example: My boss is making my life a living hell because he’s constantly criticizing me.

meaning: “me to swim” (as the object in: jemandem das Schwimmen beibringen = to teach someone to swim).
additional_notes: Used with the verb phrase „(jemandem) etwas beibringen“ (“to teach (someone) something”). „mir“ is dative (“to me”), and „das Schwimmen“ is the thing being taught (“swimming”). Word order often: „Er/Sie bringt mir das Schwimmen bei.“
target_language_example: Meine Mutter hat mir das Schwimmen beigebracht.
native_language_example: My mother taught me to swim.

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression. mir is the dative form of ich and usually means "to me" or "for me"; das means "that" or sometimes "it." Together they are a very common object combination with many verbs: gib mir das = "give me that," sag mir das = "tell me that," kauf mir das = "buy that for me."
target_language_example: Kannst du mir das erklären?
native_language_example: Can you explain that to me?

meaning: "your hand (to me)" (used with verbs like "give" or "hold").
additional_notes: This is a common phrase fragment in requests like "Gib mir deine Hand" (Give me your hand) or "Reich mir deine Hand" (Hold out your hand to me). "mir" is the dative form of "ich" (= to me), and "deine Hand" means "your hand" (informal singular "you").
target_language_example: Gib mir deine Hand, bitte.
native_language_example: Give me your hand, please.

meaning: 'me the …' (dative "mir" + accusative masculine "den") used when someone does something to/for me involving a specific masculine thing.
additional_notes: Common pattern with verbs that take two objects: a person in the dative (recipient/affected person) + a thing in the accusative (direct object). Example: "Gib mir den Rucksack" = "Give me the backpack." The "den" is for masculine nouns in the accusative (e.g., der Rucksack → den Rucksack). Word order is often "mir den + noun" when the noun comes right after, but you can also say "Gib mir den Rucksack" or "Gib den Rucksack mir" (less common/emphatic).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir den Schlüssel geben?
native_language_example: Can you give me the key?

meaning: “my arm” (used with a dative pronoun, typically when something happens to your arm).
additional_notes: German often uses a dative pronoun (mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch) + a definite article + a body part instead of a possessive (“mein Arm”), especially with injuries/accidents: „Ich brach mir den Arm.“ = “I broke my arm.” It can also appear with certain requests/gestures, e.g. „Gib mir den Arm.“ = “Give me your arm (to hold/support).”
target_language_example: Ich fiel und brach mir den Arm.
native_language_example: I fell and broke my arm.

meaning: 'my back' (literally: 'me the back', used with a body part).
additional_notes: Used with many verbs that involve touching or doing something to someone’s body (e.g., streicheln, massieren, waschen, kratzen). German often uses the dative pronoun (mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen) + the definite article (den Rücken) instead of a possessive like “my back”.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir den Rücken massieren?
native_language_example: Can you massage my back?

meaning: 'me the way' / 'to show (point) me the way'.
additional_notes: Dative phrase: mir = “to me”, den Weg = “the way/path”. Common with verbs like zeigen or weisen: „Er zeigt mir den Weg.“ = “He shows me the way.” It can also appear in more figurative expressions like „sich den Weg freischießen“ (“to shoot/force one’s way through”).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir den Weg zur U-Bahn zeigen?
native_language_example: Can you show me the way to the subway?

meaning: 'me the way to the …' (used when asking for directions).
additional_notes: This is a common sentence chunk used with verbs like *zeigen* (to show) or *erklären* (to explain): *Kannst du mir den Weg zum Bahnhof zeigen?* It uses dative *mir* (“to me”). *zum* = *zu dem* and is used with masculine/neuter places (*zum Bahnhof*, *zum Hotel*). For feminine places, use *zur* = *zu der* (*zur Schule*).
target_language_example: Können Sie mir den Weg zum Bahnhof zeigen?
native_language_example: Can you show me the way to the train station?

meaning: (to) me the way to the train station.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like „sagen“ (tell) or „zeigen“ (show) when asking for directions: „Können/Könnten/Würden Sie mir den Weg zum Bahnhof sagen/zeigen?“ Here „mir“ = to me, „den Weg“ = the way, „zum Bahnhof“ = to the train station (zu + dem). You can swap „zum Bahnhof“ for another place (e.g., „zum Hotel“, „zur Apotheke“).
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, können Sie mir den Weg zum Bahnhof zeigen?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you show me the way to the train station?

additional_notes: Used when someone does something to/for you involving a specific feminine noun (singular) or plural noun: **jemand gibt/zeigt/verkauft/schickt mir die/den/das …**. Here **mir** is the indirect object (= to me), and **die** is the definite article for what is being given/sold/etc. (often the direct object).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir die Adresse schicken?
native_language_example: Can you send me the address?

meaning: “my hair” expressed with the dative pronoun mir in common German constructions with body parts (literally “to me the hair”).
additional_notes: German frequently uses a dative pronoun (mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen) with body parts when the action affects the person: „Ich wasche mir die Haare“ = literally “I wash myself the hair,” meaning “I wash my hair.” The same structure is also used when someone does it for you: „Schneid mir die Haare“ = “Cut my hair (for me).” It can also appear in idioms, e.g. „Ich hätte mir die Haare raufen können“ (“I could have torn my hair out” in frustration).
target_language_example: Ich wasche mir die Haare.
native_language_example: I’m washing my hair.

additional_notes: German often uses the dative pronoun (mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen) with body parts instead of a possessive (meine/deine …), especially with actions done to yourself or to someone else: „Ich wasche mir die Hände.“ = „I wash my hands.“ / „Er legte mir die Hände auf die Schultern.“ = „He put his hands on my shoulders.“
target_language_example: Ich trockne mir die Hände ab.
native_language_example: I dry my hands.

meaning: (to put) the blame on me; (to blame) me.
additional_notes: Usually appears as part of a larger verb phrase such as „mir die Schuld geben“ (to blame me) or „mir die Schuld in die Schuhe schieben“ (to pin the blame on me). „mir“ is dative (“to/on me”), and „die Schuld“ is “the blame/guilt.” Often followed by „für …“ (“for …”) to specify what the blame is for.
target_language_example: Hör auf, mir die Schuld zu geben, nur weil du es verpasst hast.
native_language_example: Stop blaming me just because you missed it.

meaning: "(to) me the truth" (as in: "tell me the truth").
additional_notes: Usually used with verbs like **sagen** or **erzählen**: **mir die Wahrheit sagen/erzählen** = “tell me the truth.” **mir** is dative (“to me”), and **die Wahrheit** is the thing being told (accusative). You’ll also see it after verbs like **glauben**: **mir die Wahrheit glauben** = “believe me (that it’s) the truth.”
target_language_example: Bitte sag mir die Wahrheit.
native_language_example: Please tell me the truth.

additional_notes: Used when asking or insisting that someone be honest with you. "mir" = "to me" (dative), and the verb phrase is "die Wahrheit sagen". Commonly used with modal verbs (e.g., "können", "müssen") or in questions (e.g., "Wird er mir die Wahrheit sagen?").
target_language_example: Du kannst mir die Wahrheit sagen.
native_language_example: You can tell me the truth.

meaning: to/for me the whole time; to me all along
additional_notes: A common combination of **mir** (dative “to/for me”) + **die ganze Zeit** (“the whole time”). It’s often used to express that something was continuously happening or was true throughout a period: *Der folgt mir die ganze Zeit.* It can appear in the middle of the clause depending on German word order (especially in subordinate clauses): *Endlich begreife ich, was du mir die ganze Zeit sagen wolltest.*
target_language_example: Der folgt mir die ganze Zeit.
native_language_example: He keeps following me the whole time.

meaning: 'this book to me' / 'for me, this book' (dative recipient + direct object).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like **leihen/ausleihen** to show who receives the book. In **Bitte leihe mir dieses Buch**, **mir** = 'to me' (the person getting it), **dieses Buch** = the thing being lent. Common patterns: **jdm. etw. leihen** (lend someone something) and **sich etw. ausleihen** (borrow something for oneself), e.g. **Ich leihe mir dieses Buch aus** / **Könnte ich mir dieses Buch ausleihen?**.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir dieses Buch bis morgen leihen?
native_language_example: Can you lend me this book until tomorrow?

meaning: 'I don't care' / 'it doesn't matter to me'.
additional_notes: Used to say you’re indifferent about something. Often appears as a short standalone answer (“Mir egal.”) or with a clause: “Mir egal, was …” (“I don’t care what …”), “Mir egal, ob …” (“I don’t care whether …”), “Es ist mir egal, was Sie denken” (“I don’t care what you think”). Note the dative pronoun: mir = “to me”. Can sound blunt; add “ist” for a slightly fuller form: “(Es) ist mir egal.”
target_language_example: Es ist mir egal, wo wir essen.
native_language_example: I don’t care where we eat.

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression. mir is the dative form of ich ('to me' or 'for me'), and ein means 'a/an' or 'one' before a noun. Together they often appear with verbs like geben, holen, kaufen, or anbieten: Gib mir ein Buch = 'Give me a book.' In some contexts, especially with verbs like ich kaufe mir ein ..., it can mean 'for myself' rather than literally 'to me'.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir ein Glas Wasser bringen?
native_language_example: Can you bring me a glass of water?

additional_notes: Used with the dative pronoun **mir** (“for me”) plus **ein Stück** (“a piece”). Often appears with verbs like **(sich) holen** or **kaufen** to mean you get/buy something *for yourself*: **Ich hole mir ein Stück (Kuchen).** In requests, **mir** means “for me”: **Gib mir ein Stück Holz.** Usually you add what the piece is of (e.g., **ein Stück Kuchen**, **ein Stück Land**, **ein Stück Holz**).
target_language_example: Ich nehme mir ein Stück Kuchen.
native_language_example: I’ll take a piece of cake (for myself).

meaning: "me a piece of paper" (usually as part of a request).
additional_notes:
This is a sentence fragment you’ll often see after a verb like geben/bringen/reichen (“to give/bring/hand”).
- mir = “to me” (dative object)
- ein Stück Papier = “a piece of paper” (thing being given, accusative)
Typical full sentence: „Gib mir ein Stück Papier.“
target_language_example: Kannst du mir ein Stück Papier geben?
native_language_example: Can you give me a piece of paper?

additional_notes: Used with verbs like **rufen** (call), **bestellen** (order), **suchen** (find): *Jemand ruft/bestellt/sucht mir ein Taxi.* Here **mir** is dative (“for me”). Related: **Ich nehme mir ein Taxi** = “I’ll get/take a taxi (for myself).”
target_language_example: Er rief mir ein Taxi.
native_language_example: He called me a taxi.

additional_notes: Used in the fixed, polite phrase (often formal): „Es ist/war mir ein Vergnügen …“ = “It is/was a pleasure for me …”. You can say it after meeting someone, saying goodbye, or thanking someone. Grammar note: „mir“ is dative (“for me”), so you can also hear „Es war uns ein Vergnügen“ (“It was a pleasure for us”).
target_language_example: Es war mir ein Vergnügen, Sie kennenzulernen.
native_language_example: It was a pleasure to meet you.

meaning: 'me a little' / 'for me, a bit' (dative + “a little”).
additional_notes: Used with verbs that take the dative object (mir = “to me”), often meaning “do something for me a little”: Spiel mir ein bisschen … (“Play me a little …”). With feelings/fit descriptions it can mean “for me”: Das ist mir ein bisschen zu eng (“That’s a bit too tight for me”). Word order can vary in real speech (e.g., Hilf mir ein bisschen).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir ein bisschen Wasser geben?
native_language_example: Can you give me a little water?

additional_notes: Used with a following noun (often neuter: *ein neues Handy/Wörterbuch/Motorrad/Hobby*) to show who benefits from the action. Very common with verbs like **(sich) kaufen** and **(sich) suchen**: *Ich kaufe mir …* / *Ich muss mir … suchen.* Here **mir** is dative (“for me / for myself”), not the direct object.
target_language_example: Ich kaufe mir ein neues Fahrrad.
native_language_example: I’m buying myself a new bike.

additional_notes: Here, "mir" is the dative pronoun meaning "for me / to me" and it often shows that you’re doing something for yourself, especially with verbs like "(sich) kaufen" or "(sich) zulegen". In full sentences you’ll often see: "mir + (ein) + noun" (e.g., "Ich kaufe mir ..." = "I’m buying myself ...").
target_language_example: Zu meinem Geburtstag kaufe ich mir ein neues Auto.
native_language_example: For my birthday, I'm buying myself a new car.

meaning: 'me a few / a couple (of …)' (to me, a few).
additional_notes: Used with a verb (often a request) to mean you want/need a small number or amount of something for yourself. "mir" is the dative pronoun "to me/for me" and "ein paar" means "a few/a couple"; it’s usually followed by a plural noun ("ein paar Minuten", "ein paar Fragen").
target_language_example: Können Sie mir ein paar Minuten geben?
native_language_example: Can you give me a couple of minutes?

meaning: “to/for me a …” (indicating you are the recipient).
additional_notes: Used with verbs that involve giving/sending/saying/recommending something to someone. **mir** is the dative pronoun “to me/for me,” and **eine** is “a/an” for feminine nouns (accusative), e.g., *eine Postkarte, eine Unterkunft, eine Bemerkung, eine Freude*. Common in polite requests: *Können Sie mir eine … empfehlen?* / *Schicken Sie mir eine …*
target_language_example: Kannst du mir eine Adresse schicken?
native_language_example: Can you send me an address?

meaning: “an honor (to me)” (as in: “It’s/It was/It would be an honor for me”).
additional_notes: Used almost always in the fixed phrase **„Es ist/war/wäre mir eine Ehre, …“** to express respectful, often formal politeness (sometimes old-fashioned), e.g. accepting an invitation, thanking someone, or showing high respect. Common patterns: **Es war mir eine Ehre.** (“It was an honor.”) / **Es wäre mir eine Ehre, wenn …** (“It would be an honor if …”).
target_language_example: Es wäre mir eine Ehre, Ihnen zu helfen.
native_language_example: It would be an honor to help you.

mir eine Liste, was ich alles

target_language_multi_word_term: (Schreib/Schreibt) mir eine Liste, was ich alles … soll.
meaning: “Write me a list of everything I should …”
additional_notes: Used to ask someone to write down all the things you need to do/buy/etc. "alles" adds emphasis: "everything / all the things". "Schreib" is informal singular (to one person); "Schreibt" is either plural (to several people) or formal "Sie" in writing (often capitalized: "Schreiben Sie").
target_language_example: Schreib mir eine Liste, was ich alles einpacken soll.
native_language_example: Write me a list of everything I should pack.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like **schicken** (to send) or **schreiben** (to write): **Schick/Schicken Sie/Schickt mir eine Nachricht!** = “Send me a message!” The **mir** is the dative pronoun “to me.”
target_language_example: Bitte schick mir eine Nachricht, wenn du angekommen bist.
native_language_example: Please send me a message when you’ve arrived.

additional_notes: "mir" is the dative form of "ich" (= to/for me). This phrase is usually part of a sentence with a verb like "bringen" (to bring) or "einschenken" (to pour). Word order can change depending on the sentence: e.g., "Sie brachte mir eine Tasse Tee" / "Sie hat mir eine Tasse Tee gebracht."
target_language_example: Kannst du mir eine Tasse Tee bringen?
native_language_example: Can you bring me a cup of tea?

meaning: “me a …” / “to me a …” (masculine accusative object after a verb like give/bring).
additional_notes: Used when something is done or given to you: **mir** = “to me” (dative), **einen** = “a/an” for a masculine noun in the accusative (the thing being given). Common with verbs like **geben** (to give), **bringen** (to bring), **reichen/überreichen** (to hand over). Example pattern: **Gib/Bring mir einen + [masculine noun].**
target_language_example: Kannst du mir einen Kaffee bringen?
native_language_example: Can you bring me a coffee?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "tun" (or "machen") in requests: "Tu/Tun Sie mir einen Gefallen …". Very common to introduce what you want the person to do next, often with an imperative or with "und" (e.g., "Tu mir einen Gefallen und …"). "mir" = to me; "einen Gefallen" is accusative and stays the same while "mir" changes depending on the person (mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen).
target_language_example: Tu mir einen Gefallen und ruf mich später an.
native_language_example: Do me a favor and call me later.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to help you with something. Grammar: "jemandem (Dat.) einen Gefallen tun" → the person who benefits is in the dative (mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen/Ihnen). Politeness: "Kannst du …?" (informal), "Können Sie …?" (formal), and "Würden Sie …?" is even more polite.
target_language_example: Könntest du mir einen Gefallen tun und das Fenster schließen?
native_language_example: Could you do me a favor and close the window?

meaning: 'me a new …' / 'for me, a new …' (dative 'mir' + accusative 'einen neuen …').
additional_notes: Used when someone does something for you or gives you something: *jemand gibt/kauft/schickt/strickt mir …*. **mir** = “to me/for me”. **einen neuen** is masculine accusative and normally needs a noun after it (e.g., *einen neuen Namen*, *einen neuen Pullover*). The adjective ending changes with gender/case: *mir eine neue Jacke*, *mir ein neues Buch*, *mir neue Schuhe*.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir einen neuen Termin geben?
native_language_example: Can you give me a new appointment/date?

additional_notes: Used with a verb to make a request or suggestion sound easy and straightforward. Common patterns: „Sag es mir einfach.“ (Just tell me.), „Schreib mir einfach.“ (Just write/text me.), „Glaub/Vertrau mir einfach.“ (Just believe/trust me.). „mir“ is the dative pronoun “to me,” and „einfach“ often means “just” in this context (not only “simple”).
target_language_example: Ruf mir einfach an, wenn du Zeit hast.
native_language_example: Just call me when you have time.

additional_notes: Used when **mir** is the dative pronoun meaning “to me / for me,” and **etwas** means “something.” Common with verbs that take a dative person + an object, e.g. **mir etwas erzählen** (tell me something), **mir etwas erklären** (explain something to me), **mir etwas sagen** (say something to me), **mir etwas verheimlichen/vorenthalten** (hide/withhold something from me). Word order can vary, but often: verb + **mir** + **etwas**.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir etwas empfehlen?
native_language_example: Can you recommend something to me?

meaning: 'to … something to me' / 'to … something for me' (used before a verb).
additional_notes: This is a common pattern with a **zu-infinitive**: **mir** = “to me” (dative), **etwas** = “something”, **zu** introduces the infinitive (“to …”). You’ll often see it after **um ... zu ...** (in order to ...), or with verbs that take a dative object (e.g., *jemandem etwas erklären/zeigen/geben*). The verb comes later: *mir etwas zu erklären* = “to explain something to me.”
target_language_example: Kannst du mir etwas zu essen geben?
native_language_example: Can you give me something to eat?

additional_notes: Used when asking someone to get/make/give you food. "mir" is the dative pronoun meaning "to/for me" (often used with verbs like geben, bringen, holen, machen, besorgen). "etwas zu essen" literally means "something to eat" and works like a noun phrase.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir etwas zu essen bringen?
native_language_example: Can you bring me something to eat?

meaning: "something to drink for me" (asking for a drink).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like „geben“, „bringen“, „holen“: „Gib/Bring/Hol mir etwas zu trinken.“ „mir“ is dative = “for/to me,” and „etwas zu trinken“ means “something to drink.”
target_language_example: Können Sie mir etwas zu trinken bringen?
native_language_example: Could you bring me something to drink?

meaning: I remember; it occurs to me.
additional_notes: From the verb "einfallen" (= to come to mind). It’s used when a thought/idea suddenly comes to you. Grammar: the person is in the dative (mir/dir/ihm …) and the thing/idea is the subject: "Mir fällt ein Name ein." Common: "Mir fällt nichts ein."
target_language_example: Mir fällt ein, dass ich noch Milch kaufen muss.
native_language_example: It occurs to me that I still need to buy milk.

meaning: "not at all" (to me); "it doesn't bother me at all."
additional_notes: Used with a verb to say something is no problem for you, e.g. "Das macht mir gar nichts" (I don’t mind at all), "Das stört mir gar nichts" (That doesn’t bother me at all), or "Das ist mir gar nichts" (I’m not interested in that / that’s not for me, depending on context). "mir" can change: "dir / ihm / ihr / uns / euch / ihnen".
target_language_example: Kein Problem — das macht mir gar nichts.
native_language_example: No problem — I don’t mind at all.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **gefallen** to say you like something. The person who likes is in the **dative**: **mir** (to me), **dir** (to you), **ihm/ihr** (to him/her), **uns/euch**, **ihnen**. The thing you like is the grammatical subject, so the verb agrees with it: **Mir gefällt** der Film (singular), **Mir gefallen** die Augen / Fremdsprachen (plural).
target_language_example: Mir gefallen deine Ohrringe.
native_language_example: I like your earrings.

additional_notes: Used with gefallen to express liking, literally meaning something "pleases" you. The thing you like is the grammatical subject: Mir gefällt der Klang. For plural nouns use gefällt + plural verb: Mir gefallen die Schuhe. You can also use it with "es" + clause/infinitive: Mir gefällt es, Ski zu fahren.
target_language_example: Mir gefällt dieses Lied wirklich gut.
native_language_example: I really like this song.

meaning: “I like your …” / “I don’t like your …” (literally: “your … pleases me”).
additional_notes: Used to say you (don’t) like something about someone else. German uses the verb **gefallen** with the person in the **dative** (**mir** = “to me”) and the thing that is liked as the grammatical subject: **Deine Art gefällt mir.** The word **deine** is the possessive “your” (informal singular), usually before a feminine noun (**deine Art**, **deine Einstellung**) or plural (**deine Augen**).
target_language_example: Mir gefällt deine Stimme sehr.
native_language_example: I really like your voice.

additional_notes: Used to say you like a color (or someone’s hair color, clothes color, etc.). The verb is **gefallen**: the thing you like is the grammatical subject (**die Farbe**), and the person who likes it is in the dative (**mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen**). You can add which color with an adjective: **Mir gefällt die rote Farbe** (“I like the red color”).
target_language_example: Mir gefällt die Farbe von deinem T-Shirt.
native_language_example: I like the color of your T-shirt.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t like something. German often phrases this with **gefallen**: the thing you like is the grammatical subject. Common pattern: „Mir gefällt X nicht.“ (singular) / „Mir gefallen X nicht.“ (plural). You can also say: „Das gefällt mir nicht.“ = “I don’t like that.”
target_language_example: Der Film, mir gefällt nicht, ist zu lang.
native_language_example: The movie I don't like is too long.

additional_notes: "Mir" is the dative pronoun meaning "to me" (the person who benefits). "Geholfen" is the past participle of "helfen" and is used with "haben" to form the perfect tense: "Du hast mir geholfen" = "You helped me / have helped me." With "Sie" (formal) and plural, it becomes "Sie haben mir geholfen" / "Ihr habt mir geholfen."
target_language_example: Danke, dass du mir geholfen hast.
native_language_example: Thanks for helping me.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how you are doing, especially health or well-being. Literally it’s like “to me, it goes,” so German uses the dative: mir (to me) + geht es (is going). Common patterns: “Mir geht es gut/schlecht/besser.” You can also add words like „wieder“ (again) or „jetzt“ (now).
target_language_example: Mir geht es heute viel besser.
native_language_example: I feel much better today.

meaning: I’m doing well / I feel good.
additional_notes: Common answer to "Wie geht es dir/Ihnen?" (“How are you?”). Literally it’s like “To me it goes well” (German uses the dative: mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen). In everyday speech you often hear the shortened form "Mir geht’s gut".
target_language_example: Danke, mir geht es gut, und dir?
native_language_example: Thanks, I’m doing well—how about you?

additional_notes: Uses the dative pronoun **mir** (“to me”) with the past participle **gesagt** (from **sagen**, “to say/tell”). Very common in the perfect tense with **haben**: **Er hat mir gesagt, dass …** (“He told me that …”). Often followed by a clause or a question word: **was / dass / ob**.
target_language_example: Er hat mir gesagt, dass er heute keine Zeit hat.
native_language_example: He told me that he doesn’t have time today.

additional_notes: Used after a subject (often "Sie/Er hat …") to introduce what someone reported: "jemandem sagen, dass …" = "to tell someone that …". The clause after "dass" is a statement. In more formal/indirect reported speech, you may see Konjunktiv I in the "dass"-clause (e.g., "sie habe", "sie wolle") to show it’s reported, not directly quoted.
target_language_example: Er hat mir gesagt, daß sie später kommt.
native_language_example: He told me that she’s coming later.

additional_notes: "helfen" means "to help" and it takes the dative case. "mir" is the dative form of "ich" (me), so you use it when someone helps you: "Du willst mir helfen." You can replace "mir" with other dative pronouns/nouns (e.g., "dir", "ihm", "ihr", "uns").
target_language_example: Du willst mir helfen.
native_language_example: You want to help me.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like „sehen/schauen/gucken“ + „jemandem in die Augen“ to mean making eye contact with someone. „mir“ is the dative pronoun “to me” (= “me” here). Often used as an instruction or demand: „Sieh/Sehen Sie mir in die Augen!“
target_language_example: Kannst du mir in die Augen schauen, wenn du mit mir redest?
native_language_example: Can you look me in the eyes when you talk to me?

additional_notes: Used with verbs to indicate that something is directed at the speaker’s face (e.g., someone stares at you; wind blows at you; someone laughs/lies to your face). Common in fixed expressions like „jemandem ins Gesicht lügen“ (to lie to someone’s face) and „jemandem ins Gesicht lachen“ (to laugh in someone’s face). Grammar: „mir“ is dative (= to me) and „ins Gesicht“ is a contraction of „in das Gesicht“ (into the face).
target_language_example: Der Wind bläst mir ins Gesicht.
native_language_example: The wind is blowing in my face.

meaning: to go to the cinema/movies with me.
additional_notes: In correct German you normally say **„mit mir ins Kino gehen“** (with **mit** + dative: *mit mir*). Used in invitations or questions: **„Willst du mit mir ins Kino gehen?“**.
target_language_example: Willst du mit mir ins Kino gehen?
native_language_example: Do you want to go to the movies with me?

meaning: "I don't care" / "it doesn't matter to me."
additional_notes: Uses dative mir (“to me”) + ist egal (“is irrelevant/doesn’t matter”). Often followed by a clause with ob/was/wer/warum, etc.: Mir ist egal, ob/was/wer… It can sound blunt; for a softer tone you can say: Das ist mir egal.
target_language_example: Mir ist egal, wo wir essen gehen.
native_language_example: I don't care where we go to eat.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how you feel (temperature). German often uses this pattern: "mir ist + adjective" (literally “to me is ...”), e.g. "mir ist warm" (I’m warm), "mir ist heiß" (I’m hot). You can add a body part with "an den/der ...": "Mir ist kalt an den Händen" (My hands are cold).
target_language_example: Kannst du das Fenster schließen? Mir ist kalt.
native_language_example: Can you close the window? I’m cold.

meaning: (to be) sorry; to feel sorry for someone.
additional_notes:
Almost always used with a verb, especially in:
- **Es tut mir leid.** = “I’m sorry.” (apology)
- **X tut mir leid.** = “I feel sorry for X.” (pity/compassion)
You’ll also see other verb forms like **es täte mir leid** (would be sorry) or past **er tat mir leid** (I felt sorry for him).
target_language_example: Es tut mir leid, ich komme zu spät.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, I’m late.

meaning: "sorry about" / "sorry because of" (used to apologize for something).
additional_notes: This is usually said as **„Es tut mir leid wegen …“** (or **„Tut mir leid wegen …“** in speech). After **wegen** you often see the **genitive** in formal German (e.g., „wegen des Lärms“), while **dative** is common in everyday speech (e.g., „wegen dem Lärm“).
target_language_example: Es tut mir leid wegen der Verspätung.
native_language_example: I’m sorry about the delay.

meaning: “(to) me … just/for a moment” (softens a request).
additional_notes: Used mostly in spoken German: **mir** is the dative pronoun (“to me/for me”), and **mal** is a common modal particle that makes requests sound more casual, friendly, or less demanding (often like “just” or “for a second” in English). It doesn’t usually mean “once” literally here. Word order often stays together: *Gib mir mal …*, *Hör mir mal zu*.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir mal kurz helfen?
native_language_example: Can you help me for a moment?

meaning: “me the screwdriver (for a moment),” i.e. “hand me the screwdriver.”
additional_notes: Used inside requests like „Gib mir mal …“ / „Können Sie mir mal … geben?“ Here „mir“ is dative (“to me”), and „mal“ is a very common conversational particle that softens the request (like “just” / “for a sec”). In polite form, use „Geben Sie mir mal den Schraubenzieher.“
target_language_example: Kannst du mir mal den Schraubenzieher geben?
native_language_example: Can you hand me the screwdriver for a sec?

meaning: “(to) me the scissors, please” → “hand/pass me the scissors (for a moment)”
additional_notes: Used in requests like „Gib/Reich mir mal die Schere.“ The word „mal“ (short for „einmal“) is very common in spoken German to soften a request—similar to “just” or “for a second” in English. It usually sounds casual; in polite situations you’d use „Können Sie mir bitte die Schere geben/bringen?“
target_language_example: Gib mir mal die Schere, bitte.
native_language_example: Hand me the scissors, please.

additional_notes: Used with the dative pronoun mir (“to me/for me”) plus nicht (“not”). It often appears in common patterns like: etwas nicht erzählen/geben/sagen (don’t tell/give/say me), es erscheint mir nicht … (it doesn’t seem … to me), ich kann es mir nicht leisten (I can’t afford it), ich hätte mir nicht träumen lassen (I never would have imagined). In questions, it can also sound like a polite suggestion/request: Wollen Sie mir nicht antworten? (“Won’t you answer me?”).
target_language_example: Das ist mir nicht klar.
native_language_example: That isn’t clear to me.

additional_notes: Used with the reflexive verb **sich vorstellen** (“to imagine”). The **mir** is the dative reflexive pronoun (“to myself”). Very common in the pattern **Das kann ich mir nicht vorstellen!** = “I can’t imagine that!” / “No way!” You can follow it with **dass...**: **Ich kann mir nicht vorstellen, dass...**
target_language_example: Ich kann mir nicht vorstellen, dass er so spät noch arbeitet.
native_language_example: I can’t imagine that he’s still working so late.

additional_notes: Not a fixed idiom—it's just the dative pronoun **mir** (“to me”) + **nie** (“never”). You see it with verbs that take the dative, e.g. **jemandem zuhören** (to listen to someone): *Er hört mir nie zu.* It also appears with some reflexive verbs that use a dative pronoun, e.g. *Ich werde mir nie vergeben* (“I’ll never forgive myself”). Word order can vary: **Tom hört mir nie zu** / **Tom hört nie mir zu** (the first is more neutral).
target_language_example: Bitte hör mir nie wieder so zu spät zu.
native_language_example: Please never listen to me that late again.

additional_notes: A common sentence fragment used with the Perfekt (past) tense, usually with "haben": "Du hast mir nie gesagt, dass ..." (= You never told me that ...). "mir" is the dative pronoun meaning "to me," "nie" means "never," and "gesagt" is the past participle of "sagen" (to say/tell). Word order can vary depending on what comes first in the sentence.
target_language_example: Du hast mir nie gesagt, dass du heute keine Zeit hast.
native_language_example: You never told me that you don’t have time today.

additional_notes: Used to complain or point out that someone didn’t inform you about something. Typical structure: (ihr/Sie) habt/haben + mir + nie + gesagt, daß + clause. The verb is „sagen“ (to tell/say). „daß“ (modern spelling: „dass“) introduces a subordinate clause, so the conjugated verb goes to the end of that clause.
target_language_example: Ihr habt mir nie gesagt, daß Tom Lehrer ist.
native_language_example: You never told me that Tom is a teacher.

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression. mir is the dative form of ich and means "to me" or "for me." noch can mean "still/yet" or "another," so the exact English translation depends on context: mir noch Geld schulden = "still owe me money," mir noch eine Chance geben = "give me another chance."
target_language_example: Er schuldet mir noch zehn Euro.
native_language_example: He still owes me ten euros.

meaning: "me another (one)" (asking for one more of something).
additional_notes: Used with a noun right after it, often when ordering or requesting something: "Gib/Bring mir noch ein + [noun]". "mir" is dative = "to me"; "noch" here means "another/one more"; "ein" is the masculine/neuter "a/an" (use "eine" for feminine nouns: "mir noch eine Cola").
target_language_example: Bring mir noch ein Wasser, bitte.
native_language_example: Bring me another water, please.

additional_notes: Uses the dative pronoun mir (“to me”). Common in questions like „Was wolltest du mir sagen?“ (“What did you want to tell me?”). With „zu mir sagen“ it can also mean “call me” (a name), e.g. „Du kannst Bill zu mir sagen.“
target_language_example: Kannst du mir sagen, wie spät es ist?
native_language_example: Can you tell me what time it is?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to explain the reason for something. Common pattern: „Kannst du/Könnt ihr mir sagen, warum …?“ After „warum“, German usually uses subordinate-clause word order with the verb at the end: „…, warum Tom das tut.“ (not: „warum Tom tut das“).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir sagen, warum du heute so spät bist?
native_language_example: Can you tell me why you’re so late today?

additional_notes: Used with an indirect question introduced by **was** (“what”). **mir** is the dative pronoun (“to me”), and the verb **sagen** (“to say/tell”) is commonly used like **jemandem etwas sagen** (“to tell someone something”). In a full sentence, the **was**-clause usually goes to the end: *Kannst du mir sagen, was das ist?*
target_language_example: Kannst du mir sagen, was du heute machen willst?
native_language_example: Can you tell me what you want to do today?

additional_notes: Used to ask for instructions or an explanation. Literally it’s “tell me how one …”, and it’s followed by a normal verb clause: wie man das macht / wie man dorthin kommt / wie man ein Wort buchstabiert. Often used in polite questions with Könnten Sie …? (formal) or Könntest du …? (informal singular).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir sagen, wie man diesen Drucker benutzt?
native_language_example: Can you tell me how to use this printer?

meaning: “tell me how to get to …” (asking for directions).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like „kannst du …?“ / „können Sie …?“ / „könnt ihr …?“ to politely ask for directions. „zum“ = „zu dem“ and is used with masculine/neuter places (e.g., „zum Bahnhof“, „zum Rathaus“). For feminine places use „zur“ (e.g., „zur Schule“).
target_language_example: Können Sie mir sagen, wie man zum Bahnhof kommt?
native_language_example: Can you tell me how to get to the train station?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the location of a person/place/thing. Often appears in polite questions with "können/könnten/könntest" (e.g., "Könnten Sie mir sagen, wo …?"). In a subordinate clause after "sagen", the verb goes to the end: "… wo die Post ist".
target_language_example: Könnten Sie mir sagen, wo der Bahnhof ist?
native_language_example: Could you tell me where the train station is?

meaning: "to me before / already once (at some point earlier)."
additional_notes: Used with a verb to say someone did/said something to you earlier: **mir** = “to me” (dative), **schon mal** is a common, slightly colloquial way to mean “before / already once” (often = “at least once already”). Word order is flexible, but **mir schon mal** often sits in the middle of the sentence before the main action.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir schon mal die Adresse schicken?
native_language_example: Can you send me the address already (ahead of time / for now)?

additional_notes: Uses the dative pronoun mir (= “to me”). With körperliche/gefühlte Schwere: „Der Kopf ist mir schwer.“ / „Mein Herz wird mir schwer.“ With difficulty: „Es fällt mir schwer, …“ (= “I find it hard to …”). You can also say „jemand macht es mir schwer“ (= “someone makes it hard for me”).
target_language_example: Es fällt mir schwer, heute zu konzentrieren.
native_language_example: I find it hard to concentrate today.

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression, but a very common combination: **mir** is the dative pronoun (“to me”), and **sehr** intensifies the verb/adjective (“very / a lot”). Often used with verbs like **fehlen** (to miss): *Du fehlst mir sehr.* = “I miss you a lot.” Also common with **helfen** (help): *Das hat mir sehr geholfen.* = “That helped me a lot.” With **weh tun** (hurt): *Das tut mir sehr weh.* = “That hurts me a lot.” In sentences like *Das klingt mir sehr …*, **mir** means “to me,” but beginners will also often hear **für mich** (“for me”) in this meaning.
target_language_example: Du fehlst mir sehr.
native_language_example: I miss you a lot.

meaning: “very well for me” / “really well (for my situation)”
additional_notes:
Uses the dative pronoun mir (“to me”) to show how something is for you. Common in set phrases like:
- Es geht mir sehr gut. = I’m doing very well.
- Das passt mir sehr gut. / Um sechs passt mir sehr gut. = That suits me (very well). / Six o’clock works (really well) for me.
- Das kann ich mir sehr gut vorstellen. = I can easily imagine that.
- Hör mir sehr gut zu. = Listen to me very carefully (here sehr gut intensifies zuhör(en)).
target_language_example: Am Samstag passt es mir sehr gut.
native_language_example: Saturday works really well for me.

additional_notes: Most commonly used in the full phrase "Es tut mir sehr leid" (“I’m very sorry”). "mir" means “to me,” and "sehr" intensifies the apology (“very”). Often used to apologize or express sympathy (e.g., bad news, inconvenience).
target_language_example: Es tut mir sehr leid, ich habe deinen Termin vergessen.
native_language_example: I’m very sorry, I forgot your appointment.

additional_notes: Used with the verb phrase **sich sicher sein, dass …** (“to be sure that …”). It changes with the person: **ich bin mir sicher**, **du bist dir sicher**, **er/sie ist sich sicher**, etc. Often used with past tense too: **ich war mir sicher, dass …**. The **dass**-clause sends the verb to the end: *Ich bin mir sicher, dass er kommt.*
target_language_example: Ich bin mir sicher, dass du das schaffst.
native_language_example: I’m sure that you can do it.

additional_notes: Almost always used as part of the fixed apology phrase **„(Es) tut mir so leid.“** or **„Das tut mir so leid.“** = “I’m so sorry.” Here **mir** means “to me” (dative), and **leid** expresses regret/sorrow. You can also say **„Es tut mir leid.“** (less strong) or **„Es tut mir wirklich so leid.“** (stronger).
target_language_example: Es tut mir so leid, dass ich zu spät bin.
native_language_example: I’m so sorry that I’m late.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **versprechen** (“to promise”) with **mir** = “to me” (dative). Very common in the **Perfekt** (past) form: **(jemand) hat mir … versprochen** / **ihr habt mir … versprochen**. Often followed by **dass ...** (“that ...”) or an infinitive clause: **mir versprochen, nicht wieder ... zu tun** (“promised me not to do ... again”).
target_language_example: Du hast mir versprochen, heute pünktlich zu sein.
native_language_example: You promised me you’d be on time today.

additional_notes: From the verb **(sich) etwas vorstellen** = “to imagine/picture something.” **mir** is the dative reflexive pronoun (“to myself”), often used with *sich vorstellen*. The phrase **… als ich es mir vorgestellt hatte** is very common for comparing reality with your expectations: “... than I had imagined.” Be careful: **jemanden vorstellen** can also mean “to introduce someone,” but with **mir** (reflexive) it usually means “imagine.”
target_language_example: Der Film war spannender, als ich ihn mir vorgestellt hatte.
native_language_example: The movie was more exciting than I had imagined.

additional_notes: Most often used in the full phrase „Es tut mir wirklich leid.“ (= “I’m really sorry.”). „mir“ is dative (“to me”), and „leid tun“ is the common way to apologize or say you regret something.
target_language_example: Es tut mir wirklich leid, dass ich zu spät bin.
native_language_example: I’m really sorry that I’m late.

additional_notes: Passive structure: literally 'to me was said'. Used to report what someone told you, often without naming who. Very common with reported speech, often using the subjunctive (Konjunktiv I/II): e.g. "Mir wurde gesagt, er sei krank." You can swap in other pronouns: "dir wurde gesagt" (you were told), "ihm/ihr wurde gesagt" (he/she was told).
target_language_example: Mir wurde gesagt, dass der Termin morgen ist.
native_language_example: I was told that the appointment is tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone else told you. Literally “to me it was said, that I…”, but natural English is “I was told that I…”. Commonly followed by a modal verb such as dürfen (to be allowed to / may) or sollen (should / be supposed to). Spelling note: „daß“ is the older spelling; modern German typically uses „dass“.
target_language_example: Mir wurde gesagt, daß ich dir nicht trauen dürfe.
native_language_example: I was told that I wasn’t allowed to trust you.

additional_notes: Used to say something is bigger than what fits/suits you (often clothes or shoes). Grammar pattern: [Thing] + ist/sind + mir + zu + adjective (e.g., „Die Schuhe sind mir zu klein.“).
target_language_example: Der Pullover ist mir zu groß.
native_language_example: The sweater is too big for me.

additional_notes: Often appears when a verb has the separable prefix **zu-**, which moves to the end of the clause: **zuhören** → *Hör mir zu!* (“Listen to me!”), **zulächeln** → *Sie lächelte mir zu.* (“She smiled at me.”). Note: in *mir zu zeigen* the **zu** is the infinitive marker (“to show”), not the separable prefix.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir kurz zuhören? Hör mir zu!
native_language_example: Can you listen to me for a moment? Listen to me!

meaning: to help me (as an infinitive clause: “to help me”)
additional_notes: "mir" is the dative form of "ich" (me), because "helfen" takes the dative case (jemandem helfen). "zu helfen" is the infinitive used after verbs like "bitten" (ask), "versuchen" (try), "sich weigern" (refuse), and in purpose clauses with "um ... zu ..." (in order to). The full phrase typically appears as part of a larger sentence (e.g., "jemanden bitten, mir zu helfen").
target_language_example: Ich bat ihn darum, mir zu helfen.
native_language_example: I asked him to help me.

additional_notes: Used in a **zu + infinitive** clause after certain verbs that take a **dative person** (mir/dir/ihm …), especially **erlauben** (allow) and **verbieten** (forbid): *jdm. erlauben/verbieten, zu reden* = “allow/forbid someone to speak.” On its own, **mir zu reden** is incomplete—you need a main verb before it. If you want to say “talk to me,” you usually say **mit mir reden**.
target_language_example: Der Lehrer erlaubt mir zu reden.
native_language_example: The teacher allows me to speak.

additional_notes: Uses the infinitive with „zu“ (zu sagen = to say/tell) plus the dative pronoun „mir“ (to me). Common after verbs like „bitten“ (to ask), „weigerte sich“ (refused), or in patterns like „etwas, das du mir zu sagen hast“ (= something you have to tell me). Word order can vary: „mir zu sagen“ / „zu sagen, was …“.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir zu sagen, wie spät es ist?
native_language_example: Can you tell me what time it is?

meaning: 'for my birthday' (for me, on the occasion of my birthday).
additional_notes: Used when someone does something for you as a birthday gift or gesture. It often appears with verbs like „schenken“ (to give as a gift), „mitbringen“ (to bring), „kaufen“ (to buy), or „gratulieren“ (to congratulate). Grammar: „mir“ is the dative pronoun meaning “to/for me,” and „zum Geburtstag“ means “for/on (the occasion of) my birthday.”
target_language_example: Sie hat mir zum Geburtstag ein Buch geschenkt.
native_language_example: She gave me a book for my birthday.

additional_notes: Used to say someone did something deliberately (not by accident). Often used in questions or accusations: "Machst du das mit Absicht?" = "Are you doing that on purpose?" The opposite is "aus Versehen" (by mistake).
target_language_example: Ich habe das nicht mit Absicht gemacht.
native_language_example: I didn’t do that on purpose.

additional_notes: Used to say something wasn’t an accident. Often you’ll also hear just “mit Absicht” (without “gemacht”), or the more formal adverb “absichtlich” (intentionally). Word order is flexible in sentences, e.g. “Er hat das mit Absicht gemacht.”
target_language_example: Ich habe das nicht mit Absicht gemacht.
native_language_example: I didn’t do that on purpose.

additional_notes: Used to say that an action was intentional (not an accident). Often said as a complaint or accusation. Very common in the shorter form „mit Absicht“ (e.g., „Das war mit Absicht.“).
target_language_example: Er hat das mit Absicht getan.
native_language_example: He did that on purpose.

meaning: by far; with some distance (figuratively: from a detached perspective).
additional_notes: Most often used with superlatives/comparisons to intensify: "mit Abstand der/die/das Beste" = "by far the best". It can also mean taking a step back mentally: "die Dinge mit Abstand sehen" = "to see things with distance / more objectively".
target_language_example: Er ist mit Abstand der schnellste Läufer in unserem Team.
native_language_example: He is by far the fastest runner on our team.

additional_notes: A literal, compositional phrase meaning that something is done by seeing/looking. Most commonly appears inside longer expressions (e.g., "mit eigenen Augen" = with your own eyes; "mit offenen Augen" = with your eyes open/attentively). On its own, it can sound a bit incomplete and is usually used with an implied modifier.
target_language_example: Man muss mit Augen sehen und mit dem Kopf denken.
native_language_example: You have to see with your eyes and think with your head.

meaning: in view of; with regard to.
additional_notes: A fairly formal prepositional phrase used to introduce the aspect/topic you’re considering. Common in writing and news/business German. Often followed by a noun phrase: „mit Blick auf + Akkusativ“ (e.g., „mit Blick auf die Zukunft“). Similar in meaning to „angesichts“ (in view of) or „hinsichtlich“ (regarding).
target_language_example: Mit Blick auf das Wetter nehmen wir eine Jacke mit.
native_language_example: In view of the weather, we’re bringing a jacket.

meaning: with a kind, caring heart; kind-hearted.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is warm or compassionate despite seeming rough or rude. Often appears in phrases like „(ein) X mit Herz“ (e.g., „ein Arsch mit Herz“), meaning “a jerk with a heart (of gold)”—insulting but humorous/affectionate in context.
target_language_example: Er wirkt manchmal hart, aber er ist ein Kerl mit Herz.
native_language_example: He sometimes seems tough, but he’s a guy with a kind heart.

meaning: with the help of; using (something) as help.
additional_notes: Often used as a prepositional phrase meaning you achieve something by using a tool, resource, or person. Common patterns: "mit Hilfe + Genitive" (more formal: "mit Hilfe dieses Buches") and "mit Hilfe von + Dative" (very common: "mit Hilfe von Wörtern").
target_language_example: Mit Hilfe einer App lerne ich jeden Tag Deutsch.
native_language_example: With the help of an app, I learn German every day.

additional_notes: Used with the dative pronoun „Ihnen“ to address one person formally (or a group). Common with verbs like „sprechen/reden/unterhalten“ (to talk), „Zeit verbringen“ (to spend time), „unzufrieden sein“ (to be unhappy with), and in questions like „Was hat sie mit Ihnen gemacht?“ (= what did she do to you/with you).
target_language_example: Könnte ich kurz mit Ihnen sprechen?
native_language_example: Could I speak with you briefly?

additional_notes: Used when addressing one person politely with "Sie/Ihnen" (e.g., a stranger, customer, teacher, or someone you don’t know well). "mit" + dative → "mit Ihnen". Often appears with modal verbs: "möchte/will/wollte ... mit Ihnen reden".
target_language_example: Entschuldigen Sie, ich muss kurz mit Ihnen reden.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I need to talk to you for a moment.

additional_notes: "mit" + dative means "with" in the sense of talking to someone. "Ihnen" is the formal/polite "you" (used with strangers, customers, officials, etc.), so this phrase is common in professional or polite situations. In casual situations, you would usually say "mit dir sprechen" (to speak with you, informal).
target_language_example: Könnte ich kurz mit Ihnen sprechen?
native_language_example: Could I speak with you briefly?

meaning: “to … with you” (formal), used before an infinitive with „zu“.
additional_notes: This chunk is typically followed by an infinitive (often at the end of the clause): „mit Ihnen zu sprechen/reden/arbeiten …“. „Ihnen“ is the formal dative form of „you“ (used with people you don’t address as „du“). Word order: the main verb often comes last in German infinitive phrases (e.g., „… mit Ihnen zu sprechen“).
target_language_example: Ich freue mich, mit Ihnen zu sprechen.
native_language_example: I’m happy to speak with you.

additional_notes: A polite/formal way to introduce what you want to talk to someone about. Commonly used with verbs like „reden“ and „sprechen“: „mit Ihnen über + [topic] reden/sprechen“. „Ihnen“ is the formal “you” (used with strangers, customers, officials, etc.).
target_language_example: Könnte ich kurz mit Ihnen über Ihren Termin sprechen?
native_language_example: Could I briefly speak with you about your appointment?

additional_notes: Used with the formal possessive "Ihr-" (for "Sie" = you). "Mit" takes the dative case, so before a masculine/neuter noun you get: mit Ihrem + noun (e.g., mit Ihrem Mann, mit Ihrem Hund). In the common question "Was ist mit ...?", it often means "What about ...?" / "What’s going on with ...?" (e.g., Was ist mit Ihrem Ausflug?).
target_language_example: Kommen Sie bitte mit Ihrem Ausweis zur Rezeption.
native_language_example: Please come to reception with your ID.

meaning: "with your" (formal; used with feminine singular nouns).
additional_notes: Used with the preposition "mit" (which takes the dative case). "Ihrer" is the dative feminine singular form of the formal possessive "Ihr" (= your, addressed as "Sie"). Common patterns include: "mit Ihrer Tochter/Frau" (with your daughter/wife), "mit Ihrer Hilfe" (with your help), and "Was ist mit Ihrer ...?" meaning "What about your ...?".
target_language_example: Kommen Sie mit Ihrer Kollegin zur Besprechung?
native_language_example: Are you coming to the meeting with your colleague?
