additional_notes: Used to say something is done effortlessly or with no difficulty. Often with verbs like lernen (learn), lösen (solve), gelingen (succeed), heben (lift), springen (jump). It can emphasize that something is surprisingly easy for someone.
target_language_example: Sie hat die Prüfung mit Leichtigkeit bestanden.
native_language_example: She passed the exam with ease.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has/uses a bow and arrow (as a weapon or for hunting/sport). Often describes the method or tool you use to do something: „Ich jage/fische/schieße mit Pfeil und Bogen.“
target_language_example: Er schießt mit Pfeil und Bogen auf die Zielscheibe.
native_language_example: He shoots at the target with a bow and arrow.

meaning: Literally: “with poker this weekend”; intended meaning: “playing poker this weekend / spending this weekend with poker.”
additional_notes: As written, this is non-standard/incorrect German. The correct spelling is **Wochenende** (not *Wochende*), and you typically wouldn’t phrase it with **mit** like this. More natural options are **Wir spielen dieses Wochenende Poker.** or **Dieses Wochenende spielen wir Poker.** If you want to keep the idea of “with,” you could say **Dieses Wochenende geht’s um Poker** (more idiomatic) or **Dieses Wochenende dreht sich alles um Poker** (“this weekend is all about poker”).
target_language_example: Ich bin am Samstag **mit Poker dieses Wochende** beschäftigt.
native_language_example: On Saturday I’m busy with poker this weekend.

additional_notes: Used to say a feeling, statement, or action is justified. Often placed before an adjective/verb phrase ("mit Recht stolz", "mit Recht verärgert"). Can also be used on its own: "Und das mit Recht." = "And rightly so."
target_language_example: Du bist mit Recht wütend.
native_language_example: You’re right to be angry.

additional_notes: Describes something whose surface is covered by snow. Common with sein/war: „Der Berg ist/war mit Schnee bedeckt.“ You can intensify it with words like „ganz/gänzlich“ (completely) or time phrases like „das ganze Jahr (über)“ (all year (round)).
target_language_example: Am Morgen war die ganze Stadt mit Schnee bedeckt.
native_language_example: In the morning, the whole city was covered with snow.

additional_notes: Used to say you are sure about something. Common patterns: „Ich weiß es mit Sicherheit.“ (= I know it for sure), „Ich kann (nicht) mit Sicherheit sagen, …“ (= I can(not) say for certain …), and at the start of a sentence „Mit Sicherheit …“ (= certainly / definitely …).
target_language_example: Mit Sicherheit wird sie heute anrufen.
native_language_example: She will definitely call today.

additional_notes: Describes someone looking like they are about to cry or already crying (from sadness, emotion, or even laughter). Often used to show the emotional state while doing something: "Sie sagte/stand/ging … mit Tränen in den Augen."
target_language_example: Er verabschiedete sich mit Tränen in den Augen.
native_language_example: He said goodbye with tears in his eyes.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "füllen" (to fill) to say what something is filled with. Common patterns: "etw. mit Wasser füllen" / "etw. mit Wasser auffüllen". In these sentences, the container is in the accusative (den Eimer, die Badewanne).
target_language_example: Kannst du die Flasche mit Wasser füllen?
native_language_example: Can you fill the bottle with water?

additional_notes: Used with verbs like „waschen“ (to wash) to say what you wash something with. Common in instructions/advice (often in the imperative): „Wasch dir die Hände mit Wasser und Seife.“
target_language_example: Bitte reinigen Sie die Stelle mit Wasser und Seife.
native_language_example: Please clean the area with soap and water.

additional_notes: Uses dative after "mit" ("allem" = dative of "alles"). Common in set phrases like "mit allem ausgestattet" (fully equipped) and "mit allem fertig sein/werden" (to be finished with everything / to get everything done).
target_language_example: Die Wohnung ist mit allem ausgestattet, was du brauchst.
native_language_example: The apartment is equipped with everything you need.

additional_notes: Uses the preposition **mit** (“with”) plus **allen** (dative plural of **alle**). Often refers to being together or interacting **with all people in a group** (*mit allen Familien, mit allen Klassenkameraden*), but it can also mean “with all” in a broader sense like “provided with all information” (*mit allen Informationen*).
target_language_example: Ich habe heute mit allen aus meinem Team gesprochen.
native_language_example: I talked with everyone on my team today.

meaning: by any means (possible); using every available way.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize determination: someone will try everything to achieve a goal. Often appears with verbs like „versuchen“ (to try), „kämpfen“ (to fight), „verhindern“ (to prevent). Depending on context, it can suggest extreme measures (not necessarily illegal, but very forceful).
target_language_example: Sie will mit allen Mitteln verhindern, dass er geht.
native_language_example: She wants to prevent him from leaving by any means necessary.

meaning: "in other words" (to rephrase or sum up).
additional_notes: Used to restate what you just said more clearly, more simply, or as a conclusion. Often placed at the start of a sentence, sometimes followed by a comma: "Mit anderen Worten, ..."
target_language_example: Mit anderen Worten: Wir müssen jetzt gehen.
native_language_example: In other words: We have to leave now.

additional_notes: Used to describe doing something using both hands at the same time (e.g., holding, catching, waving). After "mit" (with), the noun is in the dative: "beiden Händen" (plural).
target_language_example: Bitte nimm die Tasse mit beiden Händen.
native_language_example: Please take the cup with both hands.

meaning: with the naked eye (without any tools like binoculars or a microscope).
additional_notes: Used to say something can (or can’t) be seen without optical aids. Often used with "sichtbar" (visible) or "sehen" (to see): "mit bloßem Auge sichtbar/nicht sichtbar".
target_language_example: Die Details sind nur mit bloßem Auge schwer zu erkennen.
native_language_example: The details are hard to make out with the naked eye alone.

meaning: with bare hands (without tools, gloves, or weapons).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone does something using only their hands—often something difficult, dangerous, or impressive. Common in contexts like fighting (“bare-knuckle”), catching something, or killing an animal. Usually appears with "mit" + dative plural: "mit bloßen Händen".
target_language_example: Er hat die Kiste mit bloßen Händen aufgemacht.
native_language_example: He opened the box with his bare hands.

meaning: 'with your' (used with masculine/neuter nouns in the dative case).
additional_notes: Used after the preposition "mit" (with), which requires the dative: "mit deinem Bruder" = "with your brother". It also appears in the pattern "das mit deinem …" meaning "the thing about your …" / "what happened with your …".
target_language_example: Kannst du morgen mit deinem Auto kommen?
native_language_example: Can you come tomorrow with your car?

additional_notes: Uses the preposition "mit" (with) + dative: "deinem Vater" (your father). Common in contexts like doing something together (arbeiten/reden mit deinem Vater) or having a situation/conflict involving him (Ärger mit deinem Vater, das mit deinem Vater…).
target_language_example: Ich möchte heute Abend mit deinem Vater sprechen.
native_language_example: I want to talk with your father this evening.

meaning: “with your …” (used with plural nouns, or masculine/neuter nouns in the dative case).
additional_notes:
Used after the preposition **mit** (“with”), which always takes the **dative**. **deinen** is the dative form of **dein-** (“your”, informal singular). You use **mit deinen** before:
- **plural nouns**: *mit deinen Hausaufgaben* (with your homework)
- **masculine/neuter dative** (less common as a fixed phrase without the noun shown): e.g., *mit deinem Bruder* (with your brother), *mit deinem Kind* (with your child)
Contrast: **mit deiner** (feminine singular) and **mit deinem** (masc./neut. singular).
target_language_example: Spielst du oft mit deinen Freunden Fußball?
native_language_example: Do you often play soccer with your friends?

additional_notes: Used with verbs that take "mit" (which requires the dative case): *mit deinen Eltern*. Common patterns: **mit deinen Eltern sprechen** = talk to your parents; **Schwierigkeiten/Stress mit deinen Eltern haben** = have difficulties/stress with your parents; **mit deinen Eltern zusammenleben** = live together with your parents; **Wie verstehst du dich mit deinen Eltern?** = How do you get along with your parents? Also in **Was ist mit deinen Eltern?** it means “What’s going on with your parents?” / “What about your parents?”
target_language_example: Ich verstehe mich gut mit deinen Eltern.
native_language_example: I get along well with your parents.

additional_notes: Used to say you do something together with your friends. After the preposition **mit** (“with”), German uses the **dative** case, so it’s **deinen Freunden** (plural dative of *deine Freunde*). You can swap *deinen* for other possessives: *mit meinen Freunden* (with my friends), *mit seinen Freunden* (with his friends).
target_language_example: Ich gehe heute mit deinen Freunden ins Kino.
native_language_example: I’m going to the cinema today with your friends.

additional_notes: “Mit” always takes the dative case. “Deiner” is the dative form of “deine” and is used before a feminine singular noun (e.g., mit deiner Vermutung, mit deiner Geschichte). It’s used when speaking to one person informally (du), not formally (Sie).
target_language_example: Ich bin mit deiner Antwort nicht ganz zufrieden.
native_language_example: I’m not completely satisfied with your answer.

meaning: with your work (job/task you are doing).
additional_notes: Used with verbs and expressions that take **mit + dative** to show what you’re dealing with or working on. Common patterns: **fertig sein mit deiner Arbeit** (to be finished with your work), **zufrieden sein mit deiner Arbeit** (to be satisfied with your work), **weitermachen mit deiner Arbeit** (to continue with your work), **aufhören mit deiner Arbeit** (to stop working), **vorankommen mit deiner Arbeit** (to make progress with your work). Here **deiner** is dative feminine (die Arbeit).
target_language_example: Ich bin noch nicht mit deiner Arbeit fertig.
native_language_example: I’m not finished with your work yet.

additional_notes: Uses the preposition "mit" (+ dative: "deiner Frau") to talk about being together/doing something together with someone. In questions like "Alles in Ordnung mit deiner Frau?" or "Was ist mit deiner Frau?", it can also mean "what about your wife?/what’s going on with your wife?" depending on context.
target_language_example: Kommst du heute mit deiner Frau zur Party?
native_language_example: Are you coming to the party today with your wife?

additional_notes: Used when someone is talking to their mother (mit deiner Mutter reden) or making plans involving her (mit deiner Mutter verabredet sein). Also appears in questions like „Was wird mit deiner Mutter?“ meaning “What about your mother?/What will happen to your mother?” Note: „deiner“ is dative feminine of „dein“ because it follows „mit“ (a dative preposition).
target_language_example: Kannst du später noch mal mit deiner Mutter sprechen?
native_language_example: Can you talk to your mother again later?

additional_notes: A very common combination of mit + dem. mit always takes the dative case, and dem is the dative singular form of the definite article for masculine and neuter nouns. It often translates directly as "with the," but in some expressions English may use a different phrasing, such as mit dem Bus = "by bus" or mit dem Trinken aufhören = "stop drinking."
target_language_example: Ich spreche mit dem Lehrer nach dem Unterricht.
native_language_example: I'm talking with the teacher after class.

additional_notes: Used with the pattern **(mit + Dativ) fertig sein** to say you’re done with something: *mit der Arbeit fertig*, *mit den Hausaufgaben fertig*. Often appears in questions like **Bist du schon …?** (“Are you already …?”).
target_language_example: Ich bin noch nicht mit dem Abendessen fertig.
native_language_example: I’m not finished with dinner yet.

meaning: by car; in a car (using the car as transport).
additional_notes: Used with "mit" + dative to say how someone travels or is transported. Often answers "Wie?" (How?/By what means?). You can swap in other transport words: "mit dem Bus", "mit dem Fahrrad", "mit der Bahn".
target_language_example: Wir fahren morgen mit dem Auto nach Berlin.
native_language_example: We’re going to Berlin tomorrow by car.

additional_notes: Used to say you travel to a place by car. Structure: **mit + dative** (*mit dem Auto*) + **nach + place** (*nach Berlin/nach Japan*). **Nach** is commonly used with cities and countries (usually without an article).
target_language_example: Wir fahren morgen mit dem Auto nach Berlin.
native_language_example: We’re driving to Berlin tomorrow.

meaning: to go/commute to work by car.
additional_notes: Used to say how you travel to your workplace. Often with verbs like fahren (to drive/go), zur Arbeit fahren (drive to work), or zur Arbeit kommen (get/come to work). “Mit dem Auto” = by car; “zur Arbeit” = to work (zu + der Arbeit → zur Arbeit).
target_language_example: Morgen fahre ich nicht mit dem Auto zur Arbeit, sondern mit dem Bus.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’m not going to work by car, but by bus.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (e.g., fahren, kommen) to say how you travel. It’s the dative form after "mit" (mit + dem = dative): "mit dem Bus". Common in questions about directions: "Wie komme ich mit dem Bus ...?"
target_language_example: Wir fahren morgen mit dem Bus zur Arbeit.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re going to work by bus.

additional_notes: Used to say you travel using the bus as your means of transportation, followed by a destination with **nach** (typical for cities/countries without an article). Often used with verbs like **fahren** (to go/drive/ride) or **kommen** (to come/arrive).
target_language_example: Ich fahre morgen mit dem Bus nach Berlin.
native_language_example: I'm going to Berlin by bus tomorrow.

mit dem Bus oder mit dem Zug

target_language_multi_word_term: mit dem Bus oder mit dem Zug
additional_notes: Used to talk about how someone travels (their means of transportation). The pattern is **mit + dem** (dative) for masculine nouns like **der Bus** → **mit dem Bus**, **der Zug** → **mit dem Zug**. Often used in questions about how someone got somewhere or what they usually take.
target_language_example: Kommt ihr lieber mit dem Bus oder mit dem Zug?
native_language_example: Do you prefer to come by bus or by train?

meaning: “by bus to the …” (going to a place by bus).
additional_notes: Used to say how you travel to a destination. It combines: **mit dem Bus** = “by bus” + **zum** (= **zu dem**) which is used before masculine/neuter places in the dative (e.g., **zum Bahnhof**, **zum Hotel**). For feminine places you use **zur** (= **zu der**), e.g., **mit dem Bus zur Schule**.
target_language_example: Wir fahren mit dem Bus zum Bahnhof.
native_language_example: We’re going by bus to the train station.

meaning: to go to work by bus.
additional_notes: Used to say how someone commutes to work. Often used with verbs like „fahren“ (go/ride/drive) or „kommen“ (come). „mit dem Bus“ = by bus; „zur Arbeit“ = to work (to the workplace).
target_language_example: Ich fahre jeden Tag mit dem Bus zur Arbeit.
native_language_example: I go to work by bus every day.

additional_notes: Common way to say how you travel to school. Uses dative after "mit" (mit dem Bus). "zur" = "zu der" (= to the). Often used with "fahren" (to go/drive/ride).
target_language_example: Heute fahre ich mit dem Bus zur Schule.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to school by bus.

meaning: with the result; with the outcome.
additional_notes: Used to say how someone feels about the final result of something (e.g., a test, decision, work, match). Very common with feelings like zufrieden/unzufrieden (satisfied/unsatisfied) or glücklich (happy): „mit dem Ergebnis zufrieden/unzufrieden sein“.
target_language_example: Wir sind mit dem Ergebnis sehr zufrieden.
native_language_example: We are very satisfied with the result.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "sein" (to be): "Ich bin/war mit dem Ergebnis zufrieden." The thing you’re satisfied with comes after "mit" and is in the dative case (e.g., "mit dem Ergebnis"). You can swap in other nouns: "mit der Antwort zufrieden", "mit dem Service zufrieden".
target_language_example: Bist du mit dem Ergebnis zufrieden?
native_language_example: Are you satisfied with the result?

meaning: finished eating; done with the meal.
additional_notes: Used with **sein/werden** to say you are (or become) done eating: **Ich bin mit dem Essen fertig.** You can also use it with **bis** (“until”): **Warte(n) Sie, bis ich mit dem Essen fertig bin.** Common in everyday conversation; **fertig sein mit + dative** means “to be finished with” something.
target_language_example: Ich bin gleich mit dem Essen fertig.
native_language_example: I’ll be finished eating in a moment.

additional_notes: Used to say how someone travels (their means of transport). Often used with verbs of going/coming/traveling like „fahren“, „kommen“, „hingefahren“, „gefahren“. Literally „with the bicycle“, but in English it’s usually “by bike” or “on a bike.”
target_language_example: Heute fahre ich mit dem Fahrrad zur Arbeit.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to work by bike.

meaning: to go to school by bike.
additional_notes: Used to say how you travel to school. Pattern: „mit dem Fahrrad“ = by bike; „zur Schule“ = to school (zu + der). Often used with fahren/go verbs (fahren, gehen, kommen).
target_language_example: Wir fahren heute mit dem Fahrrad zur Schule.
native_language_example: Today we’re going to school by bike.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like „zeigen“ or „deuten“ to say you point at someone/something. Often appears as „mit dem Finger auf jemanden/etwas zeigen“ (= to point at someone/something), which can sound rude in many situations.
target_language_example: Bitte zeig nicht mit dem Finger auf mich.
native_language_example: Please don’t point your finger at me.

additional_notes: Used to say how you travel (means of transportation). You often see it with verbs like reisen (to travel) or fahren (to go/travel), and it contrasts with options like mit dem Zug (by train) or mit dem Auto (by car).
target_language_example: Wir reisen morgen mit dem Flugzeug nach Berlin.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re traveling to Berlin by plane.

additional_notes: Used to ask or say what someone did, plans to do, or what happened to a specific sum of money (often implying responsibility or suspicion). Common with verbs like „tun“ (do), „vorhaben“ (plan), and in questions like „Was ist mit dem Geld passiert?“ (What happened to the money?).
target_language_example: Was machst du mit dem Geld?
native_language_example: What are you doing with the money?

additional_notes: Means you are accompanied by the dog, especially when going out (often implying taking the dog for a walk): „mit dem Hund ausgehen / mit dem Hund rausgehen“. Uses dative after „mit“, so it’s „dem Hund“ (not „der Hund“). In questions like „Was ist mit dem Hund?“ it means “What’s wrong/what’s going on with the dog?”
target_language_example: Ich gehe heute Abend mit dem Hund spazieren.
native_language_example: I’m going for a walk with the dog this evening.

meaning: "with the boy" (sometimes: "about/with the boy" in questions like "Was ist mit dem Jungen ...?").
additional_notes: "Mit" takes the dative case, so "der Junge" becomes "dem Jungen". Common with verbs like "sprechen" (to talk) → "mit dem Jungen sprechen" (talk to/with the boy), and with "Schluss machen mit ..." (to break up with ...) → "Schluss machen mit dem Jungen". In "Was ist mit dem Jungen passiert?", it means "What happened to the boy?" / "What’s going on with the boy?"
target_language_example: Ich gehe heute mit dem Jungen ins Kino.
native_language_example: I’m going to the cinema with the boy today.

additional_notes: Used to describe actions done using the head, especially gestures like **mit dem Kopf schütteln** (to shake your head = ‘no’) and **mit dem Kopf nicken** (to nod your head = ‘yes’/agreement), or physical contact like **mit dem Kopf gegen etwas schlagen** (to hit your head against something). Often the verb makes the meaning clear.
target_language_example: Er schüttelt mit dem Kopf, weil er nicht einverstanden ist.
native_language_example: He shakes his head because he doesn’t agree.

meaning: with the knife; using a knife.
additional_notes: Uses "mit" + dative ("dem Messer") to say you do something using a knife as a tool, or to warn someone to be careful when handling it ("Vorsicht mit ...").
target_language_example: Schneid das Brot bitte mit dem Messer.
native_language_example: Please cut the bread with the knife.

additional_notes: Used when you compare something (a copy, translation, scan, etc.) to the original source/version. Often appears with verbs like „vergleichen“ (to compare) and „übereinstimmen“ (to match).
target_language_example: Bitte vergleichen Sie das Dokument mit dem Original.
native_language_example: Please compare the document with the original.

additional_notes: Used to say how you travel (your mode of transport). Often with verbs like fahren/kommen/sein: „mit dem Rad fahren“ (to ride a bike), „mit dem Rad kommen“ (to come by bike). Also appears as „mit dem Fahrrad“ (same meaning).
target_language_example: Heute komme ich mit dem Rad zur Arbeit.
native_language_example: Today I’m coming to work by bike.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like **aufhören** (to stop/quit) and **anfangen** (to start): **mit dem Rauchen aufhören** = “to quit smoking”, **mit dem Rauchen anfangen** = “to start smoking”. After **mit**, German uses the **dative**: *mit dem Rauchen*.
target_language_example: Ich will mit dem Rauchen aufhören.
native_language_example: I want to quit smoking.

additional_notes: Used with the verb „aufhören“ + „mit“ + dative to say you stopped doing an activity: „mit dem Rauchen aufhören“ (to stop/quit smoking). Often appears in the perfect tense: „Ich habe … aufgehört.“ In questions: „Haben Sie … aufgehört?“
target_language_example: Ich habe vor einem Jahr mit dem Rauchen aufgehört.
native_language_example: I quit smoking a year ago.

meaning: to quit smoking; to stop smoking.
additional_notes: Pattern: "mit" + dative + "aufhören" = to stop doing an activity (e.g., "mit dem/der + [noun/gerund-like noun] aufhören"). Here, "das Rauchen" is a nominalized verb meaning "smoking," so "mit dem Rauchen aufhören" literally corresponds to "to stop with the smoking" → "to quit smoking." Common forms: "Hör mit dem Rauchen auf!" (Quit smoking!) and "Ich will mit dem Rauchen aufhören." (I want to quit smoking).
target_language_example: Als Erstes musst du mit dem Rauchen aufhören.
native_language_example: First of all, you have to quit smoking.

additional_notes: Uses the verb phrase „mit etwas aufhören“ = “to stop (doing) something.” Here: „mit dem Rauchen“ (with smoking) + „aufhören“. Often appears after verbs like „versuchen“ (try), „beschließen“ (decide), „raten“ (advise), „gezwungen sein“ (be forced), or „sich bemühen“ (make an effort). In many sentences you’ll see it as „aufzuhören“ (zu + infinitive) at the end: „Ich versuche, mit dem Rauchen aufzuhören.“
target_language_example: Ich versuche gerade, mit dem Rauchen aufzuhören.
native_language_example: I’m trying to quit smoking right now.

additional_notes: Used to describe your body position: you are facing away from something behind you (a door, wall, camera, etc.). Grammar: "mit" + dative, so the article changes (zur = zu der; also common: "zum" = zu dem). Fixed pattern: "mit dem Rücken zur/zum + noun". Can also be used figuratively (e.g., "mit dem Rücken zur Wand" = backed into a corner / under pressure).
target_language_example: Sie saß mit dem Rücken zur Tür.
native_language_example: She sat with her back to the door.

meaning: "with this shit" / "with this crap" (used to complain and tell someone to stop).
additional_notes: Very rude/vulgar. Commonly used with commands like „Hör auf mit dem Scheiß!“ (Stop that shit!) or „Schluss mit dem Scheiß!“ (Enough of this shit!). It refers to whatever annoying behavior, talk, or situation is happening.
target_language_example: Hör auf mit dem Scheiß und konzentrier dich.
native_language_example: Stop that shit and focus.

additional_notes: Used with actions done using an animal’s tail, especially dogs (e.g., „mit dem Schwanz wedeln“ = to wag the tail). In German, „Schwanz“ can also be a vulgar word for a penis in other contexts, but in these examples it clearly means an animal’s tail.
target_language_example: Der Hund wedelt mit dem Schwanz, wenn er mich sieht.
native_language_example: The dog wags its tail when it sees me.

additional_notes: Used with "mit" + dative to say how you travel (means of transport). Common with verbs like "kommen" (to come), "fahren" (to go/drive/ride), and with time questions like "Wie lange braucht/dauert es …?".
target_language_example: Wir fahren heute mit dem Taxi nach Hause.
native_language_example: We’re going home by taxi today.

additional_notes: Used to say you use a taxi as your means of transport. It often answers the question „Wie fährst du?“ (How are you going?). You can also say „Wir fahren mit dem Taxi“ (We’re going by taxi).
target_language_example: Weil der letzte Bus schon weg war, musste ich mit dem Taxi fahren.
native_language_example: Because the last bus had already gone, I had to go by taxi.

additional_notes: Uses the separable verb **aufhören** (“to stop”). Common pattern: **mit + dative + infinitive** → *mit dem Trinken aufhören* (“stop drinking”). Often used after verbs like **jemandem raten** (to advise someone) or **jemanden dazu bringen** (to get someone to do something).
target_language_example: Er hat beschlossen, mit dem Trinken aufzuhören.
native_language_example: He decided to stop drinking.

meaning: by train; on the train (as a means of travel).
additional_notes: Used with verbs of travel/movement like fahren, kommen, ankommen, abfahren to say the mode of transport. Literally “with the train,” but in English it’s usually “by train.” Often contrasts with other options: mit dem Auto, mit dem Bus, etc.
target_language_example: Ich fahre morgen mit dem Zug nach Berlin.
native_language_example: I’m going to Berlin by train tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say you use the train as your means of transport. Often answers the question "Wie fährst du?" (How are you traveling?) or "Fährst du mit dem Zug?" (Are you going by train?). You can swap in other transport: "mit dem Bus/Auto/der U-Bahn fahren".
target_language_example: Wir sollten mit dem Zug fahren.
native_language_example: We should go by train.

additional_notes: Used to say you travel somewhere by train. "mit dem Zug" = "by train". "zur" is a contraction of "zu der" and is used before feminine nouns (or plural in some set phrases). The phrase is incomplete on its own—you need to add a destination, e.g. "zur Arbeit", "zur Schule", "zur Universität".
target_language_example: Ich fahre jeden Tag mit dem Zug zur Arbeit.
native_language_example: I go to work by train every day.

meaning: with all that money (i.e., using/doing something with it).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like „machen“ or „wollen“ to ask what someone did with a large amount of money or what they intended to do with it. Often appears in questions: „Was hat sie mit dem ganzen Geld gemacht?“ / „Was wollte er mit dem ganzen Geld?“ It can also show up in „Was ist mit dem ganzen Geld passiert …?“ (= What happened to all the money …?), which is about the money’s fate, not what someone used it for.
target_language_example: Was willst du mit dem ganzen Geld machen?
native_language_example: What do you want to do with all that money?

additional_notes: "Mit dem" is the contraction of "mit" + "dem" (dative). It’s used (1) after verbs that take "mit" to mean "with that/this" (often referring back to something already mentioned): "mit dem aufhören" = stop doing that; "mit dem auskommen" = manage with that/what we have; "Was ist los mit dem?" = what’s wrong with him/it. (2) In relative clauses meaning "with whom/which": "ein Freund, mit dem er sprechen konnte" = a friend (that) he could talk to. It can refer to a masculine person (him) or a neuter thing (it), depending on context.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir sagen, was ich mit dem machen soll?
native_language_example: Can you tell me what I should do with it?

additional_notes: Used when you refer back to a specific thing/action/content that’s described by a relative clause with "was" (e.g., "was Tom geschrieben hat" = "what Tom wrote"). "mit" takes the dative case, so you often see "mit dem" before the "was"-clause. Common with verbs like "einverstanden sein" (to agree), "aufhören" (to stop), or "tun" (to do) when you mean "with what someone did/said/wrote."
target_language_example: Ich bin nicht zufrieden mit dem, was er gesagt hat.
native_language_example: I’m not happy with what he said.

meaning: "with whom he talks" / "with whom he can talk" (depending on the verb form).
additional_notes: This is a relative-clause phrase. **mit** takes the dative case, so the relative pronoun is **dem** (dative, masculine/neuter: “whom/which”). In correct sentences you’ll usually see a conjugated verb like **mit dem er redet** (“with whom he talks”) or an extra verb that allows the infinitive **reden**, e.g. **mit dem er reden kann** (“with whom he can talk”).
target_language_example: Das ist der Mann, mit dem er reden kann.
native_language_example: That’s the man he can talk to.

meaning: "with which I" / "with that I" (introduces a relative clause).
additional_notes: Used in a relative clause to refer back to a masculine or neuter noun (e.g., der Zug, der Bus, das Auto). The preposition „mit“ always takes the dative case, so you get „mit dem“ (not *mit den* or *mit der*). Often translates as “that/which I (travel) with/on/in,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Das ist der Bus, mit dem ich jeden Tag zur Arbeit fahre.
native_language_example: That’s the bus that I take to work every day.

additional_notes: Used before plural nouns in the dative case after the preposition "mit". Often describes someone/something ("das Mädchen mit den langen Haaren" = "the girl with the long hair"), or is used in set expressions/commands like "Hoch mit den Armen!" ("Hands up!") and "Zur Hölle mit den …!" ("To hell with …!").
target_language_example: Ich gehe mit den Kindern in den Park.
native_language_example: I'm going to the park with the children.

meaning: (have) done with the books; (have) done to/with the books.
additional_notes: Used with **machen** in the pattern **Was hast/haben … mit + Dativ gemacht?** to ask what someone did with something (where they put it, how they used it, whether they sold/returned/threw it away, etc.). Here **mit den Büchern** is dative plural of **die Bücher**.
target_language_example: Was hast du mit den Büchern gemacht, die ich dir geliehen habe?
native_language_example: What did you do with the books I lent you?

additional_notes: Literally means you have/are carrying/using eggs (dative plural after „mit“). Common in instructions: „Misch den Reis mit den Eiern …“ (= mix the rice with the eggs). In some contexts, „Eier“ is also slang for testicles (“balls”), so phrases like „der mit den Eiern“ can be a crude/teasing way to refer to a man; the intended meaning depends on context.
target_language_example: Misch das Gemüse mit den Eiern in der Pfanne.
native_language_example: Mix the vegetables with the eggs in the pan.

additional_notes: Used with the adjective "zufrieden" + "mit" + dative to say you are satisfied with something. Here, "den Ergebnissen" is dative plural of "die Ergebnisse" (the results). You can swap in other nouns: "mit dem Service zufrieden", "mit meiner Note zufrieden".
target_language_example: Ich bin mit den Ergebnissen zufrieden.
native_language_example: I’m satisfied with the results.

additional_notes: Used to describe doing something using your fingers (often with a body movement), e.g. tapping/drumming on a surface (mit den Fingern auf den Tisch), snapping/cracking your fingers, feeling for something in the dark, or running your fingers through your hair. "den" is dative plural after "mit".
target_language_example: Sie klopfte ungeduldig mit den Fingern auf den Tisch.
native_language_example: She tapped her fingers impatiently on the table.

additional_notes: Used with "mit" + dative plural ("den Händen") to say you do something using your hands (instead of a tool), or to specify that something is done by hand. Often used with verbs like essen (eat), machen (do/make), schlagen (hit/beat), fühlen (feel). You can also say "mit der Hand" for one hand.
target_language_example: Ich esse das lieber mit den Händen.
native_language_example: I prefer to eat that with my hands.

additional_notes: Uses the preposition "mit" (with) + dative: "den Kindern" is dative plural of "die Kinder". Often describes doing something together with the children (e.g., Zeit mit den Kindern verbringen). In questions like "Was ist mit den Kindern?", it can mean "What about the children?" or "What’s wrong with the kids?" depending on context.
target_language_example: Am Wochenende gehe ich oft mit den Kindern in den Park.
native_language_example: On the weekend I often go to the park with the kids.

meaning: with the people; with those people.
additional_notes: "Mit" + dative plural "den Leuten". Used to mean being together with a group (going somewhere with them), talking/working with them, or doing something to/with them (often: treating people in a certain way: "Das kann man nicht mit den Leuten tun" = you can’t do that to people/them). Often followed by a clarifier like "vom Theater", "da hinten", "im Keller".
target_language_example: Ich gehe heute Abend mit den Leuten aus dem Kurs etwas trinken.
native_language_example: I’m going out for a drink tonight with the people from the class.

additional_notes: Used to describe or identify a person by a visible feature. It comes after the noun (“das Mädchen mit den langen Haaren”) or can stand on its own with an article/pronoun (“die mit den langen Haaren” = “the one with long hair”). The adjective ending changes with the case: langen (dative plural after mit + den).
target_language_example: Kennst du den Mann mit den langen Haaren?
native_language_example: Do you know the man with long hair?

additional_notes: Used with a plural noun to introduce a relative clause: "die Leute, mit denen ich arbeite" = "the people I work with." It’s the dative plural form of the relative pronoun after the preposition "mit". It can also stand alone to mean "with them/those people": "Mit denen habe ich nichts zu tun" = "I have nothing to do with them."
target_language_example: Das sind die Freunde, mit denen ich oft unterwegs bin.
native_language_example: Those are the friends I often go out with.

meaning: with whom/with which he (referring to a plural group).
additional_notes: Used in a relative clause. "mit" always takes the dative case, so the relative pronoun is "denen" (dative plural of "die"). It refers back to a plural noun like "die Leute" (the people) or "die Kollegen" (the colleagues): "die Leute, mit denen er …" = "the people (whom) he … with".
target_language_example: Das sind die Freunde, mit denen er jedes Wochenende Fußball spielt.
native_language_example: Those are the friends he plays soccer with every weekend.

additional_notes: Usually means 'with the'. After mit, German uses the dative case, so der here is the feminine singular dative form of die. It is used for accompaniment (mit der Familie), means or body parts (mit der rechten Hand, mit der Zunge), and descriptions like der Mann mit der grünen Jacke.
target_language_example: Sie spricht mit der Lehrerin.
native_language_example: She is speaking with the teacher.

additional_notes: Used to state someone’s purpose or planned goal. It’s typically followed by an infinitive with „zu“ (e.g., „mit der Absicht, ... zu ...“) or sometimes by a „dass“-clause. Formal/neutral in tone.
target_language_example: Sie kam mit der Absicht, sich zu entschuldigen.
native_language_example: She came with the intention of apologizing.

meaning: with the work; on the job/task.
additional_notes: Used with the preposition **mit** (+ dative), often to say you’re starting something (**mit der Arbeit anfangen**), helping with something (**mit der Arbeit helfen**), or giving an evaluation (**zufrieden mit der Arbeit sein**). **Arbeit** can mean a specific task/piece of work or your work/job, depending on context.
target_language_example: Ich bin sehr zufrieden mit der Arbeit.
native_language_example: I’m very satisfied with the work.

additional_notes: Used with **sein** (e.g., *ich bin, wir sind*) to say you’ve completed your work/task. You can add a time (*gegen Mitternacht*) or a limit (*für heute*) and you can also use it with **vorhaben/planen**: *Ich hatte vor, mit der Arbeit fertig zu sein* (“I planned to be done with work”).
target_language_example: Bist du schon mit der Arbeit fertig?
native_language_example: Are you done with work already?

additional_notes: Used to describe doing something using your hand(s), often meaning “manually” (not with a tool or machine): etwas mit der Hand machen. Common in set phrases like „mit der Hand auf etw. zeigen“ (to point at something) or „jdn. mit der Hand erwischen“ (to catch someone in the act / red-handed, e.g. „mit der Hand in der Keksdose“).
target_language_example: Ich habe den Teig mit der Hand geknetet.
native_language_example: I kneaded the dough by hand.

meaning: with the police; to/with the police (when speaking/dealing with them).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like sprechen (talk), Ärger haben/kriegen (get into trouble), or dealing/being involved with police. The case changes with gender/number: mit der Polizei (singular), mit den Polizisten (plural people). Also common: zur Polizei gehen = go to the police/police station; bei der Polizei = at/with the police (as an institution).
target_language_example: Wenn du etwas gesehen hast, solltest du mit der Polizei sprechen.
native_language_example: If you saw something, you should talk to the police.

meaning: by mail; via the post (postal service).
additional_notes: Used to say something is sent or delivered using the postal service. Common with verbs like „schicken“ (to send) or „kommen“ (to arrive): „mit der Post schicken“ = send by mail; „mit der Post kommen“ = arrive in the mail / come with the mail delivery.
target_language_example: Ich schicke dir die Unterlagen mit der Post.
native_language_example: I’ll send you the documents by mail.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of travel/transport (especially **fahren**) to say how you get somewhere: **mit der U-Bahn** = using the subway. **U-Bahn** is feminine, so it’s **mit der U-Bahn** (dative after **mit**). Often followed by a destination with **zu/nach/in**: *mit der U-Bahn zur Schule / in die Stadt*.
target_language_example: Wir fahren mit der U-Bahn zum Museum.
native_language_example: We’re taking the subway to the museum.

meaning: over time; as time goes by.
additional_notes: Used to say that something changes gradually as time passes (“with time”). In the phrase “Geh mit der Zeit!”, it means “keep up with the times” (don’t be old-fashioned).
target_language_example: Mit der Zeit gewöhnt man sich daran.
native_language_example: Over time, you get used to it.

additional_notes: Used to say you do something using your tongue (e.g., touching/feeling something in your mouth, licking, or kissing). The noun is feminine: die Zunge, so it becomes der Zunge after mit (dative).
target_language_example: Er leckt das Eis mit der Zunge.
native_language_example: He licks the ice cream with his tongue.

additional_notes: Used to say you do an action using your left hand, often with verbs like schreiben (to write), essen (to eat), halten (to hold), etc. Note: In a slightly different form, “etwas mit der linken Hand machen” can also mean doing something casually/without much effort, but in many contexts it’s simply literal.
target_language_example: Ich esse mit der linken Hand, weil meine rechte Hand verletzt ist.
native_language_example: I eat with my left hand because my right hand is injured.

meaning: "with this" (using/along with this; about what to do with this).
additional_notes: „Mit diesem …“ uses the preposition „mit“ + dative. „diesem“ is the dative form of „dieser/dieses“ for masculine or neuter nouns (e.g., „mit diesem Geld“, „mit diesem Auto“). It’s used for: (1) using something as a tool/means: „mit diesem Taschentuch …“; (2) dealing with something: „Was machst du mit diesem Geld?“; (3) describing something that goes (or clashes) with something else: „… beißt sich mit diesem …“. For feminine nouns you’d say „mit dieser …“.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir mit diesem Koffer helfen?
native_language_example: Can you help me with this suitcase?

meaning: 'with this' / 'with that' (referring to a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used with the preposition "mit" + dative. "dieser" is the dative form of "diese" (this/that) for feminine singular nouns (e.g., mit dieser Frau, mit dieser Situation). Often used for dealing/working with something ("mit dieser Situation umgehen"), having problems with something ("Probleme mit dieser Frage"), or asking what happened to/what’s wrong with something ("Was ist mit dieser ... los?").
target_language_example: Ich kann mit dieser Aufgabe nicht anfangen.
native_language_example: I can’t start with this task.

additional_notes: Usually used with **sein** or **werden**: **mit dieser Arbeit fertig sein** = to be done; **mit dieser Arbeit fertig werden** = to get/finish it. Often appears with deadlines: **bis Monatsende / um fünf Uhr**.
target_language_example: Ich bin endlich mit dieser Arbeit fertig und kann jetzt Feierabend machen.
native_language_example: I’m finally done with this work and can call it a day now.

additional_notes: Used to mean being together with, talking to, or interacting with the person addressed. mit always takes the dative case, so du becomes dir here. This is for one person addressed informally; compare mit Ihnen (formal) and mit euch (informal plural).
target_language_example: Ich spreche gern mit dir.
native_language_example: I like talking with you.

additional_notes: Usually used with a verb like **sein/stehen** (to be connected/in contact) or **bleiben** (to stay in contact), or **sich setzen** (to get in touch): *mit dir in Verbindung bleiben*, *mit dir in Verbindung stehen*, *mich mit dir in Verbindung setzen*.
target_language_example: Ich möchte mit dir in Verbindung bleiben.
native_language_example: I'd like to stay in touch with you.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of motion (e.g., fahren, gehen, kommen) to say you’re going somewhere together. "mit dir" = "with you" (dative), and "nach" is commonly used for going to cities and many countries without an article (e.g., nach Boston, nach Deutschland).
target_language_example: Ich möchte mit dir nach Boston gehen.
native_language_example: I’d like to go to Boston with you.

meaning: “(I) talk to you” / “(I’m) speaking to you.”
additional_notes: From the verb **reden** (“to talk/speak”). In German you often use **mit + Dativ** with people: **mit dir reden** = “to talk to you.” Common in reminders/scolding: **Antworte mir, wenn ich mit dir rede!** (“Answer me when I’m talking to you!”). Word order can change for emphasis: **Mit dir rede ich gar nicht** = “I’m not talking to you at all.”
target_language_example: Warum hörst du nicht zu, wenn ich mit dir rede?
native_language_example: Why don’t you listen when I’m talking to you?

meaning: to talk to you (often: to have a serious talk with you).
additional_notes: Literally “to talk with you.” Common with modal verbs like "müssen" (need to), "möchten" (would like to), and "dürfen" (may I). Often used when you want a private or important conversation: "Ich muss mit dir reden" = “We need to talk.”
target_language_example: Kann ich kurz mit dir reden?
native_language_example: Can I talk to you for a moment?

additional_notes: Present tense, 3rd person singular of "mit dir reden" (to talk to you). Used after subjects like "er/sie" or nouns: "Er redet mit dir." Often implies someone is (or isn’t) communicating with you; "nicht mehr mit dir redet" = "doesn’t talk to you anymore." Similar: "mit dir spricht" (more neutral/formal).
target_language_example: Ich begreife nicht, wieso er nicht mit dir redet.
native_language_example: I don’t understand why he isn’t talking to you.

meaning: to talk to you; to speak with you.
additional_notes: Common, polite way to ask for a conversation with one person. Often used with a time word like kurz/einmal kurz (“briefly”) or a place like draußen (“outside”). In “unter vier Augen”, it means “in private / one-on-one.”
target_language_example: Kann ich später kurz mit dir sprechen?
native_language_example: Can I talk to you briefly later?

additional_notes: This is part of the pattern **mit + Person (dative) + zu + infinitive**, used to say you do an action together with someone: **mit dir zu teilen / zu konkurrieren / zu besichtigen / zu telefonieren**. **dir** is the dative form of **du** after **mit**.
target_language_example: Ich freue mich, mit dir zu reden.
native_language_example: I’m happy to talk with you.

meaning: to talk to you / to speak with you.
additional_notes: Uses "mit" + dative (dir = to/with you). Often appears after verbs like "genießen" (enjoy), "lieben" (love), "Zeit haben" (have time), "verbieten" (forbid) with "zu" + infinitive: "Zeit haben, mit dir zu reden". You can change the pronoun: "mit Ihnen zu reden" (formal), "mit ihm/ihr/uns/euch zu reden".
target_language_example: Es war schön, mit dir zu reden.
native_language_example: It was nice talking to you.

meaning: (to have) seen (it) with one’s own eyes; witnessed firsthand.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you personally witnessed something directly (not just heard about it). Often appears with verbs like „sehen“ or „miterleben“ and can be used in statements or questions: „Hast du das mit eigenen Augen gesehen?“
target_language_example: Ich kann es kaum glauben – ich habe es mit eigenen Augen gesehen.
native_language_example: I can hardly believe it—I saw it with my own eyes.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to say that an outcome would be (or would have been) possible if there had been slightly more of something (e.g., effort, patience, caution). Very common with conditional forms like „könnte“, „hättest … geschafft“, „wäre … gewesen“.
target_language_example: Mit ein bisschen mehr Zeit könnten wir das heute noch fertig machen.
native_language_example: With a little more time, we could still finish that today.

additional_notes: Usually means "with a/an." "Mit" always takes the dative case, and "einem" is the dative form of "ein" for masculine and neuter nouns. Depending on context, it can also be understood as "by/using a" (for example, with a tool or vehicle).
target_language_example: Sie spricht mit einem Lehrer.
native_language_example: She is speaking with a teacher.

additional_notes: Used to say you do something together with a (male) friend. In German, “Freund” can mean either “friend” or “boyfriend” depending on context; for a clear “friend” (not romantic), people often say “mit einem Freund von mir” or “mit einem guten Freund.” With verbs like “sich treffen,” “mit” is very common: “sich mit einem Freund treffen” = “to meet up with a friend.”
target_language_example: Am Wochenende koche ich mit einem Freund.
native_language_example: On the weekend I’m cooking with a friend.

additional_notes: Used with the separable verb **abtrocknen** (“to dry off”). In sentences like **Ich trockne mir das Gesicht mit einem Handtuch ab**, you’ll often see a reflexive/dative pronoun (**mir/dir/sich**) showing who benefits (“I dry my face”). Word order: **trocknen ... ab** (the **ab** goes to the end in main clauses/commands).
target_language_example: Nach dem Duschen trockne ich mir die Haare mit einem Handtuch ab.
native_language_example: After showering, I dry my hair with a towel.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like beginnen (to begin), begrüßen (to greet), sich verabschieden (to say goodbye), überraschen (to surprise) to say you do something by giving a kiss. Often implies a single kiss (e.g., on the cheek), depending on context.
target_language_example: Sie verabschiedete sich mit einem Kuss.
native_language_example: She said goodbye with a kiss.

additional_notes: Used to describe the manner/tone of an action (thanking, greeting, teasing, accepting something). It often implies friendliness, warmth, or even calm acceptance (sometimes ‘taking it in stride’).
target_language_example: Er entschuldigte sich mit einem Lächeln.
native_language_example: He apologized with a smile.

additional_notes: Used to describe an abrupt change in a situation or feeling ("suddenly"), or doing something in one single action/step ("all at once", "in one go"). Often appears at the beginning of a sentence: "Mit einem Mal ...".
target_language_example: Mit einem Mal wurde es ganz still im Raum.
native_language_example: All of a sudden it became completely quiet in the room.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition **mit** (“with”), which always takes the **dative** case: **ein Mann** → **mit einem Mann**. The exact idea depends on the verb: **sprechen mit einem Mann** (talk to/with a man), **sich treffen mit einem Mann** (meet up with a man), **mit einem Mann zusammen sein** (be in a relationship / be together with a man), **mit einem Mann ausgehen** (go out/date a man).
target_language_example: Sie war lange mit einem Mann zusammen, den sie in Berlin kennengelernt hat.
native_language_example: She was together for a long time with a man she met in Berlin.

meaning: with a knife; using a knife.
additional_notes: Used with verbs to say an action is done using a knife (mit + dative): z.B. schneiden (cut), verletzen (injure), bedrohen (threaten). It can also describe having/carrying a knife: mit einem Messer in der Hand (with a knife in your hand), or a state: mit einem Messer im Rücken (with a knife in his back).
target_language_example: Kannst du das Brot mit einem Messer schneiden?
native_language_example: Can you cut the bread with a knife?

meaning: "with a knife into" (introducing where something/someone is stabbed/cut).
additional_notes: Usually used with an action verb (e.g., „stechen“ = to stab, „schneiden“ = to cut). After „in“ it typically takes the accusative to show direction/into (e.g., „in den Arm“, „in die Hand“, „in den Bauch“). On its own, the phrase is incomplete—you normally need a verb and a noun after „in“.
target_language_example: Er hat mit einem Messer in den Apfel geschnitten.
native_language_example: He cut into the apple with a knife.

additional_notes: Uses the preposition **mit** (“with”) + **dative**: **ein** → **einem** (because *Mädchen* is neuter: **das Mädchen**). Often used for doing something together or interacting (talking, dancing, going somewhere). In some contexts (e.g., **mit einem Mädchen schlafen**) it means “to sleep with a girl” (have sex with a girl).
target_language_example: Er geht morgen mit einem Mädchen ins Kino.
native_language_example: He’s going to the movies with a girl tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say you do an action using a cloth (Tuch), often for wiping/cleaning: „(ab)wischen“, „wischen“, „sich abwischen“. With „mit“ + dative: „mit einem Tuch“ (not *mit ein Tuch*).
target_language_example: Bitte wischen Sie die Arbeitsfläche mit einem Tuch ab.
native_language_example: Please wipe the work surface with a cloth.

meaning: "with a big/large …" (followed by a masculine/neuter noun).
additional_notes: Used with the preposition **mit** (+ dative) to describe something that comes along with something else: *mit einem großen Frühstück / Garten / Knall*. It’s an incomplete chunk—you normally add a noun after it. **groß** means “big/large,” not English “gross” (disgusting).
target_language_example: Er kam mit einem großen Koffer an.
native_language_example: He arrived with a big suitcase.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine noun in the dative case (e.g., after the preposition "mit" = "with"). Often describes the means/tool used ("with one hand") or being together/associated with someone/something. The noun is usually stated right after: "mit einer Hand", "mit einer Frau". In sentence 2, "mit einer anderen" means "to/with another (woman)"—"anderen" is the declined form of "andere" (another) and implies a feminine person from context.
target_language_example: Ich schreibe mit einer blauen Kugelschreiber-Mine.
native_language_example: I write with a blue ballpoint-pen refill.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is staying in bed because they have a cold. Often appears with verbs like „liegen“ (to be lying) or „bleiben“ (to stay): „Er liegt/bleibt mit einer Erkältung im Bett.“
target_language_example: Ich liege seit zwei Tagen mit einer Erkältung im Bett.
native_language_example: I've been in bed with a cold for two days.

additional_notes:
Literally just "with a woman" (mit + dative). In context it often refers to romantic or sexual involvement, depending on the verb/phrase: 
- "mit einer Frau zusammen sein" = to be in a relationship with a woman 
- "mit einer Frau schlafen" / "mit einer Frau im Bett sein" = to sleep with a woman (have sex).
target_language_example: Er ist seit zwei Jahren mit einer Frau zusammen.
native_language_example: He has been in a relationship with a woman for two years.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine noun (often omitted if clear): mit einer anderen Frau/Katze/Tätigkeit = with another woman/cat/activity. In relationship contexts it can imply "with another woman" (cheating). It can also mean "with a different/other" option or activity.
target_language_example: Ich habe ihn mit einer anderen Frau im Restaurant gesehen.
native_language_example: I saw him with another woman at the restaurant.

additional_notes: Used with more than one person in informal situations. "euch" is the plural informal form of "you," and after "mit" it is in the dative case. The formal equivalent is "mit Ihnen."
target_language_example: Ich gehe morgen mit euch ins Kino.
native_language_example: I'm going to the cinema with you all tomorrow.

meaning: with both of you (talking to two people).
additional_notes: Used when addressing exactly two people with informal/plural “ihr/euch” (not formal “Sie”). After the preposition “mit” (with), German uses the dative case, so you say “mit euch”. “beiden” emphasizes that you mean both people.
target_language_example: Ich gehe heute Abend mit euch beiden ins Kino.
native_language_example: I’m going to the movies with both of you tonight.

additional_notes: Used when speaking to more than one person you address as "ihr/euch" (friends, family, children). Often appears with modal verbs like „wollen“ (want) or „sollen“ (should), or in questions: „Warum sollte ich mit euch reden?“ = “Why should I talk to you (all)?”
target_language_example: Können wir später mit euch reden?
native_language_example: Can we talk to you all later?

additional_notes: Used when addressing more than one person ("euch" = "you" plural, dative after "mit"). Common in requests or when someone needs to discuss something, often with a serious tone: "Ich muss mit euch sprechen." You’ll also see it with modal verbs and an infinitive: "Ich hoffe, bald mit euch sprechen zu können."
target_language_example: Können wir nach dem Unterricht kurz mit euch sprechen?
native_language_example: Can we talk with you for a moment after class?

additional_notes: Literal meaning: doing something while your eyes are closed. Often used figuratively to mean you can do it easily, from habit, or without thinking much (like “I could do that in my sleep”). Can also simply describe someone lying/sitting/standing with their eyes closed.
target_language_example: Den Weg nach Hause finde ich mit geschlossenen Augen.
native_language_example: I can find the way home with my eyes closed.

additional_notes: Used to say someone does something without looking, and it’s usually followed by a target/object with **auf** (e.g., *auf das Ziel*, *auf ihn*). With **auf** meaning “at/toward,” it typically takes the accusative (e.g., *auf das Ziel*).
target_language_example: Er wirft mit geschlossenen Augen auf das Ziel.
native_language_example: He throws at the target with his eyes closed.

additional_notes: A very common combination. "mit" means "with" and always takes the dative case, so "er" becomes "ihm" here. It is used for doing something together with a male person or talking/interacting with him: "mit ihm sprechen" = "speak with him," "mit ihm gehen" = "go with him."
target_language_example: Ich möchte mit ihm ins Kino gehen.
native_language_example: I want to go to the cinema with him.

meaning: to go out with him (date him).
additional_notes: Used for dating/going on a date with a specific person. Built from: mit + dative pronoun (mit ihm/mit ihr/mit mir) + ausgehen. Often appears with verbs like bitten/fragen/versuchen and in infinitive constructions: „jemanden bitten, mit ihm auszugehen“.
target_language_example: Hat er dich gebeten, mit ihm auszugehen?
native_language_example: Did he ask you to go out with him?

meaning: (have) spoken/talked with him; (have) talked to him.
additional_notes: Used with the verb „sprechen“ in the perfect tense: „Ich habe mit ihm gesprochen“ = “I spoke/I have spoken with him.” „mit“ takes the dative, so it’s „mit ihm“ (not „mit ihn“). Common in questions: „Hast du (schon) mit ihm gesprochen?“
target_language_example: Ich habe schon mit ihm gesprochen, aber er ist sich noch nicht sicher.
native_language_example: I already talked to him, but he’s still not sure.

meaning: to talk to him; to speak with him.
additional_notes: "reden" means "to talk/speak". "mit" + dative means "with/to" someone. "ihm" is the dative form of "er" (he). Often used with "müssen" (must/have to) or "sollten" (should) to say you need to have a conversation with him, often about something important.
target_language_example: Ich muss morgen mit ihm reden.
native_language_example: I have to talk to him tomorrow.

meaning: to talk to him / speak with him.
additional_notes: Used when you want to communicate directly with a male person. "mit" takes the dative, so "er" becomes "ihm". Common with modal verbs like "müssen" (must/have to) and "wollen" (want). Word order can change in sentences (e.g., "Ich will jetzt mit ihm sprechen").
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte kurz mit ihm sprechen?
native_language_example: Can you please talk to him for a moment?

additional_notes: Usually used with the reflexive verb: **sich mit ihm treffen** = “to meet with him / meet up with him.” You conjugate **sich** to match the subject: **ich treffe mich**, **du triffst dich**, **wir treffen uns**, **ihr trefft euch**, **Sie treffen sich**. Often used for plans/appointments; with **weiter** it can mean “keep meeting him / continue seeing him.”
target_language_example: Ich muss mich unbedingt mit ihm treffen.
native_language_example: I absolutely have to meet up with him.

additional_notes: This is not usually a complete phrase by itself; it’s the start of a "zu + infinitive" construction: "mit ihm zu + Verb" (e.g., "mit ihm zu sprechen" = “to talk with him”). "Mit" always takes the dative, so "ihm" = “him” (dative).
target_language_example: Ich habe keine Lust, mit ihm zu sprechen.
native_language_example: I don't feel like talking to him.

meaning: together with him; (with sein) in a relationship with him.
additional_notes: Literally means “with him together.” With verbs like wohnen/laufen/arbeiten it simply means doing something together with him (e.g., „mit ihm zusammen wohnen“ = live together with him). With „(mit jemandem) zusammen sein“ it often means “to be together (as a couple),” i.e., dating/in a relationship.
target_language_example: Ich bin seit einem Jahr mit ihm zusammen.
native_language_example: I've been with him for a year.

additional_notes: "Mit" is followed by the dative case, so the pronoun becomes "ihnen". It can mean (1) "with them" (referring to other people/things) or (2) "with you" when speaking politely to more than one person (formal "Sie" → dative "Ihnen"). Used for being together with someone (sich mit ihnen freuen) or communicating (mit ihnen reden).
target_language_example: Kannst du mit ihnen kurz sprechen?
native_language_example: Can you talk to them briefly?

meaning: to talk to them (formal: to you all / to them).
additional_notes: "mit" + dative pronoun. "Ihnen" (capital I) is the formal "you" (singular or plural) in German, but it can also mean "to them" depending on context—often made clear by who is being addressed. Used for having a conversation, often in a direct or serious way (e.g., "Ich muss mit Ihnen reden").
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, könnte ich kurz mit Ihnen reden?
native_language_example: Excuse me, could I talk to you for a moment?

additional_notes: A very common combination of the preposition mit ('with') and the pronoun ihr. After mit, German uses the dative case, so ihr here means 'her'. It can describe being together with her, doing something alongside her, or being in a relationship with her depending on the context.
target_language_example: Ich möchte mit ihr sprechen.
native_language_example: I want to speak with her.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "sprechen" + "mit" (to talk with someone). "Ihr" is the dative form of "sie" (= her). Often appears in the perfect tense with "haben": "Ich habe mit ihr gesprochen." You can also ask questions: "Hast du mit ihr gesprochen?"
target_language_example: Ich habe gestern Abend mit ihr gesprochen.
native_language_example: I spoke with her yesterday evening.

meaning: to talk to her; to speak with her.
additional_notes: "mit" takes the dative, so "ihr" = "to/with her" (not "sie"). Very common with "reden" or "sprechen": "mit ihr reden/sprechen". Used for both a simple conversation and for addressing an issue with her (e.g., 'you should talk to her').
target_language_example: Ich muss dringend mit ihr reden.
native_language_example: I urgently need to talk to her.

additional_notes: Used when you want to talk to a female person (“ihr” = “her/to her”). The verb “sprechen” often goes with “mit” (+ dative) to mean “talk with someone”: mit ihm sprechen (with him), mit Ihnen sprechen (with you, formal), mit euch sprechen (with you all, informal). In requests it’s common in questions like “Kann ich …?” and formal “Können Sie …?”.
target_language_example: Ich möchte kurz mit ihr sprechen.
native_language_example: I'd like to speak with her briefly.

meaning: together with her; (sometimes) with her / dating her.
additional_notes: Often means being physically together with a woman/girl (accompanying her, being in the same place): „Ich war mit ihr zusammen am Fluss.“ In some contexts, especially with „sein“ (e.g., „mit ihr zusammen sein“), it can also mean being in a romantic relationship with her.
target_language_example: Ich gehe mit ihr zusammen nach Hause.
native_language_example: I’m walking home with her.

meaning: with her / with their / with your (formal).
additional_notes: "Mit" always takes the dative case. "Ihrem" is the dative form used with masculine or neuter nouns (der/das): z.B. mit ihrem Hund (der Hund), mit ihrem Auto (das Auto). It can mean "her", "their", or "your" (formal), depending on context. For feminine nouns you use "mit ihrer ..." (e.g., mit ihrer Schwester).
target_language_example: Ich spreche gerade mit ihrem Chef.
native_language_example: I’m speaking with her/their/your (formal) boss right now.

meaning: to go for a walk with her dog; to walk her dog.
additional_notes: Usually used with the verb gehen: „mit ihrem Hund spazieren gehen“. After „mit“, the noun is in the dative: „mit ihrem Hund“ (not *mit ihr Hund*). You can swap the possessive to match the person: „mit meinem/deinem/seinem/unserem Hund spazieren (gehen)“.
target_language_example: Sie geht am Abend mit ihrem Hund spazieren.
native_language_example: In the evening, she goes for a walk with her dog.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition "mit" (with), which always takes the dative case: "ihr Vater" → "mit ihrem Vater". "Ihrem" can also mean "their" or formal "your" depending on context, but in these examples it means "her" (referring to "sie").
target_language_example: Am Wochenende fährt sie mit ihrem Vater in die Stadt.
native_language_example: On the weekend she goes to the city with her father.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition "mit" (with), which always takes the dative case. "ihren" is the dative plural form of the possessive pronoun "ihr-" and can mean either "her" (of sie = she) or "their" (of sie = they), depending on context. It’s used before a plural noun: "mit ihren Katzen" = "with her cats".
target_language_example: Er kommt heute mit ihren Freunden.
native_language_example: He’s coming today with her friends.

additional_notes: "mit" (with) takes the dative case, so you say: mit + ihren Eltern. "ihren" here means "her" because the subject is "sie" (= she). If the subject is plural ("sie" = they), it can also mean "with their parents." You can swap the possessive: mit meinen/deinen/seinen/unseren Eltern.
target_language_example: Am Wochenende isst sie oft mit ihren Eltern zu Abend.
native_language_example: On the weekend she often eats dinner with her parents.

additional_notes: "mit" + dative. "ihren" is the dative plural form of "ihr" (her/their) here, and "Freunden" is plural dative of "Freund". Used to say someone is together with her friends (e.g., going out, meeting up, sitting somewhere).
target_language_example: Am Wochenende geht sie oft mit ihren Freunden ins Kino.
native_language_example: On weekends, she often goes to the movies with her friends.

additional_notes: "Mit" means "with" and takes the dative case; "ihren" is the dative plural form of "ihr" (= her), and "Freundinnen" is plural for female friends. Used when talking about a woman being together with her group of (female) friends. If the friends are mixed or you don’t want to specify gender, you can use "mit ihren Freunden" (can mean male friends or friends in general) or "mit ihren Freund*innen" (gender-inclusive writing).
target_language_example: Sie ist heute Abend mit ihren Freundinnen im Kino.
native_language_example: She’s at the movies tonight with her (female) friends.

meaning: with her children / with their children
additional_notes: Used with the preposition "mit" (with), which takes the dative case. "ihren" is the dative plural form of the possessive pronoun and can mean "her" or "their" depending on who is being talked about (e.g., "Maria" → her; "Tom und Maria" → their). "Kindern" is plural dative of "Kinder".
target_language_example: Er kommt heute mit ihren Kindern vorbei.
native_language_example: He’s stopping by today with her/their children.

additional_notes: Used after the preposition "mit" (with), which takes the dative case. "ihrer" refers to "her" and agrees with a feminine singular noun (e.g., "mit ihrer Gitarre" = with her guitar). Often appears as "mit ihrem" (masc./neut.), "mit seinen" etc., depending on the noun.
target_language_example: Er ist mit ihrer Entscheidung einverstanden.
native_language_example: He agrees with her decision.

additional_notes: Uses **mit** (“with”), which takes the **dative** case. **ihrer** is the dative form of “her” for a feminine noun (die Schwester). Common for doing something together (*spielen/gehen/reden mit ihrer Schwester*) or in phrases like **mit … verwechselt werden** (“to be confused with …”).
target_language_example: Am Wochenende geht sie mit ihrer Schwester ins Kino.
native_language_example: On the weekend she goes to the movies with her sister.

additional_notes: Used with a noun in the dative case: mit jedem Tag (each day), mit jedem Atemzug (with every breath). Very common in expressions showing something changes over time: „mit jedem Tag …“ = „each day … / more and more“. It can also mean “with anyone/everyone” when the noun is implied: „wie mit jedem anderen“ = “like with anyone else.”
target_language_example: Mit jedem Tag wird es besser.
native_language_example: It gets better each day.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re doing something with a different person than expected, or to tell someone to talk/do it with another person. After "mit" you use the dative, so it’s "mit jemand anderem" (not *mit jemand anderer*). Common with "verwechseln" (to mix up): "jemanden mit jemand anderem verwechseln" = to mistake someone for someone else.
target_language_example: Ich will darüber nicht reden—sprich bitte mit jemand anderem.
native_language_example: I don’t want to talk about it—please talk to someone else.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition **mit** + **dative** to say you do something together/with another person. **jemandem** is the dative form of **jemand** (“someone”). Common with verbs like **sprechen/reden mit jemandem** (talk to someone), **sich treffen mit jemandem** (meet up with someone), **ausgehen mit jemandem** (go out with someone).
target_language_example: Ich möchte nicht allein sein, ich will mit jemandem reden.
native_language_example: I don’t want to be alone; I want to talk to someone.

additional_notes: "mit" takes the dative case: mit jemandem (with someone), mit meiner Mutter (with my mother). Commonly used for talking to someone (often closer to "talk to" in English). You can also say "mit jemandem reden" (very similar).
target_language_example: Ich möchte mit jemandem sprechen.
native_language_example: I’d like to speak with someone.

additional_notes: Used when someone comes/goes/returns without bringing anything (e.g., no gift, no results). Often figurative: you tried, but you didn’t get/achieve anything. Common with verbs like „kommen“, „gehen“, „zurückkommen/zurückgehen“, or „dastehen“.
target_language_example: Ich kann nicht mit leeren Händen zu der Party kommen.
native_language_example: I can’t come to the party empty-handed.

meaning: "with my" (used with masculine/neuter singular nouns in the dative case).
additional_notes: Used after the preposition „mit“ (with), which always takes the dative. „meinem“ is the dative form of „mein“ for masculine or neuter singular nouns: mit meinem Bruder (brother), mit meinem Auto (car). For feminine use „mit meiner …“ (mit meiner Mutter), and for plural use „mit meinen …“ (mit meinen Freunden). Often used to talk about being together with someone, being satisfied with something, making plans, or speaking with someone.
target_language_example: Ich gehe heute Abend mit meinem Freund ins Kino.
native_language_example: I’m going to the cinema tonight with my boyfriend/friend.

additional_notes: Used to say you do something together with your brother. After **mit**, German uses the **dative** case, so it’s **meinem Bruder** (not *mein Bruder*). In some verbs, **mit** can also mean “to/with” in the sense of interacting with someone (e.g., **reden mit** = “talk to”).
target_language_example: Am Wochenende gehe ich mit meinem Bruder schwimmen.
native_language_example: On the weekend I’m going swimming with my brother.

additional_notes: Uses the preposition "mit" (+ dative case) to say you are doing something together with your dog. "meinem" is the dative form of "mein" (my), used because of "mit". Common with verbs like "gehen" (to go), "spazieren gehen" (to go for a walk), "spielen" (to play), or "sprechen" (to speak).
target_language_example: Am Wochenende fahre ich oft mit meinem Hund an den See.
native_language_example: On weekends I often go to the lake with my dog.

additional_notes: Used to say you are together with your son or doing something accompanied by him. "mit" is followed by the dative case, so "mein Sohn" becomes "meinem Sohn". Often used with verbs like gehen (to go), treffen (to meet), or müssen (must/need to).
target_language_example: Ich koche heute Abend mit meinem Sohn.
native_language_example: I’m cooking with my son this evening.

additional_notes: "Mit" takes the dative case, so "mein" becomes "meinen" when it’s plural (e.g., mit meinen Freunden = with my friends). It’s used for (1) being together/communicating with someone (mit meinen Nachbarn sprechen), and (2) tools/body parts/instruments (mit meinen Augen sehen). For feminine singular you’d say "mit meiner" (mit meiner Mutter), and for neuter/masculine singular "mit meinem" (mit meinem Bruder / mit meinem Handy).
target_language_example: Am Wochenende gehe ich mit meinen Freunden ins Kino.
native_language_example: On the weekend I go to the movies with my friends.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition **mit** (“with”), which takes the **dative** case: **meinen Eltern** (dative plural). Common with verbs like **sprechen** (to talk), **leben/wohnen** (to live), or activities: **mit meinen Eltern wandern** (go hiking with my parents). In questions like **Was ist mit meinen Eltern?**, **mit** can mean “about/with (regarding)”: “What’s going on with my parents?” / “What about my parents?”
target_language_example: Am Wochenende esse ich oft mit meinen Eltern zu Abend.
native_language_example: On the weekend I often have dinner with my parents.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition **mit** (“with”), which takes the **dative** case. That’s why it’s **meinen Freunden** (dative plural). Often used to say who you are doing something with (going out, playing, traveling, etc.).
target_language_example: Am Wochenende gehe ich mit meinen Freunden ins Kino.
native_language_example: On the weekend I’m going to the cinema with my friends.

additional_notes: Used to say you are together with your children, or that you do an activity together with them. Often follows a verb (e.g., spielen, ansehen, sein/gehen) to describe who you do it with. Case note: after "mit" you use the dative, so "meine Kinder" → "meinen Kindern".
target_language_example: Am Wochenende gehe ich oft mit meinen Kindern in den Park.
native_language_example: On the weekend, I often go to the park with my children.

meaning: "with my" (used with feminine nouns in the dative case).
additional_notes: Used after the preposition "mit" (with), which always takes the dative. "meiner" is the dative form of "meine" for feminine nouns (e.g., "mit meiner Schwester", "mit meiner Uhr"). It’s also used in fixed expressions like "stimmt etwas mit meiner ... nicht" = "something is wrong with my ...".
target_language_example: Ich gehe heute Abend mit meiner Schwester ins Kino.
native_language_example: I’m going to the cinema with my sister tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say you are together with your family or doing something in their company. "mit" takes the dative case, so "meine Familie" becomes "meiner Familie" (feminine dative). You can swap in other possessives: "mit deiner/seiner/ihrer/unserer/eurer Familie".
target_language_example: Am Wochenende esse ich oft mit meiner Familie zu Abend.
native_language_example: On the weekend I often have dinner with my family.

additional_notes: "mit" + dative. Used most often to say you are together with your mother (company): "Ich bin mit meiner Mutter hier." It can also mean "about/regarding my mother" in phrases like "das mit meiner Mutter" (= that thing about my mother), and with "passieren" it means "(to) my mother": "Was passiert mit meiner Mutter?"
target_language_example: Ich gehe heute mit meiner Mutter spazieren.
native_language_example: Today I'm going for a walk with my mother.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition **mit** (“with”), which takes the **dative** case: **meiner Schwester**. It can mean doing something together (e.g., *Ich esse mit meiner Schwester.*). In the common question **Was ist mit ...?**, it often means “What’s wrong with ...?” or “What about ...?” depending on context (e.g., *Was ist mit meiner Schwester?*).
target_language_example: Am Wochenende treffe ich mich mit meiner Schwester.
native_language_example: On the weekend I’m meeting up with my sister.

additional_notes: Literally means you are together/accompanying your daughter (e.g., going somewhere with her, speaking with her). Used with the dative case after "mit": "meiner Tochter" (from "meine Tochter"). In "mit meiner Tochter ausgehen," it can mean "to go out with my daughter" in the sense of dating.
target_language_example: Ich gehe heute mit meiner Tochter ins Kino.
native_language_example: I'm going to the movie theater with my daughter today.

additional_notes: Literally mit + mir, meaning "with me". It is used for accompaniment (Komm mit mir), being in your possession/on your person (Ich habe kein Geld mit mir), and with some verbs it corresponds to English "to me" or "with me," such as Was passiert mit mir? or Was macht das mit mir?.
target_language_example: Kommst du morgen mit mir ins Kino?
native_language_example: Are you coming to the cinema with me tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used with the verb phrase **Schluss machen (mit jemandem)** = “to break up (with someone)” or more generally “to end it.” In the perfect tense: **Er/Sie hat mit mir Schluss gemacht.** Often used for romantic relationships.
target_language_example: Ich kann es nicht glauben: Er hat gestern mit mir Schluss gemacht.
native_language_example: I can’t believe it: he broke up with me yesterday.

additional_notes: Used with **sprechen mit + dative** (mit mir = with me) to say someone spoke to you. Often appears in the **Perfekt** tense: **hat mit mir gesprochen** = “(he/she) has talked to me.” You can also use it in questions: **Hast du mit mir gesprochen?** = “Did you talk to me?”
target_language_example: Warum hast du nicht mit mir gesprochen?
native_language_example: Why didn’t you talk to me?

meaning: 'with me in/into' (together with me at a place or going to a place).
additional_notes: Used with a place to say you are together with someone there (location: usually dative, e.g. *mit mir in Boston*) or going there (movement: usually accusative, e.g. *mit mir in ein Restaurant* / *in das Konzert*). Very common in invitations and suggestions with verbs like *gehen*, *fahren*, *laufen*: *Willst du mit mir in ... gehen?*
target_language_example: Kommst du morgen mit mir in die Stadt?
native_language_example: Are you coming with me into town tomorrow?

meaning: to go to the movies/cinema with me
additional_notes: Used to invite someone to the cinema with you, typically as a question (e.g., "Möchtest du …?", "Würdest du …?") or in reported speech after "ob" (e.g., "Ich fragte, ob …"). "ins" is a contraction of "in das" meaning "to the/into the" (cinema).
target_language_example: Möchtest du mit mir ins Kino gehen?
native_language_example: Would you like to go to the movies with me?
