additional_notes: 'nach' takes the dative. In this phrase, 'der' is usually the feminine singular dative article, as in 'nach der Arbeit' or 'nach der Wahl'. It can be used for time/events ('after the election') and for movement or location ('past/after the next corner'). In the pattern 'eine/r ... nach der anderen', it means 'one ... after another'.
target_language_example: Nach der Schule gehe ich direkt nach Hause.
native_language_example: After school, I go straight home.

additional_notes: Used to say what someone does when their workday is over. It can refer to after work in general or after a specific shift/day. Often follows time expressions like „jeden Tag“ (every day) or starts questions like „Was machst du …?“
target_language_example: Nach der Arbeit gehe ich oft noch einkaufen.
native_language_example: After work, I often go shopping.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens after the school day ends. It often answers the question "Wann?" (When?) and is followed by what you do or where you go: "nach der Schule nach Hause gehen" (go home after school), "nach der Schule Hausaufgaben machen" (do homework after school).
target_language_example: Nach der Schule gehe ich meistens nach Hause und mache Hausaufgaben.
native_language_example: After school I usually go home and do homework.

additional_notes: Used with a verb like **spielen**: **nach der Schule Tennis spielen**. **nach der Schule** = “after school” (time phrase) and it often comes before the activity. You can swap in other activities: **nach der Schule Fußball/Basketball spielen**, etc.
target_language_example: Wir spielen nach der Schule Tennis.
native_language_example: We play tennis after school.

meaning: to there; over to that place (direction/movement).
additional_notes: Used with verbs of motion to indicate a destination. It often points to a place that’s farther away or specifically indicated ("dort" = "over there"), similar to "dahin". Contrast: "dort" alone is just "there" (location), while "nach dort" emphasizes going/moving there.
target_language_example: Wir gehen nach dort, wo die Berge sind.
native_language_example: We’re going over there, where the mountains are.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement to show direction: going from inside to outside (e.g., gehen/laufen nach draußen). For location (being outside), you usually use „draußen“ or „(nach) draußen“ is not used: „Ich bin draußen.“ In polite requests it can mean “on your way out”: „auf Ihrem Weg nach draußen …“.
target_language_example: Komm nach draußen, die Sonne scheint!
native_language_example: Come outside, the sun is shining!

meaning: to take/bring (someone or something) outside; to show someone out.
additional_notes: Used with an object (jemanden/etwas) to mean moving them from inside to outside. In polite/formal contexts (e.g., an office), it can mean “to escort/show someone out.” Word order varies with tense (e.g., „wird … nach draußen bringen“).
target_language_example: Meine Sekretärin wird Sie nach draußen bringen.
native_language_example: My secretary will show you out.

additional_notes: Used for leaving a building/room and going out into the open air. Very common with pets, smoking, getting fresh air, or taking a short break. Often answers the question „Wohin gehst du?“ (Where are you going?): „nach draußen“.
target_language_example: Ich will kurz nach draußen gehen, um frische Luft zu schnappen.
native_language_example: I want to go outside for a moment to get some fresh air.

additional_notes: Infinitive phrase meaning moving from inside to outside. Common after expressions like "Angst haben" (to be afraid), "vermeiden" (to avoid), or in contrasts like "statt ... zu" (instead of ...). "draußen" means "outside/outdoors" and "nach" indicates direction/movement toward a place (outside). Often contrasts with "zu Hause bleiben" (stay at home).
target_language_example: Die Leute haben noch immer Angst, nach draußen zu gehen.
native_language_example: People are still afraid to go outside.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (gehen, kommen, laufen) to show direction: you move from outside to inside. Contrast: "drinnen" alone describes location (already inside). Often used with "wieder" = "back inside again".
target_language_example: Es fängt an zu regnen, komm bitte nach drinnen.
native_language_example: It’s starting to rain—please come inside.

additional_notes: “Nach” is a preposition that takes the dative case, so you often see it as “nach einem” (masculine/neuter dative: “einem”). Common uses: time/sequence = “after a …” (Nach einem kurzen Besuch …); searching/requesting = “for a …” with verbs like “suchen nach …”, “sich umsehen nach …”, “nach … schicken” (send for). It can also mean “looks like a …” with “nach etwas aussehen” (Sieht nach einem Versehen aus?).
target_language_example: Ich suche nach einem Parkplatz.
native_language_example: I'm looking for a parking space.

meaning: to look for a parking space (spot).
additional_notes: Uses the verb "suchen" (to search/look for) with "nach" + dative: "nach einem Parkplatz". Often used with time words like "lange" (for a long time) or "ewig" (forever) to emphasize how hard it was to find parking.
target_language_example: Am Samstag mussten wir lange nach einem Parkplatz suchen.
native_language_example: On Saturday we had to look for a parking space for a long time.

meaning: "after a" (period of time); also "for a" (longing for something).
additional_notes: "Nach" takes the dative case, so with a feminine noun you often get "nach einer ..." (e.g., nach einer Weile = after a while; sich sehnen nach einer Tätigkeit = to long for an activity/job). It’s a common pattern: nach + time expression for "after", and verbs like "sich sehnen" use "nach" to mean "for".
target_language_example: Nach einer Stunde sind wir endlich angekommen.
native_language_example: After an hour, we finally arrived.

meaning: after a while; after some time.
additional_notes: Used to say that some time passes before the next thing happens. Often placed at the beginning of the sentence, but it can also come later. Similar to "nach einiger Zeit".
target_language_example: Nach einer Weile habe ich mich an den neuen Job gewöhnt.
native_language_example: After a while, I got used to the new job.

meaning: to the back; backwards (toward the rear).
additional_notes: Used to give directions about movement or position (e.g., step/move/lean back). Often contrasted with „nach vorne“ (to the front/forward).
target_language_example: Geh bitte ein Stück nach hinten.
native_language_example: Please step back a bit.

meaning: to backfire; to have the opposite effect than intended.
additional_notes: Used when a plan, idea, or action doesn’t work out and instead causes problems (often with words like „Plan“, „Aktion“, „Strategie“). It’s a common idiom and usually talks about unintended negative consequences.
target_language_example: Wenn du ihn so kritisierst, könnte das nach hinten losgehen.
native_language_example: If you criticize him like that, it could backfire.

additional_notes: **Nach** takes the dative case. **Ihrem** is the dative form of **ihr** (= her / their). It’s very common in set verb + preposition phrases, e.g. **jemanden nach etwas fragen** = to ask someone about something (*nach ihrem Alter* = about her age), and **süchtig nach etwas** = addicted to something (*süchtig nach ihrem Telefon* = addicted to her phone). Don’t confuse it with **Ihrem** (capital I), which is formal “your” (dative).
target_language_example: Ich habe sie nach ihrem Namen gefragt.
native_language_example: I asked her about her name.

meaning: after her/their; for/about her/their (depending on context).
additional_notes: "Nach" can mean (1) "after" in time (Nach ihrer Rückkehr / Nach ihrer Krankheit), (2) "for" with feelings like "Sehnsucht" (Sehnsucht nach ihrer Familie = longing for her family), and (3) "about" with verbs like "fragen" (jemanden nach ihrer neuen Stelle fragen = ask someone about her new job). "Nach" takes the dative case, so "ihrer" here is dative feminine singular (her) or dative plural (their).
target_language_example: Nach ihrer Hochzeit sind sie in eine neue Wohnung gezogen.
native_language_example: After their wedding, they moved into a new apartment.

additional_notes: Used for direction or movement toward the inside of something (a room, building, body, etc.). Common in instructions and spatial descriptions: „von außen nach innen“ = from outside to inside; „Die Tür geht nach innen auf“ = the door opens inward (toward the room). Can also be used figuratively: „nach innen schauen“ = to look inward/reflect.
target_language_example: Komm bitte nach innen, es ist kalt draußen.
native_language_example: Please come inside; it’s cold outside.

meaning: after every meal (your) teeth — usually in “die Zähne putzen” (“to brush your teeth”).
additional_notes: A common timing phrase used with reflexive “sich die Zähne putzen” (to brush one’s teeth). Word order is flexible: “Nach jeder Mahlzeit solltet ihr euch die Zähne putzen.” / “Ihr solltet euch nach jeder Mahlzeit die Zähne putzen.”
target_language_example: Ich putze mir nach jeder Mahlzeit die Zähne.
native_language_example: I brush my teeth after every meal.

meaning: to the left; left (in that direction).
additional_notes: Used for movement or direction: turning, going, running, shifting, or bending to the left. Common in instructions: „Dreh nach links!“ / „Gehen Sie … nach links.“ Can be used with verbs like gehen, rennen, drehen, abbiegen, and also to describe how something extends or curves (e.g., a river).
target_language_example: Am Ende der Straße gehst du nach links.
native_language_example: At the end of the street, you go left.

additional_notes: Used with movement or direction toward a higher place (e.g., going up stairs, going upstairs, looking up). Often used with verbs like gehen (go), kommen (come), schauen (look).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte nach oben kommen?
native_language_example: Can you please come upstairs?

additional_notes: Used to indicate movement or direction toward the right side, often with verbs like gehen (go), fahren (drive), bewegen (move), schauen (look), or as an instruction/command (e.g., "Fahr nach rechts!"). It answers the question "Wohin?" (to where?).
target_language_example: Biegen Sie an der nächsten Kreuzung nach rechts ab.
native_language_example: Turn right at the next intersection.

meaning: after his; for/asking about his (with „fragen“); addicted to his (with „süchtig“).
additional_notes: „nach“ takes the dative, so you often see it with dative possessives like „seinem“ (= his, masc./neut.). Common patterns: (1) time: „nach seinem Abschluss“ = after his graduation; (2) asking for/about: „nach seinem Namen/Anwalt fragen“ = ask for/about his name/lawyer; (3) fixed expression: „süchtig nach seinem Telefon“ = addicted to his phone.
target_language_example: Nach seinem Essen ist er sofort eingeschlafen.
native_language_example: After his meal, he fell asleep immediately.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like „(jdn.) nennen“ or „benennen“ to say someone was given the same name as an older family member. Here, „nach“ means “after” in the sense of “in honor of / following the name of,” not “afterwards in time.”
target_language_example: Er wurde nach seinem Großvater benannt.
native_language_example: He was named after his grandfather.

additional_notes: This is the preposition **nach** + **seiner** (dative masculine/neuter singular) meaning “his.” **Nach** has different meanings: (1) time: **nach seiner Operation** = “after his operation”; (2) asking/saying according to something: **nach seiner Meinung** = “for/according to his opinion”; (3) with certain verbs like **sich umsehen nach**: **nach seiner Kamera** = “for his camera.” The noun that follows is in the **dative**.
target_language_example: Nach seiner Arbeit geht Tom nach Hause.
native_language_example: After his work, Tom goes home.

meaning: "should do (afterwards / after that)" (part of a larger sentence).
additional_notes: This isn’t a fixed phrase by itself; it’s usually a fragment from something like: **was wir danach tun sollten** (“what we should do after that”) or **was wir als Nächstes tun sollten** (“what we should do next”). In German you typically say **danach** or **nachher** (“after that/later”) rather than **nach** alone in this structure.
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht, was wir danach tun sollten.
native_language_example: I don’t know what we should do after that.

additional_notes: Used with movement or direction: going/looking/heading downward (e.g., downstairs, down in an elevator). Often with verbs like gehen (go), fahren (ride/drive), schauen/blicken (look).
target_language_example: Komm nach unten, das Essen ist fertig.
native_language_example: Come downstairs; the food is ready.

additional_notes: Used for direction or movement (often with verbs like schauen/sehen, gehen, treten, machen): looking forward (eyes/gaze) or moving one step forward. Common in instructions and commands: „Augen nach vorn!“ / „Schau nach vorn!“
target_language_example: Bitte treten Sie einen Schritt nach vorn.
native_language_example: Please step one step forward.

additional_notes: Used with movement or direction: going to the front of a room/line (Geh nach vorne), looking ahead (Schau nach vorne), leaning forward (sich nach vorne beugen), or falling forward (nach vorne fallen). Often answers the question “Wohin?” (where to?).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte ein bisschen nach vorne kommen?
native_language_example: Can you please come a bit forward (towards the front)?

additional_notes: Used to say a situation continues and hasn’t changed. Often placed in the middle of the sentence: „Er ist nach wie vor …“. Similar to „immer noch“, but „nach wie vor“ is a bit more formal and emphasizes ‘just like before’.
target_language_example: Wir warten nach wie vor auf eine Antwort.
native_language_example: We are still waiting for an answer.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re making a conclusion from evidence or an impression. Often follows a noun in the dative + „nach“ (e.g., „dem Himmel nach zu urteilen“ = judging by the sky). You can also use it with „nach dem, was …“ (judging by what …).
target_language_example: Dem Verkehr nach zu urteilen, kommen wir zu spät.
native_language_example: Judging by the traffic, we’re going to be late.

additional_notes: Used to describe something that happens slowly in steps, not all at once. Often with verbs like „sich verbessern“, „sich verändern“, „steigen“ (increase), or „werden“ (become).
target_language_example: Nach und nach habe ich mich an das Wetter hier gewöhnt.
native_language_example: Little by little, I got used to the weather here.

additional_notes: Used when you look/verify something to find out if it’s true. Very common with verbs like „nachsehen“ or „schauen“: „Ich sehe/schaue nach, ob …“. In imperatives you’ll often hear: „Schau/Sieh mal nach, ob …“. The „ob“ clause functions like an English “whether/if” clause.
target_language_example: Ich sehe kurz nach, ob die Tür abgeschlossen ist.
native_language_example: I’ll quickly check whether the door is locked.

meaning: after; about; to check—what (used as a split construction where **nach** is separated from **was** by intervening words).
additional_notes: This entry covers the very common **split** pattern where **nach** belongs to a separable verb or to **nachdenken (über etw.)** and **was** introduces a clause: e.g. **nachsehen, was ...** (“check what ...”), **dem nachgehen, was ...** (“pursue/investigate what ...”), **über etw. nachdenken, was ...** (“think about what ...”). In these constructions, **nach** and **was** are not adjacent, but they function together across the clause boundary.
target_language_example: Sieh mal nach, was die Köter schon wieder haben.
native_language_example: Have a look what those mutts have got again.

additional_notes: Used to start a dependent clause (subordinate clause) about something that happened before the main action. In this clause, the verb goes to the end: „Nachdem er gegangen war, …“. Often paired with past perfect (Plusquamperfekt) to show the earlier action: „Nachdem er gegessen hatte, ging er …“.
target_language_example: Nachdem er gegessen hatte, ging er schlafen.
native_language_example: After he had eaten, he went to sleep.

additional_notes: Used when you want someone to verify something: *nachsehen, ob …* = “check whether …”. The verb *nachsehen* is separable: **Ich sehe nach, ob …** / **Kannst du nachsehen, ob …?** In subordinate clauses introduced by *ob*, the verb goes to the end: **…, ob das Paket da ist.**
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte nachsehen, ob die Tür abgeschlossen ist?
native_language_example: Can you please check whether the door is locked?

additional_notes: Used when someone checks a situation or a fact to find out if something is true. Very common in an infinitive clause with „um … nachzusehen, ob …“ (= in order to check whether/if …) or after verbs like „bitten“: „Sie bat mich nachzusehen, ob …“.
target_language_example: Er stand auf, um nachzusehen, ob er das Licht in der Küche ausgemacht hatte.
native_language_example: He got up to check whether he had turned off the light in the kitchen.

additional_notes: Used for physical closeness (nearby) or being close to achieving something (“almost there”). Often with **sein**: *Wir sind nah dran.* You can intensify it: **ganz nah dran** (“very close”), **ziemlich nah dran** (“pretty close”), **so nah dran, dass ...** (“so close that ...”). With distances you often hear **zu nah dran** (“too close”).
target_language_example: Wir sind ganz nah dran, das Problem zu lösen.
native_language_example: We’re really close to solving the problem.

additional_notes: Used to say something is close to a place/thing. It’s formed with **nahe** + a **dative** noun phrase, e.g. **nahe dem Fluss** (near the river), **nahe dem Eingang** (near the entrance). Often interchangeable with **in der Nähe von** + dative.
target_language_example: Das Hotel liegt nahe dem Bahnhof.
native_language_example: The hotel is near the train station.

additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of **annehmen, dass ...**. Used to express an assumption or belief (often without being sure). Common in writing and storytelling; in everyday speech people also often use **habe angenommen, dass ...** (Perfekt). Word order: **Ich nahm an, dass + verb at the end** (e.g., „… dass er kommt“).
target_language_example: Ich nahm an, dass du heute keine Zeit hast.
native_language_example: I assumed you don’t have time today.

additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of "ein Taxi nehmen" = "to take a taxi." It’s common in written narration (stories, news). In everyday speech, Germans often use the perfect tense instead: "hat ein Taxi genommen" (has taken/got a taxi).
target_language_example: Wegen des Regens nahm ein Taxi zu nehmen keine Option, also nahm ein Taxi er trotzdem.
native_language_example: Because of the rain, taking a taxi wasn’t an option, but he took a taxi anyway.

meaning: “took a …” (simple past of *nehmen* + a masculine direct object).
additional_notes: *nahm* is the simple past of *nehmen* (“to take”). It’s used with an object in the accusative: *nahm einen* + masculine noun (e.g., *einen Zug*, *einen Kredit*). Often it appears with separable verbs where another part comes later, e.g. *einen Kredit aufnehmen* → *Er nahm einen Kredit auf* (“He took out a loan”).
target_language_example: Sie nahm einen Schluck Wasser.
native_language_example: She took a sip of water.

additional_notes: Used in narratives to say that a man/boy took something that belongs to him. In many common phrases you’ll see it with a separable prefix later in the sentence, e.g. **nahm seine Brille ab** = “took off his glasses.” Word order: **nahm** (verb) + **seine** + noun, and the prefix (**ab**) comes at the end of the clause.
target_language_example: Er nahm seine Jacke ab, weil es warm war.
native_language_example: He took off his jacket because it was warm.

additional_notes: Used when a male person (or masculine/neuter noun) is the subject and he took something that is 'his' (direct object in the accusative): *Er nahm seinen Bruder mit* (He took his brother along), *Er nahm seinen Helm ab* (He took off his helmet). Also appears in the fixed expression *nahm seinen Ursprung (in ...)* = 'originated (in ...)'.
target_language_example: Er nahm seinen Schlüssel aus der Tasche.
native_language_example: He took his key out of his pocket.

meaning: “took (for oneself)”; often used as “took time off / took a day off.”
additional_notes: Simple past (Präteritum) of the reflexive verb phrase **sich nehmen** (“to take for oneself”). Very common with **frei**: **sich frei nehmen** = to take time off (work/school). Often used with a time expression: **einen Tag / eine Woche frei**.
target_language_example: Tom nahm sich einen Tag frei.
native_language_example: Tom took a day off.

meaning: took their own life; committed suicide.
additional_notes: Präteritum (simple past) of the reflexive expression „sich das Leben nehmen“ (= to kill oneself). „nahm“ agrees with the subject: „Er nahm sich das Leben“, „Sie nahm sich das Leben“. This is a serious, sensitive topic; alternatives include „Suizid begehen“ (more formal) or „sich umbringen“ (more direct/harsh).
target_language_example: Maria nahm sich das Leben.
native_language_example: Maria took her own life.

meaning: soaking wet; wet to the skin.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone or something is completely wet (usually from rain, getting splashed, falling in water, etc.). Often follows forms of „sein/werden“ (e.g., „Ich bin …“, „Er wurde …“).
target_language_example: Nach dem Spaziergang im Sturm waren wir nass bis auf die Haut.
native_language_example: After the walk in the storm, we were soaking wet.

meaning: to take off your wet clothes.
additional_notes: Uses the separable verb „ausziehen“ (to take off clothes). In the present tense, „aus“ often goes to the end: „Zieh dir die nassen Sachen aus.“ Often paired with „… und trockene anziehen“ (…and put on dry ones). „ausziehen“ can also mean “to move out,” but with clothes it means “to take off.”
target_language_example: Nach dem Regen habe ich mir die nassen Sachen ausgezogen.
native_language_example: After the rain, I took off my wet clothes.

meaning: next to / beside the (masculine or neuter noun, dative).
additional_notes: Used to say something is located next to something else. It uses the dative form of “der/das” → “dem” (e.g., neben dem Kühlschrank, neben dem Hotel). With feminine nouns you’ll often see “neben der …”, and with plural “neben den …”.
target_language_example: Mein Fahrrad steht neben dem Eingang.
native_language_example: My bike is standing next to the entrance.

additional_notes: From the verb **annehmen**. Very common for making a guess or stating what you think is probably true. Often used as **Ich nehme an, dass ...** (“I assume that ...”) or **Ich nehme an, ...** (informal, without *dass*). Note: *annehmen* can also mean “to accept” (e.g., an offer), but in these examples it means “to assume.”
target_language_example: Ich nehme an, dass du heute keine Zeit hast.
native_language_example: I assume you don’t have time today.

additional_notes: This is the 1st-person singular of **nehmen** used with German word order (verb in position 2). It’s common when choosing or ordering something (**Eine nehme ich.** = “I’ll take one.”), talking about what you take/use (**Da nehme ich den Larousse.**), routines (**Jeden Abend nehme ich ein Bad.**), or transport (**Zuerst nehme ich den Bus...**). In questions it can mean “Am I taking...?” (**Nehme ich dir nicht den Platz weg?**).
target_language_example: Den Kaffee nehme ich, bitte.
native_language_example: I’ll take the coffee, please.

additional_notes: Used to show you’re guessing or not 100% sure. Often added at the end of a sentence like a tag (similar to “I guess”): „…, nehme ich an.“ Literally it’s „(das) nehme ich an“ (“I assume that”). You’ll also see: „Ich nehme an, dass …“ (“I assume that …”).
target_language_example: Du kommst morgen, nehme ich an.
native_language_example: You’re coming tomorrow, I assume.

additional_notes: “Nehmen Sie …” is the polite/formal imperative (addressing someone as Sie). It’s common in instructions and requests: medicine (“Nehmen Sie Ihre Tabletten!”), directions (“Nehmen Sie die nächste Straße rechts!”), and set phrases like “Nehmen Sie Platz!” = “Have a seat.” It also combines with prefixes/particles: “mitnehmen” → “Nehmen Sie … mit!” (“take … along”), “annehmen” → “Nehmen Sie … an!” (“accept …”).
target_language_example: Nehmen Sie bitte noch ein Glas Wasser.
native_language_example: Please have another glass of water.

meaning: formal command: “take your …” / “put your …” (for a masculine thing).
additional_notes: Used with **Sie** (formal “you”) in instructions/requests. **Ihren** is the accusative form of “your” for a **masculine** noun (e.g., *Ihren Hut, Ihren Mantel*). The exact meaning of *nehmen* depends on context: it can mean “take” (*Nehmen Sie Ihren Mantel!*), or “take off” when paired with **ab** (*Nehmen Sie Ihren Hut ab!*), or “put/leash” in set phrases (*Nehmen Sie Ihren Hund an die Leine!*).
target_language_example: Nehmen Sie Ihren Mantel bitte mit.
native_language_example: Please take your coat with you.

additional_notes: Used to invite someone to sit down, especially in formal situations (e.g., offices, waiting rooms, meetings). It’s the polite/formal imperative with "Sie"; a more casual version is "Nimm Platz" (to one person you’re on du-terms with) or "Nehmt Platz" (to a group). Often said with "Bitte".
target_language_example: Bitte nehmen Sie Platz.
native_language_example: Please have a seat.

additional_notes: Used with formal **Sie** to give instructions or polite commands. **Den** is the accusative form of **der** for masculine nouns (and also used for some plural forms in the dative, though the examples here are accusative). Common in signs and directions: **Nehmen Sie den Notausgang!** = “Take the emergency exit!”
target_language_example: Nehmen Sie den zweiten Gang links.
native_language_example: Take the second street on the left.

additional_notes: Used with **Sie** (formal “you”) to give instructions. Very often it’s the start of a **separable verb** phrase, where the prefix comes later: **Nehmen Sie die Maske ab.** (abnehmen = take off), **Nehmen Sie die Sendung auf.** (aufnehmen = record), **Nehmen Sie die Person fest.** (festnehmen = arrest), **Nehmen Sie die Haufen auf!** (pick up).
target_language_example: Nehmen Sie die Schuhe bitte aus dem Regal.
native_language_example: Please take the shoes from the shelf.

additional_notes: This is the formal (Sie) imperative of **sich nehmen** (“to take for oneself”). It’s used with an object: **Nehmen Sie sich das Geld** (take the money), **Nehmen Sie sich die Zeit** (take the time), **Nehmen Sie sich so viel, wie Sie brauchen** (take as much as you need / help yourself). In the fixed phrase **sich ein Beispiel an jemandem nehmen**, it means “to follow someone’s example.”
target_language_example: Nehmen Sie sich ruhig noch ein Stück Kuchen.
native_language_example: Go ahead and help yourself to another piece of cake.

additional_notes: Form of the verb "nehmen" (to take) with "wir" (we). It can be a simple statement about what you (plural) will take/do (e.g., "Morgen nehmen wir...") or, very commonly, a suggestion/question in the "wir"-form meaning "Shall we...? / Let’s...?" (e.g., "Nehmen wir die Wette an?" = "Shall we accept the bet?"). Word order helps: starting the sentence with "Nehmen wir ...?" usually signals a suggestion/question.
target_language_example: Nehmen wir den Bus oder die Bahn?
native_language_example: Shall we take the bus or the train?

meaning: “take your …” (command to more than one person).
additional_notes: This is the imperative (command) form for “ihr” (you plural/informal): nehmt = “take!” and eure = “your” (plural or feminine noun). It’s used to tell a group to take/bring something (“Nehmt eure Sachen raus.”) or to remove something (“Nehmt eure Maske ab.”).
target_language_example: Nehmt eure Jacken mit!
native_language_example: Take your jackets with you!

meaning: "do you (all) take" / "are you (all) taking" (2nd person plural of *nehmen*).
additional_notes: Used when speaking to more than one person (*ihr* = “you” plural). It’s a common way to ask what someone is taking/choosing/using: *Welchen Zug nehmt ihr?* (“Which train are you taking?”), *Welches nehmt ihr?* (“Which one are you taking?”). With *nehmen*, the meaning depends on context: taking medicine/food (*Medikamente nehmen*, *Flüssigkeit zu sich nehmen*), removing something (*den Ring abnehmen*), taking time off (*sich frei nehmen*), or participating (*teilnehmen*).
target_language_example: Welchen Bus nehmt ihr nach Hause?
native_language_example: Which bus are you taking home?

meaning: to tend to (do something); to be prone to.
additional_notes: Used to describe a general tendency or typical behavior. Commonly followed by an infinitive clause with „zu“: „… neigen dazu, zu + Infinitiv“ or with a reflexive verb: „… neigen dazu, sich …“. Can refer to individuals or groups (e.g., „Viele Leute neigen dazu …“).
target_language_example: Wir neigen dazu, Fehler zu machen.
native_language_example: We tend to make mistakes.

meaning: tends to; is prone to (has a habit/likelihood of doing something).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive clause: „jemand/etwas neigt dazu, + zu + Verb“. It describes a typical tendency or habitual behavior, not a one-time action. Often translates to “tends to” or “is prone to”.
target_language_example: Er neigt dazu, sein Versprechen zu vergessen.
native_language_example: He tends to forget his promise.

additional_notes: Used when speaking respectfully to a man (e.g., to an officer, customer, or superior). In German writing you often see a comma: “Nein, Sir, …”. Similar to “Nein, Herr …” (No, Mr. …).
target_language_example: Nein, Sir, ich kann Ihnen dabei leider nicht helfen.
native_language_example: No, sir, unfortunately I can’t help you with that.

meaning: "No, but ..." (used to disagree, correct, or add a contrasting point).
additional_notes: Common in conversation at the start of a sentence. It can answer someone directly ("No, but...") or be used even without an explicit question to introduce a mild objection, correction, or contrasting comment—often with a slightly emphatic tone (similar to "No, but really..." / "Come on, but...").
target_language_example: Nein, aber das habe ich dir doch schon gestern erklärt.
native_language_example: No, but I already explained that to you yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to politely decline an offer, invitation, help, or something you don’t want. Often followed by a reason: “Nein, danke, ich habe …”. You’ll also hear it without a comma (“Nein danke”). “Oh nein, danke.” can sound more emphatic/surprised but is still polite.
target_language_example: Nein, danke, ich möchte nichts trinken.
native_language_example: No, thanks, I don’t want anything to drink.

additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence to reject or correct what was just said or assumed. Often followed by a verb phrase: “Nein, das ist … / das gibt es … / das wird …”. In speech there’s usually a pause after “Nein”.
target_language_example: Nein, das stimmt nicht.
native_language_example: No, that's not true.

meaning: "No, that is…" (used to deny/correct or clarify).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a reply to say something is not true or to correct information: "Nein, das ist es nicht." (= "No, it isn’t."). You can follow it with an adjective ("… furchtbar", "… zu groß"), a noun phrase ("… sein Name"), or "kein" + noun ("… kein Problem").
target_language_example: Nein, das ist nicht richtig.
native_language_example: No, that’s not correct.

additional_notes: Use this to correct someone when they name the wrong thing: "Nein, das ist kein X." It uses "kein" (the negative form of "ein") with masculine or neuter nouns in the nominative (e.g., kein Hund, kein Haus). For feminine nouns, use "Nein, das ist keine …"; for plural, "Nein, das sind keine …".
target_language_example: Nein, das ist kein Hund, das ist ein Wolf.
native_language_example: No, that's not a dog, that's a wolf.

additional_notes: Used to deny or correct something someone said or assumed. It’s usually followed by a noun or adjective: “Nein, das ist nicht mein Auto.” / “Nein, das ist nicht richtig.” In spoken German you often add emphasis: “Nein, das ist nicht so.”
target_language_example: Nein, das ist nicht richtig.
native_language_example: No, that’s not correct.

meaning: “No, that was …” (to correct or deny something about the past).
additional_notes: Used to contradict what someone just said or assumed, usually followed by a noun/pronoun/adjective phrase (e.g., “Nein, das war ich nicht.” / “Nein, das war kein Zufall.”). “Das” = “that,” and “war” is the simple past of “sein” (to be).
target_language_example: Nein, das war nicht mein Handy.
native_language_example: No, that wasn’t my phone.

meaning: "No, that would…" (used to say what would happen in a hypothetical situation).
additional_notes: Used to reject an idea and explain a likely consequence. "würde" is the Konjunktiv II form of "werden" and often corresponds to English "would". It can be followed by an infinitive (sometimes omitted when clear from context), e.g. "Nein, das würde nie funktionieren."
target_language_example: Nein, das würde zu lange dauern.
native_language_example: No, that would take too long.

meaning: "No, you…" (an emphatic way to contradict or stop someone and tell them what they must/should do).
additional_notes: Used when speaking directly to someone (du = informal "you") to strongly disagree, correct them, or give a firm instruction. Often followed by a statement or command: "Nein, du bleibst …" / "Nein, du sollst …". In writing, it’s commonly separated by a comma to show a pause and emphasis.
target_language_example: Nein, du gehst jetzt nach Hause.
native_language_example: No, you’re going home now.

meaning: "No, you are …" (used to correct or contradict someone).
additional_notes: Used to disagree with what someone said or assumed, and then state what’s true instead. It’s usually followed by an adjective or a longer phrase. "du bist" is the informal singular form of "to be" (sein): *ich bin, du bist, er/sie/es ist*.
target_language_example: Nein, du bist nicht zu spät.
native_language_example: No, you’re not late.

additional_notes: Used to answer or correct something in conversation: you say "Nein" and then continue with a full sentence where the subject is "er" (he). Often separated by a comma in writing: "Nein, er ...".
target_language_example: Nein, er hat heute keine Zeit.
native_language_example: No, he doesn't have time today.

meaning: "No, it …" (starting a reply that corrects or disagrees).
additional_notes: Used at the beginning of a sentence to contradict what someone said or assumed. It’s usually followed by a full clause like "Nein, es ist …" (“No, it is …”), "Nein, es ist nicht …" (“No, it isn’t …”), or another verb phrase such as "Nein, es tut mir leid …" (“No, I’m sorry …”).
target_language_example: Nein, es ist keine gute Idee.
native_language_example: No, it’s not a good idea.

meaning: "No, it’s …" (used to correct or disagree, then add information).
additional_notes: Used when you want to say “no” and then explain what the situation really is. Common with adjectives or short statements: “Nein, es ist alles gut.” / “Nein, es ist fertig.” You can also use it with negation: “Nein, es ist nicht …”. In speech, there’s often a pause after “Nein”.
target_language_example: Nein, es ist nicht teuer.
native_language_example: No, it’s not expensive.

meaning: "No, I …" (used to start a negative reply about yourself).
additional_notes: Used when answering a question or correcting someone: you begin with "Nein," and then continue with "ich" + verb (e.g., "Nein, ich bin …", "Nein, ich bleibe …"). The comma is common in writing; in speech there’s usually a short pause.
target_language_example: Nein, ich habe heute keine Zeit.
native_language_example: No, I don’t have time today.

meaning: "No, I am …" (used to deny or correct, then say what you are/feel).
additional_notes: Used when replying to something and correcting it: start with "Nein" and follow with a statement about yourself using "ich bin". "bin" is the 1st-person singular of "sein" (to be). It’s followed by an adjective (alleine, zufrieden) or a noun with an article/possessive (sein Freund).
target_language_example: Nein, ich bin müde.
native_language_example: No, I am tired.

additional_notes: Used to deny a statement about your identity or a condition/state. It’s a common answer pattern: "Nein, ich bin nicht + [noun/adjective]." With nouns (who/what you are), you often add an article: "Nein, ich bin nicht der/die/das ...". With adjectives (how you are), no article: "Nein, ich bin nicht müde."
target_language_example: Nein, ich bin nicht der neue Mitarbeiter.
native_language_example: No, I’m not the new employee.

additional_notes: Used to start a negative reply and then add what you have/feel/need. “hab” is a very common spoken/colloquial short form of “habe” (ich habe). Often followed by expressions like “Angst haben” (to be afraid), “Hunger haben” (to be hungry), or objects: “Ich hab kein Geld.”
target_language_example: Nein, ich hab heute keine Zeit.
native_language_example: No, I don’t have time today.

meaning: “No, I have …” (a way to start a negative answer).
additional_notes: Used at the beginning of a reply to contradict/deny something or to answer “Have you…?” questions. It’s usually followed by (1) a past participle to form the present perfect (Perfekt): “Nein, ich habe es nicht gefunden.” or (2) a noun/object: “Nein, ich habe dir etwas mitgebracht.” In German you often add “nicht” (not) or “nichts” (nothing) later in the sentence to make the meaning clearly negative.
target_language_example: Nein, ich habe heute keine Zeit.
native_language_example: No, I don’t have time today.

meaning: "No, I mean..." (used to correct or clarify).
additional_notes: Used in conversation when you want to correct a misunderstanding or specify what you really meant. It’s often followed by a pronoun/noun (e.g., „Nein, ich meine sie.“ = “No, I mean her.”) or by a full clause (e.g., „Nein, ich meine, dass …“ / „Nein, ich meine, …“). Common in spoken German as a self-correction or clarification.
target_language_example: Nein, ich meine morgen, nicht heute.
native_language_example: No, I mean tomorrow, not today.

additional_notes: Used to refuse or decline something and immediately give a reason/obligation. Commonly followed by an infinitive (e.g., arbeiten, los, essen) or a noun phrase (e.g., die Reifen überprüfen). In speech, it often implies “sorry, I can’t (because I have to…).”
target_language_example: Nein, ich muss jetzt gehen.
native_language_example: No, I have to go now.

additional_notes: Used to firmly reject something and immediately state your own intention or desire. Often followed by an infinitive (e.g., „Nein, ich will gehen.“ = “No, I want to go.”) or an object (e.g., „Nein, ich will das.“ = “No, I want that.”). In the given examples it’s commonly followed by „nicht“ to refuse: „Nein, ich will das nicht.“
target_language_example: Nein, ich will das nicht machen.
native_language_example: No, I don't want to do that.

additional_notes: Used to strongly refuse, correct someone, or stop/interrupt them (often like “no, no—”). Can also sound reassuring when calming someone down (tone matters). Often followed by an instruction: “Nein, nein, bleib hier.”
target_language_example: Nein, nein, das ist nicht nötig.
native_language_example: No, no, that’s not necessary.

meaning: "No, no, that's …" (used to correct, reassure, or react strongly).
additional_notes: A common spoken pattern at the start of a sentence. It can (1) correct a misunderstanding ("No, no, that’s not what I mean"), (2) reassure someone ("No, no, that doesn’t matter"), or (3) emphasize a positive reaction ("No, no, that’s wonderful!"). Tone depends on context; it’s usually friendly and conversational.
target_language_example: Nein, nein, das ist nicht schlimm.
native_language_example: No, no, that’s not bad / it’s not a big deal.

additional_notes: Saying "nein" three times is a common way to make the refusal or warning much stronger. Depending on tone, it can mean: a firm rejection ("Absolutely not"), alarm ("Oh no"), or stopping someone ("Don’t do that"). You can repeat it more or fewer times: "Nein, nein!" / "Nein, nein, nein, nein!"
target_language_example: Nein, nein, nein — das machen wir auf keinen Fall.
native_language_example: No, no, no — we’re definitely not doing that.

additional_notes: Repeating „nein“ is a common way to strongly refuse, protest, or show shock/disbelief. More repetitions usually mean stronger emotion; it’s most common in spoken German (or informal writing) and the tone depends on context (angry, urgent, or sometimes playful).
target_language_example: Nein, nein, nein, nein! Das machen wir nicht.
native_language_example: No, no, no, no! We’re not doing that.

additional_notes: Used to strongly refuse, correct, or stop something: "Nein" rejects, and "nicht" negates what follows. Common in spoken German when you interrupt or contradict someone: "Nein, nicht so!" (= No, not like that!). It can also mean "No, not really" when followed by an adverb like "wirklich".
target_language_example: Nein, nicht so laut sprechen!
native_language_example: No, don't speak so loudly!

meaning: "No, just/only …" (to limit or correct what was said).
additional_notes: Used when you answer "no" and then add a restriction or clarification. Often followed by a noun phrase or infinitive (e.g., "nur unterschreiben" = "just sign"), or "nur, dass …" meaning "only that …" / "just that …".
target_language_example: Nein, nur kurz – ich habe gleich einen Termin.
native_language_example: No, just briefly—I have an appointment soon.

additional_notes: Used at the start of a reply to say that something is not true, followed by "sie" as the subject. "Sie" can mean "she", "they", or the formal "you" depending on context; in these examples it means "she". Often followed by a verb: "Nein, sie ist ..." / "Nein, sie geht ...".
target_language_example: Nein, sie kommt heute nicht.
native_language_example: No, she isn’t coming today.

additional_notes: Used to contradict, correct, or refuse something and then state your own plan/need: "Nein, wir ..." + verb. Often said with a short pause after "Nein" for emphasis (like "No—WE..."). Common in conversations when responding to a suggestion, assumption, or order.
target_language_example: Nein, wir bleiben hier und warten.
native_language_example: No, we’re staying here and waiting.

additional_notes: A polite way to refuse or decline an offer, invitation, or help. Often used on its own (“Nein danke!”) or followed by a short reason (“Nein danke, ich habe Kopfschmerzen.”). In writing, you’ll often see a comma after “Nein” (Nein, danke), but the fixed phrase is also commonly written without it as “Nein danke”.
target_language_example: Nein danke, ich habe Kopfschmerzen.
native_language_example: No, thanks, I have a headache.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone what name to use for you in a polite/formal situation (Sie-form). Often combined with "bitte": "Nennen Sie mich bitte …". With "nicht" it means “don’t call me …”.
target_language_example: Nennen Sie mich bitte Frau Schneider.
native_language_example: Please call me Mrs. Schneider.

meaning: 'do you call' / 'do you name' (you = informal singular).
additional_notes: Used in questions with the verb "nennen" (to call/name). Often appears as: (1) "Wie nennst du ...?" = "What do you call ...?" (asking for the name/term), or (2) "Das nennst du ...?" = "You call that ...?" which is often rhetorical/critical (showing surprise or disagreement).
target_language_example: Das nennst du pünktlich?
native_language_example: You call that being on time?

additional_notes: Used with an indefinite subject “man” (= “one/people”). Common patterns: (1) “Wie nennt man …?” = “What do you call …?” (asking for the word/name). (2) “Das nennt man …” = “That’s what you call …” (often to praise or comment on something).
target_language_example: Wie nennt man das auf Deutsch?
native_language_example: What do you call that in German?

additional_notes: From the verb **nennen** (to call/name). **Bitte nennt mich …** is an **informal plural** request to a group (friends, classmates): “Please call me …”. With a subject, it can also mean “calls me”: **Er nennt mich …** (“He calls me …”). For one person politely, you’d usually say **Nennen Sie mich …**.
target_language_example: Bitte nennt mich Alex.
native_language_example: Please call me Alex.

additional_notes: Used with the verb „sein“ (to be) to describe someone’s emotional state (feeling anxious/uneasy). It commonly appears in an infinitive clause after verbs like „scheinen“ (to seem): „Er scheint nervös zu sein.“ You can add intensifiers like „ein wenig“ (a little), „sehr“ (very), or „überaus“ (extremely).
target_language_example: Tom scheint sehr nervös zu sein, weil er gleich ein Vorstellungsgespräch hat.
native_language_example: Tom seems to be very nervous because he has a job interview in a moment.

additional_notes: Used to comment on or thank someone for a kind action: **(Das ist) nett von dir/euch/ihm/ihr/ihnen.** Often appears with **Wie nett von …!** (“How nice of …!”). The person is introduced with **von** + dative pronoun/name.
target_language_example: Das ist sehr nett von dir, dass du mich abholst.
native_language_example: That’s very nice of you to pick me up.

additional_notes: Used to thank someone for something kind they did or said. "Ihnen" is the formal “you” (to one person or a group). Common patterns: "Das ist (sehr/unheimlich) nett von Ihnen" and "Es war nett von Ihnen, …".
target_language_example: Das war wirklich nett von Ihnen, mir zu helfen.
native_language_example: That was really nice of you to help me.

additional_notes: Used to thank someone or show appreciation for a kind action or comment. Often appears as: „(Es war) nett von dir, … zu …“ (“It was nice of you to …”) or as an exclamation: „Wie nett von dir!“ (“How nice of you!”).
target_language_example: Das ist echt nett von dir, mir zu helfen.
native_language_example: That’s really nice of you to help me.

meaning: 'nice of you (to do something) for me' / 'kind of you (to help me)'.
additional_notes: Used to thank someone or show appreciation for something they do for you. Pattern: (Das/Es) ist/war (sehr) nett von dir, mir + zu-infinitive ("… zu helfen") or + noun phrase ("mir ein Geschenk zu machen"). In exclamations you can also say: "Wie nett von dir, mir zu helfen!"
target_language_example: Es ist wirklich nett von dir, mir beim Umzug zu helfen.
native_language_example: It’s really nice of you to help me with the move.

additional_notes: Used to thank or react positively to something someone (a group, or someone you address with ihr) did or said. Often appears as: „Das ist (echt/sehr) nett von euch.“ / „Es war nett von euch, …“ / „Wie nett von euch!“
target_language_example: Wie nett von euch, dass ihr uns geholfen habt!
native_language_example: How nice of you all to help us!

additional_notes: Used with a person (often in dative): "nett zu + jemandem". It describes how you behave toward someone: "Sei nett zu ihr" = "Be nice to her."
target_language_example: Bitte sei nett zu deinem Bruder.
native_language_example: Please be nice to your brother.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "sein" (or "war", "bist", etc.): "jemand ist nett zu mir" = someone is kind toward me. "zu" here means "to/toward" a person (often "nett zu + dative").
target_language_example: Danke, dass du immer nett zu mir bist.
native_language_example: Thanks for always being nice to me.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone's character or behavior as friendly, kind, or pleasant. Commonly appears with another verb (e.g., scheinen, versuchen) and with a complement like „zu jemandem“ or „jemandem gegenüber“ (e.g., „nett zu jemandem sein“ = to be nice to someone).
target_language_example: Dein Vater scheint nett zu sein.
native_language_example: Your father seems to be nice.

additional_notes: A friendly, approving way to talk about a man. Often used with an article: „(ein) netter Kerl“. Words like „ganz“ and „sehr“ intensify it: „ein ganz/sehr netter Kerl“ = “a really/very nice guy.” „Kerl“ is a bit colloquial, but not rude in this context.
target_language_example: Er ist ein wirklich netter Kerl und hilft immer.
native_language_example: He’s a really nice guy and always helps.

additional_notes: A friendly, positive way to describe someone’s character. Usually used with an article: „ein netter Mensch“ (a nice person). „Mensch“ is masculine (der Mensch), and the adjective changes with case/article: „ein netter Mensch“, „der nette Mensch“, plural „nette Menschen“.
target_language_example: Er ist ein netter Mensch und hilft gerne.
native_language_example: He’s a nice person and likes to help.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "versuchen" (to try) or "probieren" (to try): "Hast du versucht, den Router neu zu starten?" It means turning a device off and on again, or restarting it so it starts fresh. The separable verb is "neu starten"; in an infinitive construction with "zu" it becomes "neu zu starten".
target_language_example: Ich versuche, mein Handy neu zu starten.
native_language_example: I’m trying to restart my phone.

additional_notes: Most commonly means a new job/position (“eine neue Arbeit haben”). In some contexts it can also mean new work/tasks, but for jobs German often also uses “ein neuer Job” or “eine neue Stelle”. “Arbeit” is feminine: die Arbeit, eine neue Arbeit, seine neue Arbeit.
target_language_example: Ich fange nächste Woche eine neue Arbeit an.
native_language_example: I’m starting a new job next week.

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb "(neue) Freundschaften schließen" = "to make new friends / form new friendships." It often comes up when talking about moving somewhere new, starting school, or meeting people.
target_language_example: In einer neuen Stadt ist es nicht immer leicht, neue Freundschaften zu schließen.
native_language_example: In a new city, it’s not always easy to make new friends.

additional_notes: Used when talking about someone having changed their hair style or gotten a haircut. Often appears with the verb „haben“ (Du hast eine neue Frisur.) or with „eine neue Frisur“ as an object (eine neue Frisur wagen = to dare/try a new hairstyle). „Frisur“ is feminine: die Frisur, eine neue Frisur, meine neue Frisur.
target_language_example: Gefällt dir meine neue Frisur?
native_language_example: Do you like my new haircut?

additional_notes: An infinitive phrase with „zu“ („… zu lernen“ = “to learn …”). Often used after another verb (e.g., „Ich versuche/plane/hoffe, eine neue Sprache zu lernen.“) or as a subject („Eine neue Sprache zu lernen ist…“).
target_language_example: Ich versuche, eine neue Sprache zu lernen.
native_language_example: I'm trying to learn a new language.

additional_notes: In the examples, **neuen Anzug** is in the **accusative** (direct object) masculine form: *einen neuen Anzug*. The base form is **der neue Anzug** (nominative). Often used with verbs like **kaufen** (to buy), **anziehen** (to put on/wear), and **anfertigen lassen** (to have [it] made). You may hear both **Wie finden Sie ...?** (formal) and **Wie findest du ...?** (informal) for “What do you think of ...?”
target_language_example: Für die Hochzeit brauche ich einen neuen Anzug.
native_language_example: For the wedding I need a new suit.

additional_notes: A common past-action phrase built with the verb **kaufen** (to buy). It usually appears with **haben** in the Perfekt tense: **Ich habe einen neuen Computer gekauft.** Note the adjective ending: **einen neu**en** Computer** (masculine accusative after *einen*).
target_language_example: Ich habe mir einen neuen Computer gekauft.
native_language_example: I bought myself a new computer.

meaning: to introduce (one’s) new friend / new boyfriend.
additional_notes: Uses the verb **vorstellen** in the sense of **introducing someone**: *jemanden vorstellen* (to introduce someone). **Freund** can mean either **friend** or **boyfriend**; context usually makes it clear. Often used with a possessive: *meinen neuen Freund vorstellen* (introduce my new boyfriend/friend) or with the person you’re introducing them to: *meinen neuen Freund meinen Eltern vorstellen* (introduce my new boyfriend to my parents).
target_language_example: Ich möchte dir meinen neuen Freund vorstellen.
native_language_example: I’d like to introduce you to my new boyfriend/friend.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **treffen** (“to meet”) in the **Perfekt** (present perfect): **(jemanden) treffen → ich habe … getroffen**. The person met takes the **accusative** case. **Nachbarn** can be **plural** (“neighbors”) or **singular masculine** (“neighbor”) depending on the article/determiner: **meine neuen Nachbarn** (plural) vs. **meinen neuen Nachbarn** (singular masculine).
target_language_example: Hast du schon deine neuen Nachbarn getroffen?
native_language_example: Have you met your new neighbors yet?

additional_notes: Used with masculine accusative articles/pronouns (e.g., "einen/meinen/den neuen Wagen") because "Wagen" is masculine (der Wagen). Often means a (new) car, though "Wagen" can also mean a vehicle/wagon in some contexts. In the nominative it’s "ein neuer Wagen"; in the dative: "mit einem neuen Wagen".
target_language_example: Ich habe mir gestern einen neuen Wagen gekauft.
native_language_example: I bought myself a new car yesterday.

additional_notes: "Roman" in German means "novel" (a work of fiction). Don’t confuse it with English "Roman" (related to ancient Rome). Often used when talking about a new book by an author or a recently released novel. Note: in many sentences you’ll also see the inflected form (e.g., "einen neuen Roman"), but the base term is "neuer Roman".
target_language_example: Ihr neuer Roman erscheint nächste Woche.
native_language_example: Her new novel is coming out next week.

additional_notes: Means a car that is new (often: newly bought). In German, adjectives change endings: with "ein" you say "ein neues Auto" (neuter noun "das Auto"); with "sein" you say "sein neues Auto".
target_language_example: Ich habe mir ein neues Auto gekauft.
native_language_example: I bought myself a new car.

additional_notes: An infinitive phrase. In a full sentence, you usually add an article: „ein neues Auto kaufen“. After a modal verb (möchten, wollen, können, müssen), the verb „kaufen“ often stays in the infinitive at the end: „Ich möchte ein neues Auto kaufen.“
target_language_example: Ich möchte ein neues Auto kaufen.
native_language_example: I’d like to buy a new car.

additional_notes: "Neues" is the neuter form of "neu" (new) to match "das Buch" (neuter). Often used with an article or possessive: "ein neues Buch" (a new book), "mein/dein/sein neues Buch" (my/your/his new book).
target_language_example: Ich habe ein neues Buch gekauft.
native_language_example: I bought a new book.

additional_notes: "Neues" is the neuter form of "neu" (new) to match "das Fahrrad" (bike). Often used with verbs like "kaufen" (to buy), "haben" (to have), and "(sich) leisten" (to afford), e.g., "Ich kann mir kein neues Fahrrad leisten."
target_language_example: Ich spare für ein neues Fahrrad.
native_language_example: I'm saving for a new bike.

additional_notes: Used with the adjective "neu" (new) plus the neuter noun "das Haus" (house/home). In the nominative/accusative with no article, it becomes "neues Haus" ("-es" ending). With an article or possessive, the ending changes: "das neue Haus", "sein neues Haus", "unser neues Haus".
target_language_example: Wir ziehen nächste Woche in unser neues Haus ein.
native_language_example: We’re moving into our new house next week.

additional_notes: A common fragment meaning that someone has built a new house. In a full sentence you usually add an article and use the perfect tense: **Ich habe ein neues Haus gebaut.** (built = *haben* + past participle *gebaut*). You can also use simple past in writing: **Ich baute ein neues Haus.**
target_language_example: Wir haben letztes Jahr ein neues Haus gebaut.
native_language_example: We built a new house last year.

additional_notes: "Kleid" means "dress" (a noun). "Neu" is an adjective; with "ein" it becomes "ein neues Kleid" (neuter: das Kleid). With a possessive (mein/ihr/sein…) it’s also "mein/ihr neues Kleid". You can change the adjective: "ein schönes Kleid" (a nice dress).
target_language_example: Ich habe ein neues Kleid gekauft.
native_language_example: I bought a new dress.

additional_notes: Used to state a time. Often with **um** for “at” (e.g., *um neun Uhr*). In time ranges you’ll see **von … bis …** (“from … to …”), and you can also see it without **um**, especially in informal speech (e.g., *Ich komme neun Uhr*).
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns um neun Uhr vor dem Museum.
native_language_example: We’re meeting at nine o’clock in front of the museum.

additional_notes: Used to state someone’s age. With "sein" it describes how old someone is ("Er ist neunzig Jahre alt"). With "werden" it means to turn/reach that age ("Er wird neunzig Jahre alt"), and in the past it can mean someone lived to that age ("Er wurde neunzig Jahre alt").
target_language_example: Meine Nachbarin ist neunzig Jahre alt und sehr aktiv.
native_language_example: My neighbor is ninety years old and very active.

additional_notes: Used to contrast two clauses: something is not the case (or not done), but something else is. Typically you say it as a pattern: „nicht …, aber …“. In writing, there’s usually a comma before „aber“ when it connects two clauses.
target_language_example: Ich gehe heute nicht, aber morgen habe ich Zeit.
native_language_example: I’m not going today, but I have time tomorrow.

meaning: 'not that …' / 'so that … not' (to prevent a misunderstanding or warn about a possible outcome).
additional_notes: Used to add a clarification like English “not that …” (often with Konjunktiv II: „Nicht, dass du denkst, …“). It can also introduce a warning meaning “so that you don’t … / in case …” (common in spoken German: „Beeil dich, nicht dass du den Zug verpasst.“).
target_language_example: Nicht, dass du denkst, ich hätte keine Lust – ich bin nur müde.
native_language_example: Not that you think I don’t feel like it—I’m just tired.

meaning: "that you ..." after a negative (e.g., "I don’t know/think/say that you...").
additional_notes: German often uses a subordinate clause with "dass" (= "that") after verbs like wissen (to know), merken (to notice), sagen (to say), erlauben (to allow). When the main clause is negative, you’ll often see "nicht, dass Sie ..." meaning "not ... that you ..." / "... that you ..." in English: "Ich wusste nicht, dass Sie ..." = "I didn’t know (that) you ...". The comma before "dass" is required. This is different from "Nicht dass ..." meaning "in case ..." (a warning), which is used in other contexts.
target_language_example: Ich glaube nicht, dass Sie heute Zeit haben.
native_language_example: I don’t think you have time today.

meaning: "that you ... not" / "that you don't ..." (used to introduce a 'dass'-clause).
additional_notes: Used before a subordinate clause with **dass** when the main verb expresses things like **not believing** or **not wanting** something: *Ich fasse es nicht, dass du ...* = “I can’t believe (that) you ...”; *Ich wollte nicht, dass du ...* = “I didn’t want you to ...”. In writing there is usually a comma before **dass**: *Ich fasse es nicht, dass du ...*. In the **dass**-clause, the conjugated verb typically goes to the end: *... dass du morgen kommst*.
target_language_example: Ich will nicht, dass du so spät nach Hause gehst.
native_language_example: I don’t want you to go home so late.

additional_notes: Used when the main clause is negated (nicht) and is followed by a subordinate clause with dass + subject er. Very common after verbs/phrases like wissen (to know), glauben (to think), wollen (to want), sich freuen (to be happy), sehen (to see): e.g., „Ich glaube nicht, dass er …“ = “I don’t think (that) he …”, „Ich will nicht, dass er …“ = “I don’t want him to …”. In the dass-clause, the conjugated verb goes to the end.
target_language_example: Ich glaube nicht, dass er heute kommt.
native_language_example: I don’t think he’s coming today.

meaning: “not that it …” / “(did) not … that it …” (with dass = “that”).
additional_notes: Used with the conjunction **dass** to introduce a subordinate clause. With verbs like **sagen / wissen / wollen**, it means “not (say/know/want) that it …”. The clause usually has **verb at the end** (e.g., *… dass es so schlimm ist*). A comma typically comes before **dass**.
target_language_example: Ich hoffe nicht, dass es heute regnet.
native_language_example: I hope it doesn’t rain today.

additional_notes: Used as an aside to correct a possible misunderstanding or to add a limitation: „Nicht, dass ich …“ = “Not that I … (but …)”. The verb goes to the end of the clause (subordinate clause word order): „Nicht, dass ich das wüsste.“ Note: Without the comma and in a different structure, „nicht, dass ich …“ can also appear as part of „nicht wollen, dass ich …“ = “(to) not want me to …”.
target_language_example: Nicht, dass ich mich beschweren will, aber das ist zu teuer.
native_language_example: Not that I want to complain, but that’s too expensive.

additional_notes: Used with a verb like "glauben", "bedeuten", or "vergessen" to introduce a "dass"-clause and negate it: "Ich glaube nicht, dass man..." = "I don’t think that people/you (in general)...". Here "man" means "one/people/you" in a general sense. Common in reminders too: "Vergiss/ Vergessen Sie nicht, dass man..." = "Don’t forget that (in general) ...".
target_language_example: Das heißt nicht, dass man keine Fehler machen darf.
native_language_example: That doesn’t mean you’re not allowed to make mistakes.

meaning: "not that she/they …" (used to say you don’t think/want/claim that she/they …).
additional_notes: Often introduces a subordinate clause with "dass" after verbs like "denken" (to think), "glauben" (to believe), "wollen" (to want), or "sich beklagen" (to complain): "Ich denke nicht, dass sie …" = "I don’t think she …". "sie" can mean "she" (singular) or "they" (plural)—the verb form in the clause helps you tell which.
target_language_example: Ich glaube nicht, dass sie heute kommt.
native_language_example: I don’t think she’s coming today.

meaning: "(that) we don't …" / "not that we …" (introduces a negative "dass"-clause about what we do/think).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like glauben, denken, wissen, finden, mögen, etc. The main clause is negative (e.g., "Du glaubst nicht …"), and then you add a dass-clause: "…, dass wir …". In the dass-clause, the conjugated verb goes to the end: "Du glaubst nicht, dass wir Zeit haben."
target_language_example: Ich glaube nicht, dass wir heute kommen können.
native_language_example: I don’t think we can come today.

additional_notes: Used when you negate a verb like wollen/möchten (to want), hoffen (to hope), glauben (to think/believe), etc., and then add a dependent clause with daß/dass. The comma is required: „Ich will nicht, daß …“. Modern spelling is „dass“ (instead of „daß“).
target_language_example: Ich will nicht, daß du dich verletzt.
native_language_example: I don't want you to get hurt.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like „wissen“, „verstehen“, „sagen“ to introduce an indirect yes/no question: „Ich weiß nicht, ob …“ (“I don’t know whether/if …”). The comma often comes before „ob“, and the verb usually goes to the end of the „ob“-clause.
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht, ob der Laden heute geöffnet ist.
native_language_example: I don’t know if the shop is open today.

meaning: "..., right?" / "..., isn’t it?" (a tag question asking for confirmation).
additional_notes: Used at the end of a sentence to check/confirm what you just said, often when you expect the listener to agree. Very common in spoken German. It usually follows a negative statement (with nicht/kein), but you can also hear it after positive statements in casual speech.
target_language_example: Du hast keinen Hunger, nicht, oder?
native_language_example: You’re not hungry, right?

additional_notes: Used when you *don’t know, don’t understand, or can’t explain the reason*. Typically follows verbs like **wissen**, **verstehen**, **begreifen**: **Ich weiß nicht, warum ...** / **Wir verstehen nicht, warum ...**. The comma is common because **warum** introduces a subordinate clause (**..., warum + verb at the end**). It can also stand alone: **Ich weiß nur nicht, warum.**
target_language_example: Ich verstehe nicht, warum er so spät kommt.
native_language_example: I don’t understand why he’s coming so late.

additional_notes: This is the combination of the negation **nicht** with the question/relative word **was** (“what”). It commonly appears in sentences with verbs like **wissen** (to know), **denken** (to think), **erzählen** (to tell): **Ich weiß nicht, was …** = “I don’t know what …”. It can also start a short correction/contrast: **Nicht, was wir uns erhofft hatten.** = “Not what we had hoped for.”
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht, was ich tun soll.
native_language_example: I don’t know what I should do.

additional_notes: Used with an indirect clause starting with **was ich …** ("what I …"). In German, indirect questions/clauses use **verb at the end**: *Ich wusste nicht, was ich sagen sollte.* It can also be used in commands to push back: *Sag/Erzähl mir nicht, was ich …* ("Don’t tell me what to …").
target_language_example: Sag mir nicht, was ich fühlen soll!
native_language_example: Don’t tell me what I should feel!

meaning: "not what she/they …" (introduces a "what"-clause after a negation).
additional_notes: Used with a comma before a "was"-clause, often after verbs like "wissen" (to know) or statements like "Es stimmt nicht, was sie sagt". "sie" can mean "she" or "they" depending on context. The rest of the clause usually continues with a verb: "… was sie sagen/tun/bedeuten".
target_language_example: Ich verstehe nicht, was sie meint.
native_language_example: I don't understand what she means.

additional_notes: Used to deny a reason that someone might assume: "nicht, weil X" = "not because X". Often followed by a contrasting true reason with "sondern weil ..." ("but because ..."). The comma is common when the speaker pauses: "Nicht, weil ..." can also start a sentence fragment for emphasis.
target_language_example: Ich sage das nicht, weil ich böse bin, sondern weil ich helfen will.
native_language_example: I'm not saying that because I'm angry, but because I want to help.

additional_notes: Used to say something does NOT happen under a certain condition. Often appears as a short, emphatic answer at the beginning of a sentence: "Nicht, wenn ..." (= "Not if/when ..."). The comma is common when "nicht" is set off for emphasis; without emphasis you’ll also see: "..., wenn ... nicht ..." depending on word order.
target_language_example: Nicht, wenn ich morgen früh arbeiten muss.
native_language_example: Not if I have to work early tomorrow.

meaning: "don’t you know who …?" (introducing an indirect question with wer).
additional_notes: Used after a verb like wissen/kennen to introduce an indirect question: „(Weißt/Wissen) du/Sie nicht, wer …?“ The comma often comes before „wer“ because it starts the embedded question clause. „wer“ changes case depending on its role: wer (nom.), wen (acc.), wem (dat.).
target_language_example: Weißt du nicht, wer dir geholfen hat?
native_language_example: Don’t you know who helped you?

additional_notes: Used after verbs like **wissen** (to know): **Du weißt nicht, wer ich bin.** The comma is typical because **wer ich bin** is an embedded question/subordinate clause (“who I am”). Often used when someone doesn’t recognize you, or (with **Ich**) to express confusion about your identity.
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, Sie kennen mich nicht, wer ich bin.
native_language_example: Sorry, you don’t know who I am.

additional_notes: Used when someone doesn’t know, doesn’t understand, or can’t explain *how* something happens/is done. The comma usually appears because the “wie …” part is a subordinate clause (often with verbs like: wissen, verstehen, erklären, glauben). It can also stand alone as “Ich weiß nicht, wie.” = “I don’t know how.”
target_language_example: Ich verstehe nicht, wie das passiert ist.
native_language_example: I don’t understand how that happened.

meaning: "(don’t) know where" (introduces an indirect question about location).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like *wissen* (to know) or *sagen* (to tell) to introduce an indirect question: *Ich weiß nicht, wo …* = “I don’t know where …”. The *wo*-clause is a subordinate clause, so the verb usually goes to the end: *Ich weiß nicht, wo er wohnt.*
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht, wo die nächste U-Bahn-Station ist.
native_language_example: I don’t know where the nearest subway station is.

additional_notes: Used before an adjective/adverb (or a quantity phrase like "viele") to soften it: "not too/that". Often implies something is limited or moderate (e.g., not many, not big, not important).
target_language_example: Die Aufgabe war nicht allzu schwierig.
native_language_example: The task wasn’t too difficult.

meaning: “not …” with separable verbs that have the prefix “an-” (e.g., not start/turn on, not last, not bite).
additional_notes: In many German separable verbs, the prefix “an-” moves to the end of the clause: *Das Auto springt nicht an* (“The car doesn’t start”). Here *nicht* negates the verb, and *an* is the separated prefix. The exact meaning depends on the full verb: *nicht anhalten* (not last), *jemandem etwas nicht antun* (not do something to someone), *nicht anspringen/angehen* (not start/turn on), *nicht anbeten* (not worship/adore), *nicht anbeißen* (not take the bait / not bite).
target_language_example: Mein Handy geht nicht an.
native_language_example: My phone won’t turn on.

meaning: “no other way / can’t be helped” or “not any different”.
additional_notes: Often used to say something cannot be changed: „Geht nicht anders.“ = “There’s no other way / It can’t be helped.” It can also mean “not any different” in comparisons or results: „Es wird (dadurch) nicht anders.“ = “It won’t be any different (because of that).” In „nicht anders verdient“, it means “deserve no better.”
target_language_example: Ich würde gern kommen, aber es geht nicht anders.
native_language_example: I’d like to come, but there’s no other way (I can’t).

meaning: not answer the phone (not pick up).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "gehen" ("ans Telefon gehen") to mean answering a ringing phone. In questions like "Warum gehst du nicht ans Telefon?", it often expresses impatience or concern that someone isn’t picking up.
target_language_example: Ich kann gerade nicht ans Telefon gehen.
native_language_example: I can’t answer the phone right now.

additional_notes: “Nicht” negates phrases that use the preposition/particle “auf”. It can mean literally “not on” with locations (nicht auf dem Tisch), and it also appears with many verbs that take “auf” (e.g., auf etwas achten = pay attention to; auf jemanden hören = listen to; auf eine Frage antworten = answer a question; auf etwas treten/schlagen = step/hit on/onto; auf einen Namen kommen = remember/think of a name). The exact English translation depends on the verb.
target_language_example: Bitte tritt nicht auf das Gras.
native_language_example: Please don’t step on the grass.

additional_notes: Used to say that a person, thing, or option is missing from an official or expected list (guest list, signup list, menu/options list, etc.). Often appears with „stehen“: „(nicht) auf der Liste stehen“ = “to be (not) on the list.” Can also be used as a short standalone reply: „Nicht auf der Liste.“
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, Ihr Name steht nicht auf der Liste.
native_language_example: Sorry, your name isn't on the list.

meaning: “not on/onto the …” (used before a feminine/plural noun in the accusative).
additional_notes: Used with verbs that take **auf + Akkusativ** to show movement/impact onto something, especially in warnings/commands: **Nicht auf die Flammen treten!** (“Don’t step on the flames!”), **nicht auf die Decke schlagen** (“don’t hit the blanket/ceiling”). It can also appear as part of set phrases like **etw. auf die Probe stellen** (“to put sth to the test”): **Stell … nicht auf die Probe.**
target_language_example: Bitte nicht auf die Blumen treten.
native_language_example: Please don’t step on the flowers.

meaning: 'not on me' (e.g., 'don’t count on me / don’t wait for me / don’t listen to me').
additional_notes: Used with verbs that take **auf + accusative (Akk.)**: **auf mich** = “on me / for me.” Common patterns: **(nicht) auf mich zählen** = (not) count on me; **(nicht) auf mich warten** = (not) wait for me; **(nicht) auf mich hören** = (not) listen to me / obey me. Word order can vary, e.g. **Hör nicht auf mich!** or **Er hört nicht auf mich.**
target_language_example: Zähl heute bitte nicht auf mich.
native_language_example: Please don’t count on me today.

additional_notes: Used to weaken/soften a statement. Often with adjectives/adverbs ("nicht besonders interessant/einfach/gut") or with verbs of liking ("jdn. nicht besonders mögen" = not like someone very much). Depending on context, it can sound mildly negative ("Sieht nicht besonders aus" = It doesn’t look like much).
target_language_example: Heute bin ich nicht besonders motiviert.
native_language_example: Today I’m not particularly motivated.

additional_notes: Used either as (1) an order: „Nicht bewegen!“ = “Don’t move!”, often in urgent situations or when taking a photo; or (2) with a body part or reflexive „sich“: „Ich kann meine Hände/Beine nicht bewegen.“ = “I can’t move my hands/legs.” In commands to a person, you also often hear „Beweg dich nicht!“ or „Du sollst dich nicht bewegen!“
target_language_example: Nicht bewegen! Ich mache schnell ein Foto.
native_language_example: Don’t move! I’m taking a quick photo.

additional_notes: Often used to ask someone not to be angry: „Sei mir nicht böse“ = “Don’t be mad at me” (literally “Don’t be angry to me”). Common with dative pronouns like mir/dir/ihr/ihm. Also in phrases like „nicht böse gemeint“ / „nicht böse meinen“ = “not meant in a bad way” / “I didn’t mean it badly.”
target_language_example: Sei mir nicht böse, ich habe es wirklich vergessen.
native_language_example: Don’t be mad at me, I really forgot.

meaning: "not talk about it" / "not talk about that."
additional_notes: Used to refuse or avoid discussing a topic. "darüber" refers back to something already mentioned ("about it/that"). Often used with softeners like "lieber" (rather) or "vielleicht" (maybe) to sound more polite: "Ich möchte lieber nicht darüber reden."
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, ich kann nicht darüber reden.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can't talk about it.

meaning: "You can't be serious." / "You must be kidding."
additional_notes: Used to express disbelief, shock, or annoyance at what someone just said or did. Very common in the pattern "Das ist (doch/wohl) nicht dein Ernst!" The add-ons "doch" and "wohl" make it sound more emphatic. Colloquial and can sound quite accusatory depending on tone.
target_language_example: Nicht dein Ernst – du hast schon wieder den Schlüssel verloren?
native_language_example: You can’t be serious—you lost the key again?

additional_notes: Used to say a person or thing is not unique in a situation: someone/something else also exists or did the same. It often appears as: „Du bist nicht der/die Einzige …“ (you’re not the only one …), „Ich bin nicht der/die Einzige.“ (I’m not the only one.), or „Das war nicht der einzige Grund.“ (That wasn’t the only reason.). The word changes for gender and case: der Einzige (male), die Einzige (female), das Einzige (neuter, usually with things/ideas), and plural: die Einzigen. Example: „Du bist nicht die Einzige, die so denkt.“
target_language_example: Du bist nicht der Einzige, der einen Fehler gemacht hat.
native_language_example: You’re not the only one who made a mistake.

additional_notes: Used with a following infinitive clause (often with „zu“), e.g. „nicht die Absicht, … zu + infinitive“. It’s a formal/neutral way to say you don’t plan to do something, or that you didn’t mean to do something (often in apologies: „Ich hatte nicht die Absicht, … zu verletzen.“).
target_language_example: Ich habe nicht die Absicht, heute länger zu bleiben.
native_language_example: I have no intention of staying longer today.

additional_notes: Often used to say something is difficult, challenging, or complicated. It can describe a task (Es war nicht einfach, ...), a situation (Das wird nicht einfach sein.), or people/behavior (Sie sind nicht einfach = “They’re difficult / not straightforward”). In speech you can stress it for emphasis: Das ist wirklich nicht einfach.
target_language_example: Es ist nicht einfach, eine neue Sprache zu lernen.
native_language_example: It’s not easy to learn a new language.

meaning: “not just like that”; “not simply / not that easily (without reason or consequences)”
additional_notes: Used to say something can’t happen or be done casually, without explanation, permission, or consequences. Often with verbs like passieren, wegbleiben, einsperren, wegwerfen: „Das kann man nicht einfach so …“ = “You can’t just … (like that).” Related: „einfach so“ alone often means “just (like that), for no particular reason.”
target_language_example: Du kannst nicht einfach so gehen, ohne etwas zu sagen.
native_language_example: You can’t just leave like that without saying anything.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is true even in the smallest/least expected case (“not even X”). Can also mean “not even once” with time/amount expressions (e.g., nicht einmal eine Stunde / nicht einmal einen Monat). Often appears with a noun/pronoun: „nicht einmal seine Mutter“.
target_language_example: Ich hatte nicht einmal Zeit, mich zu verabschieden.
native_language_example: I didn’t even have time to say goodbye.

meaning: “not for me” / “not for my benefit” (often: “no thanks, not for me”).
additional_notes: Used to refuse something politely (especially after an offer), or to say something isn’t meant for you or isn’t done for your benefit. Often contrasts with “für dich / für ihn / für sie” etc.: „Wir machen das für dich, nicht für mich.“
target_language_example: Nein danke, das ist nicht für mich.
native_language_example: No thanks, that’s not for me.

additional_notes: Used to soften a statement or say something is only partly true/finished (often with adjectives or verbs): „nicht ganz verstanden“ = didn’t fully understand; „nicht ganz ehrlich“ = not entirely honest; „nicht ganz unrecht“ = not completely wrong. In fixed phrases like „nicht ganz auf dem Damm“ it means someone isn’t feeling well / isn’t back to normal.
