target_language_example: Ich bin nicht ganz sicher, ob das stimmt.
native_language_example: I’m not quite sure if that’s true.

additional_notes: Used to say something is insufficient in amount/quantity/degree. Often followed by an infinitive clause (e.g., „nicht genug zu essen“ = not enough to eat) or „für + Akkusativ“ (e.g., „nicht genug für dich“ = not enough for you). In „Ich kann Sie nicht genug loben“, it’s an idiomatic intensifier meaning “I can’t praise you enough” (i.e., very much).
target_language_example: Wir haben nicht genug Zeit, um alles zu erledigen.
native_language_example: We don’t have enough time to get everything done.

additional_notes: Used to express very strong gratitude. Commonly said as: „Ich kann dir/Ihnen (gar) nicht genug danken (für …).“ Use „dir“ for friends/family and „Ihnen“ for formal situations. „gar“ intensifies it (“really/absolutely”).
target_language_example: Ich kann dir gar nicht genug danken für alles, was du getan hast.
native_language_example: I really can’t thank you enough for everything you’ve done.

additional_notes: Used to say that the amount/quantity/degree is insufficient. Typically placed before the thing that is lacking (nicht genug Orangen) or before a noun like Zeit/Geld/Licht (nicht genug Zeit/Geld/Licht). Often used with verbs as an adverb: sich nicht genug Mühe geben (not make enough effort).
target_language_example: Ich habe nicht genug Zeit, um heute zu kommen.
native_language_example: I don't have enough time to come today.

additional_notes: Used to deny having said something. The verb changes with the subject (ich habe/du hast/er hat … nicht gesagt, dass …). In speech you often hear the shorter form: „Ich hab nicht gesagt, dass …“. The clause after „dass“ goes to the end in German: „… dass ich dich liebe / dass jemand dabei getötet wird“.
target_language_example: Ich habe nicht gesagt, dass du schuld bist.
native_language_example: I didn’t say that it was your fault.

additional_notes: Used with **es** to mean you didn’t succeed in doing something: **Ich habe es nicht geschafft.** Often appears with past tenses (**haben** + **geschafft**) or conditional (**hätte(n) … nicht geschafft**) and can be followed by **zu + infinitive**: **Ich habe es nicht geschafft, anzurufen.**
target_language_example: Ich habe es heute nicht geschafft, dich anzurufen.
native_language_example: I didn’t manage to call you today.

additional_notes: Past participle of "sehen" used with "haben" (e.g., "Ich habe ihn nicht gesehen" = "I didn’t see him / I haven’t seen him"). Very common in questions asking if someone has seen a person/thing: "Hast du X nicht gesehen?" (sometimes implies surprise: "You didn’t see X?").
target_language_example: Hast du meinen Schlüssel nicht gesehen?
native_language_example: Haven’t you seen my key?

additional_notes: Used to say something is bad/unsatisfactory (Das ist nicht gut.) or that something doesn’t sound/look good (Das klingt/sieht nicht gut aus.). With feelings/health it often means “not well” (Ich fühle mich nicht gut.). It can also be used with “in/bei” to mean “not good at” (Ich bin nicht gut im… / Ich bin nicht gut bei…).
target_language_example: Heute geht es mir nicht gut.
native_language_example: I’m not feeling well today.

meaning: not good; not going well; not approved of.
additional_notes: Used to say something is going badly (often with verbs like "laufen" or "ausgehen": "Es läuft nicht gut", "Das geht nicht gut aus"). It can also mean something was poorly received ("nicht gut ankommen") or that you don’t approve of something ("Das heiße ich nicht gut" = "I don’t approve of that").
target_language_example: Die Verhandlungen laufen nicht gut.
native_language_example: The negotiations aren’t going well.

meaning: to not help; to be unable to help.
additional_notes: Used to say someone doesn’t help or can’t help. Often appears with a modal verb like „können“: „nicht helfen können“ = “to be unable to help.” In questions and statements with a modal, the infinitive „helfen“ goes to the end: „Kann er nicht helfen?“ / „Ich kann nicht helfen.“
target_language_example: Ich kann dir leider nicht helfen.
native_language_example: Unfortunately, I can't help you.

meaning: 'not here to' (not here in order to).
additional_notes: Used to say what someone is NOT present for, often to clarify intentions. It’s typically followed by an infinitive verb (sometimes with an object): „Ich bin nicht hier, um zu helfen.“ / „Ich bin nicht hier, um Ihnen zu helfen.“ Also common in questions: „Bist du nicht hier, um …?“
target_language_example: Ich bin nicht hier, um zu streiten.
native_language_example: I'm not here to argue.

meaning: to not be here; to not be allowed/supposed to be here.
additional_notes: Literally “not here be.” Often used with modal verbs like dürfen (to be allowed to) or sollen (to be supposed to) to say someone is not allowed or not supposed to be in this place. With du/Sie/wir it changes by the modal verb, not by this phrase: Du darfst nicht hier sein! / Sie dürfen nicht hier sein! / Wir sollen nicht hier sein.
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich darf nicht hier sein.
native_language_example: Sorry, I'm not allowed to be here.

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb **lassen**: **jemanden (nicht) im Stich lassen**. It means you will stay reliable and support the person, especially when it matters. Common in requests and promises: **Lass/Bitte lass mich nicht im Stich!**
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, ich lasse dich nicht im Stich.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I won’t let you down.

additional_notes: Used to say something is true only sometimes (not in every case). Often appears with general statements ("X ist nicht immer …") or habits/routines ("Er macht das nicht immer"). In questions like "Können Sie das nicht immer?", it can suggest surprise/complaint: “Can’t you always do that?”.
target_language_example: Ich habe nicht immer Zeit, dir zu helfen.
native_language_example: I don't always have time to help you.

meaning: "not always like that" / "not always this way."
additional_notes: Used to say a situation or behavior is not constant, or to push back against a generalization ("It isn’t always like that"). With people, it can be an admonition: "Don’t always be like that!" (Seid… = informal plural; Seien Sie… = formal). Often implies “stop doing that so often.”
target_language_example: Sei nicht immer so ungeduldig!
native_language_example: Don’t always be so impatient!

additional_notes: Used to negate something with in. With the dative, it usually means not in a place or location (nicht in Boston). With the accusative, it often means not into / not to when there is movement or direction (nicht in die Schule gehen).
target_language_example: Ich gehe heute nicht in die Stadt.
native_language_example: I'm not going into town today.

meaning: “out of the question” / “no way” (not an option).
additional_notes: Usually used in the set phrase **(gar/überhaupt) nicht in Frage kommen** (“to be completely out of the question”), often to strongly refuse an idea or say something is not possible/acceptable. Can also be used alone as **Kommt nicht in Frage!**
target_language_example: Für mich kommt das nicht in Frage.
native_language_example: That’s out of the question for me.

meaning: not OK; not working properly; wrong.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is wrong, off, or not functioning correctly. Often appears with "etwas/irgendwas ist ... nicht in Ordnung" (something is not right) or "Ist etwas ... nicht in Ordnung?" (Is something wrong?). Commonly used with "mit" + dative: "Mit der Waschmaschine ist etwas nicht in Ordnung" = There’s something wrong with the washing machine.
target_language_example: Mit deinem Handy ist etwas nicht in Ordnung.
native_language_example: There’s something wrong with your phone.

meaning: not in peace / not undisturbed; unable to do something without being bothered.
additional_notes: Used to say you can’t do something calmly because of noise, interruptions, or people bothering you. Very common with the verb "lassen": "Lass mich in Ruhe!" = "Leave me alone!" / "Stop bothering me!".
target_language_example: Ich kann mich hier nicht in Ruhe konzentrieren.
native_language_example: I can’t concentrate here in peace.

meaning: "not into the" / "not in the" (with a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used to negate going/moving/putting something into a place or situation. "in den" is "in + den" (accusative masculine), typically used with movement/change of location (e.g., gehen/fahren/steigen/stellen). For location without movement you often use dative: "nicht in dem" (often shortened to "nicht im").
target_language_example: Bitte stell das nicht in den Schrank.
native_language_example: Please don’t put that into the cupboard.

meaning: 'not in the' / 'not within' (used before a feminine noun in the dative).
additional_notes: Often appears in set expressions that describe something being outside a scope, power, reach, or state. Common patterns: „nicht in der Geschichte“ (= not part of the story), „nicht in der Macht von …“ (= not in someone’s power), „nicht in der Reichweite von …“ (= not within someone’s reach), „nicht in der Stimmung (für) …“ (= not in the mood (for) …). It’s literally „nicht“ + „in“ + „der“ (feminine dative: in der + noun).
target_language_example: Ich bin heute nicht in der Stimmung für ein langes Gespräch.
native_language_example: I’m not in the mood for a long conversation today.

additional_notes: Used to say someone cannot do something (because of ability, circumstances, health, etc.). Very common with an infinitive clause: „nicht in der Lage sein, + zu + Infinitiv“ (e.g., „Er ist nicht in der Lage, zu kommen.“). It can also be used without a verb in the phrase, relying on context: „Er ist nicht in der Lage dazu.“
target_language_example: Ich bin heute nicht in der Lage, dir zu helfen.
native_language_example: I'm not able to help you today.

meaning: not at school; absent from school.
additional_notes: Used to say someone didn’t attend school on a particular day/period. Very common with forms of "sein" (war, bist, wart): "Ich war nicht in der Schule" = "I wasn’t at school." Often followed by a reason with "weil" (because) or "wegen" + Genitive/Dative (because of).
target_language_example: Heute bin ich nicht in der Schule, weil ich einen Arzttermin habe.
native_language_example: Today I’m not at school because I have a doctor’s appointment.

meaning: not in town; out of town.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is not currently in the city/town (often because they’re traveling). Common with time expressions like "diese Woche" or "letzte Woche". You can also use it in longer clauses like "solange ich nicht in der Stadt bin" (“as long as I’m out of town”).
target_language_example: Ich bin am Wochenende nicht in der Stadt.
native_language_example: I’m out of town this weekend.

meaning: "not into the" / "not to the" (with in + accusative feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used with verbs that involve entering, being allowed in, putting something in, or making it into a group/place (e.g., „nicht in die Disko lassen“ = not let someone into the club; „nicht in die Datenbank kriegen“ = can’t get it into the database; „es nicht in die Mannschaft schaffen“ = not make it onto the team). Grammatically, „in die“ is the contraction of „in“ + accusative feminine article „die“, so it’s followed by a feminine noun (or plural „die“).
target_language_example: Ich darf heute Abend nicht in die Bar.
native_language_example: I’m not allowed into the bar tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say something won’t take much time, often to reassure someone ("It shouldn’t take long"). With future meaning you’ll often hear: „Es wird nicht lange dauern.“ You can also use it about how long something will last: „Das kann nicht lange dauern“ = “That can’t last long.”
target_language_example: Warte kurz, das wird nicht lange dauern.
native_language_example: Wait a moment, it won’t take long.

additional_notes: Used to say something is hard to do or hard to deal with. Very common in the pattern: „Es ist/war nicht leicht (für jdn), …“ = “It’s/was not easy (for someone) to …”. Also: „jdn/etw macht es (jdm) nicht leicht“ = “someone/something doesn’t make it easy (for someone)” (i.e., makes it harder).
target_language_example: Es ist nicht leicht für mich, so früh aufzustehen.
native_language_example: It’s not easy for me to get up so early.

meaning: to not like; to not be able to stand (someone/something).
additional_notes: Most often used with "können" ("Ich kann … nicht leiden") to express strong dislike or intolerance. It can be about a person ("Ich kann ihn nicht leiden"), a thing/food ("Ich kann Kaffee nicht leiden"), or a situation introduced with "wenn"/"dass" ("Ich kann es nicht leiden, wenn …" / "…, dass …"). Stronger than simple "nicht mögen" and often close to "can't stand".
target_language_example: Ich kann es nicht leiden, wenn man zu spät kommt.
native_language_example: I can’t stand it when people are late.

additional_notes: Used to say a state, situation, or rule has ended. Often placed before the part it negates (e.g., adjective/verb phrase): „Ich bin nicht länger müde.“ / „Er kann das nicht länger ertragen.“ Common in writing and formal speech; in everyday conversation people also say „nicht mehr“.
target_language_example: Wir können nicht länger warten.
native_language_example: We can’t wait any longer.

additional_notes: Used to say something stops being true or an action shouldn’t/ can’t continue. Often placed before the verb or at the end of the sentence: „Er arbeitet nicht länger hier.“ / „Er arbeitet hier nicht länger.“
target_language_example: Ich wohne nicht länger in Berlin.
native_language_example: I don’t live in Berlin anymore.

meaning: "not even"; in questions often "not even/at least" (showing surprise, annoyance, or impatience).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something doesn’t happen or isn’t true to the smallest degree. Common in statements: „Du kennst nicht mal …“ = “You don’t even know …”. In questions it can sound like a complaint or request for permission: „Darf ich dich nicht mal anrufen?“ ≈ “Can’t I even call you?” / “Can’t I at least call you (once)?”
target_language_example: Ich habe heute nicht mal Zeit für einen Kaffee.
native_language_example: I don't even have time for a coffee today.

additional_notes: Used when something used to be true or happen before, but is now no longer true or happening. It can also mean something will not happen again. Very common with verbs: Ich wohne nicht mehr hier. Compare it with noch nicht, which means 'not yet'.
target_language_example: Ich wohne nicht mehr in Berlin.
native_language_example: I don't live in Berlin anymore.

additional_notes: Used with **sein** to say someone/something is **no longer the way it used to be**: *Er ist nicht mehr, was er war.* Also common with **wissen** (*nicht mehr wissen, was …*) to mean **to no longer know / not remember what …**: *Ich weiß nicht mehr, was er gesagt hat.* The comma is typical when a **was-clause** follows.
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht mehr, was ich dir gestern geschrieben habe.
native_language_example: I can’t remember what I wrote to you yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to set an upper limit: "nicht mehr als zehn" = at most ten. You can also use it in comparisons: "nicht mehr als dir" = no more than you (do). Often followed by a number, an amount of money, or expressions like "nötig" (necessary).
target_language_example: Ich brauche nicht mehr als fünf Minuten.
native_language_example: I need no more than five minutes.

meaning: not there anymore; no longer around/present.
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something was present before but is now gone. With things it can simply mean it has disappeared (“Der Hubschrauber war nicht mehr da.”). With people it can mean they have left, or (especially “Sie/Er ist nicht mehr da.”) it can be a gentle way to say someone has died. Often used with forms of “da sein/da gewesen sein” (to be/have been there).
target_language_example: Als ich zurückkam, war mein Handy nicht mehr da.
native_language_example: When I came back, my phone wasn’t there anymore.

additional_notes: Used to say something has changed and isn’t the same as before, often with forms of "sein" (ist/war): "X ist nicht mehr das, was es (einmal/früher) war." The clause after "was" often uses "war" to refer to the past state.
target_language_example: Meine Lieblingsband ist nicht mehr das, was sie früher war.
native_language_example: My favorite band is no longer what it used to be.

meaning: “haven’t seen (someone/something) anymore / since then” (no longer saw / haven’t seen again).
additional_notes: Uses **nicht mehr** (“no longer / not anymore”) with **gesehen** (past participle of **sehen**, “to see”). Often appears with the **Perfekt**: *Ich habe ihn nicht mehr gesehen* (“I haven’t seen him anymore / again”). Very commonly used with time expressions like **seit** (“since”) or **schon lange** (“for a long time”). In narrative style you may also see it with **wurde/ward**: *Seitdem wurde/ward er nicht mehr gesehen* (“Since then he was not seen again”).
target_language_example: Seit dem Umzug habe ich meine Nachbarn nicht mehr gesehen.
native_language_example: Since the move, I haven’t seen my neighbors anymore.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is not in a place (or situation) anymore. The key part is "nicht mehr" = "no longer / not anymore"; it often comes right before a prepositional phrase like "in + Dativ" (in Australia, in public, etc.). Word order: subject + verb + nicht mehr in + place.
target_language_example: Wir sind nicht mehr in der Innenstadt.
native_language_example: We’re no longer in the city center.

additional_notes: Used to say that something will happen soon (often with "(es) dauert nicht mehr lange" = "it won’t take much longer"), or that something/someone won’t last much longer (e.g., a car, a battery, your patience). Often used without a verb as a short warning: "Nicht mehr lange jetzt."
target_language_example: Es ist nicht mehr lange bis wir ankommen.
native_language_example: It won’t be much longer until we arrive.

meaning: "not anymore / no longer (able/willing) to keep up/participate" (usually with a verb).
additional_notes: This is a common spoken chunk that typically appears with verbs like **mitkommen** (come along/keep up), **mitmachen** (join in/participate), or **mitbekommen** (catch/understand). Very common: **Ich komme nicht mehr mit.** = “I can’t keep up / I’m not following anymore.”
target_language_example: Ich komme nicht mehr mit—kannst du bitte langsamer sprechen?
native_language_example: I’m not following anymore—can you please speak more slowly?

meaning: to not see (someone/something) anymore; (also) to not be able to stand (someone) anymore.
additional_notes: Used with a direct object: jemanden/etwas nicht mehr sehen. Literal meaning: you no longer see something (e.g., because it’s gone or too dark). Common figurative meaning (often in spoken German): you’re fed up with someone—“I can’t stand him/her anymore.” Often appears as: Ich kann ihn/sie nicht mehr sehen.
target_language_example: Ich kann ihn nicht mehr sehen.
native_language_example: I can’t stand him anymore.

additional_notes: Used to say something is no longer the same degree as before. Often followed by an adjective/adverb or a comparison: “nicht mehr so + Adjektiv/Adverb (wie früher / wie …)”. Example patterns: “nicht mehr so stark”, “nicht mehr so oft”, “nicht mehr so bitter”. Sometimes “so” refers back to a situation already mentioned: “Jetzt ist es nicht mehr so” = “Now it’s not like that anymore.”
target_language_example: Ich bin nicht mehr so müde wie gestern.
native_language_example: I’m not as tired as yesterday anymore.

additional_notes: Used before a "zu"-infinitive to say something is not possible anymore or won’t happen anymore. Very common with an implied passive meaning: "nicht mehr zu reparieren/erkennen" = "can’t be repaired/recognized anymore". With a normal verb it can simply mean "not to (do something) anymore" (e.g., "ihm nicht mehr zu begegnen" = "not to run into him anymore"). The infinitive goes to the end: "… nicht mehr zu + Infinitiv".
target_language_example: Die Tür ist nicht mehr zu öffnen.
native_language_example: The door can’t be opened anymore.

additional_notes: Used with a verb of motion (e.g., gehen, kommen) or with können to say someone no longer returns or is no longer able to return. Often implies it’s no longer possible or it’s final/irreversible (e.g., after leaving, after a point of no return). Common patterns: „Er geht nicht mehr zurück.“ / „Sie kam nicht mehr zurück.“ / „Wir können nicht mehr zurück!“
target_language_example: Ich kann nicht mehr zurück, der letzte Zug ist schon weg.
native_language_example: I can’t go back anymore; the last train has already gone.

additional_notes: Used to negate actions that take **mit** (“with”), especially with people: **nicht mit jemandem spielen/reden/schlafen** = not play/talk/sleep with someone. The person after **mit** is in the **dative** (e.g., *mit meinem Vater*). Often used in phrases like **nicht mit jemandem reden** (“don’t talk to someone”) as a reprimand.
target_language_example: Ich rede nicht mit dir, wenn du so gemein bist.
native_language_example: I’m not talking to you if you’re being so mean.

additional_notes: *Mit dem* is **mit + dem** (dative case), used with **masculine/neuter** nouns: *mit dem Zug* (by train), *mit dem Motor* (with the engine). With transport it often means **"by"** (*nicht mit dem Boot* = not by boat). It also appears in set phrases like **"nicht mit etw. rechnen"** (not to expect/count on something): *Ich hatte nicht mit dem Problem gerechnet.*
target_language_example: Ich komme heute nicht mit dem Auto.
native_language_example: I’m not coming by car today.

meaning: "not with you" / "not to you" (often: "not talking to you").
additional_notes: Uses the preposition "mit" (with) + "dir" (you, dative). Common in negatives like "Ich rede nicht mit dir" (= I’m not talking to you) and in contrasts: "Mit ihm ..., nicht mit dir" (= with him ..., not with you). Also appears in the fixed question "Was stimmt nicht mit dir?" meaning "What’s wrong with you?" (can sound accusatory; stronger with swear words like "zur Hölle").
target_language_example: Ich will jetzt nicht mit dir darüber sprechen.
native_language_example: I don’t want to talk to you about it right now.

meaning: “not with me” / “not when it comes to me” (often: “not with me!” = “not going to happen with me”).
additional_notes: Used either literally (“not with me”) or as an emphatic refusal/protest: “Not with me!” / “Don’t count on me (to accept that).” Common with verbs like rechnen (to count on/expect): „nicht mit mir gerechnet“ = “didn’t count on me.” Word order can vary: „Mit mir nicht!“ is also common for emphasis.
target_language_example: Wenn du denkst, dass ich das einfach akzeptiere: nicht mit mir!
native_language_example: If you think I’ll just accept that: not with me!

additional_notes: Used with verbs like **mitgehen**/**mitkommen** (often split: *ich gehe/komme … mit*) to say you are **not** joining others. Typical in invitations/plans: *Kommst du mit?* → *Ich komme nicht mit.*
target_language_example: Heute Abend gehe ich nicht mit ins Kino.
native_language_example: I’m not coming along to the cinema tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say that something cannot be done or cannot happen (often because of rules, circumstances, or limitations). Common in neutral/formal statements like „Das ist/war/wird nicht möglich (sein).“
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, heute ist das leider nicht möglich.
native_language_example: Sorry, unfortunately that isn’t possible today.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of motion like kommen (to come) or gehen (to go) to say someone is not going/coming home. Often implies the direction/destination “home” (nach Hause), not the location “at home” (zu Hause). Word order: it’s usually "nicht" + destination ("nicht nach Hause").
target_language_example: Ich gehe heute nicht nach Hause, ich übernachte bei einem Freund.
native_language_example: I'm not going home today; I'm staying overnight at a friend's place.

additional_notes: Used to say something should not be repeated (often as a warning, request, or complaint). It can stand alone as an exclamation or be added to a sentence: „Mach das nicht noch einmal.“
target_language_example: Mach das nicht noch einmal!
native_language_example: Don’t do that again!

additional_notes: Used to say something should not be repeated. Often follows the verb: "Mach das nicht noch mal!" = "Don’t do that again!". In questions it can mean "(Could you) do it again/one more time?" depending on intonation and context: "Können Sie nicht noch mal (…)?".
target_language_example: Bitte mach das nicht noch mal.
native_language_example: Please don’t do that again.

additional_notes: Used to add extra information: 'not only X, (but) also Y'. Very often paired with "sondern auch" (or just "sondern") in the same sentence. Can also be used more generally to mean 'not just' (e.g., "Es geht nicht nur mir so" = 'It’s not just me').
target_language_example: Das ist nicht nur teuer, sondern auch schlecht gemacht.
native_language_example: That’s not only expensive, but also badly made.

nicht nur Englisch, sondern auch Französisch

target_language_multi_word_term: nicht nur Englisch, sondern auch Französisch
meaning: not only English, but also French.
additional_notes: Pattern: "nicht nur X, sondern auch Y" = "not only X, but also Y". Use it to add a second item that is also true (languages, skills, facts, etc.). Often used with verbs like "sprechen" or "können" when talking about languages.
target_language_example: Ich spreche nicht nur Englisch, sondern auch Französisch.
native_language_example: I speak not only English, but also French.

additional_notes: Used to say that something isn’t required or can be skipped. Often appears as a short reply: “Nicht nötig.” or with “sein”: “Das wird nicht nötig sein.” (That won’t be necessary). Can also be followed by “zu” + infinitive: “Nicht nötig, zu …” / “Es ist nicht nötig, zu …”.
target_language_example: Nicht nötig, ich kann das selbst machen.
native_language_example: No need, I can do that myself.

meaning: to not be necessary; to not be needed.
additional_notes: Used to say something won’t be required. Very common with the future: „Das wird nicht nötig sein.“ (= “That won’t be necessary.”). „nötig“ = necessary; „sein“ changes with the subject (ist/war/wird ... sein).
target_language_example: Mach dir keine Sorgen — das wird nicht nötig sein.
native_language_example: Don’t worry — that won’t be necessary.

additional_notes: Used to stress that something is necessary or must be included before an action happens. Often followed by a noun/pronoun: „nicht ohne meinen Ausweis“, „nicht ohne dich“. It can also be used as a short/elliptical warning or condition: „Nicht ohne den Fahrer.“ (= not without the driver).
target_language_example: Ich gehe nicht ohne meinen Ausweis ins Hotel.
native_language_example: I’m not going into the hotel without my ID.

meaning: not without reason; for good reason.
additional_notes: Used to say there is a real/justified reason for something (often implying suspicion, praise, or a situation is understandable). Can appear mid-sentence ("Er ist nicht ohne Grund …") or at the start for emphasis ("Nicht ohne Grund …").
target_language_example: Ich mache mir nicht ohne Grund Sorgen um dich.
native_language_example: I’m not worried about you without reason (I have good reason to worry about you).

additional_notes: Often used to say something is factually wrong (an answer, a statement) or that something is morally/socially wrong or inappropriate ("Das ist nicht richtig" = "That’s not right"). It can also soften criticism with "nicht richtig" meaning "not really" or "not quite" in some contexts.
target_language_example: Das klingt nicht richtig, lass uns das nochmal prüfen.
native_language_example: That doesn’t sound right—let’s check that again.

meaning: to not say (something); not to tell.
additional_notes: Uses **nicht** to negate the verb **sagen** (“to say/tell”). Often with an object like **das/es**: *Das darfst du nicht sagen* (“You mustn’t say that”). In instructions it can appear as an infinitive: *Nicht sagen, nur merken* (“Don’t say it, just remember”). Can also mean someone is unable or unwilling to say something: *Sie können es nicht sagen* (“You can’t/won’t say it”).
target_language_example: Bitte nicht sagen, was ich dir erzählt habe.
native_language_example: Please don’t say what I told you.

meaning: to not sleep; to be unable to sleep.
additional_notes: Used with können to say you can’t sleep: „Ich kann nicht schlafen.“ You can also use it as a short statement (dropping „ich“): „Kann nicht schlafen.“ Often followed by a reason with „wegen“ (because of) or „sodass“ (so that).
target_language_example: Ich kann heute Nacht nicht schlafen, weil ich zu viel Kaffee getrunken habe.
native_language_example: I can't sleep tonight because I drank too much coffee.

additional_notes: Used to give mild praise or say something is better than expected. Can stand alone as a reaction ("Nicht schlecht!"). Often means "quite good" rather than literally "not bad."
target_language_example: Die Idee ist nicht schlecht, aber wir brauchen noch mehr Zeit.
native_language_example: The idea isn’t bad, but we still need more time.

meaning: “not again” / “not already again!” (complaining that something is happening again).
additional_notes: A common exclamation when you’re annoyed, tired, or frustrated that something is repeating. Often said on its own (“Nicht schon wieder!”) or followed by a name (“Nicht schon wieder, Dora.”) or “bitte.” Stronger than just “nicht wieder” and has a dramatic “ugh, this again?” feeling.
target_language_example: Nicht schon wieder! Ich habe meinen Schlüssel schon wieder vergessen.
native_language_example: Not again! I forgot my key again.

additional_notes: Depending on context, it can mean (1) uncertain/not confident about something (often with sein: „Da bin ich nicht sicher.“), or (2) unsafe/not protected (often about a place or situation: „In diesem Land ist man nicht sicher.“).
target_language_example: Ich bin mir nicht sicher, ob das der richtige Weg ist.
native_language_example: I'm not sure if that's the right way.

additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty about something. It’s often followed by a full clause (subject + verb), and the verb typically goes to the end of the clause after „ob“. Tense changes with context (e.g., „bin“ present, „war“ past).
target_language_example: Wir sind nicht sicher, ob der Laden heute geöffnet ist.
native_language_example: We’re not sure if the shop is open today.

additional_notes: Usually limits the degree of something: nicht so + adjective/adverb means "not so / not as" (often with wie: nicht so jung wie ... = "not as young as ..."). It can also mean "not like that" in commands or criticism, as in Red nicht so = "don't talk like that" or Ändere deinen Plan nicht so oft = "don't change your plan so often."
target_language_example: Das Wetter ist heute nicht so gut.
native_language_example: The weather isn't so good today.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is different from what someone expected, wanted, or described. It is often followed by a clause with a verb at the end: „nicht so, wie ich gedacht habe“ (not the way I thought). Common with verbs like „sein“, „laufen“, „kommen“: „Es ist nicht so, wie es aussieht.“
target_language_example: Das ist nicht so, wie ich es mir vorgestellt habe.
native_language_example: That’s not the way I imagined it.

meaning: "not like that" / "don’t (do) that like that" (with a separable-verb prefix ending in -an).
additional_notes: You’ll often see this in commands with separable verbs whose prefix is **an-**. In the imperative, **an** goes to the end: **Fass mich nicht so an!** (Don’t touch me like that!), **Sieh mich nicht so an!** (Don’t look at me like that!). With **sich anstellen**, **Stell dich nicht so an!** means “Stop making such a fuss / Don’t be so dramatic.” Note: **Gib nicht so an!** is a different verb (**angeben** = to show off), but it follows the same word order pattern (prefix **an** at the end).
target_language_example: Schau mich nicht so an!
native_language_example: Don’t look at me like that!

meaning: not that easy; not so simple.
additional_notes: Used to say something is difficult or more complicated than it seems. Often appears as a standalone comment (Das ist nicht so einfach.) or in comparisons: nicht so einfach, wie ... (“not as easy as ...”).
target_language_example: Das Problem ist nicht so einfach, wie du denkst.
native_language_example: The problem isn’t as simple as you think.

additional_notes: Used to say something is smaller (in size) or shorter (in height) than expected or than something/someone else. Often appears in comparisons with **wie** (“as … as”): **nicht so groß wie …** = “not as big/tall as …”. You can also use it without a comparison: **Das Zimmer ist nicht so groß.**
target_language_example: Der Koffer ist nicht so groß wie meiner.
native_language_example: The suitcase isn’t as big as mine.

additional_notes: Used to make a comparison with "wie". The pattern is: "(nicht) so + adjective + wie + noun/pronoun". With "nicht", it means something is less (big/fast/expensive, etc.) than the other thing.
target_language_example: Mein Zimmer ist nicht so groß wie dein Zimmer.
native_language_example: My room is not as big as your room.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is going poorly or less good than expected, often with verbs like *gehen* (to be doing/feeling) and *laufen* (to be going). It can also be used for comparisons: *nicht so gut wie …* (“not as good as …”).
target_language_example: Mir geht es heute nicht so gut.
native_language_example: I’m not feeling so well today.

additional_notes: Used to compare two things, often with the second part implied or stated (e.g., not as good as earlier / usual / me). The comparison part comes after wie; you can also use it as a short answer: „Nicht so gut wie sonst.“
target_language_example: Der Film war nicht so gut wie das Buch.
native_language_example: The movie wasn’t as good as the book.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to slow down or calm down (physically or in conversation/action). Often sounds like a mild warning or admonition, and can be said sharply: "Moment, nicht so hastig!" = "Wait, not so fast!"
target_language_example: Nicht so hastig—wir haben noch Zeit.
native_language_example: Not so fast—we still have time.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone they shouldn’t (advice) or aren’t allowed to (rule) stay up late. Common with modal verbs like sollen (should) and dürfen (be allowed to). The verb aufbleiben (“to stay up”) is separable in finite forms (Ich bleibe auf), but in the infinitive it stays together (aufbleiben), as in this phrase.
target_language_example: Du solltest nicht so lange aufbleiben.
native_language_example: You shouldn’t stay up so late.

additional_notes: Used to reassure someone or downplay a problem: "Das ist nicht so schlimm" = "It’s not that bad." Often used in comparisons: "nicht so schlimm wie ..." = "not as bad as ..." You can also say it alone as a response: "Nicht so schlimm!" = "No worries!/It’s okay!"
target_language_example: Mach dir keine Sorgen — das ist nicht so schlimm.
native_language_example: Don’t worry — it’s not that bad.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to slow down or wait a moment. Often said on its own as an exclamation (“Nicht so schnell!”), or followed by a name (“Nicht so schnell, Clark!”). It can also be used in comparisons: “Ich bin nicht so schnell wie du” = “I’m not as fast as you.”
target_language_example: Nicht so schnell — ich muss erst meine Jacke holen.
native_language_example: Not so fast—I have to get my jacket first.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to slow down (running, speaking, acting too quickly), or more generally to say something won’t happen as quickly as expected. Often said as a short warning/request: “Nicht so schnell!” Polite with "bitte" and/or "Sie"; can also sound scolding depending on tone.
target_language_example: Nicht so schnell—ich kann dir nicht folgen.
native_language_example: Not so fast—I can’t follow you.

additional_notes: Used to reassure someone or downplay difficulty. Often said as a comment: „Das/Es ist (doch) nicht so schwer.“ (= It’s really not that hard.) Can also appear in comparisons: „nicht so schwer, wie …“ (= not as hard as …).
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, das ist nicht so schwer.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it’s not that hard.

meaning: “not so much / not that much” (often: “don’t … so much”).
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to reduce the amount of something (drinking, eating, talking, spending, etc.). Often follows an imperative: „Trink/Iss/Red/Arbeite nicht so viel.“ You can also use it in statements: „Ich trinke nicht so viel.“
target_language_example: Iss nicht so viel, sonst wird dir schlecht.
native_language_example: Don’t eat so much, or you’ll feel sick.

meaning: “not so much / not so many”; “not that much.”
additional_notes: Used to advise someone to do less of something (often with sollen/solltest: “You shouldn’t ... so much”), or to say an amount was small (“It wasn’t that much”). As an exclamation (“Nicht so viel!”) it means “Not so much!” / “Don’t do so much!” or “Take it easy.”
target_language_example: Iss nicht so viel, sonst wird dir schlecht.
native_language_example: Don’t eat so much, or you’ll feel sick.

meaning: not that far / not so far.
additional_notes: Used to say a place isn’t very far away, or that something hasn’t progressed very far yet. Common with verbs like sein (Es ist nicht so weit.), gehen/fahren (Wir müssen nicht so weit gehen/fahren.), or in phrases like noch nicht so weit (not that far yet).
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, es ist nicht so weit bis zum Bahnhof.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it’s not that far to the train station.

additional_notes: Used to downplay something or reassure someone that it isn’t a big deal. Often said on its own as a short reply (“Nicht so wichtig!”). You can also add it after a thing: “Das ist nicht so wichtig.”
target_language_example: Mach dir keine Sorgen — das ist nicht so wichtig.
native_language_example: Don’t worry — it’s not that important.

additional_notes: Used with a dative person: jemandem nicht trauen = “not trust someone.” Common in advice/warnings (often with sollen: Du sollst ihm nicht trauen.). Don’t confuse with sich trauen (“to dare”) or sich trauen lassen (“to get married”).
target_language_example: Ich habe Sie gewarnt, daß Sie ihm nicht trauen sollen.
native_language_example: I warned you that you shouldn’t trust him.

meaning: not for nothing; not in vain; not for free.
additional_notes: Commonly means there was a good reason or a worthwhile result ("not for nothing / not in vain"). With work or effort it can also mean "not for free" (i.e., you expect payment or something in return). Often implies justification: something happened or was done with purpose.
target_language_example: Er hat nicht umsonst so lange gelernt – er hat die Prüfung bestanden.
native_language_example: He didn’t study that long for nothing—he passed the exam.

additional_notes: Used as a reminder or warning. It can stand alone as an instruction (“Nicht vergessen!”) or be used with what you should remember, often with an infinitive + zu (“Nicht vergessen, deiner Mutter zu schreiben.”) or with a clause introduced by dass (“Nicht vergessen, dass …”). In polite/formal speech you may hear: “Sie dürfen nicht vergessen, …”.
target_language_example: Nicht vergessen, morgen den Müll rauszubringen!
native_language_example: Don’t forget to take out the trash tomorrow!

additional_notes: Used to say there is only a small amount/number, or that little is happening or possible. Common in phrases like: „nicht viel übrig (bleiben)“ (not much left), „nicht viel los“ (not much going on), „nicht viel machen/können“ (can’t do much), and „sich nicht viel ändern“ (not much changes). Also in fixed expression „(Es) lässt nicht viel zu wünschen übrig“ = “there’s not much to complain about / it’s pretty good.”
target_language_example: Heute ist nicht viel los, also bleibe ich zu Hause.
native_language_example: There’s not much going on today, so I’m staying home.

meaning: not to move; not to make any progress.
additional_notes:
Used with verbs like „sich bewegen“, „sich rühren“ or „kommen“.

1) Literally: not leaving the spot (a command like “Don’t move!”): „Rühr dich nicht vom Fleck!“
2) Figuratively: being stuck / not getting anywhere (no progress): „Ich komme nicht vom Fleck.“
target_language_example: Wir arbeiten seit Stunden daran, aber wir kommen einfach nicht vom Fleck.
native_language_example: We’ve been working on it for hours, but we just aren’t making any progress.

additional_notes: Most often used at the end of a statement to seek confirmation or agreement (like “right?” / “isn’t it?”). In this use it’s a fixed phrase and doesn’t literally mean “not true.” It can also be used normally to mean something is not true: „Das Gerücht ist offensichtlich nicht wahr.“
target_language_example: Du kommst morgen auch, nicht wahr?
native_language_example: You’re coming tomorrow too, right?

meaning: to not be true; (as an exclamation) “That can’t be true!”
additional_notes: Used either literally (“It isn’t true”) or as a strong reaction to surprising/bad news. Very common in the pattern: „Das kann (doch) nicht wahr sein!“ = “That can’t be true!” / “You’ve got to be kidding!”
target_language_example: Das kann doch nicht wahr sein!
native_language_example: That can’t be true!

additional_notes: Used to say something is at a short distance. Common patterns: „nicht weit von hier/da“ (not far from here/there), „nicht weit nach …“ (not far to …). It can also mean “can’t be far (away)” when guessing someone/something is close: „Sie kann nicht weit sein.“ With „genug“ it means “not far enough” (e.g., far enough away): „nicht weit genug“.
target_language_example: Der Supermarkt ist nicht weit von unserer Wohnung.
native_language_example: The supermarket isn’t far from our apartment.

meaning: not far away; not far from here/there.
additional_notes: Used to say that a place (or sometimes a point in time) is nearby. Often followed by a preposition like „von“: „nicht weit entfernt von …“ (= not far from …).
target_language_example: Der Bahnhof ist nicht weit entfernt.
native_language_example: The train station is not far away.

meaning: no less than; nothing less than.
additional_notes: Used for emphasis to say a number/amount is surprisingly large, or that something is exactly as serious/extreme as stated ("nothing less than..."). Often placed at the start of a sentence for dramatic emphasis, especially with numbers.
target_language_example: Es waren nicht weniger als zwanzig Leute auf der Party.
native_language_example: There were no less than twenty people at the party.

additional_notes: Common in two patterns: (1) before a zu-infinitive: „nicht zu + Verb“ = not to do something (e.g., „nicht zu verkaufen“). (2) with a destination/person (often after verbs like gehen/kommen) + dative: „nicht zu + jemandem/etwas“ = not to (someone/somewhere). Also appears in the phrase „(nicht) zu jemandem passen“ = (not) to match/go with someone/something.
target_language_example: Vergiss nicht, heute nicht zu spät nach Hause zu kommen.
native_language_example: Don’t forget not to come home too late today.

additional_notes: Used with "sein" or "war" to say someone isn’t/wasn’t at home (e.g., not in their house/apartment). It can also be used more generally to mean someone is absent/unavailable. Common warning: "Mach(t) das nicht zu Hause nach!" = “Don’t try this at home!”
target_language_example: Ich rufe später noch mal an, weil er gerade nicht zu Hause ist.
native_language_example: I’ll call again later because he isn’t at home right now.

additional_notes: Used before an adjective or adverb to soften it: "nicht zu aggressiv" = "not too aggressive". Here "zu" means "too" as an intensifier (not the infinitive marker "zu" like in "zu gehen"). Common in advice/requests to say something shouldn’t be done excessively: "nicht zu ernst", "nicht zu oft".
target_language_example: Mach dir nicht zu viele Sorgen.
native_language_example: Don’t worry too much.

meaning: “not too close / don’t come too close.”
additional_notes: Used as a warning or instruction about distance, often with verbs like „kommen“: „Komm mir nicht zu nahe!“ (= Don’t come too close to me!). It commonly takes a dative person („mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen“). In the set phrase „jemandem nicht zu nahe treten“, it means “not to offend someone / not to step on someone’s toes.”
target_language_example: Komm dem Hund nicht zu nahe.
native_language_example: Don’t get too close to the dog.

additional_notes: Used to say or ask that someone should arrive on time (or at least not after the expected time). Often with the purpose phrase "um nicht zu spät zu kommen" ("so as not to be late"). With a destination you typically use: "(nicht) zu spät + zu/zur/zum + [place/event]" (e.g., "nicht zu spät zur Schule/zum Termin"). In questions it can be a reminder: "Kommst du nicht zu spät?" ≈ "You’re not going to be late, are you?"
target_language_example: Wir müssen jetzt los, damit wir nicht zu spät zum Termin kommen.
native_language_example: We have to leave now so that we don’t arrive too late for the appointment.

meaning: “not to go too far” (cross a line / overdo it).
additional_notes: Used to warn someone to stay within limits—about behavior, words, criticism, jokes, demands, or sometimes physical distance. Often used as advice or a boundary; also common in the imperative: „Geh nicht zu weit.“
target_language_example: Pass auf, dass du mit deinen Witzen nicht zu weit gehen wirst.
native_language_example: Be careful that you won’t go too far with your jokes.

additional_notes: Usually appears before an infinitive: "nicht zu kommen" = "not to come," "nicht zu vergessen" = "not to forget." After "brauchen," it often means "don’t need to" ("Du brauchst nicht zu kommen" = "You don’t need to come"). In some set expressions like "nicht zu fassen," it means something like "impossible to grasp/believe." Be careful: in verbs like "zuhören," the "zu" belongs to the verb, so "du hörst nicht zu" means "you’re not listening," not this pattern.
target_language_example: Ich versuche, nicht zu lachen.
native_language_example: I'm trying not to laugh.

meaning: “(do) not allow/let them/her …” (as in: “don’t let it happen that she/they …”).
additional_notes: This comes from the separable verb **zulassen** (“to allow/permit”): **nicht zulassen, dass …** = “not allow that … / not let … happen.” In the examples, **zu** is separated from **lassen**: *Ich lasse nicht zu, dass …* / *Lass nicht zu, dass …* / *Lassen Sie nicht zu, dass …* / *Lasst nicht zu, dass …*. **dass** introduces a clause with the verb at the end.
target_language_example: Lass nicht zu, dass sie dich unterbrechen.
native_language_example: Don’t let them interrupt you.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive + zu after verbs like versprechen (to promise), bitten (to ask), erlauben (to allow), or in polite requests (Würde es dir/euch etwas ausmachen …?). Often means “please don’t smoke (here)” when talking about a place (e.g., in diesem Zimmer).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte daran denken, hier nicht zu rauchen?
native_language_example: Can you please remember not to smoke here?

additional_notes:
Often appears in two common patterns:
1) **um nicht zu sagen + stronger word** = “if not to say …” / “not to say …” (you first use a mild description, then correct/strengthen it: *warm, um nicht zu sagen heiß*).
2) **jemandem etwas nicht sagen** = “not to tell someone something” (keeping information from them). Also used alone as **Mehr brauche ich nicht zu sagen** = “I don’t need to say any more.”
target_language_example: Das war unhöflich, um nicht zu sagen gemein.
native_language_example: That was rude—if not downright mean.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (usually with a previous “das/es” = “it/that”) to say that something should not be done. Common after verbs like raten (to advise), brauchen (to need), beschließen (to decide), bitten (to ask), auffordern (to tell/urge). Word order: “… das nicht zu tun.” or with es: “… es nicht zu tun.”
target_language_example: Bitte vergiss nicht, das nicht zu tun.
native_language_example: Please don’t forget not to do that.

additional_notes: Used mostly in questions to check a possibility or make a tentative guess, often with a hint of “I hope so” or “I’m just checking.” Very common with tags like „oder?“ / „oder?“: „Du bist nicht zufällig …, oder?“ Literal meaning is closer to “not coincidentally,” but in everyday speech it often means “by any chance.”
target_language_example: Hast du nicht zufällig ein Ladekabel dabei?
native_language_example: You don’t happen to have a charging cable with you, do you?

meaning: “not allow/permit that …” (refuse to let something happen).
additional_notes: Used to say you will not allow a certain action or situation. It’s typically followed by a subordinate clause introduced by “dass” describing what must not happen. Common patterns include “Ich werde … nicht zulassen, dass …” (I won’t allow …) and “Wir dürfen/können … nicht zulassen, dass …” (we must/can’t allow …).
target_language_example: Wir dürfen nicht zulassen, dass diese Probleme unser Projekt beeinflussen.
native_language_example: We must not allow these problems to affect our project.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement/going (especially "gehen" and "kommen"): "nicht zur Schule gehen/kommen" = to not go/come to school. "zur" = "zu der" (to the), and with "Schule" it usually means going to school (attending) rather than going into the school building.
target_language_example: Ich gehe heute nicht zur Schule, weil ich krank bin.
native_language_example: I’m not going to school today because I’m sick.

additional_notes: Commonly used to give a moderately positive评价: “Not bad!” / “Looks pretty good.” Also appears in the fixed phrase “(etwas) nicht übel nehmen” = “not to take (something) badly / not to be offended” (e.g., “Ich hoffe, du nimmst mir das nicht übel.”).
target_language_example: Dein Ergebnis ist nicht übel.
native_language_example: Your result isn’t bad.

additional_notes: Used when you negate an entire group of things and then describe that group with a relative clause: "Es gibt nichts, was ..." = "There is nothing that ..." Often followed by a verb at the end of the clause (e.g., "... was ich tun kann"). You can also use it at the start of a sentence for emphasis: "Nichts, was du sagst, ...".
target_language_example: Es gibt nichts, was ich heute noch erledigen muss.
native_language_example: There’s nothing I still have to do today.

meaning: nothing but; only (used to downplay or dismiss something).
additional_notes: Used before a noun (often with an article) to say something is simply and exclusively that thing—often with a critical, dismissive, or emphatic tone. Common variant: "nichts anderes als" (= "nothing other than").
target_language_example: Das ist nichts als Ausreden.
native_language_example: That’s nothing but excuses.

meaning: (in „Das geht dich/Sie nichts an“) “none of your business”; (in „nichts anfassen / nichts anrühren“) “don’t touch anything.”
additional_notes:
Common patterns:
- „Das geht dich/Sie (gar) nichts an.“ = “That’s none of your business.” (can sound firm/rude; works with du/ihr/Sie: dich/euch/Sie)
- With verbs like „anfassen“ or „anrühren“: „Fass/Rühr da nichts an.“ = “Don’t touch anything / don’t mess with that.”
It’s not the preposition „an“ by itself that means this—these meanings come from fixed verb phrases (especially „jdn. nichts angehen“ and „nichts anfassen/anrühren“).
target_language_example: Das geht dich nichts an, das ist privat.
native_language_example: That’s none of your business, it’s private.

additional_notes: Used to say there is no alternative, no other option, or that someone knows/does/thinks about only one thing (often with verbs like kennen, sehen, haben, denken, sagen). It can sound like a complaint or criticism in questions like „Kannst du nichts anderes sagen?“ (= Can’t you say anything else?).
target_language_example: Ich habe nichts anderes zu essen.
native_language_example: I have nothing else to eat.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone does only one thing (and no other activity). Often appears with verbs like "tun" (e.g., "Er tut nichts anderes, als …") followed by "als" + infinitive: "… als fernzusehen / sich zu beschweren / an sie zu denken". In everyday speech, you may also hear it without the comma.
target_language_example: Ich tue heute nichts anderes, als zu Hause zu bleiben.
native_language_example: Today I’m doing nothing but staying at home.

meaning: 'nothing but / nothing other than'; emphasizes that something is simply that (and not more).
additional_notes: Used to stress that someone/something does only one thing or that something is essentially just that thing. Often followed by an infinitive with "zu" ("nichts anderes als zu + Infinitiv": Das Baby tut nichts anderes als zu weinen.) or by a noun ("nichts anderes als + Nomen": Ein Lebenslauf ist nichts anderes als Werbung.). In past tense you may see "tat" (ich tat nichts anderes als ...).
target_language_example: Am Wochenende habe ich nichts anderes als geschlafen.
native_language_example: On the weekend I did nothing but sleep.

meaning: “no other choice (left)” / “nothing else left to do.”
additional_notes: Usually used with "(jdm.) bleibt ... übrig" (literally: “remains left”), often in fixed phrases like "Es bleibt uns nichts anderes übrig". It expresses that you have to accept a situation and do something because there are no alternatives (often reluctant/resigned).
target_language_example: Mir bleibt nichts anderes übrig, als zu warten.
native_language_example: I have no other choice but to wait.

additional_notes: Used with bleiben (e.g., „Es bleibt mir/dir/uns nichts anderes übrig, als …“) to say there is only one possible option left. After „als“ you usually use an infinitive with „zu“ (e.g., „als zu warten“, „als dich zu entschuldigen“).
target_language_example: Nach dem Unfall blieb uns nichts anderes übrig, als die Polizei zu rufen.
native_language_example: After the accident, we had no choice but to call the police.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that there is absolutely nothing (that you want, fear, value more, etc.). Common in patterns like: „Es gibt nichts auf der Welt, das …“ (“There’s nothing in the world that …”) and „Nichts auf der Welt ist wichtiger als …“ (“Nothing in the world is more important than …”). Also used in the fixed phrase „Um nichts auf der Welt“ = “for nothing in the world / no way / under no circumstances.”
target_language_example: Nichts auf der Welt kann mich davon abhalten, dir zu helfen.
native_language_example: Nothing in the world can stop me from helping you.

meaning: No way! / Absolutely not! (a firm refusal)
additional_notes: Used as a strong, often abrupt way to reject something or stop someone. Common as a standalone exclamation (“Nichts da!”) or at the start of a sentence followed by what must happen instead (often with an imperative), e.g. “Nichts da, wir gehen jetzt!”
target_language_example: Nichts da, du gehst jetzt sofort ins Bett!
native_language_example: No way—you’re going to bed right now!

meaning: to not be able to help it; to not be at fault
additional_notes: Used to say someone is not responsible for a bad situation or problem. Often about things you can’t control (e.g., illness, delays, accidents). Common patterns: „Ich kann nichts dafür.“ / „Er kann nichts dafür.“ / „Dafür kann ich nichts.“
target_language_example: Ich kann nichts dafür können, dass der Zug zu spät ist.
native_language_example: I can’t help it / It’s not my fault that the train is late.

meaning: "nothing against it" / "don’t mind"; also in set phrases: "can’t do anything about it".
additional_notes:
Common patterns:
- (etwas) nichts dagegen haben + dass/zu… = to not mind / to have no objection ("Ich habe nichts dagegen, dass du kommst.")
- nichts dagegen einzuwenden haben = to have nothing to object to (more formal)
- nichts dagegen tun/machen können = to be unable to change the situation / can’t do anything about it. "dagegen" refers to a specific thing/situation mentioned or understood from context.
target_language_example: Ich habe nichts dagegen, wenn du das Fenster aufmachst.
native_language_example: I don’t mind if you open the window.

meaning: to have nothing to do with it; to not be involved.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is not connected to a situation, decision, or problem. Often appears as: „Ich habe nichts damit zu tun.“ (I have nothing to do with it.) You can also use it with past tense: „Er hatte nichts damit zu tun.“ (He had nothing to do with it.)
target_language_example: Ich habe nichts damit zu tun, dass die Tür kaputt ist.
native_language_example: I have nothing to do with the door being broken.

meaning: "none of it / nothing of it"; "not any of that".
additional_notes: Used to refer back to something already mentioned (an idea, plan, facts, etc.). Common with verbs like wissen/verstehen/sagen: „nichts davon wissen“ (to know nothing about it), „nichts davon verstehen“ (to understand none of it), „nichts davon sagen“ (to say nothing about it). It can also mean “you get nothing out of it” with haben: „Du hast nichts davon, …“ = “It doesn’t benefit you to …”.
target_language_example: Ich habe nichts davon gehört.
native_language_example: I haven’t heard anything about it.

additional_notes: Commonly used to say someone isn’t at fault or hasn’t made a mistake. Built from: "nichts" (nothing) + "falsch" (wrong) + "gemacht" (done/made, past participle of "machen"). Often appears with "haben": "Ich habe nichts falsch gemacht." / "Er hat nichts falsch gemacht."
target_language_example: Keine Sorge — du hast nichts falsch gemacht.
native_language_example: Don’t worry — you did nothing wrong.

meaning: "No offense" / "don’t take it the wrong way."
additional_notes: A set phrase used to soften criticism or an awkward comment—often before or after saying something negative (frequently with "aber": "Nichts für ungut, aber …"). It signals you don’t want to upset the other person, though it can still sound blunt depending on tone.
target_language_example: Nichts für ungut, aber ich glaube, das ist keine gute Idee.
native_language_example: No offense, but I think that’s not a good idea.

additional_notes: Past tense of “nichts sagen” (to say nothing). Used to state that someone didn’t tell you something or didn’t speak up. Common in questions and reproaches ("Warum/Wieso hast du mir nichts gesagt?") and in regrets ("Hätt ich doch bloß nichts gesagt!" = “If only I hadn’t said anything!”). Word order can change: “Ich habe dir nichts gesagt” (I didn’t tell you anything) vs. “Ich habe nichts gesagt” (I didn’t say anything).
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, ich habe dir nichts gesagt.
native_language_example: Sorry, I didn’t tell you anything.

additional_notes: Uses the verb **geschehen** (“to happen”) with **nichts** (“nothing”). Often used to reassure someone with **jemandem wird nichts geschehen** (“nothing will happen to someone,” dative: *mir/dir/ihr/ihm/uns/euch/ihnen*). Very common in the phrase **als ob nichts geschehen wäre** (“as if nothing had happened”).
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, dir wird nichts geschehen.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, nothing will happen to you.

meaning: “nothing more / nothing else / no longer anything.”
additional_notes: Used with **mehr** (“more/anymore”) to say that there is nothing left, nothing else to add, or that something doesn’t happen anymore. Common patterns: **nichts mehr + Verb** (Ich weiß nichts mehr. = I don’t know anything anymore.), **von jemandem nichts mehr hören** (not hear from someone anymore), **nichts mehr zu + Infinitiv** (nichts mehr zu essen = nothing left to eat).
target_language_example: Ich kann dir nichts mehr helfen.
native_language_example: I can’t help you anymore.

meaning: haven’t heard from him anymore / since then.
additional_notes: Used to say there has been no news or contact from him after a certain time or event. Common with time expressions like „seitdem“, „seit“, „seither“, „schon seit …“.
target_language_example: Seit dem Umzug habe ich nichts mehr von ihm gehört.
native_language_example: I haven’t heard from him since he moved.

meaning: “nothing left to …” / “no more … to …” (with an infinitive).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive at the end of the clause to say there is nothing remaining to do, say, fear, discover, etc. Common pattern: “Es gibt nichts mehr zu + Infinitiv” (There’s nothing left to + verb), “Du hast nichts mehr zu + Infinitiv” (You have nothing left to + verb), “Wir haben nichts mehr zu + Infinitiv” (We have nothing more to + verb).
target_language_example: Ich habe nichts mehr zu sagen.
native_language_example: I have nothing left to say.

additional_notes: Used to say there are no more tasks or actions needed. Common with forms like: „Es gibt nichts mehr zu tun.“ (There’s nothing left to do.) or „Ich habe nichts mehr zu tun.“ (I have nothing left to do.) „mehr“ = “any more / left”. The verb is „tun“ (to do); with „zu tun“ it’s an infinitive phrase (“to do”).
target_language_example: Wir sind fertig – es gibt nichts mehr zu tun.
native_language_example: We’re finished—there’s nothing left to do.

meaning: "nothing to do with me"; "not related to me".
additional_notes: Used to say something is not your responsibility, not your concern, or not connected to you. Often appears as: "Das hat nichts mit mir zu tun" (That has nothing to do with me) or "jdn. nichts mit jdm. zu tun haben" (to have nothing to do with someone). With "haben" it can also mean wanting no contact/relationship: "Sie will nichts mit mir zu tun haben" = she wants nothing to do with me.
target_language_example: Bitte frag jemand anders — das hat nichts mit mir zu tun.
native_language_example: Please ask someone else—that has nothing to do with me.

additional_notes: Used to say that no incident occurred, often to reassure someone (e.g., after a scare): „Es ist nichts passiert.“ It can also be used in the present as an exclamation meaning “Nothing’s happening!” or “Nothing happened!” (depending on context). With dative pronouns it can mean “nothing happened to him/her/etc.”: „Ihm ist nichts passiert.“
target_language_example: Keine Sorge—mir ist nichts passiert.
native_language_example: Don’t worry—nothing happened to me.

meaning: to do nothing; to not do anything (often: not do anything to someone).
additional_notes: Most commonly means “do nothing” (no action). With a dative object (mir/dir/ihm/ihr/euch/ihnen), it often means “not do anything to (someone),” i.e., not harm them: „Ich werde dir nichts tun.“ You may also see „nichts tun können“ = “can’t do anything (about it).”
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, ich werde dir nichts tun.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I won’t do anything to you.

meaning: "nothing about" / "nothing from" (i.e., no news/contact from someone; or no knowledge of something).
additional_notes: Used mainly in two ways: (1) with verbs like "hören" or "sehen" to mean you haven’t heard/seen anything from someone (= no news/contact): "Ich habe nichts von ihm gehört." (2) with verbs like "wissen" to mean you know nothing about a plan/idea/topic: "Ich wusste nichts von Ihrem Plan." It can also refer to parts of a set: "Nichts von beiden" (= neither), "Nichts von dem, was …" (= nothing of what …).
target_language_example: Seit Wochen habe ich nichts von meiner Freundin gehört.
native_language_example: I haven’t heard from my friend in weeks.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like wissen (to know), erzählen (to tell), sagen (to say) to mean someone knows/tells nothing about something: „Ich weiß nichts von der Sache.“ It can also mean something is not recorded or mentioned: „In der Akte steht nichts von der alten Schule.“ The noun after it is feminine (der + noun).
target_language_example: Bitte erzähl ihr nichts von der Überraschung.
native_language_example: Please don’t tell her anything about the surprise.

meaning: haven’t heard from him / haven’t heard anything about him.
additional_notes: Uses the pattern „(nichts/etwas) von jemandem hören“ (dative) to mean you got no news or contact from/about someone. Often used in the perfect tense: „Ich habe (noch/schon lange/seitdem) nichts von ihm gehört.“
target_language_example: Ich habe seit Wochen nichts von ihm gehört.
native_language_example: I haven’t heard from him in weeks.

additional_notes: Used to downplay something (“It’s nothing serious”) or to say something is the only thing needed/true. Very common pattern: „nichts weiter (tun), als …“ = “do nothing but … / all you have to do is …”. Also „nichts weiter als …“ = “nothing but … / nothing more than …”.
target_language_example: Du musst nichts weiter tun, als hier zu unterschreiben.
native_language_example: All you have to do is sign here.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say there is nothing to do/fear/forgive, etc.: „nichts zu + Infinitiv“ = “nothing to + verb.” Common fixed phrase: „Nichts zu danken.“ = “Don’t mention it / You’re welcome.”
target_language_example: Du hast nichts zu befürchten.
native_language_example: You have nothing to fear.

additional_notes: Used to say there is no food available, or that someone has no food. Grammatically it’s the negation "nichts" + "zu" + infinitive (here: "essen") meaning “nothing to [do]”. Common with verbs like haben/geben: "Ich habe nichts zu essen" (I have nothing to eat), "Es gibt nichts zu essen" (There’s nothing to eat).
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, ich habe heute nichts zu essen.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have nothing to eat today.

meaning: to say nothing; to have nothing to say.
additional_notes: Used in two common ways: (1) choosing not to tell someone something: „jemandem nichts sagen“ (often with promises/oaths: „versprechen/schwören, jemandem nichts zu sagen“). (2) having no comment or nothing to contribute: „Ich habe (dazu) nichts zu sagen.“ You can also use it as a question: „Habt ihr nichts zu sagen?“ = “Don’t you have anything to say?”
target_language_example: Bitte sag ihm nichts zu sagen, bis ich da bin.
native_language_example: Please tell him to say nothing until I’m there.

meaning: “nothing to do” / “not to be involved (with something)”.
additional_notes: Common in two situations: (1) having no tasks/being idle: „Ich habe heute nichts zu tun.“ (2) denying involvement or responsibility, often with „damit“ or „mit + Dativ“: „Damit habe ich nichts zu tun.“ / „Ich habe mit der Sache nichts zu tun.“
target_language_example: Am Wochenende finde ich es schön, einfach nichts zu tun.
native_language_example: On the weekend, I think it’s nice to just do nothing.

additional_notes: Used to say you aren’t hiding any secrets or doing anything wrong, often as a reassurance or defense. Very common with forms of haben (e.g., Ich habe/du hast/er hat …) and also in reported speech with Konjunktiv (e.g., er sagte, er habe/hätte nichts zu verbergen).
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, ich habe nichts zu verbergen.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I have nothing to hide.

additional_notes: Used with forms of "haben" (e.g., "Ich habe nichts zu verlieren") to say there’s no real risk or nothing left that could be lost—often to encourage taking a chance or because the situation can’t get much worse.
target_language_example: Probier es ruhig—du hast doch nichts zu verlieren.
native_language_example: Go ahead and try it—you’ve got nothing to lose.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like „wissen“ (to know), „erzählen“ (to tell), „verraten“ (to reveal), „sagen“ (to say) to mean you have (or share) no information about a person/thing/topic. Common pattern: „(jemand) weiß nichts über (jemanden/etwas)“.
target_language_example: Ich weiß nichts über diesen Film.
native_language_example: I don’t know anything about this movie.

additional_notes: This is a common sentence pattern: a main clause with **nie** (“never”) is followed by a comma and a subordinate clause starting with **was** (“what”). It often appears after verbs like **wissen** (to know), **sagen** (to say/tell), or **tun** (to do): *Ich weiß nie, was …* / *Er sagt nie, was …*.
target_language_example: Ich weiß nie, was ich als Nächstes tun soll.
native_language_example: I never know what I should do next.

meaning: “never been there” / “as if it never existed (or happened).”
additional_notes: Literally “never there been.” Used to say something wasn’t present, or (often with *als wäre…*) that something is treated as if it never existed or happened: *als wäre es nie da gewesen* (“as if it was never there”). Note: as an adjective meaning “unprecedented,” German usually writes it as one word: *nie dagewesen* (e.g., *ein nie dagewesener Erfolg*).
target_language_example: Am nächsten Tag war die Kiste weg, als wäre sie nie da gewesen.
native_language_example: The next day the box was gone, as if it had never been there.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something does not happen at any time (nie) and with any thing/information (etwas). Often appears with a verb: "Er sagt mir nie etwas" = he never tells me anything. In German you usually don’t add another "nicht" with this: "nie etwas" already makes the sentence negative.
target_language_example: Ich vergesse nie etwas Wichtiges.
native_language_example: I never forget anything important.

additional_notes: Used with the passive of "gebären" (to give birth): "geboren werden" = to be born, so "nie geboren worden" = to have never been born. Often appears in the subjunctive to express regret or a strong threat: "Ich wünschte, ich wäre nie geboren worden" (I wish I had never been born) / "Du wirst dir wünschen, du wärst nie geboren worden" (You’ll wish you’d never been born). In statements about records/status you may see it with "war": "Er war offiziell nie geboren worden" (officially, he had never been born).
target_language_example: Sie sagte, sie wünschte, sie wäre nie geboren worden.
native_language_example: She said she wished she had never been born.

additional_notes: Used with the verb „mögen“ in the present perfect (Perfekt): „ich habe … nie gemocht“ = “I never liked …”. Often appears as „noch nie gemocht“ to mean “have never liked (up to now)”. Typically takes a direct object in the accusative (a person or thing you don’t like).
target_language_example: Ich habe Kaffee nie gemocht.
native_language_example: I never liked coffee.

meaning: "never said" (used to deny having said something).
additional_notes: Often appears in the present perfect: "Das habe ich nie gesagt" = "I never said that." Used to contradict someone or to emphasize that something was not mentioned. With "hätte" it can appear as reported/conditional speech: "Er behauptet, dass er das nie gesagt hätte" = "He claims he would never have said that / that he never said that."
target_language_example: Das habe ich nie gesagt – du hast mich falsch verstanden.
native_language_example: I never said that—you misunderstood me.

additional_notes: Used with the perfect tense of "sehen" (haben + gesehen) to say someone has never seen something/someone up to now. Word order is usually: subject + haben + object + nie + gesehen (e.g., "Ich habe ihn nie gesehen."), but "nie" can also come before the object for emphasis.
target_language_example: Ich habe diesen Film nie gesehen.
native_language_example: I've never seen this movie.

additional_notes: Used to strongly deny something, express that something is impossible, or emphasize that you would never do something. Often used with past tense (“Nie im Leben habe ich …”) or as a short exclamation (“Nie im Leben!” = “No way!”).
target_language_example: Nie im Leben würde ich das tun.
native_language_example: I would never do that (no way).

meaning: 'never in' (not at any time in a place).
additional_notes: Used to say someone has never been to / never lived in / never arrived in a particular place. Often appears split in a sentence: „Ich war nie in Amerika.“ / „Er ist nie in New York gewesen.“ With verbs of living or arriving, German commonly uses „in“ (e.g., „in Australien leben“, „in Australien ankommen“).
target_language_example: Ich bin nie in Berlin gewesen.
native_language_example: I have never been to Berlin.

additional_notes: Used with verbs that take an indirect object in the dative (jemandem = “to someone”). Often appears in the middle of the sentence: subject + auxiliary + nie + jemandem + (object) + past participle (e.g., „Er hat es nie jemandem gesagt.“). The words don’t have to be right next to each other, but this is a very common pairing.
target_language_example: Ich habe nie jemandem davon erzählt.
native_language_example: I never told anyone about it.

meaning: never again; no longer (from now on).
additional_notes: Used to say something will not happen anymore starting now (often a strong promise, decision, or threat). It can stand alone as an emphatic answer: “Nie mehr.” You’ll also often hear it with extra emphasis like “nie mehr wieder” (“never ever again”), and it commonly goes with the imperative: “Lüg mich nie mehr an.”
target_language_example: Ich komme nie mehr zu spät.
native_language_example: I’ll never be late again.

additional_notes: Often used to say something will not happen again in the future ("never again"). It can also mean someone/something is no longer seen/doesn’t return (often with a tragic or final tone), e.g. "nie mehr gesehen". Common with future forms like "wird ... nie mehr" or "werde ... nie mehr".
target_language_example: Bitte mach das nie mehr!
native_language_example: Please never do that again!

additional_notes: Used to express that someone will not say something at any time (often because they refuse, it would be untrue, or they want to keep it secret). Common in strong statements like "Das werde ich nie sagen!" = "I would never say that!" In future contexts it can also imply "will never tell" (e.g., "Er wird euch nie sagen ...").
target_language_example: Ich werde dir nie sagen, wie alt ich bin.
native_language_example: I’ll never tell you how old I am.

meaning: 'never like that' / 'never so' (in that way or to that degree).
additional_notes: Used with comparisons or descriptions to say something has never happened in that way/at that level. Common patterns: (1) comparison: „nie so … wie …“ = never as … as … (e.g., „nie so geliebt wie dich“). (2) with an article: „nie so ein(e/n) …“ = never such a … / never a … like that (e.g., „nie so einen schönen Sonnenuntergang“). (3) with verbs: „nie so gemacht/gesagt“ = would never have done/said it like that.
target_language_example: Ich habe dich noch nie so glücklich gesehen.
native_language_example: I've never seen you this happy.

additional_notes: An emphatic way to say something will definitely not happen or that you will definitely not do/believe something. Often used in spoken German, sometimes as a standalone exclamation (“Nie und nimmer!”).
target_language_example: Das mache ich nie und nimmer.
native_language_example: I would never ever do that.

additional_notes: Means you will always remember someone/something. Common with future forms like „Ich/Wir werde(n) … nie vergessen“ and with objects: „dich/Sie/es“ or „deine/Ihre Freundlichkeit“.
target_language_example: Ich werde dich nie vergessen.
native_language_example: I will never forget you.

meaning: never again; never (ever) again in the future.
additional_notes: Used to say something must not happen again, or that something did not happen again after a certain point (often about seeing/hearing from someone). With future intentions it often appears as a promise or resolution: „Ich werde nie wieder …“.
target_language_example: Ich mache diesen Fehler nie wieder.
native_language_example: I’ll never make that mistake again.

additional_notes: This isn’t usually complete by itself. It’s most common with verbs that take **an** (meaning “about/to”), e.g. **an jdn/etw denken** (to think about), **an jdn/etw glauben** (to believe in), **sich an jdn/etw erinnern** (to remember). Pattern: **nie wieder an + noun/pronoun** (often with a verb like *denken*).
target_language_example: Ich will nie wieder an dich denken.
native_language_example: I never want to think about you again.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t want to do something again together with a person, or you don’t want to deal with something again. It’s often said as an incomplete sentence, with the rest understood from context (e.g., "Nie wieder mit dir!" = “Never again with you!” / “I’m never doing that with you again!”). Put a noun or pronoun after "mit" (mir, dir, ihm/ihr, uns, euch, ihnen).
target_language_example: Nie wieder mit dir in dieses Restaurant!
native_language_example: Never again with you in this restaurant!

additional_notes: Often used as a strong statement that you don’t want to see someone again (e.g., as a threat or when throwing someone out): „Ich will dich hier nie wieder sehen!“ It can also be neutral/sad about not meeting again: „Wir werden sie wohl nie wieder sehen.“ Word order changes with pronouns and tense (e.g., „Ich werde dich nie wieder sehen.“ / „Sie würden sich nie wieder sehen.“).
target_language_example: Ich werde dich nie wieder sehen.
native_language_example: I will never see you again.

additional_notes: Used to promise, vow, or strongly say you won’t repeat an action. It often appears with a direct object like „das“/„es“: „Das/Es werde ich nie wieder tun.“ You can change tense or add modals: „Ich will/muss/darf … nie wieder tun.“
target_language_example: Ich würde es nie wieder tun.
native_language_example: I would never do it again.

additional_notes: Used to express that you don’t want to meet or see a person anymore. Often said strongly or emotionally (e.g., after an argument). The core verb is "wiedersehen" (“to see again”); "nie" (“never”) makes it final.
target_language_example: Nach dem Streit wollte sie ihn nie wiedersehen.
native_language_example: After the argument, she never wanted to see him again.

additional_notes: Often used with "Es ist nie zu spät, ..." to encourage someone that there’s still time to do something (e.g., change your mind, start something new). It can also describe punctuality: "nie zu spät (kommen)" = to never be late.
target_language_example: Es ist nie zu spät, neu anzufangen.
native_language_example: It’s never too late to start over.

additional_notes: Used to say something has not happened/been seen/experienced at any time earlier. Often appears with the past tense (Perfekt/Präteritum), and it can be placed before the verb phrase: „Ich habe das nie zuvor gesehen.“
target_language_example: So etwas habe ich nie zuvor erlebt.
native_language_example: I have never experienced something like that before.

additional_notes: Used to say you shouldn’t rule something out completely, because things can change and something unexpected might still happen. Often used as advice or as a comment when something seems unlikely but possible.
