target_language_example: Ich dachte, ich würde nie nach Berlin ziehen, aber man soll niemals nie sagen.
native_language_example: I thought I’d never move to Berlin, but you should never say never.

additional_notes: Used to say that no other person (besides the one already mentioned) is involved or allowed. Often with modal verbs like darf/kann/könnte, or with weiß/hat gesehen, etc. In speech you may also hear the shorter form „niemand sonst“.
target_language_example: Ich will das mit niemand anders besprechen.
native_language_example: I don’t want to discuss that with anyone else.

additional_notes: Used to say that no person did something (often in the Perfekt tense): **niemand** (nobody) + **hat** (has) + past participle at the end of the clause. Common with verbs that form the Perfekt with **haben** (e.g., *angerufen, gefragt, gesehen, besucht*).
target_language_example: Niemand hat mir heute geantwortet.
native_language_example: No one answered me today.

additional_notes: Used to say that there is no person who is able to do something. In statements, the conjugated verb (here: "kann") stays in 2nd position, so "Niemand" often comes first: "Niemand kann ...". The infinitive usually goes to the end: "Niemand kann alles wissen."
target_language_example: Niemand kann heute kommen.
native_language_example: No one can come today.

meaning: “no one anymore” / “nobody (does it) anymore” / “no one left.”
additional_notes: Used to express that from now on there is no person who does something anymore, or that no person remains in a place. Typical position is after the verb or toward the end of the clause: „Hier wohnt niemand mehr.“ Note: in object position, German usually uses the accusative form „niemanden“ (so it won’t appear as the exact string „niemand mehr“): e.g., „Ich kenne niemanden mehr.“
target_language_example: In dem Gebäude lebt niemand mehr.
native_language_example: No one lives in that building anymore.

additional_notes: Used to say that no one wants a certain thing to happen. It’s followed by a subordinate clause with **dass** (“that”), and the verb in that clause goes to the end (e.g., **…, dass du das machst/tust**). **möchte** is the polite/soft form of **will** (“wants / would like”).
target_language_example: Niemand möchte, dass wir zu spät kommen.
native_language_example: Nobody wants us to be late.

additional_notes: Used to say that zero people in your group ("uns") did something or are something. It’s usually the subject of the sentence and is followed by a verb in 3rd person singular: "Niemand von uns hat/ist/weiß ...". You can also use it with reflexive verbs: "..., dass niemand von uns sich setzen konnte."
target_language_example: Niemand von uns kann heute kommen.
native_language_example: None of us can come today.

additional_notes: Used to say that no person has the information. Often followed by a statement (Niemand weiß das.) or by a clause starting with **dass/ob/wie/warum** etc.: **Niemand weiß, ob… / dass… / wie…**. In these clauses, the verb goes to the end (**…dauern wird**).
target_language_example: Niemand weiß, wann der Zug ankommt.
native_language_example: Nobody knows when the train will arrive.

meaning: “no one knows what …” (introduces an unknown outcome or situation).
additional_notes: Often used to say the result, future, or situation is uncertain. The comma is standard before the clause with “was”. Common continuations include: “... als Nächstes passieren wird” (will happen next), “... die Zukunft bringt” (the future holds), “... mit ihm geschehen ist” (what happened to him), “... aus ihm geworden ist” (what became of him).
target_language_example: Niemand weiß, was morgen passieren wird.
native_language_example: No one knows what will happen tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say that the location of someone/something (or where something happens) is unknown. It’s usually followed by a clause with the verb at the end: „Niemand weiß, wo er/sie/es ist.“ You’ll also see it as a question: „Niemand weiß, wo …?“ (expressing surprise/concern).
target_language_example: Niemand weiß, wo mein Schlüssel ist.
native_language_example: No one knows where my key is.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that a person (often the one you’re talking to) has the most knowledge or experience about something. Very common as a lead-in to add what they know best: “Niemand weiß das besser als du: Wie funktioniert das?” You can change the pronoun (Sie/du/er/sie/wir/ihr) or replace it with a name.
target_language_example: Niemand weiß das besser als du: Wie läuft der Kurs wirklich ab?
native_language_example: No one knows that better than you: what is the course really like?

additional_notes: Used to say that no one wants something to happen or to do something. After "will" (from "wollen" = to want), German typically uses an infinitive at the end of the clause: "Niemand will gehen." = "Nobody wants to go."
target_language_example: Niemand will heute arbeiten.
native_language_example: Nobody wants to work today.

additional_notes: Used with the future meaning of **werden** (“will”). The main verb usually goes to the end: **Niemand wird dich verstehen.** (“No one will understand you.”). It can also be used with a past participle to form the passive: **Niemand wird verletzt.** (“No one will be hurt.”).
target_language_example: Niemand wird dir helfen, wenn du nicht fragst.
native_language_example: No one will help you if you don’t ask.

meaning: “nobody’s home” (no one is at home; sometimes: someone seems mentally absent).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like „scheinen“ or in the pattern „Es sieht aus, als wäre niemand zu Hause“ to say it seems no one is in. In everyday speech it can also be said about a person to mean they’re not paying attention or seem “not all there.”
target_language_example: Ich habe geklingelt, aber es war niemand zu Hause.
native_language_example: I rang the doorbell, but nobody was home.

meaning: "no one (to) whom" / "no one to turn to."
additional_notes: Used with a relative clause to refer back to "niemanden" (nobody): "niemanden, an den ..." = "no one (that) ... to." The preposition depends on the verb; with sich an jdn wenden (to turn to someone), it’s an + accusative: an den (masc.), an die (fem.), an das (neut.), an die (pl.). Often used with Hilfe/um Hilfe: "niemanden, an den er sich um Hilfe wenden kann" = "no one he can turn to for help."
target_language_example: Ich habe niemanden, an den ich mich wenden kann.
native_language_example: I have no one I can turn to.

meaning: “no one who …” (referring to a male person: “no one who …”).
additional_notes: Used with a relative clause to say there is nobody who does/can do something. Grammar: "niemanden" is accusative (object). The relative pronoun agrees with the missing person: der (masc.), die (fem.), das (neut.), die (plural). Examples: "Ich habe niemanden, der mir hilft." / "Ich habe niemanden, die mir hilft." (for a woman).
target_language_example: Wir haben niemanden, der uns heute fahren kann.
native_language_example: We have no one who can drive us today.

additional_notes: Used when you want to say you don’t have a person to do something with. It commonly appears with a relative clause: „Ich habe niemanden, mit dem ich …“ (= I have no one to/with whom I can …). The form changes with gender/case: „niemanden, mit dem“ (masc./neut. dative), „niemanden, mit der“ (fem. dative), „niemanden, mit denen“ (plural dative).
target_language_example: Ich habe niemanden, mit dem ich heute Abend ins Kino gehen kann.
native_language_example: I have no one to go to the movies with tonight.

additional_notes: Imperative (du-form) of **nehmen**: **nimm** = “take”. **die** is the accusative article for **feminine singular** (die Pizza, die Brille, die Maske) or **plural** (die drei). Often used with separable verbs/particles: **nimm … ab** (“take … off”) and **nimm … mit** (“take … with you”).
target_language_example: Nimm die Jacke mit!
native_language_example: Take the jacket with you!

additional_notes: Imperative of the reflexive verb phrase „sich (etwas) nehmen“: „Nimm dir …“ = “help yourself / go ahead and take …”. Common with food/drinks („Nimm dir etwas vom Kuchen!“) and with time or breaks: „Nimm dir Zeit“ = “take your time”, „Nimm dir ein paar Tage frei“ = “take a few days off”. The „dir“ is a dative pronoun (“for yourself”).
target_language_example: Nimm dir ruhig noch ein Stück Brot.
native_language_example: Go ahead and take another piece of bread.

additional_notes: Imperative form of "mitnehmen" (to take along). Said when you want someone to include you when they go somewhere. Often followed by a destination: "Nimm mich mit nach Hause!" You can also use the polite form: "Nehmen Sie mich mit."
target_language_example: Wenn du zum Supermarkt gehst, nimm mich mit.
native_language_example: If you’re going to the supermarket, take me with you.

additional_notes: From the verb **nehmen** (“to take”), **nimmst du** asks what someone takes/uses/chooses. Common meanings in everyday German: taking/bringing someone along (**Nimmst du mich mit?**), taking medicine (**Nimmst du deine Medikamente?**), taking/using transport (**Nimmst du den Zug? / ein Taxi?**), choosing one option (**Nimmst du die rote oder die blaue?**). It’s addressed to one person you say **du** to (friends, family, kids).
target_language_example: Nimmst du heute das Auto oder den Bus?
native_language_example: Are you taking the car or the bus today?

meaning: “Will you take me with you?” / “Can I come with you?”
additional_notes: From the separable verb **mitnehmen** (“to take along”). Used to ask someone if you can come along (in a car, to an event, to another place, etc.). Often followed by **nach** + city/country (e.g., *nach Rom*) or **zu(m/zur)** + place/activity (e.g., *zum Kämpfen*, *zur Party*).
target_language_example: Nimmst du mich mit zur Arbeit?
native_language_example: Will you take me with you to work?

additional_notes: "nippen an" means to sip slowly, usually from a drink. It’s often used with "an" + dative, so you’ll see forms like: an meinem/deinem/ihrem/seinem … (e.g., "an ihrem Kaffee"). "nippte" is simple past (Präteritum) of "nippen".
target_language_example: Sie nippte an ihrem Glas Wasser.
native_language_example: She sipped at her glass of water.

meaning: "sipped (at) his" (took small sips from his drink).
additional_notes: Used with the verb **nippen an + dative** to mean taking small, slow sips from a drink. **nippte** is simple past (Präteritum) of *nippen*; **seinem** is dative masculine/neuter and changes with the noun: *an seinem Kaffee/Wein/Getränk* (masc./neut.), but *an seiner Cola* (fem.). Typically used with a drink, but can also be used figuratively in some contexts.
target_language_example: Tom nippte an seinem Kaffee und sah aus dem Fenster.
native_language_example: Tom sipped his coffee and looked out the window.

meaning: used like “(still) remember what …” / “do you remember what …?”
additional_notes: Often used in the pattern **(Weißt/Wisst) du/ihr noch, was …?** to ask if someone remembers a specific detail. With **ich weiß noch, was …**, it means “I still remember what …”. With **immer noch** it means “still” in the sense of “even now” (e.g., *Fragst du dich immer noch, was …?* = “Are you still wondering what …?”).
target_language_example: Weißt du noch, was der Arzt gesagt hat?
native_language_example: Do you remember what the doctor said?

meaning: 'still (remember/know) how …' / 'do you still remember what … was like?'.
additional_notes: Used when you’re asking or stating that someone still remembers something from the past. Often appears with verbs like (sich) erinnern and wissen: „Erinnerst du dich noch, wie …?“ / „Ich weiß noch, wie …“. The comma before „wie“ is typical because „wie …“ introduces an embedded (indirect) question/clause.
target_language_example: Weißt du noch, wie wir uns kennengelernt haben?
native_language_example: Do you still remember how we met?

additional_notes: Used to say someone hasn’t died (often after an accident, illness, or danger). Common with verbs like „sein“: „Er ist noch am Leben.“ Also used with „Glück haben“ to mean someone survived: „Er hat Glück, noch am Leben zu sein.“
target_language_example: Nach dem Unfall ist sie zum Glück noch am Leben.
native_language_example: After the accident, luckily she is still alive.

meaning: still / yet … (with an = on/about; often: still remember/think of).
additional_notes:
Used when something is still true or still happens, with a phrase introduced by **an**.
- With **denken an + Akk.** / **sich erinnern an + Akk.**: **noch an** = “still (think of / remember)”.
  Example pattern: *Denkst du noch an …?* / *Erinnern Sie sich noch an …?*
- With time expressions: **noch an + Dat.** can mean “not (even) on … yet/ever”: *noch an keinem Tag* = “not on a single day (ever)”.
- With **beteiligt an + Dat.**: *noch an … beteiligt* = “still involved in …”.
target_language_example: Denkst du noch an mich?
native_language_example: Do you still think of me?

additional_notes: Used to ask or talk about more items beyond the ones already mentioned. Often comes before a plural noun: „noch andere Hobbys/Symptome/Gedichte“. Can also appear with articles/pronouns: „noch andere(n)“ depending on case (e.g., „Kennst du noch andere?“).
target_language_example: Gibt es noch andere Fragen?
native_language_example: Are there any other questions?

additional_notes: Used to compare and intensify: something is better than before/than another option. Often used in recommendations or upgrades ("X ist gut, noch besser ist Y") and also as a stand-alone reaction ("Noch besser!" / "Noch besser sogar!").
target_language_example: Wir könnten den Bus nehmen, aber noch besser wäre es, zu Fuß zu gehen.
native_language_example: We could take the bus, but even better would be to go on foot.

additional_notes: Used to say a person is still present (not left yet) or that something still exists/is standing. Often answers the question "Ist er/sie/es noch da?" (= Is he/she/it still here/there?).
target_language_example: Bist du morgen noch da oder fährst du schon heute ab?
native_language_example: Will you still be here tomorrow, or are you leaving already today?

additional_notes: Used with the reflexive verb: **sich (an etw.) erinnern** = “to remember (something)”. **noch** adds the idea of “still” (you remember it even now). **daran** refers back to something (“to it/that”) and often introduces a clause with **wie/wo/was** etc. Common pattern: **Kannst du dich noch daran erinnern, ...?** (informal **du**) / **Können Sie sich noch daran erinnern, ...?** (formal **Sie**).
target_language_example: Kannst du dich noch daran erinnern, wie er heißt?
native_language_example: Do you still remember what his name is?

meaning: on top of that; besides that (often emphasizing an extra, sometimes surprising/annoying point).
additional_notes: Used to add an additional fact after already mentioning something: "..., und noch dazu ..." = "..., and on top of that ...". It often strengthens the statement (sometimes like "to make matters worse"). It can also be used with "bereit" to mean "ready for that as well / ready on top of everything else".
target_language_example: Ich habe heute viel Arbeit, und noch dazu ist mein Computer kaputt.
native_language_example: I have a lot of work today, and on top of that my computer is broken.

meaning: another three days; three more days.
additional_notes: Used with time periods to mean an additional amount of time from now or from a reference point (often with verbs like bleiben, warten, dauern). It implies the time continues beyond what was expected or already counted. You can add words like „länger“ to stress the extension: „noch drei Tage länger“ = “three more days longer.”
target_language_example: Ich muss noch drei Tage hier bleiben.
native_language_example: I have to stay here for another three days.

additional_notes: Used to add one more of something. It often comes before a noun ('noch ein Kaffee' = 'another coffee'), with quantity expressions like 'noch ein paar' ('a few more'), or in set phrases like 'noch ein Mal' ('once more'). The article changes with gender and case: noch eine, noch einen, etc.
target_language_example: Ich nehme noch ein Stück Kuchen.
native_language_example: I'll have another piece of cake.

additional_notes: Used when you want an additional beer (after you’ve already had one, or you’re adding one more to an order). Very common in restaurants/bars. Word order can vary: "noch ein Bier, bitte"; polite requests often use "Könnte ich bitte …?" or "Ich hätte gern …". In casual speech you may hear "Hol mir mal noch ein Bier!" (informal, can sound like an order).
target_language_example: Könnte ich bitte noch ein Bier haben?
native_language_example: Could I please have another beer?

meaning: another / one more glass of wine.
additional_notes: Uses "noch ein …" to ask for or describe an additional item beyond what you already had (e.g., an extra drink). Common with verbs like "trinken" (drink), "bekommen" (get), and "(sich) einschenken" (pour oneself). In offers or questions: "Möchtest du noch ein Glas Wein?"
target_language_example: Ich hätte gern noch ein Glas Wein, bitte.
native_language_example: I’d like another glass of wine, please.

additional_notes: Most often used with **sein**: **(Er/Ich war) noch ein Kind** = “(He/I was) still a child / just a child (at that time).” Depending on context, **noch ein** can also mean “another” (one more), e.g. **noch ein Kind verlieren** can mean “to lose another child.”
target_language_example: Ich war damals noch ein Kind und habe das nicht verstanden.
native_language_example: Back then I was still a child and didn’t understand that.

meaning: another piece of cake (one more piece).
additional_notes: Used when offering or asking for an additional serving of cake. "noch" = "another/one more" here; "ein Stück" means "a piece" (common with food like cake, pizza, bread). Often appears in polite requests with "Darf ich/Kann ich ... haben?" or when offering with "Möchtest du/Wollen Sie ...?".
target_language_example: Ich nehme noch ein Stück Kuchen, bitte.
native_language_example: I’ll have another piece of cake, please.

meaning: a little bit more; a little longer.
additional_notes: Used to say there is still a small amount left, or that you want to do something a bit more/longer. Common with nouns (noch ein bisschen Wein) and with verbs (noch ein bisschen arbeiten/schlafen). Often sounds polite/softening in offers and requests.
target_language_example: Kannst du noch ein bisschen langsamer sprechen?
native_language_example: Can you speak a little more slowly?

meaning: a little longer / a bit more.
additional_notes: Used to say you want something to continue for a short time, or you want a small additional amount. Often said on its own as a request: "Noch ein bisschen!" (= "A bit more!" / "Just a little longer!").
target_language_example: Kannst du noch ein bisschen langsamer sprechen?
native_language_example: Can you speak a little more slowly?

meaning: a little longer; a bit more.
additional_notes: Used with time or actions to mean “just a little more / a little longer.” Common with verbs like bleiben/dableiben (“stay”), warten (“wait”), nachdenken (“think about it”). In modern spelling you’ll often see: „noch ein bisschen“.
target_language_example: Kannst du noch ein bißchen warten?
native_language_example: Can you wait a little longer?

additional_notes: Used to say there are some additional items or tasks still left (more than before). Typically followed by a plural noun: „noch ein paar Termine / Briefe / Bäume“. Similar in meaning to „ein paar … mehr“.
target_language_example: Ich brauche noch ein paar Minuten.
native_language_example: I need a few more minutes.

additional_notes: Used when you want to ask additional questions after you’ve already discussed something. Common in polite conversation and in meetings/interviews. You’ll often hear it with a verb: „Ich habe noch ein paar Fragen.“
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich habe noch ein paar Fragen.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have a few more questions.

additional_notes: Used to say you will wait/stay for an additional short time. Common with verbs like bleiben (to stay) and warten (to wait). In speech you’ll also hear: noch ein paar Tage lang (“for a few more days”).
target_language_example: Können wir noch ein paar Tage hier bleiben?
native_language_example: Can we stay here for a few more days?

additional_notes: Used to say you want/add/need some additional amount (usually small). It’s often followed by a plural noun ("noch ein paar Jahre" = “a few more years”), or used alone when the noun is clear from context ("Ja, noch ein paar."). You can also add "Mal" for repetition: "noch ein paar Mal" = “a few more times.”
target_language_example: Kannst du noch ein paar Minuten warten?
native_language_example: Can you wait a few more minutes?

meaning: “a few more minutes” / “a few minutes longer.”
additional_notes: Used to ask for or give a little extra time. Often with verbs like geben (to give), warten (to wait), bleiben (to stay). “noch” adds the idea of “still/another/more.” Common in polite requests: “Geben Sie mir noch ein paar Minuten.”
target_language_example: Können wir noch ein paar Minuten warten?
native_language_example: Can we wait a few more minutes?

additional_notes: Used to say something should continue for a short additional time. Often with verbs like „bleiben“ (stay) or with „darüber nachdenken“ (think about it): „Denk noch ein paar Tage darüber nach.“ Can also appear in the pattern „Noch ein paar Tage, und …“ meaning “In a few more days, … / Just a few more days and …”.
target_language_example: Ich brauche noch ein paar Tage, um alles zu organisieren.
native_language_example: I need a few more days to organize everything.

additional_notes: Used with feminine nouns (eine) to mean an additional one: *noch eine Kopie / Flasche / Nacht / Chance*. It can also stand alone when the noun is understood: *Bitte noch eine.* Often means “one more” in requests (*Noch eine Flasche, bitte.*) or “another” in the sense of “an additional/different one” (*Es wird sich noch eine Gelegenheit ergeben.*).
target_language_example: Können wir noch eine Flasche Wasser kaufen?
native_language_example: Can we buy another bottle of water?

additional_notes: Used when asking for or offering an additional opportunity to try again, often after a mistake. Very common with verbs like „geben“ (to give): „Jemandem noch eine Chance geben“ = “to give someone another chance.” „Noch“ here means “still/yet/another,” emphasizing “one more.”
target_language_example: Kannst du mir bitte noch eine Chance geben?
native_language_example: Can you please give me another chance?

additional_notes: Used when offering or suggesting an extra serving, often coffee or tea. “noch” = “another/one more” in this context. You’ll often hear it in polite questions with Sie (Möchten/Trinken Sie …?) or casual with du (Möchtest/Trink …?).
target_language_example: Möchtest du noch eine Tasse Tee?
native_language_example: Would you like another cup of tea?

meaning: another cup of coffee; one more cup of coffee.
additional_notes: Used when offering or asking for an additional serving. Here, "noch" means "another / one more" (not "still"), especially with food and drinks. Common in polite questions like "Möchten Sie noch …?"
target_language_example: Ich hätte gern noch eine Tasse Kaffee, bitte.
native_language_example: I’d like another cup of coffee, please.

meaning: another cup of tea (one more cup).
additional_notes: "noch" means "another/one more" here, used to ask for or offer an extra serving. Common in polite questions with "Möchtest du …?" or "Wollt ihr …?" and in requests like "Gib mir …".
target_language_example: Kann ich bitte noch eine Tasse Tee haben?
native_language_example: Could I please have another cup of tea?

meaning: for a while longer; for a bit longer.
additional_notes: Used to say something will continue for some more time. Very common with verbs like bleiben (stay), dauern (take/last), warten (wait), and with modal verbs (kann/muss/sollte). Often implies “not just now—some more time.”
target_language_example: Ich warte noch eine Weile auf dich.
native_language_example: I’ll wait for you a little longer.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine accusative noun (einen + noun), e.g. „noch einen Tee“, „noch einen Tag“. With „noch“ it can mean (1) adding one more (“one more/another”), or (2) something is still available/left (“still a”), especially in questions and statements like „Gibt es noch einen…?“ / „Wir haben noch einen…“. For other genders/cases you’ll see forms like „noch eine“, „noch ein“, „noch einem“, etc.
target_language_example: Ich nehme noch einen Kaffee, bitte.
native_language_example: I’ll have another coffee, please.

additional_notes: Used to ask to repeat something (“Could you say that again?”) or to say something happens another time/once more (often: “noch einmal + verb”). It can also mean “again” in the sense of coming back or doing something another time.
target_language_example: Kannst du das bitte noch einmal sagen?
native_language_example: Can you say that again, please?

additional_notes: Used with another verb/plan to say you want to make another attempt. Often appears after a verb like „ich will/ich werde …“ or with „es“: „Ich will es noch einmal versuchen.“ Similar: „es nochmal versuchen“ (more casual) or „es erneut versuchen“ (more formal).
target_language_example: Ich will es morgen noch einmal zu versuchen.
native_language_example: I want to try again tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "überdenken" (to rethink / to think over). "noch einmal" adds the idea of doing it again—often after getting new information or having doubts. Common with decisions, plans, and offers: "den Plan / das Angebot noch einmal überdenken".
target_language_example: Ich habe die Entscheidung noch einmal überdacht.
native_language_example: I’ve rethought the decision.

meaning: a little longer; a bit longer.
additional_notes: Used to say someone should continue doing something for a short additional time. "noch" adds the idea of "still/yet" (additional time), and "etwas" softens it to mean "a little/a bit". Common with verbs like bleiben (stay), warten (wait), schlafen (sleep), halten (hold).
target_language_example: Können wir noch etwas länger warten?
native_language_example: Can we wait a little longer?

meaning: “some more” / “anything else” (a bit more of something).
additional_notes: Used when asking for or referring to an additional amount of something (often food/drink): “Haben wir noch etwas …?” = “Do we have any … left?” With verbs like “nachschenken” it means “pour me a bit more.” It can also mean “there’s still a bit of … (left/on it)” as in “noch etwas … an deinen Lippen.”
target_language_example: Kann ich noch etwas Wasser haben?
native_language_example: Can I have some more water?

meaning: "something else" / "a bit more" / "still something" (depending on context).
additional_notes: Used when adding an extra point ("And another thing..."), asking/offering an additional item ("Would you like some more...?"), or meaning "still" with feelings or actions ("I still feel something..."). With time/amounts it can mean "a bit longer" or "a little more" (e.g., "noch etwas warten" = wait a bit longer).
target_language_example: Hättest du noch etwas Zeit für mich?
native_language_example: Do you still have some time for me?

additional_notes: Used to ask or talk about an additional item, idea, or option besides what’s already mentioned. Often in questions: "Gibt es noch etwas anderes ...?" (= Is there anything else ...?). "noch" adds the sense of "still/yet/in addition," and "etwas anderes" means "something else".
target_language_example: Hast du noch etwas anderes, das du sagen möchtest?
native_language_example: Do you have anything else you’d like to say?

meaning: to say one more thing; to add something.
additional_notes: Used when you want to add additional information (often important) before ending a conversation: "Ich muss/möchte dir noch etwas sagen" = "I still need/want to tell you something." In questions (often formal with "Sie"): "Möchten Sie noch etwas sagen?" = "Would you like to add anything (else)?"
target_language_example: Bevor du gehst, muss ich dir noch etwas sagen.
native_language_example: Before you go, I still need to tell you something.

meaning: "anything else to …" / "still something to …" (followed by an infinitive).
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive with "zu" to say there is one more thing to do, or to ask if someone wants/needs something else. Very common in questions and polite offers (often with "Haben Sie …?").
target_language_example: Haben Sie noch etwas zu trinken?
native_language_example: Would you like anything else to drink?

additional_notes: Used to say there is still an extra five minutes left, or to suggest waiting/sleeping a bit longer. Often used with verbs like schlafen (sleep) or warten (wait): „noch fünf Minuten schlafen/warten“. „Noch“ here means “still/yet/more,” and the exact meaning depends on context (remaining time vs. additional time).
target_language_example: Können wir noch fünf Minuten warten?
native_language_example: Can we wait another five minutes?

additional_notes: Used to say something hasn’t happened/been done up to now. Often adds emphasis: 'not yet at all / not even yet'. Common with verbs like denken, wissen, können, fertig sein, etc.
target_language_example: Ich habe noch gar nicht gegessen.
native_language_example: I haven’t eaten yet (at all).

additional_notes: Used to say someone hasn’t gotten up yet (often later than expected). Common in questions with "sein" (to be): "Bist du noch im Bett?" It can sound mildly surprised or impatient depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Ich bin noch im Bett, ich stehe gleich auf.
native_language_example: I’m still in bed; I’ll get up in a moment.

additional_notes: Used when a state or action continues up to now or up to another point in time. It is very similar to immer noch and often adds a slightly emphatic sense of 'still'.
target_language_example: Ich warte noch immer auf deine Antwort.
native_language_example: I'm still waiting for your answer.

additional_notes: Used with the common pattern **Angst haben** (“to be afraid”): **noch immer Angst haben** = “to still be afraid.” You can add what you’re afraid of with **vor + dative** (e.g., *vor Spinnen*) or with **davor, … zu + infinitive** (e.g., *davor, nach Hause zu gehen*). **Noch immer** emphasizes that the fear continues up to now.
target_language_example: Ich habe noch immer Angst, allein nach Hause zu gehen.
native_language_example: I'm still afraid to go home alone.

additional_notes: Used to say something continues up to the present. Often followed by a state with **in + dative**, e.g. **noch immer in jemanden verliebt/verknallt sein** (“still in love with someone”), or with fixed phrases like **noch immer in Gebrauch sein** (“still in use”). Similar to **immer noch**, but **noch immer** can sound a bit more emphatic (“still, after all this time”).
target_language_example: Bist du noch immer in ihn verliebt?
native_language_example: Are you still in love with him?

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that a negative situation continues up to the present moment. Common with verbs like wissen, verstehen, können, or with states like klar/überzeugt/verheiratet. Word order: it often sits before the main verb or adjective it negates (e.g., „ist noch immer nicht klar“, „kann noch immer nicht …“).
target_language_example: Ich habe noch immer nicht verstanden, was du meinst.
native_language_example: I still haven't understood what you mean.

additional_notes: “noch” expresses that something continues up to now (“still”) or emphasizes that it remains true even now (“even today”). “in der” means “in the” with dative feminine nouns (e.g., in der Medizin, in der Straße/Wohnung). Often used with places or fields: “Wohnt er noch in der …?” = “Does he still live in …?”
target_language_example: Arbeitest du noch in der gleichen Firma?
native_language_example: Do you still work at the same company?

additional_notes: Used to refer to an additional person beyond the one(s) already mentioned, or to ask if any other person is present/doing something. Very common in questions and offers: „Ist noch jemand da?“ = “Is anyone else there?” / „Noch jemand Kaffee?“ = “Anyone else (want) coffee?” With objects it often appears as „noch jemand(en)“ or expanded as „noch jemand anderen / noch jemand anderem“ depending on case.
target_language_example: Ist noch jemand hungrig, oder wollen wir schon bestellen?
native_language_example: Is anyone else hungry, or should we order already?

meaning: 'not (by) a long way yet'; 'still a long time (to go)'.
additional_notes: Used (1) with time/duration questions or statements to mean it will still take a long time: "Dauert es noch lange?" / "Bis ... ist es noch lange hin." Also used (2) with negation to mean "that doesn’t automatically mean..." / "not necessarily": "Das macht dich noch lange nicht zu ..." and patterns like "Nur weil ..., ist ... noch lange nicht ...".
target_language_example: Nur weil er laut spricht, hat er noch lange nicht recht.
native_language_example: Just because he speaks loudly doesn’t mean he’s right.

additional_notes: Common everyday form of "noch einmal". Used when something happens one more time or is repeated: "Erklär es noch mal" = "Explain it again." In questions like "Was war noch mal ...?" it can sound like "again" or "remind me". In quantity phrases such as "noch mal so viele," it means an additional equal amount.
target_language_example: Kannst du das bitte noch mal sagen?
native_language_example: Can you say that again, please?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to repeat an action: *Kannst du das noch mal machen?* = “Can you do that again?” Often written/spoken as **noch mal** or **nochmal**. **das** = “that” (the action), and **es** = “it”. Works in informal (**du/ihr**) and formal (**Sie**) situations.
target_language_example: Können Sie das bitte noch mal machen?
native_language_example: Could you please do that again?

additional_notes: Used when you want to restart something from a certain point, very often with phrases like „von vorne“ (from the beginning) or „von Anfang an“ (from the start). „noch mal“ is a common, more casual form of „noch einmal“ (once again).
target_language_example: Wir fangen noch mal von vorne an.
native_language_example: We'll start again from the beginning.

meaning: again from the beginning; start over.
additional_notes: Used when you want to repeat something from the start (an explanation, a task, a process). Common in spoken German; "noch mal" = short for "noch einmal". Often said as a stand-alone request/command: "Noch mal von vorn!" You can also pair it with verbs like "anfangen" or "beginnen": "noch mal von vorn anfangen/beginnen".
target_language_example: Kannst du das bitte noch mal von vorn erklären?
native_language_example: Can you please explain that again from the beginning?

additional_notes: Used to say you want or notice an additional amount beyond what already exists. Often expresses an increase or extra items/information: "Ich will noch mehr ..." (I want even more ...), "Es gibt noch mehr ..." (There are even more ...). With negatives/exclamations it can mean "no more": "Nicht noch mehr!"
target_language_example: Kann ich noch mehr Wasser haben?
native_language_example: Can I have some more water?

additional_notes: "noch" adds the idea of "still/yet" (there are additional ones), and "mehr" means "more". Often used at the end of an explanation or meeting: "Haben Sie noch mehr Fragen?" (formal) / "Habt ihr noch mehr Fragen?" (to a group) / "Hast du noch mehr Fragen?" (to one person, informal). You can also use it as a statement: "Ich habe noch mehr Fragen."
target_language_example: Haben Sie noch mehr Fragen, oder soll ich weitermachen?
native_language_example: Do you have any more questions, or should I continue?

additional_notes: Used when you already have/need/ask for money and you want an extra amount beyond that. Often sounds like an emphasis: "more than before" or "more than expected" ("wirklich noch mehr Geld?" = "really even more money?").
target_language_example: Ich brauche noch mehr Geld, um die Rechnung zu bezahlen.
native_language_example: I need even more money to pay the bill.

additional_notes: Used when you need additional time beyond what was already expected or given. Often with verbs like „brauchen“ (to need) or „bekommen“ (to get): „Er braucht noch mehr Zeit.“ = he still needs more time.
target_language_example: Können wir noch mehr Zeit bekommen?
native_language_example: Can we get even more time?

additional_notes: Used to increase the amount/degree compared to what already exists or was mentioned. Common with comparisons and desires/plans: "Ich mag X, aber Y mag ich noch mehr" (I like Y even more), "Wir brauchen/ müssen noch mehr ..." (we need to do even more), "Es tut noch mehr weh" (it hurts even more).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte noch mehr Wasser holen?
native_language_example: Can you please get even more water?

additional_notes: Used to say that something has not happened, is not known, or is not possible so far. Very common with the present tense. In English, it often translates as "not yet," but sometimes "still not" fits better depending on context.
target_language_example: Ich bin noch nicht fertig.
native_language_example: I'm not finished yet.

additional_notes: Used to say something (a task, work, food, a project, a person getting ready) isn’t done at the moment, but is expected to be done later. Common pattern: „noch nicht + adjective“ (e.g., „noch nicht da“ = not here yet). „fertig“ can mean both “finished” and “ready,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Ich bin noch nicht fertig, gib mir bitte fünf Minuten.
native_language_example: I’m not finished yet—please give me five minutes.

meaning: "not even (yet)" (emphasizes that something hasn’t happened/been done at all).
additional_notes: Colloquial version of "noch nicht einmal". Used to stress that something is missing or unfinished, often with a surprised/critical tone: "Ich habe noch nicht mal Zeit" = "I don’t even have time." It can refer to an action not started/done yet or something you don’t have yet.
target_language_example: Ich habe noch nicht mal gefrühstückt.
native_language_example: I haven’t even had breakfast yet.

meaning: not ready yet / not there yet.
additional_notes: Used to say that a point in time hasn’t come yet, or that someone/something hasn’t reached the needed stage (development, progress, emotional readiness). Often said about plans or events ("Es ist noch nicht so weit.") or about people/things being ready ("Ich bin noch nicht so weit.").
target_language_example: Ich kann dir noch nichts sagen – ich bin noch nicht so weit.
native_language_example: I can’t tell you anything yet—I’m not ready yet.

additional_notes: Used to say that something has not happened at any time up to now. Often appears with the present perfect, but it can also be used for emphasis in comparisons, as in wie noch nie = "like never before."
target_language_example: So etwas habe ich noch nie gesehen.
native_language_example: I've never seen anything like that before.

meaning: "never (ever) a / never once a" (up to now).
additional_notes: Used to say that something has not happened at any time up to now. It’s the pattern "noch nie" + verb (often in the perfect tense) + "ein" + noun (usually accusative): "Ich habe noch nie ein … gesehen/gehört/gegessen." You can swap "ein" for other articles/quantities: "noch nie eine …", "noch nie einen …", "noch nie …" (no article).
target_language_example: Ich habe noch nie ein E-Book gelesen.
native_language_example: I’ve never read an e-book.

additional_notes: Used with the present perfect or past perfect to say something has never happened up to now/that point in time: "Ich habe noch nie einen …" / "Er hatte noch nie einen …". The key part is "noch nie" = "never (yet)". "einen" is just the masculine accusative form of "ein"; depending on the noun it can change to "noch nie eine" (feminine) or "noch nie ein" (neuter).
target_language_example: Ich habe noch nie einen Herzinfarkt gehabt.
native_language_example: I have never had a heart attack.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that up to now, there has been zero experience with something. Often appears with the present perfect (Perfekt): „Ich habe noch nie etwas …“ = “I have never … anything.” You’ll frequently see it with verbs like „gehört“ (heard of), „gegessen“ (eaten), „gemacht“ (done), etc. Word order can vary depending on what follows (e.g., „noch nie etwas von … gehört“).
target_language_example: Ich habe noch nie etwas von diesem Buch gehört.
native_language_example: I’ve never heard of this book.

additional_notes: Used to say you have never heard something at any time up to now (often meaning “I’ve never heard of that”). Very common with "Das habe ich ja noch nie gehört!" to show surprise or disbelief. You can also use it alone as a short reply: "Noch nie gehört."
target_language_example: Von dieser Band habe ich noch nie gehört.
native_language_example: I’ve never heard of this band.

additional_notes: Uses the passive voice: **geküsst worden** = “been kissed” (literally “kissed been”). It’s often used with **sein** in the past: **Ich war noch nie geküsst worden.** = “I had never been kissed.” With **so** (“like that / that way”), it emphasizes the manner: **So bin/war ich noch nie geküsst worden.** = “I’ve never been kissed like that before.”
target_language_example: Sie war noch nie geküsst worden, bis sie ihn traf.
native_language_example: She had never been kissed until she met him.

additional_notes: Used to say something has never happened up to now (“noch nie” = “never before / not once yet”). It’s commonly used with the present perfect: **Ich habe … noch nie gemacht** / **Das wurde noch nie gemacht** (passive: “That has never been done”). Word order: **noch nie** usually comes before the past participle (**gemacht**) or near the end of the clause.
target_language_example: Ich habe das noch nie gemacht, aber ich kann es versuchen.
native_language_example: I’ve never done that before, but I can try.

additional_notes: Used with the present perfect (Perfekt) to say that something has not happened at any time up to now: (ich) habe … noch nie gesehen. Often appears with etwas/so etwas (“something like that”): So etwas habe ich noch nie gesehen. “Noch nie” is stronger than just “nie” because it emphasizes “up to now”.
target_language_example: Ich habe das noch nie gesehen.
native_language_example: I’ve never seen that before.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that something has never happened before, often with the present perfect ("Ich habe …") or past perfect ("Ich hatte …"). "Im Leben" adds extra emphasis to "noch nie". Sometimes "(in) meinem" is implied rather than said: "Noch nie im Leben …". (Note: if you see this phrase in sentences containing insults/slurs, that offensive language is separate from the phrase itself.)
target_language_example: So etwas habe ich noch nie im Leben gesehen.
native_language_example: I have never seen anything like that in my life.

meaning: “never (before) in / to” (has never been to a place; has never seen something in a situation).
additional_notes: Used to say something has not happened at any time up to now. Often with the present perfect for life experience ("Ich war/Ich bin noch nie in ... gewesen") and with the past perfect to talk about an earlier point in the past ("hatte noch nie in ... gesehen"). Word order: "noch nie" usually comes before the place phrase with "in" ("noch nie in Frankreich").
target_language_example: Ich bin noch nie in Deutschland gewesen.
native_language_example: I have never been to Germany.

additional_notes: Used to say you have never done something to any person up to now, usually with the present perfect (Perfekt) or past perfect (Plusquamperfekt): **Ich habe / hatte noch nie jemanden + past participle** (e.g., *getroffen, geküsst, enttäuscht*). **noch nie** emphasizes “not at any time up to now,” and **jemanden** is the accusative form meaning “someone/anyone” (the person affected by the verb).
target_language_example: Ich habe noch nie jemanden so sehr vermisst.
native_language_example: I’ve never missed anyone this much.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something has never happened or been experienced to this degree before. Very common in comparisons with adjectives/adverbs: "noch nie so + adjective/adverb" (e.g., "noch nie so klar", "noch nie so sauer"). Often paired with "in meinem ganzen Leben" (“in my whole life”) for extra emphasis.
target_language_example: Ich war noch nie so müde wie heute.
native_language_example: I’ve never been this tired before.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something has not happened at any time in the past until that moment: *Ich habe das noch nie zuvor gemacht* = “I’ve never done that before.” Often appears with past tenses (Perfekt/Präteritum) and can be placed in the middle of the sentence near the verb.
target_language_example: Ich habe so etwas noch nie zuvor gesehen.
native_language_example: I’ve never seen anything like that before.

meaning: still in time; just in time (before it’s too late).
additional_notes: Used when there is (or was) a deadline or danger of being too late. "noch" emphasizes that there’s still time left; "rechtzeitig" means on time/in good time. Very common with verbs like "schaffen" (manage), "kommen" (arrive), or "helfen" (help) in urgent situations.
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, wir sind noch rechtzeitig angekommen.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, we arrived just in time.

additional_notes: Used to say a situation could become more bad than it already is, or to warn not to make things worse. Common with verbs like „werden“ (to become) and „machen“ (to make): „noch schlimmer werden“ = to get even worse; „(etwas) noch schlimmer machen“ = to make (something) even worse.
target_language_example: Bitte sag es ihr nicht jetzt — das würde alles noch schlimmer machen.
native_language_example: Please don’t tell her now — that would make everything even worse.

additional_notes: Used to say that a lot of work/tasks are not finished yet. Very common with verbs like „haben“ (Ich habe noch viel zu tun), „bleiben“ (Es bleibt noch viel zu tun), or „geben“ (Es gibt noch viel zu tun).
target_language_example: Wir können noch nicht gehen – wir haben noch viel zu tun.
native_language_example: We can’t leave yet—we still have a lot to do.

additional_notes: Used when there is an additional task, issue, piece of information, or question besides what was just mentioned. Often introduces a new topic: „Oh, und da wäre noch was anderes.“ In questions it can sound critical or challenging: „Kannst du noch was anderes als Nein sagen?“ Note: „was“ is informal spoken German for „etwas“, so „noch etwas anderes“ is more neutral/formal.
target_language_example: Ich habe gerade keine Zeit, ich muss noch was anderes erledigen.
native_language_example: I don’t have time right now; I still have something else to take care of.

additional_notes: Used to say that the right time hasn’t come yet. Often appears with "sein" ("Es ist noch zu früh") and can be followed by "für" + noun ("noch zu früh für die Rente") or an implied action ("Dafür ist es noch zu früh" = It’s still too early for that).
target_language_example: Wir können noch nicht gehen—es ist noch zu früh.
native_language_example: We can’t leave yet—it’s still too early.

meaning: still (go) to school; still in school (not graduated yet).
additional_notes: Used with a verb like gehen/fahren to say someone is still attending school (as opposed to having finished school). Word order: "Gehst du noch zur Schule?" = "Are you still in school?"
target_language_example: Ich gehe noch zur Schule, aber nächstes Jahr mache ich meinen Abschluss.
native_language_example: I still go to school, but next year I’ll graduate.

additional_notes: Used to push someone to finally act or hurry up. Often said with impatience/pressure and can sound rude depending on tone and context. You may also hear it with an added verb: "Nun mach schon, spring!" (= "Come on, jump!").
target_language_example: Nun mach schon, wir haben keine Zeit!
native_language_example: Come on, hurry up—we don't have time!

meaning: 'just' / 'simply' (that’s how it is), often with resignation.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is a fact and can’t really be changed, often sounding a bit resigned or matter-of-fact: "So ist es nun mal." It can also stress that something has a certain priority or importance: "Das hat nun mal Priorität." Common in spoken German.
target_language_example: Ich kann das nicht ändern – so ist es nun mal.
native_language_example: I can’t change that—that’s just how it is.

additional_notes: Used as a discourse marker when you pause to think, soften what you’re about to say, or admit something with mild reluctance (sometimes like “well, I mean…” or “I guess…”). It can also stand alone (“Nun ja.”) to express uncertainty or a noncommittal reaction.
target_language_example: Nun ja, ich bin mir nicht sicher, ob das eine gute Idee ist.
native_language_example: Well, I’m not sure if that’s a good idea.

meaning: “only that … / just that …” (introduces a limited condition, wish, or the only relevant point).
additional_notes: Used with a dass-clause to express that one thing is the only requirement/goal/important point: „Ich will nur, dass …“ = “All I want is that …”. With a pause/comma („Nur, dass …“) it can also add a correction or limitation, similar to “except that / it’s just that …”.
target_language_example: Ich will nur, dass du mir zuhörst.
native_language_example: All I want is for you to listen to me.

meaning: “just/only that you …” (often: “I just want you to …”).
additional_notes: Used with a clause starting with **dass du ...** to limit what someone wants/says to one point: **Ich will nur, dass du ...** = “I only want you to ... / I just want you to ...”. In questions like **Wie kam es nur, dass du ...?**, **nur** works as an intensifier meaning “(how) on earth / ever”.
target_language_example: Ich will nur, dass du mir Bescheid gibst.
native_language_example: I just want you to let me know.

meaning: “only to … / just to …” (used to express purpose, often with the sense that it’s the only reason, or with an ironic/disappointing outcome).
additional_notes: Used to introduce an infinitive clause with „zu“ (purpose): „Er kommt nur, um zu helfen.“ With the comma, „nur, um“ often marks a clause break and can emphasize restriction or an ironic result, especially sentence-initial: „Nur, um dann …“ (= “only to then …”). In standard German, the comma is common when „um … zu“ introduces an infinitive clause; many speakers may omit the comma in simpler sentences, but „nur, um“ with a comma is idiomatic for emphasis.
target_language_example: Ich bin nur hier, nur, um dir zu helfen.
native_language_example: I’m only here, just to help you.

additional_notes: Used to say something is true or happens for one limited reason, often implying that this reason is not enough to justify a conclusion ("Just because X, doesn’t mean Y"). Common pattern: „Nur, weil …, heißt das nicht, dass …“. The comma marks a pause/emphasis; in everyday writing you’ll also see „nur weil“ without the comma.
target_language_example: Nur, weil es teuer ist, heißt das nicht, dass es gut ist.
native_language_example: Just because it's expensive doesn't mean it's good.

additional_notes: Used to express a condition or the only situation in which something happens. It often sets a limit: something is true/done exclusively under that condition. Word order: in a main clause you’ll often see it as “Ich … nur, wenn …” (comma before wenn; the verb goes to the end in the wenn-clause).
target_language_example: Ich komme nur, wenn du Zeit hast.
native_language_example: I’m coming only if you have time.

additional_notes: Used to say something was meant as a joke and not seriously (often after teasing or a sarcastic comment). You’ll also hear: „Ich mach(e) nur Spaß.“ and „War nur Spaß.“ It’s informal and common in spoken German.
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, das war nur Spaß.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I was just kidding.

meaning: "only" / "just" (used with "an" = about / in / on / at, depending on the verb).
additional_notes: Used to narrow the focus to one thing or person in common patterns like: „nur an etwas interessiert sein“ (= only interested in something), „nur an etwas/jemanden denken“ (= think only about something/someone), and „es liegt nur an dir“ (= it depends only on you / it's up to you). The preposition „an“ takes accusative with „denken an“ (Ich denke an dich) and dative with „interessiert an“ (interessiert an Macht).
target_language_example: Er denkt nur an sich.
native_language_example: He only thinks about himself.

additional_notes: Used to limit something strictly to a specific thing, followed by a relative clause with "was" (often with a comma): "nur das, was ich will" = "only what I want". Often expresses emphasis: not more than that.
target_language_example: Ich sage nur das, was ich sicher weiß.
native_language_example: I only say what I know for sure.

meaning: “just/only the red button” (i.e., you only need to press the red button).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like **drücken** (to press) and often after **nur** with **müssen** or **brauchen** to mean “all you have to do is…”. Common patterns: **Du musst nur den roten Knopf drücken.** / **Du brauchst nur den roten Knopf zu drücken.** (with *brauchen* you typically use **zu + infinitive**).
target_language_example: Sie müssen nur den roten Knopf drücken, dann geht es los.
native_language_example: You just have to press the red button, then it starts.

meaning: “only the …” (used with feminine singular nouns or plural nouns).
additional_notes: Used to limit something to one specific thing or group (“only those/the ones”). Grammar: **die** can be (1) feminine singular (“die Fassade”) or (2) plural (“die Batterien”, “die Überschriften”). Word order can shift for emphasis, e.g. **Nur die Fassade** wurde renoviert / Renoviert wurde **nur die Fassade**.
target_language_example: Ich brauche nur die Schlüssel, nicht die Dokumente.
native_language_example: I only need the keys, not the documents.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone is telling the truth and not lying or exaggerating. Often appears with verbs like sagen/sprechen (to say/speak) or as a strong statement by itself. Word order can vary (e.g., "Ich sage nur die Wahrheit"), and it can be used in a serious or dramatic tone.
target_language_example: Ich will nur die Wahrheit wissen.
native_language_example: I just want to know the truth.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the number is small or limited. Often answers “how many/how long?” and can refer to a quantity (nur drei Brote) or a duration (nur drei Monate). Word order: usually “nur” directly before the number it limits.
target_language_example: Ich habe nur drei Fragen.
native_language_example: I only have three questions.

additional_notes: Used to limit or downplay something: 'just/only a ...'. This exact form appears before certain singular nouns; the article changes with gender and case, so you may also see forms like 'nur eine' or 'nur einen'.
target_language_example: Ich bin nur ein Student.
native_language_example: I'm just a student.

additional_notes: Used to say something wasn’t meant seriously, often after a remark that could be taken as offensive, alarming, or threatening. Common in the pattern: „Das war/ist nur ein Scherz.“ You can also hear the shortened spoken version: „War nur ein Scherz.“
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, das war nur ein Scherz.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it was just a joke.

additional_notes: Used to say that something isn’t real or didn’t really happen, often for reassurance (e.g., after a nightmare) or in a philosophical/figurative way (“maybe everything is just a dream”). Often appears with “(es war/ist) nur ein Traum”.
target_language_example: Keine Sorge — das war nur ein Traum.
native_language_example: Don’t worry — it was just a dream.

additional_notes: Used to say the amount or degree is small. Common with quantities (food, money, time) and with skills or intensity ("nur ein bisschen Französisch", "nur ein bisschen gerannt"). "nur" adds the idea of "only/just" (nothing more).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir nur ein bisschen helfen?
native_language_example: Can you help me just a bit?

meaning: only a little; just a bit.
additional_notes: Used to downplay the amount/degree of something. "nur" = only/just, "ein bisschen" = a little/a bit. Often used alone as a short answer (e.g., "Nur ein bisschen.") or before a verb to mean you’re doing something a small amount ("Wir räumen nur ein bisschen auf.").
target_language_example: Ich spreche nur ein bisschen Deutsch.
native_language_example: I speak only a little German.

meaning: only a few; just a couple (of).
additional_notes: Used to say the amount/number is small and limited. It’s often followed by a plural noun: „nur ein paar Bissen/Lieder/Sätze/Antworten“. With people you may also hear „nur ein paar wenige Leute“ (= only a very few people).
target_language_example: Ich brauche nur ein paar Minuten.
native_language_example: I only need a few minutes.

additional_notes: Used to say something takes a short time or that you can stay for a short time. Often with verbs like dauern (to take), bleiben (to stay), warten (to wait). Note: vor Ihnen/euch = “before you” (formal/plural informal), often meaning “a few minutes earlier than you.”
target_language_example: Warte bitte, es sind nur ein paar Minuten.
native_language_example: Please wait, it’s only a few minutes.

meaning: only a few; just a couple (of).
additional_notes: Used to say the number/amount is small, often to downplay it or reassure someone. It can be followed by a plural noun (nur ein paar Leute/Schritte/Stiche) or by “von” + pronoun/noun (nur ein paar von uns). Often implies “not many / not much more than that.”
target_language_example: Ich brauche nur ein paar Minuten.
native_language_example: I only need a few minutes.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that there is exactly a single item/instance. "Eine" is the feminine form of "one/a" and is used with feminine nouns (often the noun is understood from context, e.g., "nur eine (Sache/Frage/Socke)"). With other genders/cases you’ll see forms like "nur ein" (masc./neut.), "nur einen" (acc. masc.), "nur einem" (dat.).
target_language_example: Ich brauche nur eine Minute.
native_language_example: I only need one minute.

additional_notes: Used to say there’s only one question left (“Es bleibt nur eine Frage.”) or to soften what you’re asking (“Ich habe nur eine Frage …”). In replies like “War ja nur eine Frage.” it downplays the question: “It was just a question,” often after someone reacts strongly.
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich habe nur eine Frage: Wo ist die Toilette?
native_language_example: Sorry, I just have one question: where is the bathroom?

meaning: "only a matter of time" (it will happen sooner or later).
additional_notes: Used to say an event is inevitable; often followed by a clause with "bis" ("until") or "bevor" ("before"). Can appear as "(Es) ist/war nur eine Frage der Zeit" or as a shortened comment: "..., nur eine Frage der Zeit."
target_language_example: Es ist nur eine Frage der Zeit, bis sie es herausfinden.
native_language_example: It’s only a matter of time until they find out.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to wait briefly or to say you only have a short amount of time. Common as a standalone phrase (“Nur eine Minute!”) in both formal (Sie) and informal (du/ihr) situations.
target_language_example: Nur eine Minute, ich komme sofort!
native_language_example: Just a minute, I’ll be right there!

additional_notes: Used to say there is just one of something. "Nur" = "only/just" and "einen" is the masculine accusative form of "ein" (e.g., einen Mond, einen Bruder, einen Muffin). For feminine/neuter or different cases, the form changes (e.g., "nur eine" Idee, "nur ein" Kind, "nur einem" Freund).
target_language_example: Ich habe nur einen Euro dabei.
native_language_example: I only have one euro with me.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens one single time (or just one time in total). With a time expression it can mean "only once every..." (e.g., "nur einmal alle hundert Jahre" = "only once every hundred years"). In general statements it often means "only once in life" (e.g., "Man ist nur einmal jung" = "You’re only young once").
target_language_example: Ich war nur einmal in Berlin.
native_language_example: I’ve only been to Berlin once.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something takes a very short time, or as a request for a brief moment (e.g., asking someone to wait). Can refer to time needed (“Ich brauche nur fünf Minuten.”) or time after an event (“nur fünf Minuten nach Spielbeginn” = only five minutes after the start of the game). Often said on its own as a short request: “Nur fünf Minuten.”
target_language_example: Warte bitte nur fünf Minuten, dann bin ich fertig.
native_language_example: Please wait just five minutes, then I’ll be done.

additional_notes: Used to limit something to a specific purpose, person, or time period: "nur für eine Woche" = only for a week. Very common with amounts/resources to show how long they last: "Das Essen reicht nur für eine Woche" (The food is only enough for a week). In the pattern "nur für ein(e) ...!" it can also add emphasis in exclamations: "Was war ich nur für ein Narr!" = What a fool I was!
target_language_example: Ich bin nur für zwei Tage in Berlin.
native_language_example: I'm only in Berlin for two days.

meaning: "only for a few" / "just for a couple of" (followed by a plural noun, often time).
additional_notes: Used to say something lasts or applies for a short time/quantity. Usually followed by a plural noun: "nur für ein paar Tage" (only for a few days), "nur für ein paar Minuten" (just for a couple of minutes). "ein paar" means "a few / a couple of" and is common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ich bleibe nur für ein paar Tage in Berlin.
native_language_example: I’m only staying in Berlin for a few days.

additional_notes: Used to compare amounts or degree, usually in the pattern „nur halb so + adjective/adverb + wie …“ (only half as … as …) or „nur halb so viel(e) + noun + wie …“ (only half as much/many … as …). Often implies something is 50% of someone else’s amount/degree.
target_language_example: Ich bin nur halb so schnell wie du.
native_language_example: I’m only half as fast as you.

additional_notes: Used to say something is possible/true only if a certain thing is included or available. Common in phrases like "nur mit Mühe" / "nur mit großen Schwierigkeiten" (= only with difficulty). Can also mean you are speaking/communicating exclusively with someone/something: "Ich rede nur mit dir" (= I’m only talking to you).
target_language_example: Ohne Passwort kommst du nur mit Hilfe rein.
native_language_example: Without a password, you can only get in with help.

meaning: only ... left/remaining; just ... more (and then no more).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that a number/amount/time has become very small compared to before: *Es sind nur noch drei da* (“There are only three left”). Often refers to what remains after a reduction, or what will happen from now on (sometimes like “only anymore”): *Ich trinke nur noch Wasser* (“I only drink water now”). Word order: usually placed before the quantity/time/thing that remains.
target_language_example: Wir haben nur noch zehn Minuten.
native_language_example: We only have ten minutes left.

meaning: only three more / just three left.
additional_notes: Used to say that the remaining amount is three (e.g., three items left, three minutes left, three stops left). Often said when counting down or emphasizing that not much is left. Word order can vary by context (e.g., „Es sind nur noch drei.“ / „Nur noch drei Tage!“).
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, es sind nur noch drei Minuten bis wir da sind.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it’s only three more minutes until we’re there.

additional_notes: “nur noch + time/amount” is a very common pattern meaning “only … left” or “just … more.” It often appears with “bis + event” (Nur noch drei Tage bis Weihnachten.) or with an infinitive phrase like “zu leben” (to live): “nur noch drei Tage zu leben haben” = “to have only three days left to live.” You can swap the number/time unit: nur noch zwei Wochen, nur noch fünf Minuten, etc.
target_language_example: Ich habe nur noch drei Tage Zeit, das Projekt fertig zu machen.
native_language_example: I only have three days left to finish the project.

additional_notes: Used to say there is just one remaining (often with verbs like bleiben: "Es bleibt nur noch ein ..."). It can also mean there’s just one more step/action needed: "Nur noch ein Schritt ...". With nouns it’s often followed by a singular noun: "nur noch ein Tag / ein Schritt". In phrases like "nur noch ein Schatten (ihrer selbst)", it means someone has become only a weak remnant of what they were.
target_language_example: Es ist nur noch ein Platz frei.
native_language_example: There’s only one seat left.

meaning: just one more; only one left; now only a (single) …
additional_notes: Used when there is exactly one item/person/step remaining ("only one left"), or when something has been reduced to just one thing/state ("nothing but a …"). The form "eine" is for feminine nouns; with masculine/neuter you’ll see "nur noch ein".
target_language_example: Ich habe nur noch eine Frage.
native_language_example: I only have one question left.

meaning: only very rarely anymore; hardly ever now.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens much less often than before. �nur noch� = �only� / �only anymore� (now compared to earlier), and �sehr selten� = �very rarely�. Often used with everyday habits or repeated actions.
target_language_example: Seit dem Umzug sehen wir uns nur noch sehr selten.
native_language_example: Since the move, we only see each other very rarely anymore.

additional_notes: Often used with verbs like (sich) lassen, können, or kommen to say something is difficult to do or happens only slowly. It means “not easily,” and can also express that something is hard to imagine or understand ("Ich kann mir das nur schwer vorstellen").
target_language_example: Der Text ist nur schwer zu verstehen.
native_language_example: The text is hard to understand.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens infrequently. Common in statements about habits or general frequency (often with the present tense). Word order: it can go after the verb or later in the sentence depending on what you emphasize (e.g., „Er schreibt nur selten.“ / „…aber ich sehe sie nur selten.“).
target_language_example: Ich esse nur selten Fleisch.
native_language_example: I only rarely eat meat.

meaning: (in exclamations) ‘ever/possibly’ to express disbelief or reproach: “How could … be so …?”
additional_notes: Often used in emotional questions with "Wie konnte/könntest du/Sie/ich/wir nur so … sein?" It adds emphasis (surprise, shock, criticism) and doesn’t mean “only so” here. Common with adjectives like "blind", "grausam", "dumm", "naiv".
target_language_example: Wie konntest du nur so unhöflich sein?
native_language_example: How could you possibly be so rude?

meaning: to be so stupid (said in shock/criticism: “How could … be so stupid?”)
additional_notes: Most often used in the pattern „Wie konnte(n/st) … nur so dumm sein?“ to express disbelief, frustration, or criticism about someone’s mistake. „nur“ here doesn’t mean “only” literally; it intensifies the question (like “ever/possibly”). „dumm“ is quite blunt, so it can sound rude if said directly to someone.
target_language_example: Wie konntet ihr nur so dumm sein und das Passwort weitergeben?
native_language_example: How could you be so stupid and give out the password?

additional_notes: Often used in the pattern **„Es geht (nur) um …“** to say what something is (only) about: **„Es geht nur um Aufmerksamkeit.“** = “It’s only about attention.” It can also appear before **um** with verbs that take **um**, e.g. **„sich kümmern um …“** (to take care of …): **„Ich hätte mich nur um mich kümmern sollen.“** = “I should only have taken care of myself.” Here **nur** limits the focus to that one thing/person.
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, es geht nur um ein paar Details.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it’s only about a few details.

additional_notes: Used with plural countable nouns to emphasize that the number is small. Often followed by a plural noun (e.g., „nur wenige Studenten“) and the verb is typically plural. Can also stand alone when the noun is clear from context: „Nur wenige haben es geschafft.“
target_language_example: Nur wenige Leute wissen davon.
native_language_example: Only a few people know about it.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the number of people is small. Often followed by a verb in plural (e.g., „nur wenige Menschen wissen …“). You can also use it with other nouns: „nur wenige Bücher“, „nur wenige Tage“ (only a few books/days).
target_language_example: Nur wenige Menschen haben genug Zeit für ihre Freunde.
native_language_example: Only a few people have enough time for their friends.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the number is small/limited. Often followed by a noun ("nur zwei Minuten", "nur zwei Restaurants") or used on its own when the noun is understood ("Es gibt nur zwei.").
target_language_example: Wir haben nur zwei Tickets, also können nur zwei Leute mitkommen.
native_language_example: We only have two tickets, so only two people can come along.

additional_notes: Used to say something lasts for a limited time period of two days, or that only two days remain. Often appears with time-related verbs like „gelten“/„gültig sein“ (to be valid) or with „es bleiben …“ (… remain).
target_language_example: Der Pass ist nur zwei Tage gültig.
native_language_example: The pass is only valid for two days.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the week after the current one. Often appears without an article ("nächste Woche"), but you may also hear "in der nächsten Woche" (= sometime next week). With appointments it can be used like a time adverb: "Wir sehen uns nächste Woche."
target_language_example: Ich habe nächste Woche einen Arzttermin.
native_language_example: I have a doctor’s appointment next week.

additional_notes: Used when saying you will go/travel somewhere next week: **nächste Woche** (next week) + **nach** + destination. **nach** is used with most cities and many countries **without an article** (nach Berlin, nach Kanada). With countries/places that take an article, you usually use **in** + article instead (e.g., *nächste Woche in die Schweiz*). Often appears with verbs like **fahren**, **reisen**, **fliegen**, **müssen**.
target_language_example: Wir fliegen nächste Woche nach Spanien.
native_language_example: We’re flying to Spain next week.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the week after the current one. It can be used with or without a verb: "Nächste Woche bin ich dort." / "Nächste Woche." You can also use it in the dative with a preposition: "in der nächsten Woche" (often a bit more formal or specific).
target_language_example: Nächste Woche habe ich einen Termin.
native_language_example: Next week I have an appointment.

additional_notes: In public transport you often hear/see **Nächste Haltestelle: …** (“Next stop: …”). The form **nächsten Haltestelle** is typically used with a preposition + article, e.g. **an der nächsten Haltestelle** (“at the next stop”) or **bis zur nächsten Haltestelle** (“until the next stop”). On its own, you’ll more commonly see **nächste Haltestelle**.
target_language_example: An der nächsten Haltestelle müssen wir umsteigen.
native_language_example: At the next stop we have to change (transfer).

additional_notes: Used to talk about something happening in the month after the current one. Often appears without an article as a time expression: „nächsten Monat“ (= next month). You can also say „im nächsten Monat“ (in the next month), but „nächsten Monat“ is the most common for plans. With „bis zum nächsten Monat“ it means “by next month” / “until next month”.
target_language_example: Nächsten Monat fange ich einen neuen Job an.
native_language_example: Next month I’m starting a new job.

meaning: “next month to (a destination)” / “going/traveling to … next month”.
additional_notes: Used when you mention a time + a destination: **nächsten Monat** (next month) + **nach** + place. **Nach** is used mainly with **cities** and **most countries** (usually **without an article**): *nach Boston, nach Australien*. If the place has an article, you typically use **in**: *in die Schweiz*, *in die USA*. In the examples it often appears with verbs like **fahren** (to go/drive/travel) or **müssen** (to have to).
target_language_example: Ich fliege nächsten Monat nach Berlin.
native_language_example: I’m flying to Berlin next month.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a point in time. Often appears without a preposition: „nächsten Montag“ (common in everyday speech). With a preposition it’s usually „am nächsten Montag“ (literally “on the next Monday”). Depending on context, it can mean the nearest upcoming Monday.
target_language_example: Ich habe nächsten Montag einen Arzttermin.
native_language_example: I have a doctor’s appointment next Monday.

additional_notes: Used to say that something will happen (or someone will be) on the next Monday, in a specific location. Word order: time phrase first ("nächsten Montag"), then location with "in" + place (e.g., "in Berlin", "in Boston"). "Nächsten" is the accusative form because "Montag" is implied as the time when something happens.
target_language_example: Wir sind nächsten Montag in Berlin.
native_language_example: We’ll be in Berlin next Monday.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the morning after a referenced day or event. Often appears with a preposition and case ending, e.g. **am nächsten Morgen** (= on the next morning; dative) or **den nächsten Morgen** in some contexts (accusative).
target_language_example: Am nächsten Morgen gehen wir zum Bahnhof.
native_language_example: The next morning we’re going to the train station.

additional_notes: Refers to the Sunday that comes next (often the upcoming Sunday). You can use it without an article as a time expression: „nächsten Sonntag“. With prepositions like „auf“ (postponed to), it’s common to use the accusative: „auf den nächsten Sonntag verschieben“.
target_language_example: Können wir uns nächsten Sonntag treffen?
native_language_example: Can we meet next Sunday?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the day after a reference point (often “tomorrow” from the perspective of that moment). Commonly used with prepositions like „am nächsten Tag“ (on the next day) or „bis zum nächsten Tag“ (until the next day). Note: „nächsten Tag“ often appears with a case ending depending on the sentence (e.g., „nächster Tag“, „nächsten Tag“).
target_language_example: Am nächsten Tag sind wir früh losgefahren.
native_language_example: The next day we left early.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens (or you do something) again on the following day. Often used with a verb: „Ich komme nächsten Tag wieder.“ In correct standard German you’ll also see: „am nächsten Tag wieder“ (“again the next day”) or „den nächsten Tag wieder“ depending on context.
target_language_example: Ich rufe dich nächsten Tag wieder an.
native_language_example: I’ll call you again the next day.

additional_notes: Used with travel/departure verbs like „abreisen“, „abfahren“, or „abfliegen“ (often with „am“: „am nächsten Tag wieder ab“). Here „ab“ is short for the idea of departing/going away again.
target_language_example: Wir kommen am Montag an und reisen am nächsten Tag wieder ab.
native_language_example: We arrive on Monday and leave again the next day.

additional_notes: Used to say someone left (a place) on the following day, often after a short visit. "abreisen" means "to depart/leave (on a trip)" and in the Perfekt it’s usually formed with "sein": "ist abgereist". "wieder" here means "again" (not "back"—for "back" you’d often use "zurück").
target_language_example: Er ist am nächsten Tag wieder abgereist.
native_language_example: He left again the next day.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the year after the current one. Often used with future plans or predictions; it can appear at the beginning of the sentence ("Nächstes Jahr ...") or later ("... nächstes Jahr ..."). Capitalize "Jahr" because it’s a noun; "nächstes" changes depending on gender/case (e.g., "nächsten Monat").
target_language_example: Nächstes Jahr mache ich einen Deutschkurs.
native_language_example: Next year I’m taking a German course.

meaning: "next year in …" (talking about where/when something will happen next year).
additional_notes: Used to set the time as next year and then add a place or time period with "in". Often followed by a location ("in Berlin") or a month/season (usually "im Mai", "im Sommer" = "in + dem" → "im"). With places, "in" typically takes the dative for a stationary location (e.g., "in Berlin").
target_language_example: Nächstes Jahr in Berlin besuche ich meine Freunde.
native_language_example: Next year in Berlin I’m visiting my friends.

additional_notes: Used to talk about going/moving/traveling to a place next year. Typically followed by a place name with **nach** (e.g., nach Frankreich, nach Boston, nach Australien). Often used with verbs like **fahren**, **gehen**, **ziehen**.
target_language_example: Wir fliegen nächstes Jahr nach Spanien.
native_language_example: We’re flying to Spain next year.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the next occasion something happens. Common in reminders, promises, warnings, or plans. Often used without an article: „Nächstes Mal …“ (not *„das nächstes Mal“).
target_language_example: Nächstes Mal komme ich früher.
native_language_example: Next time I’ll come earlier.

additional_notes: Used to invite someone to do an activity together at the next weekend. "nächstes Wochenende" is a common time expression (often without a preposition), and "mit uns" means "with us" ("uns" = "us"). It typically comes before the activity: "nächstes Wochenende mit uns + [Verb] gehen".
target_language_example: Hast du Lust, nächstes Wochenende mit uns ins Kino zu gehen?
native_language_example: Do you feel like going to the movies with us next weekend?

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that will happen on the next occasion (often implying a future attempt or opportunity). Often said at the start of a sentence: „Nächstes Mal mache ich das anders.“
target_language_example: Nächstes Mal machen wir das zusammen.
native_language_example: Next time we’ll do that together.
