It comes from „sich rühren“ = “to move,” even though „rühren“ by itself often means “to stir” (like stirring soup). Common with negatives: „Rührt euch nicht vom Fleck!" = “Don’t move an inch!”
target_language_example: Rührt euch jetzt endlich, wir sind spät dran!
native_language_example: Move it already, we’re running late!

meaning: abbrev.: “see there / see (the referenced entry)” ("siehe dort").
additional_notes: Used mainly in dictionaries, glossaries, and older/academic texts as a cross-reference. It tells you to look up the information at another place/entry that has just been mentioned.
target_language_example: Für weitere Details, s. d.
native_language_example: For more details, see there / see the referenced entry.

additional_notes: Uses the informal singular imperative "sag" (spoken to someone you address as "du"). It introduces a "dass" clause: after "dass", the conjugated verb typically goes to the end (e.g., "Sag, dass du morgen kommst."). For formal/polite, use "Sagen Sie, dass Sie...".
target_language_example: Sag, dass du morgen keine Zeit hast.
native_language_example: Say that you don’t have time tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to inform you once a condition is met or something happens. Very common in everyday speech. You can also say "Gib Bescheid, wenn ..." (same meaning; a bit more neutral/polite).
target_language_example: Sag Bescheid, wenn du fertig bist.
native_language_example: Let me know when you’re done.

additional_notes: Imperative with **du** (informal singular) from **sagen** + **es**. Used to prompt someone to speak or to say something in a certain way (e.g., **Sag es auf Französisch.** = “Say it in French.”). In phrases like **Ich sag es mal so**, it means “I’ll put it this way.”
target_language_example: Sag es mir bitte ehrlich.
native_language_example: Please tell me honestly.

additional_notes: Imperative form of "sagen" (to say/tell) addressed to "du" (one person you know well). "es" = "it" (the thing/information), "mir" = "to me." Often used with "bitte" to be polite ("Sag es mir bitte") or with strong words to sound angry/urgent ("Verdammt, sag es mir!"). For formal/polite address use: "Sagen Sie es mir."
target_language_example: Sag es mir bitte, wenn du Bescheid weißt.
native_language_example: Please tell me when you know.

additional_notes: Imperative (command) form of **sagen** addressed to **du** (one person you’re on informal terms with). **ihm** means “to him” (dative pronoun). Often followed by what you want to say: a noun phrase (**Sag ihm die Wahrheit.**) or a clause (**Sag ihm, dass … / was …**).
target_language_example: Sag ihm bitte, dass ich später anrufe.
native_language_example: Please tell him that I’ll call later.

additional_notes: Used to report or pass on a message to a male person (ihm = “to him”). It’s the informal imperative form of sagen (“to say/tell”) addressed to one person: sag! For more polite/formal situations you can say: Sagen Sie ihm, dass… After it, you use a dass-clause with verb at the end: …dass ich beschäftigt bin.
target_language_example: Sag ihm, dass ich später zurückrufe.
native_language_example: Tell him that I’ll call back later.

meaning: "tell him to ..." (asking you to pass on an instruction).
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to give a message/instruction to a male person (ihm = “to him”). After this, German often uses “er soll + infinitive” to report what someone should do (indirect command). Common with: aufhören (stop), bleiben (stay), herkommen (come here), abhauen (leave/get out).
target_language_example: Sag ihm, er soll mich nachher anrufen.
native_language_example: Tell him to call me later.

additional_notes: Uses the verb **sagen** in the **du** imperative: **Sag ...!** It introduces a **dass**-clause ("that"-clause), and you write a comma before **dass**. The **dass**-clause usually has the verb at the end: *Sag ihnen, dass sie warten sollen.* For a formal version, use **Sagen Sie ihnen, dass ...**
target_language_example: Sag ihnen, dass ich später komme.
native_language_example: Tell them that I’m coming later.

additional_notes: Imperative of sagen used when speaking to one person in the informal du form. ihr here means "to her" (dative), so the phrase is used to tell someone to say something to a female person.
target_language_example: Sag ihr bitte die Wahrheit.
native_language_example: Tell her the truth, please.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to pass a message to a woman/girl (“ihr” = “to her”). “Sag” is the informal (du) imperative of “sagen” (to say/tell), so it’s used with friends/family/children. The “dass” clause gives the message, and the verb in that clause usually goes to the end: „Sag ihr, dass ich komme.“
target_language_example: Sag ihr, dass ich später zurückrufe.
native_language_example: Tell her that I’ll call back later.

additional_notes: Used to pass on a message to a female person (“ihr” = “to her”). Follow it with a full clause where “ich” (I) is the subject. Often introduces what you want someone to report: Sag ihr, dass ich keine Zeit habe. (Tell her that I don’t have time.)
target_language_example: Sag ihr, dass ich später anrufe.
native_language_example: Tell her that I’ll call later.

additional_notes: Used when giving an instruction through someone else: you tell a person (du-form) to pass on a request/order to “her” (ihr). Often followed by an infinitive at the end: „Sag ihr, sie soll warten.“ You can also say „Sag ihr, dass sie … soll“, but „dass“ is often omitted in spoken German. Note: „sag“ is informal (to one person you address as „du“).
target_language_example: Sag ihr, sie soll mich später zurückrufen.
native_language_example: Tell her to call me back later.

meaning: “hey, tell me…” / “say…” (to get someone’s attention; often shows surprise or annoyance).
additional_notes: Literally “say (to me)”, from "sagen". Used a lot in spoken German to start a question or comment, like “hey” or “so…”. Tone depends on context: it can sound neutral/curious, surprised (“Sag mal!” = “Wait a second!”), or irritated (“Sag mal, will die mich verarschen?”). Often followed by a question, but it can also stand alone as an exclamation.
target_language_example: Sag mal, hast du kurz Zeit?
native_language_example: Hey, do you have a moment?

meaning: “Hey, are you …?” / “Tell me, are you …?” (often sounding annoyed or shocked).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a question, often rhetorically, when you’re surprised, irritated, or can’t believe what someone did. It’s informal and can sound confrontational depending on tone. Literally: “say (to me), are you …”.
target_language_example: Sag mal, bist du sicher, dass das eine gute Idee ist?
native_language_example: Hey, are you sure that’s a good idea?

meaning: "Hey, what…?" / "Tell me, what…?" (used to introduce a question, often with surprise or concern).
additional_notes: Common conversational opener before a question. It can sound slightly impatient, nosy, or worried depending on tone and context. Very often followed by questions like „Was ist los (mit …)?“ or „Was geht (mit …)?“. Literally it’s „say (to me)“ + „what“, but it’s mainly used like an English „hey“ or „so“ to get someone’s attention.
target_language_example: Sag mal, was ist denn passiert?
native_language_example: Hey, what happened?

meaning: "Say, where…?" / "Hey, where…?" (casual way to ask where something/someone is or where something comes from).
additional_notes: "Sag mal" literally means "say (to me)" and is used to get someone’s attention before a question. It often sounds informal and can hint at surprise, impatience, or "come on…" depending on tone. Commonly followed by questions like "wo ist…?", "wo sind…?", or "woher…?"
target_language_example: Sag mal, wo ist mein Handy schon wieder?
native_language_example: Hey, where is my phone again?

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "(du) sagst" + "mir" (to me). It’s the imperative used when speaking to one person you address as du. Often followed by a question word (wie, wann, woher) or a clause with wenn (“tell me if/when…”). For polite/formal, use "Sagen Sie mir …"; for plural informal, "Sagt mir …".
target_language_example: Sag mir bitte, was los ist.
native_language_example: Please tell me what's going on.

additional_notes: Used to ask for a reason/explanation. It’s the imperative of "sagen" (du-form): "Sag mir …" + an indirect question with "warum". In standard word order, the verb goes to the end: "Sag mir, warum das so wichtig ist." In speech you may also hear a direct-question order after the comma ("Sag mir, warum ist das so wichtig?"), but the indirect form is more typical in writing.
target_language_example: Sag mir, warum du so spät bist.
native_language_example: Tell me why you're so late.

meaning: “tell me why you …” (asking for an explanation).
additional_notes: Used to press someone to explain their reason. It starts with the imperative **Sag mir** (“Tell me”) and is followed by the indirect question **warum du …** (“why you …”). In German, **warum** introduces a subordinate clause, so the conjugated verb usually goes to the end: **Sag mir, warum du das denkst.**
target_language_example: Sag mir, warum du heute nicht kommen kannst.
native_language_example: Tell me why you can’t come today.

additional_notes: Uses the informal (du) imperative of sagen: "sag". It’s followed by a comma and then a subordinate clause starting with "was"; in that clause, the verb usually goes to the end (e.g., "Sag mir, was du willst.").
target_language_example: Sag mir, was du heute Abend machen willst.
native_language_example: Tell me what you want to do tonight.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone (du-form) to tell you information about what they did/said/saw/heard, etc. It’s an imperative: sag mir … (“tell me …”), followed by an indirect question: was du … (“what you …”). In writing you often see a comma, but in English you usually drop it: “Tell me what you saw.”
target_language_example: Sag mir, was du heute gemacht hast.
native_language_example: Tell me what you did today.

meaning: "tell me who" (asking for a person’s identity).
additional_notes: Used to ask who someone is or who did something. "Sag mir" is an informal/neutral imperative to one person (du); more formal: "Sagen Sie mir, wer ...". The clause after "wer" takes normal word order: "wer gewonnen hat", "wer du bist".
target_language_example: Sag mir, wer heute kommt.
native_language_example: Tell me who is coming today.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to explain a method or way to do something. It uses the informal/“du” imperative (sag). For a more formal/polite version, use “Sagen Sie mir, wie …” or “Sag mir bitte, wie …”.
target_language_example: Sag mir, wie ich dorthin komme.
native_language_example: Tell me how to get there.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to give you the location of something/someone, or to say where something happened. Commonly followed by a full clause with the verb at the end (e.g., „Sag mir, wo du bist.“). In questions like „Sag mir, wo ich … soll“, it can also mean asking where you should go next.
target_language_example: Sag mir, wo die nächste U-Bahn-Station ist.
native_language_example: Tell me where the nearest subway station is.

meaning: let me know; tell me (when something happens).
additional_notes: Common, friendly way to ask someone to inform you. Often used with a time/condition clause (e.g., "Wenn ... , sag mir Bescheid!"). You can also say "Gib mir Bescheid" (same meaning). Formal: "Sagen Sie mir Bescheid."
target_language_example: Sag mir Bescheid, wenn du angekommen bist.
native_language_example: Let me know when you arrive.

additional_notes: Common way to ask someone to inform you once something happens or is decided. Uses the idiom „Bescheid sagen“ (= to let someone know / give someone notice). You can also say „Gib mir Bescheid, wenn du …“ (same meaning).
target_language_example: Sag mir Bescheid, wenn du Zeit hast.
native_language_example: Let me know when you have time.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone you address as du to tell you something. "Sag" is the informal (du) imperative of "sagen" (to say/tell). Often followed by a noun ("die Wahrheit") or a question word + clause ("warum/was/wie ..."). For formal/polite situations use: "Sagen Sie mir bitte ...". Common extension: "Sag mir bitte Bescheid" = "Please let me know."
target_language_example: Sag mir bitte, wann du Zeit hast.
native_language_example: Please tell me when you have time.

additional_notes: Direct command using the informal imperative of "sagen" (du-form): "Sag ...!" Often used when you think someone is hiding something. You can also say "Sagen Sie mir die Wahrheit" in formal situations.
target_language_example: Bitte, sag mir die Wahrheit—was ist passiert?
native_language_example: Please, tell me the truth—what happened?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone (with du) to be direct and give information. Common before a subordinate clause with was (“what”), e.g., “Sag mir einfach, was passiert ist.” If you’re speaking formally (Sie), use: “Sagen Sie mir einfach, was …”
target_language_example: Sag mir einfach, was du brauchst.
native_language_example: Just tell me what you need.

meaning: "Come on, tell me already!" (urging someone to speak).
additional_notes: Used to push someone to finally say something—often because you’re impatient or curious. Common with intensifiers like „Jetzt sag schon!“, „Na los, sag schon!“ or followed by an indirect question: „Sag schon, was du gesehen hast.“
target_language_example: Sag schon, was ist passiert?
native_language_example: Come on, what happened?

additional_notes: An imperative with du: **Sag** = “tell (me/us)”. **uns** is “us”. After the comma, **was** introduces an indirect question (“what ...”). You can swap the object: **Sag mir, was ...** (tell me what ...), **Sagt uns, was ...** (tell us, plural/you all). Often used when someone wants an explanation or answer right now.
target_language_example: Sag uns, was du gesehen hast.
native_language_example: Tell us what you saw.

additional_notes: Common spoken/written contraction of the du-imperative „sag es“. The apostrophe shows that the „e“ in „es“ is dropped: „Sag’s mir!“ = „Sag es mir!“. Used to tell someone to say something, often in phrases like „Sag’s auf Deutsch!“ or „Wenn du Hilfe brauchst, sag’s (einfach)!“.
target_language_example: Wenn du es weißt, sag’s mir bitte.
native_language_example: If you know it, please tell me (say it to me).

additional_notes: From **sagen** (to say/tell) + **dir** (to you). Often used to stress that you’re sure about something, similar to English “I’m telling you” / “believe me.” You’ll also see it as **ich sage dir ...** (I tell you ...) or in the imperative **Sag(’ ) dir ...** / **Sag mir ...** depending on the pronoun.
target_language_example: Ich sage dir, das wird heute noch passieren.
native_language_example: I’m telling you, it’s still going to happen today.

additional_notes: Just the verb sagen with ich. Because German often puts the verb before the subject after another element, you will often see sage ich where English would simply say I say. It can also be used parenthetically for emphasis, especially in phrases like sage ich dir = I'm telling you.
target_language_example: Dann sage ich nichts mehr.
native_language_example: Then I won’t say anything more.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a full clause after the verb sagen (“to say/tell”), typically with a comma before dass: „Ich muss sagen, dass …“. In everyday speech, dass is often omitted: „Ich muss sagen, ich komme später.“ Note: conjugated forms (e.g., „ich sage“, „er sagte“, „wir sagen“) are common; the entry form „sagen, dass“ represents the pattern.
target_language_example: Ich muss sagen, dass ich euch beneide.
native_language_example: I have to say that I envy you.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what someone says/claims about “you” with a dass-clause. After „dass“, German word order changes: the conjugated verb usually goes to the end (e.g., „…, dass du recht hast.“). „du“ is informal “you”; you can swap it for another subject (er/sie/wir/etc.).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir sagen, dass du morgen Zeit hast?
native_language_example: Can you tell me that you have time tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect statement about a male person ("er" = "he"). After „sagen, dass …“, German often puts the verb at the end of the clause: „… dass er nie sein Dorf verlassen hat.“ In speech, „dass“ is sometimes left out: „Er sagt, er kommt später.“
target_language_example: Ich muss dir sagen, dass er heute keine Zeit hat.
native_language_example: I have to tell you that he doesn’t have time today.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you want to communicate about yourself, often with a person in the dative: „jdm. sagen, dass ich …“ = “tell someone that I …”. The verb is conjugated to match the subject (ich sage, du sagst, er/sie sagt, wir sagen, ihr sagt, sie/Sie sagen).
target_language_example: Kannst du ihr sagen, dass ich heute nicht kommen kann?
native_language_example: Can you tell her that I can’t come today?

additional_notes: Used to report what someone claims or states. "sagen" is "to say/tell"; "dass" introduces an indirect statement (“that …”); "sie" can mean “they” or “she” depending on context. Word order: the verb in the "dass"-clause goes to the end (e.g., „… dass sie kommen.“).
target_language_example: Sie sagen, dass sie heute keine Zeit haben.
native_language_example: They say that they don’t have time today.

additional_notes: Used when introducing a subordinate clause with **dass** (“that”) and the subject **wir** (“we”): **(jemandem) sagen, dass wir …**. Often used to share information or opinions (e.g., *Ich wollte dir sagen, dass wir …*). Word order: the main clause has **sagen**, and in the **dass**-clause the verb goes to the end (*dass wir nach Toronto ziehen*).
target_language_example: Kannst du ihnen sagen, dass wir später kommen?
native_language_example: Can you tell them that we’re coming later?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a statement in a subordinate clause with **daß** (traditional spelling; modern standard spelling is usually **dass**). You normally put a **comma** before daß, and the **conjugated verb goes to the end** of the daß-clause: „Ich sage, daß ich heute keine Zeit **habe**.“ Often used with a person in the dative: „jemandem sagen, daß …“.
target_language_example: Wie oft muß ich Ihnen noch sagen, daß Sie hier drin nicht rauchen sollen?
native_language_example: How many more times do I have to tell you that you’re not supposed to smoke in here?

meaning: to say/tell (someone) why; to explain why.
additional_notes: Used when asking someone to explain the reason for something. Often appears in questions with "kannst/können/könntest ... sagen, warum ...?". Typically you include the person being told in the dative: "Sag mir/uns/ihm/ihr, warum ...".
target_language_example: Kannst du mir sagen, warum du heute nicht kommst?
native_language_example: Can you tell me why you’re not coming today?

additional_notes: Used when “what” introduces a clause after a verb of speaking: „sagen, was …“. Very common in phrases like „sagen, was du willst“ (“say what you want”) or „sagen, was passiert ist“ (“say what happened”). Here „was“ means “what” (not “that”).
target_language_example: Du kannst sagen, was du denkst.
native_language_example: You can say what you think.

additional_notes: Used when someone is going to explain or report something: „… sagen, was Sie + verb …“. It introduces an indirect clause with „was“ (“what”). „Sie“ is the formal “you” (often used with strangers, customers, officials); in informal speech you’d use „du“: „sagen, was du …“.
target_language_example: Können Sie mir sagen, was Sie brauchen?
native_language_example: Can you tell me what you need?

additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect question or statement about information from the speaker, often followed by a verb at the end of the clause: „… sagen, was ich weiß/denke/brauche/fühle.“ A comma is required before „was“. The person you’re speaking to can be added: „Kannst du mir sagen, was ich tun soll?“
target_language_example: Kannst du mir sagen, was ich tun soll?
native_language_example: Can you tell me what I should do?

additional_notes: Used when asking or deciding to explain an event. The person you tell is usually in the dative: mir/dir/uns/ihm/ihr/Ihnen. Common in questions and polite requests (e.g., „Könntest du …?“ / „Würden Sie mir bitte …?“).
target_language_example: Können Sie mir sagen, was passiert ist?
native_language_example: Can you tell me what happened?

meaning: to tell (someone) what she/they should/did/want to do.
additional_notes: Used with the verb „sagen“ + an object (e.g., „ihr“, „ihnen“, a name) and a „was“-clause: „jemandem sagen, was sie …“. In the „was“-clause, the verb usually goes to the end (e.g., „was sie tun soll“, „was sie getan hat“). „sie“ can mean “she” or “they” (and „Sie“ with a capital S is formal “you”).
target_language_example: Kannst du ihm sagen, was sie gesagt hat?
native_language_example: Can you tell him what she said?

additional_notes: Common in questions about what to reply in a situation: **Was soll ich (ihm/ihr) sagen, wenn …?** = “What should I tell him/her when/if …?” The **wenn**-clause usually comes at the end, and the verb goes to the end of that clause (e.g., *wenn ich ihn treffe*). Also appears in the idiom **von Glück sagen können, wenn …** meaning “to be lucky if … / to count yourself lucky if …”.
target_language_example: Was soll ich dir sagen, wenn du wieder zu spät kommst?
native_language_example: What should I tell you when you’re late again?

additional_notes: Used with an indirect question starting with **wie** (“how”). Common patterns: **jemandem sagen, wie …** = “tell someone how …” (often giving instructions or explaining), and **nicht sagen können, wie …** = “can’t say how …” (to emphasize feelings/degree). It can also be used to ask for an estimate: **Was würdest du sagen, wie …?** = “What would you say, how …?”
target_language_example: Kannst du mir sagen, wie ich zum Bahnhof komme?
native_language_example: Can you tell me how to get to the train station?

additional_notes: Used with an object (often in dative) + "sagen" and an indirect question with "wo". Common patterns: „Kannst du mir sagen, wo … ist?“ / „Ich kann nicht sagen, wo … ist.“ The verb often goes at the end of the „wo“-clause: „…, wo der Bahnhof ist.“
target_language_example: Kannst du mir sagen, wo die Toilette ist?
native_language_example: Can you tell me where the restroom is?

meaning: to tell (someone) where the nearest … is.
additional_notes: Used to ask for directions or locations. Common polite forms: “Können Sie mir (bitte) sagen …?” (formal) and “Könnt ihr mir sagen …?” / “Kannst du mir sagen …?” (informal). The thing you’re looking for is a noun phrase like “die nächste Tankstelle / Bushaltestelle / Kirche”. Word order: “…, wo die nächste ___ ist?”
target_language_example: Können Sie mir bitte sagen, wo die nächste Apotheke ist?
native_language_example: Could you please tell me where the nearest pharmacy is?

additional_notes: Used to politely (but firmly) tell one person to speak or to pass on information. It’s the imperative of "sagen" with the formal "Sie". Often followed by an object (mir/ihm/ihr/uns) and/or a clause: "Sagen Sie mir, ..." / "Sagen Sie ihm, dass ...". In questions like "Warum sagen Sie das?" it means "why are you saying that?".
target_language_example: Sagen Sie mir bitte, wie ich zum Bahnhof komme.
native_language_example: Please tell me how to get to the train station.

additional_notes: Imperative form used when speaking politely to one person ("Sie"). "es" refers to some information already known from context (e.g., the reason, the truth, the name). Often used to urge someone to speak up; particles like "doch" or "schon" add impatience/encouragement ("Come on, say it!").
target_language_example: Sagen Sie es bitte direkt.
native_language_example: Please say it directly.

additional_notes: Used when addressing someone with formal „Sie“ and asking/telling them to pass a message to a male person („ihm“ = to him). Often followed by a clause with „dass …“ or a question word: „Sagen Sie ihm, dass … / wo … / was …“.
target_language_example: Sagen Sie ihm bitte, dass ich später zurückrufe.
native_language_example: Please tell him that I’ll call back later.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to give you information. It’s the imperative of **sagen** addressed to **Sie** (formal “you”), plus **mir** (“to me”). Often followed by a question word or a comma + clause: *Sagen Sie mir, wann/wo/warum …*.
target_language_example: Sagen Sie mir bitte, wo der Bahnhof ist.
native_language_example: Please tell me where the train station is.

additional_notes: Used to politely (and sometimes firmly) ask someone to explain or specify something. "Sagen Sie" is the formal imperative (Sie-form) of "sagen" (to say/tell), and "mir" means "to me." It’s typically followed by a full clause: "... was Ihr Plan ist" (what your plan is). In informal speech with friends you’d usually say: "Sag mir, was ...".
target_language_example: Sagen Sie mir, was genau passiert ist.
native_language_example: Tell me what exactly happened.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask for information or an opinion. It’s in the formal "Sie" form, so you use it with strangers, customers, officials, etc. The verb is an imperative: "Sagen Sie …!" and it’s followed by an indirect question starting with "was Sie …" (what you …).
target_language_example: Sagen Sie mir, was Sie heute vorhaben.
native_language_example: Tell me what you’re planning to do today.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask for instructions or an explanation. It’s the formal form (Sie) used with strangers, in customer service, etc. Typically followed by a subordinate clause with the verb at the end: „… wie ich … komme“, „… wie man … benutzt“. Often used with „bitte“ for extra politeness.
target_language_example: Bitte sagen Sie mir, wie ich zum Flughafen komme.
native_language_example: Please tell me how to get to the airport.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to give you a location or point out where something/someone is. "Sie" makes it formal (to a stranger, official, etc.). Often followed by a full clause with the verb at the end: "Sagen Sie mir, wo die Polizeiwache ist." You can also use it in a broader sense to mean "tell me where I'm wrong" (explain what the mistake is).
target_language_example: Sagen Sie mir, wo der Bahnhof ist, bitte.
native_language_example: Please tell me where the train station is.

additional_notes: Uses the formal "Sie" form (for strangers, customers, officials, etc.). Often followed by a question word (wie/was/welcher…) or by "Bescheid" ("Sagen Sie mir bitte Bescheid" = “Please let me know”). Word order can also be "Sagen Sie bitte mir…" but "Sagen Sie mir bitte…" is very common.
target_language_example: Sagen Sie mir bitte, wo die Toilette ist.
native_language_example: Please tell me where the restroom is.

additional_notes: Uses the formal "Sie" form, so it’s appropriate for strangers, customers, officials, etc. Often followed by what you should tell: a noun ("die Wahrheit"), or a clause with a question word/"dass" ("Sagen Sie uns, wer Sie sind." / "Sagen Sie uns, dass ..."). Word order note: if a verb comes at the end of the clause ("wo ... versteckt ist"), that’s normal in German after a comma.
target_language_example: Sagen Sie uns bitte, wie wir Ihnen helfen können.
native_language_example: Please tell us how we can help you.

meaning: “to tell (someone) already / to just say it” (often with an impatient or urging tone)
additional_notes: Most commonly appears in the imperative (**Sag schon! / Sagen Sie schon!**) to push someone to finally say something (because they’re hesitating or keeping you in suspense). **schon** adds impatience/pressure, similar to “already,” “come on,” or “just” in English. The base form **sagen schon** is less common on its own, but occurs in subordinate clauses or with modal verbs (e.g., **Du musst es sagen schon** is unidiomatic; prefer **Du musst es schon sagen**).
target_language_example: Du solltest mir endlich sagen schon, was los ist.
native_language_example: You should finally tell me already what’s going on.

meaning: “should have said” / “was supposed to say” (expressing what would have been better or expected).
additional_notes: Most often used with the subjunctive past (Konjunktiv II + hätten): **hätte/hättest/hätten … sagen sollen**. It talks about a past situation and implies regret, criticism, or that something was expected: *Das hättest du nicht sagen sollen* = “You shouldn’t have said that.” Word order: *Du hättest es ihm sagen sollen* (“You should have told him”).
target_language_example: Wir hätten dir die Wahrheit sagen sollen.
native_language_example: We should have told you the truth.

meaning: to want to say; to mean (to say)
additional_notes: Used to express what someone intends to express or is trying to convey, often equivalent to “mean” in English. Common in questions and with object clauses ("was ... sagen wollen"): e.g., "Ich verstehe, was Sie sagen wollen." Grammatically: infinitive "sagen" + modal verb "wollen"; in subordinate clauses the finite verb "wollen" typically comes at the end.
target_language_example: Ich verstehe, was Sie sagen wollen.
native_language_example: I understand what you mean.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what someone would say in an imagined situation, to make a statement sound less direct, or in indirect questions (often after *was*, *wer*, *wie*, etc.). It can also appear with expressions like *als ob* (“as if”) and *Angst haben, dass ...* (“to be afraid that ...”). Word order: the conjugated helper *würde* typically goes in the verb position, and *sagen* stays in the infinitive at the end of the clause.
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht, was er dazu sagen würde.
native_language_example: I don’t know what he would say about that.

additional_notes: From the verb "sagen" (to say/tell): "du sagst" = you say; in questions "Sagst du ...?" = Are you saying ...? Often used to challenge or clarify what someone means ("Ein Fluch, sagst du?") or in requests: "Sagst du mir Bescheid ...?" = Will you let me know ...? Can also mean "tell" with an indirect object: "Sagst du es mir?" = Will you tell me?
target_language_example: Sagst du mir bitte, was passiert ist?
native_language_example: Will you please tell me what happened?

meaning: “what do you say to that?” / “what do you think about it?”
additional_notes: Used to ask someone for their reaction or opinion about something that was just said/proposed. Often appears in questions like “Was sagst du dazu?” (What do you say to that?) or after a suggestion: “Ich könnte morgen kommen—was sagst du dazu?” Word order is inverted (verb first) because it’s a question.
target_language_example: Ich habe zwei Karten fürs Konzert – was sagst du dazu?
native_language_example: I have two tickets for the concert—what do you say to that?

meaning: "do you tell me" / "will you tell me" (addressing one person).
additional_notes: From "(du) sagst" (you say/tell) + "mir" (to me). It’s commonly used in questions and requests: "Sagst du mir ...?" = "Can/Would you tell me ...?" In yes/no questions, the verb often comes first (Sagst du mir ...?). You’ll also see it with "Bescheid" in the fixed phrase "Sagst du mir Bescheid?" = "Will you let me know?"
target_language_example: Sagst du mir bitte, wo der Bahnhof ist?
native_language_example: Can you please tell me where the train station is?

additional_notes: Used with the verb **sagen** (“to say”) to introduce a subordinate clause with **dass** (“that”). In writing, you usually put a comma before **dass**: *Er sagt, dass …* In **dass**-clauses, the verb typically goes to the end: *… dass sie keine Zeit hat.* In informal speech, **dass** is often omitted: *Er sagt, sie hat keine Zeit.*
target_language_example: Sie sagt, dass sie morgen keine Zeit hat.
native_language_example: She says that she doesn’t have time tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to report what a man/boy says. After „dass“ (that), German usually sends the conjugated verb to the end of the clause: „Er sagt, dass er müde ist.“ You can replace „er“ with „sie“ (she) or „ich“ (I), etc., depending on who is speaking.
target_language_example: Sie sagt, dass er heute keine Zeit hat.
native_language_example: She says that he doesn’t have time today.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone says. After **dass**, the verb in the clause typically goes to the end: **Sie sagt, dass ich morgen komme.** In speech, **dass** is sometimes omitted: **Sie sagt, ich komme morgen.** (then the clause has normal word order).
target_language_example: Er sagt, dass ich heute früher nach Hause gehen soll.
native_language_example: He says that I should go home earlier today.

additional_notes: Used to report what a woman has said (indirect/reported speech). It’s common to put a comma before „dass“. After „dass“, German often uses normal word order (verb later): „… dass sie viel zu tun hat.“ You may also see the subjunctive (Konjunktiv I) in more formal reporting: „… dass sie Französisch studiere.“
target_language_example: Er sagt, dass sie morgen keine Zeit hat.
native_language_example: He says that she doesn’t have time tomorrow.

meaning: "says (that) you…" (introducing what someone tells you to do).
additional_notes: Used with reported instructions/commands: "Er sagt, du sollst …" = "He says you should/are supposed to …". The comma often appears before a full clause (common in writing), and the verb in the next clause typically comes at the end: "du sollst/du musst …".
target_language_example: Sie sagt, du sollst jetzt nach Hause gehen.
native_language_example: She says you should go home now.

meaning: “(he) says that he …” (reporting what a man says).
additional_notes: Used in indirect/reported speech. The comma often introduces the reported clause (especially in writing): „Tom sagt, er …“. In the second part, German keeps main-clause word order (verb in 2nd position): „er wurde …“, „er will …“. In everyday speech you may also hear „Tom sagt, dass er …“ (with „dass“ = “that”), where the verb goes to the end.
target_language_example: Sie sagt, er hat keine Zeit.
native_language_example: She says (that) he doesn’t have time.

meaning: “says (that) he has” in reported/indirect speech using Konjunktiv I (subjunctive I).
additional_notes: Used to report what someone claims without presenting it as a direct quote or as a confirmed fact (common in journalism and formal reporting). After „sagt,“ German often uses Konjunktiv I: „er habe“ (instead of indicative „er hat“). Related patterns: „sagt, er sei…“ (is), „sagt, er werde…“ (will), „sagt, er könne…“ (can).
target_language_example: Tom sagt, er habe Maria im Park gesehen.
native_language_example: Tom says he saw Maria in the park.

additional_notes: Used for indirect speech (reported speech) with **Konjunktiv I**: **habe** is the Konjunktiv I form of **haben** (instead of **hat**). It’s common in formal writing and news reports to show you’re reporting what someone said, not stating it as a fact. In everyday speech, many people also say: **Er sagt, er hat ...**
target_language_example: Tom sagt, er habe mit der Angelegenheit nichts zu tun.
native_language_example: Tom says he has nothing to do with the matter.

additional_notes: Used to report what a man claims/says, often in news-like or neutral reporting. The verb form „könne“ is Konjunktiv I (subjunctive) and signals that you’re reporting someone’s statement without confirming it. With a named person you’ll also see: „Tom sagt, er könne …“. In everyday speech, many speakers also use the indicative: „Er sagt, er kann …“.
target_language_example: Sie sagt, er könne morgen kommen.
native_language_example: She says (that) he can come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone says without quoting them directly. "sei" is Konjunktiv I (subjunctive) of "sein" and is common in indirect speech, especially after verbs like "sagen" and in phrases like "Man sagt, ..." (= people say / it is said). In everyday speech, many speakers also use the indicative: "Er sagt, er ist ..."
target_language_example: Sie sagt, er sei schon zu Hause.
native_language_example: She says (that) he is already at home.

additional_notes: Used in reported (indirect) speech: first clause with "sagt" (says), then a comma, then a new clause with "er will" (he wants). In English, "that" is often optional. You can replace the subject as needed (e.g., "Sie sagt, sie will...", "Tom sagt, er will...") and change the verb phrase that follows "will".
target_language_example: Tom sagt, er will nach Boston gehen.
native_language_example: Tom says he wants to go to Boston.

additional_notes: Used to report what a man said, often in news/reporting style. "wolle" is Konjunktiv I of "wollen" and shows you are reporting someone’s statement (not necessarily saying it’s true). In everyday speech, many people also say: "Er sagt, er will ..."
target_language_example: Sie sagt, er wolle morgen vorbeikommen.
native_language_example: She says he wants to stop by tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone says, often with a comma and a clause starting with "es" ("it"). German can use this without "dass" ("that"): "Er sagt, es ist zu spät." = "He says (that) it’s too late." "Sagt," can also be the imperative (plural/formal): "Sagt, es ist dringend." = "Say/Tell (them) it’s urgent."
target_language_example: Sie sagt, es regnet später.
native_language_example: She says (that) it will rain later.

additional_notes: Used to introduce reported speech: someone (often named before) says that she did/wants something. In German you often see a comma before the reported clause: „Maria sagt, sie …“. In more formal/written German, the verb in the reported clause is often in Konjunktiv I (e.g., „sie wolle“, „sie habe“) to show it’s reported, not necessarily a fact.
target_language_example: Er sagt, sie habe heute keine Zeit.
native_language_example: He says (that) she doesn’t have time today.

additional_notes: Used with the impersonal pronoun "man" (= one/you/people) to ask for the usual/correct way to say something or to refer to what people commonly say. Very common in questions like "Sagt man das so?" (Is that how you say it?) and "Wie sagt man…?" (How do you say…?).
target_language_example: Wie sagt man das auf Deutsch?
native_language_example: How do you say that in German?

additional_notes: Used when asking for a translation into another language. Very common in the pattern: „Wie sagt man das auf Englisch/Deutsch/Spanisch?“ = “How do you say that in English/German/Spanish?” The language comes after „auf“ (e.g., „auf Deutsch“).
target_language_example: Wie sagt man das auf Deutsch?
native_language_example: How do you say that in German?

additional_notes: From **sagen** (to say/tell). **Das sagt mir (et)was** means “That tells me something” or “That rings a bell / means something to me” (you understand it or recognize it). **Sagt mir ...** can also be an imperative (often to a group or as a polite/formal command): “Tell me ...”.
target_language_example: Das sagt mir nichts.
native_language_example: That doesn’t mean anything to me / That doesn’t ring a bell.

meaning: “tell me what …” (asking for instructions or information).
additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect question with **was** (“what”). **Sagt** is the **ihr** (informal plural) imperative of *sagen* (“to say/tell”), so it’s used when speaking to more than one person you address as **ihr**. For one person: **Sag mir, was …**; formal: **Sagen Sie mir, was …**.
target_language_example: Sagt mir, was ich als Nächstes machen soll.
native_language_example: Tell me what I should do next.

additional_notes: Used to address a group (ihr = “you all”) and introduce an indirect question. It’s followed by a verb at the end of the clause (e.g., wisst, gesehen habt, hört, davon haltet). Common for asking people to describe what they know/see/hear or to give their opinion.
target_language_example: Sagt mir, was ihr heute gelernt habt.
native_language_example: Tell me what you learned today.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said: "[Person] sagte, dass + clause". In everyday speech, the clause often uses normal word order (e.g., "..., dass ich mich verspäte"), but in more formal writing or reported speech you may see subjunctive I forms (e.g., "..., dass er geholfen habe").
target_language_example: Er sagte, dass er heute keine Zeit hat.
native_language_example: He said that he doesn’t have time today.

additional_notes: Used to report what a man or boy said. The comma before „dass“ is required. After „dass“, German word order changes: the conjugated verb usually goes to the end of the clause (e.g., „dass er heute keine Zeit hat“). In indirect speech you may also see Konjunktiv forms like „sei“.
target_language_example: Sie sagte, dass er keine Zeit habe.
native_language_example: She said that he didn’t have time.

meaning: 'said (that) there is/it is…' (reporting what someone said).
additional_notes: Used to introduce reported speech: someone "said that…". After "dass" (that), the verb usually goes to the end of the clause (e.g., "sicher sei", "wahr sein könnte", "zu spät sei"). "es" can mean "it" (it is…) or act as a dummy subject meaning "there" (there is/are…).
target_language_example: Er sagte, dass es heute zu kalt sei, um schwimmen zu gehen.
native_language_example: He said that it was too cold to go swimming today.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said about you, often followed by a subordinate clause where the verb goes to the end: "Er sagte, dass ich ...". In everyday speech, people often skip "dass": "Er sagte, ich sehe anders aus." Tense in the reported clause can shift (e.g., "... dass ich anders aussehe" vs. "... dass ich anders aussehen würde").
target_language_example: Der Arzt sagte, dass ich mehr Wasser trinken soll.
native_language_example: The doctor said that I should drink more water.

additional_notes: Used when reporting what a woman/girl said. It’s followed by a **dass**-clause; the verb usually goes to the **end** of that clause: „… dass sie krank **ist**.“ In formal written German, reported speech often uses **Konjunktiv I**: „… dass sie krank **sei**.“
target_language_example: Er sagte, dass sie heute keine Zeit hat.
native_language_example: He said that she doesn’t have time today.

meaning: "said that she …" (introducing what she said; often followed by a reflexive verb).
additional_notes: Used to report what a woman/girl said (indirect/reported speech). After **dass** (“that”), German normally sends the main verb to the end of the clause: *Sie sagte, dass sie sich freue.* The **sich** is a reflexive pronoun (“herself”) and appears because many common verbs are reflexive in German (e.g., *sich freuen* = “to be happy/glad”, *sich wünschen* = “to wish”, *sich langweilen* = “to be bored”, *sich fühlen* = “to feel”). In reported speech you may see **Konjunktiv I** forms like *freue, wünsche*.
target_language_example: Sie sagte, dass sie sich heute nicht gut fühlt.
native_language_example: She said that she doesn’t feel well today.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said. It’s followed by a subordinate clause introduced by „daß“ (old spelling; modern spelling: „dass“), which sends the conjugated verb to the end of the clause. A comma is normally used before „daß“.
target_language_example: Maria sagte, daß sie sich schwach fühle.
native_language_example: Maria said (that) she felt weak.

additional_notes: Used to report what a woman said: a main clause with sagte (“said”) followed by a daß/dass-clause. In written German, daß is the older spelling; modern spelling is dass. In reported speech you may see Konjunktiv I/II (e.g., habe, hätte, fühle) to show it’s indirect speech.
target_language_example: Er sagte, daß sie morgen keine Zeit habe.
native_language_example: He said that she doesn’t have time tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to introduce reported speech (what someone said about you). In German you often see a comma before the clause: „Er sagte, du …“. After it, German commonly uses Konjunktiv I (reported-speech form), e.g. „du seist …“ instead of „du bist …“.
target_language_example: Sie sagte, du hättest keine Zeit.
native_language_example: She said that you didn’t have time.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone else said about you. Very often followed by a past action: "Sie sagte, du hättest ...". The form "hättest" is Konjunktiv II and is common in indirect speech (especially in writing/news) to show it’s reported information, not the speaker’s direct claim. In more direct/colloquial speech you may also hear: "Sie sagte, du hast ...".
target_language_example: Er sagte, du hättest den Schlüssel verloren.
native_language_example: He said you had lost the key.

additional_notes: Used to introduce reported speech after a verb like „sagen“. Very often the following verb is in the subjunctive (Konjunktiv) in writing and news-style German (e.g., „er freue sich“, „er ziehe“, „er würde …“), similar to English “he said (that) he was/would …”.
target_language_example: Sie sagte, er habe keine Zeit.
native_language_example: She said (that) he didn’t have time.

additional_notes: Used after a reporting verb like „sagen“ to introduce what someone reported. „habe“ is Konjunktiv I of „haben“ and is common in indirect speech (especially in news/reporting) to show it’s reported information. In English you usually use “said (that) he had …”, often without a special verb form. The comma is typical: „Tom sagte, er habe …“.
target_language_example: Sie sagte, er habe keine Zeit.
native_language_example: She said he didn’t have time.

additional_notes: Used to report what a man said, often in writing (news, formal narration). The verb form **habe** is **Konjunktiv I** of *haben* and signals indirect speech (not the speaker’s claim). Often **dass** is omitted: *Er sagte, (dass) er habe …* In everyday speech people also commonly use indicative: *Er sagte, er hat …*
target_language_example: Sie sagte, er habe keine Zeit.
native_language_example: She said (that) he had no time.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said. The form **er liebe** is **Konjunktiv I** (reported/indirect speech) and is common in writing and formal speech; in everyday conversation you’ll often hear **Er sagte, er liebt mich** or **Er sagte, dass er mich liebt**. Word order: you can omit **dass** and keep the comma: **Er sagte, er liebe mich.**
target_language_example: Sie sagte, er liebe mich nicht mehr.
native_language_example: She said he didn’t love me anymore.

additional_notes: Used to report what a man said, without quoting him directly. After verbs like "sagen" (to say), German often uses the subjunctive I form "sei" (from "sein") in indirect speech: "Er sagte, er sei müde". In English you typically translate it as "he said (that) he was/is …" depending on context.
target_language_example: Sie sagte, er sei krank und könne nicht kommen.
native_language_example: She said (that) he was sick and couldn’t come.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said, often in indirect/reported speech. Here, **wolle** is **Konjunktiv I** of **wollen** and is common in news or formal writing to show it’s reported information (not necessarily the speaker’s own statement). In everyday speech, many people also use **er wollte** instead.
target_language_example: Sie sagte, er wolle später anrufen.
native_language_example: She said he wanted to call later.

meaning: “said (that) …” (introducing reported speech, often with a dummy “it”).
additional_notes: Used after a subject (Er/Ich/Tom …) to report what someone said: „Er sagte, es …“. The comma is normal in German before a clause like this. „es“ is often just a placeholder subject in expressions like „es tut mir leid“ (I’m sorry), „es dauert …“ (it takes …), „es regnet“ (it’s raining). In reported speech you may see Konjunktiv forms, especially in writing: „er sagte, es könne … / es seien … / es würde …“.
target_language_example: Sie sagte, es sei zu spät.
native_language_example: She said it was too late.

meaning: 'said that it was' (reported speech, often using Konjunktiv I).
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said, especially in news or formal writing. After "sagte," German often uses Konjunktiv I to show it’s reported information (not necessarily confirmed): "es sei" = "it is/was" in reported speech. In everyday speech you also often hear Indicative: "Er sagte, es ist/war wichtig."
target_language_example: Die Zeugin sagte, es sei dunkel gewesen.
native_language_example: The witness said that it had been dark.

meaning: “said (that) I …” (introducing what someone said about you).
additional_notes: Used to report speech: **X sagte, ich …** = “X said (that) I …”. In German, reported speech often uses **Konjunktiv** after *sagte* (e.g., *ich sei/könne/hätte/sähe/soll*). The comma is common because the quoted/reported part is a separate clause; in English you usually add **that** (optional).
target_language_example: Sie sagte, ich sei zu spät.
native_language_example: She said (that) I was late.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone told you to do. It uses the subjunctive form of "sollen" (Konjunktiv) to show indirect speech (you’re repeating their words, not stating it as your own command). In conversation you may also hear: "Er/ Sie hat gesagt, ich soll ..."
target_language_example: Der Arzt sagte, ich solle mehr Wasser trinken.
native_language_example: The doctor said I should drink more water.

additional_notes: Used to report what a woman said: "X sagte, sie …". In formal written German, the part after the comma is often in reported-speech verb forms (Konjunktiv I), e.g. "sie habe", "sie sei", "sie müsse", "sie freue sich". In everyday speech you often hear indicative instead: "Sie sagte, sie hat/ist/muss …".
target_language_example: Er sagte, sie komme heute später.
native_language_example: He said (that) she would come later today.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said. After a reporting verb like „sagte“, German often uses Konjunktiv I for indirect speech: „sie habe“ (instead of „sie hat/hatte“). It’s very common in news/reporting and formal writing. The comma before „sie“ is required in this structure.
target_language_example: Er sagte, sie habe keine Zeit.
native_language_example: He said (that) she had no time.

meaning: 'said that she has' (reported speech; Konjunktiv I).
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said indirectly. After verbs like „sagen“, German often uses Konjunktiv I (here: „habe“) instead of the normal „hat“, especially in writing and news-style speech. In English you usually translate it as “said that she has …” or often “said that she had …” depending on context.
target_language_example: Er sagte, sie habe keine Zeit.
native_language_example: He said that she has no time. / He said that she had no time.

meaning: "said (that) she was / is" (reported speech, Konjunktiv I).
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said without quoting them directly. German often uses Konjunktiv I for reported speech: "sie sei" (from "sie ist"). In English this is usually just "she was/is" depending on context: "Maria sagte, sie sei müde" = "Maria said (that) she was tired." Common in news and formal writing, but also used in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Er sagte, sie sei krank und könne nicht kommen.
native_language_example: He said (that) she was sick and couldn't come.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said. "wolle" is Konjunktiv I of "wollen" and is common in indirect/reported speech (especially in writing/news). In everyday speech you’ll also hear: "Sie sagte, dass sie … will/wollte."
target_language_example: Er sagte, sie wolle später anrufen.
native_language_example: He said she wanted to call later.

additional_notes: “sagte” is the simple past (Präteritum) of **sagen** (“to say/tell”). **ihm** is the dative pronoun meaning **“to him”**. Often used to introduce what someone said, followed by a comma and a clause: *Er sagte ihm, dass …* (“He told him that …”). In spoken German, you often hear *hat ihm gesagt* instead of *sagte ihm*.
target_language_example: Ich sagte ihm, dass ich heute keine Zeit habe.
native_language_example: I told him that I don’t have time today.

additional_notes: Used to report advice, instructions, or a request to a man in the past. "sagte" = "said/told" (simple past of *sagen*). "ihm" = "to him" (dative). "er solle" is Konjunktiv I (often used in reported/indirect speech) and corresponds to "he should" / "he is supposed to". You can swap in other pronouns: *sagte ihr, sie solle...* (told her she should...), *sagte ihnen, sie sollten...* (told them they should...).
target_language_example: Ich sagte ihm, er solle früher nach Hause gehen.
native_language_example: I told him he should go home earlier.

additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of "(jemandem) sagen" = "to tell (someone)". Used when reporting what someone said to you. Very often followed by a clause ("..., dass ..." or just ", ...") and in reported speech you may see Konjunktiv (e.g., "sie seien", "du wärest").
target_language_example: Er sagte mir, dass er morgen keine Zeit hat.
native_language_example: He told me that he doesn’t have time tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said to you. "sagte" is the simple past of "sagen" (to say/tell); "mir" = to me; "dass" introduces a subordinate clause (often with the verb at the end: "..., dass er kommt."). In everyday speech, Germans often use the present perfect instead: "Er hat mir gesagt, dass ...".
target_language_example: Er sagte mir, dass er heute keine Zeit hat.
native_language_example: He told me that he doesn’t have time today.

meaning: “told me that he …” / “said to me that he …”
additional_notes: Used to report what a man said. It’s the past tense of **sagen** (“to say/tell”) + indirect object **mir** (“to me”) + a **dass**-clause. In a **dass**-clause, the conjugated verb goes to the end: *Er kommt.* → *Er sagte mir, dass er kommt.*
target_language_example: Sie sagte mir, dass er später kommt.
native_language_example: She told me that he’s coming later.

meaning: “(She) told me that she …” / “(She) said to me that she …”
additional_notes: Used to introduce reported speech in the past: someone said something to you, and you report it with a daß-clause. Modern spelling is usually “dass” instead of “daß”, but “daß” is still seen in older texts or by those using traditional spelling. In more formal reported speech, the verb in the daß-clause is often in the subjunctive (Konjunktiv I/II), e.g., „sie habe…“, „sie sei…“; in everyday speech, indicative forms are also common.
target_language_example: Maria sagte mir, daß sie dich angerufen habe.
native_language_example: Maria told me that she had called you.

additional_notes: Used to introduce reported speech (what a man said). It’s a common storytelling pattern: *Jemand sagte mir, er …* (“Someone told me he …”). Often followed by a verb phrase: *… kommt später / … hat keine Zeit / … sei krank* (the last one uses subjunctive in more formal reporting).
target_language_example: Er sagte mir, er kommt später.
native_language_example: He told me he’s coming later.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said. "sei" is Konjunktiv I of "sein" (to be) and is common in indirect/reported speech, especially in writing and formal speech. In everyday conversation, many speakers also use indicative: "Er sagte mir, er ist …".
target_language_example: Sie sagte mir, er sei schon zu Hause.
native_language_example: She told me (that) he was already at home.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said to you. After the comma, German often uses reported speech (especially in writing) with **Konjunktiv I** (e.g., *ich sei, ich müsse*) and puts the verb at the end of the clause. In everyday speech you may also hear *sagte mir, dass ich …*.
target_language_example: Sie sagte mir, ich solle früher ins Bett gehen.
native_language_example: She told me (that) I should go to bed earlier.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone advised or instructed you to do. The verb after the comma is often in the subjunctive (Konjunktiv) in indirect speech: “ich solle …” (= “that I should …”). Common with advice/instructions (often from a doctor, boss, parent, etc.).
target_language_example: Meine Mutter sagte mir, ich solle früher ins Bett gehen.
native_language_example: My mother told me I should go to bed earlier.

meaning: "told me I should …" (indirect/reported instruction, often with a reflexive verb).
additional_notes: Used to report what someone instructed or advised you to do. German often uses Konjunktiv (here: "solle") in reported speech: "Er sagte mir, ich solle …" = "He told me I should … / to …". The "mich" is the start of a reflexive verb phrase (e.g., mich benehmen = behave, mich treffen = meet up, mich fernhalten = stay away).
target_language_example: Der Arzt sagte mir, ich solle mich ausruhen.
native_language_example: The doctor told me I should rest.

additional_notes: Used to introduce reported speech: someone tells you something about a woman/girl (“sie” = “she”). Often you can omit “dass” (“that”) after “sagen”: “Er sagte mir, sie komme später.” In the reported clause, the verb typically goes at the end (e.g., „… sie brauche …“, „… sie lebe …“, „… sie wolle …“).
target_language_example: Er sagte mir, sie komme heute nicht.
native_language_example: He told me (that) she isn’t coming today.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said. After "sagte mir" (told me), German often uses **Konjunktiv I** for indirect speech: **sie sei** = reported form of **sie ist**. In everyday speech, many people also say **sie ist** instead of **sie sei**, but **sie sei** is common in writing and more formal narration. The comma before the reported clause is typical: "Sie sagte mir, sie sei …"
target_language_example: Er sagte mir, sie sei krank.
native_language_example: He told me (that) she was sick.

additional_notes: Used to report what a group of people said. After „sagten“ you often get a comma and then a clause starting with „sie“ (= they). In reported speech German commonly uses Konjunktiv (e.g., „sie hätten“, „sie würden“) to show it’s someone else’s words.
target_language_example: Die Nachbarn sagten, sie hätten gestern nichts gehört.
native_language_example: The neighbors said (that) they didn’t hear anything yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to report what other people said. In indirect/reported speech German often uses the subjunctive (Konjunktiv) to show it’s someone else’s statement: "sie hätten" is Konjunktiv II of "sie haben" and often corresponds to English "they said they had ..." (or sometimes "they said they have ...", depending on context). The comma before "sie" is typical when introducing a reported clause.
target_language_example: Die Zeugen sagten, sie hätten nichts gesehen.
native_language_example: The witnesses said they hadn't seen anything.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone else claimed. The verb form „seien“ is Konjunktiv I (indirect/reported speech) of „sein“ (“to be”) and is common in news and formal writing. In everyday speech, many people also use the indicative: „Sie sagten, sie sind …“.
target_language_example: Sie sagten, sie seien schon fertig.
native_language_example: They said they were already finished.

additional_notes: Used to report what several people said in the past: **sagten** = “said” (simple past, plural), and **sie wollten** = “they wanted” + an action (often an infinitive like *gehen*, *aussteigen*, *nach Hause*). The comma separates the main clause from the reported-speech clause; **dass** (“that”) is often omitted here: *Sie sagten, (dass) sie wollten …*
target_language_example: Die Kinder sagten, sie wollten nach Hause gehen.
native_language_example: The kids said they wanted to go home.

additional_notes: Uses the simple past of the separable verb **ansehen** (to look at): **er/sie sah** … **an**. **mich** is the accusative pronoun “me”. Often used in storytelling to link two actions: “He/She looked at me and (then) …”.
target_language_example: Er sah mich an und sagte nichts.
native_language_example: He looked at me and said nothing.

meaning: "looked as if / looked like" (describing an impression).
additional_notes: From the verb "aussehen" (to look/appear). Used to say someone/something gives the impression that something is true, often followed by "ob" ("als ob") or a subjunctive form (e.g., „als wäre/als würde/als sei …“). It’s about appearance, not certainty.
target_language_example: Sie sah aus, als wäre sie krank.
native_language_example: She looked as if she were sick.

additional_notes: Used with **aus** to talk about someone’s appearance or how they seem: **jemand sah sehr + Adjektiv + aus** (“someone looked very + adjective”). It’s the simple past of **aussehen** (to look/seem): **sah … aus**.
target_language_example: Er sah sehr müde aus.
native_language_example: He looked very tired.

meaning: "realized/accepted that" (came to understand and admit that).
additional_notes: "einsehen" means to realize and also to admit/accept something (often after doubt or a mistake). "sah ein" is simple past (Präteritum) of "einsehen". Very common in writing and storytelling; in conversation you may also hear "hat eingesehen, dass" (present perfect).
target_language_example: Sie sah ein, dass sie sich geirrt hatte.
native_language_example: She realized/accepted that she had been wrong.

additional_notes: Simple past of the separable verb „fernsehen“ (to watch TV). In the simple past, it is commonly split: „sah … fern“. Present: „ich sehe fern“; perfect: „ich habe ferngesehen“.
target_language_example: Ich sah fern, bevor ich ins Bett ging.
native_language_example: I watched TV before I went to bed.

additional_notes: Used to report that someone noticed/realized something: "Er sah, dass …". "sah" is the simple past (Präteritum) of "sehen" and is common in writing and storytelling; in everyday speech, people often use "hat gesehen, dass …" instead.
target_language_example: Ich sah, dass die Tür offen war.
native_language_example: I saw that the door was open.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone observed. After "sah" (simple past of "sehen" = to see), German uses a comma and a "wie"-clause describing the action you saw: "Er sah, wie …". In the "wie"-clause, the verb typically goes to the end (e.g., "wie er die Straße überquerte"). Often translates naturally as “saw (that)” in English.
target_language_example: Ich sah, wie der Bus an der Haltestelle anhielt.
native_language_example: I saw the bus stop at the bus stop.

additional_notes: Common pattern: **sehen + , wie + subject + verb** to describe watching an action happen. In English you often translate it as **“(someone) saw him + verb”** rather than “saw how he…”. Tense changes with the subject (e.g., *ich sah*, *sie sah*).
target_language_example: Ich sah, wie er die Tür aufmachte.
native_language_example: I saw him open the door.

additional_notes: *Sah* is the Präteritum (simple past) of *sehen* (“to see”), common in written stories and reports. *Ihn* is the accusative form meaning “him” (referring to a masculine person/thing). You’ll often see it in sentences like *Sie sah ihn das Fenster aufbrechen* (“She saw him break open the window”), where *jemanden etwas tun sehen* = “to see someone do something.”
target_language_example: Ich sah ihn gestern im Park.
native_language_example: I saw him yesterday in the park.

additional_notes: Often used to describe checking both directions (for example, before crossing a street). In the past tense: "(er/sie) sah ...". In the present tense you’ll often see: "Er sieht nach links und rechts."
target_language_example: Sie sah nach links und rechts, bevor sie die Straße überquerte.
native_language_example: She looked left and right before she crossed the street.

additional_notes: Typically appears with **um**: **sah sich … um** (“looked around”). With **nach + dative**, it often implies searching: **sah sich nach einem Platz / nach seiner Kamera um**. Because German separates verb particles, **sah sich** may be split from **um** in the clause (with **um** usually near the end).
target_language_example: Tom sah sich nach einem Platz zum Sitzen um.
native_language_example: Tom looked for a place to sit.

additional_notes: Präteritum (simple past) of the reflexive verb **sich umsehen** (“to look around”). Used when someone turns their head/body to check their surroundings (e.g., to find someone, to see what’s happening, to make sure they’re alone). In other tenses you’ll often see the separable prefix at the end: **Er sieht sich um. / Er hat sich umgesehen.**
target_language_example: Tom sah sich um, aber Maria war bereits weg.
native_language_example: Tom looked around, but Maria was already gone.

meaning: “(they) saw each other” / “(they) looked at each other.”
additional_notes: “sahen” is the simple past (Präteritum) of “sehen” (to see). With “einander” it expresses a mutual action (“each other”). Very commonly this appears as part of the separable verb “ansehen” (to look at): “(sie) sahen einander an” = “they looked at each other,” where “an” moves to the end of the clause in the past tense. On its own, “sahen einander” can be understood as “saw each other,” but many contexts prefer adding “an” to clearly mean “looked at each other.”
target_language_example: Tom und Maria sahen einander an; dann blickten sie zurück zu Johannes.
native_language_example: Tom and Maria looked at each other; then they looked back at Johannes.

meaning: “looked at each other” / “watched (something)” (simple past of sich ansehen).
additional_notes: From the verb **sich ansehen** (separable: *sehen … an*). With no object or with *einander*, it usually means **they looked at each other**: *Sie sahen sich an.* With an object, it means **they watched/checked out something**: *Sie sahen sich eine Dokumentation an.* *sahen* = simple past for *sie/Sie/wir*; *sich* is the reflexive pronoun (here often meaning “each other”).
target_language_example: Als er den Raum betrat, sahen sich alle kurz an.
native_language_example: When he entered the room, everyone briefly looked at each other.

additional_notes: Used with the verb aussehen (“to look/appear”) in simple past, 3rd person plural (sie sahen) + als to introduce an appearance-based assumption. The following clause often uses Konjunktiv II (e.g., als wären/würden …) to signal uncertainty; als ob is also common in speech/writing.
target_language_example: Tom und Maria sahen aus, als würden sie sich gleich küssen.
native_language_example: Tom and Maria looked as if they were about to kiss.

additional_notes: Common, everyday way to say someone is angry with/at someone. Used with **sauer auf + accusative person**: *sauer auf mich/dich/ihn/sie/uns/euch/Sie*. Similar to **wütend auf mich** (stronger/more direct: “furious at me”).
target_language_example: Bitte sei nicht sauer auf mich.
native_language_example: Please don’t be mad at me.

additional_notes: Used to say someone was sitting on something. "saß" is the simple past of "sitzen" (to sit). "auf" usually takes the dative here (location): "auf einer Bank", "auf dem Tisch".
target_language_example: Er saß auf dem Stuhl und wartete.
native_language_example: He sat on the chair and waited.

meaning: “sat on the” (past tense of *sitzen* + *auf dem* = “on the”).
additional_notes: *Saß* is the simple past of **sitzen** (“to sit”). **Auf dem** is **auf + dem** (dative masculine/neuter), used with things you are located on (e.g., *auf dem Klo*, *auf dem Sofa*, *auf dem Rand*). In casual speech you may hear **auf’m** or **aufm** instead of *auf dem*. With feminine nouns it becomes **auf der** (e.g., *auf der Bank*).
target_language_example: Er saß auf dem Sofa und las ein Buch.
native_language_example: He sat on the couch and read a book.

additional_notes: "saß" is the simple past of "sitzen" (to sit). It describes a state/position in the past. "auf einem Stuhl" means "on a chair" (literally: "on a chair"). You can change who is sitting by changing the subject (e.g., "Ich saß...", "Er saß...").
target_language_example: Ich saß auf einem Stuhl und wartete.
native_language_example: I sat on a chair and waited.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone sitting while their eyes are closed (e.g., resting, thinking, dozing, or listening). The verb form depends on the subject: er saß / sie saß (past tense of "sitzen" = to sit). You can also add a place: „im Sessel“, „auf der Bank“, or „da“ (= there).
target_language_example: Sie saß mit geschlossenen Augen im Zug und hörte Musik.
native_language_example: She sat on the train with her eyes closed and listened to music.

additional_notes: Past tense of **sitzen** (“to sit”) + **neben** (“next to/beside”). With location, **neben** usually takes the **dative** case: *neben mir, neben ihr, neben einem großen Typ*. Used to say someone was seated next to someone/something.
target_language_example: Ich saß neben meinem Freund im Kino.
native_language_example: I sat next to my friend at the cinema.

additional_notes: "saßen" is the simple past of "sitzen" (to sit). Use "auf" + dative with surfaces/places you sit on (e.g., auf der Bank, auf der Erde, auf der Treppe). "auf der" is used with feminine nouns (die Bank, die Erde, die Treppe) and also when the noun is feminine in dative after "auf".
target_language_example: Wir saßen auf der Bank und haben geredet.
native_language_example: We sat on the bench and talked.

meaning: “(they) sat / were sitting on a …” (with a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Past tense of **sitzen** (“to sit”). **auf** + dative is used for location (“on”/“sitting on”), so you often get **auf einer** before feminine dative nouns like **auf einer Bank** (on a bench), **auf einer Mauer** (on a wall), **auf einer Decke** (on a blanket).
target_language_example: Wir saßen auf einer Decke und haben gepicknickt.
native_language_example: We sat on a blanket and had a picnic.

additional_notes: Used to express regret or disappointment about a situation, followed by a clause with "dass" (verb goes to the end). Often stands alone as an exclamation: "Schade!" You can use it with formal (Sie) or informal (du) speech.
target_language_example: Schade, dass wir heute kein gutes Wetter haben.
native_language_example: It's a shame that we don't have good weather today.

additional_notes: Colloquial short form of "schaffe ich" (from "schaffen" = to manage, to accomplish). Often used with "es": "Schaff ich (es) nicht" = "I can’t do it." With "schon" it can sound reassuring/confident: "Das schaff ich schon" = "I’ll manage that." In other contexts it can mean "I manage to...": "Ich schaff(e) es nicht, ..." = "I can’t manage to..."
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, das schaff ich heute noch.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll manage that today.

meaning: "I can't do it / I won't manage (it)."
additional_notes: Spoken, contracted form of "(Das) schaffe ich nicht." You often leave out "das" when it’s clear from context. Used to say you can’t manage a task, don’t have time/energy, or it’s too difficult. In more formal speech/writing: "Das schaffe ich nicht."
target_language_example: Heute schaff ich nicht, den Bericht fertig zu machen.
native_language_example: I can’t manage to finish the report today.

meaning: “can you do it / will you manage (to)?”
additional_notes: From the verb "schaffen" (to manage, to accomplish). "es" is a dummy pronoun meaning “it” (the task/situation). Very often used with an infinitive clause: "Schaffst du es, ... zu ...?" = “Can you manage to …?” In negative form: "Schaffst du es nicht, ..." = “If you don’t manage to …” / “Can’t you manage to …?”
target_language_example: Schaffst du es, morgen früher aufzustehen?
native_language_example: Can you manage to get up earlier tomorrow?

additional_notes: You usually complete it with a separable particle: **an / ein** = turn on, **aus** = turn off. In a full sentence, the particle often comes at the end: *Schalte bitte das Licht an/aus/ein.* Common as a polite request at home or at work.
target_language_example: Wenn du gehst, schalte bitte das Licht aus.
native_language_example: When you leave, please turn the light off.

additional_notes: “Schalten Sie …” is the polite/formal imperative with Sie (you). It’s commonly used with particles like **aus** (off) and **an** (on): **Schalten Sie das Licht aus.** / **Schalten Sie es wieder an.** In spoken German it can sound like a firm instruction, especially without **bitte**.
target_language_example: Schalten Sie bitte Ihr Handy aus.
native_language_example: Please turn off your phone.

additional_notes: Uses the verb *schalten* in the simple past (*schaltete*). In everyday speech, Germans often use the perfect tense instead: *Ich habe das Licht an-/ausgeschaltet.* You’ll usually see it with a separable prefix or particle: *das Licht an/aus schalten* or *das Licht ein/ausschalten* (= to switch the light on/off). Word order: *Ich schaltete das Licht an.*
target_language_example: Ich schaltete das Licht aus, bevor ich ging.
native_language_example: I turned off the light before I left.

meaning: "look at" / "take a look at" (du-imperative, used with "... an").
additional_notes: This is part of the separable, reflexive verb phrase "sich etw. ansehen" (= to look at something). In the du-command you typically say: "Schau dir + [thing/person] + an." Example pattern: "Schau dir den Einband an." (More formal: "Schauen Sie sich ... an.")
target_language_example: Schau dir das mal an!
native_language_example: Take a look at that!

additional_notes: Imperative of „sich etwas ansehen“ (to look at something). „dir“ is the reflexive pronoun (to yourself), used with informal „du“. Often said to get someone’s attention to something you want them to see. Variations: „Schau dir mal das an!“ (a bit more casual/soft), formal: „Schauen Sie sich das an.“
target_language_example: Schau dir das an—der Hund kann die Tür aufmachen!
native_language_example: Look at that—the dog can open the door!

additional_notes: Common spoken phrase used to draw attention to something you’re about to show, point out, or comment on. Often used at the start of a sentence, sometimes with an exclamation mark or semicolon, and it can be followed by a noun or a whole clause (e.g., “Schau mal, was …”). Slightly casual but not rude.
target_language_example: Schau mal, wie schön der Sonnenuntergang ist!
native_language_example: Look, how beautiful the sunset is!

additional_notes: Used with **Sie** (formal “you”) as a polite command/request. It’s usually part of the separable verb **sich etwas anschauen**: **Schauen Sie sich … an!** (= “Look at …!”). The **sich** is a reflexive pronoun that goes with this verb pattern and doesn’t translate literally into English.
target_language_example: Schauen Sie sich das bitte einmal an.
native_language_example: Please take a look at that.

additional_notes:
Polite command using **Sie** (formal “you”), used when speaking to strangers, customers, etc. Often followed by:
- **... genauer hin** = “look more closely”
- **... mal her** = “look here (for a moment)”
It can also introduce what you’re about to say: **Schauen Sie, …** = “Look, … / See, …”.
target_language_example: Schauen Sie bitte hier auf den Bildschirm.
native_language_example: Please look here at the screen.

meaning: “look (at …),” said to more than one person (you all).
additional_notes: Used in the plural imperative (command/request) with the reflexive pronoun euch. It’s often followed by a separable verb prefix like in **schaut euch … an** (“look at …”). You can also use it as an excited prompt: **Schaut euch das an!** = “Look at that!”
target_language_example: Schaut euch bitte die Speisekarte an.
native_language_example: Please look at the menu.

meaning: to get divorced; to have a divorce finalized.
additional_notes: Used reflexively with sich: sich scheiden lassen = to get divorced. Often followed by von + dative to say who you divorce: sich von seiner Frau scheiden lassen. In perfect tense it’s commonly hat sich ... scheiden lassen (or hatte ... scheiden lassen in past perfect).
target_language_example: Nach zehn Jahren Ehe haben sie sich scheiden lassen.
native_language_example: After ten years of marriage, they got divorced.

meaning: to get divorced (to have a divorce finalized).
additional_notes: Usually used reflexively: **sich scheiden lassen** = “to get divorced.” The form **scheiden zu lassen** typically appears when it depends on another verb (e.g., *planen/vorhaben/entscheiden*, etc.): **Er plant, sich scheiden zu lassen.** In everyday German, it often implies going through the legal divorce process, not just separating.
target_language_example: Sie hat beschlossen, sich scheiden zu lassen.
native_language_example: She decided to get divorced.

additional_notes: Used to express that something appears to be the case, without full certainty. Formed with the verb "scheinen" + "zu" + infinitive (here: "sein"). Common patterns include "Er/Sie scheint ... zu sein" and "Es scheint ... zu sein".
target_language_example: Er scheint zu sein, was er vorgibt.
native_language_example: He seems to be what he claims to be.

additional_notes: Used to describe sunny weather. Word order can change: “Die Sonne scheint.” (most common) and “Heute scheint die Sonne.” Also note the vulgar idiom “Ihm scheint die Sonne aus dem Arsch.” meaning someone has everything going their way / is extremely lucky (very rude).
target_language_example: Heute scheint die Sonne, aber es ist kalt.
native_language_example: The sun is shining today, but it’s cold.

additional_notes: Uses **scheinen** (“to seem/appear”) + **zu sein** (“to be”). It expresses an assumption based on appearances or limited information, not a confirmed fact. **Scheint** is the 3rd person singular form (er/sie/es scheint).
target_language_example: Er scheint reich zu sein, aber er ist sehr sparsam.
native_language_example: He seems to be rich, but he’s very frugal.

additional_notes: Very vulgar and aggressive. Used to dismiss someone/something or say it doesn’t matter. Usually followed by an accusative object (e.g., „Scheiß auf deinen Boss!“). You’ll also hear „Scheiß drauf!“ (= “Fuck it.”).
target_language_example: Scheiß auf den Stress, wir gehen nach Hause.
native_language_example: Screw the stress, we’re going home.

additional_notes: Very vulgar, angry way to say you don’t care about someone/something or you reject it. Used as an exclamation. It’s short for the pattern „Scheiß auf + Akkusativ“ (e.g. „Scheiß auf den Verein!“, „Scheiß auf das Geld!“, „Scheiß auf die Regeln!“). Here „den“ is masculine accusative (“that guy/that thing”).
target_language_example: Scheiß auf den Plan — wir machen es anders.
native_language_example: Screw the plan—we’re doing it differently.

additional_notes: "Schicken" means "to send"; "Sie" is the formal "you". Used for polite instructions or requests (often with "bitte"). Common patterns: "Schicken Sie + object" (Send/dispatch + something/someone), "Schicken Sie + jemanden + zu mir" (Send someone to me), "Schicken Sie mir + etwas" (Send me something).
target_language_example: Schicken Sie mir bitte die Unterlagen per E-Mail.
native_language_example: Please send me the documents by email.
