additional_notes: Uses the verb **scheinen** (“to seem”) in the simple past (**schien**) + adjective (**überrascht**) + **zu sein** (“to be”). It expresses an *impression* rather than a confirmed fact. Common pattern: **[Person] schien + Adjektiv + zu sein** (e.g., *schien müde zu sein* = “seemed to be tired”).
target_language_example: Er schien überrascht zu sein, als ich plötzlich anrief.
native_language_example: He seemed to be surprised when I called suddenly.

meaning: to go to sleep; to go to bed.
additional_notes: Common everyday phrase meaning you’re going to bed for the night. Often used with a modal verb (e.g., müssen/wollen/sollen) or with time words: „Ich muss jetzt schlafen gehen.“ You can also say „ins Bett gehen“ (= to go to bed), which focuses more on going to bed physically.
target_language_example: Ich muss wirklich schlafen gehen, ich bin total müde.
native_language_example: I really have to go to sleep; I’m totally tired.

additional_notes: Used with forms of „sein“ (to be) to describe someone’s mood: „Ich bin/sie ist schlecht gelaunt.“ Often strengthened with words like „sehr“, „total“, „recht“, or „so“ (e.g., „recht schlecht gelaunt“ = rather in a bad mood).
target_language_example: Heute bin ich schlecht gelaunt, weil ich kaum geschlafen habe.
native_language_example: Today I’m in a bad mood because I barely slept.

meaning: badly about other people; to speak ill of others.
additional_notes: Usually used with verbs like „reden/sprechen“: „schlecht über andere reden/sprechen“ = criticize others or say negative things about them (often like gossiping, especially „hinter jemandes Rücken“ = behind someone’s back).
target_language_example: Bitte rede nicht schlecht über andere.
native_language_example: Please don’t speak badly about other people.

additional_notes: Often used with verbs like **finden** or **für ... halten**: *Ich finde das eine schlechte Idee.* / *Er hält das für eine schlechte Idee.* Very common as **keine schlechte Idee** (“not a bad idea”), which usually means “actually, that’s pretty good.”
target_language_example: Ich glaube, das ist eine schlechte Idee.
native_language_example: I think that’s a bad idea.

additional_notes: Used with "haben" (to have) to say someone is in a bad mood: "Ich habe schlechte Laune." You can also say "schlechte Laune haben" (to be in a bad mood). Often with reasons or time words: "Ohne Frühstück...", "heute Morgen...".
target_language_example: Ich habe heute schlechte Laune, weil ich zu wenig geschlafen habe.
native_language_example: I’m in a bad mood today because I didn’t sleep enough.

additional_notes: Used to introduce or talk about something unpleasant. Often said with an article: „eine schlechte Nachricht“ (a piece of bad news). Plural: „schlechte Nachrichten“ (bad news items). Common phrase: „Ich habe eine schlechte Nachricht.“
target_language_example: Ich habe leider eine schlechte Nachricht: Der Zug hat Verspätung.
native_language_example: Unfortunately, I have some bad news: the train is delayed.

additional_notes: A common phrase to introduce unpleasant or disappointing information. Often used with "Ich habe ..." (I have ...) or "Das sind ..." (That’s ...), and sometimes paired with "gute Nachrichten" (good news): "Ich habe gute und schlechte Nachrichten."
target_language_example: Leider habe ich schlechte Nachrichten: Der Zug fällt heute aus.
native_language_example: Unfortunately I have bad news: the train is cancelled today.

meaning: 'of bad weather' / 'because of the bad weather' (genitive form of 'bad weather').
additional_notes: This is the genitive form of *schlechtes Wetter* (“bad weather”). You often see it after prepositions like **aufgrund** (because of) and **trotz** (despite): *aufgrund des schlechten Wetters*, *trotz des schlechten Wetters*.
target_language_example: Trotz des schlechten Wetters sind wir spazieren gegangen.
native_language_example: Despite the bad weather, we went for a walk.

additional_notes: Usually used with "sein": "(jemand) ist schlechter Laune" = "(someone) is in a bad mood". Often used with intensifiers like "ziemlich" (pretty) or "gerade" (at the moment), and in questions: "Bist du schlechter Laune?" / formal "Sind Sie schlechter Laune?".
target_language_example: Ich bin heute etwas schlechter Laune, weil ich schlecht geschlafen habe.
native_language_example: I’m in a bit of a bad mood today because I slept badly.

additional_notes: Used to judge someone’s character or morality. Often appears with the indefinite article (ein schlechter Mensch) or in negation (kein schlechter Mensch). You can also say it about yourself: "Ich bin kein schlechter Mensch" (I’m not a bad person) or "Ich komme mir wie ein schlechter Mensch vor" (I feel like a bad person).
target_language_example: Er will kein schlechter Mensch sein.
native_language_example: He doesn’t want to be a bad person.

meaning: a sore loser (someone who reacts badly to losing).
additional_notes: Used to criticize someone who can’t accept defeat (e.g., gets angry, complains, makes excuses). Often used with “sein” (Tom ist ein schlechter Verlierer) or as a warning/command: “Sei kein schlechter Verlierer.”
target_language_example: Du hast nur ein Spiel verloren—sei kein schlechter Verlierer.
native_language_example: You only lost one game—don’t be a sore loser.

additional_notes: Used with „ein“ or „ohne“ to talk about guilt: „ein schlechtes Gewissen haben“ (to feel guilty) and „jemandem ein schlechtes Gewissen machen“ (to make someone feel guilty, to guilt-trip someone).
target_language_example: Ich kann das nicht tun, ohne ein schlechtes Gewissen zu haben.
native_language_example: I can’t do that without feeling guilty.

additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of the separable verb „einschlafen“ (= to fall asleep). In the present tense it splits: „Ich schlafe ein.“ In the perfect tense: „Ich bin eingeschlafen.“ Often used with time words like „als“ (when), „ehe“ (before), „kaum dass“ (hardly when).
target_language_example: Ich schlief ein, während ich den Film schaute.
native_language_example: I fell asleep while I was watching the movie.

additional_notes: “schlief ein” is the simple past of the separable verb “einschlafen” (to fall asleep). In the past tense, the prefix splits off: ich schlief ein. “während” is a conjunction meaning “while/during (the time that)”, and it introduces what was happening at the same time. After “während”, German often uses another clause with a verb (often at the end in more formal word order).
target_language_example: Ich schlief ein, während ich ein Buch las.
native_language_example: I fell asleep while I was reading a book.

meaning: slept soundly (was in a deep sleep).
additional_notes: Common way to say someone was sleeping very deeply and wasn’t easily woken up (often used with interruptions like noise, a phone ringing, etc.). It’s the simple past of "schlafen" (to sleep). You can also say in the present: "Er schläft tief und fest."
target_language_example: Ich klopfte an die Tür, aber er schlief tief und fest.
native_language_example: I knocked on the door, but he was fast asleep.

additional_notes: Imperative form of "(du) schließt" from "schließen" (to close). It’s directed to one person you address with "du" (friends, family, kids). With "Sie" (formal), you would say: "Schließen Sie die Tür." You’ll often hear it with extra words like "bitte" (please), "zu" (shut it/close it), or "hinter dir" (behind you).
target_language_example: Schließ die Tür hinter dir, wenn du gehst!
native_language_example: Close the door behind you when you leave!

additional_notes: Used for comparisons with adjectives/adverbs: "X ist schlimmer als Y" (= X is worse than Y). You can also start a sentence with it for emphasis (often in an incomplete comparison): "Schlimmer als Ungeziefer, ...". "viel schlimmer als" = "much worse than".
target_language_example: Das Wetter ist heute schlimmer als gestern.
native_language_example: The weather is worse today than yesterday.

additional_notes: Uses the reflexive verb "sich einschließen" (= to lock oneself in). It usually means someone goes into a room (here: the bathroom) and locks the door from the inside so they can’t (or don’t want to) come out. In past tense you’ll often see it as "schloss sich ... ein" (Präteritum of "schließen").
target_language_example: Er schloss sich im Badezimmer ein, weil er allein sein wollte.
native_language_example: He locked himself in the bathroom because he wanted to be alone.

additional_notes: Used with a direct object that takes *die* (e.g., *die Tür*, *die Augen*). *schloss* is the simple past form and is common in written narratives; in everyday speech you often hear the present perfect: *Er hat die Tür geschlossen.*
target_language_example: Er schloss die Fenster, bevor er ging.
native_language_example: He closed the windows before he left.

additional_notes: Narrative phrase used to describe a sequence of actions. **schloss** is simple past of **schließen** (“to close”); **die Augen** = “the eyes”. In English you usually add a possessive (“his/her eyes”), even though German often uses **die** here.
target_language_example: Er schloss die Augen und lächelte leise.
native_language_example: He closed his eyes and smiled softly.

additional_notes: Simple past (Präteritum) of "die Tür schließen" (to close the door). Common in written German and storytelling; in everyday speech you often hear the perfect: "Er/Sie hat die Tür geschlossen."
target_language_example: Er schloss die Tür, damit es leiser wurde.
native_language_example: He closed the door so it would get quieter.

additional_notes: This is typically used with a reflexive pronoun: **schloss die Tür hinter sich** (“closed the door behind himself/herself/themself”). **schloss** is the simple past (Präteritum) of **schließen** (“to close”). In the present/perfect you’ll often hear: **Er schließt die Tür hinter sich. / Er hat die Tür hinter sich geschlossen.**
target_language_example: Er schloss die Tür hinter sich und ging weg.
native_language_example: He closed the door behind him and left.

additional_notes: Präteritum (simple past) of the separable verb phrase „die Tür zuschlagen“ = to slam the door shut, often expressing anger, frustration, or emphasis. Present: „Ich schlage die Tür zu.“ Perfekt: „Ich habe die Tür zugeschlagen.“
target_language_example: Tom stürmte in sein Büro und schlug die Tür zu.
native_language_example: Tom stormed into his office and slammed the door shut.

additional_notes: "schlug" is the simple past (Präteritum) of **schlagen** (to hit/strike). **mit der Faust** means "with the fist" and often appears with **auf + accusative** to specify what was hit (e.g., *auf den Tisch* = onto the table). Present tense: *Er/Sie schlägt mit der Faust ...*
target_language_example: Der Sprecher schlug mit der Faust auf den Tisch.
native_language_example: The speaker hit the table with his fist.

additional_notes: Used to say someone suggested an idea or plan. Very often followed by a comma and an infinitive clause with "zu" (e.g., "schlug vor, eine Pause zu machen") or by a "dass"-clause / indirect suggestion (e.g., "schlug vor, ich solle ...").
target_language_example: Sie schlug vor, früher nach Hause zu gehen.
native_language_example: She suggested going home earlier.

additional_notes: This is the 2nd-person singular (du) present tense of "schlafen" (to sleep), used in questions. It can mean (1) right now: "Are you sleeping (already)?" or (2) in general/habitually: "Do you sleep (well)?" It also appears in phrases like "mit jemandem schlafen" meaning "to sleep with someone" (have sex). Word order in questions: verb first (schläfst) + subject (du).
target_language_example: Hey, schläfst du schon?
native_language_example: Hey, are you asleep already?

meaning: "(he/she) sleeps on the ..." (on top of something).
additional_notes: "schläft" is 3rd-person singular of "schlafen" (to sleep). "auf dem" means "on the" with dative case, used for location (where?), e.g. "auf dem Sofa" (on the couch). For movement onto something, German often uses accusative: "auf den" (onto the). This phrase is incomplete by itself—you need a noun after it (e.g., "Sofa", "Boden", "Stuhl").
target_language_example: Er schläft auf dem Sofa.
native_language_example: He sleeps on the couch.

meaning: is fast asleep; is sleeping deeply and soundly.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "schlafen" to emphasize that someone is sleeping very deeply and is hard to wake up. Often describes a calm, uninterrupted sleep (e.g., in bed, on the sofa, etc.).
target_language_example: Bitte sei leise — er schläft tief und fest.
native_language_example: Please be quiet—he’s fast asleep.

meaning: to have something cut (by someone else).
additional_notes: Uses "lassen" to show you arrange for someone else to do the cutting (often at the hairdresser). Common pattern: "sich die Haare schneiden lassen" = to get your hair cut. You can add an adjective for the result: "kurz schneiden lassen" = have it cut short.
target_language_example: Maria hat sich die Haare kurz schneiden lassen.
native_language_example: Maria had her hair cut short.

additional_notes: Used with the impersonal subject "es" for weather: "Es schneit." In yes/no questions, the verb comes first: "Schneit es (hier)?" You can add time/place words: "Im Januar schneit es" / "Bei uns schneit es oft."
target_language_example: Schneit es morgen in Berlin?
native_language_example: Is it going to snow in Berlin tomorrow?

meaning: "does it snow here?" / "it snows here" (depending on context).
additional_notes: From the verb "schneien" (to snow). With normal word order you often get a statement: "Hier schneit es (oft)." With inverted word order you get a yes/no question: "Schneit es hier (oft)?" You can add time/frequency words like "im Winter" (in winter), "oft" (often), "selten" (rarely), "jemals/je" (ever).
target_language_example: Schneit es hier im Januar oft?
native_language_example: Does it snow here often in January?

meaning: to do (something) quickly; to hurry up (and get it done).
additional_notes: Common in everyday speech. Often used when urging someone to speed up and finish something promptly; also used about doing a task quickly. In imperatives you’ll often hear the separated form: "Mach das schnell" or "Mach schnell", but the full term appears as "schnell machen" in sentences like "Ich muss das schnell machen."
target_language_example: Ich muss das schnell machen, sonst verpassen wir den Zug.
native_language_example: I have to do this quickly, otherwise we’ll miss the train.

additional_notes: Used to describe running at a high speed. In comparisons you’ll often see it with words like „so“ (so fast), „genauso“ (just as fast), and „wie“ (as/like): „so schnell … wie …“.
target_language_example: Ich muss schnell rennen, sonst verpasse ich den Bus.
native_language_example: I have to run fast, otherwise I'll miss the bus.

additional_notes: Used to express urgency. Often appears with verbs like „kommen“, „machen“, or „schicken“: „Komm bitte so schnell wie möglich.“ You may also hear „so schnell wie möglich“ (very common) with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Bitte antworte so schnell wie möglich.
native_language_example: Please reply as quickly as possible.

additional_notes: Used with the comparative form of an adjective/adverb + „als“ to compare two people/things: „X ist schneller als Y.“ After „als“, you often use the nominative (like English subject form): „schneller als ich/du/er wir/sie/Sie“. It can also be used more generally to mean “quicker than” (not only literal running speed).
target_language_example: Ich bin heute schneller als gestern.
native_language_example: I'm faster today than yesterday.

meaning: “faster than” (used to compare speed or how quickly something happens).
additional_notes: Used in comparisons: X ist/geht/rennt/läuft schneller als Y. With pronouns, you’ll often see the dative: schneller als mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch. Also common in the phrase schneller als man denkt (“faster than you think”).
target_language_example: Kannst du das schneller als ich machen?
native_language_example: Can you do that faster than me?

additional_notes: "schon" means "already" and "angefangen" is the past participle of "anfangen" (to start). It’s typically used with "haben" in the present perfect to say something has already begun (often earlier than expected). Common patterns: "Hast du schon angefangen?" (Have you started yet/already?) and "Es hat schon angefangen zu ..." (It has already started to ...).
target_language_example: Ich habe schon angefangen, den Bericht zu schreiben.
native_language_example: I’ve already started writing the report.

meaning: “already the whole … / all … (for a while)” (used with a time period, e.g., day, week).
additional_notes: This phrase is normally completed by a noun like "Tag" (day), "Woche" (week), "Morgen" (morning): "schon den ganzen Tag" = "all day already" / "for the whole day (so far)". "schon" adds emphasis: something has been true for the entire period up to now.
target_language_example: Ich warte schon den ganzen Tag auf deinen Anruf.
native_language_example: I’ve been waiting for your call all day.

meaning: (already) all afternoon; for the whole afternoon (up to now).
additional_notes: Used with the present tense to emphasize that something has been going on since earlier in the afternoon and is still happening now. "schon" adds the idea of duration/"for quite a while". Often also said as "schon den ganzen Nachmittag lang" ("all afternoon long").
target_language_example: Ich warte schon den ganzen Nachmittag auf deinen Anruf.
native_language_example: I've been waiting for your call all afternoon.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something has been happening continuously since earlier today and is still true now. Often placed before what you’re doing/feeling: “Ich suche schon den ganzen Tag …” = “I’ve been looking all day …”.
target_language_example: Ich warte schon den ganzen Tag auf deinen Anruf.
native_language_example: I’ve been waiting for your call all day.

meaning: "all along" / "the whole time" (for a while already).
additional_notes: Used to say something has been true, happening, or intended continuously up to now (often for longer than expected). "schon" adds the sense of "already". Often used with the present perfect or simple past, and with verbs like warten, fragen, wissen, wollen, erwarten.
target_language_example: Ich wusste schon die ganze Zeit, dass du recht hast.
native_language_example: I knew all along that you were right.

meaning: "already a name for" (have you already chosen a name for …?).
additional_notes: Used when asking whether someone has already decided on a name for a person, baby, project, pet, etc. Very common with a verb like "haben" or "aussuchen/ausgesucht": "Habt ihr schon einen Namen für … (ausgesucht)?" The word "schon" implies it might be expected by now or you’re curious if the decision has been made yet.
target_language_example: Hast du schon einen Namen für deinen Hund?
native_language_example: Have you already chosen a name for your dog?

additional_notes: Often used in questions about past experience, especially with the perfect tense: Hast du das schon einmal gemacht? = Have you ever done that? Literally it is like “already once,” so in statements it can also mean “once before.”
target_language_example: Hast du dieses Lied schon einmal gehört?
native_language_example: Have you heard this song before?

additional_notes: Usually appears in questions about whether someone has visited a place before. It often continues with a location (e.g., "auf Mallorca", "auf einem Konzert") and commonly pairs with verbs like "sein" (Warst du schon einmal auf …?) or "gewesen" (Ich bin schon einmal auf … gewesen).
target_language_example: Warst du schon einmal auf Mallorca?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Mallorca?

meaning: "ever (before) on a …" / "have you ever been on a …?" (fragment).
additional_notes: This is an incomplete phrase you’ll usually see in questions with a noun after it and a verb later, especially **gewesen**: **Warst du schon einmal auf einem Schiff/Flugzeug/Konzert?** = “Have you ever been on a ship/plane/to a concert?” Literally it’s “already once on a …”, but in English it often corresponds to “ever (before) …”. **auf einem** is dative; the noun after it is typically masculine/neuter (einem Zug, einem Schiff, einem Festival).
target_language_example: Warst du schon einmal auf einem Kreuzfahrtschiff?
native_language_example: Have you ever been on a cruise ship?

meaning: "ever" / "(at least) once" (used to ask about past experience).
additional_notes: Common in questions about whether someone has had a certain experience before. Pattern: "Haben/Hast/Habt ... schon einmal + ein/eine + Nomen + Partizip II?" (e.g., geschrieben, gebaut, gegessen, gesehen). It often corresponds to English "Have you ever…?" or "Have you ever once…?".
target_language_example: Hast du schon einmal ein deutsches Lied gesungen?
native_language_example: Have you ever sung a German song?

meaning: "ever" (have you ever…?) with a feminine noun.
additional_notes: Used in questions with "haben" to ask whether someone has done/experienced something at least once before. "schon einmal" literally means "already once," but in many questions it corresponds to English "ever." The "eine" changes with the noun (e.g., "schon einmal einen" for masculine, "schon einmal ein" for neuter, or no article in the plural).
target_language_example: Hast du schon einmal eine Schildkröte gesehen?
native_language_example: Have you ever seen a turtle?

meaning: "ever a" / "once before a" (introduces a masculine noun in the accusative).
additional_notes: Used in questions and statements to ask or say whether someone has ever done/seen/experienced something at least once before. The key phrase is "schon einmal" = "ever/once before"; "einen" is the masculine accusative form of "ein" and changes with the noun (e.g., "schon einmal eine Katze" / "schon einmal ein Auto").
target_language_example: Hast du schon einmal einen Film auf Deutsch gesehen?
native_language_example: Have you ever watched a movie in German?

meaning: “ever/a (before) a letter” (usually as part of a question like “Have you ever written a letter?”).
additional_notes: This is a sentence fragment. "schon einmal" means “ever / before (at least once)”, and "einen Brief" is “a letter” (accusative). You’ll typically see it after a verb, especially in questions: "Hast du schon einmal einen Brief geschrieben?" = “Have you ever written a letter?”
target_language_example: Hast du schon einmal einen Brief geschrieben?
native_language_example: Have you ever written a letter?

additional_notes: Used to ask whether someone has seen a person or thing at some point in the past (at least once). Often used in questions with "schon einmal" = "ever/before". Word order: "Haben Sie ... schon einmal gesehen?" (formal) vs. "Habt ihr ... schon einmal gesehen?" (informal plural "you").
target_language_example: Hast du diesen Film schon einmal gesehen?
native_language_example: Have you ever seen this movie before?

meaning: “ever (before) in the …” (used to ask if someone has experience in a place/field).
additional_notes: Used with the present perfect to ask about past experience: "Hast du schon einmal im + [Bereich/Ort] + gearbeitet/tätig gewesen?" Here, "schon einmal" means “ever/at some point before,” and "im" = "in dem" (in the). Often followed by a noun like "im Verkauf" (in sales).
target_language_example: Hast du schon einmal im Ausland gearbeitet?
native_language_example: Have you ever worked abroad?

additional_notes: Used to talk about having visited a place at least once in your life or once before now. Common with the verb "sein" (to have been): "Bist du schon einmal in … gewesen?" = "Have you ever been to …?" In statements: "Ich war schon einmal in …" = "I've been to … before / once."
target_language_example: Bist du schon einmal in den USA gewesen?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to the USA?

additional_notes: Used when asking whether someone has previously thought about an option or possibility. It’s the past participle of the common phrase "in Erwägung ziehen" (= to consider). Often used in questions with "Hast/Habt du/ihr schon einmal ...?" and followed by an infinitive with "zu" (e.g., "... in Erwägung gezogen, umzuziehen?").
target_language_example: Hast du schon einmal in Erwägung gezogen, den Job zu wechseln?
native_language_example: Have you ever considered changing jobs?

additional_notes: Used most often in questions like "Warst du schon einmal in der Schweiz?" to ask whether someone has been somewhere before. "schon einmal" = 'ever/once before', and "in der" is 'in the' with a feminine noun in the dative case (e.g., in der Schweiz, in der Stadt, in der Schule). Often followed by a place/event noun.
target_language_example: Warst du schon einmal in der Schweiz?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Switzerland?

meaning: 'ever in a' / 'have you ever been in a…' (talking about past experience).
additional_notes: Used to ask whether someone has had the experience of being in a certain place or type of place. Often comes with a verb like "sein" (to be): "Warst du schon einmal in einem …?" = "Have you ever been in a …?". "schon einmal" literally means "already once" but is often best translated as "ever" in questions.
target_language_example: Warst du schon einmal in einem Museum?
native_language_example: Have you ever been in a museum?

additional_notes: Used in questions (and statements) about past experience. **schon einmal** means 'ever' or 'before/once in your life' (not necessarily 'already'). **jemanden** is accusative ('someone') and will be followed by a verb phrase, often in the **Perfekt**: *Hast du schon einmal jemanden …?* / *Haben Sie schon einmal jemanden …?*
target_language_example: Hast du schon einmal jemanden singen hören?
native_language_example: Have you ever heard someone sing?

additional_notes: Used mostly in questions to ask whether someone has ever done something before together with a person (mit Tom) or involving a group (mit Kindern). It often suggests “at least once before” in your life so far. Word order: schon einmal comes after the auxiliary (hast/habt/haben/warst), and mit introduces the person/group you did it with.
target_language_example: Bist du schon einmal mit deiner Schwester gereist?
native_language_example: Have you ever traveled with your sister?

additional_notes: Used in questions with a form of **sehen** (e.g., *Hast du…? Habt ihr…? Haben Sie…?*) to ask whether someone has ever witnessed a person dancing. **schon einmal** means “ever / at any time before.” Word order: *jemanden* + *schon einmal* + *tanzen sehen* (e.g., *Hast du ihn schon einmal tanzen sehen?*).
target_language_example: Hast du sie schon einmal tanzen sehen?
native_language_example: Have you ever seen her dance?

meaning: 'ever' (as in: 'have you ever heard of a ...?')
additional_notes: Usually part of the pattern: „Hast du schon einmal von einer/einem … gehört?“ = “Have you ever heard of a …?” The „von“ takes the dative case: „von einer“ is used before a feminine noun (or a noun used as feminine). For masculine/neuter you use „von einem“.
target_language_example: Hast du schon einmal von einer Geisterstadt gehört?
native_language_example: Have you ever heard of a ghost town?

meaning: “to have ever seen (someone) cry / to have seen (someone) cry before.”
additional_notes: Used with a person/object in the accusative: jemanden (schon einmal) weinen sehen. In questions, *schon einmal* often means “ever / before” (not literally “already once”). The verb pattern is **sehen + infinitive** (“see someone do something”): *Hast du mich schon einmal weinen sehen?* Word order: the person usually comes before *weinen sehen*.
target_language_example: Hast du Anna schon einmal weinen sehen?
native_language_example: Have you ever seen Anna cry?

additional_notes: Used with the verb **vorhaben** (“to plan/to intend”). In the present tense, **vorhaben** splits: **haben ... vor**. **etwas** is a placeholder for “something,” and **schon** adds the idea of “already” (e.g., asking if someone has already made plans). Often used in questions about holidays, weekends, etc.
target_language_example: Ich habe am Wochenende schon etwas vor.
native_language_example: I already have plans for the weekend.

additional_notes: Used to ask or state that someone is finished earlier than expected, or to politely check if they’re done (e.g., in a shop, restaurant, at work). “schon” adds the idea of “already/by now,” and “fertig” means “finished/ready.” Often used in questions like “Bist du schon fertig?” or polite “Sind Sie schon fertig?”
target_language_example: Bist du schon fertig, oder brauchst du noch fünf Minuten?
native_language_example: Are you already done, or do you still need five minutes?

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize a negation, often after a first negative statement: "X nicht, (und) Y schon gar nicht" = "not X, and certainly not Y / let alone Y". It highlights that the second thing is even less likely/less acceptable than the first.
target_language_example: Ich habe heute keine Zeit, und morgen schon gar nicht.
native_language_example: I don't have time today, and certainly not tomorrow (let alone tomorrow).

additional_notes: Used with the Perfekt tense to say someone has eaten earlier than now. Often answers the question of whether the person is still hungry or whether food is still needed. In questions like "Hast du schon gegessen?", it can also mean "Have you eaten yet?" depending on context. Word order is flexible: "Ich habe schon gegessen" / "Ich habe gegessen" (but "schon" adds the idea of 'already').
target_language_example: Ich habe schon gegessen, danke.
native_language_example: I've already eaten, thanks.

additional_notes: Used when you’re reminding someone that you already told them the information that follows. Typical patterns: „Ich habe dir/Ihnen schon gesagt, was …“ (I already told you what …). Often used with „doch“ to sound more emphatic/insistent: „Ich habe doch schon gesagt, was …!“
target_language_example: Ich habe dir schon gesagt, was du jetzt tun sollst.
native_language_example: I already told you what you should do now.

additional_notes: Used with the present perfect (haben + gesehen) to say you’ve already watched/seen/checked something. In questions, it often means “have you seen it yet/already?” depending on context and tone. Word order is flexible in speech (e.g., „Hast du das schon gesehen?“ / „Hast du schon das gesehen?“).
target_language_example: Ich habe den Film schon gesehen, aber ich schaue ihn gern nochmal.
native_language_example: I've already seen the movie, but I like watching it again.

additional_notes: Used to reassure someone, calm them down, or to say “don’t worry about it / never mind.” Often said as a quick response on its own (“Schon gut!”). Depending on tone it can also sound like “Alright, alright” (to stop a discussion).
target_language_example: Schon gut, ich mache das gleich.
native_language_example: It’s okay, I’ll do it in a moment.

meaning: always; ever since (as long as one can remember).
additional_notes: Used to say something has been true for a very long time and still is (a long-standing habit, condition, or dream). It often appears with past tenses or the present to emphasize continuity: „Ich wollte das schon immer.“ = “I’ve always wanted that.”
target_language_example: Ich wollte schon immer nach Berlin fahren.
native_language_example: I’ve always wanted to go to Berlin.

meaning: “always (been) like this/that” (since as long as you can remember).
additional_notes: Used to say something has been the same for a long time (often “all along”). Commonly used in questions about whether someone/ something has always had a certain quality: “War sie schon immer so …?” It can sound accusatory or emphatic depending on tone.
target_language_example: Ich mache das schon immer so.
native_language_example: I’ve always done it like this.

meaning: “It’s okay / it’s all right / no problem.”
additional_notes: Used to reassure someone or to say you accept something (e.g., after an apology or when someone is worried). The word “schon” makes it sound more calming/assuring, like “it’s really fine.” Often said alone: “Schon in Ordnung.”
target_language_example: Tut mir leid! – Schon in Ordnung, kein Problem.
native_language_example: Sorry! – It’s okay, no problem.

meaning: for a long time (already); for a long while.
additional_notes: Used to say something has been true/going on for a long time up to now. Very common in questions about duration (e.g., relationships, knowing someone, living somewhere): „Kennst du ihn schon lange?“ Often implies “already” (= longer than expected): „Der ist doch schon lange tot.“
target_language_example: Ich war schon lange nicht mehr in Berlin.
native_language_example: I haven’t been to Berlin for a long time.

meaning: "for a long time in" (asking how long someone has been in a place).
additional_notes: Used with the present tense to ask about duration up to now. Common in questions like: „Bist du schon lange in …?“ (informal) / „Sind Sie schon lange in …?“ (formal). It can refer to being somewhere temporarily (e.g., traveling) or living there, depending on context.
target_language_example: Bist du schon lange in Berlin?
native_language_example: Have you been in Berlin for a long time?

meaning: “not for a long time anymore” / “haven’t … in a long time.”
additional_notes: Used to say something hasn’t been true or hasn’t happened for a long time up to now. Very common with the present perfect (ich habe … schon lange nicht mehr gemacht) or with the present tense to describe a current state (wir wohnen da schon lange nicht mehr = we don’t live there anymore, and it’s been that way for a long time). Often implies a change happened long ago.
target_language_example: Ich habe schon lange nicht mehr so gut geschlafen.
native_language_example: I haven’t slept this well in a long time.

meaning: "a long time ago / for a long time already" (sooner than expected).
additional_notes: Used to stress that something happened long ago or has been the case for a long time already—often implying “by now” or “it should have happened earlier.” Common in statements like: Ich habe das schon längst gemacht. / Das hätte schon längst passieren müssen.
target_language_example: Wir hätten schon längst losfahren sollen.
native_language_example: We should have left a long time ago (by now).

additional_notes: Used a lot in spoken German to say you’ll do something now as a first step, earlier than others, or ahead of time: *Ich gehe schon mal rein* (= I’ll go in first/now). With imperatives it often means “go ahead and …”: *Deck schon mal den Tisch!* It can also mean “to start getting used to something”: *Er kann sich schon mal dran gewöhnen.*
target_language_example: Ich rufe schon mal ein Taxi, dann müssen wir später nicht warten.
native_language_example: I’ll call a taxi now/in advance so we don’t have to wait later.

additional_notes: "schon mal" is short for "schon einmal" and is very common in spoken German. In questions it often means "ever" or "have you ever…?" The "einen" is the masculine accusative form of "ein" and changes depending on the noun (e.g., "schon mal eine Katze" (fem.), "schon mal ein Auto" (neut.), or plural "schon mal welche").
target_language_example: Hast du schon mal einen E-Scooter gefahren?
native_language_example: Have you ever ridden an e-scooter?

additional_notes: "schon mal" is a common, slightly colloquial way to say "schon einmal" ("already/once"), and in this phrase it means "at some earlier time" = "before." It’s often used with the present perfect: "Ich habe X schon mal gesehen" ("I’ve seen X before"). As a short question, "Schon mal gesehen?" means "Have you seen it before?"
target_language_example: Ich glaube, wir haben uns schon mal gesehen.
native_language_example: I think we’ve seen each other before.

meaning: “ever / at some point before in the …” (talking about past experience).
additional_notes: Used mostly in questions to ask whether someone has had an experience before: **Warst du schon mal im Kino?** = “Have you ever been to the movies?” **schon mal** means “ever / before / at some point,” and **im** is **in dem** (“in the”). Often used with **sein** or **haben** in the Perfekt/Präteritum.
target_language_example: Warst du schon mal im Krankenhaus?
native_language_example: Have you ever been in the hospital?

additional_notes: Used to ask or say whether someone has had the experience of being in a certain place at least once. Very common with travel/experience questions, often in the present perfect: „Bist du schon mal in X gewesen?“ It can also appear with simple past: „Warst du schon mal in X?“ The place comes after „in“ (usually dative: in Italien, in Japan).
target_language_example: Bist du schon mal in Berlin gewesen?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Berlin?

additional_notes: Used mainly in questions to ask whether someone has tried something at least once up to now. It’s a common, slightly colloquial phrasing; the more formal version is „schon einmal versucht“. Often followed by an infinitive clause: „… versucht, + zu + infinitive“ (e.g., „… versucht, an nichts zu denken?“).
target_language_example: Hast du das schon mal versucht?
native_language_example: Have you ever tried that before?

additional_notes: "Schon" adds the idea of “already / up to now,” and "oft" means “often.” Together, "schon oft" is used to say something has happened many times before now (often with the feel of “this isn’t new” or “I’ve experienced this before”). Common with the present perfect: "Ich habe ... schon oft ...".
target_language_example: Das habe ich schon oft gemacht.
native_language_example: I’ve already done that many times.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize duration up to now. "schon" adds the idea of "already" (it has been that long), and it often comes before the time phrase: "Ich bin schon sehr lange hier." Can be used in statements and questions, and with present tense to describe something that started in the past and is still true now.
target_language_example: Wir kennen uns schon sehr lange.
native_language_example: We've known each other for a very long time.

additional_notes: Used with a time period to say that something started in the past and is still true/going on now. Often emphasizes that it feels like a long time (“already”). Common with present tense in German: "Ich warte schon seit dreißig Minuten" = “I’ve been waiting for 30 minutes.”
target_language_example: Ich kenne sie schon seit zwei Jahren.
native_language_example: I’ve known her for two years (already).

meaning: for years now; already for years.
additional_notes: Used to say something started years ago and is still true/continuing. Common with the present tense (or present perfect) and often placed near the time expression: „Ich wohne schon seit Jahren hier.“
target_language_example: Ich kenne diese Familie schon seit Jahren.
native_language_example: I’ve known this family for years now.

additional_notes: Used to stress that something has been going on for a long time (hours) and is still continuing now. Often expresses impatience or surprise. Typically used with the present tense in German: „Er wartet schon seit Stunden.“
target_language_example: Wir warten schon seit Stunden auf den Bus.
native_language_example: We’ve been waiting for the bus for hours now.

additional_notes: Used to say something started at “three” and is still true now. It normally needs a time unit or context after it, e.g. „schon seit drei Uhr“ (since three o’clock), „schon seit drei Jahren“ (for three years), or „schon seit drei Tagen“ (for three days). „schon“ adds emphasis: ‘already/for quite a while.’
target_language_example: Ich warte schon seit drei Uhr.
native_language_example: I’ve been waiting since three o’clock.

meaning: for three years already (for the past three years).
additional_notes: Used with the present tense to say an action/state started three years ago and is still true now. "seit" = since/for (time duration), and "schon" adds emphasis like “already/as long as”.
target_language_example: Ich lerne schon seit drei Jahren Deutsch.
native_language_example: I've been learning German for three years already.

meaning: “for three days already” (and it’s still going on).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something started three days ago and continues up to now. Often appears with the present tense in German (e.g., „Ich warte schon seit drei Tagen.“ = “I’ve been waiting for three days already”). You can swap in other time periods: „schon seit einer Woche / seit zwei Stunden / seit Jahren“.
target_language_example: Ich habe schon seit drei Tagen Kopfschmerzen.
native_language_example: I’ve had a headache for three days already.

meaning: 'for a ... already' / 'already for a ...' (indicates a continuing duration).
additional_notes: Used with a time expression (often feminine nouns in the dative after "seit"), e.g. "schon seit einer Stunde/seit einer Woche/seit einer Weile". It means something started in the past and is still true now, often with the feeling of "longer than expected".
target_language_example: Ich warte schon seit einer Stunde auf den Bus.
native_language_example: I’ve been waiting for the bus for an hour already.

meaning: for a long time already; for a long time now.
additional_notes: Used to say something started long ago and has been true/going on up to now (or up to the time being talked about). Often with the present tense in German: "Ich wohne schon seit langem hier" = "I’ve lived here for a long time." Similar to "seit langem", but "schon" adds emphasis: “already/for quite a while.”
target_language_example: Ich suche schon seit langem einen neuen Job.
native_language_example: I've been looking for a new job for a long time.

meaning: for over a month already; (has) been (that way) for over a month already.
additional_notes: Used with the present tense to say a situation started in the past and is still true now (e.g., ist … verschwunden / ist … arbeitslos / hat … keine Arbeit). “schon” adds emphasis (“already/as long as”), “seit” means “since/for” with a time period, and “über” means “over/more than.” Word order is flexible: “Schon seit über einem Monat …” or “… schon seit über einem Monat.”
target_language_example: Ich warte schon seit über einem Monat auf eine Antwort.
native_language_example: I’ve been waiting for an answer for over a month already.

additional_notes: Used to say that a situation, performance, or someone’s health/feelings has improved compared to before (often compared to yesterday, earlier, or a previous attempt). Common with verbs like „gehen“ (Es geht mir …) and „sich fühlen“ (Ich fühle mich …).
target_language_example: Danke, mir geht es heute schon viel besser.
native_language_example: Thanks, I’m already feeling much better today.

additional_notes: Short, spoken form of „schon etwas vorhaben“. Used in questions to ask if someone is free at a certain time. Often said with „heute Abend / nachmittags“ etc. „was“ = informal for „etwas“.
target_language_example: Ich kann nicht mitkommen, ich habe heute Abend schon was vor.
native_language_example: I can't come along; I already have plans this evening.

additional_notes: Used very often with "sein" (e.g., "Er ist schon weg") to say someone/something has already left or is no longer there. It can also mean that something has already been used up/consumed or is missing (e.g., "Die Hälfte ist schon weg"). In questions, it can express surprise that someone is leaving early: "Du willst schon weg?"
target_language_example: Sorry, der letzte Bus ist schon weg.
native_language_example: Sorry, the last bus is already gone.

meaning: again (already again); once more (often: annoyingly/surprisingly soon).
additional_notes: Used when something happens again sooner than expected, often with an annoyed, tired, or surprised tone. Common in questions/exclamations ("Schon wieder?") and in short comments like "Schon wieder weg" (= gone again already).
target_language_example: Du bist schon wieder zu spät!
native_language_example: You're late again (already again)!

additional_notes: Used to say someone is in trouble once more, often with a tone of surprise, annoyance, or “not again.” Common with verbs like „in Schwierigkeiten kommen/geraten“ (to get into trouble) and „in Schwierigkeiten stecken“ (to be stuck in trouble). „schon wieder“ emphasizes repetition and can suggest it happens too often.
target_language_example: Er ist schon wieder in Schwierigkeiten, weil er zu spät gekommen ist.
native_language_example: He’s in trouble again because he arrived late.

additional_notes: Used to say or ask whether someone has eaten lunch already. "schon" = "already"; "zu Mittag" = "for lunch / at noon"; "gegessen" is the past participle of "essen" (to eat). Usually appears with "haben" in the present perfect: "Ich habe schon zu Mittag gegessen." In the past perfect it’s "hatte ... gegessen" (had already eaten).
target_language_example: Wir haben schon zu Mittag gegessen, aber wir können später noch einen Kaffee trinken.
native_language_example: We’ve already eaten lunch, but we can still have a coffee later.

additional_notes: “Sie” is the formal “you” (used with strangers, in service situations, or professionally). With “schreiben,” it can be an imperative: “Schreiben Sie …!” (“Write …!”), often softened with “bitte.” It can also be the normal present tense for formal “you”: “Schreiben Sie …?” (“Do you write …?” / “Are you writing …?”).
target_language_example: Schreiben Sie bitte Ihre E-Mail-Adresse hier auf.
native_language_example: Please write your email address down here.

meaning: “do you write…?” / “are you writing…?” (2nd person singular question).
additional_notes: Question form of **du schreibst** (“you write/you’re writing”), with the verb first. Used to ask about a habit (**Schreibst du Kurzgeschichten?** = “Do you write short stories?”) or something happening now, often with **gerade/jetzt** (**Schreibst du gerade einen Brief?** = “Are you writing a letter right now?”). Can take objects or question words: **Was schreibst du? Worüber schreibst du?**
target_language_example: Schreibst du heute Abend noch eine E-Mail?
native_language_example: Are you writing another email tonight?

additional_notes: Used with the verb „schreiben“ + dative to say who you’re writing to. „seinen Eltern“ = “his parents” (dative plural). Often followed by what is being written: „… einen Brief / eine Nachricht“.
target_language_example: Er schreibt seinen Eltern jeden Sonntag eine Nachricht.
native_language_example: He writes to his parents a message every Sunday.

additional_notes: Typically used in the pattern: „[Person] schrie, so laut [Person/Pronoun] konnte.“ = “(Someone) shouted as loudly as (they) could.” The second clause usually ends with „konnte“ and changes with the subject: ich konnte, du konntest, er/sie/es konnte, wir konnten, ihr konntet, sie konnten.
target_language_example: Das kleine Mädchen schrie, so laut es konnte.
native_language_example: The little girl shouted as loudly as she could.

additional_notes: Describes someone urgently shouting to get assistance. "schrie" is the simple past (Präteritum) of "schreien" (to shout/scream). The base expression is "um Hilfe schreien" (to cry for help).
target_language_example: Sie schrie um Hilfe, doch niemand kam.
native_language_example: She cried for help, but nobody came.

additional_notes: "schrieb" is the simple past (Präteritum) of "schreiben" (to write). It’s common in written narration and also fairly common with "ich" in spoken German. You can add the recipient with "an" + accusative (e.g., "schrieb einen Brief an meine Oma"). You can specify the language with "auf Deutsch/auf Englisch". Note: German "Brief" means a (mail) letter, not English "brief".
target_language_example: Ich schrieb einen Brief auf Englisch.
native_language_example: I wrote a letter in English.

additional_notes: "schrieb" is the simple past (Präteritum) of "schreiben" (to write). Pattern: "(jemand) schrieb einen Brief an (jemanden)" = someone wrote a letter to someone. The recipient comes after "an" and is typically accusative (e.g., an meine Mutter, an Jim, an die Polizei, an sich selbst). Note: German "Brief" means "letter" (not English "brief"), so this is a false cognate.
target_language_example: Ich schrieb einen Brief an Jim.
native_language_example: I wrote a letter to Jim.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "sein": "(jemand) ist schuld daran" = someone is responsible for causing something bad. Very often followed by a "dass"-clause: "Du bist schuld daran, dass ...". You can also put the real cause in front: "Schuld daran waren ..." = "... were to blame."
target_language_example: Ich bin nicht schuld daran, dass der Bus zu spät kam.
native_language_example: It’s not my fault that the bus was late.

meaning: to be to blame; to be at fault.
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something caused a problem or is responsible for a bad result. Common patterns: „Wer ist schuld?“ (Who’s to blame?), „X ist schuld.“ (X is to blame.), „an etw. schuld sein“ / „daran schuld sein“ (to be to blame for something), and „schuld sein, dass …“ (to be the reason that …).
target_language_example: Ich will nicht schuld sein, dass wir zu spät sind.
native_language_example: I don’t want to be to blame for us being late.

additional_notes: From the verb „schulden“ (to owe). It’s usually used with an explicit subject: „Du schuldest mir …“ and often followed by an amount or something owed: „Du schuldest mir 10 Euro / einen Gefallen.“ The person owed to is in the dative („mir“, „dir“, „ihm/ihr“).
target_language_example: Du schuldest mir noch 10 Euro.
native_language_example: You still owe me 10 euros.

additional_notes: Used in legal contexts, especially in court rulings and news reports. It describes the result of a trial: someone is officially judged guilty of a crime (often followed by "wegen" + genitive/dative or "für" + accusative, e.g., "wegen Betrugs").
target_language_example: Der Angeklagte wurde wegen Betrugs schuldig befunden.
native_language_example: The defendant was found guilty of fraud.

meaning: to be guilty; to owe (someone something).
additional_notes: Used in two common ways: (1) legal/moral guilt: „Er ist schuldig.“ = „He is guilty.“ (2) owing a person something: „Ich bin dir 10 Euro schuldig.“ = „I owe you 10 euros.“ In the ‘owe’ meaning, it’s often used with a person in the dative (mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen).
target_language_example: Ich bin dir 10 Euro schuldig sein.
native_language_example: I owe you 10 euros.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s hair color. With plural "Haare" you typically use "haben": "Ich habe schwarze Haare." You may also hear "dunkle, fast schwarze Haare" for “dark, almost black hair.”
target_language_example: Meine Schwester hat schwarze Haare und braune Augen.
native_language_example: My sister has black hair and brown eyes.

meaning: blacklist; a list of people/things that are banned or not trusted.
additional_notes: Used for an official or unofficial list of people, companies, websites, etc. that are excluded, blocked, or considered suspicious. Often appears with verbs like „auf die schwarze Liste setzen“ (to blacklist) or „auf der schwarzen Liste stehen“ (to be blacklisted).
target_language_example: Die Firma steht auf der schwarzen Liste und darf nicht mehr liefern.
native_language_example: The company is on the blacklist and is no longer allowed to deliver.

additional_notes: A noun phrase: "schwarz" (black) + "das Loch" (hole). Used mostly in science/astronomy contexts; can also be used figuratively for something that seems to swallow things up (e.g., money, time), though that’s more context-dependent.
target_language_example: Ein schwarzes Loch hat eine so starke Gravitation, dass nicht einmal Licht entkommen kann.
native_language_example: A black hole has such strong gravity that not even light can escape.

additional_notes: Used to say something is difficult for you, either physically (too heavy) or mentally/emotionally. Often appears as (1) “Es ist schwer für mich, …” + infinitive (to do something), or (2) “zu schwer für mich, um … zu …” (too difficult/heavy for me to…).
target_language_example: Es ist schwer für mich, so früh aufzustehen.
native_language_example: It’s hard for me to get up so early.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive with **zu**: **schwer zu + Verb** (e.g., *schwer zu lernen* = hard to learn, *schwer zu entfernen* = hard to remove). Often appears in the pattern **Es fällt jemandem schwer, ... zu ...** (“Someone finds it hard to ...”). With **zu haben**, it commonly means “hard to get” (or “playing hard to get”).
target_language_example: Dieses Wort ist schwer zu übersetzen.
native_language_example: This word is hard to translate.

additional_notes: Used to say something seems unlikely or surprising. Often appears with an introductory phrase like „(Ich finde / Mir fällt es) schwer zu glauben, dass …“ = “(I find it / I have a hard time) believing that …”.
target_language_example: Es ist schwer zu glauben, dass er schon 30 ist.
native_language_example: It’s hard to believe that he’s already 30.

additional_notes: Used to say something is difficult to understand (a book, music, poems, a situation, etc.). Often used as: „X ist (sehr) schwer zu verstehen.“ You can intensify with „sehr“ (very).
target_language_example: Die Erklärung ist schwer zu verstehen.
native_language_example: The explanation is hard to understand.

additional_notes: Used to describe the severity of an injury (often in accidents or emergencies). It can be used in statements and questions: "Ist er schwer verletzt?" = "Is he seriously injured?" You can intensify it with "sehr" (very): "sehr schwer verletzt".
target_language_example: Nach dem Unfall war der Fahrer schwer verletzt.
native_language_example: After the accident, the driver was seriously injured.

additional_notes: Used to describe a severe injury, often in news or accident contexts. Typically appears with "sein/werden" (e.g., "Er wurde schwer verletzt" = "He was seriously injured").
target_language_example: Bei dem Sturz wurde sie schwer verletzt.
native_language_example: She was seriously injured in the fall.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is difficult for you personally. Often appears in patterns like: „Es ist schwierig für mich, …“ (It’s hard for me to …) or with „zu“: „zu schwierig für mich“ (too difficult for me). You can replace „mich“ with other people: „schwierig für dich/ihn/sie/uns/euch/Sie“.
target_language_example: Es ist schwierig für mich, Deutsch schnell zu sprechen.
native_language_example: It’s hard for me to speak German quickly.

additional_notes: Common way to talk about the activity of going somewhere (pool, lake, etc.) to swim. Typically used with modal verbs or future context: „Ich will/möchte/kann/werde schwimmen gehen.“ You can add where with „im/am + Dativ“ (e.g., „im See“, „am Strand“) and who with „mit + Dativ“ (e.g., „mit einem Freund“, „mit uns“).
target_language_example: Wollen Tom und Maria nächstes Wochenende mit uns schwimmen gehen?
native_language_example: Do Tom and Maria still want to go swimming with us next weekend?

additional_notes: Uses the modal verb "können" (to be able to/can) with the infinitive "schwimmen" (to swim). In main clauses, the finite form of "können" is in position 2 and "schwimmen" goes to the end (e.g., "Ich kann schwimmen."). With future meaning it often appears as "wird ... schwimmen können" (= "will be able to swim").
target_language_example: Jeder sollte schwimmen können.
native_language_example: Everyone should be able to swim.

additional_notes: Used with another verb (e.g., Lust haben, vorhaben, vorschlagen, jemandem raten) to express the plan/idea of going to swim. The structure is an infinitive with „zu“ + „gehen“ and is similar to English “to go + [activity]” (e.g., „joggen zu gehen“, „einkaufen zu gehen“).
target_language_example: Wir planen, morgen früh schwimmen zu gehen.
native_language_example: We’re planning to go swimming tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Usually used as part of the reflexive verb "sich schämen" (to be ashamed). In the 1st person singular: "Ich schäme mich." Often followed by "für" + accusative ("Ich schäme mich für meinen Fehler." = I’m ashamed of my mistake) or "wegen" + genitive/dative in everyday speech ("wegen dem/ des Fehlers").
target_language_example: Ich schäme mich für das, was ich gesagt habe.
native_language_example: I’m ashamed of what I said.

additional_notes: Used as a polite greeting when you meet someone (often again) in formal situations. It uses the formal “Sie” (not “du”). You’ll often hear it shortened to just “Schön, Sie zu sehen!” or expanded as “Es ist schön, Sie zu sehen!”.
target_language_example: Guten Tag, Frau Müller — schön, Sie zu sehen.
native_language_example: Good afternoon, Ms. Müller — nice to see you.

meaning: 'nice/beautiful, but …' (a compliment followed by a contrast/criticism).
additional_notes: Used to acknowledge something positive ("schön") and then add a limitation or objection with "aber". Common in evaluations and polite refusals: "Es ist schön, aber …" / "Das ist zwar schön, aber …". In writing, a comma often comes before "aber" when it links two main clauses.
target_language_example: Das ist schön, aber ich habe leider keine Zeit.
native_language_example: That’s nice, but unfortunately I don’t have time.

additional_notes: Used with a "dass"-clause. (1) As a polite/friendly remark: "Schön, dass Sie/du da sind/bist" = “Nice to have you here / Glad you’re here.” (2) With "so schön, dass …" it expresses a result: “so beautiful that …”. The verb goes to the end of the "dass"-clause.
target_language_example: Schön, dass du Zeit hast.
native_language_example: Nice that you have time / Glad you have time.

additional_notes: Used to express pleasure or appreciation about what someone (addressed as Sie) is doing or that they are present. Common with verbs like „da sein“ (be here), „wieder da sein“ (be back), „helfen“ (help), etc. In informal speech with friends you’d usually say „Schön, dass du …“.
target_language_example: Schön, dass Sie heute Zeit haben.
native_language_example: I’m glad you have time today.

additional_notes: Used to express that you’re happy about what the other person did or that they’re present. Typically followed by a verb at the end of the clause: „Schön, dass du gekommen bist!“ (“Glad you came!”), „Schön, dass du wieder da bist!“ (“Nice to have you back!”).
target_language_example: Schön, dass du Zeit hast!
native_language_example: Nice / glad that you have time!

additional_notes: Used as a friendly opener in phrases like „Schön, dich zu sehen/kennenzulernen/zu hören.“ It’s short for „(Es ist) schön, dich …“ and is typically followed by an infinitive with „zu“. You’ll also hear it in the past („War schön, dich gekannt zu haben.“) as a farewell, sometimes sincerely and sometimes ironically.
target_language_example: Schön, dich wiederzusehen!
native_language_example: Nice to see you again!

additional_notes: A common, polite phrase when you meet someone (or are introduced) for the first time. Often said as an exclamation: "Schön, dich kennenzulernen!" You can also use the more formal version with "Sie": "Schön, Sie kennenzulernen." Literally it means "(It’s) nice to get to know you."
target_language_example: Hallo, ich bin Mark. Schön, dich kennenzulernen!
native_language_example: Hi, I'm Mark. Nice to meet you!

meaning: "Nice to see you." / "Good to see you."
additional_notes: Used as a friendly greeting when you meet someone (again). Often said as a full sentence ("Es ist schön, dich zu sehen!") or shortened ("Schön, dich zu sehen!"). "dich" is informal (to one person you address as "du"); for formal use: "Schön, Sie zu sehen." You can intensify it with words like "so" or "wie" ("So/WIe schön, dich zu sehen!").
target_language_example: Schön, dich zu sehen! Wie geht’s dir?
native_language_example: Nice to see you! How are you?

additional_notes: Used to say something sounds so positive that you doubt it’s real. Very often appears in the pattern „(fast) zu schön, um wahr zu sein“ with verbs like „klingen“ (to sound) or „scheinen“ (to seem).
target_language_example: Der Preis ist zu schön, um wahr zu sein.
native_language_example: The price is too good to be true.

additional_notes: Used to say that a situation is pleasant or would be pleasant. Common patterns: „Es ist schön, wenn …“ (general statement) and „Wäre (wirklich) schön, wenn …“ (a wish/hope, often like “It would be nice if …”). You can also start a sentence with „Schön, wenn …“ as a shorter, more conversational version (sometimes even slightly ironic depending on tone/context).
target_language_example: Es wäre schön, wenn du morgen Zeit hättest.
native_language_example: It would be nice if you had time tomorrow.

meaning: “It would be nice if …” (often expressing a wish, sometimes with a skeptical/“if only” tone).
additional_notes: Short for „Schön wäre es, wenn …“. Used to say you’d like something to be true or happen; depending on context it can sound like wishful thinking (maybe unlikely). Usually followed by a subjunctive form like „wäre“, „könnte“, etc.
target_language_example: Schön wär’s, wenn wir morgen frei hätten.
native_language_example: It would be nice if we had tomorrow off.

meaning: “If only I …” / “Yeah, that’d be nice if I …” (wishful thinking; not true).
additional_notes: Used to express a wish or an unrealistic/ironic idea. Often implies “but that’s not the case.” "wär’s" is a spoken contraction of "wäre es". Typically followed by the subjunctive (Konjunktiv II): "wenn ich … wäre/hätte/könnte".
target_language_example: Schön wär’s, wenn ich morgen frei hätte.
native_language_example: If only I had tomorrow off. (That would be nice, but I don’t.)

additional_notes: Used to compliment someone’s eyes; often sounds a bit personal or flirtatious depending on the situation. Usually appears with a form of "haben" (e.g., "Du hast schöne Augen") or in the exclamation "Was für schöne Augen du hast!".
target_language_example: Du hast wirklich schöne Augen.
native_language_example: You have really beautiful eyes.

additional_notes: "schöne" is the adjective "schön" (beautiful/nice) with an ending because it comes before the noun. Common in descriptions, often with "es gibt" (there are) or exclamations like "Was für schöne Blumen!" (What beautiful flowers!).
target_language_example: Sie hat mir schöne Blumen geschenkt.
native_language_example: She gave me beautiful flowers as a gift.

meaning: beautiful woman; pretty wife (depending on context).
additional_notes: Means a woman who is beautiful/pretty. With possessives like "seine" it often refers to someone’s wife/partner (e.g., "seine schöne Frau" = “his beautiful wife”), but it can also simply describe any woman ("eine schöne Frau"). Adjective endings change: eine schöne Frau, die schöne Frau, seine schöne Frau.
target_language_example: Auf dem Foto sieht man eine schöne Frau in einem roten Kleid.
native_language_example: In the photo you can see a beautiful woman in a red dress.

additional_notes: This is not a fixed idiom; it’s a sentence fragment built from **schöne** (beautiful) + **Rosen** (roses) + **gesehen** (seen, past participle of *sehen*). It’s typically used with an auxiliary verb in the Perfekt tense, e.g. **Ich habe ... gesehen** (“I saw / I have seen ...”).
target_language_example: Ich habe im Park schöne Rosen gesehen.
native_language_example: I saw beautiful roses in the park.

additional_notes: "schöne" is the adjective "schön" (beautiful/pretty) with the ending -e because it comes after an article like "eine" (eine schöne Stadt). Used to compliment or describe a city. You can intensify it with "sehr" (very): "eine sehr schöne Stadt".
target_language_example: Das ist eine schöne Stadt, besonders im Frühling.
native_language_example: That’s a beautiful city, especially in spring.

additional_notes: Used as a friendly wish or farewell, especially in the phrases “Schönen Abend noch!” (Have a nice evening!) and as a short goodbye “Schönen Abend!” It can also be literal, describing an evening that is pleasant/beautiful (e.g., “an einem so schönen Abend…”).
target_language_example: Ich muss los—schönen Abend noch!
native_language_example: I have to go—have a nice evening!

meaning: 'have a nice day' (often as a short farewell).
additional_notes: Used when saying goodbye, often as the phrase "Schönen Tag noch!" (= "Have a nice day!" / "Have a nice rest of your day!"). It’s polite and common in shops, phone calls, and service situations. You’ll also hear "Schönen Tag!" on its own.
target_language_example: Tschüss, und schönen Tag noch!
native_language_example: Bye, and have a nice day!

meaning: “Have a nice day” / “Have a good rest of your day.”
additional_notes: A polite, friendly goodbye said when leaving (often after “Danke”). Literally “(a) nice day still,” meaning you wish the other person a pleasant remainder of the day. You can also say “Schönen Tag noch!” on its own, or use variants like “Schönen Abend noch” (have a nice evening) and “Schönes Wochenende noch” (have a nice weekend).
target_language_example: Danke für Ihre Hilfe—schönen Tag noch!
native_language_example: Thanks for your help—have a nice day!

additional_notes: Used to compliment someone’s name (often after hearing it). In speech you might also hear it without a verb as a short comment: “Schöner Name.” Depending on tone, it can also be mildly sarcastic (“Yeah, great name...”). Grammar note: this is the nominative form; you may see other endings like “ein schöner Name” (with “ein”) or “einen schönen Namen” (accusative).
target_language_example: —Ich heiße Lina. —Schöner Name!
native_language_example: —My name is Lina. —Nice name!

additional_notes: Used to compare two things/people. It’s the comparative form of schön + als (than). You can strengthen it with words like „noch“ (even) and „sogar noch“ (even more): „noch schöner als …“. Common patterns: „X ist schöner als Y.“ / „schöner als je zuvor“ = "more beautiful than ever before."
target_language_example: Das neue Kleid ist noch schöner als das alte.
native_language_example: The new dress is even nicer than the old one.

additional_notes: "schönes" is the neuter form of "schön" (beautiful). You use it with neuter nouns like "das Land". Depending on context, "Land" can mean a country (e.g., Germany as a nation) or simply land/the countryside.
target_language_example: Deutschland ist ein schönes Land.
native_language_example: Germany is a beautiful country.

additional_notes: A common compliment. Used with the verb "haben" (to have): "Er/Sie hat ein (sehr) schönes Lächeln." Adjective ending changes with gender/case (e.g., "ein schönes Lächeln" because "Lächeln" is neuter).
target_language_example: Du hast ein schönes Lächeln.
native_language_example: You have a nice smile.

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase for pleasant weather (often sunny, warm, and dry). Common with "sein" (Heute ist schönes Wetter), "geben" (Morgen gibt es schönes Wetter), and in forecasts (Es wurde schönes Wetter vorhergesagt). Note the adjective ending changes with grammar: e.g., "schönes Wetter" (nom./acc.), but "bei schönem Wetter" (dat.).
target_language_example: Glaubst du, dass es morgen schönes Wetter gibt?
native_language_example: Do you think there will be nice weather tomorrow?

additional_notes: A common wish/greeting used on Fridays or when saying goodbye before the weekend. Often said on its own (“Schönes Wochenende!”). You can make it more formal by adding a verb: “Ich wünsche Ihnen ein schönes Wochenende.” (formal) / “Ich wünsche dir/euch ein schönes Wochenende.” (informal).
target_language_example: Schönes Wochenende! Wir sehen uns am Montag.
native_language_example: Have a nice weekend! See you on Monday.

additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of "den Kopf schütteln". Used to show disagreement, disbelief, or that something is not true/acceptable—often without speaking. You can change the subject (er/sie) and the tense: "Er schüttelt den Kopf" (present), "Er hat den Kopf geschüttelt" (spoken past).
target_language_example: Sie schüttelte den Kopf und sagte: „Nein, das stimmt nicht.“
native_language_example: She shook her head and said, “No, that’s not true.”

additional_notes: Used to talk about a length of time (duration) or an age difference. Often used with time expressions like "seit" (for six years), "vor" (six years ago), or with "alt/älter" (six years old/older). In phrases like "Im Mai sind es sechs Jahre", it means "It will have been six years (by May)."
target_language_example: Ich wohne seit sechs Jahren in Berlin.
native_language_example: I’ve been living in Berlin for six years.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a time period (duration) or a deadline/remaining time. Often appears with time expressions like „sechs Monate lang“ (for six months) or with „noch“ to mean “another/only six months left” (e.g., „nur noch sechs Monate“). It can also be used in legal contexts for a sentence or probation period.
target_language_example: Ich bin seit sechs Monaten in Berlin.
native_language_example: I’ve been in Berlin for six months.

meaning: for six months (for a duration of six months).
additional_notes: Used to express how long something lasts. It often follows the time period: „sechs Monate lang“ = literally “six months long.” You can replace the number/time unit: „zwei Tage lang“, „drei Jahre lang“. In speech and writing you may also see „sechs Monate“ without „lang“ when the duration is clear.
target_language_example: Ich war sechs Monate lang krank.
native_language_example: I was sick for six months.

additional_notes: You often see "sechs Monaten" after prepositions that require the dative, especially time expressions like "seit" (for/since), "vor" (ago), and "in" (in/within). Examples: "seit sechs Monaten" = for six months, "vor sechs Monaten" = six months ago, "in sechs Monaten" = in/within six months.
target_language_example: Ich lerne seit sechs Monaten Deutsch.
native_language_example: I’ve been learning German for six months.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration of time ("for six hours") or a time interval/frequency, often with "alle": "alle sechs Stunden" = "every six hours." Can also be used in commands: "Warte/Warten Sie sechs Stunden!" = "Wait six hours!"
target_language_example: Bitte warten Sie sechs Stunden, bevor Sie wieder essen.
native_language_example: Please wait six hours before eating again.

additional_notes: Used to say the time. Often appears with prepositions like „um“ (at), „bis“ (until), „von … bis …“ (from … to …), „vor“ (before), and „spätestens“ (at the latest/by). To be more specific, you can add „morgens“ (in the morning) or „abends“ (in the evening): „sechs Uhr morgens/abends“.
target_language_example: Können wir uns um sechs Uhr treffen?
native_language_example: Can we meet at six o’clock?

meaning: 'up at six o’clock' (awake/out of bed at 6:00).
additional_notes: Often used with verbs like „sein“ or „stehen“ (short for the idea of „auf sein/aufstehen“). Common patterns: „um sechs Uhr auf sein“ = to be up at six; „um sechs Uhr aufstehen“ = to get up at six. You’ll frequently see it with „um“ before the time: „um sechs Uhr …“.
target_language_example: Ich bin jeden Tag um sechs Uhr auf.
native_language_example: I’m up at six o’clock every day.

meaning: "I look at" / "I watch" (as part of *mir … ansehen*).
additional_notes: *Sehe mir* is usually not used alone—it's part of the separable verb **sich etwas ansehen** (to look at/watch something). In the full sentence you typically have **Ich sehe mir + [object] + an**: **mir** = “(to) myself” (dative reflexive pronoun), and **an** goes to the end of the clause.
target_language_example: Ich sehe mir den Film an.
native_language_example: I'm watching the movie.

additional_notes: Used in the pattern **(Immer/Jedes Mal/Wenn) ich [etwas/jemanden] sehe, erinnere ich mich an [Akk.]** to say that seeing something/someone triggers a memory/association. **sich erinnern an** takes **an + accusative** (e.g., *an ihn, an meinen Vater, an die Straßen*).
target_language_example: Wenn ich dieses Lied höre oder dich sehe, erinnere ich mich an unseren Sommerurlaub.
native_language_example: When I hear this song or see you, I remember our summer vacation.

meaning: “I see” / “do I look … ?” (with verb-first word order).
additional_notes: From the verb „sehen“ (to see), 1st person singular present: „ich sehe“. In main clauses, German often puts another element first, so you get inversion: „Da sehe ich …“, „Jeden Morgen sehe ich …“. In yes/no questions the verb comes first: „Sehe ich nicht aus, als ob …?“ (= “Don’t I look as if …?”). With „aussehen“ you’ll often see: „Wie sehe ich aus?“ (= “What do I look like?”).
target_language_example: Heute sehe ich meine Freunde erst am Abend.
native_language_example: Today I don’t see my friends until the evening.

additional_notes: This is the formal (Sie) imperative of the reflexive verb **sich ansehen** (“to look at”). In real sentences you usually see the separable prefix **an** at the end: **Sehen Sie sich das an.** You use it to politely ask someone to view or inspect something (a film, photos, a section of a document, etc.).
target_language_example: Sehen Sie sich bitte die Bilder an.
native_language_example: Please take a look at the pictures.

additional_notes: Used with a "dass"-clause to state what someone observes or understands. It can refer to something visually evident ("Everyone can see that …") or to realizing something from the situation ("Tom could see that …"). In the future ("Du wirst sehen, dass …"), it often means "you’ll see / you’ll find that …".
target_language_example: Jeder kann sehen, dass es Lippenstift ist.
native_language_example: Everyone can see that it’s lipstick.

meaning: to see/check whether; to find out if.
additional_notes: Used when you want to check something or find out whether something is true. It’s often used with verbs like „(ich will) sehen“ / „(wir wollten) sehen“ and followed by an „ob“-clause (a yes/no question in indirect form): „… ob er kommt“, „… ob das stimmt“. Common in the fixed phrase „Mal sehen, ob …“ = “Let’s see if …”.
target_language_example: Ich will nur sehen, ob er mich wirklich liebt.
native_language_example: I just want to see whether he really loves me.

meaning: to see what … / to find out what …
additional_notes: Used when you want to look at or discover information about something. It’s typically followed by a subordinate clause introduced by **was** (“what”), so you usually write a **comma** before **was** and the verb often goes to the **end** of the clause: *Ich wollte sehen, was passieren würde.*
target_language_example: Wir werden sehen, was morgen passiert.
native_language_example: We’ll see what happens tomorrow.

meaning: to see how (something turns out / happens).
additional_notes: Common with verbs like wollen/werden: "Ich will sehen, wie …" / "Wir werden sehen, wie …". It introduces an indirect question or subordinate clause with "wie" (“how”), so you typically write a comma before "wie" when it starts that clause.
target_language_example: Wir werden sehen, wie alles läuft.
native_language_example: We’ll see how everything goes.

additional_notes: Used when you want to know or find out the place/location of something (often with a clause: „sehen, wo … ist/war/endete“). Can also mean to make out visually where something is or where something ends.
target_language_example: Komm, wir gehen raus und sehen, wo der Bus hält.
native_language_example: Come on, let’s go outside and see where the bus stops.

additional_notes: Formal address (Sie). Used as a polite command (Sehen Sie sich das an. = “Take a look at that.”) or as a question to check understanding (Sehen Sie den Unterschied? = “Do you see the difference?”). It can also appear parenthetically as a discourse marker meaning “you see,” when explaining something (…, sehen Sie, …).
target_language_example: Sehen Sie, was ich meine?
native_language_example: Do you see what I mean?

additional_notes: This is the formal command form (to one person) of the reflexive verb with “sich”: usually **sich ansehen** (“to look at / view”) as in **Sehen Sie sich das an.** and **sich umsehen** (“to look around”) as in **Sehen Sie sich in Ruhe um!**. It’s often used with separable parts like **… an** or **… um** at the end of the sentence.
target_language_example: Sehen Sie sich bitte diese Fotos an.
native_language_example: Please take a look at these photos.

meaning: to look like; to resemble; to appear to be.
additional_notes: Used to compare appearance to something/someone: "X sieht aus wie Y" (X looks like Y). It can also describe someone’s apparent state: "Du siehst aus wie jemand, der Hilfe braucht" (You look like someone who needs help). Conjugate "sehen" to match the subject: ich sehe aus, du siehst aus, er/sie/es sieht aus, wir sehen aus, ihr seht aus, sie/Sie sehen aus. "wie" is followed by a noun/pronoun or a clause.
target_language_example: Sie sehen aus wie jemand, der Hilfe braucht.
native_language_example: You look like someone who needs help.

meaning: "see each other" (in Wir sehen uns…); also "see us" (in Sie sehen uns…).
additional_notes: Most commonly used as part of the goodbye phrase **Wir sehen uns …** meaning “See you … / We’ll see each other …” with a time word like **bald** (soon), **nachher** (later), **morgen** (tomorrow), **wieder** (again). In other subjects (e.g., **Sie sehen uns**), it can simply mean “They/You see us.”
target_language_example: Okay, wir sehen uns morgen!
native_language_example: Okay, see you tomorrow!

meaning: "we’ll see each other" / "see you"; also "shall we take a look…?" (with a separable verb).
additional_notes: From "wir sehen uns" = "we see each other". Common for arranging a meeting or saying goodbye: "Dann sehen wir uns …" / "Sehen wir uns später?". In questions it often starts a separable verb with a reflexive pronoun, e.g. "Sehen wir uns das an?" (ansehen = to look at) or "Zuerst sehen wir uns um" (sich umsehen = to look around).
target_language_example: Alles klar, dann sehen wir uns morgen um zehn.
native_language_example: All right, then I’ll see you tomorrow at ten.

meaning: longs for; yearns for; misses (someone/something deeply).
additional_notes: From the reflexive verb phrase „sich nach etwas/jemandem sehnen“. It expresses a strong emotional desire or longing. Used with „nach“ + dative: „Sie sehnt sich nach Liebe.“ / „Tom sehnt sich nach dir.“ (dir = dative).
target_language_example: Jeder Mensch sehnt sich nach Liebe.
native_language_example: Every person longs for love.

additional_notes: A repeated intensifier used to strongly emphasize an adjective/adverb (similar to “really, really” in English). It’s common in spoken German and informal writing; you can repeat it even more times for extra emphasis ("sehr, sehr, sehr"). In formal writing you’d more often use words like "sehr" once or "äußerst"/"extrem".
target_language_example: Ich bin sehr, sehr müde.
native_language_example: I’m very, very tired.

additional_notes: "Sehr" intensifies the adjective "alt" (old). Common for people, buildings, cities, objects, etc. With "schon" (already), it often means something feels outdated or has been around a long time: "Mein Handy ist schon sehr alt."
