additional_notes: Often used with **machen**: **seinen Abschluss machen** = “to graduate” / “to get one’s degree” (from school, university, etc.). With **von/an** you can mention the institution: **sein Abschluss von der Universität** / **sein Abschluss an einer Universität**.
target_language_example: Er hat letztes Jahr seinen Abschluss an der Universität gemacht.
native_language_example: He graduated from the university last year.

meaning: 'his parents' (often in the dative: 'to/for his parents').
additional_notes: „seinen Eltern“ is the plural form of „seine Eltern“ (= his parents). The -n often appears because it’s commonly used in the dative case (e.g., „mit seinen Eltern“, „es seinen Eltern sagen“). Depending on the verb/preposition, it can also be accusative (e.g., „seinen Eltern besuchen“ = to visit his parents). For other possessors: „ihren Eltern“ (her/their parents), „meinen Eltern“ (my parents), „deinen Eltern“ (your parents).
target_language_example: Ich telefoniere jeden Sonntag mit seinen Eltern.
native_language_example: I talk on the phone with his parents every Sunday.

meaning: his friends (dative plural: to/for/with his friends).
additional_notes: "Seinen" is the masculine/neuter possessive pronoun "his" in the dative plural, and "Freunden" is the dative plural of "Freund". You often see this after dative prepositions (e.g., "bei seinen Freunden" = at his friends’ place/with his friends) or with verbs that take an indirect object (e.g., "seinen Freunden helfen" = help his friends).
target_language_example: Er hat seinen Freunden ein Geschenk gekauft.
native_language_example: He bought his friends a present.

meaning: “his dog” (accusative: his dog as the object).
additional_notes: “Seinen” is the masculine accusative form of “sein” (his). You use “seinen Hund” when the dog is what someone has, brings, feeds, names, looks for, ties up, etc. In the nominative (subject) it’s “sein Hund” (e.g., “Sein Hund ist süß.”).
target_language_example: Er sucht seinen Hund im Park.
native_language_example: He’s looking for his dog in the park.

meaning: "his hat"; in the expression "(vor …) seinen Hut ziehen": to take off your hat (to …) / to show respect.
additional_notes: Most commonly this is a straightforward possessive noun phrase: "sein" (his) + "Hut" (hat). In "seinen Hut ziehen" it’s an idiom meaning to express admiration or respect (often with "vor" + dative: "vor jemandem/etwas").
target_language_example: Vor deiner Leistung zieht jedermann seinen Hut.
native_language_example: Everyone takes their hat off to your achievement.

meaning: "his coffee" (as the direct object of a verb).
additional_notes: Used when referring to a male person’s coffee as the object in a sentence. It’s the accusative form of the masculine noun Kaffee: sein Kaffee (nominative/subject) → seinen Kaffee (accusative/direct object). Common with verbs like trinken (to drink), mögen (to like), in etwas geben (to add/put into), and austrinken (to finish). Often paired with descriptors like schwarz (black, no milk) and ohne Zucker (without sugar).
target_language_example: Er trinkt seinen Kaffee immer schwarz.
native_language_example: He always drinks his coffee black.

additional_notes: Used when 'his children' is in the dative case, often after common patterns like: jemandem etwas geben (Er gab seinen Kindern …), zu + Dativ (streng zu seinen Kindern), and mit + Dativ (mit seinen Kindern). The base form is seine Kinder (accusative/nom.), but it becomes seinen Kindern in the dative.
target_language_example: Er liest seinen Kindern jeden Abend eine Geschichte vor.
native_language_example: He reads his children a story every evening.

meaning: his suitcase (accusative: the suitcase is the object).
additional_notes: "Seinen" is the masculine accusative form of "sein" (his). You use it when "Koffer" is the direct object: jemanden bitten, seinen Koffer zu tragen (to carry his suitcase); seinen Koffer abstellen (to set/put it down); seinen Koffer auf das Bett stellen (to put it onto the bed); seinen Koffer auspacken (to unpack it).
target_language_example: Er trägt seinen Koffer zum Auto.
native_language_example: He carries his suitcase to the car.

meaning: his head; (in set phrases) his life.
additional_notes: Often literally (body part): e.g., „den Kopf schütteln“ = to shake your head. In idioms it can mean someone’s life: „jemanden den Kopf kosten“ = to cost someone his life; „seinen Kopf retten“ = to save his life. In a bounty/hunt context: „eine Belohnung für seinen Kopf“ = a reward/bounty for capturing or killing him.
target_language_example: Sie schüttelte seinen Kopf nicht, sondern ihren eigenen.
native_language_example: She didn’t shake his head, but her own.

meaning: one’s living; one’s livelihood (money to live on).
additional_notes: Most commonly used with **verdienen**: **seinen Lebensunterhalt verdienen** = “to earn a living.” Often followed by **mit + Dativ** to say how you earn it: **seinen Lebensunterhalt mit etwas verdienen** (e.g., *mit Singen*). The possessive changes with the person/grammar (**meinen/deinen/seinen/ihren/unseren/euren/ihren Lebensunterhalt**).
target_language_example: Er verdient seinen Lebensunterhalt mit Singen.
native_language_example: He earns his living by singing.

additional_notes: "seinen" is the masculine accusative possessive determiner for "sein" (his). You often see it after verbs that take a direct object, especially with actions you do to/with a coat: anziehen (put on), ausziehen (take off), aufhängen (hang up), zuknöpfen (button up). The noun is "der Mantel" (coat).
target_language_example: Er hat seinen Mantel vergessen.
native_language_example: He forgot his coat.

additional_notes: “Seinen” is the masculine accusative form of “sein” (“his”). You use “seinen Namen” when “name” is the direct object (e.g., write/know/remember/say his name). Common patterns: „seinen Namen schreiben“, „seinen Namen kennen“, „sich an seinen Namen erinnern“, „auf seinen Namen kommen“ (= to remember/think of his name).
target_language_example: Ich kann mir seinen Namen nicht merken.
native_language_example: I can't remember his name.

meaning: his place / his seat; (figuratively) his place/role.
additional_notes: Literally “his place” (sein + Platz). Commonly refers to a physical spot or seat (jemandem seinen Platz überlassen = to give someone your seat; etwas an seinen Platz stellen = to put something back where it belongs). Can also be figurative for someone’s role/standing (seinen Platz im Volk verdienen = to earn one’s place among the people). The possessive changes with gender/case (z.B. seinen/ihren/meinen Platz).
target_language_example: Tom überließ mir seinen Platz und setzte sich näher an den Ausgang.
native_language_example: Tom gave me his seat and sat closer to the exit.

meaning: his umbrella (masculine accusative; used as the direct object, e.g., the thing being lost/forgotten/opened, etc.).
additional_notes: "seinen" is the masculine accusative form of "sein" (his). "Regenschirm" is masculine (der Regenschirm). Use it when the umbrella is the direct object: *seinen Regenschirm verlieren/vergessen/öffnen/liegenlassen*. It changes with case: *sein Regenschirm* (nom.), *seinen Regenschirm* (acc.), *seinem Regenschirm* (dat.). The possessor can also change: *meinen/deinen/ihren Regenschirm*, etc.
target_language_example: Tom hat seinen Regenschirm im Bus vergessen.
native_language_example: Tom forgot his umbrella on the bus.

additional_notes: Used when a male person owns the umbrella and it is the direct object of the sentence (after many verbs, e.g., haben, wiederhaben, ausleihen). The possessive pronoun changes with case: der Schirm (nom.) → seinen Schirm (acc.).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte seinen Schirm mitnehmen?
native_language_example: Can you please take his umbrella with you?

meaning: his son (accusative: as the direct object).
additional_notes: Used when “his son” is the direct object of the verb (e.g., sehen, nennen, verlieren, beschützen). The possessive pronoun changes with case and gender: nominative *sein Sohn*, accusative *seinen Sohn*, dative *seinem Sohn*. *sein* can mean “his” (or “its” for things).
target_language_example: Er besucht seinen Sohn jedes Wochenende.
native_language_example: He visits his son every weekend.

additional_notes: Used when “his father” is the direct object of the verb (e.g., sehen, besuchen, vertreten). It’s the accusative form of "sein Vater"; the possessive pronoun changes with case: nominative "sein Vater" (his father), accusative "seinen Vater" (his father), dative "seinem Vater" (to/for his father).
target_language_example: Er besucht seinen Vater am Wochenende.
native_language_example: He visits his father on the weekend.

additional_notes: "Wagen" is a common word for “car/vehicle” (similar to "Auto"). "Seinen" is the masculine accusative form of "sein" (“his”) and is used when the car is the direct object (e.g., "Er parkt seinen Wagen" = “He parks his car”).
target_language_example: Er hat seinen Wagen vor dem Haus geparkt.
native_language_example: He parked his car in front of the house.

meaning: “his car and drove …” (a sentence fragment: someone drove away/left by car).
additional_notes: This isn’t a fixed phrase; it’s usually part of a longer sentence like: „Er stieg in seinen Wagen und fuhr los.“ (= He got into his car and drove off.) „seinen Wagen“ is accusative (masculine: der Wagen → seinen Wagen) and often means “his car.”
target_language_example: Er stieg in seinen Wagen und fuhr los.
native_language_example: He got into his car and drove off.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "verpassen" (to miss) plus a possessive pronoun (meinen/deinen/seinen/ihren/unseren/euren/Ihren) and an object like "Zug". Often appears in the Perfekt tense: "Ich habe meinen Zug verpasst." You can add time words like "gerade (eben)" (just now) or "soeben" (just now).
target_language_example: Tom hat gerade eben seinen Zug verpasst und muss auf den nächsten warten.
native_language_example: Tom just missed his train and has to wait for the next one.

meaning: "his own" (emphasizing that it belongs to him personally).
additional_notes: Used to stress that something is specifically his, not someone else’s. It changes with gender/case: z.B. „sein eigener Sohn“ (nom.), „seinen eigenen Sohn“ (acc.), „seinem eigenen Sohn“ (dat.); also „seine eigene …“ (fem.) / „sein eigenes …“ (neut.). Often used with family, name, mistakes, way, things, etc.
target_language_example: Er will seinen eigenen Schlüssel haben.
native_language_example: He wants to have his own key.

meaning: 'his work' / 'his job' (in dative or genitive form).
additional_notes: “seiner” is the masculine/neuter dative or genitive form of “sein” (his). “Arbeit” is feminine, so it becomes “Arbeit” with the ending shown by “seiner.” You often see it after certain prepositions (e.g., “außer” + dative: “außer seiner Arbeit”) or with adjectives/expressions that take the genitive (e.g., “(etwas) überdrüssig sein” + genitive: “seiner Arbeit überdrüssig”).
target_language_example: Außer seiner Arbeit hat er kaum Zeit für Freunde.
native_language_example: Besides his work, he hardly has time for friends.

additional_notes: “seiner” is the masculine/neuter form of “sein-” (“his”), and it changes depending on case. You often see “seiner Familie” in the dative after certain prepositions (e.g., mit seiner Familie = with his family; von seiner Familie = from his family; bei seiner Familie = at/with his family) or as an indirect object (e.g., seiner Familie Geld schicken = to send his family money). It can also appear in the genitive to mean “of his family,” though that’s less common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Er hat seiner Familie sofort geschrieben.
native_language_example: He wrote to his family right away.

meaning: to/from/with his wife (his wife, in the dative case).
additional_notes: "Seiner" is the dative form of "sein" (his) with the feminine noun "Frau" (wife). You’ll see it (1) with an indirect object: "Er gab seiner Frau …" and (2) after dative prepositions like "gegenüber", "vor", and "von" (as in the examples). The exact English translation depends on the verb or preposition (e.g., "to his wife", "from his wife", "in front of his wife").
target_language_example: Ich habe seiner Frau zum Geburtstag Blumen gekauft.
native_language_example: I bought flowers for his wife for her birthday.

meaning: to his girlfriend / with his girlfriend (dative: “his girlfriend”).
additional_notes: “Seiner Freundin” is the dative form of “seine Freundin” (“his girlfriend”). It’s used after certain prepositions (e.g., mit = with) and with verbs that take an indirect object in the dative (e.g., jemandem schreiben = to write to someone, jemandem einen Antrag machen = to propose to someone). Note: “Freundin” can mean “girlfriend” or “(female) friend” depending on context; here it clearly means “girlfriend.”
target_language_example: Er hat mit seiner Freundin telefoniert.
native_language_example: He talked on the phone with his girlfriend.

additional_notes:
"Seiner" is the masculine/neuter possessive form of "sein" (= his). With "Mutter" (feminine), you commonly see:
- dative: "seiner Mutter" = "to/for his mother" (e.g., "Er schrieb seiner Mutter einen Brief.")
- genitive: "seiner Mutter" = "of his mother" (e.g., "ein Bild seiner Mutter", "der Platz seiner Mutter").
Which meaning it has depends on the verb or noun it goes with.
target_language_example: Ich habe seiner Mutter gestern Blumen gegeben.
native_language_example: I gave his mother flowers yesterday.

additional_notes: This is the genitive case of *seine Rede* (“his speech”). It’s common after prepositions like **während** (“during”) and **nach** (“after”): *während seiner Rede*, *nach seiner Rede*. You may also see **in seiner Rede** (“in his speech”), where *in* takes the dative, so it’s not genitive.
target_language_example: Nach seiner Rede klatschten alle begeistert.
native_language_example: After his speech, everyone applauded enthusiastically.

additional_notes: "seiner" is the possessive pronoun “his,” declined to match the feminine noun "die Tasche" (dative/genitive feminine singular). You’ll often see it with prepositions like "in" (+ dative for location): "in seiner Tasche" = “in his pocket/bag.” "Tasche" can mean a bag (handbag, backpack pocket, etc.) and sometimes “pocket,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Ich habe meinen Schlüssel in seiner Tasche gefunden.
native_language_example: I found my key in his pocket/bag.

meaning: “his daughter” (in the dative case: “to/for/with his daughter”).
additional_notes: "Seiner" is the dative form of "sein" (his) for feminine nouns like "die Tochter". You use "seiner Tochter" after many verbs that take an indirect object (e.g., "jemandem etwas kaufen/schicken") and after dative prepositions like "mit". It can mean "to his daughter," "for his daughter," or "with his daughter," depending on the verb/preposition.
target_language_example: Er hat seiner Tochter zum Geburtstag ein Buch geschenkt.
native_language_example: He gave his daughter a book for her birthday.

additional_notes: This is the genitive case of "seine Unschuld" (his innocence). It’s often used after nouns (e.g., "Beweise seiner Unschuld" = evidence of his innocence) or with certain expressions like "sich seiner Unschuld bewusst sein" (to be aware of one’s innocence). It can also mean "of one’s innocence" depending on context (not only literally "his").
target_language_example: Es gibt keine Beweise seiner Unschuld.
native_language_example: There is no evidence of his innocence.

meaning: “of his life” (genitive: belonging/relating to his life).
additional_notes: Used with nouns to describe a part of someone’s life or something connected to their life. Common patterns: „zu Anfang seines Lebens“ (at the beginning of his life), „unter Einsatz seines Lebens“ (risking his life), „die Liebe seines Lebens“ (the love of his life). Changes with gender/number: „ihres Lebens“ (of her life), „deines Lebens“ (of your life), etc.
target_language_example: Das war der wichtigste Tag seines Lebens.
native_language_example: That was the most important day of his life.

additional_notes: This is the genitive form of „sein Vater“ (masculine). It shows possession or a relationship: „der Ruhm seines Vaters“ = “his father’s fame”, „der Tod seines Vaters“ = “his father’s death”. In everyday spoken German, people often use „von seinem Vater“ instead of the genitive, but the genitive is common in writing and more formal speech.
target_language_example: Er wohnt im Haus seines Vaters.
native_language_example: He lives in his father’s house.

additional_notes: "seines" is the genitive form of "sein" (his). "Wagen" means “car/vehicle” in many contexts. This phrase is used to show possession after another noun (e.g., "die Motorhaube seines Wagens" = “the hood of his car”).
target_language_example: Die Farbe seines Wagens ist blau.
native_language_example: The color of his car is blue.

meaning: for years; for many years (since years ago).
additional_notes: Used with the present tense (or present perfect) to say something started years ago and is still true now: „Ich kenne sie seit Jahren.“ In negatives it often means you haven’t done something for years up to now: „Ich war seit Jahren nicht mehr hier.“
target_language_example: Wir warten seit Jahren auf eine Lösung.
native_language_example: We’ve been waiting for a solution for years.

additional_notes: Used with the present tense to say something started months ago and is still true now (Ich warte seit Monaten.). With a negative, it often means you have not done/seen something for months (Ich habe ihn seit Monaten nicht gesehen.). Emphasizes a long ongoing period.
target_language_example: Ich suche seit Monaten einen neuen Job.
native_language_example: I’ve been looking for a new job for months.

additional_notes: Used with a noun phrase in the dative (dem/der/den) to mark a starting point in time or an event: seit dem letzten Sonntag, seit dem Umzug, seit dem Skandal. Often implies the action/state continues up to now. At the start of a sentence, it can come first: „Seit dem Umzug …“. Don’t confuse with „seitdem“ (one word), which means “since then” and is used without a noun (e.g., „Seitdem gehe ich nicht mehr hin.“).
target_language_example: Seit dem Unfall habe ich weniger Zeit.
native_language_example: Since the accident, I have less time.

additional_notes: Used with **seit** (“since”) to say when something started and is still true now. Often you’ll see it expanded as **seit drei Uhr** (“since three o’clock”) or with a time unit: **seit drei Jahren** (“for three years / since three years ago”). **Seit** is followed by the dative (e.g., **seit dem Montag**).
target_language_example: Ich warte seit drei Uhr.
native_language_example: I’ve been waiting since three o’clock.

meaning: for three years; since three years ago (continuing until now).
additional_notes: Use **seit + time period** to say something started in the past and is still true now. It’s common with the present tense in German: *Ich wohne seit drei Jahren hier.* You can swap in other durations: *seit zwei Wochen, seit einem Monat, seit vielen Jahren*.
target_language_example: Ich arbeite seit drei Jahren in Berlin.
native_language_example: I’ve been working in Berlin for three years.

meaning: "for three years in" (from three years ago until now, in a place).
additional_notes: Used to say someone has been in a location for a period of time up to the present. German often uses the present tense with "seit": e.g., "Ich wohne/arbeite/bin seit drei Jahren in …". Replace the number/time unit as needed: "seit zwei Wochen in", "seit fünf Monaten in".
target_language_example: Ich wohne seit drei Jahren in Hamburg.
native_language_example: I've been living in Hamburg for three years.

meaning: for three months; since three months ago.
additional_notes: Used with the present tense to say an action/state started three months ago and is still true now (duration up to the present). It can also answer “Seit wann?” (“Since when?”) and often comes at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis.
target_language_example: Ich arbeite seit drei Monaten hier.
native_language_example: I’ve been working here for three months.

meaning: for three days (since three days ago; still ongoing).
additional_notes: Used with actions or states that started three days ago and continue up to now. Typically used with the present tense in German (e.g., „Wir sind seit drei Tagen hier.“). For completed past events, German usually uses „vor drei Tagen“ (three days ago) instead.
target_language_example: Ich bin seit drei Tagen krank.
native_language_example: I’ve been sick for three days.

meaning: for three weeks; since three weeks ago.
additional_notes: Used with the present tense to describe something that started in the past and is still true now (duration up to the present). You can swap in other time periods: seit zwei Tagen, seit einem Jahr. Word order is flexible: Er ist seit drei Wochen krank / Seit drei Wochen ist er krank.
target_language_example: Ich lerne seit drei Wochen Deutsch.
native_language_example: I’ve been learning German for three weeks.

meaning: for a month; since a month ago.
additional_notes: Used with the present tense to say something started one month ago and is still true/ongoing now ("Seit einem Monat wohne ich hier."). With the simple past (Präteritum) it can describe something that was ongoing at that time ("Sie waren mir seit einem Monat auf der Spur.").
target_language_example: Seit einem Monat lerne ich Deutsch.
native_language_example: I’ve been learning German for a month.

additional_notes: Used to say how long something has been happening, with a feminine noun in the dative case ("einer" = dative feminine of "eine"). Common with time expressions: "seit einer Woche" (for a week), "seit einer Stunde" (for an hour). For masculine/neuter you use "seit einem" (e.g., "seit einem Jahr").
target_language_example: Ich warte seit einer Stunde auf den Bus.
native_language_example: I’ve been waiting for the bus for an hour.

meaning: for an hour; for the past hour (since an hour ago).
additional_notes: Used with **seit** + **dative** to say something started in the past and is **still happening now**. Common with the present tense in German: *Wir warten seit einer Stunde.* (= We’ve been waiting for an hour.)
target_language_example: Der Bus ist seit einer Stunde zu spät.
native_language_example: The bus has been late for an hour.

meaning: for a week; since a week ago (up to now).
additional_notes: Used with „seit“ + dative to say something started one week ago and is still true now. Often used with the present tense in German (English often uses present perfect): „Ich bin seit einer Woche krank.“ = “I’ve been sick for a week.”
target_language_example: Ich warte seit einer Woche auf deine Antwort.
native_language_example: I’ve been waiting for your reply for a week.

meaning: sick for a week; has been sick for a week.
additional_notes: Uses **seit** (“since”) + a time period to show something started in the past and is still true now. German often uses the **present tense** here: *Sie ist seit einer Woche krank.* In English you usually say “has been sick for a week.” You can also add location/position: *seit einer Woche krank im Bett liegen* = “to have been sick in bed for a week.”
target_language_example: Ich bin seit einer Woche krank und bleibe heute zu Hause.
native_language_example: I’ve been sick for a week and I’m staying home today.

meaning: for some time (now); for quite a while.
additional_notes: Used with "seit" to say that something started in the past and is still true up to now. In German this often goes with the present tense (or present perfect), where English might use "have been"/"has been" + duration: "Seit einiger Zeit habe ich Probleme" = "I’ve been having problems for a while."
target_language_example: Seit einiger Zeit arbeite ich jeden Tag länger.
native_language_example: I’ve been working longer every day for quite a while now.

additional_notes: Used with the present tense to describe something that started yesterday and is still true now (a continuing situation). You can also use it with the simple past/perfect when talking about what has happened in that time period. Similar patterns: seit heute, seit letzter Woche, seit 2020.
target_language_example: Ich habe seit gestern Kopfschmerzen.
native_language_example: I’ve had a headache since yesterday.

additional_notes: Used with an action/state that started today and is still true now (often with present tense): „Ich bin seit heute hier.“ It can also be used alone as a short answer to mean “Since today.”
target_language_example: Ich habe seit heute ein neues Handy.
native_language_example: As of today, I have a new phone.

meaning: since this morning (from this morning until now).
additional_notes: Used with **seit** + a point in time to say when something started and that it continues up to now. Often used with the present tense in German (e.g., *Er arbeitet seit heute Morgen.*), even though English typically uses the present perfect (“has been working since this morning”).
target_language_example: Ich warte seit heute Morgen auf deinen Anruf.
native_language_example: I’ve been waiting for your call since this morning.

meaning: for a long time (now); for a long time already.
additional_notes: Used with the present perfect or present tense to say an action/state started in the past and continues up to now. Often appears as "schon seit langem" (= for a long time already).
target_language_example: Wir wollen uns seit langem wiedersehen.
native_language_example: We’ve been wanting to see each other again for a long time.

meaning: since last (used with a time word).
additional_notes: Used with „seit“ to say something started in the past and is still true now. It’s followed by a time expression in the dative: „seit letztem Sonntag/Monat/Jahr/Mittwoch“. In writing and careful speech you’ll often also see „seit dem letzten …“ (same meaning).
target_language_example: Ich habe seit letztem Sommer keinen Urlaub gemacht.
native_language_example: I haven’t taken a vacation since last summer.

meaning: since last year (from last year until now).
additional_notes: Used with the present tense to describe something that started last year and is still true now. It refers to a starting point in time (last year). Word order is flexible: “Seit letztem Jahr wohnt er in …” or “Er wohnt seit letztem Jahr in …”.
target_language_example: Ich arbeite seit letztem Jahr bei dieser Firma.
native_language_example: I've been working at this company since last year.

meaning: for many years (since a long time ago).
additional_notes: Use with the present tense to say an action/state started in the past and is still true now: „Ich wohne hier seit vielen Jahren.“ = “I have lived here for many years.” It often answers “Seit wann?” (“Since when?”). Can also be used with a negative to show something hasn’t happened for a long time: „Ich habe sie seit vielen Jahren nicht gesehen.“
target_language_example: Wir sind seit vielen Jahren befreundet.
native_language_example: We’ve been friends for many years.

additional_notes: Used to ask about the starting point of a situation or action. Often refers to something that began in the past and is still true now (e.g., with the present tense in German: „Seit wann bist du hier?“). It can also express surprise or skepticism, similar to “Since when do you…?” in English.
target_language_example: Seit wann arbeitest du hier?
native_language_example: Since when have you worked here?

meaning: 'Since when have you been…?' / 'How long have you been…?'.
additional_notes: Used to ask from what point in time something has been true (often with a tone of surprise or curiosity). It’s followed by an adjective or situation: seit wann bist du hier/da?, seit wann bist du verheiratet?, seit wann bist du so gut darin?
target_language_example: Seit wann bist du schon hier?
native_language_example: How long have you been here? / Since when have you been here?

meaning: "Since when is/has ...?" (asking from what point in time something has been true).
additional_notes: Use this to ask when a state started and is still the case now. It’s common with situations/conditions (hier, verheiratet, zusammen, wichtig, weg, krank). The answer is often a time expression with „seit“ (e.g., „seit gestern“, „seit 2020“) or „schon seit …“. Word order: „Seit wann ist + subject + …?“. In context it can also sound surprised/critical (“Since when do you care?”).
target_language_example: Seit wann ist der Laden geschlossen?
native_language_example: Since when has the shop been closed?

meaning: "since how many" (used to ask how long something has been true).
additional_notes: Used in questions with a time unit in the dative plural (e.g., seit wie vielen Jahren/Tagen/Wochen …?). Often the rest of the sentence is in the present tense: "Seit wie vielen Jahren wohnst du hier?" = "How many years have you lived here?"
target_language_example: Seit wie vielen Jahren lernst du Deutsch?
native_language_example: How many years have you been learning German?

meaning: "for how many years" / "since how many years ago" (asking how long something has been the case).
additional_notes: Used to ask about duration from a starting point in the past up to now. Common with the present tense in German: "Seit wie vielen Jahren bist du schon …?" = "How many years have you been …?" Also appears inside longer sentences (indirect questions): "wer weiß, seit wie vielen Jahren …" = "who knows how many years …".
target_language_example: Seit wie vielen Jahren wohnst du schon in Berlin?
native_language_example: How many years have you been living in Berlin?

meaning: “for how many days (now)?” / “how many days has it been since…?”
additional_notes: Used to ask about a duration starting in the past and continuing up to now. It’s commonly followed by a present-tense verb (e.g., „Seit wie vielen Tagen trägst du …?“) or appears with a perfect tense to ask how long since something last happened (e.g., „Seit wie vielen Tagen hast du nichts gegessen?“).
target_language_example: Seit wie vielen Tagen wartest du schon auf eine Antwort?
native_language_example: How many days have you been waiting for an answer?

meaning: for ten years; since ten years ago.
additional_notes: Used with the preposition „seit“ + a time period to say something started in the past and is still true now (often with present tense): „Ich lebe seit zehn Jahren hier.“ It can also appear in „zum ersten Mal seit zehn Jahren …“ = “for the first time in ten years …”.
target_language_example: Ich arbeite seit zehn Jahren bei dieser Firma.
native_language_example: I’ve been working at this company for ten years.

additional_notes: Used to say something started at 2:00 and is still true now. Often said more fully as "seit zwei Uhr" (since two o’clock). With other time units you add the unit: "seit zwei Tagen" (for two days / since two days ago), "seit zwei Jahren" (for two years).
target_language_example: Ich warte seit zwei Uhr auf dich.
native_language_example: I’ve been waiting for you since two o’clock.

meaning: for two years; since two years ago.
additional_notes: Uses **seit** (+ dative) to mark a starting point in the past that **continues up to now**. Very common with the **present tense in German** where English often uses the present perfect: *Ich kenne sie seit zwei Jahren* = “I’ve known her for two years.”
target_language_example: Ich wohne seit zwei Jahren in Berlin.
native_language_example: I've been living in Berlin for two years.

meaning: “for (the past) two months” / “since two months ago” (continuing until now).
additional_notes: Used with **seit** + a time period to say something started in the past and is still true now. In German you often use the present tense: *Ich wohne hier seit zwei Monaten* (literally “I live here since two months”).
target_language_example: Ich warte seit zwei Monaten auf eine Antwort.
native_language_example: I’ve been waiting for an answer for two months.

meaning: for over a year (up to now).
additional_notes: Used with the present tense (or present perfect) to say something started more than a year ago and is still true/ongoing now. Literally it’s like “since over a year,” but in natural English you usually say “for over a year.”
target_language_example: Ich wohne seit über einem Jahr in Berlin.
native_language_example: I’ve been living in Berlin for over a year.

meaning: for over a month; since more than a month ago.
additional_notes: Used with the present tense to say something started in the past and is still true now. After „seit“, German uses the dative case: „einem Monat“ (not *einen Monat*). Often answers the question „Seit wann?“ (Since when?/For how long?).
target_language_example: Ich lerne seit über einem Monat Deutsch.
native_language_example: I’ve been learning German for over a month.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a time clause that marks the starting point of something that began in the past and continues up to now. Very common with the present perfect (Perfekt) or simple past (Präteritum) in the since-clause: „Seit ich ihn kennengelernt habe, …“. Often paired with „schon“ for emphasis: „schon seit ich klein war“ (= ever since I was little).
target_language_example: Seit ich in Berlin wohne, fahre ich jeden Tag mit der U-Bahn.
native_language_example: Since I’ve been living in Berlin, I take the subway every day.

additional_notes: Usually used with an article and often a preposition: **am selben Tag** (= on the same day), **an demselben Tag** (more formal), **den selben Tag** (accusative, e.g. as an object). Note spelling: you may also see **denselben Tag** written as one word (especially in more formal/written German).
target_language_example: Wir sind am selben Tag angekommen.
native_language_example: We arrived on the same day.

additional_notes: Often used as advice or a reminder not to just follow others: „Du musst selbst denken!“ = “You have to think for yourself.” Related but different: „an dich selbst denken“ means “to think of yourself / look out for yourself” (i.e., don’t always put others first).
target_language_example: Glaub nicht alles im Internet – du musst selbst denken!
native_language_example: Don’t believe everything on the internet—you have to think for yourself!

additional_notes: Introduces a condition that does not change the main statement: something will happen or be true despite that condition. Often paired with the main clause stating what happens anyway (e.g., "..., selbst wenn ..."). Can also be used alone in short replies, meaning roughly "Even if (that’s true)...".
target_language_example: Ich helfe dir, selbst wenn ich wenig Zeit habe.
native_language_example: I’ll help you even if I have little time.

meaning: your own fault; you only have yourself to blame.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is responsible for a bad outcome because of their own actions or choices. Often sounds blaming, dismissive, or unsympathetic. In everyday speech, the shorter variant “selbst schuld” is more common than “selbst die Schuld”.
target_language_example: Wenn du deine Schlüssel liegen lässt, bist du selbst die Schuld.
native_language_example: If you leave your keys lying around, it’s your own fault.

additional_notes: Used to talk generally about unusual, unexplained, or unexpected events or situations. Often appears with verbs like passieren (to happen) or geschehen (to occur), and can sound a bit mysterious: Hier geschehen seltsame Dinge. Note: seltsam means “strange/weird,” Dinge means “things.”
target_language_example: Seit dem Stromausfall passieren hier seltsame Dinge.
native_language_example: Since the power outage, strange things have been happening here.

additional_notes: This is the declined form of "seltsamer Traum" ("a strange dream"). You’ll often see "seltsamen Traum" after verbs that take the accusative, e.g. "einen seltsamen Traum haben" (to have a strange dream) or "einen seltsamen Traum träumen" (to dream a strange dream).
target_language_example: Ich hatte letzte Nacht einen seltsamen Traum.
native_language_example: I had a strange dream last night.

additional_notes: Du-imperative of **sich setzen** (“to sit down”). Used when speaking to one person you address as **du** (friends, family, kids). Polite/formal version: **Setzen Sie sich (bitte).** You can add a place: **Setz dich hierhin/auf den Stuhl/zu mir.**
target_language_example: Setz dich bitte kurz hin und ruh dich aus.
native_language_example: Sit down for a moment and rest.

additional_notes: Imperative (du-form) of „sich auf etwas setzen“: telling one person to sit on a specific place/object. Often followed by a noun: „Setz dich auf den Stuhl!“ Also commonly shortened to „Setz dich!“ when the surface/place is obvious.
target_language_example: Setz dich auf den Stuhl, bitte.
native_language_example: Sit down on the chair, please.

additional_notes: Du-imperative of **(sich) hinsetzen**. Used when speaking to one person you address as **du** (friends, family, children). It can sound neutral, firm, or rude depending on tone/context. Polite/formal: **Setzen Sie sich hin.** Plural (to a group): **Setzt euch hin.**
target_language_example: Setz dich hin und entspann dich kurz.
native_language_example: Sit down and relax for a moment.

additional_notes: Polite/formal imperative of **sich setzen** (“to sit down”). Common when speaking to strangers, customers, or in formal situations. Often followed by a place: **Setzen Sie sich auf die Bank.** You may also hear **Setzen Sie sich (bitte) hin.** Note: in phrases like **sich mit jemandem in Verbindung setzen**, **setzen** means “to get in contact,” but that’s a different expression than “setzen Sie sich” on its own.
target_language_example: Setzen Sie sich bitte, ich komme gleich zu Ihnen.
native_language_example: Please have a seat; I’ll be with you in a moment.

additional_notes: Formal ("Sie") imperative used to tell someone to return to a seated position. Very often said as "Setzen Sie sich wieder hin!" ("hin" emphasizes the motion of sitting down). For friends/family you’d typically use "Setz dich wieder (hin)!".
target_language_example: Bitte setzen Sie sich wieder hin, wir fangen gleich an.
native_language_example: Please sit down again, we’ll start in a moment.

meaning: “Sit down!” (spoken to two or more people).
additional_notes: Imperative of **sich setzen** for **ihr** (plural “you”). Often used when inviting people to take a seat. You’ll also hear it softened with particles like **doch** (“go on”), **nur** (“just”), or **schon** (“go ahead/already”): *Setzt euch doch/nur/schon.* Note: in phrases like **sich in Verbindung setzen** (“to get in touch”), **setzen** has a different meaning than “sit.”
target_language_example: Kommt rein und setzt euch bitte.
native_language_example: Come in and please sit down.

additional_notes: Usually used with the separable verb **aufsetzen**: **Er setzte seinen Hut auf.** In the past tense, **setzte ... auf** means “put on” (literally “set ... on”). You’ll also see **wieder** (“again/back on”) when someone puts it on again: **Er setzte seinen Hut wieder auf.**
target_language_example: Er setzte seinen Hut auf, bevor er hinausging.
native_language_example: He put on his hat before he went outside.

additional_notes: Simple past of the separable, reflexive verb phrase „sich die Brille aufsetzen“ (present: „Er setzt sich die Brille auf.“). In main clauses the prefix „auf“ is separated and goes to the end. „sich“ is reflexive (dative here), and „die Brille“ is what’s being put on.
target_language_example: Tom setzte sich die Brille auf und fing an zu lesen.
native_language_example: Tom put on his glasses and started to read.

additional_notes: Past tense (simple past) of the reflexive verb **sich setzen** (“to sit down”). It describes the action of moving into a sitting position, often with a place: **sich auf den Boden/Stuhl setzen**. Contrast: **saß** = “was sitting” (already seated).
target_language_example: Er setzte sich neben mich und wartete.
native_language_example: He sat down next to me and waited.

additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of **sich an + Akkusativ setzen** (“to sit down at/next to”). Used when someone moves into a sitting position at a place like a table, desk, or piano: **Er setzte sich an den Tisch.** (movement → **an** + accusative).
target_language_example: Er setzte sich an den Tisch und begann zu essen.
native_language_example: He sat down at the table and started eating.

additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of "sich auf etw. setzen" = to sit down on something (a bench, bed, chair, etc.). It’s reflexive: "sich" changes with the person (ich setzte mich…, du setztest dich…, er/sie setzte sich…). Often used in storytelling and written German; in everyday speech you also hear Perfekt: "Er hat sich auf die Bank gesetzt."
target_language_example: Sie setzte sich auf den Stuhl und wartete.
native_language_example: She sat down on the chair and waited.

additional_notes: Past tense of the reflexive verb „sich setzen“ (to sit down). It’s used when someone moves into a sitting position next to someone/something. After „neben“ (next to), German typically uses the dative case for a fixed position: „neben mich/dir/ihn/sie …“.
target_language_example: Er setzte sich neben seine Freundin.
native_language_example: He sat down next to his girlfriend.

meaning: (used with certain reflexive verbs) to make sure/verify that …; (with certain impersonal constructions) it turns out that …
additional_notes:
This pattern appears when a reflexive/impersonal verb is followed by a subordinate clause introduced by „dass“.
Common examples:
- „sich vergewissern, dass …“ = to make sure/verify that …
- „(es) ergibt sich, dass …“ = it turns out that … / it becomes clear that …
Grammar note: In the „dass“-clause, the conjugated verb goes to the end (e.g., „… dass er ausgegangen war“).
target_language_example: Bitte vergewissern Sie sich, dass Ihr Sicherheitsgurt fest geschlossen ist.
native_language_example: Please make sure that your seat belt is securely fastened.

meaning: “(to do something) in order to …” after a reflexive verb.
additional_notes: Used to express purpose: a reflexive verb in the main clause + a comma + „um … zu“ + infinitive. The comma before „um“ is required. Example pattern: „Er bückte sich, um … zu …“ (= He bent down in order to …).
target_language_example: Tom bückte sich, um eine Münze aufzuheben.
native_language_example: Tom bent down in order to pick up a coin.

meaning: to make an effort; to try hard
additional_notes: A common reflexive phrase: *ich gebe mir Mühe, du gibst dir Mühe, er/sie gibt sich Mühe*. Often used with **bei** (for a task) or with an infinitive clause: *Ich gebe mir Mühe, pünktlich zu sein.*
target_language_example: Ich muss mich wirklich Mühe geben, jeden Tag Deutsch zu lernen.
native_language_example: I really have to make an effort to learn German every day.

additional_notes: Reflexive expression: sich Sorgen machen (um + accusative) = to worry about someone/something (e.g., Ich mache mir Sorgen um dich.). "sich Sorgen" is also used (often in subordinated clauses or infinitive constructions) and is understood from context.
target_language_example: Es hat keinen Sinn, sich Sorgen darum zu machen.
native_language_example: There’s no point in worrying about it.

additional_notes: Reflexive phrase; typically used with a dative reflexive pronoun (mir/dir/sich/uns/euch): Ich mache mir Sorgen. Often followed by "um" + accusative to specify what/who: sich Sorgen machen um die Kinder. Common as an imperative: Mach dir keine Sorgen!
target_language_example: Ich werde mich nicht um dich sorgen; ich will mir keine Sorgen machen.
native_language_example: I won’t worry about you; I don’t want to worry.

additional_notes: Reflexive phrase meaning that the subject is worried. Use the correct reflexive pronoun (ich mache mir Sorgen … / du machst dir Sorgen …), or use this verb phrase directly: „Ich sorge mich um …“. It is followed by „um“ + accusative: „sich Sorgen um + Akk.“. Closely related: „sich um etwas/jemanden sorgen“ (to take care of / to look after; context-dependent), while „sich Sorgen um“ clearly focuses on worrying.
target_language_example: Ich sorge mich um dich.
native_language_example: I’m worried about you.

meaning: to take your time; not rush.
additional_notes: Reflexive expression (ich lasse mir Zeit, du lässt dir Zeit, etc.). Often used as an encouragement or request: „Lass dir Zeit!“ = “Take your time.” Can also imply someone is being slow/delaying: „Er lässt sich Zeit.“ = “He’s taking his time / he’s in no hurry.”
target_language_example: Du kannst dich mit der Antwort ruhig noch etwas Zeit lassen; wir haben es nicht eilig.
native_language_example: You can take your time with the reply; we’re not in a hurry.

meaning: to take your time; to make time (for something).
additional_notes: Reflexive phrase used when you don’t want to hurry or when you deliberately set aside time for something. Commonly used with "für" + accusative: "Ich nehme mir Zeit für …" Also used as a polite suggestion or encouragement: "Nehmen Sie sich Zeit."
target_language_example: Ich möchte mir am Wochenende Zeit nehmen, um meine Familie zu besuchen.
native_language_example: I’d like to take time this weekend to visit my family.

meaning: to present/describe/register oneself as; as (in disguise/role).
additional_notes: Used with reflexive verbs to say what role or identity someone takes on. Common patterns: „sich als + Nomen verkleiden“ (to dress up as), „sich als + Nomen bezeichnen“ (to describe oneself as), „sich als + Nomen melden“ (to sign up/volunteer as). The noun after „als“ is usually without an article when it’s a role (e.g., „als Freiwilliger“, „als König“).
target_language_example: Sie hat sich als Lehrerin vorgestellt.
native_language_example: She introduced herself as a teacher.

meaning: to turn out to be true
additional_notes: Used when something (a prediction, rumor, statement, assumption) is later confirmed to be true. Pattern: „X erweist sich als wahr“ = “X turns out to be true.” Often used in past: „X hat sich als wahr erwiesen.“
target_language_example: Deine Prophezeiung hat sich als wahr erwiesen.
native_language_example: Your prophecy turned out to be true.

meaning: reflexive pronoun + „am“ (= an dem): used to indicate that something happens to oneself at/on a specific body part, or (less commonly) that one complains/acts at a specific place.
additional_notes:
Common patterns:
- Body part: *sich am Kopf kratzen* (scratch your head), *sich am Bein weh tun* (hurt your leg), *sich am Handgelenk verletzen* (injure your wrist).
- Place (with certain verbs like *sich beklagen*): *sich am Empfang beklagen* (complain at reception).
- Warming oneself: *sich am Feuer die Hände wärmen* (warm your hands by the fire).
Note: English often omits the reflexive idea; German typically requires *sich* with these verbs/phrases.
target_language_example: Roger rutschte auf dem Eis aus und tat sich am Bein weh.
native_language_example: Roger slipped on the ice and hurt his leg.

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression by itself. It appears with many reflexive verbs, usually with an accusative noun or pronoun after an, as in sich an jemanden wenden, sich an etwas halten, or sich an etwas gewöhnen. The full verb gives the exact meaning, but this pattern often shows the person or thing someone turns to, sticks to, or gets used to.
target_language_example: Es dauert oft eine Weile, sich an den neuen Job zu gewöhnen.
native_language_example: It often takes a while to get used to the new job.

meaning: “(to) oneself on/at the …” (reflexive + an + dative, with a feminine noun). Used in expressions like hurting yourself on something or being/doing something at a place.
additional_notes: This is a common pattern with many verbs that take **sich + an + dative**. It often expresses (1) injury/contact with something: **sich an der Hüfte verletzen** (hurt your hip), **sich an der Kante schneiden** (cut yourself on the edge), **sich an der heißen Suppe die Zunge verbrennen** (burn your tongue on hot soup); or (2) location/activity at a place: **sich an der Theke unterhalten** (chat at the counter). Here **der** is the dative feminine article (e.g., *die Kante → an der Kante*, *die Theke → an der Theke*, *die Hüfte → an der Hüfte*).
target_language_example: Ich habe gesehen, wie Tom sich an der Theke mit dir unterhalten hat.
native_language_example: I saw Tom chatting with you at the counter.

meaning: reflexive + “an” + accusative: “to / at / onto (someone/something)”—meaning depends on the verb.
additional_notes: “sich an + Akk.” is a common pattern used with many verbs. Typical meanings: • sich an etw. gewöhnen = to get used to something • sich an jdn./etw. wenden = to turn to / contact someone (often for help or information) • sich an etw. halten = to follow / stick to rules/laws • sich an etw. machen = to get to work on something • sich an etw. fassen = to touch / grab something. The noun after “die” is in the accusative (e.g., an die Gesetze, an die Öffentlichkeit).
target_language_example: Bitte halten Sie sich an die Regeln.
native_language_example: Please follow the rules.

meaning: reflexive pronoun + separable prefix “an-” appearing in split separable verbs (e.g., „sich anziehen“, „sich anschnallen“, „sich anfühlen“).
additional_notes:
„Sich an“ is usually not a standalone phrase; it’s the reflexive pronoun („sich“) plus the separated prefix „an“ placed at the end of the clause.

Common patterns:
- **sich anschnallen** = to buckle up: „Bitte schnallen Sie sich **an**.“
- **sich anziehen** = to get dressed: „Er zog sich **an**.“
- **es bietet sich an** = it’s a good idea / it suggests itself: „Es bietet sich **an**, dass …“
- **sich ankuscheln** = to snuggle up to: „Katzen kuscheln sich **an** …“
- **sich anstellen** = to line up: „Stellen Sie sich **an**.“
- **sich anfühlen** = to feel (like): „Wie fühlt es sich **an** …?“
target_language_example: Bitte schnallen Sie sich an.
native_language_example: Please buckle up.

additional_notes: Usually used in the perfect tense with a reflexive dative pronoun: „Ich habe es mir anders überlegt.“ = “I changed my mind about it.” The pronoun changes with the person (mir/dir/sich/uns/euch/sich). Often refers to a decision you made earlier and then reversed.
target_language_example: Er hat sich anders überlegt und kommt doch mit.
native_language_example: He changed his mind and is coming along after all.

meaning: reflexive pronoun + „auf“ (often + Akkusativ): a common pattern used with certain verbs to connect the action to what someone is preparing for, focusing on, or looking forward to.
additional_notes: „sich auf …“ is usually not a standalone phrase; it appears with specific reflexive verbs. Common examples: „sich vorbereiten auf“ (+Akk) = to prepare for, „sich freuen auf“ (+Akk) = to look forward to, „sich konzentrieren auf“ (+Akk) = to concentrate on. In other contexts, „auf“ can also mark location (often + Dativ), e.g. „Sie trafen sich auf der Straße“ (met on/in the street). The case depends on the governing verb/expression; with the ‘prepare/look forward/focus’ meanings it’s typically accusative.
target_language_example: Er freute sich auf ein Wiedersehen mit ihr.
native_language_example: He was looking forward to seeing her again.

meaning: (pattern) oneself on/onto the; also (with certain verbs) to/for the (masculine accusative noun).
additional_notes: This is not a standalone phrase but a common pattern: reflexive verb + „auf“ + accusative masculine article „den“. Often it’s physical position or movement onto something (e.g., „sich legen/setzen auf den …“ = to lie down/sit down on …). With some verbs it’s abstract: „sich auf den … vorbereiten“ = to prepare for …; „sich auf den … auswirken“ = to have an effect on … . The noun after „den“ is masculine and in the accusative case (e.g., „den Bauch“, „den Kampf“, „den Unterricht“).
target_language_example: Es ist gar nicht leicht, sich auf den Unterricht vorzubereiten.
native_language_example: It’s not easy to prepare for class.

meaning: onto one’s back / on one’s back
additional_notes: Used with reflexive verbs to describe changing position so that you end up lying on your back (e.g., sich legen, sich drehen). With verbs like (sich) klopfen, it can also mean patting yourself on the back (self-praise). The reflexive pronoun changes with the subject: ich lege mich…, du legst dich…, er/sie/es legt sich…, wir legen uns…, ihr legt euch…, sie/Sie legen sich….
target_language_example: Er legte sich auf den Rücken.
native_language_example: He lay down on his back.

meaning: to set off; to start one’s journey (to leave and go).
additional_notes: Reflexive expression; conjugates with the subject (ich mache mich, du machst dich, wir machen uns, etc.). Often followed by a destination using "nach" (cities/countries) or "zu" (people/places): "Wir machen uns auf den Weg nach Berlin / zu unseren Freunden." It highlights the moment of departure/setting out rather than the whole trip.
target_language_example: Wir müssen los; wir werden uns jetzt auf den Weg machen.
native_language_example: We have to go; we’re going to set off now.

meaning: “oneself … on the …” / “(to/for oneself) … on the …” (reflexive pronoun + “on the” with a feminine noun, typically dative for location).
additional_notes:
This isn’t a complete fixed phrase by itself—it's a common pattern made of two parts:
- **sich** is a reflexive pronoun used with many verbs (e.g., *sich waschen* = “to wash oneself”, *sich übergeben* = “to vomit”).
- **auf der** means **“on the”** with **feminine singular nouns** in the **dative** when describing location/position (*auf der Erde*, *auf der Motorhaube*, *auf der Rückbank*).
- Often contrasted with **auf die** (accusative) for movement/direction (*sich auf die Bank setzen* = “to sit down onto the bench”) vs. **auf der** (dative) for location (*auf der Bank sitzen* = “to be sitting on the bench”).
target_language_example: Tom briet sich auf der Motorhaube seines Wagens ein Ei.
native_language_example: Tom fried himself an egg on the hood of his car.

meaning: “(to) oneself onto/on the …” / “(to) oneself for the …” — reflexive pronoun + **auf die** (Accusative) used with many verbs to indicate movement onto something or orientation/focus toward something (with a feminine singular or plural noun).
additional_notes: **sich** is a reflexive pronoun whose form depends on the subject (e.g., *ich setze **mich***, *er setzt **sich***, *wir setzen **uns***). **auf die** is **auf + Accusative**, commonly used for **movement/direction** (e.g., sitting/lying down onto a surface) or **aiming/focusing toward** something. For a static location without movement, German often uses **auf + Dative** (e.g., *auf der Bank* = on the bench). The noun following **die** will be feminine singular (*die Bank*) or plural (*die Fingernägel*).
target_language_example: Tom und Maria setzten sich auf die Parkbank.
native_language_example: Tom and Maria sat down on the park bench.

meaning: A reflexive pattern meaning “to (rely/lean) on a …” or “to agree on a …,” depending on the verb used (sich + Verb + auf + Akkusativ: einen/eine/ein …).
additional_notes:
This is a productive pattern: **sich + Verb + auf + Akkusativ (einen/eine/ein …)**. The meaning comes from the verb:
- **sich auf etw. stützen** = to lean/rely on something (*auf einen Stock*)
- **sich auf etw. einigen** = to agree on something (*auf einen Preis*, *auf einen Termin*)
- Fixed expression: **sich auf einen Schlag ändern** = to change all at once
Article varies by gender in the accusative: **einen** (masc.), **eine** (fem.), **ein** (neut.).
target_language_example: Tom und Maria einigten sich auf einen Preis.
native_language_example: Tom and Maria agreed on a price.

meaning: "(to get) oneself out of the … / from the …" (used with a reflexive verb).
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase by itself: it’s a building block used with a reflexive verb (e.g., sich retten, sich befreien, sich lösen) plus a masculine/neuter noun in the dative after "aus" ("dem" = "the"). It expresses moving/escaping out of something: "sich aus dem + noun".
target_language_example: Er rettete sich aus dem brennenden Haus.
native_language_example: He saved himself from the burning house.

meaning: reflexive + bei = to do something (e.g., apologize/thank/complain) to/with someone.
additional_notes: Used with reflexive verbs that take "bei" to mark the person you direct the action toward. Common with: sich (bei jdm.) entschuldigen (apologize to), sich (bei jdm.) bedanken (thank), sich (bei jdm.) beschweren (complain to). The person is in the dative: bei Tom, bei jemandem, bei der Chefin. Word order in questions: "Hast du dich bei Tom entschuldigt?"
target_language_example: Ich finde, Sie sollten sich bei Tom entschuldigen.
native_language_example: I think you should apologize to Tom.

meaning: “oneself with/at me” → used with certain reflexive verbs to mark “to me / with me” as the person addressed (e.g., *sich bei jemandem entschuldigen* = “to apologize to someone”; *sich bei jemandem erkundigen* = “to inquire with someone / ask someone”).
additional_notes: *bei* + dative often means “at/with (someone)”. In combinations like *sich bei jemandem entschuldigen* and *sich bei jemandem erkundigen*, it identifies the person you apologize to or the person you ask. *mir* is the dative form of *ich* (“me”).
target_language_example: Ich möchte, dass Tom sich bei mir entschuldigt.
native_language_example: I want Tom to apologize to me.

additional_notes: Used with a reflexive verb plus **beim** (= **bei dem**) to express that something happens to someone during an activity. Typical pattern: **sich + Verb + beim + [nominalized verb/activity noun]** (e.g., *sich verletzen beim Tanzen* = to hurt oneself while dancing). Often used with verbs like **sich verletzen** (injure oneself), **sich übergeben** (vomit), **sich amüsieren** (have fun), **sich abwechseln** (take turns).
target_language_example: Sie verletzte sich beim Tanzen.
native_language_example: She hurt herself while dancing.

meaning: “oneself … it/that” in reflexive constructions: a reflexive pronoun (often dative) + “das” as the thing affected/obtained/remembered/arranged; sometimes “sich” is part of the verb and “das” is the subject (e.g., „Verbessert sich das …?“).
additional_notes: Common uses: (1) accidental harm/impact to a body part: „Er hat sich das Knie gestoßen.“ (= he banged his knee). (2) having something done for yourself: „Sie hat sich das Klavier stimmen lassen.“ (= she had the piano tuned). (3) getting/buying/ordering something for yourself: „Er hat sich das Auto gekauft.“ (4) memorizing/keeping something in mind: „sich das Gespräch merken“ (= to remember the conversation). Also note: in sentences like „Verbessert sich das Sehvermögen …?“ the „sich“ is inherent to the verb „sich verbessern“ (to improve), and „das“ is the grammatical subject, not an object.
target_language_example: Er hat sich das Knie am Stuhl gestoßen.
native_language_example: He banged his knee on the chair.

meaning: to break one’s leg (used with verbs like „brechen“).
additional_notes: Used with a reflexive pronoun (mir/dich/sich/uns/euch/sich) plus the body part in the accusative: „Ich habe mir **sich das Bein** …“ is not possible; correct is e.g. „Ich habe **mir das Bein** gebrochen.“ In third person you get the exact sequence „sich das Bein“: „Er/Sie hat **sich das Bein** gebrochen.“ This is the common German pattern for injuries to body parts.
target_language_example: Tom hat sich das Bein gebrochen.
native_language_example: Tom broke his leg.

additional_notes: Usually used in the perfect tense with a reflexive pronoun in the dative: „Ich habe mir das Bein gebrochen.“ (mir/dir/sich/uns/euch). You can swap „Bein“ with other body parts (e.g., „Arm“).
target_language_example: Er hat sich das Bein gebrochen und kann nicht laufen.
native_language_example: He broke his leg and can’t walk.

meaning: to (do something to) your hair; used to indicate an action affecting one’s own hair (literally “to oneself the hair”).
additional_notes: Common German pattern: reflexive pronoun (sich/mir/dir/uns/euch) + definite article + body part (das Haar) instead of a possessive (“my/your hair”). Used with many hair-related verbs, e.g. sich das Haar bürsten (brush your hair), sich das Haar waschen (wash your hair), sich das Haar färben (dye your hair), sich das Haar schneiden lassen (have your hair cut). Note: in a full sentence the reflexive pronoun changes with the subject (ich: mir, du: dir, er/sie: sich, etc.), but the dictionary form is “sich …”.
target_language_example: Maria schaute in den Spiegel, während sie sich das Haar bürstete.
native_language_example: Maria looked in the mirror while she brushed her hair.

meaning: “(to) oneself, (one’s) life” — used inside common expressions about someone’s life (usually with a verb).
additional_notes:
Not typically used alone; it appears with verbs, e.g.:
- „sich das Leben schwer machen“ = to make life difficult for yourself
- „sich das Leben leicht machen“ = to make life easy for yourself
- „sich das Leben nehmen“ = to take your own life (very sensitive/serious topic)
Grammar: „sich“ is the reflexive pronoun (myself/yourself/etc.) and changes with the person (mir/dir/sich/uns/euch/sich) in many full expressions.
target_language_example: Mach dir nicht so oft sich das Leben schwer.
native_language_example: Don’t make life so difficult for yourself so often.

meaning: to shave one’s beard / to let one’s beard grow (reflexive + dative construction).
additional_notes: Occurs with verbs like rasieren (to shave), abrasieren (to shave off), wachsen lassen (to let grow). The reflexive pronoun (mich/dich/sich/uns/euch/sich) marks the person, and the dative article (den Bart) is the thing affected. Typical patterns: „Er rasiert sich den Bart.“ / „Sie lässt sich den Bart wachsen.“
target_language_example: Tom rasiert sich den Bart.
native_language_example: Tom shaves his beard.

meaning: “one’s head” in a reflexive body-part construction (e.g., to shave/bump one’s head); also used in the idiom „sich den Kopf zerbrechen“ = “to rack your brains / puzzle something out”.
additional_notes: German often uses a reflexive pronoun + definite article with body parts: „Ich habe **mir den Kopf** gestoßen“ (literally “I bumped myself the head”). The pronoun is typically dative (mir/dir/sich/uns/euch). In „sich den Kopf zerbrechen“ the meaning is idiomatic: to think very hard about a problem.
target_language_example: Er hat sich den Kopf rasiert.
native_language_example: He shaved his head.

meaning: to be aware of the danger
additional_notes: Fixed pattern: „jemand ist sich (Genitiv) bewusst“ = someone is aware/conscious of something. Here: „sich der Gefahr bewusst (sein)“. Often used with modals (müssen/sollen): „Er muss sich der Gefahr bewusst sein.“ In spoken German, some speakers use a dative construction (e.g., „sich der Sache bewusst sein“ remains standard in careful writing).
target_language_example: Er muss sich der Gefahr bewusst sein, bevor er weitergeht.
native_language_example: He has to be aware of the danger before he goes on.

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression, but a common pattern with a reflexive pronoun before a feminine singular or plural noun. German often uses this with body parts, clothing, and personal items where English prefers a possessive: sich die Hände waschen = wash one's hands. It can also simply be part of a reflexive verb, as in sich die Speisekarte ansehen. The pronoun changes with the subject (mir/dir/sich/uns/euch/sich), and die changes with the noun (for example den/das with other nouns).
target_language_example: Sie wäscht sich die Hände vor dem Essen.
native_language_example: She washes her hands before eating.

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb **aufsetzen**: **sich die Brille aufsetzen**. In everyday speech you often hear it split: **Setz dir die Brille auf!** The pronoun is typically **dative** (mir/dir/sich): *Ich setze mir die Brille auf.*
target_language_example: Wenn du das Kleingedruckte lesen willst, solltest du dir zuerst **sich die Brille auf** setzen.
native_language_example: If you want to read the fine print, you should first put on your glasses.

meaning: “one’s hair” (used with a reflexive verb, e.g., to wash/dye one’s hair).
additional_notes: Common German pattern for body parts: use a reflexive pronoun + definite article (die) instead of a possessive. You typically use it with verbs like waschen (to wash) or färben (to dye): „Ich wasche mir die Haare.“ / „Sie hat sich die Haare gefärbt.“ The reflexive pronoun changes with the subject (ich mir, du dir, er/sie sich, wir uns, ihr euch, Sie sich).
target_language_example: Er hat sich die Haare braun gefärbt.
native_language_example: He dyed his hair brown.

meaning: (to) one’s hands (used with a reflexive verb: wash/rub/wipe your hands).
additional_notes: Common reflexive+dative pattern for body parts: the person is the indirect object (mir/dir/sich …) and the body part takes the definite article (die Hände), not a possessive (*meine Hände*) in most everyday sentences. Typical verbs: sich die Hände waschen/abwischen/reiben. Note: the base form is given as *sich*, but in a sentence it conjugates (mir/dir/sich/uns/euch/sich).
target_language_example: Tom vergaß, sich die Hände zu waschen.
native_language_example: Tom forgot to wash his hands.

meaning: “(to have) taken the trouble (to do something)” / “(to have) gone to the effort.”
additional_notes: Used with a reflexive pronoun (ich/du/er/sie/wir/ihr/Sie): *Ich habe mich die Mühe gemacht …*, *Hast du dich die Mühe gemacht …?* Often used to thank someone (*Danke, dass Sie sich die Mühe gemacht haben …*) or to complain that someone didn’t bother (*Niemand hat sich die Mühe gemacht zu fragen.*). Typically followed by **zu + infinitive** or a clause explaining what was done. Common in the perfect tense (*hat sich … gemacht* / *haben sich … gemacht*).
target_language_example: Er hat sich die Mühe gemacht, mich am Bahnhof zu verabschieden.
native_language_example: He took the trouble to see me off at the train station.

meaning: to make the effort; to take the trouble (to do something).
additional_notes: Used with a reflexive pronoun (ich mache mir, du machst dir, er/sie macht sich, wir machen uns, ihr macht euch, sie machen sich) and often followed by "zu" + infinitive: "sich die Mühe machen, etwas zu tun". Very common in negatives or requests: "Mach dir nicht die Mühe" (= don’t bother). Polite/formal enough for everyday use.
target_language_example: Könntest du bitte sich die Mühe machen, mir die Adresse zu schicken?
native_language_example: Could you please take the trouble to send me the address?

meaning: (as in „sich die Zähne putzen“) ‘(to) brush one’s teeth’ / literally ‘(to) brush oneself the teeth’.
additional_notes: Common German pattern: reflexive pronoun (mich/dich/sich/uns/euch/sich) + body part with the definite article (die Zähne), often with a dative pronoun (mir/dir/sich/uns/euch/sich): „Ich putze mir die Zähne.“ / „Er putzt sich die Zähne.“ In natural English you usually use a possessive: “brush my/your/his teeth.”
target_language_example: Er putzt sich die Zähne.
native_language_example: He brushes his teeth.

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression. Sich is a reflexive pronoun (himself/herself/itself/themselves, depending on the subject), and ein means "a/an." This combination often appears when someone does something for themselves, as in sich ein Eis kaufen = "to buy oneself an ice cream." But sometimes sich simply belongs to a reflexive verb, so the exact meaning depends on the whole sentence.
target_language_example: Er kauft sich ein neues Auto.
native_language_example: He's buying himself a new car.

meaning: to buy yourself a car; to buy a car for yourself.
additional_notes: Infinitive construction with the reflexive pronoun „sich“ to emphasize that the purchase is for one’s own benefit. Commonly used after verbs of intention/plan (e.g., „beabsichtigen“, „vorhaben“) or in purpose clauses with „um … zu“. In a main clause, German often uses a dative pronoun instead: „Ich kaufe mir ein Auto.“
target_language_example: Beabsichtigen Sie, sich ein Auto zu kaufen?
native_language_example: Do you intend to buy yourself a car?

meaning: to get yourself a glass (to drink), e.g. to order or pour yourself a glass (of something).
additional_notes: Used with a verb plus a reflexive dative pronoun (mir/dir/sich/uns/euch/sich): e.g. „sich ein Glas einschenken“ (pour yourself a glass) or „sich ein Glas bestellen“ (order yourself a glass). „ein Glas“ refers to a serving/quantity (a glass of something), not merely the physical object.
target_language_example: Tom bestellte sich ein Glas Apfelsinensaft und eine Tasse Kaffee.
native_language_example: Tom ordered himself a glass of orange juice and a cup of coffee.

additional_notes: Used with the verb „kaufen“ to mean buying something for yourself. „sich“ is a reflexive pronoun in the dative (mir/dir/sich/uns/euch/sich), and „ein neues“ changes to match the noun’s gender/case, e.g. „ein neues Handy“ (neuter), „eine neue Jacke“ (feminine), „einen neuen Mantel“ (masculine).
target_language_example: Er will sich ein neues Handy kaufen.
native_language_example: He wants to buy himself a new phone.

additional_notes: Pattern: **sich** (reflexive dative: “for yourself”) + **ein paar** (“a few”) + a noun, commonly used with verbs like **holen** (get), **nehmen** (take), **kaufen** (buy). In many sentences, **sich** changes form depending on the subject (e.g., *ich hole **mir** ein paar…*, *du holst **dir** ein paar…*).
target_language_example: Ich nehme mir ein paar Minuten.
native_language_example: I’ll take a few minutes for myself.

meaning: to get/make yourself a cup (of something, e.g. coffee/tea).
additional_notes: This is an incomplete phrase that’s typically followed by what the cup contains (e.g. "Kaffee", "Tee") and a verb like "machen" (make) or "holen" (get). "sich" is the reflexive pronoun and changes by person (mir/dir/sich/uns/euch/sich): e.g. "Ich mache mir eine Tasse Kaffee." The bare sequence "sich eine Tasse" is most naturally used together with an infinitive construction like "sich eine Tasse (Tee/Kaffee) machen/holen".
target_language_example: Ich gehe in die Küche, um mir sich eine Tasse Tee zu machen.
native_language_example: I’m going to the kitchen to make myself a cup of tea.

meaning: “(to) get/buy/find oneself a …” (do something for one’s own benefit).
additional_notes: Used with a reflexive dative pronoun (mir/dir/sich/uns/euch/sich) plus an accusative masculine noun: “sich einen + Nomen”. Often appears with verbs like “kaufen” (buy), “suchen” (look for), “nehmen” (take), “holen” (get). It emphasizes that the action is done for oneself: “Tom kauft sich einen Anzug” ≈ “Tom buys himself a suit” (not just “Tom buys a suit”).
target_language_example: Tom kauft sich einen Anzug.
native_language_example: Tom is buying himself a suit.

meaning: "to have decided" / "to have made up one’s mind".
additional_notes: Perfect tense of the reflexive verb **sich entscheiden** (haben + sich + entschieden). Often followed by **zu + infinitive** ("decided to...") or **für + Akkusativ** ("decided on/for...").
target_language_example: Sie hat sich entschieden, Tom zu heiraten.
native_language_example: She decided to marry Tom.

additional_notes: Uses the reflexive pronoun (mir/dir/sich/uns/euch/sich) to show it’s for yourself (or themselves). Often used with verbs like holen, machen, kaufen, bestellen: „Ich hole mir etwas zu essen.“ The „zu“ + infinitive („zu essen“) works like an adjective meaning “to eat” = “for eating”.
target_language_example: Ich hole mir schnell, um mich zu stärken, sich etwas zu essen.
native_language_example: I’ll quickly get myself something to eat to regain strength.

meaning: reflexive pronoun + „für“ (accusative), used in many common verb patterns to mean things like “be interested in,” “consider oneself,” “apologize for,” or “be suitable for,” depending on the verb.
additional_notes: „sich“ changes with the subject (ich mich, du dich, er/sie/es sich, wir uns, ihr euch, sie/Sie sich). „für“ takes the accusative: für mich/dich/ihn/sie/es/uns/euch/sie/Sie. Common combinations: sich interessieren für (+Akk) = to be interested in; sich (für etw.) entschuldigen = to apologize for; sich (für jdn./etw.) halten = to consider oneself (to be) / think oneself; sich eignen für = to be suitable for.
target_language_example: Er scheint sich für sie zu interessieren.
native_language_example: He seems to be interested in her.

meaning: Used inside common *sich für + Akk.* structures meaning “to be interested in / decide on / apply for / opt for the …” (with a masculine accusative noun: *den*).
additional_notes: This is not a complete phrase on its own; it’s a chunk that typically needs a verb to form a full expression (e.g., *sich für den Kurs interessieren*, *sich für den Salat entscheiden*, *sich für den Job bewerben*). *Sich* is the reflexive pronoun (“myself/yourself/…”), and *für den* means “for the” with masculine nouns in the accusative. With other genders, change *den* to *die/das* (e.g., *für die Arbeit*, *für das Ticket*).
target_language_example: Er interessiert sich für den Kurs.
native_language_example: He is interested in the course.

additional_notes: Used with reflexive verbs to show that two or more people do the action to one another (mutual action). It often comes after the verb: „Sie helfen sich gegenseitig.“ In subordinate clauses it can come earlier: „…, weil sie sich gegenseitig helfen.“ Note: the reflexive pronoun changes with person/number (mich/dich/sich/uns/euch/sich), but the core term is commonly given as „sich gegenseitig“.
target_language_example: Sie bewundern sich gegenseitig.
native_language_example: They admire each other.

meaning: to have been mistaken; to have been wrong.
additional_notes: Past participle of the reflexive verb „sich irren“ (usually used with „haben“): „Ich habe mich geirrt.“ You use it to admit that your belief/guess/assumption was wrong. Common with: „Ich glaube, ich habe mich geirrt.“
target_language_example: Er hat sich geirrt – der Zug fährt erst um 9 Uhr.
native_language_example: He was mistaken—the train doesn’t leave until 9 o’clock.

additional_notes: Perfect tense of the reflexive verb **sich ändern** (“to change”). Used when something changes (often by itself or over time), not when someone changes something deliberately (that’s **etw. ändern**). Common patterns: **etw. hat sich geändert** (“something has changed”), **Haben sich deine Pläne geändert?** (“Have your plans changed?”).
target_language_example: Viele Dinge haben sich geändert, wissen Sie.
native_language_example: Many things have changed, you know.

meaning: to make a big effort; to try very hard.
additional_notes: Used with the reflexive verb "sich Mühe geben" (= to make an effort). "große" intensifies it: "a lot of effort." Common patterns: "Ich gebe mir (große) Mühe" / "Gib dir Mühe!" / "Sie geben sich große Mühe, aber …" Often followed by "zu" + infinitive: "sich große Mühe geben, etwas zu tun."
target_language_example: Sie scheinen sich große Mühe zu geben.
native_language_example: They seem to be making a big effort.

additional_notes: Common fixed phrase with a reflexive pronoun + „Sorgen“ + „um“ + accusative. Conjugation pattern: ich mache mir…, du machst dir…, er/sie macht sich…, wir machen uns…, ihr macht euch…, sie/Sie machen sich…. The worried-about person/thing follows with „um“ + accusative (um dich/um ihn/um Maria/um den Hund).
target_language_example: Tom macht sich große Sorgen um Maria.
native_language_example: Tom is very worried about Maria.

meaning: to do well / feel good / turn out well (used with reflexive verbs to express that someone/something is doing or working well).
additional_notes: Used as **sich gut + verb** to say someone performs well or something functions/sells well. Common patterns: **sich gut schlagen** (do well/hold up), **sich gut verkaufen** (sell well), **sich gut machen** (do well / look good), **sich gut anfühlen** (feel good), **sich gut auskennen** (know a place/topic well), **sich gut um jdn. kümmern** (take good care of someone). The reflexive pronoun changes with the subject (ich **mich**, du **dich**, er/sie/es **sich**, wir **uns**, ihr **euch**, sie/Sie **sich**). Note: the fixed idea is “reflexive pronoun + gut”; the exact pronoun depends on the subject.
target_language_example: Für sein Alter hat Tom sich gut geschlagen.
native_language_example: For his age, Tom did well / held up well.

meaning: to get along well with (someone); to be on good terms with (someone).
additional_notes: Usually appears as **sich gut mit + Dat. verstehen** (common) or **sich gut mit + Dat. vertragen**. It’s reflexive: *ich verstehe **mich** gut mit …, du verstehst **dich** gut mit …, er/sie versteht **sich** gut mit …, wir verstehen **uns** gut mit …, ihr versteht **euch** gut mit …, sie/Sie verstehen **sich** gut mit …*. The person/group after **mit** takes the dative: *mit meinem Nachbarn, mit meinen Freunden, mit der Chefin*. Not a literal “understand”; it means “get along.”
target_language_example: Verstehen Sie sich gut mit Ihren Nachbarn?
native_language_example: Do you get along well with your neighbors?

meaning: used with certain verbs to express the idea of moving into a resting/down position (“to … down”), e.g., **sich hinlegen** = “to lie down,” **sich hinknien** = “to kneel down.”
additional_notes: Pattern: reflexive pronoun (mich/dich/sich/uns/euch/sich) + **hin**, most commonly with verbs of placing oneself somewhere (especially **legen**, **knien**, sometimes **setzen** in some regions). In imperatives, the reflexive pronoun is often visible: **Legen Sie sich hin!** (formal) / **Leg dich hin!** (informal). **hin** here is not usually translated word-for-word; it contributes the sense of “down/into position.”
target_language_example: Er ging ins Nebenzimmer und legte sich hin.
native_language_example: He went into the next room and lay down.

additional_notes: This is usually part of a longer verb phrase like "sich hinter dem Auto verstecken" (to hide behind the car). "hinter" is a two-way preposition: with location (no movement) it often uses dative ("hinter dem …"); with movement it uses accusative ("hinter den …"). "dem" is dative for masculine/neuter "der/das" nouns.
target_language_example: Das Kind versteckt sich hinter dem Vorhang.
native_language_example: The child is hiding behind the curtain.

meaning: “oneself in the …” — a very common grammatical pattern: reflexive **sich** + **im** (“in the”, contraction of **in dem**) as part of a larger phrase/verb construction.
additional_notes:
**sich im** is not a fixed idiom on its own; it normally appears inside longer expressions with reflexive verbs or set phrases.

- **im** = **in dem** (“in the”)
- **sich** changes with the subject (mich/dich/sich/uns/euch/sich; in dative often **mir/dir/sich** etc.).

Common patterns:
- **sich im Nebel auflösen** = “to dissolve/vanish in the fog”
- **sich im Klaren sein (über …)** = “to be clear/aware (about …)” (often with **sich** in dative: *ich bin mir…, sind Sie sich…*)
target_language_example: Der Junge sagte, das Taxi habe sich im Nebel aufgelöst.
native_language_example: The boy said the taxi had vanished in the fog.
