target_language_example: Ich habe heute so viel zu tun, dass ich keine Zeit für ein Treffen habe.
native_language_example: I have so much to do today that I don’t have time to meet up.

meaning: so many; that many (with plural nouns).
additional_notes: Used with plural countable nouns to express a large number or to compare quantities. Often answers or asks “how many?” (Wie viele?) and can be intensified (e.g., “so viele … wie …” = “as many … as …”). In imperatives it can mean “don’t/mention/eat so many …”.
target_language_example: Ich habe heute so viele E-Mails bekommen.
native_language_example: I got so many emails today.

meaning: “as many books as …” (a comparison of quantity).
additional_notes: Used in the pattern **so viele + plural noun + wie** to compare amounts: **so viele Bücher wie er** = “as many books as he (has)”. Very often you’ll see **so viele … wie möglich** (“as many … as possible”) or **(zwei)mal so viele … wie** (“(two) times as many … as”). The verb often comes at the end in the **wie**-clause: **… wie du kannst**.
target_language_example: Ich will dieses Jahr so viele Bücher wie möglich lesen.
native_language_example: I want to read as many books as possible this year.

additional_notes: Used to express that there are a lot of questions (often: curiosity, uncertainty, or too few answers). Common patterns: „Ich habe so viele Fragen.“ (I have so many questions.) and „so viele … wie …“ = “as many … as …” (e.g., „Stell so viele Fragen, wie du willst!“ = Ask as many questions as you want!).
target_language_example: Ich habe so viele Fragen, aber keine Zeit.
native_language_example: I have so many questions, but no time.

additional_notes: Used with plural countable nouns (or with a plural idea) to indicate a quantity. Often points to a number just mentioned or implied by context ("exactly so many again" = the same number again). In comparisons you’ll also see it in patterns like “so viele … wie …” (“as many … as …”).
target_language_example: Ich habe so viele Fragen, aber keine Zeit.
native_language_example: I have so many questions, but no time.

meaning: “so much (that) I …” / “so many things that I …”
additional_notes: Used to say you have a lot to say/do/feel, often followed by a verb like sagen (to say), erzählen (to tell), erklären (to explain), fragen (to ask), or anvertrauen (to confide). "so vieles" can mean “so much” or “so many things” depending on context, and "was" here means “that/which.”
target_language_example: Es gibt so vieles, was ich noch lernen muss.
native_language_example: There’s so much I still have to learn.

additional_notes: Refers to a thing/action of that kind, often with surprise, criticism, or disbelief. Common in spoken German; more formal/neutral is "so etwas". Often used with verbs like "machen", "tun", "sagen", "passieren" (e.g., "So was passiert.").
target_language_example: Ich habe noch nie so was erlebt.
native_language_example: I’ve never experienced anything like that.

additional_notes: Colloquial short form of "so etwas von". Used to strongly emphasize an adjective or description (often negative): "so was von schlecht/peinlich/fies" = "so incredibly bad/embarrassing/mean". It can also be used on its own after a statement for emphasis ("Aber so was von!") meaning "Absolutely! / Totally!".
target_language_example: Der Film war so was von langweilig.
native_language_example: The movie was so incredibly boring.

additional_notes: Often used to talk about reaching a point in time or progress/state. With time: "Es ist (noch) nicht so weit" = "It’s not time yet." With progress/being ready: "(schon) so weit sein" = "to be that far along / to be ready."
target_language_example: Bist du schon so weit, oder brauchst du noch fünf Minuten?
native_language_example: Are you ready yet, or do you need five more minutes?

meaning: to go so far (as to); to go to the point of (doing something)
additional_notes: Often used figuratively to express that someone does something extreme or takes something to a certain point. Common patterns: „Er/Sie geht so weit, dass …“ and „Er/Sie geht (sogar) so weit, zu + Infinitiv“. Can also be used literally about distance in some contexts, but the figurative meaning is very common.
target_language_example: Er kann so weit gehen, dass er seine Freunde anlügt.
native_language_example: He can go so far as to lie to his friends.

meaning: to be ready; to have reached the point (where something happens).
additional_notes: Used when something is now at the required stage or the moment has come. Very common in the fixed phrase "Es ist so weit" = "The time has come / It’s happening (now)." You can also say "Ich bin so weit" (I’m ready) or "Bist du so weit?" (Are you ready?) in everyday situations.
target_language_example: Ich muss nur noch meine Jacke anziehen, dann werde ich so weit sein und wir können losgehen.
native_language_example: I just need to put on my jacket, then I’ll be ready and we can leave.

additional_notes: Used for progress or distance (literal or figurative): Wir sind so weit gekommen. With “gut” it often means “so far, so good” (So weit gut?). In comparisons it appears as “so weit … wie …” = “as far as … as … / as much as …”: Wir treiben uns so weit, wie wir können.
target_language_example: So weit ist alles in Ordnung, aber wir sind noch nicht fertig.
native_language_example: So far everything is fine, but we’re not finished yet.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize how important something is. Very common in questions like „Warum ist das so wichtig?“ (“Why is that so important?”). Also used in comparisons with „wie“: „X ist so wichtig wie Y“ (“X is as important as Y”). With negation it can downplay something: „Das ist nicht so wichtig“ (“It’s not that important”).
target_language_example: Warum ist dir das so wichtig?
native_language_example: Why is that so important to you?

additional_notes: Used to compare things or people: "so wie X" = "like X / the way X (does/ is)". It can introduce a whole clause ("so wie du es gesagt hast" = "just as you said") or appear in set phrases like "So wie die Dinge stehen" = "as things stand".
target_language_example: Mach es so wie ich es dir gezeigt habe.
native_language_example: Do it the way I showed you.

additional_notes: Used to compare someone/something to the person you’re talking to, or to describe how someone does something. Common uses: (1) similarity: "Er ist mehr so wie du." (more like you). (2) manner/way: "Ich kann nicht drüber lachen so wie du." (I can’t laugh about it the way you do). It can also introduce a clause fragment for emphasis, e.g. "So wie du die Mädchen beschützt hast …" In full clauses, the verb goes to the end in the part after it when a verb is present.
target_language_example: Ich kann nicht drüber lachen so wie du!
native_language_example: I can’t laugh about it the way you do!

meaning: like before; as it used to be.
additional_notes: Used to compare the present (or future) to an earlier time, often with a nostalgic tone. Very common with "wieder" (again) when talking about returning to a previous state: "Alles wird wieder so wie früher."
target_language_example: Ich vermisse die Zeiten, als alles so wie früher war.
native_language_example: I miss the times when everything was like it used to be.

meaning: like me; just as I am/do.
additional_notes: Used to compare someone/something to yourself. Often means “just like me” (emphasizing similarity): „Tom will so wie ich sein.“ It can also introduce a comparison clause in longer sentences (often with a verb added): „so wie ich es gesagt habe“ = “just like I said.”
target_language_example: Mach es so wie ich: langsam und genau.
native_language_example: Do it like me: slowly and carefully.

additional_notes: Used to describe seeing or understanding something in a particular way, often stressing reality or truth: "so ... wie es ist" = "as it is". Pattern: (etw.) so sehen, wie + clause (often with "es/sie"): "die Dinge so sehen, wie sie sind".
target_language_example: Ich versuche, die Situation so zu sehen, wie sie wirklich ist.
native_language_example: I’m trying to see the situation the way it really is.

additional_notes: Used with a following clause introduced by **als** or **als ob**: **so tun, als ob ...** (“pretend as if ...”). Very common for saying someone is acting like something is true when it isn’t. Often followed by Konjunktiv (subjunctive), especially with **als ob** (e.g., *als ob ich keine Zeit hätte*).
target_language_example: Hör auf, so zu tun, als ob du mich nicht kennen würdest.
native_language_example: Stop pretending like you don’t know me.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to point to a certain type or to emphasize your reaction: neutral (“so ein Laden” = a shop like that) or exclamatory/complaining (“So ein Mist!” = What rubbish!). It changes with gender/case: so ein (m./n.), so eine (f.), so einen (m. acc.), etc.
target_language_example: So ein Auto habe ich noch nie gesehen.
native_language_example: I've never seen a car like that.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun to emphasize intensity, often in exclamations (approval or annoyance): "So eine Demütigung!" = "Such a humiliation!" / "What a humiliation!". With other genders: "so ein" (masc./neut.) and plural: "so welche/solche".
target_language_example: So eine Frechheit habe ich noch nie erlebt!
native_language_example: I’ve never experienced such cheekiness / nerve!

additional_notes: Used before a masculine noun in the accusative case to emphasize what kind of thing/person it is, often expressing surprise, admiration, or annoyance: *so einen Traum* (“such a dream”), *so einen Stuss* (“such nonsense”). It often refers to something just mentioned, obvious from context, or meant as an exaggeration. Form changes with gender/case (e.g., *so ein Auto*, *so eine Idee*).
target_language_example: So einen Tag habe ich lange nicht erlebt.
native_language_example: I haven’t experienced a day like that in a long time.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an unspecified thing or situation, often one that was just mentioned or is understood from context. In "mit so etwas rechnen" it means “to expect something like that” (usually something unpleasant).
target_language_example: Mit so etwas habe ich nicht gerechnet.
native_language_example: I didn’t expect something like that.

additional_notes: Used to say something is similar to something else, but not exactly the same (an approximation or comparison). It’s often followed by a noun or noun phrase: „Ist das so etwas wie …?“ = “Is that kind of like …?” It can also be used in statements like „Es gibt (nicht) so etwas wie …“ = “There is (no) such thing as …”.
target_language_example: Brauchen wir so etwas wie einen Plan?
native_language_example: Do we need something like a plan?

meaning: "something like that"; "stuff like that" (also: "such a ...!" for emphasis).
additional_notes: Literally "so something" (= "such something"). Very common in spoken German. Often refers back to an idea or situation: "so was" = "that kind of thing". It can also be used as an exclamation for strong emphasis (often with "von"): "So was (von)!" ≈ "No way!" / "That’s unbelievable!" / "So very ...!" (depending on context).
target_language_example: So was habe ich noch nie erlebt.
native_language_example: I've never experienced anything like that.

meaning: "not something like that" / "not like that" (used to say someone wouldn’t do/say such a thing, or to tell someone not to say/do it).
additional_notes: Uses the informal/colloquial "so was" (= "so etwas", "something like that"). Often appears with verbs like "tun" (do) or "sagen" (say): "Er würde so was nicht tun" = "He wouldn’t do something like that"; "Sag so was nicht!" = "Don’t say that!". The "nicht" negates the whole idea: 'not something like that'.
target_language_example: Ich würde so was nicht sagen.
native_language_example: I wouldn’t say something like that.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an approximate example or category when you can’t (or don’t want to) name it exactly. Often introduces a noun: "so was wie eine Pistole" (= something like a gun). It can also introduce an abstract idea: "so was wie Trauer" (= something like grief). With "gibt es nicht", it means "there is no such thing as ...": "So was wie einen Ex-Marine gibt es nicht." (= There’s no such thing as an ex-Marine.) In speech it’s very common to shorten "so etwas" to "so was".
target_language_example: Ich brauche so was wie einen Plan, bevor wir losfahren.
native_language_example: I need something like a plan before we set off.

additional_notes: Used as a spoken transition to move on to what comes next (often in instructions, demonstrations, or when getting people’s attention). It can sound like “So, now…” in English, but it’s often closer in tone to “Alright, now…” or “Okay then, now…”. Usually followed by what should happen next.
target_language_example: So, jetzt machen wir weiter mit der nächsten Aufgabe.
native_language_example: Alright, now we’ll continue with the next task.

meaning: "Is that so?" / "Well, well." (often skeptical or ironic).
additional_notes: Used as a reaction to what someone just said or did. Depending on tone, it can sound merely interested ("I see") or clearly suspicious/ironic ("Oh really?"). It’s common in spoken German; repeated forms like "So, so, so!" add emphasis.
target_language_example: So, so, du hast also schon wieder verschlafen?
native_language_example: Oh really, you overslept again?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a time clause with "sobald" (= as soon as). It’s a subordinating conjunction, so the verb in the "sobald"-clause goes to the end: "sobald ich nach Hause kam". The clause can come first or second; if it comes first, the main clause verb comes right after: "Sobald ich Zeit habe, rufe ich dich an."
target_language_example: Sobald ich fertig bin, komme ich runter.
native_language_example: As soon as I’m finished, I’ll come down.

meaning: to stop it immediately; to stop doing that right away.
additional_notes: Used to tell someone to stop what they’re doing right now. „damit“ refers to the action/activity (roughly “with that” → “doing that”). Often appears with a modal verb (müssen/sollen): „Du musst sofort damit aufhören.“ / „Sie sollten sofort damit aufhören.“
target_language_example: Du musst sofort damit aufhören.
native_language_example: You have to stop it immediately.

meaning: to the hospital immediately / right away.
additional_notes: Used for urgent situations where someone needs to go to the hospital. Often appears with verbs like müssen (must/need to) or fahren (drive/go). Note the motion phrase: ins = in das (into the). If someone is already there, you usually say im Krankenhaus (in the hospital).
target_language_example: Du musst sofort ins Krankenhaus.
native_language_example: You have to go to the hospital right away.

additional_notes: Used to show urgency, often in commands or strong advice. Typically used with motion verbs like gehen (to go) or kommen (to come): „Geh/komm sofort nach Hause!“ In German, „nach Hause“ means “(to) home” (going home), not “at home” (zu Hause).
target_language_example: Ich muss sofort nach Hause, es ist etwas passiert.
native_language_example: I have to go home immediately; something happened.

additional_notes: Used with haben to strongly emphasize how afraid someone is: Ich habe solche Angst. Here solche means “such” (that kind/so much) and agrees with the noun: Angst is feminine singular, so it’s usually solche Angst. Often followed by an infinitive clause with zu: solche Angst, (etwas) zu tun.
target_language_example: Ich habe solche Angst, alleine nach Hause zu gehen.
native_language_example: I’m so scared to walk home alone.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a general category of actions/events/objects similar to what was just mentioned or is understood from context. Often used when speaking generally (sometimes with a critical or dismissive tone). It’s the plural of "so ein Ding" ("a thing like that").
target_language_example: Ich mag solche Dinge nicht.
native_language_example: I don’t like things like that.

additional_notes: Used to refer to events or objects in a general way, often to say that something is normal or happens sometimes. It can point back to something mentioned or understood from context ("things like that").
target_language_example: Mach dir keine Sorgen—solche Sachen passieren manchmal.
native_language_example: Don’t worry—things like that happen sometimes.

additional_notes: Used to ask for clarification about the implication of what someone said (often with surprise, doubt, or disbelief). Very common in spoken German, usually followed by a full clause: “Soll das heißen, dass …?” or without “dass” in colloquial speech: “Soll das heißen, du kommst nicht?”
target_language_example: Soll das heißen, dass wir morgen nicht kommen können?
native_language_example: Does that mean we can’t come tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to ask for advice or permission about what you should do next. It’s the verb "sollen" (to be supposed to / should) + "ich" (I) in a question, often followed by an infinitive: "Soll ich gehen?" (= Should I go?).
target_language_example: Soll ich dir helfen?
native_language_example: Should I help you?

additional_notes: Used to politely offer help or ask what you should do for someone. It uses the modal verb „sollen“ in a question: „Soll ich …?“. „Ihnen“ is the formal/polite dative form of “you” (to/for you), used with strangers, customers, or in professional situations. Often followed by an infinitive at the end: „Soll ich Ihnen helfen?“ / „Soll ich Ihnen das bringen?“
target_language_example: Soll ich Ihnen die Tür aufhalten?
native_language_example: Should I hold the door open for you?

meaning: “Should I…?” / “Do you want me to…?” (offering or asking what to do with it/that).
additional_notes: Used to ask for instructions or to offer help. "soll" expresses what is expected/desired (often by the other person), not what you are able to do ("kann"). "das" refers to something specific (“it/that”), often an object: "Soll ich das hierhin stellen?" = “Should I put it here?” You can add details like a verb or place: "Soll ich das für Sie machen?", "Soll ich das irgendwo hinbringen?"
target_language_example: Soll ich das Fenster zumachen?
native_language_example: Should I close the window?

meaning: "Should I … you?" / "Do you want me to … (for you)?"
additional_notes: Used to offer to do something for someone (often something helpful or caring). It’s the start of a question and needs a main verb at the end: “Soll ich dich abholen?” (= Should I pick you up?). Word order: Soll + ich + dich + (other info) + verb.
target_language_example: Soll ich dich nach Hause bringen?
native_language_example: Should I take you home?

meaning: “Should I … ?” (offering/asking what you should do with *the* … / *them*).
additional_notes: Used to ask for instructions or to offer help. **Soll ich …?** is like “Should I…?” or “Do you want me to…?”. **die** is the definite article in the accusative for **feminine singular** (“the [feminine noun]”) or **plural** (“the [plural noun]”), and it can also act like a pronoun meaning **“them”** when the noun is understood from context.
target_language_example: Soll ich die Tasche tragen?
native_language_example: Should I carry the bag?

meaning: “Should I … for you?” / “Do you want me to … for you?”
additional_notes: Used to offer or suggest doing something for the other person (dir = “to you” informal singular). Often followed by an infinitive phrase (e.g., „… helfen?“, „… etwas zeigen?“) or a noun phrase (e.g., „… was erzählen?“). Depending on tone/context, it can be a genuine offer or a slightly teasing/ironic suggestion.
target_language_example: Soll ich dir die Tür aufmachen?
native_language_example: Should I open the door for you?

meaning: "Should I (do) it?" / "Do you want me to (do) it?"
additional_notes: Used to ask for advice or permission before doing something. It’s usually followed by an infinitive verb at the end: "Soll ich es aufmachen?" (Should I open it?). "Es" means "it" and refers to something already known from context; in short questions you can also hear "Soll ich es?" meaning "Should I do it?"
target_language_example: Soll ich es dir erklären?
native_language_example: Should I explain it to you?

meaning: “Should I … for you (all)?” / “Do you want me to … ?” (offering or asking if you should do something).
additional_notes: Used with a verb to offer help or ask for permission/confirmation: “Soll ich euch helfen?” = “Should I help you (all)?” Here, “euch” is the informal plural “you” (to a group). For one person you’d say “Soll ich dir …?” and for formal “you” you’d say “Soll ich Ihnen …?”.
target_language_example: Soll ich euch die Tür aufhalten?
native_language_example: Should I hold the door open for you (all)?

meaning: "Should I … him?" / "Am I supposed to … him?"
additional_notes: Used to ask whether you should do something to/for a male person (or a masculine noun). "soll" is from the modal verb "sollen" (often about advice, suggestion, or what someone wants you to do). "ihn" is the accusative form of "er" (= him). It’s usually followed by another verb in the infinitive at the end: "Soll ich ihn anrufen?"
target_language_example: Soll ich ihn später noch einmal anrufen?
native_language_example: Should I call him again later?

additional_notes: Combination of soll (from sollen) + das. Das often refers to a whole situation, action, or idea. In questions, this pattern often asks about purpose, meaning, or likely result, often with some surprise or annoyance: Was soll das? = 'what's that supposed to mean?' In statements, it can simply mean 'should that' or 'is not supposed to'.
target_language_example: Wie soll das funktionieren?
native_language_example: How is that supposed to work?

meaning: “Is that really supposed to…?” (expressing surprise, disbelief, or annoyance).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a question to challenge or criticize what someone did/said. It’s built from "sollen" (to be supposed to) + "das" (that/this) + the particle "denn" (adds emphasis in questions). Often followed by more information, e.g. "Soll das denn ein Witz sein?" or "Soll das denn funktionieren?"
target_language_example: Soll das denn ein Witz sein?
native_language_example: Is that supposed to be a joke?

meaning: "does that mean…?" / "what’s that supposed to mean?"
additional_notes: Used to ask for the meaning/implication of what someone said, often with surprise, doubt, or annoyance. Commonly appears in questions like: „Soll das heißen, dass …?“ (= “Does that mean that …?”) and „Was soll das heißen?“ (= “What’s that supposed to mean?”).
target_language_example: Soll das heißen, dass du morgen nicht kommst?
native_language_example: Does that mean you’re not coming tomorrow?

meaning: “What’s that supposed to mean?” / “What are you doing?” (annoyed or surprised).
additional_notes: Usually used in the full question: „Was soll denn das?“. It’s a common spoken reaction when you think something is pointless, rude, or strange. „denn“ is a modal particle that adds emotion (often impatience/irritation) and doesn’t translate directly.
target_language_example: Was soll denn das? Hör sofort auf damit!
native_language_example: What’s that supposed to be? Stop that right now!

additional_notes: Used to ask what the right thing to do is, or what someone expects you to do. It’s the modal verb **sollen** in a question with **ich** (“I”): **Soll ich + (object) + verb…?** Often implies asking for advice, instructions, or permission (similar to “Shall I…?” / “Should I…?”).
target_language_example: Soll ich das Fenster aufmachen oder zu lassen?
native_language_example: Should I open the window or leave it closed?

meaning: "am I supposed to (do) that?" / "how am I supposed to (do) that?"
additional_notes: Built from "sollen" (to be supposed/expected to) + "ich" (I) + "das" (that/it). It’s used to ask what you’re expected to do, or to express doubt/annoyance in questions like "Wie soll ich das …?" (How am I supposed to …?) or "Wieso soll ich das …?" (Why am I supposed to …?). Often followed by an infinitive: "Soll ich das sagen/erledigen/machen?" In some contexts it can also mean "Should I …?"
target_language_example: Soll ich das jetzt bezahlen oder später?
native_language_example: Am I supposed to pay for that now or later?

meaning: "What am I supposed to…?" / "Should I really…?" (with emphasis).
additional_notes: Used to start a question with the modal verb "sollen" (duty/expectation) plus the particle "denn", which adds emotion (surprise, impatience, doubt) and makes it sound more like "So what am I supposed to do (then)?". Common in spoken German; "denn" usually doesn’t translate directly.
target_language_example: Soll ich denn alleine alles machen?
native_language_example: Am I really supposed to do everything by myself?

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to ask what you should do for someone or to offer to do something: "Soll ich dir (mal) helfen/etwas zeigen/vorlesen?" It can also sound annoyed or rhetorical in complaints: "Wie oft soll ich dir noch sagen …?" Word order can change in questions with a question word: "Welche Seite soll ich dir vorlesen?"
target_language_example: Soll ich dir die Adresse aufschreiben?
native_language_example: Should I write down the address for you?

additional_notes: Uses the modal verb **sollen** to ask what you’re supposed to do / what would be advisable. **mich** is the reflexive pronoun (“myself”) and is needed with many verbs (e.g., **sich treffen** = to meet, **sich ausruhen** = to rest, **sich wehren** = to defend oneself, **sich kümmern** = to take care of, **sich freuen/erfreuen** = to be glad/enjoy). In other persons it changes: **sollst du dich…?**, **soll er/sie sich…?**
target_language_example: Soll ich mich bei dir melden, wenn ich angekommen bin?
native_language_example: Should I message you when I arrive?

meaning: "one should" / "you're supposed to" (general advice or a general rule).
additional_notes: Uses the impersonal pronoun "man" (= one/people/you in general) with "sollen" to express what is recommended, expected, or considered the right thing to do. Often used in proverbs and general statements: "Das soll man nicht tun." In questions it means "Why should one...?")
target_language_example: Wie soll man das denn wissen?
native_language_example: How is one supposed to know that?

additional_notes: Used to ask for agreement, make a suggestion, or ask whether it is a good idea for us to do something. It is the question form of wir sollen and is usually followed by another verb in the infinitive: Sollen wir gehen? In some contexts, especially with a question word, it can also mean 'are we supposed to ...?' as in Wann sollen wir gehen? Tone matters: in hostile contexts it can sound like a threat or challenge.
target_language_example: Sollen wir morgen früher losfahren?
native_language_example: Shall we leave earlier tomorrow?

meaning: "should we now…?" / "are we supposed to… now?"
additional_notes: Used to ask what the right next step is. Often expresses uncertainty, worry, or disbelief (can be rhetorical): "Sollen wir jetzt etwa aufgeben?" = "Are we really supposed to give up now?". Put it before the verb phrase you’re asking about (e.g., "Sollen wir jetzt gehen?", "Wie sollen wir jetzt …?" = "How are we supposed to … now?").
target_language_example: Sollen wir jetzt nach Hause gehen?
native_language_example: Should we go home now?

meaning: “shall we / should we … (ourselves/us)?”—used before a reflexive verb to suggest or ask what to do.
additional_notes: Used to make a suggestion or ask for a plan (“Shall we…?”) when the following verb is reflexive and needs **uns** (e.g., **uns anziehen** = get dressed, **uns treffen** = meet up, **uns in Verbindung setzen** = get in touch). The **uns** can mean “ourselves” or just “us,” depending on the verb.
target_language_example: Sollen wir uns heute Abend treffen?
native_language_example: Shall we meet up this evening?

meaning: "is said to" / "is apparently supposed to" (reported information + uncertainty).
additional_notes: Used when you pass on something you’ve heard (not something you know for sure). "sollen" signals reported speech/rumor (“they say…”), and "wohl" adds uncertainty (“apparently / probably”). Common in news, gossip, and indirect claims: "Er soll wohl krank sein" = you heard he’s ill, but you’re not certain.
target_language_example: Sie sollen wohl morgen nach Berlin fahren.
native_language_example: They’re said to be going to Berlin tomorrow (apparently).

meaning: “should be abolished / should be done away with.”
additional_notes: Used to express an opinion or recommendation that something (a law, punishment, custom, rule, tradition) ought to be ended. Grammar: "sollte" (soft, polite 'should') + passive infinitive "abgeschafft werden" (“to be abolished”). Often used in debates or formal discussions.
target_language_example: Diese Regel sollte abgeschafft werden.
native_language_example: This rule should be abolished.

additional_notes: Used mainly in questions to ask for advice, suggestions, or what the right thing to do is: Sollte ich ...? = 'Should I ...?' It can also be rhetorical, especially in questions like Wieso sollte ich? ('Why should I?'). In a normal statement, the order is ich sollte ....
target_language_example: Sollte ich jetzt gehen?
native_language_example: Should I go now?

additional_notes: Used to ask for advice or what would be appropriate to do. "Sollte" is Konjunktiv II of "sollen" and often sounds a bit more polite/tentative than "Soll ich …?". It’s followed by a reflexive verb, so the pronoun changes with the person (e.g., "solltest du dich …?", "sollten wir uns …?"). Common with verbs like "bedanken", "ausruhen", "wenden".
target_language_example: Sollte ich mich bei der Lehrerin entschuldigen?
native_language_example: Should I apologize to the teacher?

additional_notes: Uses the modal verb "sollen" in Konjunktiv II ("sollte") with the impersonal subject "man" (= “one/you/people in general”). It’s common for giving general recommendations, rules, or best practices. In questions ("Wie oft sollte man …?") it asks what is recommended. Often followed by an infinitive at the end: "sollte man + … + machen/nehmen/umsetzen".
target_language_example: Im Winter sollte man sich warm anziehen.
native_language_example: In winter, you should dress warmly.

additional_notes: Uses **Sie** (formal “you”) with **sollten** (Konjunktiv II of *sollen*) to give polite advice/recommendations, or to sound less direct than *Sie sollen …*. Often followed by an infinitive: *sollten Sie heute vorbeikommen* (“you should stop by today”). Can also appear in questions, sometimes rhetorically: *Warum sollten Sie das tun?* (“Why would/should you do that?”).
target_language_example: In diesem Fall, meine ich, sollten Sie heute vorbeikommen.
native_language_example: In that case, I think you should stop by today.

meaning: "should" (giving advice/recommendation) used with a reflexive pronoun ("oneself/yourself/themselves").
additional_notes: Common in polite advice, especially with "Sie": "Sie sollten sich ...". The reflexive pronoun changes with the subject: ich sollte mich, du solltest dich, er/sie sollte sich, wir sollten uns, ihr solltet euch, Sie sollten sich. "Sollten" is Konjunktiv II of "sollen" and often sounds like a gentle recommendation.
target_language_example: Sie sollten sich bei Tom entschuldigen.
native_language_example: You should apologize to Tom.

additional_notes: From the modal verb **sollen** in **Konjunktiv II** (**sollten**) + **wir** (“we”). It’s commonly used to make **suggestions** or give **advice** (often softer/more polite than *wir müssen* “we have to”). It can appear in statements (*Das sollten wir …*) or in questions (*Wie sollten wir …?* = “How should we …?”).
target_language_example: Sollten wir jetzt losgehen, oder wollen wir noch warten?
native_language_example: Should we leave now, or do we want to wait a bit longer?

meaning: “you should …” (giving advice), often with a reflexive verb.
additional_notes: Used with "du" to recommend something: "Du solltest dich …". "Solltest" is the Konjunktiv II of "sollen" and sounds a bit softer/more polite than "Du sollst …". The "dich" is the reflexive pronoun and changes with the person (ich: mich, du: dich, er/sie/es: sich, wir: uns, ihr: euch, sie/Sie: sich). Common with reflexive verbs like "sich ausruhen" (to rest), "sich setzen" (to sit down), "sich schlafen legen" (to go to bed).
target_language_example: Du solltest dich warm anziehen, es ist kalt draußen.
native_language_example: You should dress warmly; it’s cold outside.

additional_notes: This is a common frame used before a verb that takes "sich" + "bei" (dative), especially "sich bei jemandem melden" (to get in touch / report to someone). Grammar: "solltest" = "should" (du-form), "dich" = reflexive pronoun, and "bei" is followed by dative (e.g., "bei mir", "bei deiner Mutter", "bei der Polizei").
target_language_example: Du solltest dich bei der Polizei melden.
native_language_example: You should contact the police / report to the police.

additional_notes: Form of the modal verb *sollen* in 2nd person singular, past subjunctive/conditional (*du solltest*). Often used for advice (*Du solltest mehr schlafen.*). With inversion it can start a question (*Solltest du das wirklich tun?* = “Should you really do that?”) and it can also introduce a conditional idea, especially in more formal writing (*Solltest du Hilfe brauchen, ruf mich an.* = “If you should need help, call me.”).
target_language_example: Solltest du Hilfe brauchen, sag bitte Bescheid.
native_language_example: If you need help, please let me know.

additional_notes: "Solltet ihr" is the Konjunktiv II form of "ihr sollt" and is often used to give advice, recommendations, or a polite-sounding instruction to a group of people you address as "ihr" (informal plural “you”). It’s common in statements like "Das solltet ihr wissen" (“You should know that”).
target_language_example: Solltet ihr Fragen haben, sagt mir bitte Bescheid.
native_language_example: If you have any questions, please let me know.

meaning: “but also” (adds a second thing, usually after „nicht nur …“).
additional_notes: Most often used in the pattern „nicht nur X, sondern auch Y“ = “not only X, but also Y”. „sondern“ contrasts/corrects the first part and „auch“ adds the extra item. Word order: „nicht nur“ comes before the first item; „sondern auch“ introduces the second item, which can be a noun, adjective, verb phrase, etc.
target_language_example: Sie spricht nicht nur Deutsch, sondern auch Englisch.
native_language_example: She speaks not only German, but also English.

additional_notes: Used with a negative (nicht/kein/nichts) to mean “nothing else” besides what was mentioned: „Ich habe sonst nichts …“ = “I don’t have anything else …”. As a short question („Und sonst nichts?“) it can mean “Anything else?” or “Is that all?”.
target_language_example: Hast du sonst nichts im Kühlschrank?
native_language_example: Do you have anything else in the fridge?

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that, apart from the person/thing already mentioned, there is nobody else. Often appears in relative clauses like „was sonst niemand …“ (= „what no one else …“).
target_language_example: Das weiß sonst niemand.
native_language_example: No one else knows that.

additional_notes: Used to ask about additional things or people beyond what has already been mentioned. Common in questions with words like etwas/irgendwas/irgendwelche (“anything/any”) or wer/wem (“who/whom”). Often implies “besides that” or “in addition.”
target_language_example: Brauchen Sie sonst noch etwas?
native_language_example: Do you need anything else?

additional_notes: Used in questions to ask if there is more information, another request, or something additional. Very common in conversations and in service situations (e.g., a cashier or waiter asking if you need anything else). Often appears as a short question: „Sonst noch etwas?“
target_language_example: Kann ich dir sonst noch etwas helfen?
native_language_example: Can I help you with anything else?

meaning: 'anyone else' (in addition to the people already mentioned).
additional_notes: Used mostly in questions to ask whether there is another person besides those already involved (e.g., another speaker, another injured person). Often placed near the beginning of the sentence or used alone as a short question: "Sonst noch jemand?"
target_language_example: Hat sonst noch jemand eine Frage?
native_language_example: Does anyone else have a question?

additional_notes: Used mostly in questions to ask if there is another person besides the ones already mentioned. "jemanden" is accusative (direct object), so it goes with verbs like fragen (ask), sehen (see), verdächtigen/in Verdacht haben (suspect), etc. Similar word order: "Hast du sonst noch jemanden …?"
target_language_example: Hast du sonst noch jemanden eingeladen?
native_language_example: Did you invite anyone else?

additional_notes: Used to ask if there’s something additional. Depending on tone and context, it can be polite and helpful (e.g., in service situations: "Kann ich sonst noch was für dich tun?") or impatient/curt (e.g., "Sonst noch was?" = "Anything else?" as in "Are you done?"). Often shortened to just "Sonst noch was?"
target_language_example: Brauchen Sie sonst noch was?
native_language_example: Do you need anything else?

additional_notes: Colloquial. Used to widen options or refer vaguely to other things: "Einen Drink oder sonst was?" (= a drink or something/whatever). In questions it can mean "anything else?" or "anything else at all?" ("Hast du sonst was gesehen...?" / "Sonst was?"). With "zu ... fähig" it means "capable of anything". In the fixed phrase "wie sonst was" it’s an intensifier meaning "like crazy / like hell" (very strongly).
target_language_example: Willst du noch etwas essen oder sonst was?
native_language_example: Do you want to eat something else or anything like that?

additional_notes: Used mostly in questions to ask whether there is another person besides the ones already mentioned. Often appears as "Sonst noch wer?" or "War sonst wer da?". "Sonst" = "else/otherwise" and "wer" = "who", but in English you normally translate it as "anyone else" rather than "else who".
target_language_example: Kommt sonst wer mit?
native_language_example: Is anyone else coming along?

meaning: to take care of; to make sure/ensure (that something happens).
additional_notes: Used with **für + accusative** (für wen/was): *für die Kinder sorgen* = take care of the children. It can also mean “ensure/provide” in the sense of making something happen: *für Ordnung sorgen* = make sure there is order. Not the same as English “to worry for” (even though **sorgen** alone is related to “worries”).
target_language_example: Ich muss für das Essen sorgen.
native_language_example: I have to take care of the food.

meaning: to be ready / to have come this far (to the point where…).
additional_notes: Usually used as: **(schon) soweit sein**. It often describes progress or being at a certain stage: **Ich bin (noch nicht) soweit.** = “I’m (not) ready yet.” With **dass** it means “to be at the point where…”: **Ich bin soweit, dass …** = “I’ve gotten to the point where …”. Often spelled as two words (**so weit sein**) as well; spelling varies, but meaning is the same.
target_language_example: Ich bin noch nicht soweit, dass ich alleine fahren kann.
native_language_example: I’m not ready yet to drive on my own.

meaning: "so far, so good" (up to this point everything is okay).
additional_notes: Used to say that things have gone well up to now, often implying that problems could still come later. Common in spoken German and informal writing, but not slang.
target_language_example: Der Umzug ist stressig, aber soweit so gut.
native_language_example: The move is stressful, but so far so good.

meaning: "as far as I know" / "to the best of my knowledge."
additional_notes: Used to show that you’re not 100% sure and you’re sharing what you currently believe to be true. Often placed at the beginning of the sentence, but it can also be inserted mid-sentence with commas.
target_language_example: Soweit ich weiß, beginnt der Kurs um neun Uhr.
native_language_example: As far as I know, the course starts at nine o’clock.

meaning: “As far as I know, there is/there are …”
additional_notes: Used to politely say something is true to the best of your knowledge (you’re not 100% sure). After „gibt es“ you use the accusative: „gibt es einen Fehler“ / „gibt es eine Lösung“ / „gibt es keine Zeit“. Often followed by „nur“, „keine“, etc.
target_language_example: Soweit ich weiß, gibt es hier keinen Supermarkt in der Nähe.
native_language_example: As far as I know, there isn’t a supermarket nearby.

meaning: "as far as I know, ... is" (to the best of my knowledge).
additional_notes: Used to introduce information you believe is true, but you’re not 100% sure. Often followed by a statement with "ist" because you’re talking about a fact/state (e.g., someone is happy/sick/retired). You can also use it without "ist" ("Soweit ich weiß, ...").
target_language_example: Soweit ich weiß, ist der Supermarkt sonntags geschlossen.
native_language_example: As far as I know, the supermarket is closed on Sundays.

meaning: 'As far as I know, he is …' (to the best of my knowledge).
additional_notes: Used to show you’re not 100% sure and are giving the information based on what you currently know. Often used at the start of a sentence: “Soweit ich weiß, ist er …”. After the comma, German word order is normal: verb first in a statement (“ist er …”). You can swap the subject: “Soweit ich weiß, ist sie … / sind sie … / ist das …”.
target_language_example: Soweit ich weiß, ist er heute im Büro.
native_language_example: As far as I know, he’s in the office today.

meaning: 'both English and …' (used to say someone does/has two things).
additional_notes: This is part of the pattern **sowohl A als auch B** = **both A and B**. It emphasizes that *both* items are true. Word order: the verb usually comes right after the subject, and the pair **sowohl … als auch** stays with the two items: *Er spricht sowohl Englisch als auch Deutsch.*
target_language_example: Ich spreche sowohl Englisch als auch Spanisch.
native_language_example: I speak both English and Spanish.

additional_notes: Uses the paired structure „sowohl … als auch …“ to mean “both … and …”. Put the first item after „sowohl“ and the second after „als auch“. You can replace the languages with other nouns, verbs, or adjectives (e.g., „sowohl lesen als auch schreiben“ = “both read and write”).
target_language_example: Sie spricht sowohl Französisch als auch Englisch sehr gut.
native_language_example: She speaks both French and English very well.

additional_notes: Usually appears as **die sozialen Medien** (plural). The ending changes with the case: **die sozialen Medien** (nominative/accusative), **der sozialen Medien** (genitive), **den sozialen Medien** (dative). Common with prepositions like **in/auf/über** (e.g., *auf den sozialen Medien* = on social media; *über die sozialen Medien* = via/through social media).
target_language_example: Viele Jugendliche verbringen jeden Tag viel Zeit in den sozialen Medien.
native_language_example: Many teenagers spend a lot of time on social media every day.

additional_notes: Usually used in the plural: „soziale Medien“ = “social media.” „Medium“ is neuter (das Medium); singular is less common and often refers to one specific platform (e.g., one app/website).
target_language_example: Für viele Jugendliche ist ein soziales Medium ein wichtiger Teil des Alltags.
native_language_example: For many teenagers, a social media platform is an important part of everyday life.

additional_notes: Common verb + language pattern: "[Sprache] sprechen" (e.g., "Deutsch sprechen", "Englisch sprechen"). When referring to the language as a noun, it’s usually capitalized ("Spanisch"); in the fixed pattern with the verb, you will also commonly see "Spanisch sprechen". This entry uses the exact term as given: "spanisch sprechen".
target_language_example: Ich kann spanisch sprechen.
native_language_example: I can speak Spanish.

additional_notes: Used for walking as a relaxed activity (often in a park, along the beach, etc.), not mainly for getting somewhere. Conjugate only the verb gehen (ich gehe spazieren, wir sind spazieren gegangen). You can add a place: im Park/am Strand spazieren gehen.
target_language_example: Lass uns morgen früh am Strand spazieren gehen.
native_language_example: Let’s go for a walk on the beach early tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like „mögen“, „lieben“, „Lust haben“ or „pflegen“ to express the activity of taking a walk. The „zu“ + infinitive („zu gehen“) is common after many verbs/expressions to mean “to (do something)”. Often you’ll add where/when: „im Park“, „am Abend“, „morgens“.
target_language_example: Wir haben Lust, heute Abend im Park spazieren zu gehen.
native_language_example: We feel like going for a walk in the park this evening.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone (one person you address as du) whether they play an instrument, a sport, or a game. It’s the verb spielen (“to play”) in 2nd person singular (du spielst) with inversion for a question: Spielst du …?
target_language_example: Spielst du ein Instrument?
native_language_example: Do you play an instrument?

additional_notes: Used with a subject in 3rd person singular (er/sie/es or a name): **spielt** is the present-tense form of **spielen** (“to play”). **jeden Tag** means “every day” (accusative after a time expression). Often followed by a sport or game: *spielt jeden Tag Fußball/Tennis*.
target_language_example: Meine Schwester spielt jeden Tag Klavier.
native_language_example: My sister plays the piano every day.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is not important or not relevant to the situation. Often said as (1) "Das spielt keine Rolle" = "That doesn't matter" or (2) "Es spielt keine Rolle, ..." / "Spielt keine Rolle, ..." = "It doesn't matter (that/what/if) ...". "Rolle" literally means "role," but here the whole phrase means "be important / make a difference."
target_language_example: Es spielt keine Rolle, ob du heute oder morgen kommst.
native_language_example: It doesn't matter whether you come today or tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to praise someone’s performance in games or sports, or how well they play an instrument. "spielt" is the 3rd-person singular of "spielen" (to play): "Er/Sie spielt sehr gut." You can also use it with a name or a team: "Die Mannschaft spielt sehr gut."
target_language_example: Sie spielt sehr gut Klavier.
native_language_example: She plays the piano very well.

additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of **mit jemandem sprechen** (“to speak with someone”). **Mit** is followed by the **dative** case: *sprach mit mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen*; *sprach mit Maria / mit den Freunden*. It can also be used with **mit + noun** to describe how someone spoke: *sprach mit fester Stimme* (“spoke in a firm voice”).
target_language_example: Einer der Soldaten sprach mit mir.
native_language_example: One of the soldiers spoke with me.

additional_notes: "sprachen" is the simple past (Präteritum) of "sprechen" for "they" (or a plural subject like "Tom und Maria"). It’s commonly used in writing or storytelling. It is followed by "über" + accusative to say what the conversation topic was: "über Politik", "über mich", "über die Zukunft".
target_language_example: Wir sprachen über das Wetter, während wir warteten.
native_language_example: We talked about the weather while we were waiting.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **springen** in the simple past (**sprang**) to describe someone/something jumping out of a place/container. **aus** takes the **dative** case, so masculine/neuter nouns often appear as **aus dem** (“out of the”). For feminine nouns: **aus der**; plural: **aus den**.
target_language_example: Das Kind sprang aus dem Auto.
native_language_example: The child jumped out of the car.

additional_notes: "sprang" is the simple past of "springen" (to jump). "über" means "over/across." "den" is the accusative masculine form of "der" (the), used because the thing being jumped over is a direct object (e.g., "den Hund", "den Graben"). With other nouns, the article changes: "über das" (neuter), "über die" (feminine/plural).
target_language_example: Der Junge sprang über den Zaun.
native_language_example: The boy jumped over the fence.

additional_notes: This is the formal (Sie) form of the verb sprechen (“to speak”). It’s used when addressing strangers, customers, or in professional settings. In questions it often means “Do you speak …?” (e.g., a language). As an imperative, it can mean “Please talk/speak …” (e.g., Sprechen Sie mit ihm! = “Talk to him!”). With aus Erfahrung it means “from experience” (Sprechen Sie aus Erfahrung? = “Are you speaking from experience?”).
target_language_example: Sprechen Sie bitte langsamer.
native_language_example: Please speak more slowly.

additional_notes: Used when addressing someone politely (Sie = formal “you”), especially strangers or in service situations. In questions it’s often preceded by Entschuldigung/Verzeihung (“Excuse me”). Without a question mark it can sound like an instruction (“Speak English!”); to soften it, use a question intonation or add bitte.
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, sprechen Sie Englisch, bitte?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you speak English, please?

meaning: "talk to" / "speak with" (formal: addressing one person as "you").
additional_notes: Used with the formal "Sie" form (e.g., to a stranger, customer, or in polite situations). It’s typically followed by the person you’re talking to: "Sprechen Sie mit Tom." To specify the topic, you can add "über + Akk.": "Sprechen Sie mit niemandem darüber."
target_language_example: Gehen Sie und sprechen Sie mit Tom!
native_language_example: Go and talk to Tom!

meaning: to talk about; to speak about.
additional_notes: Used with a topic introduced by the preposition **über** (typically **über + Akkusativ**: *über das Wetter sprechen*, *über ihn sprechen*). Word order can vary (e.g., *Über ... sprechen wir*), but the core collocation is **sprechen über**.
target_language_example: Wir sprechen über deine Pläne.
native_language_example: We’re talking about your plans.

additional_notes: Present tense of **sprechen** with **ihr** (“you all/you guys”). Often used in questions (verb first): **Sprecht ihr Deutsch?** = “Do you guys speak German?” It can also mean “are you talking (about…)” depending on what follows: **über** (about), **von** (about/which), **mit** (with), **aus (persönlicher) Erfahrung** (from (personal) experience). Uses **ihr**, not the formal **Sie**.
target_language_example: Sprecht ihr auch Englisch?
native_language_example: Do you guys also speak English?

additional_notes: Used to ask what a group of people you address as "ihr" (friends, classmates, kids, etc.) is talking about. It goes with "über" + accusative (e.g., über Tom, über sie, über etwas). You can also say: "Sprecht ihr gerade über …?" (right now) or "Worüber sprecht ihr?" (What are you talking about?).
target_language_example: Sprecht ihr über etwas Bestimmtes?
native_language_example: Are you talking about something specific?

meaning: Talk to me. / Speak to me.
additional_notes: Imperative (command/request) using the informal "du" form: "sprich" (from "sprechen"). Use it with friends, family, kids, or when speaking informally; for a formal/polite version say "Sprechen Sie mit mir." Often used when someone wants an answer or wants to start/continue a conversation.
target_language_example: Bitte, sprich mit mir.
native_language_example: Please, talk to me.

additional_notes: An imperative using du-form: sprich = "speak/talk". Used to scold someone for their tone, rudeness, or disrespect. Usually followed by a pronoun or noun in the dative: mit mir/dir/ihm/ihr, mit meiner Mutter, etc. You can also say: "Sprich nicht so mit mir!"
target_language_example: Sprich nicht so mit deinem Bruder!
native_language_example: Don’t talk to your brother like that!

additional_notes: From "sprechen" (to speak/talk). Used to ask someone if they speak a language (often followed by a language: „Sprichst du Deutsch?“) or to ask about what they’re talking about (e.g., „Von wem sprichst du?“ = “Who are you talking about?”). It’s informal because it uses „du“ (used with friends, family, kids, etc.); the formal version is „Sprechen Sie …?“
target_language_example: Sprichst du Englisch?
native_language_example: Do you speak English?

additional_notes: A common question when you want to check if someone can speak English. Uses informal/singular “du”; for a polite/formal version say “Sprechen Sie Englisch?”
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, sprichst du Englisch?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you speak English?

additional_notes: Used with the verb „sprechen“ to say what language someone speaks. It changes with the subject: ich spreche Englisch, du sprichst Englisch, er/sie spricht Englisch, wir sprechen Englisch, ihr sprecht Englisch, sie/Sie sprechen Englisch. You can add adverbs like „flüssig“ (fluently) or list multiple languages with „und“.
target_language_example: Sie spricht Englisch flüssig.
native_language_example: She speaks English fluently.

additional_notes: Used with the verb „sprechen“ (to speak) + a language. The verb changes with the subject: ich spreche, du sprichst, er/sie/es spricht, wir sprechen, ihr sprecht, sie/Sie sprechen. You can add adverbs like „auch“ (also), „natürlich“ (of course), „ziemlich gut“ (pretty well), or comparisons like „genau so gut wie …“ (just as well as …).
target_language_example: Meine Schwester spricht Französisch, aber ich spreche nur Englisch.
native_language_example: My sister speaks French, but I only speak English.

additional_notes: Used to compare language ability, often with **als** (“than”): *Er spricht besser Französisch als ich.* You can also add what it’s being compared to: *… als Englisch.* If **als** introduces a full clause, a comma is used: *…, als er glauben machen will.*
target_language_example: Sie spricht besser Französisch als Deutsch.
native_language_example: She speaks French better than German.

additional_notes: Used to say someone’s language ability is the same as someone else’s. It’s typically followed by a comparison with **wie**: **Er spricht genauso gut Englisch wie du.** You can also place the language after **gut**: **Er spricht genauso gut wie du Englisch.**
target_language_example: Sie spricht genauso gut Deutsch wie ihr Bruder.
native_language_example: She speaks German just as well as her brother.

additional_notes: Used with "man" (impersonal subject meaning "people/one") to say what language is spoken in a place or in general. Common pattern: "In/Hier + spricht man + Sprache." You can also use it in questions: "Wie viele Sprachen spricht man ...?"
target_language_example: In der Schweiz spricht man Deutsch, Französisch und Italienisch.
native_language_example: In Switzerland people speak German, French, and Italian.

additional_notes: Uses the impersonal pronoun „man“ (= people/one) to talk generally about what language is spoken in a country/region. Often used in statements like „Deutsch spricht man in …“ and in questions like „Welche Sprache spricht man in …?“ In English you’d usually say “People speak … in …” or “... is spoken in ...”.
target_language_example: Deutsch spricht man in Deutschland, Österreich und der Schweiz.
native_language_example: People speak German in Germany, Austria, and Switzerland.

spricht nicht nur Englisch, sondern auch

target_language_multi_word_term: spricht nicht nur Englisch, sondern auch
additional_notes: This uses the common pattern **nicht nur …, sondern auch …** to add extra information (“not only … but also …”). Here it’s used with **sprechen** to list more than one language. The second part (**sondern auch …**) typically names the additional language.
target_language_example: Er spricht nicht nur Englisch, sondern auch Italienisch.
native_language_example: He speaks not only English, but also Italian.

additional_notes: Used with **über + accusative** to say someone never talks about a topic. **seine** is the possessive for **his** (or **their**) with masculine/neuter nouns in the accusative (e.g., *seinen Bruder*, *seine Arbeit*, *sein Leben*). In full sentences you often add the subject first: *Er spricht nie über seine …*
target_language_example: Er spricht nie über seine Vergangenheit.
native_language_example: He never talks about his past.

additional_notes: Used with a language name after it: „spricht sehr gut Deutsch/Englisch/Japanisch“. The verb changes with the subject (ich spreche, du sprichst, er/sie spricht), but „sehr gut“ stays the same.
target_language_example: Meine Schwester spricht sehr gut Deutsch.
native_language_example: My sister speaks German very well.

additional_notes: Used with forms of „sein“ (ich bin/du bist/wir sind … spät dran) to say you’re late or don’t have much time left. Often used for appointments, meetings, deadlines, or when you need to hurry. You can intensify it with „schon“ (already) or „zu“ (too): „Ich bin schon spät dran.“ / „Wir dürfen nicht zu spät dran sein.“
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich bin spät dran — der Bus hatte Verspätung.
native_language_example: Sorry, I'm running late — the bus was delayed.

additional_notes: Used to say something continues until very late at night. Often used with verbs like arbeiten (to work), feiern (to party/celebrate), lernen (to study), or reden (to talk): „Wir haben spät in die Nacht gefeiert.“
target_language_example: Wir haben gestern spät in die Nacht geredet.
native_language_example: We talked late into the night yesterday.

additional_notes: Inverted word order of the more common "Es ist spät." This inversion can sound a bit poetic or emphatic (e.g., in storytelling, songs, or to stress that it’s already late).
target_language_example: Spät ist es schon – wir sollten nach Hause gehen.
native_language_example: It’s late already—we should go home.

meaning: to arrive late; to be late.
additional_notes: Used to say someone arrives later than planned. Often used with more context: „spät kommen“ (to be late) vs. „zu spät kommen“ (to be too late, e.g., for a train/meeting). In the past tense you’ll often see „(zu) spät gekommen“ (e.g., „Ich bin spät gekommen.“).
target_language_example: Ich werde heute spät kommen.
native_language_example: I will arrive late today.

additional_notes: Used with motion verbs like kommen/gehen/fahren to say someone arrives at home late. "nach Hause" means "(to) home" (direction). Don’t confuse it with "zu Hause" = "at home" (location). You can add intensifiers like "sehr" (very) or give a time: "um Mitternacht" (at midnight).
target_language_example: Ich bin gestern spät nach Hause gekommen.
native_language_example: I got home late yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens or someone does something at a very late hour during the night (often implying “too late” or unusual). Often used with "bis" (bis spät nachts = until late at night) or "so" (so spät nachts = so late at night).
target_language_example: Bitte ruf mich nicht so spät nachts an.
native_language_example: Please don’t call me so late at night.

additional_notes: Used to say someone arrives late to a lesson. Common with verbs like „kommen“ or „sein“: „Ich komme spät zum Unterricht.“ / „Er ist heute spät zum Unterricht gekommen.“ In many contexts you’ll also hear „zu spät zum Unterricht“ (= too late for class).
target_language_example: Ich bin heute spät zum Unterricht gekommen.
native_language_example: I arrived late for class today.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like **sein** or **kommen** to say you are arriving late at your workplace. **zur** is a contraction of **zu der** (to the) and is used because **Arbeit** is feminine (**die Arbeit**). Common patterns: **Ich bin spät zur Arbeit.** / **Ich komme spät zur Arbeit.**
target_language_example: Ich komme heute spät zur Arbeit.
native_language_example: I’m coming to work late today.

additional_notes: Used to say someone arrives at school late, often with verbs like "sein" or "kommen": "Ich bin spät zur Schule" (common but incomplete) is usually said as "Ich bin spät zur Schule gekommen" or more naturally "Ich bin zu spät zur Schule gekommen" (= I came to school too late).
target_language_example: Ich bin heute zu spät zur Schule gekommen.
native_language_example: I came to school too late today.

additional_notes: Used with "sein" in the perfect tense to say someone arrived at school late: "Ich bin spät zur Schule gekommen." The "zur" is short for "zu der" and is used with destinations (going/coming to a place).
target_language_example: Ich bin heute spät zur Schule gekommen.
native_language_example: I came to school late today.

meaning: to call later; to call back later.
additional_notes: Used when you want to make a phone call at a later time. With the separable verb **anrufen**, the verb often splits in a main clause (e.g., *Ich rufe dich später an.*), but the exact phrase **später anrufen** stays together in infinitive constructions (e.g., after modal verbs like *können* or *sollen*, or in subordinate clauses).
target_language_example: Können Sie mich später anrufen?
native_language_example: Could you call me later?

meaning: to come from; to originate from.
additional_notes: Used to state the origin of people, things, traditions, or words/ideas. Very common for people’s roots (often like “to be originally from”) and for etymology. Typically followed by a place/country/region or a language: aus Australien, aus Boston, aus China; aus dem Latein(ischen). In the present tense with plural subjects you’ll see the exact form “stammen aus” (e.g., meine Eltern stammen aus …); with singular subjects it becomes “stammt aus”.
target_language_example: Meine Eltern stammen aus Australien.
native_language_example: My parents come from Australia.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the origin of people, things, or backgrounds. It’s followed by **aus + dative**: *Er stammt aus Berlin.* / *Das Gemüse stammt aus der Region.* Also common for family or social background: *Sie stammt aus einer großen Familie.*
target_language_example: Dieses Rezept stammt aus meiner Heimat.
native_language_example: This recipe comes from my hometown.

additional_notes: Used to link two actions: first someone gets up (from sitting/lying), then they do the next action. It’s the simple past of the separable verb **aufstehen**: **(er/sie) stand … auf**. In sentences, **stand** comes early and **auf** goes to the end of the clause; **und** connects the next verb/action.
target_language_example: Ich stand auf und machte das Fenster auf.
native_language_example: I stood up and opened the window.

meaning: "stood up and went" (got up and left/went somewhere).
additional_notes: A common story/narration sequence in the simple past (Präteritum): **stand auf** is the Präteritum of **aufstehen** (a separable verb: *auf* goes to the end), and **ging** is the Präteritum of **gehen**. Often followed by a destination: *zur Tür*, *ans Fenster*, or used alone to mean someone left.
target_language_example: Sie stand auf und ging nach Hause.
native_language_example: She stood up and went home.

additional_notes: Used to say someone got up early with a purpose. It’s the past tense (Präteritum) of "früh aufstehen" (to get up early): "ich stand … auf", "sie/er stand … auf". "um … zu" introduces the purpose/goal (like "in order to"). In everyday speech, many people also use Perfekt: "Ich bin früh aufgestanden, um …".
target_language_example: Ich stand früh auf, um vor der Arbeit noch zu joggen.
native_language_example: I got up early to go jogging before work.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone/something being positioned next to something (often right at an edge or surface): *an der Tür* (at the door), *an der Spüle* (by the sink), *an der Straßenecke* (at the street corner). With a fixed location, *an* takes the dative case: *an der* (feminine nouns), *an dem* = *am* (masculine/neuter), *an den* (plural).
target_language_example: Sie stand an der Bushaltestelle und wartete.
native_language_example: She stood at the bus stop and waited.

meaning: “was standing in the shower” (often: “was taking a shower”).
additional_notes: Literally “stood under the shower.” In everyday use it usually implies the person was showering. “stand” is the simple past (Präteritum) of “stehen” and is common in written narration; in speech you also hear: “Er hat unter der Dusche gestanden.”
target_language_example: Als ich die Tür öffnete, stand er unter der Dusche.
native_language_example: When I opened the door, he was in the shower.

meaning: “died of/from” (a cause) or “died on” (a specific day).
additional_notes: “Starb” is the simple past of *sterben* (“to die”). With **an + dative**, it often gives the cause of death: *an Krebs, an Sauerstoffmangel, an einer Krankheit*. It can also use **an + dative** for a point in time like a day/date: *an ihrem Geburtstag* (“on her birthday”).
target_language_example: Mein Großvater starb an Krebs.
native_language_example: My grandfather died of cancer.

additional_notes: "starb" is the simple past of "sterben" (to die). In German you often say "an" + illness/cause of death: "an Krebs sterben" = to die of cancer. In everyday speech you’ll also hear the perfect tense: "Er ist an Krebs gestorben."
target_language_example: Ihre Mutter starb an Krebs.
native_language_example: Her mother died of cancer.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **sterben** + **an** + dative to name the cause of death (often an illness, injury, or overdose). Here **starb** is simple past (“died”), and **einer** is dative feminine/indefinite (“a/an”), e.g. **an einer Lungenentzündung**. Other forms: **stirbt an …** (present), **ist an … gestorben** (present perfect).
target_language_example: Er starb an einer schweren Krankheit.
native_language_example: He died of a serious illness.

additional_notes: “starb” is the simple past of “sterben” (to die). With “vor” + a time period, it means “... ago” (e.g., „vor einem Jahr“ = a year ago). With “vor” + an event/noun, it means “before” (e.g., „vor meiner Ankunft“ = before my arrival).
target_language_example: Meine Großmutter starb vor drei Jahren.
native_language_example: My grandmother died three years ago.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something has sufficient strength, power, or intensity. Often followed by an infinitive with „um … zu …“: „stark genug, um … zu …“ (strong enough to …). With drinks like coffee, „stark“ means strong in taste/caffeine.
target_language_example: Ich bin noch nicht stark genug, um den Koffer allein zu tragen.
native_language_example: I'm not strong enough yet to carry the suitcase by myself.

meaning: to make (someone/something) strong; to stand up for / advocate (for something).
additional_notes: Used both literally ("jemanden stark machen" = to strengthen someone) and idiomatically, especially in the pattern "sich für + Akkusativ stark machen" meaning to advocate for a cause or support/defend someone.
target_language_example: Ich will mich für bessere Arbeitsbedingungen stark machen.
native_language_example: I want to advocate for better working conditions.

meaning: of heavy rain (genitive: “because of / despite heavy rain”).
additional_notes: “starken Regens” is the genitive form of “starker Regen” (heavy rain). It’s commonly used after prepositions that often take the genitive, especially **wegen** (because of) and **trotz** (despite): **wegen starken Regens**, **trotz des starken Regens**. In everyday speech you may also hear the dative: **wegen starkem Regen**.
target_language_example: Wegen starken Regens bleibt der Park heute geschlossen.
native_language_example: Because of heavy rain, the park is closed today.

meaning: "you are" (2nd-person singular of *stecken*), used for where you are, whether you’re stuck, or whether you’re involved.
additional_notes: *Steckst du* is the present-tense form of **stecken** for **du** (“you”). It shows up in several common expressions: **Wo steckst du?** = “Where are you?” (often: “Where are you hiding/where have you got to?”); **Du steckst in der Klemme.** = “You’re in a jam / you’re stuck (in a difficult situation).”; **Du steckst dahinter.** = “You’re behind it (responsible for it).”; and it can also mean “you put something into something” depending on context (e.g., *Du steckst den Schlüssel ins Schloss.*).
target_language_example: Wo steckst du? Ich warte schon seit zehn Minuten.
native_language_example: Where are you? I’ve been waiting for ten minutes already.

additional_notes: Du-imperative of the separable verb **aufstehen** (“to stand up / get up”). Often used to tell one person to stand up physically or get out of bed. In speech you may also hear **Steh auf!** or more emphatically **Steh doch auf!**. Can sound harsh depending on tone or if combined with insults.
target_language_example: Steh auf, wir müssen jetzt los!
native_language_example: Get up, we have to leave now!

additional_notes: Imperative of **aufstehen** (“to stand up / to get up”), used when speaking to **one person** (du). Often used to tell someone to get up from sitting/lying down, or to get out of bed. Common with urging phrases like **Komm schon** (“come on”) or **Na los** (“go on/come on”).
target_language_example: Steh auf, wir müssen jetzt gehen!
native_language_example: Get up, we have to go now!

meaning: to stop (and stay standing); to stand still.
additional_notes: Often used as an imperative command ("Bleib stehen!" / "Stehen bleiben!") meaning "Stop!"—e.g., police, parents, or in urgent situations. It literally combines "stehen" (to stand) + "bleiben" (to stay), and implies not moving forward.
target_language_example: Bitte stehen bleiben—der Zug fährt gleich ab.
native_language_example: Please stay where you are—the train is about to depart.

meaning: 'are you standing?' / 'do you stand (for/in line)?' / 'what are you into?' (depending on context).
additional_notes: "stehst du" is the 2nd-person singular form of "stehen" (you stand/are standing). The meaning depends a lot on what comes with it: (1) "Auf was/was für … stehst du?" = 'What … are you into?' (colloquial, about tastes). (2) "Auf wessen Seite stehst du?" = 'Whose side are you on?' (3) "Wie lange stehst du da …?" = 'How long have you been standing there …?' (4) "Wofür stehst du an?" uses "anstehen" = 'to queue/wait in line for'.
target_language_example: Auf welche Musik stehst du gerade?
native_language_example: What kind of music are you into right now?

meaning: gets up every morning (literally: “stands every morning”).
additional_notes: Most commonly part of the separable verb "aufstehen" (= to get up). In a main clause, "steht" is the conjugated verb and the particle "auf" goes to the end: "Er steht jeden Morgen um acht Uhr auf." "jeden Morgen" means “every morning.” Without "auf," "steht" can also literally mean “stands,” but in everyday use with a time expression like this it usually implies getting up when completed with "auf."
target_language_example: Er steht jeden Morgen um acht Uhr auf.
native_language_example: He gets up every morning at eight o’clock.

meaning: “is/stands on the …” (location); also “is at stake” in fixed phrases (e.g., auf dem Spiel stehen).
additional_notes: Literal use: for where an object is placed, with a dative noun after „auf dem“ (e.g., auf dem Herd = on the stove). Figurative: in the idiom „auf dem Spiel stehen“ it means something important is at risk/at stake.
target_language_example: Das Glas steht auf dem Tisch.
native_language_example: The glass is on the table.

additional_notes: From the verb "stehen" (to suit, to look good on someone). Very common with clothes/colors: "Das steht dir gut." It can also be used in fixed expressions like "(Etwas) steht dir ins Gesicht geschrieben" = "(Something) is written all over your face" (your expression clearly shows it).
target_language_example: Die Farbe steht dir wirklich gut.
native_language_example: That color really suits you.

additional_notes: Used to compliment someone’s appearance, especially clothes, colors, or accessories. The thing that looks good is the subject: "Blau steht dir gut" = “Blue suits you.” Often said as "Das steht dir gut!" (“That looks good on you!”).
target_language_example: Die Jacke steht dir gut.
native_language_example: The jacket looks good on you.

meaning: “is in the … / is written (said) in the …” or literally “is standing in the …”.
additional_notes: From the verb **stehen** (“to stand”). With a place, it’s literal: **Tom steht in der Zimmerecke** = “Tom is standing in the corner of the room.” With books, documents, or text, German often uses **stehen** to mean something is written/mentioned there: **Das steht in der Bibel** = “That’s written in the Bible.” It’s usually followed by a feminine noun in the dative (e.g., **in der Bibel**, **in der Zeitung**, **in der E-Mail**).
target_language_example: Das steht in der E-Mail.
native_language_example: It says that in the email.

meaning: “is right at the door” (literally) / “is just around the corner; is coming very soon” (figuratively).
additional_notes: Used literally when something is physically in front of the door, and very commonly figuratively for events/seasons that are approaching soon (e.g., Herbst, Halloween, Weihnachten). In the figurative sense, it means it will happen very soon, like “just around the corner.” Note: the phrase inflects with the subject (e.g., *stehen vor der Tür* with plural subjects), but this entry focuses on the exact form *steht vor der Tür*.
target_language_example: Halloween steht vor der Tür, also sollten wir alles vorbereiten.
native_language_example: Halloween is just around the corner, so we should prepare everything.

additional_notes:
Used to say that something is being offered for sale (e.g., a house, apartment, furniture). You conjugate the verb: 
- Das Auto steht zum Verkauf. (The car is for sale.)
- Die Autos stehen zum Verkauf. (The cars are for sale.)
Also common on signs/ads: „Zum Verkauf“ = “For sale”.
target_language_example: Dieses Fahrrad steht zum Verkauf.
native_language_example: This bicycle is for sale.

additional_notes: Imperative form of "einsteigen" (to get in/board). Used to tell someone to get into a car, taxi, bus, etc. Very common with urging words like "komm" or "los". You can also say "Steigen Sie ein!" for formal/polite.
target_language_example: Steig ein, wir fahren jetzt los.
native_language_example: Get in, we're leaving now.

meaning: formal command: “get on/in”, “get off/out”, “change/transfer”, or “mount/climb onto”.
additional_notes: “Steigen Sie …” is the polite/standard imperative with Sie (used for strangers and in announcements). The exact meaning usually comes from a separable prefix or preposition: **steigen Sie ein** = get in/on (a car/train/bus), **steigen Sie aus** = get out/off, **steigen Sie um** = change/transfer (trains/buses), **steigen Sie auf** (e.g., *auf das Pferd*) = mount/climb onto. Often used with places like *an der nächsten Haltestelle/Station* (“at the next stop/station”).
target_language_example: Steigen Sie hier ein und steigen Sie an der nächsten Station um.
native_language_example: Get on here and transfer at the next station.

meaning: “Get in.” / “Step in.” (polite command, e.g. into a car/boat/train).
additional_notes: Polite imperative using Sie (formal “you”). Comes from the separable verb einsteigen (“to get in/board”): in commands, the prefix splits off → steigen … ein. Commonly used when inviting or ordering someone to enter a vehicle (car, taxi, boat, train) or sometimes a room.
target_language_example: Bitte steigen Sie ein, der Zug fährt gleich ab.
native_language_example: Please get in; the train is leaving soon.

additional_notes: Du-imperative of **sich stellen** (“to stand/position oneself”). Very common with a place: **Stell dich da vorne hin.** / **Stell dich an die Wand.** / **Stell dich in die Schlange.** With a thing/person (dative) it can mean “face/confront”: **Stell dich der Sache!** Note: **Stell dich mal an!** comes from **sich anstellen** and is often colloquial for “Don’t make such a fuss / stop acting so difficult” (context decides whether it’s “line up” or “make a fuss”).
target_language_example: Stell dich bitte in die Schlange.
native_language_example: Please get in line.

additional_notes: Imperative of the separable verb „sich vorstellen“ (to imagine). Used to ask someone to picture a situation: „Stell dir vor, du wärst …“. It can also be an exclamation meaning “Guess what!” or “Can you believe it?”—often said on its own: „Stell dir vor!“
target_language_example: Stell dir vor, wir gewinnen morgen das Spiel!
native_language_example: Imagine we win the game tomorrow!

additional_notes: Imperative of (sich) etwas vorstellen (“to imagine”). Very common to introduce a hypothetical situation or a surprising story: “Stell dir vor, …”. Often followed by a comma and a full clause. You can also say “Stell dir das mal vor!” = “Just imagine that!”
target_language_example: Stell dir vor, morgen ist schon Urlaub!
native_language_example: Imagine it—tomorrow is already vacation!

meaning: polite command form of „stellen“: “(please) put/place/set …” (and in some fixed phrases: “connect” / “make sure”).
additional_notes:
„Stellen Sie …“ is the formal (Sie) imperative. Very common with locations: „Stellen Sie die Eier in den Kühlschrank.“ (= put/place). Also appears in set phrases:
- „jemanden zu … durchstellen“ = to put someone through (on the phone)
- „Stellen Sie sicher, dass …“ = make sure that …
- „wegstellen“ (often as „Stellen Sie … weg!“) = put away.
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, stellen Sie bitte sicher, dass das Fenster zu ist.
native_language_example: Excuse me, please make sure the window is closed.

additional_notes: This uses the formal imperative with **Sie** (used with strangers, customers, etc.). **stellen** often means to place something somewhere in an upright/positioned way, and it commonly appears with a location phrase: **auf** (+ accusative) = onto, **ins** (= in das, + accusative) = into, **dorthin/dahin zurück** = back there.
target_language_example: Stellen Sie das Buch bitte zurück ins Regal.
native_language_example: Please put the book back on the shelf.

additional_notes:
This is the polite command form (Sie) of **sich stellen**. It’s usually completed with a place or a prefix verb:
- **Stellen Sie sich an.** = Queue up.
- **Stellen Sie sich (in einer Reihe) auf.** = Line up.
- **Stellen Sie sich vor.** = Introduce yourself / Imagine (depending on context).
So **stellen Sie sich** by itself often feels unfinished; you typically add **an/auf/vor** or a location.
target_language_example: Stellen Sie sich bitte hierhin.
native_language_example: Please stand here.

additional_notes: Used with Sie (formal “you”). Very common as an invitation to imagine a scenario: “Stellen Sie sich vor, …” = “Imagine (that) …”. It can also mean “Introduce yourself” (e.g., at a meeting or interview): “Bitte stellen Sie sich vor.” In the “imagine” meaning, it’s often followed by a whole clause (with commas), and can also be used with “wie” (“how/what it’s like”): “Stellen Sie sich vor, wie …”.
