additional_notes: Used to say something happened repeatedly. Often appears with verbs like „wiederholen“ (repeat), „treffen“ (meet), „erlauben“ (allow), or in passive sentences („ist … gebeten worden“). You can also intensify it: „so viele Male, wie nötig“ = “as many times as necessary.”
target_language_example: Ich habe dich schon viele Male angerufen.
native_language_example: I’ve called you many times already.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a large number of people in general (not specific individuals). Often the subject of a sentence. Note: "Menschen" means "people/humans" (not just "men").
target_language_example: In der Stadt sind heute viele Menschen unterwegs.
native_language_example: There are many people out and about in the city today.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has many difficulties, troubles, or issues. Often appears with verbs like haben (to have), bereiten (to cause someone problems), and sich um ... kümmern (to take care of/deal with).
target_language_example: Wir haben im Moment viele Probleme mit dem Computer.
native_language_example: We have a lot of problems with the computer at the moment.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "sprechen" (to speak) or "können" (to be able to) to say someone speaks/knows many languages. The adjective "viele" changes depending on case and gender (e.g., "viele Sprachen" in nominative/accusative; "in vielen Sprachen" = in many languages).
target_language_example: Sie spricht viele Sprachen, aber Deutsch lernt sie gerade erst.
native_language_example: She speaks many languages, but she’s only just starting to learn German.

additional_notes: Used to say there are a lot of stars. "Viele" is the plural form meaning "many/a lot of"; "Sterne" is the plural of "Stern" (star). Common with "es gibt" (there are): "Es gibt viele Sterne."
target_language_example: Heute Nacht sieht man viele Sterne.
native_language_example: Tonight you can see many stars.

additional_notes: Used to say something takes/lasts many hours, often emphasizing that it’s a long time. Common with verbs like "dauern" (to last), "warten" (to wait), and "brauchen" (to need).
target_language_example: Ich habe viele Stunden für die Hausaufgaben gebraucht.
native_language_example: I needed many hours for the homework.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how much time you spend doing something each day. "viele Stunden" describes a duration (many hours). "am Tag" is short for "an dem Tag" and often means "a day / per day" in this kind of time expression (similar to "pro Tag"). Common pattern: "Ich + verb + [viele Stunden] + am Tag."
target_language_example: Ich arbeite viele Stunden am Tag.
native_language_example: I work many hours a day.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how much time someone spends regularly (e.g., working, studying, training). Often appears with verbs like „arbeiten“, „lernen“, „trainieren“: „Ich arbeite viele Stunden pro Woche.“ You’ll also commonly see it in questions: „Wie viele Stunden pro Woche …?“
target_language_example: Ich arbeite viele Stunden pro Woche.
native_language_example: I work many hours per week.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a large number of days in general (often without giving an exact number). In questions, it commonly appears as "wie viele Tage ...?" = "how many days ...?". You’ll often see it with a relative clause: "viele Tage, an denen ..." = "many days on which ...".
target_language_example: Ich war viele Tage unterwegs.
native_language_example: I was traveling for many days.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a large quantity of coffee, focusing on the number of cups. After quantities like "viele", the noun is plural ("Tassen"). "Kaffee" is often used without an article here and means "(of) coffee"—similar to saying "cups of coffee" in English.
target_language_example: Ich trinke jeden Tag viele Tassen Kaffee.
native_language_example: I drink many cups of coffee every day.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to emphasize variety within a large number: "viele verschiedene Ursachen" (= many different causes, not just many causes). The adjective "verschieden" changes ending like other adjectives depending on the noun phrase (e.g., "viele verschiedene Sorten", "viele verschiedenen Sorten" in some contexts).
target_language_example: In der Klasse gibt es viele verschiedene Sprachen.
native_language_example: There are many different languages in the class.

meaning: "many are" (talking about many people or things).
additional_notes: Used when „viele“ (“many”) is the subject and the verb is „sein“ (“to be”) in the plural: „Viele sind …“. It’s commonly followed by an adjective („Viele sind nicht einverstanden.“), a place/situation („Viele sind im Urlaub.“), or a past participle („Viele sind hier umgekommen.“). Often refers to people, but it can also refer to things depending on context.
target_language_example: Viele sind heute krank.
native_language_example: Many are sick today.

meaning: Thank you very much; many thanks.
additional_notes: A common, polite way to express strong thanks. Often used on its own ("Vielen Dank!") or with an addressee ("Vielen Dank, Beatrice."). You can also say "Habt vielen Dank!" to thank a group (using "ihr").
target_language_example: Vielen Dank für deine Hilfe!
native_language_example: Thank you very much for your help!

meaning: "thank you very much for" / "many thanks for".
additional_notes: Used to thank someone for a thing, help, or action, followed by a noun or pronoun: „Vielen Dank für deine Hilfe.“ For a whole clause, you often use „Vielen Dank dafür, dass …“ (e.g., „Vielen Dank dafür, dass du gekommen bist.“).
target_language_example: Vielen Dank für Ihre Nachricht.
native_language_example: Thank you very much for your message.

additional_notes: Used with time expressions to mean “for many years / many years ago.” Common patterns: „seit vielen Jahren“ = for many years (since many years ago, continuing to now); „vor vielen Jahren“ = many years ago; „nach so vielen Jahren“ = after so many years. Note the dative plural: „in/seit/vor/nach vielen Jahren“.
target_language_example: Ich wohne seit vielen Jahren in Berlin.
native_language_example: I’ve been living in Berlin for many years.

additional_notes: Dative plural of **viele Leute** (“many people”). You often see **vielen Leuten** after dative prepositions like **mit** (with), **von** (by/from), or in set patterns like **aus wie vielen Leuten besteht ...?** (“how many people is ... made up of?”). **Leuten** is the dative plural form of **Leute**.
target_language_example: Ich spreche jeden Tag mit vielen Leuten.
native_language_example: I talk to many people every day.

additional_notes: Used when the noun phrase is in the dative plural, often after prepositions like in/aus/mit/zu: „in vielen Ländern“ (in many countries), „aus vielen Ländern“ (from many countries), „mit vielen Ländern“ (with many countries). In questions you often see „wie vielen Ländern…?“ = „in how many countries…?“
target_language_example: In vielen Ländern gibt es unterschiedliche Traditionen.
native_language_example: In many countries there are different traditions.

additional_notes: A common, polite way to thank someone. You can say it on its own, add a name ("Vielen Dank, John."), or use it with „für“ + noun to say what you’re thanking them for ("Vielen Dank für Ihre Empfehlung."). Often followed by a response like „Gern geschehen.“
target_language_example: Vielen Dank für Ihre Hilfe!
native_language_example: Thank you very much for your help!

meaning: “Thank you very much for …” (followed by a clause).
additional_notes: Used to thank someone for a specific action, with the reason expressed in a full sentence after „dass“ (that). Often followed by past tense: „dass Sie/du … gemacht haben/hast“. Choose „Sie“ for formal and „du“ for informal situations.
target_language_example: Vielen Dank, dass Sie mir so schnell geantwortet haben.
native_language_example: Thank you very much for replying so quickly.

meaning: “Thank you very much for…” (polite/formal, addressing “you” as Sie).
additional_notes: Used to thank someone politely and introduce a reason with dass + a full clause. Common in formal situations or when speaking to someone you don’t know well (e.g., a customer, a neighbor, an older person). After „dass“, the verb goes to the end of the clause: „…dass Sie gekommen sind.“
target_language_example: Vielen Dank, dass Sie sich so viel Zeit genommen haben.
native_language_example: Thank you very much for taking so much time.

meaning: “Thank you very much that …” / “Thank you very much for … (doing something).”
additional_notes: Used to thank someone for a specific action, followed by a full clause introduced by „daß“ (older spelling; today usually spelled „dass“). Often followed by perfect tense for something already done („… daß du gewartet hast“) or present tense for something ongoing („… daß du mir hilfst“). Can be used with formal „Sie“ or informal „du/ihr“ depending on the rest of the sentence.
target_language_example: Vielen Dank, daß Sie mir geholfen haben!
native_language_example: Thank you very much for helping me!

additional_notes: Used to express strong thanks for a specific thing. It’s followed by a noun/pronoun (often in the accusative), e.g. für deine Hilfe, für alles, für die Einladung. In speaking you’ll also hear the shorter “Danke für …”; “Vielen Dank” is a bit more formal/polite.
target_language_example: Vielen Dank für deine Zeit und deine Geduld.
native_language_example: Thank you very much for your time and your patience.

additional_notes: Used in polite/formal situations when addressing one person with “Sie/Ihr” (e.g., in emails, at events, to customers/strangers). It is usually followed by a noun: Vielen Dank für Ihre Einladung / Ihre Unterstützung / Ihre Zeit. For informal “you,” use: „Vielen Dank für deine …“.
target_language_example: Vielen Dank für Ihre Zeit und Ihre Hilfe.
native_language_example: Thank you very much for your time and your help.

additional_notes: Used to warmly thank someone for something that belongs to them or that they did. It’s followed by a feminine noun in the singular (e.g., deine Hilfe, deine Unterstützung) or a plural noun (e.g., deine Kommentare, deine Fragen). Because it uses deine (du-form), it’s for friends, family, classmates, etc. (Formal would be: „Vielen Dank für Ihre …“).
target_language_example: Vielen Dank für deine Hilfe!
native_language_example: Thank you very much for your help!

meaning: "Thanks a lot for the ..." (feminine noun or plural).
additional_notes: A very common, polite way to thank someone. It’s typically followed by a noun phrase in the accusative (e.g., die Hilfe, die Unterstützung, die schnelle Antwort). Use it in emails and everyday speech. With masculine/neuter nouns you change "die" to "den/das" (e.g., Vielen Dank für den Anruf / für das Geschenk).
target_language_example: Vielen Dank für die Einladung!
native_language_example: Thanks a lot for the invitation!

meaning: in many respects; in many ways.
additional_notes: Used (almost always with the preposition "in") to say that something is true from several different angles/aspects: "in vielerlei Hinsicht". Common in more formal or written German. The noun "Hinsicht" means "respect/aspect" (not "insight").
target_language_example: In vielerlei Hinsicht war die Reise ein Erfolg.
native_language_example: In many respects, the trip was a success.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause with an unspecified set of things: "vieles" = "a lot / many things" (neuter). It’s commonly followed by a clause with "was ich ..." (what/that I ...), e.g., "Vieles, was ich sage, stimmt". The verb usually comes at the end of the relative clause.
target_language_example: Vieles, was ich heute gelernt habe, war neu für mich.
native_language_example: Many things that I learned today were new to me.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a guess or uncertainty about yourself, often followed by an adjective or description (e.g., „zu streng“, „älter“). Word order matters: because „Vielleicht“ comes first, the verb comes second: „Vielleicht bin ich …“ (not *„Vielleicht ich bin …“). In speech/writing, it’s often shortened to „Vielleicht bin ich’s…“ (= „Vielleicht bin ich es…“). Particles like „ja“ can be added ("maybe, actually"): „Vielleicht bin ich ja …“.
target_language_example: Vielleicht bin ich heute einfach müde.
native_language_example: Maybe I’m just tired today.

additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty about something you (might) have done or a situation that (might) be true. Very commonly followed by a past participle to form the present perfect: “Vielleicht habe ich es vergessen” = “Maybe I forgot (it).”
target_language_example: Vielleicht habe ich die E-Mail schon geschickt.
native_language_example: Maybe I already sent the email.

additional_notes: Used to guess or say you’re not sure. After "vielleicht", German keeps the verb in 2nd position, so you get "Vielleicht hat er ...". It’s often followed by a past participle (Perfekt): "Vielleicht hat er es vergessen" (= maybe he forgot it).
target_language_example: Vielleicht hat er keine Zeit gehabt.
native_language_example: Maybe he didn’t have time.

additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty or possibility. “Vielleicht” often comes first in the sentence; then the verb “ist” (is) comes next, followed by the subject (word order: Vielleicht + ist + Subject + …). You can use it with any subject: Vielleicht ist er müde. / Vielleicht ist es wahr.
target_language_example: Vielleicht ist es morgen kalt.
native_language_example: Maybe it’ll be cold tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to speculate or soften a statement. It’s often followed by a noun or clause: "Vielleicht ist das nur eine Illusion" (“Maybe that’s just an illusion”). Word order is normal German main-clause order with the verb in position 2 ("ist"). In speech you may also hear the contraction "Vielleicht ist’s das …".
target_language_example: Vielleicht ist das die beste Lösung.
native_language_example: Maybe that's the best solution.

additional_notes: Used to guess or speculate about a man’s situation/identity/state. Often followed by an adjective, a place, or a noun: *vielleicht ist er zu Hause* (maybe he’s at home), *vielleicht ist er ein Spion* (maybe he’s a spy). Can also appear as a tentative question in speech/writing (sometimes with a question mark) to suggest a possibility.
target_language_example: Vielleicht ist er krank und kommt später.
native_language_example: Maybe he’s sick and will come later.

additional_notes: Used to suggest a possible explanation or guess about a situation. Often followed by a noun or phrase ("Vielleicht ist es das Alter"), a place/time phrase ("im Koffer", "zu früh"), or an expression like "an der Zeit" (= time to...). You can also negate it: "Vielleicht ist es nicht ..." (= maybe it’s not ...).
target_language_example: Vielleicht ist es besser, wenn wir morgen darüber sprechen.
native_language_example: Maybe it’s better if we talk about it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to express a possibility about what you are able to do, often as a tentative offer to help. The modal verb comes early: "Vielleicht kann ich dir helfen" (literally: "Maybe can I help you"). You can add "ja" to sound more tentative or encouraging: "Vielleicht kann ich ja helfen."
target_language_example: Vielleicht kann ich dir später beim Umzug helfen.
native_language_example: Maybe I can help you with the move later.

meaning: “maybe you can …” (a polite, tentative suggestion or request).
additional_notes: Used to soften a request or suggestion and make it sound less direct. It’s often followed by an infinitive verb at the end: „Vielleicht kannst du mir helfen?“ / „Vielleicht kannst du morgen vorbeikommen?“ In more polite/formal situations you can also say „Vielleicht könnten Sie …“ (to a stranger) or „Könntest du vielleicht …?“
target_language_example: Vielleicht kannst du mir heute Abend kurz helfen?
native_language_example: Maybe you can help me briefly tonight?

additional_notes: Used to suggest an idea gently or politely, often when making plans, offering help, or proposing a solution. It can be followed by an infinitive (e.g., helfen, reden, zusammenarbeiten) or a full clause.
target_language_example: Vielleicht können wir morgen darüber sprechen.
native_language_example: Maybe we can talk about it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to make a suggestion gently and politely. It often introduces an idea without sounding too direct, and is commonly followed by a time/activity (e.g., Freitag, morgen, dieses Wochenende, zusammen lernen). Verb order: in a main clause with "vielleicht" first, the conjugated verb comes second: "Vielleicht könnten wir …".
target_language_example: Vielleicht könnten wir nach der Arbeit einen Kaffee trinken.
native_language_example: Maybe we could have a coffee after work.

additional_notes: Used to make a gentle suggestion about your own actions (often with a verb in the infinitive at the end): „Vielleicht sollte ich + Infinitiv …“ (e.g., „… lernen/gehen/anrufen“). „sollte“ is Konjunktiv II of „sollen“ and sounds softer/less definite than „ich soll“.
target_language_example: Vielleicht sollte ich heute früher ins Bett gehen.
native_language_example: Maybe I should go to bed earlier today.

additional_notes: Used to soften advice or a recommendation. Grammatically, it’s often **sollten** (Konjunktiv II of **sollen**) + infinitive: **Vielleicht sollten wir gehen.** You can use it with different subjects: **Vielleicht sollten Sie … / Vielleicht sollten wir … / Vielleicht sollten sie …**.
target_language_example: Vielleicht sollten wir später noch einmal darüber sprechen.
native_language_example: Maybe we should talk about it again later.

additional_notes: Used to give advice or make a gentle recommendation in a polite/formal way. "Sie" is the formal "you" (to a stranger, customer, older person, etc.). Word order: "Vielleicht sollten Sie + infinitive" (e.g., "… anrufen", "… warten", "… hingehen").
target_language_example: Vielleicht sollten Sie den Arzt anrufen.
native_language_example: Maybe you should call the doctor.

meaning: maybe we should… / perhaps we should…
additional_notes: Used to make a gentle suggestion for what the group ("we") should do. "sollten" is the subjunctive form of "sollen" and often sounds like English "should" (a recommendation, not a strict obligation). It’s commonly followed by an infinitive at the end of the clause: "Vielleicht sollten wir gehen."
target_language_example: Vielleicht sollten wir morgen früher losfahren.
native_language_example: Maybe we should leave earlier tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to give advice in a soft, non-direct way. It’s formed from "vielleicht" (maybe) + "solltest" (you should, subjunctive of "sollen") + "du" (you). Often followed by an infinitive at the end of the clause: "Vielleicht solltest du mit ihr reden."
target_language_example: Vielleicht solltest du morgen früher ins Bett gehen.
native_language_example: Maybe you should go to bed earlier tomorrow.

meaning: "maybe you (all) should" (a suggestion/advice to a group).
additional_notes: Used to politely suggest what a group of people ("ihr" = you plural/informal) should do. "Solltet" is Konjunktiv II of "sollen" and softens the advice (less direct than "ihr sollt"). Often followed by an infinitive at the end: "... fragen/arbeiten/unterhalten/nachdenken".
target_language_example: Vielleicht solltet ihr früher losfahren, wenn es regnet.
native_language_example: Maybe you should leave earlier if it’s raining.

meaning: “four eyes”; usually refers to a private one-on-one talk (in the phrase „unter vier Augen“).
additional_notes: Most often used as part of „unter vier Augen“ (= literally “under four eyes”), meaning only two people are present and you speak privately/confidentially. On its own, „vier Augen“ is just the literal “four eyes.”
target_language_example: Können wir das kurz unter vier Augen besprechen?
native_language_example: Can we discuss that briefly in private (just the two of us)?

additional_notes: Usually said as **„unter vier Augen sprechen“** (“to speak under four eyes”), meaning only two people are present and the conversation is confidential. Often used when you want to discuss something sensitive without others listening.
target_language_example: Können wir kurz unter vier Augen sprechen?
native_language_example: Can we talk in private for a moment?

additional_notes: Used to say a duration (how long something lasts: „dauerte vier Jahre“), a frequency (how often: „alle vier Jahre“ = every four years), or an age (how old someone was: „vier Jahre alt“ = four years old). With time expressions, German often uses the accusative without a preposition for duration (e.g., „Er lebte vier Jahre dort.“).
target_language_example: Ich habe vier Jahre in Berlin gelebt.
native_language_example: I lived in Berlin for four years.

additional_notes: Used to say someone’s age. With "sein" (ist) it describes a current age; with "werden" (wird/werde) it means turning four (on a birthday). Often used with "schon" (already) or "erst" (only).
target_language_example: Mein Neffe ist vier Jahre alt.
native_language_example: My nephew is four years old.

additional_notes: Used with certain time expressions that take the dative plural "Jahren" (from "Jahr"). Common patterns: "mit vier Jahren" = at the age of four; "seit vier Jahren" = for/since four years (still continuing); "vor vier Jahren" = four years ago.
target_language_example: Ich lerne seit vier Jahren Deutsch.
native_language_example: I’ve been learning German for four years.

additional_notes: Used to say a duration or time span. Often appears as an accusative time expression answering “How long?” (e.g., „vier Tage im Bett“, „vier Tage durch/ lang“), or in time clauses like „vier Tage, nachdem …“ (“four days after …”).
target_language_example: Wir bleiben nur vier Tage in Berlin.
native_language_example: We’re only staying four days in Berlin.

meaning: four-leaf clover (a symbol of good luck).
additional_notes: Literally “four-leaf clover.” Used when talking about luck, lucky charms, or something rare and fortunate. Grammar note: it’s an adjective + noun; as a standalone noun phrase you’ll also see it with an article (e.g., „ein vierblättriges Kleeblatt“).
target_language_example: Ich habe ein vierblättriges Kleeblatt gefunden.
native_language_example: I found a four-leaf clover.

meaning: "fourth mistress" / "fourth wife (in rank)" (a form of address).
additional_notes: Used to address a woman who is the fourth-ranked wife/concubine in a household (often in historical or fictional settings with multiple wives). It’s a respectful title + ordinal number (erste/zweite/dritte/vierte Herrin). In modern everyday German, this is unusual; you’ll mostly see it in period dramas, novels, or translations.
target_language_example: Vierte Herrin, der Tee ist fertig.
native_language_example: Fourth Mistress, the tea is ready.

meaning: “fourth sister” (used as a form of address).
additional_notes: Used to address a woman who is considered the “fourth sister” within a group (e.g., sisters in a family or community), where “fourth” reflects her rank/order among the sisters. Often used directly when speaking to her (like a title/name), so you may see it with a comma: „Vierte Schwester, …“.
target_language_example: Vierte Schwester, kannst du kurz hierherkommen?
native_language_example: Fourth sister, can you come here for a moment?

additional_notes: An adverbial phrase used to emphasize total agreement, full dedication, or full availability. Common with verbs like „zustimmen“ (agree) and the expression „jdm. voll und ganz zur Verfügung stehen“ (to be fully at someone’s disposal/available).
target_language_example: Ich unterstütze dich dabei voll und ganz.
native_language_example: I fully support you in that.

additional_notes: Usually used with the preposition phrase **mit vollem Mund** (“with a full mouth”), especially in warnings or rules like **Nicht mit vollem Mund sprechen!** (“Don’t talk with your mouth full!”). **vollem** is the dative form of **voll** because it follows **mit** (mit + dative).
target_language_example: Sprich bitte nicht mit vollem Mund.
native_language_example: Please don’t talk with your mouth full.

additional_notes: Used with forms of "sein" (to be) or "sich fühlen" (to feel) to describe someone’s mood/condition. Grammatically it’s "voll" + genitive: "voller" is the common form before a noun ("voller Energie", "voller Freude").
target_language_example: Nach dem Kaffee bin ich wieder voller Energie.
native_language_example: After the coffee, I’m full of energy again.

additional_notes: Used with sein: „X ist/sind vom Aussterben bedroht“ = X could disappear completely. Common in news and nature contexts when talking about species/animals (Art, Tiere). Past: „war/waren vom Aussterben bedroht“.
target_language_example: Viele Insektenarten sind vom Aussterben bedroht.
native_language_example: Many insect species are endangered.

additional_notes: "vom" = "von dem" and is used for movement/starting point away from a place. Often used with verbs like "abfahren" (depart), "kommen" (come), "gehen" (go), and in distance/time phrases like "vom Bahnhof zur Schule" (from the station to the school). Also appears in "vom Bahnhof aus" = "starting from the station".
target_language_example: Vom Bahnhof aus sind es nur zehn Minuten zu Fuß bis zum Hotel.
native_language_example: From the train station, it’s only a ten-minute walk to the hotel.

additional_notes: "vom" = "von dem" (from the). Used with movement away from a tree, often when someone/something falls or takes something off it (e.g., apples). Common with verbs like "fallen" (to fall) or "(etwas) stehlen/pflücken" (to steal/pick).
target_language_example: Die Katze sprang vom Baum herunter.
native_language_example: The cat jumped down from the tree.

additional_notes: Literal meaning: someone falls down from a tree (often with details like kopfüber/kopf voran = headfirst). It can also be used idiomatically as a slightly rude comment meaning someone is acting clueless/crazy/out of touch (similar to “Were you dropped on your head?”), depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: Das Kind ist vom Baum gefallen, aber zum Glück ist nichts passiert.
native_language_example: The child fell from the tree, but luckily nothing happened.

additional_notes: Used for something/someone hit by a lightning strike, often in the passive: „X wurde vom Blitz getroffen.“ (X was struck by lightning). You’ll also hear the related idiom „wie vom Blitz getroffen“ meaning “as if struck by lightning” (suddenly shocked/surprised).
target_language_example: Der Baum wurde letzte Nacht vom Blitz getroffen.
native_language_example: The tree was struck by lightning last night.

additional_notes: „vom“ = contraction of „von dem“ (dative). Most often used with movement or action verbs to show someone/something ends up off the roof: „(vom Dach) springen“ (jump off), „(vom Dach) stoßen“ (push off), „sich (vom Dach) stürzen“ (throw oneself off), „jdn. (vom Dach) kriegen“ (get someone off the roof). In some contexts, „vom Dach“ can also mean “about the roof” with verbs like „halten von“ (= think of), e.g. „Was haltet ihr vom Dach?“ = “What do you think of the roof?”
target_language_example: Die Katze ist vom Dach gefallen.
native_language_example: The cat fell off the roof.

additional_notes: "vom" is a common contraction of "von dem" (dative). Use it to talk about a starting point (e.g., traveling from the airport) or where someone/something is picked up ("jemanden vom Flughafen abholen"). It can also mean “of the airport” in contexts like "ein Foto vom Flughafen" (= a photo of the airport).
target_language_example: Wir nehmen ein Taxi vom Flughafen zum Hotel.
native_language_example: We’re taking a taxi from the airport to the hotel.

additional_notes: Contraction of „von dem Himmel“. Used literally with verbs like „fallen“ (to fall) or „kommen“ (to come): „vom Himmel fallen/kommen“ = to fall/come from the sky. Also appears in the common idiom „das Blaue vom Himmel versprechen“ = to promise the impossible / make unrealistic promises.
target_language_example: Plötzlich fielen große Tropfen vom Himmel.
native_language_example: Suddenly big drops fell from the sky.

meaning: 'off the horse' / 'from the horse' (i.e., from on top of a horse).
additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement or accidents to describe leaving the horse: e.g. fallen/stürzen/geworfen werden (fall off/be thrown off) or steigen (get off). It’s the contraction of „von dem Pferd“ and refers to movement away from the horse’s back.
target_language_example: Nach dem Ausritt stieg sie vom Pferd.
native_language_example: After the ride, she got off the horse.

meaning: to fall off a chair (often because of laughing hard or being shocked).
additional_notes: Literally means “(to have) fallen from the chair.” Often used with **fast** (“almost”) to show something nearly happened: **…dass er fast vom Stuhl gefallen wäre** (“…that he would have almost fallen off his chair”). In the past tense it commonly uses **sein**: **Ich bin vom Stuhl gefallen.**
target_language_example: Ich musste so lachen, dass ich fast vom Stuhl gefallen wäre.
native_language_example: I laughed so hard that I almost fell off my chair.

meaning: from the beginning; right from the start.
additional_notes: Used to say something was true or happened starting at the very beginning and continuously since then (often with verbs like sagen, wissen, verstehen, klar sein). It can also emphasize that there was no change later: it was already like that at the start.
target_language_example: Ich wusste von Anfang an, dass das nicht klappt.
native_language_example: I knew from the beginning that it wouldn’t work.

meaning: from beginning to end; all the way through.
additional_notes: Used to say something is told, read, watched, or done completely, without skipping any parts. Often goes with verbs like erzählen (tell), lesen (read), ansehen (watch).
target_language_example: Wir haben den Film von Anfang bis Ende gesehen.
native_language_example: We watched the movie from beginning to end.

additional_notes: Used when you mean talking/meeting directly with someone, not by phone, email, etc. Often used with verbs like sprechen (talk) or sich treffen (meet). It can also describe two people standing directly opposite each other ("face to face").
target_language_example: Lass uns das lieber von Angesicht zu Angesicht klären.
native_language_example: Let’s clear this up face to face (in person).

additional_notes: Used in the passive voice to say who did the abducting: **von** + dative (agent) + **entführen** (“to abduct/kidnap”). Common full forms: **Er wurde von Außerirdischen entführt.** (simple past passive) / **Er ist von Außerirdischen entführt worden.** (perfect passive).
target_language_example: Sie behauptet, sie sei von Außerirdischen entführt worden.
native_language_example: She claims she was abducted by aliens.

meaning: from scratch; completely/from the ground up.
additional_notes: Used to say something is learned, built, redone, or changed thoroughly and fundamentally (not just small improvements). Common with verbs like lernen, aufbauen, überarbeiten, verändern.
target_language_example: Wir haben die Website von Grund auf neu aufgebaut.
native_language_example: We rebuilt the website from scratch.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s inherent traits or original background/training (what they are “from the start”). Often used with professions or characteristics: "Er ist von Haus aus Ingenieur" (He’s an engineer by training/originally), "Sie ist von Haus aus sehr ruhig" (She’s naturally very calm).
target_language_example: Er ist von Haus aus Informatiker, arbeitet aber jetzt als Lehrer.
native_language_example: He’s a computer scientist by training, but now he works as a teacher.

additional_notes: Used to say something is meant genuinely and with strong feeling (often gratitude, wishes, apologies, or concern). Common with verbs like „danken“ (Ich danke dir/Ihnen von Herzen) or phrases like „Es muss von Herzen kommen“ to emphasize sincerity.
target_language_example: Ich wünsche dir von Herzen alles Gute.
native_language_example: I sincerely wish you all the best.

additional_notes: Polite/formal way to say "from you" when addressing one person formally or more than one person formally. "Von" takes the dative, so the pronoun is "Ihnen".
target_language_example: Ich habe lange nichts von Ihnen gehört.
native_language_example: I haven't heard from you in a long time.

von Ihnen sagen, was passiert ist

target_language_multi_word_term: von Ihnen sagen, was passiert ist
meaning: (Can) one of you tell me what happened?
additional_notes: Used in questions to ask someone from a group (“von Ihnen” = “one of you” in formal/polite address) to explain what happened (“was passiert ist”). Often appears as: „Kann mir jemand/irgendjemand von Ihnen sagen, was passiert ist?“ Variants like „irgendwer/wer“ are more casual than „jemand“.
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, kann mir jemand von Ihnen sagen, was passiert ist?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can one of you tell me what happened?

meaning: from year to year; year by year (gradually over time).
additional_notes: Used to describe something that changes gradually as time passes, typically increasing or decreasing each year. Often appears with verbs like „steigen“ (rise/increase), „sinken“ (fall/decrease), „sich erhöhen“ (increase), or „sich verbessern“ (improve).
target_language_example: Die Situation wird von Jahr zu Jahr besser.
native_language_example: The situation is getting better year by year.

additional_notes: Used to say a quality is natural/inborn rather than learned or caused by outside influence. Often appears with verbs like „sein“ (to be) or „können“ (can): „Er ist von Natur aus ruhig.“
target_language_example: Ich bin von Natur aus neugierig.
native_language_example: I’m naturally curious.

additional_notes: Means doing something again from the beginning, often after it ended or failed. Common with verbs like beginnen (start), machen (do), anfangen (begin), lesen (read). Often interchangeable with „noch einmal“, but „von Neuem“ emphasizes a fresh restart.
target_language_example: Wir müssen von Neuem anfangen.
native_language_example: We have to start over.

meaning: to be useful; to be of use.
additional_notes: A slightly formal way to say something is helpful or beneficial. Often used with a dative person (mir/dir/ihm/ihr/Ihnen/uns/euch/ihnen) and with modal verbs like „könnte/kann/wird … von Nutzen sein“. Common patterns: „etwas könnte (jemandem) von Nutzen sein“ and „für + Akk“ can also appear (e.g., „für Sie“).
target_language_example: Die Tipps könnten dir bei der Prüfung von Nutzen sein.
native_language_example: The tips could be useful to you for the exam.

meaning: from day to day; more and more with each passing day.
additional_notes: Used to say something changes gradually over time (often getting better/worse/stronger) as days pass. Common with comparatives like „besser“, „schlimmer“, „kälter“, or verbs like „wachsen“.
target_language_example: Von Tag zu Tag fühle ich mich sicherer auf Deutsch.
native_language_example: Day by day, I feel more confident in German.

meaning: from time to time; now and then; occasionally.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens sometimes, but not regularly. It often goes with the present tense for a general habit (Ich treffe ihn von Zeit zu Zeit …) or with the past to describe repeated actions in the past (Von Zeit zu Zeit blieb er stehen …). You can put it in the middle of the sentence or at the beginning for emphasis.
target_language_example: Von Zeit zu Zeit gehe ich alleine spazieren.
native_language_example: From time to time I go for a walk alone.

meaning: (all) by itself; on its own (without help).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens automatically or independently, without someone doing it or helping. Often with verbs like „gehen“, „fahren“, „fliegen“, „passieren“, „kommen“, „sich entscheiden“. In questions it can imply “without anyone doing anything?” (e.g., „Ging nicht von allein, oder?“).
target_language_example: Keine Sorge — das regelt sich von allein.
native_language_example: Don’t worry — it’ll sort itself out.

additional_notes: Used to compare one person/thing with the whole group: superlatives like der/die/das + -ste often go with it ("der größte von allen" = "the biggest of all"). It can also start the sentence: "Von allen Jungs ..." = "Out of all the boys ...".
target_language_example: Sie ist die schnellste von allen Läuferinnen.
native_language_example: She is the fastest of all the runners.

meaning: from all sides; from every direction.
additional_notes: Used to say something surrounds, comes from, or affects someone/something in every direction (physically or figuratively, e.g., “criticized from all sides”). Often used with verbs like „umgeben sein“ (to be surrounded), „angreifen“ (to attack), and „kritisieren“ (to criticize).
target_language_example: Wir wurden von allen Seiten beobachtet.
native_language_example: We were being watched from all sides.

additional_notes: Used after a superlative to mean “of all (the ones in the group)”: das beste/ billigste/ interessanteste von allen. With passive verbs like „respektiert/geliebt/gehört“, it can mean “by everyone” (agent): „Er wird von allen respektiert.“
target_language_example: Das ist der schönste Park von allen.
native_language_example: That’s the nicest park of all.

additional_notes: Used to describe something seen, done, or affecting something from the outside (often contrasted with „von innen“ = from inside). Common with verbs like „anschauen“ (look at), „verschlossen“ (locked), and in phrases like „Druck von außen“ (outside pressure).
target_language_example: Man kann das Schild von außen gut lesen.
native_language_example: You can read the sign well from outside.

meaning: from then on; from that point onward.
additional_notes: Used to mark a turning point in time: something happens, and after that moment the new situation continues. Often refers back to a specific event or point in a story (similar to "ab dann").
target_language_example: Von da an ging alles viel schneller.
native_language_example: From then on, everything went much faster.

additional_notes: Means leaving a place and going away from it. It’s a fixed, old-fashioned/literary expression (often in stories), commonly used with verbs like „ziehen“ or „(sich) machen“: „von dannen ziehen“, „sich von dannen machen“. In everyday speech you’d more often say „weggehen“, „gehen“, or „davongehen“.
target_language_example: Nach dem Streit ging er schweigend von dannen.
native_language_example: After the argument, he left in silence.

meaning: "from your" / "of your" (used with a masculine or neuter noun in the dative).
additional_notes: "von" takes the dative case. "deinem" is the dative form of "dein" for masculine/neuter nouns (e.g., von deinem Wein, von deinem Schiff). It’s used for source/origin ("ein Schluck von deinem Wein"), talking about something/someone related to you ("etwas von deinem Traum" = something about your dream), and with some verbs/phrases like "abhängen von" ("hängt von deinem Erfolg ab" = depends on your success) or "sich befreien von" (free yourself from your curse).
target_language_example: Ich habe von deinem Plan gehört.
native_language_example: I heard about your plan.

meaning: “of/from your” (used with a feminine noun in the dative).
additional_notes: Used with the preposition **von** (“from/of”), which takes the **dative** case. **deiner** is the dative form of **dein-** (“your”) for **feminine singular** nouns (e.g., *Straße, Tasche, Wohnung*): *von deiner Straße* = “of/from your street.” It can also appear in other contexts (e.g., genitive), but after **von** it’s dative.
target_language_example: Ich habe ein Foto von deiner Wohnung gesehen.
native_language_example: I saw a photo of your apartment.

meaning: “from the” / “about the” (masculine or neuter noun, dative).
additional_notes: Contraction of "von" + "dem" (often shortened to "vom" in everyday speech). Used with "von" to express origin/source ("copies from the letter"), topic/reporting ("tell about the case"), separation/relief ("free me from the curse"), or a starting point in time ("from that moment on"). Refers to a specific masculine/neuter noun in the dative case.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir noch mal von dem Plan erzählen?
native_language_example: Can you tell me about the plan again?

additional_notes: Used with verbs like **sprechen (von)**, **hören (von)**, **erzählen (von)** to mean “about.” It takes **dative**: **von dem Unfall**. In everyday speech and writing, it’s often contracted to **vom Unfall**.
target_language_example: Tom hat mir eben von dem Unfall erzählt.
native_language_example: Tom just told me about the accident.

meaning: “of whom/which”, “about whom/which”, or “from which” (relative clause connector).
additional_notes: Used to refer back to a masculine or neuter noun (der/das) in a relative clause. It’s the contraction of “von + dem” (dative). Common with verbs like sprechen/reden von (talk about), erzählen von (tell about), and also to express “from which” or “with which” (connection/source). For feminine/plural: von der, von denen.
target_language_example: Das ist der Film, von dem ich dir gestern erzählt habe.
native_language_example: That’s the movie I told you about yesterday.

meaning: “of what” / “of that which” (referring back to a previously mentioned thing/amount, then linking it to a clause).
additional_notes: Used to connect a quantity/portion (e.g., einiges, die Hälfte, ein Teil, kein Wort, das Doppelte) to a relative clause: "[quantity] von dem, was + clause" = "[quantity] of what + clause." Grammatically, "von dem" refers back to a neuter singular idea/amount ("dem" = dative), and "was" introduces the relative clause meaning "what/that which." Common in careful, written, or neutral speech.
target_language_example: Kein Wort von dem, was Tom sagte, war wahr.
native_language_example: Not a word of what Tom said was true.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the content of what someone has said/done, often after words like nichts (nothing), vieles (a lot), einiges (some), nur (only): nichts/vieles/einiges von dem, was Sie sagen/tun/sagten. "Sie" is the formal "you" (to a stranger, customer, official, etc.).
target_language_example: Ich glaube nur wenig von dem, was Sie mir erzählt haben.
native_language_example: I only believe a little of what you told me.

meaning: "from/of what she/they …" (introduces a clause about something).
additional_notes: Used to link something to a whole idea or action described in the following clause. It commonly appears after nouns/adjectives like "das Gegenteil von …" (the opposite of …), "überrascht von …" (surprised by …), or with comparisons like "das Doppelte von …" (double of …). "sie" can mean "she" or "they" depending on context.
target_language_example: Ich war schockiert von dem, was sie gesagt hat.
native_language_example: I was shocked by what she said.

meaning: "about whom/which I" (referring back to a masculine/neuter noun).
additional_notes: Used in relative clauses to refer to something already mentioned: der/das + von dem ich ... It’s the relative pronoun (von dem) plus subject (ich), often with verbs like sprechen/erzählen: „der Junge, von dem ich gesprochen habe“ = “the boy I talked about.” For feminine/plural you use „von der ich“ / „von denen ich“.
target_language_example: Das ist das Buch, von dem ich dir erzählt habe.
native_language_example: This is the book I told you about.

meaning: “that I told you about” / “about which I told you” (formal “you”).
additional_notes: Used in a relative clause to refer back to a masculine or neuter noun (der/das) and means “about which.” Literally it’s “from which I (to) you…,” but in English you usually translate it as “that/which … about.” Grammar: “von” takes the dative case, so the relative pronoun is “dem” (not “den”). “Ihnen” is the formal dative “to you” (Sie-form). Often followed by a verb like “erzählen” (to tell).
target_language_example: Das ist der Arzt, von dem ich Ihnen gestern erzählt habe.
native_language_example: That’s the doctor I told you about yesterday.

von dem ich dir erzählt habe

target_language_multi_word_term: von dem ich dir erzählt habe
meaning: “that I told you about” (literally: “about which I told you”).
additional_notes: Used in relative clauses to refer back to a noun (person/thing) you mentioned before. You choose the form based on the noun: von dem (masculine/neuter), von der (feminine), von denen (plural). It’s common after expressions like “Das ist …,” “Der Mann …,” “Das Buch …”.
target_language_example: Das ist der Film, von dem ich dir erzählt habe.
native_language_example: That’s the movie I told you about.

meaning: 'from the' / 'of the' (used with plural or formal 'you').
additional_notes:
Combination of the preposition **von** + **den** (dative plural of **der/die/das**, or dative plural of formal **Sie**). Commonly used:
- for **partitives/selection**: *von den vier Jahreszeiten* = “of the four seasons” (among them)
- for **origin/source**: *von den Toten* = “from the dead”.
Grammar note: **von** takes the **dative**. With singular masculine/neuter you usually see the contraction **vom** (= *von dem*), but there is **no** contraction for *von den*.
target_language_example: Von den Kindern hat nur eins Zeit.
native_language_example: Of the children, only one has time.

additional_notes: Used with plural "die" to refer back to a previously mentioned group of people/things. Common uses: (1) comparison: "X unterscheidet sich von denen ..." = "X is different from those ..."; (2) partitive: "einer/eins von denen" = "one (of) those"; (3) in a relative clause: "..., von denen ..." = "..., of whom/which ...".
target_language_example: Ich kenne ein paar Leute, von denen du viel lernen kannst.
native_language_example: I know a few people you can learn a lot from.

additional_notes: Combination of von + the feminine dative article der. Most often it means movement away from or origin/source ('from the'). With some verbs and expressions, it can be closer to 'of the' or 'about the'.
target_language_example: Sie kommt gerade von der Schule nach Hause.
native_language_example: She is just coming home from school.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement to say you’re leaving work or returning home after work (e.g., „von der Arbeit nach Hause“, „von der Arbeit zurückkommen“). „von“ takes the dative case, so it’s „der Arbeit“.
target_language_example: Ich komme heute spät von der Arbeit nach Hause.
native_language_example: I’m coming home late from work today.

meaning: from the bridge / off the bridge.
additional_notes: Used with movement away from a place: **von + dative** (here: *die Brücke* → *von der Brücke*). It can mean being on the bridge as a viewpoint (*Fotos von der Brücke*) or moving/falling/jumping off it (*von der Brücke springen/stürzen*). In contexts like *sich von der Brücke stürzen*, it can refer to suicide.
target_language_example: Wir schauen uns die Stadt von der Brücke aus an.
native_language_example: We’re looking at the city from the bridge.

von der Hand in den Mund

target_language_multi_word_term: von der Hand in den Mund
meaning: living hand to mouth; living paycheck to paycheck.
additional_notes: An idiom meaning you have barely enough money for basic needs, with little or no savings (you spend what you earn right away). Used with "leben": "(von der Hand in den Mund) leben".
target_language_example: Nach der Miete bleibt uns fast nichts übrig – wir leben von der Hand in den Mund.
native_language_example: After rent, we have almost nothing left—we’re living paycheck to paycheck.

additional_notes: Used to show distance or origin relative to the coastline. Common with words like "entfernt" (away) and verbs like "liegen": "X liegt ... von der Küste entfernt" = "X is ... away from the coast." It can also describe origin: "Leute von der Küste" = "people from the coast."
target_language_example: Das Hotel liegt nur fünf Minuten von der Küste entfernt.
native_language_example: The hotel is only five minutes away from the coast.

additional_notes: Used to show that something/someone is taken from a list. Common with **(jdn./etw.) von der Liste streichen** = “to cross (someone/something) off the list / remove from the list”, and with **(etw.) von der Liste wählen** = “to choose (something) from the list.”
target_language_example: Bitte streichen Sie meinen Namen von der Liste.
native_language_example: Please remove my name from the list.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something has been removed from a list, often implying it was deleted or deliberately taken off. It’s the past participle of „von der Liste streichen“ (to cross off/remove from the list) and is commonly used in passive sentences: „Du wurdest von der Liste gestrichen“ (You were removed from the list).
target_language_example: Aus Versehen wurde ich von der Liste gestrichen.
native_language_example: I was accidentally crossed off the list.

additional_notes: Literally "von" = "from/by" and "der Polizei" = "the police" (dative). Very common in the passive to show who does the action: "wurde von der Polizei festgenommen" = "was arrested by the police". With "sein" it can mean belonging/working there: "Sind Sie von der Polizei?" = "Are you with the police?"
target_language_example: Er wurde von der Polizei kontrolliert.
native_language_example: He was checked by the police.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "kommen" (to come), "anrufen" (to call), etc. to mean someone/something is coming or contacting you from the school ("ein Anruf von der Schule"). With "abgehen" it means leaving school / dropping out. With nouns like "Abwesenheit" it means being absent from school ("Abwesenheit von der Schule").
target_language_example: Meine Schwester ist heute von der Schule nach Hause gekommen.
native_language_example: My sister came home from school today.

additional_notes: Used to describe going/being on the way from school back home. Often appears with movement or travel phrases like "auf dem Weg ..." (on the way), and verbs like "gehen" (go/walk), "kommen" (come), "fahren" (go/drive). "von" + dative: "von der Schule" (from the school); "nach" + dative: "nach Hause" (to home).
target_language_example: Ich gehe jeden Tag von der Schule nach Hause.
native_language_example: I go home from school every day.

meaning: from the street/road; off the street/road.
additional_notes: Used with movement/change-of-position verbs to show something/someone moving away from the street/road (often with runter: runter von der Straße! = Get off the road!). Also used to show distance/position relative to a road: einige Meter von der Straße entfernt = a few meters away from the road. With picking something up: von der Straße aufheben = pick up from the street.
target_language_example: Runter von der Straße, da kommt ein Auto!
native_language_example: Get off the road, a car is coming!

additional_notes: Used to say where someone/something is coming from. "von" takes the dative case, so "die Universität" becomes "von der Universität" (often shortened in speech to "von der Uni"). "Uni" is a very common, slightly informal short form for "Universität" (like English "uni").
target_language_example: Ich komme gerade von der Uni.
native_language_example: I’m just coming from the university.

meaning: from the wall; off the wall.
additional_notes: Used to say something moves/comes away from a wall, or is removed/taken down from a wall. Common with verbs like (ab)prallen (to bounce off), entfernen (to remove), and abnehmen/nehmen (to take down/off).
target_language_example: Kannst du das Bild von der Wand nehmen?
native_language_example: Can you take the picture off the wall?

meaning: of/about the world; from the world.
additional_notes: Literally “from the world.” Often used with verbs like **(etw.) von der Welt tilgen/verbannen** (“to wipe/banish (something) from the world”). It’s also common after nouns/verbs to mean “about the world,” e.g. **eine Vorstellung von der Welt** (“an idea of the world”), **(viel) von der Welt sehen/wissen** (“to see/know (a lot) of the world”).
target_language_example: Sie will mehr von der Welt sehen.
native_language_example: She wants to see more of the world.

meaning: from the other side of the (…)
additional_notes: Used to describe something located or happening on the opposite side of something. It’s followed by a noun in the genitive case: des + masculine/neuter noun (e.g., des Flusses, des Parks). With a feminine or plural noun, it becomes: von der anderen Seite der (e.g., der Straße, der Berge).
target_language_example: Wir hören Musik von der anderen Seite des Flusses.
native_language_example: We can hear music from the other side of the river.

meaning: "of this" / "from this" (referring to a masculine/neuter noun).
additional_notes: Used with the preposition "von" + dative to show origin, source, or relation: "von diesem Dokument" = "of/from this document". "Diesem" is the dative form of "dieser" for masculine/neuter nouns; for feminine/plural you’ll see "von dieser" / "von diesen".
target_language_example: Ich brauche eine Kopie von diesem Vertrag.
native_language_example: I need a copy of this contract.

additional_notes: Combination of the preposition "von" + "dir" (dative of "du"). Common uses: (1) origin/source: "eine Antwort von dir" = an answer from you; (2) topic: "von dir erzählen / von dir reden" = talk about you; (3) depends on: "Das hängt von dir ab" = That depends on you; (4) distance from: "weit weg von dir" = far away from you; (5) separation: "sich von dir verabschieden" = say goodbye to you.
target_language_example: Das hängt ganz von dir ab.
native_language_example: That depends entirely on you.

meaning: “(I/we) expect/require (from) you to …” (introduces what is expected of you).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like **erwarten** (to expect) or **verlangen** (to demand): **[Verb] von dir, dass du + Nebensatz**. The **dass**-clause explains the expectation/requirement, and the verb in the **dass**-clause goes to the end: *… dass du pünktlich **bist***.
target_language_example: Ich erwarte von dir, dass du pünktlich bist.
native_language_example: I expect you to be on time.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "träumen" (to dream). The structure is "von + dative" (here: "von dir" = about you) plus the past participle "geträumt" in the perfect tense: "Ich habe von dir geträumt." Word order can change with time phrases: "Letzte Nacht habe ich von dir geträumt."
target_language_example: Ich habe letzte Nacht von dir geträumt.
native_language_example: I dreamed about you last night.

additional_notes: Used to describe the origin or starting point of something (where someone/something comes from, escapes from, speaks from, etc.). Refers to a place that’s already known from context (dort = “there”). Often contrasts with "von hier" (“from here”).
target_language_example: Wir kommen später von dort zurück.
native_language_example: We’ll come back from there later.

additional_notes: von takes the dative case, so ein becomes einem here. It is often used for the doer in passive sentences (for example, 'von einem Hund angegriffen' = 'attacked by a dog'), but depending on context it can also mean 'of a/an' or sometimes 'about a/an'.
target_language_example: Sie wurde von einem Arzt untersucht.
native_language_example: She was examined by a doctor.

meaning: "from a car" (sometimes "by a car" in passive sentences).
additional_notes: "von" + dative ("einem Auto") often means origin/source ("from a car"). In passive constructions it can indicate the agent/cause, similar to English "by": e.g., "Er wurde von einem Auto angefahren" = "He was hit by a car."
target_language_example: Er wurde von einem Auto angefahren.
native_language_example: He was hit by a car.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "werden" to form the passive: "jemand wird von einem Auto angefahren" = someone gets hit by a car. "fast" adds “almost/nearly”: "fast von einem Auto angefahren". Common in accident/news contexts; "anfahren" means to hit/knock someone down with a vehicle.
target_language_example: Der Mann wurde gestern Abend von einem Auto angefahren.
native_language_example: The man was hit by a car last night.

meaning: (to) have been hit/struck by a car.
additional_notes: This is the passive past form of **anfahren** (“to hit/strike (someone) with a vehicle”). It’s built with **werden**: *jdn. anfahren* → *von einem Auto angefahren werden* (present passive) → *von einem Auto angefahren worden* (“have/was been hit by a car”). **von + dative** names who/what caused it (*von einem Auto*, *von einem Bus*). Often appears with **fast / beinahe** (“almost”) or in the conditional: **wäre … angefahren worden** (“would have been hit”).
target_language_example: Sie ist gestern auf dem Zebrastreifen fast von einem Auto angefahren worden.
native_language_example: Yesterday she was almost hit by a car at the crosswalk.

meaning: to be run over by a car.
additional_notes: Passive-style phrase: "von" + dative marks the agent (who/what does it). Often used for accidents: "Er wurde von einem Auto überfahren." You can replace "einem Auto" with another vehicle (z.B. "von einem Bus").
target_language_example: Der Hund wurde von einem Auto überfahren.
native_language_example: The dog was run over by a car.

additional_notes: Used to say the source/origin of something (a letter, help, money, a borrowed item) is a friend. It can also mark the doer in passive sentences: "Sie wurde von einem Freund betrogen" = "She was cheated on/by a friend."
target_language_example: Ich habe das Buch von einem Freund bekommen.
native_language_example: I got the book from a friend.

meaning: from another planet (often said jokingly: very strange / out of touch).
additional_notes: Literally refers to extraterrestrials (“aliens from another planet”). In everyday speech it can also be used humorously to say someone’s idea or behavior seems so odd that they must be “from another planet.” Used with verbs like kommen (“to come”): „Kommst du von einem anderen Planeten?“
target_language_example: Die Idee ist so komisch – bist du von einem anderen Planeten?
native_language_example: That idea is so weird—are you from another planet?

meaning: "from a" / "by a" (referring to a feminine noun, dative).
additional_notes: Used with feminine singular nouns in the dative case: von + einer + [feminine noun]. Often means "from" (origin/source: von einer Freundin) or "by" in the passive voice (agent: von einer süßen Kellnerin begrüßt). Common feminine nouns: die Freundin, die Universität, die Person, die Brücke, die Kellnerin.
target_language_example: Ich habe den Tipp von einer Kollegin bekommen.
native_language_example: I got the tip from a (female) colleague.

additional_notes: Used in the passive to say someone received a bee sting. Common patterns: „Wurdest du (schon mal) von einer Biene gestochen?“ (Were you ever stung by a bee?) and „Ich bin von einer Biene gestochen worden.“ (I was stung by a bee).
target_language_example: Ich bin gestern im Garten von einer Biene gestochen worden.
native_language_example: I was stung by a bee in the garden yesterday.

additional_notes: Uses the informal plural pronoun euch ('you all'). With von, it often means 'of you' in expressions like einige von euch ('some of you'), after judgments like nett von euch ('nice of you'), or after nouns to show possession, as in Freunde von euch ('friends of yours'). Formal equivalent: von Ihnen.
target_language_example: Einige von euch sprechen schon gut Deutsch.
native_language_example: Some of you already speak German well.

meaning: 'of you two' / 'from the two of you'.
additional_notes: Used when speaking to two people (euch = you [plural, informal]) and referring to one or both of them. Common with questions like "Wer/Was/Wie viele von euch beiden ...?" or with "eine/einer von euch beiden" (= one of you two).
target_language_example: Kann einer von euch beiden mir kurz helfen?
native_language_example: Can one of you two help me for a moment?

meaning: with all my/your/one’s heart; sincerely, wholeheartedly.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize deep, genuine feelings (thanks, love, wishes, dedication). Often appears with verbs like danken (to thank), lieben (to love), wünschen (to wish), and widmen (to dedicate). The pronoun is usually understood from context (e.g., 'Ich danke dir …' = 'with all my heart').
target_language_example: Wir gratulieren euch von ganzem Herzen.
native_language_example: We congratulate you with all our hearts / wholeheartedly.

additional_notes: Often used after a noun to mean it belongs to yesterday: „die Sendung von gestern“ = “yesterday’s show”, „die Eier von gestern“ = “the eggs from yesterday”. In expressions like „Der/die … von gestern!“ it can mean someone is behind the times (similar to “yesterday’s man/woman”).
target_language_example: Hast du noch das Brot von gestern?
native_language_example: Do you still have yesterday’s bread?

meaning: to be very useful; to be of great use.
additional_notes: Used to say something will help a lot. Often appears with a dative pronoun/person (mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/Ihnen): „Das wird dir von großem Nutzen sein.“ More formal-sounding than simply „(sehr) nützlich sein“. Commonly used in the future with „wird … sein“, but can be used in other tenses too.
target_language_example: Die Tipps werden uns bei der Prüfung von großem Nutzen sein.
native_language_example: The tips will be very useful for us in the exam.

additional_notes: Used to say something starts/leaves/moves away starting at this location (e.g., a train departs from here). With verbs like „verschwinden/weggehen/gehen“ it means leaving this place: „Ich verschwinde von hier“ = “I’m getting out of here.”
target_language_example: Kannst du mich von hier aus sehen?
native_language_example: Can you see me from here?

meaning: from here; from where we are (starting from this point).
additional_notes: Used to talk about what you can see/hear/reach starting from your current location. Often with verbs like sehen (see), hören (hear), erkennen (make out), erreichen (reach). It can also be used more generally for “from this standpoint,” but most commonly it’s literally about physical location.
target_language_example: Von hier aus kannst du den Bahnhof in fünf Minuten zu Fuß erreichen.
native_language_example: From here, you can reach the train station on foot in five minutes.

meaning: "From here, you can …" (literally: "from here, one can …").
additional_notes: Used to say what is possible or visible from a particular place. "von hier aus" means "from here / from this spot" (with the idea of a starting point), and "man" is the general/impersonal "you/one" (not a specific person). Often followed by a verb like "sehen" (to see): "Von hier aus kann man … sehen."
target_language_example: Von hier aus kann man die Berge gut sehen.
native_language_example: From here, you can see the mountains well.

meaning: 'from here to' (describing a distance, travel time, or cost).
additional_notes: Used with a destination that usually follows (often introduced by nach/zu/in), e.g. "von hier bis nach Berlin", "von hier bis zum Bahnhof", "von hier bis in die Stadt". Common in questions about how far it is, how long it takes, or how much it costs to get somewhere.
target_language_example: Wie lange dauert es von hier bis zum Bahnhof?
native_language_example: How long does it take from here to the train station?

meaning: "from here to ..." (indicating a range or distance).
additional_notes: Used to describe a span from the speaker’s current location (hier) to an endpoint introduced by "zu" (often a place, sometimes a point in time/extent). Common with distances and routes: "von hier bis zu + place".
target_language_example: Von hier bis zum Bahnhof sind es zehn Minuten zu Fuß.
native_language_example: From here to the train station, it’s a ten-minute walk.

additional_notes: A distance/direction phrase: von + place (dative) + bis zu(m) + destination (dative). Often used when asking or telling how long it takes (e.g., „Wie lange braucht man …?“ / „Es dauert …“), frequently with „zu Fuß“ (on foot). „zum" = „zu dem" (masculine/neuter); with feminine destinations you’ll see „bis zur …“ (zu der).
target_language_example: Wie lange dauert es zu Fuß von hier bis zum Bahnhof?
native_language_example: How long does it take on foot from here to the train station?

meaning: 'away from here' (at a distance from this place).
additional_notes: Used to say how far something is from where you are now. Very common with distances (e.g., „zwei Kilometer von hier entfernt“) and with „(nicht) weit“: „nicht weit von hier entfernt“ = not far from here. Often appears with „sein“: „X ist … von hier entfernt.“
target_language_example: Die Apotheke ist nur fünf Minuten zu Fuß von hier entfernt.
native_language_example: The pharmacy is only a five-minute walk away from here.

meaning: to get out of here; to leave quickly (often urgently).
additional_notes: Literally “to disappear from here.” Used to tell someone to leave a place, often because it’s dangerous, unwanted, or time to go. Common with müssen/sollten (e.g., „Wir müssen/sollten von hier verschwinden.“). Can sound strong as an order, especially with an exclamation mark.
target_language_example: Es wird gleich Ärger geben—wir müssen von hier verschwinden.
native_language_example: There’s going to be trouble any minute—we have to get out of here.

additional_notes: Used to describe movement or an approach coming from behind someone/something (often with verbs like „kommen“, „sich anschleichen“, „sich heranschleichen“). It can also mean doing something starting from the back side. In some contexts (e.g., talking about sex), „von hinten“ can mean “from behind” in a sexual position and may sound suggestive.
target_language_example: Pass auf — jemand kommt von hinten!
native_language_example: Watch out—someone’s coming from behind!

additional_notes: Uses the preposition "von" + dative pronoun "ihm" (him). Common meanings: (1) source/origin: "Ich habe es von ihm erfahren." = I found out from him; "ein Brief von ihm" = a letter from him. (2) topic: "von ihm sprechen/erzählen" = talk/tell about him. (3) sometimes with passive/"lassen": "sich von ihm küssen lassen" = let him kiss you.
target_language_example: Ich habe das Geschenk von ihm bekommen.
native_language_example: I got the gift from him.

additional_notes: Used with a thing you receive: "etwas von ihm bekommen" (e.g., eine Antwort, einen Brief, ein Geschenk). Word order changes in questions: "Hast du ... von ihm bekommen?". "bekommen" here means "receive/get" (not "become").
target_language_example: Ich habe gestern eine Nachricht von ihm bekommen.
native_language_example: I received a message from him yesterday.

meaning: heard from him; heard any news about/from him.
additional_notes: Used with hören + von (+ dative) to ask/report whether you’ve had any contact or information. Very common in the pattern „(etwas) von jemandem hören“ = to hear from someone / to hear something about someone (news, updates). Often used with time expressions like „in letzter Zeit“ (lately).
target_language_example: Ich habe seit Wochen nichts von ihm gehört.
native_language_example: I haven't heard from him in weeks.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition **von** + dative plural pronoun **ihnen** (“them”). It can mean **from them** (source: *Wir hörten es von ihnen.*) or **of them** (belonging/responsibility: *ein Fehler von ihnen* = “a mistake of theirs”). Also appears in polite phrases like **Das war recht von Ihnen!** (“That was very kind of you!”), where **Ihnen** is the formal “you” (capitalized).
target_language_example: Ich habe es von ihnen erfahren.
native_language_example: I found out about it from them.

meaning: from her; of her (away from her).
additional_notes: "von" + dative pronoun "ihr" (her). Often marks the source/origin (e.g., a message coming from her): "eine Antwort von ihr" = "an answer from her". It’s also used in some fixed verb phrases to mean “away from her,” e.g. "den Blick von ihr lassen" = "to take your eyes off her."
target_language_example: Ich habe heute eine Nachricht von ihr bekommen.
native_language_example: I got a message from her today.

additional_notes: Used to say that she is the source/giver of something. Very common with objects: „Ich habe das von ihr bekommen.“ = “I got that from her.” In questions: „Hast du was von ihr bekommen?“ = “Did you get anything from her?” Grammar tip: „von“ takes the dative case → „ihr“ (her, dative).
target_language_example: Ich habe die Nachricht von ihr bekommen.
native_language_example: I got the message from her.

meaning: heard from her; heard about her.
additional_notes: Past form of the verb phrase „von jemandem hören“. It can mean (1) getting news/updates from someone (“hear from her”) or (2) hearing information about someone (“hear about her”). Often used with „nichts“: „Ich habe nichts von ihr gehört“ = “I haven’t heard from/about her.”
target_language_example: Ich habe seit Wochen nichts von ihr gehört.
native_language_example: I haven’t heard from her in weeks.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition **von** + **dative**. **ihrem** is the dative form of **ihr** (“her/its”), used with **masculine or neuter nouns** (e.g., *von ihrem Großvater*, *von ihrem Können*). **von + dative** can show (1) where something comes from (*from*), (2) what someone is distracted from, and very often (3) the agent in the passive (*by*): *Sie wurde von ihrem Chef angeschrien.*
target_language_example: Sie war von ihrem Ergebnis überrascht.
native_language_example: She was surprised by her result.

additional_notes: Uses **von** (+ dative) to show who something comes from or who is involved. **ihrem** is dative of **ihr** (“her”). **Freund** can mean either “friend” or “boyfriend” depending on context. Also used with verbs like **(sich) trennen von** (“to separate/break up with”). Word order can vary: *ein Geschenk von ihrem Freund* or *von ihrem Freund ein Geschenk*.
target_language_example: Sie hat das Buch von ihrem Freund bekommen.
native_language_example: She got the book from her boyfriend/friend.

additional_notes: "von" takes the dative case, so "ihrer" is the dative form of "sie" as a possessive meaning "her" or "their" (feminine singular noun or plural noun). It’s used for origin/source ("von ihrer neuen Arbeit erzählen" = talk about her new job), cause/experience ("bewegt von ihrer Freundlichkeit" = moved by her kindness), opinion/assessment ("halten von ihrer Entdeckung" = think of her discovery), and in passive-like meaning with people ("von ihrer Großmutter großgezogen" = raised by her grandmother).
target_language_example: Ich habe das Geschenk von ihrer Schwester bekommen.
native_language_example: I got the gift from her sister.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens/works from the inside of a room, building, object, or body. Very common with doors/locks: "von innen geöffnet/verschlossen/aufschließen" = opened/locked/unlocked from the inside (not from the outside). Also used figuratively: "Schönheit kommt von innen" = beauty comes from within.
target_language_example: Die Fenster lassen sich nur von innen öffnen.
native_language_example: The windows can only be opened from the inside.

additional_notes: Used to mark a change that begins at the present moment and continues into the future. Often followed by a present or future statement (e.g., with "musst", "wirst", or simple present in German).
target_language_example: Von jetzt an gehe ich jeden Tag zu Fuß zur Arbeit.
native_language_example: From now on, I’m walking to work every day.

meaning: from a very young age; since childhood.
additional_notes: Used to say something has been true since someone was little (habits, upbringing, character traits). Often with "schon": "schon von klein auf" = "since I/they were little".
target_language_example: Ich spiele schon von klein auf Klavier.
native_language_example: I’ve played the piano since I was very young.

additional_notes:
Used with the preposition **von** + **dative** to mean:
- **source/origin**: *von meinem Freund* = from my friend
- **possession/connection** (often like “of”): *ein Bild von meinem Wagen* = a picture of my car
- **topic** after verbs like **erzählen (von)**, **sprechen (von)**: *von meinem Problem* = about my problem
**meinem** is the dative form of **mein** for **masculine or neuter singular** nouns. (Feminine: *von meiner*; plural: *von meinen*.)
target_language_example: Kannst du mir von meinem Urlaub erzählen?
native_language_example: Can you tell me about my vacation?

additional_notes: Used with the preposition **von** (+ dative) to show a starting point or reference point: distance **from** your house, directions **from** your house, or location relative to it. Often appears with **aus** (e.g., **von meinem Haus aus**) meaning “starting from my house / from where my house is.” (Note: **von dem** is often shortened to **vom**, but with **meinem** you keep **von meinem**.)
target_language_example: Von meinem Haus aus dauert es nur zehn Minuten bis zum Bahnhof.
native_language_example: From my house, it only takes ten minutes to get to the train station.

meaning: "from my son" / "about my son" (depending on the verb).
additional_notes: Uses **von + dative** (**meinem Sohn** is dative). With some verbs it means **from** (source/origin): *Ich habe das von meinem Sohn.* = “I got that from my son.” With other verbs it means **about** (topic): *Sprich nicht von meinem Sohn.* = “Don’t talk about my son.” It can also appear in set patterns like **enttäuscht von** (“disappointed with/by”).
target_language_example: Ich habe das Geschenk von meinem Sohn bekommen.
native_language_example: I got the gift from my son.

meaning: by my father; from my father.
additional_notes: Uses **von + dative** (mein Vater → **meinem Vater**). Often means **“by”** to name the doer in the **passive** (Das Haus wurde von meinem Vater gestrichen = “The house was painted by my father”). It can also mean **“from”** to show the source/origin, e.g. a gift or something you received (ein Geschenk von meinem Vater = “a gift from my father”), or authorship (ein Buch von meinem Vater = “a book by my father”).
target_language_example: Der Brief ist von meinem Vater.
native_language_example: The letter is from my father.

additional_notes: "von" takes the dative case, so it becomes "von meiner" before a feminine noun (e.g., "von meiner Mutter", "von meiner Freundin"). It can mean (1) origin/source: "I got it from my…", (2) distance/avoidance with verbs like "sich fernhalten": "Stay away from my…", and (3) “of” in expressions like "überzeugt von": "convinced of my…". In "von ... sprechen", it means “talk about …”.
target_language_example: Ich habe den Rat von meiner Mutter bekommen.
native_language_example: I got the advice from my mother.

meaning: from my mother / by my mother; about my mother.
additional_notes: “von” + dative (“meiner Mutter”) is used in a few common ways: (1) origin/possession: “Fotos von meiner Mutter” = photos of/from my mother; “Briefe von meiner Mutter” = letters from my mother. (2) agent in the passive: “ist von meiner Mutter benutzt worden” = was used by my mother. (3) topic: “so von meiner Mutter reden” = talk about my mother like that. In speech, “Von meiner Mutter, ja.” can be a short confirming answer (“From my mother, yes.”).
target_language_example: Das Geschenk ist von meiner Mutter.
native_language_example: The gift is from my mother.

meaning: to tell (someone) about my trip; to report on my trip.
additional_notes: Used with a person in the dative (mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen) and the topic with **von + dative**: *jemandem von etwas berichten*. You can make it more polite or more forceful with **Lassen Sie mich …** (formal) / **Lass mich …** (informal singular) / **Lasst mich …** (informal plural).
target_language_example: Nach dem Urlaub möchte ich meinen Freunden von meiner Reise berichten.
native_language_example: After the vacation, I’d like to tell my friends about my trip.

additional_notes: A common phrase with von + the dative pronoun mir. It usually shows source or origin: something comes from you, was given by you, or was borrowed from you. In some contexts, especially passive-style expressions, it can also mean "by me".
target_language_example: Das Geschenk ist von mir.
native_language_example: The gift is from me.

meaning: “fine by me” / “as far as I’m concerned” (I don’t mind).
additional_notes: Used to give permission or show indifference/acceptance: “Okay, if that’s what you want.” It can also widen an option: “on Monday, or (if you prefer) on Tuesday.” Often sounds slightly reluctant depending on tone (similar to “if you insist”).
target_language_example: Von mir aus können wir auch später anfangen.
native_language_example: Fine by me—we can also start later.

meaning: from morning to evening; all day long.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something lasts the whole day, typically with the idea of working or doing something continuously from the morning until the evening. Often paired with verbs like arbeiten (to work) or lernen (to study).
target_language_example: Ich habe heute von morgens bis abends gelernt.
native_language_example: I studied today from morning to evening (all day long).

additional_notes: Used to say that something will change and be true or happen beginning at this moment and continuing into the future. Often followed by a present or future idea: "Von nun an mache/werde ich ..." It can appear at the start of the sentence for emphasis.
target_language_example: Von nun an esse ich kein Fleisch mehr.
native_language_example: From now on, I won't eat meat anymore.

meaning: from above; (figuratively) from higher authority (“from the top”).
additional_notes: Used literally for physical position or movement (e.g., looking/hearing from a higher place, ‘von oben nach unten’ = from top to bottom). Figuratively it means an instruction/order coming from superiors (e.g., ‘ein Befehl/eine Anordnung von oben’ = an order from higher up). Often contrasts with ‘von unten’ (from below).
target_language_example: Von oben sieht die Stadt ganz anders aus.
native_language_example: From above, the city looks completely different.

meaning: from above (downwards); condescendingly (“looking down on someone”).
additional_notes: Used as an adverb phrase. Literally describes something moving/falling down from above: „Ein Stein fiel von oben herab.“ Figuratively, it describes an arrogant, patronizing attitude—often with verbs like „jemanden von oben herab behandeln/anschauen“ (“to treat/look at someone condescendingly”).
target_language_example: Er sprach von oben herab mit den neuen Kollegen.
native_language_example: He spoke condescendingly to the new colleagues.

additional_notes: "von" + dative. "seinem" is the dative form of "sein" (= his) for masculine/neuter nouns (e.g., von seinem Text, von seinem Motorrad). Used for: (1) origin/source or “a (photo/picture) of his …”, (2) separation/movement away (e.g., getting off something), (3) being impressed/affected by something, and (4) asking an opinion: "Was hältst du von seinem …?"
target_language_example: Ich habe viel von seinem neuen Projekt gehört.
