native_language_example: I’ve heard a lot about his new project.

meaning: from his father; (in passive) by his father.
additional_notes: "von" + dative shows the source/origin of something (e.g., inheriting or taking over something from someone). It can also name the agent in a passive sentence: "Er ist von seinem Vater ..." = "He was ... by his father." (Here: "seinem Vater" is dative masculine; the base form is "sein Vater".)
target_language_example: Er hat das Haus von seinem Vater geerbt.
native_language_example: He inherited the house from his father.

meaning: "from his" / "of his" (used before a plural noun).
additional_notes: "von" is a preposition that usually takes the dative case. "seinen" is the dative plural form of "sein" (his), used with plural nouns (often masculine/neuter in dative plural). Common uses: source/origin ("von seinen Händen" = from his hands), belonging/selection ("eines von seinen Autos" = one of his cars), and fixed patterns like "abhängig von seinen …" (dependent on his …) or "leben von seinen …" (live on/from his …).
target_language_example: Sie bekommt Hilfe von seinen Freunden.
native_language_example: She gets help from his friends.

meaning: from his parents; by his parents (as the source/origin).
additional_notes: Uses the preposition „von“ + dative to express source/origin or dependence/separation (e.g., „abhängig/unabhängig von …“, „getrennt von …“). „seinen“ is masculine/neuter dative plural possessive here and changes with person/gender/number (e.g., „von ihren Eltern“, „von seiner Mutter“).
target_language_example: Er ist völlig von seinen Eltern abhängig.
native_language_example: He is completely dependent on his parents.

additional_notes: Uses dative plural after "von" (Freunden). In passive sentences, "von" often marks the doer/agent = "by" ("Er wurde von seinen Freunden ausgelacht" = "He was laughed at by his friends"). In other contexts it can mean origin/source = "from" ("Hilfe von seinen Freunden" = "help from his friends").
target_language_example: Er hat das Geschenk von seinen Freunden bekommen.
native_language_example: He got the present from his friends.

meaning: "about his" / "of his" (von + dative; refers to something that belongs to him).
additional_notes: Used when a verb or noun takes "von" (with dative). Common patterns: **von seiner Arbeit erzählen** = talk about his job; **ein Bild von seiner Katze** = a picture of his cat. **seiner** is the dative feminine form of **sein** (“his”), used with feminine nouns like **die Arbeit**, **die Katze**, **die Vergangenheit**.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir von seiner Familie erzählen?
native_language_example: Can you tell me about his family?

meaning: from his family; of his family.
additional_notes: Uses the preposition „von“ + dative („seiner Familie“). It can mean (1) source/origin: getting something from his family („Geld von seiner Familie“), (2) belonging to a group: nobody in his family („Niemand von seiner Familie“), or (3) separation: living separated from his family („von seiner Familie getrennt“).
target_language_example: Er bekommt viel Unterstützung von seiner Familie.
native_language_example: He gets a lot of support from his family.

meaning: from his wife; (with some verbs) about his wife.
additional_notes: Uses "von" + dative: "seiner Frau" (his wife). Depending on the verb, it can mean (1) "from" (e.g., Geld von seiner Frau borgen = borrow money from his wife), (2) "separated/divorced from" (e.g., getrennt von seiner Frau; sich von seiner Frau scheiden lassen), or (3) "about" (e.g., schlecht von seiner Frau sprechen = speak badly about his wife).
target_language_example: Er hat ein Geschenk von seiner Frau bekommen.
native_language_example: He got a gift from his wife.

meaning: by/from/about his girlfriend (depending on the verb).
additional_notes: "von" + dative. Common uses: (1) In the passive, it can mark the doer/agent: "Er wurde von seiner Freundin verlassen" = "He was left by his girlfriend." (2) It can mean "from" with receiving/getting: "eine Nachricht von seiner Freundin" = "a message from his girlfriend." (3) Some verbs take "von" to mean "about/of": "träumen von" = "to dream about." "seiner" is the masculine/neuter dative form of "sein" (his).
target_language_example: Er hat eine Nachricht von seiner Freundin bekommen.
native_language_example: He got a message from his girlfriend.

meaning: “from his mother” (source/origin); sometimes “of his mother” (about/depicting her).
additional_notes: Uses "von" + dative ("seiner Mutter") to show where something comes from or who it is inherited/learned/received from: "von seiner Mutter geerbt" (inherited from his mother), "von seiner Mutter eine Tracht Prügel bekommen" (got a beating from his mother). With things like photos or stories, "von" can mean "of/about": "Fotos von seiner Mutter" = photos of his mother.
target_language_example: Ich habe das von seiner Mutter gehört.
native_language_example: I heard that from his mother.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "(jdn.) von etw. überzeugen" (to convince someone of something). Literally "from his innocence" in German structure, but in English it’s usually "of his innocence". After "von" you use the dative: "von seiner Unschuld" (masc./neut. dative), "von ihrer Unschuld" (fem. dative).
target_language_example: Die Anwältin konnte den Richter von seiner Unschuld überzeugen.
native_language_example: The lawyer was able to convince the judge of his innocence.

meaning: by itself; on its own (without help).
additional_notes: Used when something happens automatically or without anyone doing it. With people, it can mean they figured something out on their own (without being told). Often used with verbs like gehen (Das Licht ging von selbst aus.), sich schließen (Die Tür schließt sich von selbst.), or kommen (auf etwas von selbst kommen = to figure something out by oneself).
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, das Problem löst sich von selbst.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, the problem will solve itself.

meaning: from oneself; (often) out of one’s mouth / on one’s own initiative.
additional_notes: Common in set phrases. With verbs like „etwas von sich geben“ it means to say/utter something (often: to blurt something out): „Er gab einen Kommentar von sich.“ As a short answer „Von sich aus.“ means “on their own” / “of their own accord” (not because someone told them).
target_language_example: Sie hat von sich aus angerufen.
native_language_example: She called on her own initiative.

meaning: "of us" / "from us" ("one/some/how many of us"; "away from us").
additional_notes: Very common with quantities and superlatives: "einer von uns" (one of us), "einige von uns" (some of us), "wie viele von uns" (how many of us), "der Beste von uns" (the best of us). Also used with distance: "(zwei Häuser) von uns entfernt" = "(two houses) away from us". With "wissen von" it means "to know about": "Wissen sie von uns?" = "Do they know about us?"
target_language_example: Nur einer von uns hat die Antwort.
native_language_example: Only one of us has the answer.

meaning: “of the two of us” / “between the two of us” (the two people: you and me).
additional_notes: Literally “from us both.” Used to compare or refer to something involving exactly two people (usually the speaker + one other person): e.g., *Von uns beiden ist sie die Ältere* (“Of the two of us, she’s the older one”). It can also mean “between the two of us” in the sense of sharing something: *Das bleibt von uns beiden geheim* (“Let’s keep that between the two of us”).
target_language_example: Von uns beiden kann er am besten Deutsch sprechen.
native_language_example: Of the two of us, he can speak German the best.

meaning: to let us help (you/them); to allow yourself/yourselves to be helped by us.
additional_notes: Usually used with a reflexive pronoun: „sich von uns helfen lassen“ = literally “to have oneself helped by us.” Common in advice/requests (often with müssen/sollten). Conjugate „lassen“ and match the reflexive pronoun: ich lasse **mich**, du lässt **dich**, er/sie/es lässt **sich**, wir lassen **uns**, ihr lasst **euch**, Sie/sie lassen **sich**.
target_language_example: Sie müssen sich von uns helfen lassen.
native_language_example: You must let us help you.

meaning: "from our" / "of our" (with a masculine or neuter noun).
additional_notes: Used with the preposition "von" + dative. "Unserem" is the dative form of "unser" for masculine/neuter nouns (e.g., von unserem Vater, von unserem Haus). "Von" often expresses origin (from), perspective/starting point, or a relation like "of"—and in everyday German it can sometimes be used where English would use "of" or where German could also use the genitive.
target_language_example: Ich habe das von unserem Lehrer gehört.
native_language_example: I heard that from our teacher.

additional_notes: Used for physical position/direction (something comes/is seen/gets pushed from below). Often appears with a direction phrase like „von unten nach oben“ (“from bottom to top”) or with verbs like „kommen“, „stoßen“, „hoch(arbeiten)“. In some contexts it can also mean “from downstairs” (from a lower floor).
target_language_example: Der Lärm kommt von unten.
native_language_example: The noise is coming from downstairs (from below).

meaning: from the beginning; from the front.
additional_notes: Used for starting over (often with verbs like „anfangen/beginnen“: „von vorn anfangen“ = start again from the beginning). It can also mean entering/reading from the front: „von vorn rein“ (come in from the front), „von vorn lesen“ (read from the start). Common fixed phrase: „von vorn bis hinten“ = from start to finish / through and through.
target_language_example: Ich habe mich vertan—wir müssen von vorn anfangen.
native_language_example: I made a mistake—we have to start over from the beginning.

additional_notes: Used to say you start at the beginning again (e.g., after a mistake) or from the front/start of something. Common with verbs like anfangen/beginnen (to begin) and with the pattern “von vorne bis hinten” = “from front to back / from start to finish.” As an answer by itself (“Von vorne.”), it means “Start again from the beginning.”
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich habe dich nicht verstanden—kannst du bitte von vorne anfangen?
native_language_example: Sorry, I didn’t understand you—can you please start again from the beginning?

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "anfangen" or "beginnen" to say you will restart completely (not just continue where you left off). Often intensified as "ganz von vorne an" (right from the start) or combined with "noch mal / noch einmal" (again).
target_language_example: Können wir bitte von vorne an anfangen?
native_language_example: Can we please start over from the beginning?

meaning: to start over; to start again from the beginning.
additional_notes: Used when you want to restart a task, conversation, or explanation from the beginning (often because something went wrong or wasn’t understood). Commonly combined with "noch mal / noch einmal" (= again): "Können wir noch mal von vorne anfangen?"
target_language_example: Sorry, ich habe es nicht verstanden—können wir von vorne anfangen?
native_language_example: Sorry, I didn’t understand—can we start over?

meaning: "yeah right" / "as if" (used to reject what was just said or implied).
additional_notes: Very common in spoken German and informal writing. Used to express disbelief, contradiction, or sarcasm. Often comes after the word/idea you’re rejecting (e.g., "Abmachung, von wegen.") or on its own: "Von wegen!"
target_language_example: Du meinst, er kommt pünktlich? Von wegen!
native_language_example: You think he’ll be on time? Yeah right!

meaning: from a distance; from far away.
additional_notes: Used to say something is seen, noticed, or done when you are not close. Often with verbs like aussehen (to look), beobachten (to watch), grüßen (to greet), scheinen (to seem). Common pattern: „Von weitem betrachtet, ...“ = “Seen from a distance, ...”.
target_language_example: Von weitem konnte ich nicht erkennen, wer es war.
native_language_example: From a distance, I couldn't tell who it was.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition **von** to ask about the source, origin, or reference point (e.g., which platform/book/planet). **von** takes the **dative**, so it becomes **von welchem** for **masculine/neuter singular** nouns. For feminine: **von welcher**; for plural: **von welchen**.
target_language_example: Von welchem Land kommst du?
native_language_example: Which country are you from?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the person something comes from or originates with (a gift, an idea, information, etc.). It’s the combination of the preposition "von" (from) + "wem" (whom, dative). Often used alone as a follow-up question: "Von wem?" = "From who(m)?"
target_language_example: Von wem hast du die Nachricht gehört?
native_language_example: Who did you hear the news from?

meaning: "Who did you get (it) from...?" / "From whom did you...?"
additional_notes: A question starter used to ask about the source of something. It’s incomplete on its own and is typically followed by an object or past participle, e.g. "Von wem hast du das?" (Who did you get that from?) or "Von wem hast du das gehört?" (Who did you hear that from?). "von" + "wem" is dative and means "from whom".
target_language_example: Von wem hast du das Geschenk bekommen?
native_language_example: Who did you get the gift from?

additional_notes: Used for movement or origin starting at home: leaving home, coming from home, etc. It can also mean something comes from a person's home or family environment, as in habits or behavior learned at home.
target_language_example: Er kommt direkt von zu Hause.
native_language_example: He's coming directly from home.

meaning: from home; working/doing something from home.
additional_notes: Used to say you do an activity while staying at home, often with work ("von zu Hause aus arbeiten" = "to work from home"). It goes with verbs like arbeiten, lernen, telefonieren, bestellen, etc. It can be moved in the sentence like other adverbs: "Ich arbeite von zu Hause aus." / "Von zu Hause aus arbeite ich ..."
target_language_example: Ich kann heute von zu Hause aus lernen.
native_language_example: I can study from home today.

meaning: from excitement / nervousness (so that you react strongly).
additional_notes: Used to say that excitement or nervousness is the cause of a reaction (e.g., jumping up and down, not being able to sleep, barely being able to control yourself). Often appears with verbs like hüpfen, nicht schlafen können, sich kaum halten können, außer sich sein. Similar: „vor Freude“ (from joy), „vor Angst“ (from fear).
target_language_example: Ich konnte vor Aufregung kaum sprechen.
native_language_example: I could hardly speak from excitement/nervousness.

meaning: before nightfall / before it gets dark.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens earlier than the moment when darkness begins (around sunset). Common with arrival/return plans and deadlines: „Wir müssen vor Einbruch der Dunkelheit zurück sein.“ Often paired with „noch“ for emphasis: „noch vor Einbruch der Dunkelheit“ = “before it gets dark (still in time)”.
target_language_example: Lass uns vor Einbruch der Dunkelheit nach Hause gehen.
native_language_example: Let’s go home before it gets dark.

meaning: with joy; out of joy (because of happiness).
additional_notes: Used to express that someone does something because they feel very happy. Often used with strong reactions like tanzen (dance), springen (jump), lachen (laugh), weinen (cry), schreien (shout). The preposition "vor" can mean "from/out of" with feelings: vor Angst (out of fear), vor Wut (with anger).
target_language_example: Die Kinder sprangen vor Freude, als sie die gute Nachricht hörten.
native_language_example: The children jumped for joy when they heard the good news.

meaning: 'in court' / 'before a court' (in a legal case).
additional_notes: Used in legal contexts for court proceedings (not the food meaning of "Gericht"). Common with verbs like "kommen" (to end up in court), "gehen" (to go to court), and "aussagen" (to testify in court).
target_language_example: Der Zeuge muss morgen vor Gericht erscheinen.
native_language_example: The witness has to appear in court tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with feelings like "Angst haben" or "ängstlich sein": "Angst vor + dative". Here, "Hunden" is dative plural of "Hund". It means being afraid of dogs (not the literal sense of "in front of dogs").
target_language_example: Ich habe Angst vor Hunden, besonders wenn sie bellen.
native_language_example: I’m afraid of dogs, especially when they bark.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened a short time ago (in the recent past). Often placed near the verb, but it can also start a sentence for emphasis: "Vor Kurzem ...". Common in both spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Ich bin vor Kurzem nach Berlin gezogen.
native_language_example: I moved to Berlin recently.

meaning: on site; at the location (there in person).
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is physically at the place where something is happening, or where work is done (e.g., police on site, a video recorded on location). Often contrasts with doing something remotely.
target_language_example: Die Techniker sind schon vor Ort und prüfen die Anlage.
native_language_example: The technicians are already on site and are checking the system.

additional_notes: Used with feelings like "Angst" (fear), "Ekel" (disgust), or "Respekt" (respect): "Angst vor Schlangen" = "fear of snakes". Here "vor" takes the dative; plural is "Schlangen".
target_language_example: Ich habe Angst vor Schlangen.
native_language_example: I’m afraid of snakes.

meaning: "out of worry about" / "because of concern for".
additional_notes: Used to say that worry about someone or something is the reason for an action or feeling. Common pattern: "vor Sorge um + jemanden/etwas" (accusative). Example meanings: "Ich kann vor Sorge um dich nicht schlafen" = I can’t sleep because I’m worried about you.
target_language_example: Ich konnte vor Sorge um meine Tochter kaum schlafen.
native_language_example: I could hardly sleep out of worry about my daughter.

meaning: of spiders / from spiders (used after words like “fear” or “disgust”).
additional_notes: Uses the preposition **vor** (+ dative) to say what you’re afraid of or disgusted by: **Angst vor Spinnen** (fear of spiders), **Ekel vor Spinnen** (disgust at spiders). Literally **vor** means “in front of / before,” but in this context it’s best translated as “of/from.” Note: **Spinnen** (capital S) = “spiders”; **spinnen** (verb) can mean “to spin” or informally “to be crazy.”
target_language_example: Ich habe Angst vor Spinnen.
native_language_example: I'm afraid of spiders.

additional_notes: Used after certain verbs to show the reason or emotion behind a strong reaction, e.g. „zittern vor Wut“ (to tremble with rage), „kochen vor Wut“ (to be boiling with rage), „außer sich vor Wut“ (to be beside oneself with rage). It’s not about physical location; it expresses how strongly someone feels anger.
target_language_example: Sie schrie vor Wut und knallte die Tür zu.
native_language_example: She shouted with rage and slammed the door.

additional_notes: Used to highlight what is most important or the main focus. It can modify a noun phrase (often with a specific example): „Ich mag Obst, vor allem Äpfel.“ It can also be used at the start of a sentence as a discourse marker meaning “above all / first of all” to introduce the main point or a key question.
target_language_example: Vor allem im Winter ist es hier sehr kalt.
native_language_example: Especially in winter, it’s very cold here.

meaning: “in front of the” / “before the” (with masculine or neuter nouns).
additional_notes: “vor” takes the dative when it means location (where?): vor dem Kino (= in front of the cinema). It can also mean time: vor dem Sommer (= before the summer). “dem” is the dative form of “der/das” (masculine/neuter). Often used in fixed phrases like “vor dem Gesetz” (= before the law).
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns vor dem Restaurant.
native_language_example: We’ll meet in front of the restaurant.

additional_notes: Used with an action to say it happens earlier than dinner. It’s a time phrase with the preposition "vor" + dative: "vor dem" + noun (here: "Abendessen").
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte vor dem Abendessen den Müll rausbringen?
native_language_example: Can you please take out the trash before dinner?

meaning: in front of the train station.
additional_notes: A location phrase: "vor" + dative means "in front of" (outside, near the entrance). "dem" is the dative form of "der" because "Bahnhof" is masculine (der Bahnhof). Often used for meeting points or where taxis wait.
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns vor dem Bahnhof um acht.
native_language_example: We’ll meet in front of the train station at eight.

additional_notes: Literally “before the eating/meal.” Used for actions you do beforehand (often hygiene): vor dem Essen die Hände waschen. Grammar: vor + dative → dem (from das Essen). You can also use it with other nouns: vor dem Schlafengehen (before going to sleep).
target_language_example: Ich putze mir vor dem Essen die Zähne.
native_language_example: I brush my teeth before eating.

vor dem Essen die Hände waschen

target_language_multi_word_term: vor dem Essen die Hände waschen
meaning: to wash your hands before eating.
additional_notes: Used for hygiene advice or rules. Often used with modal verbs like sollten (“should”) and with dative reflexive pronouns: ich wasche mir…, du wäschst dir…, wir waschen uns…, ihr wascht euch…, Sie waschen sich… Can also be used as a polite question (e.g., Wo kann ich mir … waschen?).
target_language_example: Du solltest dir vor dem Essen die Hände waschen.
native_language_example: You should wash your hands before eating.

meaning: in front of the TV; watching TV.
additional_notes: Literally means “in front of the television.” Often used to describe where someone is sitting/lying (e.g., on the couch) and commonly implies they’re watching TV or spending time watching TV (e.g., Zeit vor dem Fernseher verbringen).
target_language_example: Ich habe gestern Abend zwei Stunden vor dem Fernseher gesessen.
native_language_example: I sat in front of the TV for two hours last night.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens earlier than breakfast (time expression). With the dative: vor + dem + Frühstück (das Frühstück). Often used with daily routines (shower, walk, take medicine, etc.).
target_language_example: Ich trinke vor dem Frühstück ein Glas Wasser.
native_language_example: I drink a glass of water before breakfast.

meaning: 'in front of the house' (outside, by the house).
additional_notes: "vor" + dative (dem Haus) describes a location in front of something. Often used for where someone/something is or stops (e.g., a bus stops in front of the house). Not to be confused with "vor das Haus" (accusative), which means movement to in front of the house.
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte vor dem Haus warten?
native_language_example: Can you please wait in front of the house?

meaning: from the rain; against the rain (protected from rain).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like „schützen“ or „sich schützen“ to say someone/something is protected from rain. It literally means “before the rain,” but in this context it means “from/against the rain.” Often paired with an object like „Schirm/Regenschirm“, „Jacke“, or „Dach“.
target_language_example: Wir haben die Fahrräder vor dem Regen untergestellt.
native_language_example: We put the bikes under cover to protect them from the rain.

meaning: before going to sleep; before bedtime.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something you do shortly before you go to bed. Often used with a regular habit (e.g., "Ich lese vor dem Schlafengehen") or a suggestion/plan ("Wollen wir ...?").
target_language_example: Ich trinke vor dem Schlafengehen noch einen Tee.
native_language_example: I drink a tea before going to sleep.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is standing/doing something in front of a mirror, often while getting ready (hair, makeup, clothes) or practicing (e.g., speaking, singing, facial expressions). It commonly goes with verbs like stehen (to stand), sich fertig machen (to get ready), üben (to practice).
target_language_example: Ich mache mich vor dem Spiegel fertig.
native_language_example: I’m getting ready in front of the mirror.

meaning: before the storm (literally); often: a calm period before trouble or intense activity.
additional_notes: Literal meaning: time before a real storm/weather event (often with verbs like Angst haben vor dem Sturm). Figurative meaning: “the calm before the storm,” i.e., a quiet moment before something stressful, dramatic, or busy begins. Grammar: vor + dative → vor dem Sturm (dem = dative of der Sturm).
target_language_example: Genieß die Pause vor dem Sturm.
native_language_example: Enjoy the break before the storm.

meaning: "of death" (e.g., fear of death); also "before death."
additional_notes: Most often used with nouns like Angst/Furcht: **Angst/Furcht vor dem Tod** = “fear of death” (here **vor** + dative expresses what you’re afraid of). It can also be used in a more general sense meaning “before death” or “in the face of death,” e.g. **Vor dem Tod sind alle gleich** (“In the face of death, everyone is equal”).
target_language_example: Viele Menschen haben Angst vor dem Tod.
native_language_example: Many people are afraid of death.

meaning: before going to bed; before bedtime.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something you do as part of your evening routine. Literally “before the going-to-bed” (vor + dem + Zubettgehen). Often pairs with habits like duschen (shower), baden (bathe), lesen (read), Zähne putzen (brush teeth).
target_language_example: Ich trinke vor dem Zubettgehen immer noch einen Tee.
native_language_example: I always drink a tea before going to bed.

meaning: in front of the; before the; from the (to protect/hide/flee).
additional_notes: “Vor” is a two-way preposition. With **Accusative** (like “vor den” = plural masculine/neuter accusative), it often shows **movement/direction** to a position in front of something (e.g., *sich vor den Spiegel stellen*). It’s also used in common patterns meaning **protection or escape from** something/someone (*schützen vor*, *fliehen vor*, *sich verstecken vor*), and it can mean **earlier than** (*vor den anderen ankommen* = arrive before the others) or **in front of others / in the presence of others** (*vor den anderen blamieren*).
target_language_example: Stell dich bitte vor den Spiegel.
native_language_example: Please stand in front of the mirror.

meaning: in front of (someone), in full view (of someone).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens while someone is watching—often emphasizing that it’s public or inappropriate (e.g., “vor den Augen der Kinder” = “in front of the children”). Typically followed by a genitive noun (vor den Augen der Familie/der Nation) or “von” + dative (vor den Augen von Gyges).
target_language_example: Er wurde vor den Augen aller verhaftet.
native_language_example: He was arrested in full view of everyone.

additional_notes: Used especially with a hand: „die Hand vor den Mund halten/nehmen“ = to cover your mouth (e.g., when coughing, sneezing, yawning, or to hide a smile). Often appears with a reflexive pronoun: „Halt dir / sich die Hand vor den Mund.“
target_language_example: Bitte halte dir die Hand vor den Mund, wenn du hustest.
native_language_example: Please cover your mouth with your hand when you cough.

additional_notes: "vor" can describe place ('in front of') or time ('before'). In these examples, "der" is the dative feminine form of 'the', as in "vor der Disko" and "vor der Wahl". After some verbs, especially "warnen vor", English often translates it less literally: "vor der Gefahr warnen" = 'warn about/against the danger'.
target_language_example: Wir warten vor der Schule.
native_language_example: We're waiting in front of the school.

additional_notes: Used to say something should happen earlier than it gets dark. With time expressions, "vor" usually takes the dative case: "vor der Dunkelheit". A common, slightly more formal variant is "vor Einbruch der Dunkelheit" (= before nightfall).
target_language_example: Wir müssen vor der Dunkelheit zu Hause sein.
native_language_example: We have to be home before dark.

meaning: to wait for someone in front of the school.
additional_notes: Used with the verb **warten**: **vor der Schule auf jemanden warten**. **vor** + dative indicates location here (in front of the school), and **auf** + accusative is required with **warten** to mark the person you’re waiting for (**auf jemanden** = for someone). You can replace **jemanden** with a pronoun or noun, e.g., **auf ihn/sie/euch/Sie** or **auf meine Freundin**.
target_language_example: Ich habe gesehen, wie du vor der Schule auf jemanden gewartet hast.
native_language_example: I saw how you waited for someone in front of the school.

meaning: in front of the door; (figuratively) just around the corner / about to happen.
additional_notes: Literal: the place immediately outside a door (often used with verbs like stehen, warten). Figurative: used with things like events or time periods to mean they’re coming very soon (e.g., Die Ferien stehen vor der Tür). You’ll often also hear it with draußen: draußen vor der Tür.
target_language_example: Ich warte kurz vor der Tür.
native_language_example: I’ll wait outside the door for a moment.

meaning: to be (standing) at the door; (figuratively) to be just around the corner / imminent.
additional_notes: Literal: someone is right outside or in front of the door (often implying they’re about to come in). Figurative: used with events or times to mean they’re coming very soon (e.g., holidays, exams: „Die Prüfung steht vor der Tür.“). Note: In the figurative use, German commonly puts the subject first ("Die Prüfung steht vor der Tür"), but the fixed term is still "vor der Tür stehen".
target_language_example: Die Prüfung wird bald vor der Tür stehen, ich muss lernen.
native_language_example: The exam will soon be just around the corner; I have to study.

meaning: in front of you; ahead of you; (figurative) still to come for you.
additional_notes: Literally describes position: something/someone is directly in front of you (often with movement: laufen vor dir). Figuratively, it can mean your future is still ahead of you: Du hast (noch) viel vor dir. Also used with some verbs to mean “of you,” especially with fear: Angst haben vor dir = “to be afraid of you” (vor + dative).
target_language_example: Keine Sorge — du hast noch alles vor dir.
native_language_example: Don’t worry — you still have everything ahead of you.

meaning: "three (units of time) ago" (used with a time word).
additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened: **vor drei Tagen / Wochen / Monaten / Jahren** = three days/weeks/months/years ago. It’s usually followed by a plural time unit in the dative case (often identical to the plural form): **vor drei Tagen**. On its own (**vor drei**) is incomplete; you normally need to add what kind of time (days, weeks, etc.).
target_language_example: Ich war vor drei Wochen in Berlin.
native_language_example: I was in Berlin three weeks ago.

additional_notes: Used with a past tense to say something happened three years before now. With "vor" + a time period (dative): vor einem Jahr, vor zwei Wochen, vor drei Monaten, etc. You can often place it at the beginning or end of the sentence.
target_language_example: Vor drei Jahren habe ich angefangen, Deutsch zu lernen.
native_language_example: Three years ago, I started learning German.

additional_notes: Used to say when and where something happened: "vor drei Jahren" = "three years ago" and "in" introduces the place (city/country). Word order is flexible, but this pattern is common: time phrase + in + place.
target_language_example: Ich war vor drei Jahren in Berlin.
native_language_example: I was in Berlin three years ago.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened a certain amount of time before now. Pattern: „vor + time (dative)“ (e.g., vor einem Jahr, vor zwei Wochen, vor drei Monaten). Often used with the simple past (Präteritum) or present perfect (Perfekt).
target_language_example: Wir sind vor drei Monaten umgezogen.
native_language_example: We moved three months ago.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened three hours before now (or before another reference time). Common with the simple past/perfect: „Ich habe … vor drei Stunden …“. You can place it at the start for emphasis: „Vor drei Stunden habe ich …“.
target_language_example: Wir haben vor drei Stunden gegessen.
native_language_example: We ate three hours ago.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happened 3 days before now (or before another reference point in the sentence). With a specific past event, German often uses simple past ("ging") or present perfect ("habe gelesen"). Pattern: "vor + time period" (vor zwei Wochen, vor einem Jahr).
target_language_example: Ich habe ihn vor drei Tagen zum letzten Mal gesehen.
native_language_example: I last saw him three days ago.

additional_notes: Time expression with **vor + dative** to say how long ago something happened. With plural time units like **Wochen**, the form stays the same in dative: **vor drei Wochen** (not *vor drei Wochens*). You can swap the number: **vor zwei Wochen**, **vor vier Wochen**, etc.
target_language_example: Wir sind vor drei Wochen umgezogen.
native_language_example: We moved three weeks ago.

additional_notes: Used with a time unit to say how long ago something happened: "vor ein paar Tagen/Wochen/Monaten/Jahren". It’s a common time expression with "vor" + a time span (past).
target_language_example: Wir sind vor ein paar Tagen umgezogen.
native_language_example: We moved a few days ago.

additional_notes: Used with "vor" + a time expression to say how long ago something happened. Often with past tense (Perfekt/Präteritum): "Ich habe/hatte … vor ein paar Minuten …". Similar patterns: "vor einer Stunde" (an hour ago), "vor zwei Tagen" (two days ago).
target_language_example: Wir haben vor ein paar Minuten angefangen.
native_language_example: We started a few minutes ago.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened a small number of days in the past. It’s a common, neutral time phrase; you can also say "vor ein paar Wochen/Monaten" (a few weeks/months ago). In speech you may also hear "vor ein paar Tage(n)"; standard German is "vor ein paar Tagen" (dative plural after "vor").
target_language_example: Wir haben uns vor ein paar Tagen gesehen.
native_language_example: We saw each other a few days ago.

additional_notes: Used to place an event in the past, typically an indefinite time around 2–5 years before now. It often answers “Wann?” (When?) and commonly goes with the simple past (Perfekt/Präteritum). Word order: it can come at the beginning or later in the sentence (e.g., “Vor ein paar Jahren habe ich …” / “Ich habe … vor ein paar Jahren …”).
target_language_example: Vor ein paar Jahren habe ich hier gewohnt.
native_language_example: A few years ago, I lived here.

meaning: '...ago' / 'a short time before' (with a masculine/neuter time expression).
additional_notes: Used with time expressions in the dative to say when something happened earlier than now: vor einem Jahr (a year ago), vor einem Monat (a month ago), vor einem Augenblick (a moment ago). For feminine nouns it becomes vor einer (vor einer Woche = a week ago), and plural is vor (vor zwei Tagen = two days ago).
target_language_example: Wir haben uns vor einem Monat kennengelernt.
native_language_example: We met a month ago.

meaning: a year ago; one year earlier (than now/then).
additional_notes: Used to say that something happened exactly one year before a reference point. Often paired with a time word like heute/gestern (e.g., heute vor einem Jahr = “this day a year ago”). Can also be used more loosely to mean “about a year ago.”
target_language_example: Heute vor einem Jahr habe ich meinen neuen Job angefangen.
native_language_example: This day a year ago, I started my new job.

additional_notes: "Vor" is a preposition that usually takes the dative case for location/time. "Vor einer" is used when the following noun is feminine (e.g., *vor einer Minute*, *vor einer Prüfung*, *vor einer schwierigen Entscheidung*). With time expressions it often means "ago" (*vor einer Weile* = "a while ago"). With events it can mean "before" (*vor einer Prüfung* = "before an exam"). With objects/situations it can mean "in front of" or "facing" (*vor einer Entscheidung stehen* = "to be facing a decision").
target_language_example: Ich war vor einer Stunde schon zu Hause.
native_language_example: I was already at home an hour ago.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened very recently in the past. Often with simple past/Perfekt: „Er war vor einer Minute hier.“ You can replace „einer Minute“ with other times: „vor zwei Minuten“, „vor einer Stunde“, etc. In contrast, „in einer Minute“ means “in one minute” (in the future).
target_language_example: Ich habe ihn vor einer Minute gesehen.
native_language_example: I saw him a minute ago.

additional_notes: Used with the dative after "vor" to say how long before now something happened. Often goes with past tense (Perfekt/Präteritum) and can come at the beginning or in the middle of the sentence.
target_language_example: Ich habe ihn vor einer Stunde gesehen.
native_language_example: I saw him an hour ago.

meaning: a week ago (one week before now/then).
additional_notes: Used with a time point in the past to say something happened one week earlier. Often with the simple past (Präteritum) or present perfect (Perfekt): „Ich habe … vor einer Woche …“. Also used with due dates/expected events: „Es war vor einer Woche fällig“ = it was due a week ago.
target_language_example: Wir sind vor einer Woche nach Berlin gezogen.
native_language_example: We moved to Berlin a week ago.

additional_notes: Used with past events to say something happened 30 minutes earlier. Often answers the question "Wann?" (When?) and is placed like a time expression: "Er ist vor einer halben Stunde gegangen." You can change the amount of time: "vor einer Stunde" (an hour ago), "vor zwei Stunden" (two hours ago).
target_language_example: Ich habe ihn vor einer halben Stunde gesehen.
native_language_example: I saw him half an hour ago.

meaning: "a few … ago" / "some … ago" (with a time expression).
additional_notes: Used with a plural time unit to say how long ago something happened: vor einigen Tagen (a few days ago), vor einigen Wochen (some weeks ago). It’s followed by dative plural: einigen Tagen, einigen Wochen.
target_language_example: Ich bin vor einigen Tagen nach Berlin gezogen.
native_language_example: I moved to Berlin a few days ago.

additional_notes: Time expression for something that happened in the past. Uses dative plural after "vor": "vor einigen Jahren" (not *vor einige Jahre*). Often used with past tense (Perfekt or Präteritum).
target_language_example: Vor einigen Jahren habe ich in Berlin gearbeitet.
native_language_example: A few years ago, I worked in Berlin.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened some months before now. It’s a time expression: vor (+ dative) + einem/einigen + time unit. Variations: „vor einem Monat“ (a month ago), „vor zwei Monaten“ (two months ago). Word order is flexible: „Ich habe ihn vor einigen Monaten gesehen.“ / „Vor einigen Monaten habe ich ihn gesehen.“
target_language_example: Vor einigen Monaten habe ich hier gewohnt.
native_language_example: A few months ago, I lived here.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened a few days in the past. Often placed at the beginning of the sentence (then the verb comes second: "Vor einigen Tagen habe ich ...") or later in the sentence ("... ist vor einigen Tagen passiert").
target_language_example: Vor einigen Tagen habe ich ihn in der Stadt gesehen.
native_language_example: I saw him in town a few days ago.

additional_notes: Used to say how long before now something happened. Often placed at the beginning of a sentence for emphasis ("Vor fünf Jahren ..."), or after the verb ("... ist vor fünf Jahren ..."). In questions it can show surprise or ask for confirmation ("Vor fünf Jahren?").
target_language_example: Vor fünf Jahren bin ich nach Berlin gezogen.
native_language_example: Five years ago I moved to Berlin.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened in the recent past. Often placed after the verb or at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis (then the verb comes second): „Vor kurzem habe ich …“.
target_language_example: Wir haben uns vor kurzem in Berlin gesehen.
native_language_example: We saw each other in Berlin recently.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened far in the past. Often placed near the beginning of the sentence for emphasis ("Vor langer Zeit ..."), or in the middle after the verb ("... ist vor langer Zeit passiert").
target_language_example: Vor langer Zeit habe ich hier gewohnt.
native_language_example: A long time ago, I lived here.

meaning: 'in front of my house' (outside, on the street side).
additional_notes: Uses the preposition "vor" (in front of) with the dative: "vor" + dative answers "where?" (location), e.g. "vor meinem Haus". For motion to a place, German often uses accusative: "vor mein Haus" (rare in everyday speech here; more common: "vor mein Haus" = to in front of my house). You can swap "meinem" for other possessives: "vor deinem Haus", "vor ihrem Haus".
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns um acht vor meinem Haus.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at eight in front of my house.

meaning: in front of me; ahead of me; (hidden) from me.
additional_notes: Literal meaning is “before me.” Used for physical position (“Tom steht direkt vor mir.” = right in front of me), for things that are coming up in time/tasks (“Ich habe eine lange Fahrt vor mir.” = I have a long drive ahead of me), and with verbs like „verstecken“ to mean keeping something from you (“etwas vor mir verstecken”). Note: „vor“ can look like English “for,” but it means “before/in front of.”
target_language_example: Ich habe heute noch viel Arbeit vor mir.
native_language_example: I still have a lot of work ahead of me today.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. With present perfect/simple past: an action happened six months ago (Ich habe vor sechs Monaten aufgehört...). With past perfect: it was already true six months ago (Ich hatte vor sechs Monaten... = I had/had had...). Not to be confused with in sechs Monaten (= in six months, from now).
target_language_example: Wir sind vor sechs Monaten nach Berlin gezogen.
native_language_example: We moved to Berlin six months ago.

meaning: ahead of (oneself); in progress/going on (especially in the phrase „vor sich gehen“ = to happen, to be going on).
additional_notes: Used with reflexive pronouns that match the subject: ich habe … vor mir, du hast … vor dir, er/sie/es hat … vor sich, wir haben … vor uns, ihr habt … vor euch, sie/Sie haben … vor sich. Common patterns: (1) „etw. vor sich haben“ = to have something ahead of you (often about the future): „Er hat eine strahlende Zukunft vor sich.“ (2) „Was geht hier vor sich?“ / „Hier geht etwas Seltsames vor sich.“ = What’s going on here? / Something strange is happening here. In these expressions, „sich“ refers back to the subject.
target_language_example: Er hat eine strahlende Zukunft vor sich.
native_language_example: He has a bright future ahead of him.

meaning: "is going on / is happening" (what’s really happening).
additional_notes: Used mostly with „was … vor sich geht“ to ask or say what is happening, often when it’s unclear or secretive: „Keiner weiß, was hier/da/hinter geschlossenen Türen vor sich geht.“ It can also be used for thoughts/feelings: „was in ihrem Kopf vor sich geht“ = what’s going on in her head. Base verb: „vor sich gehen“; in main clauses it splits: „Was geht hier vor sich?“
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht, was hier vor sich geht.
native_language_example: I don’t know what’s going on here.

additional_notes: Comes from the verb phrase „vor sich gehen“ (= to happen, to be going on). „vor sich ging“ is the simple past (Präteritum) form used in narration/writing. Very common in sentences like „… um zu sehen, was (da/dort/hier) vor sich ging.“ Often used when someone wants to find out what was happening, especially something unusual.
target_language_example: Ich lief sofort nach unten, um nachzusehen, was da vor sich ging.
native_language_example: I ran downstairs immediately to check what was going on there.

additional_notes: Used as an adverbial phrase, often in the pattern “vor sich hin + verb” to describe an action continuing quietly, absent-mindedly, or without a clear goal. Common with verbs like träumen, starren, murmeln, summen, arbeiten. Depending on the verb, English translations include “to oneself,” “away,” or “into space.”
target_language_example: Er starrte vor sich hin und sagte kein Wort.
native_language_example: He stared into space and didn’t say a word.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like pfeifen (whistle), summen (hum), reden/murmeln (talk/mumble), niesen/husten (sneeze/cough) to show the action happens in a low-key way, often without paying much attention and not directed at other people. It can also suggest something is going on continuously in the background.
target_language_example: Sie murmelte vor sich hin, während sie ihre Sachen suchte.
native_language_example: She was mumbling to herself while she was looking for her things.

additional_notes: Used with a past event to say how long ago it happened. Pattern: „vor + time period (dative)“ (e.g., vor einer Woche, vor zwei Monaten, vor sieben Jahren).
target_language_example: Ich bin vor sieben Jahren nach Berlin gezogen.
native_language_example: I moved to Berlin seven years ago.

meaning: in front of us; ahead of us.
additional_notes: Used for physical position (something is in front of you) and for what is coming in the future (what lies ahead). Also used with verbs like „sich verstecken vor …“ / „fliehen vor …“ meaning “to hide from” / “to flee from” someone (here: from us).
target_language_example: Ich sehe schon das Ziel vor uns.
native_language_example: I can already see the destination ahead of us.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened four years before now. It can go at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis (Vor vier Jahren ...) or after the verb/object (… vor vier Jahren). You can swap the number: vor zwei Jahren (two years ago), vor zehn Jahren (ten years ago).
target_language_example: Vor vier Jahren habe ich in Berlin gewohnt.
native_language_example: Four years ago, I lived in Berlin.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happened ten years before now (or before another reference point in the sentence). Often used for comparisons with the present: „… wie vor zehn Jahren“ = “…than ten years ago.”
target_language_example: Ich habe vor zehn Jahren in Berlin studiert.
native_language_example: I studied in Berlin ten years ago.

additional_notes: This is the pattern **vor + number**. With a **time period** it means **“… ago”**: *vor zwei Sekunden* = “two seconds ago”, *vor zwei Jahren* = “two years ago”. With a **point in time** (clock time, a deadline) it means **“before …”**: *vor zwei Uhr* = “before two o’clock”, *vor zwei Uhr dreißig* = “before 2:30”. With nouns it can also mean **“in front of / facing”** in some contexts, but in your examples it means “before” (time) or “two …”. The noun after *vor* is typically in the dative plural: *vor zwei Sekunden*, *vor zwei Sachen*.
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte vor zwei Uhr hier sein?
native_language_example: Can you please be here before two o’clock?

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. It’s built with **vor + time period** (e.g., *vor einem Jahr* = a year ago, *vor drei Tagen* = three days ago). The noun is in the dative after **vor** (*vor zwei Jahren*, not *vor zwei Jahre*).
target_language_example: Vor zwei Jahren bin ich nach Berlin gezogen.
native_language_example: Two years ago I moved to Berlin.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. With a past event, German often puts the time phrase first (Vor zwei Monaten habe ich …), but it can also come later (… hat vor zwei Monaten …). You can swap the number: vor drei Tagen (three days ago), vor einem Jahr (one year ago).
target_language_example: Vor zwei Monaten bin ich nach Berlin gezogen.
native_language_example: I moved to Berlin two months ago.

additional_notes: Used with the past tense to say something happened two days before now. It can appear at the start of the sentence for emphasis ("Vor zwei Tagen ...") or later in the sentence ("... vor zwei Tagen"). Related patterns: "vor einem Tag" (one day ago), "vor drei Wochen" (three weeks ago).
target_language_example: Vor zwei Tagen habe ich meinen Schlüssel verloren.
native_language_example: Two days ago I lost my key.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened two weeks before now (a point in the past). With other time amounts: vor drei Tagen (three days ago), vor einem Jahr (a year ago).
target_language_example: Wir haben uns vor zwei Wochen zum ersten Mal getroffen.
native_language_example: We met for the first time two weeks ago.

additional_notes: Used to say that something sometimes (or rarely/often) happens. Very often you’ll add an adverb like **selten** (rarely), **oft** (often), **manchmal** (sometimes): *Es kommt selten vor, dass …* = “It rarely happens that …”. The verb **vorkommen** is separable: *Es kommt … vor* + **dass**-clause.
target_language_example: Es kommt manchmal vor, dass ich den Schlüssel vergesse.
native_language_example: It sometimes happens that I forget the key.

meaning: pros and cons; advantages and disadvantages.
additional_notes: Used when weighing different options or making a decision. Usually appears as a set phrase (often with an article): "die Vor- und Nachteile". Note the hyphen in writing: "Vor- und Nachteile" stands for "Vor- und Nachteile" (= "Vorteile und Nachteile").
target_language_example: Wir sollten die Vor- und Nachteile vergleichen, bevor wir entscheiden.
native_language_example: We should compare the pros and cons before we decide.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive clause: **vorhaben, … zu + Infinitiv**. Typical pattern: **Ich habe vor, … zu + Infinitiv** (present: *habe vor*; past: *hatte vor*). It expresses an intention or plan, often not yet fixed. The *zu*-infinitive usually comes at the end of the clause; a comma is often used before the *zu*-phrase, especially when it’s longer.
target_language_example: Wir haben vorhaben zu reisen, sobald wir Urlaub bekommen.
native_language_example: We intend to travel as soon as we get vacation time.

meaning: to start over; to start from the beginning.
additional_notes: Often used with "(noch) mal" and/or "von" → "(noch) mal von vorne anfangen" = "start over again". It can refer to restarting a task/process or resetting a relationship/conversation. "von vorne" literally means "from the front/beginning."
target_language_example: Wenn wir einen Fehler gemacht haben, können wir einfach noch mal von vorne anfangen.
native_language_example: If we made a mistake, we can just start over.

meaning: to be careful; to be cautious.
additional_notes: Used to warn someone or to remind yourself to avoid danger or mistakes. Often with "bei" + noun (e.g., "beim Autofahren") or with "wenn" (when) / "damit" (so that) clauses. You can also specify what to be careful about with "vorsichtig sein, was ...".
target_language_example: Sie müssen vorsichtig sein, wenn Sie die Treppe hinuntergehen.
native_language_example: You must be careful when you go down the stairs.

meaning: to be more careful; to be more cautious.
additional_notes: Used to advise or warn someone to use more care. Often appears with modal verbs like "sollen" or "müssen": "Du solltest vorsichtiger sein" (You should be more careful), "Er muss vorsichtiger sein" (He has to be more careful). "vorsichtiger" is the comparative of "vorsichtig" (careful).
target_language_example: In Zukunft solltest du wohl etwas vorsichtiger sein.
native_language_example: In the future you should probably be a bit more careful.

meaning: “(to have) completely lost your mind” (said to someone: “Are you crazy?!”).
additional_notes: Used as a sharp, often rhetorical question to show shock, anger, or disbelief at what someone is doing or suggesting. It can sound quite rude or aggressive. Often appears with a pronoun/auxiliary: „Hast du völlig den Verstand verloren?“ / „Haben Sie völlig den Verstand verloren?“ (formal).
target_language_example: Willst du ohne Helm Motorrad fahren? Hast du völlig den Verstand verloren?
native_language_example: You want to ride a motorcycle without a helmet? Have you completely lost your mind?

additional_notes: Command telling one person to wake up. It’s the imperative of the separable verb „aufwachen“: „wach“ + „auf“. Often used with names or terms of address (e.g., „Mama“, „Schätzchen“). For more than one person, use „Wacht auf!“; formal singular „Wachen Sie auf!“
target_language_example: Wach auf, wir sind schon da!
native_language_example: Wake up, we’re already here!

additional_notes: Used in an infinitive construction with „zu“ + bleiben. Common after verbs like „versuchen“ (to try) or in purpose clauses with „um … zu …“: „Ich trinke Kaffee, um wach zu bleiben.“
target_language_example: Du musst versuchen, wach zu bleiben.
native_language_example: You have to try to stay awake.

additional_notes: Imperative of **aufwachen** (to wake up), addressed to **du** (one person you’re on first-name/"du" terms with). Can be literal (stop sleeping) or figurative ("wake up!" = pay attention/realize what’s happening). For formal or plural: **Wachen Sie auf!** (formal), **Wacht auf!** (you all).
target_language_example: Wach auf, wir sind schon spät dran!
native_language_example: Wake up, we're already running late!

meaning: to be true; to be real (actually the case).
additional_notes: Used to state or question whether something is true. Common with questions or negation: "Kann das wahr sein?" (Can that be true?), "Das kann nicht wahr sein." (That can’t be true.). In exclamations like "Das darf doch nicht wahr sein!" it expresses shock/annoyance: “This can’t be happening/This can’t be true!”
target_language_example: Kann das wahr sein?
native_language_example: Can that be true?

meaning: to come true; to become reality (said of wishes, dreams, hopes, predictions, etc.).
additional_notes: Used for wishes, dreams, hopes, predictions, plans, etc. Grammar: the verb splits in many tenses: present/future often wird ... wahr or wird ... wahr werden; past wurde ... wahr. Common with modals: kann/könnte ... wahr werden = can/could come true. Note: You typically say a wish/dream wird wahr / wird wahr werden (not *macht wahr).
target_language_example: Dein Wunsch könnte wahr werden.
native_language_example: Your wish could come true.

additional_notes: An infinitive phrase used after verbs/adjectives like scheinen (to seem), glauben (to believe), behaupten (to claim), or expressions like den Eindruck erwecken, ... zu sein (“to give the impression of being ...”). Often appears as: Das scheint wahr zu sein. / Das ist weit davon entfernt, wahr zu sein (“That’s far from being true.”).
target_language_example: Es klingt zu gut, um wahr zu sein.
native_language_example: It sounds too good to be true.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an ideal, deep, genuine kind of love (often in romantic stories). You can use it as a noun phrase ("wahre Liebe") or with "Das nennt man …" (= "That’s what you call …").
target_language_example: Sie glaubt an wahre Liebe.
native_language_example: She believes in true love.

additional_notes: Used with the pattern **jemanden dazu zwingen, etwas zu tun** = “to force someone to do something.” **dazu** points forward to the **zu + infinitive** action (often explicitly stated: *dazu zwingen, das zu tun*). Word order: modal/auxiliary + adverb (*wahrscheinlich*) + **dazu zwingen**.
target_language_example: Sie könnten ihn wahrscheinlich dazu zwingen, die Wahrheit zu sagen.
native_language_example: They could probably force him to tell the truth.

additional_notes: Used with another verb (often in invitations/plans) to say you’re going hiking: z. B. „Hast du vor, …?“ (Do you plan to…?) or „Hättest du Lust, …?“ (Would you like to…?). „wandern“ means hiking (walking in nature), not just wandering around aimlessly.
target_language_example: Hast du Lust, am Samstag wandern zu gehen?
native_language_example: Do you feel like going hiking on Saturday?

additional_notes: Used to mean it doesn’t matter when something happens—at any time. Often introduces a subordinate clause: „Wann auch immer du Zeit hast, …“. It can also stand alone as a short answer meaning “whenever”.
target_language_example: Ruf mich an, wann auch immer du Hilfe brauchst.
native_language_example: Call me whenever you need help.

additional_notes: Used to ask about the starting time/date of an event or period (movie, game, trip, vacation, performance, etc.). The verb is "beginnen" (to begin); in a question, the conjugated verb comes second: "Wann beginnt der Film?" You can swap in different subjects (der Film, das Spiel, dein Urlaub, Ihre Reise).
target_language_example: Wann beginnt der Unterricht?
native_language_example: When does the class start?

meaning: “when did you…?” / “when were you…?” (asking about a past time).
additional_notes: Used to ask at what time or on what date something happened, often with the Perfekt (past) tense: "Wann bist du … gewesen/gegangen/gekommen/aufgestanden?". With verbs that use "haben" in the past, you’ll say "Wann hast du …?" instead (e.g., "Wann hast du das gemacht?").
target_language_example: Wann bist du gestern nach Hause gekommen?
native_language_example: When did you come home yesterday?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the time/date someone arrived in or moved to a place. It’s typically followed by a city/country and a verb like **gekommen** (came/arrived), **gezogen** (moved), or **gefahren** (went/traveled). **nach** is used with most cities and countries (e.g., *nach Berlin, nach Australien*).
target_language_example: Wann bist du nach Berlin gezogen?
native_language_example: When did you move to Berlin?

additional_notes: Used to ask for departure time in timetables and public transport. It’s normally followed by a masculine noun like der Bus / der Zug, or you add the noun right after: „Wann fährt der Bus/Zug?“ Often paired with „ab“: „Wann fährt der Bus ab?“
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, wann fährt der Zug nach Berlin ab?
native_language_example: Excuse me, when does the train to Berlin leave?

meaning: 'when do you go / leave' (when are you going to...).
additional_notes: Used to ask at what time/date someone is going somewhere or doing an activity with gehen + a destination or activity (e.g., nach Hause, zur Schule, ins Bett, mit jemandem essen). Very common in everyday planning. For a more formal/polite version (e.g., to strangers), use „Wann gehen Sie ...?“.
target_language_example: Wann gehst du heute nach Hause?
native_language_example: When are you going home today?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the time of a past action in the polite/formal form ("Sie"). It’s typically followed by a past participle (Perfekt), e.g. "Wann haben Sie angefangen?" / "Wann haben Sie es gekauft?" In spoken German this is a very common way to ask "when did you…?"
target_language_example: Wann haben Sie das letzte Mal Ihren Arzt gesehen?
native_language_example: When did you last see your doctor?

additional_notes: A polite/formal question using "Sie" to ask when someone began doing something. Often followed by an infinitive with "zu" (e.g., "angefangen, Deutsch zu lernen") or a main clause alone ("Wann haben Sie angefangen?").
target_language_example: Wann haben Sie angefangen, Deutsch zu lernen?
native_language_example: When did you start learning German?

wann haben Sie das letzte Mal

target_language_multi_word_term: wann haben Sie das letzte Mal
additional_notes: Used to ask about the most recent time someone did something. It’s a formal/polite question with “Sie” (used with strangers, in service situations, interviews, etc.). The verb usually goes at the end of the clause: „Wann haben Sie das letzte Mal … gemacht/gekauft/gehört?“
target_language_example: Wann haben Sie das letzte Mal Urlaub gemacht?
native_language_example: When was the last time you took a vacation?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the most recent time someone did something. Common in conversation, interviews, and questionnaires. After this phrase you typically add a past action, often in the Perfekt: „… gegessen/getragen/gebadet/geschlafen/gemacht?“ Note: In standard German spelling this is usually written and capitalized as „Wann haben Sie das letzte Mal …?“.
target_language_example: wann haben Sie das letztemal in einem Zelt geschlafen?
native_language_example: When was the last time you slept in a tent?

meaning: “When did you …?” (formal), often with a reflexive verb (“… yourself”).
additional_notes: Used to ask about the time of a past action in the Perfekt: **Wann haben Sie …?** The **Sie** is the polite/formal “you.” The **sich** appears with reflexive verbs (e.g., **sich rasieren** = to shave, **sich streiten** = to argue, **sich etw. zulegen** = to get/buy oneself something). Word order typically continues with the rest of the verb phrase and any objects: **Wann haben Sie sich das letzte Mal rasiert?**
target_language_example: Wann haben Sie sich entschieden, Deutsch zu lernen?
native_language_example: When did you decide to learn German?

meaning: 'when did you (all) ...?' (asking about time in the past).
additional_notes: Used to ask when something happened, addressing a group ("ihr" = you all) or using informal plural "you". Often followed by the Perfekt: "habt" + past participle (e.g., "Wann habt ihr es gemerkt?"). It can also be used with an infinitive phrase after a verb like "anfangen": "Wann habt ihr angefangen, ... zu ...?"
target_language_example: Wann habt ihr die Tickets gekauft?
native_language_example: When did you (all) buy the tickets?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the time or moment when a group of people ("ihr" = you all) began doing something. "angefangen" is the past participle of "anfangen" (to start), used here with "habt" (Perfekt): "habt ihr angefangen" = "did you start". Often followed by an infinitive with "zu" (e.g., "angefangen, Deutsch zu lernen") or a comma before the infinitive clause.
target_language_example: Wann habt ihr angefangen, zusammen zu arbeiten?
native_language_example: When did you (all) start working together?

additional_notes: Used to ask when something last happened, addressing two or more people informally ("ihr"). In standard German spelling/capitalization, this is usually written: „Wann habt ihr das letzte Mal …?“ (with „letzte Mal“ as two words and „Wann“ capitalized). The verb phrase typically uses Perfekt, with the past participle at the end: „Wann habt ihr das letzte Mal Spargel gegessen?“
target_language_example: wann habt ihr das letztemal Spargel gegessen?
native_language_example: When was the last time you ate asparagus?

meaning: “When did you (all) … ?” (informal plural, often with a reflexive verb).
additional_notes: Used to start a question in the past (Perfekt): **Wann** (when) + **habt** (have) + **ihr** (you, plural informal) + **euch** (yourselves/each other). Common with reflexive verbs like **sich streiten** (argue), **sich verfahren** (get lost while driving), **sich verirren** (get lost), **sich kennenlernen** (meet/get to know each other). In English you usually translate it with **“When did you … ?”** rather than a literal “When have you … ?”.
target_language_example: Wann habt ihr euch das letzte Mal gesehen?
native_language_example: When did you last see each other?

additional_notes:
Used to ask about the time of a past action. It’s followed by a past participle (Perfekt), often with a helping verb: 
- **Wann hast du** das gemacht? (haben + gemacht)
- **Wann hast du dich** schlafen gelegt? (reflexive + gelegt)
For plural/formal: **Wann habt ihr …? / Wann haben Sie …?**
target_language_example: Wann hast du Zeit, darüber zu reden?
native_language_example: When do you have time to talk about it?

additional_notes: A common question asking about the time someone began doing something. Uses the present perfect: **hast** (from *haben*) + **angefangen** (past participle of *anfangen*, “to start”). Often followed by **…, [activity] zu + infinitive** (e.g., *Deutsch zu lernen*) or another infinitive (e.g., *Golf zu spielen*).
target_language_example: Wann hast du angefangen, in Berlin zu wohnen?
native_language_example: When did you start living in Berlin?

wann hast du das letzte Mal

target_language_multi_word_term: wann hast du das letzte Mal
additional_notes: Used to ask about the most recent time someone did something. It’s typically followed by a past participle at the end of the sentence (Perfekt), e.g., „… gekauft?“, „… geschlafen?“. You can change „du“ to other people: „Wann haben Sie das letzte Mal …?“ (formal), „Wann hast ihr das letzte Mal …?“ (you plural).
target_language_example: Wann hast du das letzte Mal im Restaurant gegessen?
native_language_example: When was the last time you ate at a restaurant?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the most recent time someone did something. Note: Standard spelling is usually „Wann hast du das letzte Mal …?“ (two words: „letzte Mal“). Your given form „letztemal“ is commonly seen in informal writing, but is nonstandard. It’s typically followed by a past participle at the end of the clause: „… gebadet?“, „… um Hilfe gebeten?“
target_language_example: Wann hast du das letztemal gebadet?
native_language_example: When was the last time you bathed?

wann hast du das letztemal einen

target_language_multi_word_term: wann hast du das letztemal einen
meaning: "When was the last time you …?" (asking when you last did something; followed by a masculine noun phrase and then the rest of the verb phrase).
additional_notes: This is a common question pattern. Standard spelling/capitalization is usually: "Wann hast du das letzte Mal einen …?" ("letzte Mal" as two words; "Wann" capitalized). In your provided term, "letztemal" is written as one word and in lowercase; it will still be understood, but it’s nonstandard. After "einen" you typically add a masculine noun (e.g., "Anzug", "Besen", "Ölwechsel") and then the verb/past participle (e.g., "getragen", "benutzt", "machen lassen").
target_language_example: wann hast du das letztemal einen Anzug getragen?
native_language_example: When was the last time you wore a suit?

additional_notes: Used to ask when someone last did something that takes a reflexive pronoun ("sich" = "yourself"). It’s commonly followed by a past participle in the perfect tense: "Wann hast du dich verlaufen?" (= When did you get lost?). Often appears with time phrases like "das letzte Mal" (the last time) or "zuletzt" (most recently).
target_language_example: Wann hast du dich das letzte Mal bei deinen Eltern gemeldet?
native_language_example: When did you last check in with your parents?

target_language_multi_word_term: Wann hast du dich das letzte Mal …?
additional_notes: This is a common question pattern. You add an action after it (often a reflexive verb, so you see "dich"): e.g., "Wann hast du dich das letzte Mal ausgeruht?" = "When was the last time you rested?" The version "wann hast du dich das" by itself is incomplete; it normally needs "letzte Mal" and then a verb/phrase to finish the sentence.
target_language_example: Wann hast du dich das letzte Mal so gefühlt?
native_language_example: When was the last time you felt like this?

meaning: "When did you (last) …?" (asking about something you did for yourself).
additional_notes: Used to ask about the time of a past action (usually in the Perfekt tense). The word „dir“ is a dative reflexive pronoun (“for yourself”) and is common with personal-care actions, especially when something is done to you or for you: „sich die Nägel machen lassen“, „sich die Haare schneiden lassen“, etc. Often followed by „das letzte Mal“ (“the last time”).
target_language_example: Wann hast du dir das letzte Mal die Haare schneiden lassen?
native_language_example: When did you last get your hair cut?

meaning: “When did you … him?” (asking about the time of a past action involving him).
additional_notes: Used to ask *when* something happened with a male person ("ihn" = “him”). The phrase is typically followed by a past participle in the **Perfekt** tense, e.g. "Wann hast du ihn gesehen?" (“When did you see him?”). Word order: **Wann** + **hast** (auxiliary) + **du** + **ihn** + **Partizip II**.
target_language_example: Wann hast du ihn angerufen?
native_language_example: When did you call him?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the time something happened. You usually add a past participle (or other verb form) at the end: "Wann hast du sie gekauft?" = "When did you buy it?". "sie" can mean "her," "it" (for feminine nouns), or "them" depending on context. In formal speech, use "Wann haben Sie sie …?".
target_language_example: Wann hast du sie zum ersten Mal getroffen?
native_language_example: When did you meet her for the first time?

meaning: “When did you last have that?” / “When was the last time you had …?”
additional_notes: A casual question with du, used to ask about the last time someone had or experienced something. Very often followed by letzte Mal + noun/phrase: „Wann hattest du das letzte Mal …?“ (e.g., „eine Erkältung“, „einen freien Tag“).
target_language_example: Wann hattest du das letzte Mal Urlaub?
native_language_example: When was the last time you had a vacation?

meaning: “when is/was …?” (asking about the time of an event).
additional_notes: Used to ask when something happens or happened. Often followed by the subject and a verb in the past (ist … gegangen/angekommen/gewesen/krank geworden) or with a time expression (Wann ist eure Unterrichtsstunde zu Ende?). In questions, German typically uses verb-second order, but with a question word like „wann“ the verb comes right after it: „Wann ist …?“.
target_language_example: Wann ist der Zug angekommen?
native_language_example: When did the train arrive?

meaning: 'when are we coming?' / 'when do we arrive?'
additional_notes: A question with **wann** (“when”) + **kommen** (“to come”). Very often you’ll hear it with **an** (as in the examples): **Wann kommen wir an?** = “When do we arrive?” You can add a destination with **in** + city/country: **Wann kommen wir in Berlin an?** or **zu Hause** for “at home”.
target_language_example: Wann kommen wir am Bahnhof an?
native_language_example: When do we arrive at the train station?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the time/date of someone’s arrival. "Sie" is the formal “you” (to a stranger, customer, etc.). It’s often followed by a place or phrase like "zurück" (back) and "aus dem Urlaub" (from vacation): "Wann kommen Sie zurück?" / "Wann kommen Sie zurück nach …?" / "Wann kommen Sie aus … zurück?".
target_language_example: Wann kommen Sie zurück nach Deutschland?
native_language_example: When are you coming back to Germany?

additional_notes: A common question using **wann** (“when”) + **kommst du** (“are you coming/coming back”). Often followed by a place or direction: **heim** (home), **zurück/wieder** (back/again), **nach** + country/city (to). You can make it more polite/formal with **Wann kommen Sie …?**
target_language_example: Wann kommst du zurück?
native_language_example: When are you coming back?

additional_notes: A common question to ask about someone’s return. Often followed by a place: **nach** + city/country (z.B. *nach Boston*), **nach Hause** (home), or **zur** + place/event like work (*zur Arbeit*). You may also hear **zurück** added for emphasis (*Wann kommst du wieder zurück?*), but **wieder** alone already implies “back/again.”
target_language_example: Wann kommst du wieder nach Hause?
native_language_example: When are you coming home again?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the time someone or something arrives. Often followed by a person/thing (Wann kommt Papa?/die Post?) or combined with an adverb like "zurück" (Wann kommt er zurück? = When is he coming back?). In main clauses, the verb stays in 2nd position: "Wann kommt ...?"
target_language_example: Wann kommt der Bus?
native_language_example: When is the bus coming?

meaning: "When are you (plural) coming?" / "When will you (plural) come?"
additional_notes: Used to ask about the time a group of people is arriving/coming back/coming over. "ihr" is the informal plural "you" (talking to two or more people you address with du). Often followed by a destination or direction: "nach Hause" (home), "zurück" (back), "mich besuchen" (visit me). In real sentences, it may appear as "Wann kommt ihr ...?" with extra info at the end.
target_language_example: Wann kommt ihr heute Abend nach Hause?
native_language_example: When are you coming home tonight?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the time something happens or happened. "ihr" is informal plural "you" (talking to more than one person). "seid" is the 2nd-person plural form of "sein" (to be) and is often used with a past participle to form the spoken past (Perfekt) with movement/change-of-state verbs: "Wann seid ihr angekommen?" = "When did you arrive?". Word order is typically: "Wann" + verb ("seid") + subject ("ihr") + ...
target_language_example: Wann seid ihr gestern Abend zurückgekommen?
native_language_example: When did you come back yesterday evening?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the time/date of something involving the listener, using formal "Sie" (you). In questions, the verb comes before the subject: "Wann sind Sie ...?" Often followed by a past participle for the perfect tense (e.g., "angekommen", "gegangen") or an adjective (e.g., "beschäftigt").
target_language_example: Wann sind Sie verfügbar?
native_language_example: When are you available?

meaning: "When should I …?" / "When am I supposed to …?"
additional_notes: Used to ask for the right time to do something, often when someone expects you to do it or you need instructions. Uses the modal verb "sollen" (ich soll), which can mean "should" or "be supposed to". You normally follow it with an infinitive at the end: "Wann soll ich kommen?"
target_language_example: Wann soll ich die Unterlagen mitbringen?
native_language_example: When should I bring the documents?

additional_notes: Used to ask for both the time (wann?) and the place (wo?) of an event, often together in one question: "Wann und wo ...?".
target_language_example: Kannst du mir sagen, wann und wo wir uns treffen?
native_language_example: Can you tell me when and where we're meeting?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the most recent time something happened. Often followed by a clause with „dass …“ or „als …“ (especially in speech/writing: „Wann war das letzte Mal, dass/als du …?“). You can also use it with formal „Sie“: „Wann war das letzte Mal, dass Sie …?“
target_language_example: Wann war das letzte Mal, dass du im Meer geschwommen bist?
native_language_example: When was the last time you swam in the sea?

wann warst du das letzte Mal

target_language_multi_word_term: wann warst du das letzte Mal
additional_notes: A common question pattern for asking about someone’s most recent experience. It uses the simple past of sein (warst du = were you). You normally add an activity or place after it (e.g., am Strand, in Boston, segeln).
target_language_example: Wann warst du das letzte Mal im Kino?
native_language_example: When was the last time you were at the movies?

meaning: “When was the last time you were …?” / “When was the last time you …?”
additional_notes: Common question pattern to ask about someone’s most recent time doing something or being somewhere. Typically used with places (in/im/beim + noun) or activities (often with an infinitive like „rudern“). Note: Standard spelling is usually „das letzte Mal“ (two words, capitalized in German), but this entry keeps the provided form „das letztemal“.
target_language_example: wann warst du das letztemal im Kino?
native_language_example: When was the last time you were at the movies?

meaning: “When were you (plural) the last time …?” / “When was the last time you all …?”
additional_notes: Used to ask a group of people (ihr = you all) when they most recently did something or were somewhere. In standard German spelling, this is usually written and capitalized as: „Wann wart ihr das letzte Mal …?“ (two words: letzte Mal). Your term is kept exactly as given. Typical pattern: wann wart ihr das letztemal + location/prepositional phrase (e.g., im Kino) or + activity (e.g., mit Tom zelten).
target_language_example: wann wart ihr das letztemal im Kino?
native_language_example: When was the last time you all were at the cinema?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the time of a future action in a polite/formal way. "Sie" is the formal "you" (one person or multiple people). The verb comes right after "werden" at the end (e.g., "Wann werden Sie nach Berlin fahren?"). In everyday speech you may also hear "Wann werden Sie ...?" as a slightly formal alternative to "Wann ...?"
target_language_example: Wann werden Sie die Unterlagen schicken?
native_language_example: When will you send the documents?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the timing of a future action when speaking to two or more people informally ("ihr"). "werdet" is the 2nd person plural form of "werden" and is often used to form the future: "Wann werdet ihr kommen?" = “When will you come?” ("werden" can also mean “to become,” but in these questions it usually marks the future.)
target_language_example: Wann werdet ihr wieder zu Hause sein?
native_language_example: When will you be home again?

additional_notes: Used to ask when something will happen. It’s often followed by the subject (or a passive construction): „Wann wird es beginnen?“ / „Wann wird das Buch veröffentlicht?“ In German you can also form a similar question with „Wann findet … statt?“ depending on the verb.
target_language_example: Wann wird der Film anfangen?
native_language_example: When will the movie start?

meaning: “When will you …?” (asking about the time when someone will do something).
additional_notes: Used to ask about the timing of a future action. It’s built from: „wann“ = when, „wirst“ = will (2nd person singular of „werden“), „du“ = you. Usually followed by an infinitive (often at the end): „Wann wirst du kommen?“ = When will you come? In casual speech, people also use present tense: „Wann kommst du?“
target_language_example: Wann wirst du ankommen?
native_language_example: When will you arrive?

meaning: 'when was ...?' (asking about a past event/date; often passive).
additional_notes: Used to start questions about when something happened in the past, often in the passive voice: "Wann wurde + noun + Partizip II?" = "When was ... (done/built/founded)?"
